# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."

# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.

# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.

# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.

# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

The Verge attributes FTX's quick rise as an industry force at least in part to that appetite for attention: Bankman-Fried gave interviews freely and quickly rose to public prominence, positioning himself as an important, boyish face for crypto even though FTX hadn't been in the business as long as competing exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Gemini. At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.

# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. # The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."

# Bankman-Fried's Decision To Testify Backfired

The Verge's trial reporter argued that Bankman-Fried's choice to take the stand was a net loss for his defense: like Theranos' Elizabeth Holmes before him, he got on the stand to speak directly to his state of mind in a way no other witness can, but telling your side of the story opens you to a great many questions you might not want to answer on cross-examination — and, having watched a lot of crosses, she called Sassoon's the nastiest she had ever seen.

The warrant is what the charges turn on. The case hinged on conspiracy and intentional deceit: just losing $8 billion is not a crime, though it is very embarrassing, but if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing and how safe FTX was, that is a crime. Because state of mind was the contested issue, his own testimony became the evidence, and it did not hold: Sassoon had established the day before that he has a long history of dishonesty, and on October 31st, through a set of questions about what he did and did not do, she established that the story he told on direct examination was absurd. After a brief redirect by his own lawyers, resplendent with word salad, Bankman-Fried stepped down and the defense rested.

The direct examination had already supplied grounds. Beyond the two obvious lies the reporter counted him telling on the stand — about Alameda Research's name and about "allow_negative" — she was struck by how little he seemed to know about his own companies: apparently Singh, Wang, and Ellison were out there just doing whatever their little hearts desired, because Bankman-Fried was a CEO, but definitely not the kind that pays any attention to money at his crypto trading firm and futures exchange.

# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.

# VC And Lender Testimony As Collateral Risk For Crypto

The Verge argued that calling lenders, venture capitalists and customers to testify — necessary to establish the basis for some charges — might create collateral damage for the crypto industry beyond Bankman-Fried himself.

The grounds are the shape of the indictment and who it drags in: prosecutors allege that Bankman-Fried lied to FTX investors, so some of those investors may be called on to testify, which is not the kind of thing VC big shots generally enjoy. The worked example is Sequoia Capital: if Sequoia did due diligence around its investment in FTX, whatever Bankman-Fried told its partners could be important — was FTX already sending Alameda customer funds at that point, did Bankman-Fried know, and did he tell the VCs at the time? If he told them it wasn't happening, that would establish intent. Hermine Wong, the former head of policy at Coinbase and a former SEC regulator, adds that Binance was also an early investor in FTX and that former executives may be called on to testify as well.

# The Risk That Bankman-Fried Implicates The Whole Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that Bankman-Fried's own defense could damage crypto's public perception far beyond his case, because his post-collapse behavior suggests he's something of a wild card.

The grounds are the defenses available to him: he may suggest he was acting on the advice of his lawyers, but he may also introduce other evidence that could be troublesome — implying that he was engaged in standard industry behavior, or that everything that happened was Binance's fault. That may be risky, but "we already know that Bankman-Fried loves risk." Hermine Wong frames the danger as a question: "Is he going to throw the entire industry under the bus? An idea like, 'Everyone was doing this, it's not fair I'm the only one who was charged?'" That may not fly in a court of law, but it could absolutely damage public perception of crypto at large. The precedent is his own conduct: just before he was arrested, Bankman-Fried brought forward messages from a crypto group chat in testimony he planned to give before Congress, in which he primarily blames Binance and his lawyers at the firm Sullivan & Cromwell. Other group chat messages may be brought into evidence during the trial, which Wong says could be embarrassing for the whole industry: "You can imagine some of these founders, CEOs, people of that echelon talk to each other somewhat informally about what's going on. If it seems like his peer group supported him, or worse, fawned over him, that's a real problem for the industry's reputation."

# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.

# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.

# Lobbying and Political Donations

Lobbying and political donations, in the corpus, are the practice of routing money to political candidates, parties, or officials to gain influence with regulators and lawmakers.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's use of FTX- and Alameda-linked funds for political spending during his rise, which became a prosecution theme at his fraud trial: TechCrunch reports he "had close ties to U.S. regulators and government officials, many of whom he donated to," and that Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" surfaced his "attempt to buy off Trump to get him to not run again for president" by discussing with Mitch McConnell how to "fund political candidates who were looking to offset Trump's influence in the Republican Party." At trial, prosecutor Thane Rehn told the jury Bankman-Fried used stolen customer funds to "donate millions to political candidates," and Nishad Singh, described as a longtime family friend of Bankman-Fried, pleaded guilty to charges that included counts "around his political donations." The practice also extended to those around Bankman-Fried: The Verge names "Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap" among the entities caught up in the case.

## Key Characteristics

- **Funding source under dispute** — the prosecution's theory was that the political donations were financed with misappropriated FTX customer deposits, not Bankman-Fried's own money.
- **Instrument of influence, not charity** — donations to candidates and officials are described alongside efforts to buy access (e.g., the reported offer to Trump), distinguishing them from Bankman-Fried's professed effective-altruism philanthropy.
- **Bipartisan reach** — the reporting describes both engagement with Democratic-aligned regulators/officials and an attempt to influence a Republican presidential race, i.e., donations spanning both parties.
- **Legal exposure** — political donations became a distinct criminal count (against Nishad Singh) and a recurring prosecution talking point against Bankman-Fried, showing the practice can carry direct legal consequences when the underlying funds are alleged to be stolen.
- **Family/associate involvement** — the practice was not confined to Bankman-Fried himself; his mother Barbara Fried's PAC, Mind the Gap, is named as part of the same political-spending network.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.



---


# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.



---


# Trump's Other Criminal and Civil Cases 2023

Letitia James' lawsuit is one of several legal headaches for Trump as he campaigns for a return to the White House in 2024. He has been indicted four times in the six months to September 2023 — accused in Georgia and Washington, D.C., of plotting to overturn his 2020 election loss; in Florida of hoarding classified documents; and in Manhattan of falsifying business records related to hush money paid on his behalf.

Separately, the Trump Organization was convicted of tax fraud in 2022 in an unrelated criminal case for helping executives dodge taxes on extravagant perks such as Manhattan apartments and luxury cars, and the company was fined $1.6 million. One of the executives, Trump's longtime finance chief Allen Weisselberg, pleaded guilty and served five months in jail; he is a defendant in James' lawsuit and gave sworn deposition testimony for the case in May.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.

# The Crown Season Six: Release and Premise

The Crown season six is the final season of Netflix's royal drama, split into two parts: the first four episodes arrived on Netflix on Thursday 16 November 2023, and the last six episodes followed on 14 December. It carries the show into the late Nineties and early Noughties — described in one account as the late 1990s to the mid-2000s — so that events are depicted on screen which many of the public will remember well.

The first part of the season takes place in the summer of 1997. It sees Prince Charles (Dominic West) building on his relationship with Camilla Parker Bowles (Olivia Williams), while Princess Diana (Elizabeth Debicki) sparks up a romance with film producer Dodi Fayed (Khalid Abdalla); the season also features the pair's death in a car crash in Paris, and includes the lead-up to that fatal 1997 crash.

The season opens with Diana whisking her sons — Prince William (played by Rufus Kampa) and Prince Harry (played by Fflyn Edwards) — away on summer holiday to Saint-Tropez, France. After staying several days on Mohamed Al Fayed's yacht, the boys return home to London, where their father, the then-Prince of Wales, accompanies them to Balmoral Castle to vacation with the rest of the royal family in Scotland. The first four episodes are available to stream on Netflix in the US and UK.



---


# Diana's Final Phone Call With William and Harry

Episode three of The Crown season six depicts what the show presents as Princess Diana's final conversation with her sons, and many viewers called it the most devastating moment in the entire series.

In the episode, Diana's partner Dodi Fayed (played by Khalid Abdalla) surprises her with a quick trip to Paris, France. The princess is keen to return home to the United Kingdom and eager to speak to her sons over the phone; a mob of paparazzi following the couple delays Diana's scheduled phone call with William and Harry, until she is able to catch them again later that evening. William, then 15, and Harry, then 12, ask over the phone when their mother will be coming back home from Paris. "I'm coming home tomorrow, and I'm seeing you both tomorrow night," Diana replies, in an episode that also takes place on the same day as her fatal car crash later that evening.

The boys then ask Diana whether she plans on marrying Dodi, given that their relationship has been plastered all over the tabloids. "Well, you know better than to believe the papers," she tells William, before adding: "I'm emphatically not going to marry Dodi. To be honest, I can't wait to come home." When William asks his mother if she is doing "okay", Diana tells her eldest son: "I'm okay. It's just a bit mad here. I don't really understand how I ended up here. Mummy just needs to make some changes to her life, that's all. But that's not your problem, that's mine." Before saying goodbye she reminds them she will see them the next day — a day that never comes: "I'll see you both tomorrow night. Just the three of us."

The moment tugged on the heartstrings of many viewers, who took to social media to share their reactions. "The last phone call between Harry, William and Diana broke my heart," one fan wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter. "That precious phone call between Diana and her sons," said someone else. "Don't mind me, I'm just gonna cry in one corner." A third user commented: "The last call between Harry, William and Diana is heartbreaking."



---


# Prince William at Balmoral After Diana's Death

It is true that William and Harry initially stayed at Balmoral with their grandmother following Diana's death, though it is not known whether William went missing as The Crown depicts.

In the drama, after learning of Diana's death from his father at the royal residence of Balmoral in Scotland, William (Rufus Kampa) is left heartbroken with grief and angry at his family's response to it. At one point Charles is informed that the prince is not in his room and that "no one can find him", prompting Charles and Prince Harry to look for him and a subsequent hunt across the grounds for the young royal. He is not located, but later walks back to the house of his own accord, drenched in rain. "14 hours, that poor boy was gone," the Queen later says.

William himself has spoken about that period. During a visit to Scotland in 2021, he recalled the experience as one of the "saddest" moments of his life. "I was in Balmoral when I was told that my mother had died. Still in shock, I found sanctuary in the service at Crathie Kirk that very morning," he recalled. "And in the dark days of grief that followed, I found comfort and solace in the Scottish outdoors. As a result, the connection I feel to Scotland will forever run deep."



---


# Queen Elizabeth's Reluctance to Accept Camilla

It took a while for Queen Elizabeth and Camilla to grow close, and according to historian Robert Lacey the Queen was reluctant to accept Charles's request to be more accommodating to Camilla — going further, in the record, than The Crown shows: unlike in the drama, she is said to have once referred to Camilla as "that wicked woman" to Charles's face.

As The Crown season six begins, Charles is frustrated at the public for demonising Camilla long after his split from Diana. He asks the Queen whether she had received the invitation to Camilla's 50th birthday; she says she has, but cannot attend as she is in Derbyshire. When Charles points out that plans "can always be changed", she replies: "Why would we want to change it?" She does not attend, but later tells Prince Philip that she does not want Camilla to be considered "wicked, because she's not", or to be unkind to her.

The relationship changed over time. The Queen grew to become closer to Camilla, and despite an announcement in 2005 that Camilla would become the Princess Consort rather than Queen Consort, it was announced that Camilla would be queen seven months before Elizabeth's death.



---


# The Crown: Diana and a Role With the Blair Government

The Crown's depiction of Diana seeking a formal role with Tony Blair's government tracks the historical record. In episode one, Diana visits Tony (Bertie Carvel) and Cherie Blair (Lydia Leonard) with William after asking for a meeting with him; recalling their discussion to the Queen, Blair says that Diana feels she "still has a lot to offer the country as a public servant", that she had asked whether there was a way to work with the government on "a more formal basis", and that any "official role" would be appreciated.

Following Diana's death, Downing Street confirmed that she had visited Blair at Chequers with her son a few weeks before, where they discussed a special role for her as an overseas "ambassador" for Britain. Diana told a journalist at the time that the prime minister had recognised her skills and asked her to undertake "missions" abroad for Britain.



---


# The Crown: The Fact-Versus-Fiction Criticism

The criticism levelled at The Crown attacks the premise that a dramatisation set close to living memory can be relied on to read as fiction: as Netflix's acclaimed royal drama moves closer to the present day, the line between fact and fiction feels ever more blurred.

The objection does not deny that Peter Morgan's show has always presented a dramatised take on real-life events. It targets the inference that the dramatised framing is therefore self-evident to viewers — many have argued that viewers struggle to tell the difference between the real royal family and the events on the show.

The proposed remedy, and Netflix's refusal of it, is part of the same dispute: when season five arrived in 2022 there were calls for the show to include a "fictional explainer", something Netflix did not do.



---


# Dodi Fayed's Engagement Ring on the Night of the Crash

In real life Dodi Fayed did not propose to Diana on the night of the Paris crash, as The Crown depicts — but at the 2007 inquest into the death, the jury were shown CCTV footage of him buying an engagement ring worth £11,600 in a jewellers across the square from the Ritz on the afternoon of the crash.

The Crown's version has Dodi bursting into tears going for dinner at the Ritz, then moving upstairs and proposing with a ring Diana had previously pointed out when they sheltered from crowds in a Monte Carlo jewellery shop. She tells him to get up off his knee: "I know the whole world is wondering if we're going to get married, but that's not a reason to actually do it." They then share a drink and a bittersweet conversation about how they need to live their lives going forward.

The ring in the record was later believed to have been delivered to their room before they went to Dodi's flat, where a ring bearing the words "Dis-moi Oui" ("Tell me Yes") — also the name of episode three — was later recovered, alongside a receipt for a "bague de fiançaille" (engagement ring). Speaking at the inquest, his father Mohamed claimed that the pair had met the jeweller in Monte Carlo during the holiday on the yacht, and that he believed Dodi planned to propose that night.



---


# Kelly Fisher's Engagement to Dodi Fayed

The Crown's depiction of Dodi Fayed's American fiancée comes close to the truth as told by model Kelly Fisher, who claimed to have been engaged to Dodi when he met Diana.

When viewers first meet Dodi in The Crown, he is in Paris with a woman with short, blonde hair — not Diana, but an American woman he says he is picking out fabric for a Malibu home with and marrying in three weeks. His father Mohamed is unimpressed, calling him to Saint Tropez to meet a "special guest" and leave his "gold-digger" fiancée — whom he also calls "Madame Bikini" — behind. The model later confronts Dodi, asking if he was with Diana when he leaves her to go see his father, and Diana also alludes to a "lawsuit" between Dodi and his ex.

In the record, Fisher had previously modelled for brands such as Victoria's Secret and magazines including Elle and Marie Claire. As in The Crown, Fisher — who met Fayed in July 1996 — was on another Fayed yacht when Dodi and Diana were first photographed. She staged a press conference announcing that she was filing a breach-of-contract lawsuit against Dodi, after he allegedly asked her to stop modelling as much and prioritise the relationship. Through tears, she claimed he had proposed to her (something his family denied) and promised to buy her a house in Malibu. She dropped the lawsuit following Dodi's death.



---


# Diana and the Paparazzi on the Fayed Yacht

The Crown shows Diana as both hounded by and complicit with the photographers around Dodi's father's yacht in France, and the historical accounts cited alongside it support the second half of that picture.

In the drama, when Dodi and Diana first spend time together on the yacht, the paparazzi are never far away. When William refuses to go outside until the photographers leave them alone, Diana takes a boat out to visit them. Wearing a swimming costume, she tells them: "We're having a lovely time, apart from one little thing: you lot." "Don't be like that, you love us really," they reply. She asks them to leave her alone as they are "freaking out" her sons, before telling one photographer — whom she knows by name — that if they go away, "you're going to get a big surprise with the next thing I do". She then poses for them in her swimsuit, but complains in a later episode that they can "never relax" with the press "constantly" around.

Former Vanity Fair editor Tina Brown, who wrote the controversial 2007 book Diana Chronicles, claimed that Diana would often tip off the press and "couldn't resist giving them the images they wanted", including on the boat. Photographer Daniel Pirrie, who ended up selling the photo of the kiss, claimed that Diana herself invited him to photograph her on holiday with Dodi in France that summer. "She told me she'd be on the yacht somewhere in the Mediterranean," he told The Daily Mail in 2013. "She let me know she was going to be on a tender going out to the yacht. I think overall, she was happy with all the pictures taken that summer… I knew that Diana had wanted [the kiss photo] to be taken."



---


# Mohamed Al Fayed and the Dodi-Diana Kiss Photo

It is not known whether Mohamed Al Fayed was as instrumental in securing the famous photo of Dodi and Diana kissing as The Crown suggests, but accounts published after his death in 2023 describe him boasting about engineering the couple's romance.

Throughout season six, Mohamed al Fayed (Salim Daw) is shown as heavily invested in his son Dodi's relationship with Diana, even ringing up the maid to ask if they have been "intimate". In Arabic, he then asks his secretary whether they can find him an Arabic photographer — "not just any idiot with a long lens", but "the best photographer on the Meditarranean".

Following the Harrods owner's death in 2023, biographer Tom Bower recalled in The Times how Al-Fayed "gleefully" showed him the photographs of Dodi and Diana and allegedly "revealed how he had rapidly bought a yacht suitable for his son's seduction of her".



---


# Elizabeth Debicki on Recreating the Paparazzi Pursuit

Australian actor Elizabeth Debicki, who took over the role of Diana from Emma Corrin in season five, said the scene was "difficult to recreate" — especially with her character being hounded by the paparazzi.

"It was heavy and very manic, and incredibly invasive. And it had a kind of pressure to it," Debicki said in an interview with Netflix. "At times it's almost like an animalistic response to being pursued, by that many actors playing the press, because there's nowhere you can go and you only have to be in a situation like that for about a minute, before you realise this is completely unbearable."



---


# Diana and Dodi's Paris Car Crash, 1997

In both The Crown and in real life, Diana and Dodi Fayed — along with their chauffeur, Henri Paul — were killed on 31 August 1997 when their Mercedes-Benz was pursued by paparazzi and crashed in the Pont de l'Alma tunnel in Paris. Diana, a mother of two, was 36 years old.

The fatal car crash was recreated in the very first scene of season six. The incident itself is not shown on-screen: a car carrying Diana and Dodi is seen speeding past a man walking his dog, before entering the tunnel, and as the vehicle's horn blares he calls emergency services on his cell phone.



---


# Nyad

Nyad, a biographical sports drama available to stream on Netflix in early November 2023, runs 2 hours 1 minute, is directed by Jimmy Chin and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, and stars Jodie Foster, Annette Bening, and Rhys Ifans.

Polygon's weekend roundup describes it as the — questionably — true story of swimmer Diana Nyad, who swam from Cuba to Florida at 64 years old, among many other swimming accomplishments. Netflix's own synopsis, reproduced in Polygon's November catalog listing, gives different particulars: it calls the film the remarkable true story of an athlete who, at the age of 60 and with the help of her best friend and coach, commits to achieving her life-long dream of a 110-mile open ocean swim from Cuba to Florida.



---


# Fan Reactions To Owen Teale After Jon Snow's Death Scene

Owen Teale braced for hostility after Jon Snow's death was broadcast, expecting irate Game of Thrones fans who would hate him for "killing the goodness"; instead he was asked for endless selfies and impromptu recitations of Ser Alliser Thorne catchphrases such as "For the Watch!" or "Bas-terd!", The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 20 October 2023.

Once, a drunk emerged from a restaurant and stumbled towards Teale brandishing a knife; the actor braced himself, but the man simply wanted "Ser Alliser" to hold the utensil to his throat for a photo. On a visit to Uluru with his family, the tour guide caught sight of his face and exclaimed, "what are you doing here?" — "He just kept staring at me and I realised it was an Alliser Thorne thing," says Teale. "I said, 'I'm not going to kill anyone, I'm just an actor'. But it clearly troubled him that this person who had committed this awful crime had suddenly appeared." Teale has the grace to admit he enjoys this new level of celebrity: "People seem to realise that without the darkness of people like Ser Alliser, Jon Snow couldn't have shone as brightly as he did."

He was well into his 50s when he landed his highest-profile role, but it would be wrong to think of him as a late starter: in 1989, not long out of drama school, he starred in the hit television adaptation of Catherine Cookson's romance The Fifteen Streets, alongside Sean Bean, another young working-class actor who went on to become a leading man in Hollywood before playing Ned Stark in Game of Thrones. Asked whether he ever wishes he had followed Bean's trajectory, Teale replies: "Oh god, yeah. Absolutely. You instinctively think [playing leading men] will lead to feelings of success. But it never came my way. My cut of my jib wasn't quite right. It's about what your face does on screen I guess."



---


# Owen Teale's Missed Leading Man Opportunities

Owen Teale had several chances to become a leading man and each fell away — financing collapsed, an American star was demanded, and he chose family over Hollywood networking — The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 20 October 2023.

When The Fifteen Streets attracted a massive TV audience in Britain, Teale was offered a lead role in a movie playing a bare knuckle fighter, but the financing fell through and he signed up for a four-year stint with the Royal Shakespeare Company instead. Years later a producer offered him the lead in a big film being shot in Britain, but the money men demanded an American star and William Hurt got the gig. When Teale won a Tony Award in 1997 for his performance in Ibsen's A Doll's House, he was told he needed to spend time in Hollywood wooing producers and decided to fly home to his family in London instead: "My wife was about to give birth, so I said 'I'm off'. I'm sure part of it was I just didn't believe that I was going to waltz into leading man roles in Hollywood." Despite the plaudits, awards and steady offers of work, the piece observes, he has never been certain of his gifts — probably why he is so consistently good, since complacency is not in his nature.

He is far better at recognising brilliance in others, such as Toni Collette, with whom he worked on Dream Horse, a 2020 movie about an unlikely champion racehorse. "Toni just raised my game. That's a huge talent, huge," he says, shaking his head in wonder. "I recently received an award from BAFTA for the film and part of me thinks they should give it to Toni." He is happiest in a room full of actors working on a play, a film or a TV production: "What turns me on is the thought of collaborating with talented people. I'm very sociable with the rest of the company and fully intend to do that when I come to Melbourne."

# How Will Smith And Jada Pinkett Smith Met And Married In 1997

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith met when she auditioned for the role of his girlfriend on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air; she did not get the part, but the two hit it off — even though Smith was married to Sheree Zampino at the time, with whom he shares son Trey. Smith later described the moment of recognition on Pinkett Smith's Red Table Talk in 2018: "I had a realisation I wasn't with the person I was supposed to be with. I was sitting in a [bathroom] stall and I was crying and laughing uncontrollably, and I knew [Jada] was the woman I was supposed to be with."

The pair only began seriously dating in 1995, after Smith finalised his divorce from Zampino. He proposed in November 1997 and they married just one month later, in Baltimore. # The Roland Doe Case and The Exorcist

Perhaps the most famous instance of purported demonic possession connected to Ouija board usage was the case of "Roland Doe", a young teenage boy from Maryland, who underwent numerous major exorcisms in 1949, said Fr. Dan Reehil.

Doe's story was adapted into the 1971 book "The Exorcist" by William Peter Blatty, which was then made into the 1973 movie starring Ellen Burstyn and Linda Blair.



---


# Expert Disagreement Over What The Oscars Slap Meant Given The Separation

Dating coach Jacob Lucas attacks the sincerity premise behind Will Smith's 2022 Oscars outburst, arguing that the newly revealed separation makes the reaction implausible as a husband's defence. "That's a weird reaction to have somebody who you've been broken up with for six years, you know?" he asked. "So, were they really broken up or is Jada saying that as an attention-seeking thing?" His challenge cuts both ways: either the couple were not genuinely separated, or Jada Pinkett Smith's account of the separation is itself being questioned.

Relationship expert Susan Winter takes the opposite reading of the same incident, holding that it demonstrates rather than undermines the strength of the commitment. "I feel as though Will has a tremendous love and commitment to Jada, as well as to the marriage and the family unit," she said. "The pride that he takes in defending his wife is extraordinary, almost to the detriment of his image, at times." ---


# Kevin Federline's Marriage To Victoria Prince

Victoria Prince is Kevin Federline's wife, a volleyball player he married in 2013 after moving on from his relationship with Britney Spears. The couple share two daughters. The two Independent accounts, published two days apart in October 2023, give their names and ages slightly differently: the 18 October piece calls them Jordan, 10, and Peyton, eight, while the 20 October piece gives their full names as Jordan Kay, 12, and Peyton Marie, nine.

The marriage is presented as the post-divorce chapter of the Spears-Federline story: after the divorce, the two appeared to be co-parenting amicably, seen supporting their boys at soccer and football games, and Federline moved on to Prince.



---


# Jada Pinkett Smith's 2023 Disclosure Of A Seven-Year Separation

Jada Pinkett Smith revealed in October 2023 that she and her husband Will Smith had been separated for the previous seven years — that is, since 2016 — while remaining married. The disclosure came in an interview with People given while she was promoting her memoir Worthy; The Independent's timeline piece dates the publication to 11 October, while its other reports on the same interview date it 10 October. Pinkett Smith, 52, said of her 26-year marriage to the 55-year-old actor that the couple are "still figuring it out": "We've been doing some really heavy-duty work together. We just got deep love for each other and we are going to figure out what that looks like for us."

She anchored the timeline to the 2022 Academy Awards, when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock after the comedian made a joke about her appearance: at that moment, she said, the pair had already been separated for six years. The revelation was treated as major news — "sent shockwaves around the world," in The Independent's phrasing — because both Smiths had previously doubled down on their stance against divorce, so a lengthy separation raised a new question: when should a couple simply get a divorce?



---


# The King Of Comedy (1983) As A Box Office Flop

Illustrating the slang term "slept on" during her TikTok quiz, Francesca Scorsese told her father: "King of Comedy was slept on," referring to his 1983 film starring Robert De Niro. The King of Comedy received mostly positive reviews from critics on release but was a flop at the box office.

Scorsese corrected the framing from his own memory of the reception: "People hated it when it came out," he said, before turning towards the camera. "It was the flop of the year, that's what it was called on Entertainment Tonight, New Year's Eve '83 to '84. It's okay, it's alright."

# Britney Spears' Unconfirmed Romances With Wade Robson And Colin Farrell

Two of the romances attributed to Britney Spears in the early 2000s were never confirmed by either party. Shortly after her breakup from Justin Timberlake, Spears was rumoured to be dating Wade Robson, a dancer and choreographer who appeared in the music video for her 2009 song "(You Drive Me) Crazy"; neither Spears nor Robson confirmed the rumours.

The quote was reported by People in 2003.



---


# Will Smith's Slap Of Chris Rock At The 2022 Oscars

In March 2022, at the 94th annual Academy Awards, Will Smith walked onto the stage and slapped the comedian Chris Rock, then yelled at him to "keep my wife's name out your f***ing mouth." The altercation followed Rock's joke — "Jada, I love you. GI Jane 2, can't wait to see you" — referring to Jada Pinkett Smith's shaved head, which is a result of her alopecia. It quickly became the most talked-about moment of the evening, with the pair initially appearing to laugh off the tense moment. Later that night, while accepting the award for Best Actor, Smith became teary and said he was a "fierce defender of his family."

The incident was reassessed in October 2023 after Pinkett Smith revealed the couple had been separated since 2016 and so were separated at the time of the ceremony. UK-based dating coach Jacob Lucas, quoted by The Independent, tied part of the surrounding controversy to that timing and questioned Smith's behaviour and word choice at the awards given the separation.

# UK Dementia Burden and Projections

About a million people are living with dementia in the UK, and this is expected to rise to about 1.7 million by 2040; last year dementia took the lives of 66,000 people in England and Wales, and it is now the leading cause of death in Britain, with Alzheimer's accounting for two-thirds of cases.

The prospect of the new drugs has raised hopes that, after years of effort, scientists may be closing in on ways to directly tackle the UK's dementia crisis — a crisis whose projected growth the article describes as carrying potentially grim consequences.



---


# Justin Timberlake's Apology And Support For Britney Spears

Justin Timberlake publicly apologised to Britney Spears on Instagram in 2021 after the documentary Framing Britney, which addressed the public scrutiny Spears faced during the 2000s, prompted criticism of how he had behaved following their breakup. Neither had ever acknowledged the rumours about why they split. His apology read: "I've seen the messages, tags, comments, and concerns and I want to respond. I am deeply sorry for the times in my life where my actions contributed to the problem, where I spoke out of turn, or did not speak up for what was right. I understand that I fell short in these moments and in many others and benefited from a system that condones misogyny and racism."

# The Fan Movement And The 2021 End Of Britney Spears' Conservatorship

According to The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account of *The Woman in Me*, Spears first learned of the blossoming fan movement questioning her conservatorship from a nurse, called 911 in June 2021 to report her father for conservatorship abuse days before a probate court hearing, and was granted her freedom in November 2021.

A nurse showed her the fan movement that was spreading awareness of its suspicions that all was not right with the arrangement. Of speaking publicly at that point she writes: "My voice had been used for me and against me so many times that I was afraid nobody would recognise it now if I spoke freely."

When freedom came in November 2021, she says she felt shock, relief, elation, sadness and joy.

# The Stepfather's Role After a Father's Death

The Reddit poster gave the family background behind the aisle decision: she lost the father of her children — Calla and Hawthorn — when they were six and eight, and remarried four years later, and it was made clear to the children from the outset that her second husband "was not going to be filling the role of a dad in their lives".

Her partner "was fine with that, as long as he was respected and they could work toward being a caring family".

The bond with the late father remained the stronger one. While she had a close relationship with Calla, it was "extremely tough" for her child to lose her father, and while Calla has a good relationship with her stepfather, "it comes nowhere close to the bond she had with her dad". Taylor Swift liked and commented on the viral TikTok of three young fans struggling to open her "1989 (Taylor's Version)" CD, writing "Wait, this is amazing", FOX News Lifestyle reported on 11 November 2023.

# Young Swifties Struggle To Open The 1989 (Taylor's Version) CD

A group of 11- and 12-year-old "Swifties" went viral after a TikTok video captured their attempts to open a "1989 (Taylor's Version)" compact disc, FOX News Lifestyle reported on 11 November 2023.

"The girls knew what a CD was, but we had to borrow Grandma and Grandpa's CD player to let them fully experience it," Schmidt shared. # Taylor Swift And Joe Alwyn's Relationship And Breakup

In April 2023 it was revealed that Taylor Swift and British actor Joe Alwyn had broken up after six years of dating. The former couple were notoriously private: the Conversations with Friends star had previously said he did not want to discuss the relationship because doing so "feeds into a weird part of the culture."

# Taylor Swift Named Time's 2023 Person Of The Year

Time named Taylor Swift its 2023 Person of the Year, announcing the choice on Wednesday 6 December 2023. The magazine said the honour followed an "editors' assessment of the individual who most shaped the headlines over the previous 12 months, for better or for worse," and explained its selection this way: "While her popularity has grown across the decades, this is the year that Swift, 33, achieved a kind of nuclear fusion: shooting art and commerce together to release an energy of historic force." She was chosen from a strong list of contenders that included Chinese President Xi Jinping, King Charles III, the live-action Barbie movie, and Vladimir Putin.

The recognition came at the end of a whirlwind year in which her Eras Tour dominated ticket sales. Swift told Time: "This is the proudest and happiest I've ever felt, and the most creatively fulfilled and free I've ever been. Ultimately, we can convolute it all we want, or try to overcomplicate it, but there's only one question... Are you not entertained?"

# How Taylor Swift And Travis Kelce's Relationship Began

Taylor Swift, 33, revealed in her December 2023 Time interview — her first time publicly speaking about Travis Kelce — that the relationship began in July 2023, after he confessed on his podcast that he had tried and failed to give her a friendship bracelet with his phone number on it during one of her Eras Tour shows. We would never be psychotic enough to hard launch a first date," she said. # The Masters Dispute And The "Taylor's Version" Re-Recordings

When music mogul Scooter Braun acquired Taylor Swift's longtime label, Big Machine Records, in 2019, he also gained the rights to the master recordings of Swift's first six studio albums; in November 2020 Braun sold those masters to an investment fund in a deal believed to be worth over $300 million. Swift responded by re-recording her catalogue, and by the end of 2023 had released four "Taylor's Version" albums: Fearless (Taylor's Version) in April 2021, Red (Taylor's Version) in November 2021, Speak Now (Taylor's Version) in July 2023, and 1989 (Taylor's Version) in October 2023.

The Independent suggests it was that decision to re-record the catalogue that catapulted Swift into her 2023 success. Asked by Time about the success of her tour, Swift traced it back to two ordeals: "It's not lost on me that the two great catalysts for this happening were two horrendous things that happened to me. The first was getting cancelled within an inch of my life and sanity. The second was having my life's work taken away from me by someone who hates me."

Two months after ending her engagement to Jason Trawick, Britney Spears began dating David Lucado, who worked at a legal firm; she announced their split in August 2014 by tweeting "Ahhhh the single life!", and her representative confirmed to People: "Yes, she's single." Speculation that Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift were dating began in July 2023, when Kelce confessed that he had tried and failed to give Swift a friendship bracelet bearing his phone number at one of her Eras Tour concerts; he later invited her on his podcast to one of his games at Arrowhead Stadium, an invitation she famously accepted on 24 September 2023, and she had attended three more of his games by 25 November 2023.

Kelce first told the bracelet story to his brother on their podcast back in July. "I was disappointed that she doesn't talk before or after her shows, because she has to save her voice for the 44 songs that she sings," he explained. # Style: Named For Harry Styles, Explained As A Song About Fashion

Style is an epic aural painting of windswept coastlines and propulsive wanderlust, supposedly named for Harry Styles, with whom Taylor Swift had a brief relationship in 2012 — many of 1989's songs were supposedly inspired by that relationship. Swift's own account differs: she says the song was inspired by fashion, and how certain items like a black dress or red lipstick will "never go out of style", which prompted her to write about the people who'll always be part of your life even after the flame of romantic love wanes. The BBC notes that this all sounds like a classic piece of deflection to a probing journalist.

Whichever interpretation you prefer, the song marks a shift in Swift's psychology, as she briefly admits to having been unfaithful — the discriminating feature that separates it from her earlier writing. "I would never have said anything like that on a previous album," she told Ryan Seacrest. "My previous albums have always been, 'I was right, you were wrong'. What happens when you grow up is you realise that the rules in a relationship are very blurred. It gets very complicated, very quickly."

The BBC reported this on 13 October 2023, with the article itself noting a publication date of 27 October for the album's return.

This re-recording is described as the biggest and riskiest part of the project. Earlier remakes in the campaign were largely made with a live band, whereas 1989's pop landscapes are full of squelchy, processed synths and treated vocals, which makes them harder to reproduce faithfully. Alongside the re-recorded album, fans can hear five new tracks from the star's vault, expanding on the themes and relationships she explored on the original. The artwork for the re-recorded version has a beach vibe, in contrast to the Polaroid aesthetics of the original.

# Wildest Dreams: Imagining The End Before The Relationship Begins

Wildest Dreams is defined by anticipatory disillusion — Taylor Swift imagines the end of a relationship before it has truly begun, asking her partner, when it all goes wrong, "Say you'll remember me / Standing in a nice dress / Staring at the sunset." It belongs to a wider strand on 1989 in which growing up means letting go of youthful optimism: on one hand she has developed an ability to laugh off her critics, on the other she seems increasingly jaded about love.

Swift described the shift in her own terms to Rolling Stone: "The way I used to approach relationships was very idealistic. I used to go into them thinking, 'Maybe this is the one - we'll get married and have a family, this could be forever'. Whereas now I go in thinking, 'How long do we have on the clock before something comes along and puts a wrench in it, or your publicist calls and says this isn't a good idea?'" An early draft of the lyrics had the couple fleeing the city and blotting out the pressures of the world, an idea which eventually resurfaced in I Know Places.

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce appeared together publicly through the autumn of 2023, at his games, at her concerts, and away from both. Afterwards Chariah Gordon, the partner of Kelce's teammate Mecole Hardman Jr, posted an Instagram picture of Swift standing next to Kelce and reaching to kiss his cheek. Kelce also responded warmly when a fan shouted "Let's go Taylor's boyfriend" while he waited for an elevator, smiling slightly and pumping his fist into the air.

The couple were also photographed together away from stadiums, including a date earlier that month in New York City after their surprise appearances on the season 49 premiere of Saturday Night Live.
