# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# ChatGPT FAQ: Basics And Definitions

ChatGPT is a general-purpose chatbot developed by tech startup OpenAI that uses artificial intelligence to generate text after a user enters a prompt; it runs on GPT-4, a large language model that uses deep learning to produce human-like text. GPT stands for Generative Pre-Trained Transformer.

The boundary against the wider category matters: a chatbot can be any software or system that holds dialogue with a person and does not necessarily have to be AI-powered — there are rules-based chatbots that give canned responses to questions — whereas ChatGPT is AI-powered and uses LLM technology to generate text after a prompt. ChatGPT was released for public use on November 30, 2022. Both the free version of ChatGPT and the paid ChatGPT Plus are regularly updated with new GPT models, and the most recent model is GPT-4; the free version requires only a sign-in. There is a free ChatGPT app, at launch limited to U.S. iOS users, with OpenAI saying an Android version is "coming soon," and there is an API, released March 1, 2023.

Anyone can use ChatGPT, and more and more tech companies and search engines are using the chatbot to automate text or quickly answer user questions and concerns. Multiple enterprises use it, although others limit use of the tool. Microsoft announced at its 2023 Build conference that it is integrating its ChatGPT-based Bing experience into Windows 11; the Brooklyn-based 3D display startup Looking Glass uses ChatGPT to produce holograms you can communicate with; and the nonprofit organization Solana integrated the chatbot into its network with a ChatGPT plug-in geared toward end users to help onboard into the web3 space.

# ChatGPT Web Browsing And Plugins

OpenAI formally launched an internet-browsing feature for ChatGPT, ending the chatbot's confinement to training data up to September 2021 — a launch that came some three weeks after the feature was re-introduced in beta following several months in hiatus.

The path there ran through plugins and a withdrawal. OpenAI first connected ChatGPT to the internet by launching plugins, extending the bot's functionality by granting it access to third-party knowledge sources and databases, including the web; plugins were available in alpha to ChatGPT users and developers on the waitlist, with OpenAI saying it would initially prioritize a small number of developers and premium ChatGPT Plus subscribers before rolling out larger-scale and API access. OpenAI then announced that ChatGPT Plus subscribers could use a feature in the app called Browsing, which allows ChatGPT to search Bing for answers; it is enabled from the New Features section of app settings by selecting "GPT-4" in the model switcher and choosing "Browse with Bing" from the drop-down list, and it is available on both the iOS and Android apps. That web browsing capability for Plus subscribers, offered in July, was taken away after users exploited it to get around paywalls.

OpenAI posted on Twitter/X on September 27, 2023 that "ChatGPT can now browse the internet to provide you with current and authoritative information, complete with direct links to sources. It is no longer limited to data before September 2021."

# GPT Model Lineage And The ChatGPT Launch

GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) is the large language model that ChatGPT runs on, and OpenAI had been developing it since 2016 — unveiling GPT-1 in 2018 and iterating it to GPT-3 by June 2020. With the November 30, 2022 release of GPT-3.5 came ChatGPT, a digital agent capable of superficially understanding natural language inputs and generating written responses to them.

The first iteration's limits were plain: it was rather slow to answer and couldn't speak to questions about anything that happened after September 2021, not to mention its issues answering queries with misinformation during bouts of "hallucinations." Even so, that kludgy first iteration demonstrated capabilities far beyond what other state-of-the-art digital assistants like Siri and Alexa could provide — the discriminating feature that set it apart from what came before.

# ChatGPT's Launch And Its First Year Of Evolution

ChatGPT, OpenAI's viral AI chatbot, turned one on November 30, 2023. A year earlier OpenAI released it as a "low-key research preview," reportedly spurred in part by an intense rivalry with AI startup Anthropic. The goal, OpenAI leadership told the OpenAI rank-and-file at the time, was to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI to inform the development of OpenAI's future models.

Initially a basic free-to-use, web-based and chat-focused interface on top of one of OpenAI's existing models, GPT-3.5, ChatGPT would go on to become the company's most popular product ever — and the fastest-growing consumer app in history. Sam Altman marked the anniversary on X: "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning's launch. what a year it's been…"

In the months following its launch, ChatGPT gained paid tiers with additional features, including a plan geared toward enterprise customers. OpenAI also upgraded ChatGPT with web searching, document analyzing and image creating capabilities via DALL-E 3. And, leaning on speech recognition, voice synthesis and text-image understanding models developed in house, OpenAI gave ChatGPT the ability to "hear," "speak," "see" and take actions.

# Meta's Open Source AI Strategy And Motives

TechCrunch reads the AI Alliance release's closing jab — its contrast with a vision that would relegate AI innovation to a small number of closed, proprietary companies — as saying a lot about Meta's ulterior motives.

# Google's Gemini Model Family And Its Capability Claims

Gemini is Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled in the first week of December 2023 and meant to power a range of products and services including Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor. # Product Launch

## Definition

Across this corpus, "launch" (and "launched") is used to describe a company unveiling, announcing, or first shipping a new product, feature, or device — the corpus does not itself define the term, but consistently applies it to this announce-and/or-ship moment (see Context).

## Background (external)

ProductPlan's product-management glossary defines a product launch as "a business's planned and coordinated effort to debut a new product to the market and make that product generally available for purchase," noting that launches also build anticipation, gather early-adopter feedback, and generate momentum beyond simply enabling sales (ProductPlan, accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.productplan.com/glossary/product-launch/).

## Context

Across the corpus, launches recur as the mechanism by which companies move a product from development into the market, and the term covers a spectrum from a single press event to a multi-year rollout. Google's annual hardware event unveiled the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro alongside the Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds and Pixel Watch 2, showing that a single launch event can bundle several products at once. Apple's "Scary Fast" event was anticipated as the venue for unveiling M3-powered MacBook Pros, a refreshed iMac, and new USB-C accessories, illustrating that launches are often previewed and rumored before the event itself. Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" was "first announced in September" and only became available afterward, alongside the Echo Pop Kids speakers being "available for purchase" at $49.99 — showing the announce-then-ship pattern explicitly. OpenAI's ChatGPT similarly moved through staged launches: an initial November 2022 release, then a paid ChatGPT Plus tier and plug-in/API support unveiled in March 2023, then further features (Enterprise, browsing, voice, GPTs) rolled out through the rest of the year. Valve's Steam Deck OLED was announced at a press event ahead of its device launch, with press being told units would be "available to order" on a specific date and begin shipping shortly after. Keep Labs' medication-storage device took years between its 2019 preorder campaign and "this week started shipping its first product to consumers," showing a launch can be delayed substantially between announcement and actual availability.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-stage structure** — an "unveiling" or announcement stage (often at a press or hardware event) is followed by a separate "available for purchase" or shipping stage, and the gap between them can range from days to years, as with Keep Labs' multi-year gap between its 2019 preorder campaign and 2023 shipping date.
- **Bundling** — a single launch event frequently introduces multiple products or features together, as Google did with the Pixel 8 line, Android 14, and several accessories in one hardware event.
- **Pre-launch anticipation** — launches are frequently preceded by rumors and analyst predictions about what will be unveiled, as with the expected Apple "Scary Fast" event coverage of M3 chips and MacBook Pro refreshes before the event occurred.
- **Staged/iterative rollout** — for software products like ChatGPT, "launch" is not a single moment but a sequence of feature releases (Plus tier, plugins, Enterprise, voice, GPTs) unveiled over many months following the initial debut.
- **Concrete availability signals** — corpus reporting marks a launch's completion with specific, checkable facts: a price, an order date, or a shipping date, e.g. the Steam Deck OLED being "available to order on November 16th" with shipping "as orders start to roll in," or the Echo Pop Kids being "available for purchase, starting at $49.99."

# The Competitive Response To ChatGPT Across The AI Industry

ChatGPT became priority number one at OpenAI — not simply a one-off product but a development platform to build upon — and, as often happens in a competition-driven marketplace, it shifted the focus at other AI firms and research labs too.

Google scrambled to launch a response to ChatGPT, eventually releasing Bard, a more or less comparable AI chatbot, in February 2023. Countless other ChatGPT rivals and derivatives have arrived to market since, most recently Amazon Q, a more business-oriented take on ChatGPT. # ChatGPT Adoption Milestones And Usage Statistics

Roughly a year after its release, ChatGPT had 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also revealed that over two million developers use the platform, including more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies.

Two other markers frame that scale. OpenAI hit the one-year anniversary of ChatGPT: what began as a "low-key research preview" evolved into a powerhouse that changed the AI industry forever, and Altman looked back on the night before its launch in a post on X on November 30, 2023 — "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning's launch. what a year it's been…" Meanwhile neither Apple nor Google chose an AI app as its app of the year for 2023, despite the success of ChatGPT's mobile app, which became the fastest-growing consumer application in history before that record was broken by Meta's Threads.

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# ChatGPT Legal And Privacy Controversies

ChatGPT has generated a run of legal and privacy controversies: an Australian mayor publicly announced he may sue OpenAI for defamation over ChatGPT's false claims that he had served time in prison for bribery, which would be the first defamation lawsuit against the text-generating service, and there have been other cases of ChatGPT accusing individuals of false crimes.

The libel exposure follows from how the models work: they do not know or care whether something is true, only that it looks true — a problem when the output is used for homework, and potentially libel when it accuses someone of a crime they did not commit. How troubling statements produced by ChatGPT will be handled was expected to play out over the following months as tech and legal experts tackled the fastest moving target in the industry. As of the article, there were no lawsuits specifically targeting ChatGPT, but OpenAI is involved in at least one lawsuit with implications for AI systems trained on publicly available data, which would touch on ChatGPT. There are also plagiarism issues: text-generating AI models like ChatGPT have a tendency to regurgitate content from their training data. Copyright in output sits with the user — the person who requested the input from ChatGPT is the copyright owner.

On privacy, OpenAI has said that individuals in "certain jurisdictions" such as the EU can object to the processing of their personal information by its AI models by filling out a form — the "OpenAI Personal Data Removal Request" — which includes the ability to request deletion of AI-generated references about them, although OpenAI notes it may not grant every request since it must balance privacy requests against freedom of expression "in accordance with applicable laws." In its privacy policy OpenAI makes a passing acknowledgement of the objection requirements attached to relying on "legitimate interest," pointing users to instructions on how to opt out of use of their information to train its models. ChatGPT chats are not public, but OpenAI disclosed a bug, since fixed, that exposed the titles of some users' conversations to other people on the service.

Other controversies span platforms and schools. Discord integrated OpenAI's technology into its bot Clyde, and two users tricked Clyde into providing instructions for making methamphetamine and napalm. CNET found itself in controversy after Futurism reported the publication was publishing articles under a mysterious byline completely generated by AI, and Red Ventures, the private equity company that owns CNET, was accused of using ChatGPT for SEO farming even where the information was incorrect. Several major school systems and colleges, including New York City Public Schools, have banned ChatGPT from their networks and devices, claiming the AI impedes the learning process by promoting plagiarism and misinformation — a claim not every educator agrees with.

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. # ChatGPT Overview And Significance

ChatGPT is OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot, and it has taken the world by storm: what started as a tool to hyper-charge productivity through writing essays and code from short text prompts has evolved into a behemoth used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies for far more wide-ranging needs.

That growth propelled OpenAI itself into becoming one of the most-hyped companies in recent memory, even though CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return raised concerns about the company's direction and opened the door for competitors. Whatever the nefarious side of ChatGPT, it was clear that AI tools were not going away anytime soon: since its initial launch nearly a year earlier, ChatGPT had hit 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI was investing heavily in it.

The capability boundary at the time was defined by model access and modality. # Independent Research And Reviews Of ChatGPT's Flaws

Independent researchers and advocacy groups repeatedly found ChatGPT and GPT-4 to be flawed in ways OpenAI's own launches did not resolve — on child safety, on toxicity, and on the vision-enabled multimodal model.

An independent review from Common Sense Media, a nonprofit advocacy group, found that ChatGPT could potentially be harmful for younger users, flagging it as potentially unsafe for kids; ChatGPT got an overall three-star rating in the report, with its lowest ratings relating to transparency, privacy, trust and safety. On multimodality, OpenAI announced that GPT-4 with vision would become available alongside the upcoming launch of the GPT-4 Turbo API, but some researchers found that the model remained flawed in several significant and problematic ways.

Two toxicity findings stand out. A Microsoft-affiliated scientific paper examined the "trustworthiness" — and toxicity — of LLMs including GPT-4; because GPT-4 is more likely to follow the instructions of "jailbreaking" prompts, the co-authors claim it can be more easily prompted than other LLMs to spout toxic, biased text. Separately, a study co-authored by scientists at the Allen Institute for AI showed that assigning ChatGPT a "persona" through the ChatGPT API — for example "a bad person," "a horrible person" or "a nasty person" — increases its toxicity sixfold; the co-authors also found that having the chatbot pose as certain historical figures, gendered people and members of political parties increased its toxicity, with journalists, men and Republicans in particular causing the model to say more offensive things than it normally would. That research was conducted using the latest version, but not the model then in preview based on GPT-4.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

# GPT Model Releases From GPT-3.5 To GPT-4

ChatGPT first launched to the public as OpenAI quietly released GPT-3.5: the model broke cover with ChatGPT, a fine-tuned version of GPT-3.5 that is essentially a general-purpose chatbot able to engage with a range of topics including programming, TV scripts and scientific concepts.

Writers everywhere rolled their eyes at the new technology, much as artists did with OpenAI's DALL-E model, but the chat-style iteration seemingly broadened its appeal and audience. GPT-4 followed on March 14: a powerful image- and text-understanding AI model, released to paying ChatGPT Plus users and through a public API, with developers able to sign up on a waitlist to access the API.



---


# OpenAI Developer Platform And API Releases

OpenAI progressively opened its models to developers through paid APIs and fine-tuning programmes, beginning with a paid API for ChatGPT — a move toward monetization whose initial customers included Instacart, Snap (Snapchat's parent company) and Quizlet.

Model access followed. OpenAI announced the general availability of GPT-4: starting July 6, all existing OpenAI developers "with a history of successful payments" could access GPT-4, with access planned for new developers by the end of July. OpenAI said it would in future allow developers to fine-tune GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 Turbo — one of the original models powering ChatGPT — with their own data, as had long been possible with several of OpenAI's other text-generating models, and that the capability should arrive later that year. It then brought fine-tuning to GPT-3.5 Turbo: companies using the model through the API can make it better follow specific instructions, such as always responding in a given language, improve its ability to consistently format responses, and hone the "feel" of its output, such as tone, so it better fits a brand or voice; most notably, fine-tuning lets customers shorten text prompts to speed up API calls and cut costs. OpenAI partnered with Scale AI to allow companies to fine-tune GPT-3.5, though it was unclear whether OpenAI was developing an in-house tuning tool to complement platforms like Scale AI or to serve a different purpose. Fine-tuning costs were $0.008 per 1K tokens for training, $0.012 per 1K tokens for usage input and $0.016 per 1K tokens for usage output. A GPT-4 fine-tuning programme followed, but unlike the GPT-3.5 programme it involves more oversight and guidance from OpenAI teams, largely because of technical hurdles.

OpenAI also extended the platform beyond text. DALL-E 3, its text-to-image model, became available via an API after first coming to ChatGPT-4 and Bing Chat, and OpenAI released a text-to-speech API, the Audio API, offering six preset voices and two generative AI model variants.

# Model Fine-Tuning

## Definition

In the corpus, model fine-tuning is the OpenAI capability that lets companies using GPT-3.5 Turbo or GPT-4 through the API continue training the model on their own data so it better fits their use case. In the corpus's most concrete example, OpenAI's fine-tuning of GPT-3.5 Turbo lets companies using the model through the API make it better follow specific instructions — such as always responding in a given language, formatting responses consistently, or matching a brand's tone — and shorten text prompts to speed up API calls and cut costs.

## Context

The corpus documents fine-tuning as a capability OpenAI progressively opened to developers alongside its paid APIs. OpenAI first brought fine-tuning to GPT-3.5 Turbo, partnering with Scale AI so companies could fine-tune the model, at published costs of $0.008 per 1K tokens for training, $0.012 per 1K tokens for usage input, and $0.016 per 1K tokens for usage output. It later extended fine-tuning to GPT-4, though the GPT-4 program involves more oversight and guidance from OpenAI teams than the GPT-3.5 program, largely due to technical hurdles. Separately, in TechCrunch's October 2023 survey of AI investors, fine-tuning is named as one of the distinct layers of the emerging LLM stack — alongside models and pre-training solutions — that sits in the middle layer connecting foundation models to specialized applications, together with prompt engineering and model orchestration.

## Key Characteristics

- **Continues training an existing model on customer data** — fine-tuning takes a model the customer already accesses through the API (e.g., GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4) and continues training it on data the customer supplies.
- **Improves instruction-following and output style** — it can make a model better follow specific instructions, consistently format responses, and match a desired tone or brand voice.
- **Reduces prompt length and cost** — because the desired behavior is trained into the model, fine-tuning lets customers shorten text prompts, which speeds up API calls and cuts per-call cost.
- **Priced separately from inference** — OpenAI charged distinct per-token rates for fine-tuning training versus using (input/output) the fine-tuned model.
- **Oversight scales with model capability** — OpenAI applied more oversight and guidance to the GPT-4 fine-tuning program than to the GPT-3.5 program, citing technical hurdles.
- **A distinct layer of the LLM stack** — investors surveyed by TechCrunch treat fine-tuning tools as their own layer of the GenAI tech stack, separate from foundation model providers and end-user applications.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, OpenAI's own documentation describes fine-tuning more generally as letting a developer "take an OpenAI base model, provide the kinds of inputs and outputs you expect" so the model is adapted to a specific task rather than replaced with a newly trained one (OpenAI, "Model optimization," accessed 2026-09-02, https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization).

# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.

# OpenAI's Founding And Its 2023 Board Crisis

The Rosewood hotel dinner led to the creation of a startup called OpenAI later that year; backed by hundreds of millions of dollars from Elon Musk and other funders, the lab promised to protect the world from Larry Page's vision. Thanks to its ChatGPT chatbot, OpenAI has fundamentally changed the technology industry and introduced the world to the risks and potential of artificial intelligence, and it is valued at more than $US80 billion, about $A123 billion, according to two people familiar with the company's latest funding round. Musk and Sam Altman's partnership did not survive, and the two have since stopped speaking. Altman's own gloss on such splits: "There is disagreement, mistrust, egos. The closer people are to being pointed in the same direction, the more contentious the disagreements are. You see this in sects and religious orders. There are bitter fights between the closest people."

The month before the 9 December 2023 article, that infighting came to OpenAI's boardroom: rebel board members tried to force out Altman because they believed they could no longer trust him to build AI that would benefit humanity, and over five chaotic days OpenAI looked as if it were going to fall apart until the board, pressured by giant investors and by employees who threatened to follow Altman out the door, backed down. The drama gave the world its first glimpse of the bitter feuds among those who will determine the future of AI, but years before the near meltdown there was a little-publicised but ferocious competition in Silicon Valley for control of the technology now quickly reshaping the world, from how children are taught to how wars are fought. That earlier story begins with DeepMind: five years before the Napa Valley party and two before the cat breakthrough on YouTube, Demis Hassabis, a 34-year-old neuroscientist, walked into a cocktail party at Peter Thiel's San Francisco town house and realised he had hit pay dirt, because there in Thiel's living room, overlooking the city's Palace of Fine Arts and a swan pond, was a chessboard; Hassabis had once been the second-best player in the world in the under-14 category, and said "I was preparing for that meeting for a year. I thought that would be my unique hook in: I knew that he loved chess."

# GPTs: OpenAI's Custom Chatbots And The Dev Day Announcements

GPTs are OpenAI's tool for building custom conversational, action-taking AI systems powered by OpenAI's models, including the models underpinning ChatGPT. They were announced at OpenAI's first-ever developer conference, held Monday, November 6, 2023, where the Microsoft-backed AI startup announced a host of new products — the more notable being tools to create custom "GPTs" (that is, domain-specific chatbots), new text-to-speech models, an API for the text-to-image model DALL-E 3, and an improved version of OpenAI's flagship model GPT-4, called GPT-4 Turbo.

What distinguishes a GPT from a prompt is that the knowledge is built in. With GPTs, a user can train a model on a cookbook collection, for example, so that it can answer questions about ingredients for a specific recipe; or they can give a model their company's proprietary codebases so that developers can check their style or generate code in line with best practices. Some of the initial GPTs, all created by OpenAI, include a Gen Z meme translator, a coloring book and sticker creator, a data visualizer, a board game explainer and a creative writing coach. ChatGPT can accomplish these tasks given carefully engineered prompts and foreknowledge, but purpose-built GPTs drastically simplify things — and might just kill the cottage industry that emerged around creating and editing prompts to feed to ChatGPT.

The consequence TechCrunch draws for ChatGPT itself is a change of role: with GPTs, ChatGPT could become more a gateway to a broader ecosystem of AI-powered chatbots than the end-all-be-all. GPTs introduce a level of personalization far beyond that ChatGPT offers today, and — once OpenAI sorts out its capacity issues — TechCrunch expects an explosion of creativity there. Will ChatGPT be as visible as it once was after GPTs flood the marketplace? Perhaps not; but it will not go away, it will simply adapt and evolve, no doubt in ways not even its creators can anticipate.

# OpenAI's Nonprofit-To-For-Profit Structure

OpenAI started out as a nonprofit when it launched with financial backing from Tesla CEO Elon Musk and others, with stated aims to "advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return." That changed in 2018, when it incorporated a for-profit business, OpenAI LP, and shifted nearly all its staff into that business, not long after releasing its first generation of the GPT large language model for mimicking human writing.

Around the same time, Musk — who had co-chaired its board with Altman — resigned from the board, in a move OpenAI said would eliminate a "potential future conflict for Elon" due to Tesla's work on building self-driving systems. The resulting arrangement is a split one: OpenAI's board has preserved its nonprofit governance structure, while the startup it oversees has increasingly sought to capitalize on its technology by tailoring its popular chatbot to business customers.

# OpenAI's Updated Preparedness Framework

OpenAI's "Preparedness Framework," described in a new document and blog post covered on 18 December 2023, is the company's internal process for identifying, analyzing, and deciding what to do about "catastrophic" risks inherent to the models it is developing. The update is part of an expansion of OpenAI's internal safety processes to fend off the threat of harmful AI: a new "safety advisory group" will sit above the technical teams and make recommendations to leadership, and the board has been granted veto power — though whether it will actually use that power is another question entirely.

TechCrunch's framing is that policies like these normally do not warrant coverage, since in practice they amount to closed-door meetings with obscure functions and responsibility flows that outsiders will seldom be privy to. What makes this one worth examining is the recent leadership fracas at OpenAI and the evolving AI risk discussion, given that OpenAI is the world's leading AI development company.

The report notes that the framework appears to have been retooled after November's shake-up, which removed the board's two most "decelerationist" members: Ilya Sutskever, who remained at the company in a somewhat changed role, and Helen Toner, who left entirely.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had previously pointed to industry-wide GPU shortages for the service's spotty performance, and producing its own processors might mitigate those supply issues while potentially lowering the current four-cent-per-query cost of operating the chatbot to something more manageable.

# The Microsoft-OpenAI Partnership And Microsoft's Response To The Firing

Microsoft is OpenAI's largest corporate backer — it had poured $13 billion into OpenAI as of November 2023 and holds what amounts to a 49% stake — and its public response to Altman's firing was to reaffirm the partnership and to back interim CEO Mira Murati rather than to intervene.

The relationship has three visible features in this account: the scale of the investment, a long-term agreement giving Microsoft access to OpenAI's technology, and deep product integration. Frank Shaw, Microsoft's chief communications officer, said: "We have a long-term partnership with OpenAI and Microsoft remains committed to Mira and their team as we bring this next era of AI to our customers." CEO Satya Nadella then published a fuller statement: "As you saw at Microsoft Ignite this week, we're continuing to rapidly innovate for this era of AI, with over 100 announcements across the full tech stack from AI systems, models and tools in Azure, to Copilot. Most importantly, we're committed to delivering all of this to our customers while building for the future. We have a long-term agreement with OpenAI with full access to everything we need to deliver on our innovation agenda and an exciting product roadmap; and remain committed to our partnership, and to Mira and the team. Together, we will continue to deliver the meaningful benefits of this technology to the world."

The partnership's limits also showed. Microsoft's stock price fell more than 1% in the last 30 minutes of trading after Altman's departure was announced, and Axios reported that Microsoft was notified Altman would be leaving only "minutes" before the public announcement. OpenAI's press relations declined to comment beyond the official blog post.

# ChatGPT Subscription Tiers And Pricing

ChatGPT is sold in a ladder of paid tiers on top of the free chatbot: ChatGPT Plus at $20 per month, a previewed ChatGPT Business tier, and ChatGPT Enterprise — with the tiers distinguished mainly by data-usage policy, control over end users, and access to the newest models.

The ladder was built in stages. OpenAI first said it was "starting to think about how to monetize ChatGPT" in an announcement on the company's official Discord server, posting a waitlist for a version to be called ChatGPT Professional; the waitlist document listed benefits including no "blackout" windows, no throttling and an unlimited number of messages — "at least 2x the regular daily limit." A month later OpenAI launched a pilot subscription plan, ChatGPT Plus, starting at $20 per month. # Sam Altman Fired As OpenAI CEO In November 2023

Sam Altman was fired as CEO of OpenAI late on Friday, November 17, 2023, by the board of directors of OpenAI, Inc. — the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that acts as the governing body for OpenAI, the startup behind ChatGPT, GPT-4 and DALL-E 3. He both left the company's board of directors and stepped down as CEO, with chief technology officer Mira Murati stepping in as interim CEO.

OpenAI announced the shake-up in a post on its official blog; the company's management team was made aware shortly after. The blog post said Altman's departure followed a "deliberative review process by the board" which concluded that Altman "wasn't consistently candid in his communications" with other board members, "hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities," and that the board "no longer has confidence in [Altman's] ability to continue leading OpenAI." In a joint statement the board wrote that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity," said it remained "fully committed to serving this mission," thanked Altman for "his many contributions to the founding and growth of OpenAI," and said that "we believe new leadership is necessary as we move forward" and that Mira, "as the leader of the company's research, product, and safety functions," was "exceptionally qualified" as interim CEO. OpenAI said it would begin a formal search for a permanent CEO immediately.

Altman responded on X: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later." The removal came unexpectedly. OpenAI had just hosted its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, the week before with Altman emceeing; Altman had spoken at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference and at an Oakland, California event on the Thursday. According to The Verge and The New York Times, citing multiple internal sources, OpenAI employees learned of Altman's firing when it was announced publicly. # Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# Regulatory Investigations Into OpenAI In 2023

OpenAI faced regulatory action on several fronts in 2023: Italy ordered ChatGPT blocked over GDPR concerns, Poland opened its own GDPR investigation, China's licensing regime pushed ChatGPT clients out of the App Store, and the FTC was reported to be investigating the chatbot's statements about people.

Italy moved first. Italy's data protection authority ordered OpenAI to stop processing people's data locally with immediate effect, saying it was concerned the ChatGPT maker was breaching the EU's General Data Protection Regulation and opening an investigation; OpenAI began geoblocking access to ChatGPT in Italy. The DPA then laid out what OpenAI needed to do for the order to be lifted, giving OpenAI a deadline of April 30 to complete the regulator's compliance demands, with a slightly more generous timeline of May 15 for a local radio, TV and internet awareness campaign. Poland's authority publicly announced it had opened an investigation regarding ChatGPT, accusing the company of a string of breaches of the GDPR.

In China, multiple generative AI apps were removed from Apple's China App Store ahead of the country's latest generative AI regulations, set to take effect August 15. Apple wrote in a letter to OpenCat, a native ChatGPT client: "As you may know, the government has been tightening regulations associated with deep synthesis technologies (DST) and generative AI services, including ChatGPT. DST must fulfill permitting requirements to operate in China, including securing a license from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). Based on our review, your app is associated with ChatGPT, which does not have requisite permits to operate in China."

In the United States, the FTC was reportedly in at least the exploratory phase of an investigation into whether ChatGPT made "false, misleading, disparaging or harmful" statements about people. TechCrunch reporter Devin Coldewey noted that such an investigation does not appear out of thin air — the FTC does not look around and say "That looks suspicious"; generally a lawsuit or formal complaint is brought to its attention and the practices described imply that regulations are being ignored, much as a person suing a supplement company over pills that made them sick can prompt an FTC investigation because there is evidence the company lied about side effects. Separately, FTC chair Lina Khan and fellow commissioners warned House representatives in a congressional hearing that modern AI technologies like ChatGPT could be used to "turbocharge" fraud: "AI presents a whole set of opportunities, but also presents a whole set of risks," Khan said. "And I think we've already seen ways in which it could be used to turbocharge fraud and scams. # ChatGPT Adoption Milestones And Usage Statistics

# Generative AI

## Definition

In the corpus, "generative AI" is the umbrella label applied to the 2023 AI boom's content-producing systems — OpenAI's ChatGPT (built on GPT-3.5/GPT-4) and Adobe's Firefly image and vector-graphics models are the flagship examples named — rather than a term the corpus itself formally defines.

## Context

The corpus treats "generative AI" as the umbrella term for the mainstream AI boom of 2023, distinct from the EU AI Act's regulatory term "general purpose AI" (GPAI), which lawmakers deliberately chose as a more technology-neutral label for "the most powerful models behind the current boom in generative AI tools" so the law would not be pinned to one architecture like transformers (doc_0525).
OpenAI built ChatGPT specifically "to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI," and its free, chat-based interface is credited with "taking generative AI mainstream" as a consumer product rather than a research artifact (doc_0047).
Enterprise adoption is depicted as cautious relative to vendor hype: a Morgan Stanley survey found 56% of CIOs said generative AI was affecting investment priorities, but only 4% had launched significant projects, most still in evaluation or proof-of-concept (doc_0160).
The technology spans well beyond chatbots — Adobe's Firefly generative AI models generate images and vector graphics for creative software (doc_0043), and Amazon executive Tye Brady discussed generative AI alongside humanoid robots and mobile manipulation as an input to robotics work (doc_0528).
The same capability that drives adoption also drives the corpus's recurring regulatory and creative-industry concerns: the EU warned that "widely accessible generative AI tools" pose disinformation risks to elections (doc_0248), and the National Music Publishers Association called generative AI "the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed" in its copyright submission to the US Copyright Office (doc_0271).

## Key Characteristics

- **Illustrated by content-producing examples rather than defined outright** — the corpus shows the term through instances of new text, images, and vector graphics being produced from a prompt, illustrated by ChatGPT's text generation (doc_0048) and Firefly's image/vector generation (doc_0043).
- **Consumer breakout via chat interfaces** — ChatGPT's free, web-based chat interface is what took generative AI "mainstream," reaching the fastest adoption of any consumer app (doc_0047, doc_0048).
- **Enterprise adoption lags vendor hype** — large-company CIOs report slow, cautious rollout despite heavy vendor promotion, weighing API/SaaS costs against ROI (doc_0160).
- **Distinct from but overlapping "general purpose AI"** — EU lawmakers deliberately avoided calling the underlying models "generative AI" in law, choosing "general purpose AI" instead to stay technology-neutral rather than tied to transformer-based architectures (doc_0525).
- **Applies across domains beyond chatbots** — spans creative tools (Adobe Firefly) and robotics (Amazon's mobile manipulation work), per the corpus (doc_0043, doc_0528).
- **Focus of copyright and disinformation controversy** — named by the NMPA as a threat to the "human creative class" via unlicensed training data (doc_0271), and flagged by the EU as an election-disinformation risk requiring safeguards (doc_0248).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "generative AI" as a familiar shorthand without formally defining it. Per IBM, generative AI "is artificial intelligence (AI) that can create original content — such as text, images, video, audio or software code — in response to a user's prompt or request," distinguishing it from AI systems built only to classify or act on existing data (IBM, *What is generative AI?*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# GPTs: OpenAI's Custom Chatbots And The Dev Day Announcements

GPTs are OpenAI's tool for building custom conversational, action-taking AI systems powered by OpenAI's models, including the models underpinning ChatGPT. They were announced at OpenAI's first-ever developer conference, held Monday, November 6, 2023, where the Microsoft-backed AI startup announced a host of new products — the more notable being tools to create custom "GPTs" (that is, domain-specific chatbots), new text-to-speech models, an API for the text-to-image model DALL-E 3, and an improved version of OpenAI's flagship model GPT-4, called GPT-4 Turbo.

What distinguishes a GPT from a prompt is that the knowledge is built in. With GPTs, a user can train a model on a cookbook collection, for example, so that it can answer questions about ingredients for a specific recipe; or they can give a model their company's proprietary codebases so that developers can check their style or generate code in line with best practices. Some of the initial GPTs, all created by OpenAI, include a Gen Z meme translator, a coloring book and sticker creator, a data visualizer, a board game explainer and a creative writing coach. ChatGPT can accomplish these tasks given carefully engineered prompts and foreknowledge, but purpose-built GPTs drastically simplify things — and might just kill the cottage industry that emerged around creating and editing prompts to feed to ChatGPT.

The consequence TechCrunch draws for ChatGPT itself is a change of role: with GPTs, ChatGPT could become more a gateway to a broader ecosystem of AI-powered chatbots than the end-all-be-all. GPTs introduce a level of personalization far beyond that ChatGPT offers today, and — once OpenAI sorts out its capacity issues — TechCrunch expects an explosion of creativity there. Will ChatGPT be as visible as it once was after GPTs flood the marketplace? Perhaps not; but it will not go away, it will simply adapt and evolve, no doubt in ways not even its creators can anticipate.

# ChatGPT Web Browsing And Plugins

OpenAI formally launched an internet-browsing feature for ChatGPT, ending the chatbot's confinement to training data up to September 2021 — a launch that came some three weeks after the feature was re-introduced in beta following several months in hiatus.

The path there ran through plugins and a withdrawal. OpenAI first connected ChatGPT to the internet by launching plugins, extending the bot's functionality by granting it access to third-party knowledge sources and databases, including the web; plugins were available in alpha to ChatGPT users and developers on the waitlist, with OpenAI saying it would initially prioritize a small number of developers and premium ChatGPT Plus subscribers before rolling out larger-scale and API access. OpenAI then announced that ChatGPT Plus subscribers could use a feature in the app called Browsing, which allows ChatGPT to search Bing for answers; it is enabled from the New Features section of app settings by selecting "GPT-4" in the model switcher and choosing "Browse with Bing" from the drop-down list, and it is available on both the iOS and Android apps. That web browsing capability for Plus subscribers, offered in July, was taken away after users exploited it to get around paywalls.

OpenAI posted on Twitter/X on September 27, 2023 that "ChatGPT can now browse the internet to provide you with current and authoritative information, complete with direct links to sources. It is no longer limited to data before September 2021."

# Sam Altman Fired As OpenAI CEO In November 2023

Sam Altman was fired as CEO of OpenAI late on Friday, November 17, 2023, by the board of directors of OpenAI, Inc. — the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that acts as the governing body for OpenAI, the startup behind ChatGPT, GPT-4 and DALL-E 3. He both left the company's board of directors and stepped down as CEO, with chief technology officer Mira Murati stepping in as interim CEO.

OpenAI announced the shake-up in a post on its official blog; the company's management team was made aware shortly after. The blog post said Altman's departure followed a "deliberative review process by the board" which concluded that Altman "wasn't consistently candid in his communications" with other board members, "hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities," and that the board "no longer has confidence in [Altman's] ability to continue leading OpenAI." In a joint statement the board wrote that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity," said it remained "fully committed to serving this mission," thanked Altman for "his many contributions to the founding and growth of OpenAI," and said that "we believe new leadership is necessary as we move forward" and that Mira, "as the leader of the company's research, product, and safety functions," was "exceptionally qualified" as interim CEO. OpenAI said it would begin a formal search for a permanent CEO immediately.

Altman responded on X: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later." The removal came unexpectedly. OpenAI had just hosted its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, the week before with Altman emceeing; Altman had spoken at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference and at an Oakland, California event on the Thursday. According to The Verge and The New York Times, citing multiple internal sources, OpenAI employees learned of Altman's firing when it was announced publicly. The same change also saw co-founder Greg Brockman step down as chairman of the board while remaining OpenAI's president, reporting to Murati.

# The Microsoft-OpenAI Partnership And Microsoft's Response To The Firing

Microsoft is OpenAI's largest corporate backer — it had poured $13 billion into OpenAI as of November 2023 and holds what amounts to a 49% stake — and its public response to Altman's firing was to reaffirm the partnership and to back interim CEO Mira Murati rather than to intervene.

The relationship has three visible features in this account: the scale of the investment, a long-term agreement giving Microsoft access to OpenAI's technology, and deep product integration. Frank Shaw, Microsoft's chief communications officer, said: "We have a long-term partnership with OpenAI and Microsoft remains committed to Mira and their team as we bring this next era of AI to our customers." CEO Satya Nadella then published a fuller statement: "As you saw at Microsoft Ignite this week, we're continuing to rapidly innovate for this era of AI, with over 100 announcements across the full tech stack from AI systems, models and tools in Azure, to Copilot. Most importantly, we're committed to delivering all of this to our customers while building for the future. We have a long-term agreement with OpenAI with full access to everything we need to deliver on our innovation agenda and an exciting product roadmap; and remain committed to our partnership, and to Mira and the team. Together, we will continue to deliver the meaningful benefits of this technology to the world."

The partnership's limits also showed. Microsoft's stock price fell more than 1% in the last 30 minutes of trading after Altman's departure was announced, and Axios reported that Microsoft was notified Altman would be leaving only "minutes" before the public announcement. OpenAI's press relations declined to comment beyond the official blog post.

# OpenAI's Nonprofit-To-For-Profit Structure

OpenAI started out as a nonprofit when it launched with financial backing from Tesla CEO Elon Musk and others, with stated aims to "advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return." That changed in 2018, when it incorporated a for-profit business, OpenAI LP, and shifted nearly all its staff into that business, not long after releasing its first generation of the GPT large language model for mimicking human writing.

Around the same time, Musk — who had co-chaired its board with Altman — resigned from the board, in a move OpenAI said would eliminate a "potential future conflict for Elon" due to Tesla's work on building self-driving systems. The resulting arrangement is a split one: OpenAI's board has preserved its nonprofit governance structure, while the startup it oversees has increasingly sought to capitalize on its technology by tailoring its popular chatbot to business customers.

In the days after his firing, Sam Altman's destination was genuinely unsettled: on November 20, 2023 he and Greg Brockman announced they would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research team, yet on the same day both were reported to be still open to returning to OpenAI, and Altman was separately telling investors he planned to launch a new venture.

# Large Language Model (LLM)

## Definition

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to learn from enormous amounts of digital text — Wikipedia articles, digital books, message boards — so that it can generate text on its own.

## Context

The corpus traces the term to OpenAI's GPT-3, described as the neural network Dario Amodei's team built by analysing "countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards" so it "could generate text on its own," released in the summer of 2020; it also "had the unfortunate habit of making things up." ChatGPT itself runs on GPT, the LLM lineage OpenAI had developed since 2016, iterating from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-3 (June 2020) before GPT-3.5 powered ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. In the venture-capital view of the AI market, LLMs sit at the base "foundation model" layer of a broader stack — models, pre-training solutions, fine-tuning tools, middle-layer tooling, and end-market applications — with providers such as OpenAI's GPT-4, Google's Bard, and Anthropic's Claude expected to consolidate into an oligopolistic structure resembling the cloud-provider market. OpenAI's GPT-X models are repeatedly described as proprietary LLMs that other companies build businesses on top of, a dependency that became visible when the November 2023 OpenAI board upheaval led customers to contact rival LLM providers (Anthropic, Google, Cohere) out of concern for continuity.

## Key Characteristics

- **Trained on enormous text corpora** — LLMs learn by analysing vast amounts of digital text (Wikipedia, books, message boards) rather than following hand-written rules.
- **Generative** — once trained, an LLM can generate text on its own in response to a prompt.
- **Prone to fabrication and privacy leakage** — GPT-3 had "the unfortunate habit of making things up," and a Google DeepMind-led test found that prompting ChatGPT to repeat a word endlessly caused OpenAI's LLM to surface private, identifiable information (email addresses and similar) from its training data; a separate Microsoft-affiliated study found GPT-4 more easily "jailbroken" into unsafe outputs than other LLMs.
- **Costly to run and usage-priced** — LLM economics are dominated by compute cost (OpenAI was reported to spend roughly $700,000/day on compute), which is why LLM providers commonly bill by token/usage rather than flat SaaS pricing.
- **Anchors a layered AI stack** — LLMs form the "foundation model" layer beneath middle-layer tooling (fine-tuning, prompt engineering, model orchestration, observability) and top-layer applications that startups build against.
- **Split between proprietary and open approaches** — OpenAI's GPT-X models are proprietary LLMs, contrasted in the corpus with Meta's Llama family and other efforts pushing more "open" LLM development, a split that intensified after a leaked internal Google memo argued neither OpenAI nor Google had a durable "moat" against open-source LLMs.

# The OpenAI Crisis As A Case Against Centralized AI Control

The claim is that the OpenAI debacle exposes a structural risk in depending on a centralized proprietary AI player. The situation remained fluid as of November 21, 2023, with any number of potential outcomes still on the table, but the whole debacle has shone a spotlight on the forces that control the burgeoning AI revolution, leading many to question what happens if you go all-in on a centralized proprietary player and things then go belly-up.

Mark Surman, president and executive director at the Mozilla Foundation, put the ground this way to TechCrunch: "The OpenAI / Microsoft drama underlines one of the big near-term risks with AI — that this next wave of technology is controlled by the same tiny set of players who have shaped that last era of the internet. We might have a chance of avoiding this if GPT-X were responsibly open sourced, giving researchers and startups a shot at making this technology safer, more useful and more trustworthy for people everywhere." The warrant is that concentration of control is itself the hazard, and open sourcing distributes it.

TechCrunch qualifies the claim: it is still too early to make any surefire claims on what impact the OpenAI fallout will have on LLM development and uptake in the future, and Altman and Brockman are undoubtedly steady hands for a commercial AI startup who may even return to steward OpenAI. But some might argue it is unhealthy that so much focus lies on just a handful of people — and it is telling that their departure has created such widespread havoc.

# Model Fine-Tuning

## Definition

In the corpus, model fine-tuning is the OpenAI capability that lets companies using GPT-3.5 Turbo or GPT-4 through the API continue training the model on their own data so it better fits their use case. In the corpus's most concrete example, OpenAI's fine-tuning of GPT-3.5 Turbo lets companies using the model through the API make it better follow specific instructions — such as always responding in a given language, formatting responses consistently, or matching a brand's tone — and shorten text prompts to speed up API calls and cut costs.

## Context

The corpus documents fine-tuning as a capability OpenAI progressively opened to developers alongside its paid APIs. OpenAI first brought fine-tuning to GPT-3.5 Turbo, partnering with Scale AI so companies could fine-tune the model, at published costs of $0.008 per 1K tokens for training, $0.012 per 1K tokens for usage input, and $0.016 per 1K tokens for usage output. It later extended fine-tuning to GPT-4, though the GPT-4 program involves more oversight and guidance from OpenAI teams than the GPT-3.5 program, largely due to technical hurdles. Separately, in TechCrunch's October 2023 survey of AI investors, fine-tuning is named as one of the distinct layers of the emerging LLM stack — alongside models and pre-training solutions — that sits in the middle layer connecting foundation models to specialized applications, together with prompt engineering and model orchestration.

## Key Characteristics

- **Continues training an existing model on customer data** — fine-tuning takes a model the customer already accesses through the API (e.g., GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4) and continues training it on data the customer supplies.
- **Improves instruction-following and output style** — it can make a model better follow specific instructions, consistently format responses, and match a desired tone or brand voice.
- **Reduces prompt length and cost** — because the desired behavior is trained into the model, fine-tuning lets customers shorten text prompts, which speeds up API calls and cuts per-call cost.
- **Priced separately from inference** — OpenAI charged distinct per-token rates for fine-tuning training versus using (input/output) the fine-tuned model.
- **Oversight scales with model capability** — OpenAI applied more oversight and guidance to the GPT-4 fine-tuning program than to the GPT-3.5 program, citing technical hurdles.
- **A distinct layer of the LLM stack** — investors surveyed by TechCrunch treat fine-tuning tools as their own layer of the GenAI tech stack, separate from foundation model providers and end-user applications.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, OpenAI's own documentation describes fine-tuning more generally as letting a developer "take an OpenAI base model, provide the kinds of inputs and outputs you expect" so the model is adapted to a specific task rather than replaced with a newly trained one (OpenAI, "Model optimization," accessed 2026-09-02, https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization).

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# Independent Research And Reviews Of ChatGPT's Flaws

Independent researchers and advocacy groups repeatedly found ChatGPT and GPT-4 to be flawed in ways OpenAI's own launches did not resolve — on child safety, on toxicity, and on the vision-enabled multimodal model.

An independent review from Common Sense Media, a nonprofit advocacy group, found that ChatGPT could potentially be harmful for younger users, flagging it as potentially unsafe for kids; ChatGPT got an overall three-star rating in the report, with its lowest ratings relating to transparency, privacy, trust and safety. On multimodality, OpenAI announced that GPT-4 with vision would become available alongside the upcoming launch of the GPT-4 Turbo API, but some researchers found that the model remained flawed in several significant and problematic ways.

Two toxicity findings stand out. A Microsoft-affiliated scientific paper examined the "trustworthiness" — and toxicity — of LLMs including GPT-4; because GPT-4 is more likely to follow the instructions of "jailbreaking" prompts, the co-authors claim it can be more easily prompted than other LLMs to spout toxic, biased text. Separately, a study co-authored by scientists at the Allen Institute for AI showed that assigning ChatGPT a "persona" through the ChatGPT API — for example "a bad person," "a horrible person" or "a nasty person" — increases its toxicity sixfold; the co-authors also found that having the chatbot pose as certain historical figures, gendered people and members of political parties increased its toxicity, with journalists, men and Republicans in particular causing the model to say more offensive things than it normally would. That research was conducted using the latest version, but not the model then in preview based on GPT-4.
