# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.



---


# Epic's Rebuttal Of Google's Leaked Email Summary

Pressed with the suggestion that the email Epic accused Google of leaking showed Epic was itself interested in a special deal, Tim Sweeney attacked the premise of the characterisation: Google did not leak the email, he said — it leaked "their ridiculously biased summary of it" to Abner Li at 9to5Google.

He supported the leak claim with trial testimony: Don Harrison testified that he didn't think Google leaked to the press, and was then presented with a document including Google's press team and Sameer Samat, head of all Android, summarising the articles that appeared as a result of Google's leaking of Epic's plans to the press. On the substance of the email, Sweeney said it is in evidence and is the same one he had already described: right before Christmas-ish 2019, with the new Marvel season and a lineup of Star Wars content planned, he asked Google's executives to let Fortnite come to the Google Play Store using Epic's own payment method and to open up the use of their own payment methods to all developers, not just Epic. The interviewer conceded the point, saying he had read that email in court and had not realised it was the same one, because it was so far off from what he had heard described as a "special billing exception."



---


# Platform Owners Should Treat Developers As Partners

Tim Sweeney argued that any tech company, Apple and Google included, would be much better off in the long term if it viewed developers as awesome partners and did everything it could to support and empower them rather than get in their way financially — and said the opposite behavior at Apple and Google is what has disappointed him most.

His grounds are a comparison and a diagnosis. The comparison is Microsoft: even at the peak of the antitrust trial against Microsoft, he said, Microsoft was awesome to developers — always respectful, giving developers a great deal and treating them as partners — so that even as Microsoft was crushing corporate competitors, the developer experience was excellent. The Verge appended an editor's note that Netscape might feel differently. The diagnosis is that Google and Apple both treat developers as adversaries, trying to attack developer revenue streams and prevent them from competing with the platforms' own products, and have built massive self-preferencing schemes around excluding developers and disadvantaging third parties — which Sweeney calls very shortsighted. The warrant is that a platform's own long-term position improves when its developers thrive, and Sweeney offers Epic's own conduct as the demonstration: this has been Epic's philosophy with Unreal Engine and the Epic Games Store, where Epic wants to be "a cool partner that helps other companies succeed the way we do." He suspected such a philosophy change at Apple and Google may only come with a generational change in the companies' management.



---


# The Epic v. Apple Ruling And Its Limited Weight Here

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. She also decided that Epic violated its developer agreement with Apple and would have to pay.

Epic did win something. Rogers barred Apple from keeping iPhone users in the dark about alternate ways they can pay for apps, and may have even allowed developers to add their own payment mechanisms.

The precedent's reach into the Google trial is limited in two specific ways. First, that was a different case — and it is not over until the Supreme Court weighs in or declines to take a look. Second, Google cannot tell jurors that Apple won its case, or that other plaintiffs settled; the judge in this case says so. Epic declined to answer on the record when asked about the Apple outcome.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# The $360 Million Activision Payment And Its Evidentiary Weakness

The counter to Epic's headline number attacks the factual premise beneath it: the $360 million refers to an alleged payment that kept Activision from opening an app store that could compete with Google Play, but Activision told The Verge in 2022 that it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store" — and Google says it is now armed with the evidence to prove it.

Epic itself conceded a related point. On Monday Epic's attorney admitted Google "was too clever" to draw up contracts that specifically forced developers not to compete with the Play Store, so it is not clear how much of Epic's evidence will hold up on closer examination.

The narrative advantage may nonetheless survive the evidentiary weakness. The overall story Epic tells is compelling, and it is not clear Google's opening statement countered it: Google spent its 45 minutes attempting to explain that its dominance over the Android app market is not anything nefarious but simply the natural outcome of Google fiercely competing with the iPhone and its iOS App Store, where Google would like the court to believe the competition truly lies.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# Simple Versus Complicated: Assessing The Opening Arguments

The claim after day one is that Epic's chances look better than they should, because the case may come down to simplicity: Google spent most of its first day attempting to explain complicated ins and outs of business, while Epic was able to paint a black-and-white picture of good and evil with itself as the clear underdog.

The starting expectation ran the other way. Walking into the courtroom on Monday morning it seemed impossible — if Epic could not prove Apple's walled iOS garden is a monopoly, how could the comparatively open Google do worse against the windmill-tilting Fortnite developer? The warrant that reverses that expectation is about jury persuasion rather than legal merit: a clearer picture beats a more accurate but more complicated one.

Things got complicated for both parties when the first two witnesses — Epic Games Store head Steve Allison and Yoga Buddhi CEO Benjamin Simon, who also appeared in the earlier Epic v. Apple trial — took the stand. Both Epic and Google spent a long, long time on subtle lines of questioning: you really had to read between the lines to see that Epic was trying to make a point about how Google's 70/30 revenue split is probably based on an arbitrary decision Valve made two decades ago with Steam, or that Google was trying to make the point that Epic, too, likely believed an app store provides more value than just payment processing and maybe deserves more money.



---


# Epic v. Google Is A Jury Trial

Epic and Google have to convince a jury, not the judge, which is totally different from how the Apple case played out — that one was a "bench trial."

The consequence is that persuasion cuts both ways and is hard to predict. All the evidence of tricky deals inside Google might sway a jury against the company; alternatively, Google scaremongering that sideloaded apps equal gaping security holes might sway a jury against Epic. Who knows.

The jury is also sealed off from coverage: Judge Donato explicitly told jurors they are in a "news-free bubble" through mid-December.



---


# Recommendation Algorithm

## Definition

Across the corpus, "recommendation algorithm" (and the closely related notion of algorithmic ranking/curation) names the automated mechanism a platform uses to control the visibility of content, products, or posts — and by extension, the mechanism regulators, courts, and users scrutinize when they suspect a platform is suppressing or favoring particular items.
No single corpus document offers a formal definition of the term; instead each shows the mechanism at work in a different dispute: Amazon's marketplace search ranking and "other products you may like" widget, Instagram's Stories/feed visibility, U.S. platforms' content-moderation feed curation, and Google's Featured Snippets extraction.

## Context

The corpus shows the same underlying mechanism operating across very different platform types, and shows regulators and courts converging on it from different angles.
On Amazon's marketplace, the EU's antitrust objections to the iRobot acquisition center on Amazon's ability to foreclose a rival's *algorithmic visibility* — delisting rival products, reducing their ranking in organic and paid results, excluding them from the "other products you may like" widget, or denying them labels like "Amazon's Choice" — since RVC buyers in France, Germany, Italy, and Spain rely on that in-marketplace ranking both for product discovery and for the final purchase decision.
The same document notes that Amazon's marketplace was separately designated a core platform service under the EU's Digital Markets Act, which imposes restrictions on self-preferencing.
On Meta's Instagram, users and digital-rights groups suspect a comparable but content-moderation-flavored version of the same idea — "shadowbanning" — where an algorithmic process silently lowers a post's visibility (e.g., Palestine-related Stories) without an explicit takedown.
In the U.S. Supreme Court's NetChoice cases (challenging Texas's HB 20 and Florida's SB 7072), the fight is over whether a platform's curation of what appears in a user's feed — a process now largely conducted algorithmically, generally with light human intervention or oversight — is a First-Amendment-protected editorial act that states cannot compel platforms to individually explain post-by-post.
Google's Featured Snippets, which algorithmically extract answers directly from publishers' web pages into search results, are cited in a news-publisher antitrust suit as a related mechanism: an algorithm that decides what content a user sees without the user visiting the original source, which publishers say siphons off their traffic and ad revenue.

## Key Characteristics

- **Ranking, not binary inclusion** — the algorithm typically operates on relative visibility (higher/lower placement in organic or paid results, inclusion in a "you may like" widget) rather than simple on/off access, which is what makes self-preferencing and shadowbanning hard to prove or disprove.
- **Automated with limited human oversight** — described in the NetChoice case as a process "largely conducted algorithmically now — generally with light human intervention or oversight," which is central to arguments that mandated per-decision human explanations would be impractical at the scale of "millions and millions of pieces of content a day."
- **Commercial leverage point** — on marketplaces, control over the recommendation algorithm doubles as a competitive lever: a platform that also sells its own products can use ranking, delisting, and widget exclusion to foreclose rivals, per the EU's ability-and-incentive theory of harm against Amazon.
- **Contestable but opaque** — content creators and merchants can suspect suppression (shadowbanning, reduced marketplace visibility) but the underlying ranking logic is not published, so claims tend to rely on circumstantial or anecdotal patterns rather than direct evidence.
- **Distinct from explicit content removal** — reduced algorithmic visibility (shadowbanning, lower ranking) is a softer, less visible action than outright delisting or takedown, and is treated differently in both platform policy and legal argument.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the general computer-science term for this kind of system is a "recommender system" (also called a recommendation algorithm, engine, or platform): a type of information filtering system that suggests items most relevant to a particular user, predicting user preferences to help them choose from large sets of options such as products, media, or content.
Source: "Recommender system," Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommender_system.

- [The University Response Gap To Faculty Online Abuse](university_response_gap_to_faculty_online_abuse.md)



---


# Epic's Argument That Google Blocks Alternative Android App Stores

Epic will attempt to demonstrate that Google makes it hard for alternative app stores to succeed and reach consumers. Its headline ground is a distribution fact: 90% of apps are still downloaded through Google Play.

The mechanism Epic offers to explain that share is contractual. Google bundles the Play Store with other Google apps that Android OEMs (original equipment manufacturers) have to agree to in order to use Android. Epic will also bring up "Anti-Fragmentation Agreements" (AFAs) that prevent the OEMs from modifying Android to allow for frictionless downloading of apps outside of Google Play. The warrant is that if OEMs are contractually barred from making outside downloading frictionless, rival stores cannot reach consumers on comparable terms, and Play's share follows from the contracts rather than from consumer preference.

Epic will offer two concrete instances. It will specifically reference an agreement it had made with the OEM OnePlus, to make Epic games available on its devices through the Epic Games app; OnePlus had to cancel the deal over concerns that the arrangement would have it bypassing the Google Play Store. The case will also examine a deal between Google and Samsung that Epic says was designed to prevent the Galaxy Store from being a competitive threat and to require Google Play Billing on apps distributed by Samsung.



---


# The FTC's Antitrust Lawsuit Against Amazon

The Federal Trade Commission's sweeping 172-page antitrust lawsuit, filed in late September 2023, accuses Amazon of wielding its monopoly power to squeeze merchants and thwart rivals, which the agency alleges has led to artificially inflated prices and a degraded shopping experience for consumers.

The mechanism the FTC describes is an "anti-discounting strategy" backed by a "massive web-crawling apparatus that constantly tracks online prices" to stifle competition: Amazon punishes third-party sellers who offer cheaper products elsewhere by threatening to disqualify them from appearing in the buy box if it detects a lower price, and losing the buy box is an "existential threat" to sellers' businesses, the complaint alleges. The end result, the FTC argues, is elevated prices across the web — the company steadily hikes the fees it charges sellers and prevents them from discounting on other sites, so sellers often inflate their prices off Amazon, creating an "artificial price floor everywhere." The FTC is seeking to hold Amazon liable for allegedly violating anti-monopoly law but has not yet outlined the specific remedies it believes would best resolve its concerns; in antitrust cases, remedies are often determined only after a court finds the defendant liable. Amazon general counsel David Zapolsky responded in a blog post that third-party sellers set their own prices on the marketplace and that the company invests in tools to help sellers offer "competitive prices": "Even with those tools, some of the businesses selling on Amazon might still choose to set prices that aren't competitive. Just like any store owner who wouldn't want to promote a bad deal to their customers, we don't highlight or promote offers that are not competitively priced." Zapolsky argued the lawsuit could force Amazon to stop highlighting low prices, "a perverse result that would be directly opposed to the goals of antitrust law."

# Valve's Future Handheld And Hardware Plans

While there are no concrete updates on future hardware developments, Valve engineer Pierre-Loup Griffais noted that, so long as interest in handheld gaming remains high, the company has "plans for successive generations of handhelds." For now, Griffais explained, it's important to Valve that developers don't need to "split their attention" between different performance targets.

Asked about the potential for future hardware — like a return of the Steam Machine or an updated Steam Controller — there were no firm updates, but there does seem to be something happening. Griffais agreed that enabling the Steam Deck to work as a hybrid living room console was a "side goal" of the team, and noted that everything Valve does to improve SteamOS will benefit other devices. Coomer added that Valve is still working internally on "a bunch of controllers and prototypes": if SteamOS is being used on larger displays, the team would want to augment that experience with better input options. "We don't have any announcements on that front, but it's why we're building prototypes and thinking about the future there," Coomer said.



---


# Handheld PC Gaming Market Growth

The argument is that the Steam Deck's own success created the component supply that made the OLED model possible. According to the developers Engadget spoke with at Valve, this is the definitive version of the Steam Deck — the HDR OLED model is what they would have released the first time around, if the technology had existed before 2022.

The grounds are the market's pace: the handheld market has evolved quickly, and in just over a year the Steam Deck proved there's widespread demand for handheld PCs, with its success helping drive chip makers and display manufacturers to build hardware specifically for high-fidelity mobile play. The warrant is that this supply-side shift benefits the whole category, not only Valve: this is great news for Valve and the Steam Deck, and also the other handhelds coming out of companies like Ayaneo, ASUS, Ayn, Logitech, Retroid and Razer — and, joking, maybe even Playdate will get an HDR OLED display one day, though Playdate is literally perfect.



---


# Steam Deck OLED Review Verdict

Engadget's verdict, scoring the Valve Steam Deck OLED 89, is that this isn't the Steam Deck 2 some are waiting for — it's just a welcome improvement on an already good device, at $549 at Steam. The pros listed are improved battery life, bright and smooth visuals, better thermals, feeling less top-heavy, and a long charging cable; the cons are that it is still ridiculously large — "Seriously it's so big."

The grounds are the specific gains: the Steam Deck OLED is the facetuned, photoshopped, spit-shined version of Valve's handheld, and it features tangible, clever improvements, with the updated display as the highlight while things like faster charging, improved antennas and smoother haptics are welcome bonuses. The larger warrant is strategic: more importantly, this is Valve renewing its commitment to portable PC gaming, and that's a relief to see, since the Steam Deck is the granddaddy of handheld PCs and Valve has the resources to continue innovating in this space. For now, the OLED model is a half-step toward the Steam Deck 2, which may be the final version of the device — unless Valve finally learns how to count to three.



---


# Steam Deck OLED Improves Much More Than Its Screen

Polygon's reviewer reports that the Steam Deck OLED, which arrived the week before the 2023-11-09 piece, reads as though the Steam Deck team collected a laundry list of complaints about the original and responded to all of them one by one.

The reviewer's baseline is the original Steam Deck, released by Valve in early 2022 and described as his favorite video game console — the first device that let him play the bulk of his sprawling collection of video games wherever he liked — but with gripes: he tended to bundle it with a huge portable power supply, and could not quite shirk how much better games looked on the family's OLED TV. At first glance it appears Valve cribbed from Nintendo's playbook with the Switch OLED, upgrading the screen but not the guts: in raw power the Steam Deck OLED is identical to the original, which Valve says is meant in part to keep giving developers a single optimisation target, while promising that the Steam Deck 2 — which the company hopes to release in two to three years — will have a generational power leap. Everything else, though, improved: longer battery life, faster Wi-Fi, and a stand-alone Bluetooth module. The screen is not merely OLED but HDR OLED — described as the first HDR OLED screen on any gaming portable — with a peak brightness of 1,000 nits for HDR content and 600 nits for SDR, against the original screen's 400 nits peak. And with all of these additions, the Steam Deck OLED is somehow lighter. The reviewer's advice to those who have never tried a Steam Deck is not to wait for the sequel.



---


# Steam Deck Game Compatibility Labels

Valve's compatibility labels are markers on Steam games signifying how well they'll work on the handheld, with four levels: unknown, unsupported, playable and verified.

The discriminating line runs between the top two: playable games generally come with a small caveat, like having to deploy the on-screen keyboard, while verified games have been fully optimized for portable play. Currently, more than 10,000 titles on Steam fall under the playable or verified labels, with more added every day.



---


# Steam Deck OLED As A Mid-Cycle Refresh

The first thing to know about the Steam Deck OLED is that it's not the Steam Deck 2: it is a mid-cycle refresh from Valve, similar to the Switch OLED upgrade, but with a lot more going on internally. Its screen is better, its battery life is better, its thumbsticks are better, the haptics are better, and its chip and thermals are better. One thing that hasn't changed is its form factor — this is still one of the biggest babies on the handheld block.

Engadget's launch coverage on 2023-11-09 frames it the same way: it might not look like a big change from the outside, but the Steam Deck OLED is a thorough mid-cycle refresh of a machine that's not even two years old, and at the same time Valve is also adjusting the configuration of its entry-level model, making it a far more compelling option. At an event held for press prior to the device's launch, Greg Coomer, a product designer at Valve, called the new model "the definitive version of the Steam Deck," explaining that the device contains many things the company wanted to include at the LCD model's launch but wasn't able to, along with some additions based on community feedback.



---


# Steam Deck OLED Models And Pricing

Valve kept Steam Deck pricing the same as the original line while increasing storage at every tier, and set the Steam Deck OLED on sale from November 16, 2023 through the Steam storefront.

The three models are $649 for the 1 TB OLED, up from 512 GB at that price; $529 for the 512 GB OLED, up from 256 GB; and $399 for a 256 GB non-OLED Steam Deck, up from 64 GB. For a limited time the company also offered a special edition 1 TB Steam Deck OLED with a translucent shell for $679, sold only in the U.S. and Canada — a limited run Polygon's reviewer predicted would sell like hotcakes, prompting Valve to reconsider the definition of "limited supply." Polygon discloses that the hardware was reviewed with a unit provided by Valve, and that Vox Media has affiliate partnerships which do not influence editorial content though the company may earn commissions on products purchased via affiliate links.



---


# Steam Deck OLED Pricing And Lineup

The Steam Deck OLED goes on sale on November 16th at 1pm ET, with Valve holding units ready to ship that same day, and it starts at $549, replacing all but the entry-level model in the range. Valve says the lineup moving forward is: 256GB Steam Deck LCD at $399, 512GB Steam Deck OLED at $549, and 1TB Steam Deck OLED at $649. There is also a limited edition 1TB OLED version — priced at $680 in the review and $679 in the launch coverage — that comes with a special carrying case, a translucent gray body and orange accents.

Valve has lowered the price of its LCD lineup and will sell through its backstock of 64GB and 512GB models until they're all gone: the 64GB LCD Steam Deck, previously sold at $399, drops to $349, and the 512GB LCD, previously $649, drops to $499, after which both lines will be discontinued — though Valve says it will continue to support all LCD models with software updates. So the long-term lineup starts at the same $399 price, which gets the old LCD Steam Deck but with 256GB of storage instead of 64GB; the new step-up model costs $20 more at $549 but comes with an OLED display, the hardware improvements and double the storage; and the range still tops out at $649, now with 1TB of storage instead of 512GB, an improved carry case that can pop out into a slimmer shell that's smaller and easier to fit in a bag, and the same anti-glare etched glass as the outgoing 512GB LCD model. The updated pricing on the existing LCD models is already in effect.



---


# Steam Deck OLED Hardware Refinements

Beyond the screen, the Steam Deck OLED adds a gaggle of minor physical upgrades that Polygon argues matter as much as the headline change. Since the original Steam Deck launched Valve has been improving the hardware through updates — its team estimates around 300 to date — and that continues for both models, with the original getting a fresh BIOS update to align it with some of the OLED's upgrades, including some battery life improvement, though not the OLED model's 30-50% jump.

Some changes demand new hardware. The Steam Deck OLED includes a Wi-Fi 6E radio, useful if you have a modern router and connection to make use of it, and a dedicated Bluetooth module, which allows improved audio quality with wireless headphones, the option to wake the Steam Deck from a controller, and the capability to connect many Bluetooth controllers for multiplayer. The haptics are noticeably improved with a wider frequency range, and the touchscreen is markedly better — responsive to the point where the reviewer no longer feels the need to plug in a USB-C keyboard to type a few words. Valve also claims the device is more repairable, which the reviewer did not have occasion to test, with parts again sold through iFixit. He did enjoy the new power supply, with faster charging — 45 minutes gets you from 20% to 80% — and a 2.5-meter cable that stretches the length of his couch. One charming detail: the carrying case now has a tinier carrying case within it, with the bulky original recommended for the cautious and the slim case for tossing the Deck in a backpack for a day trip.



---


# Steam Deck OLED's Custom AMD APU

The Steam Deck OLED has a die-shrunk version of the custom AMD APU found in the original Steam Deck — same CPU and GPU, just more efficient, produced on a 6nm process rather than the older 7nm process. Manufacturers typically use die-shrinks to either improve performance or efficiency, and Valve has chosen the latter; the max frequency of both the GPU and CPU is identical between the LCD and OLED models.

This is the process Sony takes advantage of to build the PS4 Slim and PS5 Slim, but instead of collapsing the Steam Deck around smaller hardware, Valve chose to add a bigger battery and larger fan to its existing chassis. For developers, this means the device has the same performance targets as the original and there's no need to create games specifically for the new hardware — a single performance target to tune for. In the end, the device weighs about 30 grams less than the original model, or the equivalent of five quarters.

Polygon's reviewer concedes that for an existing Steam Deck owner the OLED model is technically an incremental improvement, but argues that the screen and the battery may still justify the double dip — and that for a heavy user the upgrade is inescapable.

For readers who do not already own a Steam Deck the argument is simpler and unconditional: the reviewer repeats that this is his favorite console ever, and it just got better.

# Game Patch Notes

## Definition

Neither corpus article uses the phrase "patch notes," but both document the same underlying pattern: a studio bundling a slate of changes — new content, rebalancing, and quality-of-life fixes — under a single named or numbered update tied to a release date.
Polygon's Diablo 4 coverage lists that pattern for "Season 2"/"Season of Blood": leveling speed, new endgame bosses, a Nightmare Dungeon rework, mount handling, and Renown/gem-Stash changes, all bundled to arrive together on Oct. 17 (doc_0533).
Polygon's games-of-the-year piece shows the same pattern for Cyberpunk 2077's named "Patch 2.0," a systems-revamping update shipped alongside — but distinct from — the paid Phantom Liberty expansion (doc_0213).

## Context

The corpus's clearest example is Diablo 4's Season 2 update, "Season of Blood," reported by Polygon on 2023-10-04: alongside new vampire powers, Blizzard shipped a broad slate of quality-of-life changes covering leveling speed, endgame bosses, Nightmare Dungeon design, mount handling, and the Renown and gem/Stash systems, all set to arrive together on Oct. 17 as one seasonal patch.

Polygon's broader 2023 games-of-the-year piece shows the same pattern in a second game: Cyberpunk 2077's Phantom Liberty expansion arrived "alongside the sweeping Patch 2.0," which revamped the base game's role-playing progression systems, improved enemy AI, and "course-corrected a litany of other details" — a patch bundled with, but distinct from, the paid DLC content it accompanied.

## Key Characteristics

- **Versioned or seasonal framing** — changes are grouped under a single identifier (Patch 2.0, Season 2/"Season of Blood") rather than released piecemeal, per doc_0533 and doc_0213.
- **Mix of change types** — a single patch bundles new content (Diablo 4's five endgame bosses), rebalancing (faster leveling, reworked Nightmare Dungeon affixes), and quality-of-life fixes (Renown carryover, gems no longer taking bag space), per doc_0533.
- **Developer-explained rationale** — studios attach commentary to justify changes, as when Diablo 4's game director Joe Shely and associate director Joe Piepiora told Polygon the quality-of-life focus came from finally having time to react to player feedback, unlike the rushed first season (doc_0533).
- **Distinct from paid content** — a patch can ship independently of or alongside paid expansions; Cyberpunk 2077's Patch 2.0 revamped core systems while Phantom Liberty (the paid DLC) added new story content, and reviewers credit the patch as much as the DLC for the game's improved reception (doc_0213).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, this kind of update bundle has a generic industry name: release notes (also called patch notes).
Per Wikipedia, release notes "describe important information about a distribution of a hardware or software product" and typically include "a list of what is new in the release, including bug fixes and new features" (Wikipedia, "Release notes," accessed 2026-09-02).

Engadget argues that even with improvements to the battery, thermals and weight distribution, the Steam Deck OLED is still more of a Wii U than a Vita: it's a beast of a handheld, and it makes the most sense as a portable console to use around the house rather than a truly travel-ready device.

# Polygon's Thesis That 2023 Games Broke the Scope-Versus-Scale Tradeoff

Polygon's claim, in its 2023-10-31 best-video-games-of-the-year piece, is that for the first year in recent memory scale did not necessitate tradition and scope did not preclude getting weird: in 2023 nothing was sacred in video games, and so they felt more vibrant than ever.

The grounds are a series of cases spanning budget tiers. Among the more "focused" games, Dredge begins as a lonely fishing sim before transforming into something otherworldly, Humanity morphed from a pensive art project into an all-out war, and Dave the Diver is not so much about being a diver as it is about running a sushi restaurant, or hunting for alien artifacts, or conversing with said aliens. This amorphousness was not confined to newcomers: Larian Studios, fresh off two years of early-access development and riding the reputation garnered from Divinity: Original Sin 2, released a role-playing game in which you can kill off nearly every main character the moment you meet them; Remedy Entertainment made a sequel that is equal parts horrifying, hilarious, fun, and fabulous; and Nintendo, in another banner year, finally let go and let players toy with the digital molecules of its most revered series.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is that these examples span every size of developer, every genre, and every tier of budget — so the weirdness cannot be dismissed as the province of small or low-risk projects. Polygon's summary, credited to Mike Mahardy, is that it is intoxicating to see developers of all sizes mining the depths of interactive design, branching this way and that as they follow their respective veins of gold, and that they are nowhere near the bottom of that expanse — a heartening thought. The piece also notes the platform context in passing: whether you booted up your Steam Deck for a cross-country flight or hid your Switch off screen during a boring Zoom meeting, the game you returned to was rarely the one you left behind.

# Product Launch

## Definition

Across this corpus, "launch" (and "launched") is used to describe a company unveiling, announcing, or first shipping a new product, feature, or device — the corpus does not itself define the term, but consistently applies it to this announce-and/or-ship moment (see Context).

## Background (external)

ProductPlan's product-management glossary defines a product launch as "a business's planned and coordinated effort to debut a new product to the market and make that product generally available for purchase," noting that launches also build anticipation, gather early-adopter feedback, and generate momentum beyond simply enabling sales (ProductPlan, accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.productplan.com/glossary/product-launch/).

## Context

Across the corpus, launches recur as the mechanism by which companies move a product from development into the market, and the term covers a spectrum from a single press event to a multi-year rollout. Google's annual hardware event unveiled the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro alongside the Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds and Pixel Watch 2, showing that a single launch event can bundle several products at once. Apple's "Scary Fast" event was anticipated as the venue for unveiling M3-powered MacBook Pros, a refreshed iMac, and new USB-C accessories, illustrating that launches are often previewed and rumored before the event itself. Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" was "first announced in September" and only became available afterward, alongside the Echo Pop Kids speakers being "available for purchase" at $49.99 — showing the announce-then-ship pattern explicitly. OpenAI's ChatGPT similarly moved through staged launches: an initial November 2022 release, then a paid ChatGPT Plus tier and plug-in/API support unveiled in March 2023, then further features (Enterprise, browsing, voice, GPTs) rolled out through the rest of the year. Valve's Steam Deck OLED was announced at a press event ahead of its device launch, with press being told units would be "available to order" on a specific date and begin shipping shortly after. Keep Labs' medication-storage device took years between its 2019 preorder campaign and "this week started shipping its first product to consumers," showing a launch can be delayed substantially between announcement and actual availability.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-stage structure** — an "unveiling" or announcement stage (often at a press or hardware event) is followed by a separate "available for purchase" or shipping stage, and the gap between them can range from days to years, as with Keep Labs' multi-year gap between its 2019 preorder campaign and 2023 shipping date.
- **Bundling** — a single launch event frequently introduces multiple products or features together, as Google did with the Pixel 8 line, Android 14, and several accessories in one hardware event.
- **Pre-launch anticipation** — launches are frequently preceded by rumors and analyst predictions about what will be unveiled, as with the expected Apple "Scary Fast" event coverage of M3 chips and MacBook Pro refreshes before the event occurred.
- **Staged/iterative rollout** — for software products like ChatGPT, "launch" is not a single moment but a sequence of feature releases (Plus tier, plugins, Enterprise, voice, GPTs) unveiled over many months following the initial debut.
- **Concrete availability signals** — corpus reporting marks a launch's completion with specific, checkable facts: a price, an order date, or a shipping date, e.g. the Steam Deck OLED being "available to order on November 16th" with shipping "as orders start to roll in," or the Echo Pop Kids being "available for purchase, starting at $49.99."

# Epic Games Store Growth And Diversification Beyond Games

Asked what changed after a period when Epic seemed interested in expanding outside games with acquisitions like Houseparty and Bandcamp, Tim Sweeney said Epic has gotten so much traction with Fortnite in so many different ways, and with the Epic Games Store, that it is going to continue investing heavily there.

He called the Epic Games Store "the untold success story in the background": since it launched in 2018 it now has 80 million monthly active users, against Steam's 120 million, which he read as catching up fast. He also claimed Fortnite has more concurrent users right now than all Steam games combined, and promised dramatic changes that benefit all developers over the next few years. The Verge appended an editor's note correcting the concurrency claim: Epic spokesperson Natalie Muñoz confirmed Sweeney had misinterpreted a Polygon story about Fortnite hitting 7.6 million players at a time when the entirety of Steam had 10.1 million; these days Steam generally peaks at over 30 million with valleys of 20 million, while Fortnite's valleys are closer to 3.8 million.

# Steam Deck OLED Display Upgrade

The new Steam Deck's main upgrade is its OLED screen, which replaces the original LCD and, crucially, has native support for HDR and faster frame rates. The OLED also has smaller bezels, making the display larger at 7.4 inches compared with the original 7-inch screen: the original Steam Deck had a 7-inch 800p LCD running at 60Hz, and the new model squeezes a 7.4-inch OLED screen into the same space at the same resolution but with a refresh rate of up to 90Hz.

The HDR OLED display looks fantastic, featuring a wider P3 color gamut — covering 110 percent of the P3 color space — pure blacks and a peak brightness of 1,000 nits, compared with the original max of around 400 nits. In action, this means the screen's bezels meld with the black of any game, creating a more polished frame for retro aspect ratios and providing room for higher-contrast colors. The screen on the new model doesn't support variable refresh rates (VRR), but it now tops out at 90Hz where the original could only hit 60Hz, and like all OLED screens it has near-instantaneous response times. As before, anti-glare etched glass is available, but only on the premium model. Engadget's verdict on the panel: the updated display is smooth, crisp and bright, like a perfect lemon tart.

# Steam Deck OLED Battery Life

Valve says the Steam Deck OLED battery lasts 30 to 50 percent longer than the original's depending on how you play, with an official claim of "three to 12 hours," and Engadget's November 2023 testing measured gains at the top of or above that range.

The original Steam Deck's short battery life was one of its downsides, maxing out at eight hours and only under ideal conditions. The OLED pairs a more-efficient processor with a 25 percent larger battery — 50Whr capacity against the original's 40Whr — and charges faster, going from 20 percent to 80 percent in 45 minutes by Valve's claim. Engadget tested with Hades, its reviewer's most-played game on the original: although Hades does not support HDR it pops on the OLED, with animations looking more fluid than on the LCD version, and the OLED lasted four hours and 23 minutes before dying, against two hours and 42 minutes for the original at the same settings of 800p with a 60 fps cap and similar brightness — a 62 percent improvement that surpasses Valve's own estimates. Engadget flags the confound: batteries degrade, and its LCD Steam Deck dated from the device's launch in early 2022, an 18-month-old unit at review time, which explains why its gains were more pronounced. A harsher stress test playing Elden Ring with everything maxed out gave the OLED two hours and 20 minutes, about 40 percent longer than the original. Polygon separately resolved the obvious ambiguity in Valve's 30-50% figure by asking whether the comparison was against a Steam Deck running original firmware, which had poor battery life, or the latest firmware; Valve's answer was the latter, so existing owners should expect the big improvements over their current experience. Polygon's conclusion is that the OLED screen makes for a fancier Steam Deck, but it is the battery life — plus tweaks throughout the design to carve out more of it — that lets the handheld truly deliver on its promise of a portable gaming PC.

# The Epic Games Store As A General-Purpose App Store

Asked whether a freely installable Epic store on Android would be only a game store or also an app store, Tim Sweeney rejected the premise of the label: "the Epic Games Store isn't a games store — it's the store operated by Epic Games," and Epic will host any app anybody wants, of any sort.

The discriminating feature is that the store already carries non-games today: the Brave web browser and a number of software creation tools including Unreal Engine, with more coming, including other creation tools and productivity tools. The boundary case Sweeney concedes is one of emphasis rather than scope: gaming is a market Epic is uniquely close to, so he expects Epic would likely be able to forge closer partnerships and opportunities in gaming — but the store will be open to everybody on Android as it is on PC. The question that prompted the answer contrasted Epic with Valve, which operates a store that could be both but has decided to focus exclusively on games.

# Steam Deck OLED HDR Display

The OLED panel in the new Steam Deck is lighter, thinner, and more power efficient than its LCD predecessor, as well as bigger and faster. Though the device keeps the same shape as the original, smaller screen bezels allow a slightly larger display: 7.4 inches against 7 inches.

The panel has a wider color gamut — 110% DCI-P3 — and the inky blacks OLED enthusiasts value. Its 90 Hz refresh rate is described as perfect for frame doubling from 45 frames per second, which in plainer terms means gameplay looks smoother. Polygon notes the comparison and its caveat: 90 Hz falls short of the Asus ROG Ally's 120 Hz, but the higher the frame rate the faster the battery drain, assuming you can even spot the difference between the two. The reviewer's own use case was Sega's Like a Dragon Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name, played on high settings at 60 fps while watching football and Christmas movies with family; its night sequences flaunted the OLED's dark blacks and its abundant neon signage showcased the HDR. The most welcome feat only registered later: on the original Steam Deck he had always kept the handheld plugged into an outlet when playing AAA games, whereas with the OLED model a couple of hours passed before he realised he had forgotten to connect the charger.

# Fan Opposition To Activision Console Exclusivity Risk

Not everyone greeted the Microsoft-Activision deal positively, and the objection targets the assumption that current cross-platform availability will hold: some fans do not want to see a permanent switch to Microsoft somewhere down the line.

The precedent they invoke cuts the other way from Sony's current position. Once upon a time, the Activision games Crash Bandicoot and Spyro the Dragon were PlayStation exclusives, which shows how a publisher's titles can be tied to a single console.

That worry has taken organised form: it has even led some fans to make petitions calling for Microsoft to keep the games playable on all consoles in perpetuity.
