# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# FTX's Spending Served Bankman-Fried's Status, Not Philanthropy

The Verge's reporter argued that at every turn the scams at FTX and Alameda led back to making Bankman-Fried more important — not to giving money away, as his stated Effective Altruism rationale claimed. The grounds are the pattern of what the money bought: Singh testified to more than a billion dollars spent on celebrity endorsements, which made FTX very famous even though the futures platform did not operate in the US; the political donations gave Bankman-Fried influence in the highest echelons of power; and Ellison testified to venture investments that gave him more dominance in the tech world.

The warrant joining the pattern to the conclusion is that spending reveals priorities better than statements do: it is easy to lie with words and harder to lie with money. Bankman-Fried went around telling people he wanted to make a lot of money in order to give it away, an idea of the Effective Altruism movement he affiliated himself with, but the amount he funneled to his Paper Bird vehicle alone was ten times the size of his philanthropic spending as outlined by the prosecution's expert Peter Easton — and all of it was vastly outweighed by his investments, the places where he could prove he was very smart by investing in the right companies early.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Decision To Testify Backfired

The Verge's trial reporter argued that Bankman-Fried's choice to take the stand was a net loss for his defense: like Theranos' Elizabeth Holmes before him, he got on the stand to speak directly to his state of mind in a way no other witness can, but telling your side of the story opens you to a great many questions you might not want to answer on cross-examination — and, having watched a lot of crosses, she called Sassoon's the nastiest she had ever seen.

The warrant is what the charges turn on. The case hinged on conspiracy and intentional deceit: just losing $8 billion is not a crime, though it is very embarrassing, but if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing and how safe FTX was, that is a crime. Because state of mind was the contested issue, his own testimony became the evidence, and it did not hold: Sassoon had established the day before that he has a long history of dishonesty, and on October 31st, through a set of questions about what he did and did not do, she established that the story he told on direct examination was absurd. After a brief redirect by his own lawyers, resplendent with word salad, Bankman-Fried stepped down and the defense rested.

The direct examination had already supplied grounds. Beyond the two obvious lies the reporter counted him telling on the stand — about Alameda Research's name and about "allow_negative" — she was struck by how little he seemed to know about his own companies: apparently Singh, Wang, and Ellison were out there just doing whatever their little hearts desired, because Bankman-Fried was a CEO, but definitely not the kind that pays any attention to money at his crypto trading firm and futures exchange.



---


# Gary Wang's Ownership Stake And Cooperation Deal

Gary Wang, co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX and co-founder of Alameda Research, owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX and drew a $200,000-a-year salary with no performance bonuses — though at times he was a billionaire on paper — while Bankman-Fried owned 90 percent of Alameda and 65 percent of FTX. He returned to the US on November 16th, met with the US government on November 17th without having been arrested or charged, offered to cooperate immediately, and pled guilty to various charges a month later. Wang was clear that he was cooperating because he did not want to go to jail, and said he hoped his assistance would lead a sentencing judge to be lenient.

The Verge's reporter drew from the disparity a puzzle she could not resolve: Wang took bizarre risks for a relatively small share. Bankman-Fried did not code, so none of his fingerprints are on the technical changes that let FTX allegedly defraud its customers and investors, while Wang supervised the code behind a key prosecution claim — that Alameda Research was afforded secret, special privileges with FTX's funds. When FTX went down, Wang left himself with no plausible deniability. Wang, a college roommate of Bankman-Fried's, took the stand after Adam Yedidia and, in the reporter's phrase, sang like a canary about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code.

The delivery was heavy going. On October 6th, 2023 Wang had to explain to the jury the difference between a front end and a back end, explain futures trading, and read a great deal into the record, which took a while; it was a tough day for the jury, and probably for Wang, who spoke quickly, perhaps from nerves.



---


# Can Sun's Testimony On Fabricated Justifications

Former FTX lawyer Can Sun testified that during the days in November when the exchange imploded, Bankman-Fried — then trying to raise money from the private equity group Apollo, which wanted an explanation for what had happened — came to him and asked him to come up with justifications for the missing funds. That request, Sun said, "basically confirmed my suspicions that had been rising all day" that Bankman-Fried had purloined the funds.

Sun ran Bankman-Fried through possible explanations, including a margin loan program, and explained that none of them could fit the actual situation — for instance, Alameda had borrowed more from FTX than had ever been in the margin loan program. He said Bankman-Fried acknowledged their conversation with a "yup, yup": "I was expecting a bigger response, but it was very muted." After that, Sun testified, Singh spilled the beans that Alameda had withdrawn assets that included the customer funds. Sun quit the next day, and, like Yedidia, testified with immunity.

The jury then saw the fabrication deployed in public: a Good Morning America appearance by Bankman-Fried on December 1st, 2022, in which he tried to justify the missing funds through the margin loan program. The Verge's reporter called it such a flimsy excuse that even George Stephanopoulos could see through it, and described Sun's testimony as brief and explosive.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

The Verge attributes FTX's quick rise as an industry force at least in part to that appetite for attention: Bankman-Fried gave interviews freely and quickly rose to public prominence, positioning himself as an important, boyish face for crypto even though FTX hadn't been in the business as long as competing exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Gemini. At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Defense Strategy And Appeal Groundwork

Bankman-Fried's defense can itself introduce risks for people who dealt with him, because his lawyers have several simultaneous objectives: first and foremost proving their client not guilty, but also — just in case they don't get the outcome they want — laying the groundwork for appeals and sentencing arguments.

The consequence is procedural: any piece of evidence they want to introduce for those two purposes has to come into play during the trial. Christopher LaVigne notes that Bankman-Fried's lawyers are already marking arguments that his constitutional rights are being violated by his pretrial incarceration because, among other things, his internet connection wasn't good enough for him to plan his defense — which could be grounds for an appeal.



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.



---


# Adam Yedidia's First Testimony And His Immunity Deal

Late in the afternoon of the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the government called Adam Yedidia to the stand, and lead prosecutor Danielle Sassoon disclosed that this college friend of Bankman-Fried had legal immunity during his testimony. Asked why he had made such a deal with the government, Yedidia answered: "I was concerned that I had unwittingly written code that contributed to a crime."

Yedidia, described as a fast-talking graduate of MIT, testified that he and Bankman-Fried were close friends in college. After Bankman-Fried left Jane Street — the high-frequency trading firm where the former billionaire got his start in finance after MIT — he persuaded Yedidia to join him, first as a trader at Alameda and then as a developer at FTX.

The testimony was cut short when the clock neared 4:30 p.m. and court adjourned for the day. Yedidia was scheduled to continue his testimony on Thursday, to be followed by Matt Huang, a former partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital, and then by Gary Wang, a key Bankman-Fried lieutenant and one of the government's star witnesses.



---


# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.



---


# Alameda Research's Origins And Naming

Alameda Research was the cryptocurrency trading firm Bankman-Fried started in 2017 during a crypto bull run, and it was named for Alameda County in California, where its first office was set up. Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried said he knew "basically nothing" about cryptocurrency at the time but wanted to do arbitrage on it anyway, and that he is "somewhat introverted, naturally."

The name was chosen for cover. In his own words on the stand: "Effectively, we wanted to be under the radar at that point in time. I didn't want to call it Sam's Crypto Trading Firm or anything like that. We — there are a lot of competitors and people who we didn't particularly want to know what we were building out because they would race to do it. 'Research' was a sort of generic word, which filled out the company name. And that was — it was far better than the internal name that we had at that point, which was Wireless Mouse." The Verge's reporter noted she would find this more believable had she not already watched a video, played during Gary Wang's first day of testimony with Bankman-Fried and the jury present, of Bankman-Fried explaining on a podcast that the name made it easier to get a bank account.

The founding assembled the people later charged alongside him: Bankman-Fried went on a hiring spree, taking on Wang to program the computers, then Nishad Singh about a month after founding Alameda Research, and finally Caroline Ellison. Though Bankman-Fried was CEO and also majority owner, he wanted to be clear that he did not supervise Wang's direct work. After a run of wildly successful arbitrage — 50 percent to 100 percent annualized returns, per his testimony — he decided to found a cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, figuring he would fail and putting the chance of success at 20 percent, without defining the time period he had in mind.



---


# Ellison's Risk Spreadsheet For Venture Investments

Caroline Ellison testified that she prepared a spreadsheet at Bankman-Fried's request in the fall of 2021 and shared it with him, analysing the risk to Alameda of repaying its loans if they were abruptly recalled by its lender Genesis. Bankman-Fried wanted to use $3 billion for venture investments, so Ellison ballparked what that would do to Alameda's risk: in the as-is scenario she put the chance they would not be able to meet the loan recalls at 30 percent, and if Bankman-Fried spent $3 billion on investments, the chance rose to 100 percent — even with FTX customer funds.

What made this the worst of her testimony, in The Verge's account of the October 10th, 2023 proceedings, was not the math, which seemed pretty arbitrary, but the assumption underneath it: Ellison's calculations assumed Alameda could borrow $1.8 billion in normal dollars and $1.5 billion in crypto from FTX, and the spreadsheet made this explicit with a row labeled "FTX borrows," which Ellison said were customer funds. The background condition was that Alameda was also getting loans from outside lenders such as Genesis, because when FTX started there were not a lot of customer funds to borrow.

The day ended with a document shared between Ellison and Bankman-Fried, his comments appearing in bubbles along the main text. Ellison had written that she was worried about "both actual leverage and presenting on our balance sheet." Bankman-Fried responded with a note: "Yup, and could also get worse."



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.

# The 2023 NFL Best Bets Season Record

Through eight weeks of the 2023 NFL season, Sporting News' best bets stood at 65-46-1 — a winning percentage of over .590, a number the column noted many professional bettors wish they were maintaining during a rollercoaster season. # Super Bowl

## Definition

In the corpus, the Super Bowl is the season-long reference point every team, player, and betting market is measured against — the game whose winners are still identified as "defending Super Bowl champions" months later (doc_0059) and which is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year" (doc_0201).

## Context

The corpus treats the Super Bowl as the horizon every team's season is measured against: the New York Times' Pick Six column frames one-third of the regular season through "the biggest questions facing Super Bowl contenders," ranking the Chiefs, Eagles, 49ers, Bills, Bengals, Cowboys, Ravens, Lions, Dolphins, and Jaguars by their Super Bowl odds (doc_0316).
Franchise identity is tied to it retroactively — the Cincinnati Bengals are described as having reached "a Super Bowl appearance in 2021" as the marker of the team's turnaround (doc_0071), and Travis Kelce is introduced as having "helped bring his team to Super Bowl victory in both 2020 and 2023" (doc_0044), with the Kansas City Chiefs subsequently referred to simply as "the defending Super Bowl champions" (doc_0059).
A Christmas Day matchup between the 49ers and Ravens is previewed explicitly as a "potential Super Bowl sneak peek" (doc_0003), showing how regular-season games get framed as previews of the eventual championship.

## Key Characteristics

- **Season-defining stakes** — teams and players are described relative to it long after the fact ("defending Super Bowl champions," "two-time Super Bowl MVP") (doc_0059, doc_0003).
- **Odds and futures market** — sportsbooks release "next Super Bowl champion" odds shortly after the previous Super Bowl concludes, and those odds shift through the season as teams change (doc_0061).
- **Special-event betting draw** — sportsbooks single out "Super Bowl betting lines" alongside World Series odds and March Madness as flagship special-event markets carrying their own promotional bonuses (doc_0072).
- **Peak prop-betting event** — the Super Bowl is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year," drawing "hundreds of prop bets" including exotic novelty props on the halftime show, the coin toss, and the color of the sports drink dumped on the winning coach (doc_0201).

## Background (external)

The corpus never defines "Super Bowl" itself — it only reports how teams, players, and betting markets relate to it.
Per Wikipedia, the Super Bowl is "the annual championship game of the National Football League (NFL), serving as the final game of each NFL season" (Wikipedia, *Super Bowl*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Point Spread Push And Half-Point Lines

A "push" in point spread betting is the situation where the final result of an event exactly matches the set point spread, producing neither a win nor a loss for bettors; the wagers are typically refunded, so neither the bettor nor the sportsbook wins or loses money on that bet. Sporting News illustrates it with an NFL game in which the Dallas Cowboys are favored by 7 points against the Philadelphia Eagles: if the Cowboys win by exactly 7, bettors on either team experience a push and their wagers are refunded, because the Cowboys neither exceeded nor fell short of the 7-point spread.

Sportsbooks often employ half-points in their lines precisely to avoid this outcome, since they do not want to return bets. Had the example spread been Cowboys -7.5, the game could not possibly have ended in a push; half-point lines such as 7.5 or 6.5 remove the exact-match case entirely.

A tie in the literal matchup is a distinct boundary case from a push, and many spread bets still have winners and losers when one occurs. If the Cleveland Browns are -1.5 favorites over the Baltimore Ravens and the NFL matchup ends 21-21 after overtime, the Ravens win that spread bet, because the margin of victory of 0 was narrower than 1.5.

# NFL Week 9 Player Prop Picks

Sporting News made three SuperDraft player prop picks for Week 9 of 2023: Rashee Rice OVER 45.5 receiving yards, Austin Ekeler OVER 29.5 receiving yards and Jahan Dotson OVER 45.5 receiving yards.

Ekeler (RB, Chargers @ Jets) was backed because the Chargers finally had their best player back to full health: he exploded for 123 yards and a touchdown against the Bears, a whopping 94 of them through the air as the PPR god gashed Chicago for chunk yardage several times. Dotson (WR, Commanders @ Patriots) came full circle after making the preseason sleepers column, fading into early-season obscurity and re-emerging over the previous two weeks: with Curtis Samuel clearly not right the week before, the second-year wideout caught 8 of 10 targets for 108 yards and a touchdown, a stellar encore to his Week 7 line of five catches for 43 yards. The banged-up Patriots defense would focus primarily on stopping Terry McLaurin, which should open plenty of opportunities for Dotson.

# The Taylor Swift Effect On NFL Merchandise And Ticket Sales

Since Taylor Swift attended the Chiefs game on 24 September 2023 there was a 400% increase in Travis Kelce jersey sales, according to Front Office Sports figures cited in CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023.

The same set of figures, dated 25 September, records that Kelce's podcast went No. 1 overall on Apple, he gained over 380,000 Instagram followers, and 24.3 million people watched the game, making it the No. 1 game of that week. There was also triple the "Chiefs" searches on the web and triple the Chiefs ticket sales on StubHub.

The effect extended to other teams' gates. On 26 September the timeline notes that the defending Super Bowl champions were already one of the more popular teams in the league but were becoming the hottest ticket in town, no matter what town that was: "Since Swift's appearance at the Chiefs game on Sunday, the Jets have sold more tickets for their game against the Chiefs in a single day than since the season started -- by more than double," a representative at StubHub told Town & Country magazine.

# Why Moneyline Odds Change

Lines at sports betting apps change quickly for two primary reasons — public betting and new information — and sportsbooks adjust moneyline odds to stay profitable, balance their book and reflect the most current information about an event. Before setting odds oddsmakers gather extensive data, then release the finalized odds to the public; from that point a bettor can bet immediately or wait for shifts, though predicting those shifts is challenging.

The time dimension shows how an opening price drifts. Odds for the next Super Bowl champion released shortly after the previous Super Bowl are based mostly on the recently concluded season; as the new season approaches and teams make changes, the odds adjust to perceived championship chances, and as games progress the lines keep evolving with team performances.

The mechanism has five named drivers. Public betting patterns move a line because, when a significant amount of money lands on one team or participant, sportsbooks adjust the odds to balance their liability — making the price less favorable for the heavily-bet side and more favorable for the less-bet side to encourage even betting and reduce financial risk. New information matters because changes in player injuries, player substitutions or weather conditions alter the perceived outcome, and books adjust once such information becomes public. Professional bettors move lines because large wagers from sharp bettors often reflect insights or information that can influence the odds. Initial miscalculation is a fourth driver: sometimes the opening odds are perceived as offering value, and heavy betting on one side signals that the initial price was potentially "off," prompting an adjustment. Event dynamics is the fifth, applying to live betting placed while the event is in progress, where the evolving dynamics of the match lead to frequent changes.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. # Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. # Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).
