# Connor Stalions And The In-Person Scouting Operation

Connor Stalions was the Michigan football analyst at the center of the NCAA's sign-stealing investigation, accused of buying tickets to scout future opponents in person — a practice prohibited by NCAA rules. According to ESPN.com, Stalions allegedly purchased tickets to more than 35 games involving Big Ten and potential College Football Playoff opponents. Michigan suspended him when news of his alleged involvement first broke, and he resigned on Nov. 3, 2023; the university confirmed the resignation in a statement saying only that "Connor Stalions resigned his position with Michigan Athletics this afternoon. We are unable to comment further regarding this personnel matter."

A second strand of the investigation concerns whether Stalions appeared in Chippewas gear on Central Michigan's sideline during the team's opener against Michigan State on Sept. 1. Photos surfaced of a person resembling Stalions on that sideline, and Central Michigan had not confirmed who the person was, adding another layer to a story that supplied endless meme and conspiracy material on social media. Through his lawyer, Stalions said he hoped to avoid creating more distractions for Michigan and denied that any Wolverines staffer "told anyone to break any rules."

Sporting News framed Stalions' eventual place in the story as still undetermined: he might be the fall guy who saved Michigan from further wrath from the Big Ten and the NCAA, or the reason the Wolverines' national championship season unraveled. Either way, the outlet judged that he would be one of those controversial names never forgotten, in the company of Harvey Updyke and Nevin Shapiro.

# The Big Ten's 2023 Run Of Scandals

Sporting News counted the Michigan sign-stealing affair as the fourth Big Ten football scandal in less than a calendar year. Three former Iowa football players and a student manager were charged in an illegal sports wagering scandal, with several student-athletes facing allegations of placing bets on games in which they played. Northwestern coach Pat Fitzgerald was fired on July 10 after a hazing investigation into the program, and is suing the university for wrongful termination. # The Connor Stalions Central Michigan Sideline Investigation

Central Michigan said it is investigating whether suspended Michigan staffer Connor Stalions was on the CMU sideline during the Chippewas' 1 September game at Michigan State, as reported by The New York Times on 3 November 2023.

The evidence trail is dated: screenshots of a person who looks similar to Stalions began circulating online on the Monday night, and The Athletic obtained more photos of the person on the sideline on the Tuesday. # Michigan Expected To Face No Big Ten Penalty Before The Season's End

Sources at four different Big Ten schools said they do not expect the conference to levy any sort of punishment against Michigan before the season ends, despite frustration from all corners of the conference, as reported by The New York Times on 3 November 2023.

# Michigan's 2023 Team Culture And Expectations

Sporting News argued that the 2023 Wolverines were the most mature player-led Michigan football team on the field since 1997 — the year the program beat Ohio State 20-14 in a top-five showdown and split the national championship with Nebraska — and that the win over Ohio State showed a team that no longer merely hopes to win The Game but expects to. The grounds were the season's two parallel stories: an off-field one in which the team kept overcoming obstacles, self-inflicted and otherwise, and an on-field one described as a withering march through the Big Ten toward a third straight College Football Playoff berth.

The obstacle was Jim Harbaugh's three-game suspension from the Big Ten over the illegal in-person scouting and sign-stealing operation, which dominated headlines more than the Wolverines dominated opponents in the second half of the season. Staffer Connor Stalions and assistant coach Chris Partridge were gone, and Harbaugh was suspended; he addressed the team on Friday, and McCarthy listened closely. "The one thing he said that stuck out, the whole mantra, 'The Team, The Team, The Team,'" McCarthy said. "He said we are that team."

The warrant is the pattern of who blinks in high-magnitude games. Ohio State had not lost three in a row to Michigan since 1995-97, and since 1997 the Buckeyes had found a way in these games, with 2006 and 2016 the best examples; on a stage somewhere in between those classics, the Wolverines pointed the pressure the other way. Marvin Harrison Jr. had five catches for 118 yards and a touchdown, but Michigan then ran seven minutes off the clock and added a field goal — a further point of criticism for Ryan Day and defensive coordinator Jim Knowles.

The NCAA investigation would continue too, but Sporting News concluded that the Wolverines would play out the rest of the season on their terms — and that Harbaugh returned Monday.

# The Big Ten's Head-Coach Responsibility Doctrine

The Big Ten justified suspending Jim Harbaugh without proving he knew of the sign-stealing scheme by arguing that a head coach bears responsibility for preventing such a scheme from taking place. The conference said it was "proven" that an illegal sign-stealing scheme existed, but conceded it could not prove that Harbaugh knew about it — so the punishment rested on his position rather than on his personal conduct.

The warrant joining that claim to the penalty is a claim about what a head coach represents. As reported by Stewart Mandel on Nov. 10, 2023, the Big Ten also asserted that it was not actually sanctioning Harbaugh, for whom it had no proof of wrongdoing, but that he "embodies the university for purposes of its football program." On that reading the sanction attaches to the institution and lands on the coach only because he stands for it.

# Michigan's Counterclaim That Rivals Shared Its Signs

Michigan's counter to the sign-stealing case is that it is hardly alone in trying to decipher opponents' signals, and it has shared evidence with the Big Ten and the NCAA showing that staff members at Ohio State, Purdue and Rutgers exchanged intelligence on the Wolverines' signals before the previous year's Michigan-Purdue Big Ten Championship Game. The Athletic reported that documents breaking down Michigan's signals for numerous plays were compiled by Purdue staffers ahead of that game based on information provided by Ohio State and Rutgers football personnel. The person who supplied the documents told The Athletic that he spent 10 to 12 hours per week trying to decode signals from game video, and that sharing decoded signals with other schools is a common practice.

The counterclaim does not dispose of the charge, because it attacks the wrong premise. The primary difference, per the same reporting, is that Michigan is accused of using in-person scouting — prohibited under NCAA rules for nearly 30 years — to acquire its information, rather than decoding from video.

Ohio State denied the allegation outright. Asked about the claim that Ohio State had given information about Michigan's signs to Purdue before the 2022 Big Ten championship game, coach Ryan Day said, per the Columbus Dispatch: "I can tell you this right now that nobody here did any of that. We went through and made sure we asked all the questions and got our compliance people involved. None of that came back at all. I can answer very strongly that that did not happen." Separately, Yahoo Sports reported that Day and his family have no connection to the Big Ten and NCAA investigations into Michigan; a weekend report had suggested Day may have had some involvement in the probe into the Buckeyes' arch-rivals, but the NCAA told the Big Ten there are no ties that it knows of between the Ohio State coach and the investigation.

# The Big Ten's Deliberation Over Harbaugh's Punishment

In the week before the Nov. 10, 2023 ruling, the Big Ten weighed a "range of possibilities" for punishing Jim Harbaugh, with a suspension the most-discussed option and a significant fine also under consideration. Thamel had reported on Nov. 8 that the Big Ten expected Michigan's formal response to the notice of discipline by the end of the day Wednesday and that no ruling should be expected that day, since the conference would take time to absorb it. Heather Dinich reported on Nov. 9 that commissioner Tony Petitti would not be in Dallas for that Thursday's College Football Playoff meeting, which fuelled further speculation that punishment was near.

The NCAA's findings did not implicate the head coach. Yahoo Sports reported on Monday that the NCAA had shared its investigation findings with the Big Ten and that the findings "do not connect the in-person scouting and recording of opponents' sidelines to Harbaugh." The conference nonetheless considered a suspension and could hand down punishments before the end of the week; Yahoo said a multi-game suspension was on the table and that Michigan was fully expected to fight a ban. It would have been Harbaugh's second suspension of the season, after Michigan self-imposed a three-game ban on him to start the year amid a separate NCAA investigation that found he lied to investigators.

Momentum built through consultation and public pressure. Pete Thamel said on ESPN's "College GameDay" that "Over the past few days, Petitti has spoken with the athletic directors, he's spoken with the presidents, he's spoken with the coaches. And the next steps appear that there will be some type of punishment for Michigan. The most likely scenario here is some type of suspension for Jim Harbaugh." Earlier in the week it was reported that coaches were pressing the Big Ten to punish Michigan, with Purdue's Ryan Walters publicly calling for action and saying the allegations were no longer simply allegations.



---


# NCAA Coach-To-Player Helmet Communication For Bowl Season

CBSSports.com reported on Oct. 20, 2023 that the NCAA rules committee is giving teams the option of coach-to-player helmet communication to relay plays from the sideline during bowl season that year. Sporting News expected tablets to follow inevitably, and called this the sliver of good that would come from the Michigan sign-stealing scandal.

The outlet's verdict was blunt: "It's about damn time. Death to sandwich-board playcalling, please. Bring on those playsheets where coaches simply have to cover their mouth." This, it argued, is one instance where emulating the NFL game is overdue.



---


# Michigan's Ten-Page Letter To The Big Ten

Michigan's 10-page letter to the Big Ten attacked the premise that the conference could properly discipline Harbaugh or the university before the NCAA investigation was complete. Posted in full on X by Yahoo Sports' Dan Wetzel on Nov. 9, 2023, the letter argued that the Big Ten would be acting too hastily in suspending Harbaugh or levying any punishment before a full NCAA investigation had concluded, and warned commissioner Tony Petitti against "premature" disciplinary action.

The due-process objection was procedural. Michigan said it had not had the chance to review all the evidence and respond, which oversteps the due process allowed to the university, and that Petitti should not have unilateral authority to punish violations without first a completed investigation and then a response from the Compliance and Reinstatement Committee, the body that would recommend penalties for rules violations.

The evidentiary objection attacked the factual basis. Michigan said it was aware of nothing supporting a claim that athletics personnel at Michigan committed the alleged violations, and that the rule on electronic recordings of games is limited to field equipment used by the institution for the game it is currently playing. It said it had not seen much evidence but had only heard a summary of second- and third-hand information.

The materiality objection attacked the significance of any conduct that did occur. Given the use of sign decoding by other universities, the letter said, there was little reason to believe Stalions' efforts proved meaningful, and it pointed to the teams' average margin of victory since Stalions was suspended. The information obtained was "at most a reflection of information that teams can and easily do obtain through public and permissible sources," making it "highly dubious" that Stalions' observations would have a "material effect on the integrity of the competition." The letter further alleged that in-person scouting and sign-stealing are commonplace across the NCAA — "The conference should act cautiously when setting precedent given the reality that in-person scouting, collusion among opponents, and other questionable practices may well be far more prevalent than believed" — and, per Yahoo Sports, enclosed "two attached documents of Michigan's offensive and defensive signs allegedly stolen and shared by other Big Ten teams."

Michigan submitted this response to the Big Ten's notice of discipline as a step toward resolution. ESPN reported on Wednesday that no conference ruling was expected until Thursday because the Big Ten planned to "take time to absorb" what Michigan had to say, and ESPN's Adam Rittenberg reported on Nov. 8, 2023 that the school had sent its response and that Petitti now had to decide how to proceed with potential discipline.



---


# Big Ten Commissioner Petitti's Punishment Dilemma

The New York Times set out on 3 November 2023 why any decision by Tony Petitti is constrained: the claim is that this is an unprecedented situation in which whatever he decides to do, or not do, will set a precedent, and the warrant is that the Big Ten has no investigators of its own and no punishment available that would fall only on those responsible.

The coaches' pressure supplies one side. "The Big Ten is so much more powerful than the NCAA," a third Big Ten coach said. "Why are you just sitting back and doing nothing about this? The Big Ten can't pound its chest for the last 30 years about how it does the right thing ethically (when other conferences like the SEC won't) and then have this go on. If this were a team in the bottom half of the Big Ten, would this be handled in the same way?" A source briefed on the coaches' call said Big Ten coaches are concerned about whether Michigan "should represent the Big Ten," adding: "No matter what happens, if Michigan continues to move forward, the clouds will follow. They're reading the tea leaves and wondering why the Big Ten hasn't done anything yet. Every week and every day that goes by, people are like, 'Something's gotta give.' It's getting a little bit out of hand when you see him (allegedly) on the Central Michigan sideline. The playing field is not level right now. How can you have a team that you know has a competitive advantage over you still being allowed to play? That's what the coaches are grappling with."

The constraints supply the other. The Big Ten itself doesn't have investigators, so it needs to rely upon the NCAA to do that part and to determine who else was involved in the alleged scouting scheme. And it's not clear exactly what the coaches would want the league to do to punish Michigan: banning the team from competing in the Big Ten championship, for example, would harm players who had nothing to do with the sign-stealing apparatus.



---


# November 10 Reporting On Punishment Day

On Friday, Nov. 10, 2023, reporters tracked Michigan's travel to Penn State hour by hour as the college football world waited for the Big Ten's decision, which ESPN's Heather Dinich reported was expected to be announced early Friday afternoon while the team left for State College at 1 p.m. CT ahead of Saturday's game. Dinich reported that sources indicated a Big Ten response was coming early that afternoon and that Michigan would leave at 1 and fly midafternoon out of Detroit after clearing security checks, per usual routine.

The decision came right down to the wire. Adam Rittenberg reported that Michigan's administration had not heard from the Big Ten as of that hour, that the team would begin preparations to leave for Penn State around 1 p.m. ET, and that going down to the wire with any discipline was, as several sources noted, not really fair to players. Austin Meek reported Harbaugh boarding the bus, and observers on the ground in Ann Arbor had him heading to the airport with his team as Michigan awaited word. Harbaugh's attorney Tom Mars told ESPN he fully expected Harbaugh to fly with the team: "I'm confident he's going to be on that plane one way or another."

Dinich also mapped the possible outcomes and a limit on the conference's own authority. She reported the punishment could be anything ranging from "indefinite suspension to public reprimand or lofty fine," and cautioned against assumptions while noting that a suspension was certainly on the table. She added that anything more than two games or a fine of $10,000 would require special permission from an executive board composed of league representatives.



---


# The Big Ten Suspends Jim Harbaugh For Three Games

The Big Ten officially announced that Michigan coach Jim Harbaugh would be suspended for the remaining three games of the 2023 regular season, prohibited from coaching on the sideline for the rest of that stretch, including the Wolverines' rivalry game with Ohio State. The announcement was reported by Chris Vannini on Nov. 10, 2023.

The stated basis was a conference rule violation rather than an NCAA finding. In its statement the Big Ten said Michigan had been found in violation of the Big Ten Sportsmanship Policy for conducting an "impermissible, in-person scouting operation over multiple years."



---


# Michigan's Temporary Restraining Order Against The Big Ten

Michigan filed a temporary restraining order against the Big Ten on Friday night, Nov. 10, 2023, hoping to block Jim Harbaugh's three-game suspension, but no ruling came before the Wolverines' game at Penn State and the hearing was set for Friday, Nov. 17. ESPN reported that the Nov. 17 hearing would determine whether Harbaugh returned to the field for the final two games against Maryland and No. 1 Ohio State, after the Big Ten's Friday ruling barred him from the field for the final three regular-season games over the in-person scouting and sign-stealing scandal that led to staffer Connor Stalions' resignation.

The filing itself was made in Washtenaw County Trial Court on Friday night, with Jim Harbaugh and the U-M regents as plaintiffs and the Big Ten and Tony Petitti as defendants; Chris Vannini reported on Nov. 11, 2023 that the judicial officer was Timothy P. Connors, a U-M lecturer and adjunct professor at Wayne State and Vermont, and the case was also reported to be in the hands of Judge Carol Kunhke, a Michigan alumnus. If granted, the order would have delayed the suspension, but the clock was running before Saturday's game.

The drama ran to kickoff and then ended without relief. ESPN's Pete Thamel reported it was unclear whether Harbaugh would be granted a hearing in time to coach against Penn State, saying with kickoff scheduled for noon ET that "the drama's going to go right up 'till noon." Nicole Auerbach reported on Nov. 11 that there was no ruling on the TRO filing that day, so Harbaugh would not coach against Penn State, with the school saying: "We look forward to presenting our case next week where we intend to demonstrate that the Big Ten has not acted legally or fairly." Adam Rittenberg noted that Harbaugh was not on the team bus with other coaches and players when it arrived at Beaver Stadium on Saturday morning, and Michigan offensive coordinator Sherrone Moore was set to serve as acting head coach in his absence.



---


# Reactions To Jim Harbaugh's Suspension

The suspension of Jim Harbaugh drew a wave of public responses from players, the university president, a former assistant and the school itself in the days around Nov. 10-17, 2023. Michigan released a statement expressing frustration with the Big Ten's process and said it intended to seek a court order preventing the disciplinary action from taking effect, as reported by Matt Fortuna on Nov. 10, 2023.

Players answered on social media. J.J. McCarthy and a handful of other Michigan players tweeted "Bet" at the same time on Friday night, hours after Harbaugh was suspended for the remainder of the regular season; McCarthy had earlier worn a shirt reading "Free Harbaugh" while the 59-year-old served a separate suspension at the start of the season.

Former Wolverines assistant and Harbaugh confidant Biff Poggi, in his first year as Charlotte's head coach, offered an open invitation on Friday for Harbaugh to join him on the 49ers' sidelines for their games against Rice on Saturday and at South Florida on Nov. 25, writing that it would be his honor to stand next to Harbaugh again as they had for three years.

University of Michigan President Santa Ono posted on social media the day after the Penn State win, praising the team's ability to "respond to any challenge head on with a conviction to do better and to emerge even stronger" and thanking the countless members of the Michigan family who had reached out over the weekend. The post drew immediate and extensive blowback on social media and beyond, as observers questioned Ono's tone with Michigan in the midst of a self-inflicted controversy.



---


# Michigan Drops Its Suit And Accepts The Three-Game Ban

Michigan and Jim Harbaugh dropped their litigation against the Big Ten on Thursday and accepted the three-game suspension, so Harbaugh was not on Michigan's sideline that week against Maryland or the following week against Ohio State to end the regular season. The joint resolution closed both the lawsuit and the conference's investigation.

The statement set out the terms: "This morning, the University, Coach Harbaugh, and the Big Ten resolved their pending litigation. The Conference agreed to close its investigation, and the University and Coach Harbaugh agreed to accept the three-game suspension. Coach Harbaugh, with the University's support, decided to accept this sanction to return the focus to our student-athletes and their performance on the field. The Conference has confirmed that it is not aware of any information suggesting Coach Harbaugh's involvement in the allegations. The University continues to cooperate fully with the NCAA's investigation." It continued: "The Big Ten Conference's commitment to student-athletes, sportsmanship and the commissioner's duty to protect the integrity of competition will never waver. Today's decision by the University of Michigan to withdraw its legal challenge against the conference's November 10th notice of disciplinary action is indicative of the high standards and values that the conference and the university seek to uphold, the University of Michigan is a valued member of the Big Ten Conference and the conference will continue to work cooperatively with the university and the NCAA during this process."

Before the withdrawal, Harbaugh held his usual weekly news conference on Monday but mostly avoided the only topic on anyone's mind. He initially told reporters he would speak at the scheduled Friday hearing, then backtracked and sounded uncommitted, pending legal advice. Nicole Auerbach reported on Nov. 13, 2023 that Harbaugh said he was looking for "due process," mentioning a civics class he took 40 years ago — "You're innocent until proven guilty. I'd like that opportunity." Austin Meek reported the same day that Harbaugh clarified he was not sure whether he would testify Friday: "That's not my dance floor. I've watched a lot of shows. I've watched Judge Judy a lot."



---


# Tony Petitti's Defense Of The Michigan Ruling

Sporting News argued that Big Ten commissioner Tony Petitti "did the right thing" in ruling against Michigan, because the penalty showed he was not afraid to take on one of the conference's Big Two rather than issuing a "slap on the wrist." In a letter to Michigan reported by The Athletic's Nicole Auerbach, Petitti tried to dispel any notion of favouritism: "The Conference does not play favorites among its members, nor does it take actions towards its members based on prejudgment or bias. Failing to act under the extraordinary circumstances here could lead other Conference members to reasonably conclude that the conference has chosen to favor the University over all other members." Auerbach also reported, on Nov. 10, 2023, that Petitti said in the letter that the school initially refused to consent to the Big Ten obtaining the spreadsheet and other documents from the NCAA related to its investigation.

The severity was larger than expected. Most speculation had pinned a potential Harbaugh suspension at two games, on the reasoning that the regular-season finale against No. 1 Ohio State is a huge television draw and that Petitti has a background in TV with the MLB Network. Petitti went heavy-handed instead — maybe a little too heavy, Sporting News allowed, given the pending legal response from Michigan.

The outlet also set out the risks. The Big Ten made clear that it still had not linked Harbaugh to any wrongdoing and that this was an institutional penalty based on the findings, while the NCAA would continue its own investigation into the Wolverines. The timing of Friday's announcement was poor, coming less than 24 hours before the game against Penn State. On this account Petitti upheld sportsmanship within the conference, but the ruling could lead to a long-term rift with Michigan.



---


# Warde Manuel's Rebuttal Of The Harbaugh Suspension

Michigan athletic director Warde Manuel attacked the Big Ten's suspension of Jim Harbaugh on the ground that the conference skipped the due process of a complete investigation. In a statement he did not mince words: while the program had been disappointed to hear about the allegations, he said, it also felt the conference acted before any complete investigation in suspending Harbaugh on Friday.

Manuel described the suspension as "completely unethical" and "an assault on the rights of everyone (especially in the Big Ten) to be judged by a fair and complete investigation," adding in the statement reported by Pete Thamel on Nov. 11, 2023 that he found it "completely unethical, insulting to a well-established process within the NCAA, and an assault on the rights of everyone (especially in the Big Ten) to be judged by a fair and complete investigation."

He also turned the precedent back on the conference's other members: "All of the Head Coaches in the Big Ten (some who have been accused of actively participating in the trading of signals of opponents) and my Big Ten AD colleagues can rejoice today that someone was 'held accountable,' but they should be worried about the new standard of judgment (without complete investigation) that has been unleashed in this conference."



---


# The CFP Committee's "Different Team" Justification For Florida State

The New York Times attacked the CFP committee's justification for omitting Florida State on 3 December 2023, arguing that CFP committee chair Boo Corrigan's statement — "Florida State is a different team. You look at who they are as a team without Jordan Travis — they are a different team" — is a well-informed opinion that is probably true, but is not a fact.

The premise under attack is that a team's quality without its injured starter can be reliably judged in advance. Choosing the best is entirely subjective and ultimately misleading given this is a sport that routinely features unpredictable results and unforeseen runs. The precedent cited is that the last time a team was relying on a third-string quarterback heading into the College Football Playoff — Ohio State in the inaugural season of the four-team field — it won the national title.

The rebuttal also concedes the disanalogy and then answers it. The difference between those Buckeyes and this Florida State team was that Ohio State won the Big Ten title game that year 59-0, while Florida State was in a close game with Louisville that was, quite frankly, not an enjoyable watch for people who love the excitement of big-time offense — perception, wrongly, became reality. Against that, one could make the case that Florida State is so good that it won a Power 5 conference championship game with a true freshman quarterback, and that in the CFP the Seminoles would have gotten second-string quarterback Tate Rodemaker back with a month to prepare for a semifinal game.



---


# Sherrone Moore's Turn As Michigan's Acting Head Coach

Sherrone Moore filled in for the suspended Jim Harbaugh as Michigan's coach for the Penn State game and, by Sporting News' reckoning, turned it into a fitting audition for a head-coaching job of his own. The Wolverines rushed for 227 yards — including 32 straight run plays — in grinding out a top-10 victory against the Nittany Lions at Beaver Stadium, one of the toughest environments in the FBS.

Moore was emotional afterward, complete with NSFW language. In the Fox postgame interview with Jenny Taft he made Harbaugh ever-present in the moment: "I want to thank the Lord and I want to thank Coach Harbaugh," Moore said. "I f------ love you man. I love the s--- out of you, man. I did this for you, for this university, the president, our AD. We've got the best players, best university, and the best alumni in the country. I love these guys. These f------ guys right here. These guys right here. These guys did it."

Sporting News judged that Moore would emerge as a leading candidate for some jobs as a result, a huge victory for one of the nation's top assistants.



---


# Michigan State Hires Jonathan Smith Away From Oregon State

Michigan State hired Jonathan Smith as its next football coach, the school announcing the move on Saturday, as reported by CBS Sports on 2023-11-25. Smith, 44, had spent the past six seasons as coach at Oregon State, where he guided the Beavers to 18 wins over the past two seasons, including a 10-3 mark and a No. 17 finish in the AP Top 25 during a 2022 campaign that earned him Pac-12 Coach of the Year honors. He was among the initial pool of candidates linked to the Michigan State opening after the Spartans fired fourth-year coach Mel Tucker with cause midseason amid sexual harassment allegations, and he later emerged as the leading candidate to replace Tucker during the final week of the regular season — a week in which Oregon State suffered a 31-7 loss at rival Oregon.

Michigan State athletic director Alan Haller framed the hire around Smith's record: "Jonathan has a proven track record of success, building the Oregon State program from the ground up by implementing a plan resulting in sustained historic success for the Beavers. He's been a part of championship staffs, coached in the College Football Playoff, and understands what's required to be successful at the highest level, learning from some of the game's most successful coaches." Haller added that on the field Smith's teams are tough and physical yet innovative, that Oregon State that year had controlled the line of scrimmage on both sides of the ball while ranking among the nation's leaders in both rushing offense and rushing defense, and that Smith has shown the ability both to recruit talented student-athletes who fit his system and to develop and maximize players once they're in the program. Smith, a former quarterback for the Beavers from 1998-2001, exited Oregon State with a 34-35 overall mark as coach, including a 1-1 record in bowl games, as he joined the Big Ten coaching ranks. In a statement posted to social media he thanked the players, coaches and colleagues of the last six years, said he would cherish the memories and friendships, and expressed his deepest gratitude to the people of OSU and Corvallis, noting that when he first arrived as a freshman college student he had no idea the opportunities and relationships the community would provide for him and his family.



---


# Michigan Did Not Need Harbaugh At Penn State, But Ohio State Is Different

Sporting News argued that whatever the Penn State win proved, Michigan still needs Jim Harbaugh for the Ohio State game, because the Wolverines will not be able to beat the Buckeyes the way they beat Penn State. The 20-yard box in which Michigan won at Beaver Stadium "will stretch across the entire country," and that kind of game requires a coach ready to make legacy-defining decisions.

The grounds are the quality of the opponent. Ohio State has Heisman Trophy candidate Marvin Harrison Jr., who was the separator when the Buckeyes beat Penn State 20-12 on Oct. 21, and a top-five defense as well; the rage between the rivals would reach a 1970s pitch — 1973 for those who know — as they barreled toward another 11-0 vs. 11-0 showdown at the Big House. Harbaugh reportedly watched the Penn State game from the team hotel, and after Sherrone Moore's postgame emotion, a reality set in through a brutal watch of a second half.

The stakes are national. Michigan (10-0, 7-0 Big Ten) was, on this reading, public enemy No. 1 heading into the final two weeks — "Michigan vs. Everybody" — and Ohio State and Michigan locked in their answers about hero and villain long ago. More than 17 million people watched the previous year's 45-23 Michigan victory, a game in which Connor Stalions' involvement continued to be scrutinized through a double-barrel Big Ten and NCAA investigation, and early forecasts said 20 million would tune in this year. Tony Petitti's Friday ruling sent a shockwave through the conference mainly because the third game means Harbaugh will not be on the sideline for The Game. In the short term, the College Football Playoff committee could slide Michigan up to No. 2, and the debate with the Buckeyes and No. 1 Georgia would perk up more than ever — the three best teams in the country, only one with uncertainty at head coach.

Whether Harbaugh would actually be absent was for the courts to decide, but Moore's comments suggested Harbaugh, president Santa Ono and athletic director Warde Manuel were on a united front, consequences be damned in 2024 and beyond. The conclusion: whether they admit it or not, Michigan still needs Harbaugh for those moments, especially in two weeks — and he might not be present for that one either.



---


# Television Ratings For The Ohio State-Michigan Rivalry

With or without Harbaugh, Sporting News expected The Game to draw ridiculous television ratings, and reported on Nov. 11, 2023 that the previous year's matchup drew an 8.05 Nielsen rating with 17.1 million viewers. According to Sports Media Watch, only three college football games had drawn a Nielsen rating of 5.0 or better that season: Penn State-Ohio State (5.3), Colorado-Oregon (5.2) and Ohio State-Notre Dame (5.1). Michigan-Penn State was expected to join that list on Saturday, but the intrigue around The Game could double all of those numbers.

The draw came from what was on the line. Michigan had won the last two meetings and had a chance to win three in a row in the rivalry for the first time since 1995-97; Ohio State was No. 1 in the College Football Playoff rankings; Harbaugh (2-5) and Ryan Day (1-2) both had losing records in the matchup; and the Big Ten East, the CFP and perhaps a national championship were at stake. Sporting News judged that a 10 Nielsen rating and 20 million viewers was not out of the question, with enough WWE-like promos leading up to the game to get both fan bases frothing.

qid: Which company, recently discussed on both The Verge and TechCrunch, has the capability to address Android app distribution issues and uses specific criteria to rank local search results, while also being accused of harming news publishers' profits through its business practices?
context:
# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.



---


# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. Google's execution was uneven, though — it wound up spending much of its opening statement attempting to explain away its seemingly bad behavior as normal business practices and did not always succeed out of the gate.



---


# "Go Big In Europe": Google's Post-Fine Search Quality Push

The government argued on November 10, 2023 that Google only endeavored to enhance its search engine in the European Union after it was hit by a €5 billion antitrust fine in 2018 — a claim internal documents revealed, according to Bloomberg.

The EU's antitrust order forced Google to offer Android phone users a screen with five search engine options to choose from, according to the DOJ. In response, Google enacted a plan its executives dubbed "Go Big in Europe," to enhance search results in France and Germany in 2019 and 2020 with more local content: news, post-game soccer video highlights, information on local television options for streaming, and pronunciation practice for different languages. The aim was to incentivize users to click on Google's home screen rather than the competition's.

That revelation effectively supports the Justice Department's argument that Google, without the push of competition, has little incentive to improve its products — a classic consequence in a monopoly.



---


# The Market Definition Fight In Epic v. Google

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

The relation between definition and outcome is direct. If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

Two observations sit outside the formal model but bear on how the fee looks. Google charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal or a credit card, which does seem like a lot; and though Epic cannot argue it in court, Apple was not able to explicitly justify a 30 percent fee to that case's judge. On the other hand, it does kind of seem like Epic wants something for nothing — Epic has not stated what kind of fee would actually be reasonable for Google to charge in exchange for placement in its store, and CEO Tim Sweeney seemingly suggests there should not be a Google fee at all if a developer wants to use its own payment system.



---


# Epic's Antitrust Claims Against Google Play

Epic's claim is that the Android operating system's Google Play Store constitutes an unlawful monopoly, and that Google is separately tying its Google Play payments platform to that store, keeping other potential app payment mechanisms from competing.

The grounds Epic offers are the frictions it says Google creates: Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that it has created an illegal monopoly which unjustly enriches Google while artificially driving up app prices because other stores cannot compete. The warrant joining that to the legal claim is the competitive-harm chain — no viable rival stores means no fee discipline, which means the "Google Tax" is paid either by developers or passed along to consumers. Epic wants to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods so developers are not stuck paying that tax.

Google's answer contests the warrant rather than the fees: it says Epic's demands would damage Android's ability to offer a secure user experience and to compete with Apple's iOS. Both sides agree the future of Google's app store could depend on this trial. Epic sued in 2020 after a fight over in-app purchase fees.



---


# Google's News Content Payment Deal With Canada

In November 2023, the month before the Helena World Chronicle suit was filed, Google reached an agreement with the Canadian government under which the search giant would pay Canadian media for use of their content. Under the terms of the deal, Google will provide $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) every year to news organizations in the country, with funds distributed based on the news outlets' headcount.

Negotiations with Meta over the same Canadian law were still unresolved as of mid-December 2023. Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August, in light of the pressure to pay for content under the new Canadian law.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The Epic v. Google Witness Lineup

A whole cast of intriguing people were set to be called as witnesses during the trial, going straight to the top of the org chart: Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Epic CEO Tim Sweeney are absolutely expected to attend.

# Google's Defense: Android Openness And Sideloading

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google will also attack the foreclosure premise directly. It will note that, unlike Apple, it allows apps to be sideloaded on Android devices — something Epic takes advantage of today — and that this process is streamlined and helps keep users safe. Epic will claim in response that the process is made to be overly difficult for end users, with multiple steps involved and "scare screens" that warn users of the security risks involved with sideloading.

On discovery, Epic will suggest that Google hid items by allowing execs and employees to have "off the record" chats; Google will counter this as well, saying it has provided the court with thousands of chat logs and millions of documents. Google will ultimately push the notion that this case is not about competition but about money — that is, that Epic Games wants to reach the Play Store's 2.5 billion users without having to pay. As a Google blog post by Wilson White, VP, Government Affairs & Public Policy, put it: "Android's choice and flexibility work well for consumers and developers of all sizes. # Revenue Split

## Definition

A revenue split, in the corpus, is the percentage pair — such as 70/30, 50/50, or 95/5 — by which a platform and a counterparty divide proceeds: Google's revenue share agreements (RSAs) with Android device makers and carriers, Google's 70/30 app-store split with developers, and Twitch's and Kick's subscription-revenue splits with streamers.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces across three unrelated disputes that share the same underlying mechanic: dividing proceeds between a platform and a counterparty. In the US v. Google antitrust trial, Google's revenue share agreements (RSAs) pay Android device makers and wireless carriers like Verizon a cut in exchange for setting Google Search and Chrome as defaults. In the Epic v. Google trial, Epic argued that Google's 70/30 app-store revenue split with developers is likely descended from an arbitrary decision Valve made with Steam two decades earlier, rather than from any principled calculation of the value Google's store provides. On the creator-platform side, Twitch's default subscription revenue split for Partners is 50/50, with a premium 70/30 tier once offered to select streamers before Twitch discontinued it in favor of ad revenue; rival platform Kick instead lures streamers away with a 95/5 split.

## Key Characteristics

- **Expressed as a ratio** — revenue splits are stated as two percentages that sum to 100, such as 70/30, 50/50, or 95/5, denoting each party's share.
- **Applies across different platform relationships** — the corpus shows the same mechanic governing device-maker default agreements (Google RSAs), app-store developer terms (Google/Epic 70/30), and creator subscription payouts (Twitch, Kick).
- **A lever platforms adjust unilaterally** — Twitch changed its subscription split from a 70/30 deal for select streamers to a 50/50 default, then introduced the Partner Plus program to restore a 70/30 rate for qualifying creators, showing the split is a platform-controlled term rather than a fixed market rate.
- **A point of leverage in competitive disputes** — Epic used the 70/30 app-store split's arbitrary Valve/Steam origin to challenge Google's justification for its rate, and Kick's more generous 95/5 split is a stated draw for streamers dissatisfied with Twitch's terms.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "revenue split" and "revenue share" only in the specific device-maker, app-store, and creator-payout deals described above, without defining the general concept. Outside the corpus, revenue sharing is defined as the distribution of the total revenue generated by the sale of goods and services among stakeholders or contributors, distinct from profit sharing (which splits only what remains after costs) (Wikipedia, "Revenue sharing," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenue_sharing).

# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# MADA And RSA: Google's Two Android Distribution Agreements

Google binds Android device makers through two distinct contract types, described at trial on November 8, 2023 by Jamie Rosenberg, a Google employee who focuses on Android and Google Play, testifying in Google's defense. A mobile app distribution agreement (MADA) requires Android smartphone makers — like Samsung or Oppo — to pre-load a bundle of 11 Google apps on the device, including Search, Chrome and Play. Rosenberg's discriminating point about MADA is that the pre-loaded apps do not have to be the default choices.

A revenue share agreement (RSA) is the second and separate instrument. RSAs run with smartphone makers and also with wireless carriers such as Verizon, and unlike MADAs they do require the counterparty to set Google search and the Chrome web browser as defaults. So the boundary between the two is pre-installation versus default status: MADA buys presence on the device, RSA buys the default slot.

Rosenberg defended the arrangement on two grounds — that Google apps like Search are "best in class," and that the RSAs motivate other companies to make or sell more Android devices. He framed the broader competitive setting by saying the competition between Google and Apple is "as intense as it gets," per Bloomberg.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# The SEO Naming Effect On Customer Acquisition

The Verge argued that Thai Food Near Me's name really did help the restaurant — but not through the mechanism its owners intended. The initial SEO "hack" was likely technically ineffective, but it was memorable and funny, and the joke led to many, many, many articles and forum posts about the restaurant's name, which tipped the SEO scales in its favor; all of that content, including The Verge's own story, will help the restaurant's prominence on Google platforms. One SEO trick, the reporter wrote, has eaten another.

The grounds for saying the direct hack failed are a test and a concession. A Google Maps search for "Thai food near me" from the reporter's home in Brooklyn yielded plenty of options literally near her but not Jirapraphanan's business a few miles away. Robert Sampson, a co-owner who handles much of the back-end work including SEO, followed the online discussion about the utility of the name and conceded part of it: "The people who said that [the name is] not such a good idea… I think they're responding more from a national brand campaign. It is true that if you're in California, and you type 'Thai food near me,' you're going to have a little bit of a hard time finding us. But for local search, I think the name works really well." Danny Sullivan's position was that a "near me" name is not a silver bullet for gaming the search algorithm.

The warrant connecting name to durable ranking is the feedback loop that follows a first visit. As with Thai Food Near Me, the most powerful thing an SEO-driven name might be able to do is get customers in the door; from there it is up to the business to give them a good experience, whether that is a great plate of pad see ew or the perfect haircut, and then the cycle continues — happy customers leave good reviews, and good reviews help the business's Google Maps profile rank higher. Felix Silva also uploads high-quality photos and videos to his page and shares updates, another SEO move, since some experts say active profiles can improve a business's rankings.

# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.

# Google Play Billing And The User Choice Billing Alternative

Google Play's billing arrangement, as of November 2023, has two tiers. The baseline requires apps to use Google's own first-party billing system and charges app developers a 15% to 30% commission on the sales it processes. The alternative is User Choice Billing, a program still in pilot testing, open to all developers who sell apps in the 35 markets where it is then available, including the U.S., which reduces the standard commission by 4% for companies who choose to use their own payment processing solution. ## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

# iPhone Setup And The Absence Of A Search Engine Choice Screen

Eddy Cue acknowledged on the stand that the ISA didn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup — and said he wouldn't want to do that anyway, because "we try to get people up and running as fast as possible" and "setup is just critical stuff."

Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw built to that answer through a series of questions about the iPhone setup process, using three screenshots: the Appearance screen that appears when you first boot up an iPhone so you can pick font sizes, the location-tracking prompt that appears when you open Maps, and the App Tracking Transparency pop-up that tells you when an app wants to collect your data. Cue objected to all of these being considered part of setup, but Bellshaw's point was that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, and that search could be one of them. Cue argued that showing people a bunch of search engines they had never heard of would just be a bad user experience — even he couldn't remember the names of some of the alternatives to Google — and said, "We make Google be the default search engine because we've always thought it was the best. We pick the best one and let users easily change it." The Verge noted that "easily" is a persistent point of contention in the trial: DuckDuckGo's CEO, who testified the week before, claimed it takes "too many steps" to switch.

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. # The Market Definition Fight In Epic v. Google

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

The relation between definition and outcome is direct. If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

Two observations sit outside the formal model but bear on how the fee looks. Google charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal or a credit card, which does seem like a lot; and though Epic cannot argue it in court, Apple was not able to explicitly justify a 30 percent fee to that case's judge. On the other hand, it does kind of seem like Epic wants something for nothing — Epic has not stated what kind of fee would actually be reasonable for Google to charge in exchange for placement in its store, and CEO Tim Sweeney seemingly suggests there should not be a Google fee at all if a developer wants to use its own payment system.

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. # Payment Processor

## Definition

In the corpus, a payment processor is named as one of several distinct roles a company can hold in a transaction — the entity that handles the movement of payments — separate from being the customer, the merchant, or a market maker, even when a single company (like Alameda Research for FTX, or Google Play for its app store) plays more than one of those roles at once.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term across two very different settings: crypto-market infrastructure and app-store commerce.
In the FTX criminal trial, defense counsel Mark Cohen argued that Alameda Research "acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker" — the third role described in the corpus as a "financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies."
In fintech coverage, "payment processor" describes companies such as Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; the startup Rainforest is described as competing to win software-platform business away from these "legacy processors."
In the Epic v. Google trial, Google Play's own billing system is treated as the payment processor for in-app purchases, and the antitrust dispute centers on whether Google may tie that processing to app-store access; per Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, Google charges other developers 30% but struck a special deal letting Spotify pay 0% when it processes its own payments, or 4% when it uses Google's payment service instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of several roles a single company can hold** — the FTX defense listed "customer, payment processor, and market maker" as three separate roles Alameda played for FTX, distinct from being FTX itself.
- **A fee-generating, competitive service** — Google charges up to 30% for Play billing (discounted to 4%, or waived to 0% for self-processed payments, under Spotify's special deal), and a separate "User Choice Billing" program launched in 2022 knocks only 4 percentage points off Google's standard fee for developers using their own payment system; Rainforest, Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS compete for the equivalent software-platform and merchant business.
- **Built differently for different customer types** — Rainforest founder Joshua Silver argues that existing "modern processors" (incumbents like Fiserv and FIS) were built directly for merchants, not software platforms, and have had to retrofit their systems to handle software companies' payment-processing and reporting needs — the gap Rainforest positions itself to fill.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a payment processor is generally described as the intermediary that transfers payment data and messaging between the card-issuing bank, the merchant, and the acquiring bank to authorize and settle a transaction, and is typically categorized as either front-end (handling authorization) or back-end (handling settlement) (Wikipedia, "Payment processor," accessed 2026-09-02).
