# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.

# Google's Defense That Safari Succeeded On Product Integration

Google lawyer John Schmidtlein's rebuttal attacked the DOJ's premise that Google's position on Apple devices was bought rather than earned: his overall point was that Google helped Safari succeed not by forcing Apple's hand, but by being a great product that integrated seamlessly with Apple's own stuff.

He developed it after a closed session and the lunch break by leading Eddy Cue through a history of the Google/Apple partnership and of the Safari browser. Cue testified that Safari's combination of URL and search bar was a user interface innovation and that the seamless Google integration was part of what made it work; Schmidtlein pointed out that in early promotional materials for Safari, the Google integration was nearly always mentioned. Cue supplied the origin story: "Before 2003, the way that you searched the web was you had to go in and you had to type in google.com in the URL field, or you could type in another URL. We came up with the idea that if you type anything in the URL field that's not a URL, it just goes to search."



---


# Meta's Proposal: Parental Approval For App Downloads At The App Store

Meta wants to shift the burden of monitoring social media usage among teens back to the app stores — and to parents. In a blog post published November 15, 2023, Meta's global head of Safety, Antigone Davis, argued that parents should be responsible for approving their teens' app downloads, and staked Meta's position in supporting federal legislation that would require parental approval for app downloads for users under the age of 16.

The ground Meta offered is public opinion: it pointed to recent Pew research indicating that 81% of U.S. adults were in favor of requiring parental consent for teens to create social media accounts. TechCrunch's caveat is that while this may speak to popular opinion around parental sentiment, it does not mean that parents have thought through who should be responsible for preventing or allowing teens' access to social media, or how those apps should operate to protect teens.

The warrant tying the proposal to the app stores is one of existing capability: the app stores already have age guidelines, so it would seem to follow that they should also enforce them, if enforcement is to be regulated — or that seems to be Meta's thinking. TechCrunch also notes that a policy position like this is not something that would have been rushed out in a matter of days as a PR response to Bejar's claims, but something Meta has been stewing on for some time.



---


# Epic's Antitrust Claims Against Google Play

Epic's claim is that the Android operating system's Google Play Store constitutes an unlawful monopoly, and that Google is separately tying its Google Play payments platform to that store, keeping other potential app payment mechanisms from competing.

The grounds Epic offers are the frictions it says Google creates: Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that it has created an illegal monopoly which unjustly enriches Google while artificially driving up app prices because other stores cannot compete. The warrant joining that to the legal claim is the competitive-harm chain — no viable rival stores means no fee discipline, which means the "Google Tax" is paid either by developers or passed along to consumers. Epic wants to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods so developers are not stuck paying that tax.

Google's answer contests the warrant rather than the fees: it says Epic's demands would damage Android's ability to offer a secure user experience and to compete with Apple's iOS. Both sides agree the future of Google's app store could depend on this trial. Epic sued in 2020 after a fight over in-app purchase fees.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Openness And Sideloading

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google will also attack the foreclosure premise directly. It will note that, unlike Apple, it allows apps to be sideloaded on Android devices — something Epic takes advantage of today — and that this process is streamlined and helps keep users safe. Epic will claim in response that the process is made to be overly difficult for end users, with multiple steps involved and "scare screens" that warn users of the security risks involved with sideloading.

On discovery, Epic will suggest that Google hid items by allowing execs and employees to have "off the record" chats; Google will counter this as well, saying it has provided the court with thousands of chat logs and millions of documents. Google will ultimately push the notion that this case is not about competition but about money — that is, that Epic Games wants to reach the Play Store's 2.5 billion users without having to pay. As a Google blog post by Wilson White, VP, Government Affairs & Public Policy, put it: "Android's choice and flexibility work well for consumers and developers of all sizes. We look forward to making our case in court as we fight to keep our users safe from harm, partner with developers to grow their businesses, and keep the Android ecosystem thriving and healthy for everyone."



---


# MADA And RSA: Google's Two Android Distribution Agreements

Google binds Android device makers through two distinct contract types, described at trial on November 8, 2023 by Jamie Rosenberg, a Google employee who focuses on Android and Google Play, testifying in Google's defense. A mobile app distribution agreement (MADA) requires Android smartphone makers — like Samsung or Oppo — to pre-load a bundle of 11 Google apps on the device, including Search, Chrome and Play. Rosenberg's discriminating point about MADA is that the pre-loaded apps do not have to be the default choices.

A revenue share agreement (RSA) is the second and separate instrument. RSAs run with smartphone makers and also with wireless carriers such as Verizon, and unlike MADAs they do require the counterparty to set Google search and the Chrome web browser as defaults. So the boundary between the two is pre-installation versus default status: MADA buys presence on the device, RSA buys the default slot.

Rosenberg defended the arrangement on two grounds — that Google apps like Search are "best in class," and that the RSAs motivate other companies to make or sell more Android devices. He framed the broader competitive setting by saying the competition between Google and Apple is "as intense as it gets," per Bloomberg.



---


# Anti-Steering Rules

## Definition

Anti-steering rules, as the corpus uses the term, are restrictions that PayPal — and, earlier, Visa and Mastercard — impose on the merchants who accept their payment methods, alleged in a 2023 consumer class action to stifle competition from lower-cost payment platforms such as Stripe and Shopify.

## Context

The corpus introduces the term through a 2023 class-action lawsuit against PayPal: consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman allege that PayPal's anti-steering rules stifle competition against lower-cost payment platforms such as Stripe and Shopify, and that PayPal has subjected consumers to excess charges when purchasing from merchants that accept PayPal or Venmo. The attorneys who filed the suit placed PayPal's rules in a lineage going back to the card networks: "Visa and MasterCard once imposed similar anti-steering rules on merchants accepting their cards but, after the Justice Department sued the networks for antitrust violations, they agreed in 2010 to eliminate their anti-steering rules as part of the settlement. With payments transitioning into the digital realm, PayPal has simply ripped a page right from the Visa and MasterCard [sic] playbook." Antitrust litigator Patrick McGahan framed the underlying tension as structural rather than PayPal-specific: platform companies that act as gatekeepers in a market will keep drawing antitrust suits over the fees they charge, and PayPal can be expected to respond that its own fees are themselves driven by the card schemes (Visa, Mastercard, American Express) that set the terms it operates under.

## Key Characteristics

- **Merchant-facing restriction** — the rule binds merchants who accept a given payment method, not consumers directly, by limiting the merchant's ability to steer buyers elsewhere.
- **Fee insulation** — the effect alleged is that the rules stifle competition from lower-cost platforms, letting the rule-setter avoid price competition on its fees.
- **Precedent in card networks** — Visa and Mastercard imposed similar anti-steering rules on merchants before agreeing, in a 2010 Justice Department antitrust settlement, to eliminate them.
- **Migrates across payment eras** — the lawsuit's framing treats PayPal's digital-era rules as a continuation of the same practice the card networks used, rather than a new phenomenon.
- **Tied to gatekeeper status** — commentary on the suit links anti-steering rules to a platform's position as a fee-charging gatekeeper between merchants and payment systems, and to who bears responsibility when fees are themselves imposed further up the chain (e.g., by card schemes).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the U.S. Supreme Court examined the same kind of restriction in the 2018 antitrust case *Ohio v. American Express Co.*: American Express's merchant contracts contained anti-steering provisions that "prohibit merchants from avoiding fees by discouraging customers' American Express card use at the point of sale," and the Court held, 5–4 in an opinion by Justice Thomas decided June 25, 2018, that these provisions did not violate federal antitrust law.
(Source: SCOTUSblog, "Ohio v. American Express Co." case page, accessed 2026-09-02: https://www.scotusblog.com/case-files/cases/ohio-v-american-express-co/)

# Apple's Privacy Stance Versus Google's Default Payments

Meagan Bellshaw's privacy line of questioning attacked the premise that Apple chose Google because Google had the best product: if Apple genuinely regards Google as bad on privacy, then something other than product quality must explain why Apple gives Google a central place on its platform.

Bellshaw asked Cue whether Apple believes user privacy is important, to which he said, "Absolutely." She then showed a series of emails and slides in which Cue and Apple railed against Google's privacy policies, and Cue readily agreed with them: "We've always thought we had better privacy than Google." He said one provision of the ISA was that Google had to allow people to search without logging in, and that Apple has done things in Safari and around its platforms to make it harder for Google or anyone else to track users. Bellshaw never quite said it, but The Verge read the DOJ's implication as this: Google is a privacy menace anathema to everything Apple believes is important to its users, yet Apple gives it that central place because Google pays so handsomely. She then asked Cue to review some of Apple's financial filings and whether it is true that the ISA represents a significant portion of Apple's profits. Cue's rebuttal was that this is not how Apple looks at it, because the framing doesn't account for all the work Apple did to make its platform so appealing that an agreement like this could work as well as it does.



---


# Temu As The Top US iPhone App Of 2023

Temu, the Chinese e-commerce company, is Apple's most downloaded free app in the U.S. for 2023. Apple released an App Store feature on 12 December 2023 showcasing the top iPhone apps of the year, free and paid, as measured by app installs — its proxy for overall popularity. In that ranking, apps from Chinese-based companies have taken over spots previously held by U.S. tech giants like Meta and Google, with CapCut and TikTok, both from Beijing-based ByteDance, coming in at No. 3 and No. 5 respectively.

TechCrunch suggests the negative attention TikTok received during the year may account for its slip from being the No. 1 app last year to No. 5 this year, but says U.S. consumers have not sworn off Chinese apps by the looks of things, given Temu's No. 1 position.

Engagement data supports the point: figures from Apptopia, reported by Bloomberg, noted that consumers were spending 18 minutes per day in Temu's app compared with 10 minutes in Amazon, with younger users spending even more, at 19 minutes per day on average. While Temu attracts users with in-app games, its real draw may be its bargain prices, which have more appeal during an economic downturn, and it is also a heavily marketed app, just as TikTok was in the months leading up to its No. 1 ranking last year.



---


# The $360 Million Activision Payment And Its Evidentiary Weakness

The counter to Epic's headline number attacks the factual premise beneath it: the $360 million refers to an alleged payment that kept Activision from opening an app store that could compete with Google Play, but Activision told The Verge in 2022 that it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store" — and Google says it is now armed with the evidence to prove it.

Epic itself conceded a related point. On Monday Epic's attorney admitted Google "was too clever" to draw up contracts that specifically forced developers not to compete with the Play Store, so it is not clear how much of Epic's evidence will hold up on closer examination.

The narrative advantage may nonetheless survive the evidentiary weakness. The overall story Epic tells is compelling, and it is not clear Google's opening statement countered it: Google spent its 45 minutes attempting to explain that its dominance over the Android app market is not anything nefarious but simply the natural outcome of Google fiercely competing with the iPhone and its iOS App Store, where Google would like the court to believe the competition truly lies.



---


# Project Liberty: Epic's Deliberate Payment Bypass

Epic is the studio behind Fortnite, the extraordinarily popular free-to-play game, which makes money by selling in-game items with its virtual currency V-Bucks; until August 13th, 2020, if a player used an Android or iOS device and installed the game through an official app store, buying V-Bucks triggered an in-app payment fee to Google or Apple — fees critics call the "Google tax" or the "Apple tax," and which Epic definitely was not a fan of.

August 13th, 2020 was a very busy day. Epic announced it was bypassing Apple and Google's app store fees, deploying a hotfix update to Fortnite without either company's knowledge that let players buy V-Bucks directly through its own payment processing option at a discount. Apple and Google almost immediately reacted by kicking Fortnite off their app stores for breaking the rules. Then Epic was ready and waiting with two lawsuits and an attack ad depicting a Fortnite hero throwing a unicorn-llama hammer into a giant screen reminiscent of Apple's famous "1984" Macintosh ad. It was a striking publicity blitz followed by a lot of slow-moving court proceedings: the Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021 and a ruling came down that September, mostly decided in Apple's favor, though both parties are waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in, while the Google one was delayed again and again.

The premeditation is documented, and Google is countersuing over it. At trial Google pointed out how Epic hatched a secret plan called "Project Liberty" to quietly update Fortnite with code to bypass app store fees, get its app kicked off Apple's and Google's app stores, and sue. It showed out-of-context quotes from internal Epic communications — phrases like "How do we not look like the bad guys?", "Just planting the nefarious seed now" and "I mean everything we're attempting is technically a violation of Google's policy, right?" — to suggest Epic knew it was breaking bad at the time. An email from Epic CEO Tim Sweeney reads: "Here is our official plan for communicating with Google about bypassing the Google Play Store: SAY NOTHING TILL IT SHIPS."

Epic did not try to hide it in court. Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening statement, so by the time Google raised it, it had already been an hour since Epic admitted it intentionally broke Google's rules. "Epic decided to stand up because that's what you do to a bully," Bornstein told the jury.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Google's Zero Percent Play Billing Deal With Spotify

The second piece of trial evidence Tim Sweeney called astonishing was the Spotify deal: Google gave Spotify a 0 percent fee and let Spotify process its own payments, keeping 100 percent — an arrangement Google did for Spotify and for nobody else.

Sweeney framed Spotify as the one company with negotiating power comparable to Fortnite's, and faulted it for using that power to cut a special deal with Google instead of fighting for the good of all developers. His summary of the consequence: "If you're a smaller developer than Spotify, you get screwed." He added that when Spotify does use Google's own payment service, it pays 4 percent rather than the 30 percent Google forces other developers to pay — and said that is what the rate should be, calling four percent "a perfectly reasonable rate for an unbundled payment system."



---


# Platform Owners Should Treat Developers As Partners

Tim Sweeney argued that any tech company, Apple and Google included, would be much better off in the long term if it viewed developers as awesome partners and did everything it could to support and empower them rather than get in their way financially — and said the opposite behavior at Apple and Google is what has disappointed him most.

His grounds are a comparison and a diagnosis. The comparison is Microsoft: even at the peak of the antitrust trial against Microsoft, he said, Microsoft was awesome to developers — always respectful, giving developers a great deal and treating them as partners — so that even as Microsoft was crushing corporate competitors, the developer experience was excellent. The Verge appended an editor's note that Netscape might feel differently. The diagnosis is that Google and Apple both treat developers as adversaries, trying to attack developer revenue streams and prevent them from competing with the platforms' own products, and have built massive self-preferencing schemes around excluding developers and disadvantaging third parties — which Sweeney calls very shortsighted. The warrant is that a platform's own long-term position improves when its developers thrive, and Sweeney offers Epic's own conduct as the demonstration: this has been Epic's philosophy with Unreal Engine and the Epic Games Store, where Epic wants to be "a cool partner that helps other companies succeed the way we do." He suspected such a philosophy change at Apple and Google may only come with a generational change in the companies' management.



---


# Epic's Jury Verdict Against Google, December 2023

On Monday, a federal jury sided with Fortnite maker Epic Games in its fight to break Google's control over Android apps, surprising the world. The nine-person jury decided that Google has an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems, and that Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The outcome was striking because "walled garden" rival Apple almost entirely won a similar case two years earlier. For Tim Sweeney, this was, at last, a win.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# Eddy Cue's Testimony In US V. Google

Eddy Cue took the stand as a witness in US v. Google, the landmark antitrust trial over Google's search business, and arrived with two messages: Apple believes in protecting its users' privacy, and it also believes in Google — whether those two statements can be simultaneously true became the question of the day.

Cue is one of the highest-profile witnesses in the case so far, in part because the deal between Google and Apple, which makes Google the default search engine on all Apple devices and pays Apple billions of dollars a year, is central to the US Department of Justice's case against Google. The Verge set the scene in the Washington, DC courtroom, where the screens had briefly malfunctioned and left witnesses with only binders before the tech came back up, showing an image of three iPhones each demonstrating a part of the phone's setup process. Cue, in a dark suit, squinted at the monitor and said, "The resolution on this is terrible. You should get a Mac," drawing laughs in an otherwise staid and quiet courtroom; Judge Amit Mehta, presiding over the case, leaned into his microphone and answered, "If Apple would like to make a donation…", drawing bigger ones, before everybody got back down to business.

Most US stocks slipped in the overnight Wall Street session reported on 5 December 2023, though the market stayed near its highest level in 20 months after a mixed set of reports that kept alive questions about whether the world's largest economy can pull off a perfect landing in which it kills high inflation but avoids a recession. Wall Street advanced overnight with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq touching three-week highs as dovish comments from Fed officials pushed Treasury yields lower; following remarks from other top Fed officials on Monday, Atlanta Fed President Raphael Bostic said the US central bank did not need to raise interest rates any further, and that he saw no recession ahead.

# US Government Shutdown Risk And The Market History Of Shutdowns

Besides high interest rates, a long list of other worries was tugging at Wall Street in late September 2023, the most immediate being the threat of another US government shutdown as Capitol Hill threatened a stalemate that could shut off federal services across the country. Wall Street has dealt with such shutdowns before, and stocks have historically been turbulent in the run-up to them, according to Lori Calvasina, strategist at RBC Capital Markets: looking at the seven shutdowns that lasted 10 days or more since the 1970s, she found the S&P 500 dropped an average of roughly 10 per cent in the three months heading into them, but stocks managed to hold up rather well during the shutdowns themselves, falling an average of just 0.3 per cent before rebounding meaningfully afterward.

Wall Street was also contending with higher oil prices, shaky economies around the world, a strike by US autoworkers that could put more upward pressure on inflation, and a resumption of US student-loan repayments that could dent spending by households.

# Federal Reserve Rate Path Expectations Late 2023

By early December 2023 traders widely expected the Federal Reserve to hold its key interest rate steady at its meeting the following week before potentially cutting rates in March, according to data from CME Group, and Fed officials had recently hinted that the federal funds rate may already be at its peak, above 5.25 per cent, up from nearly zero early in 2022. Fed Chair Jerome Powell and others nevertheless warned Wall Street against being overzealous in its predictions about how early a cut could happen.

The bond market moved with those expectations. With inflation down from its peak two summers earlier, Wall Street was hopeful the Fed might be done with its market-shaking hikes. Investors were looking for a slowdown in the job market that came through employers cutting back on open positions rather than laying off workers, and the report cited showed employers advertised just 8.7 million jobs on the last day of October, down 617,000 from a month earlier. US Treasury yields continued to sag from the heights reached during late October: the 10-year yield fell to 4.18 per cent from 4.26 per cent late on the Monday, after having been above 5 per cent and at its highest level in more than a decade during October. The two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks Fed expectations, fell from 4.61 per cent just before the economic reports to 4.57 per cent, yo-yoed, and then eased back to 4.57 per cent. Lower yields were one reason cryptocurrency prices had been rising, alongside excitement about a possible bitcoin exchange-traded fund that helped send bitcoin above $US43,000 ($65,600); Robinhood Markets reported a roughly 75 per cent jump in crypto trading volumes during November from a month earlier, said customers added about $US1.4 billion in net deposits during the month, and its own stock rose 10.3 per cent.

A month earlier, in early November 2023, the same expectations were forming from a lower base. Before that week, stocks had been struggling under the weight of rapidly rising Treasury yields catching up to the Fed's main interest rate, which was above 5.25 per cent and at its highest level since 2001. Higher rates and yields slow the economy, hurt investment prices and raise the risk of something breaking in the financial system, such as the three high-profile US bank failures that rattled markets during the spring. "It was really fear that the Fed was going to go too far," said Katie Nixon, chief investment officer for Northern Trust Wealth Management. The Fed had applied that pressure intentionally, hoping to starve inflation of its fuel and to cool the job market, particularly pay raises, because it feared too-strong pay gains could create a vicious cycle keeping inflation high. Analysts said the Friday jobs report offered encouraging signals, with average hourly earnings rising less in October from September than expected, though it did not mean the job was done. Treasury yields tumbled immediately after that report, with the 10-year easing to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday and from more than five per cent the previous week, when it hit its highest level since 2007. Traders then moved up expectations for the first Fed cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data. A separate report that Friday from the Institute for Supply Management said growth in US services industries such as finance and construction was weaker than economists expected and suggested a slight easing in prices.

# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.

# ASX Stock And Sector Moves, Late September 2023

REITs, up 0.4 per cent, was the strongest sector on the Australian index in the session reported on 2023-09-26, as Goodman added 0.5 per cent and Dexus climbed 2.8 per cent. In company news, ETF provider Betashares, which manages $30 billion in funds, reached an agreement to acquire Bendigo and Adelaide Bank's superannuation business, its first venture into the superannuation sector and part of what Betashares said was a longer-term strategy to expand into the broader financial sector; shares in Bendigo increased 0.6 per cent on the news.

Among the laggards, casino operator Star Entertainment Group's shares hit an all-time low of 60¢ after it raised $565 million, closing the session 16 per cent weaker at 63¢; Star, which raised $800 million in February, had to return to the market for fresh funding and is hoping to raise $750 million at a share price of 60¢ a share. Healthcare heavyweight CSL shed 1.4 per cent, weighing down the healthcare sector, and insurers IAG (down 2.6 per cent) and Suncorp (down 2 per cent) gave back some of their gains from Tuesday. Gold miners Newcrest (down 2.1 per cent) and Evolution (down 3.5 per cent) were also among the biggest large-cap decliners after the spot gold price dropped 0.9 per cent overnight. Information technology, down 1.1 per cent, was the weakest sector on the local bourse, with WiseTech losing 1.4 per cent.

# Bank Of America's Warning Of More Housing "Turbulence"

A Bank of America team led by U.S. economist Jeseo Park warned in the week of 2023-10-06 that there is more "turbulence" coming for the housing market because of high mortgage rates: "With rates likely staying higher for longer, we are cautious of potential turbulence ahead," the group wrote. The grounds are the persistence of high rates rather than a repeat of a past crash — the team said they were getting an eerie feeling of "déjà vu," but it was not 2008 that came to mind, it was the 1980s.

The forecast attached to this warning is qualified. Bank of America had previously forecast 0% home price growth and falling home sales for the full year 2023, but it did not offer a new prediction in its latest note. The warrant joining the rate outlook to the housing outlook runs the other way as well: eventually, as inflation fades and leads the Fed to cut interest rates, housing affordability will improve. "At that stage, we should see a more stable and healthy housing market," Park and her team wrote. "Until then, hang tight, it may be a bumpy ride."

# Wall Street Movers At The End Of September 2023

Blue Apron soared 134.5 per cent after the meal kit company said it was being bought by Wonder Group for $US13 per share in cash in a deal valued at $US103 million ($160.2 million), while energy producers were on the losing end, hurt by the slide in oil's price.

Energy stocks in the S&P 500 fell 2 per cent as a group, more than double the loss of any of the other 10 sectors that make up the index; ExxonMobil fell 1.6 per cent and Schlumberger dropped 4.3 per cent — though energy stocks remain the market's standout performers since the summer. Shares of Ford and General Motors slipped after the United Auto Workers said it would expand its limited strike to include another facility for each, with Ford down 1.1 per cent and GM down 0.6 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 slipped 11.65 points to 4288.05, the Dow dropped 158.84 to 33,507.50, and the Nasdaq added 18.05 to 13,219.32. In sharemarkets abroad, indexes were modestly higher in Europe after exchanges were closed across much of Asia.

# ASX Decliners In The Session Before The October 2023 RBA Meeting

On the Monday before the Reserve Bank's Tuesday meeting, Treasury Wine Estates (down 1.9 per cent) and Woolworths (down 1.2 per cent) dragged the consumer staples sector (down 1.1 per cent) lower, with Pilbara Minerals (down 2.1 per cent) and Qantas (down 1.5 per cent) also among the biggest large-cap decliners.

Stronger iron ore prices helped to bolster the local bourse on Monday but not enough to offset the prospect of higher-for-longer interest rates ahead of the RBA meeting. Iron ore heavyweights advanced after the iron ore price increased 1.4 per cent overnight, with lithium miner Liontown resisting the downward momentum of lithium prices, which dropped to their lowest level in two years.



---


# Robyn Davidson's Memoir, Published October 2023

Robyn Davidson's memoir, published by Bloomsbury at $34.99 on 3 October, tells the story of her life from childhood and beyond — largely avoiding the desert trip with her camels that made Tracks famous — The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its defining move is that omission: "You've read the book, you've seen the film – Tracks – but here is the story of Robyn Davidson's life from childhood, largely avoiding that trip across the desert with her camels, and beyond to a life of more travel, houses, lovers and family."

The book's centre is family, and particularly her mother, who took her own life at 46 and about whom Davidson has previously been unable to write to her own satisfaction. She is acutely aware that her version of the truth "can bury another's", but this one is hers.



---


# The Seven, Chris Hammer's Crime Novel

Chris Hammer's latest crime novel, published by Allen & Unwin at $32.99 on 3 October, brings back Nell Buchanan and Ivan Lucic for a murder case involving one of the seven families who rule the Yuwonderie district like a fiefdom, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its place in his output is the roundup's framing: it is hard to believe Scrublands, Hammer's first crime novel, was published only five years earlier, and since then the former journo has followed the crime writer's timetable of a book a year. The returning detectives were met in Treasure & Dirt and Tilt.

The reviewer's expectation of the genre is stated plainly: "You can expect dark secrets to emerge and herrings to be red."



---


# US Jobs And Services Data In Early October 2023

Wednesday's ADP report suggested private employers added 89,000 jobs last month, a much sharper slowdown in hiring than the 140,000 economists expected. The report does not have a perfect track record in predicting what the more comprehensive jobs report from the US government will say, which was due to arrive on the Friday. Mike Loewengart, head of model portfolio construction at Morgan Stanley Global Investment Office, said that "if Friday's report also shows the labour market is cooling, stock investors may worry a little less about indefinitely higher interest rates".

A second report on the economy said growth in US services industries slowed in September by a touch more than economists expected. The figures were reported by The Age on 4 October 2023 alongside a note that oil prices slumped overnight.



---


# The Oil Slump And House Speaker Vacancy, Early October 2023

Oil prices tumbled on Wednesday 4 October 2023, taking some heat off inflation: benchmark US crude fell $US5.01 to settle at $US84.22 per barrel for its worst drop in just over a year, having topped $US93 the previous week, while Brent crude, the international standard, lost $US5.11 to $US85.81. Prices for crude had been generally charging higher from $US70 during the summer following announcements of production cuts by some oil-producing countries. The services report of the same day offered hints of sticky pressure on inflation, with prices paid by services companies rising last month at a similar rate as in August.

Wall Street was also absorbing the ouster of Kevin McCarthy as speaker of the House of Representatives. The unprecedented move to remove a speaker likely does not change much in the short term, with funding for the US government set until 17 November, but according to economists at Goldman Sachs, "a leadership vacuum in the House raises the odds of a government shutdown when the current funding extension expires"; a shutdown would drag on the US economy and raise the risk of a recession, though financial markets have held up relatively well through past shutdowns. On Wall Street, big tech stocks helped support the market after leading it lower a day earlier, since they tend to move more sharply with expectations for rates because high-growth stocks are seen as some of the biggest victims of high yields, while stock indexes abroad were mixed across much of Europe.

# Charlotte Wood's October 2023 Novel

Charlotte Wood's novel, published by Allen & Unwin at $32.99 on 3 October, is another reckoning with a mother's death — this time in fiction — in which a woman arrives at some sort of religious community having turned her back on her husband, their life and the metropolis, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

The questions the book poses are what she is fleeing and what her demons are. It is not all peace and tranquillity in the community, which has collective crises to deal with, while her previous life will not leave her alone.

Written in spare prose, the reviewer says, "the consistently brilliant Wood delivers yet again".

# Holiday Season Stress And The Question Of Partner Introductions

The holiday season is often perceived as the most wonderful time of year, but survey data says otherwise for a large minority: in a recent poll by the American Psychological Association, cited by The Independent in December 2023, 41 per cent of US adults said their stress levels increased from November to January compared with other months of the year, and nearly 50 per cent of Americans described their stress level during the season as "moderate."

That backdrop is what makes introducing a new partner to your family over the holidays a genuine question rather than an obvious opportunity. People approaching Christmas, Hanukkah or New Year carry different concerns — from family drama at the dinner table to small spats with a mother about decorations — which raises the question of whether you really want to bring a partner into the mix. The Independent's framing is that while it is important to introduce your loved ones to your significant other eventually, relationship experts believe there are discussions to have beforehand, especially during the holidays.

# The Verge Staff Favorites Black Friday Roundup

Black Friday and Cyber Monday may be in the past, but some sales are still hanging around — although maybe not for long — and The Verge points readers to the rest of the Cyber Monday deals still available for more leftovers across all categories.

The roundup's premise is a recurring feature: every month or so The Verge asks its staff about their favorite stuff — pet toys, travel aids, kitchen gadgets, or straightforward tech — and the results are usually very different, very interesting, and a lot of fun.

In celebration of the annual post-Thanksgiving sales, the staff looked through recent "favorites" articles and found deals on a lot of the tech, kitchen tools, travel aids, and pet toys they like — listed in case readers had previously thought "well, that sort of sounds good, but it's a bit pricey," or "that's pretty cheap, but maybe I'll wait until the price goes down some more." Much of the gear is still discounted from Cyber Monday.

# Preparing Both Partner And Family Before A Holiday Introduction

Relationship experts told The Independent that the preparation for introducing a partner to your family at the holidays happens in a set order, and before anyone travels. The precondition is clarity between the couple: Saba Lurie, a licensed marriage and family therapist at Take Root Therapy in California, says there is no right or wrong time for the introduction, but the intentions behind it must be clear — you should already have discussed where the relationship is headed. Step one is then to brief your partner on the purpose: "I think you should tell the person why you're bringing them home for the holidays, so you're on the same page about the intentions and what's motivating the decision to include," Lurie said. Step two is to brief them on the family they are walking into: "Sometimes it can be helpful for them to know about the dynamics that they're stepping into and how they can best support you. Frankly, they should be aware if there is tension or if there is stress within your family."

Step three runs the other way. Rachel Zar, a licensed marriage and family therapist at Spark Chicago Therapy, says the family needs advance notice too: "If there's something about your partner that could be surprising to your family, or that's a notable difference from who someone you've brought home before, tell your relatives that. Let's set your family and partner up for success." Step four is to say how you want your family to include your partner — for example by incorporating your partner's family traditions into your own celebration. The limit on the procedure is oversharing: Zar advises against telling too much before Christmas, since you still want your family and partner to connect in person rather than hearing about each other through the grapevine. Zar also sets the context for why the preparation matters — every family is different, but problems arise mainly because we put too much pressure on having a joyful holiday: "I think anytime that emotions are heightened, with the holidays certainly being one of those times, our expectations are really high. We're expecting it to be this joyful, happy, perfect occasion. So, we sometimes forget that the holidays come with a lot of stress."

# Thanksgiving Observance Outside the United States

Thanksgiving is not observed only in America: while it is one of the most important cultural holidays in the United States, Canada also has its own Thanksgiving Day, held on the second Monday in October, and Liberia celebrates Thanksgiving on the first Thursday of November.

The distinguishing feature between these observances is therefore the date rather than the existence of the holiday — the American fourth-Thursday-in-November timing is one national convention among several.

Plauché and Johnson, the two borrowers Fortune profiled on 2023-12-23, are just two of those millions. # Friendsgiving Alternative Activity Ideas

For a Friendsgiving that is not a sit-down dinner, the options below can be chosen instead of hosting a big meal; the enabling precondition throughout is that Friendsgiving is not necessarily held on the Thanksgiving holiday itself, which frees the date and the venue.

Visit a holiday market. While Christmas is still over a month away, many cities in the US already have their holiday-themed markets up and running, so a Friendsgiving held off the holiday can be used as an opportunity to check out new shops. In New York City, Bank of America hosts its annual Winter Village at Bryant Park in Manhattan, where a wide variety of food vendors lets a group pick dinner and dessert, and vendors also sell goods from ornaments to jewellery to scarves — a chance to do some early holiday shopping.

Host a movie marathon at home. This is the budget-friendly indoor alternative to a big dinner: with the help of friends, make a list of any horror, romance or comedy films to watch for the day, and top the activity off by supplying an assortment of snacks or cooking a meal together. Options can match the Thanksgiving theme, with films like A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood (2019), Toy Story (1995), Addams Family Values (1993) and A Charlie Brown Thanksgiving (1973), and Christmas films can be added to the mix, including Elf (2003), It's A Wonderful Life (1947) and Steel Magnolias (1989).

Go on a hike — this one is weather-dependent, so check the conditions outside first. Whether at a local park or a trail an hour or so away, hiking is the perfect daytime activity for a friend group of any size.

Bake or decorate treats. This is another easy indoor activity: make a pie from scratch or simply frost ready-bake sugar cookies, which gives the group something interactive to do together. Treats can be chosen on theme with the fall and winter seasons, from baking an apple crisp to decorating gingerbread cookies.

Run a Turkey Trot. Whether before, during, or after Thanksgiving Day, many cities in America host an annual Turkey Trot run, and the length varies — from a 5K to a half marathon — so the group can pick what it prefers. In New York City in 2023, one Turkey Trot was held at Flushing Meadows-Corona Park on 25 November, with participants running for the Rolling Thunder organisation, a non-profit "for mainstream athletes who are developmentally disabled or have other special needs".

Host an at-home wine tasting. A night out at the bars can get expensive depending on the venue, and a trip to a winery can rack up a hefty bill and is not the most enjoyable activity in cold weather — which is the reason to host your own instead. Everyone brings a different type of wine, from red to white, and the group tries a few sips from each bottle; a big wine fan may end up discovering a new favourite brand. A homemade charcuterie board, filled with different meats and cheeses, can be prepared to pair with the wine.

Play an outdoor game. If the friends have a fun, competitive side, the group can host the event in any big outdoor space — a local park or a friend's backyard. Football in particular meets the typical theme of Thanksgiving, as a beloved tradition on the actual holiday is to watch a sports game with the family.

Hold an early gift exchange. The winter holidays are still weeks away, but Friendsgiving can be used to host the annual exchange: many friend groups in the US opt for the budget-friendly Secret Santa format, where each person is randomly assigned someone to give a gift to and, during the exchange, reveals that they are that person's "secret Santa" before handing over the present.

# Giving Experiences Instead Of Material Gifts

Another way to save money at the holidays is to skip material gifts and grant your time instead — in many cases your family would rather spend quality time with you.

Credit Karma's Courtney Alev recommended planning low-cost activities such as a hike with your family or attending a free event in your city. Other options she listed include a holiday movie marathon with your friends, a free museum with your parents, or a volunteering day with your family.

# Livestreaming

## Definition

In the corpus, livestreaming is used both as a distinct product category and as a feature bolted onto other apps: Twitch is covered as a dedicated livestreaming platform whose creator monetization is a recurring news topic (doc_0401, doc_0551), while Facebook, Instagram, and the Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses treat livestreaming as one feature among several rather than the product itself (doc_0335, doc_0364).

The corpus does not otherwise supply a formal definition of the term; see Background (external) for a general definition.

## Context

In the corpus, livestreaming shows up both as a distinct product category — Twitch positions itself as a livestreaming platform whose creator economy, subscription tiers, and monetization policy fights with streamers define much of its news coverage — and as a feature that other products bolt on: the Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses let a wearer livestream directly to Facebook or Instagram, and Blizzard held a livestream ahead of Diablo 4's Season of Blood to reveal quality-of-life changes. Meta explicitly named its Facebook and Instagram livestreaming functions as a moderation priority during the Israel-Hamas war, treating the feature as a specific risk surface distinct from ordinary posts. TwitchCon 2023's announcement that Twitch now permits simulcasting — streaming to Twitch and rival livestreaming platforms at the same time — shows livestreaming platforms directly competing for the same broadcasting creators, with Kick named as a competitor.

## Key Characteristics

- **Real-time and continuous** — unlike a VOD or a pre-recorded clip, a livestream is watched as it happens, which is why Meta describes "watching for" hostage footage in real time rather than reviewing it after upload.
- **Platform-gated by design** — the Ray-Ban Meta glasses can livestream, but only to Meta's own Facebook and Instagram, not to Twitch or TikTok, illustrating how a livestreaming feature can be walled off to a single ecosystem.
- **A moderation-risk surface** — Meta prioritized "checks on livestreaming functions" specifically, separate from its general Violence and Incitement policy, because live broadcast can surface real-time abuse (e.g., hostage footage) before moderators can intervene.
- **Multi-platform / simulcastable** — Twitch's 2023 policy change to allow simulcasting acknowledges that streamers livestream to more than one platform at once, and that livestreaming platforms compete directly for the same creator base (Twitch vs. Kick).
- **Supported by dedicated hardware** — accessories like Elgato's Stream Deck exist specifically to give livestreamers one-button macros and shortcuts during a livestream.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, live streaming is generally defined as the real-time (or near real-time) transmission of video or audio over the internet, distinguished from video-on-demand or pre-recorded clips by its live, ongoing nature, and spans uses such as social media, video gaming, sports coverage, and lifecasting on platforms including Facebook Live, YouTube, Twitch, and Kick (Wikipedia, "Live streaming," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_streaming).

# Why Introducing A Partner To Your Family Can Deepen The Relationship

Relationship experts argue that letting a partner see you with your family — including the awkward parts — deepens the relationship rather than endangering it, because the act is a vulnerable one. "I think introducing a significant other to family is a really vulnerable act, and that vulnerability is going to be what allows for greater intimacy," Saba Lurie told The Independent. "When your significant other sees you with your family, they may see another side of you that they may not have had access to before."

The obvious objection — that a partner may discover your relationships with your parents and extended family are complex — is answered by framing that discovery as evidence of self-knowledge, provided you have explained the family dynamics in advance. "I think that we tend to be our best relational self when we've really done the work around understanding all of our past relationships," Rachel Zar explained. "You can tell your partner: 'I don't have a close relationship with my brother, and here's why. Here are the intentional choices that I've made around it.' Or you can say: 'Here's my chosen family. These are the people who are important to me.' Your significant other will see that you've been introspective and have takeaways around how you've navigated your family's origin." The conclusion carries a condition and a limit: as long as the couple have discussed their relationship expectations both before and during the holidays, the introduction may deepen the relationship and be a step in the right direction — or it may simply be an opportunity to bring two important people in your life together. And the timing remains the couple's own call: "I don't think there's ever going to be a perfect time for folks," Lurie said. "I think it'll depend on the relationship between the two partners and also on the family dynamics, and what feels more comfortable for all parties. I don't think there's going to be a right or wrong time for the introduction."

# Logistics And Check-Ins During A Holiday Family Visit

Beyond the initial conversations, relationship experts told The Independent that two practical steps remain when bringing a partner home for the holidays. The first is settling logistics in advance: if you are travelling, you may need to decide on sleeping arrangements — potentially staying somewhere other than a parent's house — in order to minimise family stress. "It would be really helpful to have conversations beforehand, so it's clear what you are agreeing or not agreeing to," said Saba Lurie. "For example, if your family isn't comfortable with you bringing someone home and sleeping in the same bedroom, then you and your partner may stay elsewhere. But those would be conversations that you all need to have together. It really depends on your relationship with your family and with your partner."

The second is checking in with your partner during the visit itself, including some quality time together, so that any family drama that arises does not damage the relationship. "I'd recommend pulling your partner aside and saying: 'How are we doing?' Like a temperature check," Lurie added. "Those are points where the two of you can come and remind each other: 'We are a team in this.' Or, the two of you could go on a walk and separate from the family, just for a little bit of time to reset within the relationship."

The Govee Envisual TV backlight kit adds drama and atmosphere to nightly viewing by using a mountable camera to track what is on your screen, then projecting a matching light show behind the TV — almost as if the colors were bleeding off the screen.

# Blink Video Doorbell And Outdoor 4 Deal

The Blink Video Doorbell bundled with the latest Blink Outdoor security camera was available on Amazon for $89.99 — $90 off, down from $180, a 50 percent discount — as reported on October 28th, 2023, alongside continuing half-price offers on other Blink security cameras and video doorbells, including the Blink Mini cameras. The Verge pitched the bundle as a way to keep track of all the ghosties and ghoulies about to visit your front door on Halloween.

Both are 1080p cameras with tech that lets you clearly see trick-or-treaters after the sun goes down, plus support for motion detection and two-way audio. The battery-powered Blink Outdoor 4 also covers a wider field of view and supports person detection, which the prior model did not.

As budget picks they lack some premium features, including smart alerts, and you have to pay extra for features like cloud-based storage — but otherwise, The Verge wrote, they are a pair of great security devices that will protect your home just fine for years to come. The Blink Video Doorbell is described as the best budget-friendly buzzer, offering motion-activated recording and alerts, night vision, two-way audio, and up to two years of battery life.

# Google Pixel Watch First-Gen Deal

Verge readers could save an extra $80 on the already discounted first-generation Google Pixel Watch by using promo code VERGEPIX80 at Wellbots, dropping the checkout price to $199.99 — down from $350, a 43 percent discount — as reported on October 28th, 2023. That is not bad, the writer noted, considering Google's first-gen smartwatch retailed for $349.99 when it launched a little over a year earlier. The 41mm wearable has a beautiful domed display and native Fitbit integration for health tracking, and comes with six months of Fitbit Premium and three months of YouTube Music.

The first-gen Pixel Watch may not be as capable as the new Google Pixel Watch 2, but the two share strengths: both offer health and fitness-tracking features powered by Fitbit, allowing special features like FDA-cleared EKGs, and both support Google services like Google Assistant and Google Wallet. Thanks to the new Wear OS 4 update, the older model also gets access to the Google Calendar app, Gmail, and the new Safety Check feature introduced with the newer wearable.

There are trade-offs. The Pixel Watch 2 offers superior battery life, whereas the last-gen model struggles to last a full day, and the newer wearable adds Sleep Profiles, abnormal heart rate tracking, and nightly SpO2 features. If you are comfortable with these omissions, The Verge concluded, the first-gen model is still a good wearable to buy at this price.

# Polygon's Halloween Countdown Calendar

For the past three years as of 2023-10-10, Polygon has put together a Halloween countdown calendar: the staff selects 31 of its top horror-themed or Halloween-adjacent picks across movies and TV throughout the month of October, all of them available to watch at home. The outlet brought the format back again for 2023, this time with a whole new batch of films and shows to choose from.

The mechanics are daily: every day for the month of October, Polygon adds a new recommendation to the countdown and tells readers where they can watch it. The invitation is to curl up on the couch, dim the lights, and grab some popcorn for a marathon of horrific delights.

The countdown sits alongside Polygon's year-round horror coverage rather than replacing it — the outlet also runs lists of the best horror movies you can stream at home, the best horror movies on Netflix, and the best horror movies of the year ranked by scariness. The stated reason for the separate seasonal format is that Halloween is an especially spooky time of year and warrants special attention and celebration.

# Smart Home Device

## Definition

A smart home device is a connected household product — a speaker, camera, thermostat, light, plug, lock, sprinkler controller, or storage container — that can be controlled remotely (typically via a smartphone app or voice assistant) and often coordinates with other such devices through a shared smart home platform.

## Context

The corpus covers smart home devices mainly as a deal category in seasonal shopping roundups: The Verge devotes an entire Prime Day roundup (doc_0205) to smart home products, grouping the category into robot vacuums, security cameras and doorbells, smart speakers and displays, and smart lighting/locks/thermostats/sprinklers/plugs — all controllable from a phone and, increasingly, interoperable through a common home-automation platform.

The Verge's Black Friday under-$25 roundup (doc_0090) similarly carves out a "Smart home tech" section for budget smart plugs and a smart lamp, placed right alongside networking gear like a Wi-Fi extender.

The term also surfaces as a regulatory subject: the EU's antitrust probe into Amazon's iRobot acquisition explicitly gathered views from market participants including "suppliers of RVCs and other smart home devices," treating robot vacuum cleaners as one instance of the broader smart-home-device category.

Keep Labs' medicine-storage device (the Keep) shares the same connected-appliance characteristics described above — an app to unlock the lid, plus a scale and phone notifications to track medication use — even though its own category (secure medical storage) is unusual for a smart home device.

## Key Characteristics

- **Remote/app control** — devices are opened, adjusted, or monitored via a companion smartphone app (e.g., the Keep's lid opens via an app button; the Meross smart garage door controller lets you control your garage door from anywhere, and the MyQ Chamberlain Smart Garage Control opens the garage door from any location using a smartphone).
- **Voice-assistant integration** — many devices work with a voice assistant such as Amazon's Alexa; the Echo smart speaker is described as "a great way to get started with the smart home" and doubles as a smart home hub.
- **Interoperability via shared protocols** — devices such as the Govee LED Strip Light M1 and the Google Nest Thermostat support the Matter protocol specifically so a single hub can control gadgets from different manufacturers ("a wide array of smart home platforms" / "every major smart home platform, including Apple Home").
- **Hub/bridge role** — some devices (the fourth-gen Echo) act as more than an endpoint: it is also a Matter controller, Thread border router, and Zigbee bridge, connecting other gadgets to the home network.
- **Regulatory relevance beyond consumer tech** — the category is broad enough to draw antitrust scrutiny of channel access: the EU's iRobot probe frames robot vacuum cleaners as one of the "other smart home devices" whose competing suppliers depend on Amazon's marketplace for distribution.

# Australian Christmas Retail Spending Outlook For 2023

Australian Retailers Association chief Paul Zahra said that "last year, Christmas spending was bolstered by a record freedom spending phenomenon with delayed overseas travel, whereas this year shoppers are expected to be much more conservative with their budgets", as cost-of-living pressures put a lid on spending, with shoppers tipped to cut back on hospitality, home goods and clothes purchases. The comment was The Age's quote of the day on 4 October 2023.

The same edition's "you may have missed" item recorded that Qantas' freight division has suffered a catastrophic system failure that left dead bodies, live animals and perishable food unable to be collected from airports.

# Holiday 2023 Shipping Deadline Planning

The Verge's December 18, 2023 guide collects the upcoming domestic shipping deadlines for various retailers and shipment carriers, so readers sending gifts via traditional mail can ensure packages arrive before Christmas, Kwanzaa, or whatever holiday they celebrate this time of year.

Its framing is the annual pattern the deadlines are meant to defuse: the same thing happens year after year, as things get busy with work, school, and life in general until you're suddenly up against the clock racing your gifts to the local post office, FedEx store, or UPS location. The stated purpose is to help with planning your next move as you begin sending out holiday packages and, hopefully, to avoid some holiday stress.

# Thanksgiving 2023 Retail Closure Policy

Because Thanksgiving Day is a federal holiday in the US, some stores shut down completely on the holiday — and for the two largest chains this is now a standing policy rather than a one-off: both Target and Walmart announced permanent closures on the holiday in 2020, with the policy remaining in place ever since.

The origin of that policy was the pandemic. The outbreak had initially pushed these chains to close their doors on Thanksgiving in order to limit crowding and spread out the shopping season.

The closure is not universal, and it is short. Not all grocery stores remain closed on Thanksgiving Day — there are some retailers that shoppers could visit on the morning of the holiday, in preparation for the annual feast — and once Thanksgiving Day comes to a close, many stores reopen on the Friday, operating during their earlier or usual business hours in preparation for some of the biggest sales of the year.



---


# Thanksgiving: The American Holiday

Thanksgiving is a national holiday in the United States, celebrated every fourth Thursday in November — falling on Thursday 23 November in 2023 — and it is a cultural holiday that symbolises peace, thankfulness, and the beginning of the holiday season. Although Thanksgiving may originally have had religious significance, the day has become a mostly secular holiday.

Food is arguably the main component of the day. Americans start preparing their menus weeks ahead, with the requisite turkeys and stuffing ingredients likely already purchased, and on the day itself they are hard at work preparing dinner, with foods on the menus ranging from a roasted turkey to a green bean casserole. Aside from the dishes served in the lavish feast, which can vary based on families' cultures and traditions, the holiday is a beloved time of year when Americans come together to celebrate what they are thankful for, either with family or friends, and to commemorate all that they are grateful for.

Most Americans consider the holiday a day to gather and express their thanks through food, family, and football — with multiple NFL teams playing on the holiday. During some Thanksgiving celebrations, people write down what they are thankful for and then read aloud from the pieces of paper. Following Thanksgiving, the month-long shopping season for the winter holidays begins, with Black Friday kicking it off.



---


# Thanksgiving's Black Friday Opening As Consumerism Critique

Eli Roth argues that the Black Friday sale that opens Thanksgiving is not just spectacle but a critique of a rigged economy — the frenzy, he told The Age on 15 November 2023, is driven less by greed than by people who are "paid shit" and can only afford Christmas gifts on one sale day a year.

The grounds are in the film's construction. The idea gives Thanksgiving its raucous opening, what The Age calls possibly the most horribly enjoyable 13 minutes of a film all year — a sick and clever movement that launches the action amid the craze of a Black Friday sale. In the great tradition of seasonal horror classics, the move lets Roth critique the gross commercialisation of the holiday, tap into the era's increasingly stoked class divisions, and evoke the horror genre's rich legacy: the hordes of rampaging shoppers rushing the shopping mall feel like a direct nod to George Romero's anti-capitalist screed Dawn of the Dead (1978). "I love Dawn of the Dead, zombies running the mall, and very much in line with Romero's views on consumerism run amok. That's what it's all about," says Roth. "There's a real darkness underneath it and it's not just people's greed that's behind [the frenzy of these] Black Friday sales. People are paid shit now so there's no middle class any more so they desperately need these Black Friday sales in order to get all the Christmas gifts for their kids, otherwise they can't afford them. So then you have the very few at the top sitting in their mansions watching all the rats fighting over these crumbs, and there's something really sick about that, that everyone's been reduced to fighting for televisions and electronics because the only way they can afford them is on this one sale day, while the few at the top get richer and richer."

The warrant is the horror genre's long history of reflecting the tumult and anxieties of the wider culture that produced it — the opening scenes of crazed shoppers pressed against the jagged glass of the mall also evoke images from the US's January 6 riots, while later scenes of armed school students anxiously and awkwardly defending themselves against a crazed killer feel like they engage with US gun control rhetoric. Roth himself resists over-reading it: "Look, I want it to be where we're in the world of the movie, we're not in the real world. I want people to escape into a rollercoaster ride and have a fun time with the movie. But certainly, if you want to write a film school thesis about it, everything's there." For such a horror tragic, he says, the first goal is always "great kills".

# DraftKings Week 14 DFS Quarterback And Running Back Picks

Sporting News built its Week 14 DraftKings DFS lineup around quarterback Justin Fields of the Bears ($6,800) and running backs Christian McCaffrey ($9,200) and Alvin Kamara ($8,200), publishing on Dec. 7, 2023.

The framing was that most season-long fantasy leagues were entering their final week of the regular season, and if a team was not going to qualify, DFS was where every week is a new season: managers do not have to sweat injury reports, make difficult trades, or concern themselves with bad matchups, and instead get to enjoy each week as a new opportunity.

Fields (Bears vs. Lions) was picked because the Lions might have control over the NFC North but their defense was losing steam as the season progressed — Detroit appeared well on their way to a dominant victory over New Orleans until they let the 2023 Saints march back into it, alarming with that version of Derek Carr leading the charge — and Fields recently had success against the divisional foe, rushing for 104 yards and tossing a touchdown in Week 11, so the dual-threat quarterback should be in line for a great day at home.

McCaffrey (49ers vs. Seahawks) was the splurge: fantasy's best running back had been a little rich all season, but the 49ers were coming off an emotional win over the Eagles after stomping the Seahawks on Thanksgiving and were trying to track down the top spot in the NFC while leaning on their stars; McCaffrey had just rushed for over 100 yards and two touchdowns against that same defense two weeks earlier, and his floor remained at the penthouse with a ceiling stretching to the moon. Kamara (Saints vs. Panthers) was backed despite the Saints' quarterback problem and an offense stuck in quicksand: Derek Carr would likely be out with a concussion, leaving Jameis Winston to start, and Kamara remained a fixture as arguably the team's top runner and receiver thanks to his work as a security blanket for whichever quarterback was under center; with the Panthers remaining terrible at defending running backs, Sporting News penciled him in for at least 100 total yards and a touchdown.

# Kyler Murray Cardinals Hot Seat
