# Can Sun's Testimony On Fabricated Justifications

Former FTX lawyer Can Sun testified that during the days in November when the exchange imploded, Bankman-Fried — then trying to raise money from the private equity group Apollo, which wanted an explanation for what had happened — came to him and asked him to come up with justifications for the missing funds. That request, Sun said, "basically confirmed my suspicions that had been rising all day" that Bankman-Fried had purloined the funds.

Sun ran Bankman-Fried through possible explanations, including a margin loan program, and explained that none of them could fit the actual situation — for instance, Alameda had borrowed more from FTX than had ever been in the margin loan program. He said Bankman-Fried acknowledged their conversation with a "yup, yup": "I was expecting a bigger response, but it was very muted." After that, Sun testified, Singh spilled the beans that Alameda had withdrawn assets that included the customer funds. Sun quit the next day, and, like Yedidia, testified with immunity.

The jury then saw the fabrication deployed in public: a Good Morning America appearance by Bankman-Fried on December 1st, 2022, in which he tried to justify the missing funds through the margin loan program. The Verge's reporter called it such a flimsy excuse that even George Stephanopoulos could see through it, and described Sun's testimony as brief and explosive.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# Bail

## Definition

Bail is the term the corpus uses for Sam Bankman-Fried's pretrial release from custody: a $250 million bond that let him live under house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto instead of in jail while awaiting trial, and which a U.S. judge revoked in August 2023 (doc_0010, doc_0226).

## Context

The corpus's clearest illustration is Sam Bankman-Fried's case: after being arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022 and extradited to the U.S., he was released on a $250 million bail bond and confined to house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto (doc_0010). That release was not permanent — a U.S. judge revoked his bail in August 2023 after he was accused of intimidating former Alameda CEO Caroline Ellison by leaking her private diary, leaving him in custody by the time his fraud trial began that October (doc_0010, doc_0226). Bail is also treated as something a court can simply refuse to grant: one recap of the FTX saga notes flatly that "SBF has been denied bail" (doc_0030). The concept resurfaces around Bankman-Fried's co-defendants, where house arrest — the condition often attached to bail — is described as a lighter alternative to imprisonment that cooperating felons like Gary Wang, Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison might still face even without prison time (doc_0121).

## Key Characteristics

- **Conditional, not unconditional freedom** — release on bail came bundled with restrictions (house arrest at a fixed address) rather than free movement (doc_0010).
- **Financially secured** — Bankman-Fried's release required a $250 million bail bond, tying his liberty to a monetary guarantee (doc_0010).
- **Revocable** — a judge can revoke bail mid-proceedings for conduct that violates its terms, as happened after the Ellison intimidation allegations, moving the defendant from house arrest to detention (doc_0010, doc_0226).
- **Discretionary and sometimes denied outright** — courts can decline to grant bail at all, as they did for Bankman-Fried at least once during his case (doc_0030).
- **Distinct from post-conviction outcomes** — bail concerns pretrial release, while house arrest can separately appear as a possible post-conviction alternative to imprisonment for cooperating defendants (doc_0121).

## Background (external)

The corpus never defines "bail" itself — it only reports how bail applied in Bankman-Fried's case.
Per Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute, bail is "the money a defendant pays as a guarantee that they will show up in court at a later date," and release can be "conditioned on certain behavior of the defendant," such as staying away from an alleged victim (Cornell Law School LII, *Wex: bail*, accessed 2026-09-02).
A defendant's failure to comply "triggers the bond obligation and allows the court to keep any money given as security" (Cornell Law School LII, *Wex: bail*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.



---


# SBF's Arrest And Bail

Bankman-Fried was arrested in December 2022 in the Bahamas, where FTX was based, and was then extradited to the U.S. to face a number of criminal charges. He was released on a $250 million bail bond and remained under house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto. TechCrunch set out the sequence on 2023-10-01.

That release did not hold. It was revoked in August, after he was accused of intimidating Alameda's former CEO, Caroline Ellison, by leaking her private diary.



---


# Adam Yedidia's First Testimony And His Immunity Deal

Late in the afternoon of the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the government called Adam Yedidia to the stand, and lead prosecutor Danielle Sassoon disclosed that this college friend of Bankman-Fried had legal immunity during his testimony. Asked why he had made such a deal with the government, Yedidia answered: "I was concerned that I had unwittingly written code that contributed to a crime."

Yedidia, described as a fast-talking graduate of MIT, testified that he and Bankman-Fried were close friends in college. After Bankman-Fried left Jane Street — the high-frequency trading firm where the former billionaire got his start in finance after MIT — he persuaded Yedidia to join him, first as a trader at Alameda and then as a developer at FTX.

The testimony was cut short when the clock neared 4:30 p.m. and court adjourned for the day. Yedidia was scheduled to continue his testimony on Thursday, to be followed by Matt Huang, a former partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital, and then by Gary Wang, a key Bankman-Fried lieutenant and one of the government's star witnesses.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Post-Bankruptcy Media Tour

After FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried went on an extensive media tour, doing interviews with The New York Times' Andrew Ross Sorkin and Good Morning America — and he kept giving interviews even under house arrest, including with The New Yorker.

The Verge's reading of his motive: Bankman-Fried seemed to think that if he just explained things, everyone would understand that what he did was a mistake, not a crime.

# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.



---


# The OpenAI Board's Firing Of Sam Altman

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said on Friday, 2023-11-17, that it had pushed out its co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after a review found he was "not consistently candid in his communications" with the board of directors. "The board no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI," the artificial intelligence company said in a statement. Mira Murati, OpenAI's chief technology officer, would take over as interim CEO effective immediately while the company searched for a permanent replacement.

OpenAI declined to answer questions on what Altman's alleged lack of candor was about; the statement said only that his behavior was hindering the board's ability to exercise its responsibilities. Altman posted on X that Friday: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later."



---


# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# Altman's Argument On AI's Promise And Existential Risk

Sam Altman predicted that AI will prove to be "the greatest leap forward of any of the big technological revolutions we've had so far."

He paired that claim with its counterweight rather than leaving it alone: he also acknowledged the need for guardrails, calling attention to the existential dangers future AI could pose.



---


# Greg Brockman Departure From OpenAI

OpenAI's longtime president and co-founder Greg Brockman was first removed as chairman of the board and then resigned from the company outright, citing "today's news" — the firing of Sam Altman on Friday, November 17, 2023.

By Brockman's own account, he got a text from OpenAI chief scientist and co-founder Ilya Sutskever shortly after noon on the Friday asking for a quick call. After Brockman sent a Google Meet link, he was told that he was being removed from the board as chairman "but was vital to the company and would retain his role" as president, and that Altman had been fired. Brockman then announced his resignation from OpenAI, sending a memo internally and publishing the text on X: "After learning today's news, this is the message I sent to the OpenAI team." He also posted jointly with Altman that "Sam and I are shocked and saddened by what the board did today," thanking the people they had worked with at OpenAI, their customers and their investors, and saying they were "still trying to figure out exactly" what had happened.

Brockman's account also places events the day before, on November 16: according to his post on X, Sutskever texted Altman on the Thursday evening about scheduling a Friday noon call, and Brockman alleges that Mira Murati, OpenAI's CTO and now interim CEO, was informed on Thursday night that Altman would be fired. Three senior OpenAI researchers resigned after Brockman, including director of research Jakub Pachocki and head of preparedness Aleksander Madry.



---


# OpenAI Employee Revolt And Sutskever's Reversal

Nearly 500 of OpenAI's roughly 770 employees signed a letter saying they might quit unless the startup's board resigned and reappointed the ousted Sam Altman — a number that climbed to over 650 later that Monday — and, remarkably, the signatories included Ilya Sutskever, the chief scientist who had taken part in the removal.

Sutskever publicly reversed himself, publishing a post on X suggesting that he regretted his decision to remove Altman and that he would do everything in his power to reinstate Altman as CEO: "I deeply regret my participation in the board's actions. I never intended to harm OpenAI. I love everything we've built together and I will do everything I can to reunite the company." This was a reversal of the position he had taken days earlier. At an OpenAI all-hands meeting on the Friday afternoon, Sutskever had defended Altman's ouster, dismissing suggestions that pushing Altman out amounted to a "hostile takeover" and claiming that it was necessary to protect OpenAI's mission of "making AI beneficial to humanity."



---


# OpenAI Board Composition And The Helen Toner Dispute

At the time of Sam Altman's ouster in November 2023, OpenAI's board of directors consisted of OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, tech entrepreneur Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner, the director of strategy at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology — and a clash between Altman and Toner is reported to have contributed to the crisis.

The New York Times reported that, before his ousting, Altman made a move to push out board member Helen Toner because he thought a paper she had co-written was overly critical of OpenAI. That, among other issues, led to OpenAI's predicament. The Times also indicated that negotiations to hire Altman back were continuing, but that one major sticking point remaining was "guardrails" intended to improve Altman's communication with the board.



---


# Sam Altman Fired As OpenAI CEO In November 2023

Sam Altman was fired as CEO of OpenAI late on Friday, November 17, 2023, by the board of directors of OpenAI, Inc. — the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that acts as the governing body for OpenAI, the startup behind ChatGPT, GPT-4 and DALL-E 3. He both left the company's board of directors and stepped down as CEO, with chief technology officer Mira Murati stepping in as interim CEO.

OpenAI announced the shake-up in a post on its official blog; the company's management team was made aware shortly after. The blog post said Altman's departure followed a "deliberative review process by the board" which concluded that Altman "wasn't consistently candid in his communications" with other board members, "hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities," and that the board "no longer has confidence in [Altman's] ability to continue leading OpenAI." In a joint statement the board wrote that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity," said it remained "fully committed to serving this mission," thanked Altman for "his many contributions to the founding and growth of OpenAI," and said that "we believe new leadership is necessary as we move forward" and that Mira, "as the leader of the company's research, product, and safety functions," was "exceptionally qualified" as interim CEO. OpenAI said it would begin a formal search for a permanent CEO immediately.

Altman responded on X: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later." The removal came unexpectedly. OpenAI had just hosted its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, the week before with Altman emceeing; Altman had spoken at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference and at an Oakland, California event on the Thursday. According to The Verge and The New York Times, citing multiple internal sources, OpenAI employees learned of Altman's firing when it was announced publicly. The same change also saw co-founder Greg Brockman step down as chairman of the board while remaining OpenAI's president, reporting to Murati.



---


# Sam Altman's Side Ventures: Helion, Retro And Worldcoin

Altman has a number of possible next steps after leaving OpenAI, because even while running the company he placed large bets on several other ambitious projects.

Among them are Helion Energy, for developing fusion reactors that could produce prodigious amounts of energy from the hydrogen in seawater, and Retro Biosciences, which aims to add 10 years to the human lifespan using biotechnology. Altman also co-founded Worldcoin, a biometric and cryptocurrency project that has been scanning people's eyeballs with the goal of creating a vast digital identity and financial network.



---


# Sam Altman's Next Move After The OpenAI Firing

In the days after his firing, Sam Altman's destination was genuinely unsettled: on November 20, 2023 he and Greg Brockman announced they would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research team, yet on the same day both were reported to be still open to returning to OpenAI, and Altman was separately telling investors he planned to launch a new venture.

On November 20 Altman, Brockman and colleagues announced they would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research team, with Satya Nadella leaving the door open to other OpenAI staffers and saying they would be given the resources they needed should they choose to join. As reported by The Verge, however, Altman's move to Microsoft was not a done deal — both Altman and Brockman remained open to returning to OpenAI if the remaining board members who initially fired him stepped aside. At the same time, according to The Information, Altman had been telling investors he was planning to launch a new venture, with Brockman expected to join the effort in whatever form it took — possibly an AI chip startup. Altman also posted on X on November 18: "i love you all. today was a weird experience in many ways. but one unexpected one is that it has been sorta like reading your own eulogy while you're still alive. the outpouring of love is awesome. one takeaway: go tell your friends how great you think they are."

Nadella himself hedged. In a series of interviews he stepped back from earlier reporting that Altman and Brockman were headed to Microsoft, telling CNBC: "Obviously, we want Sam and Greg to have a fantastic home if they're not going to be in OpenAI," and saying he was "open" to them settling at Microsoft or returning to OpenAI should the board and employees support the move.



---


# Greg Brockman's Account Of Altman's Removal

Greg Brockman, OpenAI co-founder and the board's chairman, rejected the board's framing of an orderly leadership transition in which he would step down as chairman but remain as president: later on X, formerly Twitter, he posted a message he had sent to OpenAI employees in which he wrote, "based on today's news, i quit." "Sam and I are shocked and saddened by what the board did today," Brockman wrote — contesting the premise that the decision reflected a considered board judgment they were party to.

His account of the process supplies the grounds. In an X post on Friday night, Brockman said Altman was asked to join a video meeting at noon that Friday with the company's board members, minus Brockman, during which OpenAI co-founder and Chief Scientist Ilya Sutskever informed Altman he was being fired. Brockman added that he was informed of his own removal from the board in a separate call with Sutskever a short time later.



---


# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."



---


# Analyst Assessment Of Altman's Departure Impact

Gartner analyst Arun Chandrasekaran argued that Altman's exit "is indeed shocking as he has been the face of" generative AI technology — the ground for the shock being his public role rather than any operational gap.

Chandrasekaran qualified the consequence for the company itself: OpenAI still has a "deep bench of technical leaders," but its next executives will have to steer it through the challenges of scaling the business and meeting the expectations of regulators and society.



---


# OpenAI's Board Composition In November 2023

The OpenAI board that fired Sam Altman consisted, the company said, of OpenAI's chief scientist Ilya Sutskever plus three non-employees.

Those three were Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, tech entrepreneur Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner of the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology.



---


# The Analyst View That Altman's Exit Was Not A Business Problem

Forrester analyst Rowan Curran speculated that Altman's departure, "while sudden," did not likely reflect deeper business problems — attacking the inference from a shocking exit to trouble in the company's technology or commercial position.

"This seems to be a case of an executive transition that was about issues with the individual in question, and not with the underlying technology or business," Curran said.



---


# Theory: An AGI And Mission Rift Between Altman And The Board

The proposition is that Altman's zeal for AGI, even absent a secret project or agreement, led to a major rift between him and the board. Altman is a proud techno-optimist and often speaks fondly of the possibilities of AGI, or artificial general intelligence, a theoretical software system that achieves human-like intellect and versatility. The board's statement pointedly includes that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity" and that new leadership was necessary.

The supporting observation is a directional one: it has been obvious to all that Altman took the company in a much more corporate direction from its origins, changing its legal status and aggressively pursuing enterprise and consumer applications, which does not sound a lot like the "mission" the board wants to advance.

What counts against it is timing. This shift did not happen today, and it certainly does not seem like a plausible reason for abruptly firing the CEO and a few others on a beautiful fall Friday afternoon — a gradual drift does not explain an abrupt dismissal.



---


# Theory: A Financial Mismatch At OpenAI

The proposition is that some major mismatch in the financial department was the cause for dismissal. Could OpenAI be losing even more money than Altman admitted or projected? It seems impossible, TechCrunch writes, but the costs of running this operation have no precedent, nor really does the operation itself.

A variant, offered as purely speculative: what if Altman had been secretly pursuing an internal project, perhaps at significant cost, against the advice of the board and without the necessary safety measures that probably should accompany such research? It sounds a little wild, but firing your CEO like this is also a little wild.

What weighs against the family of financial theories is the difficulty of concealment: it is hard to imagine what Altman could have kept from the board and CTO that would be so damning. A separate possibility is that Altman was making personal investments in a way the board disagreed with — with OpenAI poised to be a kingmaker in the field, he would certainly be in a position of power. One would think that, as an ideologically driven person already rich beyond belief and at the head of the world's leading AI company, Altman would have risen beyond having to do this kind of side deal, or at the very least that scrutiny on him and those close to him would prevent them. But one can never be sure.



---


# OpenAI Board Negotiations Over Altman Reinstatement

Over the weekend that followed Sam Altman's firing, OpenAI's board held on-and-off talks about bringing him back as CEO; the talks repeatedly stalled, and at one point it was confirmed that Altman would not return and that new leadership would take hold.

The sequence ran roughly as follows. Investors — reportedly furious at the turn of events — exerted pressure on OpenAI's board to reinstate Altman, going so far as to recruit Microsoft, with Satya Nadella said to be sympathetic. On November 18 The Verge reported that the board had agreed in principle to resign and to allow Altman and Brockman to return, but it waffled, missing a deadline by which many OpenAI staffers were set to leave the company; Altman was said to be ambivalent about coming back and to be asking for "significant" governance changes. Bloomberg, citing sources close to the matter, reported that the board was in talks with Altman about returning as CEO as soon as that week, with discussions involving Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, one current board member, and possibly other directors. On November 19 The Information reported that Altman was expected to meet at OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters as executives pushed to have him reinstated, with Brockman invited to join though it was unclear whether he would.

Negotiations then hit a snag: Bloomberg reported that Brad Lightcap and Mira Murati, among others, were pushing the board to reinstate Altman, but the directors resisted, and as of midday Sunday the board had not resigned out of concern over who could replace them and was vetting candidates — one possible new addition being Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor. Later, according to The Information citing an internal memo sent by Sutskever, Altman would not be returning as CEO, and OpenAI appointed Emmett Shear, the co-founder of video streaming site Twitch, as interim CEO, replacing Murati. A number of investors and OpenAI employees had tried to bring Altman back after the sudden firing, but following a weekend of negotiations it was confirmed that he would not return; what that meant for ChatGPT's future and for the OpenAI DevDay announcements remained to be seen.



---


# Sam Altman's Firing And Reinstatement

OpenAI's plans were very nearly smashed to pieces just before Thanksgiving when the OpenAI board of directors fired Sam Altman, arguing that he had not been "consistently candid in his communications with the board."

That firing didn't take. Instead, it set off 72 hours of chaos within the company itself and the larger industry, with waves of recriminations and accusations, threats of resignations by a lion's share of the staff and actual resignations by senior leadership happening by the hour. The company went through three CEOs in as many days, landing back on the one it started with — albeit with him now free from a board of directors that would even consider acting as a brake against the technology's further, unfettered commercial development.



---


# Theory: A Long-Term Strategy Disagreement Over OpenAI's Economics

The proposition is that Altman and the board fell out over when OpenAI's money-losing growth strategy has to end. Despite being the hottest tech company in the world and everyone talking about ChatGPT, OpenAI is not exactly a sound business: it is shoveling money into the furnace as fast as it can by serving, by all accounts, a fantastically expensive product at bargain-bin prices. That is all well and good for a year or two, but at some point that strategy changes from a growth hack to an existential liability — so could Altman and the board have had irreconcilable differences on where that point lies?

TechCrunch judges this unlikely, and gives the disconfirming evidence: the company has been very deliberately pursuing this very publicly, confidently and on a long-term basis. Altman and the board seem to be in sync on this, at least for the present.



---


# Theory: Copyright Liability Over OpenAI's Training Data

The proposition is that the board acted over mounting accusations that OpenAI's product was built on a dataset including thousands or millions of copyrighted works, with the CEO systematically downplaying the potential liability. TechCrunch's reporter notes that Altman told him at OpenAI's Dev Day earlier that month that the company does not want to incur any copyright problems by using datasets of pirated books, but that a lot of research he had been reading contradicts that, as does pretty much every AI data scientist he talks to. It is exceedingly hard to imagine that OpenAI built GPT-3 with the copyrighted books database, as seems to be the case, but not GPT-4 or succeeding models.

The framing of the hypothesis is a question about the board's likely reaction: if you were the board and facing those accusations, and your CEO had systematically downplayed the potential liability, how would you feel? "I'd feel very hurt."

What works against it is again the succession. If copyright liability was the reason, it seems unlikely that the board would promote the CTO; presumably OpenAI's Chief Science Officer Ilya Sutskever would also have been in the know, and he is still on the board.



---


# OpenAI's Founding And Its 2023 Board Crisis

The Rosewood hotel dinner led to the creation of a startup called OpenAI later that year; backed by hundreds of millions of dollars from Elon Musk and other funders, the lab promised to protect the world from Larry Page's vision. Thanks to its ChatGPT chatbot, OpenAI has fundamentally changed the technology industry and introduced the world to the risks and potential of artificial intelligence, and it is valued at more than $US80 billion, about $A123 billion, according to two people familiar with the company's latest funding round. Musk and Sam Altman's partnership did not survive, and the two have since stopped speaking. Altman's own gloss on such splits: "There is disagreement, mistrust, egos. The closer people are to being pointed in the same direction, the more contentious the disagreements are. You see this in sects and religious orders. There are bitter fights between the closest people."

The month before the 9 December 2023 article, that infighting came to OpenAI's boardroom: rebel board members tried to force out Altman because they believed they could no longer trust him to build AI that would benefit humanity, and over five chaotic days OpenAI looked as if it were going to fall apart until the board, pressured by giant investors and by employees who threatened to follow Altman out the door, backed down. The drama gave the world its first glimpse of the bitter feuds among those who will determine the future of AI, but years before the near meltdown there was a little-publicised but ferocious competition in Silicon Valley for control of the technology now quickly reshaping the world, from how children are taught to how wars are fought. That earlier story begins with DeepMind: five years before the Napa Valley party and two before the cat breakthrough on YouTube, Demis Hassabis, a 34-year-old neuroscientist, walked into a cocktail party at Peter Thiel's San Francisco town house and realised he had hit pay dirt, because there in Thiel's living room, overlooking the city's Palace of Fine Arts and a swan pond, was a chessboard; Hassabis had once been the second-best player in the world in the under-14 category, and said "I was preparing for that meeting for a year. I thought that would be my unique hook in: I knew that he loved chess."



---


# The Microsoft-OpenAI Partnership And Microsoft's Response To The Firing

Microsoft is OpenAI's largest corporate backer — it had poured $13 billion into OpenAI as of November 2023 and holds what amounts to a 49% stake — and its public response to Altman's firing was to reaffirm the partnership and to back interim CEO Mira Murati rather than to intervene.

The relationship has three visible features in this account: the scale of the investment, a long-term agreement giving Microsoft access to OpenAI's technology, and deep product integration. Frank Shaw, Microsoft's chief communications officer, said: "We have a long-term partnership with OpenAI and Microsoft remains committed to Mira and their team as we bring this next era of AI to our customers." CEO Satya Nadella then published a fuller statement: "As you saw at Microsoft Ignite this week, we're continuing to rapidly innovate for this era of AI, with over 100 announcements across the full tech stack from AI systems, models and tools in Azure, to Copilot. Most importantly, we're committed to delivering all of this to our customers while building for the future. We have a long-term agreement with OpenAI with full access to everything we need to deliver on our innovation agenda and an exciting product roadmap; and remain committed to our partnership, and to Mira and the team. Together, we will continue to deliver the meaningful benefits of this technology to the world."

The partnership's limits also showed. Microsoft's stock price fell more than 1% in the last 30 minutes of trading after Altman's departure was announced, and Axios reported that Microsoft was notified Altman would be leaving only "minutes" before the public announcement. OpenAI's press relations declined to comment beyond the official blog post.



---


# OpenAI Denial Of Malfeasance In Altman Ouster

OpenAI's own management pushed back against the inference that Sam Altman had been fired for wrongdoing, stating definitively that the board's decision was not a response to malfeasance and framing it instead as a communication breakdown.

The rebuttal came in an internal memo obtained by Axios and sent on the Saturday morning after the firing by OpenAI COO Brad Lightcap. Lightcap said the previous day's announcement "took [the management team] by surprise" and that management had had "multiple conversations with the board to try to better understand the reasons and process behind their decision," with discussions still ongoing as of Saturday morning. "We can say definitively that the board's decision was not made in response to malfeasance or anything related to our financial, business, safety, or security/privacy practices," Lightcap added. "This was a breakdown in communication between Sam and the board … We still share your concerns about how the process has been handled, are working to resolve the situation, and will provide updates as we're able."

The premise this attacks is the natural reading of the board's stated grounds — that a CEO removed for not being "consistently candid" must have done something wrong in the company's financial, business, safety or security and privacy conduct. Lightcap's memo concedes the communication problem while denying the conduct problem, and it also concedes that management itself did not understand the board's reasoning at the time.



---


# OpenAI Board's Merger Approach To Anthropic

During the leadership crisis, OpenAI's board of directors approached Dario Amodei, the co-founder and CEO of rival large-language model developer Anthropic, about a potential merger of the two companies, according to a report by The Information.

The approach was part of an effort by OpenAI to persuade Amodei to replace Altman as CEO. Amodei quickly turned down the CEO offer.



---


# OpenAI Share Sale And Valuation Risk After The Firing

The planned sale of OpenAI employee shares that would have valued the startup at about $86 billion was put in jeopardy by Altman's firing.

The Information, speaking to three sources formerly with the company, reported that they no longer expected the sale — led by Thrive Capital — to happen, or, if it did happen, expected it to come with a lesser valuation because of the recent turn of events. Money was also implicated in the causes as well as the consequences: at the time of the firing it was unclear what missteps Altman might have made helming OpenAI, but they evidently related to his relationship with OpenAI's unusual board makeup and corporate governance structure — and perhaps to OpenAI's active talks to raise substantial new capital.



---


# Theory: A Security Or Privacy Incident At OpenAI

The proposition is that OpenAI experienced a major, perhaps pervasive, security issue that Altman downplayed. The circumstantial support: Microsoft reportedly suspended use of ChatGPT internally a few days before the firing, and OpenAI subsequently stopped allowing new signups. If there was a serious security problem in its biggest product and Altman downplayed it, that would obviously create distrust with the board. There is also the potential for misuse at scale with the enormous amount of personal data that travels through OpenAI's APIs and services.

What works against this theory is the identity of the replacement. CTO Mira Murati was just elevated to interim CEO in Altman's place, and it seems unlikely that anything security-related would go through the CEO and not the CTO, or that the two would be at odds to the point where one could be fired like this and the other swapped in to clean up the mess. As the board's statement notes, Murati is in charge of product and safety, among other things, so any significant snafu in that department would reflect on her as well as Altman.



---


# The GPT-4 Demonstration To Bill Gates

Over dinner, Bill Gates told Sam Altman and Greg Brockman that he doubted large language models could work, and said he would stay sceptical until the technology performed a task that required critical thinking, such as passing an Advanced Placement biology test. Five months later, on 24 August 2022, Altman and Brockman returned and brought along an OpenAI researcher named Chelsea Voss, who had been a medallist in an international biology Olympiad as a high schooler; Satya Nadella and other Microsoft executives were there too.

On a huge digital display on a stand outside Gates' living room, the OpenAI crew presented a technology called GPT-4. Brockman gave the system a multiple-choice advanced biology test and Voss graded the answers. The first question involved polar molecules, groups of atoms with a positive charge at one end and a negative charge at the other; the system answered correctly and explained its choice. "It was only trained to provide an answer," Brockman said. "The conversational nature kind of fell out, almost magically." In other words, it was doing things they hadn't really designed it to do.



---


# Criticism Of The Focus On Far-Off AI Risk, And The FTC Probe

Some computer scientists have criticized the focus on far-off risks — the existential dangers Altman called attention to — as distracting from the real-world limitations and harms of current AI products. The premise attacked is that future catastrophic risk is the most urgent thing to attend to.

The concrete present-day case is already before a regulator: the U.S. Federal Trade Commission has launched an investigation into whether OpenAI violated consumer protection laws by scraping public data and publishing false information through its chatbot.



---


# The OpenAI Crisis As A Case Against Centralized AI Control

The claim is that the OpenAI debacle exposes a structural risk in depending on a centralized proprietary AI player. The situation remained fluid as of November 21, 2023, with any number of potential outcomes still on the table, but the whole debacle has shone a spotlight on the forces that control the burgeoning AI revolution, leading many to question what happens if you go all-in on a centralized proprietary player and things then go belly-up.

Mark Surman, president and executive director at the Mozilla Foundation, put the ground this way to TechCrunch: "The OpenAI / Microsoft drama underlines one of the big near-term risks with AI — that this next wave of technology is controlled by the same tiny set of players who have shaped that last era of the internet. We might have a chance of avoiding this if GPT-X were responsibly open sourced, giving researchers and startups a shot at making this technology safer, more useful and more trustworthy for people everywhere." The warrant is that concentration of control is itself the hazard, and open sourcing distributes it.

TechCrunch qualifies the claim: it is still too early to make any surefire claims on what impact the OpenAI fallout will have on LLM development and uptake in the future, and Altman and Brockman are undoubtedly steady hands for a commercial AI startup who may even return to steward OpenAI. But some might argue it is unhealthy that so much focus lies on just a handful of people — and it is telling that their departure has created such widespread havoc.

# Capital Rotation from China into Japanese Assets

One of the most significant changes, according to asset managers quoted by the Financial Times on 1 October 2023, is a fundamental shift in the way global funds now look at China — and the mechanism runs directly to Japan's benefit. The geopolitics of US-China tensions, chip wars, decoupling and "friendshoring" seem in particular to be working significantly in Japan's favour: Asia-focused global investment is rotating out of China and into Tokyo stocks, real estate and other assets, just as large parts of corporate Japan are engaging more actively with shareholders than at any time in the past.

The push side of the model is China's loss of sheen after years of stunning growth and investor attention. Its economy is growing more slowly and the expected post-pandemic rebound is proving elusive. # Kishida's Pitch to Global Investors 2023

Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida was preparing, in the week of 1 October 2023, to make his strongest ever push for a bet on Asia's biggest advanced economy, as BlackRock founder Larry Fink and other heads of global funds gathered in Tokyo for a series of events to attract investment. # The USD Fund Copycat Playbook In China

USD-denominated funds in China have long operated on a benchmark model: draw inspiration from Silicon Valley startups and use them as templates for investment targets back home. They would seek out the equivalents of Facebook, Amazon and Uber on the other side of the Pacific Ocean and hope they become winners in the country's largely untapped internet market.

The range over which that model worked was two decades. Since their entry into China in the late 1990s, American venture capital firms — led by powerhouses like Sequoia Capital, IDG Capital and GGV — have played a major role in funding high-risk, high-reward startups in the country's consumer internet sector.

The relationship now hangs in the balance as changes at home and abroad diminish the pool of investment opportunities for outside financiers. This dealmaking strategy of American funds in China has become less effective in the face of shifting global and domestic landscapes; driven by a confluence of factors, from China's crackdown on the tech industry to escalating U.S.-China tensions, some of these investors are now turning their gaze to opportunities abroad, tracing the footsteps of a new generation of Chinese-founded startups that are expanding overseas.

# Venture Capital

## Definition

In the corpus, venture capital (VC) names the money that specialist VC firms — and the individual "venture capitalists" and partners who run them — put into privately held startups, tracked through a sequence of named funding rounds (seed, pre-Series A, Series A through E and beyond) from Thiel's early backing of DeepMind through FTX's $400 million Series C.

## Context

The corpus shows venture capital operating at both ends of the startup lifecycle. Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. Later-stage venture capital appears in FTX's $400 million Series C round that pushed its valuation to $32 billion, and in Rainforest's Accel-led $8.5 million seed round alongside Bolt's earlier $355 million Series E. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# The Outlook For US-China VC Dealmaking

There are no signs that USD funds' dealmaking in China will bounce back to its heights in the foreseeable future. The PitchBook report predicts that VC activity with U.S. participation in China during 2023 will hit a nine-year low, followed by a decade low in 2024.

Many Chinese general partners have already been sourcing capital from the Middle East, which might eventually limit the impact of U.S. investors' pullback. But the open question is whether Chinese tech firms, now under a new stringent regulatory regime, can deliver the same level of strong growth and returns they experienced in the previous laissez-faire era.

If the U.S. market turns out to be too challenging to penetrate due to competitive and geopolitical factors, there are still other markets to explore. Japan, known for its openness to new technologies, has been particularly popular among China's SaaS startups venturing abroad; sniffing opportunity, China's USD fund managers, still anchored in the Middle Kingdom, will likely follow them to the neighboring country or any other market that will help hedge against uncertainties presented at home and abroad.

# Why USD Funds Follow Chinese Founders Abroad

The claim is that the diaspora financing gap is the natural hunting ground for USD fund managers looking beyond China. "It's just a lot easier to raise their first round from China's USD funds," said a former investor at one of China's top VC firms. "In some sense, the entrepreneurs are taking these investors on an international expedition."

The grounds for why they cannot simply compete for American deals instead are twofold. Besides the low-hanging fruit of the diaspora community, Chinese VCs flying in from Beijing and Shanghai have limited avenues to source deals in the U.S.: American startups are courted by a plethora of local investors, let alone the geopolitical risks of accepting Chinese-managed money. These parachuting investors also run into competition from local investors already tailored to U.S.-China cross-border opportunities, most famously UpHonest Capital.

The warrant is a claim about what venture investing actually depends on: "VCs thrive on information arbitrage. In the U.S., we don't really have that same extensive network as at home," said an investor from the China arm of a global VC firm who now spends a third of their time abroad. Lacking that network locally, the diaspora is where their information advantage still holds.

# Family Offices and the "This Time Is Different" Test for Japan

Large global funds are not the only investors whose interest in Japan has been piqued, says Keith Truelove, head of global markets at UBS Securities Japan: "There is still a lot of dry powder on the sidelines. There is a lot of interest in Japan from family offices and from high net worth individual investors, who value wealth preservation more highly than institutional investors — it's really taking off now."

The condition those investors applied before committing was sustainability rather than short-term return. "They took their time to decide if it was safe to invest in Japan again, because they need to get confidence in the idea that the Japan story will be more sustainable this time," Truelove adds. He notes that Japan has offered investors a number of false dawns over the years, and that the bar for deciding that 'this time is different' remains high.

# USD Funds In China Turn To Overseas Deals

On a weekday afternoon at Red Rock Coffee, the café known for spotting venture capitalists in Silicon Valley, one is likely to overhear a few conversations in Mandarin. With China reopening its borders in spring 2023 following three years of COVID-19 restrictions, managers of U.S. funds in the country have been flocking to the Bay Area.

The trips themselves are not new; their purpose is. While these trips were routine before the pandemic, they have now taken on a fresh purpose of discovering deals beyond China.

As China's domestic investment appeal wanes, some investors start to look for opportunities beyond its borders. Rather than a complete departure, they are merely following the footsteps of Chinese talent who have already embarked on global expansion.

# Japanese Corporate Governance Reform and Shareholder Alignment

Japanese companies are increasingly aligning themselves with the interests of shareholders in a way that once seemed unlikely, and the Financial Times reports a generational mechanism behind it. Companies that replace their chief executive on five or seven year cycles now have leaders who reached their positions after the establishment of Japan's stewardship code in 2014 and corporate governance code in 2015, and many have a very different view of the role of a chief executive than their predecessors did.

The effect on investors runs through consistency of signal rather than any single reform. "I think that Japan, in terms of the unifying message that companies and the Tokyo Stock Exchange are sending out, now gives a lot more confidence about where they are deploying capital," says Kirk Neureiter of Fidelity Management & Research Japan. "So people looking at the region are finding Japan incrementally more attractive. I've never seen such a consensus around what needs to be done for Japanese companies to improve capital efficiency and returns on capital."



---


# Japan Asset Management Reform and NISA Expansion

Japan's government initiatives to make Tokyo more attractive for foreign asset managers have two components, reported by the Financial Times on 1 October 2023. Prime minister Fumio Kishida has promised major reform of the country's $5tn asset management industry, which would ease regulations that had made it difficult for foreign and new players to enter. Separately, the government plans to expand the Nippon Individual Savings Account (Nisa) tax-free investment scheme from the following year, in a bid to unlock $14tn in household financial assets that has long sat in cash and bank deposits.

These initiatives aid the efforts of Japanese businesses to demonstrate better governance. The distinguishing feature investors draw from the combination is a change in kind, not degree: "This is completely different from before," says Stefanie Drews, president of Nikko Asset Management. "In the past, allocation to Japan had been tactical but this time it is strategic and that is why it is much more meaningful."

# Chinese USD Fund Managers' Transitory Phase

The premise under attack is that the Bay Area influx represents a strategic pivot. Venturing out of China is not a "pivot" for the USD fund managers, said one of the investors TechCrunch spoke to; rather, the partners and their associates are mostly looking for something to get their hands on in the midst of a tepid market. Some are contemplating a career change, but it is difficult to find any job that matches their enviable pay.

The motive that investor offers is closer to reconnaissance than redeployment: "Chinese VCs are most anxious about the U.S. building cars behind closed doors. They don't want to fall behind, especially given the speed AI is evolving, so they are going to the Bay Area to figure it out themselves."

There is also a mundane explanation for the timing. The recent influx of Chinese VCs into the Bay Area should be viewed in a broader context: many of these investors, who have family ties in the U.S., have been going stateside regularly for years, and COVID-19 — which shut down trans-Pacific flights and introduced costly and harsh quarantines — created a pent-up demand for travel. Naturally, many investors rushed to the Bay Area as soon as the borders reopened, but the surge in activity might soon start to subside, said a partner who spent the past summer in California.



---


# Haigui And Guihai: The Returnee Founder Cycle

Haigui are Chinese founders who "return from overseas" — a homophone of "sea turtles." Many in the current generation of globalizing Chinese founders studied or worked overseas, and, captivated by the Chinese internet's rapid growth, returned home in the late 2010s to join the likes of Tencent, Baidu, Alibaba and ByteDance; having gained an insider's look into Chinese tech titans, they set out on their own entrepreneurial journey with the hope of becoming the next Jack Ma, the founder of Alibaba.

Guihai are the same people going the other way — those who "return overseas." Their dreams started to crumple following the fall from grace of Ma, whose Ant Group and Alibaba became prominent targets of China's tech crackdown; they soon realized that China had entered a new era, where the regulatory hurdles for running a startup have significantly heightened. Not every startup has the resources to pursue a dual-market strategy, so many "sea turtles" wound up leaving China again. While foreign markets present their own sets of challenges — competition and skepticism toward outsiders — these entrepreneurs perceive a broader, more predictable opportunity in AI in the West. That reversal of their trajectory earned them the moniker guihai.

This wave differs from earlier ones in when the expansion happens. Chinese startups have a long history of going abroad, and every wave has assumed its own approach: previously, many companies would venture out only after succeeding in China, whereas these days more are eyeing global expansion from day one, sometimes even skipping their home market.



---


# The Scale Of Israel's Technology Sector In 2022

Technology is, without question, a giant part of Israel's economy: in 2022 it contributed more than 18% of the country's GDP, the most of any single sector, according to the latest annual report from the Israel Innovation Authority at the time of writing in October 2023. A total of 14% of Israeli citizens work in high tech, which in a country of just 9.2 million people works out to about 1.3 million.

The startup base is correspondingly large. The active number of startups in the country is 9,000, third-highest in the world after the Bay Area and NYC, and over the last five years those startups collectively brought $95 billion into the country by way of venture capital. Combining the business development of startups with the larger tech companies operating in Israel — Intel, Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and many others have operations there — they collectively exported $71 billion in the prior year, 48.3% of the total amount exported across all industries.

These figures are the pre-war baseline, and the article's own caveat is that all of them are going to be significantly lower this year, not least because the disruptions of the war are coming directly on the heels of a major protest movement.

The context for that qualification is that the world was still coming to terms with Hamas' deadly attacks on Israelis the previous weekend, and with everything that had unfolded in the aftermath, including the barrage of retaliation strikes on Gaza. TechCrunch was explicit that the ramifications for the technology ecosystem pale in comparison to the human toll the fighting is taking on both sides, and that the industry is worth considering only because it bears on how the wider region will weather the destruction and one day recover. In such a small country, just about everyone knows someone who was directly affected by the attacks, or someone involved in the subsequent defense and retaliation — and often all three.

# Roblox's China Strategy And Tencent

Asked at the Code Conference where Roblox stands in China — a big part of its growth narrative at its IPO, mentioned many times in the prospectus via a joint venture with Tencent that was shut down without explanation less than a year after the company went public — David Baszucki said Tencent continues to be an amazing partner and that Roblox is being very, very careful in China. The dynamics there have gone to the point where, rather than envisioning a fully connected-type network, the company has to imagine an autonomous network: it is modernizing its infrastructure to the point where it can literally print a copy of Roblox in China and bring it to market there.

Asked what an "autonomous version" of Roblox means, Baszucki said that as with any other platform or social media-type company, looking back over the last three to four years shows less and less information going back and forth between the US and China, to the point where he thinks the future will be very little going back in a China situation. Asked directly whether Roblox has given up on China, he answered: "Absolutely not. No." The interviewer also noted that Roblox's head of China is now its head of Japan.



---


# China's Tech Crackdown And Investor Exit Risk

In recent years, Beijing's sweeping tech crackdowns have introduced a new sense of uncertainty to investors, and the mechanism running from crackdown to investor loss operates through the exit.

The two reference cases define the risk. VCs fear that their portfolio companies might encounter a fate akin to that of Ant Group, whose colossal initial public offering was called off, and Didi, which weathered an extensive data security probe that eventually led to its delisting from New York.

The structural consequence is the closure of the route investors depended on: with China tightening its grip on overseas IPOs, investors who once relied on taking Chinese firms public in the U.S. are no longer assured of an exit channel.



---


# SoftBank Corp's Majority Stake In Cubic Telecom

Cubic Telecom, which provides a software-based networking solution for vehicles and other devices to link up with mobile networks in whichever country they happen to be, picked up €473 million ($513 million at the time) from SoftBank Corp, which took a 51% stake in the Dublin-based startup, valuing it at just over $1 billion (€927 million).

That effectively makes Cubic Telecom a consolidated subsidiary of SoftBank. Barry Napier stays on as CEO and will have a seat on the board; Daichi Nozaki, SoftBank's SVP of global business, plus two other SoftBank-appointed people, still unnamed, will join the board, with the remaining three board seats occupied by existing Cubic Telecom investors, which include CARIAD (the Volkswagen Group) and Qualcomm.

An important distinction: the investment comes from SoftBank Corp, not SoftBank Group, nor the company's storied Vision Fund known — and occasionally notorious — for its outsized venture deals. In this case the Japanese telecoms and IT division in Tokyo is putting in the money as a strategic investment. "In line with our 'Beyond Japan' strategic growth initiative, we are extremely pleased to be teaming up with Cubic Telecom to make a full-fledged entry into the fast-growing market for high-value IoT asset connectivity," said Junichi Miyakawa, president and CEO of SoftBank Corp, in a statement.



---


# China Versus Overseas: The Dual-Market Strategy

For Chinese AI startups the two markets impose incompatible cost structures, which is why the choice is usually binary. To launch an AI service in China, for example, a company needs to navigate a multitude of complications, which can include obtaining a license for its large language model, seeking regulatory approval for its algorithms, and implementing a costly censorship mechanism to comply with censorship requirements.

The relation between those costs and funding conditions forces a pick. "You need to pick sides. You either focus on China or go overseas, otherwise, you end up doing double the workload but with a lot less funding secured from the last two years," said one of the five China-based VCs TechCrunch interviewed for the story; it also spoke to six diaspora Chinese entrepreneurs, and due to the sensitivity of the topic all of them asked to remain anonymous.

The range over which the dual approach remains viable is narrow, and requires a specific corporate structure: some ambitious, well-funded AI startups want to target both sides, and to that end they would create two entities each tailored to the Chinese and non-Chinese markets, while raising capital in USD and RMB separately.



---


# GM And Honda End Their Affordable EV Program

General Motors and long-time partner Honda have ended plans to build millions of affordable and smaller electric vehicles, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-30. The reasons given are that the automakers are coming to terms with high interest rates and battery costs coupled with softening EV demand.

TechCrunch places the cancellation in a run of similar decisions that week, asking: "Anyone spotting a trend here?"



---


# US Outbound Investment Restrictions On China

Washington has stepped up restrictions on the flow of U.S. money into China amid an escalating tech war between the two superpowers. In August 2023, President Joe Biden signed an executive order barring U.S. investments in three strategically critical sectors in China: artificial intelligence, quantum computing and semiconductors.

The effect on behavior is caution while the scope is unclear. As USD funds in China await further clarity on the scope of the ban, they are practicing more discretion than ever before, slowing down capital deployment even amidst a global AI fervor that has given rise to a parallel AI universe in China.

At the same time, domestic RMB funds play an increasing role in funding critical tech sectors. Zhipu AI, one of China's most ambitious challengers to OpenAI, for instance, raised financing in RMB instead of USD.



---


# Chinese Capital Stigma In US Fundraising

A founder's Chinese links now operate as a screening filter in US fundraising, and the filter's scope keeps widening. Even having the Chinese branches of famed American VCs listed on the cap table might deter U.S. investors from funding Chinese founders in their backyard, three founders said; local investors are now shunning Chinese "links," of which the definition is ever evolving and broadening, at all costs to avoid geopolitical risks.

The reputational asymmetry compounds it. At home, the Western-educated and -trained Chinese entrepreneurs are darlings of local VCs; in Silicon Valley, they are little known to investors. Occasional media reports that stress their Chinese background further erode trust in potential investors and customers at a time when concerns about national security already run high.

A San Francisco-based Chinese founder set out the conditions under which the filter can be passed: "If you speak like a local, know how to pitch like a confident Silicon Valley founder, have not taken any money from Chinese VCs, have all your staff in the U.S., have generated good traction in the local market, and are working on getting a green card, you might get a chance to raise local money. Don't even think about it if you still run your R&D out of China."

# Israel's Startup Funding Decline Before The War

Startup investment in Israel was already far below the prior year before the fighting began: as TechCrunch's Anna Heim reported in July, a provisional tally of $3.2 billion for the first half of the year meant funding activity in Israel had dropped by 73% compared with the same period in 2022, according to IVC data. Other countries and regions reported similar declines in their private-market capital flows that year, so the fall was not unique to Israel.

The decline had a political prelude. The tech industry led opposition to the government's bid for judicial reform and, even before the fighting started, it was voting with its feet, with some companies and investors already refusing to do business in the country with the prospect of the reforms getting pushed through. That effort was in turn brought to a halt, because people on the two sides of that debate were then standing together for what they saw as the significantly bigger fight and threat.

By the sixth day of the war, many people were being called up to the reserves or volunteering to help in other ways, and with the tech industry skewing younger it was estimated that anywhere between 10% and 30% of all of Israel's tech employees were getting mobilized. More than 500 VCs had pledged their support of those efforts as well; the signatories wrote, "In the spirit of peace and unity, we encourage the global venture community to support and engage with Israeli startups, entrepreneurs, and investors as they navigate through these challenging times."

TechCrunch spoke to a number of startup founders, PR people who work with startups, and investors to understand the on-the-ground situation for Israeli entrepreneurs, and the predominant response was that the businesses have to continue to operate as best they can, to help ensure the economic viability of the country.

The Verdane-Meltwater deal underscores two themes in European tech and VC: tech companies continue to see huge pressure on their valuations, and investors are structuring deals to de-risk as private equity fills the gap left by shrinking venture funding.

On valuations, the evidence is Meltwater's own numbers: its market cap of just under $600 million is actually less than the company raised over the years when it was a privately held startup — over $700 million per PitchBook data — and less than half of its valuation when it went public in December 2020 at over $1 billion. On dealmaking, the market is particularly tight in Europe: VC firm Atomico's annual deep dive into the European funding landscape, put together with a number of third-party research firms and participation from others in the ecosystem, found that funding in 2023 halved to just $43 billion, and private equity firms are making a much bigger appearance in deals to make up some of the drop from VC.

The warrant linking those conditions to the deal's unusual shape is de-risking. It is notable that Verdane opted to invest in Fountain Venture rather than directly in Meltwater: that gives Verdane not only the stake in Meltwater but also a stake in Jobylon and whatever else Fountain and Lyseggen find interesting, which in turn de-leverages a focus on just one business. Verdane itself has only recently started to spread its wings to invest in startups across all of Europe and beyond, so tying up with a partner to help direct it is a very de-risked approach to take while trying to be more ambitious.

# Hikvision Video Surveillance Company Profile

Hikvision is one of the world's largest makers of video surveillance equipment, based in Hangzhou, China, and it is among the vendors behind the surveillance cameras deployed in the occupied Palestinian territories.

What distinguishes it from other camera vendors is its record: the company has been accused of aiding what the US has categorized as a genocide. It is already infamous among international human rights groups, has been blacklisted by the US, and has been identified by the UK as a security threat, in both cases for being complicit in China's repression of the Uyghur ethnic minority.

The company's headquarters are in Hangzhou, in eastern China's Zhejiang province.

CRED grew its operating revenue by a staggering 255% to $168.1 million in the financial year ending March, as the fintech startup found rising adoption of its lending and commerce offerings among India's affluent individuals.

The Bengaluru-headquartered startup, which garners an unusually high level of attention, had a total income of about $50 million in the financial year ending March of the prior year, and $11.4 million in the year before that.

The figures were reported by Manish Singh.

# Stellantis' Leapmotor Stake And Joint Venture

Stellantis made a €1.5 billion deal ($1.59 billion) to take a 20% stake in Chinese electric vehicle maker Zhejiang Leapmotor Technologies, just days after ending manufacturing in the country, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-30.

---


# 10 Minute School's Pre-Series A Investor Syndicate

10 Minute School's new pre-Series A round, reported on 2023-10-12, came from a combination of private and government investors and was led by Conjunction Capital. Participation came from returning investor Peak XV's Surge (formerly Sequoia Capital India), the Bangladesh government's sovereign venture fund Startup Bangladesh Limited, CRED founder and CEO Kunal Shah, MyAsiaVC managing partner Sajid Rahman, and several local angel investors.

The mix of a sovereign fund, a regional scale-up program, individual founder-operators and local angels is what marks the round out. Conjunction Capital managing partner Kirill Kozhevnikov framed the investment as an entry into a new market, saying in an investor quote, "This marks our first venture into the Bangladesh market, and we are confident that this partnership will redefine the education landscape in the country."

# Nike Greater China Sales Recovery

Nike's sales in China grew by 5% compared with the year-ago period to $1.7 billion in its fiscal first quarter ended 31 August 2023, falling short of the $1.8 billion analysts had expected, according to StreetAccount.

The comparison base matters: during the previous quarter ended 31 May, Nike saw China sales jump 16% year-on-year, but those numbers were against easy comparisons because the region was still under Covid-related lockdown orders during the prior year. While Nike remains bullish on China, the region's economic recovery has so far been a mixed bag — following a sluggish July, retail sales picked up during August to rise 4.6% compared with the prior year, beating expectations of 3% growth forecast by Reuters.

CEO John Donahoe, who said he had travelled to China twice in the previous four months, expressed confidence: "We feel good about the market there and our position. Frankly, a couple things stand out. One, sport is back in China, you can just feel it, and that gives us great confidence about the future and the Chinese consumer in our segment, regardless of the macroeconomic outlook there."



---


# Israeli Founders And Investors On Operating Through The War

Israeli startup founders and their investors told TechCrunch in October 2023 that, alongside the war effort, keeping the businesses running mattered, and they expected the immediate commercial damage to fall on product development rather than sales. For most Israeli startups the customer base is global and for many the go-to-market teams are in the U.S. and hence not directly affected by the war, so the current situation may slow down product development but won't directly affect sales in the short run.

Lazer Cohen, whose company Concrete Media works with many startups, said people are contributing however they can while the businesses also need to keep running: "Looking at our clients and my agency, 10-25% of Israeli team members have been called up to reserve duty." Others on the team were helping by donating blood, hosting survivors of the attacks, packing supplies for soldiers, or covering for a team member who was called up. Cohen framed continued operation as an obligation: "As we come out of the initial shock and horror of the attack, many tech workers and executives see it as their duty to keep the tech industry up and running. Technology is Israel's biggest export and the main engine of our economy and with a long and difficult war ahead, it's crucial that we keep working and innovating."

Customers had been understanding for the most part, but companies were working to continue operating under difficult conditions. Sharon Seeman, a partner at YL Ventures, stressed that companies maintain communication with customers: "Ensuring the continuity of business operations is vital for Israeli startups in maintaining their customer relationships."

The trickier question was deferred rather than answered. Startups eventually come around to the inevitable cadence of their existence — raising money to scale their operations, then doubling down and scaling those operations — and the article left open how that would play out with would-be startup investors and the LPs of those investors should the region and country continue to be at war.

Investors quoted took the long view. OurCrowd founder and CEO Jon Medved believes the ecosystem will remain resilient: "There is no doubt that in the long run — a year or more — Israel's tech ecosystem will emerge from this war, stronger, bigger, with more investment and returns for investors," pointing to proven resilience in past conflicts with Hamas and to Israel's focus on deep tech, semiconductors, AI, mobility, fintech, cybersecurity, quantum, agtech, the cloud, devops and clean energy. Oren Yunger, managing partner at GGV, said his firm will do what it takes to make sure the Israeli startups in its portfolio don't go bankrupt because of the war: "I can say with absolute confidence — even if we don't know how long it's going to take and who's going to be affected — I am 100% sure that none of our companies will go bust as a result from this moment in time."

# Britney Spears On Virginity Marketing And Timberlake's Cheating Claim

Spears writes in *The Woman in Me*, as reported by The Guardian on 24 October 2023, that she was actively marketed as a virgin — an "archaic premise" that turned a 16-year-old's sexuality into a timebomb — and that she was relieved rather than wounded when Justin Timberlake told the world they had had a sexual relationship.

The fixation on her "purity" took "the focus off me as a musician and a performer", she writes: "All some reporters could think of to ask me was whether or not my breasts were real (they were, actually) and whether or not my hymen was intact." In fact, she writes happily, she first slept with her older brother's best friend when she was 14. When Timberlake told the world she had cheated on him, she was all but emblazoned with a scarlet letter and knew she was powerless against that narrative — "I don't think Justin realised the power he had in shaming me. I don't think he understands to this day" — but she welcomed his disclosure of their sexual relationship: "To be honest with you, I liked that Justin said that.
