She could not, however, escape the cycle Timberlake set in motion. She describes her 2004 Onyx Hotel tour in the aftermath as "too sexual, for a start. Justin had embarrassed me publicly, so my rebuttal onstage was to kind of go there a little bit, too. But it was absolutely horrible."

# Britney Spears On Body Scrutiny And Diet Control

The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account of *The Woman in Me* reports that Spears' body was treated as public property "from day one" and that, once she was under the conservatorship, her father policed her weight and every calorie she ate was recorded.

Between the videos for her debut single Baby, One More Time and Sometimes, the media noted her changing physique and concluded that the 16-year-old must have had breast implants rather than simply going through puberty. She noticed that talkshow hosts asked her about her chest while her boyfriend Justin Timberlake was asked serious questions about his music. Writing about shaving her head in a salon in 2007, she frames it as a "fuck you" to impossible beauty standards: "I'd smiled politely while TV show hosts leered at my breasts, while American parents said I was destroying their children by wearing a crop top."

That brief moment of freedom did not last: a year later she was ambushed into the conservatorship, which also exercised jurisdiction over her body. "No matter how much I dieted and exercised, my father was always telling me I was fat," she writes; punishing gym routines left her feeling "out of my mind", and her diet was monitored along with every other detail of her life while she went through the motions of her Las Vegas residency. "My body was strong enough to carry two children and agile enough to execute every choreographed move perfectly onstage. And now here I was, having every calorie recorded so people could continue to get rich off my body." On the other side of the conservatorship, she writes, freedom looks like being able to gain weight without anyone "shouting at me", eating chocolate again, and posting selfies — nude or clothed — on Instagram; people who do not understand the last of these, she suggests, have not been "photographed by other people thousands of times, prodded and posed for other people's approval".

# How Kevin Federline Came To Have Custody Of Britney Spears' Sons

Kevin Federline met Britney Spears in 2004 at a nightclub, and months later they were married. They welcomed two sons, Preston and Jayden, before divorcing in 2007. At the time of the divorce they split custody, but a few months later Federline received sole physical custody because of what a judge called Spears' "habitual, frequent and continuous use of controlled substances and alcohol". In 2008, when Spears began experiencing trouble with her mental health, Federline was awarded sole legal custody as well, with Spears given visitation rights.

In her recently released memoir, "The Woman in Me", Spears claimed she agreed to her conservatorship for her kids: "Because I played by the rules, I was reunited with my boys." She eventually gained more custody, though Federline has remained the boys' primary caregiver and they have lived with him since the divorce; earlier this year they moved to Hawaii with Spears' approval.

After years of getting along, some tension began to show in 2022, when Spears and Federline both shared negative posts on social media about the other, which they both deleted. Soon after, Preston and Jayden did a rare interview with ITV to discuss the situation. Jayden clarified there was "no hate" involved towards anyone, but said "it will take a lot of time and effort" to fix their relationship with their mother: "I 100% think this can be fixed. It's just going to take a lot of time and effort. I just want her to get better mentally. When she gets better, I really want to see her again." Directly to Spears, he said: "I love you a lot, I hope for the best for you. Maybe one day we can sit down like this and talk again." They reportedly haven't seen each other since early last year.

# Britney Spears And Sam Asghari: Marriage And Divorce

Sam Asghari filed for divorce from Britney Spears in August 2023 after only 14 months of marriage, listing the date of separation as 28 July 2023 and citing "irreconcilable differences." The two had met in 2016, when Asghari was cast as Spears' love interest in the music video for "Slumber Party," from her 2016 album Glory; they made the relationship Instagram official in 2017 and supported each other through milestones including the 29th annual GLAAD Media Awards, where Spears accepted the Vanguard Award for her work promoting equality and acceptance. In April 2022 Spears announced she was pregnant with her third child and their first together, but the following month said in an Instagram statement that she had suffered a miscarriage; the couple wrote: "We have lost our miracle baby."

They married that June at her California home in Los Angeles, a lavish ceremony one month after the miscarriage announcement, with a guest list that included Selena Gomez, Paris Hilton, Drew Barrymore, Madonna, and Donatella Versace, who designed the wedding dress. Spears' close family — her mother Lynne, father Jamie, sister Jamie-Lynn, and her two sons — were not present. In August 2023, months after Asghari had shut down speculation about a divorce, TMZ claimed he had confronted Spears about rumours she had cheated on him; the fitness instructor filed the same day. His statement read: "After six years of love and commitment to each other my wife and I have decided to end our journey together. We will hold onto the love and respect we have for each other and I wish her the best always. S*** happens. Asking for privacy seems ridiculous so I will just ask for everyone including the media to be kind and thoughtful." Days before the memoir's release he told TMZ, on 13 October, that he had obtained an early copy and was not worried about being painted negatively: "I already read it and I'm very proud of her. She put a lot of work into it, and it was very hard. I'm definitely excited, and I'm extremely proud of her. It was a very tough one [to write]." Fans had previously praised him for his continuing support of Spears through her conservatorship and custody battle. Spears' two children, Sean, 18, and Jayden, 17, are shared with her second ex-husband, Kevin Federline.

# Britney Spears' Memoir On Early Fame And The Loss Of Freedom

In *The Woman in Me*, as summarised by The Guardian on 24 October 2023, Britney Spears describes how fame converted her childhood escape into confinement: by the age of 16 she was "public property", unable to go outside without being mobbed, and her love of singing and dancing had become a lucrative resource for other people.

Spears writes that as a child she escaped a difficult home life — her alcoholic father often rowing with her mother — into the outdoors, which "gave me a sense of aliveness and danger", and that performing made her feel invincible. By the time of her second album she wanted for so little; skinny-dipping with her dancers after playing Rock in Rio in January 2001 is one of her happiest memories, "a taste of rebellion and freedom, but I was just having fun and being a 19-year-old". After her split from Justin Timberlake she dreamed about quitting pop and opening a shop, and writes with hindsight that she "hadn't given myself enough time to heal from the breakup" — yet her requests for a break were not only turned down but interpreted as a potential sign of sedition to be quashed and interrogated.

In that restrictive environment small kindnesses took on outsized significance, such as Paris Hilton encouraging her "to have fun for the first time in a long time", which led to infamous nights out with the heiress and Lindsay Lohan; once again Britney was seen as stepping out of bounds and potentially damaging her earning potential. One night, after her mother babysat her sons, she returned home tipsy and Lynne Spears screamed at her: "The shame I felt killed my heart. I stood there, reeling, and thought, OK, I guess it's forbidden for me to party." As the restrictions tightened she acted out, and ended up legally denied her freedom for 13 years under a conservatorship controlled by her father.



---


# Britney Spears' Estrangement From Her Family

In *The Woman in Me*, as reported by The Guardian on 24 October 2023, Spears concludes that she made peace with her family in the sense that she "realised I never wanted to see them again, and I was at peace with that" — a break she traces to a lifetime of being made to feel she was not enough.

She writes about her father's alleged alcoholism, neglect and brutal standards, and about a mother who always made her feel less-than. She is unsparing about her younger sister, whom she characterises as a brat spared the pain of Britney's impoverished childhood because of Britney's success: "My mom and I had to witness the ugliness and the violence without believing that there was anywhere else to go." Even once she was the biggest pop star in the world her parents still seemed to have an undue say in running her career, including making her sit for humiliating TV interviews — why exactly that was remains unanswered in the book. Her father seized control legally with the imposition of the conservatorship, telling her, chillingly, "I am Britney Spears now", and her family appear to live off her dime while she lived an extraordinarily restricted life.

Returning home from the forced stint in a brutal rehab facility, she found that her parents had thrown away her childhood things, including a binder full of her poetry: "I felt an overwhelming sadness. I thought of the pages I'd written through tears. I never wanted to publish them or anything like that, but they were important to me. And my family had thrown them in the trash, just like they'd thrown me away." She resolved to start over with a new notebook, and writes that she is working to feel "more compassion than anger" towards them: "It's not easy."



---


# Britney Spears' 55-Hour Marriage To Jason Alexander

Jason Alexander was Britney Spears' first husband: the two married at a wedding chapel in Las Vegas in 2004 and annulled the marriage only 55 hours after the ceremony. Alexander returned to the news in 2022 when he tried to attend Spears' wedding to Sam Asghari, and could be heard in a video saying he was going to crash the nuptials. "She's my first wife, my only wife," he reportedly told security. "I'm her first husband, I'm here to crash the wedding."

Alexander was arrested for trespassing, vandalism, and battery over the incident. A security guard later revealed in court that when Alexander crashed the wedding he also tried to enter Spears' bedroom.

# The Spears-Federline Child Support And Custody Disputes

In 2018 Kevin Federline asked Britney Spears for an extra $20,000 a month in child support, then, after months of court discussions, rejected her counter-proposal and doubled his request to $40,000 a month; a settlement was finally reached in September 2018, with Spears raising her payments to Federline from $20,000 to $35,000 a month.

The custody balance shifted the following year. Amid her father's health crisis and ongoing emotional distress, Spears voluntarily checked into a mental health treatment facility in 2019. Federline's attorney Mark Kaplan told Entertainment Tonight: "Kevin commends Britney for recognising that she needs to take a step back and that she is taking the reasonable steps to dealing with her situation in a responsible way. He wishes everyone well." That same year, Federline was granted 70 per cent custodial rights and Spears 30 per cent.



---


# The Fan Movement And The 2021 End Of Britney Spears' Conservatorship

According to The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account of *The Woman in Me*, Spears first learned of the blossoming fan movement questioning her conservatorship from a nurse, called 911 in June 2021 to report her father for conservatorship abuse days before a probate court hearing, and was granted her freedom in November 2021.

A nurse showed her the fan movement that was spreading awareness of its suspicions that all was not right with the arrangement. Of speaking publicly at that point she writes: "My voice had been used for me and against me so many times that I was afraid nobody would recognise it now if I spoke freely."

When freedom came in November 2021, she says she felt shock, relief, elation, sadness and joy.



---


# Britney Spears' Conservatorship Under Jamie Spears

Britney Spears' conservatorship was a legal arrangement, entered into in February 2008, under which her father Jamie Spears took complete control over her assets. It followed a mental breakdown in 2008 that saw her placed on a 5150 psychiatric hold and left Kevin Federline with sole custody of their sons. The defining feature of the arrangement was the transfer of control not only over her finances but over her personal life, and it lasted until November 2021, when Spears was granted her freedom from it.

The turning point was Spears' testimony at her conservatorship hearing in June 2021, when she spoke publicly about her experience for the first time and called for those involved to be "put in jail." Federline expressed support for her after the testimony, saying he "only hopes the best for her because when the best for her is achieved, it's the best for their kids." His lawyer added in a statement at the time: "The best thing would be for their mom to be healthy and happy. And if either of those things aren't true, it doesn't provide for the best setting for custody to be exercised."



---


# Britney Spears On Music Making From Baby One More Time To Blackout

Per The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account of the memoir, Spears says the period around Baby, One More Time was "probably the moment in my life when I had the most passion for music", and the only album she discusses in any detail afterwards is 2007's Blackout.

Early on she loved making music: she told producer Max Martin she wanted to sound more R&B than straight pop, listened to Tainted Love the night before recording Baby, One More Time and stayed up late so she would sound as gravelly and "fried" as Marc Almond. She was a studio perfectionist who would stay in the booth for hours, and the school setting and uniforms of the Baby video were her idea. "I was unknown and I had nothing to lose if I messed up," she writes.

After that, her music barely features in the book — there is a nod to her breaking records, and the era-defining Toxic is dispensed with in a sentence. Blackout, the cult favourite made at the height of her public struggles yet full of potential, is the exception: the studio was a refuge from the paparazzi hounding her outside, and while the messy DIY video for the single Gimme More may be "by far the worst video I've ever shot in my life", its scrappiness meant "more interesting people started noticing and wanting to work with me". There is some later love for 2016's Glory, and she writes proudly about her 2022 collaboration with Elton John, but says she has no plans to make music at the moment.



---


# Arrested Development: Britney Spears' Child-Robot Model Of The Conservatorship

The Guardian's 24 October 2023 reading of *The Woman in Me* frames Spears' life as a structure of arrested development: she was "never allowed to be a real child, nor a real adult", and the conservatorship pushed her into what she calls a "child-robot" state in which she vacillated between girl, teenager and woman.

The relation holds across three phases she describes. In early fame, her 2001 single I'm Not a Girl, Not Yet a Woman is read as her most prescient recording, and after her split from Timberlake she likens herself to Benjamin Button: "Somehow that year, in becoming more vulnerable I started to feel like a child again." In the postnatal-depression phase the split deepens — "It was as if some part of me became the baby," she writes in an apologetic section about transferring her frustrations on to her interior decorator, "One part of me was a very demanding grown woman yelling about white marble, while another part of me was suddenly very childlike."

In the conservatorship phase she not only regresses but feels dehumanised by constant scrutiny: "I became a robot. But not just a robot – a sort of child-robot. The conservatorship stripped me of my womanhood, made me into a child." The vacillation, she says, is hard to explain — it followed "the way they had robbed me of my freedom … They wanted me to be wild onstage, the way they told me to be, and to be a robot the rest of the time." The model therefore holds only within the terms of her own memoir, as her account of how loss of freedom mapped onto loss of adulthood.

Golf bets are typically placed on professional tournaments, including PGA and DP World Tour events, and the popular options are a distinct set of market types. Bet to Win means picking a specific golfer to win the entire tournament. Betting Against the Field means wagering on a golfer to outperform the rest of the players. # Moneyline Outcomes: Win, Loss, Draw And Push

A moneyline wager can end in several ways: the most straightforward outcomes are a win or a loss, determined by whether the team or individual you backed was victorious or defeated, and there is also the possibility of a draw if the event ends in a tie. Winning is simply a matter of picking the eventual winner — bet on Boxer B in a bout between Boxer A and Boxer B, and if Boxer B wins you are paid based on the odds at the time you placed the wager. A loss means the side you backed did not win: bet $100 on Team A in an NBA game and, if Team B wins, the bet on Team A loses.

Some sports price the draw as its own selection. In soccer especially, games can end in a draw and bettors can wager on that outcome, so a moneyline typically shows three sets of odds — one for each team to win and one for the draw. For a match between Team A and Team B, the odds might read Team A +150, Draw +220, Team B +180; a $100 wager on "Draw" that lands returns $220 in profit on top of the $100 stake, totaling $320, while a win by either team loses the $100.

A tie handled as a "push" is a different case, and the scope condition matters. When a push occurs bettors are refunded their original wager, with no money won or lost; but sports that typically allow a tie, like soccer, often offer the draw as a bet instead, and if the game ends in a draw and you did not bet that option, you lose. It is therefore essential to understand the specific rules of the sportsbook and the sport to know how ties are handled. Finally, in most sports and with most sportsbooks — including new betting sites — overtime or any extra time or tiebreakers do count toward a moneyline bet, though you should always check your sportsbook's specific rules.

# Sports Betting Odds

## Definition

Sports betting odds are the numbers a sportsbook posts alongside a wager to show the payout a bettor stands to win relative to their stake, and they are set by oddsmakers using computer models and analytics before being released to the public. The same underlying odds concept takes different shapes depending on the bet type — a moneyline price on who wins outright, a point spread price on a handicapped margin, and a totals (over/under) price on the combined score — and can be displayed in American, decimal, or fractional format.

## Context

In the corpus, odds are the common thread across every major bet type: moneylines, point spreads, totals, and prop bets all price outcomes with the same odds conventions, and combined-market previews such as college bowl coverage post moneyline, spread, and total odds side by side for a single game. Odds are not static — sportsbooks move them ("line movement") in response to public betting patterns, injury or roster news, and sharp/professional money, with the goal of balancing action on both sides of a bet so the book keeps its built-in profit regardless of outcome. Because different sportsbooks can carry different odds for the same event, bettors practice "line shopping" — comparing odds and lines across multiple sportsbooks before wagering to find the best price. Odds also extend beyond single games into futures and award markets, such as season-long odds on the NFL MVP race between Brock Purdy and Lamar Jackson.

## Key Characteristics

- **American odds format dominates U.S. listings** — a negative number (e.g., -110) shows the favorite and how much must be wagered to profit $100; a positive number (e.g., +250) shows the underdog and how much a $100 wager profits.
- **Three display formats carry the same price** — American, decimal (multiply the odds by the stake for total payout), and fractional (numerator = profit, denominator = stake) are alternative notations for identical odds.
- **Odds move for identifiable reasons** — sportsbooks shift a line or its odds because of lopsided public betting, new information (injuries, weather), sharp bettor action, or a perceived initial mispricing.
- **Odds differ by bet type but share the sign convention** — moneyline odds price the outright winner, point spread odds price a handicapped margin near even money, and totals odds price the over/under of a combined score; all three commonly display as American odds.
- **Line shopping exploits cross-sportsbook odds variance** — because oddsmakers and sportsbooks don't always move in lockstep, checking odds at multiple books before betting can secure a better price on the same wager.

# Why Moneyline Odds Change

Lines at sports betting apps change quickly for two primary reasons — public betting and new information — and sportsbooks adjust moneyline odds to stay profitable, balance their book and reflect the most current information about an event. Before setting odds oddsmakers gather extensive data, then release the finalized odds to the public; from that point a bettor can bet immediately or wait for shifts, though predicting those shifts is challenging.

The time dimension shows how an opening price drifts. Odds for the next Super Bowl champion released shortly after the previous Super Bowl are based mostly on the recently concluded season; as the new season approaches and teams make changes, the odds adjust to perceived championship chances, and as games progress the lines keep evolving with team performances.

The mechanism has five named drivers. Public betting patterns move a line because, when a significant amount of money lands on one team or participant, sportsbooks adjust the odds to balance their liability — making the price less favorable for the heavily-bet side and more favorable for the less-bet side to encourage even betting and reduce financial risk. New information matters because changes in player injuries, player substitutions or weather conditions alter the perceived outcome, and books adjust once such information becomes public. Professional bettors move lines because large wagers from sharp bettors often reflect insights or information that can influence the odds. Initial miscalculation is a fourth driver: sometimes the opening odds are perceived as offering value, and heavy betting on one side signals that the initial price was potentially "off," prompting an adjustment. Event dynamics is the fifth, applying to live betting placed while the event is in progress, where the evolving dynamics of the match lead to frequent changes.

# Moneyline Odds Examples By Sport

Typical moneyline prices look the same across sports — a minus number on the favorite, a plus number on the underdog — but the shape of the market varies with the sport, most obviously where draws or large fields exist. In an NFL game between the Dallas Cowboys (-130) and the New York Giants (+110), the Cowboys are the favorites: a $130 bet on Dallas returns $100 profit if they win, while a $100 wager on the Giants earns $110 profit on an upset. An NBA game between the Los Angeles Lakers (-150) and the Miami Heat (+130) works the same way, with $150 on the Lakers profiting $100 and $100 on the Heat profiting $130.

Baseball and hockey illustrate slight favorites and even money. For an MLB game with the New York Yankees at -120 and the Boston Red Sox at +100, the Yankees are slight favorites — a $120 bet returns $100 profit — while the Red Sox are at even odds, so a $100 bet also returns $100 profit. For an NHL game with the Toronto Maple Leafs at -140 and the Chicago Blackhawks at +120, $140 on Toronto profits $100 and $100 on Chicago profits $120.

Soccer adds a third selection. In an MLS match between the Seattle Sounders (+110), the Draw (+230) and Atlanta United (+140), neither team is a clear favorite though the Sounders have slightly better odds: $100 on Seattle profits $110, $100 on the draw profits $230 if the match ends tied, and $100 on Atlanta profits $140. In soccer, the possibility of a draw is a common outcome to bet on, which is different from many other major sports.

Combat sports, tennis and golf round out the pattern. A UFC fight between Conor McGregor (-200) and Dustin Poirier (+170) pays $100 profit on a $200 bet on McGregor and $170 profit on a $100 bet on Poirier. A tennis match between Serena Williams (-150) and Maria Sharapova (+130) makes Williams the favorite, with $150 on her profiting $100 and $100 on Sharapova profiting $130. PGA Tour odds price individual golfers to win a tournament — Tiger Woods +500, Rory McIlroy +600 — so a $100 bet profits $500 or $600 respectively; in golf, with usually many players in the field, the odds can be much higher than in head-to-head matchups.

# The Moneyline Bet

Every moneyline bet has a favorite and an underdog as determined by the sportsbook, "favorites" and "underdogs" referring to the perceived stronger and weaker participants respectively. # Over/Under Betting In MMA, Tennis And Golf

In individual sports the over/under line is denominated not in combined points but in the sport's own unit of duration or performance: rounds in MMA, games or sets in tennis, and strokes relative to par in golf.

In an MMA context, over/under bets often refer to the duration of the fight rather than points or scores. In a UFC bout between Fighter A and Fighter B the bookmaker sets an over/under line at 2.5 rounds; a bettor who believes both fighters have aggressive styles and the fight will end early bets the "under." If the fight ends midway through the second round by knockout or submission, the total rounds would be 1.5, below the set total of 2.5, so the "under" wins. Conversely, if the fight extends beyond the midway point of the third round, "over" bets win.

At tennis betting sites, over/under betting typically revolves around the total number of games or sets played in a match. In a Grand Slam match between Player A and Player B the bookmaker sets the total at 40.5 games for the entire match; a bettor anticipating a closely contested match with many extended sets bets the "over." With set scores of 7-5, 6-7, 7-6 and 6-4, the combined total is 42 games, which exceeds 40.5, so the "over" wins.

At golf betting sites, over/under betting often pertains to a golfer's score for a specific round or the entire tournament relative to par. In a major tournament where Rory McIlroy is playing, the bookmaker sets an over/under line at 69.5 strokes for his first-round score; a bettor who analyses the challenging course conditions and expects difficulties bets the "under," predicting 69 strokes or fewer. If McIlroy concludes the round with a 68 — 3 under par on a par-71 course — the "under" wager wins; if he shoots 70 or higher, those who bet the "over" win.

# Totals Bet Outcomes: Push And Overtime

An over/under wager has three potential outcomes: if the combined score exceeds the set total, the "over" bet wins; if the score is below the set total, the "under" bet wins; and if the combined score of the game matches the total exactly, the bet is typically considered a "push" and the wager is refunded.

A push therefore occurs when the combined score of a game matches the set total established by the bookmaker, meaning bettors neither win nor lose and their original wager is returned. To avoid this outcome, most sportsbooks employ half-points in their totals: by setting a total at 200.5 instead of 200, sports betting sites ensure that a game's combined score cannot possibly match the set total exactly.

Overtime is a separate boundary case. In most sports and with the majority of sportsbooks, overtime does count toward a totals wager; Sporting News advises always checking the specific rules of the sportsbook you are betting with to confirm, but says overtime is generally included in totals wagers.

For tennis, Sporting News uses a match between Serena Williams and Maria Sharapova: if Williams is a -4.5 favorite, she must win by a 5-game margin for her bettors to win. Set handicaps work similarly but focus on the number of sets won by each player.

For golf, betting often centers on outright winners or head-to-head matchups, with stroke handicap as the spread-like alternative. # Point Spread Bet Definition

A point spread bet is a wager on the difference in score between two teams (or players) in a specific game or event, in which bookmakers assign the favored team a point spread or handicap intended to equalize the odds against the less-favored team. To place one, a bettor selects either the favored team or the underdog and predicts whether that side will surpass or fall short of the given spread; the odds on both sides are set to try to even out the money wagered on each.

The discriminating features are the two symbols and what they oblige each side to do. The "(-)" symbol denotes the favorite — the team expected to win, typically assigned a negative point value indicating the number of points by which it must win for a bet on it to succeed; the favorite has points deducted. The "(+)" symbol denotes the underdog — the team expected to lose, typically assigned a positive point value indicating the number of points it may lose by and still win the bet; the underdog has points added. Covering the spread means a team has surpassed the expectations the spread set and so won the bet: for the favorite, winning by more than the specified number of points; for the underdog, either winning outright or losing by fewer points than the spread. If the underdog wins the contest outright, it is also the spread winner.

The term "against the spread" carries two senses that mark a boundary case. Most generally, betting against the spread simply means placing a point spread bet at all — betting the underdog to win outright or lose by fewer points than specified, or betting the favorite to win by a margin greater than specified. In a secondary definition that distinguishes betting "with the spread" from betting "against the spread," the latter term means specifically that you are betting on the underdog. # The Exorcist III

The Exorcist III, written and directed by William Peter Blatty — the original screenwriter of The Exorcist and author of the novel it was based on — is, in Polygon's judgment, the sequel that came closest to capturing the same lightning in a bottle as William Friedkin's original, which nearly 50 years after its theatrical release has withstood the test of time as one of the most terrifying and influential horror films in American cinema. It was the Oct. 31 pick in Polygon's 2023-10-10 Halloween Countdown, listed on Prime Video and the Criterion Channel.

When a series of gruesome murders matching the modus operandi of an infamous serial killer begins to terrorize the city of Georgetown, Lt. William F. Kinderman, played by George C. Scott, investigates the psych ward of a local hospital in search of leads. Confronted with a suspect whose appearance matches that of his late friend Father Damien Karras, Kinderman is thrust into a battle for his very soul as he confronts an evil beyond his comprehension.

Polygon's Toussaint Egan calls the production history a tangled mess of false starts, studio interference, and thwarted artistic ambitions: it was originally conceived with Friedkin in mind to return as director, but he left over creative differences with Blatty; John Carpenter was at one time tapped to direct before he too stepped aside to let Blatty take the reins; and financier Morgan Creek Productions demanded Blatty reshoot the final act, which originally ended without an exorcism. Even so, Egan calls it a fascinating and terrifying film in its own right, with a hodgepodge of fascinating creative choices and literary dialogue that makes it feel like a sister piece to Blatty's The Ninth Configuration — maybe not the Exorcist sequel audiences at the time wanted, but still a damn fine picture.

Starring Sam Neill, Julie Carmen and Jurgen Prochnow, and watchable on YouTube, it follows insurance investigator John Trent (Neill), who is hired to find a missing famous horror novelist; things become increasingly unhinged as the plots of the author's books and the various monsters seem to invade the real world.

Neill, a staple of this list, is absolutely fantastic responding to the horrors of hell, slowly becoming exactly as off-kilter as they are: by the third act the door to hell is halfway open and Trent is ready to dive headfirst into the void, which the reviewer says is honestly how every movie's third act should go. Its place in Carpenter's work is specific — this is the third film in his apocalypse trilogy, which also includes two other stone-cold classics, The Thing and Prince of Darkness, which are not on the list but which the reviewer recommends anyway.

# The Roland Doe Case and The Exorcist

Perhaps the most famous instance of purported demonic possession connected to Ouija board usage was the case of "Roland Doe", a young teenage boy from Maryland, who underwent numerous major exorcisms in 1949, said Fr. Dan Reehil.

Doe's story was adapted into the 1971 book "The Exorcist" by William Peter Blatty, which was then made into the 1973 movie starring Ellen Burstyn and Linda Blair.

# Overlord (2018 Nazi Zombie Film)

Overlord is a slept-on genre-mashing gem that places a cast of excellent actors about to do bigger things — Jovan Adepo, Wyatt Russell, John Magaro, Pilou Asbæk, and more — and up-and-coming director Julius Avery, of The Pope's Exorcist, behind Nazi lines during World War II, where the Nazis are up to more than usual: there be zombies in these labs. It was the Oct. 24 pick in Polygon's 2023-10-10 Halloween Countdown, listed on Paramount Plus and Pluto TV.

On the eve of D-Day, a group of Allied paratroopers are sent into Germany on a covert mission. Things go wrong instantly when their plane crashes, and they soon discover twisted Nazi experiments after connecting with the residents. Things get bloody fast, with great action from second unit director Shaun O'Dell, of The Woman King and Brotherhood of the Wolf, and stunt coordinator Jo McLaren of Heart of Stone.

Polygon's Pete Volk calls it a gleeful, intentionally ridiculous Nazi-zombie-bashing time with tight direction and a fantastic group of actors, recommended for anyone who loves the Wolfenstein games, Call of Duty's Zombies mode, or B-movies with A-movie production.

# Polygon's Selection Process for the Best Movies of 2023

Polygon builds its best-movies-of-the-year list by having each of the staff's film fans create an individual ballot of their top movies every year, with an option to rank the entries numerically or simply weight them; those ballots are then used to generate a collective list, weighted by strength of opinion so that a much-seen mainstream movie does not gain too much advantage over a terrific but underseen indie. The result is then published, with the top 10 picks on each staffer's list listed in the comments.

The eligibility rule is that any movie released in the US during that calendar year qualifies. A stated limitation follows from the publication timing: because the list is published in early December, some December releases are underrepresented.

Polygon frames the exercise as inherently difficult, likening a collaborative best-movies list to forming a committee to definitively rank apples and oranges — how to account for personal tastes, or for access when a given movie is only available in certain markets at certain times, or for the fact that the entries are so qualitatively different they have little in common. The weighted-ballot procedure exists to accommodate that spread: the staff describes its collective tastes as eclectic, with some hungriest for action, horror, epic fantasy, or challenging science fiction, some preferring complicated drama or dark neo-noir, and others drawn to musicals, comedy, animated adventures, and other lighter fare. The best-of-the-year list is meant to reflect that range.

# Hellraiser: Clive Barker's Lament Configuration And The Cenobites

Hellraiser is Clive Barker's 1987 directorial debut, adapting his own 1986 novella The Hellbound Heart, starring Andrew Robinson, Clare Higgins and Ashley Laurence, and available on Prime Video, AMC+, Shudder, Tubi, Pluto and Hoopla. Polygon calls it easily the best and most enduring of the Hellraiser movie series and a must-watch for horror fans.

The core narrative concerns Larry and Julia Cotton, a married couple who move into the home of Larry's recently deceased brother Frank, with whom Julia had a previous affair. After Frank is inadvertently resurrected by a drop of blood spilled by Larry on the floor of the house's attic, he seduces Julia into luring new men to the house so he can drain their life force and fully regain his mortal form.

Surrounding that story is the Lament Configuration, a puzzle box Frank acquired before his untimely death: when solved, it conjures hellish beings known as Cenobites to the mortal plane of existence, which indulge in hellish exercises of sadomasochistic mutilation.

# The Barbenheimer Phenomenon of 2023

In 2023, beleaguered movie theaters got a boost from the Barbenheimer phenomenon: film fans made an event out of seeing two radically different movies back-to-back — a slyly satirical movie about a living fashion toy and a heavy, grim historical drama about the father of the atomic bomb. Polygon reported this in its best-movies-of-2023 write-up on 2023-10-07.

Polygon's account allows that Barbie and Oppenheimer do have a clear theme in common while insisting they remain radically different movies. The observation the outlet draws from the pairing is that the way the two collectively dominated the 2023 box office and the cultural discussion is a strong reminder that regardless of tone or topic, a great story told passionately stands out — cinephiles can be drawn to just about any movie in any genre if it is well crafted and engaging, no matter what kind of fruit it is.

# Five Nights at Freddy's Movie Development and Release

The possessed-animatronics horror video game Five Nights at Freddy's is less than a decade old, but a movie version had been in the works almost since the game launched — a protracted development process Polygon recounted on 2023-10-26.

Warner Bros. bought the movie rights in 2015, and the project moved over to Blumhouse a couple of years later. Game creator Scott Cawthon wrote and rewrote the script, while kid-horror filmmakers including Gil Kenan of Monster House and Chris Columbus of Gremlins and the first Harry Potter and Percy Jackson movies signed on and jumped off the project.

Finally, under director Emma Tammi, the film hit theaters simultaneously with a Peacock streaming debut. Polygon framed its accompanying Q&A as extremely spoiler-light and aimed at people other than the franchise's most hardcore fans, deliberately not digging into the considerable FNAF lore and focusing instead on who the film is for and what to expect.

# Scorsese's Maximalist, Improvisational Late Style

Where aging has meant settling for more routine and less challenging stories and shots on a tight production schedule for certain older filmmakers — Polygon names Clint Eastwood — Scorsese went in the other direction, into a maximalist, improvisational late style. The account is Polygon's, published 2023-10-26.

The Departed is the first case. From the outside it appears to be a cynical, domestic remake of a Hong Kong cops-and-robbers shootout, but Scorsese makes it his own and breathes bizarre life and energy into it: it contains the continuity errors, quick cutting, both rhythmic and arrhythmic needle bombs, and goofball humor his movies had not featured since Goodfellas. That earlier film essentially birthed an entire genre of filmic language, and The Departed goes a step beyond the original, being constantly rewritten and adjusted with the actors on the fly — exhilarating seat-of-the-pants filmmaking that Scorsese and his longtime creative partner, editor Thelma Schoonmaker, wrangled into a coherent film.

He brought the same cokey, maximalist energy to The Wolf of Wall Street, a pointed comedy as wildly, masterfully off the rails and improvisational as anything he has done, with Jonah Hill perhaps smuggling in a touch of Judd Apatow's "keep the camera rolling" ethos. Established-filmmaker confidence — and a touch of "eh, why not?" thinking — shows as DiCaprio's Ferrari changes color mid-narration during a highway blowjob, and when DiCaprio addresses the camera directly urging the audience not to worry about specific plot points. Polygon calls it a miracle that Scorsese and Schoonmaker produced a masterpiece out of the chaotic pieces of that production, again in post and with ample voice-over, with the shoot taking on something of a religious quality in the participants' retelling.

What grounds the style is the framing. Scorsese is telling a familiar story audiences have come to expect from him, about criminals and the pleasure they take in committing crimes and reaping the benefits; the brilliance is how he mines filmgoers' long relationship with his work, repurposing the style and tone of his gangster classics and inserting it into the world of finance. As he has done effectively since Casino, Scorsese weaponizes postmodernism, using viewers' presumed existing familiarity with his films as context — you do not get the full gale force of the film, its pleasures, or its overarching point without him reaching back to his past work and relying on viewers to recognize his voice in the storytelling.

# Certified Copy (Abbas Kiarostami)

Certified Copy is a romance directed by the late Abbas Kiarostami, whom Polygon calls one of the most masterful directors of his time; the film stars Juliette Binoche and William Shimell and was available to watch for free on Tubi as of the 2023-10-25 roundup.

The film follows two people: a French antique dealer, played by Binoche and described as arresting as always, and a British writer played by famed opera baritone William Shimell, who meet in Tuscany while the latter is promoting his new book. That book, also titled Certified Copy, puts forth the argument that there is no such thing as a "copy" in art, because even reproductions are original works. The two debate this idea as the question of what is "real" gets called into question — even the very nature of their own relationship.

Polygon's Pete Volk describes it as a gorgeous film led by two unforgettable performances and the kind of masterpiece that will linger for years, depicting humanity at its most impenetrably complex in a way that lays bare fears and hopes while remaining warm, charming, and delightfully funny. He calls it one of a kind but also in conversation with many other films about love and art — after all, every copy is its own original work.

Passages is Ira Sachs' film starring Franz Rogowski, Ben Whishaw, and Adèle Exarchopoulos, which Polygon calls perhaps the platonic ideal of an arthouse film. It ranked 48 on the best movies of 2023 list of 2023-10-07 and was available on Mubi or for digital rental/purchase.

The ingredients Polygon names are a messy love triangle, set in Paris, shot through with explicit sex and arresting fashion choices.

Critic Oli Welsh's defense of the film is unfussy: sometimes you just want to watch complicated hot people — Adèle Exarchopoulos, Ben Whishaw, and Franz Rogowski in this case — messing with each other's heads in tops their characters could not possibly afford, and there is nothing wrong with that.

# Are You There God? It's Me, Margaret

Kelly Fremon Craig's adaptation of Judy Blume's coming-of-age novel, starring Abby Ryder Fortson, Rachel McAdams, and Benny Safdie, is called a gem by Polygon. It ranked 29 on the outlet's best movies of 2023 list of 2023-10-07 and was available on Starz or for digital rental/purchase.

Polygon notes the book's standing: Blume's novel is one of the most challenged in the country because of its direct discussion of puberty, but it is also a staple of children's literature.

# Skinamarink (Kyle Edward Ball)

Skinamarink is Kyle Edward Ball's feature debut and, in Polygon's judgment, hands down the most peculiar and divisive horror film to come out in 2023 — and also one of the best. It ranked 30 on the outlet's best movies of 2023 list of 2023-10-07 and was available on Hulu, AMC Plus, Shudder, or for digital rental/purchase; the cast is Lucas Paul, Ross Paul, and Dali Rose Tetreault.

The premise is that a pair of siblings awake in the middle of the night to find their home transformed into an inescapable nightmare of yawning hallways, dimly lit corridors, and looming walls devoid of any windows or doors. As they search aimlessly for safety and familiarity, the children find they are not alone in the house, haunted by an unknowable entity that seems to feed on their fear as it twists their lives into ever more frightening shapes — or maybe not, since the film's narrative is notoriously sparse and open to interpretation. The effect is nonetheless one of the most unsettling scenarios seen that year.

Polygon's Halloween Countdown write-up of 2023-10-10 calls it one of the most polarizing horror releases of 2023 and describes its method: the film eschews the formal conventions of traditional cinematography and plot, consisting instead of a series of canted-angle shots of dark hallways and yawning darkness that force the audience to ruminate on the horrors that lie therein. The critic adds that he vibed with it heavily and, unsurprisingly, also enjoyed Ball's 2020 short film Heck.

# Polygon's Halloween Countdown Calendar

For the past three years as of 2023-10-10, Polygon has put together a Halloween countdown calendar: the staff selects 31 of its top horror-themed or Halloween-adjacent picks across movies and TV throughout the month of October, all of them available to watch at home. The outlet brought the format back again for 2023, this time with a whole new batch of films and shows to choose from.

The mechanics are daily: every day for the month of October, Polygon adds a new recommendation to the countdown and tells readers where they can watch it. The invitation is to curl up on the couch, dim the lights, and grab some popcorn for a marathon of horrific delights.

The countdown sits alongside Polygon's year-round horror coverage rather than replacing it — the outlet also runs lists of the best horror movies you can stream at home, the best horror movies on Netflix, and the best horror movies of the year ranked by scariness. The stated reason for the separate seasonal format is that Halloween is an especially spooky time of year and warrants special attention and celebration.



---


# Scorsese's Late Career Refutes Tarantino's Claim That Directors Do Not Get Better

Polygon's 2023-10-26 piece attacks the premise behind Quentin Tarantino's 2021 defense of his intention to make "just" 10 movies and retire: "I know film history, and from here on in, directors do not get better." The counter is that this view of both artistry and film is squarely at odds with Martin Scorsese's historic body of work.

The specific premise under attack is the claim of inevitable late-career decline. Scorsese had already made his 10th feature-length narrative film by 1986; he is now 80 years old, and his 27th, Killers of the Flower Moon, is a strong argument that directors are still capable of groundbreaking greatness late in life — and, in Scorsese's case, of continued exhilarating experimentation and discovery.

Polygon presses the point further: since the year 2000, Scorsese has curated a 23-year career within a career, and the quality and variety of his films have come not in spite of his age and experience but because of it. His movies have never been more relevant than in the past two decades, and with each subsequent release, as his career winds down, critical appreciation for him grows — Scorsese worship being the one remaining form of gerontocracy America is perfectly content with, and with good reason.

The mechanism the piece identifies is autonomy. This century Scorsese has zigged and zagged as always, but because he is following his own varied interests rather than moving from compromise to compromise as he once had to in order to keep working: an artist who spent the first 30 years of his career desperate for autonomy finally got it, and now takes full advantage — telling difficult stories, setting his own mega-budgets, and demanding every minute of run time he feels each picture demands. He has used that autonomy to revisit his work and revise the record, creating great new films and adding crucial addendums to past work while blazing new trails and adding layers to his style. Remarkably, the control that eluded him when he was younger has made his films more consistently collaborative and creative, more fluid and alive than he was often allowed to be before the 2000s, with the earned confidence of an artist who knows he will find something great in post. Polygon concludes that this should give Tarantino cause to reconsider, alongside any artist or critic who thinks the creative spark has an expiration date.



---


# When Evil Lurks (Demián Rugna)

When Evil Lurks is Demián Rugna's gory possession movie starring Ezequiel Rodríguez, Demián Salomón, and Luis Ziembrowski, ranked 33 on Polygon's best movies of 2023 list of 2023-10-07 and available on Shudder, AMC Plus, or for digital rental/purchase.

Polygon argues the film is not just the usual barrage of religious imagery and religious anxiety: it is much more concerned with bigger, sadder thoughts on the ways institutions keep failing people, and the ways people fail each other and themselves.

Ezequiel Rodríguez gives a mesmerizing performance as Argentinian farmer Pablo, a man estranged from his wife and in denial about his own responsibilities; when a demonic presence starts stalking his rural county, he runs to his ex-wife and the city and brings the curse along with him. Polygon calls it a shocking film that crosses lines in unusual ways for horror, particularly around horrors visited on children and animals, but says what really makes it land is how well realized all the human drama is, more so than the demon drama.



---


# Tubi's Free Ad-Supported Streaming Movie Catalog

Tubi is Fox's ad-supported free streaming service, and it holds one of the most vast libraries of any streaming service, with thousands upon thousands of movies available to watch at home. The defining features are that it is free, ad-supported, owned by Fox, and enormous in scale.

The size of the catalog is what makes curation difficult. Writing for Polygon on 2023-10-25, the author reported that when building a list of the best movies on the service, they looked up their "liked" films on Letterboxd that were currently on Tubi and more than 100 showed up — an illustration offered explicitly as not an exaggeration. The response was to narrow the field down to a group of excellent movies drawn from a variety of moods, cultures, and eras.

The catalog is treated as a living list rather than a fixed one. Polygon said it would continue to update its Tubi picks over time, building out a full catalog of excellent free movies to watch at home; the latest update at the time added Planet Terror as an editor's pick.



---


# The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes

The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes is Francis Lawrence's Hunger Games prequel starring Rachel Zegler, Tom Blyth, and Peter Dinklage, which Polygon calls a rare meaningful prequel that bolsters the existing narrative. It ranked 46 on the best movies of 2023 list of 2023-10-07 and was in theaters.

Polygon's Petrana Radulovic frames it against the series as a whole: The Hunger Games is one of the few series where the movies are often just as good as the books, and the new prequel — which focuses on a young President Snow, played excellently by Tom Blyth — is no exception.

What distinguishes it is a particular attention to detail and some masterful songs that really color the world.



---


# M3GAN (2023 AI Horror Film)

M3GAN, directed by Gerard Johnstone and starring Allison Williams, Violet McGraw, and Amie Donald, is a refreshingly goofy — and fairly creepy — spin on the "AI is going to murder us all" horror trope. Polygon ranked it 34 on its best movies of 2023 list published 2023-10-07, and listed it as available on Prime Video or for digital rental/purchase.

Polygon frames the film against its moment: 2023 was such a big year for big conversations about AI, including AI art, AI writing, and AI style theft, that a fresh wave of AI-kills-us-all horror movies was no surprise.

The premise is that when a tech whiz played by Allison Williams has to take responsibility for her dead sister's kid, she distances herself by building a robot to handle parenting for her, and it goes badly. Scripted by Akela Cooper with the same shamelessly messy, giddy verve she brought to Malignant, M3GAN is described as a good time for knowledgeable horror fans, packed with referential humor but still channeling real anxiety about the place computers have in people's lives and how far that will eventually go.



---


# The Thing: A Paranoid Thriller Premise Wrapped In Alien Gore

The Thing is John Carpenter's postmodern creature feature, starring Kurt Russell, Wilford Brimley and Keith David, and available on Peacock. It takes the idea of alien monsters and makes them simultaneously more recognisable and more gross and unworldly than in any other movie in history; the second adaptation of the novella Who Goes There?, it remains thrilling, terrifying and absolutely disgusting more than 40 years after its release.

The setup: a group of researchers work at an Antarctic base when a dog from a local Norwegian camp rushes in, with Norwegian men hot on its heels trying to kill it by any means necessary. Once the American crew takes the dog in and shelters it, they discover it is an alien that can transform into any living creature, mimicking it perfectly — which makes every one of them a suspect. That is one of the great paranoid thriller premises of all time, and it just so happens to also be filled with gross and fantastic alien gore. There's nothing quite like The Thing.



---


# Scorsese's Self-Implication in Killers of the Flower Moon

Polygon's claim, published 2023-10-26, is that Killers of the Flower Moon is a classic Scorsese Catholic reckoning in which the director expresses guilt and culpability as a beneficiary of inequality — a level of awareness that goes beyond the introverted morality plays he grappled with earlier in his career, and a mature framing of the individual and the responsibilities we have toward one another on a societal scale.

The grounds are both textual and literal. This time Scorsese is concerned with white supremacy and systemic racism, full of unsparing and punishing conclusions and self-recriminations in the wake of George Floyd's death and the 2020 protests; in a press conference on Oct. 16 he described the film as "a story of complicity, a story of sin by omission." And in the movie's closing minutes he literally puts himself squarely in the frame.

The warrant is contested, and Polygon says so. In a charitable light, adding himself to the movie as the voice of its final reckoning is a bold statement of accountability; in an uncharitable light it plays as performative, like an older relative getting worked up over a police brutality Facebook post. Polygon concludes it is too early to decide how the film tags into our present historical moment or how it will be remembered, with many viewings and conversations ahead.



---


# Apostle (Gareth Evans)

Apostle is Gareth Evans' Netflix-exclusive folk horror film — a grimy, extremely gory period piece that goes to startling extremes — and the Oct. 5 pick in Polygon's 2023-10-10 Halloween Countdown.

Polygon opens with a warning not to confuse Gareth Edwards, director of The Creator and Rogue One: A Star Wars Story, with Gareth Evans, director of the Raid movies: viewers who do may sit down expecting expansive, detail-driven science fiction and be unpleasantly surprised.

The film deliberately starts in roughly the same place as the classic 1973 suspense thriller The Wicker Man, with a lone man heading to a remote Welsh island after getting a letter suggesting his sister is being held there against her will by a dangerous cult. Worming his way into the community by pretending to be a convert, Thomas — played by Dan Stevens, even more feral and intense than he is in The Guest or Beauty and the Beast — inevitably discovers a lot of nasty work going on. Critic Tasha Robinson writes that Evans charts his own course, veering far from the Wicker Man mold into much bloodier territory while taking advantage of some of the same ideas: the ominous isolation of the island, the close-knit secrecy of its community, and the predatory ideas that have flourished there under charismatic leadership. Stevens is particularly terrific, lunging from one scene to the next like a humanoid wolf who can barely contain his bloodlust, and Thomas has plenty of closely held secrets of his own; Evans' commitment to violent mayhem gives the film memorable moments likely to haunt you later, in the dark.



---


# John Wick: Chapter 4

John Wick: Chapter 4 is Chad Stahelski's fourth entry in the saga about the boogeyman of assassins in a world full of them, starring Keanu Reeves, Donnie Yen, and Ian McShane. Polygon ranked it 12 on its best movies of 2023 list of 2023-10-07 and listed it on Starz or for digital rental/purchase.

Polygon's premise summary is that John Wick has only ever wanted to fuck off and retire, and no one seems to get the message. The film reaches a staggering crescendo, somehow managing to run faster and hit harder than three previous movies dedicated to constant escalation.

Facing off against action legends Donnie Yen and Scott Adkins, Keanu Reeves pushes John Wick harder and farther than before, in a film that critic JR describes as raging against the untouchably wealthy and their expectation that the world be in their service.



---


# Infinity Pool (Brandon Cronenberg)

Infinity Pool is Brandon Cronenberg's third film, starring Alexander Skarsgård, Mia Goth, and Cleopatra Coleman, ranked 41 on Polygon's best movies of 2023 list of 2023-10-07 and available on Hulu or for digital rental/purchase.

Its premise is that death does not have to be real in the world of the film — at least not if you are rich enough to turn it into a fun night out. Polygon says the film, from the director of 2020's stellar Possessor, gazes into the bizarre void of identity and wonders what happens when it gazes back.

Polygon's Austen Goslin calls it queasy and fascinating, and perhaps 2023's most nihilistic view of wealth, while naming the real selling point as the go-for-broke central performances by Mia Goth and Alexander Skarsgård.



---


# The Movie's Simplified Lore Cuts Against the "For the Fans" Framing

Polygon's 2023-10-26 guide pushes back on the premise that the Five Nights at Freddy's movie was made purely to please longtime fans: fans hungering for an exploration or expansion of the game series' continuing mythology should prepare themselves to see something more simplified.

As is typical enough for an adaptation, some of the more complicated lore has been stripped out, though it could probably be reintroduced in any sequel.

The consequence undercuts the producer's stated approach directly: this does make the movie more accessible for franchise newcomers, whether Blum wanted that or not. Polygon adds a second disappointment for fans — they might expect more screen time than they actually get for the core animatronics team of Freddy, Bonnie, Chica, Foxy, and Carl the Cupcake.



---


# Silent Hill (2006 Film Adaptation)

Silent Hill is the 2006 film adaptation of the video game series, and Polygon argues it deserved so much better than the moment it arrived in. It was the Oct. 20 pick in the 2023-10-10 Halloween Countdown, listed on Peacock.

Polygon situates it in a no man's land for horror movies: by 2006 audiences were four years out from the blockbuster prestige of Gore Verbinski's The Ring and the J-horror import boom that followed it in America, and only just beginning to transition into the Saw-dominated years of "realistic" horror, still almost a decade away from the arthouse horror boom that would kick off closer to 2014 with films like It Follows.

The story follows Rose, whose daughter Sharon is plagued with awful episodes of sleepwalking and nightmares about the mysterious abandoned town of Silent Hill. Rose brings Sharon to the town in a last-ditch attempt to find answers, but things go horribly wrong when the fog-shrouded town seems to transport them, along with police officer Cybil Bennett, to a new monstrous dimension; meanwhile Rose's husband Christopher sets off to Silent Hill to find his family. Inside the town the film takes the most inspiration from the games, with some of Silent Hill's most recognizable enemies and monsters chasing Cybil, Sharon, and Rose through the town and eventually into the iconic Pyramid Head — segments critic AG calls impressively scary and steeped in the dreadful atmosphere that made the games famous.

Goslin's favorite part comes when Christopher arrives: rather than finding his family, all he finds is an abandoned mining town, so for most of the movie the women's frantic running and hiding from monsters is paralleled by Christopher wandering the exact same areas, filled with a dreadful sense that his family is close but completely unable to see them or the horrors threatening to kill them. He calls it not a subtle metaphor for the differences in the ways men and women go through the world, but an effective one that creates a level of crushing existential terror and defeat few movies ever come close to.



---


# Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem

Mutant Mayhem, directed by Jeff Rowe with Seth Rogen as executive producer and voiced by Micah Abbey, Shamon Brown Jr., Nicolas Cantu, and Brady Noon, asserts itself as one of the most visually impressive animated films of the post-Into the Spider-Verse era. Polygon ranked it 28 on its best movies of 2023 list of 2023-10-07 and listed it on Paramount Plus or for digital rental/purchase.

A modern reboot of the classic TMNT origin story, the film emphasizes the fact that everyone's favorite anthropomorphic reptilian warriors are, well, teenagers, with all the stupid, fun-loving shenanigans that come with being an adolescent.

Polygon's Toussaint Egan writes that from the character designs and lighting to the action sequences and soundtrack, everything in the film pops with its own unique oddball charm that breathes new life into a beloved franchise — a certified banger whether you are new to the Turtles or a longtime fan.
