# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Search As Private Infrastructure, Not A Public Library

The claim is that routing nearly all online information through a single private company has left us arguably worse off than before, because information that is controlled by a private business will always be subject to that business's bottom line — which is exactly why most countries around the world have libraries that are public institutions.

The grounds are a comparison with what the internet was supposed to be. In the beginning it was seen as an improvement on the spirit of the public library: an opportunity to transcend the gatekeepers controlling who could publish a book, allowing mankind to fully connect and share knowledge. Instead, nearly all online information runs through a single company, which assumes a veneer of civic utility, of impassive authority, when it is very much not a neutral entity.

Matt Cutts supplies the insider warrant that the veneer is doing work. "There were so many true believers at Google in the early days," he said. "As companies get big, it gets harder to get things done. Inevitably, people start to think about profit or quarterly numbers." He claimed that, at least while he was there, search quality always came before financial goals, but he believes the public underestimates how Google is shaping what they see: "I deeply, deeply, deeply believe search engines are newspaper-like entities, making editorial decisions." He speculated that the company did not want the public to think too hard about how search works because that awareness "encourages regulators and makes people realize, 'Oh, there's a lot of money here.'"

The consequence is epistemic rather than commercial. There has always been advertising and polemics from cranks, scammers, and liars, but now we see this stuff surfacing alongside truth and we cannot tell the difference, so we move through our lives with a greater sense of distrust and fear and insecurity. At the end of the day, it is Google's world, and the SEOs are only living in it.



---


# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.



---


# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.



---


# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.



---


# Google's Most Lucrative Search Terms, Unsealed At Trial

Judge Amit Mehta ruled to make public a list that provides a glimpse of which search terms make Google the most money: 20 terms that were lucrative for the week of September 22, 2018. Revenue per search term, how many queries each of those terms got, and a separate list of popular search terms ordered by queries rather than revenue were all redacted, so the disclosure is a bare ranking without magnitudes.

The visible list, in order, is: iPhone 8; iPhone 8 plus; Auto insurance; Car insurance; Cheap flights; Car insurance quotes; DirecTV; Online colleges; AT&T; Hulu; iPhone; Uber; Spectrum; Comcast; Xfinity; Insurance quotes; Free credit report; Cheap car insurance; AARP; LifeLock.

TechCrunch read little surprise into it. Google and Apple have a long and mutually beneficial relationship even while competing, so three Apple search-related queries bringing in the big bucks is unsurprising — not least since September 22, 2017 was the official release date of the iPhone 8. Queries like "car insurance," "cheap flights" and "credit report" are perennial favorites and speak to how much Google dominates vertical search, that is, search in very specific market categories. As for LifeLock, the big Equifax data breach of 2017 was a hot topic in September 2017 and LifeLock was making a big push to win business with people who wanted to buy identity theft protection.



---


# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.



---


# The SEO-Algorithm Update Cycle

Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# The Defense Of SEO As Legitimate Work

Barry Schwartz rejects the premise that the industry is filled with con artists: "There are a lot of scammers in every single business. It's just easier to call yourself an SEO than a doctor." Schwartz is an unbelievably fast talker and a prolific writer who has spent the past two decades covering SEO for the trade rag Search Engine Land, and both in conversation and in his work he has defended SEO as a legitimate, dignified pursuit: "The search community is filled with hard-working individuals working to help their clients' websites succeed in Google Search. That success is not done through dark, corrupt or shady tactics but rather hard, smart and thorough work."

Several people made a similar point: the best SEOs are the ones that follow Google's rules, which essentially ask you to make amazing websites without even thinking about Google. You are not supposed to make any attempt to artificially boost a website's ranking; you are supposed to be designing websites for human readers, not for the algorithm — and many SEOs do exactly this kind of work, rewriting copy, making a site load more quickly, and so on.

The defense has a limit the article presses on. The existence of good SEOs does not negate the presence of scammers and idiots and people who get ahead by violating Google's terms of service, just as the mild-mannered teacher's pet in a classroom does not negate the obnoxious shouting of the kids who refuse to behave; a few loud kids can easily drown everyone else out. Even Schwartz acknowledged the effect rule-breaking SEOs have had on the internet experience. Asked how he himself would find a reliable attorney — lawyers, accountants and contractors being particularly lucrative SEO customers because they are eager for attention from people going online for local recommendations — he answered: "I don't know if you can trust anything you read online. Maybe you ask a friend."



---


# "Go Big In Europe": Google's Post-Fine Search Quality Push

The government argued on November 10, 2023 that Google only endeavored to enhance its search engine in the European Union after it was hit by a €5 billion antitrust fine in 2018 — a claim internal documents revealed, according to Bloomberg.

The EU's antitrust order forced Google to offer Android phone users a screen with five search engine options to choose from, according to the DOJ. In response, Google enacted a plan its executives dubbed "Go Big in Europe," to enhance search results in France and Germany in 2019 and 2020 with more local content: news, post-game soccer video highlights, information on local television options for streaming, and pronunciation practice for different languages. The aim was to incentivize users to click on Google's home screen rather than the competition's.

That revelation effectively supports the Justice Department's argument that Google, without the push of competition, has little incentive to improve its products — a classic consequence in a monopoly.



---


# SEOs Also Say Search Results Have Improved

The strongest challenge to the article's premise is that Sullivan was not the only person insisting search results have improved significantly: out of the dozen-plus SEOs the writer spoke with at length, nearly every single one said search results are way better than they used to be — just objectively more accurate, more useful, more difficult to manipulate.

What gives that testimony force is the absence of an incentive to flatter Google. Except for Sullivan, these were not people with a reason to praise the company; if anything, these were folks who lamented how much harder it had become for them to take advantage of Google.

The effect on the writer was disorientation rather than conviction. This was not what she had been noticing, and certainly not what she had been hearing from friends and journalists and friends who are journalists. Were all of us wrong, or engulfed in some kind of Baader-Meinhof frequency bias delusion? Had she been researching a nonexistent problem? Were Google results actually amazing? Truly, she had lost the plot — was the premise of the piece completely off, and was she the asshole who deserved to be attacked by an alligator?



---


# Firefox's Yahoo Default Search Switch, As Recounted By Mitchell Baker

On November 1, 2023, Mozilla CEO Mitchell Baker provided a defense of Google's quality as a search engine, even in "competitive" environments, by recounting how Mozilla "failed" when it switched Firefox's default search engine from Google to Yahoo. Baker was providing a recorded deposition for Google's defense, and she noted that Mozilla's users apparently wanted and expected Google.

The backstory: Yahoo inked a deal with Mozilla back in 2014 to pay the browser maker $375 million annually to be the default search engine on Firefox, at a time when Google was offering $276 million, said Baker. TechCrunch's verdict was that it was a bad deal.

Baker's account of why, according to Bloomberg: "I felt strongly that Yahoo was not delivering the search experience we needed and had contracted for." Yahoo had promised to reduce the number of ads and offer less user tracking, she said, but ended up gradually serving users more ads anyway. "The number of users who stayed with Firefox declined noticeably during the years when Yahoo was the default," said Baker.



---


# Expedia's Testimony On Google Ad Costs And Organic Listings

On November 1, 2023, Barry Diller, chair of Expedia and IAC, testified about his concerns that the increasing number of ads in search results was having an impact on organic listings. Quoting a letter he had written to Google back in 2019, per Bloomberg: "I must say I'm on the edge of revolt now that Google's actions are so punitive, not just for Expedia but also for IAC and all the players that depend upon something of a level playing field." Google CEO Sundar Pichai fired back that Google's travel listings was one of the most popular experiences the company built.

Expedia executives also testified about the cost of ads and how increases had no impact on search results. On October 19, 2023, Expedia's former chief operating officer, Jeff Hurst, told the court that the company's ad fees increased tenfold, from $21 million in 2015 to $290 million in 2019, and yet Expedia's traffic from Google did not increase. The implication was that this was due to direct competition from Google itself; Hurst pointed out that Google began sharing its own flight and hotel data in search results in that period, according to The Seattle Times.



---


# Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.



---


# Deft's Revenue Model And Pricing Tiers

Deft does not show ads on its platform — the discriminating feature against the incumbents it criticizes. It relies on affiliate commissions to generate revenue, but wants subscriptions to be its primary revenue driver.

Deft is currently testing two paid tiers: a $10 a month plan, which will offer better search customization to filter out some brands, and a $20 per month plan, which will enable a personal shopping service that will continue to look for suitable products even after you stop searching manually.

Its roadmap moves outward from its own site: Deft aims to release a browser extension that helps users search for products by the end of 2023 or early 2024, and in the next three years wants to build and release search APIs that other e-commerce sites could use.



---


# Google's Denial That Search Quality Has Declined

Danny Sullivan rejects the premise that Google results have gone downhill — because they have not, he insisted; if anything, search results have gotten a lot better over time, and anyone who thought search quality was worse needed to take a hard look in the mirror.

His alternative explanation puts the change in the users, not the engine: "We have an entire generation that grew up expecting the search box to do the work for them," he said. "We might do a better job of matching for a bulk of people, but for people who are super sensitive, when they have that fail moment, now it becomes, 'All my searches aren't good.'" The problem was not Google; the problem was not SEOs; the problem was kids these days.

He also rejects the secondary charge of reduced transparency. Speaking on the phone with a communications chaperone on the line, Sullivan came across as angry and defensive, annoyed that anyone would think his era at Google has been less transparent than Cutts': "We have reams of help documents! We have more people assigned to work with SEOs than we did when Matt worked here!" He is frustrated that people want to know every last detail about Google's algorithm because even "if we listed all one thousand of the ranking signals" and how much each was worth, that would not actually help SEOs do their jobs better anyway.

The interest that qualifies the denial is stated plainly: of course Sullivan would say this — he works for Google. The contrast with Cutts is what many SEOs pointed to as a turning point emblematic of Google's transition from idealistic startup to one of the most valuable and powerful companies to ever exist: over the phone Cutts came off as humble and thoughtful, acknowledging the nuances and challenges of the search engine business, while Sullivan sounded like an impatient corporate stooge, trying to gaslight the writer into believing the sky was red.



---


# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# The 2016 ISA Renegotiation And Its Revenue-Share Dispute

Eddy Cue testified that when Apple and Google renegotiated the ISA, Apple wanted a higher percentage of the revenue Google made from the Apple users it directed to the search engine, while Sundar Pichai wanted to keep the deal as it was; the two eventually compromised on some other number that was not disclosed in open court, and Google has been paying Apple that amount since.

Discussion of specific numbers was reserved for closed court sessions. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw asked Cue whether he would have walked away from the deal if the two sides couldn't agree on a revenue-share figure, and Cue said he had never really considered that an option: "I always felt like it was in Google's best interest, and our best interest, to get a deal done." Cue also argued that the deal was about more than economics, that Apple never seriously considered switching to another provider or building its own search product, and that "certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time" — adding that there still isn't one.

# YouTube's AI Music Incubator And Its Rightsholder Pledges

During its period of discussions with the majors, YouTube made a series of announcements aimed at the biggest issue for any rightsholder regarding AI-driven voice replication of artists: their ability to police it.

In August, YouTube and Universal Music Group jointly announced that the video platform was launching an "AI Music Incubator" — a program by which new tools and innovations would be developed at YouTube in close conjunction with artists and the music business; to progress the incubator, YouTube said it was working behind the scenes with a number of UMG-affiliated artists. Also in August, YouTube publicly committed to three principles or pledges behind its development of music-based generative AI tools. These pledges promised "appropriate protections… for music partners who decide to participate" in such tools, and promised "invest[ment] in the AI-powered technology" that, among other things, would help YouTube "protect our community of viewers, creators, artists and songwriters… [from] trademark and copyright abuse" — all of which seemed to hint at a desire to build a "Content ID"-style system on YouTube to control and police content made by cloning artists' voices. Then, earlier in November, YouTube announced it was developing a specific system for music partners allowing them to request the removal of content on its platform that "mimics an artist's unique singing or rapping voice."



---


# UMG And WMG's Licensing Of "Dream Track"

Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group both dipped a toe into YouTube's "Dream Track" experiment — though not without caution — with UMG granting a limited license.

Sir Lucian Grainge, Chairman and CEO of Universal Music Group, said of the decision: "We have a fundamental responsibility to our artists to ensure the digital ecosystem evolves to protect them and their work against unauthorized exploitation, including by generative AI platforms. At the same time, we must help artists achieve their greatest creative and commercial potential – in part by providing them access to the kind of opportunities and cutting-edge creative tools made possible by AI." Robert Kyncl, CEO of Warner Music Group and an ex-high flyer at YouTube, commented: "With each major leap in technology, the music industry navigates a fresh set of challenges and opportunities. It's not always the case that, from the outset, tech platforms partner with artists, songwriters, labels, and publishers to experiment, iterate, and find possible solutions. YouTube is taking a collaborative approach with this Beta. These artists are being offered the choice to lean in, and we're pleased to experiment and find out what the creators come up with."

# YouTube's "Dream Track" Voice Cloning Experiment

On November 16, 2023 YouTube unveiled "Dream Track," an experiment enabling creators to clone the vocals, via AI tech and with official consent, of well-known stars.

Charlie Puth's voice is on there. John Legend's voice is on there. Demi Lovato's voice is on there. In fact the voices of a number of well-known recording artists signed to Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group — or labels within each major — are on there. Something conspicuous is not: any endorsement whatsoever from the world's second-biggest recording company, Sony Music Entertainment, or its artists.



---


# Which Artists Joined "Dream Track", And The Licensing Questions That Follow

MBW's closing observation is that the artists who agreed, with their record companies, to enter the YouTube "Dream Track" trial are stars — but in the case of both Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group they are, currently anyway, not the biggest megastars on either company's books.

The reasoning is that you might not expect, at this early stage, for the likes of UMG to put forward Drake, Taylor Swift, or The Beatles — or for WMG to put forward Ed Sheeran or Dua Lipa — to be guinea pigs in any early AI music experiments, even ones run by "friends" of the music industry like YouTube. From that observation MBW raises two open questions: whether there have been significant licensing payments made by YouTube to UMG and WMG for the right to play with the AI vocals of artists who have signed off on Dream Track thus far, and if so, whether these payments are being placed against any as-yet-unrecouped advances that some of these artists may have on their label accounts. More broadly, MBW poses a bigger question: when the day comes that YouTube asks the world's biggest superstars to wholeheartedly embrace "Dream Track", will Google's recent US Copyright Office filing give those superstars — and their record companies — pause for thought?



---


# Google's Copyright Filing Against YouTube's Music Reassurances

MBW's counter to the idea that YouTube's rightsholder assurances settle the matter is that Google's take on copyright "harvesting" by generative AI models sits in odd contrast to the copyright-related reassurances YouTube was careful to make to the music industry during the pre-development, development, and trial launch of "Dream Track."

The premise attacked is that the platform relationship and the parent company's legal position can be read separately. MBW's sources close to Sony Music were keen to point out that the company's general ongoing relationship with YouTube and YouTube Music is a harmonious one — YouTube is now the second largest commercial partner of the major record companies, with a stated ambition to catch up with Spotify in the years ahead, and says it paid out over USD $6 billion to music rightsholders in the year to end of June 2022, with around $2 billion of that coming just from ads on user-generated content. However, the October US Copyright Office filing from Google has definitely put the cat amongst the pigeons at Sony Music HQ, as MBW is sure it has at the other two major record companies, because of its position that "Any prohibition or limitation on the use of copyrighted materials for purposes of AI training would undermine the purpose of copyright and foreclose the many opportunities that come with this technology." As well as part-explaining Sony Music's refusal to be included in Dream Track thus far, Google's USCO filing also perhaps explains the careful words selected by Robert Kyncl and especially Sir Lucian Grainge in their respective comments endorsing YouTube's AI experiment — Grainge's statement, after all, began: "We have a fundamental responsibility to our artists to ensure the digital ecosystem evolves to protect them and their work against unauthorized exploitation, including by generative AI platforms…"

# Sony Music's Absence From "Dream Track"

Dennis Kooker's public statements on AI arrived a week after MBW pointed out a notable lack of endorsement from Sony Music Entertainment, and its artists, of YouTube's experimental AI project "Dream Track," which lets creators clone the vocals of successful musicians.

The initial cohort of stars involved in the project included recording artists signed to Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group — or labels within each of those two majors — but no Sony Music artists. In its earlier report MBW suggested that YouTube parent Google's recent submission to the United States Copyright Office, made in response to a request for written submissions as part of a study around copyright law and policy issues raised by AI systems, may have influenced Sony's absence from Dream Track.

# Sony Music's "Artist-Led" Approach To AI

Sources close to Sony Music's HQ in New York have suggested to MBW that the company is taking an "artist-led" approach to its experiments with any AI platform that can manipulate the work or voice of its roster — which is offered as the explanation for why Sony did not join Universal and Warner in "Dream Track."

The grounds are that Sony did not decline on principle. MBW understands that Sony Music, the recorded music arm of Sony Music Group, had like Universal and Warner been in discussions for months with YouTube over potentially licensing the experiment, and the company had shown its own willingness to experiment with generative AI music platforms that same week via an announcement about a project with David Gilmour, The Orb, and AI company Vermillio. In the case of Dream Track, MBW understands, Sony first offered the opportunity to participate to a number of its artists, but this group of acts did not show enthusiasm about participating. MBW notes that if one of these artists was Bad Bunny, signed to Sony's The Orchard, the reluctance is easy to see: the Puerto Rican superstar had expressed fury the other week about a popular track on TikTok that had cloned his vocal stylings via AI.

# Sony Music's Pipeline Of AI Startup Partnerships

Kooker said Sony Music has "roughly 200 active conversations taking place with startups and established players" right now about building new AI-related products and tools, and that some of these conversations "also include potential equity investments which would accelerate the development of these companies."

He framed this as the optimistic counterweight to the harms: despite the negative impacts of AI, including unauthorized clones and low-quality AI music, there are still "many positive and optimistic developments to highlight," and he highlighted legitimate AI startups and established firms "with music ideas that want to partner with the industry." The products under discussion range from tools for "creative or marketing assistance," to tools that "potentially give us the ability to better protect artist content or find it when used in an unauthorized fashion," as well as "brand new products that have never been launched before."

# Sony Music's Deepfake Takedowns And Support For The No FAKES Act

Dennis Kooker reported in his November 29, 2023 speech that Sony Music Entertainment has to date sent "close to 10,000 takedowns to a variety of platforms hosting unauthorized deepfakes that SME artists asked us to take down."

He openly discussed the company's efforts to get unauthorized AI content removed from platforms online, and named the obstacle: "platforms are quick to point to the loopholes in the law as an excuse to drag their feet or to not take the deepfakes down when requested." Kooker commended the No FAKES Act policy drafted by senators earlier in 2023, which he explained "would create a federal property right in one's voice or visual likeness and protect against unauthorized AI-generated replicas."

# Thesis That Music Labels Are Headed for Irrelevance

The argument, common among music business observers from the world of tech, is that record labels could in the long term be headed for irrelevance. Its grounds are the arrival of digital platforms, including open ones like YouTube and SoundCloud, together with the proliferation of indie music distribution platforms such as DistroKid and TikTok's SoundOn.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is a claim about what labels are for: in a world where anyone can record music using a desktop audio workstation (DAW) and upload it directly to YouTube, or to Spotify via a distribution platform, labels have little left to do. Recording and distribution — the functions the label historically supplied — are available to any artist directly, so on this reasoning the label's remaining role shrinks toward nothing. Music Business Worldwide presented this as the speculation that tech-world observers "like to" make, and as the position Warner Music Group CEO Robert Kyncl was answering at the Code Conference in September 2023.

# YouTube Content ID as Blueprint for AI Rights Management

Robert Kyncl's model treats the solutions built for user-generated content as a "blueprint" that can be applied to AI-generated content on platforms. The analogy has three parts: the explosion of AI use among the public maps onto the explosion of user-generated content (UGC) a decade or two ago; just as UGC often infringed copyright, AI threatens the rights of artists and music rights holders; and therefore the same class of remedy should apply.

The remedy he describes is YouTube's Content ID. "When YouTube was formed… people started to upload content, including copyrighted material, which, obviously, put YouTube into hot water with lots of different copyright holders. And I had the privilege of working through a lot of that and fix it up. But we made a very important decision, which was to go above and beyond the law, and build a fingerprinting software that allowed us to track the copyright on our platform, and then have commercial relationship[s] with copyright holders to send them the money. Out of that we built a multi-billion-dollar business, which now is a multi-billion-dollar business per year. And it was an incredible new revenue stream for everyone. AI is that with new super tools." Content ID scours uploaded videos for copyrighted content, video and audio, then offers the copyright owner the option to monetise that video or to request that it be taken down — a system that has essentially allowed YouTube users to upload content without paying much attention to copyright while ensuring copyright owners are paid.

Two conditions bound the model. First, the same thoughtfulness must be applied to AI as was applied to UGC, and "we have to make sure that artists have a choice" — detection alone is not the point; owner election between monetisation and takedown is. Second, refusal is not available as a strategy: "You have to embrace technology, because it's not like you can put technology in a bottle. The genie is not going back."

Universal Music Group, Concord Music Group and ABKCO filed a lawsuit against AI developer Anthropic seeking potentially tens of millions of dollars for the alleged "systematic and widespread infringement of their copyrighted song lyrics."

Music Business Worldwide noted on 2023-11-30 that the fair use argument Anthropic had advanced in its submission to the US Copyright Office could yet come into play in the company's legal battle with Universal.

# AI Developers Should Be Required To License Training Material

The NMPA's second demand is that AI developers be required to license the materials they use for training and keep records of them — not that music never be used for AI training, but that developers license it, not unlike how streaming services, bars and restaurants, or movie producers license music.

Many key players in the music industry and beyond have been adamant that using copyrighted works to train AI algorithms without authorization is copyright infringement, and a number of lawsuits have been launched against AI companies on these grounds. The NMPA's grounds for feasibility are practical: "Licensing musical works before training use is both required and practicable," the submission states, adding that "there are well developed processes in place for technology ventures to obtain free market licenses on a large scale." Scale is the operative condition, given that AI algorithms such as large language models are trained on countless millions or even billions of pieces of digital data. The NMPA points to existing activity as evidence that work on licensing "is already underway," citing news reports earlier in 2023 that UMG, along with Warner Music Group, were in talks with Google to secure licenses for artists' vocals and musical melodies to create AI-generated songs.

# The US Copyright Office's 2023 Study Of AI And Copyright

The US Copyright Office is spearheading one of the key US efforts to address AI and copyright: in the summer of 2023 it issued a call for submissions on the issue of AI and copyright, with the goal of putting together a study to "help assess whether legislative or regulatory steps in this area are warranted."

The call for submissions came as legislators and regulators around the world grappled with the many issues that had emerged since AI technology "went mainstream" about a year earlier. Numerous businesses involved in AI, and those with substantial copyright holdings, submitted their thoughts on the issue — including Universal Music Group and AI developer Anthropic.



---


# UMG's USCO Filing Rejecting Fair Use For AI Training

Universal Music Group's response to the US Copyright Office rejected the notion that using copyrighted material to train large language models is "fair use" — a position MBW called unsurprising and the starkest possible contrast to Google's assertion that prohibiting or limiting the use of copyrighted materials for AI training would undermine the purpose of copyright and foreclose the opportunities of the technology.

The filing's own example puts the claim bluntly: "The wholesale appropriation of UMG's enormous catalog of copyright-protected sound recordings and musical compositions to build multibillion commercial enterprises [in AI] is anything but fair use."



---


# Kooker's Rebuttal Of The Tech Industry's "Distorted View Of Copyright"

Dennis Kooker used his November 29, 2023 speech to attack the premise of the tech industry's Copyright Office submissions directly, telling Senators that "based on recent Copyright Office filings it is clear that the technology industry and speculative financial investors would like governments to believe in a very distorted view of copyright."

He commented directly on the flurry of submissions to the USCO from the tech industry at the end of October, in what may have been a nod to Google's filing and its "fair use" position. The premise he identified and rejected was this: "[That view is] one in which music is considered fair use for training purposes and in which certain companies are permitted to appropriate the entire value produced by the creative sector without permission, and to build huge businesses based on it without paying anything to the creators concerned."

# Kyncl Prediction: Music Is the First Industry to Feel AI's Impact

Robert Kyncl's proposition, put at the Code Conference in September 2023, is that the music business will be out ahead of other industries in exploiting the potential of AI, and — out of necessity — also ahead on the question of how to regulate and monetise the use of AI by non-rights-holders. He attached a date to it: asked when that sea change would occur, he said "I would say within the next year you will see lots of evolution around AI… What you will likely see is increasing quality at a very fast pace."

His reasoning is structural rather than accidental. "Music – because it's so broadly distributed and it's so well aligned with the internet, because it's short format, it lends itself to recommendations, it's on all platforms – is generally first in most transformations and most innovations. So it digitizes first." He generalises from the previous cycle: "Whatever happened to the music industry 20 years ago is starting to happen in the movies and TV shows now. In the meantime, music emerged out of [digitization] better and stronger and more resilient. So, I would imagine the same will happen here, which is we'll likely be first."

The hypothesis is falsifiable on two fronts as stated. It fails if other industries, rather than music, lead on both exploiting and regulating AI; and it fails on its own timetable if the year following September 2023 does not bring the predicted rapid evolution and fast-rising quality in AI. Because the argument rests on music's broad distribution, short format and recommendation-friendliness, an AI transformation that arrives first in a long-format medium would also count against the mechanism he proposes.

# AI Copyright And Training Disputes

Universal Music Group's answer to generative AI trained on its catalogue rejects the premise that such training is a neutral technical act, recasting it as a choice of allegiance: "The training of generative AI using our artists' music . . . begs the question as to which side of history all stakeholders in the music ecosystem want to be on: the side of artists, fans and human creative expression, or on the side of deep fakes, fraud and denying artists their due compensation," the label said after a song using AI to imitate Drake and The Weeknd, two of its artists, went viral.

A second objection cuts against the label framing itself. These same conversations and contradictions are manifesting across creative industries, but artists themselves don't always have a seat at the table — so an industry-level statement of grievance is not the same thing as artists speaking for themselves. Independent artists in particular are learning that their voices resonate louder when coming together across disciplines to push back against what Holland describes as an "extraordinary spectrum of exploitation" that leverages their work.

The dispute is not confined to music. In a roundtable hosted by the FTC that same week, the agency brought together figures from across creative industries — from voice acting and science fiction to screenwriting, music, illustration and even fashion — to delve into how generative AI is affecting creatives. TechCrunch reported the exchange on 2023-10-06.

# Sony Music's Generative AI Principles For Congress

Dennis Kooker, Sony Music Entertainment's President of Global Digital Business & US Sales, asked Congress at the November 29, 2023 AI Insight Forum to embrace a set of five principles around generative AI, on the argument that "if copyrights are protected and enforced appropriately, we are at the beginning of a multi-decade marathon that will change the creative and commercial landscape for music."

The framing condition Kooker set is that "Music is a tremendous driver for AI technology, and AI technology presents a tremendous opportunity for the creative development of music. But these opportunities must be grounded by the human creators' vision with the machine assisting, not with the machine replacing the human creator." The principles are: Assure Consent, Compensation, and Credit — "New products and businesses built with music must be developed with the consent of the owner and appropriate compensation and credit. It is essential to understand why the training of AI models is being done, what products will be developed as a result, and what the business model is that will monetize the use of the artist's work. Congress and the agencies should assure that creators' rights are recognized and respected." Confirm That Copying Music to Train AI Models is Not Fair Use — "Even worse are those that argue that copyrighted content should automatically be considered fair use so that protected works are never compensated for usage and creators have no say in the products or business models that are developed around them and their work. Congress should assure and agencies should presume that reproducing music to train AI models, in itself, is not a fair use." Prevent the Cloning of Artists' Voices and Likenesses Without Express Permission — "We cannot allow an artist's voice or likeness to be cloned for use without the express permission of the artist. This is a very personal decision for the artist. Congress should pass into law effective federal protections for name, image, and likeness." Incentivize Accurate Recordkeeping — "Correct attribution will be a critical element to artists being paid fairly and correctly for new works that are created. In addition, rights can only be enforced around the training of AI when there are accurate records about what is being copied. Otherwise, the inability to enforce rights in the AI marketplace equates to a lack of rights at all, producing a dangerous imbalance that prevents a thriving ecosystem. This requires strong and accurate record keeping by the generative AI platforms, a requirement that urgently needs legislative support to ensure incentives are in place so that it happens consistently and correctly." And Assure Transparency for Consumers and Artists — "Transparency is necessary to clearly distinguish human-created works from AI-created works. The public should know, when they are listening to music, whether that music was created by a human being or a machine." MBW summarised the intended effect: "The principles will ensure that intellectual property businesses can succeed in this new world alongside tech partners, further advancing investment and expanding economic opportunities."



---


# The EU AI Act's Training Data Disclosure Rule

The European Union's proposed AI Act contains a rule that would require AI developers to disclose whether their AI had been trained on copyrighted materials — going some, if not all, of the way toward the transparency regime the NMPA sought.

As of MBW's 2023-11-30 report the Act was still the subject of back-and-forth negotiations between the European Commission and the European Parliament, so the rule was proposed rather than in force. Transparency in the use of AI is also becoming a rule on social media sites where AI-generated content is likely to appear: both TikTok and YouTube have passed rules requiring AI-generated content to be labeled as such.



---


# The EU-US Asymmetry In Recorded Music Performance Rights

At the heart of the dispute is a difference in how the US and the EU pay artists for terrestrial (non-satellite) radio broadcasts of music and recorded music played in bars and restaurants.

In Europe, when recorded music is played over terrestrial radio or in venues, performance rights payments must be made to the artists and labels behind the recording, as well as to the songwriters and publishers who own the composition behind the recording. In the US, by contrast, performance rights payments are made only to the songwriters and publishers, and not to artists and labels.



---


# The Material Reciprocity Principle In Music Royalties

Because of the EU-US asymmetry, European countries largely followed the "reciprocity principle" written into international copyright treaties such as the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty of 1996: in those countries where artists and labels are paid performance rights, there was no obligation to pay US artists and labels, since European artists did not receive those payments from airplay in the US.

The artists' groups' statement defends the principle in general terms, saying it "has proven vital in raising the level of copyright protection across the globe for decades."



---


# The Digital-First Artist Development Model

The success of "Si No Estás" illustrates how much artist development has changed: social media and digital music services have now become the number one source of music discovery, and Believe has developed an innovative, AI and data-driven expertise to develop tracks and artists that Alejandra Olea describes as unique in the music industry.

The model's components and their relations are stated together: the key to success is great partnerships with the artist and their label, and being able to combine strong AI data-driven expertise to maximise momentum for an artist and a track at the right time with the right tools and the right partnerships, supported by both local and global teams. Olea singles out the last element as particularly important and truly one of Believe's strengths, being able to mobilise teams multi-locally and globally to accompany audience development for artists. The forward-looking claim attached to the model is that this is only the beginning for Iñigo Quintero and that Believe anticipates many more successes like his in future.



---


# Deepfakes And Unauthorized Voice Clones Harm Artists

Kooker argued that the "more dire outputs of early generative AI technology are deep fakes and unauthorized voice clones" of artists, and that in the United States artists are not adequately protected from these deepfakes.

The grounds are economic and reputational. "An artist literally makes their livelihood from their voice," he said. "Deep fakes intentionally exploit an artist's talent and reputation to steal that income stream. Every stream of a deep fake takes streams and royalty payments away from the legitimate artist. Deepfakes are also misleading and confusing to consumers and music fans who are not typically interested in supporting fake versions of their favorite artist." He set this against a qualified optimism: while "the music industry sees great potential with various forms of AI technology in this early phase of AI," so far "the available generative AI products are not delivering on the expected promise of new products in creative industries," because some generative AI platforms "are not expanding the business model or enhancing human creativity."



---


# Google's USCO Filing On AI Training And Fair Use

On October 30, Google — the parent of YouTube within Alphabet Inc. — issued a filing with the US Copyright Office outlining its core position on "Artificial Intelligence and Copyright," arguing that the ingestion of copyrighted material for the training of generative AI platforms should not be hampered by copyright law.

The claim rests on transformation: "The doctrine of fair use [within existing US copyright law] provides that copying for a new and different purpose is permitted without authorization where — as with training AI systems — the secondary use is transformative and does not substitute for the copyrighted work." The warrant is an analogy to reading: "If [AI] training could be accomplished without the creation of copies, there would be no copyright questions here. Indeed that act of 'knowledge harvesting'… like the act of reading a book and learning the facts and ideas within it, would not only be non-infringing, it would further the very purpose of copyright law. The mere fact that, as a technological matter, copies need to be made to extract those ideas and facts from copyrighted works should not alter that result." Google then pre-empts the market-harm objection: "Some might object to this logic in the context of generative AI systems, arguing that even if such a system produces content that is not substantially similar to any of the content it was trained on, the output of that model might compete in the marketplace with works used for training… This argument misunderstands both the nature of the fair use inquiry and the creative markets that copyright is intended to protect. Even if generative-AI-assisted outputs do compete with existing works that were used in training, or with future works by the authors of those works, the pro-competitive nature of copying for the purpose of 'knowledge harvesting' has traditionally been a reason to favor a holding of fair use, not a reason to reject it." The conclusion is the kicker: "Any prohibition or limitation on the use of copyrighted materials for purposes of AI training would therefore undermine the purpose of copyright and foreclose the many opportunities that come with this technology." To be fair to Google, its submission also notes the importance of US copyright law, including as applied to generative AI, striking "the right balance between the legitimate interests of rightsholders and the equally legitimate interests of the public and succeeding generations of creators." The contents of the document caused some alarm at Sony Music HQ and, MBW reported, effectively scuppered any chance that Sony Music would get involved with "Dream Track" at that juncture. Google was just one of various tech giants and AI companies that submitted responses to the USCO, among them Anthropic and Stability AI.



---


# Robert Kyncl, Warner Music Group CEO

Robert Kyncl is the CEO of Warner Music Group, and the defining feature of his profile in the music business is that he came to it from 'Big Tech' — specifically from YouTube, where he was Chief Business Officer. That background is why, in the months before September 2023, he had been keeping a close eye on AI in the music industry.

His current role explains a second position associated with him: he has been pushing for price hikes at music streaming services. Both themes — AI in music, and streaming pricing — came up during Kyncl's Q&A session at the Code Conference in Laguna Niguel, California, on Tuesday 26 September 2023, as reported by Music Business Worldwide two days later.



---


# Generative AI

## Definition

In the corpus, "generative AI" is the umbrella label applied to the 2023 AI boom's content-producing systems — OpenAI's ChatGPT (built on GPT-3.5/GPT-4) and Adobe's Firefly image and vector-graphics models are the flagship examples named — rather than a term the corpus itself formally defines.

## Context

The corpus treats "generative AI" as the umbrella term for the mainstream AI boom of 2023, distinct from the EU AI Act's regulatory term "general purpose AI" (GPAI), which lawmakers deliberately chose as a more technology-neutral label for "the most powerful models behind the current boom in generative AI tools" so the law would not be pinned to one architecture like transformers (doc_0525).
OpenAI built ChatGPT specifically "to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI," and its free, chat-based interface is credited with "taking generative AI mainstream" as a consumer product rather than a research artifact (doc_0047).
Enterprise adoption is depicted as cautious relative to vendor hype: a Morgan Stanley survey found 56% of CIOs said generative AI was affecting investment priorities, but only 4% had launched significant projects, most still in evaluation or proof-of-concept (doc_0160).
The technology spans well beyond chatbots — Adobe's Firefly generative AI models generate images and vector graphics for creative software (doc_0043), and Amazon executive Tye Brady discussed generative AI alongside humanoid robots and mobile manipulation as an input to robotics work (doc_0528).
The same capability that drives adoption also drives the corpus's recurring regulatory and creative-industry concerns: the EU warned that "widely accessible generative AI tools" pose disinformation risks to elections (doc_0248), and the National Music Publishers Association called generative AI "the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed" in its copyright submission to the US Copyright Office (doc_0271).

## Key Characteristics

- **Illustrated by content-producing examples rather than defined outright** — the corpus shows the term through instances of new text, images, and vector graphics being produced from a prompt, illustrated by ChatGPT's text generation (doc_0048) and Firefly's image/vector generation (doc_0043).
- **Consumer breakout via chat interfaces** — ChatGPT's free, web-based chat interface is what took generative AI "mainstream," reaching the fastest adoption of any consumer app (doc_0047, doc_0048).
- **Enterprise adoption lags vendor hype** — large-company CIOs report slow, cautious rollout despite heavy vendor promotion, weighing API/SaaS costs against ROI (doc_0160).
- **Distinct from but overlapping "general purpose AI"** — EU lawmakers deliberately avoided calling the underlying models "generative AI" in law, choosing "general purpose AI" instead to stay technology-neutral rather than tied to transformer-based architectures (doc_0525).
- **Applies across domains beyond chatbots** — spans creative tools (Adobe Firefly) and robotics (Amazon's mobile manipulation work), per the corpus (doc_0043, doc_0528).
- **Focus of copyright and disinformation controversy** — named by the NMPA as a threat to the "human creative class" via unlicensed training data (doc_0271), and flagged by the EU as an election-disinformation risk requiring safeguards (doc_0248).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "generative AI" as a familiar shorthand without formally defining it. Per IBM, generative AI "is artificial intelligence (AI) that can create original content — such as text, images, video, audio or software code — in response to a user's prompt or request," distinguishing it from AI systems built only to classify or act on existing data (IBM, *What is generative AI?*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Federal Reserve Rate Path Expectations Late 2023

By early December 2023 traders widely expected the Federal Reserve to hold its key interest rate steady at its meeting the following week before potentially cutting rates in March, according to data from CME Group, and Fed officials had recently hinted that the federal funds rate may already be at its peak, above 5.25 per cent, up from nearly zero early in 2022. Fed Chair Jerome Powell and others nevertheless warned Wall Street against being overzealous in its predictions about how early a cut could happen.

The bond market moved with those expectations. With inflation down from its peak two summers earlier, Wall Street was hopeful the Fed might be done with its market-shaking hikes. Investors were looking for a slowdown in the job market that came through employers cutting back on open positions rather than laying off workers, and the report cited showed employers advertised just 8.7 million jobs on the last day of October, down 617,000 from a month earlier. US Treasury yields continued to sag from the heights reached during late October: the 10-year yield fell to 4.18 per cent from 4.26 per cent late on the Monday, after having been above 5 per cent and at its highest level in more than a decade during October. The two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks Fed expectations, fell from 4.61 per cent just before the economic reports to 4.57 per cent, yo-yoed, and then eased back to 4.57 per cent. Lower yields were one reason cryptocurrency prices had been rising, alongside excitement about a possible bitcoin exchange-traded fund that helped send bitcoin above $US43,000 ($65,600); Robinhood Markets reported a roughly 75 per cent jump in crypto trading volumes during November from a month earlier, said customers added about $US1.4 billion in net deposits during the month, and its own stock rose 10.3 per cent.

A month earlier, in early November 2023, the same expectations were forming from a lower base. Before that week, stocks had been struggling under the weight of rapidly rising Treasury yields catching up to the Fed's main interest rate, which was above 5.25 per cent and at its highest level since 2001. Higher rates and yields slow the economy, hurt investment prices and raise the risk of something breaking in the financial system, such as the three high-profile US bank failures that rattled markets during the spring. "It was really fear that the Fed was going to go too far," said Katie Nixon, chief investment officer for Northern Trust Wealth Management. The Fed had applied that pressure intentionally, hoping to starve inflation of its fuel and to cool the job market, particularly pay raises, because it feared too-strong pay gains could create a vicious cycle keeping inflation high. Analysts said the Friday jobs report offered encouraging signals, with average hourly earnings rising less in October from September than expected, though it did not mean the job was done. Treasury yields tumbled immediately after that report, with the 10-year easing to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday and from more than five per cent the previous week, when it hit its highest level since 2007. Traders then moved up expectations for the first Fed cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data. Foreign-exchange strategists at Bank of America wrote in a BofA Global Research report that for investors around the world the "Fed matters more than other central banks" and weak US data is "the only game-changer for markets". A separate report that Friday from the Institute for Supply Management said growth in US services industries such as finance and construction was weaker than economists expected and suggested a slight easing in prices.
