# US Treasury Yields And Fed Rate Expectations In October 2023

The mechanism linking data to yields to stocks ran in both directions during October 2023. On 4 October, the yield on the 10-year Treasury, the centrepiece of the bond market, pulled back from its highest level since 2007, down to 4.73 per cent from 4.80 per cent late on the Tuesday, with shorter- and longer-term yields also easing to allow more oxygen for the stock market. Yields fell following reports indicating a slowing US economy, the first suggesting that hiring by employers outside the government was much weaker than expected; on Wall Street that is currently good news because a cooling job market could mean less upward pressure on inflation, which in turn could convince the Federal Reserve to take it easier on interest rates. After already raising its main interest rate to the highest level since 2001, the Fed had indicated it may keep its overnight rate higher next year than earlier expected, and Treasury yields had correspondingly snapped higher as traders accept a new normal of high rates for longer; the Fed pays particular attention to the job market because too much strength there could drive wages much higher, which it fears could keep inflation well above its target of 2 per cent.

By 12 October the same mechanism was running the other way. The stock market has largely been taking its cue from the bond market recently, and weak results announced in the afternoon for an auction of 30-year Treasury bonds sent yields of all kinds higher; higher yields can knock down prices for stocks and slow the economy by making borrowing more expensive. Yields had already been rising in the morning after a report showing consumer-level inflation a touch higher than economists expected, raising worries about the Fed keeping its main interest rate high for a long time as it tries to undercut inflation by knocking down investment prices and slowing the economy. The report also had encouraging nuggets: after ignoring prices for food and fuel, which Fed officials see as a better predictor of where inflation is heading, prices consumers paid were in line with expectations and continued to decelerate from earlier months. A second report said slightly fewer US workers than expected applied for unemployment benefits, indicating a job market with few lay-offs and therefore strength for the overall economy, though it could also add fuel to upward pressure on inflation. After the reports the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.7 per cent from 4.56 per cent late Wednesday, and the two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks expectations for the Fed, climbed to 5.06 per cent from 4.99 per cent, with yields still down slightly for the week after regressing from more-than-decade highs following speeches that investors saw as hints the Fed may not raise its main overnight rate further. The big jump for the 10-year yield since the summer has pulled mortgage rates to their highest levels since the turn of the millennium, and such moves could slow the economy without requiring more Fed hikes; Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said nothing in Thursday's inflation report should sway the Fed one way or the other on what it will do on 1 November, calling the data "reassuringly uneventful".



---


# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.



---


# US Home Prices Peaked In June 2022 And Returned To A Record High By July 2023

National U.S. home prices did not peak until June 2022 — even as mortgage rates soared and purchase applications plummeted amid the Federal Reserve's first interest rate hikes — and although prices fell more than 5% from that peak by January 2023, they returned to a record high in July 2023. This is the observation that has so far vindicated the majority of real estate veterans, who despite a widely bearish industry outlook avoided arguing that home prices would drop the way they did during the 2008 crash that kicked off the Global Financial Crisis.

The backdrop, as of the reporting date of 2023-10-06, is that housing market pessimists had been sounding the alarm for years about a pending crash in U.S. residential real estate. Even before the Fed began hiking interest rates to fight inflation in 2022 — pushing mortgage rates to a 23-year high in October 2023 — years of surging home prices had left some experts warning that the housing market was a massive bubble ready to pop.



---


# The Wall Street September 2023 Selloff And Bond Yields

September 2023 brought a loss of 5.2 per cent so far for the S&P 500, putting it on track to be the worst month of the year by far, as the realisation set in that the Federal Reserve would indeed keep interest rates high for a long time. That growing understanding sent yields in the bond market to their highest levels in more than a decade, which in turn undercut prices for stocks and other investments.

Treasury yields rose again on Tuesday, 2023-09-26, following a mixed batch of reports on the economy: the yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.55 per cent from 4.54 per cent late on Monday and is near its highest level since 2007, up sharply from about 3.5 per cent in May and from 0.5 per cent about three years ago. One economic report that Tuesday showed confidence among consumers was weaker than economists expected — concerning because strong spending by US households has been a bulwark keeping the economy out of a long-predicted recession.

# US Jobs And Services Data In Early October 2023

Wednesday's ADP report suggested private employers added 89,000 jobs last month, a much sharper slowdown in hiring than the 140,000 economists expected. The report does not have a perfect track record in predicting what the more comprehensive jobs report from the US government will say, which was due to arrive on the Friday. Mike Loewengart, head of model portfolio construction at Morgan Stanley Global Investment Office, said that "if Friday's report also shows the labour market is cooling, stock investors may worry a little less about indefinitely higher interest rates".

A second report on the economy said growth in US services industries slowed in September by a touch more than economists expected. The figures were reported by The Age on 4 October 2023 alongside a note that oil prices slumped overnight.

# Housing Affordability Is Worse Now Than At The 2006 Peak

Roger Ashworth, a managing director at Goldman Sachs, argued in a credit strategy research paper released in mid-October 2023 that although some economic factors are stronger today than during the Global Financial Crisis, housing affordability is undeniably worse: "While housing and more generally consumer fundamentals are in a much stronger position today, affordability for the incremental buyer is worse than it was at the peak in 2006 before the crash." The claim is deliberately narrow — it is about the incremental buyer's affordability, not about overall fundamentals, which he grants are stronger.

The proximate causes cited are the same constraints that have held all year. "As has been the case throughout this year, limited inventory and low housing affordability continue to hamper home sales," NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement, adding a policy conclusion: "The Federal Reserve simply cannot keep raising interest rates in light of softening inflation and weakening job gains." The Fed had raised rates several times in 2023, with Chair Jerome Powell arming his "higher for longer" stance.

# Bank Of America's Warning Of More Housing "Turbulence"

A Bank of America team led by U.S. economist Jeseo Park warned in the week of 2023-10-06 that there is more "turbulence" coming for the housing market because of high mortgage rates: "With rates likely staying higher for longer, we are cautious of potential turbulence ahead," the group wrote. The grounds are the persistence of high rates rather than a repeat of a past crash — the team said they were getting an eerie feeling of "déjà vu," but it was not 2008 that came to mind, it was the 1980s.

The forecast attached to this warning is qualified. Bank of America had previously forecast 0% home price growth and falling home sales for the full year 2023, but it did not offer a new prediction in its latest note. The warrant joining the rate outlook to the housing outlook runs the other way as well: eventually, as inflation fades and leads the Fed to cut interest rates, housing affordability will improve. "At that stage, we should see a more stable and healthy housing market," Park and her team wrote. "Until then, hang tight, it may be a bumpy ride."

# ASX Outlook And RBA Rate Expectations At End-September 2023

The Australian sharemarket was set to retreat with futures pointing to a fall of 38 points, or 0.5 per cent, at the open, after Wall Street closed out its worst month and quarter of the year with more losses on Friday.

Most sectors traded lower, but interest-rate sensitive sectors including healthcare and consumer companies were among the weakest amid expectations that the RBA would keep rates on hold in October; the National Australia Bank has forecast another rate hike to 4.35 per cent in November. # The 1980s, Not 2008, Is The Better Analogy For Today's Housing Market

Bank of America economists argued in a Thursday note that "Looking back at previous housing recessions, we think the 1980s are a better analogy for today's market than the 2008 housing crash." The grounds they gave are structural: back in the early 1980s, just like today, home prices had boomed for years before Fed officials were ultimately forced to hike interest rates aggressively in an attempt to fight inflation.

First American chief economist Mark Fleming made the same case in a Tuesday report titled "1980s Déjà Vu for the Housing Market," arguing from the absence of the specific 2000s failure modes: "Today's housing market isn't anything like the housing market of the mid-2000s. The housing market today is not overbuilt, nor is it driven by loose lending standards, subprime mortgages, or homeowners who are highly leveraged." The claim is offered with a scope qualification — the housing market today isn't identical to that of the '80s, but it's pretty close — and with a demographic warrant: in a lot of ways, millennials are being forced to follow the housing journey of their boomer parents as they face a frozen, unaffordable market with rising interest rates, as noted by both BofA Research economist Jeseo Park and Fleming.

# Volcker's And Powell's Rate-Hiking Cycles Compared

The consumer price index rose at a peak of around 14% in 1980 before then-Fed Chair Paul Volcker's hawkish policies sent mortgage rates to 18% within a year — cooling inflation but sparking a recession, and causing a serious downturn in housing in which home sales and building levels cratered while national home prices actually remained stable. At the start of Volcker's term as Fed chair in August 1979 the median U.S. home sales price was $64,700, and even after a near doubling of mortgage rates that figure rose to $69,400 by the second quarter of 1981. A second account puts the average 30-year fixed mortgage peaking at about 18% by late 1981, and records that home sales activity plummeted from 1978 to 1982, with existing-home sales dropping 50% over that period according to the Office of Policy Development and Research.

Over the 18 months preceding October 2023, current Fed chair Jerome Powell has been following a very similar game plan, raising interest rates aggressively to quash inflation and setting the tone for the most aggressive global hiking of rates in the modern era. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate, the most common type in the U.S., soared from 3.8% in March 2022 to over 7.5% by 2023-10-06, and by the week of 2023-10-20 mortgage rates hit 8%, the highest in more than 20 years. This in turn slowed mortgage purchase applications and caused home sales to plummet, just as in the '80s; but home prices, echoing the dynamic of that era, have yet to collapse. # Bank of Israel Interest Rate Policy During the War

Asked what the Bank of Israel should do at its interest rate decision on 23 October 2023, Leo Leiderman argued for holding: "As for cutting the interest rate, it's too early to consider that. The current interest rate is at the right level for the state of the economy, and together with the policy on exchange rates, it contributes to ensuring financial stability."

It was still too early to tell how the war would affect the rate of inflation in the short and medium term: just as there are new inflationary factors, such as the depreciation of the shekel, there will also be factors working in the opposite direction, given the expected decline in private consumption, tourism and other items.

His second ground extends his fiscal reasoning to monetary policy: as with fiscal policy, a country at war is allowed to deviate temporarily from the set inflation target. He judged that at the moment there was no surge in inflation expectations, and that the investment community is aware of the existence of index-linked assets and the exchange rate that can assist in hedging inflation risk. # Why 2023 Is Not A Repeat Of The 2008 Housing Crash

Against the premise that today's housing market is heading for a 2008-style crash, Bank of America's Jeseo Park and her team concluded flatly: "We reiterate that we do not expect another housing crash like 2008." The attacked premise is the assumed similarity of conditions — the 2008 crash was fueled by the collapse of subprime mortgages, and the real estate market of that era was very different from what Bank of America's experts see today.

The specific rebuttals are four. There are no "noticeable signs" of excess housing development today like there were back then. Households are not nearly as burdened by mortgage debt: household mortgage debt represented roughly 65% of U.S. consumers' disposable income in the second quarter, compared to 100% before the Global Financial Crisis. The ratio of Americans' mortgage debt to their real estate assets — loan-to-value — was just 27% in the second quarter, compared to over 40% in 2008 and roughly 50% in 2010, on Bank of America's data. And new legislation enacted since the GFC has helped prevent worst-case scenarios, most obviously by leaving far fewer risky adjustable-rate mortgages, which can lead to higher default rates when interest rates rise: they now represent less than 5% of total purchase and refinance loans, compared with over 35% at the peak of the pre-GFC housing cycle.



---


# Simply Homes' Interest-Rate Underwriting Resilience

Simply Homes CEO Brian Bagdasarian argues that his company has been less affected by the macro environment than other proptech firms because it factored in the possibility of high interest rates very early on in its model. Many proptech companies struggled, or outright shut down, in 2023, in large part due to sky-high interest rates.

His first ground is conservative underwriting: "Everything is underwritten to a worst-case scenario. A lot of first generation ibuyers never underwrote interest rate risk. But we started with that. We made sure our large return rates were inclusive of high interest rates that still allowed us to operate profitably."

His second is the predictability of the revenue: "The other piece of that is we have highly stable income — because the way that Housing Choice Voucher works is that the tenant pays 30% of their adjusted monthly income. The voucher covers the balance. So it's highly predictable income."



---


# From The Zero-Rate Era To 8% Mortgage Rates

The path from 2010 to the 8% mortgage of October 2023 runs through a single policy regime and its reversal. In 2010, the last time existing home sales were so low, the global economy was on life support and the Fed slashed interest rates down to zero to revive the flatlining patient — fueling an "everything bubble" that inflated all kinds of assets along the way, not least housing. That zero-rate regime persisted until the highest inflation in 40 years surprised many economists and prompted the massive series of rate hikes that produced the once-unthinkable 8% mortgage.

Some onlookers had anticipated the level if not the cause: Zillow warned in May 2023 that housing would enter a "deep freeze" if the debt limit standoff failed to resolve and America defaulted, since that would send mortgage rates up to 8%. The default was averted, yet 8% mortgage rates arrived anyway. The account's own framing of the resulting market is that this isn't like 2008 or 2010 again — it calls instead for a 1980s history lesson.



---


# The Mortgage Rate Lock-In Effect Freezing US Home Sales

The rate lock-in effect works like this: out of fear of losing their lower interest rates, current homeowners are resistant to putting their homes on the market, which produces abysmal inventory levels and leaves fewer and fewer properties exchanging hands. More than 90% of existing-home owners are locked into mortgage rates below 6%, Odeta Kushi, deputy chief economist at First American, told Fortune. "These homeowners do not have a financial incentive to sell," Kushi says. "The combination of reduced affordability and an even stronger rate lock-in effect suppresses home sales because you can't buy what's not for sale, even if you can afford it."

The mechanism inverts the usual relationship between rates and prices. "Unlike the turn of the millennium, house prices today are rising alongside mortgage rates, primarily due to low inventory," Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist, said in a statement released Sept. 29, 2023. "These headwinds are causing both buyers and sellers to hold out for better circumstances."



---


# The Post-Tightening Monetary Policy Autopsy Of 2023

After the most aggressive monetary-tightening campaign in four decades, academics and economic practitioners are running autopsies on what could have prevented the cost-of-living crisis and how to ensure the same mistakes won't be repeated. Markets have scrambled to price in high-for-longer interest rates, with a new war in the Middle East adding yet more risk to an already uncertain outlook confronting central bankers as they gather for their penultimate meetings of a tumultuous year.

The policy navel-gazing centers on three debates: how much flexibility central banks can allow in reaching their inflation targets, the effectiveness of asset purchases in the policy mix, and the merits of monetary and fiscal coordination. Bloomberg surveyed economists from around the world to gather views on those three debates. Their verdict: central banks won't break their economies in a rush to hit inflation targets, QE will be used more sparingly in the future, and fiscal policy risks countering the work of monetary authorities.



---

On the Australian sharemarket session reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 5 December 2023, Perpetual was the standout gainer, climbing 6.3 per cent after announcing a strategic review of its three-pronged corporate structure that might see it demerge its corporate trust and wealth management businesses and create a more focused asset manager. Gold miner Newmont was down 1.25 per cent, Origin Energy fell 0.4 per cent, Mercury NZ declined 0.3 per cent and Argo Investments traded 0.1 per cent lower.

Moomoo market strategist Jessica Amir attributed the local market's outperformance of global equities on the Wednesday session to the National Accounts figures, which pointed to the Reserve Bank potentially hitting pause on lifting interest rates. "We know economic growth is slowing, Australian unemployment is likely to pick up next year and inflation is likely to fall," Amir said, adding that this "trifecta" pointed towards the RBA stopping rate rises and then potentially moving to cut, which was what the market had priced in that day.

# The EU's Urgent Warning Letter To X

The European Union fired a public warning at Elon Musk-owned X (formerly Twitter) for failing to tackle illegal content circulating on the platform in the wake of Saturday's deadly attacks on Israel by Hamas terrorists based in the Gaza Strip — an "urgent" letter from internal market commissioner Thierry Breton that TechCrunch described as a very swift test of the bloc's newly updated content moderation rulebook. Breton shared the letter publicly, tweeting on October 10, 2023: "Following the terrorist attacks by Hamas against 🇮🇱, we have indications of X/Twitter being used to disseminate illegal content & disinformation in the EU. Urgent letter to @elonmusk on #DSA obligations". TechCrunch's later account places the letter on the Wednesday.

The letter's substance was twofold. Breton said the bloc had seen "indications" from "qualified sources" that X was being used to disseminate illegal content and disinformation in the EU following Saturday's attacks, then reminded X of the DSA's "very precise obligations" on content moderation: "When you receive notices of illegal content in the EU, you must be timely, diligent and objective in taking action and removing the relevant content when warranted." Separately, the European Commission raised concerns about the spread of disinformation on X related to the terrorist attacks and their aftermath.

On the disinformation side Breton was specific about what had been reported and what he wanted done: "Public media and civil society organisations widely report instances of fake and manipulated images and facts circulating on your platform in the EU, such as repurposed old images of unrelated armed conflicts or military footage that actually originated from video games. This appears to be manifestly false or misleading information," he wrote. "I therefore invite you to urgently ensure that your systems are effective, and report on the crisis measures taken to my team."

TechCrunch's own characterisation of the platform at that moment was blunter than the letter's: rather than tackling the problem, it wrote, X "appears to be turning into an engine of disinformation" — one that had demonstrably enabled the very swift amplification of a smorgasbord of toxic fakes around the Israel-Hamas war, falsehoods that might be trying to manipulate opinion around the conflict, or otherwise exploit horrific events to drive engagement (clickbait) or for even more cynical and potentially harmful ends.

# Disinformation

## Definition

Disinformation is false or misleading content spread online — distinct from the illegal-content category (like terrorism or hate speech) in that, per the corpus's account of EU regulation, disinformation "is not illegal in the EU per se," yet still counts as a *systemic risk* that large platforms must assess and mitigate.

## Context

The corpus's central storyline is the EU's escalating regulatory pressure on X (formerly Twitter) over disinformation tied to the Israel-Hamas war: the Commission's October 2023 warning and formal information request to Musk accused X of being used "to disseminate illegal content and disinformation" following the Hamas attacks, and a EU-commissioned study later found X had "the largest ratio of mis/disinformation posts" among major platforms.
Because X is a Digital Services Act (DSA) "very large online platform" (VLOP), the obligation to mitigate disinformation risk is legally binding on it even though the underlying falsehoods are not themselves illegal; the EU's voluntary Code of Practice on Disinformation (which Musk pulled X out of earlier in 2023) is treated by the Commission as a signal of DSA compliance on this exact risk.
Disinformation also surfaces as a generative-AI worry: Suleyman warned DeepMind's ethics board that AI "could lead to an explosion in disinformation," EU commissioner Vera Jourova flagged AI-generated disinformation as an election threat, and early fears that ChatGPT would be used "to generate disinformation on a massive scale" pushed European policymakers toward mandating security assessments of generative AI products.
Real-world examples in the corpus include a video-game clip falsely presented as Hamas missile footage circulating on X, and misinformation described as "rampant on social media" during the Gaza crisis, prompting some users to turn to Snap Map for unmediated, firsthand footage instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **Not illegal per se in the EU** — disinformation is treated as a systemic risk to be mitigated, not content that platforms are legally required to remove the way they must remove illegal content.
- **Distinct from "misinformation" but often paired with it** — the corpus uses both terms (e.g., "mis/disinformation posts," Mozilla's content-policy list of "misinformation" as a harm category), generally without a sharp technical distinction, though disinformation carries a stronger connotation of deliberate falsehood or manipulation (e.g., "Kremlin propaganda").
- **A VLOP systemic-risk obligation** — under the DSA, platforms designated VLOPs (like X) must proactively assess and mitigate disinformation risk, which is what makes an EU formal-information request or investigation possible even absent an illegal-content finding.
- **Measurable and comparable across platforms** — the EU's Code of Practice enabled a pilot study producing "structural indicators" (e.g., how easily disinformation content is found, how much engagement it gets) that let regulators rank X as worst among mainstream platforms.
- **A named risk of generative AI** — beyond social-media falsehoods, the corpus repeatedly frames disinformation as a downstream risk of AI text/image generation (ChatGPT, deepfakes), motivating both EU AI-Act-era safeguards and industry-side labeling commitments.

# X Found To Have The Worst Disinformation Ratio In EU Analysis

X, formerly Twitter, was called out in the European Union for having the worst ratio of disinformation and misinformation to posts not spreading falsehoods among mainstream social networks.

The finding came in a September 2023 speech by EU commissioner for values and transparency Vera Jourova, discussing the latest updates from platforms signed up to combat disinformation under a beefed-up EU Code of Practice linked to compliance with the bloc's legally binding Digital Services Act. X's poor performance was assessed during a pilot phase of testing of a new methodology developed by Code signatories. "A big novelty under the Code is now the publication of the first set of structural indicators such as how easy it is to find disinformation content, how much engagement such content receives or indicators about sources. These indicators — developed by the signatories — constitute an unprecedented and novel insight into disinformation on online platforms," she said. "Such insight is crucial to understand how effective platforms efforts are to fight this threat even more efficiently. This is a very valuable industry proposal that has great potential while it has to be still further developed. Here, signatories have decided to run a pilot phase in three Member States to evaluate the methodology on two of those indicators. X, former Twitter, who is not under the Code any more is the platform with the largest ratio of mis/disinformation posts."

X was contacted for a response to the EU's analysis of the ratio of disinformation it is spreading, and replied with an automated email reading: "Busy now, please check back later." The finding fits a wider pattern: consistent moderation, fact-checking investment and researcher data access are areas where X under new owner Elon Musk has moved out of step with EU expectations on countering disinformation, suggesting that X — designated by the EU as a VLOP under the DSA back in April — continues to put itself squarely in the Commission's crosshairs, including over its priority issue of tackling Kremlin propaganda.

# EU Enforcement Steps Against X Over DSA Compliance

Between 10 and 13 October 2023 the European Union escalated against Elon Musk-owned X in two steps: a public warning letter on Wednesday from internal market commissioner Thierry Breton, and then, late on Thursday, a formal request for information sent by the Commission under the Digital Services Act. Crucially, no investigation had been opened at that point — EU officials confirmed to TechCrunch that an investigation had not been taken, and TechCrunch substantially revised its original report to make clear that a formal request for information, while it could prefigure a formal announcement of an investigation, is not yet that formal technical step.

The warning came first. In his "urgent" letter, shared on X by Breton himself, the bloc sent the strongest signal yet that it believed Musk's platform was in breach of the DSA — though this was by no means Musk's first warning. Breton wrote that the EU had "indications" that X was being used to disseminate illegal content and disinformation in the EU following Saturday's attacks, then reminded the company of the DSA's "very precise obligations" on content moderation: "When you receive notices of illegal content in the EU, you must be timely, diligent and objective in taking action and removing the relevant content when warranted," he warned, adding, "We have, from qualified sources, reports about potentially illegal content circulating on your service despite flags from relevant authorities." He also took issue with a change X had made the previous night to the public interest policy under which it judges newsworthiness — the test for whether posts that infringe its rules may nonetheless remain on the site — which Breton said had left "many European users uncertain" about how X applies its own rules. That matters under the DSA because the regulation requires platforms to be clear and transparent about their rules and how they apply them, "particularly relevant when it comes to violent and terrorist content that appears to circulate on your platform." Breton further said X should have "proportionate and effective mitigation measures" in place to tackle "the risks to public security and civic discourse stemming from disinformation." The EU asked Musk to make contact with relevant law enforcement authorities and Europol and to "ensure that you respond promptly to their requests", flagged unspecified additional DSA compliance issues his team would raise "shortly" — "with a specific request" — and gave Musk a deadline of 24 hours to respond, stipulating that his answer would be added to the bloc's assessment file on X's DSA compliance. The letter closed: "I remind you that following the opening of a potential investigation and a finding of non-compliance, penalties can be imposed."

The formal request for information followed. It came after the Wednesday warning about reports of illegal content and disinformation targeting the Israel-Hamas war circulating on the platform, and after Twitter's CEO sent a high-level, non-specific response to that warning. The Commission said it was looking at X's compliance with the DSA across a number of areas — its policies and practices regarding notices on illegal content; complaint handling; risk assessment; and measures to mitigate the risks identified. In its press release the EU wrote that "This request follows indications received by the Commission services of the alleged spreading of illegal content and disinformation, in particular the spreading of terrorist and violent content and hate speech," adding that the ask also addressed other aspects of DSA compliance.

The request carried explicit deadlines and consequences. X had until October 18 to provide information about "the activation and functioning of X's crisis response protocol", and until October 31 to respond to the other requests. "Based on the assessment of X replies, the Commission will assess next steps," the Commission wrote. "This could entail the formal opening of proceedings pursuant to Article 66 of the DSA." The regulation also includes powers to impose fines for "incorrect, incomplete or misleading information in response to a request for information", and the EU added that "In case of failure to reply by X, the Commission may decide to request the information by decision. In this case, failure to reply by the deadline could lead to the imposition of period penalties." TechCrunch noted that the pace at which regulators were moving was a strong indication of the bloc's direction of travel, and that its revised report also corrected an error in the original which had referred to Interpol rather than Europol.

# The EU's First Formal DSA Proceeding, Against X

On 18 December 2023 the European Commission announced the opening of a "formal proceeding" against Elon Musk's X, making it the first confirmed investigation opened by the European Union under its rebooted digital rulebook, the Digital Services Act (DSA). The investigation will look at whether the social networking platform may have breached rules linked to risk management, content moderation, dark patterns, advertising transparency and data access for researchers.

The Commission set out the evidentiary basis for the step: "On the basis of the preliminary investigation conducted so far, including on the basis of an analysis of the risk assessment report submitted by X in September, X's Transparency report published on 3 November, and X's replies to a formal request for information, which, among others, concerned the dissemination of illegal content in the context of Hamas' terrorist attacks against Israel, the Commission has decided to open formal infringement proceedings against X under the Digital Services Act."

The EU added that "if proven, these failures would constitute infringements of Articles 34(1), 34(2) and 35(1), 16(5) and 16(6), 25(1), 39 and 40(12) of the DSA," and said it will now carry out an in-depth investigation "as a matter of priority." Internal market commissioner Thierry Breton announced the same day that the proceedings covered a suspected breach of obligations to counter illegal content and disinformation, a suspected breach of transparency obligations, and suspected deceptive design of the user interface.

# The Digital Services Act

The Digital Services Act (DSA) is the European Union's pan-EU content moderation rulebook: a regulation that places governance obligations on digital services and platforms carrying user-generated content, with the aim of ensuring companies respond to reports of illegal content, and that layers heavier duties on the largest platforms. Its baseline obligations apply to digital services and platforms generally — respond diligently to notices of illegal content, clearly communicate terms and conditions to users, and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement of those terms.

The discriminating feature of the regime is its second tier. Platforms designated as "very large online platforms" (VLOPs) carry additional obligations to identify and mitigate systemic risks such as disinformation, gender-based violence, or negative effects on the exercise of fundamental rights. The Commission designated 19 VLOPs in April 2023, including Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram; X is also a designated VLOP. Compliance for VLOPs kicked in over the summer of 2023 — TechCrunch dates Meta's compliance start to August.

The regime's boundary case is disinformation itself. Unlike terrorism content, disinformation is not illegal in the EU per se. The DSA therefore does not reach it through the illegal-content removal route at all; it reaches it through the systemic-risk route, obliging a VLOP such as X to mitigate the risks attached to harmful falsehoods while separately acting diligently on reports of genuinely illegal content. The two duties run on different legal tracks even when they concern the same posts.

Penalties for confirmed breaches can be as high as 6% of global annual turnover, and the bloc holds a further power, in extremis, to block access to a service in the region for repeated infringements — meaning a platform that repeatedly fails to correct course could be shut off in the EU. TechCrunch illustrates the scale on both ends: Elon Musk last projected revenues of about $3 billion for 2023 for X, which by that example would cap a fine at up to $180 million, while in Meta's case the same 6% ceiling could run to multiple billions.

The regulation also contains a "crisis response" mechanism (Article 36) which enables the Commission to adopt rapid-fire measures on larger platforms in situations of "serious threat", such as war. As of TechCrunch's October 2023 reporting this part of the regulation was not yet operative: it would not start operating until February 17 of the following year, because it requires an advisory body — the European Board for Digital Services — to be operational before it can recommend that the Commission adopt a crisis response mechanism, and the Board's set-up was itself waiting on Member States to establish national Digital Services Coordinators, the bodies that oversee DSA compliance for non-VLOPs.

# Musk's Removal Of Trust Signals And The Turn To Community Notes

Under Elon Musk, X has pushed the use of an existing crowdsourced fact-checking feature, rebranded as Community Notes, which essentially seeks to outsource the issue to an arm's-length process of aggregating views from platform users, some of which may be appended as contextual notes to dubious tweets.

At the same time, Musk set about removing signals Twitter users were previously able to rely on to help assess the quality of information tweets contained — removing state-affiliated media labels from propaganda outlets and replacing legacy account verifications with pay-to-play. A report by misinformation watcher NewsGuard, published the same day as the EU's disinformation analysis, found that Musk's decision to remove labels denoting state-run or government-affiliated media accounts led to a surge in propaganda spreading on X, with Russia's RT seeing the biggest gains per the analysis.

# Platform Transparency After X Went Private

An EU investigation would, indirectly, be a key way for the public to gain significantly more transparency around how X is being used — and abused. That is TechCrunch's claim about what regulatory scrutiny of the platform would deliver beyond any compliance finding.

The grounds are a change in X's corporate status. Since Musk took Twitter private, the company no longer produces quarterly earnings reports, and it is not held as closely to account as a result.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is the substitution of one disclosure channel for another. Public-company reporting is what ordinarily forces periodic, public disclosure about a platform's operations and scale; taking the company private removed that channel and the accountability pressure attached to it. A regulatory investigation compels disclosure through a different route, so it would restore to public view information about the platform's use and abuse that the market no longer extracts.

# Musk's Position On Disinformation

Musk's answer to the EU's warning did not dispute the regulator's authority so much as the premise underneath it: that "disinformation" is a category anyone can independently arbitrate. Replying on X to journalist Glenn Greenwald — who had attacked the DSA as a "censorship law" that he claimed would be used to "punish X" — Musk avoided expressing the same trenchant criticism of the EU's approach and instead invited relativism, writing: "Let the public hear exactly what this disinformation consists of and decide for themselves."

That reply attacks the EU's inferential step rather than its legal one. The bloc's demand that X be "effective" against disinformation presupposes that false content can be identified as such by some competent party, so that a platform's failure to act on it is a measurable compliance gap. Musk's move was to sow doubt that disinformation is something that can be independently arbitrated at all, implying that fact-checking is merely a convenient exercise for targeting different opinions — essentially echoing Greenwald's position — by claiming that "many times" the "official fact-checker" has been found making false statements, before adding, for plausible deniability, the rhetorically empty offer that "Maybe this is the case here, maybe not". If no arbiter is trustworthy, the adjudication the EU's obligation depends on cannot be performed, and the public becomes the only judge.

TechCrunch treats this as of a piece with a wider mismatch. A rule of law clash between Musk and the EU had looked increasingly inevitable in recent months, and had indeed been predicted by some industry watchers since rumours of the billionaire's plan to take over Twitter emerged the previous year; asking Musk to be "effective" against disinformation, the publication wrote, is a bit like asking the sea to stop moving. Musk's extremely iterative — or just plain erratic and arbitrary — management style is so far from the responsive and responsible qualities the EU's rulebook demands of digital leaders that TechCrunch found it hard to see how the clash could end well for either side. But this is how the regulatory dance must go, and after the dance comes the denouement: if a DSA breach is confirmed, enforcement follows, and actual penalties might be a bit harder for Musk to troll.

A second exchange illustrates the practical cost of the position. Musk chipped into a conversation in which an X user had commented on a screengrab of an apparent exchange of threats between Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Khamenei, and an official Israeli government account in relation to the war, writing: "Amazing to see this exchange!" The irony, TechCrunch notes, is that Musk's destruction of Twitter's legacy verification of notable accounts means you can't, at a glance, be sure whether the exchange really happened — so the "decide for themselves" standard is being applied on a platform whose own authenticity signals he removed.

# EU Warning On Deepfake Election Risks

The European Union warned in September 2023 that more needs to be done to address the risks that widely accessible generative AI tools may pose to free and fair debate in democratic societies, with the bloc's values and transparency commissioner Vera Jourova highlighting AI-generated disinformation as a potential threat to elections ahead of the pan-EU vote to choose a new European Parliament the following year.

Giving an update on the bloc's voluntary Code of Practice on Disinformation in a speech, Jourova welcomed initial efforts by a number of mainstream platforms to address the AI risks by implementing safeguards to inform users about the "synthetic origin of content posted online," as she put it, but said more must be done. "These efforts need to continue and intensify considering the high potential of such realistic AI products for creating and disseminating disinformation. The risks are particularly high in the context of elections," she warned. "I therefore urge platforms to be vigilant and provide efficient safeguards for this in the context of elections."

The commissioner noted she was meeting representatives of ChatGPT maker OpenAI later that day to discuss the issue. The AI giant is not a signatory to the bloc's anti-disinformation Code as yet, so is likely to be facing pressure to get on board with the effort.

# The Scope Of The EU's DSA Investigation Into X

Per the Commission, the EU's investigation of X covers four areas. The first is compliance with DSA obligations related to countering the dissemination of illegal content in the EU, notably in relation to the risk assessment and mitigation measures adopted by X, as well as the functioning of the notice and action mechanism for illegal content in the EU mandated by the DSA, including in light of X's content moderation resources.

The second is the effectiveness of measures taken by X to combat information manipulation, with a focus on the effectiveness of its "Community Notes" system of crowdsourcing fact-checking to aggregated views of users, who may vote to label disputed tweets with additional context. The EU said the probe will also look at the effectiveness of related policies mitigating risks to civic discourse and electoral processes.

The third is transparency requirements, with a focus on "suspected shortcomings" by X in giving researchers access to publicly accessible data as mandated by Article 40 of the DSA, and suspected shortcomings in its ads repository, the ads transparency library the regulation also mandates. The fourth is suspected deceptive design elements in X's user interface, notably in relation to checkmarks linked to certain subscription products, the so-called Blue checks.

# X's Revenue Decline And The Information-Network Decay Argument

Charging all users for access to X could be the final nail in the coffin of the platform as a real-time information network, because it risks triggering a further and final exodus of the remaining legacy users whose knowledge and engagement lent Twitter its original value.

The grounds are financial. Subscription revenues to the revamped Twitter Blue paid offering, now called X Premium, do not appear to have been substantial enough to plug the advertising gap, which may explain Musk's recent suggestion that he plans to charge all users a small fee. The warrant joining that to the conclusion is a claim about what makes an information network work: a bona fide information network depends on a critical mass of genuine users to pay attention and contribute value and vitality — its life-blood. Remove the paywall-averse legacy users and disinformation and spammers may rush in to fill the gap, generating a parody of activity; without the genuine users, X really will mark the spot of Twitter's demise.

# Digital Services Act Obligations For Very Large Online Platforms

The EU's Digital Services Act places an obligation on so-called very large online platforms (VLOPs) to assess societal risks attached to their use of algorithms and to put in place "reasonable, proportionate and effective mitigation measures" for identified risks, with their reporting and mitigation plans subject to independent audit and oversight by the Commission.

Back in April 2023, X/Twitter was named as one of 19 larger platforms that face the strictest level of regulation under the DSA. The bloc's executive, which also devised the anti-disinformation Code, is responsible for oversight of VLOPs' compliance with the DSA, and has powers under the law to fine violators up to 6% of global annual turnover; the Commission has previously wanted that not following the Code of Practice on Disinformation would be factored into its assessments. The key distinction is that the Code is voluntary while compliance with the DSA is not: the DSA is now legally binding on X/Twitter, including in particular the obligation on VLOPs to mitigate the risks their platforms pose for the spread of disinformation. On timing, the Commission noted that the TrustLab study to measure two Structural Indicators covers signatories of the Code at the time of the launch of the exercise, which then included X/Twitter, and that during this period the DSA had not entered into force yet for VLOPs and VLOSEs including X/Twitter. The Commission said it could not comment further on the substance of the risk assessments, that it was analysing available information on a range of issues and in close contact with X but could not comment on specifics and timelines, and that — as stated by Commissioner Thierry Breton — minor protection and integrity of elections are priorities in the enforcement of the DSA.

One practical limit on the deterrent: while the price for X ignoring the EU's warnings on disinformation could be steep, its ad revenue has cratered since Musk's takeover as a result of his failure to tackle toxicity and harmful disinformation encouraging an advertiser exodus, and shrinking earnings would effectively downsize any future penalties X could face under the DSA.

# Disinformation On X After The Hamas Attacks On Israel

In the days after Saturday's Hamas attacks on Israel, posts identified as false circulated widely on X, including footage repurposed from a video game and clips entirely unrelated to the conflict. TechCrunch reported the pattern in two articles, on 10 and 13 October 2023, drawing on fact-checkers, public media, civil society organisations and X's own safety account.

The observed content fell into several kinds. Graphic videos apparently showing terrorist attacks on civilians circulated on X from Saturday onward. Alongside them were posts purporting to show footage from the attacks inside Israel, or from Israel's subsequent retaliation on targets in the Gaza Strip, which fact-checkers identified as false. A number of videos posted since the attacks were identified as entirely unrelated to the conflict — including footage filmed the previous month in Egypt, and a clip from the video game Arma 3 posted with the false claim that it showed Hamas missile attacks on Israel. Shayan Sardarizadeh (@Shayan86) flagged the Arma 3 clip on October 9, 2023: "This video certainly doesn't show a new air assault on Israel by Hamas militants, because it's actually from the video game Arma 3."

The volume was substantial. In remarks via X's safety account, the company reported more than 50 million posts globally over the past two days that referenced the weekend's terrorist attack, underlining the scope of content generated.

Two conditions shaped the environment. First, the attacks themselves: Hamas militants inside Gaza got past border fences and mounted a series of surprise attacks on Israeli civilians and tourists, after which Israel's prime minister declared "we are at war" and its military retaliated by firing scores of missiles into the Gaza Strip. By Thursday afternoon, per TechCrunch's 13 October report, Hamas' attack had killed more than 1,200 people according to the Israeli Military, and at least 1,537 people had been killed in Gaza by Israel's retaliatory strikes according to the Gaza Ministry of Health. Second, amplification on the platform itself: Eliot Higgins (@EliotHiggins) wrote on October 10, 2023 that "a totally false claim about Israel bombing a church in Gaza" had gone viral "thanks to multiple blue tick accounts repeating an unverified claim that had no evidence to back it up", adding that "Musk has created a fundamental issue with Twitter's credibility in moments of crisis."

X's owner was himself part of the observed pattern: at one point Musk recommended that people follow accounts that had posted antisemitic comments and false information in the past, though he subsequently deleted the tweet in which he made the suggestion. A Wired report published the day before TechCrunch's 10 October article summed up the situation on the platform under the headline "The Israel-Hamas War Is Drowning X in Disinformation."

# Kremlin Propaganda And Platform Countermeasures

EU values and transparency commissioner Vera Jourova warned in September 2023 that platforms must concentrate efforts to combat the spread of Kremlin propaganda, including in the context of looming EU elections the following year with the risk of Russia stepping up its election interference efforts.

"One of my main messages to the signatories is to be aware of the context. Russian war against Ukraine, and the upcoming EU elections next year, are particularly relevant, because the risk of disinformation is particularly serious," she said. "The Russian state has engaged in the war of ideas to pollute our information space with half-truth and lies to create a false image that democracy is no better than autocracy. Today, this is a multi-million euro weapon of mass manipulation aimed both internally at the Russians as well as at Europeans and the rest of the world. We must address this risk. The very large platforms must address this risk. Especially that we have to expect that the Kremlin and others will be active before elections. I expect signatories to adjust their actions to reflect that there is a war in the information space waged against us and that there are upcoming elections where malicious actors will try to use the design features of the platforms to manipulate."

The Commission's early analysis of Big Tech's Code reports produced three concrete counts. YouTube shut down more than 400 channels between January and April 2023 which were involved in coordinated influence operations linked to the Russian state-sponsored Internet Research Agency, and removed ads from almost 300 sites linked to state-funded propaganda sites. TikTok's fact-checking efforts now cover Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian and 17 European languages, including through a new partnership with Reuters; "In this context, 832 videos related to the war have been fact-checked, of which 211 have been removed," Jourova noted. And Microsoft reported that Bing Search had either promoted information or downgraded questionable information in relation to almost 800,000 search queries related to the Ukraine crisis.

# Community Notes

## Definition

Community Notes is X's (formerly Twitter's) crowdsourced fact-checking feature, which lets platform users add context to questionable posts: users vote to label disputed tweets, and the aggregated result may be appended to the post as a contextual note.

## Context

In the corpus the feature recurs as X's central, and contested, answer to disinformation risk after Elon Musk's takeover.

# Content Moderation

## Definition

Content moderation, as the corpus uses the term, is the mix of platform policy and enforcement — written rules like Meta's Violence and Incitement policy and Community Guidelines, human reviewers, automated systems, and crowdsourced tools like X's Community Notes — that decides what user-generated content stays visible and how a platform acts on notices of illegal or rule-breaking material.

## Context

In the corpus, content moderation surfaces mainly as the practice EU regulators scrutinize under the Digital Services Act (DSA): the DSA's "very precise obligations" require platforms to be "timely, diligent and objective" in acting on notices of illegal content, and the European Commission's formal DSA proceeding against X names "content moderation" as one of the specific areas under investigation, alongside risk management, dark patterns, advertising transparency, and researcher data access (doc_0024; doc_0153).
It also appears as a site of contested practice and bias: Meta's moderation of Palestinian-related content during the Israel-Hamas war produced widespread allegations of shadowbanning and inconsistent enforcement across Arabic versus Hebrew content (doc_0106), while Meta separately described tightening its livestreaming and hostage-content moderation in direct response to that same conflict (doc_0335).

## Key Characteristics

- **Policy plus enforcement** — moderation combines written rules (e.g. Meta's Violence and Incitement policy, Community Guidelines) with mechanisms to act on them: human reviewers, automated classifiers, and appeals processes (doc_0335; doc_0106).
- **Legally obligated for large platforms under the DSA** — the DSA requires timely, diligent, objective action on illegal-content notices, and imposes added systemic-risk mitigation duties (e.g. disinformation) on very large online platforms like X and Meta (doc_0024; doc_0335).

- **Prone to inconsistency and bias** — Meta's own third-party report found Arabic content flagged as violating at higher rates than Hebrew content, and attributed this to uneven language/dialect resources and reviewer training rather than deliberate policy (doc_0106).
- **Contested as speech regulation** — in the US, whether moderation decisions constitute protected "editorial judgment" under the First Amendment is the central legal question in the Texas/Florida social-media laws before the Supreme Court (doc_0256).
- **A competitive and reputational lever** — platforms position their moderation stance (heavy vs. light) as a market differentiator (doc_0508; doc_0405), though the corpus notes stricter moderation alone did not guarantee growth for at least one platform, Pebble, which shut down after never gaining more than 20,000 users (doc_0026).

# Very Large Online Platform (VLOP)

## Definition

A Very Large Online Platform (VLOP) is a service designated by the European Commission under the EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) as carrying obligations beyond the DSA's baseline, on the grounds of its scale. Designation is the discriminating feature: the DSA's general duties apply to digital services broadly, but a platform once designated a VLOP additionally must identify and mitigate the *systemic risks* its service poses — disinformation, threats to fundamental rights, and, for algorithmic services, the societal risks attached to their recommender systems. The parallel designation for search engines is the Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE).

## Context

In the corpus the term appears as the tier that triggers DSA enforcement against the largest platforms. The Commission designated Meta's Facebook and Instagram as VLOPs earlier in 2023, and designated X (formerly Twitter) a VLOP in April 2023; VLOP compliance obligations took effect over the summer of 2023. The Commission is the *sole enforcer* of the DSA over VLOPs, which is the basis on which it opened its own request for information and later a formal investigation into X, and weighed in on Meta's advertising consent model. Designation is also what obliges these platforms to mitigate the disinformation risks the EU raised around upcoming elections, and it is why the Commission treats the (voluntary) Code of Practice on Disinformation as underpinning the DSA, with its stated intention to transform the Code into a Code of Conduct forming part of a co-regulatory framework for addressing disinformation risks.

## Key Characteristics

- **Designation, not self-classification** — a service becomes a VLOP by a Commission decision, and only then carries the extra duties.
- **Systemic-risk duty** — beyond acting on illegal content, a VLOP must assess and mitigate systemic risks such as disinformation, even where the underlying content (e.g. disinformation) is not itself illegal in the EU.
- **Sole-enforcer model** — the European Commission, not national regulators, enforces the DSA against VLOPs directly.
- **Penalty exposure** — confirmed DSA breaches by a VLOP can draw fines of up to 6% of global annual turnover, with service blocking possible for repeated infringement.
- **Search-engine analogue** — VLOSEs are the equivalent designation for very large search engines, subject to the same systemic-risk logic.

## Background (external)

The corpus names VLOP designation but does not state the numeric threshold that triggers it. Per the European Commission, the DSA sets the bar at more than **45 million average monthly active users in the EU** (European Commission, *DSA: Very Large Online Platforms and Search Engines*, accessed 2026-09-02), and the first batch of VLOP/VLOSE designations was issued on **25 April 2023** (European Commission, *List of designated VLOPs and VLOSEs*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# The EU CSAM Scanning Proposal

The EU CSAM-scanning proposal is a controversial proposed law on the scanning of child sexual abuse material spearheaded by the European Union's home affairs commissioner, Ylva Johansson, whose final shape is still being determined by the European Council and MEPs as co-legislators — and which, as of TechCrunch's report of 25 October 2023, had become the subject of a Commission investigation into whether its own promotional advertising broke EU digital rules.

The immediate occasion for that definition is an admission. Johansson confirmed the Commission is investigating whether or not it broke recently updated digital governance rules when her department ran a microtargeted political ad campaign aiming to drive support for the proposal. At a committee hearing in the European Parliament that day she deflected MEPs' enquiries for her to give more details about the ad campaign.

The rule in question is the Digital Services Act, which includes provisions relating to online advertising — among them a prohibition on the use of sensitive personal data, such as political opinions, for targeting ads. The ads in question ran on X (formerly Twitter), which is already expected to be compliant with the DSA, having been designated by the Commission as a so-called Very Large Online Platform (VLOP) back in April.

The boundary case that makes the proposal distinctive is institutional rather than technical: the Commission itself not only proposed the DSA but is responsible for oversight of VLOPs' DSA compliance. If EU officials have used X's ad-targeting tools to break the bloc's own digital rulebook, it is the very definition of an awkward situation — the author, the enforcer and the suspected infringer being the same institution.

The campaign that triggered the investigation was found from outside. Its existence was spotted the previous month by technologist Danny Mekić, and an article with his findings ran in the Dutch newspaper De Volkskrant earlier in October 2023. Using the public ad transparency tools the DSA requires VLOPs to provide, Mekić found the Commission had run a paid advertising campaign on X targeting users in the Netherlands, Sweden, Belgium, Finland, Slovenia, Portugal and the Czech Republic — countries that were not supportive of Johansson's CSAM-scanning proposal according to leaked minutes from a September 14 meeting of the European Council, a co-legislative body that is involved, along with MEPs, in determining the final shape of the CSAM law.

Two features of the campaign's content distinguish it from routine institutional communication. Per Mekić, the campaign, which apparently racked up millions of views on X, insinuated that opponents of the proposed legislation did not want to protect children — messaging he dubbed "a form of emotional blackmail". The ads also included what he suggested is a misleading claim that the majority of Europeans support the proposal, based on a survey that highlighted "only the benefits but not the drawbacks of the proposed legislation"; other surveys, by the research firms YouGov and Novus, that highlighted the drawbacks showed "virtually no support" for the plan among the European population.

# X's Moderation Capacity After The Musk Takeover

X's capacity to act on content reports is best understood as a set of substitutions made since Musk's takeover the previous year: in-house enforcement capacity was cut, legacy policies and verification were removed, a crowdsourced mechanism was installed as the main response to disinformation, and the EU's voluntary disinformation Code was exited. TechCrunch's reporting in October 2023 describes each element and how they connect.

The first element is headcount. X's ability to respond internally to reports of content problems was drastically pared back after Musk's takeover, which saw major layoffs, including in content moderation and human rights, as part of the new billionaire owner's bid to improve the platform's profitability. Musk also ripped up a bunch of legacy content moderation policies and slashed in-house enforcement teams. The relation here is direct: the profitability motive is what drives the reduction in enforcement capacity.

The second element is signal quality. Musk ended legacy account verification and turned the Blue Check system into a game of pay-to-play, one of a series of changes that, in TechCrunch's account, make it harder for users to locate quality information on X — which is why the publication says Musk has painted the largest target on X when it comes to DSA enforcement.

The third element is the replacement mechanism. X has been pushing Community Notes — which crowdsources additional context to add to questionable tweets — as its main response to disinformation risks, promoting this decentralised, crowdsourced alternative in place of the in-house teams it cut. TechCrunch's reading of that substitution is sharply critical: it essentially outsources responsibility for dealing with tricky issues like disinformation to users, in what looks suspiciously like another gambit to eke out extra engagement and farm confusion by applying a philosophy of extreme relativism, so that culture warriors are encouraged to keep forever fighting for their own "truth" in the comments.

The fourth element is the regulatory posture around all of this. Earlier in 2023 Musk pulled X out of the EU's Code of Practice on online disinformation — in TechCrunch's words, a very clear thumb of the nose to EU regulators. That move did not change the binding position, and Breton said so in response to X leaving the voluntary Code: "Obligations remain. You can run but you can't hide." The range over which the model holds is therefore bounded on both ends — it describes X from Musk's takeover the previous year through the October 2023 reporting, and it applies to voluntary commitments only; the statutory DSA duties survive the exit.

# EU Demands On Fact-Checking And Researcher Data Access

In her September 2023 speech on the disinformation Code, EU commissioner Vera Jourova urged Code signatories to go further in two specific areas: fact-checking coverage and researcher access to platform data.

She called, yet again, for more consistent moderation and investment in fact-checking, especially in smaller Member States and languages. She also criticized platforms over access to data, saying they must step up efforts to make sure researchers are empowered to scrutinize disinformation flows "and contribute to the necessary transparency."



---


# The Contested Evidence On Social Media Harm

Buck records a reasonable counter-discussion about how many of our problems can really be laid at the feet of social media: the research on the impacts of social media on political dysfunction, mental health, and society writ large does not paint a neat portrait.

The objection attacks the causal premise rather than the description of the media ecology. Scholars have argued that putting too much emphasis on the platforms can be too simplistic and reeks of technological determinism, and have also pointed out that cultures like the United States' and the legacy media have a long history with post-truth.

That literature sits alongside a substantial body of work outlining the contours and dynamics of the current media ecology and what it does: Siva Vaidhyanathan's Antisocial Media, Safiya U. Noble's Algorithms of Oppression, Geert Lovink's Sad by Design, Shoshana Zuboff's Surveillance Capitalism, Richard Seymour's The Twittering Machine, Tim Hwang's Subprime Attention Crisis, Tressie McMillan Cottom's writing on how to understand the social relations of Internet technologies through racial capitalism, and many more. Buck's own position concedes the uncertainty without abandoning the concern: there are certainly dynamics going on that we did not anticipate, and we do not seem quite sure what to do with them, even with multiple areas of scholarship in communication, disinformation, and social media and democracy working on these inquiries for years.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Why Traditional E-Commerce Search Has Degraded

Deft co-founder Zach Hudson told TechCrunch that there are a few plaguing problems with the traditional search experience that prevent users from finding a suitable item — that is, the claim is that search has gotten worse, not that users have gotten worse at searching.

He offers three grounds, each a different actor degrading the result set: "You have companies like Google and Amazon that continue to push the most relevant listings down so they can make more advertising dollars. Some easy searches are now hard because marketers have learned how to game these search engines. Plus, now you have AI content that is putting the burden on users to separate fact from fiction," he said.

The warrant tying them together is that each mechanism moves cost onto the user: platform ad incentives bury relevance, SEO gaming inflates the noise, and AI-generated content shifts verification work to the person searching.

# The SEO-Algorithm Update Cycle

Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."

# Firefox's Decline: The Chrome Share Alternative Explanation

TechCrunch attacks the causal premise in Mozilla's Yahoo story — the inference that Firefox lost users *because* Yahoo was the default. As it puts it, that is not the full story.

Two grounds are offered. First, Yahoo was already well behind Google in terms of search technology at that point, so the switch conflated the default change with a pre-existing quality gap. Second, and more damaging to the inference, Firefox itself was very well behind Chrome: Chrome ended 2014 with nearly 50% market share and ended 2017 — when Google got prime default search position on Firefox — at nearly 65% of all web browser usage on desktop, with mobile even more skewed to Chrome. In other words, the number of Firefox users might have been declining for other reasons.

The counter also flags the interest at stake: pushing the blame on Yahoo certainly works in Google's favor here, since the story is being told in Google's defense.

# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.
