# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.

# Google's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

In its report to the EU disinformation Code, Google — an early adopter of generative AI in search via its Bard chatbot — discusses "recent progress in large-scale AI models" which it suggests has "sparked additional discussion about the social impacts of AI and raised concerns on topics such as misinformation."

Google summarised its approach: "Google is committed to developing technology responsibly and has published AI Principles to guide our work, including application areas we will not pursue," adding, "We have also established a governance team to put them into action by conducting ethical reviews of new systems, avoiding bias and incorporating privacy, security and safety. Google Search has published guidance on AI-generated content, outlining its approach to maintaining a high standard of information quality and the overall helpfulness of content on Search. To help address misinformation, Google has also announced that it will soon be integrating new innovations in watermarking, metadata, and other techniques into its latest generative models. Google also recently joined other leading AI companies to jointly commit to advancing responsible practices in the development of artificial intelligence which will support efforts by the G7, the OECD, and national governments. Going forward we will continue to report and expand upon Google developed AI tools and are committed to advance bold and responsible AI, to maximise AI's benefits and minimise its risks."

On forward commitments over the next six months, Google's report states it has no additional measures planned for YouTube. With generative image capabilities rolling out internally over the next year, it commits Google Search to leveraging the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard to add metadata tags to images generated by Google AI, and notes: "Creators and publishers will be able to add a similar markup to their own images, so a label can be displayed in Search to indicate the images as AI generated."

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# "Go Big In Europe": Google's Post-Fine Search Quality Push

The government argued on November 10, 2023 that Google only endeavored to enhance its search engine in the European Union after it was hit by a €5 billion antitrust fine in 2018 — a claim internal documents revealed, according to Bloomberg.

The EU's antitrust order forced Google to offer Android phone users a screen with five search engine options to choose from, according to the DOJ. In response, Google enacted a plan its executives dubbed "Go Big in Europe," to enhance search results in France and Germany in 2019 and 2020 with more local content: news, post-game soccer video highlights, information on local television options for streaming, and pronunciation practice for different languages. The aim was to incentivize users to click on Google's home screen rather than the competition's.

That revelation effectively supports the Justice Department's argument that Google, without the push of competition, has little incentive to improve its products — a classic consequence in a monopoly.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

# Prediction: AI-Generated Content Will Overwhelm Search

Daron Babin's proposition is that Google results will soon be even worse, dominated entirely by AI-generated crap designed to please the algorithms, produced and published at volumes far beyond anything humans could create — far beyond anything we had ever seen before.

The mechanism he gives is cost collapse at the bottom of the market: "All the assholes that are out there paying shitty link-building companies to build shitty articles now they can go and use the free version of GPT."

The prediction's strong form is that the volume is unstoppable: "They're not gonna be able to stop the onslaught of it," he said, then laughed and laughed, thinking about how puny and irrelevant Google seemed in comparison to the next generation of automated SEO. "You can't stop it!" What would falsify it is exactly that — Google proving able to stop the onslaught, so that results are not dominated by machine-produced content.

# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

# Google Warps The Web It Observes

The article's central claim is that Google, not the SEOs, defined the shape of the modern internet: you cannot be the most powerful observer in the world for two decades and not deeply warp what you are looking at.

The grounds are the structural impossibility built into Google's founding goal. The company started with a noble cause — trying to make the internet easier to navigate at scale — and did accomplish that, but in doing so it inadvertently and profoundly changed how the internet looked. The problem lay in Google trying to be an objective and neutral arbiter of an information landscape that was meant to pretend it did not exist: you cannot design a free, automated system to help people find information without some people trying to game that system.

The warrant that shifts responsibility away from practitioners is a comparison of scale and agency. For the past 25 years the internet as we know it has been almost entirely defined and controlled by Google; what the SEOs do matters for all of us on a daily basis, distorting how we perceive the world in ways we can hardly begin to imagine or understand, yet any money any SEO has made is a fraction of a crumb compared to Google's 10-layer cake. The company brings in hundreds of billions of dollars a year, profits that skew Google's choices and priorities — as Google's founders themselves wrote back in 1997, "we expect that advertising funded search engines will be inherently biased towards the advertisers and away from the needs of the consumers."

The writer reaches this position by way of Lily Ray, who seemed the most reasonable person she had spoken to — even granting that Ray calls herself a "thought leader" and changed her last name to improve her personal branding by more closely associating herself with her grandmother's uncle, the artist Man Ray. Maybe some people would say that is the kind of absurd behavior that merits being attacked by an alligator, but the writer was beginning to come down on the side of the SEOs, who seemed to have a lot less agency than she had first imagined.

# Google's Defense That Search Defaults Are Easy To Change

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. On Google's blog, president of global affairs Kent Walker said the search product was the favourite of users, browsers and device makers simply because it was the best in the business: "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," and "this lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today." Walker's supporting evidence is revealed preference when Google is not the default: when Mozilla made Yahoo! the default on Firefox, most users changed it to Google; and people setting up a Windows device frequently sidestep the Microsoft default — "Google" was the number one search query on Bing in 2021 — despite Microsoft making that very annoying to do. The Age's writer called this a compelling point, familiar to anyone who has dodged Microsoft's pleading while setting Chrome and Google as defaults on a new PC, but countered that all of these arguments ignore that Google and its competitors are not on an even playing field: the question remains why users prefer Google, and if the answer is that Google is simply better, the further question is whether that is down to its scale, longevity, ubiquity and all the user data it sucks up, which no other company could possibly match.

# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.

During Pichai's testimony, the DOJ touched on Google's policy of deleting internal chat messages despite the company being subject to a litigation hold. # Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Alphabet Q3 2023 Earnings Preview

Alphabet was set to announce its Q3 results during Tuesday 24 October 2023's post-market session, with the search-engine giant having outperformed the broader market index at a 55% growth rate that year, surpassing the S&P 500's 12%.

Following the company's upbeat Q2 results, investment firm Bank of America said it was expecting "favorable" headlines, due in part to strength in YouTube, search and artificial intelligence. Just a few days before the earnings report, Seeking Alpha's Quant Rating system changed its view from Strong Buy to Hold, while Wall Street analysts maintained a bullish view with a Strong Buy rating.

Consensus EPS estimates were $1.45 and consensus revenue estimates $75.73B. On the earnings insight, Google had topped EPS expectations in 4 of the past 8 quarters, beating revenue estimates in 5 of those reports.



---


# Mass-Generated AI SEO Spam And The Churn-And-Burn Strategy

The second major reason Google results feel different lately is SEO — specifically the obnoxious-kid-refusing-to-behave-in-class kind. Google is harder to game now, but the sheer volume of SEO bait being produced is so massive and so complex that Google is overwhelmed. "It's exponentially worse," Lily Ray said. "People can mass auto-generate content with AI and other tools," and "in many cases, Google's algorithms take a minute to catch onto it."

The rule-breaking itself is not new. "SEO that goes against Google's guidelines, it's not new," Ray explained; a decade ago it used to be called "black hat" SEO, in comparison to search engine-approved "white hat" tactics, and Google has gotten better over time at catching SEOs playing tricks on the algorithm. Although many of us may have rosy memories of how magical and cool Google seemed in the early days, most SEOs consider the years between 2003 and 2011 to be the boom times, when you could still get a fake corporate website listed above the real corporate website, and you could mess with the search results for a major political figure such that something sexual or racist would come up first.

The economics of the current wave explain its persistence. Eventually a site filled with computer-generated nonsense designed to maximize SEO will get removed from search results, Ray explained, but while it is up, the creator might make as much as $50,000 or $100,000 a month. A lot of the people who do this live cheaply overseas in places like Bali and Chiang Mai. "They make a bunch of money, that site dies, and they go do it again," she said. "It's like a churn and burn strategy. So if people are seeing those results, it can be very frustrating for users 'cause it's like, 'This is terrible.'" The future Babin had cackled about at the alligator party was already here: we humans and our pedestrian questions were getting caught up in a war of robots fighting robots, of Google's algorithms trying to find and stop the AI-enabled sites programmed by SEOs from infecting our internet experience.



---


# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.



---


# Search As Private Infrastructure, Not A Public Library

The claim is that routing nearly all online information through a single private company has left us arguably worse off than before, because information that is controlled by a private business will always be subject to that business's bottom line — which is exactly why most countries around the world have libraries that are public institutions.

The grounds are a comparison with what the internet was supposed to be. In the beginning it was seen as an improvement on the spirit of the public library: an opportunity to transcend the gatekeepers controlling who could publish a book, allowing mankind to fully connect and share knowledge. Instead, nearly all online information runs through a single company, which assumes a veneer of civic utility, of impassive authority, when it is very much not a neutral entity.

Matt Cutts supplies the insider warrant that the veneer is doing work. "There were so many true believers at Google in the early days," he said. "As companies get big, it gets harder to get things done. Inevitably, people start to think about profit or quarterly numbers." He claimed that, at least while he was there, search quality always came before financial goals, but he believes the public underestimates how Google is shaping what they see: "I deeply, deeply, deeply believe search engines are newspaper-like entities, making editorial decisions." He speculated that the company did not want the public to think too hard about how search works because that awareness "encourages regulators and makes people realize, 'Oh, there's a lot of money here.'"

The consequence is epistemic rather than commercial. There has always been advertising and polemics from cranks, scammers, and liars, but now we see this stuff surfacing alongside truth and we cannot tell the difference, so we move through our lives with a greater sense of distrust and fear and insecurity. At the end of the day, it is Google's world, and the SEOs are only living in it.

# The Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act Of 2023

Tuesday's Senate AI forum followed the recent introduction of new AI legislation dubbed the Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act of 2023 (S. 3050), co-sponsored by Senators Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Mike Rounds (R-SD), Charles Schumer (D-NY) and Todd Young (R-IN).

The bill proposes AI bug bounty programs and would require a vulnerability analysis study for AI-enabled military applications. Its passage into law would also launch a report into AI regulation in the financial services industry, as well as a second report on data sharing and coordination.

The financial-services provision lands on a problem the SEC's own chairman has been lamenting. "It's frankly a hard challenge," SEC Chairman Gary Gensler told The Financial Times recently, speaking on the challenges the financial industry faces in AI adoption and regulation. "It's a hard financial stability issue to address because most of our regulation is about individual institutions, individual banks, individual money market funds, individual brokers; it's just in the nature of what we do."



---


# The Biden AI Executive Order Of October 2023

The Biden Administration unveiled its next steps in addressing and regulating artificial intelligence development on Monday: an expansive executive order (EO) that seeks to establish further protections for the public as well as improve best practices for federal agencies and their contractors.

The order is framed as a whole-of-government instrument. "The President several months ago directed his team to pull every lever," a senior administration official told reporters on a recent press call. "That's what this order does, bringing the power of the federal government to bear in a wide range of areas to manage AI's risk and harness its benefits ... It stands up for consumers and workers, promotes innovation and competition, advances American leadership around the world and like all executive orders, this one has the force of law."

Its provisions are phased rather than immediate. The actions will be introduced over the next year, with smaller safety and security changes happening in around 90 days and more involved reporting and data transparency schemes requiring nine to 12 months to fully deploy. To keep that schedule, the administration is also creating an "AI council," chaired by White House Deputy Chief of Staff Bruce Reed, who will meet with federal agency heads to ensure the actions are being executed on time.



---


# Critical Infrastructure And CBRN Provisions Of The AI Executive Order

The executive order encourages the Departments of Energy and Homeland Security to address AI threats "to critical infrastructure, as well as chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and cybersecurity risks," and it attaches those standards to money: "Agencies that fund life-science projects will establish these standards as a condition of federal funding, creating powerful incentives to ensure appropriate screening and manage risks potentially made worse by AI." In short, any developers found in violation of the EO can likely expect a prompt and unpleasant visit from the DoE, FDA, EPA or other applicable regulatory agency, regardless of their AI model's age or processing speed.

The order also looks to use AI defensively. In an effort to proactively address the decrepit state of America's digital infrastructure, it seeks to establish a cybersecurity program, based loosely on the administration's existing AI Cyber Challenge, to develop AI tools that can autonomously root out and shore up security vulnerabilities in critical software infrastructure. It remains to be seen whether those systems will be able to address the concerns of misbehaving models that SEC head Gary Gensler recently raised.



---


# Foundation Model Reporting And Red-Team Disclosure Under The EO

The executive order sets out a reporting procedure for the most capable AI systems: a company developing any foundation model that poses a serious risk to national security, national economic security, or national public health and safety must notify the federal government when training the model, and must share the results of all red-team safety tests — and that information must be shared prior to the model being made available to the public, which could help reduce the rate at which companies unleash half-baked and potentially deadly machine learning products. The legal instrument used to compel this is the Defense Production Act.

Alongside red-team results, the EO also requires disclosure of the system's training runs — essentially its iterative development history. The purpose officials gave for the sequencing is verification: "What that does is that creates a space prior to the release… to verify that the system is safe and secure." The EO more broadly directs the establishment of new standards for AI safety and security, including reporting requirements for developers whose foundation models might impact national or economic security, and those requirements also apply in developing AI tools to autonomously implement security fixes on critical software infrastructure.

The procedure has a deliberately narrow scope. Administration officials were quick to point out that the reporting requirement will not affect any AI models currently available on the market, nor independent or small- to medium-size AI companies going forward, because the threshold for enforcement is quite high. It is geared specifically at the next generation of systems that the likes of Google, Meta and OpenAI are already working on, with enforcement on models starting at 10^26 petaflops — a capacity currently beyond the limits of existing AI models. "This is not going to catch AI systems trained by graduate students, or even professors," the administration official said.

The order was cast as a step past voluntary measures. "In response to the President's leadership on the subject, 15 major American technology companies have begun their voluntary commitments to ensure that AI technology is safe, secure and trustworthy before releasing it to the public," the senior administration official said. "That is not enough."



---


# The CPPA's Risk-Based Approach Versus The EU AI Act

The CPPA's approach to regulating ADMT is risk-based, per Soltani. That echoes another piece of in-train EU legislation, the AI Act — a dedicated risk-based framework for regulating applications of artificial intelligence which has been on the table in draft form since 2021 but is now at a delicate stage of co-legislation, with the bloc's lawmakers clashing over the not-so-tiny detail of how, or even whether, to regulate Big AI, among several other policy disputes on the file.

The relation TechCrunch draws between the two is one of comparative advantage under discord: given the disagreement around the EU's AI Act, as well as the ongoing failure of US lawmakers to pass a comprehensive federal privacy law — since there is only so much presidential Executive Orders can do — there is a plausible prospect of California ending up as one of the top global rulemakers on AI.

That relation holds only over a limited range. The impact of California's AI rules is likely to remain local, given its focus on affording protections and controls to state residents. In-scope companies might choose to go further, such as offering the same package of privacy protections to residents of other US states, but that is up to them; the bottom line is that the CPPA's reach and enforcement is tied to the California border.



---


# The EU AI Office And Its Scientific Advisory Panel

The AI Act will be implemented through a new AI Office set up within the EU's executive, which will coordinate with the Member State oversight bodies that will need to enforce the rules on AI firms and will oversee the most advanced AI models, including by contributing to fostering standards and testing practices — with a scientific panel of independent experts appointed to advise it about GPAI models.

Per internal market commissioner Thierry Breton, work to implement the agreement starts immediately with the set up of the AI Office. "We will welcome new colleagues… a lot of them," said Breton. "We will work — starting tomorrow — to get ready." The AI Office will play a key role in setting risk classification thresholds for GPAIs, but the Commission confirmed there is no budget nor headcount defined for the expert body as yet. Asked about resourcing, a Commission official said it will be decided in the future by the EU's executive taking "an appropriate and official decision," adding: "The idea is that we can create a dedicated budget line for the Office and that we will be able also to recruit the national experts from Member States if we wish to on top of contractual agents and on top of permanent staff. And some of these staff will also be deployed within the European Commission."

The scientific advisory panel, which the law will also establish, is meant to help the Office better understand the capabilities of advanced AI models for the purpose of regulating systemic risk. "We have identified an important role for a scientific panel to be set up where the scientific panel can effectively help the Artificial Intelligence Office in understanding whether there are new risks that have not been yet identified," the official noted. "And, for example, also flag some alerts about the models that are not captured by the FLOP threshold that for certain reasons could actually give rise to important risks that governments should should look at."



---


# Civil Rights, Privacy And Consumer Protections In The AI Executive Order

The executive order extends anti-discrimination guidance to "landlords, federal benefits programs and federal contractors" to prevent AI systems from exacerbating discrimination within their spheres of influence, and directs the Department of Justice to develop best practices for investigating and prosecuting civil rights violations related to AI — including, per the announcement, "the use of AI in sentencing, parole and probation, pretrial release and detention, risk assessments, surveillance, crime forecasting and predictive policing, and forensic analysis."

That builds on earlier work. The first Blueprint for an AI Bill of Rights, released by the White House last October, directed agencies to "combat algorithmic discrimination while enforcing existing authorities to protect people's rights and safety," the administration official said. "But there's more to do."

On privacy, the EO calls for prioritizing federal support to accelerate development of privacy-preserving techniques that would let future large language models be trained on large datasets without the current risk of leaking personal details those datasets might contain. Such solutions could include "cryptographic tools that preserve individuals' privacy," developed with assistance from the Research Coordination Network and the National Science Foundation. The order also reiterates its calls for bipartisan legislation from Congress addressing the broader privacy issues AI systems present for consumers.

In healthcare, the EO states that the Department of Health and Human Services will establish a safety program that tracks and remedies unsafe, AI-based medical practices. Educators will also see support from the federal government in using AI-based educational tools like personalized chatbot tutoring.



---


# Organized Labor's Pushback On AI Deployment

Organized labor's argument, voiced by AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler at the conclusion of Tuesday's Senate AI forum, is that AI's effect on workers depends entirely on whether workers are included in the process: "If we fail to involve workers and unions across the entire innovation process, AI will curtail our rights, threaten good jobs and undermine our democracy. But the responsible adoption of AI, properly regulated, has the potential to create opportunity, improve working conditions and build prosperity."

The grounds Shuler offered are that the technology is already being used against workers — "Working people are fighting back against artificial intelligence and other technology used to eliminate workers or undermine and exploit us" — so the warrant joining grounds to claim is that regulation plus worker participation is what separates the beneficial deployment path from the harmful one, rather than the technology itself deciding the outcome.

The same argument came from inside the industry. While Andreessen calls for AI advancement at any cost and Tegmark continues to advocate for a developmental "time out," rank-and-file AI industry workers pressed their own case ahead of the forum: on Monday, employees from two dozen leading AI firms published an open letter to Senator Schumer demanding Congress act to safeguard their livelihoods from the "dystopian future" that Andreessen's screed would require. "Establishing robust protections related to workplace technology and rebalancing power between workers and employers could reorient the economy and tech innovation toward more equitable and sustainable outcomes," the letter's authors argue. The previous month, Senator Ed Markey (D-MA) and Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) had called on leading AI companies to "answer for the working conditions of their data workers, laborers who are often paid low wages and provided no benefits but keep AI products online."



---


# Worker Protections And Federal AI Hiring In The Executive Order

The Biden administration concedes that while the AI revolution is a decided boon for business, its capabilities make it a threat to worker security through job displacement and intrusive workplace surveillance, and the EO seeks to address these issues with "the development of principles and employer best practices that mitigate the harms and maximize the benefit of AI for workers," an administration official said. "We encourage federal agencies to adopt these guidelines in the administration of their programs."

The order also directs the Department of Labor and the Council of Economic Advisors to study how AI might affect the labor market and how the federal government might better support workers "facing labor disruption" going forward. Administration officials also pointed to the potential benefits AI might bring to the federal bureaucracy, including cutting costs and increasing cybersecurity efficacy. "There's a lot of opportunity here, but we have to ensure the responsible government development and deployment of AI," an administration official said.

On hiring, the administration launched a new federal jobs portal on Monday, AI.gov, offering information and guidance on available fellowship programs for people looking for work with the federal government. "We're trying to get more AI talent across the board," an administration official said. "Programs like the US Digital Service, the Presidential Innovation Fellowship and USA jobs — doing as much as we can to get talent in the door." The White House is also looking to expand existing immigration rules to streamline visa criteria, interviews and reviews for people trying to move to and work in the US in these advanced industries.



---


# EU Lawmaker Reactions To The AI Act Deal

Carme Artigas, Spain's secretary of state for digital and AI issues, who led the Council's negotiations on the file as Spain held the rotating Council presidency since the summer, hailed the agreement on the heavily contested file as "the biggest milestone in the history of digital information in Europe" — both for the bloc's single digital market and, she suggested, "for the world."

"We have achieved the first international regulation for artificial intelligence in the world," Artigas announced during a post-midnight press conference to confirm the political agreement, adding, "We feel very proud." She predicted the law would support European developers, startups and future scale-ups by giving them "legal certainty with technical certainty."

Speaking on behalf of the European Parliament, co-rapporteurs Dragoș Tudorache and Brando Benifei said their objective had been to deliver AI legislation ensuring the ecosystem developed with a "human centric approach" that respects fundamental rights and European values, and they cited the inclusion in the agreed text of a total ban on the use of AI for predictive policing and for biometric categorization as major wins. "Finally we got in the right track, defending fundamental rights to the necessity that is there for our democracies to endure such incredible changes," said Benifei, who just a few weeks earlier had sounded doubtful a deal could be found. "We are the first ones in the world to have a horizontal legislation that has this direction on fundamental rights, that supports the development of AI in our continent, and that is up to date to the frontier of the artificial intelligence with the most powerful models under clear obligation. So I think we delivered." Tudorache added: "We have always been questioned whether there is enough protection, whether there is enough stimulant for innovation in this text, and I can say, this balance is there. We have safeguards, we have all the provisions that we need, the redress that we need in giving trust to our citizens in the interaction with AI, in the products in the services that they will interact with from now on. We now have to use this blueprint to seek now global convergence because this is a global challenge for everyone. And I think that with the work that we've done, as difficult as it was — and it was difficult, this was a marathon negotiation by all standards, looking at all precedents so far — but I think we delivered." The EU's internal market commissioner Thierry Breton described the agreement, clinched a little before midnight Brussels time, as "historic": "It is a full package. It is a complete deal. And this is why we spent so much time. This is balancing user safety, innovation for startups, while also respecting… our fundamental rights and our European values."



---


# The Schatz-Kennedy AI Labeling Act

Senators Brian Schatz (D-HI) and John Kennedy (R-LA) introduced legislation on Tuesday that would provide more transparency on AI-generated content by requiring clear labeling and disclosures — technology that could resemble the Content Credentials tag the C2PA and CAI industry advocacy groups are developing.

The bill, which its sponsors call the Schatz-Kennedy AI Labeling Act, would require generative AI system developers to clearly and conspicuously disclose AI-generated content to users. Those developers, and their licensees, would also have to take "reasonable steps" to prevent "systematic publication of content without disclosures." The bill would additionally establish a working group to create non-binding technical standards to help social media platforms automatically identify such content.

Schatz framed the measure plainly in a press statement: "Our bill is simple. If any content is made by artificial intelligence, it should be labeled so that people are aware and aren't fooled or scammed." Speaking on the Senate floor the same Tuesday, he added that the bill "puts the onus where it belongs: on the companies and not the consumers," and argued that "labels will help people to be informed. They will also help companies using AI to build trust in their content."



---


# Reaction To Biden's AI Order

Respondents to Biden's AI executive order attacked the premise that an executive order alone is a sufficient regulatory response, arguing that its breadth is real but its depth is not, and that the substantive work still requires Congress. Senator Mark Warner of Virginia said he was "impressed by the breadth" of the order, though, he implies, not the depth: "I am also happy to see a number of sections that closely align with my efforts around AI safety and security and federal government's use of AI," he said in a statement. "At the same time, many of these just scratch the surface – particularly in areas like health care and competition policy. While this is a good step forward, we need additional legislative measures, and I will continue to work diligently…" TechCrunch's own reading is that given the state of the legislature and the fact that an incredibly contentious election period is upcoming, it will be a miracle if any substantive law whatsoever is passed in the near future, let alone a potentially divisive and complex bill like AI rules.

Paul Barrett, deputy director of the NYU Stern Center for Business and Human Rights, acknowledged both sides of the issue and attacked the inference that direction of travel equals capacity to act. "President Biden is sending a valuable message that certain AI systems create immediate risks that demand immediate attention. The administration is moving in the right direction," he wrote. "But today is just the beginning of a regulatory process that will be long and arduous–and ultimately must require that the companies profiting from AI bear the burden of proving that their products are safe and effective, just as the manufacturers of pharmaceuticals or industrial chemicals or airplanes must demonstrate that their products are safe and effective. Without fresh resources provided by Congress, it's not clear that the federal government has the resources to assess the vastly complicated training process or the adequacy of red-teaming and other necessary testing."

A more favorable reading came from Sheila Gulati, co-founder of Tola Capital, who said the EO showed a "clear intention to walk the line of promoting innovation while protecting citizens." "It is most essential that we don't prevent agile innovation by startups. Putting AI explainability at the forefront, taking a risk-based approach with more focus on areas where harm or bias could be at play, and bringing security and privacy to the center of focus are all sensible steps," she told TechCrunch. "With this executive order and the standards implications through NIST, we would anticipate leadership from standards bodies versus legislators in the near term." It is worth mentioning as well that the federal government is a major customer of today's AI and tech products, and any company that intends to keep them as a customer will want to color inside the lines for the immediate future. Bob Cattanach, partner at legal mega-firm Dorsey and Whitney, added that the timing feels slightly off.



---


# EU AI Act Two-Tier Rules For General Purpose AI

The EU AI Act deal creates a "two-tier" system of guardrails for general purpose AIs (GPAIs) — the foundational models underpinning the viral boom in generative AI applications like ChatGPT — with a low risk tier and a high risk tier, and the trigger between them determined by an initial compute threshold set out in the law.

Low tier GPAIs face only lighter transparency requirements: model makers must draw up technical documentation and produce and publish detailed summaries about the content used for training in order to support compliance with EU copyright law, and there are obligations to apply watermarking to generative AI outputs. The high tier applies to "high-impact" GPAIs, defined as those where the cumulative amount of compute used for their training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than 10^25 FLOPs — models considered to have "high impact capabilities" and so-called "systemic risk." These face ex ante-style regulatory requirements to assess and mitigate systemic risks, meaning they must proactively test model outputs to shrink risks of actual, or "reasonably foreseeable," negative effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or society as a whole. The parliament wrote: "If these models meet certain criteria they will have to conduct model evaluations, assess and mitigate systemic risks, conduct adversarial testing, report to the Commission on serious incidents, ensure cybersecurity and report on their energy efficiency. MEPs also insisted that, until harmonised EU standards are published, GPAIs with systemic risk may rely on codes of practice to comply with the regulation."

The rules have two boundaries. Foundational models and GPAIs that have been commercialized face regulation under the Act, but R&D is not intended to be in scope of the law; and fully open sourced models will have lighter regulatory requirements than closed source ones, per the pronouncements made on the day of the deal.



---


# AI Training Transparency And Recordkeeping Requirements

The NMPA argues for a new regulation requiring AI developers to keep records of what data their algorithms ingested: "Transparency and recordkeeping requirements are needed to disincentivize infringing activity and to support enforcement activities by copyright owners."

The grounds are an enforcement problem the submission makes repeatedly: enforcing copyright against AI algorithms could be exceedingly difficult for rights holders, because "reverse-engineering" an AI algorithm to prove it was trained on content the developer had no right to is no easy task — save for when the AI produces a work substantially similar to the original, as in the lawsuits currently pending against AI companies. The NMPA also specifies who should bear the duty: "The primary parties who should be required to maintain records under a transparency and recordkeeping scheme are developers of AI models, those who use existing AI models to develop new AI tools and those who broker datasets for use in AI training."



---


# Google's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

In its report to the EU disinformation Code, Google — an early adopter of generative AI in search via its Bard chatbot — discusses "recent progress in large-scale AI models" which it suggests has "sparked additional discussion about the social impacts of AI and raised concerns on topics such as misinformation."

Google summarised its approach: "Google is committed to developing technology responsibly and has published AI Principles to guide our work, including application areas we will not pursue," adding, "We have also established a governance team to put them into action by conducting ethical reviews of new systems, avoiding bias and incorporating privacy, security and safety. Google Search has published guidance on AI-generated content, outlining its approach to maintaining a high standard of information quality and the overall helpfulness of content on Search. To help address misinformation, Google has also announced that it will soon be integrating new innovations in watermarking, metadata, and other techniques into its latest generative models. Google also recently joined other leading AI companies to jointly commit to advancing responsible practices in the development of artificial intelligence which will support efforts by the G7, the OECD, and national governments. Going forward we will continue to report and expand upon Google developed AI tools and are committed to advance bold and responsible AI, to maximise AI's benefits and minimise its risks."

On forward commitments over the next six months, Google's report states it has no additional measures planned for YouTube. With generative image capabilities rolling out internally over the next year, it commits Google Search to leveraging the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard to add metadata tags to images generated by Google AI, and notes: "Creators and publishers will be able to add a similar markup to their own images, so a label can be displayed in Search to indicate the images as AI generated."



---


# EU AI Act Political Agreement, December 2023

European Union lawmakers clinched a political deal on a risk-based framework for regulating artificial intelligence late on Friday, December 8, 2023, after marathon "final" talks which stretched to almost three days — meaning a pan-EU AI law is definitively on the way.

The file was originally proposed back in April 2021, and it took months of tricky three-way negotiations to get a deal over the line. Giving a triumphant but exhausted press conference in the small hours of Friday night/Saturday morning local time, key representatives for the European Parliament, Council and the Commission — the bloc's co-legislators — hailed the agreement as hard fought, a milestone achievement and historic, respectively. Taking to X to tweet the news, the EU's president Ursula von der Leyen — who made delivering a regulation to promote "trustworthy" AI a key priority of her term when she took up the post in late 2019 — lauded the political agreement as a "global first": "The EU AI Act is a global first. A unique legal framework for the development of AI you can trust. And for the safety and fundamental rights of people and businesses. A commitment we took in our political guidelines – and we delivered. I welcome today's political agreement."

The deal is billed by the bloc as the world's first comprehensive law for regulating artificial intelligence, and the Commission has confirmed that it includes powers for the Commission to adapt the pan-EU AI rulebook to keep pace with developments in the cutting-edge field.



---


# The CPPA's ADMT Rulemaking Timeline

The draft proposal marks the start of the CPPA's rulemaking process, with a consultation process — which will include a public component — set to kick off in the weeks after November 27, 2023. So it is still a ways off a final text. A spokeswoman for the CPPA said it was unable to comment on a possible timeline for the rulemaking, but noted this is something that will be discussed at the upcoming board meeting on December 8.

If the Agency is able to move quickly, TechCrunch judges it possible it could have a regulation finalized in the second half of 2024. There would obviously need to be a grace period before compliance kicks in for in-scope companies, so 2025 looks like the very earliest for a law to be up and running — and who knows how far developments in AI will have moved on by then.



---


# EU AI Act Phased Entry Into Force Timeline

The AI Act's compliance demands enter into force in phases after the law is adopted: six months until rules on prohibited use cases kick in, 12 months for transparency and governance requirements, and 24 months for all other requirements — so the full force of the EU's AI Act may not be felt until 2026.

Several steps stand before that clock starts. The final text must be compiled — the task facing the bloc over the coming weeks after the marathon 38-hour talks that ended on Friday night — and translated into Member States' languages, then affirmed by final votes in the parliament and Council, after which there is a short period before the text of the law is published in the EU's Official Journal and another before it comes into force. The consolidated text was expected to emerge in January or February, and it would be worth scrutinizing since there could still be devils lurking in the detail even though the EU's executive seemed keen to put key details out there in spite of there being no final text yet. Despite the EU visibly patting itself on the back over securing a deal on world-first AI rules, the lawmaking process was not quite at the end of the road; but given how much division and disagreement there had been over how, or even whether, to regulate AI, the biggest obstacles were dismantled by the political deal and the path to passing the Act in the coming months looked clear.

Within the phased approach, 24 months are allowed before the high-risk rules will apply for GPAIs, while the list of strictly prohibited use-cases applies sooner — just six months after the law enters into force. That could potentially mean bans on certain "unacceptable risk" uses of AI, such as social scoring or Clearview AI-style selfie scraping for facial recognition databases, get up and running in the second half of 2024, assuming no last-minute opposition to the regulation springs up within the Council or Parliament.



---


# CCPA To CPPA: The Regulatory Lineage Behind The ADMT Rules

The CPPA's bid to tackle AI follows the introduction of GDPR-inspired privacy rules back in 2019, with the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) coming into effect in early 2020. Since then the Agency has been pushing to go further, and in fall 2020 a ballot measure secured backing from state residents to reinforce and redefine parts of the privacy law. The new measures laid out in draft to address automated decisionmaking are part of that effort — so the ADMT rules are an implementation of an existing statute, not a new law.

"The proposed regulations would implement consumers' right to opt out of, and access information about, businesses' uses of ADMT, as provided for by the [CCPA]," the CPPA wrote in a press release. "The Agency Board will provide feedback on these proposed regulations at the December 8, 2023, board meeting, and the Agency expects to begin formal rulemaking next year."

In parallel, the regulator is considering draft risk assessment requirements intended to work in tandem with the planned ADMT rules: "Together, these proposed frameworks can provide consumers with control over their personal information while ensuring that automated decisionmaking technologies, including those made from artificial intelligence, are used with privacy in mind and in design," it suggests. Vinhcent Le, member of the regulator's board and of the New Rules Subcommittee that drafted the proposed regulations, added: "Once again, California is taking the lead to support privacy-protective innovation in the use of emerging technologies, including those that leverage artificial intelligence. These draft regulations support the responsible use of automated decisionmaking while providing appropriate guardrails with respect to privacy, including employees' and children's privacy."

# Generative AI

## Definition

In the corpus, "generative AI" is the umbrella label applied to the 2023 AI boom's content-producing systems — OpenAI's ChatGPT (built on GPT-3.5/GPT-4) and Adobe's Firefly image and vector-graphics models are the flagship examples named — rather than a term the corpus itself formally defines.

## Context

The corpus treats "generative AI" as the umbrella term for the mainstream AI boom of 2023, distinct from the EU AI Act's regulatory term "general purpose AI" (GPAI), which lawmakers deliberately chose as a more technology-neutral label for "the most powerful models behind the current boom in generative AI tools" so the law would not be pinned to one architecture like transformers (doc_0525).
OpenAI built ChatGPT specifically "to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI," and its free, chat-based interface is credited with "taking generative AI mainstream" as a consumer product rather than a research artifact (doc_0047).
Enterprise adoption is depicted as cautious relative to vendor hype: a Morgan Stanley survey found 56% of CIOs said generative AI was affecting investment priorities, but only 4% had launched significant projects, most still in evaluation or proof-of-concept (doc_0160).
The technology spans well beyond chatbots — Adobe's Firefly generative AI models generate images and vector graphics for creative software (doc_0043), and Amazon executive Tye Brady discussed generative AI alongside humanoid robots and mobile manipulation as an input to robotics work (doc_0528).
The same capability that drives adoption also drives the corpus's recurring regulatory and creative-industry concerns: the EU warned that "widely accessible generative AI tools" pose disinformation risks to elections (doc_0248), and the National Music Publishers Association called generative AI "the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed" in its copyright submission to the US Copyright Office (doc_0271).

## Key Characteristics

- **Illustrated by content-producing examples rather than defined outright** — the corpus shows the term through instances of new text, images, and vector graphics being produced from a prompt, illustrated by ChatGPT's text generation (doc_0048) and Firefly's image/vector generation (doc_0043).
- **Consumer breakout via chat interfaces** — ChatGPT's free, web-based chat interface is what took generative AI "mainstream," reaching the fastest adoption of any consumer app (doc_0047, doc_0048).
- **Enterprise adoption lags vendor hype** — large-company CIOs report slow, cautious rollout despite heavy vendor promotion, weighing API/SaaS costs against ROI (doc_0160).
- **Distinct from but overlapping "general purpose AI"** — EU lawmakers deliberately avoided calling the underlying models "generative AI" in law, choosing "general purpose AI" instead to stay technology-neutral rather than tied to transformer-based architectures (doc_0525).
- **Applies across domains beyond chatbots** — spans creative tools (Adobe Firefly) and robotics (Amazon's mobile manipulation work), per the corpus (doc_0043, doc_0528).
- **Focus of copyright and disinformation controversy** — named by the NMPA as a threat to the "human creative class" via unlicensed training data (doc_0271), and flagged by the EU as an election-disinformation risk requiring safeguards (doc_0248).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "generative AI" as a familiar shorthand without formally defining it. Per IBM, generative AI "is artificial intelligence (AI) that can create original content — such as text, images, video, audio or software code — in response to a user's prompt or request," distinguishing it from AI systems built only to classify or act on existing data (IBM, *What is generative AI?*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Second Senate AI Insight Forum, October 2023

Senator Charles Schumer (D-NY) hosted Silicon Valley's AI leaders on Tuesday as the US Senate reconvened its AI Insight Forum for a second time, and on leaving the meeting Schumer told the assembled press that "it is clear that American leadership on AI can't be done on the cheap," reporting that almost all of the experts in the forum called for robust, sustained federal investment in the private and public sectors to achieve American-led transformative and sustainable innovation in AI.

The guest list for this second session included manifesto enthusiast Marc Andreessen and venture capitalist John Doerr, along with Max Tegmark of the Future of Life Institute and NAACP CEO Derrick Johnson. According to a release from Schumer's office, the agenda covered "the transformational innovation that pushes the boundaries of medicine, energy, and science, and the sustainable innovation necessary to drive advancements in security, accountability, and transparency in AI."

On cost, National Security AI Commission estimates put the required federal investment at around $32 billion a year. Schumer believes those funding challenges can be addressed by "leveraging the private sector by employing new and innovative funding mechanisms — like the Grand Challenges prize idea." He framed the goal as a balance: "We must prioritize transformational innovation, to help create new vistas, unlock new cures, improve education, reinforce national security, protect the global food supply, and more," but in doing so "we must act sustainably in order to minimize harms to workers, civil society and the environment." As he put it, "We need to strike a balance between transformational and sustainable innovation. Finding this balance will be key to our success."

Schumer closed by saying the participants would leave "with a deeper understanding of how to approach American-led AI innovation," and that the conversation would continue "in weeks and months to come — in more forums like this and committee hearings in Congress — as we work to develop comprehensive, bipartisan AI legislation."

# Technology Neutrality: How The Online Safety Act Covers AI Content

The Online Safety Act attempts to address online harms in a "technology neutral" way, Whitehead says, regardless of how they have been created — so although artificial intelligence is not emphasized in Ofcom's consultation, that does not mean AI-generated content falls outside the rules.

The discriminating test is the harm, not the tool. AI-generated CSAM would be in scope by virtue of it being CSAM, and a deepfake used to conduct fraud would be in scope by virtue of the fraud. As Whitehead puts it: "We're not regulating the technology, we're regulating the context."

# TikTok's Synthetic Media Policy And Disinformation Measures

TikTok's report to the EU disinformation Code focuses on AI-generated content in the context of ensuring the "integrity" of its services, flagging a recent update to its community guidelines which also saw it modify its synthetic media policy "to address the use of content created or modified by AI technology on our platform."

The core rule is proactive disclosure: "While we welcome the creativity that new AI may unlock, in line with our updated policy, users must proactively disclose when their content is AI-generated or manipulated but shows realistic scenes," TikTok writes. It adds: "We continue to fight against covert influence operations (CIO) and we do not allow attempts to sway public opinion while misleading our platform's systems or community about the identity, origin, operating location, popularity, or purpose of the account. CIOs continue to evolve in response to our detection and networks may attempt to reestablish a presence on our platform. This is why we continue to iteratively research and evaluate complex deceptive behaviours and develop appropriate product and policy solutions. We continue to provide information about the CIO networks we identify and remove in this report and within our transparency reports here."

Commitment 15 in TikTok's report signs the platform up to "tak[ing] into consideration transparency obligations and the list of manipulative practices prohibited under the proposal for Artificial Intelligence Act." Under that pledge it lists being a launch partner of the Partnership on AI's "Responsible Practices for Synthetic Media" and contributing to the development of "relevant practices," and joining "new relevant groups" such as the Generative AI working group which started work that month. In the next six months it says it wants to further strengthen enforcement of its synthetic media policy and explore "new products and initiatives to help enhance our detection and enforcement capabilities" in this area, including in user education.

# FTC Generative AI Roundtable

At the FTC's conversation on generative AI and the creative industries, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-06, chair Lina Khan set out the agency's framing: "I know that generative AI in particular poses a unique set of opportunities and challenges to creative industries. We've already heard significant concerns about how these technologies could virtually overnight significantly disempower creators and artists who may watch their life's creation be appropriated into models over which they have no control."

The concerns raised by participants clustered on two points. In the comments, representatives from myriad creative communities expressed concerns around opt-out requirements that by default train AI models on artists' original work, and around how existing copyright law could be a useful if not comprehensive tool for setting out regulatory guardrails.

A representative with the WGA used the conversation to say the fight was not finished by collective bargaining: while striking writers obtained their own protections in a newly won agreement, the fight for artists' livelihoods "doesn't stop at the bargaining table."

Whether Congress mobilizes in time to address mounting concerns around AI and creative industries or not, for its part the FTC does appear to be very tuned into the technology's risks — and the power of bringing voices together across industries. FTC commissioner Rebecca Slaughter put the agency's position in categorical terms: "Art is fundamentally human. Humans may use technology to assist in creating art, but something cannot be art without human input. Technology is, by definition, not human . . . humans may endeavor to make generative AI that is ever more intelligent, [but] it cannot and will not replace human creativity."

# EU AI Act Watermarking And Transparency Obligations

Under the AI Act there is an obligation to try to watermark generative AI-produced text "on the basis of the latest state of the art technology that is available," as a Commission official put it when fleshing out details of the agreed watermarking obligations.

The obligation sits in an article that was already in the original Commission version of the risk-based framework presented back in April 2021, which focused on transparency requirements for technologies such as AI chatbots and deepfakes — but which will now also apply generally to general purpose AI systems.

The standard is deliberately relative to the state of the art rather than absolute, because the technology is uneven: "At the moment, technologies are much better at watermarking videos and audio than watermarking text," the official said. "But what we ask is the fact that this watermarking takes place on the basis of state of the art technology — and then we expect, of course, that over time the technology will mature and will be as [good] as possible."

# Microsoft's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

Microsoft — a major investor in OpenAI which has also baked generative AI capabilities into its own search engine — claims in its EU disinformation Code report that it is taking "a cross product whole of company approach to ensure the responsible implementation of AI."

The report flags Microsoft's "Responsible AI Principles," which it says it developed into a Responsible AI standard v.2, and Information Integrity Principles "to help set baseline standards and guidance across product teams." Microsoft continues: "Recognizing that there is an important role for government, academia and civil society to play in the responsible deployment of AI, we also created a roadmap for the governance of AI across the world as well as creating a vision for the responsible advancement of AI, both inside Microsoft and throughout the world, including specifically in Europe," committing to continue building on these efforts by developing new tools — such as Project Providence with Truepic — and inking partnerships, the examples it gives being the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) to combat the rise of manipulated or AI created media, EFE Verifica to track false narratives spreading in Spain, Latin America and Spanish-speaking populations, and Reporters Sans Frontières to use their Journalism Trust Initiative dataset in Microsoft products. "These partnerships are part of a larger effort to empower Microsoft users to better understand the information they consume across our platforms and products," it suggests, also citing media literacy campaigns and "cyber-skilling" which it says are "not designed to tell individuals what to believe or how to think; rather, they are about equipping people to think critically and make informed decisions about what information they consume."

On Bing Search, where Microsoft was quick to embed generative AI features — leading to some embarrassing early reviews which demonstrated the tool producing dubious content — the report claims a raft of mitigating measures: applying its AI principles during development and consulting with experts; engaging in pre-launch testing and a limited preview period and phased release; the use of classifiers and metaprompting, defensive search interventions, enhanced reporting functionality, and increased operations and incident response; and updating Bing's terms of use to include a Code of Conduct for users. The report also claims Microsoft has set up a "robust user reporting and appeal process to review and respond to user concerns of harmful or misleading content." For the next six months, the report does not commit Bing Search to any specific additional steps to address risk attached to the use of generative AI — Microsoft says only that it is keeping a watching brief: "Bing is regularly reviewing and evaluating its policies and practices related to existing and new Bing features and adjusts and updates policies as needed."
