# Data Privacy

## Definition

Data privacy, across the corpus, is the recurring dispute over whether companies may collect, track, or profile people's personal information without their knowledge or consent.

That dispute plays out as regulatory enforcement against platforms: GDPR action against Meta's consentless ad tracking (doc_0107), COPPA litigation over Meta's collection of data from children under 13 (doc_0304), a "mass breach of privacy" allegation against TikTok's pre-consent tracking pixel (doc_0189), and California's CPPA extending opt-out and access rights to AI-based profiling (doc_0164).

## Context

In the corpus, data privacy surfaces as the recurring fault line between platforms that monetize personal data and the regulators pushing back on non-consensual collection. Norway's Datatilsynet issued an emergency GDPR ban on Meta running "personalized ads" without consent, then referred the case to the EU's Board to make the ban permanent across the single market, because Meta kept running tracking ads despite the order and a rejected court challenge (doc_0107). California's CPPA is drafting rules that would give residents opt-out and access rights over "automated decisionmaking technology," explicitly modeled on GDPR and expected to draw pushback from adtech and AI firms like Meta and OpenAI (doc_0164). The Age's investigation found TikTok's tracking pixel scraping site visitors' names, emails, and phone numbers before users clicked "I consent," prompting an Australian senator to call it a "mass breach of privacy" and demand a regulatory probe (doc_0189). Meta separately faces a 42-state lawsuit alleging it violated COPPA — the US law restricting data collection from children under 13 and requiring parental consent — by knowingly letting millions of underage users onto Instagram and Facebook while collecting their personal information (doc_0304).

## Key Characteristics

- **Consent is the legal hinge** — GDPR, as applied against Meta in Norway, turns on whether a company has a valid legal basis (consent, not "legitimate interest" or "contractual necessity") before tracking or profiling users for ads (doc_0107).
- **Pre-consent collection is the specific harm alleged against TikTok** — its pixel captured form-field data "often before clicking 'I consent'," unlike Google's and Meta's pixels, which the same test showed firing only after consent (doc_0189).
- **Children are a protected, heavily litigated category** — COPPA restricts data collection from users under 13 and requires verifiable parental consent, and Meta's alleged evasion of that requirement (ignoring reports, not disabling accounts, avoiding "actual knowledge") is the specific violation named in the unredacted lawsuit (doc_0304).
- **Regulators are extending consent/access rights into AI** — California's CPPA is drafting opt-out and access rights over automated decisionmaking technology and AI-based profiling, explicitly borrowing from GDPR's model (doc_0164).
- **Enforcement can escalate beyond a single national regulator** — Norway's local DPA used an emergency GDPR mechanism to bypass the "one-stop-shop" rule and force an EU-wide decision on Meta, showing that a single country's action can become bloc-wide policy (doc_0107).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the general legal concept the enforcement actions above are built on is the definition of "personal data" under GDPR.

GDPR.eu describes personal data as "any information that relates to an individual who can be directly or indirectly identified," a category spanning obvious identifiers like names and emails as well as location data and other online identifiers (GDPR.eu, "What Is GDPR, the EU's New Data Protection Law?", published by Proton AG with EU Horizon 2020 co-funding, accessed 2026-09-02: https://gdpr.eu/what-is-gdpr/).

# Irish DPC's Assessment Of Meta's Consent Model

Meta's lead regulator in the EU for the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC), told TechCrunch: "Meta notified the DPC on July 27 of its intention to implement an alternative, consent-based model in which users would be given a choice between ads-funded versions of its platforms, and subscription versions in which, in return for payment of monthly fee, it is said that users will not receive targeted advertising."

The regulator also set out the timing and its cause: "While February 2024 was initially identified by Meta as the earliest date by which its consent model would be operational, it agreed to bring forward that date to November 2023 at the direction of the DPC, the DPC having been concerned to ensure that changes would be implemented to the platforms as soon as practicable in light of earlier findings to the effect that Meta had failed to demonstrate its entitlement to rely on the legal bases on which it was then relying when processing users' data for behavioural advertising purposes. These included findings made by the Court of Justice of the European Union when delivering judgment on July 4, 2023 in a case in which the Court examined the legal bases on which Meta's processing of users' data for behavioural advertising purposes is grounded." On the review itself: "Acting in consultation with its fellow European supervisory authorities, the DPC has been engaged in a detailed regulatory assessment of the consent-based model since it was first proposed by Meta in July. That exercise is being led by the DPC, reflecting its position as Lead Supervisory Authority for Facebook and Instagram in Europe. The exercise has not yet concluded, and no findings have been made to date. It is due to be completed shortly, at which point the DPC will notify Meta if it considers that the manner in which its new user offerings are to be implemented is compatible with Meta's obligations under GDPR." So Meta's move hasn't been signed off by data protection authorities as yet, and further regulatory interventions could follow — Norway's DPA, which has a local ban order on Meta's tracking ads, told TechCrunch it's concerned about the subscription plan, saying it has doubts as to whether it would constitute valid consent.

# Sports Betting Odds

## Definition

Sports betting odds are the numbers a sportsbook posts alongside a wager to show the payout a bettor stands to win relative to their stake, and they are set by oddsmakers using computer models and analytics before being released to the public. The same underlying odds concept takes different shapes depending on the bet type — a moneyline price on who wins outright, a point spread price on a handicapped margin, and a totals (over/under) price on the combined score — and can be displayed in American, decimal, or fractional format.

## Context

In the corpus, odds are the common thread across every major bet type: moneylines, point spreads, totals, and prop bets all price outcomes with the same odds conventions, and combined-market previews such as college bowl coverage post moneyline, spread, and total odds side by side for a single game. Odds are not static — sportsbooks move them ("line movement") in response to public betting patterns, injury or roster news, and sharp/professional money, with the goal of balancing action on both sides of a bet so the book keeps its built-in profit regardless of outcome. Because different sportsbooks can carry different odds for the same event, bettors practice "line shopping" — comparing odds and lines across multiple sportsbooks before wagering to find the best price. Odds also extend beyond single games into futures and award markets, such as season-long odds on the NFL MVP race between Brock Purdy and Lamar Jackson.

## Key Characteristics

- **American odds format dominates U.S. listings** — a negative number (e.g., -110) shows the favorite and how much must be wagered to profit $100; a positive number (e.g., +250) shows the underdog and how much a $100 wager profits.
- **Three display formats carry the same price** — American, decimal (multiply the odds by the stake for total payout), and fractional (numerator = profit, denominator = stake) are alternative notations for identical odds.
- **Odds move for identifiable reasons** — sportsbooks shift a line or its odds because of lopsided public betting, new information (injuries, weather), sharp bettor action, or a perceived initial mispricing.
- **Odds differ by bet type but share the sign convention** — moneyline odds price the outright winner, point spread odds price a handicapped margin near even money, and totals odds price the over/under of a combined score; all three commonly display as American odds.
- **Line shopping exploits cross-sportsbook odds variance** — because oddsmakers and sportsbooks don't always move in lockstep, checking odds at multiple books before betting can secure a better price on the same wager.

# Line Shopping: Comparing Sportsbooks To Maximize Your Return

"Line shopping" means researching several different sportsbooks to compare odds, so you find the best price for the bets you were already planning to make and maximize your potential return. Not all sportsbook betting odds are created equal, so if you are willing to put in some legwork you can shop for the best lines.

# The Timing Trade-Off In Rookie Of The Year Futures Betting

There is a fixed trade-off in when to bet NBA Rookie of the Year futures: the earlier you bet, the better the odds, but you bet without much information that could be key to an educated decision; conversely, if you wait for the data you need for an informed bet, the odds tighten and you see less of a return.

The mechanism is symmetric between bettor and book. When the lines are first released, the season has not started, so there are no statistics, trends or player news — the pre-season odds are so favorable precisely because even the oddsmakers lack the data to craft more specific lines. Once the season starts and you can see how the rookies are performing, you can gather the relevant data; but sportsbooks are gathering the same information and tighten the Rookie of the Year lines in response. So while you can better guess who will hoist the Wilt Chamberlain Trophy, the odds are tighter and your potential return reduced.

Stated as pros and cons: betting early gives an opportunity to find better value and betting odds that are fresh and unadjusted, but carries much higher risk because a player's performance, health and team dynamic can change through the season, and offers limited information. Waiting gives a lot more information for an informed bet and avoids betting on a player not remotely in contention, but reduces the opportunity to find value and the odds may not be as favorable. The range over which this holds is bounded by the individual: it is always important to take your risk tolerance into consideration while weighing the potential rewards, and no matter when you decide to wager, always gather as much information as possible before risking your money.

# How Sportsbooks Set And Move Betting Lines

The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services to set their lines and odds, while other sports betting apps simply copy those lines. The oddsmakers and services use computer models and algorithms that consider analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, matchup data and more to develop the lines and odds. Those lines are then subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that emerges before the game, and a book will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side.

The governing objective is balance rather than prediction. Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet, because that lets the book earn the small profit built into the odds and lines without worrying about which side wins. Sportsbooks want even betting so much that they will move a line or change the odds specifically to draw more bets to the other side.

The relation that matters to a bettor is that books do not all move together. The betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook: one book may be forced to move a line or change the odds because of the money it has taken while another is not, and the lines and odds may even differ right from the jump. That divergence is what creates the chance to book a bet at improved odds or a more favorable line.

The range over which this holds is narrow and specific. When a line moves for a legitimate reason such as an injury or roster move, every sportsbook jumps on board, and it is difficult to find value; when a line moves because of betting patterns, only the sportsbook that saw that betting makes the change, and that is the opportunity. Line shopping is the tool for spotting the second kind: choose a side, shop around at online sportsbooks, compare the lines and odds, and pounce when you find one offering something different and more favorable to your viewpoint.

# Point Spread Odds And Line Movement

Alongside a point spread, sportsbooks attach odds indicating the potential payout relative to the amount wagered, and those odds sit close to even because the spread itself is designed to level the playing field between the two teams. The same payout can be expressed in several formats: American (for example -110 or +110), Decimal (for example 1.91), and Fractional (for example 10/11), each a different way of stating the same potential return.

Point spread odds are not fixed once set; the shifts are commonly called "line movement." Lines move when the point spread or the odds attached to a particular bet change after sportsbooks have initially set them, and Sporting News identifies several drivers. The most common cause is an imbalance in the money being wagered on one side: if a significant majority of bettors back one team to cover, the top sports betting apps adjust the spread to make the other side more appealing and thereby balance the betting action. A second driver is unexpected events — injuries to key players, changes in team strategy, or significant weather events that might affect a game's outcome; for instance, if a star quarterback is announced as injured days before a big game, the spread might shift in favor of the opposing team. A third driver is information and public perception: when a piece of news or a prevailing sentiment about a team's increased chances of winning gains traction, it influences how people bet and leads sportsbooks to adjust their lines accordingly.

Every sportsbook sets its own line on each market, so it is important to find the best odds in order to maximise your return when you win; many bettors use multiple sportsbooks to "shop" for lines, and there are sites that allow you to compare odds from multiple sportsbooks. Fourth, markets. Each sportsbook will allow you to bet on different games and events — "markets" — in different ways, and in addition to common bets like spread, total and moneyline, you'll want an app with same game parlays, props, futures and other fun bet types.

The procedure assumes an operating precondition stated by the third criterion: because pricing varies between books, the method works best when the bettor is willing to hold accounts at more than one sportsbook rather than choosing a single app once.



---


# Four Sportsbooks For NBA MVP Futures Betting

The Sporting News names four favourite sportsbooks for placing MVP futures bets — DraftKings, FanDuel, BetMGM and Caesars — distinguished mainly by usability and the breadth of their markets.

The DraftKings app is one of the most prominent in the US, offering bets for just about any market including the NBA MVP award and known for its ease of use, with top features including live betting options and a diverse prop betting selection. FanDuel is touted as one of the industry's most user-friendly and best sports betting apps and has built a massive following; beyond a packed futures menu that includes NBA MVP, it has a noteworthy selection of player props and a same-game parlay feature.

BetMGM trades ease of use for depth: the app may take a little getting used to, but the sheer number of betting opportunities is fantastic, and popular features such as "edit my bet" and "easy parlay" have helped make it a leading sportsbook in many states where sports betting is legal. Caesars sits at the opposite end — the betting app may be basic, but the simplicity is part of the draw for customers, along with an outstanding selection of competitive odds, and Caesars also provides NBA betting promos and more sports betting bonuses and promotions for existing customers.



---


# DraftKings Sportsbook In Kentucky

DraftKings is a sportsbook with roots in daily fantasy sports whose defining feature among Kentucky books is a rewards program aimed especially at daily fantasy players, as described by CBS Sports on 13 October 2023.

The rewards mechanism is the discriminating detail: rewards points are earned for most wagers and can be redeemed for free bets, merchandise, or daily fantasy entries in any sport DraftKings offers. Beyond that it offers a variety of betting markets — thousands of ways to bet on sports, including pick'em and props pools — with a wagering menu that includes live and in-game bets, cross-sports parlays and moneylines, and it is known for frequent and generous profit boosts that customers can use on specific bet types, including same game parlays. At the time of writing, new customers could bet $5 and receive $200 in free bets with the current promotion.

The report frames the appeal as giving bettors more ways to "have skin in the game" and get closer to the games they love.



---


# Prop Bet Examples By Sport

Every major sport with odds at the best sports betting apps will have prop bets, and the shape of those props follows each sport's statistics. The NBA offers a wide range, varying from player to team bets and leaning heavily on the statistical side of the game: how many points a player will score, the number of assists or three-pointers a player will have, which player will score the first basket. Team props are also available, such as whether a team will lead at the end of a certain quarter, or an over/under on the total number of points a team will score.

The NFL is the king of sports betting, and NFL betting sites have no qualms about showcasing every possible bet type. Bettors find many prop opportunities, especially for the Super Bowl; during the regular season one of the most popular options is the "anytime touchdown scorer" bet, where you wager on a player to score a touchdown at any point in the game, and other props focus on one team or both teams.

Baseball, hockey and soccer follow the same logic on their own stat lines. MLB props focus primarily on individual players and statistical achievements such as home runs, RBI and strikeouts — an over/under for a starting pitcher's strikeouts, or the number of bases a hitter will reach. NHL sites carry the props you would expect from a major North American league, such as player assists or a certain player scoring a goal, plus shots on goal, team goals in a game, and which team will score first. In Major League Soccer, where demand has increased as the sport's popularity grows nationwide, props often focus on individual accomplishments such as scoring a goal or collecting an assist, and also include how many cards the two teams will combine to draw or a team's total number of corner kicks.



---


# The Three Staple NBA Bet Types: Point Spreads, Moneylines And Totals

For anyone new to NBA betting the staple wager types are point spreads, moneylines and over/unders. NBA point spreads bet on games via margins of victory or loss: if the New York Knicks are -7.5 favorites over the Miami Heat, the Knicks need to win by 8 points to win a spread bet, while the Heat can lose by up to 7 points or win outright. NBA moneylines are the simplest form of betting — you pick the winner of the game and are paid based on the odds when you finalize your bet slip, with favorites shown at negative odds such as -135 and underdogs at positive odds such as +165. NBA over/under bets, also known as totals, focus on the combined point total of the two teams, with winners and losers irrelevant: if the over/under in Knicks vs. Heat is 211.5 points, the over needs the teams to combine for 212 or more, while the under needs 211 or fewer.

These sit inside a much wider menu. With legal sports betting available in over 30 states, the NBA gives bettors plenty of games, teams and players across hundreds of odds markets — moneylines, totals and point spreads, plus player props for scoring, rebounding and assists, and futures bets such as odds to win the Eastern Conference or individual awards like NBA MVP. Bettors will want to find the best NBA betting lines night after night as well as futures markets from NBA Finals odds to Rookie of the Year odds, and any online betting site will offer plenty of odds to choose from.



---


# NBA In-Game Betting: Wagering While The Game Unfolds

In-game betting, also known as live betting, allows you to bet on a game while it is unfolding, and it has exploded nationwide thanks to the increased popularity of online sports betting apps. The action is fast and the odds are constantly shifting, making for a new way to enjoy the flow of a game while staying engaged as a bettor.

Depending on the sportsbook there is usually a strong variety of live betting opportunities. These include game and player prop bets such as whether the next bucket will be worth one, two or three points; bets on the team leading at the end of the current quarter; bets on whether there will be a comeback victory; and wagers boiled down to the results of the next possession.

The most popular sportsbook apps — DraftKings, FanDuel and BetMGM — offer NBA in-game betting, though each has its own lines and betting opportunities.



---


# Live In-Play Golf Betting

Live betting offers the opportunity to bet on golf tournaments as they unfold, with the main options covering the overall tournament victor, winners of individual rounds, and direct head-to-head matchups. Using a sportsbook app streamlines the process and gives immediate access to fluctuating, real-time odds.

The most lucrative live bets in golf often revolve around backing players who have had a slow start but have the talent to stage a comeback.

The live odds set by sportsbooks for golf events are determined by continually evaluating player performance alongside considerations such as course dynamics, prevailing weather, and player stamina.



---


# Totals Bet Outcomes: Push And Overtime

An over/under wager has three potential outcomes: if the combined score exceeds the set total, the "over" bet wins; if the score is below the set total, the "under" bet wins; and if the combined score of the game matches the total exactly, the bet is typically considered a "push" and the wager is refunded.

A push therefore occurs when the combined score of a game matches the set total established by the bookmaker, meaning bettors neither win nor lose and their original wager is returned. To avoid this outcome, most sportsbooks employ half-points in their totals: by setting a total at 200.5 instead of 200, sports betting sites ensure that a game's combined score cannot possibly match the set total exactly.

Overtime is a separate boundary case. In most sports and with the majority of sportsbooks, overtime does count toward a totals wager; Sporting News advises always checking the specific rules of the sportsbook you are betting with to confirm, but says overtime is generally included in totals wagers.

qid: Has the stance of the Federal Reserve on interest rates as reported by The Sydney Morning Herald remained the same between the article published on October 1, 2023, suggesting smaller future rate cuts, and the one from November 5, 2023, indicating a continuation of rate increases?
context:
# Federal Reserve Rate Path Expectations Late 2023

By early December 2023 traders widely expected the Federal Reserve to hold its key interest rate steady at its meeting the following week before potentially cutting rates in March, according to data from CME Group, and Fed officials had recently hinted that the federal funds rate may already be at its peak, above 5.25 per cent, up from nearly zero early in 2022. Fed Chair Jerome Powell and others nevertheless warned Wall Street against being overzealous in its predictions about how early a cut could happen.

The bond market moved with those expectations. With inflation down from its peak two summers earlier, Wall Street was hopeful the Fed might be done with its market-shaking hikes. Investors were looking for a slowdown in the job market that came through employers cutting back on open positions rather than laying off workers, and the report cited showed employers advertised just 8.7 million jobs on the last day of October, down 617,000 from a month earlier. US Treasury yields continued to sag from the heights reached during late October: the 10-year yield fell to 4.18 per cent from 4.26 per cent late on the Monday, after having been above 5 per cent and at its highest level in more than a decade during October. The two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks Fed expectations, fell from 4.61 per cent just before the economic reports to 4.57 per cent, yo-yoed, and then eased back to 4.57 per cent. Lower yields were one reason cryptocurrency prices had been rising, alongside excitement about a possible bitcoin exchange-traded fund that helped send bitcoin above $US43,000 ($65,600); Robinhood Markets reported a roughly 75 per cent jump in crypto trading volumes during November from a month earlier, said customers added about $US1.4 billion in net deposits during the month, and its own stock rose 10.3 per cent.

A month earlier, in early November 2023, the same expectations were forming from a lower base. Before that week, stocks had been struggling under the weight of rapidly rising Treasury yields catching up to the Fed's main interest rate, which was above 5.25 per cent and at its highest level since 2001. Higher rates and yields slow the economy, hurt investment prices and raise the risk of something breaking in the financial system, such as the three high-profile US bank failures that rattled markets during the spring. "It was really fear that the Fed was going to go too far," said Katie Nixon, chief investment officer for Northern Trust Wealth Management. The Fed had applied that pressure intentionally, hoping to starve inflation of its fuel and to cool the job market, particularly pay raises, because it feared too-strong pay gains could create a vicious cycle keeping inflation high. Analysts said the Friday jobs report offered encouraging signals, with average hourly earnings rising less in October from September than expected, though it did not mean the job was done. Treasury yields tumbled immediately after that report, with the 10-year easing to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday and from more than five per cent the previous week, when it hit its highest level since 2007. Traders then moved up expectations for the first Fed cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data. Foreign-exchange strategists at Bank of America wrote in a BofA Global Research report that for investors around the world the "Fed matters more than other central banks" and weak US data is "the only game-changer for markets". A separate report that Friday from the Institute for Supply Management said growth in US services industries such as finance and construction was weaker than economists expected and suggested a slight easing in prices.



---


# How Treasury Yields And "Higher For Longer" Transmit To Equities

Treasury bonds are seen as some of the safest investments possible, and when they pay higher yields, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments — which is a big reason why the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent.

The chain running into those yields is the Federal Reserve's stance. Treasury yields have been climbing sharply as Wall Street accepts a new normal in which the Fed is likely to keep interest rates high for longer; the Fed is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target, and its main tool of high interest rates does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the previous week that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The data cuts both ways within this model. Friday's economic data showed that not only was inflation a touch cooler than expected in August, so was growth in spending by US consumers, which can be a positive for inflation because it means not as many dollars are pouring into purchases and that in turn could give companies less encouragement to raise prices further — but it may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession.



---


# US Treasury Yields And Fed Rate Expectations In October 2023

The mechanism linking data to yields to stocks ran in both directions during October 2023. On 4 October, the yield on the 10-year Treasury, the centrepiece of the bond market, pulled back from its highest level since 2007, down to 4.73 per cent from 4.80 per cent late on the Tuesday, with shorter- and longer-term yields also easing to allow more oxygen for the stock market. Yields fell following reports indicating a slowing US economy, the first suggesting that hiring by employers outside the government was much weaker than expected; on Wall Street that is currently good news because a cooling job market could mean less upward pressure on inflation, which in turn could convince the Federal Reserve to take it easier on interest rates. After already raising its main interest rate to the highest level since 2001, the Fed had indicated it may keep its overnight rate higher next year than earlier expected, and Treasury yields had correspondingly snapped higher as traders accept a new normal of high rates for longer; the Fed pays particular attention to the job market because too much strength there could drive wages much higher, which it fears could keep inflation well above its target of 2 per cent.

By 12 October the same mechanism was running the other way. The stock market has largely been taking its cue from the bond market recently, and weak results announced in the afternoon for an auction of 30-year Treasury bonds sent yields of all kinds higher; higher yields can knock down prices for stocks and slow the economy by making borrowing more expensive. Yields had already been rising in the morning after a report showing consumer-level inflation a touch higher than economists expected, raising worries about the Fed keeping its main interest rate high for a long time as it tries to undercut inflation by knocking down investment prices and slowing the economy. The report also had encouraging nuggets: after ignoring prices for food and fuel, which Fed officials see as a better predictor of where inflation is heading, prices consumers paid were in line with expectations and continued to decelerate from earlier months. A second report said slightly fewer US workers than expected applied for unemployment benefits, indicating a job market with few lay-offs and therefore strength for the overall economy, though it could also add fuel to upward pressure on inflation. After the reports the 10-year Treasury yield rose to 4.7 per cent from 4.56 per cent late Wednesday, and the two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks expectations for the Fed, climbed to 5.06 per cent from 4.99 per cent, with yields still down slightly for the week after regressing from more-than-decade highs following speeches that investors saw as hints the Fed may not raise its main overnight rate further. The big jump for the 10-year yield since the summer has pulled mortgage rates to their highest levels since the turn of the millennium, and such moves could slow the economy without requiring more Fed hikes; Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, said nothing in Thursday's inflation report should sway the Fed one way or the other on what it will do on 1 November, calling the data "reassuringly uneventful".



---


# ASX Outlook And RBA Rate Expectations At End-September 2023

The Australian sharemarket was set to retreat with futures pointing to a fall of 38 points, or 0.5 per cent, at the open, after Wall Street closed out its worst month and quarter of the year with more losses on Friday.

Most sectors traded lower, but interest-rate sensitive sectors including healthcare and consumer companies were among the weakest amid expectations that the RBA would keep rates on hold in October; the National Australia Bank has forecast another rate hike to 4.35 per cent in November. On Wall Street the S&P 500 slipped 0.3 per cent with the majority of stocks within the index sinking, the Dow Jones fell 0.5 per cent and the Nasdaq composite edged 0.1 per cent higher. Solid gains for stocks early on faded as pressure built from within the bond market: after easing earlier in the day on encouraging signals about inflation, Treasury yields got back to rising as the day progressed, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury returned to 4.58 per cent, where it was late Thursday, after dipping to 4.52 per cent — again near its highest level since 2007.



---


# What Drove The ASX Rally On 10 October 2023

TMS Capital portfolio manager Ben Clark attributed the Australian sharemarket's strength to three things acting together: a calming bond market, a positive lead from Wall Street, and positive news out of China.

He set out how each fed through. "The bond market is retracing," he said. "There's also been strength in resource stocks amid rumours that the Chinese government might launch a substantial stimulus package." On the rates channel, Clark said interest-rate sensitive sectors climbed on increased probabilities of an easing in interest rates, because "Consumer discretionary and information technology companies are winners in lower-interest rate environments." Looking ahead, as more annual general meetings kicked off over the following weeks, Clark said he would be looking at trading updates, especially of companies that did not give solid guidance in their last update.



---


# The Wall Street September 2023 Selloff And Bond Yields

September 2023 brought a loss of 5.2 per cent so far for the S&P 500, putting it on track to be the worst month of the year by far, as the realisation set in that the Federal Reserve would indeed keep interest rates high for a long time. That growing understanding sent yields in the bond market to their highest levels in more than a decade, which in turn undercut prices for stocks and other investments.

Treasury yields rose again on Tuesday, 2023-09-26, following a mixed batch of reports on the economy: the yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.55 per cent from 4.54 per cent late on Monday and is near its highest level since 2007, up sharply from about 3.5 per cent in May and from 0.5 per cent about three years ago. One economic report that Tuesday showed confidence among consumers was weaker than economists expected — concerning because strong spending by US households has been a bulwark keeping the economy out of a long-predicted recession.



---


# Wall Street December 2023 Mixed Session

Most US stocks slipped in the overnight Wall Street session reported on 5 December 2023, though the market stayed near its highest level in 20 months after a mixed set of reports that kept alive questions about whether the world's largest economy can pull off a perfect landing in which it kills high inflation but avoids a recession. The S&P 500 edged down 0.1 per cent for its first back-to-back loss since October, the Dow Jones slipped 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 0.3 per cent.

Stocks fell more sharply in Asia amid worries about the health of China's economy, the world's second largest. US stocks and Treasury yields wavered after reports showed that US employers advertised far fewer jobs at the end of October than expected, while growth for services businesses accelerated more in the prior month than expected.

The underlying hope on Wall Street at the time was that the US economy was slowing from its recent hot pace by just the right amount: too much strength would give inflation more fuel, but too little would mean a recession. The Australian market's gains that day came after this mixed US session.



---


# ASX Decliners In The Session Before The October 2023 RBA Meeting

On the Monday before the Reserve Bank's Tuesday meeting, Treasury Wine Estates (down 1.9 per cent) and Woolworths (down 1.2 per cent) dragged the consumer staples sector (down 1.1 per cent) lower, with Pilbara Minerals (down 2.1 per cent) and Qantas (down 1.5 per cent) also among the biggest large-cap decliners.

Stronger iron ore prices helped to bolster the local bourse on Monday but not enough to offset the prospect of higher-for-longer interest rates ahead of the RBA meeting. Iron ore heavyweights advanced after the iron ore price increased 1.4 per cent overnight, with lithium miner Liontown resisting the downward momentum of lithium prices, which dropped to their lowest level in two years.



---


# Wall Street November 2023 Relief Rally

Wall Street closed a strong week on the Friday before this 5 November 2023 report, with the S&P 500 climbing 40.56 points, or 0.9 per cent, to 4,358.3; the Dow Jones Industrial Average gaining 222.24, or 0.7 per cent, to 34,061.32; and the Nasdaq composite jumping 184.09, or 1.4 per cent, to 13,478.28. Stocks surged through the week on rising hopes that the Federal Reserve is finally done with its market-crunching interest rate hikes aimed at getting inflation under control, with a Friday report underscoring easing inflation pressure by showing employers hired fewer workers in October than economists expected.

The report described this as a stunning turnaround from just a week earlier, when Wall Street was reeling after the S&P 500 had fallen 10 per cent below its high point for the year, sending the index into what investors call a "correction". Since then, strong profit reports helped drive some stocks to towering gains: Generac, a maker of back-up generators, soared nearly 28 per cent for its best week since its stock began trading in 2010, and Expedia Group's stronger-than-forecast report sent its stock nearly 22 per cent higher for its best week since the market was surging out of the coronavirus crash in early 2020. Even so, it was interest rates, yields and inflation that were at the centre of all the wild movements for financial markets around the world.

Excitement about a potentially easier Fed was more than enough to offset a fall for Apple, Wall Street's most influential and most valuable US stock, which fell 0.5 per cent despite reporting stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected; analysts said investors were likely disappointed with Apple's revenue forecast for the last three months of 2023.



---


# US Equity Sector Moves On 10 October 2023

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.4 per cent to 33,739.30, the S&P 500 gained 0.5 per cent and the Nasdaq Composite added 0.6 per cent, with all 11 major S&P 500 sectors advancing — materials and consumer staples led the gains while technology was the slowest gainer, and energy was among the laggards after its more than 3 per cent rally on Monday.

A measure of US-listed Chinese shares added 3 per cent amid reports that the Asian nation is considering new economic stimulus. "Policymakers have begun to acknowledge a lesser need for further policy action given financial conditions have tightened considerably after the recent surge in Treasury yields," said Ben Jeffery at BMO Capital Markets. "This acknowledgment may have reduced angst around the need for additional rate increases." Investors would be watching for any hints in the September Fed meeting minutes, due Wednesday, that would suggest the Fed may not follow through with the last rise indicated in its economic projections, according to Anna Wong at Bloomberg Economics, who noted that two critical coming indicators for the US economy — Thursday's consumer price index and Friday's University of Michigan consumer-sentiment survey — may give a more definitive read.



---


# Australian Market Resilience And The Range-Bound Reading

Novus Capital senior client adviser Gary Glover argued that the Australian sharemarket was surprisingly resilient following a negative lead from Wall Street and the latest inflation data, with markets starting to wake up to the fact that interest rates could stay higher for longer. His ground was the mismatch between the overseas move and the local one: "Considering the damage overnight in the US, Australian markets held on pretty well. I thought it would be a bigger down day across the board."

Glover characterised the market as volatile but quite range-bound, drawing an analogy to previous periods of high inflation in the 1940s and 1970s. The Wall Street lead he referred to was severe: Wall Street's ugly September got even worse on Tuesday as a sharp drop for stocks brought them back to where they were in June, with the S&P 500 tumbling 1.5 per cent for its fifth loss in the last six days, the Dow Jones dropping 1.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite losing 1.6 per cent.



---


# US Jobs And Services Data In Early October 2023

Wednesday's ADP report suggested private employers added 89,000 jobs last month, a much sharper slowdown in hiring than the 140,000 economists expected. The report does not have a perfect track record in predicting what the more comprehensive jobs report from the US government will say, which was due to arrive on the Friday. Mike Loewengart, head of model portfolio construction at Morgan Stanley Global Investment Office, said that "if Friday's report also shows the labour market is cooling, stock investors may worry a little less about indefinitely higher interest rates".

A second report on the economy said growth in US services industries slowed in September by a touch more than economists expected. The figures were reported by The Age on 4 October 2023 alongside a note that oil prices slumped overnight.



---


# Fed Dovish Comments And The Yield Retreat Of October 2023

Wall Street advanced overnight with the S&P 500 and Nasdaq touching three-week highs as dovish comments from Fed officials pushed Treasury yields lower; following remarks from other top Fed officials on Monday, Atlanta Fed President Raphael Bostic said the US central bank did not need to raise interest rates any further, and that he saw no recession ahead.

The 10-year Treasury yield came off its 16-year peak, on track for its steepest single-day drop since May as trading resumed in the US bond market, which had been closed for a holiday on Monday; ten-year yields tumbled as much as 18 basis points to 4.62 per cent. Fed swaps then showed about a 60 per cent chance the Fed would stay on hold in December, compared with 60 per cent odds on another interest rate rise by then just a week earlier. Oil edged lower, with West Texas Intermediate settling below $US86 a barrel following its biggest rally since April, and the Australian dollar was US64.20¢ at the close as the US dollar fell for a fifth straight day, its longest losing streak since July. Investors were nonetheless still closely monitoring developments in the Middle East: "Everybody has one eye on the Middle East conflict and one eye on what's happening with bond yields," said John Praveen, managing director at Paleo Leon.



---


# Housing Affordability Is Worse Now Than At The 2006 Peak

Roger Ashworth, a managing director at Goldman Sachs, argued in a credit strategy research paper released in mid-October 2023 that although some economic factors are stronger today than during the Global Financial Crisis, housing affordability is undeniably worse: "While housing and more generally consumer fundamentals are in a much stronger position today, affordability for the incremental buyer is worse than it was at the peak in 2006 before the crash." The claim is deliberately narrow — it is about the incremental buyer's affordability, not about overall fundamentals, which he grants are stronger.

The proximate causes cited are the same constraints that have held all year. "As has been the case throughout this year, limited inventory and low housing affordability continue to hamper home sales," NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement, adding a policy conclusion: "The Federal Reserve simply cannot keep raising interest rates in light of softening inflation and weakening job gains." The Fed had raised rates several times in 2023, with Chair Jerome Powell arming his "higher for longer" stance.



---


# Australian Inflation Data And The RBA's Near-Certain November Rise

GSFM investment strategist Stephen Miller said the inflation data, taken with the October Reserve Bank board meeting minutes — which revealed the board had "low tolerance for a slower return of inflation to target than currently expected" — made the possibility of an interest rate rise from the central bank in November a "near certainty."

Commodity prices nonetheless supported mining companies, as iron ore prices increased 2.9 per cent overnight, bolstering Australia's iron ore giants. This came as Chinese President Xi Jinping stepped up support for the world's second-biggest economy and major commodity trading partner for Australia, issuing additional sovereign debt, raising the budget deficit ratio and even making an unprecedented visit to the central bank. On Wall Street, the benchmark S&P 500 index closed 0.7 per cent higher ahead of tech giants Microsoft and Alphabet reporting results after the close, the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.6 per cent and the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 gained 0.9 per cent. Shares in Microsoft climbed 5 per cent in after-hours trading after the company said its sales jumped 13 per cent to $US56.5 billion ($88.9 billion) and profits climbed 27 per cent to $US22.3 billion in the three months through September.



---


# ASX November 2023 Session and RBA Rate Expectations

In the Australian session reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 5 November 2023, energy companies were the main drag on the index, down one per cent, with Woodside off 0.8 per cent, Santos down 0.4 per cent and Ampol down 1.2 per cent, alongside coal miners Yancoal (down 1.7 per cent) and Whitehaven (down 2 per cent). Lynas Rare Earths was the biggest large-cap decliner at down 3.1 per cent, while industrials fell 0.2 per cent, including Computershare (down 2.9 per cent), Seven West Holdings (down 1.9 per cent) and Worley (down 1.3 per cent).

TMS Capital portfolio manager Ben Clark said the big news for markets on the Monday was Westpac's trading update, which he said led a resurgence in the banking sector's performance. "Westpac's results were better than expected, especially because it's been a bit of a perennial underperformer in the past few years," he said, adding that it set the tone for results from NAB and ANZ due to report in the following week. Clark also described a reversal of the interest-rate trade of recent weeks: "Long-term bond yields came off quite significantly in the last few days following weaker than expected employment data on Friday, which has seen some investors swivel back into growth stocks." On his account the market had switched from pricing in an 80 per cent chance of a rate rise on the Tuesday to 50-50.

Other commentary framed the risk of a further increase. "Our view is that in the high likelihood there is another cash rate increase on Tuesday, that is going to be the nail in the coffin for consumer confidence," said CreditorWatch chief economist Anneke Thompson, amid warnings from some economists that another rate rise would dampen spending intentions just in time for Christmas. The same wrap noted that the men who built pubs and liquor juggernaut Endeavour Group into the world's largest poker machine operator had triggered a public spat over the future of a business they say has lost its way.



---


# ASX REITs And Company News, 24 October 2023

Real estate investment trusts (down 2 per cent) dropped further following the latest inflation data, with Mirvac (down 3.7 per cent) and Dexus (down 3.3 per cent) sliding lower, as the Australian sharemarket shook off a positive lead from Wall Street after hotter-than-expected inflation data raised the prospect of another interest rate rise at the Reserve Bank's next meeting.

Interest-rate sensitive sectors, including REITs and consumer companies, were among the weakest on the local bourse as investors digested the news. Dexus chief executive Darren Steinberg announced on Wednesday that he would step down next year after 11 years at the helm, and at the annual meeting in Sydney the same day the company's remuneration report received a first strike after failing to pass the 25 per cent voting threshold. Consumer staples (down 1.4 per cent) were also weaker, with Woolworths losing 2 per cent despite sales across the company rising 5.3 per cent in the 14 weeks to October, as it vowed to pass on easing costs for protein and fresh produce amid rising mortgage and rental pressures. In other company news, shares in embattled funds manager Magellan dropped 3.5 per cent after the abrupt departure of its chief executive, David George. Infratil (down 3.6 per cent), Meridian Energy (down 2.7 per cent) and Resmed (down 2 per cent) were among the biggest large-cap decliners.



---


# ASX December 2023 Session Movers

On the Australian sharemarket session reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 5 December 2023, Perpetual was the standout gainer, climbing 6.3 per cent after announcing a strategic review of its three-pronged corporate structure that might see it demerge its corporate trust and wealth management businesses and create a more focused asset manager. Endeavour shares lifted 2.4 per cent after the company forecast that earnings before interest and tax in its hotels division would grow by more than $150 million over the next five years.

Utilities and energy stocks were the weakest performers on the local bourse, rising just 0.6 per cent and 0.8 per cent respectively. Only five large-cap stocks declined outright. Evolution Mining sank a mammoth 13 per cent after raising $525 million by selling new shares to institutional investors at $3.80 a share, although the mining sector as a whole still managed to finish in positive territory. Gold miner Newmont was down 1.25 per cent, Origin Energy fell 0.4 per cent, Mercury NZ declined 0.3 per cent and Argo Investments traded 0.1 per cent lower.

Moomoo market strategist Jessica Amir attributed the local market's outperformance of global equities on the Wednesday session to the National Accounts figures, which pointed to the Reserve Bank potentially hitting pause on lifting interest rates. "We know economic growth is slowing, Australian unemployment is likely to pick up next year and inflation is likely to fall," Amir said, adding that this "trifecta" pointed towards the RBA stopping rate rises and then potentially moving to cut, which was what the market had priced in that day.



---


# US Home Prices Peaked In June 2022 And Returned To A Record High By July 2023

National U.S. home prices did not peak until June 2022 — even as mortgage rates soared and purchase applications plummeted amid the Federal Reserve's first interest rate hikes — and although prices fell more than 5% from that peak by January 2023, they returned to a record high in July 2023. This is the observation that has so far vindicated the majority of real estate veterans, who despite a widely bearish industry outlook avoided arguing that home prices would drop the way they did during the 2008 crash that kicked off the Global Financial Crisis.

The backdrop, as of the reporting date of 2023-10-06, is that housing market pessimists had been sounding the alarm for years about a pending crash in U.S. residential real estate. Even before the Fed began hiking interest rates to fight inflation in 2022 — pushing mortgage rates to a 23-year high in October 2023 — years of surging home prices had left some experts warning that the housing market was a massive bubble ready to pop.



---


# Volcker's And Powell's Rate-Hiking Cycles Compared

The consumer price index rose at a peak of around 14% in 1980 before then-Fed Chair Paul Volcker's hawkish policies sent mortgage rates to 18% within a year — cooling inflation but sparking a recession, and causing a serious downturn in housing in which home sales and building levels cratered while national home prices actually remained stable. At the start of Volcker's term as Fed chair in August 1979 the median U.S. home sales price was $64,700, and even after a near doubling of mortgage rates that figure rose to $69,400 by the second quarter of 1981. A second account puts the average 30-year fixed mortgage peaking at about 18% by late 1981, and records that home sales activity plummeted from 1978 to 1982, with existing-home sales dropping 50% over that period according to the Office of Policy Development and Research.

Over the 18 months preceding October 2023, current Fed chair Jerome Powell has been following a very similar game plan, raising interest rates aggressively to quash inflation and setting the tone for the most aggressive global hiking of rates in the modern era. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate, the most common type in the U.S., soared from 3.8% in March 2022 to over 7.5% by 2023-10-06, and by the week of 2023-10-20 mortgage rates hit 8%, the highest in more than 20 years. This in turn slowed mortgage purchase applications and caused home sales to plummet, just as in the '80s; but home prices, echoing the dynamic of that era, have yet to collapse. While home sales activity levels this low had not been seen since the 2000s, the housing market more closely mimics that of the '80s, according to a report published in the week of 2023-10-20 by Fortune 500 financial services company First American.



---


# Bank of Israel Thirty Billion Dollar FX Intervention

On the Monday of the week in which this 12 October 2023 interview was published, the Bank of Israel announced a dramatic plan to sell $30 billion of its foreign currency reserves to stabilise the shekel. By the time of the report the shekel had in fact recovered slightly and was trading at around NIS 3.96/$.

Leo Leiderman endorsed the move: "It's important to welcome the Bank of Israel's decision to intervene, as necessary, in the foreign exchange market, in order to ensure the market's regular operation." He also treated leadership continuity as stabilising, citing the decision to extend the term of Amir Yaron as governor at least for the duration of the war, and in his hope beyond it. He added that the banking system is stable with enough liquidity in the system, and that the behaviour of the investment community in Israel, including the financial institutions, indicates high confidence in the economy's resilience and financial strength — an "asset" he said a level-headed, correct economic policy must preserve.



---


# US Government Shutdown Risk And The Market History Of Shutdowns

Besides high interest rates, a long list of other worries was tugging at Wall Street in late September 2023, the most immediate being the threat of another US government shutdown as Capitol Hill threatened a stalemate that could shut off federal services across the country. Wall Street has dealt with such shutdowns before, and stocks have historically been turbulent in the run-up to them, according to Lori Calvasina, strategist at RBC Capital Markets: looking at the seven shutdowns that lasted 10 days or more since the 1970s, she found the S&P 500 dropped an average of roughly 10 per cent in the three months heading into them, but stocks managed to hold up rather well during the shutdowns themselves, falling an average of just 0.3 per cent before rebounding meaningfully afterward.

Wall Street was also contending with higher oil prices, shaky economies around the world, a strike by US autoworkers that could put more upward pressure on inflation, and a resumption of US student-loan repayments that could dent spending by households.



---


# The Case For Raising The Inflation Target

Olivier Blanchard, a former IMF chief economist, has long argued in favor of raising the inflation target, and former European Central Bank Vice President Vitor Constancio has also embraced the idea. The case comes with a strict precondition: it is a controversial view and only possible from a position of credibility, which means central banks would likely have to get inflation back to 2% first.

The supporting ground is that the environment itself has changed. Global trends suggest inflation will be stronger than in the past, with former Bank of England Governor Mark Carney among those saying rates won't return to pre-pandemic lows.



---


# The ASX And Wall Street Rebound Of 4 October 2023

IG Australia market analyst Tony Sycamore said the ASX received some relief from a rally on Wall Street following the release of cooler-than-expected US economic data which helped cap US bond yields. "Much has been written about the unrelenting rise in long-term US interest rates threatening prospects of a soft landing and raising doubts around equity market valuations," he said. "This was stopped in its tracks overnight following the release of a considerably weaker employment, and ISM services purchasing managers index data topped off by a 5.6 per cent fall in the price of crude oil to below $85 per barrel." Sycamore said the property sector and the interest rate sensitive technology sector reclaimed some lost ground while banks advanced on the back of the pullback in yields, but that iron ore miners were shackled by concerns around the Chinese economy as the market braced for China's consumer purchasing index report the following week, which was expected to show inflation remaining morbid.

The local rebound came after Wall Street rose on relief from relaxing bond yields and falling oil prices. The S&P 500 climbed 0.8 per cent to claw back more than half its sharp tumble from a day earlier, which had sent it to a four-month low; the Dow Jones rose 0.4 per cent, a day after erasing the last of its gains for the year so far; and the Nasdaq composite led the market with a gain of 1.4 per cent. Stocks have struggled under the weight of soaring Treasury yields in the bond market, because high yields undercut stock prices by pulling investment dollars away from stocks and into bonds, and also crimp corporate profits by making borrowing more expensive.



---


# Bank of Israel Interest Rate Policy During the War

Asked what the Bank of Israel should do at its interest rate decision on 23 October 2023, Leo Leiderman argued for holding: "As for cutting the interest rate, it's too early to consider that. The current interest rate is at the right level for the state of the economy, and together with the policy on exchange rates, it contributes to ensuring financial stability."

His first ground is that the inflation effect of the war is indeterminate. It was still too early to tell how the war would affect the rate of inflation in the short and medium term: just as there are new inflationary factors, such as the depreciation of the shekel, there will also be factors working in the opposite direction, given the expected decline in private consumption, tourism and other items.

His second ground extends his fiscal reasoning to monetary policy: as with fiscal policy, a country at war is allowed to deviate temporarily from the set inflation target. He judged that at the moment there was no surge in inflation expectations, and that the investment community is aware of the existence of index-linked assets and the exchange rate that can assist in hedging inflation risk. The warrant tying this to a hold rather than a cut is that financial stability, not inflation, is the binding objective while the shock is unresolved.



---


# Headwinds To US Consumer Spending In Late 2023

US consumer spending growth was cooling under three named pressures — higher energy prices, student loan debt repayments, and real disposable incomes on a declining trajectory since June. "It came to a boil during a hot summer, and the temperature is really starting to come down," said Brian Jacobsen, chief economist at Annex Wealth Management, adding that the combination "doesn't bode well."

Each channel is specified. Oil prices have jumped to their highest level in more than a year, pressuring the economy by raising fuel costs for everyone: a barrel of US crude sank 92¢ on Friday to settle at $US90.79, but it is still up sharply from $US70 in June, and Brent crude, the international standard, also weakened. The resumption of US student-loan repayments may funnel more dollars away from the consumer spending that has helped keep the economy afloat. The data calendar that would test this was still ahead — the latest monthly update on the US jobs market was due the following week, with a couple of important reports on inflation coming the week after, and postponements of such reports could complicate things for the Fed, which has insisted it will make upcoming decisions on interest rates based on what incoming data say about the economy; the Fed's next meeting on rates ends on November 1. Not every reading pointed the same way: on Wall Street, Nike jumped 6.7 per cent after reporting better profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, with strength overseas helping it make up for some declines in North America.



---


# Bank Of America's Warning Of More Housing "Turbulence"

A Bank of America team led by U.S. economist Jeseo Park warned in the week of 2023-10-06 that there is more "turbulence" coming for the housing market because of high mortgage rates: "With rates likely staying higher for longer, we are cautious of potential turbulence ahead," the group wrote. The grounds are the persistence of high rates rather than a repeat of a past crash — the team said they were getting an eerie feeling of "déjà vu," but it was not 2008 that came to mind, it was the 1980s.

The forecast attached to this warning is qualified. Bank of America had previously forecast 0% home price growth and falling home sales for the full year 2023, but it did not offer a new prediction in its latest note. The warrant joining the rate outlook to the housing outlook runs the other way as well: eventually, as inflation fades and leads the Fed to cut interest rates, housing affordability will improve. "At that stage, we should see a more stable and healthy housing market," Park and her team wrote. "Until then, hang tight, it may be a bumpy ride."



---


# ASX Stock And Sector Moves, Late September 2023

REITs, up 0.4 per cent, was the strongest sector on the Australian index in the session reported on 2023-09-26, as Goodman added 0.5 per cent and Dexus climbed 2.8 per cent. In company news, ETF provider Betashares, which manages $30 billion in funds, reached an agreement to acquire Bendigo and Adelaide Bank's superannuation business, its first venture into the superannuation sector and part of what Betashares said was a longer-term strategy to expand into the broader financial sector; shares in Bendigo increased 0.6 per cent on the news.

Among the laggards, casino operator Star Entertainment Group's shares hit an all-time low of 60¢ after it raised $565 million, closing the session 16 per cent weaker at 63¢; Star, which raised $800 million in February, had to return to the market for fresh funding and is hoping to raise $750 million at a share price of 60¢ a share. Healthcare heavyweight CSL shed 1.4 per cent, weighing down the healthcare sector, and insurers IAG (down 2.6 per cent) and Suncorp (down 2 per cent) gave back some of their gains from Tuesday. Gold miners Newcrest (down 2.1 per cent) and Evolution (down 3.5 per cent) were also among the biggest large-cap decliners after the spot gold price dropped 0.9 per cent overnight. Information technology, down 1.1 per cent, was the weakest sector on the local bourse, with WiseTech losing 1.4 per cent.



---


# The ASX And Wall Street Selloff Of 12 October 2023

Hotter-than-expected inflation data and the prospect of more rate rises in the world's biggest economy weighed on sentiment in the Australian sharemarket, as interest-rate sensitive sectors such as IT and consumer discretionary dragged the index lower on the Friday. While commodity prices boosted iron ore players, company-specific news was behind some of the biggest swings: Resmed extended its losses after brokers at RBC downgraded the stock, and gold miner Newcrest stepped up after investors approved its merger with US gold mining giant Newmont.

US stocks slipped on the Thursday as the clamps tightened on Wall Street from rising yields in the bond market. The S&P 500 was 0.7 per cent lower in afternoon trading and on track to break a four-day winning streak, its longest since August; the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 204 points, or 0.6 per cent, as of 3pm Eastern time; and the Nasdaq composite was 0.8 per cent lower.



---


# Powell's Rejection Of Monetary-Fiscal Coordination

Fed Chair Jerome Powell, sitting to Christine Lagarde's right at the panel discussion, signaled he wasn't ready to rely on the kind of cooperation between monetary and fiscal policy she described as sometimes helpful.

His stated ground rejects the premise that the central bank's mandate is contingent on what fiscal authorities do: "Our assignment is to deliver price stability kind of regardless of the stance of fiscal policy."
