context:
# Google's Gemini Model Family And Its Capability Claims

Gemini is Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled in the first week of December 2023 and meant to power a range of products and services including Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor. In blog posts and press materials, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4, and it emphasised Gemini's coding capabilities and multimodal prowess, claiming that the model can understand images, audio and videos just as well as text.

The family has tiers, and only the lower one shipped. Google did not release the full model, Gemini Ultra — which is set to launch sometime in 2024 in Bard and other products — but only a "lite" version called Gemini Pro. Gemini Pro is therefore not the most capable version of Gemini, and Google compared its performance to GPT-4's predecessor, GPT-3.5, a model that was around a year old. Google nevertheless promised improvements in reasoning, planning and understanding with Gemini Pro over the previous model powering Bard, claiming Gemini Pro was better at summarizing content, brainstorming and writing.

The shipped tier is also narrower than the multimodal claims suggest: Gemini Pro is strictly text-in, text-out, and has proven to be mistake-prone. In a worse look for Google, the company was caught faking a Gemini demo by tuning text prompts with still images off camera.



---


# OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

OpenAI struck a deal with the Berlin-based news publisher Axel Springer, which owns Business Insider and Politico, to "help provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools"; under it OpenAI will train its generative AI models on the publisher's content and add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT. Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. In its first public acquisition in its seven-year history, OpenAI acquired Global Illumination, a New York-based startup leveraging AI to build creative tools, infrastructure and digital experiences; OpenAI wrote in a brief blog post, "We're very excited for the impact they'll have here at OpenAI. The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

On financing, OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27 billion to $29 billion valuation, with VC firms including Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive and K2 Global picking up new shares according to documents seen by TechCrunch, and a source saying Founders Fund was also investing. That round was separate from a large Microsoft investment announced earlier in the year, which closed in January and is believed to be around $10 billion. On trademarks, OpenAI applied for a trademark for "GPT" — Generative Pre-trained Transformer — in December, and petitioned the USPTO to speed up the process, citing the "myriad infringements and counterfeit apps" beginning to spring into existence; the petition was dismissed because OpenAI's attorneys neglected to pay an associated fee and to provide "appropriate documentary evidence supporting the justification of special action," meaning a decision could take up to five more months.



---


# Gemini Pro's News Summarization Refusals And Stale Answers

Asked to summarise topical news in early December 2023, Gemini Pro often would not do it, despite having Google Search and Google News at its disposal. It seemed loath to comment on potentially controversial news topics, instead telling users to Google it themselves.

The TechCrunch reporter tried the same prompt and got a very similar response. ChatGPT, by contrast, gave a bullet-list summary with citations to news articles.

There was one partial exception, and it exposed a second problem: Gemini Pro did provide a summary of updates on the war in Ukraine when the reporter asked for one, but the information was over a month out of date.



---


# Anecdotal Evidence Undercuts Google's Gemini Pro Claims

Against Google's promises for Gemini Pro, TechCrunch's rejoinder on 7 December 2023 was blunt: "the anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise." The counter-argument attacks the evidential basis of the launch claims rather than the model's architecture, setting user experience after release against what Google said the model would do.

The grounds are the reception of the rollout itself. A "lite" version of Gemini, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard the day before the article, and it did not take long before users began voicing their frustrations with it on X, formerly Twitter.



---


# Associated Press And OpenAI's Licensing Deal

Select news outlets proved far more amenable to OpenAI than the authors suing it. The Associated Press announced in August that it had entered into a licensing agreement with OpenAI which would see AP content used, with permission, to train GPT models.

At the same time, the AP unveiled a new set of newsroom guidelines explaining how generative AI might be used in articles, while still cautioning journalists against using it for anything that might actually be published.



---


# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.



---


# Prediction: OpenAI Becomes A Product Company

TechCrunch predicts that after the leadership shake-up in November 2023, OpenAI will be a changed company — perhaps not outwardly, but the trickle-down effect of Sam Altman being more fully in charge will be felt at every level, manifesting above all in a "ship it" mindset.

The concrete test named is the GPT store, originally planned for launch in December 2023 but understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas. TechCrunch expects the "app store for AI" to be pushed hard as the platform to get your AI toys and tools from, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models, on the reasoning that OpenAI has an excellent model to work from in Apple's and will follow it all the way to the bank.

More broadly, the prediction is that the caution and academic reserve the previous board exerted will give way to an unseemly lust for markets and customers. Other major companies with AI efforts are expected to follow the same trend — for instance, Gemini/Bard horning in on a ton of Google products — but the writer suspects it will be more pronounced at OpenAI.



---


# ChatGPT Overview And Significance

ChatGPT is OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot, and it has taken the world by storm: what started as a tool to hyper-charge productivity through writing essays and code from short text prompts has evolved into a behemoth used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies for far more wide-ranging needs.

That growth propelled OpenAI itself into becoming one of the most-hyped companies in recent memory, even though CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return raised concerns about the company's direction and opened the door for competitors. The fallout was still settling, but it might empower competitors such as Meta and its LLaMA family of large language models, or help other AI startups get attention and funding as the industry watched OpenAI implode and put itself back together. Whatever the nefarious side of ChatGPT, it was clear that AI tools were not going away anytime soon: since its initial launch nearly a year earlier, ChatGPT had hit 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI was investing heavily in it.

The capability boundary at the time was defined by model access and modality. GPT-4, which can write more naturally and fluently than previous models, remained largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users, although it could be accessed for free through Microsoft's Bing Chat in the Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome and Safari web browsers. Beyond GPT-4 and the OpenAI DevDay announcements, OpenAI had recently connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users, and with the integration of DALL-E 3, users could generate both text and images right inside ChatGPT.



---


# Why Traditional E-Commerce Search Has Degraded

Deft co-founder Zach Hudson told TechCrunch that there are a few plaguing problems with the traditional search experience that prevent users from finding a suitable item — that is, the claim is that search has gotten worse, not that users have gotten worse at searching.

He offers three grounds, each a different actor degrading the result set: "You have companies like Google and Amazon that continue to push the most relevant listings down so they can make more advertising dollars. Some easy searches are now hard because marketers have learned how to game these search engines. Plus, now you have AI content that is putting the burden on users to separate fact from fiction," he said.

The warrant tying them together is that each mechanism moves cost onto the user: platform ad incentives bury relevance, SEO gaming inflates the noise, and AI-generated content shifts verification work to the person searching.



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# The Competitive Response To ChatGPT Across The AI Industry

ChatGPT became priority number one at OpenAI — not simply a one-off product but a development platform to build upon — and, as often happens in a competition-driven marketplace, it shifted the focus at other AI firms and research labs too.

Google scrambled to launch a response to ChatGPT, eventually releasing Bard, a more or less comparable AI chatbot, in February 2023. Countless other ChatGPT rivals and derivatives have arrived to market since, most recently Amazon Q, a more business-oriented take on ChatGPT. And DeepMind, Google's premier AI research lab, is expected to debut a next-gen chatbot, Gemini, before the end of 2023.



---


# ChatGPT Legal And Privacy Controversies

ChatGPT has generated a run of legal and privacy controversies: an Australian mayor publicly announced he may sue OpenAI for defamation over ChatGPT's false claims that he had served time in prison for bribery, which would be the first defamation lawsuit against the text-generating service, and there have been other cases of ChatGPT accusing individuals of false crimes.

The libel exposure follows from how the models work: they do not know or care whether something is true, only that it looks true — a problem when the output is used for homework, and potentially libel when it accuses someone of a crime they did not commit. How troubling statements produced by ChatGPT will be handled was expected to play out over the following months as tech and legal experts tackled the fastest moving target in the industry. As of the article, there were no lawsuits specifically targeting ChatGPT, but OpenAI is involved in at least one lawsuit with implications for AI systems trained on publicly available data, which would touch on ChatGPT. There are also plagiarism issues: text-generating AI models like ChatGPT have a tendency to regurgitate content from their training data. Copyright in output sits with the user — the person who requested the input from ChatGPT is the copyright owner.

On privacy, OpenAI has said that individuals in "certain jurisdictions" such as the EU can object to the processing of their personal information by its AI models by filling out a form — the "OpenAI Personal Data Removal Request" — which includes the ability to request deletion of AI-generated references about them, although OpenAI notes it may not grant every request since it must balance privacy requests against freedom of expression "in accordance with applicable laws." In its privacy policy OpenAI makes a passing acknowledgement of the objection requirements attached to relying on "legitimate interest," pointing users to instructions on how to opt out of use of their information to train its models. ChatGPT chats are not public, but OpenAI disclosed a bug, since fixed, that exposed the titles of some users' conversations to other people on the service.

Other controversies span platforms and schools. Discord integrated OpenAI's technology into its bot Clyde, and two users tricked Clyde into providing instructions for making methamphetamine and napalm. # Google's Denial That Ad Keyword Matching Affects Organic Results

Google's official search liaison Danny Sullivan rebutted the allegation that Google manipulates search to maximise ad revenue by denying the causal link it depends on: in a post on X, he said ad systems do not affect the organic results — the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored.

"Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads," Sullivan said. "A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query." He also defended query interpretation on its own terms: "It's no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning… If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that's not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren't even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help." The Age noted the claim being answered comes from Megan Gray, herself a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google; she admits she may have misinterpreted the evidence but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. The paper granted that some search queries result in more ads than others and that which ads you get can vary wildly by request — the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads — but noted Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# ChatGPT's Launch And Its First Year Of Evolution

ChatGPT, OpenAI's viral AI chatbot, turned one on November 30, 2023. A year earlier OpenAI released it as a "low-key research preview," reportedly spurred in part by an intense rivalry with AI startup Anthropic. The goal, OpenAI leadership told the OpenAI rank-and-file at the time, was to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI to inform the development of OpenAI's future models.

Initially a basic free-to-use, web-based and chat-focused interface on top of one of OpenAI's existing models, GPT-3.5, ChatGPT would go on to become the company's most popular product ever — and the fastest-growing consumer app in history. Sam Altman marked the anniversary on X: "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning's launch. what a year it's been…"

In the months following its launch, ChatGPT gained paid tiers with additional features, including a plan geared toward enterprise customers. OpenAI also upgraded ChatGPT with web searching, document analyzing and image creating capabilities via DALL-E 3. And, leaning on speech recognition, voice synthesis and text-image understanding models developed in house, OpenAI gave ChatGPT the ability to "hear," "speak," "see" and take actions.

# Model Fine-Tuning

## Definition

In the corpus, model fine-tuning is the OpenAI capability that lets companies using GPT-3.5 Turbo or GPT-4 through the API continue training the model on their own data so it better fits their use case. In the corpus's most concrete example, OpenAI's fine-tuning of GPT-3.5 Turbo lets companies using the model through the API make it better follow specific instructions — such as always responding in a given language, formatting responses consistently, or matching a brand's tone — and shorten text prompts to speed up API calls and cut costs.

## Context

The corpus documents fine-tuning as a capability OpenAI progressively opened to developers alongside its paid APIs. OpenAI first brought fine-tuning to GPT-3.5 Turbo, partnering with Scale AI so companies could fine-tune the model, at published costs of $0.008 per 1K tokens for training, $0.012 per 1K tokens for usage input, and $0.016 per 1K tokens for usage output. It later extended fine-tuning to GPT-4, though the GPT-4 program involves more oversight and guidance from OpenAI teams than the GPT-3.5 program, largely due to technical hurdles. Separately, in TechCrunch's October 2023 survey of AI investors, fine-tuning is named as one of the distinct layers of the emerging LLM stack — alongside models and pre-training solutions — that sits in the middle layer connecting foundation models to specialized applications, together with prompt engineering and model orchestration.

## Key Characteristics

- **Continues training an existing model on customer data** — fine-tuning takes a model the customer already accesses through the API (e.g., GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4) and continues training it on data the customer supplies.
- **Improves instruction-following and output style** — it can make a model better follow specific instructions, consistently format responses, and match a desired tone or brand voice.
- **Reduces prompt length and cost** — because the desired behavior is trained into the model, fine-tuning lets customers shorten text prompts, which speeds up API calls and cuts per-call cost.
- **Priced separately from inference** — OpenAI charged distinct per-token rates for fine-tuning training versus using (input/output) the fine-tuned model.
- **Oversight scales with model capability** — OpenAI applied more oversight and guidance to the GPT-4 fine-tuning program than to the GPT-3.5 program, citing technical hurdles.
- **A distinct layer of the LLM stack** — investors surveyed by TechCrunch treat fine-tuning tools as their own layer of the GenAI tech stack, separate from foundation model providers and end-user applications.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, OpenAI's own documentation describes fine-tuning more generally as letting a developer "take an OpenAI base model, provide the kinds of inputs and outputs you expect" so the model is adapted to a specific task rather than replaced with a newly trained one (OpenAI, "Model optimization," accessed 2026-09-02, https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization).

# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.

# Large Language Model (LLM)

## Definition

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to learn from enormous amounts of digital text — Wikipedia articles, digital books, message boards — so that it can generate text on its own.

## Context

The corpus traces the term to OpenAI's GPT-3, described as the neural network Dario Amodei's team built by analysing "countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards" so it "could generate text on its own," released in the summer of 2020; it also "had the unfortunate habit of making things up." ChatGPT itself runs on GPT, the LLM lineage OpenAI had developed since 2016, iterating from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-3 (June 2020) before GPT-3.5 powered ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. In the venture-capital view of the AI market, LLMs sit at the base "foundation model" layer of a broader stack — models, pre-training solutions, fine-tuning tools, middle-layer tooling, and end-market applications — with providers such as OpenAI's GPT-4, Google's Bard, and Anthropic's Claude expected to consolidate into an oligopolistic structure resembling the cloud-provider market. OpenAI's GPT-X models are repeatedly described as proprietary LLMs that other companies build businesses on top of, a dependency that became visible when the November 2023 OpenAI board upheaval led customers to contact rival LLM providers (Anthropic, Google, Cohere) out of concern for continuity.

## Key Characteristics

- **Trained on enormous text corpora** — LLMs learn by analysing vast amounts of digital text (Wikipedia, books, message boards) rather than following hand-written rules.
- **Generative** — once trained, an LLM can generate text on its own in response to a prompt.
- **Prone to fabrication and privacy leakage** — GPT-3 had "the unfortunate habit of making things up," and a Google DeepMind-led test found that prompting ChatGPT to repeat a word endlessly caused OpenAI's LLM to surface private, identifiable information (email addresses and similar) from its training data; a separate Microsoft-affiliated study found GPT-4 more easily "jailbroken" into unsafe outputs than other LLMs.
- **Costly to run and usage-priced** — LLM economics are dominated by compute cost (OpenAI was reported to spend roughly $700,000/day on compute), which is why LLM providers commonly bill by token/usage rather than flat SaaS pricing.
- **Anchors a layered AI stack** — LLMs form the "foundation model" layer beneath middle-layer tooling (fine-tuning, prompt engineering, model orchestration, observability) and top-layer applications that startups build against.
- **Split between proprietary and open approaches** — OpenAI's GPT-X models are proprietary LLMs, contrasted in the corpus with Meta's Llama family and other efforts pushing more "open" LLM development, a split that intensified after a leaked internal Google memo argued neither OpenAI nor Google had a durable "moat" against open-source LLMs.

# Model Fine-Tuning

## Definition

In the corpus, model fine-tuning is the OpenAI capability that lets companies using GPT-3.5 Turbo or GPT-4 through the API continue training the model on their own data so it better fits their use case. In the corpus's most concrete example, OpenAI's fine-tuning of GPT-3.5 Turbo lets companies using the model through the API make it better follow specific instructions — such as always responding in a given language, formatting responses consistently, or matching a brand's tone — and shorten text prompts to speed up API calls and cut costs.

## Context

The corpus documents fine-tuning as a capability OpenAI progressively opened to developers alongside its paid APIs. OpenAI first brought fine-tuning to GPT-3.5 Turbo, partnering with Scale AI so companies could fine-tune the model, at published costs of $0.008 per 1K tokens for training, $0.012 per 1K tokens for usage input, and $0.016 per 1K tokens for usage output. It later extended fine-tuning to GPT-4, though the GPT-4 program involves more oversight and guidance from OpenAI teams than the GPT-3.5 program, largely due to technical hurdles. Separately, in TechCrunch's October 2023 survey of AI investors, fine-tuning is named as one of the distinct layers of the emerging LLM stack — alongside models and pre-training solutions — that sits in the middle layer connecting foundation models to specialized applications, together with prompt engineering and model orchestration.

## Key Characteristics

- **Continues training an existing model on customer data** — fine-tuning takes a model the customer already accesses through the API (e.g., GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4) and continues training it on data the customer supplies.
- **Improves instruction-following and output style** — it can make a model better follow specific instructions, consistently format responses, and match a desired tone or brand voice.
- **Reduces prompt length and cost** — because the desired behavior is trained into the model, fine-tuning lets customers shorten text prompts, which speeds up API calls and cuts per-call cost.
- **Priced separately from inference** — OpenAI charged distinct per-token rates for fine-tuning training versus using (input/output) the fine-tuned model.
- **Oversight scales with model capability** — OpenAI applied more oversight and guidance to the GPT-4 fine-tuning program than to the GPT-3.5 program, citing technical hurdles.
- **A distinct layer of the LLM stack** — investors surveyed by TechCrunch treat fine-tuning tools as their own layer of the GenAI tech stack, separate from foundation model providers and end-user applications.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, OpenAI's own documentation describes fine-tuning more generally as letting a developer "take an OpenAI base model, provide the kinds of inputs and outputs you expect" so the model is adapted to a specific task rather than replaced with a newly trained one (OpenAI, "Model optimization," accessed 2026-09-02, https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization).

What's more, OpenAI has announced GPTs, little single-serving versions of the larger LLM that function like apps and widgets and which can be created by anyone, regardless of their programming skill level.

# The ChatGPT Integration Wave, Early 2023

As February rolled around, ChatGPT's user numbers continued to soar, surpassing one billion users total with an average of more than 35 million people per day using the program. At this point OpenAI was reportedly worth just under $30 billion and Microsoft was doing its absolute best to cram the new technology into every single system, application and feature in its product ecosystem: ChatGPT was incorporated into BingChat, now just Copilot, and the Edge browser to great fanfare — despite repeated incidents of bizarre behavior and responses that saw the Bing program temporarily taken offline for repairs.

Other tech companies began adopting ChatGPT as well: Opera incorporating it into its browser, Snapchat releasing its GPT-based My AI assistant, which would be unceremoniously abandoned a few problematic months later, and Buzzfeed News's parent company using it to generate listicles.

# GPT Model Lineage And The ChatGPT Launch

GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) is the large language model that ChatGPT runs on, and OpenAI had been developing it since 2016 — unveiling GPT-1 in 2018 and iterating it to GPT-3 by June 2020. With the November 30, 2022 release of GPT-3.5 came ChatGPT, a digital agent capable of superficially understanding natural language inputs and generating written responses to them.

The first iteration's limits were plain: it was rather slow to answer and couldn't speak to questions about anything that happened after September 2021, not to mention its issues answering queries with misinformation during bouts of "hallucinations." Even so, that kludgy first iteration demonstrated capabilities far beyond what other state-of-the-art digital assistants like Siri and Alexa could provide — the discriminating feature that set it apart from what came before.

# Large Language Model (LLM)

## Definition

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained to learn from enormous amounts of digital text — Wikipedia articles, digital books, message boards — so that it can generate text on its own.

## Context

The corpus traces the term to OpenAI's GPT-3, described as the neural network Dario Amodei's team built by analysing "countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards" so it "could generate text on its own," released in the summer of 2020; it also "had the unfortunate habit of making things up." ChatGPT itself runs on GPT, the LLM lineage OpenAI had developed since 2016, iterating from GPT-1 (2018) to GPT-3 (June 2020) before GPT-3.5 powered ChatGPT's November 2022 launch. In the venture-capital view of the AI market, LLMs sit at the base "foundation model" layer of a broader stack — models, pre-training solutions, fine-tuning tools, middle-layer tooling, and end-market applications — with providers such as OpenAI's GPT-4, Google's Bard, and Anthropic's Claude expected to consolidate into an oligopolistic structure resembling the cloud-provider market. OpenAI's GPT-X models are repeatedly described as proprietary LLMs that other companies build businesses on top of, a dependency that became visible when the November 2023 OpenAI board upheaval led customers to contact rival LLM providers (Anthropic, Google, Cohere) out of concern for continuity.

## Key Characteristics

- **Trained on enormous text corpora** — LLMs learn by analysing vast amounts of digital text (Wikipedia, books, message boards) rather than following hand-written rules.
- **Generative** — once trained, an LLM can generate text on its own in response to a prompt.
- **Prone to fabrication and privacy leakage** — GPT-3 had "the unfortunate habit of making things up," and a Google DeepMind-led test found that prompting ChatGPT to repeat a word endlessly caused OpenAI's LLM to surface private, identifiable information (email addresses and similar) from its training data; a separate Microsoft-affiliated study found GPT-4 more easily "jailbroken" into unsafe outputs than other LLMs.
- **Costly to run and usage-priced** — LLM economics are dominated by compute cost (OpenAI was reported to spend roughly $700,000/day on compute), which is why LLM providers commonly bill by token/usage rather than flat SaaS pricing.
- **Anchors a layered AI stack** — LLMs form the "foundation model" layer beneath middle-layer tooling (fine-tuning, prompt engineering, model orchestration, observability) and top-layer applications that startups build against.
- **Split between proprietary and open approaches** — OpenAI's GPT-X models are proprietary LLMs, contrasted in the corpus with Meta's Llama family and other efforts pushing more "open" LLM development, a split that intensified after a leaked internal Google memo argued neither OpenAI nor Google had a durable "moat" against open-source LLMs.

# ChatGPT Subscription Tiers And Pricing

ChatGPT is sold in a ladder of paid tiers on top of the free chatbot: ChatGPT Plus at $20 per month, a previewed ChatGPT Business tier, and ChatGPT Enterprise — with the tiers distinguished mainly by data-usage policy, control over end users, and access to the newest models.

The ladder was built in stages. OpenAI first said it was "starting to think about how to monetize ChatGPT" in an announcement on the company's official Discord server, posting a waitlist for a version to be called ChatGPT Professional; the waitlist document listed benefits including no "blackout" windows, no throttling and an unlimited number of messages — "at least 2x the regular daily limit." A month later OpenAI launched a pilot subscription plan, ChatGPT Plus, starting at $20 per month. It then previewed ChatGPT Business, described as "for professionals who need more control over their data as well as enterprises seeking to manage their end users"; OpenAI wrote that "ChatGPT Business will follow our API's data usage policies, which means that end users' data won't be used to train our models by default," and planned to make it available in the coming months. ChatGPT Enterprise followed, able to perform the same tasks as ChatGPT — writing emails, drafting essays, debugging computer code — while adding "enterprise-grade" privacy and data analysis capabilities on top of vanilla ChatGPT, along with enhanced performance and customization options.

Capacity became a binding constraint. Following the Dev Day conference, Sam Altman announced the company was pausing new subscriptions for ChatGPT Plus because of a "surge of usage"; the temporary hold on sign-ups, together with demand for new Plus features such as making custom GPTs, led to a slew of resellers on eBay. On December 13, 2023 Altman announced sign-ups had been re-enabled: "we have re-enabled chatgpt plus subscriptions! thanks for your patience while we found more gpus." The Plus subscription includes access to GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo.

# Independent Research And Reviews Of ChatGPT's Flaws

Independent researchers and advocacy groups repeatedly found ChatGPT and GPT-4 to be flawed in ways OpenAI's own launches did not resolve — on child safety, on toxicity, and on the vision-enabled multimodal model.

An independent review from Common Sense Media, a nonprofit advocacy group, found that ChatGPT could potentially be harmful for younger users, flagging it as potentially unsafe for kids; ChatGPT got an overall three-star rating in the report, with its lowest ratings relating to transparency, privacy, trust and safety. On multimodality, OpenAI announced that GPT-4 with vision would become available alongside the upcoming launch of the GPT-4 Turbo API, but some researchers found that the model remained flawed in several significant and problematic ways.

Two toxicity findings stand out. A Microsoft-affiliated scientific paper examined the "trustworthiness" — and toxicity — of LLMs including GPT-4; because GPT-4 is more likely to follow the instructions of "jailbreaking" prompts, the co-authors claim it can be more easily prompted than other LLMs to spout toxic, biased text. Separately, a study co-authored by scientists at the Allen Institute for AI showed that assigning ChatGPT a "persona" through the ChatGPT API — for example "a bad person," "a horrible person" or "a nasty person" — increases its toxicity sixfold; the co-authors also found that having the chatbot pose as certain historical figures, gendered people and members of political parties increased its toxicity, with journalists, men and Republicans in particular causing the model to say more offensive things than it normally would. That research was conducted using the latest version, but not the model then in preview based on GPT-4.

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# ChatGPT Competitors And Alternatives

There are multiple AI-powered chatbot competitors to ChatGPT — Together, Google's Bard and Anthropic's Claude among them — and developers are creating open source alternatives, though the latter are harder, if not impossible, to run today.

Bard is the closest comparison. Much like ChatGPT, Bard is a chatbot that answers questions in natural language; Google announced at its 2023 I/O event that it would soon add multimodal content to Bard, meaning it can deliver answers in more than just text, with rich visuals — pictures for now, and later possibly maps, charts and other items. The discriminating advantage claimed for ChatGPT is time in the field: its generative AI has had a longer lifespan and thus has been "learning" for a longer period than Bard.

Two further challengers were in development. The Google-owned research lab DeepMind claimed that its next LLM would rival, or even best, ChatGPT; DeepMind is using techniques from AlphaGo — its AI system that was the first to defeat a professional human player at the board game Go — to make a ChatGPT-rivaling chatbot called Gemini. Apple is developing AI tools to challenge OpenAI, Google and others, and has created a chatbot that some engineers internally refer to as "Apple GPT," although Apple has yet to determine a strategy for releasing the AI to consumers.

# Google's Gemini Model Family And Its Capability Claims

Gemini is Google's new flagship generative AI model, unveiled in the first week of December 2023 and meant to power a range of products and services including Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor. In blog posts and press materials, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4, and it emphasised Gemini's coding capabilities and multimodal prowess, claiming that the model can understand images, audio and videos just as well as text.

The family has tiers, and only the lower one shipped. Google did not release the full model, Gemini Ultra — which is set to launch sometime in 2024 in Bard and other products — but only a "lite" version called Gemini Pro. Gemini Pro is therefore not the most capable version of Gemini, and Google compared its performance to GPT-4's predecessor, GPT-3.5, a model that was around a year old. Google nevertheless promised improvements in reasoning, planning and understanding with Gemini Pro over the previous model powering Bard, claiming Gemini Pro was better at summarizing content, brainstorming and writing.

The shipped tier is also narrower than the multimodal claims suggest: Gemini Pro is strictly text-in, text-out, and has proven to be mistake-prone. In a worse look for Google, the company was caught faking a Gemini demo by tuning text prompts with still images off camera.

# Project Hug: Google's Developer Incentive Program, As Characterized By Both Sides

Project Hug is an initiative that forms part of the Google Games Velocity Program, and it is a second set of agreements Epic will highlight — those between Google and Android app developers themselves, as distinct from Google's agreements with device makers. Its defining feature is contested, and the two characterizations mark the boundary of the concept.

Epic will cite it as an example of where Google paid competitors not to distribute their apps on Android outside of the Play Store, by targeting those developers that were most at risk of attrition from Play and then approaching them with a monetary offer. As an example, Epic will point to Activision Blizzard — the owner of King.com and maker of Candy Crush and Call of Duty — as one developer that wanted to go the route of opening its own app store. Google and Activision Blizzard then entered into a three-year agreement in January 2020, worth approximately $360 million, to keep the developer on Google Play, Epic will argue.

Google, however, will characterize this program as a way to incentivize developers to launch their apps on Android at the same time as they launch on iOS, and plans to dispute Epic's claims that it prevented developers from opening their own app stores.

# Generative AI

## Definition

In the corpus, "generative AI" is the umbrella label applied to the 2023 AI boom's content-producing systems — OpenAI's ChatGPT (built on GPT-3.5/GPT-4) and Adobe's Firefly image and vector-graphics models are the flagship examples named — rather than a term the corpus itself formally defines.

## Context

The corpus treats "generative AI" as the umbrella term for the mainstream AI boom of 2023, distinct from the EU AI Act's regulatory term "general purpose AI" (GPAI), which lawmakers deliberately chose as a more technology-neutral label for "the most powerful models behind the current boom in generative AI tools" so the law would not be pinned to one architecture like transformers (doc_0525).
OpenAI built ChatGPT specifically "to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI," and its free, chat-based interface is credited with "taking generative AI mainstream" as a consumer product rather than a research artifact (doc_0047).
Enterprise adoption is depicted as cautious relative to vendor hype: a Morgan Stanley survey found 56% of CIOs said generative AI was affecting investment priorities, but only 4% had launched significant projects, most still in evaluation or proof-of-concept (doc_0160).
The technology spans well beyond chatbots — Adobe's Firefly generative AI models generate images and vector graphics for creative software (doc_0043), and Amazon executive Tye Brady discussed generative AI alongside humanoid robots and mobile manipulation as an input to robotics work (doc_0528).
The same capability that drives adoption also drives the corpus's recurring regulatory and creative-industry concerns: the EU warned that "widely accessible generative AI tools" pose disinformation risks to elections (doc_0248), and the National Music Publishers Association called generative AI "the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed" in its copyright submission to the US Copyright Office (doc_0271).

## Key Characteristics

- **Illustrated by content-producing examples rather than defined outright** — the corpus shows the term through instances of new text, images, and vector graphics being produced from a prompt, illustrated by ChatGPT's text generation (doc_0048) and Firefly's image/vector generation (doc_0043).
- **Consumer breakout via chat interfaces** — ChatGPT's free, web-based chat interface is what took generative AI "mainstream," reaching the fastest adoption of any consumer app (doc_0047, doc_0048).
- **Enterprise adoption lags vendor hype** — large-company CIOs report slow, cautious rollout despite heavy vendor promotion, weighing API/SaaS costs against ROI (doc_0160).
- **Distinct from but overlapping "general purpose AI"** — EU lawmakers deliberately avoided calling the underlying models "generative AI" in law, choosing "general purpose AI" instead to stay technology-neutral rather than tied to transformer-based architectures (doc_0525).
- **Applies across domains beyond chatbots** — spans creative tools (Adobe Firefly) and robotics (Amazon's mobile manipulation work), per the corpus (doc_0043, doc_0528).
- **Focus of copyright and disinformation controversy** — named by the NMPA as a threat to the "human creative class" via unlicensed training data (doc_0271), and flagged by the EU as an election-disinformation risk requiring safeguards (doc_0248).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "generative AI" as a familiar shorthand without formally defining it. Per IBM, generative AI "is artificial intelligence (AI) that can create original content — such as text, images, video, audio or software code — in response to a user's prompt or request," distinguishing it from AI systems built only to classify or act on existing data (IBM, *What is generative AI?*, accessed 2026-09-02).
