# ChatGPT Adoption Milestones And Usage Statistics

Roughly a year after its release, ChatGPT had 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also revealed that over two million developers use the platform, including more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies.

Two other markers frame that scale. OpenAI hit the one-year anniversary of ChatGPT: what began as a "low-key research preview" evolved into a powerhouse that changed the AI industry forever, and Altman looked back on the night before its launch in a post on X on November 30, 2023 — "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt before the next morning's launch. what a year it's been…" Meanwhile neither Apple nor Google chose an AI app as its app of the year for 2023, despite the success of ChatGPT's mobile app, which became the fastest-growing consumer application in history before that record was broken by Meta's Threads.

Adoption among the general public is far thinner than the headline numbers suggest. Ongoing polling by Pew Research shows that although ChatGPT is gaining mindshare, only about 18% of Americans have ever actually used it — suggesting the language model is not quite as popular or threatening as some would have you think.



---


# ChatGPT Enterprise And Multimodal Features

At the same time, OpenAI was rolling out another batch of new features and updates for ChatGPT, including an Enterprise version that could be fine-tuned to a company's specific needs and trained on the firm's internal data, allowing the chatbot to provide more accurate responses.

ChatGPT's ability to browse the internet for information was restored for Plus users in September, having been temporarily suspended earlier in the year after folks figured out how to exploit it to get around paywalls. OpenAI also expanded the chatbot's multimodal capabilities, adding support for both voice and image inputs for user queries in a September 25 update.



---


# ChatGPT Overview And Significance

ChatGPT is OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot, and it has taken the world by storm: what started as a tool to hyper-charge productivity through writing essays and code from short text prompts has evolved into a behemoth used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies for far more wide-ranging needs.

That growth propelled OpenAI itself into becoming one of the most-hyped companies in recent memory, even though CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return raised concerns about the company's direction and opened the door for competitors. The fallout was still settling, but it might empower competitors such as Meta and its LLaMA family of large language models, or help other AI startups get attention and funding as the industry watched OpenAI implode and put itself back together. Whatever the nefarious side of ChatGPT, it was clear that AI tools were not going away anytime soon: since its initial launch nearly a year earlier, ChatGPT had hit 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI was investing heavily in it.

The capability boundary at the time was defined by model access and modality. GPT-4, which can write more naturally and fluently than previous models, remained largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users, although it could be accessed for free through Microsoft's Bing Chat in the Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome and Safari web browsers. Beyond GPT-4 and the OpenAI DevDay announcements, OpenAI had recently connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users, and with the integration of DALL-E 3, users could generate both text and images right inside ChatGPT.



---


# ChatGPT Custom Instructions And File Analysis

OpenAI launched custom instructions for ChatGPT so users do not have to write the same instruction prompts to the chatbot every time they interact with it, and later extended the feature to all users, including those on the free tier.

The company said the feature lets a user "share anything you'd like ChatGPT to consider in its response." For example, a teacher can say they are teaching fourth-grade math, or a developer can specify the code language they prefer when asking for suggestions; a person can also specify their family size so the text-generating AI can give responses about meals, grocery and vacation planning accordingly. The extension to the free tier allows all users to add various preferences and requirements they want the chatbot to consider when responding.

Separately, ChatGPT began testing file upload and analysis. Subscribers to ChatGPT's Enterprise Plan reported new beta features including the ability to upload PDFs to analyze and ask questions about them directly. The same rollout also means users no longer have to manually select a mode such as DALL-E or browsing when using ChatGPT — instead they are automatically switched to models based on the prompt.

qid: After the report by Fortune on September 26, 2023, claiming Donald Trump inflated the value of his Trump Tower apartment, did The Age report on November 7, 2023, maintain consistency regarding the allegations of Donald Trump's financial misrepresentations?
context:
# Trump Net Worth Valuation Dispute at Trial

Thousands of pages of exhibits detailing the performance of Donald Trump's assets, made available during the New York fraud trial, have provided a deeper look into his fortune. His 2021 statement of financial condition, filed as part of the lawsuit, pegged his net worth at $US4.5 billion. Bloomberg's calculation has consistently been below Trump's figures; at the same time, Bloomberg measured the value of some Trump properties higher than what New York state claims.

Trump took the stand and testified that the properties whose values he is accused of inflating were actually undervalued, based on the premium his "brand" adds. He also said that banks did not rely on his statements of financial condition when weighing loans: "They just weren't a very important element in banks' decision-making process," Trump told the court. "And we'll explain that as this trial goes along."

The Age's 7 November 2023 report set out New York state's valuation of four high-profile Trump properties where the prosecution alleges fraud occurred, alongside Bloomberg's own approach to assessing the assets.



---


# Trump Tower Fifth Avenue Penthouse Valuation Dispute

Among the allegations in the New York case was that Trump claimed his Trump Tower apartment in Manhattan — a three-storey penthouse replete with gold-plated fixtures — was nearly three times its actual size, and valued the property at $327 million; no apartment in New York City has ever sold for close to that amount, Attorney General Letitia James said. The Age's comparison in November 2023 listed Trump's 2021 valuation at $US131.3 million and Bloomberg's 2023 valuation at $US40 million, with no current New York estimate available.

The size inflation is documented over a specific window: between 2011 and 2016, Trump valued the apartment on the basis of it being 30,000 square feet (2,787 square metres), almost triple its actual measurement of 10,996 square feet, and because of this New York State arrived at a valuation about a third of Trump's in those years. Space inflation was not the only issue: between 2014 and 2015 Trump increased the apartment's value to $US327 million from $US200 million, which the prosecution argues was to mask a drop in the value of another of his properties. "A discrepancy of this order of magnitude, by a real estate developer sizing up his own living space of decades, can only be considered fraud," Judge Arthur Engoron wrote in his September ruling.

Bloomberg values the property using recent Trump Tower sales and those of comparable Manhattan penthouses. While some splashy residences in much newer Billionaires Row buildings have listed for well in excess of $US100 million, they typically boast higher ceilings, more up-to-date finishes, contemporary layouts, outdoor space and better views. A better comparison, the report says, would be a 9,450-square-foot penthouse in Olympic Tower, five blocks south on Fifth Avenue, on and off the market for $US35 million since 2016; or Carl Icahn's 14,000-square-foot penthouse at Museum Tower on West 53rd Street, listed for $US35 million in 2019 before he attempted to split and sell it as two apartments, both eventually delisted.



---


# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.



---


# Letitia James Asset Inflation Allegations

Letitia James, a Democrat, sued Trump and the Trump Organization a year before this September 2023 ruling, alleging a pattern of duplicity that she dubbed "the art of the steal" — a twist on the title of Trump's 1987 business memoir "The Art of the Deal."

The lawsuit accused Trump and his company of routinely inflating the value of assets like skyscrapers, golf courses and his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, padding his bottom line by billions.



---


# Trump Park Avenue Rent-Stabilised Unit Valuations

Trump Park Avenue, the residential condo tower on Manhattan's Upper East Side formerly known as the Hotel Delmonico, is not one of Trump's best-known buildings, but according to the prosecution it has been the source of some significant asset inflations. Trump's 2021 valuation was $US90.9 million, Bloomberg's 2023 valuation $US86.4 million, and New York's 2021 valuation $US80 million.

The dispute centres on rent-stabilised units. The building's value to Trump mostly stems from unsold condo units owned by the Trump Organisation and rented out, a varying number of which have been rent-stabilised, meaning tenants pay below market rates; such apartments are typically valued at a discount because tenants can stay indefinitely, sometimes even passing them on to children. In 2010, 12 rent-stabilised apartments owned by Trump were valued at an average of $US62,500 each in an appraisal provided by a real estate company; the following year Trump valued them at $US4.1 million each, more than 65 times greater, and has continued to value stabilised apartments in the building at market rates, including in his 2021 statement of financial condition. Rent-stabilised units "with a positive cash flow are often valued at 15-25 cents a dollar of the open market value, versus single digits for negative cash flow," said Jonathan Miller, president of appraiser Miller Samuel.

Trump's optimism was shown to be at least partially justified: by 2021, only five of the 12 apartments remained rent stabilised. The prosecution also claims two additional non-stabilised apartments in the building were overvalued because Trump ignored an option his daughter, Ivanka Trump, had to buy them at a price lower than the market value he used. The Age also records an assessment of the brand effect on price generally: "There would be a Trump premium because the person that would want that property is likely to be a Trump supporter," Eli Beracha said, though it is also likely that the association with Trump would turn off some buyers.



---


# Mar-a-Lago Valuation Dispute

Mar-a-Lago is the sharpest of the valuation disputes: Trump valued the Palm Beach estate as high as $739 million — more than 10 times a more reasonable estimate of its worth, Fortune reported in September 2023 — on the idea that the property could be developed for residential use, when deed terms prohibit that, Attorney General Letitia James said. The Age's November 2023 comparison put Trump's 2021 valuation at $US612.1 million, Bloomberg's 2023 valuation at $US240 million, and New York's 2021 valuation at $US27.6 million.

The gap turns on how the property may be used. Trump made a series of agreements with Palm Beach County and the National Trust for Historic Preservation for Mar-a-Lago to be used only as a club, giving up development rights, so Palm Beach values the property as a business on its tax rolls and in 2021 assessed it at $US27.6 million, lower than comparable residential properties; New York State argues this is the appraisal Trump should have been using. That figure drew objections: New York's estimated value "was a shock to the real estate community and anybody with any understanding of the island and its values," said Liza Pulitzer, a real estate agent at Brown Harris Stevens and a Palm Beach native. "It could easily fetch $US500 million or more." That assumes a buyer views it as a single-family residence; it is currently not zoned for such use, though Trump is able to reside there through a loophole designating himself an employee. Trump's legal team engaged an expert witness who argued a future buyer could do the same thing, and could reduce the club to a membership of one, though it is unclear whether Palm Beach would allow that without a change to zoning status.

The property's economics have also shifted. Historically Mar-a-Lago never made much money for the Trump Organisation, but it took in about $US41 million in revenue in 2022 according to Trump's most recent ethics disclosure, compared with $US21 million in 2019. Bloomberg values it at $US240 million based on a combination of comparable residential property sales in the area and its value as a business, reflecting uncertainty around its future status — uncertainty not shared by everyone: if the city and county allowed it, "there is no reason why it wouldn't be able to converted to a full-time private residence," said Eli Beracha, director of the Hollo School of Real Estate at Florida International University. The Age also notes the estate has been at the centre of publicised post-presidency scandals, from classified documents kept in one of its bathrooms to being the location where Trump is said to have shared nuclear submarine secrets with Australian businessman Anthony Pratt, which Trump denies.



---


# Trump's Other Criminal and Civil Cases 2023

Letitia James' lawsuit is one of several legal headaches for Trump as he campaigns for a return to the White House in 2024. He has been indicted four times in the six months to September 2023 — accused in Georgia and Washington, D.C., of plotting to overturn his 2020 election loss; in Florida of hoarding classified documents; and in Manhattan of falsifying business records related to hush money paid on his behalf.

Separately, the Trump Organization was convicted of tax fraud in 2022 in an unrelated criminal case for helping executives dodge taxes on extravagant perks such as Manhattan apartments and luxury cars, and the company was fined $1.6 million. One of the executives, Trump's longtime finance chief Allen Weisselberg, pleaded guilty and served five months in jail; he is a defendant in James' lawsuit and gave sworn deposition testimony for the case in May.



---


# 40 Wall Street Valuation Dispute

For 40 Wall Street, Trump's flagship lower Manhattan office tower, Trump's 2021 valuation was $US664 million and Bloomberg's 2023 valuation $US270 million, with no current New York estimate available. New York State argues that in valuing the building Trump consistently ignored more conservative appraisals he had received from professionals: 40 Wall Street was appraised by a real estate company at $US200 million in 2011 and $US220 million in 2012, yet Trump valued the property in financial statements at $US524.7 million and $US527.2 million respectively for those years.

Bloomberg uses a capitalisation of net income approach. Valuations for commercial offices across the board have taken a hit in the 18 months to November 2023 amid rising interest rates and a lacklustre corporate leasing market, but 40 Wall Street has its own problems: tenant departures meant occupancy slid to 77 per cent in June, down from 98 per cent in 2015, and its net operating income is only 61 per cent of what was projected by underwriters. "There's not a lot of leasing velocity down there," said Albert Sultan, a broker at Kassin Sabbagh Realty; the financial district used to offer a lower cost for tenants, but with Midtown rents declining, "there's no reason to go downtown."

A further liability sits in the lease terms: the property is subject to a ground lease that resets in 2032 at either 6 per cent of the land value or 85 per cent of its rent in the prior year, which based on current rent means the ground lease would jump to $US30 million from about $US2.6 million now.



---


# Engoron's "Fantasy World" Finding on Trump Financial Statements

Judge Arthur Engoron's finding is that Trump's conduct went beyond boasting into legal violation: beyond mere bragging about his riches, Trump, his company and key executives repeatedly lied about them on his annual financial statements, reaping rewards such as favourable loan terms and lower insurance premiums.

Those tactics crossed a line and violated the law, the judge said, rejecting Trump's contention that a disclaimer on the financial statements absolved him of any wrongdoing.

The warrant he offers is that the defence position requires an internally incoherent picture of valuation and responsibility. "In defendants' world: rent regulated apartments are worth the same as unregulated apartments; restricted land is worth the same as unrestricted land; restrictions can evaporate into thin air; a disclaimer by one party casting responsibility on another party exonerates the other party's lies," Engoron wrote in his 35-page ruling. "That is a fantasy world, not the real world."



---


# Trump Motions to Dismiss the Fraud Case Rejected

Trump's lawyers asked the judge to throw out the case, and he denied the request. Their arguments attacked the attorney general's standing and the timing of the claims: they contend that James was not legally allowed to file the lawsuit because there is no evidence that the public was harmed by Trump's actions, and they also argued that many of the allegations in the lawsuit were barred by the statute of limitations.

Engoron, noting that he had "emphatically rejected" those arguments earlier in the case, equated them to the "time-loop in the film 'Groundhog Day.'"



---


# Letitia James' History of Investigating Trump

Letitia James, who campaigned for office as a Trump critic and watchdog, started scrutinising his business practices in March 2019, after his former personal lawyer Michael Cohen testified to Congress that Trump exaggerated his wealth on financial statements provided to Deutsche Bank while trying to obtain financing to buy the NFL's Buffalo Bills.

Her office had previously sued Trump for misusing his own charitable foundation to further his political and business interests. Trump was ordered to pay $2 million to an array of charities as a fine, and the charity, the Trump Foundation, was shut down.



---


# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Wall Street November 2023 Relief Rally

Wall Street closed a strong week on the Friday before this 5 November 2023 report, with the S&P 500 climbing 40.56 points, or 0.9 per cent, to 4,358.3; the Dow Jones Industrial Average gaining 222.24, or 0.7 per cent, to 34,061.32; and the Nasdaq composite jumping 184.09, or 1.4 per cent, to 13,478.28. Stocks surged through the week on rising hopes that the Federal Reserve is finally done with its market-crunching interest rate hikes aimed at getting inflation under control, with a Friday report underscoring easing inflation pressure by showing employers hired fewer workers in October than economists expected.

The report described this as a stunning turnaround from just a week earlier, when Wall Street was reeling after the S&P 500 had fallen 10 per cent below its high point for the year, sending the index into what investors call a "correction". Since then, strong profit reports helped drive some stocks to towering gains: Generac, a maker of back-up generators, soared nearly 28 per cent for its best week since its stock began trading in 2010, and Expedia Group's stronger-than-forecast report sent its stock nearly 22 per cent higher for its best week since the market was surging out of the coronavirus crash in early 2020. Even so, it was interest rates, yields and inflation that were at the centre of all the wild movements for financial markets around the world.

Excitement about a potentially easier Fed was more than enough to offset a fall for Apple, Wall Street's most influential and most valuable US stock, which fell 0.5 per cent despite reporting stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected; analysts said investors were likely disappointed with Apple's revenue forecast for the last three months of 2023.

# Michael Wolff On Fox News And Rupert Murdoch

Michael Wolff's latest book, published by The Bridge Street Press at $34.99 and out at the time of writing, turns his blowtorch on Fox News and the recently retired Rupert Murdoch — "two players who had massive roles in getting Trump into power" — The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its defining characteristic, per the reviewer, is the author's method: "One thing you can be sure of in a Michael Wolff book is plenty of controversial detail and quotes that are not always fully substantiated and sourced."

Its place in his output is also noted: the American writer has tackled the Donald Trump White House in three books and has already written a couple about Murdoch, to whom he now returns. "Next year? Surely not," the reviewer adds.

# Gen Z: Definition And Formative Events

Gen Z, as characterized in this account, is the cohort aged 11 to 26 as of October 2023 and the first fully digital native generation — the feature that discriminates it from every earlier cohort is not the scale of the history it has lived through but that it has been plugged into the world through the internet from such a young age. Social media posts are its lingua franca, and the "disturbing images" warning is one it is used to encountering there.

The formative events listed are dense. This generation has already lived through a once-per-century pandemic; the Jan. 6 insurrection, an event unseen for centuries in American politics, when armed right-wing extremists stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 following the election defeat of former President Donald Trump; the first major European ground war since World War II, in Ukraine; and market crashes in 2008 and 2020 that recall the Great Depression. Three years before the article, as Gen Z emerged into young adulthood, online videos of the murder of George Floyd shook the country in May 2020, resulting in a summer of violent Black Lives Matter protests and riots. School shootings have only increased in frequency since Columbine in 1999, with more students documenting the terror on their phones and sharing it online — one of them, the Parkland shooting of 2018, tragically created the first spokespeople of the post-millennial generation. Most recently, on Saturday, 2023-10-07, the Islamic militant group Hamas launched an unprecedented attack on Israel, resulting in the worst war the region has seen in 50 years; in three days more than 1,500 people died on both sides, and graphic, difficult-to-watch videos blanketed the internet.

The boundary case the account itself raises is that every generation has lived through era-defining historical events: millennials remember the 9/11 terrorist attacks and the U.S. invasion of Iraq, and baby boomers lived through the civil rights movement and the Vietnam War. What sets Gen Z apart is the medium — experiencing it all through videos, images, and articles online, which is shaping their mental health, workplace attitudes, and financial habits in visible ways.

# Trump Disclaimer Defence and Its Rejection

Trump's defence attacked the premise that his financial statements could be relied on at all: he denied wrongdoing, arguing in sworn testimony that it did not matter what he put on his financial statements because they carry a disclaimer saying they should not be trusted. He told James at an April deposition, "You don't have a case and you should drop this case," adding: "Do you know the banks were fully paid? Do you know the banks made a lot of money? Do you know I don't believe I ever got even a default notice, and even during COVID, the banks were all paid? And yet you're suing on behalf of banks, I guess. It's crazy. The whole case is crazy."

Engoron rejected that argument when the defence previously sought to have the case thrown out. The judge said the disclaimer on the financial statements "makes abundantly clear that Mr. Trump was fully responsible for the information contained within" them, and that "allowing blanket disclaimers to insulate liars from liability would completely undercut" the "important function" that such statements serve "in the real world."

# Argument That a Trump Presidency Would Not Doom Ukraine

Kurt Volker challenges the premise that a Trump election victory would mean abandonment of Ukraine, while conceding that it would make future funding uncertain. "I doubt that even if Trump were elected that he would abandon support for Ukraine overall, because it would be a disaster for U.S. interests, and it would appear to be a failure," he told CNBC. "You'd have these images of Russians overrunning places, and brutality and so forth, so I don't think he wants that."

The attack is on the inference from Trump's past relations with Moscow to a wholesale cut-off, not on the observation that his intentions are unclear: "But it's not clear exactly what he would do to try to end the war." For his part, Trump has said he would be able to resolve the Ukraine war "in one day" if reelected, saying he would convince the leaders of Ukraine and Russia to make a deal.

# Housing Affordability Is Worse Now Than At The 2006 Peak

Roger Ashworth, a managing director at Goldman Sachs, argued in a credit strategy research paper released in mid-October 2023 that although some economic factors are stronger today than during the Global Financial Crisis, housing affordability is undeniably worse: "While housing and more generally consumer fundamentals are in a much stronger position today, affordability for the incremental buyer is worse than it was at the peak in 2006 before the crash." The claim is deliberately narrow — it is about the incremental buyer's affordability, not about overall fundamentals, which he grants are stronger.

The proximate causes cited are the same constraints that have held all year. "As has been the case throughout this year, limited inventory and low housing affordability continue to hamper home sales," NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement, adding a policy conclusion: "The Federal Reserve simply cannot keep raising interest rates in light of softening inflation and weakening job gains." The Fed had raised rates several times in 2023, with Chair Jerome Powell arming his "higher for longer" stance.

# The Epoch Times, The 2020 Election And Pro-Trump Coverage

In the runup to the 2020 election, The Epoch Times directed millions of dollars in advertising toward supporting President Donald Trump's campaign and published dozens of articles parroting his lies about the election, which produced huge growth in both its audience and its coffers.

That strategy drew criticism from fact-checking groups and got the outlet banned from advertising on Facebook, but it ultimately paid off, putting the once-fringe newspaper on a path that perhaps only its leader — who claims to have supernatural powers — could have foreseen. As its marketing strategy shifted, so did its content: by 2020 it had become a megaphone for the United States' most extreme right-wing stories. There was plenty to write about, since an election marred by disinformation, the bubbling culture wars and, most helpfully for a media company missioned with ending the Chinese Communist Party, a pandemic originating in China all provided endless opportunities for takes aligned with hawkish conservatives and conspiracy theorists.

The Epoch Times was also an early and aggressive promoter of election misinformation, according to the Election Integrity Partnership, a coalition of researchers that documented misinformation around the 2020 vote. That group cited the news organization as a "repeat spreader" of false and misleading voter fraud stories, as well as a major promoter of debunked conspiracy theories about Dominion voting machines and of the "Stop the Steal" movement aimed at overturning the election results. Months after the election, The Epoch Times still refused to acknowledge the results.

# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."

# Penalties Sought in the Letitia James Civil Fraud Lawsuit

Attorney General Letitia James is seeking $250 million in penalties and a ban on Trump doing business in New York, his home state. She has asked Engoron to bar Trump and his three eldest children from ever again running a company based in New York, and to bar Trump and the Trump Organization from entering into commercial real estate acquisitions for five years, among other sanctions. The $250 million figure is the estimated worth of benefits derived from the alleged fraud, she said.

The procedural position as of 26 September 2023 was that Engoron's ruling, in a phase of the case known as summary judgment, resolves the key claim in James' lawsuit while six others remain. He was slated to hold a non-jury trial starting 2 October before deciding on those claims and any punishments he may impose, and has said the trial could last into December.

Manhattan prosecutors had looked into bringing a criminal case over the same conduct but declined to do so, leaving James to sue and seek penalties that could disrupt Trump's and his family's ability to do business in the state. James' lawsuit does not carry the potential of prison time, but could complicate Trump's ability to transact real estate deals and could also stain his legacy as a developer.

# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. # The Epoch Times' Facebook Advertising Ban, 2019

In 2019, following reporting by NBC News, Facebook found that The Epoch Times had "leveraged foreign actors posing as Americans to push political content" and banned it from future advertising, citing violations of its policies including trying to circumvent review systems.

By that year the outlet had gone mostly digital and was spending millions of dollars building a network of Facebook pages and groups and running aggressive pro-Trump ad campaigns. That move toward explicit support of Republicans ran against Li's teachings to stay away from U.S. politics, but it had been foreshadowed by Li's comments at a Falun Gong conference the year before.

The Epoch Times also employed a tactic more often associated with fake news content farms and scammers than with news organizations: it created a network of inspiring and cute-content pages, along with fake accounts, to inflate its reach.

# Bankman-Fried's Claimed Ignorance Of Alameda's Finances

Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried attacked the prosecution's premise that he knew about the hole in FTX by claiming he did not learn of the $8 billion liability associated with Alameda until October 2022, that he found it all by himself by looking at a computer database, and that when he found it he was "very surprised." The Verge's reporter recorded the claim with heavy scepticism.

The counter-argument extended to reinterpreting each earlier warning as something innocuous. On why Alameda served as FTX's "payment provider" for bank transfers, he said FTX could not get bank accounts right away and he anticipated it would take a year or two, so rather than wait he used Alameda: "My understanding at the time was that there were teams managing the process. At the time, I wasn't entirely sure what was happening." On Adam Yedidia's testimony about an August 2022 conversation regarding the enormous amount Alameda owed FTX, Bankman-Fried remembered it differently — Yedidia was just asking about Alameda's risk profile and he was not talking about insolvency at all. On the dramatic balcony conversation with Nishad Singh at their penthouse, he said Singh thought Alameda's liabilities had gotten too high and that FTX was spending too much on marketing, while Bankman-Fried still thought Alameda had more assets than liabilities so it was all fine, and besides, if Singh thought he would be better at marketing he could take it over — it did not have anything to do with the money Alameda owed FTX at all.

# Alphabet's Q3 2023 Results And Cloud Miss

Shares in Alphabet fell 6 per cent after hours after the Google parent delivered a mixed result: revenue climbed 11 per cent to $US76.7 billion with net income of $US19.7 billion thanks to a recovery in digital advertising revenue, but its closely watched cloud division — which houses its data storage business and many of its AI efforts — missed Wall Street expectations.

During trading hours the S&P 500 slipped off session highs, led by losses in energy shares as oil slid below $US84 a barrel, but once again the index found support above the key 4200 mark; Verizon Communications, 3M and General Electric climbed on bullish forecasts, while Facebook and Instagram owner Meta dropped after being sued by California and dozens of other US states over harmful youth marketing claims. Bitcoin briefly topped $US35,000, and Treasury 10-year yields edged lower following Monday's intense volatility. Investors looking to the earnings season for a dose of good news were hanging their hopes on big tech: the five biggest companies in the S&P 500 — Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and AI chipmaker Nvidia — account for about a quarter of the benchmark's market capitalisation, and their earnings were projected to jump 34 per cent from a year earlier on average, according to analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence.

# George's Claim Of Epstein's Political Influence

Denise George later testified that she thought Epstein was "flexing his political influence over or with the governor" rather than going through the usual channels — her inference from the route by which the waiver request reached her.

Given Epstein's apparent influence in the Virgin Islands, the obvious question was who would want to rock the boat, and George says she was willing to try. Around St. Thomas she has a reputation as a straightshooter, and the former public-corruption attorney stops short of pointing to official wrongdoing; but she makes clear that she, for one, wouldn't tolerate it. "If I have to lose my job to avoid being part of a conspiracy to cover something up, I would do it," George says. "My bar license, my integrity were more important to me. I wasn't going to compromise that."

# Federal Reserve Rate Path Expectations Late 2023

By early December 2023 traders widely expected the Federal Reserve to hold its key interest rate steady at its meeting the following week before potentially cutting rates in March, according to data from CME Group, and Fed officials had recently hinted that the federal funds rate may already be at its peak, above 5.25 per cent, up from nearly zero early in 2022. Fed Chair Jerome Powell and others nevertheless warned Wall Street against being overzealous in its predictions about how early a cut could happen.

The bond market moved with those expectations. With inflation down from its peak two summers earlier, Wall Street was hopeful the Fed might be done with its market-shaking hikes. Investors were looking for a slowdown in the job market that came through employers cutting back on open positions rather than laying off workers, and the report cited showed employers advertised just 8.7 million jobs on the last day of October, down 617,000 from a month earlier. US Treasury yields continued to sag from the heights reached during late October: the 10-year yield fell to 4.18 per cent from 4.26 per cent late on the Monday, after having been above 5 per cent and at its highest level in more than a decade during October. The two-year Treasury yield, which more closely tracks Fed expectations, fell from 4.61 per cent just before the economic reports to 4.57 per cent, yo-yoed, and then eased back to 4.57 per cent. Lower yields were one reason cryptocurrency prices had been rising, alongside excitement about a possible bitcoin exchange-traded fund that helped send bitcoin above $US43,000 ($65,600); Robinhood Markets reported a roughly 75 per cent jump in crypto trading volumes during November from a month earlier, said customers added about $US1.4 billion in net deposits during the month, and its own stock rose 10.3 per cent.

A month earlier, in early November 2023, the same expectations were forming from a lower base. Before that week, stocks had been struggling under the weight of rapidly rising Treasury yields catching up to the Fed's main interest rate, which was above 5.25 per cent and at its highest level since 2001. Higher rates and yields slow the economy, hurt investment prices and raise the risk of something breaking in the financial system, such as the three high-profile US bank failures that rattled markets during the spring. "It was really fear that the Fed was going to go too far," said Katie Nixon, chief investment officer for Northern Trust Wealth Management. The Fed had applied that pressure intentionally, hoping to starve inflation of its fuel and to cool the job market, particularly pay raises, because it feared too-strong pay gains could create a vicious cycle keeping inflation high. Analysts said the Friday jobs report offered encouraging signals, with average hourly earnings rising less in October from September than expected, though it did not mean the job was done. Treasury yields tumbled immediately after that report, with the 10-year easing to 4.52 per cent from 4.67 per cent late Thursday and from more than five per cent the previous week, when it hit its highest level since 2007. Traders then moved up expectations for the first Fed cut, potentially by the summer, according to CME Group data. Foreign-exchange strategists at Bank of America wrote in a BofA Global Research report that for investors around the world the "Fed matters more than other central banks" and weak US data is "the only game-changer for markets". A separate report that Friday from the Institute for Supply Management said growth in US services industries such as finance and construction was weaker than economists expected and suggested a slight easing in prices.

# Volcker's And Powell's Rate-Hiking Cycles Compared

The consumer price index rose at a peak of around 14% in 1980 before then-Fed Chair Paul Volcker's hawkish policies sent mortgage rates to 18% within a year — cooling inflation but sparking a recession, and causing a serious downturn in housing in which home sales and building levels cratered while national home prices actually remained stable. At the start of Volcker's term as Fed chair in August 1979 the median U.S. home sales price was $64,700, and even after a near doubling of mortgage rates that figure rose to $69,400 by the second quarter of 1981. A second account puts the average 30-year fixed mortgage peaking at about 18% by late 1981, and records that home sales activity plummeted from 1978 to 1982, with existing-home sales dropping 50% over that period according to the Office of Policy Development and Research.

Over the 18 months preceding October 2023, current Fed chair Jerome Powell has been following a very similar game plan, raising interest rates aggressively to quash inflation and setting the tone for the most aggressive global hiking of rates in the modern era. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate, the most common type in the U.S., soared from 3.8% in March 2022 to over 7.5% by 2023-10-06, and by the week of 2023-10-20 mortgage rates hit 8%, the highest in more than 20 years. This in turn slowed mortgage purchase applications and caused home sales to plummet, just as in the '80s; but home prices, echoing the dynamic of that era, have yet to collapse. While home sales activity levels this low had not been seen since the 2000s, the housing market more closely mimics that of the '80s, according to a report published in the week of 2023-10-20 by Fortune 500 financial services company First American.

# US Home Prices Peaked In June 2022 And Returned To A Record High By July 2023

National U.S. home prices did not peak until June 2022 — even as mortgage rates soared and purchase applications plummeted amid the Federal Reserve's first interest rate hikes — and although prices fell more than 5% from that peak by January 2023, they returned to a record high in July 2023. This is the observation that has so far vindicated the majority of real estate veterans, who despite a widely bearish industry outlook avoided arguing that home prices would drop the way they did during the 2008 crash that kicked off the Global Financial Crisis.

The backdrop, as of the reporting date of 2023-10-06, is that housing market pessimists had been sounding the alarm for years about a pending crash in U.S. residential real estate. Even before the Fed began hiking interest rates to fight inflation in 2022 — pushing mortgage rates to a 23-year high in October 2023 — years of surging home prices had left some experts warning that the housing market was a massive bubble ready to pop.

# Sports Betting Odds

## Definition

Sports betting odds are the numbers a sportsbook posts alongside a wager to show the payout a bettor stands to win relative to their stake, and they are set by oddsmakers using computer models and analytics before being released to the public. The same underlying odds concept takes different shapes depending on the bet type — a moneyline price on who wins outright, a point spread price on a handicapped margin, and a totals (over/under) price on the combined score — and can be displayed in American, decimal, or fractional format.

## Context

In the corpus, odds are the common thread across every major bet type: moneylines, point spreads, totals, and prop bets all price outcomes with the same odds conventions, and combined-market previews such as college bowl coverage post moneyline, spread, and total odds side by side for a single game. Odds are not static — sportsbooks move them ("line movement") in response to public betting patterns, injury or roster news, and sharp/professional money, with the goal of balancing action on both sides of a bet so the book keeps its built-in profit regardless of outcome. Because different sportsbooks can carry different odds for the same event, bettors practice "line shopping" — comparing odds and lines across multiple sportsbooks before wagering to find the best price. Odds also extend beyond single games into futures and award markets, such as season-long odds on the NFL MVP race between Brock Purdy and Lamar Jackson.

## Key Characteristics

- **American odds format dominates U.S. listings** — a negative number (e.g., -110) shows the favorite and how much must be wagered to profit $100; a positive number (e.g., +250) shows the underdog and how much a $100 wager profits.
- **Three display formats carry the same price** — American, decimal (multiply the odds by the stake for total payout), and fractional (numerator = profit, denominator = stake) are alternative notations for identical odds.
- **Odds move for identifiable reasons** — sportsbooks shift a line or its odds because of lopsided public betting, new information (injuries, weather), sharp bettor action, or a perceived initial mispricing.
- **Odds differ by bet type but share the sign convention** — moneyline odds price the outright winner, point spread odds price a handicapped margin near even money, and totals odds price the over/under of a combined score; all three commonly display as American odds.
- **Line shopping exploits cross-sportsbook odds variance** — because oddsmakers and sportsbooks don't always move in lockstep, checking odds at multiple books before betting can secure a better price on the same wager.

# Totals Bet Outcomes: Push And Overtime

An over/under wager has three potential outcomes: if the combined score exceeds the set total, the "over" bet wins; if the score is below the set total, the "under" bet wins; and if the combined score of the game matches the total exactly, the bet is typically considered a "push" and the wager is refunded.

A push therefore occurs when the combined score of a game matches the set total established by the bookmaker, meaning bettors neither win nor lose and their original wager is returned. To avoid this outcome, most sportsbooks employ half-points in their totals: by setting a total at 200.5 instead of 200, sports betting sites ensure that a game's combined score cannot possibly match the set total exactly.

Overtime is a separate boundary case. In most sports and with the majority of sportsbooks, overtime does count toward a totals wager; Sporting News advises always checking the specific rules of the sportsbook you are betting with to confirm, but says overtime is generally included in totals wagers.

# Over/Under Totals Bet Definition

A totals bet, commonly known as an over/under bet, is a wager on the combined score of both teams in a game: bookmakers set a predicted total score, and bettors choose whether the actual combined score will surpass it ("over") or fall short of it ("under"). Rather than picking the winner or the winning margin, totals betting asks only about the game's combined score, and it sits alongside point spreads and moneylines as a favorite option in sports betting.

The discriminating feature is that the bettor's only concern is whether the final combined score falls over or under the line set by oddsmakers — the identity of the winner is irrelevant. Sporting News illustrates with an NBA game whose total is set at 210.5 points: those who bet the "over" win if the combined score of the two teams is 211 or more, while those who bet the "under" win if the score totals 210 or less. The 0.5 ensures no chance of a tie, since teams cannot score in half-points.

The category is broader than points. Over/under bets involve wagering on whether a particular number will be over or under the figure the bookmaker set, and that number can be combined points scored in a game, total rounds in a fight, or total games in a tennis match.

# Sports Betting Terminology Glossary

CBS Sports set out the top Kentucky betting terms for new bettors on 13 October 2023, defining each bet type by what the bettor is actually wagering on and, in several cases, by a worked Kentucky example.

Against the spread means that instead of betting on an exact winner, the widely popular spread bet levels the playing field by letting you wager on how many points a team will win by: in basketball, if Kentucky is the 7.5-point favorite against Louisville then Kentucky covers by winning by 8 or more, while Louisville as the 7.5-point underdog covers by winning outright or losing by 7 or fewer. Money line is an elevated outright bet with odds adjusted to reflect a favored team and an underdog: if Kentucky is a -200 favorite against Florida you'd need to bet $200 to return $100, while Florida at +200 would return $200 on a $100 bet. An outright bet is the easiest wager to place and is perfect for horse racing, one of Kentucky's biggest sporting events — bettors choose one athlete, or thoroughbred, to win an entire event. An Over/Under has the sportsbook post an estimated total of both teams' final scores, with the bettor wagering on whether the actual final will be higher or lower: if the Over/Under for a Kentucky-Louisville basketball game is 125.5, you wager on the final total being Over 126 or Under 125. A player prop projects a player's stat at the end of a game and asks you to wager over or under that projection, with popular examples being how many touchdown passes a quarterback throws or how many three-pointers a basketball player hits; Kentucky is one of the 18 states that allows prop bets on collegiate athletes.

The remaining terms describe the market's participants and mechanics. The underdog is the team deemed less likely to win based on the odds, and a bet on one typically yields a larger return than a bet on the favorite; the favorite is deemed more likely to win, and bettors often pay a premium for backing one though they more often win outright. Consensus odds are generally defined as an average of all available betting markets, since different sportsbooks may price markets variably based on the action they've taken or their own interpretation of information. Futures markets encompass almost anything outside single-game bets — total regular-season wins, championship odds, MVP odds and more. A parlay requires two or more bets within a single wager, all of which must win: wagering $100 on a three-leg parlay at 6 to 1 odds could win $600 if all three legs win. Juice, also known as the vig or vigorish, is effectively the tax oddsmakers charge for handling a wager — if a book judges a game a virtual coinflip it may price both options at -110 to give itself a 10% rake on all the action. A push is a bet where neither the bettor nor the sportsbook wins: if an over/under for total points is set at 44 and both teams combine for exactly 44, the result is a push and the principal is returned. Live or in-game betting allows bets on several different markets in real time — in basketball, on the outcome of a quarter, individual statistics and live-updated spreads and totals.

The grounds are how the lines are made and remade. Sportsbooks set game totals considering factors like recent performances, weather, and player status, and as new data emerges and betting trends develop, this line can shift — if many bettors choose the "over," the sportsbook might raise the total to balance the bets. The warrant joining grounds to claim is that line movements often reflect public betting sentiments and therefore offer insights to informed bettors: because a move encodes information the book has absorbed about data and about where the public money is, watching it tells the bettor something they did not otherwise have. Hence bettors must monitor any line changes before the game starts and strategize accordingly to optimize their betting success.

The argument stops short of endorsing either side of a totals bet in the abstract: neither wager holds a universal advantage, and success in over/under betting hinges on a thorough evaluation of both the set line and the competing teams.

# Why Moneyline Odds Change

Lines at sports betting apps change quickly for two primary reasons — public betting and new information — and sportsbooks adjust moneyline odds to stay profitable, balance their book and reflect the most current information about an event. Before setting odds oddsmakers gather extensive data, then release the finalized odds to the public; from that point a bettor can bet immediately or wait for shifts, though predicting those shifts is challenging.

The time dimension shows how an opening price drifts. Odds for the next Super Bowl champion released shortly after the previous Super Bowl are based mostly on the recently concluded season; as the new season approaches and teams make changes, the odds adjust to perceived championship chances, and as games progress the lines keep evolving with team performances.

The mechanism has five named drivers. Public betting patterns move a line because, when a significant amount of money lands on one team or participant, sportsbooks adjust the odds to balance their liability — making the price less favorable for the heavily-bet side and more favorable for the less-bet side to encourage even betting and reduce financial risk. New information matters because changes in player injuries, player substitutions or weather conditions alter the perceived outcome, and books adjust once such information becomes public. Professional bettors move lines because large wagers from sharp bettors often reflect insights or information that can influence the odds. Initial miscalculation is a fourth driver: sometimes the opening odds are perceived as offering value, and heavy betting on one side signals that the initial price was potentially "off," prompting an adjustment. Event dynamics is the fifth, applying to live betting placed while the event is in progress, where the evolving dynamics of the match lead to frequent changes.

# Over/Under Betting In MMA, Tennis And Golf

In individual sports the over/under line is denominated not in combined points but in the sport's own unit of duration or performance: rounds in MMA, games or sets in tennis, and strokes relative to par in golf.

In an MMA context, over/under bets often refer to the duration of the fight rather than points or scores. In a UFC bout between Fighter A and Fighter B the bookmaker sets an over/under line at 2.5 rounds; a bettor who believes both fighters have aggressive styles and the fight will end early bets the "under." If the fight ends midway through the second round by knockout or submission, the total rounds would be 1.5, below the set total of 2.5, so the "under" wins. Conversely, if the fight extends beyond the midway point of the third round, "over" bets win.

At tennis betting sites, over/under betting typically revolves around the total number of games or sets played in a match. In a Grand Slam match between Player A and Player B the bookmaker sets the total at 40.5 games for the entire match; a bettor anticipating a closely contested match with many extended sets bets the "over." With set scores of 7-5, 6-7, 7-6 and 6-4, the combined total is 42 games, which exceeds 40.5, so the "over" wins.

At golf betting sites, over/under betting often pertains to a golfer's score for a specific round or the entire tournament relative to par. In a major tournament where Rory McIlroy is playing, the bookmaker sets an over/under line at 69.5 strokes for his first-round score; a bettor who analyses the challenging course conditions and expects difficulties bets the "under," predicting 69 strokes or fewer. If McIlroy concludes the round with a 68 — 3 under par on a par-71 course — the "under" wager wins; if he shoots 70 or higher, those who bet the "over" win.

# How Sportsbooks Set And Move Betting Lines

The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services to set their lines and odds, while other sports betting apps simply copy those lines. The oddsmakers and services use computer models and algorithms that consider analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, matchup data and more to develop the lines and odds. Those lines are then subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that emerges before the game, and a book will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side.

The governing objective is balance rather than prediction. Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet, because that lets the book earn the small profit built into the odds and lines without worrying about which side wins. Sportsbooks want even betting so much that they will move a line or change the odds specifically to draw more bets to the other side.

The relation that matters to a bettor is that books do not all move together. The betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook: one book may be forced to move a line or change the odds because of the money it has taken while another is not, and the lines and odds may even differ right from the jump. That divergence is what creates the chance to book a bet at improved odds or a more favorable line.

The range over which this holds is narrow and specific. When a line moves for a legitimate reason such as an injury or roster move, every sportsbook jumps on board, and it is difficult to find value; when a line moves because of betting patterns, only the sportsbook that saw that betting makes the change, and that is the opportunity. Line shopping is the tool for spotting the second kind: choose a side, shop around at online sportsbooks, compare the lines and odds, and pounce when you find one offering something different and more favorable to your viewpoint.

# Totals Line Movement Drivers

The totals line can move, and Sporting News attributes that movement to four kinds of input: betting activity, injury updates, weather conditions, and other news and updates.

Betting activity is one of the most common reasons for line movement — a significant amount of money wagered on one side, either the over or the under, leads bookmakers to adjust the line to balance the action and protect themselves from potential losses. Injury updates work through the expected score: if a key player is injured or unable to play, that can influence the expected total score, leading bookmakers to adjust the line accordingly. Weather conditions matter in outdoor sports; heavy rain or snow in a football game might create expectations of a lower-scoring game, causing the line to move down. Finally, any other news that might affect team performance — changes in team strategy or recent performances — can influence totals lines.

# Moneyline Outcomes: Win, Loss, Draw And Push

A moneyline wager can end in several ways: the most straightforward outcomes are a win or a loss, determined by whether the team or individual you backed was victorious or defeated, and there is also the possibility of a draw if the event ends in a tie. Winning is simply a matter of picking the eventual winner — bet on Boxer B in a bout between Boxer A and Boxer B, and if Boxer B wins you are paid based on the odds at the time you placed the wager. A loss means the side you backed did not win: bet $100 on Team A in an NBA game and, if Team B wins, the bet on Team A loses.

Some sports price the draw as its own selection. In soccer especially, games can end in a draw and bettors can wager on that outcome, so a moneyline typically shows three sets of odds — one for each team to win and one for the draw. For a match between Team A and Team B, the odds might read Team A +150, Draw +220, Team B +180; a $100 wager on "Draw" that lands returns $220 in profit on top of the $100 stake, totaling $320, while a win by either team loses the $100.

A tie handled as a "push" is a different case, and the scope condition matters. When a push occurs bettors are refunded their original wager, with no money won or lost; but sports that typically allow a tie, like soccer, often offer the draw as a bet instead, and if the game ends in a draw and you did not bet that option, you lose. It is therefore essential to understand the specific rules of the sportsbook and the sport to know how ties are handled. Finally, in most sports and with most sportsbooks — including new betting sites — overtime or any extra time or tiebreakers do count toward a moneyline bet, though you should always check your sportsbook's specific rules.

# The Three Staple MLB Bet Types: Moneylines, Run Lines And Totals

Three of the most popular bet types for Major League Baseball games are run lines, moneylines and totals, and they are found at every online sportsbook that supports MLB betting. A moneyline wager is as straightforward as they come: you bet on which team you believe will win the game, with each team given odds indicating its perceived chances — the underdog represented by a positive (+) number and the favorite by a negative (-) number.

The run line is similar to a point spread in other sports, giving the underdog a handicap of 1.5 runs: the underdog needs to lose by one run or win outright for bets on them to succeed, while the favorite needs to win by two runs or more to cover the spread. Totals bets, also known as over/unders, focus on the combined number of runs both teams score — oddsmakers assign a total and bettors decide whether the two teams will score over or under it, with the actual winner of the game irrelevant.

# The Timing Trade-Off In Rookie Of The Year Futures Betting

There is a fixed trade-off in when to bet NBA Rookie of the Year futures: the earlier you bet, the better the odds, but you bet without much information that could be key to an educated decision; conversely, if you wait for the data you need for an informed bet, the odds tighten and you see less of a return.

The mechanism is symmetric between bettor and book. When the lines are first released, the season has not started, so there are no statistics, trends or player news — the pre-season odds are so favorable precisely because even the oddsmakers lack the data to craft more specific lines. Once the season starts and you can see how the rookies are performing, you can gather the relevant data; but sportsbooks are gathering the same information and tighten the Rookie of the Year lines in response. So while you can better guess who will hoist the Wilt Chamberlain Trophy, the odds are tighter and your potential return reduced.

Stated as pros and cons: betting early gives an opportunity to find better value and betting odds that are fresh and unadjusted, but carries much higher risk because a player's performance, health and team dynamic can change through the season, and offers limited information. Waiting gives a lot more information for an informed bet and avoids betting on a player not remotely in contention, but reduces the opportunity to find value and the odds may not be as favorable. The range over which this holds is bounded by the individual: it is always important to take your risk tolerance into consideration while weighing the potential rewards, and no matter when you decide to wager, always gather as much information as possible before risking your money.

# Favorites And Underdogs In Moneyline Odds

The favorite is the participant — team or individual — expected to win the event or matchup, and the underdog is the participant deemed less likely to win compared to the opponent. The distinction is a judgment about relative chances, and it is what the sign on a moneyline price encodes.

In moneyline odds, especially in the American odds format, the favorite is usually represented with a minus (-) sign: if Team A is a favorite listed at -150, a bettor would need to wager $150 to win $100. Underdogs, again particularly in the American format, are usually represented with a plus (+) sign: if Team B is an underdog at +130, a bettor would win $130 for every $100 staked, should Team B win.

# General MLB Betting Rules At Online Sportsbooks

Every sportsbook has terms and conditions for all bets, MLB included, and while those rules may be specific to each book, some general rules should apply everywhere. For example, MLB First 5 Innings bets are usually considered actionable after five innings of play, or 4.5 innings if the home team has the lead. Another common rule is weather-related: if a game is suspended due to rain or other conditions, delays may lead to bets being refunded depending on the circumstances and the specific rules of your sportsbook.

Other rules found at online sportsbooks for MLB betting are: wagers include extra innings unless specified otherwise; the game must start on the scheduled day (local stadium time) for bets to have action; the game must go 9 innings, or 8½ if the home team is winning, for the run line to have action; on "team to score first" wagers, once a run is scored the prop will be graded regardless of how long the game lasts; wagers on postseason baseball series are based on the team to win the series, regardless of the number of games involved; and for player props, the player must be in the starting lineup for wagers to have action.

It is important to read through the rules for baseball betting before placing your MLB bets, and they can be found in the terms and conditions section of your sportsbook's website.
