# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.



---


# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis On Sam Bankman-Fried

Michael Lewis's October 2023 book is an account of Sam Bankman-Fried, published by Allen Lane at $55 on 3 October, The Sydney Morning Herald listed on 1 October 2023.

Its subject is defined by the arc: Bankman-Fried set up his cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, in 2019 and three years later was rolling in money, but when the crypto world went pear-shaped his business hit an irreversible tailspin, and he now faces multiple charges and was due in court on 3 October.

The reviewer's warrant for reading it is the author: "If anyone can be relied on to tell this story of a financial Icarus with verve and narrative flair, it's Michael Lewis, author of Liar's Poker, Moneyball, and The Big Short." A caveat is attached — "No doubt the updated edition will have the verdict on SBF."



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."



---


# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

The Verge attributes FTX's quick rise as an industry force at least in part to that appetite for attention: Bankman-Fried gave interviews freely and quickly rose to public prominence, positioning himself as an important, boyish face for crypto even though FTX hadn't been in the business as long as competing exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Gemini. At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.



---


# Criminal Trial

## Definition

In this corpus, "criminal trial" names the government's federal prosecution of Sam Bankman-Fried in Manhattan on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, in which prosecutors presented witness testimony to prove guilt while the defense contested it, U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan presided, and a jury returned the verdict.
The corpus uses the term specifically to distinguish this proceeding — and the format of Epic Games v. Google, a civil jury trial — from non-criminal, civil proceedings such as the Trump/Engoron case, which sought financial penalties rather than imprisonment.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal criminal trial in Manhattan, on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, presided over by U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan; the trial ran roughly six weeks, opening with jury selection on October 3, 2023 and opening statements the next day, and closing in a guilty verdict on all counts.
The proceeding follows a recognizable structure the corpus documents in sequence: jury selection, opening statements from prosecution and defense, the prosecution's case (fact witnesses like Adam Yedidia and Matt Huang, cooperating former co-conspirators Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison testifying under cooperation agreements, and expert testimony from accounting professor Peter Easton), cross-examination, the defendant's own testimony and cross-examination, closing arguments, and jury deliberation toward a verdict.
The corpus also shows what a criminal trial is not, by contrast: the parallel civil case against Donald Trump before Judge Arthur Engoron was a non-jury ("bench") trial brought by the New York attorney general seeking financial penalties, not imprisonment, and the corpus notes Manhattan prosecutors had considered and declined to bring a criminal case over the same underlying conduct — the state instead pursued civil fraud remedies. Epic Games v. Google is likewise a civil antitrust jury trial (Sherman Act, Cartwright Act claims) seeking injunctive and monetary relief, not a criminal prosecution, even though it shares the jury-trial format.

## Key Characteristics

- **Adversarial structure** — a prosecution (the government, e.g. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Danielle Sassoon, Nicolas Roos, and Thane Rehn in the SBF case) argues guilt while defense counsel (Mark Cohen, Christian Everdell) argues innocence or lack of criminal intent.
- **Jury as fact-finder** — a jury, not the judge, decides guilt; in the SBF trial the jury included a train conductor and a retired investment banker, and reporters repeatedly note what testimony "the jury saw" or "the jury will have to decide."
- **Burden and standard tied to criminal charges** — the prosecution must show the defendant's conduct was not just harmful but criminal; as one account puts it, "Just losing $8 billion is not a crime... But if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing... that's a crime," turning the case on proving intentional deceit and conspiracy rather than mere loss or business failure.
- **Cooperating witnesses and immunity/plea deals** — co-conspirators such as Gary Wang, Caroline Ellison, and witnesses like Adam Yedidia testified under cooperation agreements or legal immunity, a common feature of criminal trials involving multiple alleged participants.
- **Judge as referee, not fact-finder** — Judge Kaplan ruled on objections, instructed the jury on the law, and controlled testimony (e.g., telling the jury he was the "final authority" on the definition of "market manipulation"), while leaving the guilt determination to the jury.
- **Sentencing follows conviction** — a guilty verdict is followed by a separate sentencing phase; the corpus notes SBF's charges could put him in prison for the rest of his life and co-conspirator Gary Wang faced up to 50 years pending sentencing.
- **Distinct from civil trials** — civil proceedings (Trump/Engoron, Epic v. Google) can share elements like juries or trial-style testimony but seek monetary or injunctive remedies under a different legal standard, and can proceed without a jury at all (non-jury "bench" trial).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, a criminal trial is a court proceeding, initiated only by the government, in which the prosecution must prove the defendant's guilt "beyond a reasonable doubt" — a heavier standard than in civil cases — while the jury decides guilt and the judge oversees the proceeding and, on a guilty verdict, determines the sentence (U.S. Courts, "Criminal Cases," uscourts.gov, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Bankman-Fried's Conduct On Direct Examination

On October 28th, 2023, before the cross-examination had even begun, Judge Lewis Kaplan had already instructed Sam Bankman-Fried to answer the question he was being asked by his own lawyer — which The Verge's reporter called honestly kind of incredible, a man torpedoing his own credibility on direct testimony. The count of "Objection, narrative!" to Bankman-Fried's answers, followed by "Sustained," stood at three; the main thing clear so far, she wrote, was that he really loves the sound of his own voice, and that sometimes when he says "we," he only means himself.

The scolding was a pattern across two days. The day before, during an evidentiary hearing, Bankman-Fried had been repeatedly scolded by Kaplan for not answering prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's questions on cross-examination; on this day he was scolded for not answering his own counsel Mark Cohen's questions on direct, and he occasionally interrupted Cohen with "yes" and "yup." Much of the morning went on vocabulary — explaining "Amazon Web Services" and "database" was a bit too detail-oriented — and when Bankman-Fried tried to define "market manipulation," Kaplan told the jury that he, the judge, was the final authority on that.

In fairness, the reporter added, he was clearer and much easier to understand than at the evidentiary hearing the day before, with a minimum of word salad; she could not tell whether he was more relaxed or simply more rehearsed, and said she would be watching to see whether he became much less coherent once Sassoon got him on cross. The jury watched all of it intently.



---


# Reaction To Lewis's Portrayal Of SBF

The backlash to Michael Lewis's 60 Minutes appearance attacks one specific premise of his account — that FTX was a sound business brought down only by an unwarranted loss of confidence — and, behind it, the inference that SBF's story is therefore a tragic fall rather than a fraud. The episode has fired up a lot of people, indignant at what they feel was too-easy treatment for someone who many believe brought down the whole crypto house. TechCrunch collected the reaction on 2023-10-02.

The premise is attacked head-on by Dan Held, who on October 2, 2023 quoted Lewis — "They had a great real business. If no one had cast aspersions on the business, if there hadn't been a run on customers deposits, they'd still be making tons of money" — and answered: "That's not true. They are not a bank, they're…", prefacing it with "Shameful that Michael Lewis is defending SBF." Ryan Selkis attacked the framing instead of the balance sheet, writing the same day that "The Michael Lewis interview is infuriating. SBF was a scumbag, and now we need to hear about his 'tragic fall' in the MSM because Sam told them he was an 'effective altruist' and people like Michael Lewis were so far up his ass they couldn't tell truth from fiction." Tobi Lutke attacked the coverage itself: "60 Minutes got rightly community noted here. How is it that SBF is still getting super positive media coverage when the media has nothing good to say about the founders that have actually created things and brought value into the world?"

Two qualifications sit against the backlash. Noff is defensive: she believes crypto is no worse than the stock market, which can also be manipulated and mishandled, adding that "Even when you identify corruption, I don't think that means we don't believe in the system in question." And TechCrunch's own reading is that the thing being attacked may not be quite what the critics take it for — Lewis's picture is a little less stark from the looks of the 60 Minutes episode, and it is not that clear at all whether SBF is getting a kicking or a coat of polish in the interview, given Lewis's celebration of SBF's self-proclaimed (yet not quite proven) idealism and the "Bankman-Fried-shaped hold in the world" that exists. The writer's closing point is that this confused message is very apt for cryptocurrency, where the process by which it works is forever murky and often misrepresented, at least to most people.



---


# FTX's Final Days And The Alameda Shortfall, As Wang Described Them

Much of Gary Wang's Friday testimony focused on the final days at FTX before the operation imploded: after media reports detailing Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, an emergency meeting was called between Bankman-Fried, Wang and Singh to discuss shutting down Alameda, and they decided against it because he and Bankman-Fried knew Alameda had no way to repay the roughly $14 billion hole in its books.

Wang, 30, was technology chief for FTX, which spiralled into bankruptcy in November; he spoke so fast that U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan and the prosecutor both stopped him at points to ask that he slow his pace. Prosecutors took the jury through a series of tweets beginning on Nov. 7 — posts from the company blaming bank hours for slow withdrawals, while Bankman-Fried tweeted from his personal account assuring customers that all was fine. "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine," Wang testified. On Nov. 12, after FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried asked Wang to drive with him to the Bahamas Securities Commission for a meeting; on the drive, Bankman-Fried told Wang to transfer assets to Bahamian liquidators because he believed they would allow him to maintain control of the company. Wang said he was not in the meeting with the securities authority, though Bankman-Fried's dad was present.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Post-Bankruptcy Media Tour

After FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried went on an extensive media tour, doing interviews with The New York Times' Andrew Ross Sorkin and Good Morning America — and he kept giving interviews even under house arrest, including with The New Yorker.

The Verge's reading of his motive: Bankman-Fried seemed to think that if he just explained things, everyone would understand that what he did was a mistake, not a crime.



---


# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.



---


# John J. Ray III Running The FTX Estate

What's left of FTX is now being led by John J. Ray III — the man who cleaned up Enron, and who has said FTX is worse than Enron.

Just before the trial began, the FTX lawyers filed suit against Bankman-Fried's parents, saying they should give back millions of dollars they got from their kid. Ray has also referred to Bankman-Fried's conduct as "really just old-fashioned embezzlement."



---


# Adam Yedidia's Testimony And The $8 Billion Bug

Adam Yedidia, the prosecution's second witness, testified that in June 2022 he submitted a report to Bankman-Fried on Signal showing that $8 billion in customer money held in an internal database tracking cash wired to an Alameda account called "fiat at ftx.com" was missing.

Yedidia met Bankman-Fried in college at MIT and the pair remained close friends; assuming a robotic posture on the stand, he said he worked out of FTX's Hong Kong office from January to October of 2021 and then in the Bahamas until the collapse. He referred to a group Signal thread called "People of the House," referring to Bankman-Fried's $35 million penthouse where many employees lived; on who was paying the rent, Yedidia recalled Bankman-Fried saying he "assumed it's just Alameda paying for it in the end." Yedidia said Bankman-Fried had told him, before he began working in the Bahamas in 2019, that he and Ellison had had sex, and asked whether it was a good idea for them to date — Yedidia said no, and Bankman-Fried responded that he was expecting that answer. One of Yedidia's responsibilities was fixing the bug in the code that gave Alameda preferential treatment. He said he and Bankman-Fried spoke about the missing $8 billion at the pickleball court at the resort in Nassau, Bahamas, where he asked his boss if things were OK because it "seemed like a lot of money" from FTX customers was at risk. "Sam said, we were bulletproof last year. We aren't bulletproof this year," Yedidia testified; asked when they would be bulletproof again, Bankman-Fried said he was not sure, but it might be six months to three years. Yedidia said Bankman-Fried appeared "worried or nervous," which was atypical, but that he still trusted Bankman-Fried and Ellison to "handle the situation." On cross-examination, Christian Everdell, Bankman-Fried's attorney, focused on how Yedidia was the one responsible for developing and reviewing the code.



---


# Adam Yedidia's First Testimony And His Immunity Deal

Late in the afternoon of the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the government called Adam Yedidia to the stand, and lead prosecutor Danielle Sassoon disclosed that this college friend of Bankman-Fried had legal immunity during his testimony. Asked why he had made such a deal with the government, Yedidia answered: "I was concerned that I had unwittingly written code that contributed to a crime."

Yedidia, described as a fast-talking graduate of MIT, testified that he and Bankman-Fried were close friends in college. After Bankman-Fried left Jane Street — the high-frequency trading firm where the former billionaire got his start in finance after MIT — he persuaded Yedidia to join him, first as a trader at Alameda and then as a developer at FTX.

The testimony was cut short when the clock neared 4:30 p.m. and court adjourned for the day. Yedidia was scheduled to continue his testimony on Thursday, to be followed by Matt Huang, a former partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital, and then by Gary Wang, a key Bankman-Fried lieutenant and one of the government's star witnesses.



---


# FTX's Collapse And Bankruptcy, November 2022

FTX went bankrupt on November 11th, 2022, days after Gary Wang and Bankman-Fried had determined that about $8 billion in customer money was gone. On November 7th, Bankman-Fried tweeted "FTX is fine. Assets are fine," and another tweet in the thread said "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings." Wang testified flatly: "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine because FTX did not have enough assets for customer withdrawals."

Prosecutor Thane Rehn placed the trigger in the same month: when CoinDesk published its article in November 2022, people realized FTX was a house of cards, while Bankman-Fried was tweeting "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" and "We don't invest customer assets even in treasuries."

The day after the bankruptcy, on November 12th, Bankman-Fried directed Wang to send customer funds to Bahamian regulators. Customers could not take their funds off the exchange at that point because FTX had run out of money and its servers had been shut down. Bankman-Fried and his father met with lawyers while Wang waited outside with liquidators; the US lawyers wanted the remaining FTX assets transferred to the US, but Wang testified that Bankman-Fried told him to stall the US lawyers and transfer the funds to the Bahamian regulators instead, who were more likely to let him stay in control of the company. The collapse also propagated outward: the government put Zac Prince, the founder and former CEO of crypto lender BlockFi, on the stand just long enough to blame FTX's bankruptcy for BlockFi's subsequent bankruptcy.

# Thesis That Music Labels Are Headed for Irrelevance

The argument, common among music business observers from the world of tech, is that record labels could in the long term be headed for irrelevance. Its grounds are the arrival of digital platforms, including open ones like YouTube and SoundCloud, together with the proliferation of indie music distribution platforms such as DistroKid and TikTok's SoundOn.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is a claim about what labels are for: in a world where anyone can record music using a desktop audio workstation (DAW) and upload it directly to YouTube, or to Spotify via a distribution platform, labels have little left to do. Recording and distribution — the functions the label historically supplied — are available to any artist directly, so on this reasoning the label's remaining role shrinks toward nothing. Music Business Worldwide presented this as the speculation that tech-world observers "like to" make, and as the position Warner Music Group CEO Robert Kyncl was answering at the Code Conference in September 2023.



---


# Kyncl Prediction: Music Is the First Industry to Feel AI's Impact

Robert Kyncl's proposition, put at the Code Conference in September 2023, is that the music business will be out ahead of other industries in exploiting the potential of AI, and — out of necessity — also ahead on the question of how to regulate and monetise the use of AI by non-rights-holders. He attached a date to it: asked when that sea change would occur, he said "I would say within the next year you will see lots of evolution around AI… What you will likely see is increasing quality at a very fast pace."

His reasoning is structural rather than accidental. "Music – because it's so broadly distributed and it's so well aligned with the internet, because it's short format, it lends itself to recommendations, it's on all platforms – is generally first in most transformations and most innovations. So it digitizes first." He generalises from the previous cycle: "Whatever happened to the music industry 20 years ago is starting to happen in the movies and TV shows now. In the meantime, music emerged out of [digitization] better and stronger and more resilient. So, I would imagine the same will happen here, which is we'll likely be first."

The hypothesis is falsifiable on two fronts as stated. It fails if other industries, rather than music, lead on both exploiting and regulating AI; and it fails on its own timetable if the year following September 2023 does not bring the predicted rapid evolution and fast-rising quality in AI. Because the argument rests on music's broad distribution, short format and recommendation-friendliness, an AI transformation that arrives first in a long-format medium would also count against the mechanism he proposes.



---


# AI Day Of Action Campaign

In the week of 2023-10-06, digital rights organization Fight for the Future partnered with music industry labor group United Musicians and Allied Workers to launch #AIdayofaction, a campaign that calls on Congress to block corporations from obtaining copyrights on music and other art made with AI.

The mechanism the campaign is betting on is indirect. The idea is that by preventing industry behemoths like major record labels, for example, from copyrighting music made with the assistance of AI, those companies will be forced to keep looping humans into the creative process. Those same concerns — and the same potential strategies for pushing back against the onslaught of AI — exist across creative industries, which is why the launch was pitched beyond music.

The launch landed in a moment when creative industries were grappling with AI's explosion into every artistic medium at once, and separate calls from artists warning the world to take action before it's too late were starting to converge. From fake Drake songs to stylized Instagram profile pictures, art conjured with newly sophisticated AI tools was suddenly ubiquitous — and so were conversations about how to rein in the technology before it does irrevocable harm to creative communities.

By the following week, on 2023-10-13, TechCrunch characterized the effort as a campaign that targets potential corporate abuse of AI technology while remaining realistic about the ways that musicians and some other creatives could benefit on an individual level from automating parts of their work. The stated goal is that AI tools "become ways for individual humans to make more money, work less, and compete with the corporations that exploit them."

# Sony Music's Pipeline Of AI Startup Partnerships

Kooker said Sony Music has "roughly 200 active conversations taking place with startups and established players" right now about building new AI-related products and tools, and that some of these conversations "also include potential equity investments which would accelerate the development of these companies."

He framed this as the optimistic counterweight to the harms: despite the negative impacts of AI, including unauthorized clones and low-quality AI music, there are still "many positive and optimistic developments to highlight," and he highlighted legitimate AI startups and established firms "with music ideas that want to partner with the industry." The products under discussion range from tools for "creative or marketing assistance," to tools that "potentially give us the ability to better protect artist content or find it when used in an unauthorized fashion," as well as "brand new products that have never been launched before."

# Robert Kyncl, Warner Music Group CEO

Robert Kyncl is the CEO of Warner Music Group, and the defining feature of his profile in the music business is that he came to it from 'Big Tech' — specifically from YouTube, where he was Chief Business Officer. That background is why, in the months before September 2023, he had been keeping a close eye on AI in the music industry.

His current role explains a second position associated with him: he has been pushing for price hikes at music streaming services. Both themes — AI in music, and streaming pricing — came up during Kyncl's Q&A session at the Code Conference in Laguna Niguel, California, on Tuesday 26 September 2023, as reported by Music Business Worldwide two days later.



---


# Capitol Music Group's Turnaround Results In 2023

Two years into Michelle Jubelirer's tenure, CMG had returned to calmer waters with US market share year-to-date in the high-5% region, alongside glittering successes and a promising array of new talent being primed. Jubelirer said that year-over-year market share is up by 25 per cent and that the company has moved up a notch in the label rankings, while noting she is not one to rattle off a lot of statistics. On TikTok's 2023 wrap-up lists, Capitol was the top-performing label across both the global and US lists.

Asked what she is most proud of in the past 12 months, she called it an incredible year and said that calling it the biggest, the best or the strongest would all be accurate. Her summary claim, made in the interview published 7 December 2023, is that she does not think any label group has been able to turn things around as quickly as she and her team have done in less than two years.

# Music Catalog Acquisition Market Slowdown 2023

Robert Kyncl's assessment in September 2023 was that the hot music rights acquisitions space is "likely slowing down a bit" — and that this is fine for a buyer like Warner Music Group, because it makes acquisition multiples come down.

The backdrop given is that the second half of 2022 saw a notable slowdown in music rights acquisitions, which some blamed on higher interest rates and the reduced liquidity that came with them. There had been something of a rebound in 2023, but in Kyncl's view the slowdown persisted. He explained the earlier boom as a one-off shift in seller behaviour: "I think what happened was there was an opening where artists and songwriters were suddenly open to selling catalogs, which they were not open to before. And they just created this incredible tidal wave. And these things happen in waves, ebb and flow. So I think it likely is slowing down a little bit, but that's okay. Because it makes the multiples come down a little bit more."

Asked whether that means Warner Music can buy more if multiples are low enough, Kyncl said: "Of course. We are in the business of buying catalogs, obviously. We have the publishing catalog of David Bowie, for instance, which we bought a few years ago. So yeah, we are in that business. We are in the business of administering [rights], which means collecting revenue from thousands of platforms around the world; very complicated matters. But we're also in the business of ownership."

# Why Spanish-Language Music Keeps Growing Globally

Asked what is driving the ability of Latin artists, particularly Latin American artists, to have global hits on distribution agreements without signing even licensing deals with major record labels, Alejandra Olea answers that Spanish-speaking music, from Spain and Latin America, just keeps getting bigger, and that Spanish and Latin artists have many more options to develop their audiences and monetize their music at each stage of their career.

The mechanism she gives has two linked parts. First, the world is one where music discovery and consumption are now primarily digital, artists have understood that, and they look for partners who get it too and whose expertise will allow them to leverage digital platforms to reach new and existing audiences wherever they are; artists like Iñigo Quintero and labels like Acqustic are prime examples of this profound shift within the Latin and the wider music industry. Second, the effect is strongest in Spanish-speaking markets, where music fans are among the most engaged audiences in the world, whether on digital platforms or on social media, and where music content is consumed with more frequency, in different formats, across multiple platforms and through different aspects related to the track.

# Digital Twins Deployed for Sustainability Goals

The first trend IoT Analytics highlights is that companies are deploying digital twins to meet sustainability goals, with the pursuit of those goals acting as a tailwind macro factor for the digital twin market. Sustainability was discussed in approximately 21% of recent CEO earnings calls and has remained a consistent topic throughout 2023.

The mechanism is that digital twins simulate real-world conditions and deliver real-time information, so organisations can optimise resource usage, reducing carbon emissions and improving supply and transportation networks. Survey evidence supports the link: according to Capgemini Research Institute's 2022 digital twins report, 57% of organisations agreed that one of the key drivers for their digital twin investments was improving their sustainability, and 51% agreed that digital twins would help achieve their organisation's environmental sustainability goals.

A former VP at an industrial automation vendor quoted in the report frames the scope over which the relation holds: "Digital solutions provide the visibility, analysis, and insight needed to address the challenges inherent in sustainability goals. A digital twin strategy as part of an overall digitalization plan can be a crucial capability for asset-intensive industries and needs to encompass the entire asset lifecycle, process, and value chain from design and operations through maintenance and strategic business planning." The worked example is Aden, a Chinese integrated facility service provider, which created a digital twin for one of its commercial centres in Chengdu, China, designed to help facility managers inspect, maintain and repair building assets; its 3D simulations assist managers in visualising, predicting and optimising energy consumption, with expected benefits including lower annual energy consumption, water usage and waste.

# Music Streaming Price Hikes and Emerging Market Growth

Robert Kyncl told the Code Conference in September 2023 that the opportunity ahead of the music business is twofold: "One, the continued growth in emerging markets, and also the GDPs of those countries will be rising at the same time. So there's lots of growth there. And then there is the price elasticity optimization in mature markets."

Music Business Worldwide read that last point as a reference to the price hikes seen among all the major music streaming services over the past year or so, and to the growing belief within the music industry that streaming price hikes will be sustained — evidenced recently, at the time of writing in September 2023, by Deezer's second price hike within a year.

# Kyncl Rebuttal: Labels Persist Like Ad Agencies After AdWords

Robert Kyncl's counterpoint at Code Media attacks the inference that easy direct distribution makes labels redundant, not the fact of that distribution. His parallel is the advertising industry a decade or two ago: at that time many predicted ad agencies were headed for the scrap-heap because Google's AdWords let any business set up a customised ad campaign on Google services. Yet ad agencies did not go extinct — today, Kyncl told the Code Conference audience, "they're the largest customers of companies like Google."

The mechanism he offers explains why the prediction failed. "In the year 2000, when AdWords came out, everybody was predicting their deaths because all the brands [could] just go direct to AdWords and buy ads… However, what happened was lots of different platforms emerged. Lots of ad tech emerged, complexity increased exponentially, and brands needed help with that, and the agencies provided that value." He sees a very close analogy with music: "Music is incredibly broadly distributed. Everybody on earth listens to music. We're on every platform. And the complexity is high. And the more people can upload content, and the more people can be heard, the greater the noise, which means it's harder to cut through the noise and sustain a career." Open access therefore raises, rather than removes, the value of the intermediary.

Kyncl also widened the label's job beyond breaking an artist. A label's value is not just about building an artist's career but about sustaining it once established: "When they become established, it is also hard to remain at the top. So their goals change. And again, we're there to help with that." He added later that a music artist "need[s] a team. You need an army behind you…. if you want a sustainable career, with repeatability and success." Music Business Worldwide framed this as a rational, level-headed explanation that was itself surprising coming from a techie like Kyncl.

# TikTok's Claim To Be The Driving Force Behind Music Discovery

TikTok's argument, made by Global Head of Music Ole Obermann on the back of the Luminate findings, is that "TikTok is the driving force behind music discovery in the industry, and that TikTok users are active, engaged and highly valuable drivers of music industry revenues."

The stated motive for commissioning the research was to move beyond the anecdotal: "TikTok is already famous for being the launchpad for creating viral hits and breaking new artists, but we wanted to understand how TikTok and its users impact the music industry more broadly," Obermann said in a statement, adding that "Luminate's findings prove what we had long known." MBW places the study in a pattern: it is part of an ongoing effort by TikTok to highlight its growing role in the development of global music culture, and last year TikTok released a report asserting that 13 out of the 14 songs to reach number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 in 2022 were driven by viral trends on TikTok.

# Music Streaming Resilience Versus Streaming Video Downturn

Asked at the Code Conference whether the audio streaming business is likely to go through what streaming video is going through, Robert Kyncl's answer was unequivocal: "No. Music is much more resilient."

The grounds for the question were the state of streaming video. Netflix experienced its first-ever decline in subscriptions in 2022, though it has since roared back to health; the subscriber count of Disney+ appears to be in freefall; and talk is growing about ongoing consolidation of the many streaming video services that have come online over the past several years.

Kyncl's grounds for the contrast are the scale and speed of audio subscription growth rather than any claim about video. "So first, I think what happened in the last 15 years is incredible. They had literally zero people in the subscription model and now we have 700 million people in the world in the premium experience… which is incredible." He credited the path-forging to Spotify's Daniel Ek — "And I think really credit goes to Daniel Ek for forging the path for everybody. And then companies like Apple and YouTube and Amazon following and building up the [music] business. It's pretty incredible what has happened." The warrant tying this to resilience is that a market built from zero to 700 million premium subscribers across multiple competing platforms is structurally different from the video services now consolidating.

# The Digital-First Artist Development Model

The success of "Si No Estás" illustrates how much artist development has changed: social media and digital music services have now become the number one source of music discovery, and Believe has developed an innovative, AI and data-driven expertise to develop tracks and artists that Alejandra Olea describes as unique in the music industry.

The model's components and their relations are stated together: the key to success is great partnerships with the artist and their label, and being able to combine strong AI data-driven expertise to maximise momentum for an artist and a track at the right time with the right tools and the right partnerships, supported by both local and global teams. Olea singles out the last element as particularly important and truly one of Believe's strengths, being able to mobilise teams multi-locally and globally to accompany audience development for artists. The forward-looking claim attached to the model is that this is only the beginning for Iñigo Quintero and that Believe anticipates many more successes like his in future.

# Digital Twin Market Size and Adoption 2023

IoT Analytics projects that the global digital twin market could grow at a compound annual growth rate of approximately 30% between 2023 and 2027, according to its Digital Twin Market Report 2023-2027 as summarised by IoT Business News on 18 November 2023.

Adoption data underpins that projection. 29% of global manufacturing companies have either fully or partially implemented their digital twin strategies, a noticeable increase from 20% in 2020, and the proportion of companies not contemplating implementation appears to have fallen to 9% in 2023, down from 33.6% in 2020. Supporting the trend, an analysis of job postings on SimplyHired suggests growing demand for digital twin expertise: postings mentioning "digital twin" increased by 11% in October 2023 compared with just two years prior, while openings for most other tech topics declined over the same timeframe. Among the 60 tech-related skill sets IoT Analytics tracked, digital twin-related skills experienced one of the most significant growths.

Against this backdrop the report notes eight notable trends helping to advance and promote digital twins, of which the article discusses four in detail: digital twins deployed to meet sustainability goals; digital twins employed as virtual sensors in complex conditions; partnerships between cloud hyperscalers and OT and simulation specialists; and initiatives promoting interoperability of digital twins across multifaceted systems. These trends are described as shaping the future of the market and influencing investment priorities for companies across various industries.

# Capitol Music Group's Organisational Reset Priorities

Michelle Jubelirer describes the reset she ran from day one as Chair of Capitol Music Group as an ordered set of priorities. First, signing a truly diverse array of new artists, with specific attention on building a strong presence in hip-hop and R&B; President of A&R Jeremy Vuernick has been crucial in this regard as well as overseeing the making of the records, and the precondition that made the work necessary was that the company had not been consistently competitive in these areas for a very long time, with Motown having been spun off on its own long before she took the reins, in early 2021, before returning to CMG in early 2023. Second, the company took a hard look at every aspect of the business, revamped its entire organisational structure, reset its value system and even replaced certain terminology that was outdated, all to meet the needs of the modern music business; President of Capitol Music Group Arjun Pulijal, whom Jubelirer calls her partner in all of this and a brilliant creative marketer equally adept at strategizing innovative paths for artists ranging from Ice Spice and Offset to Troye Sivan and Paul McCartney, was key to this process, and his expertise drove a new dynamic in how marketing, creative, international, digital and commerce now interact.

The operating rule that came out of the reset is that literally every plan at CMG is tailored for a specific artist or project rather than pulled from a well-worn playbook, with the focus on finding and creating opportunities that will have an impact no matter where an artist is in their development; the artist's vision still lies at the heart of every plan, but the company listens to an audience that is smarter and savvier than ever to determine whether the marketing direction is working and whether artists are properly engaged with their audience. The company strives to be ideas-driven, to have honest constructive conversations with artists and each other, to run the business efficiently, and to think constantly about where it finds real value for its artists. The remaining to-do item is prioritisation, which Jubelirer defines against the usual industry usage: companies often use the word to mean focusing on one group of artists and ignoring all the others, whereas for CMG it means defining what success can uniquely mean for each artist and then delivering it, identifying which artists will benefit from the close attention of a small group of people who bring passion and nuance to marketing and development and which others clearly need the full power of the organisation firing on all cylinders from the get-go.

# Believe's Marketing Playbook For "Si No Estás"

Believe has been working with Iñigo Quintero since March 2023, and Alejandra Olea describes the campaign as a sequence. In the initial discovery phase, the team developed the audience of the track with the label mostly through Believe's expertise in marketing on Spotify. Second, thanks to Believe's short-form video trends detection technology, the team noticed acceleration in the propagation of the track and consequently leveraged its partnership with TikTok, as well as coordinated promotion from all its teams around the world with Spotify. The precondition that makes the sequence work is Believe's global partnerships with both TikTok and Spotify, which allowed marketing and promotion campaigns to be combined in each service at local level in the key early markets of Spain, Latin America and France, as well as globally. Alongside TikTok on the social side, the company leveraged Instagram to drive engagement around Iñigo and the song globally, and its teams, which have robust video expertise for maximising content across platforms, built Iñigo's YouTube channel from the ground up, optimising it and directing traffic to it by creating the official lyric video as its first video so music fans could find and listen to his music on the platform.

The results reported are that the track has been included in over 180 playlists across all digital music partners and in over 79 playlists with over 97 million followers on Spotify alone, including reaching #1 of Spotify's Top 50 - Global for the first time ever for a Believe track, being featured on Today's Top Hits, Spotify's biggest playlist, and topping Spotify's Viral 50 and Top 50 playlists around the world; the TikTok partnership has resulted in more than 5 million creations according to MediaMatch; and the lyric video for "Si No Estás" has reached 100 million views to date, currently ranked #13 on YouTube's Top 100 Global Music Videos. The final step, in progress at the time of the interview, is a new phase to deepen and expand the success by promoting the track on more traditional media in key countries, where it is rapidly gaining radio airplay and unlocking other promotional opportunities.

# 62% Of US TikTok Users Pay For Music Streaming

According to an analysis commissioned by TikTok and carried out by US market monitor Luminate, 62% of US TikTok users pay for a music streaming service, compared to 43% of all consumers.

Music Business Worldwide's 2023-11-21 report puts that figure in context. TikTok counted 150 million users in the United States as of February 2023, which means that, read through the lens of the Luminate analysis, approximately 93 million TikTok users in the US appear to be paying for a subscription to one of the various streaming services available in the United States, including Spotify, Apple Music and others. For comparison, MBW reported in July that as of February, in the United States, Spotify counted 44.4 million paying subscribers, Spotify rival Apple Music had 32.6 million subscribers, and Amazon Music had 29.3 million subscribers. The framing MBW gives is that TikTok is in the process of reinventing itself as both a partner to music companies and a competitor to streaming and distribution services, and the analysis sheds light on why the ByteDance-owned short video platform has focused so intensely on expanding its services in the music world.

# Sub-Saharan Africa Recorded Music Market Growth

Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) was the world's fastest-growing recorded music region in 2022, recording 34.7% year-on-year growth according to IFPI figures, and by the time of this October 2023 report the growth opportunity for subscription music streaming in the region was becoming significantly clearer.

Africa-focused music streaming service Mdundo illustrates the trend: it recently reported a 239% year-on-year jump in revenue from paid subscriptions and a 23.2% year-on-year increase in monthly active users. Geographically, Mdundo's focus is on five key SSA markets — Nigeria, Kenya, Tanzania, Ghana and South Africa.

The connectivity base underpinning that opportunity is also expanding. According to a 2022 report from GSMA, 615 million people in sub-Saharan Africa are expected to sign up for mobile services by 2025, on top of the roughly 500 million already subscribed as of 2020.
