# ChatGPT Legal And Privacy Controversies

ChatGPT has generated a run of legal and privacy controversies: an Australian mayor publicly announced he may sue OpenAI for defamation over ChatGPT's false claims that he had served time in prison for bribery, which would be the first defamation lawsuit against the text-generating service, and there have been other cases of ChatGPT accusing individuals of false crimes.

The libel exposure follows from how the models work: they do not know or care whether something is true, only that it looks true — a problem when the output is used for homework, and potentially libel when it accuses someone of a crime they did not commit. How troubling statements produced by ChatGPT will be handled was expected to play out over the following months as tech and legal experts tackled the fastest moving target in the industry. As of the article, there were no lawsuits specifically targeting ChatGPT, but OpenAI is involved in at least one lawsuit with implications for AI systems trained on publicly available data, which would touch on ChatGPT. There are also plagiarism issues: text-generating AI models like ChatGPT have a tendency to regurgitate content from their training data. Copyright in output sits with the user — the person who requested the input from ChatGPT is the copyright owner.

On privacy, OpenAI has said that individuals in "certain jurisdictions" such as the EU can object to the processing of their personal information by its AI models by filling out a form — the "OpenAI Personal Data Removal Request" — which includes the ability to request deletion of AI-generated references about them, although OpenAI notes it may not grant every request since it must balance privacy requests against freedom of expression "in accordance with applicable laws." In its privacy policy OpenAI makes a passing acknowledgement of the objection requirements attached to relying on "legitimate interest," pointing users to instructions on how to opt out of use of their information to train its models. ChatGPT chats are not public, but OpenAI disclosed a bug, since fixed, that exposed the titles of some users' conversations to other people on the service.

Other controversies span platforms and schools. Discord integrated OpenAI's technology into its bot Clyde, and two users tricked Clyde into providing instructions for making methamphetamine and napalm. CNET found itself in controversy after Futurism reported the publication was publishing articles under a mysterious byline completely generated by AI, and Red Ventures, the private equity company that owns CNET, was accused of using ChatGPT for SEO farming even where the information was incorrect. Several major school systems and colleges, including New York City Public Schools, have banned ChatGPT from their networks and devices, claiming the AI impedes the learning process by promoting plagiarism and misinformation — a claim not every educator agrees with.

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# Sam Altman's Side Ventures: Helion, Retro And Worldcoin

Altman has a number of possible next steps after leaving OpenAI, because even while running the company he placed large bets on several other ambitious projects.

Among them are Helion Energy, for developing fusion reactors that could produce prodigious amounts of energy from the hydrogen in seawater, and Retro Biosciences, which aims to add 10 years to the human lifespan using biotechnology. Altman also co-founded Worldcoin, a biometric and cryptocurrency project that has been scanning people's eyeballs with the goal of creating a vast digital identity and financial network.

# The OpenAI Board's Firing Of Sam Altman

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said on Friday, 2023-11-17, that it had pushed out its co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after a review found he was "not consistently candid in his communications" with the board of directors. "The board no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI," the artificial intelligence company said in a statement. Mira Murati, OpenAI's chief technology officer, would take over as interim CEO effective immediately while the company searched for a permanent replacement.

OpenAI declined to answer questions on what Altman's alleged lack of candor was about; the statement said only that his behavior was hindering the board's ability to exercise its responsibilities. Altman posted on X that Friday: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later."



---


# Startups' Over-Reliance On OpenAI's Proprietary Models

The claim, from Luis Ceze, University of Washington computer science professor and OctoML CEO, is that "part of the frenzy around the future of OpenAI is due to too many startups over-relying on their proprietary models." The observed grounds: up until the week of the crisis OpenAI was still the AI darling everyone wanted to dance with, countless startups and scale-ups had built businesses atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT-X large language models (LLMs), and over the weekend hundreds of OpenAI customers reportedly started contacting OpenAI's rivals — which include Anthropic, Google and Cohere — concerned that their own businesses might be impacted if OpenAI were to disintegrate overnight. The panic has been palpable.

The warrant is drawn by analogy to an earlier concentration episode: there are precedents from elsewhere in the technology sphere, perhaps most notably the cloud computing industry, which became renowned for the way it locked companies in to centralized, vortex-like silos. As Ceze put it: "It's dangerous to put all your chips in one basket — we saw that in the early cloud days which led to companies shifting to multi-cloud and hybrid environments."

The prescription follows from the analogy: "Open source today offers a wide variety of models for companies to essentially diversify," Ceze added. "By doing so, these startups can quickly pivot and minimize risk. There is also a major upside — many of these models already outperform the likes of OpenAI's in terms [of] price-performance and speed."



---


# Skepticism That OpenAI's Board Will Use Its Veto

TechCrunch's objection is not to the design of OpenAI's escalation process but to the assumption that the board will actually exercise the veto it has been granted. The process is meant to short-circuit anything like what was rumored to have happened before the big drama — a high-risk product or process getting greenlit without the board's awareness or approval. But the result of that drama was the sidelining of two of the more critical voices and the appointment of some money-minded figures, Bret Taylor and Larry Summers, who are sharp but not AI experts by a long shot.

That yields the central question: if a panel of experts makes a recommendation and the CEO makes decisions based on that information, will this friendly board really feel empowered to contradict them and hit the brakes? And if it does, will anyone hear about it? Transparency is not really addressed outside a promise that OpenAI will solicit audits from independent third parties.

A second gap concerns disclosure of critical-risk findings. Suppose a model is developed that warrants a "critical" risk category. OpenAI has not been shy about tooting its horn about this kind of thing in the past — talking about how wildly powerful its models are, to the point where it declines to release them, is great advertising. But there is no guarantee that such disclosure will happen if the risks are so real and OpenAI is so concerned about them; maybe it would be a bad idea, but either way it is not really mentioned.

# Google's "No Moat" Memo On Open Source AI

A leaked internal memo from Google earlier in 2023 seemed to express fears that despite the huge advances made by proprietary LLM models from the likes of OpenAI, open source AI would ultimately trump them all. Its line: "We have no moat, and neither does OpenAI."

The memo's grounds were a specific event. It was written in reference to a foundation language model initially leaked from Meta in March 2023, which gained a fair bit of steam in a short period of time.

The warrant TechCrunch draws from that episode is about the development model rather than any single release: it highlighted the power and scalability of a more open approach to AI development, because openness enables collaboration and experimentation on a level that is not so easy to replicate with closed models.

# Sam Altman's Next Move After The OpenAI Firing

In the days after his firing, Sam Altman's destination was genuinely unsettled: on November 20, 2023 he and Greg Brockman announced they would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research team, yet on the same day both were reported to be still open to returning to OpenAI, and Altman was separately telling investors he planned to launch a new venture.

On November 20 Altman, Brockman and colleagues announced they would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research team, with Satya Nadella leaving the door open to other OpenAI staffers and saying they would be given the resources they needed should they choose to join. As reported by The Verge, however, Altman's move to Microsoft was not a done deal — both Altman and Brockman remained open to returning to OpenAI if the remaining board members who initially fired him stepped aside. At the same time, according to The Information, Altman had been telling investors he was planning to launch a new venture, with Brockman expected to join the effort in whatever form it took — possibly an AI chip startup. Altman also posted on X on November 18: "i love you all. today was a weird experience in many ways. but one unexpected one is that it has been sorta like reading your own eulogy while you're still alive. the outpouring of love is awesome. one takeaway: go tell your friends how great you think they are."

Nadella himself hedged. In a series of interviews he stepped back from earlier reporting that Altman and Brockman were headed to Microsoft, telling CNBC: "Obviously, we want Sam and Greg to have a fantastic home if they're not going to be in OpenAI," and saying he was "open" to them settling at Microsoft or returning to OpenAI should the board and employees support the move.

# OpenAI Board Negotiations Over Altman Reinstatement

Over the weekend that followed Sam Altman's firing, OpenAI's board held on-and-off talks about bringing him back as CEO; the talks repeatedly stalled, and at one point it was confirmed that Altman would not return and that new leadership would take hold.

The sequence ran roughly as follows. Investors — reportedly furious at the turn of events — exerted pressure on OpenAI's board to reinstate Altman, going so far as to recruit Microsoft, with Satya Nadella said to be sympathetic. On November 18 The Verge reported that the board had agreed in principle to resign and to allow Altman and Brockman to return, but it waffled, missing a deadline by which many OpenAI staffers were set to leave the company; Altman was said to be ambivalent about coming back and to be asking for "significant" governance changes. Bloomberg, citing sources close to the matter, reported that the board was in talks with Altman about returning as CEO as soon as that week, with discussions involving Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, one current board member, and possibly other directors. On November 19 The Information reported that Altman was expected to meet at OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters as executives pushed to have him reinstated, with Brockman invited to join though it was unclear whether he would.

Negotiations then hit a snag: Bloomberg reported that Brad Lightcap and Mira Murati, among others, were pushing the board to reinstate Altman, but the directors resisted, and as of midday Sunday the board had not resigned out of concern over who could replace them and was vetting candidates — one possible new addition being Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor. Later, according to The Information citing an internal memo sent by Sutskever, Altman would not be returning as CEO, and OpenAI appointed Emmett Shear, the co-founder of video streaming site Twitch, as interim CEO, replacing Murati. A number of investors and OpenAI employees had tried to bring Altman back after the sudden firing, but following a weekend of negotiations it was confirmed that he would not return; what that meant for ChatGPT's future and for the OpenAI DevDay announcements remained to be seen.

# OpenAI Employee Revolt And Sutskever's Reversal

Nearly 500 of OpenAI's roughly 770 employees signed a letter saying they might quit unless the startup's board resigned and reappointed the ousted Sam Altman — a number that climbed to over 650 later that Monday — and, remarkably, the signatories included Ilya Sutskever, the chief scientist who had taken part in the removal.

Sutskever publicly reversed himself, publishing a post on X suggesting that he regretted his decision to remove Altman and that he would do everything in his power to reinstate Altman as CEO: "I deeply regret my participation in the board's actions. I never intended to harm OpenAI. I love everything we've built together and I will do everything I can to reunite the company." This was a reversal of the position he had taken days earlier. At an OpenAI all-hands meeting on the Friday afternoon, Sutskever had defended Altman's ouster, dismissing suggestions that pushing Altman out amounted to a "hostile takeover" and claiming that it was necessary to protect OpenAI's mission of "making AI beneficial to humanity."

# Generative AI

## Definition

In the corpus, "generative AI" is the umbrella label applied to the 2023 AI boom's content-producing systems — OpenAI's ChatGPT (built on GPT-3.5/GPT-4) and Adobe's Firefly image and vector-graphics models are the flagship examples named — rather than a term the corpus itself formally defines.

## Context

The corpus treats "generative AI" as the umbrella term for the mainstream AI boom of 2023, distinct from the EU AI Act's regulatory term "general purpose AI" (GPAI), which lawmakers deliberately chose as a more technology-neutral label for "the most powerful models behind the current boom in generative AI tools" so the law would not be pinned to one architecture like transformers (doc_0525).
OpenAI built ChatGPT specifically "to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI," and its free, chat-based interface is credited with "taking generative AI mainstream" as a consumer product rather than a research artifact (doc_0047).
Enterprise adoption is depicted as cautious relative to vendor hype: a Morgan Stanley survey found 56% of CIOs said generative AI was affecting investment priorities, but only 4% had launched significant projects, most still in evaluation or proof-of-concept (doc_0160).
The technology spans well beyond chatbots — Adobe's Firefly generative AI models generate images and vector graphics for creative software (doc_0043), and Amazon executive Tye Brady discussed generative AI alongside humanoid robots and mobile manipulation as an input to robotics work (doc_0528).
The same capability that drives adoption also drives the corpus's recurring regulatory and creative-industry concerns: the EU warned that "widely accessible generative AI tools" pose disinformation risks to elections (doc_0248), and the National Music Publishers Association called generative AI "the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed" in its copyright submission to the US Copyright Office (doc_0271).

## Key Characteristics

- **Illustrated by content-producing examples rather than defined outright** — the corpus shows the term through instances of new text, images, and vector graphics being produced from a prompt, illustrated by ChatGPT's text generation (doc_0048) and Firefly's image/vector generation (doc_0043).
- **Consumer breakout via chat interfaces** — ChatGPT's free, web-based chat interface is what took generative AI "mainstream," reaching the fastest adoption of any consumer app (doc_0047, doc_0048).
- **Enterprise adoption lags vendor hype** — large-company CIOs report slow, cautious rollout despite heavy vendor promotion, weighing API/SaaS costs against ROI (doc_0160).
- **Distinct from but overlapping "general purpose AI"** — EU lawmakers deliberately avoided calling the underlying models "generative AI" in law, choosing "general purpose AI" instead to stay technology-neutral rather than tied to transformer-based architectures (doc_0525).
- **Applies across domains beyond chatbots** — spans creative tools (Adobe Firefly) and robotics (Amazon's mobile manipulation work), per the corpus (doc_0043, doc_0528).
- **Focus of copyright and disinformation controversy** — named by the NMPA as a threat to the "human creative class" via unlicensed training data (doc_0271), and flagged by the EU as an election-disinformation risk requiring safeguards (doc_0248).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "generative AI" as a familiar shorthand without formally defining it. Per IBM, generative AI "is artificial intelligence (AI) that can create original content — such as text, images, video, audio or software code — in response to a user's prompt or request," distinguishing it from AI systems built only to classify or act on existing data (IBM, *What is generative AI?*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Theory: Altman Circumvented The Board On A Deal

The prevailing theory floating around on November 18, 2023, based on the board's language and the way these giant tech companies work, is that Altman went around the board on a deal. "Not consistently candid" is a very diplomatic way of saying Altman lied.

The proposition: Altman — and potentially OpenAI President Greg Brockman, who stepped down as chairman simultaneously, then resigned — wanted to make a bold move that he knew the board would not like. It is not uncommon for these deals to be hammered out quietly in smoke- or vape-filled rooms and then presented as a fait accompli, but if it was controversial enough and the board found out about these maneuvers, it could be fuel for an ouster. The open question TechCrunch poses is what kind of deal would be big and dangerous enough for a summary dismissal of the CEO and famous face of the company, given the man was onstage two weeks earlier.

Microsoft is the natural candidate: few would be shocked if Microsoft, which is deeply embedded in OpenAI as an investor and customer, is a factor. Could Altman have been working with — or against — OpenAI's patron in secret? If Altman wanted to kill the golden goose by going independent, that might have activated the board's fiduciary or otherwise statutory duty; if he was negotiating some other deal, like an acquisition or deeper and more exclusive integration, it could also have caused the board to bristle, either at the idea itself or at being excluded. What would falsify it is weak: if Microsoft was as shocked as everyone else, as one report has it, it could hardly be the kind of high-stakes conspiracy some seem to be hoping for — but one must assume Microsoft would say that either way, since even if they had been working with Altman on a secret plan they could truthfully say they were surprised by his firing, and they "remain committed to our partnership."

# OpenAI Board Composition And The Helen Toner Dispute

At the time of Sam Altman's ouster in November 2023, OpenAI's board of directors consisted of OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, tech entrepreneur Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner, the director of strategy at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology — and a clash between Altman and Toner is reported to have contributed to the crisis.

The New York Times reported that, before his ousting, Altman made a move to push out board member Helen Toner because he thought a paper she had co-written was overly critical of OpenAI. That, among other issues, led to OpenAI's predicament. The Times also indicated that negotiations to hire Altman back were continuing, but that one major sticking point remaining was "guardrails" intended to improve Altman's communication with the board.

---


# Concert Film Versus Live Concert

Polygon's writer argues that seeing a concert film in a movie theater is not the same as attending a live concert but is not an inherently lesser experience either — a claim she grounds in having attended the BTS Yet to Come concert both in person and in cinemas.

Her case is that the concert film has value past its re-creation of a specific intersection of place, time, and performance: she went to theaters to relive a once-in-a-lifetime show, but the film version was also its own unique collective fan experience. The practical advantages she names are arriving at the theater just 20 minutes before showtime, being able to go with all her BTS fan friends this time, and watching in a theater full of fellow fans with BTS lightsticks in hand and a BT21 Tata headband on head, which gave the same sense of fandom camaraderie as the in-person concert. She concedes the losses: she missed some of the freedom of the in-person experience, such as choosing where to direct her attention across an expansive stage bedecked with intricate sets calling back to different eras in BTS history. But she argues the clarity and focus of detail in the film evened the score, giving a much closer view of the choreography and the members' interaction with a close-up camera intimacy she had not gotten in person, and letting her share those fandom moments not only with her cinema audience but with millions of other fans viewing the same film around the world. She adds that Yet to Come would stream on Amazon Prime Video starting November 9, further expanding the number of fans able to see it.

# Super Mario Bros. Wonder: The Verdict

The review's verdict is that Super Mario Bros. Wonder is a marvelous game: its art and animations have a level of polish practically unmatched by rival titles, and the addition of Wonder Seeds subverts your expectations and keeps this 40-year franchise feeling new and innovative.

The grounds are a three-part answer to the problem the review poses — Mario has been stomping Goombas, smashing blocks and running from left to right for damn near 40 years, so how is Nintendo supposed to keep its classic side scroller feeling fresh? First, you shift the location to a brand new kingdom; next, you introduce a bunch of new enemies and power-ups; but what really pushes things over the top is the introduction of a new mechanic that turns everything you think you know about Mario games on its head. What you get is a game that dazzles and delights while living up to its name in a variety of ways.

The warrant is comparative: in a lot of ways Wonder reminds the reviewer of his favorite 2D Mario game, Super Mario World. The one reservation is about the wait — he wishes it had not taken more than 10 years for Nintendo to create a proper sequel to its last mainline platformer — but as he concludes, if that is what it takes to get a game like this, he is happy to sit and wonder what is next for Mario.



---


# Super Mario Bros. Wonder

Super Mario Bros. Wonder, developed by Nintendo EPD for Nintendo Switch, is ranked 4 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31 — the first side-scrolling 2D platformer in the Super Mario Bros. line since New Super Mario Bros. U in 2012, and both a faithful rendition of the classic format and a complete reinvention of the series' irresistible formula.

When you activate the game's delightful whimsy via the aptly named Wonder Flower, it becomes more than a 2D platformer: a musical, a quiz show, a race, or a hidden object game, where pipes become inchworms, Piranha Plants burst into song, and Yoshi becomes a dragon. Critic N. Carpenter writes that each and every level finds some new way to delight and surprise, constantly introducing new ideas, enemies, and wrinkles only to pull back on them just when it is on the verge of becoming rote — like everything else in the Flower Kingdom, a few enemies shift and change in bizarre ways when the Wonder Flower is activated, such as Hoppo, the bouncy, round hippo equivalent that grows in size to create chaos. All of this weirdness, combined with Nintendo's platforming expertise, makes it an entrancing romp alone, with friends, or with strangers online, and the freshest Mario has felt in decades.

Polygon's 2023-10-20 couch co-op roundup adds the local multiplayer detail: Wonder brings together platforming shenanigans, silly power-ups, and lots of map secrets, and the best part is that four people can play local multiplayer, picking from classic characters including Mario, Luigi, Princess Peach, Princess Daisy, Toad, and Toadette.



---


# Super Mario Bros. Wonder's Art And Overworld Map

This might be the best Mario and friends have ever looked, and that includes recent 3D titles like Odyssey: there is just so much detail packed into every level and character, from the determined face Mario makes when he runs around to the little flames that sprout from your feet every time you jump.

Wonder's map is also surprisingly engaging. In the beginning the reviewer was not sure the ability to freely roam around added all that much, but as he progressed he found a number of secret nooks and crannies that would not have fit if the game were locked to a handful of paths. And with Wonder Flowers giving Nintendo the freedom to mix and match mechanics and enemies, there is just so much to see.



---


# Badges And Level Variety In Super Mario Bros. Wonder

Badges are Wonder's customization mechanic: they are earned by completing specific levels, and some may even be required to find secrets or reveal alternate exits. Some allow you to jump farther or float, while others make extra coins appear, and there are protective badges too — like the one that automatically saves you if you fall into lava or poison. It is a mechanic that feels inspired by recent roguelikes such as Hades, and it does a great job of adding customizability and replayability.

The level design is similarly varied. Wonder features six main worlds, each with a distinctive theme, but within those you will still run into reimagined haunted houses, pirate ships, underwater stages and more, along with a number of familiar baddies and some new foes across an incredible range of environments.

Even without the aid of a Wonder Flower, the sheer variety of level types is impressive. Alongside classic stages capped off by grabbing a flag, there are races, badge challenges, puzzle levels and more. KO Arenas let you pick your power-up of choice — Fire Flower, Elephant Suit, Bubble Mushroom or the Drill Hat — before taking down waves of enemies, while Break Time levels provide quick 30-second bursts of excitement. You will never be bored, even if you want a change from standard platform jumping.



---


# Minor Criticisms Of Super Mario Bros. Wonder

The reviewer's reservations are explicitly minor and do not disturb the overall verdict. Mummy enemies draw a complaint — pulling their wraps feels a bit tedious — and he fears the Elephant Suit might be a bit overpowered in comparison to the Drill Hat.

The other two are complaints about scarcity rather than quality: the 5-star levels and rhythm stages are so good he wishes there were more of them, and he is slightly disappointed the adorable penguins from the movie did not make an appearance somewhere in Wonder's ice levels.



---


# Wonder As A Return To 2D Mario Experimentation

Polygon argues that Super Mario Bros. Wonder shares the inventiveness of the earliest 2D Mario games and their disregard for what should and shouldn't be in a Mario game — making it, for middle-aged fans, a candidate for the first "true new Mario game" since Super Mario World in 1990. The grounds lie in a history the reviewer sets out: with each Super Mario Bros. on the NES and SNES, Nintendo's designers learned from the previous entry, cut what didn't work, made audacious additions (there was a time when adding a dinosaur named Yoshi felt like a gimmick), and gradually accumulated the pieces and tropes that would recur for the next thirty-plus years. Then, with Super Mario 64, 3D Mario games became the de facto labs for Nintendo's greatest experimentation — magical hats, water guns, galactic travel — while 2D Mario defaulted to a vessel for nostalgia, including the cheekily named New Super Mario Bros. series.

The warrant is that Wonder revives the old spirit specifically by letting the designers break their own machine. The traditional layer is intact — every level can be enjoyed as a loyal continuation of the plumber's work in the 2D platformer genre, which has kept a healthy cadence since the series debuted in 1985: dash from left to right, jump over pits, concuss enemies, collect the occasional power-up, and leap onto the flagpole that ends one level and unlocks the next. But the wonder of playing Super Mario Bros. in 1985 came from discovery, with Nintendo anticipating that players would climb outside the confines of the level and placing shortcuts in hidden crevices to reward the most rule-breaking players; badges now build on that freedom with skills that let you soar over towering enemies or use the Piranha Plant grappling hook to climb above the stage. "This is the most significant difference between 1985 and 2023," the reviewer writes: "Mario's creators have joined in the fun of breaking the machine." He imagines the game's origin as a notebook in which, since the '90s, every Nintendo developer wrote down each idea that "didn't fit the tone" or "wasn't Mario enough," until someone had the gall to say: "Let's turn this stuffed notebook of chaos into a game. Because why shouldn't Mario be an elephant? Why shouldn't Wigglers wear roller skates? And why shouldn't Luigi skydive?"



---


# Super Mario Bros. Wonder As A Send-Off For The Switch

Polygon argues that Super Mario Bros. Wonder would be a fitting last big release for the Nintendo Switch, on the grounds that the game embodies the same combination that defined the console. With rumours that the Switch's successor could arrive early the following year, the reviewer says he would be fine if Wonder were the console's final major title. The historical grounds: to survive after the Wii U, Nintendo had to bring its console and handheld designers together and create something unlike anything on the market without sacrificing what had got the company to that point — and as the sun sets on the Switch, after an unprecedented run of success and arguably the best entries in many of Nintendo's biggest franchises, Wonder arrives. "Like the Switch itself, Wonder is a collision between the traditional and the new. A game that's the same as it ever was and nothing like Mario has ever been."

The reviewer sets aside the fan question of whether Wonder is the unofficial Super Mario Bros. 5 that "dorks like me have long wanted," leaving that to the forums, and rests his praise on the experience instead: "What a joy it is to play a Mario game and not already know how to read it, to not have my muscle memory do more work than my brain." The scope conditions of the review are stated: Super Mario Bros. Wonder was released on 20 October 2023 on Nintendo Switch, and was reviewed on that console using a pre-release download code provided by Nintendo. Polygon notes that Vox Media has affiliate partnerships which do not influence editorial content, though it may earn commissions on products purchased via affiliate links.



---


# Wonder Seeds And The Transformations They Trigger

A Wonder Seed is the object that gives Super Mario Bros. Wonder its name: a Mario-sized ball of botany hidden inside each Wonder stage that, when found, morphs the environment into something quite wonderful. Choosing to seek it out — being "not too precious about video game tradition," as Polygon puts it — floods the atmosphere with lava-lamp plasma, sends gravity into convulsions, or transforms the hero into any variety of creatures or even inanimate objects, so that for a moment Mario gets to be the background. The second level of the game illustrates the range: it can become a musical, depending on whether you pursue the "Super Mario Bros." of the title or the "Wonder."

The defining property, in the reviewer's reading, is that the choice is one of "and," not "or" — the traditional and the topsy-turvy coexist. Across six worlds the creators offer a menu of familiar stages that can, if you like, be prepared with extra spice, or paired with the family-friendly equivalent of ayahuasca; the drug comparison is not flippant, since at one point Toad licks a Wonder Seed and is suddenly riding a dragon. Sometimes the effects go further and the levels themselves collapse and contort, disobeying laws established by decades of Mario games: giant, sudsy, rainbow-tinted bubbles fill a stage and burst through the ceiling, and a colossal snowball knocks down a flagpole, extending the stage beyond its official conclusion.



---


# The Wonder Flower Transformation Mechanic

The Wonder Flowers are the biggest twist in the game: in addition to the one Bowser stole, there is one hidden in almost every stage, and touching them transports you to an alternate dimension where the rules of the Marioverse have been completely rewritten.

The defining feature is unpredictability rather than a fixed effect. In one level Super Stars rain down from the sky; in another you might be transformed into a giant slime. You may also run into Wonder Flowers that convert the game from a side scroller into a top-down 2D maze, or suddenly find yourself the target in a shooting gallery. Almost every flower is different and the possibilities are seemingly endless.

The scale of the design work behind that is documented: in a recent volume of Nintendo's Ask the Developer, the reviewer learned the team had a wall of sticky notes with over 2,000 ideas — and after playing Wonder, he believes it. Wonder Flowers feel like they add an extra half a level to every stage; they are a delicious dessert on top of an already bountiful meal.



---


# How Wonder Fixes 2D Mario's Difficulty Pacing

The claim is that Nintendo has addressed a long-standing gripe about the pacing of previous 2D Marios — the removal of the rush to get to the "good stuff."

The grounds are the structural problem in earlier games. Because they are meant for both experienced gamers and children who might be new to the franchise, they often locked more challenging levels behind the story's completion, which meant the beginning of the game could be a slog as you rushed through easier levels to get to the more challenging bits.

The fix, and the warrant connecting it to the claim, is that Wonder adds difficulty ratings and hidden paths that lead to 5-star levels long before you finish the game, so the harder content is available from early on. And the reviewer adds that the harder content is well tuned: 4- and particularly 5-star levels are balanced just right, so completing one feels like a rewarding challenge without crossing over into punishing.



---


# Super Mario 3D World on Switch

Super Mario 3D World is Polygon's recommendation for anyone searching for that classic Super Mario feeling in a modern 3D world — or anyone who has always wanted to play as Mario in a cat suit. It appears in the outlet's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

Players can choose Mario, Luigi, Peach, or Toad.

Each has a slightly different perk: Luigi can get a bit more air in his jump, while Toad is a bit faster.



---


# The Flower Kingdom Premise

Super Mario Bros. Wonder starts with Mario and crew — Luigi, Peach, Toad, Yoshi, Nabbit and, for the first time, Daisy — visiting Prince Florian of the Flower Kingdom, until Bowser barges in and steals a Wonder Flower, which somehow allows him to merge with Prince Florian's castle to create a floating mecha fortress of doom. From there your job is to collect Wonder Seeds, this game's version of stars and shines, as you help the Florians restore order to their troubled land.

The setup has two subtle but important implications. The first is that you immediately learn Wonder Flowers have wild and unpredictable effects. The second is that, because you are not simply rescuing a princess trapped in a castle, the whole Flower Kingdom is working with you to take down Bowser.

That reciprocity shows up throughout. Sometimes it means rescuing trapped miners; other times the Florians are the ones helping Mario — who also has a new voice actor for the first time — by rebuilding a bridge or donating a Wonder Seed at the beginning of a new world. The friendly little flowers scattered across each level even shout words of encouragement or funny quips as you run by. The impressive part is that, even in a relatively straightforward platformer, there is a sense of community that makes this world feel more lived in than a lot of epic RPGs.



---


# Multiplayer In Super Mario Bros. Wonder

Super Mario Bros. Wonder shines as a solo experience but, like other recent 2D Mario games, supports up to four players together — a mode Polygon describes as both a delight and utter chaos. The character roster divides into two kinds. The humanoid characters (Mario, Peach, Toad and so on) are "like M&Ms": different exteriors that effectively play the same.

The critters are the discriminating case, intended for players who want a little extra help: Nabbit and Yoshi won't take damage, and the Yoshis come with their familiar tongue attack and floaty jump.



---


# The Badge System In Super Mario Bros. Wonder

The badge system is Super Mario Bros. Wonder's mechanism for optional special abilities: each unlockable upgrade or special move is assigned to a badge that can be found or purchased, and one collected badge can be selected before each stage. The abilities range from helpful (a high, floating leap) to playful (a Piranha Plant grappling hook) to silly (a triple jump tied to a musical rhythm), and Polygon's reviewer describes rotating them by need — opting for the Safety Bounce badge once later stages added instant-death bottomless pits, so that plunging into an abyss has the darkness spit you back up "like a piece of hamburger caught in its throat." The badges are worn by Prince Florian, a little royal bug who joins the journey and provides most of the conversation on the road trip, alongside very talkative flowers sprouting across every corner of the Flower Kingdom, eager to offer a tip for a metatextual wink.

Badges sit inside a wider design of considerate rather than patronising assistance: Wonder Seeds can add a splash of difficulty, but help is perpetually available — time limits are gone and extra lives can be purchased cheaply with the game's abundant purple currency. The balance question the system raises is answered by escalation: the reviewer expects many players to brag that their favourite badge is "the overpowered one," which is sort of always true, since whichever you use you will feel you have an unfair advantage as you float over chunks of the stage or vacuum coins through walls — so the designers layered on new challenges to keep Wonder inside the Goldilocks window, not too hard and not too easy.



---


# Wonder's Disposable-Idea Design As An Alternative To "Forever Games"

Polygon argues that Super Mario Bros. Wonder's willingness to squeeze each idea for its fun and then throw the rind away is a potent alternative to the current era of AAA "forever games" filled with endless lists of chores and artificial rewards — because in Wonder the reward isn't XP or limited-edition outfits, it's the play itself. The reviewer calls the creators' abundance of new ideas "unapologetically wasteful," and means it as a compliment: many gimmicks here could be stretched to fill entire games, but instead the player is lucky to see them last a few minutes.

The grounds are a worked example of how a single idea is escalated and then discarded: one stage features platforms that drop when you step on them; the next has platforms that drop only after a certain number of jumps, with a countdown clock at their centre; then a stage of platforms made of batteries, each dropping as it runs out of energy; and finally a stage in which you build the platform out of huge batteries of different shapes, growing and shrinking rapidly as it skims above a yawning abyss. The reviewer heads off the obvious objection — that such refusal to outstay a welcome means a short game — by noting that levels are everywhere: the map features six worlds, but levels are also found in the hub area and, to avoid spoilers, elsewhere. The familiar rhythms of a Mario game are broken too, with bosses appearing without warning, some worlds ending with no boss fight at all, and the occasional surprise stage materialising like a mirage.



---


# Luigi's Mansion 3

Luigi's Mansion 3 puts players in the role of Mario's taller counterpart rather than the plumber in the red hat. It appears in Polygon's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

Local co-op becomes available with player two as Gooigi, a spooky goo Luigi, after finishing the intro walkthrough and getting E. Gadd's briefcase.

Together the players platform their way through the haunted hotel to save Mario, Peach, and numerous Toads.



---


# Technology Dependence Creates Defense Blind Spots

Avner Barnea argues that relying on technology produces a specific cognitive failure: "When the thinking is that you don't need soldiers because there are monitors, you expect in advance that you will receive the warning about the threat via the technological means and no one imagines a situation in which the observation array would be neutralized. On the contrary, it is seen as invulnerable."

His grounds are that the enemy sees the same technology: "The problem begins when the enemy is also exposed to these means: RCWS are great, they are important and cost millions, but they are visible to everyone, and everyone knows where they are. Once you begin believing that the fence will stop all the relevant threats, you think even half a battalion on standby is enough. Technology greatly influences our way of thinking and is seen as the answer to everything — only no one ever asks themselves what the vulnerabilities are, and what is the backup plan for the doomsday scenario when the technology layer collapses." Barnea supports the pattern with a historical case, comparing Israel's sense of technological superiority with US activity during the Vietnam War between 1965 and 1968: "The Americans relied on massive aerial bombardment with precision bombs and napalm bombs that burned huge areas, and advocated the 'scorched earth' concept. They convinced themselves that the Vietcong could not withstand it. In practice, the North Vietnamese army studied the American activity. It dug tunnels, moved equipment and people between bombings, eventually enabling it to reach the important bases in the south of the country, and overwhelm the Americans. In fact, the US military so believed in the damage it was causing that they reported a far greater number of casualties on the other side than the actual number, which in turn created an illusion of victory. They told themselves, we have B-52 bombers, there's no way we can't win."



---


# Nostalgia-Driven Major Game Releases, 2023

TechCrunch cites three 2023 releases as evidence of gaming's turn to the familiar. This year's hit new Zelda game Tears of the Kingdom literally built a new game on top of the old one and remains a strong contender for Game of the Year.

Competition is stiff, more so now that Nintendo just casually dropped Super Mario Bros. Wonder, the first two-dimensional side-scrolling Mario game in more than a decade — another portal to the past given its departure from a long string of recent 3D Super Mario titles. Square Enix was so confident in its remake of the 1997 Japanese roleplaying mega-hit Final Fantasy VII that the reimagined version of the game comprises three standalone full-length games, each spaced a few years apart.



---


# Captain Toad: Treasure Tracker

Captain Toad: Treasure Tracker is a Wii U game whose Switch port Polygon calls full of charm, included in its 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

In an article five years before October 7, Brigadier General Eran Ortal argued that "Israeli restraint as regards proactive thwarting of offensive capabilities in the Gaza Strip stems from a clear Israeli strategy that strives to reduce the influence of the enemy on the current routine of life in Israel, even at the price of worsening of the threat in the future."

Ortal treated the policy as natural — "a Western nation cannot lead its life in an endless state of emergency" — but insisted that "alongside the understanding of the need for a containment policy, it must be recognized that the risks are high, as evidenced by the steeply worsening intensity of conflicts between Israel and the terrorist organizations in Gaza." # Strategic Surprise As A Recurring Pattern

The strategic surprise that hit the State of Israel on October 7 bears similar characteristics to the Japanese attack on the US naval base at Pearl Harbor in 1941, the Argentine surprise attack on Britain's Falkland Islands in 1982, the Al-Qaeda attack on the United States on September 11, 2001, and the spread of ISIS throughout the Middle East in 2014 — a pattern that, on the evidence cited here, better collection technology has not broken.

The irony is sharpened by timing: in the months leading up to October 7, former head of the Planning Division Major General (Res.) Giora Eiland held a series of lectures for senior officers on the reasons for the strategic surprise that fell on the IDF in the Yom Kippur War. "Not one of the officers imagined that 50 years after that mistake, it would repeat itself in exactly the same way," he tells Globes. Barnea claims that despite technological progress and sophistication, intelligence officials are questioning whether there really is a trend towards improved early detection and thwarting of strategic threats: a comprehensive study of intelligence failures in the national arena, from the fall of the Iron Curtain in 1989 to 2010, showed no improvement in providing or thwarting warnings about strategic surprises, even if the means of gathering information had improved. Four years after that study was signed, former US President Barack Obama admitted that US intelligence had not correctly assessed the severity of the threat of large parts of Iraq and Syria being occupied by ISIS.

Tarik Cyril Amar wrote: "And the intel, and the special forces training... both areas where Israel mythology will be very upset indeed." A user posting as Mjoachim said Israel's defence forces have lost their fame, noting that the IDF lost an army base and a general was captured right out of his house: "Invincible 'Merkava MK4 MBT's captured, and destroyed...what is wrong with the Israeli security and defence forces? Dr Jaswant Gandhi, a professor of management, drew a lesson for another country: the attack on Israel was a "great Mossad failure", and India had to learn a lot and keep all intelligence agencies duly greased and internecine conflict-proof. "Israel_under_attack Great #Mossad failure. GoI has to learn a lot and keep all Intelligence Agencies duly greased and internecine conflict-proof. # The Iron Dome's Strategic Paradox

The Iron Dome was built with the strategic vision of giving decision-makers breathing room — allowing them not to react immediately to rockets but to have the flexibility to react at the right time, in the right place, in a range of ways — yet its success was paradoxical: it was so successful that it not only supported the decision-making process but fundamentally changed it.

Prof. Eviatar Matania puts the paradox as follows: up until October 7, the system "served as a very successful plaster to threats to a sovereign state, because what legitimacy would a state leader have for going to war when no citizens were harmed?" Brigadier General Eran Ortal, until recently commander of The Dado Center for Interdisciplinary Military Studies, also believes technological measures such as the Iron Dome and the barrier influenced decision-making in Israel, and in his estimation helped the political echelon conduct a policy of military restraint towards the Gaza Strip, which in turn allowed Hamas to strengthen and gain offensive capabilities. But even after Iron Dome, Israel found it difficult to stand up against significant disruption of daily life on the home front: "Despite the clear threat posed by Gaza, the decision makers preferred to avoid a policy that would mean returning a large part of the country's population to the reality of air raids and disrupted daily routines. The bottom line: the Iron Dome did not change the essential strategic situation; as firepower from the Gaza Strip developed, so did the terrorist organizations' ability to control daily life in Israel's hinterland, hold it hostage, and restrain Israel from taking proactive measures against them." Ortal asks rhetorically why the relative success of the Iron Dome did not translate into restoring Israel's freedom of action against Hamas, and names three factors: first, like any operational system, Iron Dome is not perfect — the enemy studies it and develops its own challenges against it, and decision makers recognized that Israel is not hermetically protected; second, the enormous cost of deploying and operating batteries significantly impedes a policy based on continuous rounds of violence; and third, as long as rockets are intercepted in the skies over Israel and not over Gaza, the Israeli home front still experiences sirens, security rooms and shelters, and disrupted routine living — so "even the complete success of the Iron Dome left daily life on the home front in the hands of the terrorist organizations."

# Israeli Sectors Most Exposed to War Damage

Asked which industries the war would hit, Leo Leiderman put private consumption — particularly of services — at the centre: "A substantial decline can be expected in private consumption, particularly of services."

His mechanism runs through sentiment as well as income. The decline is not just because of damage to output and income but also for psychological reasons: distress, uncertainty and the possibility of prolonged reserve duty by some of the public will all affect consumer sentiment.

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. # Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.

# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.

# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.

# The Sherman Act Verdict As The First Major Tech Antitrust Win Since Microsoft

Tim Sweeney argued that the jury's finding for Epic showed "the Sherman Antitrust Act works in the new era of tech monopolies" — his grounds being that no major antitrust verdict against a tech company that meant change and benefits for everybody had landed since the 1990s and US v. Microsoft, back in the early days of the internet.

The warrant joining claim and grounds is his account of present-day harm: the industry, he said, is "being strangled by a few gatekeepers imposing insane amounts of control and extracting huge taxes," which not only raise prices for consumers but also make a lot of kinds of products simply unviable. If the statute can still reach that conduct after a three-decade gap, then it remains a working remedy, which is why he called the verdict "a great day for all developers" and "much needed by the industry." Sweeney was speaking about a trial four years in the making, tracing back to a September 2019 email produced in discovery about a plan to draw Google into a legal battle over antitrust.

# Google's Secret OEM And Carrier Deals And Its Deleted Chats

Asked what surprised him in the courtroom, Tim Sweeney said the trial confirmed practices he had suspected since around 2018 — when some people called him a conspiracy theorist for saying so — including that Google leaked Epic's conversations to reporters to get negative stories written, paid other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores, and went around paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores.

Sweeney gave a concrete instance from Epic's own experience: when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with other smartphone manufacturers such as OnePlus and with carriers of all sorts, those partners told Epic they couldn't do a deal because Google had done a secret deal with them. Instead, he said, Google employees were "rampantly destroying all their chats on these topics": long conversation threads would start to get into a spicy antitrust issue, somebody would point out that history was on, and the chat would go silent — history turned off so the documents would be destroyed. Sweeney said it was great to see all of that called out in detail at trial.

# Simple Versus Complicated: Assessing The Opening Arguments

The claim after day one is that Epic's chances look better than they should, because the case may come down to simplicity: Google spent most of its first day attempting to explain complicated ins and outs of business, while Epic was able to paint a black-and-white picture of good and evil with itself as the clear underdog.

The starting expectation ran the other way. Walking into the courtroom on Monday morning it seemed impossible — if Epic could not prove Apple's walled iOS garden is a monopoly, how could the comparatively open Google do worse against the windmill-tilting Fortnite developer? The warrant that reverses that expectation is about jury persuasion rather than legal merit: a clearer picture beats a more accurate but more complicated one.

Both Epic and Google spent a long, long time on subtle lines of questioning: you really had to read between the lines to see that Epic was trying to make a point about how Google's 70/30 revenue split is probably based on an arbitrary decision Valve made two decades ago with Steam, or that Google was trying to make the point that Epic, too, likely believed an app store provides more value than just payment processing and maybe deserves more money.

# Epic v. Google Is A Jury Trial

Epic and Google have to convince a jury, not the judge, which is totally different from how the Apple case played out — that one was a "bench trial."

The consequence is that persuasion cuts both ways and is hard to predict. All the evidence of tricky deals inside Google might sway a jury against the company; alternatively, Google scaremongering that sideloaded apps equal gaping security holes might sway a jury against Epic. Who knows.

The jury is also sealed off from coverage: Judge Donato explicitly told jurors they are in a "news-free bubble" through mid-December.
