# West Indies Win The 2023 T20I Series 3-2

West Indies beat England by four wickets in the fifth and deciding T20 international on Dec. 21, 2023, taking the series 3-2 when Shai Hope pinged Chris Woakes over extra cover for six at 19.2 overs, with West Indies 133-6.

It was the 120th six of the series, and Hope played a gem of an innings, calmly anchoring West Indies in an increasingly nervous chase with a run-a-ball 43; England fought admirably to defend a below-par total and, but for Hope, would probably have done it. Cricket on TNT Sports posted that the win claimed the series 3-2 and a white-ball clean sweep. The Guardian's report framed the finish as the sequel to a very different match: Tuesday's ludicrous, record-smashing, high-scoring entertainment had been followed on the same surface by thrilling low-scoring entertainment and a different result claimed in very different style, eventually won with four balls to spare and in the most unfitting of ways — with a massive six — by Hope, again proving himself the right man for a run chase. A series marked by stunning power hitting, roaring run rates and an unexpected midway transformation in England's performances and prospects concluded with a 3-2 triumph for West Indies, who extended their supremacy over England at home to four series in three formats across nearly five years.



---


# Andre Russell's Comeback In The First T20I

Andre Russell was named Player of the Match in the first T20I against England, taking 3-29 and smashing 29 not out off just 14 deliveries in his first T20I in over two years.

He seemed very pleased to be back in maroon, saying: "Life is so funny. Since when I got selected for the West Indies two weeks ago I've been dreaming of being man of the match." His bowling figures at the end of England's innings were 3-19, which the live blog described as balancing the attack perfectly on his comeback. As Tim Wigmore put it, Russell at his best adds so much to the West Indies side — with him at seven, and Holder, Shepherd and Hosein to follow, West Indies bat incredibly deep.



---


# Shai Hope's Anchor Innings In The T20 Decider

Shai Hope's 43 off 43 balls steered West Indies to their target in the deciding T20I, an exemplary anchoring innings that the live blog identified as the wicket England really needed.

At 16 overs West Indies were 112-4 with Hope on 29, and he opened the face to steer Rehan Ahmed for his first boundary; Rehan had struggled as the series progressed, and later in the over Powell muscled him over long-on for six, leaving West Indies 21 runs from a hat-trick of T20 series wins that year — South Africa away, India and England at home. In the 17th over, with West Indies 114-5, Hope was quietly guiding his side towards the finish line. The Guardian's report noted West Indies were 62 for three halfway through their innings, and if England had had 15 more runs at the same point they had also made a complete hash of the rest of it — a trap West Indies avoided thanks to Hope's 43-ball 43 as he again steered his side to their target. The batting display may have lacked their usual flamboyance, but until the final ball it was entirely appropriate for the occasion.



---


# Adil Rashid's T20I Milestones And Series Form

Adil Rashid reached his 100th T20I wicket in the first match of the December 2023 series against West Indies — on his 100th T20I appearance — and finished the series with eight wickets at 15 and an economy rate of 6.26.

In the first T20I in Barbados he had Kyle Mayers caught by Brook in the deep for 35 at 79-3, his 99th T20I wicket, off what was in truth a bit of a drag down but delivered from the front of the hand so it skidded on; England needed that badly. He then bowled Hetmyer's dismissal for 1 at 101-4, caught by Duckett on the midwicket sponge after Hetmyer danced out of his crease and got a good piece of the length ball — the 100th wicket, and a crucial one in the context of the game as England looked to ramp up the pressure. In the deciding fifth T20I he finished with figures of 4-0-21-2, and the live blog noted he had had a great series with those eight wickets at 15 and an absurd economy rate of 6.26, but was going to end on the losing side. The Guardian's report added that amid the wider theme of transformation Rashid's excellence remained constant: the 35-year-old, who had risen to the top of the T20 bowling rankings for the first time that Wednesday, took two wickets and conceded just 21 in the decider, while Topley was even better, also claiming a pair of victims but conceding only 17 — England took plenty of positives from the series, but the result was not one.



---


# Rehan Ahmed And Adil Rashid Through The Middle Overs

England's spinners were taken apart and then struck back through the middle of West Indies' chase in the first T20I, with Rehan Ahmed conceding nineteen in his first over before removing Nicholas Pooran.

In the seventh over Rehan bowled to Kyle Mayers, whose first ball was dragged down and launched over the midwicket boundary for six, followed by a supreme lofted drive down the ground for six more; Rehan came back with two sharply turning leg breaks before Shai Hope smeared a length ball over mid-on for the third six of the over, leaving West Indies 78-1. In the ninth over Tymal Mills replaced Rehan and started with another wide before a series of slower balls and back-of-the-hand trickery restricted Pooran and Hope, with the final ball top-edged over Buttler's head for a one-bounce four — 87-2, and West Indies needing 85 from 66 balls. In the tenth Adil Rashid was given another over after an excellent first: Pooran spotted the googly and drove it down the ground for six, singles were exchanged, and a short ball was panned into the deep for a couple, leaving West Indies 99-2 and needing 73 from 60. In the eleventh Rehan returned and had Pooran caught and bowled for 13, taking a nifty tumbling catch to his left at 100-3; Shimron Hetmyer opened his account with a single and Rehan got out of the over with three dots. In the twelfth just a single and a wicket came from the over as Hope could not break the legspin shackles, with West Indies captain Rovman Powell the new man and Buttler cranking the pressure by inserting a slip.



---


# West Indies' Death Overs Win In The First T20I

West Indies won the first T20I by four wickets when Andre Russell smashed the winning runs off Sam Curran — a length ball spanked over point for a one-bounce four — to go 1-0 up in the series.

The closing overs swung twice. In the thirteenth Rehan Ahmed had two balls left, the first flayed for four by Powell behind point and the last a dot, leaving West Indies needing 60 from 42. In the fourteenth Liam Livingstone came on instead of Rashid and kept it to singles as England tried to take the game as deep as possible and hope West Indies fluffed their lines at the death, with 55 needed from 36. Rehan then struck twice: Shai Hope, who had just hit him for six, holed out to Brook for 36 at 123-5, and Shepherd poked a leg break to Curran at slip first ball for 0 at 123-6, putting Rehan on a hat-trick. Russell faced the hat-trick ball and patted a decent delivery on the stumps back, then worked a couple; Ahmed finished with 3-39 from his four overs, leaving 47 needed from 30. In the sixteenth Livingstone conceded four singles before Rovman Powell crunched consecutive sixes down the ground for sixteen off the over — 31 needed from 24. In the seventeenth Tymal Mills conceded sixteen, including a mighty top-edged six from Powell and a short, wide ball sent to the fence, leaving 15 needed from 18. In the eighteenth Rashid was recalled and Russell smashed his googly clean out of the ground for six, then drove a four, eleven off the over leaving West Indies needing four.



---


# The Final Overs Of The T20 Series Clinch

England took two late wickets and pushed the decider into its final over, but West Indies got home with nine needed from six balls after Shai Hope had kept the requirement below a run a ball.

Reece Topley had Rovman Powell caught for 8 at short third man by Rashid, a smart low catch to his left, leaving West Indies 113-5 and needing 20 from 21 balls, with the live blog noting England had not given this up. In the 18th over Buttler gambled by continuing with the relatively expensive Rehan Ahmed and it did not come off: Hope skimmed a back cut between short third and backward point for four to move the requirement back below a run a ball, making it very hard to see how England could win. Sam Curran then conceded only one run from the first four balls of a superb penultimate over — with a short break while England called for a dry towel as the ball got very wet — leaving 10 needed from eight balls; Andre Russell then slugged a low full toss straight down the throat of Livingstone at long-on for 3, and England, behind the game throughout the innings, were again dreaming of an improbable victory with West Indies needing 10 from 7. Jason Holder was almost run out first ball of the 19th over, taking a very dodgy single to mid-off and finishing well short when Curran just failed to gather Rashid's throw, leaving nine to win from six balls with Chris Woakes to bowl; Holder then inside-edged Woakes wide of leg stump for three, which would have been four but for an outstanding stop from Rehan Ahmed, putting West Indies 127-6. The Guardian's report judged the outcome had seemed inevitable from the start: with such a meagre target West Indies needed little more than to keep their heads, and though both Topley and Curran conceded only two with their final overs to push the contest into its final over, that never looked in doubt.



---


# The Rain Delay And DLS Position In The First T20I

Rain stopped play in the first T20I with West Indies on 108-4 after 12.4 overs and requiring 64 runs off 44 balls — crucially, six runs ahead of the Duckworth Lewis Stern rate, so that if the rain did not abate the home side would take the spoils.

The heavens cracked out of nowhere and the players scurried off as the covers were hauled on, with Hope on 27 and Powell on 6. The rain then began tailing off and a rope was dragged around the outfield to take off excess water. The Guardian's man in Barbados, Simon Burnton, reported a 9.35 p.m. restart with no overs lost, putting play about eight minutes away; the live blog understood 10.10 p.m. local time — 2.10 a.m. in London — to be the cut off for the match.



---


# First T20I In Barbados: Match Summary

West Indies beat England in the first T20 international in Barbados on Dec. 12, 2023, chasing down 171 with eleven balls remaining after England collapsed from 112-2 at the ten-over mark.

The Guardian's James Wallace called it an intriguing game that set up the T20I series nicely, and a real statement laid down by Rovman Powell and his men. West Indies were up against it early, with England crunching their way to 112-2 off the first ten overs, but Jos Buttler's side managed only 59 runs off the next ten, losing eight wickets along the way. A total of 171 was thirty or more shy of where England would have liked to end up, and so it proved as West Indies showed how muscular their own batting card is — the home side cleared the ropes fourteen times compared with England's six. Andre Russell and Rovman Powell found the stands with ease at the business end of the match to get West Indies over the line. The second match of the series was to be played in Grenada on the Thursday.



---


# West Indies' Powerplay In The T20 Decider Chase

West Indies reached 39-2 at the end of the powerplay chasing 133 in the deciding T20I, after a flying start from Johnson Charles was checked by two England wickets.

Reece Topley found some early inswing to the right-handers in the first over: Brandon King survived an LBW appeal off the first ball, which was missing leg, before another inswinger to Charles ran away for four leg-byes, leaving 7-0 — every boundary hurting with such a low target. In the second over Charles, who had been player of the match when West Indies beat England at the T20 World Cup 11 years earlier with 84 off 56 balls, pulled Woakes for a big six with a hint of top edge and glided a boundary past short third man, taking it to 20-0. Topley then had King caught for 3 by Buttler at mid-on off a slog, 20-1. In the third over Nicholas Pooran launched his second ball over midwicket for six and England thought he edged the next to the keeper but ran out of time to review, leaving 30-1 with West Indies needing 103 from 17 overs. Woakes bowled Pooran for 10 at 33-2 — UltraEdge showed Pooran had edged an earlier Topley ball, but it did not matter as he tried to ride the bounce of an awkward delivery that cramped him for room, took the inside of an angled bat and ricocheted onto the stumps. The live blog noted England needed early wickets to have a realistic chance and that one more in the powerplay, before bringing on Adil Rashid, would put them right back in the game. Topley continued in the fifth over for just three runs — sensible, since the spinners would do most of the work after the powerplay, and he had quietly had a good series as comfortably the most economical seamer on either side — and in the sixth Charles mistimed a short ball from Woakes just short of Moeen in the covers, with Moeen doing well to save the boundary, capping a good England fightback in which only nine runs came in three overs.



---


# West Indies' Powerplay In The First T20I Chase

Chasing 172, West Indies finished the powerplay of the first T20I on 59-1, having come out of the traps as well as England did.

Brandon King got the home side off to a blistering start in the first over, sending Sam Curran down the ground for four and swiping a brace of sixes over mid-wicket to reach 16-0. In the second over, Will Jacks dropped short and Kyle Mayers murdered it onto the roof of the stadium, Mayers cut for three behind point and King skipped out of his crease to skim the ball for four down the ground, taking it to 30-0. In the third over Chris Woakes replaced the beleaguered Curran and struck immediately: Ben Duckett flew to his left at backward point for a spectacular diving catch off a full-blooded cut shot to dismiss King for 22, leaving West Indies 32-1; Shai Hope came in and dug out a Woakes yorker, crunching it away down the ground for four to make it 36-1. In the fourth over Tymal Mills bowled for England for the first time in eighteen months, starting with a couple of wides slanted down the leg side before Mayers pulled a short ball onto the roof for six, and Duckett then shelled a chance that smashed into his palm as he leapt to his right — West Indies 47-1. In the fifth over Hope clubbed a Woakes length ball down the ground for six to reach 56-1, and in the sixth Curran returned and conceded just three runs, with a single each to Mayers and Hope, to complete the powerplay at 59-1 with Mayers on 22 and Hope on 13.



---


# West Indies' Middle Overs In The T20 Decider Chase

Adil Rashid took two wickets through the middle overs of the decider chase — Johnson Charles for 27 and Sherfane Rutherford for 30 — but West Indies still moved to 95-4 with the run rate under control.

In the seventh over Rehan Ahmed's first over disappeared for 12: four singles and a two off the first five balls, then a no-nonsense straight six from Charles, taking West Indies to 51-2. Rashid struck straight away in the eighth, accidentally bowling a very wide, dipping full toss that Charles clunked low to Buttler at short extra cover, 54-3. Moeen replaced Rehan in the ninth and rushed through four singles. In the tenth, West Indies knew how dangerous Rashid was and were content to sit on him — the live blog thought that had been Charles' plan too before he saw a low full toss and his brain went rogue — and at drinks West Indies needed 71 from 60. England reviewed an LBW appeal against Rutherford off a Rashid legbreak that had hit him on the pad in front of middle and leg, but it was comfortably missing leg stump and England lost the review. In the eleventh, after 23 balls without a West Indian boundary, Rutherford lifted Moeen handsomely over extra cover for four. In the twelfth England appealed unsuccessfully for caught behind when Rutherford missed a swipe at Rashid and decided not to risk their last review — a good job, as there was nothing on UltraEdge — before Rutherford launched a full ball down the ground for six. In the thirteenth Rehan returned, perhaps hoping to tempt Rutherford into one big shot too many, but Hope, happily playing the anchor role, faced five of the six deliveries as England ran out of time. In the fourteenth Rutherford hooked new bowler Sam Curran for six more in an over worth 11, with Rutherford on 30 from 23 balls and Hope 19 from 28, both playing their roles to perfection. Buttler then brought Rashid back for his final over knowing it was now or never, and got an immediate reward as Rutherford smashed a drive towards short extra where Curran dived to his left for a superb catch, 95-4.



---


# England 171 All Out In The First T20I

England were bowled out for 171 with three deliveries to spare in the first T20I in Barbados, an innings of two halves that ran from 77 for no loss to all out.

Tymal Mills got a gossamer-thin edge through to Pooran to end the innings, completing what the live blog called a turnaround for West Indies, who had been staring down the barrel with England flying at 77-0 after six overs. The closing wickets came in quick succession: Liam Livingstone chopped a cutter from Andre Russell onto his stumps for 27 with England at 167-7; Rehan Ahmed followed shortly after for 1, trying to smear a length ball down the ground and finding Powell lurking ten yards in from the sponge, leaving England 169-8 and giving Russell two in the over to finish his spell — and his first T20I in two years — with figures of 3-19; and Adil Rashid went for 0, swiping at Joseph in the final over and hacking the ball onto his own stumps to make it 170-9. As Aatif Nawaz posted, England's recent white-ball approach was a variable one yielding mixed and often frustrating results.



---


# The England Camp's Verdict On The T20 Series Defeat

Jos Buttler's verdict on the Dec. 21, 2023 series defeat was that England "probably didn't adapt quickly enough with the bat," having thought 160 would have been a decent score on a used wicket, but that it was a fantastic bowling effort in which they did well to hang in the game as long as they did.

Buttler added that Phil Salt had had a brilliant series and that England found out lots about themselves as a team; on the stop-clock experiment, he said it was only in the last game that they really noticed it, and that it was good to keep the game moving. The live blog's own summary was that England's miserable white-ball year ended with another series defeat, though plenty of good had come from this series, most notably Salt's performance — and that while there were a few slots to fill, most notably at No. 3, they were in reasonable shape ahead of the next year's World Cup. Reece Topley said: "We've had some high-scoring games, but the last game was almost the complete opposite of what happened here. We were probably just under par with the first-innings score but with the ball we were excellent, pushed them right to the end. I think it's been an amazing series. Both teams have played some unbelievable cricket. I was so excited turning up today, because it was basically a final and those are the games you want to play in and be on the right side of. The bottom line is you want to win this series, I want to win every series I can for England."



---


# Australia Women's White-Ball Reset Before The 2024 T20 World Cup

Australia have spoken about shifting their mindset in white-ball cricket after the losses in England, pursuing a more attacking approach, and the three ODIs against India in the following week plus three ensuing T20s will be the first showing of that, with the hosts also a rising force in the white-ball game, as reported by The Roar on 24 December 2023.

Alyssa Healy framed the six matches as both a proving ground and a staging post. "Within our group we're really comfortable with where we're at, and the progression we're on," she said. "Ultimately there's a big T20 World Cup in Bangladesh towards the end of next year, that is a real carrot for us. These are the sort of big trophies that we're wanting to win. And yes, every series in between now and then is important, but at the same time we're building towards that World Cup."

She also set the terms on which the question of Australian supremacy should be revisited, deferring judgement rather than dismissing it: "Maybe you can ask me that (supremacy) question at the end of the six white-ball games to see how we're going and we can answer that. These next six games will probably give us a better indication about how we're tracking but also what we might need to improve on."



---


# England 132 All Out In The T20 Series Decider

England were bowled out for 132 in the deciding fifth T20I on Dec. 21, 2023, less than half the 267-3 they had made on the same surface two days earlier, leaving West Indies needing 133 to win the series.

The Guardian's live blog set the contrast starkly: Tuesday at Tarouba, England 267-3 with 19 sixes; Thursday, England 132 all out with five sixes. England assembled exactly the same players in exactly the same place and exactly the same situation — losing the toss, put in to bat — but this was an entirely different performance, on a wicket once so true that turned untrustworthy. The report suggested that as a tour enters its final days thoughts often turn to home, and perhaps the focus was not as laser-sharp as it might have been; whatever the reason, the pyrotechnics of the two previous matches never sparked. It took a fabulous delivery from Gudakesh Motie to end Phil Salt's run of absurd form with his score a modest 38, but some of the other wickets seemed a little careless: in the fourth over Jos Buttler casually turned a Jason Holder delivery to fine leg where Oshane Thomas was positioned, hands cupped, and Harry Brook tried to paddle-sweep Motie but sent the ball only a few feet into the air for an easy Nicholas Pooran catch, making it 70 for four one ball into the ninth over, at which point Liam Livingstone and Moeen Ali had to focus on disaster prevention rather than entertainment. Akeal Hosein's four overs went for just 20 and brought the wickets of Will Jacks and Moeen — the latter undone by a relay catch on the boundary after he and Livingstone added 40 for the fifth wicket — and Livingstone followed precisely two overs later, prodding the ball limply back to Motie, at which point things really fell apart, the last five wickets surrendered in 20 balls for just 11 runs. England were 109 for four after 14 overs and then the house fell down: in the 19th over Andre Russell, who bowled really well, finished with two for 25 and would have had three wickets in four balls had Hosein taken a tricky low chance at third man to dismiss Sam Curran; Adil Rashid was run out for 1 at 132-9, sacrificing himself just as in the 2019 World Cup final so that Curran could stay on strike with four balls remaining; and Curran clouted the next ball to long-off, caught by Rutherford off Holder for 12, to end the innings.



---


# India vs Australia At The 1996 World Cup

Australia beat India by 16 runs in a match described as one of the most exciting played between the two sides. Australia batted first and posted a target of 259 runs in 50 overs, courtesy of a brilliant 126 runs off 135 balls by Mark Waugh, with Venkatesh Prasad and Venkatapathy Raju picking up two wickets each for India.

India batted well courtesy of Sachin Tendulkar, who made a brilliant 90 runs off 84 balls, along with Sanjay Manjrekar, who scored 62 runs off 91 balls, but India were bowled out within 242 runs in 48 overs as Damien Fleming took five wickets for Australia.



---


# Damian Penaud's Try-Scoring Record Run

Damian Penaud's two tries against Italy on 6 October 2023 took him to second overall on France's men's try-scorers' chart with 35, three behind Serge Blanco, in a run that had seen the wing score in seven straight matches and 14 times that year.

The Guardian's judgment was that if the predatory Penaud's progress is a marker of France's hopes, their fellow title contenders should be worried; as a whole, the French machine was tuning up satisfactorily with top spot in Pool A secured, and a potential last-eight collision with Ireland or South Africa, or indeed Scotland, would be a monumental affair.

Galthié spread the credit: "It's easy to congratulate Damian for his attacking performance. But it's also easy when you have a team like that working for you. Players that become great are served by their teams; there's always a balance." The former France scrum-half added: "We're happy to qualify … We'll recuperate together, celebrate qualification, then turn to the quarter-final. For us, after a World Cup final against New Zealand [on opening night], our game next Sunday will be a second final."



---


# The Scotland Commitment Row And The Gulf In Class

Against the suggestion that Scotland's efforts at Hampden should be questioned — that a defensive collapse almost helped England towards a Team GB place at the Paris Olympics — The Guardian argues that would be unfair.

The premise it attacks is that Scotland's players were less than fully committed. The counter-grounds are, first, that the gulf in class between the European champions, ranked fourth in the world, and their neighbours to the north, ranked 23rd, is clear, and that the manager, Pedro Martínez Losa, has been unconvincing in charge — so the scoreline needs no explanation in terms of effort. Second, the accusations had already been rejected by the players: Lucy Bronze called the claim that Scotland players might feel conflicted, with Olympic qualification on the line for them as much as for England, "the rudest thing I've ever heard," and Scotland's captain Rachel Corsie called it "disrespectful" and "outrageous." Third, any doubt about Scotland's intentions was put to bed, temporarily at least, in the opening three minutes, with Bronze clattered into late twice as Scotland looked to make an early impression, that rare foray forward urged on by a vocal Scotland crowd. Wiegman, for her part, had urged her players to "go wild from the first minute" while cautioning "but you don't want to get erratic," and England came out of the blocks searching for an early goal to assert their authority. Among the crowd, after Lauren Hemp raced free on the right, a hopeful "Come on Lauren" was met with a thick, cheery Scottish "Shut up!" behind the press box.



---


# Healy's Criticism Of A One-Off Test Outside A Multi-Format Series

Australia's captain Alyssa Healy insisted the Mumbai Test should have formed part of a multi-format series, in the same way most top-tier women's tours are now conducted: the claim is that the match felt like a novelty and, in a sense, meaningless, and the warrant is that without overall series points for a trophy the contest carried nothing beyond itself.

The structural facts the report gives are that while one Test, three ODIs and three T20s will be played, each is an individual contest rather than an overarching series in the way the Ashes is decided — and that Australia had taken the trophy used for the multi-format 2021-22 series against India to be contested, only to be told by authorities that system would not be used.

Healy separated her disappointment at the result from her disappointment at the format: "I sit here disappointed that we couldn't win the Test match," she said. "But at the end of the day, we weren't necessarily playing for points, we weren't playing for overall series points for a trophy. It does make it a little bit of a novelty in a sense. The fact that it sort of feels meaningless to a sense is really disappointing to me. But in saying that we are disappointed that we couldn't get ourselves over the line."



---


# India vs Australia In The 2023 World Cup League Match

The most recent clash between the two sides before the 2023 final was the league match of that same World Cup, which India won by six wickets. Australia won the toss, chose to bat first and posted a target of 200 runs, being bowled out in 49.3 overs; David Warner scored 41 runs off 52 balls and Steven Smith 46 runs off 71 balls. For India, Ravindra Jadeja picked up three wickets, with Kuldeep Yadav and Jasprit Bumrah picking up two each.

India were in a terrible position at the start of the second innings as both openers got out for a duck and India lost three wickets for just two runs. Two brilliant and sensible innings by KL Rahul and Virat Kohli, who scored 97 runs off 115 balls and 85 runs off 116 balls respectively, took India to shore.



---


# Healy Denies The End Of Australian Women's Cricket Dominance

Alyssa Healy rejected the suggestion that the Test defeat to India showed Australia's unprecedented period of dominance was ending: her counter attacks the inference from a single result, arguing the loss is "probably not even a blip" because it came in a format and conditions the team is not familiar with.

Quizzed on the point after the loss, Healy was defiant. "It's probably not even a blip," she said. "It (Test cricket) is a format where we're not overly familiar with, in conditions that we're not familiar with. I see more positives out of this and than any sort of negativity."

She then challenged the standard being applied to the team, arguing that outside expectations have not kept pace with a squad in transition: "There is always a lot of expectation and external noise about our team and how we're performing. They are so used to seeing us winning, that I think, at times, they forget that we've actually seen quite a lot of change over the last 12 to 18 months. That kind of goes unnoticed external to our group."



---


# Healy's Case For A Three-Test Series In India

Alyssa Healy called for Australia's Test series in India to be extended to three matches after their defeat — their first in 11 Tests against India: the claim is that a three-Test tour would provide a better match-up between the two sides, and the warrant is that a one-off Test in India's home conditions makes the hosts heavy favourites, so it cannot be a true test of either side's abilities.

"It would create a real contest over three games," Healy said. "That would be an unbelievable experience for our group, and probably a true test of of both sides' abilities. The one-off Test, India playing in their home conditions, you'd expect them to be heavy favourites." She grounded the request in what the four days showed: "But the way we tried to adapt and continue to learn throughout the four days was really impressive. We would love to have another crack at it, show what we learned and put it into practice."

Healy is realistic in conceding her wish is unlikely to be granted, and the report gives the scheduling facts behind that: the last women's Test series of more than one match was way back in 2006, and India had not hosted any red-ball cricket for nine years before this summer. "The nature of the female game at the moment is it's very white-ball dominant," Healy said. "Trying to fit it all in to the calendar and fitting all the white-ball games in seems to take precedence. But you take three one-day games out, and we could probably play two more Test matches."



---


# IPL 2024 Auction: The Capped Wicketkeepers Set

The capped wicketkeepers set at the IPL 2024 auction produced only two sales, both at Rs 50 lakh: K.S. Bharat to KKR and Tristan Stubbs to Delhi Capitals. Phil Salt, Josh Inglis and Kusal Mendis all went unsold.

The sequence ran: at 3:08 PM IST Tristan Stubbs went to Delhi Capitals for Rs 50 L and Phil Salt went unsold; at 3:10 PM IST KS Bharat came up next and went to KKR for Rs 50 L; at 3:12 PM IST the Australian Josh Inglis was next at a base price of Rs 2 Cr and remained unsold; and at 3:13 PM IST Kusal Mendis also went unsold.



---


# Australia Women's Test Defeat To India In Mumbai, December 2023

Australia stumbled to their first Test defeat to India, by eight wickets in Mumbai on Sunday, after being outplayed by the hosts in foreign spinning conditions, as reported by The Roar on 24 December 2023.

The scorecard detail given is that Australia were all out for 209 in their first innings and looked far more confident in their second effort of 261 despite the wicket showing more signs of wear; the hosts then easily chased down 75 in the fourth innings.

The report places the loss against Australia's recent record. It comes after one of the more difficult periods for the side in the past six years, following the retirements of Meg Lanning and Rachael Haynes. Earlier in 2023 Australia won their fourth straight global ICC event in the 50-over World Cup, then retained the Ashes via a drawn multi-format series in England in July — a tour that included losing four of six white-ball matches, with Australia's win in the Test enough to leave them level on points with England and hold onto the trophy. The current tour of India is not a multi-format series, and the defeat in the one-off Test marks Australia's first loss in a four-day game since January 2014.



---


# The Rugby Australia High-Performance Director Role And Its Remit

The Rugby Australia director of high-performance is the position at the top of the governing body's high-performance structure, described by chief executive Phil Waugh in December 2023 as the biggest job on his leadership team in terms of its impact on the general sentiment around the game in Australia.

Three duties define the role as described. First, the director oversees all of Australia's men's and women's high-performance programs. Second, the holder is tasked with "integrating" those programs, as Rugby Australia tries to centralise all of Super Rugby's high-performance programs. Third — and perhaps most pressing at the time — the director must build a list of coaching candidates to take over from Eddie Jones, with Rugby Australia wanting the new Wallabies coach set in stone by the start of Super Rugby.

The scope conditions attached are timing and seniority. Rugby Australia always said it wanted the role filled by Christmas, and Waugh's framing sets the standard for the appointment: "It's a big job. It's the biggest job on my leadership team in terms of the impact it has on the general sentiment around the game."



---


# India vs Australia In The 2015 World Cup Semi-Final At Sydney

Australia beat India by 95 runs in the second semi-final of the 2015 World Cup in Sydney on 26 March, which Zee Business describes as Australia's revenge for the 2011 quarter-final. Australia outplayed India in almost all departments of the game: Man-of-the-Match Steve Smith scored 105 runs in 93 balls and Aaron Finch 81 runs in 116 balls, taking Australia to 328 runs for 7 wickets in 50 overs, reported elsewhere in the same publication as a target of 329 with seven wickets lost. Umesh Yadav picked up four wickets for India.

In reply India needed a few big innings but, apart from skipper MS Dhoni with 65 runs in 65 balls, Shikhar Dhawan with 45 runs in 34 balls and Ajinkya Rahane with 44 runs in 68 balls, the batting order collapsed miserably; India crumbled within 233 runs in 46.5 overs, with Dhoni the highest scorer for the Indian side. James Faulkner picked up three wickets for Australia, with Mitchell Johnson and Mitchell Starc taking two wickets each. Australia went all the way to lift their fifth ODI World Cup trophy, defeating New Zealand in the final.



---


# India vs Australia At The 1983 World Cup

India met Australia for the very first time at a World Cup in 1983 and lost that match by 162 runs. Australia posted a target of 321 runs courtesy of a brilliant 110 runs off 131 balls by Trevor Chappell, with Kapil Dev taking a fifer in that innings; India crumbled within 158 runs, with Ken MacLeay picking up six wickets for Australia.

India got their revenge in the very same World Cup, defeating the Australian side by 118 runs. India set a target of 248 runs after being bowled out in 55.5 overs, with Yashpal Sharma scoring 40 off 40 and Jeff Thompson and Rodney Hogg picking up three wickets each for Australia. Australia then crumbled within 129 runs, with Roger Binny and Madan Lal picking up four wickets for India. India went on to win their first-ever ODI World Cup, defeating the West Indies in the final.



---


# The Three Concurrent Roles Of A Manchester United Manager

Barney Ronay models the Manchester United job as three concurrent roles — managing the past, managing the dysfunction of the present, and managing the everyday metrics on which the manager is judged.

First you must manage the past, which is constantly in the room and which skews every act, achievement and expectation. Second you must manage the dysfunction of the present, which expresses itself in every detail from a leaking stadium roof to the deep ills of a playing squad peopled with squatters and long-term missteps. Finally you get to manage the everyday metrics — team, results, style, energy, messaging: win things, improve players, create a coherent and happy internal culture, but do it during an unceasing takeover circus while star players sulk and brief against you, and while the ghost of Hamlet's father still skulks in the eaves. The three hold together only under those conditions; as of the December 2023 Champions League exit, Ronay judged, this felt like the end of one thing, perhaps even the beginning of the end of something else.



---


# Samu Kerevi's 2023 Rugby World Cup Disappointment

Samu Kerevi said he did not perform at the 2023 Rugby World Cup where he wanted to, after injuries conspired to limit his potential in France, Wide World Of Sports reported on 7 October 2023.

Kerevi was photographed holding his face in disbelief in one of the defining images of the World Cup, after the Wallabies were pumped 40-6 by Wales in Lyon. The 30-year-old is undoubtedly one of the world's finest centres in peak form. "I don't think I performed where I wanted to perform at a World Cup," he said. "I hold myself to high standards and I just felt like I could have helped the team more in certain aspects ... I've been out of the game for nine months but I felt good coming into it ... I just felt like I was blowing a bit, but felt good towards the back end of a couple of games. But again, it's not where I want my performance to be."

Despite being dropped for Lalakai Foketi for the pool win against Portugal, Kerevi said he had no thoughts of following fellow Fijian-Wallaby Marika Koroibete into international retirement. He wanted to regain form at club level with Urayasu D-Rocks while keeping his hand up for Test selection. "I chose to leave Australian shores and understand the ruling around that and what it holds," he said. "I've got to perform for my club first and if you get the call up, you get the call up. If you don't, I'll take my three months break and enjoy that."

qid: Does the Fortune article suggest that Alameda Research's business practices with FTX were legal, in contrast to the TechCrunch article's focus on the valuation of Alameda Research's assets in FTT tokens?
context:
# Alameda Research

Alameda Research is the crypto-trading firm Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded in 2017, before FTX existed. FTX came two years later, in 2019, and Bankman-Fried co-founded it as a complement to Alameda — to help bring in revenue and liquidity for the trading arm. The founding order is the discriminating fact: the exchange was created to serve the trading firm, not the other way round.

The feature that later set Alameda's balance sheet apart was how much of it consisted of the affiliated exchange's own token. A report showed that Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of "unlocked FTT," alongside $2.16 billion of "FTT collateral." FTT was the token behind FTX. So the trading firm's single biggest asset was the token issued by the exchange founded to support it.



---


# The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse

FTX came apart in early November 2022 through a chain with four links: a leaked balance sheet revealed that Alameda's largest holding was FTX's own token in a quantity larger than the token's whole market, the disclosure destroyed confidence, the world's largest rival exchange pulled its holdings out, and the resulting bank run forced FTX and Alameda into Chapter 11 within days. TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account sets out the sequence: in early November 2022, that all changed.

Concerns surrounding FTX's liquidity grew after CoinDesk published a copy of Alameda's balance sheet, showing the firm held $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. The balance sheet showed that the $5.82 billion in FTT tokens that Alameda owned was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap, which was about $3 billion at the time — meaning Alameda purported to have more FTT tokens on its balance sheet than what existed in the world. Around the same time it was exposed, the world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, started pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT; Binance had held an equity position in FTX from 2019 to 2021. That withdrawal essentially triggered a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. mid-November 2022, Bankman-Fried resigned, and John J. Ray III, the Enron turnaround veteran, was appointed the new CEO.

The condition the whole mechanism rests on is the fragility of the underlying valuations. As TechCrunch put it on 2023-10-02, all of that activity came to a crashing end because the value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value — so when those valuations fell, they fell very, very hard. The chain therefore only runs as described where an asset is priced on expectation, held in size by a related party, and exposed to a counterparty large enough that its exit alone starts the run.



---


# The FTT Token And The "Sam Coins"

FTT was a token created by Bankman-Fried and Wang and issued by FTX, and it was one of several "Sam coins" — a nickname for tokens Bankman-Fried was heavily involved in and owned a lot of, either personally or through Alameda. Wang described FTT as being "sort of equity" in FTX, a characterisation The Verge's reporter suspected some crypto lawyers would dispute but that would probably please the SEC.

The distribution was lopsided from the start. Alameda got its war chest — 60 percent to 70 percent of the initial supply — for free, while seed investors got FTT at 10 cents a coin and FTT first listed at $1 a coin. Ellison testified that Bankman-Fried felt $1 per coin was psychologically important and directed her to buy up FTT using Alameda if the price fell below a dollar.

The discriminating feature of the Sam coins was that their book value was not realisable: they were almost certainly worth less than the value displayed on the balance sheet, because trying to sell them all at once would crater the prices. Bankman-Fried nonetheless directed Ellison to put those coins on the balance sheets Alameda showed to lenders, even though she felt doing so was "somewhat misleading." FTT also figures in the origin story of Alameda's negative-balance privilege: Wang said Bankman-Fried at first told him the code change letting an account go negative was to pay for expenses for the FTT token, but once implemented the ability to go negative was used for other things, including trading and unlimited withdrawals of FTX's trading fees and customer money.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse](ftx_collapse_mechanism.md)
- [Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership](sbf_and_ellison_relationship_and_alameda_leadership.md)



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.

# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. Later Alameda's balance was more negative than FTT and the trading revenue combined, and Wang had further conversations with Bankman-Fried about it. Wang testified he knew at the time that Alameda was using FTX customers' funds and that he knew it was wrong.

The same gradual accommodation shows in Ellison's account. Choking back tears, she testified: "When I started working at Alameda, I don't think I would have believed you if you told me I would be sending false balance sheets to our lenders or taking customer money, but over time, it was something I became more comfortable with."

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. # Ellison's Risk Spreadsheet For Venture Investments

Caroline Ellison testified that she prepared a spreadsheet at Bankman-Fried's request in the fall of 2021 and shared it with him, analysing the risk to Alameda of repaying its loans if they were abruptly recalled by its lender Genesis. Bankman-Fried wanted to use $3 billion for venture investments, so Ellison ballparked what that would do to Alameda's risk: in the as-is scenario she put the chance they would not be able to meet the loan recalls at 30 percent, and if Bankman-Fried spent $3 billion on investments, the chance rose to 100 percent — even with FTX customer funds.

What made this the worst of her testimony, in The Verge's account of the October 10th, 2023 proceedings, was not the math, which seemed pretty arbitrary, but the assumption underneath it: Ellison's calculations assumed Alameda could borrow $1.8 billion in normal dollars and $1.5 billion in crypto from FTX, and the spreadsheet made this explicit with a row labeled "FTX borrows," which Ellison said were customer funds. The background condition was that Alameda was also getting loans from outside lenders such as Genesis, because when FTX started there were not a lot of customer funds to borrow.

The day ended with a document shared between Ellison and Bankman-Fried, his comments appearing in bubbles along the main text. Ellison had written that she was worried about "both actual leverage and presenting on our balance sheet." Bankman-Fried responded with a note: "Yup, and could also get worse."

# Bank Run

## Definition

In the corpus, a bank run names the specific event in which rival exchange Binance's withdrawal of its remaining BUSD and FTT holdings "essentially triggered a bank run on FTX," the acute liquidity event that preceded FTX and Alameda's Chapter 11 filings.

## Context

In the corpus the term names the acute phase of FTX's November 2022 collapse: after a leaked Alameda Research balance sheet showed the firm's largest asset was billions of dollars of FTX's own FTT token — more FTT than existed in the entire market — rival exchange Binance began pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, and TechCrunch reports this action "essentially triggered a bank run on FTX." The run was the mechanism that converted a confidence crisis into an immediate liquidity failure, and it directly preceded FTX and Alameda filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in mid-November 2022.

## Key Characteristics

- **Confidence-driven, not solvency-driven at onset** — the run began once the leaked balance sheet destroyed trust in FTX/Alameda, independent of whether the underlying assets were ultimately worthless.
- **Triggered by a large counterparty's exit** — it was Binance's withdrawal of its remaining BUSD and FTT holdings, not a broad retail panic, that set off the run described in the corpus.
- **Fast-moving** — the run happened in the same early-November-2022 window as the balance-sheet leak, ahead of the Chapter 11 filings that followed in mid-November 2022.
- **Terminal for the institution** — in this case the run was followed by Chapter 11 filings for both FTX and Alameda, and Bankman-Fried's resignation.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a bank run is a general banking-system phenomenon: it occurs when many depositors, fearing a bank may fail, rush to withdraw their money at once, and because banks hold only a fraction of deposits as cash, a large enough run can become a self-fulfilling prophecy that drives the institution into sudden insolvency. (Wikipedia, "Bank run," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_run)

# FTX's Fabricated Backstop Insurance Fund

Gary Wang testified on October 6th, 2023 that FTX lied about how much money was in its backstop fund, and the court was shown the code that generated the fake number published on FTX's website: it took the daily trading volume on FTX, multiplied it by a random number, divided it by a billion, and added the result to the number already displayed on the site. That figure had nothing to do with the actual amount of money in the insurance fund.

The fund mattered because of what FTX advertised. In many crypto networks, if someone lost enough money the exchanges could stick other traders with the losses too; FTX touted its automated liquidation as the way to avoid this, so that one customer going bankrupt would not affect the others. In the process of liquidating, FTX would try to sell the collateral on the open market, and if it could not finish, backstop liquidity providers would step in — market makers, including Alameda, which could be compensated for the losses they took from the backstop fund. Wang also testified that when there was not enough money in the fund, money was moved there from Alameda's accounts in order to pay the insurance out.

The prosecution's framing was that this was not merely a matter of Alameda holding special, secret privileges: it claimed those privileges were used to obfuscate basic elements of FTX's operations, exposing the exchange's supposed selling points as a lie.

# Alameda Absorbed FTX's Losses, Including MobileCoin

Alameda Research functioned as FTX's sin-eater: when FTX took a loss, the loss was moved onto Alameda's balance sheet so that FTX would not look bad. Gary Wang testified that in 2021 FTX was facing a "several hundred million dollar" loss from an exploit in MobileCoin — apparently in April 2021, though Wang did not give a month — and Bankman-Fried directed him to have Alameda take it on instead, because FTX's balance sheets were visible to investors and Alameda's were not.

The relation was general, not a one-off. Ellison testified that her tenure as CEO of Alameda Research was an exercise in optics: when FTX took a loss in the hundreds of millions of dollars because a trader had exploited its system, Wang moved that loss onto Alameda's balance sheet, and FTX's "insurance fund," meant to keep traders from getting stuck with other traders' losses, was totally made up, with Alameda simply picking up the tab. The concealment held all the way to investors: Paradigm Capital's Matt Huang showed the court the balance sheets he had received from Bankman-Fried, and they did not include the loss, which should have appeared in the second-quarter numbers he was given — those instead showed $63 million in trading expenses and $63 million in "other expenses" for the quarter, and an estimated profit of $732 million.

Bankman-Fried offered a benign reading of the same arrangement from the stand: he said the MobileCoin loss, the one Wang said Alameda took to keep off FTX's balance sheet, was a totally innocent matter in which he thought it appropriate that Alameda take the position as a backstop liquidity provider.

# FTX's Cooperating Witnesses

FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang and Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse, and both planned to cooperate with prosecutors. TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-01 that they would be major witnesses in the trial, given their close ties to Bankman-Fried, FTX and Alameda.

The criminal charges were not their only exposure. Alongside them, Wang and Ellison face civil penalties from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

# FTX

FTX was a crypto exchange that at its height was the third-largest in the world, backed by an unusually broad investor base and carrying enormous daily trading volume. Within two years, more than 80 investors provided about $2 billion in capital to FTX, helping Bankman-Fried propel his vision into a reality.

Its funding peaked in January 2022, when the company raised $400 million in a Series C round that boosted its valuation to $32 billion — its last round of public funding. Trades on FTX climbed up to $15 billion a day, and TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 piece notes that as that activity grew, SBF also got tied up in the corridors of political power. By the time his trial began, TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account framed the whole story as one question: how did the once third-largest crypto exchange get here?

# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.

# Chapter 11 (Bankruptcy)

## Definition

Chapter 11 is the U.S. bankruptcy filing that insolvent companies in the corpus use to seek protection from creditors, and it does not guarantee a company survives: some filers are restructured under new leadership, while others wind down anyway once inside it.

## Context

In the corpus, Chapter 11 is the recurring endpoint for companies whose finances collapsed in 2022–2023. FTX and its trading-firm affiliate Alameda Research filed for Chapter 11 in the U.S. in mid-November 2022, after a published Alameda balance sheet exposed a huge FTT-token shortfall and a Binance-triggered bank run wiped out FTX's liquidity; the filing coincided with Sam Bankman-Fried's resignation as CEO and the appointment of Enron turnaround veteran John J. Ray III in his place. The same collapse pulled other crypto firms into Chapter 11: BlockFi filed in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading followed in January, both noted by TechCrunch as part of the wider fallout from FTX's collapse. Outside crypto, WeWork filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in November 2023, listing over $18.6 billion of debt; TechCrunch's Week in Review opened its coverage of the filing with "as predicted," without stating when or on what basis it had made that prediction. SmileDirectClub took the same route but did not come back from it: the company shut down three months after its Chapter 11 filing, citing $900 million of debt — showing that a Chapter 11 filing in this corpus can precede either continued operation under new leadership (FTX) or an eventual full shutdown (SmileDirectClub).

## Key Characteristics

- **Used by companies of very different scale and sector** — from a $32-billion crypto exchange (FTX) to a flexible-office-space firm carrying $18.6 billion of debt (WeWork) to a smaller consumer startup (SmileDirectClub).
- **Often accompanies a leadership change** — FTX's filing came with Bankman-Fried's resignation and Ray's appointment as the new CEO to run the estate.
- **Does not guarantee the company continues operating** — SmileDirectClub shut down three months after filing, despite having gone through Chapter 11.
- **Can spread across a sector after one high-profile filing** — BlockFi's and Genesis Global Trading's Chapter 11 filings followed FTX's within months, both noted by TechCrunch as part of the wider fallout from FTX's collapse.
- **Distinct from Chapter 7**, the other U.S. bankruptcy chapter appearing in the same corpus's 2023 tech-layoffs list, which cybersecurity startup IronNet filed as it ceased all business activities.

## Background (external)

The corpus repeatedly names "Chapter 11" as the filing route without stating what the chapter itself legally entails. Chapter 11, formally Chapter 11 of Title 11 of the U.S. Code, is the reorganization bankruptcy: it lets a debtor continue operating as a "debtor in possession" while it develops a plan to restructure its debts and pay creditors, rather than immediately liquidating its assets — which is the province of Chapter 7 instead (United States Courts, *Chapter 11 - Bankruptcy Basics*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.

# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

# Alameda's Special Privileges Written Into FTX's Code

Gary Wang told the court that Alameda received advantages through code baked into FTX's software granting it special access to the exchange — "We gave special privileges on FTX that gave unlimited withdrawals on the platform to Alameda" — privileges that ultimately resulted in Alameda owing FTX $8 billion worth of customer deposits.

The structure had several linked parts. Alameda was allowed to withdraw and transfer funds and had a $65 billion line of credit. "When customers deposited USD, it went to Alameda," Wang said. "It existed in the computer code. Alameda could have negative balances and unlimited withdrawals." That "bug" in the code was written by Nishad Singh, FTX's director of engineering, and reviewed by Wang, with Bankman-Fried calling the shots. Wang also told the court about a $1 million personal loan he received and a $200 million to $300 million loan in his name from Alameda that was never deposited into his account but was used to make investments into other companies on behalf of FTX — all done by Bankman-Fried, he testified. The escalation was visible over time: in early 2020 Wang discovered for the first time that Alameda's negative balance exceeded FTX's revenue, an indication that Alameda was taking customer funds, and he brought this to Bankman-Fried's attention several times; in late 2021 he discovered Alameda had withdrawn $3 billion from its $65 billion line of credit. The ownership and authority around it: Wang owned 10% of Alameda while his boss owned the other 90%, his compensation was a base salary of $200,000 per year plus stock, and he owned roughly 17% of FTX — and even though they were co-founders, "ultimately it was Sam's decision to make" when there were disagreements. Born in China, Wang moved to the U.S. at age 7 and grew up in Minnesota before going to MIT to study math and computer science, worked at Google after college, and first met Bankman-Fried during high school at a summer camp.

# Alameda Research's Origins And Naming

Alameda Research was the cryptocurrency trading firm Bankman-Fried started in 2017 during a crypto bull run, and it was named for Alameda County in California, where its first office was set up. Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried said he knew "basically nothing" about cryptocurrency at the time but wanted to do arbitrage on it anyway, and that he is "somewhat introverted, naturally."

The name was chosen for cover. In his own words on the stand: "Effectively, we wanted to be under the radar at that point in time. I didn't want to call it Sam's Crypto Trading Firm or anything like that. We — there are a lot of competitors and people who we didn't particularly want to know what we were building out because they would race to do it. 'Research' was a sort of generic word, which filled out the company name. And that was — it was far better than the internal name that we had at that point, which was Wireless Mouse." The Verge's reporter noted she would find this more believable had she not already watched a video, played during Gary Wang's first day of testimony with Bankman-Fried and the jury present, of Bankman-Fried explaining on a podcast that the name made it easier to get a bank account.

The founding assembled the people later charged alongside him: Bankman-Fried went on a hiring spree, taking on Wang to program the computers, then Nishad Singh about a month after founding Alameda Research, and finally Caroline Ellison. Though Bankman-Fried was CEO and also majority owner, he wanted to be clear that he did not supervise Wang's direct work. After a run of wildly successful arbitrage — 50 percent to 100 percent annualized returns, per his testimony — he decided to found a cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, figuring he would fail and putting the chance of success at 20 percent, without defining the time period he had in mind.
