# Bankman-Fried's Claimed Ignorance Of Alameda's Finances

Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried attacked the prosecution's premise that he knew about the hole in FTX by claiming he did not learn of the $8 billion liability associated with Alameda until October 2022, that he found it all by himself by looking at a computer database, and that when he found it he was "very surprised." The Verge's reporter recorded the claim with heavy scepticism.

The counter-argument extended to reinterpreting each earlier warning as something innocuous. On why Alameda served as FTX's "payment provider" for bank transfers, he said FTX could not get bank accounts right away and he anticipated it would take a year or two, so rather than wait he used Alameda: "My understanding at the time was that there were teams managing the process. At the time, I wasn't entirely sure what was happening." On Adam Yedidia's testimony about an August 2022 conversation regarding the enormous amount Alameda owed FTX, Bankman-Fried remembered it differently — Yedidia was just asking about Alameda's risk profile and he was not talking about insolvency at all. On the dramatic balcony conversation with Nishad Singh at their penthouse, he said Singh thought Alameda's liabilities had gotten too high and that FTX was spending too much on marketing, while Bankman-Fried still thought Alameda had more assets than liabilities so it was all fine, and besides, if Singh thought he would be better at marketing he could take it over — it did not have anything to do with the money Alameda owed FTX at all.



---


# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."



---


# Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership

Caroline Ellison testified that she and Bankman-Fried started sleeping together in the fall of 2018, on and off, when she was a trader and he was CEO, and that they later dated twice — first from the summer of 2020 through the summer of 2021, a relationship they agreed to keep secret though some people found out, and again from the fall of 2021 until the spring of 2022, when they lived together. She was named co-CEO of Alameda with Sam Trabucco in 2021 while she and Bankman-Fried were broken up, and CEO in 2022; the goal, Bankman-Fried told her, was to "optically" separate Alameda Research and FTX. "The whole time we were dating, he was my boss at work," she said. They broke up because she wanted more from the relationship and he was distant and not paying enough attention to her. He did not grant her equity even though she asked, telling her it would be too complicated; instead she got a $200,000 salary, even as CEO, and bonuses twice a year ranging from $100,000 to $20 million.

Bankman-Fried gave a different rationale for the handover. In 2021, he testified, FTX was growing to millions of users with $1 billion of revenue, he was working 12 to 22 hours a day and taking one day off every couple of months, and because FTX had grown so much he could no longer run both companies — so he handed Alameda off to Ellison and Trabucco, who immediately after being named co-CEO promptly drifted away to early retirement. Bankman-Fried did remain involved in hedging and risk at Alameda.

Ellison's proximity also gave her an unusual view of his character. She said Alameda was troubled from her earliest time there in 2018: "Shortly after I started, I learned the company was in worse shape than I realized." Alameda had initially been funded with loans "from acquaintances," and those loans were recalled a few weeks after she arrived; when she asked Bankman-Fried why he had not shared the company's shaky circumstances in the job offer, "He hadn't known how to tell me," she said. She described him as "very ambitious," said he told her there was a 5 percent chance he would become president of the United States, and said he told her that if there were a coin flip where tails destroyed the world and heads made the world twice as good, he would flip the coin — which he called being "risk-neutral," and which The Verge's reporter called a fancy way of saying he was a gambling addict. He made her CEO of his sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give her equity.



---


# SBF's Arrest And Bail

Bankman-Fried was arrested in December 2022 in the Bahamas, where FTX was based, and was then extradited to the U.S. to face a number of criminal charges. He was released on a $250 million bail bond and remained under house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto. TechCrunch set out the sequence on 2023-10-01.

That release did not hold. It was revoked in August, after he was accused of intimidating Alameda's former CEO, Caroline Ellison, by leaking her private diary.



---


# June 2022: Alameda's Reckoning And Lender Repayment

By 2022 Alameda's negative balance on FTX had become a cause for concern for Caroline Ellison, Nishad Singh, and Gary Wang, who built a spreadsheet to work out how negative Alameda actually was; the version shown in court ran to several pages of attempts to reconcile, and Wang figured Alameda owed FTX about $11 billion at a time when FTX's revenue was about $1.5 billion. Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried then met in the Bahamas office, where Alameda's lenders wanted their money back and Bankman-Fried directed the group to pay the lenders back using FTX customer funds.

Bankman-Fried considered shutting Alameda down and even wrote a long memo about it, but Wang testified that in a now-deleted Signal discussion of that memo he told Bankman-Fried and Singh they could not shut Alameda down because they could not repay its debt. Another empty Signal chat, with its setting to delete messages after a week, was shown to the court; its members were Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried.

Bankman-Fried's own account from the stand ran differently. He testified that in June 2022 he heard about the account called "fiat@ftx" tracking how much money Alameda owed to FTX, that he did not know what it was and did not bother to find out because he was busy, and that this was when he directed Ellison to repay Alameda's lenders because he thought Alameda was good for it. He also gave BlockFi and Voyager, two crypto lenders, some capital infusions for good measure.



---


# Allow_negative: Alameda's Exemption From FTX Liquidation

"Allow_negative" was a column in FTX's account database that exempted Alameda Research — and only Alameda — from the exchange's automated liquidation, letting Alameda hold a negative balance and withdraw money its accounts did not have. Gary Wang testified that it originated in a code commit dated July 31st, 2019 under Nishad Singh's username, titled "OTC trades and transfers to special accounts." Written in Python, it added two columns to the account database, the relevant one being "allow_negative," a toggle that when on let the account go negative; the feature was switched on the same day by a second set of code also carrying Singh's username, and Wang said he supervised.

The structure it modified was FTX's risk management. As Wang explained it, a futures exchange is the middleman that lets strangers bet with each other: it sits between the two ends of the bet, paying the winner and collecting from the loser, which is why it requires collateral, and under some circumstances it automatically sells that collateral to limit its losses. On FTX this liquidation process was automated and took about 30 seconds to find the accounts that needed to be liquidated to minimize FTX's losses. Normal customers — the defense objected to "normal" and was overruled — could be automatically liquidated, but not Alameda. Wang testified that Bankman-Fried "told me a few times to make sure that Alameda's account is never liquidated on FTX," and that "the code addition was the result of those conversations." Alongside the exemption, Alameda could place orders faster than other users and held an enormous line of credit, and the court saw evidence that users may have unwittingly deposited money into Alameda rather than FTX.

The relation holds only for Alameda: no other customer trading on FTX had allow_negative privileges, and the same day the toggle was switched on in July 2019, Bankman-Fried tweeted that Alameda "is a liquidity provider on FTX, but their account is just like everyone else's" — a tweet shown in court, and to The Verge's reporter evidence that the fraud at FTX started very early, just months after FTX was founded. Bankman-Fried offered a competing origin story from the stand: FTX's big selling point was its "risk engine," which in 2020 was "effectively sagging under the weight" of the exchange's rapid growth so that time to liquidation stretched to minutes, and at one point the engine got stuck in a catastrophic feedback loop that would have created losses in the "trillions of dollars," with Alameda teetering on the brink of a liquidation that "would have disastrous consequences" for FTX. "At the time, I wasn't entirely sure what was happening," he testified, saying that because of that experience he suggested an "alert" or "delay" to keep Alameda from being liquidated by a bug, that allow_negative was the eventual result of that conversation, and that he did not know about it until very recently. The dates do not fit: allow_negative was coded and switched on in 2019, and the code was displayed in court in front of Bankman-Fried and the jury.



---


# Alameda's $65 Billion Line Of Credit At FTX

Alameda Research held a line of credit at FTX that ultimately reached $65 billion, an effectively unlimited borrowing facility unmatched by anyone else on the exchange and carrying no requirement to post collateral. Caroline Ellison testified that there was no contract and no written terms, and that the credit line was not visible to FTX's auditors; when she raised that with Bankman-Fried, he told her not to worry about it.

The defining features are its size, its informality, and its exclusivity. Gary Wang, who set the line up, testified that it did not start that big: Bankman-Fried asked him to increase it a few times because Alameda kept running into its limits — first "a few hundred million," then a billion, then even that was not enough. It was not clear how Wang arrived at $65 billion specifically, but he said he had discussed the number with Bankman-Fried, and that other customers did not have the same privileges. Ellison said the credit was drawn in increments of $100,000 to $10 million at a time and was used primarily for trading: the effectively unlimited funds "allowed us to make profitable trades we couldn't have made otherwise."

The boundary case is the source of the capital and Bankman-Fried's disclaimed knowledge of it. Ellison testified that Alameda and FTX were initially "very integrated," run by the same team from the same office, and that when Alameda was scrounging for funds Bankman-Fried told her FTX would be a good source of capital. On the stand, Bankman-Fried denied he knew about the effectively infinite line of credit Alameda received from FTX — an argument The Verge's reporter found peculiar, summarising the take-away as that the CEO of a financial company simply did not pay attention to finances.



---


# Gary Wang's Ownership Stake And Cooperation Deal

Gary Wang, co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX and co-founder of Alameda Research, owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX and drew a $200,000-a-year salary with no performance bonuses — though at times he was a billionaire on paper — while Bankman-Fried owned 90 percent of Alameda and 65 percent of FTX. He returned to the US on November 16th, met with the US government on November 17th without having been arrested or charged, offered to cooperate immediately, and pled guilty to various charges a month later. Wang was clear that he was cooperating because he did not want to go to jail, and said he hoped his assistance would lead a sentencing judge to be lenient.

The Verge's reporter drew from the disparity a puzzle she could not resolve: Wang took bizarre risks for a relatively small share. Bankman-Fried did not code, so none of his fingerprints are on the technical changes that let FTX allegedly defraud its customers and investors, while Wang supervised the code behind a key prosecution claim — that Alameda Research was afforded secret, special privileges with FTX's funds. When FTX went down, Wang left himself with no plausible deniability. Wang, a college roommate of Bankman-Fried's, took the stand after Adam Yedidia and, in the reporter's phrase, sang like a canary about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code.

The delivery was heavy going. On October 6th, 2023 Wang had to explain to the jury the difference between a front end and a back end, explain futures trading, and read a great deal into the record, which took a while; it was a tough day for the jury, and probably for Wang, who spoke quickly, perhaps from nerves.



---


# Code Evidence Outweighs Deleted Signal Messages

The Verge's reporter argued after Gary Wang's October 6th, 2023 testimony that Bankman-Fried's vanishing Signal messages might not help him as much as he had hoped, because the durable evidence was the code — and the code implicates him even without the messages. The grounds: Wang's account was the first full account of Alameda's and FTX's entanglements heard in the trial, and it came from a co-owner of both companies; while there was evidence of the computer code that gave Alameda special privileges, there was no evidence of the conversations Wang recounted.

The warrant is that the code constrains who could have made the decisions. Wang was a dev; the money was not his area. And while Bankman-Fried can try to blame Ellison for some of the decisions, the code shows she could not have made all the calls — after all, she was not FTX's CEO, and in 2019 she was not Alameda's CEO either. Bankman-Fried also said too many things in public to too many people, so even without the smoking gun of Signal messages, it is hard to see how he was not involved.

The same logic explains Wang's own behaviour: of course he turned himself in quickly, because sooner or later someone would find his code — and Singh's, too.

context:
# Palestinian Content Moderation Distrust On Meta's Platforms

Users are also turning to Snapchat for information about Gaza as accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content fuel distrust in platforms like Instagram and Facebook.

The policies themselves are not what separates the platforms: Meta's policies are not dissimilar to Snap's Community Guidelines, which prohibit pornographic content, content that advocates or advances terrorism, and content that portrays gratuitous or graphic violence.

What differs is the volume of complaint and the resulting user behavior. Allegations of censorship against Snapchat are not as frequent as they are against Meta's platforms, but many users are still urging others to screen record Stories posted from Gaza in case they are taken down.



---


# Snapchat Design Features Alleged To Enable Drug Sales

The lawsuit against Snap claims that Snapchat's features facilitate practices like drug sales by connecting dealers to young customers while promising them safety from legal repercussions through anonymity.

Chief among those designs, according to Matthew Bergman, the lead attorney on the case, is the promise that a message will disappear not only for fellow users but also on the software's back end. That is the ground that turns a product feature into an enabler of crime: it prevents law enforcement officials from seeing the activity of a dealer even after the dealer has been identified.

The complaint names other features as problematic too: notifying individuals when another person screenshots their post, the ability to geolocate fellow users, and algorithms that suggest new connections based on demographics.



---


# Section 230

## Definition

Section 230 (of the Communications Decency Act) is a US law that shields online platforms from legal responsibility for the illegal actions of their users, and separately protects the platforms' own content moderation decisions.

## Context

In the corpus the statute surfaces in two distinct disputes. In the Snapchat fentanyl-death lawsuits, Snap's motion to dismiss cites Section 230 as its liability shield against claims that its platform facilitated illegal drug sales between users. In the Supreme Court case over the Texas and Florida content-moderation laws, Oregon Senator Ron Wyden — described as Section 230's co-author — invokes the statute's other function, protecting the moderation decisions platforms make about what content to host, arguing that the state laws would gut what Section 230 lets platforms do.

## Key Characteristics

- **Dual shield** — the corpus shows it protecting platforms on two separate fronts: liability for users' illegal conduct on the service (the drug-sale claims against Snap) and liability for how a platform moderates content (the basis of Wyden's objection to the Texas/Florida laws).
- **Conditional, not absolute, immunity** — per the Snap case, the statute "only offers immunity to companies that have acted responsibly and taken precautions to prevent illegal activity from taking place on their platforms," a condition the plaintiffs' attorney argues Snap failed to meet.
- **Legislative authorship tied to the moderation function** — Senator Ron Wyden is named in the corpus as a co-author of Section 230, invoked specifically to defend its role in enabling platforms to remove harmful content without losing legal protection.



---


# The Section 230 Defense In The Snap Fentanyl Lawsuit

Snapchat's answer to the parents' complaint attacks its legal foundation rather than its facts: the company filed a motion to dismiss citing Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which protects online platforms from being held responsible for the illegal actions of their users. A hearing on that motion was scheduled for 18 October.

The plaintiffs' rebuttal concedes the statute but disputes that Snap qualifies for its shelter. Section 230 only offers immunity to companies that have acted responsibly and taken precautions to prevent illegal activity from taking place on their platforms — something lead attorney Matthew Bergman says Snap has not done.

"It's the world's largest open-air drug market," Bergman said. "It was clearly designed with the intention of allowing and encouraging nefarious activity with a lack of record."



---


# Shadowbanning

## Definition

Shadowbanning, as TechCrunch describes it, is when a platform "shadowbans, or limits the visibility of" a user's content without the platform notifying the user that anything has been restricted, so the user only discovers it by noticing a drop in views or reach.

## Context

In the corpus the term names the central accusation in the October 2023 controversy over Meta's handling of Palestine-related content: Instagram users accused Meta of shadowbanning their Stories about Palestine, and TechCrunch frames the belief that Meta "shadowbans, or limits the visibility of," such content as longstanding rather than new to that month.
The same allegation is cited beyond Meta's own platforms as a driver of platform choice: users turned to Snapchat's Snap Map for firsthand Gaza content specifically because accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content on Instagram and Facebook had eroded their trust in those platforms.
Meta's official response did not deny that reach had dropped; it denied the mechanism, attributing the reduced Story reach specifically to a global, content-neutral bug in Stories that re-shared Reels or Feed posts, and separately attributed a different global bug — one that had prevented some users from going live — to technical error rather than deliberate suppression tied to subject matter.

## Key Characteristics

- **Covert, not disclosed** — the defining feature reporters and users pointed to is that visibility drops silently, with no notification to the affected account; Bella Hadid described being "immediately shadowbanned" and her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million" with no explanation from the platform.
- **Detected by comparison, not confirmation** — users inferred shadowbanning by comparing engagement across their own posts (e.g., a user whose Stories fell from "100s of views to zero or a handful" and rebounded only after posting unrelated content like a cat photo), since the platform provided no direct evidence of restriction.
- **Contested mechanism** — Meta disputed that the effect was shadowbanning-by-design, attributing the reduced Story reach to a bug that "affected accounts equally around the globe" and "had nothing to do with the subject matter of the content," rather than confirming intentional visibility limits.
- **Trust-eroding beyond the platform itself** — the accusation pushed users toward alternative platforms (Snap Map) even though the accused conduct occurred on Instagram and Facebook, showing shadowbanning claims can shift audience behavior across platforms, not just within one.



---


# Snap's Moderation Response To Drug Dealer Accounts

Snap's defence against the charge that it does nothing about dealers is that it moderates: after the Guardian's story published, a spokesperson said Snap works to "block search results for drug-related terms" and redirects at-risk users to resources on the dangers of fentanyl. "We have great empathy for families who have suffered unimaginable losses. At Snap, we are working hard to stop dealers from abusing our platform," the spokesperson said. Snap did not respond to the Guardian's request for comment prior to the story's release.

Parents in the suit contest that claim on the record of what actually happened when they reported dealers. Perla Mendoza, whose son Daniel (Elijah) Figueroa died after buying fentanyl-laced pills from a dealer on Snapchat, found that Snap did little to prevent illegal drug sales in the weeks and months after his death: even after she created her own account and found her son's dealer posting images with hundreds of pills, her reports to the help center went unanswered, and it took eight months for them to flag his account. "It was really disheartening," she said.

Hanh Badger's objection goes further, attacking the sufficiency of account removal as a remedy at all. "They'll just create another," she said, emphasising the need for structural reforms that clearly warn young users of dealers' predatory practices, or that make it so drugs cannot be peddled to kids on the platform in the first place. "Snapchat perpetuated this crisis," she said.



---


# The Social Media Victims Law Center's Lawsuit Against Snap

In April 2023, the relatives of more than 65 victims, represented by the Social Media Victims Law Center, filed lawsuits against Snap, the parent company of Snapchat — an app known for its disappearing messages features, and the platform used by the vast majority of the suit's victims.

The suits are one expression of a wider response by bereaved parents. In their grief, victims' parents are motivated to end this crisis to prevent another family's suffering while also giving meaning to their loss, and many have launched awareness campaigns, founded educational programs and advocated for legislative change.

What is new is the venue: some parents are now taking to the civil courts, targeting the tech giants whose platforms facilitated their children's purchases of the pills that killed them.



---


# User-Generated Content

## Definition

User-generated content (UGC), in the corpus, is the term for content that ordinary platform users — rather than the platform itself or a news organization — create and publish, such as Reels, Stories, posts, and streams.
The EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) treats UGC as a defined regulatory object, requiring "social media platforms and other services that carry user-generated content" to act on reports of illegal content and disinformation (doc_0025).
Snap itself describes the public Stories submitted to Snap Map as "authentic user-generated content" offering perspectives that traditional news outlets may not reflect (doc_0124).

## Context

The corpus treats UGC primarily as the object of content-moderation obligations and disputes rather than as a neutral technical term: the EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) explicitly regulates "how social media platforms and other services that carry user-generated content must respond to reports of illegal content," putting X under a legal obligation to act on flagged posts and mitigate disinformation risk (doc_0025).
On Meta's platforms, individual users' Reels and Stories about Palestine became the flashpoint for accusations of moderation bias, with filmmaker Khitam Jabr suspecting that her own Palestine travel Reels were restricted for 24 hours after other users reported them (doc_0106).
On Snapchat, an X user described the crowd-sourced public Stories submitted to Snap Map as "a WEALTH of real-time information" for journalists who could not get on the ground in Gaza, and Snap confirmed a "moderate" increase in Stories submissions from the region since October 7 (doc_0124).
Mozilla frames the broader problem as one of governance: today's large, advertiser-funded social networks decide how UGC is moderated and monetized, which is part of why it is building a decentralized "fediverse" alternative (doc_0026).
On Twitch, UGC is also an economic asset — streamers' broadcasts are the content being monetized, and disputes over revenue splits and the Partner Plus program center on how creators are compensated for the content they generate (doc_0401).

## Key Characteristics

- **User-originated** — the content is authored and published by ordinary platform users (e.g., Reels, Stories, posts, streams), not by the platform or a newsroom (doc_0106, doc_0124).
- **Subject to platform moderation and reporting** — UGC can be flagged, restricted, or shadowbanned by other users' reports or automated systems, as Jabr suspected happened to her Palestine travel videos (doc_0106).
- **Regulatory trigger** — under the DSA, a platform's responsibility to act on illegal UGC and disinformation is a defined legal obligation, not just a policy choice (doc_0025).
- **Real-time information source** — one X user called Snap Map's crowd-sourced Stories "a WEALTH of real-time information" for journalists who weren't on the ground in Gaza, and Snap confirmed a "moderate" rise in submissions from the region (doc_0124).
- **Monetizable** — UGC is also the basis for creator revenue-sharing arrangements, making its governance a business as well as a moderation issue (doc_0401).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "user-generated content" (UGC) — also called "user-created content" (UCC) — is generally defined as content generated by users of the Internet, such as images, videos, audio, text, testimonials, software, and user interactions (Wikipedia, "User-generated content," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User-generated_content).

# Snap Map And "Our Story"

Snap Map first launched in 2017 as a location-sharing feature that lets users see where their friends are posting Stories from, displayed on an interactive map. Users can also share their content to "Our Story," a collaborative public archive of Stories posted from popular locations, which are displayed as hotspots on a "heat map": if many users are posting Stories from around the same location, like a music festival, it will show up on the heat map.

The feature that distinguishes Our Story from an ordinary repost feed is a capture constraint. Although Snapchat is not immune to misinformation, spreading fake content via Our Story is not as easy as reposting a video on X or TikTok: users can upload content from their camera roll to their own Stories, but it will not be eligible for Our Stories.

Snap encourages users to "capture what's happening" around them to increase their chances of making it to Our Stories, and the submission guidelines say the company looks for "Snaps that provide a window into everyday life."

# Snap's Decision To Keep The Gaza Heat Map Live

Snap decided to keep Snap Map live in Gaza, a choice that stands against its own precedent. The company is not indifferent to geopolitical conflict: in 2022 Snap disabled its heat map in Ukraine as a "safety precaution," The Verge said, to prevent Russia from tracking civilian evacuations, and instead displayed a "curated feed" of public Stories.

A spokesperson for Snap told TechCrunch that Snap Map will stay live to allow users to continue sharing their experiences during the crisis, and that the company is monitoring hot spots for content that may spread misinformation or incite violence. Snap will "closely assess" if it needs to take additional action.

The spokesperson also acknowledged that Snap Map is a crucial resource for "authentic user-generated content" from perspectives that may not be reflected by traditional news outlets.

# Snap Map's History As A Civic Documentation Tool

In the years since Snap Map launched, it has become an unexpected resource for keeping up with current events and highlighting political protests. Following the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida in 2018, students used the map to document and archive the nationwide classroom walkout demanding stricter gun control. During the Black Lives Matter protests in 2020, Snapchat users posted videos expressing solidarity and recording instances of police violence against protestors.

This is also not the first time Snap Map has been used to demonstrate the disparity between Israeli cities and occupied Palestinian territories. The May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah prompted weeks of protests internationally, and violent fighting between Hamas and Israel.

The juxtaposition the heat map produced then was the point: Stories posted throughout Israel showed users washing their cars and celebrating their birthdays, while Stories posted from Gaza documented a neighborhood reduced to rubble.

# X's Revenue Decline And The Information-Network Decay Argument

Charging all users for access to X could be the final nail in the coffin of the platform as a real-time information network, because it risks triggering a further and final exodus of the remaining legacy users whose knowledge and engagement lent Twitter its original value.

The grounds are financial. Subscription revenues to the revamped Twitter Blue paid offering, now called X Premium, do not appear to have been substantial enough to plug the advertising gap, which may explain Musk's recent suggestion that he plans to charge all users a small fee. The warrant joining that to the conclusion is a claim about what makes an information network work: a bona fide information network depends on a critical mass of genuine users to pay attention and contribute value and vitality — its life-blood. Remove the paywall-averse legacy users and disinformation and spammers may rush in to fill the gap, generating a parody of activity; without the genuine users, X really will mark the spot of Twitter's demise.

# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.

# Social Networks' Drift From Connection To Algorithmic Feeds

The claim is that social networks stopped being social. At some point they were no longer about connecting with your closest friends, keeping up with long-distance family members and feeling a special connection with people you love; TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook, YouTube and X (formerly Twitter) are all slowly evolving to become the same infinite scrollable feed of algorithm-optimized short videos from top performers. TechCrunch's writer notes he had argued in a 2018 article that 2018 was "the year social networks were no longer social," and that while he is not sure 2018 was the turning point, the premise still holds up well.

The structural ground Mozilla offers is ownership and revenue: social networks are often run by large corporations — like Meta, Snap and Google — where advertisers pay the bills, which has created a world where modern social networks are profit-driven and consumer needs are not always at the forefront. The warrant is that when advertisers pay, the feed optimizes for them rather than for connection.

Mozilla dates the inflection point: this disconnect between what people want and what today's networks offer hit an inflection point in 2022, when billionaire Elon Musk bought Twitter, leading to a surge of interest in alternatives to centralized social networking including apps like Mastodon and Bluesky. Under Musk, Twitter — now called X — has prioritized "free speech" managed by crowdsourced-based moderation, and its policies have resulted in increased hate speech and toxic content on the platform, some studies have shown.

# Disinformation

## Definition

Disinformation is false or misleading content spread online — distinct from the illegal-content category (like terrorism or hate speech) in that, per the corpus's account of EU regulation, disinformation "is not illegal in the EU per se," yet still counts as a *systemic risk* that large platforms must assess and mitigate.

## Context

The corpus's central storyline is the EU's escalating regulatory pressure on X (formerly Twitter) over disinformation tied to the Israel-Hamas war: the Commission's October 2023 warning and formal information request to Musk accused X of being used "to disseminate illegal content and disinformation" following the Hamas attacks, and a EU-commissioned study later found X had "the largest ratio of mis/disinformation posts" among major platforms.
Because X is a Digital Services Act (DSA) "very large online platform" (VLOP), the obligation to mitigate disinformation risk is legally binding on it even though the underlying falsehoods are not themselves illegal; the EU's voluntary Code of Practice on Disinformation (which Musk pulled X out of earlier in 2023) is treated by the Commission as a signal of DSA compliance on this exact risk.
Disinformation also surfaces as a generative-AI worry: Suleyman warned DeepMind's ethics board that AI "could lead to an explosion in disinformation," EU commissioner Vera Jourova flagged AI-generated disinformation as an election threat, and early fears that ChatGPT would be used "to generate disinformation on a massive scale" pushed European policymakers toward mandating security assessments of generative AI products.
Real-world examples in the corpus include a video-game clip falsely presented as Hamas missile footage circulating on X, and misinformation described as "rampant on social media" during the Gaza crisis, prompting some users to turn to Snap Map for unmediated, firsthand footage instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **Not illegal per se in the EU** — disinformation is treated as a systemic risk to be mitigated, not content that platforms are legally required to remove the way they must remove illegal content.
- **Distinct from "misinformation" but often paired with it** — the corpus uses both terms (e.g., "mis/disinformation posts," Mozilla's content-policy list of "misinformation" as a harm category), generally without a sharp technical distinction, though disinformation carries a stronger connotation of deliberate falsehood or manipulation (e.g., "Kremlin propaganda").
- **A VLOP systemic-risk obligation** — under the DSA, platforms designated VLOPs (like X) must proactively assess and mitigate disinformation risk, which is what makes an EU formal-information request or investigation possible even absent an illegal-content finding.
- **Measurable and comparable across platforms** — the EU's Code of Practice enabled a pilot study producing "structural indicators" (e.g., how easily disinformation content is found, how much engagement it gets) that let regulators rank X as worst among mainstream platforms.
- **A named risk of generative AI** — beyond social-media falsehoods, the corpus repeatedly frames disinformation as a downstream risk of AI text/image generation (ChatGPT, deepfakes), motivating both EU AI-Act-era safeguards and industry-side labeling commitments.

# Meta Researchers Avoided Documenting Under-13 Users

A potential smoking gun in the lawsuit is a series of anecdotes from Meta researchers delicately avoiding the possibility of inadvertently confirming an under-13 cohort in their work.

One wrote in 2018: "We just want to make sure to be sensitive about a couple of Instagram-specific items. For example, will the survey go to under 13 year olds? Since everyone needs to be at least 13 years old before they create an account, we want to be careful about sharing findings that come back and point to under 13 year olds being bullied on the platform." In 2021, another, studying "child-adult sexual-related content/behavior/interactions," said she was "not includ[ing] younger kids (10-12 yos) in this research" even though there "are definitely kids this age on IG," because she was "concerned about risks of disclosure since they aren't supposed to be on IG at all." Also in 2021, Meta instructed a third-party research company conducting a survey of preteens to remove any information indicating a survey subject was on Instagram, so the "company won't be made aware of under 13." Later that year, external researchers provided Meta with information that "of children ages 9-12, 45% used Facebook and 40% used Instagram daily."

During an internal 2021 study on youth in social media described in the suit, researchers first asked parents if their kids were on Meta platforms and removed them from the study if so. But one researcher asked, "What happens to kids who slip through the screener and then say they are on IG during the interviews?" Instagram Head of Public Policy Karina Newton responded, "we're not collecting user names right?" — in other words, TechCrunch notes, what happens is nothing. As the lawsuit puts it: "Even when Meta learns of specific children on Instagram through interviews with the children, Meta takes the position that it still lacks actual knowledge of that it is collecting personal information from an under-13 user because it does not collect user names while conducting these interviews. In this way, Meta goes through great lengths to avoid meaningfully complying with COPPA, looking for loopholes to excuse its knowledge of users under the age of 13 and maintain their presence on the Platform."

# The Digital Services Act

The Digital Services Act (DSA) is the European Union's pan-EU content moderation rulebook: a regulation that places governance obligations on digital services and platforms carrying user-generated content, with the aim of ensuring companies respond to reports of illegal content, and that layers heavier duties on the largest platforms. Its baseline obligations apply to digital services and platforms generally — respond diligently to notices of illegal content, clearly communicate terms and conditions to users, and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement of those terms.

The discriminating feature of the regime is its second tier. Platforms designated as "very large online platforms" (VLOPs) carry additional obligations to identify and mitigate systemic risks such as disinformation, gender-based violence, or negative effects on the exercise of fundamental rights. The Commission designated 19 VLOPs in April 2023, including Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram; X is also a designated VLOP. Compliance for VLOPs kicked in over the summer of 2023 — TechCrunch dates Meta's compliance start to August.

The regime's boundary case is disinformation itself. Unlike terrorism content, disinformation is not illegal in the EU per se. The DSA therefore does not reach it through the illegal-content removal route at all; it reaches it through the systemic-risk route, obliging a VLOP such as X to mitigate the risks attached to harmful falsehoods while separately acting diligently on reports of genuinely illegal content. The two duties run on different legal tracks even when they concern the same posts.

Penalties for confirmed breaches can be as high as 6% of global annual turnover, and the bloc holds a further power, in extremis, to block access to a service in the region for repeated infringements — meaning a platform that repeatedly fails to correct course could be shut off in the EU. TechCrunch illustrates the scale on both ends: Elon Musk last projected revenues of about $3 billion for 2023 for X, which by that example would cap a fine at up to $180 million, while in Meta's case the same 6% ceiling could run to multiple billions.

The regulation also contains a "crisis response" mechanism (Article 36) which enables the Commission to adopt rapid-fire measures on larger platforms in situations of "serious threat", such as war. As of TechCrunch's October 2023 reporting this part of the regulation was not yet operative: it would not start operating until February 17 of the following year, because it requires an advisory body — the European Board for Digital Services — to be operational before it can recommend that the Commission adopt a crisis response mechanism, and the Board's set-up was itself waiting on Member States to establish national Digital Services Coordinators, the bodies that oversee DSA compliance for non-VLOPs.

# Musk's Removal Of Trust Signals And The Turn To Community Notes

Under Elon Musk, X has pushed the use of an existing crowdsourced fact-checking feature, rebranded as Community Notes, which essentially seeks to outsource the issue to an arm's-length process of aggregating views from platform users, some of which may be appended as contextual notes to dubious tweets.

At the same time, Musk set about removing signals Twitter users were previously able to rely on to help assess the quality of information tweets contained — removing state-affiliated media labels from propaganda outlets and replacing legacy account verifications with pay-to-play. A report by misinformation watcher NewsGuard, published the same day as the EU's disinformation analysis, found that Musk's decision to remove labels denoting state-run or government-affiliated media accounts led to a surge in propaganda spreading on X, with Russia's RT seeing the biggest gains per the analysis.

# Bonta: The Numbers Are For Impact, The Violation Is The Point

AG Rob Bonta's claim is that the scale of Meta's under-13 user base is rhetorical, not legal: any child at all makes the conduct illegal. It is difficult to extrapolate from the 2015 and 2020 numbers to today's, which as the evidence presented shows will almost certainly not be the whole story, but Bonta noted that the large figures are presented for impact, not as legal justification. "The basic premise remains that their social media platforms are used by millions of children under 13. Whether it's 30 percent, or 20 or 10 percent… any child, it's illegal," he said. "If they were doing it at any time, it violated the law at that time. And we are not confident that they have changed their ways."

Bonta also distinguishes the strength of the counts. The other complaints in the lengthy lawsuit have softer edges, such as the argument that use of the platforms contributes to poor body image and that Meta has failed to take appropriate measures, which is arguably not as actionable; the COPPA material is far more cut and dry. His evidence that notice was given: "We have evidence that parents are sending notes to them about their kids being on their platform, and they're not getting any action. I mean, what more should you need? It shouldn't even have to get to that point."

The warrant is a claim about design as choice: "These social media platforms can do anything they want. They can be operated by a different algorithm, they can have plastic surgery filters or not have them, they can give you alerts in the middle of the night or during school, or not. They choose to do things that maximize the frequency of use of that platform by children, and the duration of that use. They could end all this today if they wanted, they could easily keep those under 13 from accessing their platform. But they're not."

# Ed Ternan's Case Against Suing Snap

Not every bereaved parent supports the litigation. Ed Ternan, whose 21-year-old son Charlie died in April 2020 after taking a counterfeit Percocet he bought on Snapchat, sees suing the platform as counterproductive: "It feels like looking backwards," he said.

His objection targets the premise that responsibility can be located in the platform alone. Ternan, who did not join the suit, explains that losing his son — an energetic and fun-loving young man who was weeks away from graduating from UC Santa Cruz — forced him to come to terms with the several factors that came together to cause Charlie's death: the app, the dealer, the friends Charlie bought drugs alongside, and himself as a father. "What was my role as a parent?" Ternan asked.

The conclusion he reached is one that looks beyond blame. With his wife, Ternan now works full time on initiatives to educate parents on the dangers of fentanyl, and he has even worked with Snap to promote awareness campaigns and find ways to make the app safer. "It's been a very successful partnership," Ternan said.



---


# Youth Distrust Of Legacy News Media

Snap Map has served as an alternative source of eyewitness accounts during times of social unrest, as young people increasingly perceive news media reporting as "biased."

Trust in legacy media is waning in younger generations. A 2022 Pew Research Center survey found that American adults under 30 trust information from social media nearly as much as they trust information from national news outlets. A report conducted by the Knight Foundation earlier in 2023 concluded that perceptions of political bias in news have increased, and that young people hold more negative perceptions of news media than their predecessors.

The pattern combines high consumption with low trust: younger people also consume the most online news, but report the lowest trust in national news outlets.



---


# The COPPA Allegations Against Meta

The attorneys general claim Meta knowingly enrolls and collects data from children under 13 without lawful consent. "We're very bullish and confident in our COPPA allegations. Meta is knowingly taking steps that harm children, and lying about it," AG Rob Bonta told TechCrunch in an interview. "In the unredacted complaint we see that Meta knows that its social media platforms are used by millions of kids under 13, and they unlawfully collect their personal info. It shows that common practice where Meta says one thing in its public-facing comments to Congress and other regulators, while internally it says something else."

The grounds are the pairing of an omission with actual knowledge. The lawsuit argues that "Meta does not obtain—or even attempt to obtain—verifiable parental consent before collecting the personal information of children on Instagram and Facebook… But Meta's own records reveal that it has actual knowledge that Instagram and Facebook target and successfully enroll children as users." The warrant is that COPPA liability turns on knowledge: an unknowing failure to identify underage users would be a different case from one where the company's own records show it knows.

The alleged motive supplies the link between the two: while the problem of identifying kids' accounts created in violation of platform rules is certainly a difficult one, Meta allegedly opted to turn a blind eye for years rather than enact more stringent rules that would necessarily impact user numbers.



---


# The Republican State-Level TikTok Ban Push

Though opposition to TikTok has been bipartisan, the crusade to ban the platform over national security concerns is primarily led by Republicans at the state level, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-02. The article treats that position as a likely contributor to the party's social media struggles with young voters.

The observation matters because it sets the party's legislative posture against its outreach problem: the same platform Republicans are campaigning to ban is the one where the youth vote concentrates.



---


# Whose First Amendment Rights Are At Stake: Editorial Judgment

The case revolves around First Amendment rights — but, counterintuitively, it is the rights of the social media companies that are in question, not the rights of their users. The claim being litigated is that platforms themselves hold a constitutionally protected right to exercise editorial judgment over what appears on the services they own.

The grounds are how the question is actually posed. As Barrett framed it: "The question here is: Do social media companies have a First Amendment protected right to exercise what you might call editorial judgment?" — and, in the fuller version, "what you might call editorial judgment — or what you also might call content moderation — in sorting out what expression does and does not appear on the platforms that they own?"

The warrant joining the two halves is the equivalence Barrett draws between editorial judgment and content moderation. "These cases are about the First Amendment and how the First Amendment applies to social media companies. And then more specifically, what the First Amendment has to say about content moderation, which is obviously a subset, although a really big and important subset of what social media companies do," Barrett said. If moderation just is editorial judgment, then a platform's decisions about what to carry are the platform's own expression, and the users' speech rights are not what the case turns on.

The scope condition is that this remains an open question rather than a settled doctrine. In Barrett's words, "it's just not clear right now what precisely the First Amendment says about that question."



---


# ChatGPT Legal And Privacy Controversies

ChatGPT has generated a run of legal and privacy controversies: an Australian mayor publicly announced he may sue OpenAI for defamation over ChatGPT's false claims that he had served time in prison for bribery, which would be the first defamation lawsuit against the text-generating service, and there have been other cases of ChatGPT accusing individuals of false crimes.

The libel exposure follows from how the models work: they do not know or care whether something is true, only that it looks true — a problem when the output is used for homework, and potentially libel when it accuses someone of a crime they did not commit. How troubling statements produced by ChatGPT will be handled was expected to play out over the following months as tech and legal experts tackled the fastest moving target in the industry. As of the article, there were no lawsuits specifically targeting ChatGPT, but OpenAI is involved in at least one lawsuit with implications for AI systems trained on publicly available data, which would touch on ChatGPT. There are also plagiarism issues: text-generating AI models like ChatGPT have a tendency to regurgitate content from their training data. Copyright in output sits with the user — the person who requested the input from ChatGPT is the copyright owner.

On privacy, OpenAI has said that individuals in "certain jurisdictions" such as the EU can object to the processing of their personal information by its AI models by filling out a form — the "OpenAI Personal Data Removal Request" — which includes the ability to request deletion of AI-generated references about them, although OpenAI notes it may not grant every request since it must balance privacy requests against freedom of expression "in accordance with applicable laws." In its privacy policy OpenAI makes a passing acknowledgement of the objection requirements attached to relying on "legitimate interest," pointing users to instructions on how to opt out of use of their information to train its models. ChatGPT chats are not public, but OpenAI disclosed a bug, since fixed, that exposed the titles of some users' conversations to other people on the service.

Other controversies span platforms and schools. Discord integrated OpenAI's technology into its bot Clyde, and two users tricked Clyde into providing instructions for making methamphetamine and napalm. CNET found itself in controversy after Futurism reported the publication was publishing articles under a mysterious byline completely generated by AI, and Red Ventures, the private equity company that owns CNET, was accused of using ChatGPT for SEO farming even where the information was incorrect. Several major school systems and colleges, including New York City Public Schools, have banned ChatGPT from their networks and devices, claiming the AI impedes the learning process by promoting plagiarism and misinformation — a claim not every educator agrees with.



---


# The 42-State Lawsuit Against Meta Over Harms To Young Users

A coalition of 42 states and D.C. is suing Meta over its harms to teens and young users, in part referencing findings from Meta whistleblower Frances Haugen. The former employee had provided to news outlets a treasure trove of documents that appeared to indicate Meta understood the harms it was causing — including things like body image issues among teens — but did not take action. Instagram head Adam Mosseri was later hauled before Congress in December 2021 to defend the app's teen safety record, but as of November 15, 2023 legislators had not come to any decision about how to regulate teen usage of these platforms.

The suit was filed in October 2023, and a newly unredacted version reported on November 27, 2023 alleges a troubling pattern of deception and minimization in how the company handles kids under 13 on its platforms, with internal documents that appear to show the company's approach to this ostensibly forbidden demographic is far more laissez-faire than it has publicly claimed. The lawsuit alleges a wide spread of damaging practices at the company relating to the health and well-being of younger people using it: from body image to bullying, privacy invasion to engagement maximization, all the purported evils of social media are laid at Meta's door — perhaps rightly, TechCrunch notes, but it also gives the appearance of a lack of focus.

In one respect at least the documentation obtained by the attorneys general of 42 states is quite specific, "and it is damning," as AG Rob Bonta of California put it. That is in paragraphs 642 through 835, which mostly document violations of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA — a law that created very specific restrictions around young folks online, limiting data collection and requiring things like parental consent for various actions, but which a lot of tech companies seem to consider more suggestion than requirement.



---


# Editorial Judgment

## Definition

Editorial judgment is the term used in the Texas/Florida social-media Supreme Court case for social media companies' own claimed First Amendment right to decide what user expression does and does not appear on the platforms they own — a right belonging to the companies, not their users (doc_0256).

## Context

The term appears in the corpus as the crux of the First Amendment question the Supreme Court agreed to decide in the consolidated Texas and Florida cases over state laws (Texas's HB 20 and Florida's SB 7072) restricting how social media companies moderate content: "Do social media companies have a First Amendment protected right to exercise what you might call editorial judgment... in sorting out what expression does and does not appear on the platforms that they own?" (doc_0256).
NYU adjunct law professor Paul Barrett, quoted as the case's explainer, treats editorial judgment and content moderation as two names for the same activity — "what you might call editorial judgment — or what you also might call content moderation" — which is why the case is framed as testing whether content moderation itself counts as constitutionally protected speech (doc_0256).
Barrett is explicit that the underlying question is unsettled: "it's just not clear right now what precisely the First Amendment says about that question" (doc_0256).

## Key Characteristics

- **The platform's right, not the user's** — the case is counterintuitively about whether social media companies (not their users) hold a First Amendment right, since it is the companies' own curatorial decisions that the state laws restrict (doc_0256).
- **Equated with content moderation** — Barrett presents editorial judgment and content moderation as interchangeable labels for the same platform activity of "sorting out what expression does and does not appear" (doc_0256).
- **Framed as a subset of a larger question** — content moderation, and by extension editorial judgment, is described as "a really big and important subset" of what social media companies do, within the broader question of how the First Amendment applies to social media companies (doc_0256).
- **Legally unresolved** — as of the case being taken up, whether this judgment is constitutionally protected speech remained an open question rather than settled doctrine (doc_0256).
- **Consequential if rejected** — if courts find no such protected right, states could compel platforms to carry content (including misinformation and hateful content) and to give individualized explanations for removals, reshaping how moderation is practiced at scale (doc_0256).

# Player Injury Report

## Definition

A player injury report is the periodic status listing an NFL team publishes during game week (and updates live on gameday) that tags each hurt or ailing player with a practice participation note and a game-status designation such as questionable, doubtful, or out, so broadcasters and fantasy managers know who is likely to play.

## Context

The corpus shows the report operating on two timescales: the pregame weekly cycle and the in-game live update. In the weekly cycle, CBS Sports' Week 13 injury roundup (doc_0289) and Sporting News' Week 10 fantasy injury updates (doc_0288) track players through the week's practice sessions — a player who is a full participant, limited participant, or a "DNP" (did not practice) on Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday accumulates a running designation that the team finalizes before kickoff. Ja'Marr Chase's Week 10 status is a clear case: he was listed as a DNP on Wednesday, logged back-to-back limited practices, and his final active call was left until a Sunday morning pre-game workout (doc_0288). During the game itself, CBS Sports' live-blog roundup shows teams issuing real-time in-game designations — "questionable to return," "doubtful to return," "ruled out" — when a player is hurt mid-contest, as with Cooper Kupp's ankle injury and Kenneth Walker III's oblique injury in the Week 11 roundup (doc_0113). The designations also interact with roster mechanics: a player can be activated off injured reserve to play (doc_0035) or, conversely, be placed on injured reserve, as De'Von Achane was during Week 6 (doc_0149).

## Key Characteristics

- **Tiered designations** — the standard tags observed in the corpus are full participant/limited/DNP during the week, collapsing into questionable, doubtful, or out for the final pregame report (doc_0289, doc_0288).
- **Live in-game updates** — beyond the pregame report, teams issue real-time calls like "questionable to return" or "ruled out for the remainder of the contest" when a player is injured during the game itself (doc_0113).
- **Roster-status linkage** — the report intersects with injured reserve moves: players can be activated off IR to play (doc_0035) or placed on IR after a lingering issue (doc_0149).
- **Coach commentary supplements the tag** — reporters attach head-coach quotes (e.g., Achane is "day-to-day"; it would be "a little aggressive" for Jefferson to play) to the bare designation to give fantasy audiences more color than the tag alone conveys (doc_0113, doc_0288).
- **Deadline-driven finality** — some designations resolve only hours before kickoff, e.g. Justin Jefferson needing activation by a Saturday 4 p.m. ET deadline to be eligible (doc_0288).

# USMNT Substitute Ratings Against Germany, October 2023

The Sporting News rated the United States' six substitutes against Germany on Oct. 14, 2023 as Luca de la Torre 5, Cameron Carter-Vickers 7, Brenden Aaronson 7, Ricardo Pepi 5, Johnny Cardoso 6 and Kevin Paredes 5.

De la Torre, brought on to replace Gio Reyna at halftime, was unable to stem the German tide despite being a more defensive-minded option than Reyna in what should have been a swap to shore up the midfield. Carter-Vickers, on at the 65th minute, remains a top-tier centre-back in the U.S. player pool and a clear starter when healthy, with Tim Ream and even Chris Richards struggling at various stages; he came off the bench due to recent hamstring troubles but was stout in his 25 minutes, recording 22 touches, giving away possession just twice, completing two dribbles and making two clearances, and was not targeted by Germany nearly as much as the other three defenders on the pitch — a strong nod to his abilities. Aaronson, also on at 65 minutes, was probably the U.S. substitute to make the biggest impact, bright in attack, dazzling with his dribbling and helping usher the U.S. forward amid a second-half onslaught — a good showing from the Union Berlin winger who needs confidence at the moment.

Pepi entered at the same time in a far from ideal situation, coming on with the U.S. shell-shocked from the quickfire Germany double; he provided very little up front with just eight touches in 24 minutes, featured his usual pressing and came close to scoring once on a messy chance that Germany just barely cleared, but otherwise did not cause the opposing back line problems to open spaces for teammates. Cardoso, on at 75 minutes, had only 15 minutes to showcase his abilities, losing possession just once in his 10 touches and completing a tackle while also being dribbled past a few times — which begged the question why he or Lennard Maloney weren't introduced at halftime instead of de la Torre. # USMNT 1-3 Germany, Hartford, October 2023

The United States lost 3-1 to Germany at Rentschler Field in Hartford on Oct. 14, 2023, having appeared well positioned to fight with a European power through 45 minutes before the house of cards came crashing down after the break.

The U.S. entered the interval level, as a Christian Pulisic stunner was cancelled out by Ilkay Gundogan's poaching. After halftime, as Gio Reyna was withdrawn from his first start back under Gregg Berhalter to build his fitness, the U.S. midfield was overrun and the defense committed a multitude of errors, allowing the Germans to gain full control of proceedings. Goalkeeper Matt Turner summed it up afterwards: "It's frustrating because it's just little moments. Little moments made a big difference at the World Cup, and it's kinda the same story here."

# Gio Reyna's Return Under Berhalter, And His 45 Minutes Against Germany

Gio Reyna was called into the USMNT for the first time under Gregg Berhalter since their falling out at the 2022 World Cup, having recovered from a leg fracture suffered in summer Nations League duty under an interim head coach. The 20-year-old Borussia Dortmund playmaker's return was announced alongside that of defender Cameron Carter-Vickers, who had only just made his Celtic debut that season after a hamstring injury.

The working relationship had been a major talking point since the 2022 fallout: Reyna's lack of playing time at that World Cup was exacerbated by his parents' actions in the following weeks, which sparked a domestic violence investigation of Berhalter before his eventual re-hire as national team head coach. Berhalter had been forthcoming, admitting on his re-hire that the two had a "lot of work to do" while insisting time was needed to broach the situation, and later confirming they had broken the ice by phone. After the October roster release he confirmed they had spoken "weeks ago" on Zoom, said he appreciated Reyna's willingness to move forward, and — because Reyna had not yet played for his club that season — set the goal of getting him minutes so he could build fitness and return to Dortmund in the best position to begin his club campaign. Berhalter said they saw Reyna able to play three positions: central midfielder, attacking midfielder and winger, clarifying that his skill set fit a "between the lines" style of wide play rather than one glued to the touchline.

In the Oct. 14 friendly against Germany, Reyna looked sharp in the starting lineup in all the ways a young man can: unyielding energy, a surprising eagerness to cover the whole of the midfield, periodic flashes of skill, and bleach-blond hair that let viewers spot him instantly. He was exceptional throughout the first half — less influential than he might have been with greater access to the ball, but showing a welcome taste for covering ground to help on defense or retrieve the ball and launch an attack — while Weston McKennie was his typical self, particularly connecting with Christian Pulisic down the left. Playing 45 minutes was a victory of sorts after only 27 minutes in his one club appearance that season for Dortmund, having been injured in June with the U.S. and missed all of preseason and nearly two months of the Bundesliga. The one substantial element missing was being able to endure from starting to finishing. "The goal is to send him back to Dortmund in a really good spot," Berhalter said. "I think he played a good game, showed his quality. I think everyone in the first half played well. So it was good to see him, good to have him on the field." Many national team fans had sided with Reyna during the World Cup controversy; in this game they got what they argued for, but not what they wished.

# Playing Yunus Musah At No. 6 Against Germany Did Not Work

Deploying Yunus Musah in the defensive midfield role against Germany on Oct. 14, 2023 did not work, and the attempt to transform him into some semblance of Tyler Adams was almost certain to go wrong. The evidence: whenever Germany quelled an American surge in the first half and regained possession, they plowed with ease through the center of the park.

The warrant is a mismatch between the job and the player's habits. Musah is elite at maintaining possession when operating as a box-to-box midfielder, and lately his club play with Pulisic at AC Milan had put him in more of an attacking role; even granting that he might have the skill set to succeed at the No. 6, he did not appear comfortable transitioning to it on short notice. By contrast, the decision about how to replace Gio Reyna in the lineup was simple — it was always the plan for Reyna to play roughly half the game, and given the sometimes ridiculous controversy over his reserve role at the World Cup the obvious choice was to start him — whereas how to replace Adams in the formation was complex, too much so to be resolved in one afternoon.

The related claim is that removing Reyna compounded the problem: the collapse from a 1-1 halftime tie not only followed his departure but was probably connected to it, since the U.S. threatened enough with Reyna on the field to make the opposition defend more often than it preferred, while his replacement Luca de la Torre dulled the attack and did nothing to dissuade Germany's rampage toward the American net. The overall verdict is that the USMNT conjured a more compelling attack because of Reyna's presence, but the ability to control the game went missing.

# Coaching Change

## Definition

A coaching change is the replacement of a team's head coach — by firing, mutual departure, or resignation — followed by the appointment of a successor, whether an outside hire, an internal promotion, or an interim/caretaker placeholder.

## Context

The corpus documents coaching changes across sports and settings: mid-season firings in the NHL and NFL, off-season managerial exits in club and international soccer/rugby, and speculative hot-seat coverage that treats a coach's job security itself as an ongoing storyline ahead of any actual move.

The Minnesota Wild "relieved head coach Dean Evason and assistant coach Bob Woods of their duties effective immediately," naming John Hynes as Evason's successor mid-season after a losing stretch left the team "far out of the playoff picture" (doc_0340).

Manchester United's Erik ten Hag was reported to be under mounting pressure, with Sporting News laying out replacement candidates — including permanent hires like Zinedine Zidane and Julen Lopetegui and a caretaker option in club legend Michael Carrick — "if Manchester United decide to pull the plug" on his tenure (doc_0315); the same piece notes United had already cycled through eight managers, including caretakers Ryan Giggs, Ralf Rangnick, and Carrick, since Alex Ferguson's 2013 retirement.

Carolina Panthers owner David Tepper's impatience with head coach Frank Reich was framed against his earlier in-season firing of Reich's predecessor, Matt Rhule, as precedent for how quickly an owner might act (doc_0474); Yardbarker's NFC "hot seat" roundup names head coaches such as New Orleans' Dennis Allen and Chicago's Matt Eberflus as under pressure for their job status ahead of any actual move (doc_0437).

In international coaching, the Springboks' World Cup-winning head coach Jacques Nienaber and director of rugby Rassie Erasmus departed together after South Africa's 2023 Rugby World Cup triumph, and All Blacks coach Ian Foster's tenure ended the same tournament with Scott Robertson set to take over (doc_0022); U.S. Soccer's appointment of Emma Hayes away from Chelsea to lead the USWNT followed a formal, multi-round search process after the prior head coach, Vlatko Andonovski, departed following a World Cup exit (doc_0108).

## Key Characteristics

- **Trigger is performance or results** — the Wild's move came after a 5-10-4 record and a seven-game winless streak (doc_0340); the Panthers' pressure on Reich stemmed from a 1-7 record and a struggling offense (doc_0474).
- **In-season vs. off-season timing** — some changes happen mid-season as an emergency reset (Wild firing Evason, doc_0340; the precedent of Carolina firing Rhule in-season, doc_0474), while others follow a season's end (Nienaber/Erasmus and Foster departing after the World Cup final, doc_0022; Hayes's move to the USWNT set for after her Chelsea season concludes, doc_0108).
- **Successor types vary** — a permanent outside hire (John Hynes for the Wild, doc_0340; Emma Hayes for the USWNT, doc_0108), a permanent internal promotion (Evason himself had been promoted to Wild head coach after the team fired Bruce Boudreau in-season, doc_0340), or a caretaker/interim stopgap (Michael Carrick's past spells in charge of Manchester United, doc_0315).
- **"Hot seat" speculation precedes the actual move** — media coverage frequently discusses a head coach's job security, and the club's history of prior changes, well before any change occurs, treating pressure itself as newsworthy (doc_0437, doc_0474).
- **The exiting coach's own track record and contract carry forward** — Evason's Wild contract obligations continued after his firing (doc_0340), and Reich's overall coaching record was reported inclusive of a prior in-season firing by the Colts (doc_0474).

# USMNT Midfield Ratings Against Germany, October 2023

In the United States' 3-1 defeat to Germany on Oct. 14, 2023 the Sporting News rated the three central midfielders Yunus Musah 6, Weston McKennie 4 and Gio Reyna 7.

Musah did well in possession but struggled defensively — he dazzled at times on the ball but was beaten on the first Germany goal by whiffing with his slide. His nutmeg of Florian Wirtz was a highlight moment of the match and he was active on both ends of the pitch, yet a few bad giveaways or defensive moments betrayed his usual stoutness in the middle; overall the mistakes didn't detract from his performance as much as Sergino Dest's, but they were still concerning.

McKennie drew the harshest verdict. Other than a pair of critical blocks right before halftime he was a mess through the first 45 minutes, constantly unsure of where he should be as Germany built forward with incisive pace, and one of many U.S. players caught unaware on the first-half Ilkay Gundogan goal. He didn't put a first-half pass wrong, going 18-for-18 before the break and 28-for-30 overall, but his positioning was all wrong out of possession: McKennie was a sieve as the U.S. midfield was invisible defensively, leaving their defenders completely unshielded, particularly at the top of the penalty area. It was only a matter of time before the floodgates opened after halftime, and he was eventually withdrawn in what felt like one of Gregg Berhalter's only tactical substitutions of the match.

Reyna, in his first 45 minutes of international football under Berhalter since the World Cup fallout, was his usual self — drawing the attention of German defenders and proving visionary with his passing, combining with Folarin Balogun on a number of occasions on the counter in a link-up U.S. fans have been begging for. He was only fit for 45 minutes as he returns from a leg injury, but it's no coincidence that Germany truly secured midfield dominance when he came off, and the Sporting News called it a promising performance for a young playmaker who should head back to Borussia Dortmund after the international break with plenty of confidence.
