# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# FTX's Final Days And The Alameda Shortfall, As Wang Described Them

Much of Gary Wang's Friday testimony focused on the final days at FTX before the operation imploded: after media reports detailing Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, an emergency meeting was called between Bankman-Fried, Wang and Singh to discuss shutting down Alameda, and they decided against it because he and Bankman-Fried knew Alameda had no way to repay the roughly $14 billion hole in its books.

Wang, 30, was technology chief for FTX, which spiralled into bankruptcy in November; he spoke so fast that U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan and the prosecutor both stopped him at points to ask that he slow his pace. Prosecutors took the jury through a series of tweets beginning on Nov. 7 — posts from the company blaming bank hours for slow withdrawals, while Bankman-Fried tweeted from his personal account assuring customers that all was fine. "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine," Wang testified. On Nov. 12, after FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried asked Wang to drive with him to the Bahamas Securities Commission for a meeting; on the drive, Bankman-Fried told Wang to transfer assets to Bahamian liquidators because he believed they would allow him to maintain control of the company. Wang said he was not in the meeting with the securities authority, though Bankman-Fried's dad was present.

# Adam Yedidia's Testimony And The $8 Billion Bug

Adam Yedidia, the prosecution's second witness, testified that in June 2022 he submitted a report to Bankman-Fried on Signal showing that $8 billion in customer money held in an internal database tracking cash wired to an Alameda account called "fiat at ftx.com" was missing.

Yedidia met Bankman-Fried in college at MIT and the pair remained close friends; assuming a robotic posture on the stand, he said he worked out of FTX's Hong Kong office from January to October of 2021 and then in the Bahamas until the collapse. He referred to a group Signal thread called "People of the House," referring to Bankman-Fried's $35 million penthouse where many employees lived; on who was paying the rent, Yedidia recalled Bankman-Fried saying he "assumed it's just Alameda paying for it in the end." Yedidia said Bankman-Fried had told him, before he began working in the Bahamas in 2019, that he and Ellison had had sex, and asked whether it was a good idea for them to date — Yedidia said no, and Bankman-Fried responded that he was expecting that answer. One of Yedidia's responsibilities was fixing the bug in the code that gave Alameda preferential treatment. He said he and Bankman-Fried spoke about the missing $8 billion at the pickleball court at the resort in Nassau, Bahamas, where he asked his boss if things were OK because it "seemed like a lot of money" from FTX customers was at risk. "Sam said, we were bulletproof last year. We aren't bulletproof this year," Yedidia testified; asked when they would be bulletproof again, Bankman-Fried said he was not sure, but it might be six months to three years. Yedidia said Bankman-Fried appeared "worried or nervous," which was atypical, but that he still trusted Bankman-Fried and Ellison to "handle the situation." On cross-examination, Christian Everdell, Bankman-Fried's attorney, focused on how Yedidia was the one responsible for developing and reviewing the code.

# Criminal Trial

## Definition

In this corpus, "criminal trial" names the government's federal prosecution of Sam Bankman-Fried in Manhattan on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, in which prosecutors presented witness testimony to prove guilt while the defense contested it, U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan presided, and a jury returned the verdict.
The corpus uses the term specifically to distinguish this proceeding — and the format of Epic Games v. Google, a civil jury trial — from non-criminal, civil proceedings such as the Trump/Engoron case, which sought financial penalties rather than imprisonment.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal criminal trial in Manhattan, on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, presided over by U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan; the trial ran roughly six weeks, opening with jury selection on October 3, 2023 and opening statements the next day, and closing in a guilty verdict on all counts.
The proceeding follows a recognizable structure the corpus documents in sequence: jury selection, opening statements from prosecution and defense, the prosecution's case (fact witnesses like Adam Yedidia and Matt Huang, cooperating former co-conspirators Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison testifying under cooperation agreements, and expert testimony from accounting professor Peter Easton), cross-examination, the defendant's own testimony and cross-examination, closing arguments, and jury deliberation toward a verdict.
The corpus also shows what a criminal trial is not, by contrast: the parallel civil case against Donald Trump before Judge Arthur Engoron was a non-jury ("bench") trial brought by the New York attorney general seeking financial penalties, not imprisonment, and the corpus notes Manhattan prosecutors had considered and declined to bring a criminal case over the same underlying conduct — the state instead pursued civil fraud remedies. Epic Games v. Google is likewise a civil antitrust jury trial (Sherman Act, Cartwright Act claims) seeking injunctive and monetary relief, not a criminal prosecution, even though it shares the jury-trial format.

## Key Characteristics

- **Adversarial structure** — a prosecution (the government, e.g. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Danielle Sassoon, Nicolas Roos, and Thane Rehn in the SBF case) argues guilt while defense counsel (Mark Cohen, Christian Everdell) argues innocence or lack of criminal intent.
- **Jury as fact-finder** — a jury, not the judge, decides guilt; in the SBF trial the jury included a train conductor and a retired investment banker, and reporters repeatedly note what testimony "the jury saw" or "the jury will have to decide."
- **Burden and standard tied to criminal charges** — the prosecution must show the defendant's conduct was not just harmful but criminal; as one account puts it, "Just losing $8 billion is not a crime... But if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing... that's a crime," turning the case on proving intentional deceit and conspiracy rather than mere loss or business failure.
- **Cooperating witnesses and immunity/plea deals** — co-conspirators such as Gary Wang, Caroline Ellison, and witnesses like Adam Yedidia testified under cooperation agreements or legal immunity, a common feature of criminal trials involving multiple alleged participants.
- **Judge as referee, not fact-finder** — Judge Kaplan ruled on objections, instructed the jury on the law, and controlled testimony (e.g., telling the jury he was the "final authority" on the definition of "market manipulation"), while leaving the guilt determination to the jury.
- **Sentencing follows conviction** — a guilty verdict is followed by a separate sentencing phase; the corpus notes SBF's charges could put him in prison for the rest of his life and co-conspirator Gary Wang faced up to 50 years pending sentencing.
- **Distinct from civil trials** — civil proceedings (Trump/Engoron, Epic v. Google) can share elements like juries or trial-style testimony but seek monetary or injunctive remedies under a different legal standard, and can proceed without a jury at all (non-jury "bench" trial).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, a criminal trial is a court proceeding, initiated only by the government, in which the prosecution must prove the defendant's guilt "beyond a reasonable doubt" — a heavier standard than in civil cases — while the jury decides guilt and the judge oversees the proceeding and, on a guilty verdict, determines the sentence (U.S. Courts, "Criminal Cases," uscourts.gov, accessed 2026-09-02).

# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.

# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

# Code Evidence Outweighs Deleted Signal Messages

The Verge's reporter argued after Gary Wang's October 6th, 2023 testimony that Bankman-Fried's vanishing Signal messages might not help him as much as he had hoped, because the durable evidence was the code — and the code implicates him even without the messages. The grounds: Wang's account was the first full account of Alameda's and FTX's entanglements heard in the trial, and it came from a co-owner of both companies; while there was evidence of the computer code that gave Alameda special privileges, there was no evidence of the conversations Wang recounted.

The warrant is that the code constrains who could have made the decisions. Wang was a dev; the money was not his area. And while Bankman-Fried can try to blame Ellison for some of the decisions, the code shows she could not have made all the calls — after all, she was not FTX's CEO, and in 2019 she was not Alameda's CEO either. Bankman-Fried also said too many things in public to too many people, so even without the smoking gun of Signal messages, it is hard to see how he was not involved.

The same logic explains Wang's own behaviour: of course he turned himself in quickly, because sooner or later someone would find his code — and Singh's, too.



---


# Why FTX Trial Coverage Favors The Prosecution

Asked by some people why the reporting coming out of the FTX trial seemed so skewed toward the prosecution, The Verge's reporter answered that the prosecution had put together a strong, comprehensive indictment of Bankman-Fried's behavior at FTX and Alameda, while the defense had so far managed to do almost nothing in response. She said she did not know whether Cohen and Everdell had bad facts, a bad client, or were simply untalented themselves — or some combination of all three — but that she had not yet seen any good reason to doubt the very convincing story she was hearing from the prosecution.

The supporting ground is the state of the cross-examinations. Throughout the entire prosecution's case, the defense struggled to shake the credibility of witnesses such as Yedidia, Wang, and Ellison; the hits the defense made on Singh did not make her doubt the overall truth of his story — they just made her think Singh was kind of self-serving and trying to secure himself a lenient sentence. She also read Bankman-Fried's willingness to go to trial as a sign of his own belief: he must still think he can get away with it all, or he would not be dragging his closest companions' names through the mud in a jury trial.



---


# Defense Opening Statement: The Plane Metaphor

Defense attorney Mark Cohen answered the prosecution's opening not with evidence but with a metaphor: working at a startup, he told the jury with the energy of a patient father telling his obnoxious children a bedtime story, was like building a plane while flying it, and FTX the plane had flown right into the perfect storm of the crypto crash. The premise this attacks is the prosecution's claim of intentional theft — Cohen's counter was that Bankman-Fried "acted in good faith and took reasonable business measures," that FTX's and Alameda's business relationships were "reasonable under the circumstances," and, in the common white-collar defense form, that Bankman-Fried as CEO was simply too busy to oversee what everyone did every day. He also blamed Caroline Ellison and Binance CEO Changpeng "CZ" Zhao for the debacle.

The Verge's reporter judged the counter-argument self-defeating, because Cohen volunteered a fact the prosecution had not raised: FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit." That admission cuts against the good-faith premise — the lack of a risk officer kept elbowing her in the ribs as Cohen argued reasonableness, and the too-busy-to-supervise line made her more suspicious, since delegating oversight is exactly why you hire a risk officer. Cohen's own characterisation of his client worked the same way: Bankman-Fried was a math nerd who did not party, which paints a picture of someone deliberate, especially given that he left MIT immediately and went to work on Wall Street; a party-hardy trainwreck might plausibly overlook hiring a risk officer, but a deliberate person would not.

The context was that the defense had no plea to fall back on: the reporter had learned the day before that Bankman-Fried had never been offered a plea deal, since he and his attorneys had told the government they would not negotiate, which made her curious what evidence had made him so confident. The answer, she wrote, was instead a metaphor — and it is no good when your defense lawyer has just made you sound worse than the prosecution already did.



---


# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.



---


# Where FTX Customer Money Went

Expert witness Peter Easton, a Notre Dame accounting professor who had also assisted in investigating Enron and WorldCom, traced the funds behind the $11.3 billion liability that Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried had known about in June 2022, and presented the breakdown to the jury as a pie chart (the prosecution's exhibit 1045). Of that money, $1.2 billion went to repaying crypto lender Genesis; a substantial chunk went into investments including the celebrity-connected venture firm K5, the trading firm Modulo — co-founded by one of Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriends — and the AI company Anthropic.

The chart also traced money to Bankman-Fried personally and to those around him: another $413 million went directly to Bankman-Fried through his wholly-owned company Paper Bird; "outflows to insiders," which suggested Singh's not-quite-loans were included, came to $192 million; real estate accounted for another $228 million; and the donations to Gabe Bankman-Fried's Guarding Against Pandemics, combined with the philanthropy from the FTX Foundation, totaled less than $40 million.

An earlier and separate use of customer money came in the summer of 2021, when Bankman-Fried bought back FTX shares from Binance, an early investor. Ellison testified that he told her it was "really important," otherwise "Binance would do things to mess with FTX"; she told him Alameda did not have the money, so Bankman-Fried took $1 billion of FTX customer funds to buy Binance out. It was the first time Ellison recalled an amount that large, and she said it was Bankman-Fried's decision, as he was CEO of FTX.



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.

# Brock Purdy's Fantasy Outlook In Weeks 5 And 6 Of 2023

CBS Sports benched Brock Purdy in Week 5 of the 2023 season and then reversed itself in Week 6, admitting the first call was a mistake: the Week 5 argument was that Dallas' pressure plus man coverage created too much downside, and the Week 6 argument was that the author would not make the mistake of benching Purdy again after Dallas played zone and paid for it.

The Week 5 "Sit Him" case, published 4 October 2023, holds that it is safe to expect Purdy to feel a lot of pressure against the Cowboys, and that man coverage behind that pressure could create havoc that speeds him up; the column calls him consistent and the 49ers loaded, but treats this as one of those rare matchups with too much downside. After ranking him high early in the week the author moved him behind Anthony Richardson, Jordan Love and Trevor Lawrence, while keeping him ahead of Joe Burrow, Dak Prescott and Daniel Jones. The evidence for the downside: Dallas lost top cornerback Trevon Diggs and stayed red hot, leading the league in pass-rush pressure rate at 55.6% and ranking top-10 in blitz rate at 31.9%, which helped them into the top five in completion rate allowed (57.4%), passing touchdowns allowed (two) and missed tackles on pass plays (five, best in football); only Joshua Dobbs, who ran for 55 yards, had scored double-digit fantasy points against them, at 18, and their other victims were Daniel Jones, Zach Wilson and the Patriots quarterbacks. Dallas had also become one of the most aggressive defenses in the league, third from the bottom in zone-coverage snaps, having played heavy zone only in the closing quarters of blowout wins over the Giants and Jets — a completely different look from their January playoff meeting with Purdy, when they played zone on nearly 86% of snaps. In that playoff game the Cowboys pressured Purdy on 48.5% of dropbacks while blitzing just 21.2%, and Purdy completed 65% of his throws but struggled for 214 yards with no touchdowns. The counterweights the column concedes: San Francisco's 36.4% pressure rate allowed is only a shade worse than league average and is weighted by the Giants blitzing on 84.6% of Purdy's Week 2 dropbacks, a game in which Purdy still threw for 310 yards and two touchdowns without Brandon Aiyuk; Purdy had hit at least 20 fantasy points in eight of nine regular-season starts, which should be nine of nine but for a Week 2 touchdown ruled a lateral, and in nine of 11 including two playoff games, with at least 23 points in five of those nine including each of his past two; and the previous week he executed the offense flawlessly against Arizona, missing on one throw and again losing points to a pass ruled a lateral for a touchdown. His splits were strong against both man and zone — higher completion rate and yards per attempt against zone, four of his five passing touchdowns against man — but he was at his worst when pressured, completing 48.6% for 5.6 yards per attempt with a gaudy 18.9% off-target rate.

The Week 6 "Start Him" case, published 12 October 2023, is a correction. The author expected Purdy to struggle against a defense that pressured and played man; instead the Cowboys played a lot of zone and paid the price through the air, a choice a friend suggested was meant to avoid getting burned by long Christian McCaffrey runs. Against Cleveland, the combination of a hot 49ers defense and a Browns offense figuring to get stuffed should produce at least a game script for decent numbers, and the author would start Purdy over Trevor Lawrence, Geno Smith and Jared Goff. The breakdown lists San Francisco at Cleveland, the 49ers favoured by 7, an over/under of 37, an opponent ranked 1st versus quarterbacks, 16.5 projected points, an 11th quarterback ranking, and year-to-date totals of 1,271 passing yards, 24 rushing yards, 11 touchdowns, no interceptions and 23.4 fantasy points per game. In Week 5 Purdy beat one of the toughest pass rushes in football for four touchdowns on 24 attempts, with his seven incompletions comprising a drop, two balls batted at the line, a throwaway and two defensed passes, and an off-target rate of 0.0%. His 20-point streak extended to nine of 10 regular-season starts — 10 of 10 but for the lateral ruling — and 10 of 12 including playoffs, with at least 23 points in six of those 10 including each of his past three games. Cleveland has played the least zone coverage of any team in football, never even reaching 65% zone in a game and exceeding 70% in only three quarters all season, and had just watched Dallas play 90% zone while Purdy cooked them like BBQ chicken. The Browns rank third in pressure rate at 41.5% and blitz at an above-average 29.3%, but the Cowboys ranked higher and lost anyway; Purdy's pressured splits had improved to a 50% completion rate, 6.7 yards per attempt and a 15.9% off-target rate, and five of his seven passing touchdowns had come against man. Lamar Jackson's precedent is offered as the closing warrant: facing the Browns in their previous game he saw a ton of man coverage and heavy pressure yet threw two touchdowns and completed 79% of his passes for 9.8 yards per attempt without his starting left tackle and two of his top receivers, helped by his defense turning over an ill-prepared Browns offense.

# Brock Purdy Leads Lamar Jackson In The 2023 MVP Odds

According to oddschecker, as cited by Yardbarker on 2023-12-24, 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy was listed as the heavy favorite to be named league MVP at -230, while Baltimore signal-caller Lamar Jackson held the second-shortest odds at +525.

Purdy, the final pick of the 2022 NFL Draft, had seen his career unfold as if it were a fairy tale that just keeps getting more remarkable: the 23-year-old ranked first in the NFL in QBR at 76 and in touchdown passes with 29, while ranking third in passing yards with 3,795 — all especially impressive considering he was coming off offseason elbow surgery. Jackson might not have been posting the ridiculous numbers of his 2019 MVP campaign, but the adjustment in his play style in his first season under offensive coordinator Todd Monken had led to sustainable, winning football. Nevertheless, Baltimore needed an upset win for Jackson to capture another MVP Award; he had thrown for 3,105 yards and 17 touchdowns while adding 741 yards on the ground with five scores that season.



---


# Week 13 Seahawks-Cowboys: Start Dallas, Fade The Seattle Passing Game

CBS Sports argues that in the Week 13 Seahawks-Cowboys game the Dallas side of the ball should be started and the Seattle passing game faded, because the Cowboys defense should keep pressure on Geno Smith and a Seattle offense that has struggled to gain consistency over the last month. The grounds: Smith did OK completing passes when pressured last week (a 60% completion rate) but not at an efficient level (5.4 yards per attempt); only two quarterbacks have exceeded 250 yards against Dallas this year and only four have thrown multiple touchdowns against them. The warrant joining these is that the author does not like Smith's chances to do either, which hurts any upside case for any Seahawks receiver — if the quarterback cannot reach volume or touchdown thresholds, the pass-catchers downstream of him cannot either. A supporting data point on how hard Dallas is to beat through the air: Curtis Samuel was the first receiver to get 100 yards on the Cowboys this year, and it took him 12 targets and 9 catches to get there; no one else has had more than 86.

One scope condition is stated up front: both teams had a week of rest, so this should not be treated like a typical Thursday game. The resulting verdicts are STARTS — Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, Tony Pollard, DK Metcalf (as a low-end WR2), Jake Ferguson and the Cowboys DST; SITS — Tyler Lockett (flex at best), Geno Smith, Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Zach Charbonnet, Michael Gallup and the Seahawks DST; SLEEPERS — Brandin Cooks.

# Justin Fields As A Week 5 2023 Bust Candidate At Washington

CBS Sports flagged Justin Fields as a "Bust Candidate" for Week 5 of the 2023 season at Washington: the claim is that Fields is being started only for his passing, and the warrant is that a short-week trip behind the league's worst pass protection, with his designed rushing all but gone, removes the floor that usually protects his fantasy score.

The grounds separate the opponent from the circumstances. Washington itself is not that big a step-up in competition for Fields — but it is for his offensive line. The Commanders have a slightly below-average pass-rush pressure rate, with only one game all year above 30% (52.7% at Denver, where Russell Wilson still had a great game even discounting a Hail Mary touchdown catch), ranking seventh in sacks with 13 and 13th in pressures with 53, both around league average. Chicago, by contrast, ranks league-worst in pressure rate allowed at 47.4% of snaps — nearly one in every two dropbacks — and bringing back guard Teven Jenkins might help a little, but the unit is still struggling. The deep ball is the clearest upside: Washington ranks bottom-five in attempts, yards per catch and touchdowns allowed on throws of 15-plus air yards over the past three weeks, an area Fields can exploit, since he is tied for the most touchdowns on 15-plus air-yard throws this season with four and sits around league average in completion rate, attempts per game and expected points added per dropback. The weekly breakdown lists Chicago at Washington, the Commanders favoured by 6, an over/under of 44.5, an opponent ranked 23rd versus quarterbacks, 17.3 projected points, a 10th quarterback ranking, and year-to-date totals of 861 passing yards, 134 rushing yards, eight touchdowns, five interceptions and 20.4 fantasy points per game.

The bust risk rests on how Fields' Week 4 breakout was produced and on his vanished rushing. He posted his first-ever game with four passing touchdowns and over 300 yards against a Broncos defense devoid of a serious pass rush or pass-coverage skills through three quarters — a defense that had allowed season-best fantasy numbers to each of the past three quarterbacks it faced and was a terrific matchup for anybody. Once Denver generated heavy pressure in the fourth quarter Fields finished 5 of 11 for 50 yards, no touchdowns and two turnovers. On film he looked terrific for three quarters firing downfield from clean pockets, with an off-target rate of literally 0.0% and plays where he manipulated defenders with the threat of running before throwing over their heads, including Cole Kmet's short touchdown; by the fourth he was pressured, throwing off his back foot, throwing with too much velocity or out of sync with his target, and his off-target rate rose to 9.1%, closer to his 13.6% average over the first three games. The rushing collapse is the other prop removed: after seven designed runs in Week 3 he had just two designed runs in Week 4 for two total yards, and on the season 28 rushes for 134 yards and a score. Last season Washington got a season-best 57.1% pressure rate on Fields and blitzed him on 40.5% of dropbacks, and he still cleared nearly 20 fantasy points on one passing touchdown and one interception because he ran for 88 yards — the very cushion the column doubts he will have now. The verdict is comparative rather than absolute: Anthony Richardson and Jordan Love have more potential this week, Russell Wilson, Trevor Lawrence, Dak Prescott and Jared Goff do not, and you just might not have a better option than Fields.



---


# Russell Wilson Week 13: Start Him Because Volume Should Finally Meet His Efficiency

CBS Sports' Week 13 verdict on Russell Wilson is Start Him, on the argument that his elite efficiency has been held back only by attempt volume, and that the Texans matchup should supply the volume. The efficiency grounds: there is no denying he is now among the most efficient quarterbacks in the league — top five among qualifying quarterbacks in completion rate at 68.3%, first in touchdown rate at 6.3%, fourth in off-target rate at 7.8%, and he has clearly worked out his issues with his offensive line because he has landed the fourth-longest time-to-throw average at 3.14 seconds. He has done this without firing downfield a ton, ranking 32nd in passing ADOT at 6.7 yards. The stated reason it hasn't translated for Fantasy is that Wilson is averaging 29 attempts per game, and even lower over his past six games at 26.

The warrant for the change is matchup-driven: expect Wilson to throw more in what could become a shootout against the Texans, because quarterbacks against Houston are averaging 34.8 pass attempts per game and the Texans pass rush shouldn't be a problem. The conclusion is to count on Wilson for a 20-plus point game and thus start him over Kyler Murray, Baker Mayfield, Sam Howell and Jordan Love. Scope: Wilson is a Denver quarterback, #3, age 35 with 12 years of experience; the weekly breakdown lists the matchup at Houston with Houston favored by 3.5 and an over/under of 47, the opponent 10th versus quarterbacks, projected points of 17.8 and a QB rank of 10th; year-to-date he has 2,199 passing yards, 266 rushing yards, 21 touchdowns, 4 interceptions and 20.4 Fantasy points per game, with projections powered by SportsLine.

# Brock Purdy's 49ers Career Trajectory

San Francisco 49ers franchise QB Brock Purdy is arguably the best quarterback in the 2022 NFL Draft class, despite being that draft's Mr. Irrelevant. He has had a dream start to his NFL career, remaining unbeaten and being one of the better young shot callers in the league; since breaking into the starting lineup he has made a mockery of his "Mr. Irrelevant" tag. The Iowa State University alum was the first Mr. Irrelevant to make a forward pass in a regular season game successfully, and it has been up from there.

Purdy finished his rookie season with five consecutive regular-season victories, completing a 10-game winning streak by San Francisco to close the season. He carried on his regular season form to the postseason, leading the 49ers to an NFC Championship Game against the Philadelphia Eagles; unfortunately, Purdy got hurt in the game, as the 49ers fell just short of a Super Bowl LVII appearance.

So far, Purdy has started the 2023 NFL season where he left off, opening the season with a 5-0 record. As of October 2023, the San Francisco 49ers were the only franchise unbeaten in 2023 alongside their NFC foes, the Philadelphia Eagles. No quarterback has done better than Brock Purdy in his draft class.



---


# 2023 NFL MVP Favorites And The Longshot Cases For Goff And Stroud

Brock Purdy, Dak Prescott and Jalen Hurts were the current favorites for 2023 NFL MVP after Week 13, with C.J. Stroud and Jared Goff the longshots Sporting News argued bettors should consider, per its Dec. 5, 2023 awards-odds piece.

The reasoning for the board is that the MVP often ends up being someone, typically the quarterback, from one of the top-seeded teams, which is why Purdy, Prescott and Hurts sat atop betting boards after Week 13. But by that same logic, Sporting News argued, Jared Goff should be in the conversation: he had played well that season, his Lions were 9-3, described by Sporting News as poised to win the NFC South and in contention for the No. 1 seed in the conference — and compared to the 49ers, Cowboys and Eagles, Goff and the Lions may have had the easiest schedule to finish the season.

The case for C.J. Stroud rests on production and value. He led the league in passing yards, was one of four quarterbacks who had started the whole season with a passer rating over 100, and his touchdown-to-interception ratio was the best in the NFL at 4 to 1. As for the value of his play, Stroud had taken one of the worst teams in the NFL — 11 total wins over the previous three seasons — and turned it into a playoff contender and potential division champion.



---


# 49ers 42-19 Eagles, Week 13 2023

Brock Purdy threw for 314 yards and four touchdowns and Deebo Samuel scored three touchdowns as the San Francisco 49ers won 42-19 at Philadelphia on Sunday, Dec. 3, 2023, with Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts checked for a concussion during the game.

The fiery NFC championship game rematch also featured 49ers touchdowns on six straight possessions and a pair of ejections that showed this year's title game may not run again through Philly after all. The 49ers (9-3) had left Philly 10 months earlier battered in the NFC championship game behind injuries to Purdy and his backup, never standing a chance in a 31-7 loss; they spent an offseason chirping at the Birds — Samuel called one Eagles cornerback "trash" — and then entered the Linc as a rare betting favorite against a 10-win team at home. The Eagles (10-2) suffered a scare when Hurts jogged off the field in the fourth quarter and went straight to the locker room; it was not immediately clear when he was injured. He was cleared to play and returned with about 10 minutes left, by which time last season's NFL MVP runner-up found the Eagles trailing 35-13 and on their way to their first home loss of the season. Hurts hit DeVonta Smith for a two-yard touchdown on his return drive and finished 26-of-45 passing for 298 yards, while Purdy put the finishing touches on the win with a 46-yard touchdown to Samuel.

# Cowboys-49ers First Half: Two Kittle Touchdowns Build A 21-7 Lead

San Francisco led Dallas 21-7 at halftime of the Oct. 8, 2023 "Sunday Night Football" game, with George Kittle catching two touchdowns from Brock Purdy and Christian McCaffrey adding a third score. The 49ers started with the ball after a slightly late kickoff (8:23 p.m.), moved past midfield on a facemask penalty and a nine-yard pass to Brandon Aiyuk (8:25 p.m.), survived a near-fumble by Deebo Samuel that was nullified by a Dallas offsides penalty (8:27 p.m.), and scored at 8:30 p.m. when Purdy found a wide-open Kittle in the end zone to cap a well-scripted opening drive by Kyle Shanahan.

Dallas could not respond early. Three plays and two incompletions forced a punt (8:36 p.m.); Johnathan Hankins deflected a Purdy third-down pass with his helmet to force a 49ers punt (8:40 p.m.); Tony Pollard was dropped for a loss to start Dallas' second drive (8:44 p.m.); and after Lamb's first catch of the night, Nick Bosa sacked Prescott to end that drive (8:46 p.m.). Jayron Kearse recorded the Cowboys' first sack at 8:50 p.m., but Deebo Samuel made up 11 of the 12 needed yards on the next play, and Kearse then lined up offsides to extend the 49ers drive (8:54 p.m.). Purdy flipped a 3rd & 1 pass to Kyle Juszczyk (8:56 p.m.) before the drive fell apart on a delay of game penalty and a five-yard loss by McCaffrey on 3rd & 15 (8:59 p.m.). At 9:01 p.m. Pollard was stripped deep in Dallas territory and San Francisco recovered — confirmed at 9:04 p.m. — but at 9:10 p.m. Jourdan Lewis took the ball out of McCaffrey's arms to trade the fumble back. The first quarter ended 7-0.

In the second quarter Purdy hit Kittle again after some trickery at 9:14 p.m. for a 14-0 lead, set up when Fred Warner sacked Prescott to force a punt from the Cowboys' own end zone (9:13 p.m.), giving Warner a sack and a forced fumble. Dallas finally earned a first down after more than 17 minutes (9:20 p.m.), then Prescott completed passes to Brandin Cooks (9:22 p.m.) and a 20-yard third-down conversion to Jake Ferguson (9:24 p.m.) before hitting KaVontae Turpin on a 26-yard touchdown at 9:27 p.m. to make it 14-7. Pollard had just 10 yards on six touches at that point (9:23 p.m.). San Francisco answered with Aiyuk's 15-yard catch (9:31 p.m.), a 19-yard McCaffrey screen (9:35 p.m.) and Samuel's run to the one (9:37 p.m.), and McCaffrey pushed in at 9:38 p.m. for his 14th consecutive game with a touchdown and a 21-7 lead. Dallas' next drive ended on a short third-down pass to Ferguson (9:45 p.m.); the 49ers failed to convert with a low third-down throw to Aiyuk (9:52 p.m.); edge rusher Drake Jackson walked off after medical attention (9:56 p.m.); and Dre Greenlaw sacked Prescott at 9:58 p.m. as Dallas ran out the half, with the Cowboys due to receive to start the second half.

# Evaluating Brock Purdy And The San Francisco 49ers, 2023

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that Brock Purdy is a good, young quarterback well-suited to run Kyle Shanahan's offense at a high level by making quick decisions when given time to find open receivers — but not the kind of quarterback who can carry the 49ers when the supporting cast is missing.

The grounds start with what the 49ers do not have in Purdy: an AFC North-certified, weatherproof Ben Roethlisberger clone able to overpower the elements, break away from defensive linemen and thrive in the conditions Purdy faced against Cleveland. The warrant is that Purdy's effectiveness is conditional on time and on receivers getting open, which is a property of the system around him rather than of improvisation.

An NFL executive made the same point about the system's dependencies: "The 49ers knew they needed a good quarterback to win the Super Bowl, and they knew they could help Purdy be that. Give him a great receiving tight end, two good receivers and a great halfback who fits the system, and they'll get someone open on every pass play. But then Deebo Samuel gets hurt, Christian McCaffrey gets hurt, and now we don't have as many guys open. Especially when you face a defensive coordinator who says, 'You show me you can beat me throwing the ball outside the numbers — best of luck, and to do that, you are going to have to take a five-step drop and I'm going to have Myles Garrett chasing you every play.'"



---


# Joe Burrow As A Week 5 2023 Sneaky Sleeper At Arizona

CBS Sports listed Joe Burrow as a "Sneaky Sleeper" for Week 5 of the 2023 season at Arizona: the claim is that if there is a matchup in which Burrow could piece together a decent stat line, this is it, and the warrant is that the Cardinals' passive pass rush removes the pressure that had been exposing an injured Burrow.

The grounds start with Burrow's condition. The weekly breakdown lists Cincinnati at Arizona, the Bengals favoured by 3, an over/under of 44.5, an opponent ranked 25th versus quarterbacks, 20.8 projected points, a 19th quarterback ranking, and year-to-date totals of 728 passing yards, three rushing yards, two touchdowns, two interceptions and 8.9 fantasy points per game. The previous week Burrow looked like a quarterback playing on one leg — not getting much into his throws, not challenging downfield, getting the ball out as fast as he could and sensitive to pass-rush pressure, and unable to get much going even in garbage time. His air-yards profile is bleak: 1 for 4 on throws of 10-plus air yards and 0 for 2 on throws of 15-plus in that game, and 11 for 38 and 2 for 22 respectively on the season. He has thrown just two touchdowns all year, both against Baltimore in Week 2, both from inside the five-yard line and both to Tee Higgins, and his red-zone line is unfathomable at 7 of 15 with at least nine of those throws going into the end zone. Opponents had begun to sniff out his issues: the Browns and Titans generated pressure rates between roughly 38% and 42% with blitz rates of at least 31% in their wins over Cincinnati, while the Rams and Ravens barely pressured or blitzed and either lost or nearly lost.

# Most Valuable Player (MVP)

## Definition

In the corpus, MVP (Most Valuable Player) names the player judged most valuable to a team's or league's success, and the term surfaces at several distinct scopes: a formal season-long league award (NFL MVP, NBA MVP), a single-game honor (Super Bowl MVP), and an informal team-level or cross-sport label applied by media, players, and coaches.

## Context

At the league-season level, the NFL MVP and NBA MVP are formal annual awards contested among a small pool of star players. Sporting News's Dec. 5, 2023 awards-odds piece had Brock Purdy, Dak Prescott, and Jalen Hurts as the current NFL MVP favorites after Week 13, with C.J. Stroud and Jared Goff as the longshot cases. Separately, Yardbarker's Dec. 24, 2023 Christmas Day preview framed the Ravens-49ers game explicitly as "the decisive clash for the MVP Award," with Brock Purdy the heavy favorite (-230) and Lamar Jackson — the 2019 MVP — holding the second-shortest odds (+525). At the single-game level, MVP denotes a game-specific honor, as with Patrick Mahomes's two Super Bowl MVPs. At the team level, MVP is used informally by outlets like Yardbarker to name each team's most indispensable player at a season's midpoint — a designation that need not track the league-wide award and can go to a non-quarterback, as when Miami's Tyreek Hill or New England's Jabrill Peppers is named team MVP. The same informal usage crosses sports, as when an MLS goalkeeper calls forward Luciano Acosta "the MVP" of FC Cincinnati. MVP is also a standard sports-betting futures market: bettors wager on which player will win the season MVP award well before or during the season, alongside markets like Rookie of the Year and Offensive/Defensive Player of the Year.

## Background (external)

Beyond this corpus's sports-betting and news coverage, Wikipedia describes an MVP award more generally as an honor bestowed on the individual (or individuals, in case of a tie) "whose individual performance is the greatest in an entire league, for a particular competition, or on a specific team," recognizing one player's contribution within a team effort. (Source: Wikipedia, "Most valuable player," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Most_valuable_player, accessed 2026-09-02.)

## Key Characteristics

- **Multiple scopes** — the same "MVP" language covers a formal season-long league award (NFL, NBA), a single-game honor (Super Bowl MVP), and an informal team-level or sport-crossing designation used by media and players alike.
- **Voting-panel awards lack fixed criteria** — the NBA MVP, for instance, is chosen by a panel of sportswriters and broadcasters (format since 1980, weighted 5/3/1 points for first/second/third-place votes) with no set selection rulebook, which is why outcomes are notoriously hard to predict and can produce "upset" winners.
- **Quarterback bias in NFL MVP framing** — corpus coverage repeatedly frames the NFL MVP as typically going to a quarterback from a top-seeded team, to the point that a non-quarterback like Christian McCaffrey is described as facing long odds "if the MVP wasn't a quarterback-driven award."
- **Betting futures market** — MVP odds are a standing futures category at sportsbooks (alongside moneylines, spreads, and other award markets), bet on well ahead of the outcome and repriced as the season's results accumulate.
- **Team-level MVP is unofficial** — team MVP picks (e.g., Yardbarker's AFC team-by-team roundup) are editorial judgments, not sanctioned awards, and can diverge sharply from who is in the league MVP conversation.

# FTX's Fabricated Backstop Insurance Fund

Gary Wang testified on October 6th, 2023 that FTX lied about how much money was in its backstop fund, and the court was shown the code that generated the fake number published on FTX's website: it took the daily trading volume on FTX, multiplied it by a random number, divided it by a billion, and added the result to the number already displayed on the site. That figure had nothing to do with the actual amount of money in the insurance fund.

The fund mattered because of what FTX advertised. In many crypto networks, if someone lost enough money the exchanges could stick other traders with the losses too; FTX touted its automated liquidation as the way to avoid this, so that one customer going bankrupt would not affect the others. In the process of liquidating, FTX would try to sell the collateral on the open market, and if it could not finish, backstop liquidity providers would step in — market makers, including Alameda, which could be compensated for the losses they took from the backstop fund. Wang also testified that when there was not enough money in the fund, money was moved there from Alameda's accounts in order to pay the insurance out.

The prosecution's framing was that this was not merely a matter of Alameda holding special, secret privileges: it claimed those privileges were used to obfuscate basic elements of FTX's operations, exposing the exchange's supposed selling points as a lie.

# The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse

FTX came apart in early November 2022 through a chain with four links: a leaked balance sheet revealed that Alameda's largest holding was FTX's own token in a quantity larger than the token's whole market, the disclosure destroyed confidence, the world's largest rival exchange pulled its holdings out, and the resulting bank run forced FTX and Alameda into Chapter 11 within days. TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account sets out the sequence: in early November 2022, that all changed.

Concerns surrounding FTX's liquidity grew after CoinDesk published a copy of Alameda's balance sheet, showing the firm held $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. The balance sheet showed that the $5.82 billion in FTT tokens that Alameda owned was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap, which was about $3 billion at the time — meaning Alameda purported to have more FTT tokens on its balance sheet than what existed in the world. Around the same time it was exposed, the world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, started pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT; Binance had held an equity position in FTX from 2019 to 2021. That withdrawal essentially triggered a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. mid-November 2022, Bankman-Fried resigned, and John J. Ray III, the Enron turnaround veteran, was appointed the new CEO.

The condition the whole mechanism rests on is the fragility of the underlying valuations. As TechCrunch put it on 2023-10-02, all of that activity came to a crashing end because the value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value — so when those valuations fell, they fell very, very hard. The chain therefore only runs as described where an asset is priced on expectation, held in size by a related party, and exposed to a counterparty large enough that its exit alone starts the run.

# Alameda Research

Alameda Research is the crypto-trading firm Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded in 2017, before FTX existed. FTX came two years later, in 2019, and Bankman-Fried co-founded it as a complement to Alameda — to help bring in revenue and liquidity for the trading arm. The founding order is the discriminating fact: the exchange was created to serve the trading firm, not the other way round.

The feature that later set Alameda's balance sheet apart was how much of it consisted of the affiliated exchange's own token. A report showed that Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of "unlocked FTT," alongside $2.16 billion of "FTT collateral." FTT was the token behind FTX. So the trading firm's single biggest asset was the token issued by the exchange founded to support it.

# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. Later Alameda's balance was more negative than FTT and the trading revenue combined, and Wang had further conversations with Bankman-Fried about it. Wang testified he knew at the time that Alameda was using FTX customers' funds and that he knew it was wrong.

The same gradual accommodation shows in Ellison's account. Choking back tears, she testified: "When I started working at Alameda, I don't think I would have believed you if you told me I would be sending false balance sheets to our lenders or taking customer money, but over time, it was something I became more comfortable with."

# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# The FTT Token And The "Sam Coins"

FTT was a token created by Bankman-Fried and Wang and issued by FTX, and it was one of several "Sam coins" — a nickname for tokens Bankman-Fried was heavily involved in and owned a lot of, either personally or through Alameda. Wang described FTT as being "sort of equity" in FTX, a characterisation The Verge's reporter suspected some crypto lawyers would dispute but that would probably please the SEC.

The distribution was lopsided from the start. Alameda got its war chest — 60 percent to 70 percent of the initial supply — for free, while seed investors got FTT at 10 cents a coin and FTT first listed at $1 a coin. Ellison testified that Bankman-Fried felt $1 per coin was psychologically important and directed her to buy up FTT using Alameda if the price fell below a dollar.

The discriminating feature of the Sam coins was that their book value was not realisable: they were almost certainly worth less than the value displayed on the balance sheet, because trying to sell them all at once would crater the prices. Bankman-Fried nonetheless directed Ellison to put those coins on the balance sheets Alameda showed to lenders, even though she felt doing so was "somewhat misleading." FTT also figures in the origin story of Alameda's negative-balance privilege: Wang said Bankman-Fried at first told him the code change letting an account go negative was to pay for expenses for the FTT token, but once implemented the ability to go negative was used for other things, including trading and unlimited withdrawals of FTX's trading fees and customer money.

# Bank Run

## Definition

In the corpus, a bank run names the specific event in which rival exchange Binance's withdrawal of its remaining BUSD and FTT holdings "essentially triggered a bank run on FTX," the acute liquidity event that preceded FTX and Alameda's Chapter 11 filings.

## Context

In the corpus the term names the acute phase of FTX's November 2022 collapse: after a leaked Alameda Research balance sheet showed the firm's largest asset was billions of dollars of FTX's own FTT token — more FTT than existed in the entire market — rival exchange Binance began pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, and TechCrunch reports this action "essentially triggered a bank run on FTX." The run was the mechanism that converted a confidence crisis into an immediate liquidity failure, and it directly preceded FTX and Alameda filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in mid-November 2022.

## Key Characteristics

- **Confidence-driven, not solvency-driven at onset** — the run began once the leaked balance sheet destroyed trust in FTX/Alameda, independent of whether the underlying assets were ultimately worthless.
- **Triggered by a large counterparty's exit** — it was Binance's withdrawal of its remaining BUSD and FTT holdings, not a broad retail panic, that set off the run described in the corpus.
- **Fast-moving** — the run happened in the same early-November-2022 window as the balance-sheet leak, ahead of the Chapter 11 filings that followed in mid-November 2022.
- **Terminal for the institution** — in this case the run was followed by Chapter 11 filings for both FTX and Alameda, and Bankman-Fried's resignation.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a bank run is a general banking-system phenomenon: it occurs when many depositors, fearing a bank may fail, rush to withdraw their money at once, and because banks hold only a fraction of deposits as cash, a large enough run can become a self-fulfilling prophecy that drives the institution into sudden insolvency. (Wikipedia, "Bank run," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_run)

# FTX's Collapse And Bankruptcy, November 2022

FTX went bankrupt on November 11th, 2022, days after Gary Wang and Bankman-Fried had determined that about $8 billion in customer money was gone. On November 7th, Bankman-Fried tweeted "FTX is fine. Assets are fine," and another tweet in the thread said "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings." Wang testified flatly: "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine because FTX did not have enough assets for customer withdrawals."

Prosecutor Thane Rehn placed the trigger in the same month: when CoinDesk published its article in November 2022, people realized FTX was a house of cards, while Bankman-Fried was tweeting "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" and "We don't invest customer assets even in treasuries."

The day after the bankruptcy, on November 12th, Bankman-Fried directed Wang to send customer funds to Bahamian regulators. Customers could not take their funds off the exchange at that point because FTX had run out of money and its servers had been shut down. Bankman-Fried and his father met with lawyers while Wang waited outside with liquidators; the US lawyers wanted the remaining FTX assets transferred to the US, but Wang testified that Bankman-Fried told him to stall the US lawyers and transfer the funds to the Bahamian regulators instead, who were more likely to let him stay in control of the company. The collapse also propagated outward: the government put Zac Prince, the founder and former CEO of crypto lender BlockFi, on the stand just long enough to blame FTX's bankruptcy for BlockFi's subsequent bankruptcy.

# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.

# Alameda Absorbed FTX's Losses, Including MobileCoin

Alameda Research functioned as FTX's sin-eater: when FTX took a loss, the loss was moved onto Alameda's balance sheet so that FTX would not look bad. Gary Wang testified that in 2021 FTX was facing a "several hundred million dollar" loss from an exploit in MobileCoin — apparently in April 2021, though Wang did not give a month — and Bankman-Fried directed him to have Alameda take it on instead, because FTX's balance sheets were visible to investors and Alameda's were not.

The relation was general, not a one-off. Ellison testified that her tenure as CEO of Alameda Research was an exercise in optics: when FTX took a loss in the hundreds of millions of dollars because a trader had exploited its system, Wang moved that loss onto Alameda's balance sheet, and FTX's "insurance fund," meant to keep traders from getting stuck with other traders' losses, was totally made up, with Alameda simply picking up the tab. The concealment held all the way to investors: Paradigm Capital's Matt Huang showed the court the balance sheets he had received from Bankman-Fried, and they did not include the loss, which should have appeared in the second-quarter numbers he was given — those instead showed $63 million in trading expenses and $63 million in "other expenses" for the quarter, and an estimated profit of $732 million.

Bankman-Fried offered a benign reading of the same arrangement from the stand: he said the MobileCoin loss, the one Wang said Alameda took to keep off FTX's balance sheet, was a totally innocent matter in which he thought it appropriate that Alameda take the position as a backstop liquidity provider.

# Chapter 11 (Bankruptcy)

## Definition

Chapter 11 is the U.S. bankruptcy filing that insolvent companies in the corpus use to seek protection from creditors, and it does not guarantee a company survives: some filers are restructured under new leadership, while others wind down anyway once inside it.

## Context

In the corpus, Chapter 11 is the recurring endpoint for companies whose finances collapsed in 2022–2023. FTX and its trading-firm affiliate Alameda Research filed for Chapter 11 in the U.S. in mid-November 2022, after a published Alameda balance sheet exposed a huge FTT-token shortfall and a Binance-triggered bank run wiped out FTX's liquidity; the filing coincided with Sam Bankman-Fried's resignation as CEO and the appointment of Enron turnaround veteran John J. Ray III in his place. The same collapse pulled other crypto firms into Chapter 11: BlockFi filed in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading followed in January, both noted by TechCrunch as part of the wider fallout from FTX's collapse. Outside crypto, WeWork filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in November 2023, listing over $18.6 billion of debt; TechCrunch's Week in Review opened its coverage of the filing with "as predicted," without stating when or on what basis it had made that prediction. SmileDirectClub took the same route but did not come back from it: the company shut down three months after its Chapter 11 filing, citing $900 million of debt — showing that a Chapter 11 filing in this corpus can precede either continued operation under new leadership (FTX) or an eventual full shutdown (SmileDirectClub).

## Key Characteristics

- **Used by companies of very different scale and sector** — from a $32-billion crypto exchange (FTX) to a flexible-office-space firm carrying $18.6 billion of debt (WeWork) to a smaller consumer startup (SmileDirectClub).

- **Can spread across a sector after one high-profile filing** — BlockFi's and Genesis Global Trading's Chapter 11 filings followed FTX's within months, both noted by TechCrunch as part of the wider fallout from FTX's collapse.

The corpus repeatedly names "Chapter 11" as the filing route without stating what the chapter itself legally entails. Chapter 11, formally Chapter 11 of Title 11 of the U.S. Code, is the reorganization bankruptcy: it lets a debtor continue operating as a "debtor in possession" while it develops a plan to restructure its debts and pay creditors, rather than immediately liquidating its assets — which is the province of Chapter 7 instead (United States Courts, *Chapter 11 - Bankruptcy Basics*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Allow_negative: Alameda's Exemption From FTX Liquidation

"Allow_negative" was a column in FTX's account database that exempted Alameda Research — and only Alameda — from the exchange's automated liquidation, letting Alameda hold a negative balance and withdraw money its accounts did not have. Gary Wang testified that it originated in a code commit dated July 31st, 2019 under Nishad Singh's username, titled "OTC trades and transfers to special accounts." Written in Python, it added two columns to the account database, the relevant one being "allow_negative," a toggle that when on let the account go negative; the feature was switched on the same day by a second set of code also carrying Singh's username, and Wang said he supervised.

The structure it modified was FTX's risk management. As Wang explained it, a futures exchange is the middleman that lets strangers bet with each other: it sits between the two ends of the bet, paying the winner and collecting from the loser, which is why it requires collateral, and under some circumstances it automatically sells that collateral to limit its losses. On FTX this liquidation process was automated and took about 30 seconds to find the accounts that needed to be liquidated to minimize FTX's losses. Normal customers — the defense objected to "normal" and was overruled — could be automatically liquidated, but not Alameda. Wang testified that Bankman-Fried "told me a few times to make sure that Alameda's account is never liquidated on FTX," and that "the code addition was the result of those conversations." Alongside the exemption, Alameda could place orders faster than other users and held an enormous line of credit, and the court saw evidence that users may have unwittingly deposited money into Alameda rather than FTX.

The relation holds only for Alameda: no other customer trading on FTX had allow_negative privileges, and the same day the toggle was switched on in July 2019, Bankman-Fried tweeted that Alameda "is a liquidity provider on FTX, but their account is just like everyone else's" — a tweet shown in court, and to The Verge's reporter evidence that the fraud at FTX started very early, just months after FTX was founded. Bankman-Fried offered a competing origin story from the stand: FTX's big selling point was its "risk engine," which in 2020 was "effectively sagging under the weight" of the exchange's rapid growth so that time to liquidation stretched to minutes, and at one point the engine got stuck in a catastrophic feedback loop that would have created losses in the "trillions of dollars," with Alameda teetering on the brink of a liquidation that "would have disastrous consequences" for FTX. "At the time, I wasn't entirely sure what was happening," he testified, saying that because of that experience he suggested an "alert" or "delay" to keep Alameda from being liquidated by a bug, that allow_negative was the eventual result of that conversation, and that he did not know about it until very recently. The dates do not fit: allow_negative was coded and switched on in 2019, and the code was displayed in court in front of Bankman-Fried and the jury.

# Line Of Credit

## Definition

In the corpus, "line of credit" denotes the informal, undocumented facility FTX extended to its affiliated trading firm Alameda Research.

Caroline Ellison testified there was "no contract and no written terms," and that Alameda drew against it in increments of $100,000 to $10 million at a time to fund trading.

## Context

The corpus uses "line of credit" almost exclusively to describe the Alameda–FTX arrangement at the center of the SBF fraud trial. Gary Wang testified he set the facility up for Alameda and repeatedly raised its ceiling as the firm kept running against its limit — moving from "a few hundred million," to a billion, and eventually to an effectively unlimited figure that reached $65 billion. Caroline Ellison separately testified that Alameda used $14 billion drawn "as a line of credit" to repay debts to third-party lenders, on Bankman-Fried's instruction. Bankman-Fried, for his part, denied on the stand that he knew about the "effectively infinite" line of credit Alameda received from FTX, a denial The Verge's trial coverage called "peculiar," concluding that the CEO of a financial company simply didn't pay attention to finances.

## Key Characteristics

- **Draw-as-needed structure** — funds are accessed incrementally against a ceiling rather than disbursed as one loan, as when Ellison described draws of $100,000 to $10 million at a time.
- **No collateral, no contract** — Ellison testified the $65 billion facility "did not have to post collateral" and had "no contract and no written terms."
- **Escalating limit** — the ceiling was repeatedly raised over time as the borrower kept exceeding it, per Wang's account of the increases from a few hundred million to $65 billion.
- **Invisible to oversight** — the credit line "wasn't visible to FTX's auditors," per Ellison's testimony, despite its size.
- **Exclusivity** — Wang testified the facility was "unmatched by anyone else on FTX," making it a privilege specific to the affiliated firm rather than a standard customer product.

## Background (external)

The corpus illustrates the term through a single, irregular instance rather than defining it as a general banking product. Per Wikipedia, a line of credit is ordinarily a borrowing arrangement from a bank or financial institution that lets a customer access funds up to a set maximum whenever needed, is typically revolving so that repaid amounts can be redrawn without reapplying, and generally charges interest only on the amount actually withdrawn (Wikipedia, *Line of credit*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Alameda–FTX facility described in the corpus departs from that standard model in that it had no written agreement, no collateral requirement, and no independent oversight.

# Gary Wang's Cross-Examination By Everdell

Defense attorney Christian Everdell's cross-examination of Gary Wang on October 10th, 2023 attacked the premise that Alameda's ability to run a negative balance was unique to Alameda. Wang had testified the week before that Alameda got access to a special credit line and an option to take its balance into the negative without triggering liquidation, something he alleged no other FTX account received; Everdell countered by pointing to FTX's spot margin program, which let users lend each other assets for margin trading and in which it was possible to have a negative balance in a specific coin.

The Verge's reporter judged the counter incomplete rather than false: in spot margin cases it was not possible for those accounts to avoid liquidation, as Wang testified Alameda could, or to have an overall negative balance. Her read was that the defense was betting jurors would throw up their hands in confusion — Everdell could not undo the damage of the previous week's code review, but he shook the rust off long enough to make Wang sound less reliable by drowning the jury in confusing technicalities.

A second line of attack went to Wang's consistency. What Wang said in court apparently contradicted something he had told the government in earlier interviews about market making — "apparently," because Everdell was probably handing him his previous testimony to refresh his recollection while Wang insisted he did not remember, and whatever Wang was shown was not submitted as evidence or shown to the court. The reporter got the gist and bet the jury did too, calling it probably the strongest work the defense had done so far.
