# Hipgnosis Songs Fund Continuation Vote

A 'continuation vote' at Hipgnosis Songs Fund (HSF), the UK-listed music rights fund, is a vote of the firm's shareholders on whether to keep the entity going as a closed-ended investment entity — that is, as a publicly-traded bundle of music rights. It takes place at HSF's Annual General Meeting, and the 2023 vote looked likely to be held on Thursday 26 October, according to an announcement from the firm on 28 September 2023.

The 2023 vote was only "likely" rather than definite because it might still get bumped into November, and its outcome was unknown at the time of reporting, with a looming $440 million transaction that could potentially influence it. The vote itself was not a new event: it had been scheduled ever since HSF went public in 2018, five years after the float.

The changes HSF announced on 28 September invited the question of whether they amounted to concessions designed to keep investors happy and confident in long-term prospects — and voting to keep going. One such measure directly extends the mechanism: if shareholders vote at the next AGM to remain a publicly-traded fund, another continuation vote will be put to HSF shareholders at an Extraordinary General Meeting in January 2026, roughly two years later.



---


# The PhilEd Education Development Fund Proposal

PhilEd, the proposed Philippine Education Development Fund, is defined by its purpose: its role would be to fund the education dreams of all Filipinos, especially the neediest and most deserving.

The definition is drawn by analogy to a corporate finance role. When Isidro Consunji, President of DMCI Holdings, Inc., was asked by his officers what the role of his Chief Financial Officer would be, he gave a three-word answer: "Fund my dreams." PhilEd is cast in the same terms for the country's education ambitions.



---


# The Board Appoints And Oversees Its Own Valuer

The oddest thing about the board's complaint, MBW argues, is that Citrin Cooperman's valuation of Hipgnosis Songs Fund is, according to HSF's own company documentation, appointed and overseen by the HSF board itself. This attacks the implicit premise that the disputed valuation is something imposed on the board from outside, and therefore something whose failings can be laid at another party's door.

The documentary grounds are two recurring lines in HSF filings. Every annual and interim report from HSF so far states: "Portfolio Independent Valuer… Citrin Cooperman Advisors LLC, formerly Massarsky Consulting, Inc., [is] appointed by the Board to independently value the Company's Catalogues within the Portfolio." Various HSF company reports to date also state: "The [HSF] Board is ultimately and solely responsible for overseeing the valuation of the Company's investments in music catalogues and has appointed [Citrin Cooperman] to perform this specialist work."



---


# Three Filipino Education Dreams And The PhilEd Programs

The proposal maps three Filipino education dreams onto three PhilEd programs. The first dream is to enroll in a chosen course in the school of one's choice, which will be funded by the School Vouchers Program, transferred from DepEd to PhilEd. The second dream, especially for Filipino parents, is to save enough money to fund the college education of their children, hence the prevalence of pre-need Educational Plans; because most pre-need companies went into bankruptcy, causing financial ruin and emotional distress to plan holders, there has been a massive market failure and government must intervene, but the intervention should not involve the government offering educational plans, rather insuring them. Just as the Philippine Deposit Insurance Corp. insures bank deposits, PhilEd would insure educational plans, and just as PDIC is funded from premiums paid by banks, PhilEd would fund this program from premiums paid by educational plan companies; PhilEd would be ideally suited to this because it could swap failed educational plans with school vouchers from its repository.

The third dream is based on the realization of Filipino school graduates that their learning must continue after they leave their alma maters, because in this modern age the fount of personal knowledge must continuously be replenished. The parallel drawn is with healthcare: Health Maintenance Organizations continuously monitor and minister to health, so Lifelong Learning Organizations are needed to continuously monitor and minister to learning; HMOs exist in the Philippines while LLOs do not. In partnership with international development agencies and the private sector, PhilEd would create this industry, with the international development agencies providing technical assistance grants to create the developmental and regulatory framework and the private sector organizing the LLOs, while PhilEd acts as the "bastonero" or project manager, managing the project as well as mobilizing government support and assistance.

# JP Morgan's Note Against The HSF Board's Handling Of The Valuation

JP Morgan analyst Christopher Brown, one of the closest watchers of Hipgnosis Songs Fund in recent years, issued a damning note on 19 December 2023 attacking the board's attempt to shift responsibility for the valuation. He wrote that the delay "is an early blow to the credibility of the new [Hipgnosis Songs Fund] Board, and casts further doubt over the credibility of the independent valuer, Citrin Cooperman", and concluded that "[it] is up to the [Hipgnosis Songs Fund] Board to satisfy itself that the independent valuer, whom it hires, is up to the job, rather than try and pin the blame on [Hipgnosis Songs Management]", adding that in JP Morgan's view "a breakdown in the relationship between Board and manager would not be optimal for maximising shareholder value".

Brown said he was surprised that a second valuation expert had not been drafted in to value the HSF portfolio for the latest interim results, especially as Kroll had been appointed to consider the "reasonableness" of Citrin Cooperman's assumptions for HSF's previous set of results to the end of March 2023. He suggested that the easiest solution now for the board is to apply an additional discount rate to the Citrin Cooperman valuation to reflect current market uncertainty, on the basis that it is probably too late to employ another valuer, and quantified the effect: a 0.5% rise in the discount rate, from 8.5% to 9.0%, would "reduce the fair value of the [HSF] portfolio by 7.9%, which on a leveraged basis is [approximately a] 10% reduction in NAV [Net Asset Value]". Should the board go down that route he expected the shares to weaken, given that it represents another "unforced error", and he added that JP Morgan would not be surprised to see Citrin Cooperman resign, having been very publicly undermined by the board that day. Despite all this, JP Morgan retained its "overweight" rating against HSF's share price "in spite of yet another [HSF] own goal".

# The HSF Board Versus Hipgnosis Song Management

As part of its 19 December 2023 announcement, the HSF board took something of a swipe at its investment adviser, Merck Mercuriadis' Hipgnosis Song Management. HSF said that after seeing Citrin Cooperman's latest valuation and believing it to be too high, it "sought advice from Hipgnosis Song Management… which is majority owned by funds managed and/or advised by Blackstone, on their opinion on the independent valuer's valuation", and added that HSM "eventually provided an opinion, which was heavily caveated, such that the Board has concerns as to the valuation of the Company's assets in its interim results".

MBW argues that amongst all the noise around Hipgnosis Songs Fund, what will most likely interest its investors, including the likes of Investec Wealth & Investment, Aviva Investors and BlackRock, is the ongoing underlying commercial performance of the firm's copyrights. In a paper presented at the 5th Paderanga-Varela Memorial Lecture entitled "Alternate Service Delivery Systems: Health and Education", the authors looked at the Department of Health and the Department of Education as service delivery systems, delivering healthcare and education respectively, and concluded that the service delivery system of the DoH is far superior to that of the DepEd.

# Hipgnosis Songs Fund's Results Delay, December 2023

On the morning of 19 December 2023, the board of Hipgnosis Songs Fund, now led by Chairman Rob Naylor, issued a statement announcing that HSF would no longer be issuing its latest financial results that day as previously expected; the results, covering the six months to the end of September 2023, were instead expected to be published sometime before the close of 31 December.

As of 14 September 2023, Hipgnosis Songs Fund's market cap stood at approximately GBP £1.125 billion, which represented a 40% discount to the firm's 'operative Net Asset Value' of USD $2.316 billion as of the end of March that year. That operative NAV was calculated by an independent valuer, Citrin Cooperman, using a discount rate of 8.5%.

# Hipgnosis Investment Advisory Agreement Amendments

The amendments Hipgnosis Songs Fund confirmed on 28 September 2023 to its Investment Advisory Agreement (IAA) with Hipgnosis Song Management are a conditional, self-reversing termination mechanism tied to the fund's discount to NAV. They were set out in a circular to shareholders alongside a number of other new measures.

The first amendment gives HSM a 12-month notice period as HSF's investment advisor should the IAA be terminated at any point following the upcoming 2023 continuation vote. The second sets a trigger: if HSF's share price stands at an average discount to operative NAV of 10% or more across the month of January 2025 — with that NAV determined at the time of publication of HSF's interim report for the period to 30 September 2024 — the HSF board says it intends to serve notice to terminate the IAA with HSM. The board also gave itself the freedom to un-terminate the IAA during the entire notice period that would follow; for example, if notice were served at the end of January 2025, the board would have until the end of January 2026 to withdraw its termination decision.

One factor potentially making a future termination of HSM less likely is what would follow it: MBW understands that in such a scenario HSM would have a first-refusal option to acquire HSF's copyright portfolio, and could potentially turn to Blackstone — the backers of Hipgnosis Songs Capital — to find the money to pull off such an acquisition.

# Board Governance

In this corpus, board governance is illustrated by cases where a board of directors exercises (or conspicuously lacks) the power to oversee and remove a company's CEO: OpenAI's board firing Sam Altman, Flexport's board ousting Dave Clark, and FTX's absence of any board at all.

## Context

The corpus's clearest working example is OpenAI's board, which in November 2023 fired co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after "a deliberative review process" concluded he was "not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."
That framing treats board governance as a standing check on the CEO: the board's stated justification was not a business or legal failure but a breakdown in the information flow the board needs to do its job.
OpenAI's board itself sits atop a nonprofit structure that "preserved its nonprofit governance structure" even as the startup underneath pursued commercial growth, so the board's authority over the CEO ran through that nonprofit layer rather than ordinary shareholder control.
Board composition determines whose judgment gets exercised: OpenAI's board consisted of chief scientist Ilya Sutskever and three non-employee directors (Adam D'Angelo, Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner), and the subsequent standoff over reinstating Altman turned on negotiating a new board (Bret Taylor, Larry Summers, Adam D'Angelo) as a condition of his return.
The corpus also frames board governance by its absence: Paradigm co-founder Matt Huang testified he was "concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors" before investing anyway, though on cross-examination he said Bankman-Fried told him he didn't want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.
Flexport's board, by contrast, illustrates governance operating through composition rather than absence: a board "made up largely of investors who were betting on the founder" held quarterly meetings on June 1 and Aug. 31 before Clark was forced to resign on Sept. 5.

## Key Characteristics

- **Power to remove or reinstate the CEO** — OpenAI's board fired Altman outright, then negotiated the terms (including its own reconstitution) under which he could return.
- **Grounded in a formal duty to oversee, not just advise** — the board's justification for firing Altman was specifically that his conduct hindered "its ability to exercise its responsibilities," i.e., an oversight duty rather than a performance complaint.
- **Structure shapes authority** — OpenAI's nonprofit board sat above the commercial subsidiary, giving it authority that ordinary shareholder-elected boards would not have over a purely for-profit company.
- **Composition determines outcome** — who sits on the board (employee vs. non-employee directors, investor-aligned vs. independent) is itself a lever contested during crises, as seen in both the OpenAI reinstatement talks and Flexport's investor-heavy board.
- **Its absence is itself notable** — the corpus flags FTX's lack of a board of directors as a specific governance gap investors identified before FTX's collapse, distinguishing "no oversight body" from "an oversight body that failed."

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, corporate governance is generally defined as the mechanisms, processes, and relations by which corporations are directed and controlled by their boards of directors, managers, shareholders, and other stakeholders.
The widely cited Cadbury Report formulation puts it more simply: corporate governance is "the system by which companies are directed and controlled."
Source: [Corporate governance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_governance), Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02.

# Clark's Cease-And-Desist, The Political Friction, And The Firing For Cause

Clark's cease-and-desist letter cited two documents that had been presented to the board — a pre-acquisition financial analysis of the Deliverr deal, presented by the co-CEOs for board approval and shaped by multiple prior board meetings, and a review of Flexport's first-quarter numbers — both viewed by CNBC.

Clark's camp suggested other factors may have led to the abrupt firing, among them politics. Days after Clark was ousted, Petersen sent him a message, seen by CNBC, blasting one of his key female executives for wasting her days at the company on "far left-wing political activism"; the executive is a registered Republican. Trae Stephens, the Founders Fund partner, had also shared his contempt for that executive weeks before Clark's departure, a person familiar with the board told CNBC, and Stephens did not respond to a request for comment. Petersen is also a venture partner at Founders Fund, the firm started by Peter Thiel, a prominent supporter of President Trump's 2016 campaign who more recently bankrolled Senate candidates in Ohio and Arizona, and many of Thiel's closest confidantes at Founders Fund and elsewhere in venture are outspoken conservatives — though Petersen's sole public political contribution in 2023 was to a Democratic political action committee associated with Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia, and he does not talk much about politics. Clark has donated to candidates on both sides of the aisle; upon his departure The Wall Street Journal reported he was considering running for governor of Texas, but two people familiar with his thinking say that is not happening anytime soon. Flexport told CNBC that an employee's politics are not relevant in personnel decisions: "Ryan Petersen does not care at all about anyone's political or personal affiliations. That is their business. It is inappropriate for any employee to spend an excessive amount of time during work hours on activities unrelated to their role." A person familiar with the female executive said her noncorporate endeavors were largely related to charitable organizations. Clark has largely remained silent since he was forced to resign on Sept. 5, though in private he has expressed frustration at how his former team was treated, as many of his allies from Amazon who joined him at Flexport were summarily fired by Petersen shortly after his departure. On Sept. 13, Flexport chief legal counsel Chris Ferro contacted Clark to tell him his resignation a week earlier had not been accepted: instead, Flexport's board met the day after Clark resigned and voted to fire him for cause, though the board minutes did not yet reflect why. Ferro allegedly told Clark that Flexport would give him a block of 2 million shares — worth millions of dollars — if he signed a separation agreement including nondisclosure and nondisparagement clauses; Clark declined. Shortly after, Clark took the stage at the same Phoenix supply chain conference Petersen had spoken at earlier that day and did not hold back: "The only thing I really regret from the past year was I sort of picked the wrong founder. Basically, it was a place of extending my reputational halo to a group that, in my opinion, didn't deserve it. Largely, because about half the team was let go last week on Friday, the most brutal nonseverance packages I've ever seen in my life. It was about as disrespectful a way as humanly possible."

# The Private Sector's Role In Philippine Sustainable Development

Coming off the pandemic and given the current global economic climate, it is opportune for the government to proactively drive actionable policies and programs that focus on building the resiliency of the economy through sustainable development, with greater emphasis on addressing climate change. Abdul Karim Abdullah's first experience in the music industry came when a member of his fraternity, Phi Beta Sigma Fraternity Inc., booked Big Sean at his alma mater, Syracuse University. # Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 Targets

The Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 aims for a deep economic and social transformation to reinvigorate job creation and accelerate poverty reduction by steering the economy back to a high-growth path, and two main performance indicators are identified and will be monitored by the National Government.

The first is for the country to graduate into upper middle-income class status within the term of the current administration, for which the economy must grow its per capita income above the threshold set by the World Bank, a gross national income per capita of at least $4,466; in 2022 the Philippines achieved a GNI per capita of $3,950. The second is to lower the poverty level from 18.1% in 2021 to single digits by 2028, the end of the term of the current administration. Both indicators require high growth rates, and for the next year through 2028 the government pencils the growth rate between 6.5% and 8%.

# OpenAI's Nonprofit-To-For-Profit Structure

OpenAI started out as a nonprofit when it launched with financial backing from Tesla CEO Elon Musk and others, with stated aims to "advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return." That changed in 2018, when it incorporated a for-profit business, OpenAI LP, and shifted nearly all its staff into that business, not long after releasing its first generation of the GPT large language model for mimicking human writing.

Around the same time, Musk — who had co-chaired its board with Altman — resigned from the board, in a move OpenAI said would eliminate a "potential future conflict for Elon" due to Tesla's work on building self-driving systems. The resulting arrangement is a split one: OpenAI's board has preserved its nonprofit governance structure, while the startup it oversees has increasingly sought to capitalize on its technology by tailoring its popular chatbot to business customers.

# Human Capital, Institutions And Infrastructure In The Philippine Plan

The ability of people to take advantage of market opportunities arising from investment rests on human capital, which is why the first goal of the Philippine Development Plan is social transformation, including among other things sustained expenditure on social services, mainly education, health, and social protection. The plan's three goals map onto the policy objectives: the first two goals help attain the developmental objectives of efficiency and equity, which rest on the pillars of sustainability and resilience, while the third fosters societal resilience through an enabling environment encompassing institutions, macroeconomic stability, and the physical and natural environment.

Institutions are vital to economic acceleration, which is why the government's steps to enhance the ease of doing business are welcome, and infrastructure development enables an economy to sustain higher levels of growth, which in turn catalyzes yet more investment. The Public-Private Partnership Act is up for the signature of President Marcos and, if approved, is expected to further enhance the business atmosphere in mobilizing private resources for infrastructure development. The quantities that bound the plan are given together: the government aims to sustain its infrastructure program at 5-6% of GDP through 2028 amid a six-year medium-term fiscal framework that gradually narrows the deficit to 3% of GDP by 2028, down from 7.3% in 2022, so that the debt-to-GDP ratio is reduced from nearly 61% in 2022 to a more sustainable level of at most 53% by 2028.

# Philippine Investment Liberalisation And RCEP

Growth under the Philippine Development Plan is expected to be investment-led, driven by structural changes: the Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises law, which lowered the corporate income tax rate, and amendments to the Public Service Act, Foreign Investment Act and Retail Trade Liberalization Act, which further liberalized the economy. The new legislation is expected to attract more local and foreign investment, especially in the liberalized sectors, and for the energy sector in particular the PSA amendments are envisioned to help raise the capital needed to speed up the country's energy transition to renewables.

The trade leg runs through the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, a trading bloc encompassing the ten members of ASEAN and the ASEAN Plus One Free Trade Agreement partners Japan, China, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand, which is already in force for the Philippines and helps ease market access through trade and investment rules while supporting global and regional supply chains. The conditional relation is stated explicitly: the Philippines can potentially position itself as a regional manufacturing hub if the right incentives and policy measures are put in place to encourage local and foreign investors to participate. Together, trade and investment are expected to play an important role in attaining economic transformation, the second goal of the PDP.

# Israeli Tech Industry Boycott of Web Summit

In the days before 16 October 2023, a run of named technology figures publicly withdrew from Web Summit and, in several cases, pledged never to return, each citing Web Summit CEO Paddy Cosgrave's stance on the Israel–Hamas fighting. David Marcus, the longtime fintech entrepreneur and Meta executive, said in a tweet the previous day that he would never again attend, sponsor or speak at another Web Summit event: "Saddened by your ill-informed stance. You could've taken a more nuanced one, condemning these atrocities and calling for restraint. That would've been acceptable," he wrote. "You chose to support terrorists. As such I'll never attend/sponsor/speak at any of your events again." Keith Rabois, the Founders Fund partner and entrepreneur, went further than a single event, chiming in: "Will refuse to work with anyone who speaks at this conference in Qatar for the rest of my career."

Ori Goshen, the co-founder and co-CEO of AI21 Labs, announced on LinkedIn that he would no longer be giving a keynote at Web Summit, and grounded the withdrawal in two distinct complaints. "It's bad enough that summit CEO Paddy Cosgrave didn't see fit to express horror at the sickening atrocities committed by Hamas on October 7th," he said. "But as immoral as that is, Paddy Cosgrave chose to not only ignore these but instead post something against the policies of the Israeli government. Leaving aside his very partial understanding of history and geopolitics, this response was abhorrent. We at AI21 cannot be part of such indecency and moral bankruptcy. We will not attend WebSummit, and I will not give the keynote. #cancelwebsummit #standwithisrael"

The withdrawals then moved from individual companies to the state level when the Israeli ambassador to Portugal, Dor Shapiro, waded in. "Today, I wrote to the Mayor of Lisbon informing him that Israel will not participate in the #WebSummit conference due to the outrageous statements made by the conference CEO Paddy Cosgrave. Even during these difficult times, he is unable to set aside his extreme political views and denounce the Hamas terrorist activities against innocent people," he wrote, also on LinkedIn. "Dozens of companies have already canceled their participation in this conference, and we encourage more to do so."

Cosgrave's response over the same window moved in both directions. By 16 October he appeared to walk back his statement, writing nine days after Hamas invaded Israel: "We are devastated to see the terrible killings and the level of innocent civilian casualties in Israel and Gaza. We condemn the attacks by Hamas and extend our deepest sympathies to everyone who has lost loved ones. We hope for peaceful reconciliation." Under so much fire, however, he subsequently dug in his heels, tweeting afterward: "To repeat: War crimes are war crimes even when committed by allies & should be called out for what they are. I will not relent."

The planned sale of OpenAI employee shares that would have valued the startup at about $86 billion was put in jeopardy by Altman's firing.

# Notre Dame's First Quarter Against USC, Oct. 14 2023

Notre Dame led USC 7-3 after the first quarter of their Oct. 14, 2023 game, scoring first on a four-yard Sam Hartman touchdown pass to Gi'Bran Payne set up by Xavier Watts' interception, with USC answering through a Denis Lynch field goal.

Coverage picked up at 7:29 p.m. with the stadium dark as fans welcomed the Fighting Irish to the field. USC started with the ball at its own 25; MarShawn Lloyd ran up the middle for a yard on the first offensive play, and Caleb Williams scrambled for no gain on the next. At 7:37 p.m. Williams found Brendan Rice for an 11-yard gain and a first down, then over-shot Lake McRee and was picked off by Watts, who returned the ball all the way to the USC 12. Two Audric Estime runs picked up eight yards to set up third-and-2, and at 7:39 p.m. Hartman dropped back and threw to a leaping Payne, who back-pedalled into the end zone for the four-yard touchdown: Notre Dame 7, USC 0.

USC's response drive began with Zachariah Branch returning the kickoff to the USC 19. Austin Jones gained five on first down, and a defensive holding call on Notre Dame's Benjamin Morris on a second-down pass gave USC a first down at the 34. A Williams rush for four was followed by a snap infraction creating second-and-11, then a three-yard Jones run; Williams connected with Tahj Washington but the receiver was stopped three yards short of the marker, bringing out the punting unit, and Notre Dame fair caught at its own 14. Estime opened Notre Dame's next drive with an 11-yard run past the marker and caught a pass for four to set up second-and-6, but at 7:53 p.m. the Fighting Irish punted after Estime gained only a yard and Hartman's pass to Rico Flores Jr. fell incomplete.

# Turnovers, Not Yardage, Decided Notre Dame's Win Over USC

Notre Dame beat USC on Oct. 14, 2023 despite being out-gained and out-performed on third down, because a 5-0 turnover margin is difficult for any team to overcome — the claim the Sporting News advances is that field position bought by turnovers, plus pressure in the trenches, outweighed USC's statistical edges.

The grounds are the box score. In a season in which much had been made of USC's defensive woes holding back the offense, on this night it was the other way around: USC's defense held Notre Dame to just 251 total yards of offense, 51 fewer than the Trojans gained on offense, and Notre Dame converted only three of 10 third downs against USC's six of 13. The warrant joining those grounds to the conclusion is field position: the 5-0 turnover margin frequently left Notre Dame with only a short field to work with, so that the Fighting Irish started drives on average at their own 47 while the Trojans began on average at their own 28.

A second strand of the argument is that Watts made the headline-grabbing plays but a massive part of Notre Dame's defensive success came in the trenches. Notre Dame's defensive line tallied six sacks of Caleb Williams and three additional hits, frequently pressing the Trojan quarterback, and Williams finished 23-for-37 for 199 passing yards with one passing touchdown and three interceptions.

# NFL Aggressiveness Versus Traditional Game Management

A longtime NFL executive challenged the analytics-driven push toward aggressive play-calling on 16 October 2023, asking whether coaches have "come too far with coaches wanting to 'win' the game instead of sometimes being more traditional" after the Eagles threw a killer interception on third-and-9 from their own 46-yard line while protecting a 14-12 lead against the Jets with two minutes left in the fourth quarter.

The premise attacked is not that aggression is generally wrong. Most would agree teams have gotten smarter in their handling of fourth-down situations, going for it when it makes sense instead of punting almost out of habit; making the aggressive play to win can absolutely be the smart play regardless of results, and it is progress when teams seriously wrestle with these questions, not just on fourth down but in all aspects of strategy. What the exec disputes is the automatic application of that reasoning to a particular game state: Philadelphia could have run the ball on third-and-9, then punted from around midfield, leaving the Jets with barely more than a minute remaining, no timeouts and Zach Wilson behind center facing a ferocious Eagles pass rush. "Are coaches not willing to go against the slight statistical benefit that WPA (win probability added) provides?" he asked. "Is it no longer OK to let your defense win the game when it clearly has a huge talent/performance advantage? This Eagles game was 14-12, not 37-35."

The inference the counter-argument targets is the neglect of situation-specific factors. In that game the Jets' offense had netted 19 yards on its previous three possessions, producing one field goal on a drive that gained 16 of those yards; the Eagles had already suffered three turnovers, and they knew Wilson would be taking over deep in his territory with very little time remaining. "To me, these are exactly the type of factors that a coach needs to consider when deciding," the exec said. "I think they were ignored here." A veteran coach added an incentive-based explanation — critics attuned to the trend toward aggressiveness pounce when teams pass up chances to go for the kill, coaches know team owners tend to be fans rather than football strategists and listen to those criticisms, which creates an incentive to go down swinging: "Everybody thinks they are playing Brady, Manning or Rodgers in two-minute. If before the game someone offered Philly to put its defense against Zach Wilson on a need-field-goal drive starting inside his own 15 with no timeouts and a minute left, you think they would have taken it?" The base rate is thin: the situation Philly faced was the seventh time since 2000 that a team leading by 1-2 points in the final two minutes faced third down with 7-10 yards to go from the minus-40 yard line to midfield with the opponent holding no timeouts; three of the seven passed, resulting in one first down, one sack and Hurts' interception, and of those three only the Eagles lost the game.

CBS Sports benched Brock Purdy in Week 5 of the 2023 season and then reversed itself in Week 6, admitting the first call was a mistake: the Week 5 argument was that Dallas' pressure plus man coverage created too much downside, and the Week 6 argument was that the author would not make the mistake of benching Purdy again after Dallas played zone and paid for it.

# Cowboys-49ers Second Half: Three Prescott Interceptions And A 42-10 Final

San Francisco turned a 21-7 halftime lead into a 42-10 win over Dallas in the second half of the Oct. 8, 2023 "Sunday Night Football" game, aided by three Dak Prescott interceptions. Dallas started the half with the ball and Prescott hit CeeDee Lamb for a 29-yard gain into 49ers territory (10:13 p.m.), but San Francisco's defense tightened and limited the Cowboys to a Brandon Aubrey 50-yard field goal at 10:17 p.m., cutting the lead to 21-10.

Purdy hit Brandon Aiyuk for 23 yards (10:21 p.m.); an offensive holding call on Spencer Burford wiped out a 40-yard Aiyuk gain (10:23 p.m.); and Deebo Samuel went 43 yards on the very next play to put San Francisco in the red zone (10:25 p.m.). At 10:27 p.m. George Kittle caught his third touchdown of the night for a 28-10 lead. At 10:32 p.m. Prescott, heaving downfield under pressure, was intercepted by Tashaun Gipson. Purdy reached 242 yards with three touchdowns after a 19-yard catch by Jauan Jennings (10:38 p.m.), and the third quarter ended 28-10 with San Francisco a yard from a 25-point lead.

The fourth quarter was a formality. Purdy hit Kyle Juszczyk at 10:47 p.m. for the 49ers' fifth touchdown and his own fourth, making it 35-10. At 10:52 p.m. Fred Warner intercepted a deflected Prescott pass — completing a night with a sack, a forced fumble and an interception — and Jordan Mason ran in another touchdown at 10:53 p.m. for 42-10, with Leighton Vander Esch down injured. # The Baltimore Ravens' Pass-Oriented Offense Shift

The New York Times questioned on 16 October 2023 whether Baltimore's shift toward a more conventional pass offense will make the Ravens tougher to defend, noting they have never scored fewer points or amassed less offensive EPA through the first six games of a season with Lamar Jackson in the lineup.

The grounds are Jackson's changed rushing profile. He has one rush longer than 20 yards, where he had four or five by that point in previous seasons, and he is gaining at least eight yards on 15 percent of carries, half his previous rate. The schedule and injuries have played roles in the scoring decline, but the open question is whether the explosive quarterback runs are mostly in the past — and the writer is not expecting a consistent precision passing game to suddenly materialise.

An executive pressed the argument further, holding that the change subtracts more than it adds: "The defense keeps them in it, but I don't necessarily think this offensive change is going to make them any better when it counts. Lamar Jackson does not appear as dynamic as a runner, but in this offense, he does not need to be. He is regulated to pass from the pocket, but you are taking away the biggest weapon the offense had when you do that. Odell (Beckham) is not that guy anymore. Who are you truly afraid of on that offense? Nobody but Lamar, and if you are not using Lamar in a certain capacity, he becomes just like the rest of these quarterbacks around the league — hit or miss."

# Jets' Final Drive And The Spillane Interception

The Jets' late comeback bid against the Raiders on Nov. 12, 2023 died on a Robert Spillane interception at 11:16 p.m., and their last-gasp drive ended at 11:26 p.m. when Zach Wilson's final pass, thrown after he was chased out of the pocket, was batted down and the Raiders held on to win 16-12.

The sequence began with a turnover in New York's favor. At 11:03 p.m., just as the Raiders seemed to be inching toward putting the game away, Josh Jacobs lost a fumble at the Jets' 25 — forced by Jamien Sherwood and recovered by Ashtyn Davis — and the turnover went to review as a potential massive swing. At 11:06 p.m. the call on the field stood and Zach Wilson opened the drive with a throw across the middle to Lazard for 17 yards to the Jets 41. At 11:07 p.m. a three-yard catch by Garrett Wilson was followed by a quick pass to Breece Hall, who made defenders miss for 10 yards to the Raiders 46. At 11:08 p.m. Uzomah stayed up after a big hit for six yards, play stopped for an injury to Jakorian Bennett, and Wilson's deep shot to a double-covered Garrett Wilson was broken up. At 11:10 p.m. a dump-off to Tyler Conklin kept the drive alive with a first down at the 36, and at 11:11 p.m., after missing Lazard and a low Conklin catch two yards shy, Wilson connected with Garrett Wilson for six up to the 22 and a fresh set of downs at the two-minute warning.

Then came the pick. At 11:16 p.m. Hall could get only two yards on a check down to the right out to the 20, and on the next play Wilson tried to get the ball to Lazard and was intercepted by Robert Spillane, who returned it to the Raiders' 40 — with 1:14 left and the Jets holding three timeouts, the game was all but over. New York used those timeouts: at 11:17 p.m. Jacobs gained five and the Jets called a quick timeout; at 11:18 p.m. Jacobs was stuffed for no gain and the Jets used their second timeout with 1:05 left, leaving the Raiders a pivotal third-and-5. At 11:19 p.m. Las Vegas trusted O'Connell to put the game away with a pass, but his attempt to Mayer was batted down by Jermaine Johnson, saving the Jets a timeout and forcing a punt, before the Raiders took a delay of game penalty. At 11:20 p.m., even after backing up five yards, Cole still booted it too far and it bounced into the end zone for a touchback, giving the Jets the ball at the 20 with 53 seconds left. At 11:22 p.m. Wilson spiked the first pass with no one open, then hit Conklin on a dump-off for nine yards and again for an impressive leaping grab at the Raiders' 45, with the Jets using their last timeout at 12 seconds. At 11:24 p.m. the Hail Marys began, the first to Gipson sailing out of bounds, and with five seconds left the Raiders called their second timeout.

# Dallas Goedert As A Week 5 2023 Bust Candidate At The Rams

CBS Sports flagged Dallas Goedert as a "Bust Candidate" for Week 5 of the 2023 season at the Los Angeles Rams: the claim is that Goedert is a distant third in targets on the Eagles for a reason — he's not explosive in the least and the Philadelphia offense is much more concerned with its explosive components — and the warrant is that the Rams' recent tight end concessions came against secondary tight ends they barely covered, so they do not predict anything for Goedert.

The usage grounds are blunt. For three weeks in a row, with seven or fewer targets, Goedert has failed to reach even 50 receiving yards, and his target volume dipped from seven in Weeks 2 and 3 to four in Week 4, the same number as D'Andre Swift — and it shouldn't be lost on fantasy managers that since Swift became a staple in the Eagles offense, Goedert has taken a backseat. Coach Nick Sirianni again said "we need to get him the football," citing that plays designed for him wound up going to other Eagles because of how defenses played Goedert. The column's film review disputes that explanation: on his nine third-down routes in Week 4 there was nothing teams were doing to take him away, he still looked sluggish in his movements and didn't run many deeper routes, though on a couple he did get open and Jalen Hurts had better opportunities elsewhere. The mixed evidence from that game is that two targets came in the red zone and a third was a deep contested catch for 17 yards, while the fourth was dropped on a short throw. On the season Goedert has three red-zone targets and zero end-zone targets, and while there is always a shot he scores from short range, the Eagles like to run the ball near the goal line.

The matchup evidence is presented as a trap. The Rams got stung for two touchdowns to tight ends at Indianapolis the previous week, one on a 35-yard play where Mo Alie-Cox got matched up with defensive-end-turned-outside-linebacker Mike Hoecht, the other a five-yard toss to Andrew Ogletree, who ran past Hoecht off the snap for an easy score — but those players aren't considered primary tight ends like Goedert, so it's unlikely the Rams would cover Goedert the way they covered them, which is to say barely. Before Week 4, the Seahawks, Bengals and 49ers tight ends, including George Kittle, combined for eight non-PPR and 19 PPR fantasy points over three games against the Rams, whose pass stats against tight ends were much better before the Colts laid some numbers on them. The breakdown lists Philadelphia at the Rams, the Eagles favoured by 4.5, an over/under of 50.5, an opponent ranked 23rd versus tight ends, 9.3 projected points, a 12th tight end ranking, and year-to-date totals of 13 receptions on 19 targets for 88 yards, no touchdowns and 5.5 fantasy points per game. # Arizona's Scoring Plays Versus Utah

Arizona built a staggering 28-7 halftime lead over Utah on the back of a trick play, a blocked punt return and offensive touchdowns on three of four first-half drives. After failing continuously on trick plays involving receiver Tetairoa McMillan passing behind the scrimmage this season, head coach Jedd Fisch designed it again — this time to perfection — with McMillan finding a wide-open fifth-year senior Michael Wiley to score a touchdown in his last game in Tucson. Following the trickery, another huge roar of the Wildcat faithful ensued after a blocked punt and score by Anthony Ward, the first Arizona blocked punt and score since Nov. 13, 2021.

The Wildcats' momentum was rolling like a well-oiled machine on both ends of the ball in the first half, led by Michael Wiley tallying two of the offensive touchdowns, outgaining the Utes by 98 yards on the ground, and forcing the Utes into two three-and-outs, three punts and a red zone interception, headlined by captain linebacker Jacob Manu — the first Arizona linebacker interception since Anthony Pandy against USC in 2021. With rain starting to pour late in the first half in a rare Arizona "rain game", the overcast did not drive the Zona Zoo from the stadium, nor stop the Wildcats' progression. "I don't think the rain effected us at all," Fisch said.

When "Swag Surfin" by Fast Life Yungstaz came on to signal the fourth quarter — the quarter in which, going into the game, Arizona was outscoring opponents 90-37 — the Wildcats put a touchdown on the board on their first drive, a seven-play, 61-yard drive finished by a 25-yard dash and dive into the end zone by running back Jonah Coleman. The UA then ran away from the Utes, outscoring them 14-8 in the quarter and allowing only a garbage-time touchdown in the last minute to secure its 8th win of the season. The last touchdown came with backup quarterback Jayden de Laura hitting McMillan for a 51-yard score. "I wanted Jayden to go out with a touchdown pass this season," Fisch said. "I think that he deserves that."

# Sports Betting Odds

## Definition

Sports betting odds are the numbers a sportsbook posts alongside a wager to show the payout a bettor stands to win relative to their stake, and they are set by oddsmakers using computer models and analytics before being released to the public. The same underlying odds concept takes different shapes depending on the bet type — a moneyline price on who wins outright, a point spread price on a handicapped margin, and a totals (over/under) price on the combined score — and can be displayed in American, decimal, or fractional format.

## Context

In the corpus, odds are the common thread across every major bet type: moneylines, point spreads, totals, and prop bets all price outcomes with the same odds conventions, and combined-market previews such as college bowl coverage post moneyline, spread, and total odds side by side for a single game. Odds are not static — sportsbooks move them ("line movement") in response to public betting patterns, injury or roster news, and sharp/professional money, with the goal of balancing action on both sides of a bet so the book keeps its built-in profit regardless of outcome. Because different sportsbooks can carry different odds for the same event, bettors practice "line shopping" — comparing odds and lines across multiple sportsbooks before wagering to find the best price. Odds also extend beyond single games into futures and award markets, such as season-long odds on the NFL MVP race between Brock Purdy and Lamar Jackson.

## Key Characteristics

- **American odds format dominates U.S. listings** — a negative number (e.g., -110) shows the favorite and how much must be wagered to profit $100; a positive number (e.g., +250) shows the underdog and how much a $100 wager profits.
- **Three display formats carry the same price** — American, decimal (multiply the odds by the stake for total payout), and fractional (numerator = profit, denominator = stake) are alternative notations for identical odds.
- **Odds move for identifiable reasons** — sportsbooks shift a line or its odds because of lopsided public betting, new information (injuries, weather), sharp bettor action, or a perceived initial mispricing.
- **Odds differ by bet type but share the sign convention** — moneyline odds price the outright winner, point spread odds price a handicapped margin near even money, and totals odds price the over/under of a combined score; all three commonly display as American odds.
- **Line shopping exploits cross-sportsbook odds variance** — because oddsmakers and sportsbooks don't always move in lockstep, checking odds at multiple books before betting can secure a better price on the same wager.

# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."

# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.

# Adam Yedidia's First Testimony And His Immunity Deal

Late in the afternoon of the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the government called Adam Yedidia to the stand, and lead prosecutor Danielle Sassoon disclosed that this college friend of Bankman-Fried had legal immunity during his testimony. Asked why he had made such a deal with the government, Yedidia answered: "I was concerned that I had unwittingly written code that contributed to a crime."

Yedidia, described as a fast-talking graduate of MIT, testified that he and Bankman-Fried were close friends in college. After Bankman-Fried left Jane Street — the high-frequency trading firm where the former billionaire got his start in finance after MIT — he persuaded Yedidia to join him, first as a trader at Alameda and then as a developer at FTX.

The testimony was cut short when the clock neared 4:30 p.m. and court adjourned for the day. Yedidia was scheduled to continue his testimony on Thursday, to be followed by Matt Huang, a former partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital, and then by Gary Wang, a key Bankman-Fried lieutenant and one of the government's star witnesses.

# Bankman-Fried's Claimed Ignorance Of Alameda's Finances

Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried attacked the prosecution's premise that he knew about the hole in FTX by claiming he did not learn of the $8 billion liability associated with Alameda until October 2022, that he found it all by himself by looking at a computer database, and that when he found it he was "very surprised." The Verge's reporter recorded the claim with heavy scepticism.

The counter-argument extended to reinterpreting each earlier warning as something innocuous. On why Alameda served as FTX's "payment provider" for bank transfers, he said FTX could not get bank accounts right away and he anticipated it would take a year or two, so rather than wait he used Alameda: "My understanding at the time was that there were teams managing the process. At the time, I wasn't entirely sure what was happening." On Adam Yedidia's testimony about an August 2022 conversation regarding the enormous amount Alameda owed FTX, Bankman-Fried remembered it differently — Yedidia was just asking about Alameda's risk profile and he was not talking about insolvency at all. On the dramatic balcony conversation with Nishad Singh at their penthouse, he said Singh thought Alameda's liabilities had gotten too high and that FTX was spending too much on marketing, while Bankman-Fried still thought Alameda had more assets than liabilities so it was all fine, and besides, if Singh thought he would be better at marketing he could take it over — it did not have anything to do with the money Alameda owed FTX at all.

# Adam Yedidia's Testimony And The $8 Billion Bug

Adam Yedidia, the prosecution's second witness, testified that in June 2022 he submitted a report to Bankman-Fried on Signal showing that $8 billion in customer money held in an internal database tracking cash wired to an Alameda account called "fiat at ftx.com" was missing.

Yedidia met Bankman-Fried in college at MIT and the pair remained close friends; assuming a robotic posture on the stand, he said he worked out of FTX's Hong Kong office from January to October of 2021 and then in the Bahamas until the collapse. He referred to a group Signal thread called "People of the House," referring to Bankman-Fried's $35 million penthouse where many employees lived; on who was paying the rent, Yedidia recalled Bankman-Fried saying he "assumed it's just Alameda paying for it in the end." Yedidia said Bankman-Fried had told him, before he began working in the Bahamas in 2019, that he and Ellison had had sex, and asked whether it was a good idea for them to date — Yedidia said no, and Bankman-Fried responded that he was expecting that answer. One of Yedidia's responsibilities was fixing the bug in the code that gave Alameda preferential treatment. He said he and Bankman-Fried spoke about the missing $8 billion at the pickleball court at the resort in Nassau, Bahamas, where he asked his boss if things were OK because it "seemed like a lot of money" from FTX customers was at risk. "Sam said, we were bulletproof last year. We aren't bulletproof this year," Yedidia testified; asked when they would be bulletproof again, Bankman-Fried said he was not sure, but it might be six months to three years. Yedidia said Bankman-Fried appeared "worried or nervous," which was atypical, but that he still trusted Bankman-Fried and Ellison to "handle the situation." On cross-examination, Christian Everdell, Bankman-Fried's attorney, focused on how Yedidia was the one responsible for developing and reviewing the code.

# Alameda's Special Privileges Written Into FTX's Code

Gary Wang told the court that Alameda received advantages through code baked into FTX's software granting it special access to the exchange — "We gave special privileges on FTX that gave unlimited withdrawals on the platform to Alameda" — privileges that ultimately resulted in Alameda owing FTX $8 billion worth of customer deposits.

The structure had several linked parts. Alameda was allowed to withdraw and transfer funds and had a $65 billion line of credit. "When customers deposited USD, it went to Alameda," Wang said. "It existed in the computer code. Alameda could have negative balances and unlimited withdrawals." That "bug" in the code was written by Nishad Singh, FTX's director of engineering, and reviewed by Wang, with Bankman-Fried calling the shots. Wang also told the court about a $1 million personal loan he received and a $200 million to $300 million loan in his name from Alameda that was never deposited into his account but was used to make investments into other companies on behalf of FTX — all done by Bankman-Fried, he testified. The escalation was visible over time: in early 2020 Wang discovered for the first time that Alameda's negative balance exceeded FTX's revenue, an indication that Alameda was taking customer funds, and he brought this to Bankman-Fried's attention several times; in late 2021 he discovered Alameda had withdrawn $3 billion from its $65 billion line of credit. The ownership and authority around it: Wang owned 10% of Alameda while his boss owned the other 90%, his compensation was a base salary of $200,000 per year plus stock, and he owned roughly 17% of FTX — and even though they were co-founders, "ultimately it was Sam's decision to make" when there were disagreements. Born in China, Wang moved to the U.S. at age 7 and grew up in Minnesota before going to MIT to study math and computer science, worked at Google after college, and first met Bankman-Fried during high school at a summer camp.

# The FTX Trial's Stakes For The Wider Crypto Industry

The Verge argued that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty: depending on what evidence is introduced, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.

The grounds are the unpredictability of what a trial surfaces, voiced by Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point? This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out." The warrant joining that uncertainty to industry-wide stakes is that the industry's reputation is already beaten down, so evidence introduced against one exchange's founder lands on the whole sector rather than on him alone.

# Alameda Research's Origins And Naming

Alameda Research was the cryptocurrency trading firm Bankman-Fried started in 2017 during a crypto bull run, and it was named for Alameda County in California, where its first office was set up. Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried said he knew "basically nothing" about cryptocurrency at the time but wanted to do arbitrage on it anyway, and that he is "somewhat introverted, naturally."

The name was chosen for cover. In his own words on the stand: "Effectively, we wanted to be under the radar at that point in time. I didn't want to call it Sam's Crypto Trading Firm or anything like that. We — there are a lot of competitors and people who we didn't particularly want to know what we were building out because they would race to do it. 'Research' was a sort of generic word, which filled out the company name. And that was — it was far better than the internal name that we had at that point, which was Wireless Mouse." The Verge's reporter noted she would find this more believable had she not already watched a video, played during Gary Wang's first day of testimony with Bankman-Fried and the jury present, of Bankman-Fried explaining on a podcast that the name made it easier to get a bank account.

The founding assembled the people later charged alongside him: Bankman-Fried went on a hiring spree, taking on Wang to program the computers, then Nishad Singh about a month after founding Alameda Research, and finally Caroline Ellison. Though Bankman-Fried was CEO and also majority owner, he wanted to be clear that he did not supervise Wang's direct work. After a run of wildly successful arbitrage — 50 percent to 100 percent annualized returns, per his testimony — he decided to found a cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, figuring he would fail and putting the chance of success at 20 percent, without defining the time period he had in mind.

# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."



---


# The FTT Token And The "Sam Coins"

FTT was a token created by Bankman-Fried and Wang and issued by FTX, and it was one of several "Sam coins" — a nickname for tokens Bankman-Fried was heavily involved in and owned a lot of, either personally or through Alameda. Wang described FTT as being "sort of equity" in FTX, a characterisation The Verge's reporter suspected some crypto lawyers would dispute but that would probably please the SEC.

The distribution was lopsided from the start. Alameda got its war chest — 60 percent to 70 percent of the initial supply — for free, while seed investors got FTT at 10 cents a coin and FTT first listed at $1 a coin. Ellison testified that Bankman-Fried felt $1 per coin was psychologically important and directed her to buy up FTT using Alameda if the price fell below a dollar.

The discriminating feature of the Sam coins was that their book value was not realisable: they were almost certainly worth less than the value displayed on the balance sheet, because trying to sell them all at once would crater the prices. Bankman-Fried nonetheless directed Ellison to put those coins on the balance sheets Alameda showed to lenders, even though she felt doing so was "somewhat misleading." FTT also figures in the origin story of Alameda's negative-balance privilege: Wang said Bankman-Fried at first told him the code change letting an account go negative was to pay for expenses for the FTT token, but once implemented the ability to go negative was used for other things, including trading and unlimited withdrawals of FTX's trading fees and customer money.

# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Gary Wang's Ownership Stake And Cooperation Deal

Gary Wang, co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX and co-founder of Alameda Research, owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX and drew a $200,000-a-year salary with no performance bonuses — though at times he was a billionaire on paper — while Bankman-Fried owned 90 percent of Alameda and 65 percent of FTX. He returned to the US on November 16th, met with the US government on November 17th without having been arrested or charged, offered to cooperate immediately, and pled guilty to various charges a month later. Wang was clear that he was cooperating because he did not want to go to jail, and said he hoped his assistance would lead a sentencing judge to be lenient.

The Verge's reporter drew from the disparity a puzzle she could not resolve: Wang took bizarre risks for a relatively small share. Bankman-Fried did not code, so none of his fingerprints are on the technical changes that let FTX allegedly defraud its customers and investors, while Wang supervised the code behind a key prosecution claim — that Alameda Research was afforded secret, special privileges with FTX's funds. When FTX went down, Wang left himself with no plausible deniability. Wang, a college roommate of Bankman-Fried's, took the stand after Adam Yedidia and, in the reporter's phrase, sang like a canary about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code.

The delivery was heavy going. On October 6th, 2023 Wang had to explain to the jury the difference between a front end and a back end, explain futures trading, and read a great deal into the record, which took a while; it was a tough day for the jury, and probably for Wang, who spoke quickly, perhaps from nerves.

# Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.

# FTX's Final Days And The Alameda Shortfall, As Wang Described Them

Much of Gary Wang's Friday testimony focused on the final days at FTX before the operation imploded: after media reports detailing Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, an emergency meeting was called between Bankman-Fried, Wang and Singh to discuss shutting down Alameda, and they decided against it because he and Bankman-Fried knew Alameda had no way to repay the roughly $14 billion hole in its books.

Wang, 30, was technology chief for FTX, which spiralled into bankruptcy in November; he spoke so fast that U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan and the prosecutor both stopped him at points to ask that he slow his pace. Prosecutors took the jury through a series of tweets beginning on Nov. 7 — posts from the company blaming bank hours for slow withdrawals, while Bankman-Fried tweeted from his personal account assuring customers that all was fine. "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine," Wang testified. On Nov. 12, after FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried asked Wang to drive with him to the Bahamas Securities Commission for a meeting; on the drive, Bankman-Fried told Wang to transfer assets to Bahamian liquidators because he believed they would allow him to maintain control of the company. Wang said he was not in the meeting with the securities authority, though Bankman-Fried's dad was present.

# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

# Alameda Absorbed FTX's Losses, Including MobileCoin

Alameda Research functioned as FTX's sin-eater: when FTX took a loss, the loss was moved onto Alameda's balance sheet so that FTX would not look bad. Gary Wang testified that in 2021 FTX was facing a "several hundred million dollar" loss from an exploit in MobileCoin — apparently in April 2021, though Wang did not give a month — and Bankman-Fried directed him to have Alameda take it on instead, because FTX's balance sheets were visible to investors and Alameda's were not.

The relation was general, not a one-off. Ellison testified that her tenure as CEO of Alameda Research was an exercise in optics: when FTX took a loss in the hundreds of millions of dollars because a trader had exploited its system, Wang moved that loss onto Alameda's balance sheet, and FTX's "insurance fund," meant to keep traders from getting stuck with other traders' losses, was totally made up, with Alameda simply picking up the tab. The concealment held all the way to investors: Paradigm Capital's Matt Huang showed the court the balance sheets he had received from Bankman-Fried, and they did not include the loss, which should have appeared in the second-quarter numbers he was given — those instead showed $63 million in trading expenses and $63 million in "other expenses" for the quarter, and an estimated profit of $732 million.

Bankman-Fried offered a benign reading of the same arrangement from the stand: he said the MobileCoin loss, the one Wang said Alameda took to keep off FTX's balance sheet, was a totally innocent matter in which he thought it appropriate that Alameda take the position as a backstop liquidity provider.

# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.
