# Bankman-Fried And Ellison: Relationship And Alameda Leadership

Caroline Ellison testified that she and Bankman-Fried started sleeping together in the fall of 2018, on and off, when she was a trader and he was CEO, and that they later dated twice — first from the summer of 2020 through the summer of 2021, a relationship they agreed to keep secret though some people found out, and again from the fall of 2021 until the spring of 2022, when they lived together. She was named co-CEO of Alameda with Sam Trabucco in 2021 while she and Bankman-Fried were broken up, and CEO in 2022; the goal, Bankman-Fried told her, was to "optically" separate Alameda Research and FTX. "The whole time we were dating, he was my boss at work," she said. They broke up because she wanted more from the relationship and he was distant and not paying enough attention to her. He did not grant her equity even though she asked, telling her it would be too complicated; instead she got a $200,000 salary, even as CEO, and bonuses twice a year ranging from $100,000 to $20 million.

Bankman-Fried gave a different rationale for the handover. In 2021, he testified, FTX was growing to millions of users with $1 billion of revenue, he was working 12 to 22 hours a day and taking one day off every couple of months, and because FTX had grown so much he could no longer run both companies — so he handed Alameda off to Ellison and Trabucco, who immediately after being named co-CEO promptly drifted away to early retirement. Bankman-Fried did remain involved in hedging and risk at Alameda.

Ellison's proximity also gave her an unusual view of his character. She said Alameda was troubled from her earliest time there in 2018: "Shortly after I started, I learned the company was in worse shape than I realized." Alameda had initially been funded with loans "from acquaintances," and those loans were recalled a few weeks after she arrived; when she asked Bankman-Fried why he had not shared the company's shaky circumstances in the job offer, "He hadn't known how to tell me," she said. She described him as "very ambitious," said he told her there was a 5 percent chance he would become president of the United States, and said he told her that if there were a coin flip where tails destroyed the world and heads made the world twice as good, he would flip the coin — which he called being "risk-neutral," and which The Verge's reporter called a fancy way of saying he was a gambling addict. He made her CEO of his sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give her equity.

# Alameda Research

Alameda Research is the crypto-trading firm Sam Bankman-Fried co-founded in 2017, before FTX existed. FTX came two years later, in 2019, and Bankman-Fried co-founded it as a complement to Alameda — to help bring in revenue and liquidity for the trading arm. The founding order is the discriminating fact: the exchange was created to serve the trading firm, not the other way round.

The feature that later set Alameda's balance sheet apart was how much of it consisted of the affiliated exchange's own token. A report showed that Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of "unlocked FTT," alongside $2.16 billion of "FTT collateral." FTT was the token behind FTX. So the trading firm's single biggest asset was the token issued by the exchange founded to support it.

# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

# Can Sun's Testimony On Fabricated Justifications

Former FTX lawyer Can Sun testified that during the days in November when the exchange imploded, Bankman-Fried — then trying to raise money from the private equity group Apollo, which wanted an explanation for what had happened — came to him and asked him to come up with justifications for the missing funds. That request, Sun said, "basically confirmed my suspicions that had been rising all day" that Bankman-Fried had purloined the funds.

Sun ran Bankman-Fried through possible explanations, including a margin loan program, and explained that none of them could fit the actual situation — for instance, Alameda had borrowed more from FTX than had ever been in the margin loan program. He said Bankman-Fried acknowledged their conversation with a "yup, yup": "I was expecting a bigger response, but it was very muted." After that, Sun testified, Singh spilled the beans that Alameda had withdrawn assets that included the customer funds. Sun quit the next day, and, like Yedidia, testified with immunity.

The jury then saw the fabrication deployed in public: a Good Morning America appearance by Bankman-Fried on December 1st, 2022, in which he tried to justify the missing funds through the margin loan program. The Verge's reporter called it such a flimsy excuse that even George Stephanopoulos could see through it, and described Sun's testimony as brief and explosive.



---


# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.



---


# FTX's Spending Served Bankman-Fried's Status, Not Philanthropy

The Verge's reporter argued that at every turn the scams at FTX and Alameda led back to making Bankman-Fried more important — not to giving money away, as his stated Effective Altruism rationale claimed. The grounds are the pattern of what the money bought: Singh testified to more than a billion dollars spent on celebrity endorsements, which made FTX very famous even though the futures platform did not operate in the US; the political donations gave Bankman-Fried influence in the highest echelons of power; and Ellison testified to venture investments that gave him more dominance in the tech world.

The warrant joining the pattern to the conclusion is that spending reveals priorities better than statements do: it is easy to lie with words and harder to lie with money. Bankman-Fried went around telling people he wanted to make a lot of money in order to give it away, an idea of the Effective Altruism movement he affiliated himself with, but the amount he funneled to his Paper Bird vehicle alone was ten times the size of his philanthropic spending as outlined by the prosecution's expert Peter Easton — and all of it was vastly outweighed by his investments, the places where he could prove he was very smart by investing in the right companies early.



---


# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. Later Alameda's balance was more negative than FTT and the trading revenue combined, and Wang had further conversations with Bankman-Fried about it. Wang testified he knew at the time that Alameda was using FTX customers' funds and that he knew it was wrong.

The same gradual accommodation shows in Ellison's account. Choking back tears, she testified: "When I started working at Alameda, I don't think I would have believed you if you told me I would be sending false balance sheets to our lenders or taking customer money, but over time, it was something I became more comfortable with."



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# June 2022: Alameda's Reckoning And Lender Repayment

By 2022 Alameda's negative balance on FTX had become a cause for concern for Caroline Ellison, Nishad Singh, and Gary Wang, who built a spreadsheet to work out how negative Alameda actually was; the version shown in court ran to several pages of attempts to reconcile, and Wang figured Alameda owed FTX about $11 billion at a time when FTX's revenue was about $1.5 billion. Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried then met in the Bahamas office, where Alameda's lenders wanted their money back and Bankman-Fried directed the group to pay the lenders back using FTX customer funds.

Bankman-Fried considered shutting Alameda down and even wrote a long memo about it, but Wang testified that in a now-deleted Signal discussion of that memo he told Bankman-Fried and Singh they could not shut Alameda down because they could not repay its debt. Another empty Signal chat, with its setting to delete messages after a week, was shown to the court; its members were Ellison, Singh, Wang, and Bankman-Fried.

Bankman-Fried's own account from the stand ran differently. He testified that in June 2022 he heard about the account called "fiat@ftx" tracking how much money Alameda owed to FTX, that he did not know what it was and did not bother to find out because he was busy, and that this was when he directed Ellison to repay Alameda's lenders because he thought Alameda was good for it. He also gave BlockFi and Voyager, two crypto lenders, some capital infusions for good measure.

# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.

# Neural Networks And DeepMind's Atari Demonstration

A neural network is a complex algorithm created in the image of the human brain, essentially a giant mathematical system that spends days, weeks or even months identifying patterns in large amounts of digital data. First developed in the 1950s, these systems could learn to handle tasks on their own: after analysing names and addresses scribbled on hundreds of envelopes, for instance, they could read handwritten text. Flush with cash, DeepMind hired researchers who specialised in them.

DeepMind took the concept further, building a system that could learn to play classic Atari games such as Space Invaders, Pong and Breakout to illustrate what was possible. This got the attention of another Silicon Valley powerhouse, Google, and specifically Larry Page, who saw a demonstration of DeepMind's machine playing Atari games and wanted in. The boundary of what the field could then show was pushed again in the spring of 2012, when Geoffrey Hinton, a 64-year-old professor at the University of Toronto, and two graduate students published a research paper that showed the world what AI could do by training a neural network to recognise common objects such as flowers, dogs and cars.

# Gaza As A Tech Outsourcing Hub

Gaza, despite being one of the most economically challenged regions in the world, has ironically always been a tech hub — not only for Palestine and Palestinians, but also for the world, with international companies having for many years sought out a presence there to collaborate with talented tech freelancers and the startups that gradually emerged from the region. According to sources who helped build those bridges, Nvidia, famed for its role in the new AI boom, has been working with at least 100 engineers from the region for years; tragically, the initiative to employ Palestinians in this outsourcing was that of Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, whose daughter was brutally murdered in the attacks by Hamas.

The hub's scale marks its boundary. Since at least 2008, TechCrunch has been covering technology companies out of Palestine, some serving their direct audience and some serving the tech world internationally, and Silicon Valley had taken an increasing interest in Palestine as a tech hub — but like the ecosystem itself, that interest is nascent: to date, those working in the region estimate that as much as $10 million has been invested in the Palestinian tech ecosystem. Notably, in 2017, Salesforce founder and CEO Marc Benioff joined Silicon Valley luminaries in backing the first-ever coding academy to be created in Gaza.

# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.

# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.

# DeepMind's Founding And Thiel's Investment

In 2010 Demis Hassabis and two colleagues, all living in Britain, were looking for money to start building "artificial general intelligence", a machine that could do anything the brain could do, at a time when few people were interested in AI because after a half-century of research the field had failed to deliver anything remotely close to the human brain. Some scientists and thinkers had nonetheless become fixated on AI's downsides, and many, including the three young men, had a connection to Eliezer Yudkowsky, an internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher who led a community calling themselves Rationalists or, later, effective altruists; they believed AI could find a cure for cancer or solve climate change but worried that AI bots might do things their creators had not intended, arguing that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators. Peter Thiel, enormously wealthy through an early investment in Facebook and his work with Musk in the early days of PayPal, had developed a fascination with the singularity, the science-fiction trope describing the moment when intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity, and with his funding Yudkowsky had expanded his AI lab and created an annual conference on the singularity; one of Hassabis' colleagues had met Yudkowsky years before and snagged them speaking spots at that conference, ensuring an invitation to Thiel's party, where Yudkowsky introduced Hassabis to Thiel. Assuming many guests would be trying to squeeze their host for money, Hassabis' strategy was to arrange another meeting: he told Thiel there was a deep tension between the bishop and the knight, pieces carrying the same value whose strengths the best players understood to be vastly different. Charmed, Thiel invited the group back the next day, gathering in the kitchen where their host, just finished with his morning workout and still sweating in a shiny tracksuit, was handed a Diet Coke by a butler; the three made their pitch and soon Thiel and his venture capital firm agreed to put £1.4 million, about $A2.7 million, into their startup, making him their first major investor.

They named the company DeepMind, a nod to "deep learning", a way for AI systems to learn skills by analysing large amounts of data, to neuroscience, and to the Deep Thought supercomputer from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, and by the spring of 2010 they were building their dream machine, wholeheartedly believing that because they understood the risks they were uniquely positioned to protect the world. Senator Charles Schumer (D-NY) hosted Silicon Valley's AI leaders on Tuesday as the US Senate reconvened its AI Insight Forum for a second time, and on leaving the meeting Schumer told the assembled press that "it is clear that American leadership on AI can't be done on the cheap," reporting that almost all of the experts in the forum called for robust, sustained federal investment in the private and public sectors to achieve American-led transformative and sustainable innovation in AI.

# Vivek Ramaswamy's TikTok Launch

Republican presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy — who proposed raising the voting age to 25 — launched his TikTok presence with an endorsement from Jake Paul, the YouTuber turned boxer who built a content empire by marketing to children, in what TechCrunch described on 2023-10-02 as an appeal to younger voters. # DeepMind's Ethics Board And Its Single Meeting In 2015

When Musk invested in DeepMind he broke his own informal rule that he would not invest in any company he didn't run himself, and the downsides were already apparent when, only a month or so after his birthday spat with Larry Page, he again found himself face to face with his former friend. The occasion was the first meeting of DeepMind's ethics board on 14 August 2015, a board set up at the insistence of the startup's founders to ensure their technology did no harm after the sale. The members convened in a conference room just outside Musk's office at SpaceX, but that is where Musk's control ended: when Google bought DeepMind it bought the whole thing, and Musk was out, financially ahead but unhappy. Three Google executives now firmly in control of DeepMind were there, Page, Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder and Tesla investor, and Eric Schmidt, Google's chair, along with other attendees including Reid Hoffman, another PayPal founder, and Toby Ord, an Australian philosopher studying "existential risk".

The DeepMind founders reported that they were pushing ahead with their work but were aware the technology carried serious risks. Mustafa Suleyman gave a presentation called "The Pitchforkers Are Coming", telling the board that AI could lead to an explosion in disinformation and fretting that as the technology replaced countless jobs in coming years the public would accuse Google of stealing their livelihoods, so Google would need to share its wealth with the millions who could no longer find work and provide a "universal basic income". Musk agreed, but it was pretty clear the Google guests were not prepared to embark on a redistribution of their wealth: Schmidt said he thought the worries were completely overblown, and Page, in his usual whisper, agreed, arguing AI would create more jobs than it took away. Eight months later DeepMind had a breakthrough that stunned the AI community and the world, when a DeepMind machine called AlphaGo beat one of the world's best players at the ancient game of Go, a match streamed over the internet and watched by 200 million people across the globe, though most researchers had assumed AI needed another 10 years to muster the ingenuity to do that; the South Korean professional Lee Se-dol played Go against AlphaGo in March 2016.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

# Venture Capital

## Definition

In the corpus, venture capital (VC) names the money that specialist VC firms — and the individual "venture capitalists" and partners who run them — put into privately held startups, tracked through a sequence of named funding rounds (seed, pre-Series A, Series A through E and beyond) from Thiel's early backing of DeepMind through FTX's $400 million Series C.

## Context

The corpus shows venture capital operating at both ends of the startup lifecycle. Early-stage examples include Thiel's venture capital firm putting £1.4 million into the not-yet-named DeepMind, and Motier Ventures backing Mistral AI's €105 million seed round, Poolside's separate $126 million seed round, and Index Ventures leading (with Iconiq and Motier Ventures also participating in) Adaptive's seed round at a $100 million valuation — all part of "VC firms fighting for the most competitive funding rounds" in the French AI boom. Later-stage venture capital appears in FTX's $400 million Series C round that pushed its valuation to $32 billion, and in Rainforest's Accel-led $8.5 million seed round alongside Bolt's earlier $355 million Series E. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. # Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."

# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Google's Defense That Search Defaults Are Easy To Change

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. On Google's blog, president of global affairs Kent Walker said the search product was the favourite of users, browsers and device makers simply because it was the best in the business: "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," and "this lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today." Walker's supporting evidence is revealed preference when Google is not the default: when Mozilla made Yahoo! the default on Firefox, most users changed it to Google; and people setting up a Windows device frequently sidestep the Microsoft default — "Google" was the number one search query on Bing in 2021 — despite Microsoft making that very annoying to do. The Age's writer called this a compelling point, familiar to anyone who has dodged Microsoft's pleading while setting Chrome and Google as defaults on a new PC, but countered that all of these arguments ignore that Google and its competitors are not on an even playing field: the question remains why users prefer Google, and if the answer is that Google is simply better, the further question is whether that is down to its scale, longevity, ubiquity and all the user data it sucks up, which no other company could possibly match.

# Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.

# Google's Denial That Ad Keyword Matching Affects Organic Results

Google's official search liaison Danny Sullivan rebutted the allegation that Google manipulates search to maximise ad revenue by denying the causal link it depends on: in a post on X, he said ad systems do not affect the organic results — the list of blue links in search results that are not sponsored.

"Ad keyword matching is a long-standing and well-known process that is designed to connect people to relevant ads," Sullivan said. "A separate process, which has nothing to do with ads, is used to match organic results to a query." He also defended query interpretation on its own terms: "It's no secret that Google Search looks beyond the specific words in a query to better understand their meaning… If you make a spelling mistake, or search for a term that's not on a page but where the page has a close synonym, or if you aren't even sure exactly how to search for something, our meaning matching systems help." The Age noted the claim being answered comes from Megan Gray, herself a former vice-president at DuckDuckGo, a privacy-focused company founded explicitly to counter giants such as Google; she admits she may have misinterpreted the evidence but maintains that Google manipulates Search to maximise ad revenue. The paper granted that some search queries result in more ads than others and that which ads you get can vary wildly by request — the result of the keyword matching Google uses to sell ads — but noted Google denies pushing users towards the most monetisable subjects.

# Firefox's Yahoo Default Search Switch, As Recounted By Mitchell Baker

On November 1, 2023, Mozilla CEO Mitchell Baker provided a defense of Google's quality as a search engine, even in "competitive" environments, by recounting how Mozilla "failed" when it switched Firefox's default search engine from Google to Yahoo. Baker was providing a recorded deposition for Google's defense, and she noted that Mozilla's users apparently wanted and expected Google.

The backstory: Yahoo inked a deal with Mozilla back in 2014 to pay the browser maker $375 million annually to be the default search engine on Firefox, at a time when Google was offering $276 million, said Baker. TechCrunch's verdict was that it was a bad deal.

Baker's account of why, according to Bloomberg: "I felt strongly that Yahoo was not delivering the search experience we needed and had contracted for." Yahoo had promised to reduce the number of ads and offer less user tracking, she said, but ended up gradually serving users more ads anyway. "The number of users who stayed with Firefox declined noticeably during the years when Yahoo was the default," said Baker.

# Deft's Competitive Landscape: Search Incumbents

Given that it is building a search solution for e-commerce, Deft already faces challenges from Amazon and Google, both of which have shipped comparable features.

In September 2023, Amazon updated its visual search feature that lets users snap a photo of a product and search for similar items on the platform. Google released its multi-search feature in 2022, letting users fuse images and text — the same combination Deft offers.

Separately, Deft will also face competition from other startups like Objective, a Matrix Partners-backed startup building an API platform for multimodal search.

# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.

# Why Traditional E-Commerce Search Has Degraded

Deft co-founder Zach Hudson told TechCrunch that there are a few plaguing problems with the traditional search experience that prevent users from finding a suitable item — that is, the claim is that search has gotten worse, not that users have gotten worse at searching.

He offers three grounds, each a different actor degrading the result set: "You have companies like Google and Amazon that continue to push the most relevant listings down so they can make more advertising dollars. Some easy searches are now hard because marketers have learned how to game these search engines. Plus, now you have AI content that is putting the burden on users to separate fact from fiction," he said.

The warrant tying them together is that each mechanism moves cost onto the user: platform ad incentives bury relevance, SEO gaming inflates the noise, and AI-generated content shifts verification work to the person searching.

# "Go Big In Europe": Google's Post-Fine Search Quality Push

The government argued on November 10, 2023 that Google only endeavored to enhance its search engine in the European Union after it was hit by a €5 billion antitrust fine in 2018 — a claim internal documents revealed, according to Bloomberg.

The EU's antitrust order forced Google to offer Android phone users a screen with five search engine options to choose from, according to the DOJ. In response, Google enacted a plan its executives dubbed "Go Big in Europe," to enhance search results in France and Germany in 2019 and 2020 with more local content: news, post-game soccer video highlights, information on local television options for streaming, and pronunciation practice for different languages. The aim was to incentivize users to click on Google's home screen rather than the competition's.

That revelation effectively supports the Justice Department's argument that Google, without the push of competition, has little incentive to improve its products — a classic consequence in a monopoly.

# Expedia's Testimony On Google Ad Costs And Organic Listings

On November 1, 2023, Barry Diller, chair of Expedia and IAC, testified about his concerns that the increasing number of ads in search results was having an impact on organic listings. Quoting a letter he had written to Google back in 2019, per Bloomberg: "I must say I'm on the edge of revolt now that Google's actions are so punitive, not just for Expedia but also for IAC and all the players that depend upon something of a level playing field." Google CEO Sundar Pichai fired back that Google's travel listings was one of the most popular experiences the company built.

On October 19, 2023, Expedia's former chief operating officer, Jeff Hurst, told the court that the company's ad fees increased tenfold, from $21 million in 2015 to $290 million in 2019, and yet Expedia's traffic from Google did not increase. The implication was that this was due to direct competition from Google itself; Hurst pointed out that Google began sharing its own flight and hotel data in search results in that period, according to The Seattle Times.

# Fake Domain Redirects In The 1990s

One of Daron Babin's signature moves back in the '90s involved fake domain names: "I could make it look like it was somebody else, but it actually redirected to me!" What he and his competitors did was legal but well beyond what the dominant search engine allowed.

The consequences fell on users rather than on him. He never faced any consequences, but in the end internet users at large felt the effects: "It muddied up Yahoo, ultimately," he said, "but while it worked, we banked."

Babin also offered a forward-looking note the same evening: "We're entering a very weird time, technologically, with AI, from an optimization standpoint." Anyone who thought the internet was already saturated with SEO-oriented content should buckle up.

# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

# Danny Sullivan, From Journalist To Google Liaison

After Cutts left, Google replaced him with a handful of people, none of whom could quite fill his shoes: "Those personalities sometimes were standoffish," Forrester said. "Some of them were superior. Some of them were a bit too wallflower."

One of the people Google brought in was Danny Sullivan, a former journalist who started Search Engine Land — the industry publication where Schwartz works — back in the 2000s. In 2009 Sullivan was described as "the closest approximation to an umpire in the search world," so when he published "A deep look at Google's biggest-ever search quality crisis" in 2017 and then took a job as Google's public liaison for Search only a few months later, it felt to some SEOs as though a congressperson working on gun safety legislation had quit to become an NRA lobbyist.

Forrester reports the suspicion without endorsing it. "There is a thread across the industry of people who believe that Google just made Danny an offer he couldn't say no to, and it was designed essentially to take his voice out of the conversation," he said. "I don't believe that's the case," he went on, but compared to Cutts, "I think that Danny specifically stays out of a lot of public conversations because he is in those private conversations with businesses."

# The DOJ Theory That Google's Default Deals Foreclose Search Rivals

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.

# Google's Most Lucrative Search Terms, Unsealed At Trial

Judge Amit Mehta ruled to make public a list that provides a glimpse of which search terms make Google the most money: 20 terms that were lucrative for the week of September 22, 2018. Revenue per search term, how many queries each of those terms got, and a separate list of popular search terms ordered by queries rather than revenue were all redacted, so the disclosure is a bare ranking without magnitudes.

The visible list, in order, is: iPhone 8; iPhone 8 plus; Auto insurance; Car insurance; Cheap flights; Car insurance quotes; DirecTV; Online colleges; AT&T; Hulu; iPhone; Uber; Spectrum; Comcast; Xfinity; Insurance quotes; Free credit report; Cheap car insurance; AARP; LifeLock.

TechCrunch read little surprise into it. Google and Apple have a long and mutually beneficial relationship even while competing, so three Apple search-related queries bringing in the big bucks is unsurprising — not least since September 22, 2017 was the official release date of the iPhone 8. Queries like "car insurance," "cheap flights" and "credit report" are perennial favorites and speak to how much Google dominates vertical search, that is, search in very specific market categories. As for LifeLock, the big Equifax data breach of 2017 was a hot topic in September 2017 and LifeLock was making a big push to win business with people who wanted to buy identity theft protection.
