# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The SEO-Algorithm Update Cycle

Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."



---


# The Defense Of SEO As Legitimate Work

Barry Schwartz rejects the premise that the industry is filled with con artists: "There are a lot of scammers in every single business. It's just easier to call yourself an SEO than a doctor." Schwartz is an unbelievably fast talker and a prolific writer who has spent the past two decades covering SEO for the trade rag Search Engine Land, and both in conversation and in his work he has defended SEO as a legitimate, dignified pursuit: "The search community is filled with hard-working individuals working to help their clients' websites succeed in Google Search. That success is not done through dark, corrupt or shady tactics but rather hard, smart and thorough work."

Several people made a similar point: the best SEOs are the ones that follow Google's rules, which essentially ask you to make amazing websites without even thinking about Google. You are not supposed to make any attempt to artificially boost a website's ranking; you are supposed to be designing websites for human readers, not for the algorithm — and many SEOs do exactly this kind of work, rewriting copy, making a site load more quickly, and so on.

The defense has a limit the article presses on. The existence of good SEOs does not negate the presence of scammers and idiots and people who get ahead by violating Google's terms of service, just as the mild-mannered teacher's pet in a classroom does not negate the obnoxious shouting of the kids who refuse to behave; a few loud kids can easily drown everyone else out. Even Schwartz acknowledged the effect rule-breaking SEOs have had on the internet experience. Asked how he himself would find a reliable attorney — lawyers, accountants and contractors being particularly lucrative SEO customers because they are eager for attention from people going online for local recommendations — he answered: "I don't know if you can trust anything you read online. Maybe you ask a friend."



---


# What SEO Is, And Why People Hate It

Search engine optimization is the practice of telling the algorithm whatever it needs to hear for a site to appear as high up as possible in search results, leveraging Google's supposed objectivity to lure people in and then, usually, show them some kind of advertising — a business model. It is less straightforward than buying the advertising space labeled "Sponsored" above organic search results; it is more like the Wizard of Oz projecting his voice to magnify his authority.

The discriminating feature is that SEO borrows credibility from a system users believe is neutral. Over time SEO techniques have spread and become insidious, such that googling anything can now feel like looking up "sneaker" in the dictionary and finding a definition that sounds both incorrect and suspiciously as though it were written by someone promoting Nike ("footwear that allows you to just do it!"). Perhaps this is why nearly everyone hates SEO and the people who do it for a living: the practice seems to have successfully destroyed the illusion that the internet was ever about anything other than selling stuff.

The reputational context in 2023 is a broad unhappiness with finding information online, which for almost everyone means the quality of Google Search results. Users call the links that come back "absolutely unusable," "garbage," and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." Some blame Google itself, asserting that an all-powerful, all-seeing, trillion-dollar corporation with a 90 percent market share for online search is corrupting our access to the truth; others blame the SEO practitioners.

The stereotype of the practitioner is a hustler: a content goblin willing to eschew rules, morals, and good taste in exchange for eyeballs and mountains of cash — a nihilist in it for the thrills, a prankster gleeful about getting away with something. "This is modern-day pirate shit, as close as you can get," explained Cade Lee, who has over a decade working in SEO. What Lee said he has noticed most at SEO conferences and networking events is a certain arrogance: "There's definitely an ego among all of them. You succeed, and now you're a genius. Now you've outdone Google." The writer's own admitted starting position was that a bunch of megalomaniacal jerks were degrading our collective sense of reality because they wanted to buy Lamborghinis and prove they could vanquish the almighty algorithm — which, technically, constitutes many algorithms, but we think of as a single force.



---


# A Hands-On Comparison Of Google, Bing And DuckDuckGo Search

Testing Google against Bing and DuckDuckGo, The Age's writer found Google performed best on the sample query while DuckDuckGo performed less well and was harder to read, and Bing's generative-AI answers were not really there yet in practice.

On the query "kids BMX bike green," Google did pretty well, DuckDuckGo ignored the green part, and Bing Chat offered a comparison of a few options that were all too expensive; asked "any under $200?", it replied with more options that were all over $300. Bing has overhauled its layout over the past year to be very graphic and augmented by generative-AI explanations from its chatbot, and the writer liked the idea of asking follow-up questions in searches this way. The test also reminded the writer how much data Google collects — not just searches but anything said to a smart speaker and any search result or ad clicked — which will count in DuckDuckGo's favour for some people, even though that data collection is also why Google, across search, mobile widgets and other services, personalises more effectively. A final observation: the writer uses the Google Search bar as much for returning to familiar sites as for searching for information, so switching providers could be temporarily annoying simply because a new one wouldn't remember all the places they had been.



---


# iPhone Setup And The Absence Of A Search Engine Choice Screen

Eddy Cue acknowledged on the stand that the ISA didn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup — and said he wouldn't want to do that anyway, because "we try to get people up and running as fast as possible" and "setup is just critical stuff."

Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw built to that answer through a series of questions about the iPhone setup process, using three screenshots: the Appearance screen that appears when you first boot up an iPhone so you can pick font sizes, the location-tracking prompt that appears when you open Maps, and the App Tracking Transparency pop-up that tells you when an app wants to collect your data. Cue objected to all of these being considered part of setup, but Bellshaw's point was that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, and that search could be one of them. Cue argued that showing people a bunch of search engines they had never heard of would just be a bad user experience — even he couldn't remember the names of some of the alternatives to Google — and said, "We make Google be the default search engine because we've always thought it was the best. We pick the best one and let users easily change it." The Verge noted that "easily" is a persistent point of contention in the trial: DuckDuckGo's CEO, who testified the week before, claimed it takes "too many steps" to switch.

qid: After Polygon reported on October 18th that 'Wonder Seeds cause the levels in Super Mario Bros. Wonder to collapse and contort, breaking the traditional rules of Mario games,' did Engadget's review on October 20th agree or disagree on the significant change in gameplay experience introduced by the new mechanic in Super Mario Bros. Wonder?
context:
# Wonder As A Return To 2D Mario Experimentation

Polygon argues that Super Mario Bros. Wonder shares the inventiveness of the earliest 2D Mario games and their disregard for what should and shouldn't be in a Mario game — making it, for middle-aged fans, a candidate for the first "true new Mario game" since Super Mario World in 1990. The grounds lie in a history the reviewer sets out: with each Super Mario Bros. on the NES and SNES, Nintendo's designers learned from the previous entry, cut what didn't work, made audacious additions (there was a time when adding a dinosaur named Yoshi felt like a gimmick), and gradually accumulated the pieces and tropes that would recur for the next thirty-plus years. Then, with Super Mario 64, 3D Mario games became the de facto labs for Nintendo's greatest experimentation — magical hats, water guns, galactic travel — while 2D Mario defaulted to a vessel for nostalgia, including the cheekily named New Super Mario Bros. series.

The warrant is that Wonder revives the old spirit specifically by letting the designers break their own machine. The traditional layer is intact — every level can be enjoyed as a loyal continuation of the plumber's work in the 2D platformer genre, which has kept a healthy cadence since the series debuted in 1985: dash from left to right, jump over pits, concuss enemies, collect the occasional power-up, and leap onto the flagpole that ends one level and unlocks the next. But the wonder of playing Super Mario Bros. in 1985 came from discovery, with Nintendo anticipating that players would climb outside the confines of the level and placing shortcuts in hidden crevices to reward the most rule-breaking players; badges now build on that freedom with skills that let you soar over towering enemies or use the Piranha Plant grappling hook to climb above the stage. "This is the most significant difference between 1985 and 2023," the reviewer writes: "Mario's creators have joined in the fun of breaking the machine." He imagines the game's origin as a notebook in which, since the '90s, every Nintendo developer wrote down each idea that "didn't fit the tone" or "wasn't Mario enough," until someone had the gall to say: "Let's turn this stuffed notebook of chaos into a game. Because why shouldn't Mario be an elephant? Why shouldn't Wigglers wear roller skates? And why shouldn't Luigi skydive?"



---


# Wonder Seeds And The Transformations They Trigger

A Wonder Seed is the object that gives Super Mario Bros. Wonder its name: a Mario-sized ball of botany hidden inside each Wonder stage that, when found, morphs the environment into something quite wonderful. Choosing to seek it out — being "not too precious about video game tradition," as Polygon puts it — floods the atmosphere with lava-lamp plasma, sends gravity into convulsions, or transforms the hero into any variety of creatures or even inanimate objects, so that for a moment Mario gets to be the background. The second level of the game illustrates the range: it can become a musical, depending on whether you pursue the "Super Mario Bros." of the title or the "Wonder."

The defining property, in the reviewer's reading, is that the choice is one of "and," not "or" — the traditional and the topsy-turvy coexist. Across six worlds the creators offer a menu of familiar stages that can, if you like, be prepared with extra spice, or paired with the family-friendly equivalent of ayahuasca; the drug comparison is not flippant, since at one point Toad licks a Wonder Seed and is suddenly riding a dragon. Sometimes the effects go further and the levels themselves collapse and contort, disobeying laws established by decades of Mario games: giant, sudsy, rainbow-tinted bubbles fill a stage and burst through the ceiling, and a colossal snowball knocks down a flagpole, extending the stage beyond its official conclusion.



---


# Super Mario Bros. Wonder: The Verdict

The review's verdict is that Super Mario Bros. Wonder is a marvelous game: its art and animations have a level of polish practically unmatched by rival titles, and the addition of Wonder Seeds subverts your expectations and keeps this 40-year franchise feeling new and innovative.

The grounds are a three-part answer to the problem the review poses — Mario has been stomping Goombas, smashing blocks and running from left to right for damn near 40 years, so how is Nintendo supposed to keep its classic side scroller feeling fresh? First, you shift the location to a brand new kingdom; next, you introduce a bunch of new enemies and power-ups; but what really pushes things over the top is the introduction of a new mechanic that turns everything you think you know about Mario games on its head. What you get is a game that dazzles and delights while living up to its name in a variety of ways.

The warrant is comparative: in a lot of ways Wonder reminds the reviewer of his favorite 2D Mario game, Super Mario World. The one reservation is about the wait — he wishes it had not taken more than 10 years for Nintendo to create a proper sequel to its last mainline platformer — but as he concludes, if that is what it takes to get a game like this, he is happy to sit and wonder what is next for Mario.



---


# Super Mario Bros. Wonder As A Send-Off For The Switch

Polygon argues that Super Mario Bros. Wonder would be a fitting last big release for the Nintendo Switch, on the grounds that the game embodies the same combination that defined the console. With rumours that the Switch's successor could arrive early the following year, the reviewer says he would be fine if Wonder were the console's final major title. The historical grounds: to survive after the Wii U, Nintendo had to bring its console and handheld designers together and create something unlike anything on the market without sacrificing what had got the company to that point — and as the sun sets on the Switch, after an unprecedented run of success and arguably the best entries in many of Nintendo's biggest franchises, Wonder arrives. "Like the Switch itself, Wonder is a collision between the traditional and the new. A game that's the same as it ever was and nothing like Mario has ever been."

The reviewer sets aside the fan question of whether Wonder is the unofficial Super Mario Bros. 5 that "dorks like me have long wanted," leaving that to the forums, and rests his praise on the experience instead: "What a joy it is to play a Mario game and not already know how to read it, to not have my muscle memory do more work than my brain." The scope conditions of the review are stated: Super Mario Bros. Wonder was released on 20 October 2023 on Nintendo Switch, and was reviewed on that console using a pre-release download code provided by Nintendo. Polygon notes that Vox Media has affiliate partnerships which do not influence editorial content, though it may earn commissions on products purchased via affiliate links.



---


# Minor Criticisms Of Super Mario Bros. Wonder

The reviewer's reservations are explicitly minor and do not disturb the overall verdict. Mummy enemies draw a complaint — pulling their wraps feels a bit tedious — and he fears the Elephant Suit might be a bit overpowered in comparison to the Drill Hat.

The other two are complaints about scarcity rather than quality: the 5-star levels and rhythm stages are so good he wishes there were more of them, and he is slightly disappointed the adorable penguins from the movie did not make an appearance somewhere in Wonder's ice levels.



---


# The Badge System In Super Mario Bros. Wonder

The badge system is Super Mario Bros. Wonder's mechanism for optional special abilities: each unlockable upgrade or special move is assigned to a badge that can be found or purchased, and one collected badge can be selected before each stage. The abilities range from helpful (a high, floating leap) to playful (a Piranha Plant grappling hook) to silly (a triple jump tied to a musical rhythm), and Polygon's reviewer describes rotating them by need — opting for the Safety Bounce badge once later stages added instant-death bottomless pits, so that plunging into an abyss has the darkness spit you back up "like a piece of hamburger caught in its throat." The badges are worn by Prince Florian, a little royal bug who joins the journey and provides most of the conversation on the road trip, alongside very talkative flowers sprouting across every corner of the Flower Kingdom, eager to offer a tip for a metatextual wink.

Badges sit inside a wider design of considerate rather than patronising assistance: Wonder Seeds can add a splash of difficulty, but help is perpetually available — time limits are gone and extra lives can be purchased cheaply with the game's abundant purple currency. The balance question the system raises is answered by escalation: the reviewer expects many players to brag that their favourite badge is "the overpowered one," which is sort of always true, since whichever you use you will feel you have an unfair advantage as you float over chunks of the stage or vacuum coins through walls — so the designers layered on new challenges to keep Wonder inside the Goldilocks window, not too hard and not too easy.



---


# Badges And Level Variety In Super Mario Bros. Wonder

Badges are Wonder's customization mechanic: they are earned by completing specific levels, and some may even be required to find secrets or reveal alternate exits. Some allow you to jump farther or float, while others make extra coins appear, and there are protective badges too — like the one that automatically saves you if you fall into lava or poison. It is a mechanic that feels inspired by recent roguelikes such as Hades, and it does a great job of adding customizability and replayability.

The level design is similarly varied. Wonder features six main worlds, each with a distinctive theme, but within those you will still run into reimagined haunted houses, pirate ships, underwater stages and more, along with a number of familiar baddies and some new foes across an incredible range of environments.

Even without the aid of a Wonder Flower, the sheer variety of level types is impressive. Alongside classic stages capped off by grabbing a flag, there are races, badge challenges, puzzle levels and more. KO Arenas let you pick your power-up of choice — Fire Flower, Elephant Suit, Bubble Mushroom or the Drill Hat — before taking down waves of enemies, while Break Time levels provide quick 30-second bursts of excitement. You will never be bored, even if you want a change from standard platform jumping.



---


# The Wonder Flower Transformation Mechanic

The Wonder Flowers are the biggest twist in the game: in addition to the one Bowser stole, there is one hidden in almost every stage, and touching them transports you to an alternate dimension where the rules of the Marioverse have been completely rewritten.

The defining feature is unpredictability rather than a fixed effect. In one level Super Stars rain down from the sky; in another you might be transformed into a giant slime. You may also run into Wonder Flowers that convert the game from a side scroller into a top-down 2D maze, or suddenly find yourself the target in a shooting gallery. Almost every flower is different and the possibilities are seemingly endless.

The scale of the design work behind that is documented: in a recent volume of Nintendo's Ask the Developer, the reviewer learned the team had a wall of sticky notes with over 2,000 ideas — and after playing Wonder, he believes it. Wonder Flowers feel like they add an extra half a level to every stage; they are a delicious dessert on top of an already bountiful meal.



---


# How Wonder Fixes 2D Mario's Difficulty Pacing

The claim is that Nintendo has addressed a long-standing gripe about the pacing of previous 2D Marios — the removal of the rush to get to the "good stuff."

The grounds are the structural problem in earlier games. Because they are meant for both experienced gamers and children who might be new to the franchise, they often locked more challenging levels behind the story's completion, which meant the beginning of the game could be a slog as you rushed through easier levels to get to the more challenging bits.

The fix, and the warrant connecting it to the claim, is that Wonder adds difficulty ratings and hidden paths that lead to 5-star levels long before you finish the game, so the harder content is available from early on. And the reviewer adds that the harder content is well tuned: 4- and particularly 5-star levels are balanced just right, so completing one feels like a rewarding challenge without crossing over into punishing.



---


# Super Mario Bros. Wonder

Super Mario Bros. Wonder, developed by Nintendo EPD for Nintendo Switch, is ranked 4 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31 — the first side-scrolling 2D platformer in the Super Mario Bros. line since New Super Mario Bros. U in 2012, and both a faithful rendition of the classic format and a complete reinvention of the series' irresistible formula.

When you activate the game's delightful whimsy via the aptly named Wonder Flower, it becomes more than a 2D platformer: a musical, a quiz show, a race, or a hidden object game, where pipes become inchworms, Piranha Plants burst into song, and Yoshi becomes a dragon. Critic N. Carpenter writes that each and every level finds some new way to delight and surprise, constantly introducing new ideas, enemies, and wrinkles only to pull back on them just when it is on the verge of becoming rote — like everything else in the Flower Kingdom, a few enemies shift and change in bizarre ways when the Wonder Flower is activated, such as Hoppo, the bouncy, round hippo equivalent that grows in size to create chaos. All of this weirdness, combined with Nintendo's platforming expertise, makes it an entrancing romp alone, with friends, or with strangers online, and the freshest Mario has felt in decades.

Polygon's 2023-10-20 couch co-op roundup adds the local multiplayer detail: Wonder brings together platforming shenanigans, silly power-ups, and lots of map secrets, and the best part is that four people can play local multiplayer, picking from classic characters including Mario, Luigi, Princess Peach, Princess Daisy, Toad, and Toadette.



---


# Super Mario Bros. Wonder's Art And Overworld Map

This might be the best Mario and friends have ever looked, and that includes recent 3D titles like Odyssey: there is just so much detail packed into every level and character, from the determined face Mario makes when he runs around to the little flames that sprout from your feet every time you jump.

Wonder's map is also surprisingly engaging. In the beginning the reviewer was not sure the ability to freely roam around added all that much, but as he progressed he found a number of secret nooks and crannies that would not have fit if the game were locked to a handful of paths. And with Wonder Flowers giving Nintendo the freedom to mix and match mechanics and enemies, there is just so much to see.



---


# Wonder's Disposable-Idea Design As An Alternative To "Forever Games"

Polygon argues that Super Mario Bros. Wonder's willingness to squeeze each idea for its fun and then throw the rind away is a potent alternative to the current era of AAA "forever games" filled with endless lists of chores and artificial rewards — because in Wonder the reward isn't XP or limited-edition outfits, it's the play itself. The reviewer calls the creators' abundance of new ideas "unapologetically wasteful," and means it as a compliment: many gimmicks here could be stretched to fill entire games, but instead the player is lucky to see them last a few minutes.

The grounds are a worked example of how a single idea is escalated and then discarded: one stage features platforms that drop when you step on them; the next has platforms that drop only after a certain number of jumps, with a countdown clock at their centre; then a stage of platforms made of batteries, each dropping as it runs out of energy; and finally a stage in which you build the platform out of huge batteries of different shapes, growing and shrinking rapidly as it skims above a yawning abyss. The reviewer heads off the obvious objection — that such refusal to outstay a welcome means a short game — by noting that levels are everywhere: the map features six worlds, but levels are also found in the hub area and, to avoid spoilers, elsewhere. The familiar rhythms of a Mario game are broken too, with bosses appearing without warning, some worlds ending with no boss fight at all, and the occasional surprise stage materialising like a mirage.



---


# Super Mario 3D World on Switch

Super Mario 3D World is Polygon's recommendation for anyone searching for that classic Super Mario feeling in a modern 3D world — or anyone who has always wanted to play as Mario in a cat suit. It appears in the outlet's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

Players can choose Mario, Luigi, Peach, or Toad.

Each has a slightly different perk: Luigi can get a bit more air in his jump, while Toad is a bit faster.



---


# Multiplayer In Super Mario Bros. Wonder

Super Mario Bros. Wonder shines as a solo experience but, like other recent 2D Mario games, supports up to four players together — a mode Polygon describes as both a delight and utter chaos. The character roster divides into two kinds. The humanoid characters (Mario, Peach, Toad and so on) are "like M&Ms": different exteriors that effectively play the same.

The critters are the discriminating case, intended for players who want a little extra help: Nabbit and Yoshi won't take damage, and the Yoshis come with their familiar tongue attack and floaty jump.



---


# The Flower Kingdom Premise

Super Mario Bros. Wonder starts with Mario and crew — Luigi, Peach, Toad, Yoshi, Nabbit and, for the first time, Daisy — visiting Prince Florian of the Flower Kingdom, until Bowser barges in and steals a Wonder Flower, which somehow allows him to merge with Prince Florian's castle to create a floating mecha fortress of doom. From there your job is to collect Wonder Seeds, this game's version of stars and shines, as you help the Florians restore order to their troubled land.

The setup has two subtle but important implications. The first is that you immediately learn Wonder Flowers have wild and unpredictable effects. The second is that, because you are not simply rescuing a princess trapped in a castle, the whole Flower Kingdom is working with you to take down Bowser.

That reciprocity shows up throughout. Sometimes it means rescuing trapped miners; other times the Florians are the ones helping Mario — who also has a new voice actor for the first time — by rebuilding a bridge or donating a Wonder Seed at the beginning of a new world. The friendly little flowers scattered across each level even shout words of encouragement or funny quips as you run by. The impressive part is that, even in a relatively straightforward platformer, there is a sense of community that makes this world feel more lived in than a lot of epic RPGs.



---


# Luigi's Mansion 3

Luigi's Mansion 3 puts players in the role of Mario's taller counterpart rather than the plumber in the red hat. It appears in Polygon's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

Local co-op becomes available with player two as Gooigi, a spooky goo Luigi, after finishing the intro walkthrough and getting E. Gadd's briefcase.

Together the players platform their way through the haunted hotel to save Mario, Peach, and numerous Toads.



---


# Nostalgia-Driven Major Game Releases, 2023

TechCrunch cites three 2023 releases as evidence of gaming's turn to the familiar. This year's hit new Zelda game Tears of the Kingdom literally built a new game on top of the old one and remains a strong contender for Game of the Year.

Competition is stiff, more so now that Nintendo just casually dropped Super Mario Bros. Wonder, the first two-dimensional side-scrolling Mario game in more than a decade — another portal to the past given its departure from a long string of recent 3D Super Mario titles. Square Enix was so confident in its remake of the 1997 Japanese roleplaying mega-hit Final Fantasy VII that the reimagined version of the game comprises three standalone full-length games, each spaced a few years apart.



---


# Mario + Rabbids Kingdom Battle

Mario + Rabbids Kingdom Battle is a silly collaboration between Nintendo and Ubisoft that became one of the sleeper hits of its release year. It appears in Polygon's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

The squad tactics game pairs Mario and friends with their own doppelganger Rabbids against a veritable sea of evil Rabbids.

Polygon flags a scope limit on the co-op: local play is limited to five specific challenges, so the outlet would not recommend buying the game specifically for co-op alone — but those levels are especially fun, since working together changes the tactical dynamics.



---


# Rayman Legends Definitive Edition

The Definitive Edition of Rayman Legends has all of the platforming and hijinks the series is known for. It appears in Polygon's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

Players work through delightful levels and time trials, and collect to their heart's content.

Having multiple players is particularly helpful for respawning, as the game ramps up in difficulty in its later levels.



---


# Captain Toad: Treasure Tracker

Captain Toad: Treasure Tracker is a Wii U game whose Switch port Polygon calls full of charm, included in its 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

You play together in local co-op as Captain Toad and Toadette, exploring and solving your way through a series of bite-size puzzles.

Each self-contained course has little nooks and crannies to pop in and out of, and Koopas to navigate around.



---


# Super Mario Odyssey

In a sea of truly excellent Mario games, Polygon says Super Mario Odyssey stands out as the choice for the Switch, because it was released specifically with this console in mind.

The game perfectly mixes classic, whimsical Mario platforming with the expansiveness of a large world. You run around tons of different maps, some of which reference past installments of the franchise, and which include what the writer calls their favorite metropolitan area in any Switch game, New Donk City. There are lots of power-ups and critters to turn into courtesy of the partner character Cappy — at one point you play as a T-Rex — plus hidden collectibles for the exploration inclined. The objective is to collect Power Moons and save the day.



---


# Super Smash Bros. Ultimate

Super Smash Bros. Ultimate is described by Polygon as another Switch take on a stone-cold classic — Nintendo's fight-to-the-death brawler, stocked with all your favorite characters. It appears in the outlet's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

You can play with up to seven other people.

The goal is simply to survive and be the last one standing.



---


# Mario Party on Switch

The Mario Party series reigns supreme as a family-friendly, chill party time, in Polygon's assessment; it appears in the outlet's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

In this board game-style title, players pick their favorite Nintendo character and then roll the dice to land on a spot on the board.

Players compete in minigames, including a baseball-bat-swinging rhythm game, a rowboat race, snow catching, and many more.



---


# Kids' Toy And Playset Gifts 2023

The Verge's kids guide rounds up six toys: The Super Mario Bros. Movie Van Playset at $9.99+ (Amazon, Walmart, GameStop), the Pokémon Carry Case Playset at $33.99+ (Walmart, Target, Macy's), Furby at $49 (Amazon, Walmart), the Original Bazooka Bubble Gun at $32.39 (Amazon), the Nerf Perses MXIX-5000 Motorized Blaster at $59.99+ (Amazon, Walmart, Electronics Express), and the frog-green Quick Push electronic sensory fidget toy at $16.99 (Amazon).

It's been a big year for Mario — a new movie and a new Nintendo Switch game in Super Mario Bros. Wonder — so the Van Playset may scratch the itch for tykes who can't get enough of the plumber. The Pokémon Carry Case is a plastic backpack that unfolds to reveal a collapsible climbing wall, a sparring platform, and other arid environments for small two-inch plastic pokémon to play or battle in. The new Furby, a voice-activated animatronic plushie, has all kinds of responses, dances, and songs built in, and — most importantly for the guide — the resurrected '90s toy is a completely offline experience with no "smart" functionality, so a kid won't be pinging a cloud server every time they speak. The Bazooka Bubble Gun is a battery-powered blaster pumping out over 5,000 BPM — bubbles per minute. The Nerf Perses MXIX-5000 shoots soft foam balls as fast as eight pellets per second with a top-loading hopper that's equally fast and frantic to reload, with a warning to outfit kids with proper eye protection. The Quick Push froggy game with lights and sounds feels a bit like popping bubble wrap: recommended for ages three and up, and possibly a great fit for children who enjoy sensory toys.

# Game Patch Notes

## Definition

Neither corpus article uses the phrase "patch notes," but both document the same underlying pattern: a studio bundling a slate of changes — new content, rebalancing, and quality-of-life fixes — under a single named or numbered update tied to a release date.
Polygon's Diablo 4 coverage lists that pattern for "Season 2"/"Season of Blood": leveling speed, new endgame bosses, a Nightmare Dungeon rework, mount handling, and Renown/gem-Stash changes, all bundled to arrive together on Oct. 17 (doc_0533).
Polygon's games-of-the-year piece shows the same pattern for Cyberpunk 2077's named "Patch 2.0," a systems-revamping update shipped alongside — but distinct from — the paid Phantom Liberty expansion (doc_0213).

## Context

The corpus's clearest example is Diablo 4's Season 2 update, "Season of Blood," reported by Polygon on 2023-10-04: alongside new vampire powers, Blizzard shipped a broad slate of quality-of-life changes covering leveling speed, endgame bosses, Nightmare Dungeon design, mount handling, and the Renown and gem/Stash systems, all set to arrive together on Oct. 17 as one seasonal patch.

Polygon's broader 2023 games-of-the-year piece shows the same pattern in a second game: Cyberpunk 2077's Phantom Liberty expansion arrived "alongside the sweeping Patch 2.0," which revamped the base game's role-playing progression systems, improved enemy AI, and "course-corrected a litany of other details" — a patch bundled with, but distinct from, the paid DLC content it accompanied.

## Key Characteristics

- **Versioned or seasonal framing** — changes are grouped under a single identifier (Patch 2.0, Season 2/"Season of Blood") rather than released piecemeal, per doc_0533 and doc_0213.
- **Mix of change types** — a single patch bundles new content (Diablo 4's five endgame bosses), rebalancing (faster leveling, reworked Nightmare Dungeon affixes), and quality-of-life fixes (Renown carryover, gems no longer taking bag space), per doc_0533.
- **Developer-explained rationale** — studios attach commentary to justify changes, as when Diablo 4's game director Joe Shely and associate director Joe Piepiora told Polygon the quality-of-life focus came from finally having time to react to player feedback, unlike the rushed first season (doc_0533).
- **Distinct from paid content** — a patch can ship independently of or alongside paid expansions; Cyberpunk 2077's Patch 2.0 revamped core systems while Phantom Liberty (the paid DLC) added new story content, and reviewers credit the patch as much as the DLC for the game's improved reception (doc_0213).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, this kind of update bundle has a generic industry name: release notes (also called patch notes).
Per Wikipedia, release notes "describe important information about a distribution of a hardware or software product" and typically include "a list of what is new in the release, including bug fixes and new features" (Wikipedia, "Release notes," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Metroid Prime Remastered

Metroid Prime Remastered, developed by Retro Studios for Nintendo Switch, is ranked 19 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31. Polygon's claim is that few games from 2002 hold up as well as Metroid Prime, and the remastered version — surprise-dropped during February's Nintendo Direct — proves Samus Aran's first-person adventure is still worth experiencing, whether for the first time or, in the critic's case, the fourth.

Retro Studios' take on one of sci-fi's most famous intergalactic bounty hunters controversially took her out of the 2D puzzle-platformer realm that made her famous, although Metroid Fusion also came out in 2002 as a gift for the 2D Metroid purists — which critic M. Myers suggests may also be why Fusion joined Nintendo Switch Online's catalog shortly after Prime Remastered was released. By placing the player inside Samus' helmet, Metroid Prime recontextualized the bounty hunter's relationship with the hostile planets around her.

Wearing Samus' suit, aggressive alien lifeforms could now get right in the player's face, forcing dodging, strafing, and rolling in morph ball form using all three dimensions; no longer would players sit back and watch as Samus dipped her toe into a pool of lava, since in first-person, as molten fire spread over the visor, the pressure to find that Varia Suit upgrade was real. Perhaps most importantly, from behind the visor players gained the ability to scan enemies and environment, collecting and translating logs from the long-dead Chozo aliens who once inhabited these now-hostile places. Myers calls the world harsh and unrelenting, with save points at times quite far from one another, but worth buckling down and pushing through the pain points to discover its secrets.

# Epic's Antitrust Claims Against Google Play

Epic's claim is that the Android operating system's Google Play Store constitutes an unlawful monopoly, and that Google is separately tying its Google Play payments platform to that store, keeping other potential app payment mechanisms from competing.

The grounds Epic offers are the frictions it says Google creates: Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that it has created an illegal monopoly which unjustly enriches Google while artificially driving up app prices because other stores cannot compete. The warrant joining that to the legal claim is the competitive-harm chain — no viable rival stores means no fee discipline, which means the "Google Tax" is paid either by developers or passed along to consumers. Epic wants to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods so developers are not stuck paying that tax.

Google's answer contests the warrant rather than the fees: it says Epic's demands would damage Android's ability to offer a secure user experience and to compete with Apple's iOS. Both sides agree the future of Google's app store could depend on this trial. Epic sued in 2020 after a fight over in-app purchase fees.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Openness And Sideloading

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google will also attack the foreclosure premise directly. It will note that, unlike Apple, it allows apps to be sideloaded on Android devices — something Epic takes advantage of today — and that this process is streamlined and helps keep users safe. Epic will claim in response that the process is made to be overly difficult for end users, with multiple steps involved and "scare screens" that warn users of the security risks involved with sideloading.

On discovery, Epic will suggest that Google hid items by allowing execs and employees to have "off the record" chats; Google will counter this as well, saying it has provided the court with thousands of chat logs and millions of documents. Google will ultimately push the notion that this case is not about competition but about money — that is, that Epic Games wants to reach the Play Store's 2.5 billion users without having to pay. As a Google blog post by Wilson White, VP, Government Affairs & Public Policy, put it: "Android's choice and flexibility work well for consumers and developers of all sizes. We look forward to making our case in court as we fight to keep our users safe from harm, partner with developers to grow their businesses, and keep the Android ecosystem thriving and healthy for everyone."



---


# Epic's Jury Verdict Against Google, December 2023

On Monday, a federal jury sided with Fortnite maker Epic Games in its fight to break Google's control over Android apps, surprising the world. The nine-person jury decided that Google has an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems, and that Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The outcome was striking because "walled garden" rival Apple almost entirely won a similar case two years earlier. For Tim Sweeney, this was, at last, a win.



---


# The $360 Million Activision Payment And Its Evidentiary Weakness

The counter to Epic's headline number attacks the factual premise beneath it: the $360 million refers to an alleged payment that kept Activision from opening an app store that could compete with Google Play, but Activision told The Verge in 2022 that it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store" — and Google says it is now armed with the evidence to prove it.

Epic itself conceded a related point. On Monday Epic's attorney admitted Google "was too clever" to draw up contracts that specifically forced developers not to compete with the Play Store, so it is not clear how much of Epic's evidence will hold up on closer examination.

The narrative advantage may nonetheless survive the evidentiary weakness. The overall story Epic tells is compelling, and it is not clear Google's opening statement countered it: Google spent its 45 minutes attempting to explain that its dominance over the Android app market is not anything nefarious but simply the natural outcome of Google fiercely competing with the iPhone and its iOS App Store, where Google would like the court to believe the competition truly lies.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. Google's execution was uneven, though — it wound up spending much of its opening statement attempting to explain away its seemingly bad behavior as normal business practices and did not always succeed out of the gate.



---


# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.

# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Google Play Billing And The User Choice Billing Alternative

Google Play's billing arrangement, as of November 2023, has two tiers. The baseline requires apps to use Google's own first-party billing system and charges app developers a 15% to 30% commission on the sales it processes. The alternative is User Choice Billing, a program still in pilot testing, open to all developers who sell apps in the 35 markets where it is then available, including the U.S., which reduces the standard commission by 4% for companies who choose to use their own payment processing solution. Spotify and Bumble were the initial testers for the new system, first introduced in November 2022, and Match, as part of its settlement agreement, will also now take advantage of this option. Epic has declined to use it.

Google's defense of the commission rests on what it says the commission buys. It will argue that its commissions are not just tied to payment processing, but help it develop other features and controls to keep Android users safe and guide them to discovering new applications, as well as helping fund the tools and services developers need to build and grow their apps. Google also helps developers reach a broader audience beyond the mobile phone, with support for Android across platforms ranging from tablets to TVs to autos and more. And it notes that 99% of its developers qualify for a commission of 15% or less, based on their revenues — so the headline 30% is the boundary case, not the typical one.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

# The Market Definition Fight In Epic v. Google

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

The relation between definition and outcome is direct. If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

Two observations sit outside the formal model but bear on how the fee looks. Google charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal or a credit card, which does seem like a lot; and though Epic cannot argue it in court, Apple was not able to explicitly justify a 30 percent fee to that case's judge. On the other hand, it does kind of seem like Epic wants something for nothing — Epic has not stated what kind of fee would actually be reasonable for Google to charge in exchange for placement in its store, and CEO Tim Sweeney seemingly suggests there should not be a Google fee at all if a developer wants to use its own payment system.

# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Epic's Argument That Google Blocks Alternative Android App Stores

Epic will attempt to demonstrate that Google makes it hard for alternative app stores to succeed and reach consumers. Its headline ground is a distribution fact: 90% of apps are still downloaded through Google Play.

The mechanism Epic offers to explain that share is contractual. Google bundles the Play Store with other Google apps that Android OEMs (original equipment manufacturers) have to agree to in order to use Android. Epic will also bring up "Anti-Fragmentation Agreements" (AFAs) that prevent the OEMs from modifying Android to allow for frictionless downloading of apps outside of Google Play. The warrant is that if OEMs are contractually barred from making outside downloading frictionless, rival stores cannot reach consumers on comparable terms, and Play's share follows from the contracts rather than from consumer preference.

Epic will offer two concrete instances. It will specifically reference an agreement it had made with the OEM OnePlus, to make Epic games available on its devices through the Epic Games app; OnePlus had to cancel the deal over concerns that the arrangement would have it bypassing the Google Play Store. The case will also examine a deal between Google and Samsung that Epic says was designed to prevent the Galaxy Store from being a competitive threat and to require Google Play Billing on apps distributed by Samsung.

# The Epic v. Apple Ruling And Its Limited Weight Here

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. She also decided that Epic violated its developer agreement with Apple and would have to pay.

Epic did win something. Rogers barred Apple from keeping iPhone users in the dark about alternate ways they can pay for apps, and may have even allowed developers to add their own payment mechanisms.

The precedent's reach into the Google trial is limited in two specific ways. First, that was a different case — and it is not over until the Supreme Court weighs in or declines to take a look. Second, Google cannot tell jurors that Apple won its case, or that other plaintiffs settled; the judge in this case says so. Epic declined to answer on the record when asked about the Apple outcome.

# Revenue Split

## Definition

A revenue split, in the corpus, is the percentage pair — such as 70/30, 50/50, or 95/5 — by which a platform and a counterparty divide proceeds: Google's revenue share agreements (RSAs) with Android device makers and carriers, Google's 70/30 app-store split with developers, and Twitch's and Kick's subscription-revenue splits with streamers.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces across three unrelated disputes that share the same underlying mechanic: dividing proceeds between a platform and a counterparty. In the US v. Google antitrust trial, Google's revenue share agreements (RSAs) pay Android device makers and wireless carriers like Verizon a cut in exchange for setting Google Search and Chrome as defaults. In the Epic v. Google trial, Epic argued that Google's 70/30 app-store revenue split with developers is likely descended from an arbitrary decision Valve made with Steam two decades earlier, rather than from any principled calculation of the value Google's store provides. On the creator-platform side, Twitch's default subscription revenue split for Partners is 50/50, with a premium 70/30 tier once offered to select streamers before Twitch discontinued it in favor of ad revenue; rival platform Kick instead lures streamers away with a 95/5 split.

## Key Characteristics

- **Expressed as a ratio** — revenue splits are stated as two percentages that sum to 100, such as 70/30, 50/50, or 95/5, denoting each party's share.
- **Applies across different platform relationships** — the corpus shows the same mechanic governing device-maker default agreements (Google RSAs), app-store developer terms (Google/Epic 70/30), and creator subscription payouts (Twitch, Kick).
- **A lever platforms adjust unilaterally** — Twitch changed its subscription split from a 70/30 deal for select streamers to a 50/50 default, then introduced the Partner Plus program to restore a 70/30 rate for qualifying creators, showing the split is a platform-controlled term rather than a fixed market rate.
- **A point of leverage in competitive disputes** — Epic used the 70/30 app-store split's arbitrary Valve/Steam origin to challenge Google's justification for its rate, and Kick's more generous 95/5 split is a stated draw for streamers dissatisfied with Twitch's terms.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "revenue split" and "revenue share" only in the specific device-maker, app-store, and creator-payout deals described above, without defining the general concept. Outside the corpus, revenue sharing is defined as the distribution of the total revenue generated by the sale of goods and services among stakeholders or contributors, distinct from profit sharing (which splits only what remains after costs) (Wikipedia, "Revenue sharing," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenue_sharing).

# Project Liberty: Epic's Deliberate Payment Bypass

Epic is the studio behind Fortnite, the extraordinarily popular free-to-play game, which makes money by selling in-game items with its virtual currency V-Bucks; until August 13th, 2020, if a player used an Android or iOS device and installed the game through an official app store, buying V-Bucks triggered an in-app payment fee to Google or Apple — fees critics call the "Google tax" or the "Apple tax," and which Epic definitely was not a fan of.

August 13th, 2020 was a very busy day. Epic announced it was bypassing Apple and Google's app store fees, deploying a hotfix update to Fortnite without either company's knowledge that let players buy V-Bucks directly through its own payment processing option at a discount. Apple and Google almost immediately reacted by kicking Fortnite off their app stores for breaking the rules. Then Epic was ready and waiting with two lawsuits and an attack ad depicting a Fortnite hero throwing a unicorn-llama hammer into a giant screen reminiscent of Apple's famous "1984" Macintosh ad. It was a striking publicity blitz followed by a lot of slow-moving court proceedings: the Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021 and a ruling came down that September, mostly decided in Apple's favor, though both parties are waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in, while the Google one was delayed again and again.

The premeditation is documented, and Google is countersuing over it. At trial Google pointed out how Epic hatched a secret plan called "Project Liberty" to quietly update Fortnite with code to bypass app store fees, get its app kicked off Apple's and Google's app stores, and sue. It showed out-of-context quotes from internal Epic communications — phrases like "How do we not look like the bad guys?", "Just planting the nefarious seed now" and "I mean everything we're attempting is technically a violation of Google's policy, right?" — to suggest Epic knew it was breaking bad at the time. An email from Epic CEO Tim Sweeney reads: "Here is our official plan for communicating with Google about bypassing the Google Play Store: SAY NOTHING TILL IT SHIPS."

Epic did not try to hide it in court. Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening statement, so by the time Google raised it, it had already been an hour since Epic admitted it intentionally broke Google's rules. "Epic decided to stand up because that's what you do to a bully," Bornstein told the jury.
