context:
# Jada Pinkett Smith's 2023 Disclosure Of A Seven-Year Separation

Jada Pinkett Smith revealed in October 2023 that she and her husband Will Smith had been separated for the previous seven years — that is, since 2016 — while remaining married. The disclosure came in an interview with People given while she was promoting her memoir Worthy; The Independent's timeline piece dates the publication to 11 October, while its other reports on the same interview date it 10 October. Pinkett Smith, 52, said of her 26-year marriage to the 55-year-old actor that the couple are "still figuring it out": "We've been doing some really heavy-duty work together. We just got deep love for each other and we are going to figure out what that looks like for us."

She anchored the timeline to the 2022 Academy Awards, when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock after the comedian made a joke about her appearance: at that moment, she said, the pair had already been separated for six years. The revelation was treated as major news — "sent shockwaves around the world," in The Independent's phrasing — because both Smiths had previously doubled down on their stance against divorce, so a lengthy separation raised a new question: when should a couple simply get a divorce?



---


# The Smiths' 2021 Public Accounts Of Marital Strain

In late 2021 both Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith described the difficulty of their marriage in public, first on her show and then in his memoir. In an October 2021 episode of Red Table Talk, Pinkett Smith said it "takes work" to maintain a spark in the bedroom: "It's hard... the thing Will and I talk about a lot is the journey. We started in this [relationship] at a very young age, 22 years old... I think you expect your partner to know — especially when it comes to sex. It's like: 'Well, if you love me, you should know. If you love me, you should read my mind.' That's a huge pitfall."

The following month Will Smith's memoir was released, detailing several problems the couple had had over the years. He wrote that they were "suffering the brutal death of our romantic fantasies, the burning away of the idealistic illusion of the perfect marriage and the perfect family. Neither of us wanted a divorce; we knew we loved each other, and some aspects of our union were magical. But the structure of the life that we had established was strangling both of us."



---


# Jada Pinkett Smith's "Entanglement" With August Alsina

Jada Pinkett Smith confirmed in 2020 that she had had a relationship with the singer August Alsina during a period when she and Will Smith were separated, describing it on her Facebook Watch series Red Table Talk as an "entanglement." Alsina and Pinkett Smith were introduced in 2015, but it was only in 2020 that he claimed publicly that the two had dated while she was married and that the Smiths' marriage was open at the time. Alsina said Will Smith had given the pair his "blessing," explaining: "I actually sat down with Will and had a conversation due to the transformation from their marriage to life partnership that they've spoken on several times and it not involving romanticism." He added that he "totally gave myself to that relationship for years of my life and I truly and really, really deeply loved and have a ton of love for her."

Pinkett Smith's representatives called the claims "absolutely not true" on the day they surfaced. Less than two weeks later, she and Will Smith appeared together on Red Table Talk, where she confirmed the relationship but placed it inside an amicable separation that had not been disclosed to the press at the time: "We decided that we were going to separate for a period of time and you go figure out how to make yourself happy and I'll figure out how to make myself happy. From there, as time went on, I got into a different kind of entanglement with August... Yes, it was a relationship absolutely." Prompted by her husband, she confirmed it "was a relationship, absolutely." She also rejected Alsina's framing of permission, saying Will had not given it because the only person who could give her permission was herself. The episode is one of the grey areas in the couple's account of the terms of their separation.



---


# Why Will Smith And Jada Pinkett Smith Never Signed A Prenup

Jada Pinkett Smith revealed in an interview with Parade, published 13 October 2023 and given while promoting her memoir Worthy, that she and Will Smith deliberately did not sign a prenuptial agreement before their 1997 wedding, because they had already decided divorce was not in the cards for them. The Independent presents the missing prenup as of a piece with their promise not to divorce: the absence of a legal fallback was itself the commitment.

She described the decision as an unromantic, deliberate conversation rather than a wedding-day gesture: "Listen, weddings are beautiful, but they can be very romanticised. I feel that was a very real moment for the two of us to look each other in the eyes, recognise that there would be tough times in this journey and to say to each other: 'No matter what, we're going to figure it out and that's why we don't need a prenup, because I'm making a promise that divorce won't be necessary, that we will figure this out.'" She added that the promise was made "without all of the bridal wedding beauty; it was just sitting on a log in his mother's backyard, and going: 'Hey' — having to really look at the possibility of us not being together."



---


# The Smiths' Denials Of Open-Marriage, Divorce And Infidelity Rumours

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith have each publicly rejected the recurring claims made about their marriage — that it was an open relationship, that they were divorcing, and that either had been unfaithful. Pinkett Smith attacked the open-relationship premise directly on Facebook, after a quiet decade and a half spent making films and raising their children: "Here is how I will change my statement... Will and I BOTH can do WHATEVER we want, because we TRUST each other to do so. This does NOT mean we have an open relationship... this means we have a GROWN one." Her counter is that mutual freedom follows from trust, not from an open-marriage arrangement, so the inference from one to the other does not hold.

Will Smith answered the separation-and-divorce rumours in a mocking Facebook post: "Under normal circumstances, I don't usually respond to foolishness. But, so many people have extended [to] me their 'deepest condolences' that I figured — 'What the hell… I can be foolish, too!' So, in the interest of redundant, repetitious, over and over-again-ness… Jada and I are… NOT GETTING A DIVORCE!!!!!!!!!!!!!" In an interview on CBS Sunday Morning in October 2023 he also denied the infidelity premise outright: "Never. There's never been infidelity in our marriage... And we have never surprised one another with anything ever." He added that he had decided public chatter about his life "can be of a benefit to people," since "chatter is the first stage to having a real conversation and being able to truly explore if some of the things in your heart are loving, or poisonous."



---


# Will Smith's Response To Jada Pinkett Smith's Memoir Worthy

Will Smith broke his silence on his wife's memoir Worthy on 16 October 2023 in an interview with The New York Times, saying the book "kind of woke him up" and that he had come to realise she is more "resilient, clever and compassionate than he'd understood." He added: "When you've been with someone for more than half of your life, a sort of emotional blindness sets in, and you can all too easily lose your sensitivity to their hidden nuances and subtle beauties." The statement was framed as support for his partner and her success.

Before giving that statement he had appeared to mock the publicity storm surrounding the couple in a video titled "Official statement" posted on Instagram. "So, here's the thing. My opinion is... uh…" he said, before sneezing into the crook of his arm; as he sneezed, the video comically zoomed out to show several different landscapes including lakes and mountains.



---


# The Smith Children: Jaden, Willow And Trey

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith, married since 1997, share two children together — son Jaden, 25, and daughter Willow, 22 — while Will Smith also has a third child, son Trey, 30, from his first marriage to Sheree Zampino. The distinction matters for how the family is described: Jaden and Willow are the couple's own children, whereas Trey belongs to the earlier marriage and is Will's alone. Jaden, the couple's first child together, was born in July 1998; Willow was born in 2000.

Pinkett Smith credits both of her children with her own development, calling them "little gurus" who have taught her "a deep sense of self-acceptance." She made the remark in the October 2023 interviews surrounding her memoir, in which she also disclosed the couple's long separation. Speaking about that period, she insisted the marriage has never been an open one, saying that she and Will had "eliminated the chance of betrayal" while going on to live their "separate lives."



---


# Expert Disagreement Over What The Oscars Slap Meant Given The Separation

Dating coach Jacob Lucas attacks the sincerity premise behind Will Smith's 2022 Oscars outburst, arguing that the newly revealed separation makes the reaction implausible as a husband's defence. "That's a weird reaction to have somebody who you've been broken up with for six years, you know?" he asked. "So, were they really broken up or is Jada saying that as an attention-seeking thing?" His challenge cuts both ways: either the couple were not genuinely separated, or Jada Pinkett Smith's account of the separation is itself being questioned.

Relationship expert Susan Winter takes the opposite reading of the same incident, holding that it demonstrates rather than undermines the strength of the commitment. "I feel as though Will has a tremendous love and commitment to Jada, as well as to the marriage and the family unit," she said. "The pride that he takes in defending his wife is extraordinary, almost to the detriment of his image, at times." Both experts spoke to The Independent in October 2023, after the separation was disclosed.



---


# The Smiths' Promise That Divorce Would Never Be Necessary

Across their 26-year marriage Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith have argued that divorce is simply not an available outcome for them, on the grounds that they removed it as an option at the outset and have treated that promise as binding ever since. Pinkett Smith restated the claim in a preview of an interview with Today's Hoda Kotb that aired on 13 October 2023: "I made a promise that there will never be a reason for us to get a divorce. We will work through, whatever. I just haven't been able to break that promise." In the same interview she confirmed that the couple had been living "completely separate lives" for seven years, and, asked why they did not "just amicably divorce," replied simply: "We don't want to."

The warrant joining the promise to the outcome is that removing the exit changes how the couple treat the problems. Pinkett Smith recalled setting the terms before the 1997 wedding, in a 2018 Red Table Talk episode: "I told Will from the gate, I said let me tell you something: 'If you marry me, know this: we're gonna be together. We're going to be under the same roof.' For me personally, I'm not mature enough to have a divorce, I'm just not. I don't think I would ever be mature enough, I don't." Will Smith — who had divorced his first wife, Sheree Zampino, in 1994 — made the same argument in different terms. In 2006 he told MTV News: "With Jada, I stood up in front of God and said: 'Til death do us part.' So there are two possible outcomes. One, we are going to be together 'til death, or two, I am dead." On the Ellen DeGeneres Show he put it as an argument about choice architecture: "divorce just can't be an option... It's really that simple. And I think that's the problem with LA — there are so many options. So a huge part of the success for [Jada] and I is that we just removed the other options." As of October 2023 it remained unclear whether the couple planned to end their separation and live in the same home again.



---


# "Life Partnership" As The Smiths' Own Term For Their Marriage

"Life partnership" is the term Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith use for their relationship in place of a conventional marriage description, and its defining feature is unconditionality rather than cohabitation or romance. Will Smith set out the definition on TIDAL's Rap Radar podcast: he and Jada "refer to ourselves as life partners, where you get into that space where you realise you are literally with somebody for the rest of your life. There's no deal breakers. There's nothing she could do — ever. Nothing that would break our relationship. She has my support till death and it feels so good to get to that space."

Pinkett Smith used the same term as the goal of the couple's repair work. On the Today show on 16 October 2023 she told Hoda Kotb that she and the Suicide Squad actor were "working hard" and "concentrating on healing": "There's no finding another great love, and I think that's the point. It's like we are in a place now that we are in a deep, healing space. And we are really concentrating on healing the relationship between us." She added: "There's no divorce on paper. We really have been working hard. That's the whole thing. We are working very hard at bringing our relationship together. Back to a life partnership." Speaking about the family — the couple's children Jaden, 25, and Willow, 22, plus Will's 30-year-old son Trey with ex-wife Sheree Zampino — she framed the term as what the relationship has become rather than a permanent verdict: "We love our family and we love each other. It's more of a life partnership. Now, 10 years from now, Hoda, who knows?"



---


# How Will Smith And Jada Pinkett Smith Met And Married In 1997

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith met when she auditioned for the role of his girlfriend on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air; she did not get the part, but the two hit it off — even though Smith was married to Sheree Zampino at the time, with whom he shares son Trey. Smith later described the moment of recognition on Pinkett Smith's Red Table Talk in 2018: "I had a realisation I wasn't with the person I was supposed to be with. I was sitting in a [bathroom] stall and I was crying and laughing uncontrollably, and I knew [Jada] was the woman I was supposed to be with."

The pair only began seriously dating in 1995, after Smith finalised his divorce from Zampino. He proposed in November 1997 and they married just one month later, in Baltimore. Pinkett Smith was not initially enthusiastic about marrying at all: she told People in 2019, "I never wanted to get married. But my mother was like: 'You have to get married' — she's so old-school — and Will wanted a family. So I said: 'All right, maybe it's something I should do.'"



---


# Separation As An Alternative To Divorce: The "LAT" Partnership

New York City-based relationship expert Susan Winter argues that a long separation like Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith's is not a failed marriage but a recognised alternative form of one — a "living apart together" partnership — and that it can be the better choice. Speaking to The Independent in October 2023, she drew a sharp line between separation and divorce: divorce, particularly for Hollywood couples, means lengthy legal processes, from dividing financial assets to creating child custody agreements, whereas a separation carries none of that machinery. Although the terms of the Smiths' separation are not public, Winter believes they are showcasing a non-conventional relationship unfamiliar to the public, one whose visible feature is living in separate homes.

Her grounds are that the arrangement's organising purpose is continuity of the partnership rather than its dissolution: "It's an LAT partnership, meaning 'living apart together.' While everybody is at a different point as to why they are doing this, the centre point is the same: the preservation of the partnership is paramount." She attaches a scope condition to the benefit and a limit to what success looks like: "Separations can also be beneficial if both individuals are working on themselves and have the mutual goal of reuniting, or making their relationship better. However, that doesn't necessarily mean that their improved relationship will result in them living together again." The argument arises because the Smiths' seven years apart raise the general question of when couples should give up and when a separation should become a divorce — a question, the article notes, that has no simple answer.



---


# Will Smith's Baltimore Book-Event Remarks On A "Brutiful" Marriage

Speaking to a crowd at the Enoch Pratt Free Library in Baltimore, Maryland on 18 October 2023, Will Smith described his relationship with Jada Pinkett Smith as "very, very long and tumultuous," adding: "We call it 'brutiful.' It was brutal and beautiful at the same time." The 55-year-old actor appeared at the press event for his wife's book, Worthy, alongside their two children, Jaden, 25, and Willow, 22, days after she disclosed in the memoir that the couple had been separated for seven years. He opened by telling the crowd, as reported by The Baltimore Sun: "I just really wanted to come out and just be here and hold it down for you the way you have held it down for me."

At another point he called his union with Pinkett Smith, whom he married in 1997, a "sloppy public experiment in unconditional love," according to the Baltimore Banner, and said he is "happier than [he's] ever been in [his] entire life." He credited his wife's sacrifices for his career: "I have achieved every single thing I have ever wanted in my entire life. There is not one thing left that I desire in this world — all of the awards, all of the money, the family — everything I've ever dreamed. And those dreams were largely built on the foundation of Jada's sacrifices. There were many times when Jada put her career aside so I could follow the dreams of mine." He also thanked her for putting him "before herself" and for maintaining a good relationship with his ex-wife Sheree Zampino, with whom he shares 30-year-old son Trey Smith — who was also present at the event — saying that relationship had allowed all three of his children to grow up together. He closed with a question and a pledge: "Can you show up and love somebody for the rest of your life, even when you don't agree with them? Jada is the best friend I have ever had on this planet and I am going to show up for her and support her for the rest of my life."



---


# Will And Jada As A New, Unconventional Marriage Model

Relationship expert Susan Winter argues that the Smiths' seven-year separation is not a stalled marriage waiting to be repaired but a fluid arrangement outside the traditional marriage design — an evolving model that could come to serve other couples. Her starting point is a limit on what outsiders can know: the public will never fully learn what "heavy-duty work" Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith are doing in their relationship, and, she says, it is not necessarily anyone's business.

The grounds are that a couple who have already built something different have no reason to revert to the conventional form. "They're in the rough with a machete, carving a new path for themselves," Winter said. "Why would they say: 'Hey, let's go back to the house and just relax?' They're really exploring something vastly different. It doesn't end up that you go back into that little box of 'this is a marriage, we're living together'. It just doesn't do that." The Independent frames the same point as a question: if the Smiths have spent seven years apart as a married couple, why would they decide to return to a shared household?



---


# Will Smith's Slap Of Chris Rock At The 2022 Oscars

In March 2022, at the 94th annual Academy Awards, Will Smith walked onto the stage and slapped the comedian Chris Rock, then yelled at him to "keep my wife's name out your f***ing mouth." The altercation followed Rock's joke — "Jada, I love you. GI Jane 2, can't wait to see you" — referring to Jada Pinkett Smith's shaved head, which is a result of her alopecia. It quickly became the most talked-about moment of the evening, with the pair initially appearing to laugh off the tense moment. Later that night, while accepting the award for Best Actor, Smith became teary and said he was a "fierce defender of his family."

The incident was reassessed in October 2023 after Pinkett Smith revealed the couple had been separated since 2016 and so were separated at the time of the ceremony. UK-based dating coach Jacob Lucas, quoted by The Independent, tied part of the surrounding controversy to that timing and questioned Smith's behaviour and word choice at the awards given the separation.



---


# The Terms Of A Separation Agreement Determine Its Outcome

Relationship expert Susan Winter argues that what happens during a separation depends almost entirely on what the couple agreed the separation was for, so the same events — including an outside relationship — can lead to opposite outcomes. Applied to the Smiths, the point is pressed by a gap in the public record: outsiders now know that Jada Pinkett Smith and Will Smith have been separated since 2016, but the timeline of her relationship with August Alsina remains fuzzy and the terms of the separation are still unknown to the public. The Independent notes that in some cases having separate relationships can give couples the clarity they need about their marriage.

Winter's grounds are the two different agreements a separating couple might have made, which carry different implications for an affair: "What's pivotal here is, what was the agreement? Did we agree to separate to work on ourselves for the purpose of coming back together again? Did we agree to separate and just be alone for a while and not have that discussion? And in the second case, if you have an affair, sometimes it can bring you back to the original person. You can get whatever you need to achieve or gain a different perspective, allowing you to decide if you want to come back or leave for good."



---

# Tim McGraw And Faith Hill's Marriage

Tim McGraw and Faith Hill, both 56, met in 1994, began dating in 1996 and married later that same year; they share three daughters — Gracie, 26, Maggie, 25, and Audrey, 21 — and by late 2023 had been married for nearly 30 years. McGraw joked to "Entertainment Tonight Canada" about how that reads in the industry: "I don't know if there's a key. We always say we're 27 years coming up, it's like 96 in show business. It's almost like dog years."

The distinguishing feature of their account is a rule set at the start rather than a technique applied since. Although he humbly denied having any "key" to a successful marriage, McGraw named the commitment the two made at the outset: "We just made a commitment early on, when we first decided we were getting married and having kids, that we wouldn't just walk out the door when problems arose."

# Britney Spears And Kevin Federline: Marriage And Divorce

Britney Spears and Kevin Federline married in September 2004 after just three months of dating, in a surprise ceremony in Studio City, California, and Spears filed for divorce in November 2006 citing "irreconcilable differences." The two had met at a club in 2004 — Joseph's, in Hollywood — while Federline was working as a backup dancer for Justin Timberlake. Federline recalled the meeting to People in 2008: "I met her at a club in Hollywood, Joseph's. Our eyes met and that was it. We just hit it off right away. I learned real fast how much of a whirlwind the press and everything was." He was 26 at the time of the wedding; the "Toxic" and "Gimme More" singer was 22. Earlier that same year Spears had married her childhood friend Jason Alexander, a marriage annulled after 55 hours.

The couple's first child, son Sean Preston, was born weeks before their first wedding anniversary, and their second son, Jayden James, arrived in 2006. Federline was already a parent to daughter Kori Madison and son Kaleb Michael with ex-fiancée Shar Jackson — reported as 20 and 18 in the 18 October account and as 21 and 19 in the 20 October one. Spears filed for divorce just eight weeks after the birth of their second child. The initial divorce settlement, finalised in July 2007, granted the pair joint legal and physical custody of their two children, and relations appeared cordial until 2018, when Federline requested an increase of $20,000 a month in child support payments from Spears.

# Britney Spears And Justin Timberlake's Relationship

They broke up in 2002, shortly after Timberlake and his boy band NSYNC released their hit "Cry Me a River." The song's music video, which featured a woman with blonde hair, sparked rumours that the couple had split because Spears had allegedly cheated on him.

# Counter-Argument: Separations Reschedule Problems Rather Than Resolve Them

UK-based dating coach Jacob Lucas attacks the premise that an indefinite separation is a constructive alternative to divorce, arguing instead that it merely postpones the breakup. Speaking to The Independent in October 2023, he acknowledged that not all separations end in resolutions: when couples stop living together it can create an emotional disconnect, and if a lack of connection already existed before they separated, the separation does not make those issues go away. In such cases, he believes, couples may be avoiding an inevitable breakup for the sake of comfortability. "They're not resolving their problems, they're rescheduling them," he said. "So, if you separate from someone, but you live in a separate house and you're still together, it seems to me you're just not letting go of the past because you want to stick to what's familiar. People stick to what they know, and it's like you have a tether to that person. Your brain's like: 'I cannot let go of them because I am scared of the unknown.' I don't think I've ever seen a couple separate and come back again."

Lucas also attacks the second premise — that a promise never to divorce is a strength. While he agrees both parties must be invested in a relationship, he warns that promising not to get a divorce could spark feelings of resentment down the line, and that an agreement of the kind the Smiths made could create a false narrative about divorce. He notes that fans do not know why the couple made that promise. His warrant is that the stigma the promise defends against is not real: "Getting divorced shouldn't feel like a taboo because people grow apart and that's fine. People get stuck in relationships because of their friends and family or societal pressure, and they worry about getting divorced. They think a divorce has a stigma to its name, which it doesn't, and they push aside the fact that they still essentially feel trapped with someone they don't want to be with."

# Expert Signs That It Is Time To End A Marriage

Asked when a couple should stop trying, relationship expert Susan Winter argues that the threshold is exhaustion of options rather than any particular grievance: "When there is no stone left unturned, or when they have tried every single combination possible to make the relationship function and yet it doesn't, that's the time to pull the plug. They've done their individual work and they have done the work together and ended up in the same place." Her warrant is that effort must have been made both separately and jointly; only when both routes converge on the same failure is the case closed. The Independent notes that every relationship is different, whether lived in the public eye or not, and that living separately may not be an issue for some couples at all.

Dating coach Jacob Lucas offers a different, behaviour-based test: "If you feel disrespected by your partner, feel humiliated, or were cheated on, you probably feel ready to split. I also think a real big one is, if you lose sexual attraction for your partner and you've actively tried to get it back and can't, it's time to go." Applied to the Smiths, the article sets out three open possibilities — the couple could stay separated, move back in together as a married pair, or get a divorce.



---


# Britney Spears' 55-Hour Marriage To Jason Alexander

Jason Alexander was Britney Spears' first husband: the two married at a wedding chapel in Las Vegas in 2004 and annulled the marriage only 55 hours after the ceremony. Alexander returned to the news in 2022 when he tried to attend Spears' wedding to Sam Asghari, and could be heard in a video saying he was going to crash the nuptials. "She's my first wife, my only wife," he reportedly told security. "I'm her first husband, I'm here to crash the wedding."

Alexander was arrested for trespassing, vandalism, and battery over the incident. A security guard later revealed in court that when Alexander crashed the wedding he also tried to enter Spears' bedroom.



---


# Garth Brooks And Trisha Yearwood's Marriage

Garth Brooks and Trisha Yearwood married in 2005 and had been together 18 years as of the November 2023 article, with Yearwood becoming a bonus mom to his three grown daughters from his first marriage. The couple have been candid about the union, and its defining contrast is with Brooks's earlier marriage: the "Friends in Low Places" singer told Billboard of his first marriage, to Sandy Maul, which ended in a messy divorce in 2000, "I sucked at being a husband, I was horrible at it. I was horrible at being a dad. I had to get my s--- together."

Each partner offers a different account of why this marriage works. Brooks attributes it to the choice of person: "The person you're with [does make] a huge difference in your life." Yearwood, the "She's in Love With the Boy" singer, told E! News on the ACM Awards red carpet that the secret to their long-lasting marriage is that the relationship is "always a first date, you know? It just really is."



---


# The Woman In Me: Britney Spears' Memoir

The Woman in Me is Britney Spears' memoir, released on 24 October 2023 in both the US and the UK. Its publisher's press release describes it as "a brave and astonishingly moving story about freedom, fame, motherhood, survival, faith, and hope." The book is expected to cover the pivotal moments of Spears' life, including the high-profile legal battle to end her conservatorship, which was dissolved in November 2021 after 13 years.

Ahead of publication, the main point of anticipation was what the book would say about Spears' private life. Because she spent the 1990s and 2000s in heavily publicised romances, fans expected her to detail those relationships in the memoir, and in particular to share new material about her second husband, Kevin Federline.

# Kevin Federline's 2022 Comments And The Spears Camp's Rebuttal

Britney Spears and her camp rejected Kevin Federline's 2022 claim that their teenage sons were distancing themselves from her because of her social media posts, attacking both the causal premise and Federline's standing to make it public. In an August 2022 interview with ITV, Federline said the couple's sons found it "tough" seeing their mother sharing nude photos online — she had been posting such images while embracing her newfound freedom after the end of her 13-year conservatorship — adding: "I can't imagine how it feels to be a teenager having to go to high school." More than a decade after the marriage ended, the pair were still having ups and downs co-parenting their two teenage sons, Sean Preston and Jayden.

Spears attacked the causal claim in a statement on her Instagram Stories, denying that Instagram was the reason: "It saddens me to hear that my ex husband has decided to discuss the relationship between me and my children … As we all know, raising teenage boys is never easy for anyone. It concerns me the fact that the reason is based on my Instagram … It was LONG before Instagram … I gave them everything … Only one word: HURTFUL." Sam Asghari attacked the factual premise and Federline's motive, accusing him of using their sons to "vilify" his wife and claiming her ex-husband's "gravy train will end soon, which probably explains the timing of these hurtful statements"; he wrote on Instagram that "there is no validity to his statement regarding the kids distancing themselves and it is irresponsible to make that statement publicly." Spears' attorney Mathew Rosengart shifted the attack to Federline's own conduct, saying in a statement obtained by Variety that by posting private videos of Spears sternly speaking with her children without her consent he had created "legal issues" for himself: "Whether he realises it or not, Mr Federline has not only violated the privacy and dignity of the mother of his children, he has undermined his own children, whose privacy he should protect. Putting aside his ITV interview, Mr Federline's ill-advised decision to post an old video of his 11 and 12-year-old children was cruel, bottom of the barrel stuff. It was abhorrent." Rosengart added that "in addition to demeaning himself and violating societal norms, he has now also created various legal issues for himself, including, but not limited to, implicating cyber-harassment and cyber-bullying statutes, among other things."



---


# Britney Spears And Sam Asghari: Marriage And Divorce

Sam Asghari filed for divorce from Britney Spears in August 2023 after only 14 months of marriage, listing the date of separation as 28 July 2023 and citing "irreconcilable differences." The two had met in 2016, when Asghari was cast as Spears' love interest in the music video for "Slumber Party," from her 2016 album Glory; they made the relationship Instagram official in 2017 and supported each other through milestones including the 29th annual GLAAD Media Awards, where Spears accepted the Vanguard Award for her work promoting equality and acceptance. In April 2022 Spears announced she was pregnant with her third child and their first together, but the following month said in an Instagram statement that she had suffered a miscarriage; the couple wrote: "We have lost our miracle baby."

They married that June at her California home in Los Angeles, a lavish ceremony one month after the miscarriage announcement, with a guest list that included Selena Gomez, Paris Hilton, Drew Barrymore, Madonna, and Donatella Versace, who designed the wedding dress. Spears' close family — her mother Lynne, father Jamie, sister Jamie-Lynn, and her two sons — were not present. In August 2023, months after Asghari had shut down speculation about a divorce, TMZ claimed he had confronted Spears about rumours she had cheated on him; the fitness instructor filed the same day. His statement read: "After six years of love and commitment to each other my wife and I have decided to end our journey together. We will hold onto the love and respect we have for each other and I wish her the best always. S*** happens. Asking for privacy seems ridiculous so I will just ask for everyone including the media to be kind and thoughtful." Days before the memoir's release he told TMZ, on 13 October, that he had obtained an early copy and was not worried about being painted negatively: "I already read it and I'm very proud of her. She put a lot of work into it, and it was very hard. I'm definitely excited, and I'm extremely proud of her. It was a very tough one [to write]." Fans had previously praised him for his continuing support of Spears through her conservatorship and custody battle. Spears' two children, Sean, 18, and Jayden, 17, are shared with her second ex-husband, Kevin Federline.



---


# Britney Spears' Engagement To Jason Trawick

Britney Spears and Jason Trawick, a Hollywood agent who worked at WME, began dating in 2009 and became engaged in December 2011, but called off the engagement in January 2013 and announced they were going their separate ways.

Spears said in a statement sent by her representative to ABC News: "Jason and I have decided to call off our engagement. I'll always adore him and we will remain great friends." Trawick issued his own statement at the time: "As this chapter ends for us a new one begins. I love and cherish her and her boys and we will be close forever."



---


# Kevin Federline's Marriage To Victoria Prince

Victoria Prince is Kevin Federline's wife, a volleyball player he married in 2013 after moving on from his relationship with Britney Spears. The couple share two daughters. The two Independent accounts, published two days apart in October 2023, give their names and ages slightly differently: the 18 October piece calls them Jordan, 10, and Peyton, eight, while the 20 October piece gives their full names as Jordan Kay, 12, and Peyton Marie, nine.

The marriage is presented as the post-divorce chapter of the Spears-Federline story: after the divorce, the two appeared to be co-parenting amicably, seen supporting their boys at soccer and football games, and Federline moved on to Prince.



---


# Justin Timberlake's Apology And Support For Britney Spears

Justin Timberlake publicly apologised to Britney Spears on Instagram in 2021 after the documentary Framing Britney, which addressed the public scrutiny Spears faced during the 2000s, prompted criticism of how he had behaved following their breakup. Neither had ever acknowledged the rumours about why they split. His apology read: "I've seen the messages, tags, comments, and concerns and I want to respond. I am deeply sorry for the times in my life where my actions contributed to the problem, where I spoke out of turn, or did not speak up for what was right. I understand that I fell short in these moments and in many others and benefited from a system that condones misogyny and racism."

In June 2021 he also backed Spears after she testified publicly in a bid to end the conservatorship controlled by her father, Jamie Spears. At the Los Angeles court hearing, Spears alleged she had been forced to take lithium against her will and claimed the team managing her conservatorship had prevented her from having another baby by refusing to remove her IUD. Timberlake wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter: "After what we saw today, we should all be supporting Britney at this time. Regardless of our past, good and bad, and no matter how long ago it was. What's happening to her is just not right. No woman should ever be restricted from making decisions about her own body."

qid: Does the article from The Verge suggest that Google has the capability to address issues with Android app distribution and in-app payment systems, while the TechCrunch articles imply that Google's practices in both app distribution and news content distribution are anticompetitive?
context:
# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. Google's execution was uneven, though — it wound up spending much of its opening statement attempting to explain away its seemingly bad behavior as normal business practices and did not always succeed out of the gate.



---


# The Market Definition Fight In Epic v. Google

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

The relation between definition and outcome is direct. If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

Two observations sit outside the formal model but bear on how the fee looks. Google charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal or a credit card, which does seem like a lot; and though Epic cannot argue it in court, Apple was not able to explicitly justify a 30 percent fee to that case's judge. On the other hand, it does kind of seem like Epic wants something for nothing — Epic has not stated what kind of fee would actually be reasonable for Google to charge in exchange for placement in its store, and CEO Tim Sweeney seemingly suggests there should not be a Google fee at all if a developer wants to use its own payment system.



---


# Epic's Antitrust Claims Against Google Play

Epic's claim is that the Android operating system's Google Play Store constitutes an unlawful monopoly, and that Google is separately tying its Google Play payments platform to that store, keeping other potential app payment mechanisms from competing.

The grounds Epic offers are the frictions it says Google creates: Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that it has created an illegal monopoly which unjustly enriches Google while artificially driving up app prices because other stores cannot compete. The warrant joining that to the legal claim is the competitive-harm chain — no viable rival stores means no fee discipline, which means the "Google Tax" is paid either by developers or passed along to consumers. Epic wants to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods so developers are not stuck paying that tax.

Google's answer contests the warrant rather than the fees: it says Epic's demands would damage Android's ability to offer a secure user experience and to compete with Apple's iOS. Both sides agree the future of Google's app store could depend on this trial. Epic sued in 2020 after a fight over in-app purchase fees.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.



---


# Google Play Billing And The User Choice Billing Alternative

Google Play's billing arrangement, as of November 2023, has two tiers. The baseline requires apps to use Google's own first-party billing system and charges app developers a 15% to 30% commission on the sales it processes. The alternative is User Choice Billing, a program still in pilot testing, open to all developers who sell apps in the 35 markets where it is then available, including the U.S., which reduces the standard commission by 4% for companies who choose to use their own payment processing solution. Spotify and Bumble were the initial testers for the new system, first introduced in November 2022, and Match, as part of its settlement agreement, will also now take advantage of this option. Epic has declined to use it.

Google's defense of the commission rests on what it says the commission buys. It will argue that its commissions are not just tied to payment processing, but help it develop other features and controls to keep Android users safe and guide them to discovering new applications, as well as helping fund the tools and services developers need to build and grow their apps. Google also helps developers reach a broader audience beyond the mobile phone, with support for Android across platforms ranging from tablets to TVs to autos and more. And it notes that 99% of its developers qualify for a commission of 15% or less, based on their revenues — so the headline 30% is the boundary case, not the typical one.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Openness And Sideloading

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google will also attack the foreclosure premise directly. It will note that, unlike Apple, it allows apps to be sideloaded on Android devices — something Epic takes advantage of today — and that this process is streamlined and helps keep users safe. Epic will claim in response that the process is made to be overly difficult for end users, with multiple steps involved and "scare screens" that warn users of the security risks involved with sideloading.

On discovery, Epic will suggest that Google hid items by allowing execs and employees to have "off the record" chats; Google will counter this as well, saying it has provided the court with thousands of chat logs and millions of documents. Google will ultimately push the notion that this case is not about competition but about money — that is, that Epic Games wants to reach the Play Store's 2.5 billion users without having to pay. As a Google blog post by Wilson White, VP, Government Affairs & Public Policy, put it: "Android's choice and flexibility work well for consumers and developers of all sizes. We look forward to making our case in court as we fight to keep our users safe from harm, partner with developers to grow their businesses, and keep the Android ecosystem thriving and healthy for everyone."



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# Epic's Jury Verdict Against Google, December 2023

On Monday, a federal jury sided with Fortnite maker Epic Games in its fight to break Google's control over Android apps, surprising the world. The nine-person jury decided that Google has an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems, and that Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The outcome was striking because "walled garden" rival Apple almost entirely won a similar case two years earlier. For Tim Sweeney, this was, at last, a win.



---


# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.



---


# Epic's Argument That Google Blocks Alternative Android App Stores

Epic will attempt to demonstrate that Google makes it hard for alternative app stores to succeed and reach consumers. Its headline ground is a distribution fact: 90% of apps are still downloaded through Google Play.

The mechanism Epic offers to explain that share is contractual. Google bundles the Play Store with other Google apps that Android OEMs (original equipment manufacturers) have to agree to in order to use Android. Epic will also bring up "Anti-Fragmentation Agreements" (AFAs) that prevent the OEMs from modifying Android to allow for frictionless downloading of apps outside of Google Play. The warrant is that if OEMs are contractually barred from making outside downloading frictionless, rival stores cannot reach consumers on comparable terms, and Play's share follows from the contracts rather than from consumer preference.

Epic will offer two concrete instances. It will specifically reference an agreement it had made with the OEM OnePlus, to make Epic games available on its devices through the Epic Games app; OnePlus had to cancel the deal over concerns that the arrangement would have it bypassing the Google Play Store. The case will also examine a deal between Google and Samsung that Epic says was designed to prevent the Galaxy Store from being a competitive threat and to require Google Play Billing on apps distributed by Samsung.



---


# The Epic v. Google Witness Lineup

A whole cast of intriguing people were set to be called as witnesses during the trial, going straight to the top of the org chart: Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Epic CEO Tim Sweeney are absolutely expected to attend.

Beyond the two chief executives, Android co-founder Andy Rubin might be deposed, and Google says the court will hear from current Android — and Chrome, and Chrome OS — boss Hiroshi Lockheimer. Google also says representatives from Apple, Netflix, Motorola, and AT&T should testify.



---


# Project Hug: Google's Developer Incentive Program, As Characterized By Both Sides

Project Hug is an initiative that forms part of the Google Games Velocity Program, and it is a second set of agreements Epic will highlight — those between Google and Android app developers themselves, as distinct from Google's agreements with device makers. Its defining feature is contested, and the two characterizations mark the boundary of the concept.

Epic will cite it as an example of where Google paid competitors not to distribute their apps on Android outside of the Play Store, by targeting those developers that were most at risk of attrition from Play and then approaching them with a monetary offer. As an example, Epic will point to Activision Blizzard — the owner of King.com and maker of Candy Crush and Call of Duty — as one developer that wanted to go the route of opening its own app store. Google and Activision Blizzard then entered into a three-year agreement in January 2020, worth approximately $360 million, to keep the developer on Google Play, Epic will argue.

Google, however, will characterize this program as a way to incentivize developers to launch their apps on Android at the same time as they launch on iOS, and plans to dispute Epic's claims that it prevented developers from opening their own app stores.



---


# The $360 Million Activision Payment And Its Evidentiary Weakness

The counter to Epic's headline number attacks the factual premise beneath it: the $360 million refers to an alleged payment that kept Activision from opening an app store that could compete with Google Play, but Activision told The Verge in 2022 that it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store" — and Google says it is now armed with the evidence to prove it.

Epic itself conceded a related point. On Monday Epic's attorney admitted Google "was too clever" to draw up contracts that specifically forced developers not to compete with the Play Store, so it is not clear how much of Epic's evidence will hold up on closer examination.

The narrative advantage may nonetheless survive the evidentiary weakness. The overall story Epic tells is compelling, and it is not clear Google's opening statement countered it: Google spent its 45 minutes attempting to explain that its dominance over the Android app market is not anything nefarious but simply the natural outcome of Google fiercely competing with the iPhone and its iOS App Store, where Google would like the court to believe the competition truly lies.



---


# Epic's Rebuttal Of Google's Leaked Email Summary

Pressed with the suggestion that the email Epic accused Google of leaking showed Epic was itself interested in a special deal, Tim Sweeney attacked the premise of the characterisation: Google did not leak the email, he said — it leaked "their ridiculously biased summary of it" to Abner Li at 9to5Google.

He supported the leak claim with trial testimony: Don Harrison testified that he didn't think Google leaked to the press, and was then presented with a document including Google's press team and Sameer Samat, head of all Android, summarising the articles that appeared as a result of Google's leaking of Epic's plans to the press. On the substance of the email, Sweeney said it is in evidence and is the same one he had already described: right before Christmas-ish 2019, with the new Marvel season and a lineup of Star Wars content planned, he asked Google's executives to let Fortnite come to the Google Play Store using Epic's own payment method and to open up the use of their own payment methods to all developers, not just Epic. The interviewer conceded the point, saying he had read that email in court and had not realised it was the same one, because it was so far off from what he had heard described as a "special billing exception."



---


# Project Hug, Agave And Banyan

The allegations made before trial suggest Google was playing loads of dirty tricks with names like "Project Hug," "Project Agave," and "Project Banyan," with Epic claiming it has seen evidence Google was paying off game developers and phone makers not to abandon its app store — to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars.

Google allegedly even toyed with the idea of buying Epic, to keep Fortnite from inspiring other game developers to abandon ship.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. # Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Google's News Content Payment Deal With Canada

In November 2023, the month before the Helena World Chronicle suit was filed, Google reached an agreement with the Canadian government under which the search giant would pay Canadian media for use of their content. Under the terms of the deal, Google will provide $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) every year to news organizations in the country, with funds distributed based on the news outlets' headcount.

Negotiations with Meta over the same Canadian law were still unresolved as of mid-December 2023. Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August, in light of the pressure to pay for content under the new Canadian law.

# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.

# MADA And RSA: Google's Two Android Distribution Agreements

Google binds Android device makers through two distinct contract types, described at trial on November 8, 2023 by Jamie Rosenberg, a Google employee who focuses on Android and Google Play, testifying in Google's defense. A mobile app distribution agreement (MADA) requires Android smartphone makers — like Samsung or Oppo — to pre-load a bundle of 11 Google apps on the device, including Search, Chrome and Play. Rosenberg's discriminating point about MADA is that the pre-loaded apps do not have to be the default choices.

A revenue share agreement (RSA) is the second and separate instrument. RSAs run with smartphone makers and also with wireless carriers such as Verizon, and unlike MADAs they do require the counterparty to set Google search and the Chrome web browser as defaults. So the boundary between the two is pre-installation versus default status: MADA buys presence on the device, RSA buys the default slot.

Rosenberg defended the arrangement on two grounds — that Google apps like Search are "best in class," and that the RSAs motivate other companies to make or sell more Android devices. He framed the broader competitive setting by saying the competition between Google and Apple is "as intense as it gets," per Bloomberg.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# Revenue Split

## Definition

A revenue split, in the corpus, is the percentage pair — such as 70/30, 50/50, or 95/5 — by which a platform and a counterparty divide proceeds: Google's revenue share agreements (RSAs) with Android device makers and carriers, Google's 70/30 app-store split with developers, and Twitch's and Kick's subscription-revenue splits with streamers.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces across three unrelated disputes that share the same underlying mechanic: dividing proceeds between a platform and a counterparty. In the US v. Google antitrust trial, Google's revenue share agreements (RSAs) pay Android device makers and wireless carriers like Verizon a cut in exchange for setting Google Search and Chrome as defaults. In the Epic v. Google trial, Epic argued that Google's 70/30 app-store revenue split with developers is likely descended from an arbitrary decision Valve made with Steam two decades earlier, rather than from any principled calculation of the value Google's store provides. On the creator-platform side, Twitch's default subscription revenue split for Partners is 50/50, with a premium 70/30 tier once offered to select streamers before Twitch discontinued it in favor of ad revenue; rival platform Kick instead lures streamers away with a 95/5 split.

## Key Characteristics

- **Expressed as a ratio** — revenue splits are stated as two percentages that sum to 100, such as 70/30, 50/50, or 95/5, denoting each party's share.
- **Applies across different platform relationships** — the corpus shows the same mechanic governing device-maker default agreements (Google RSAs), app-store developer terms (Google/Epic 70/30), and creator subscription payouts (Twitch, Kick).
- **A lever platforms adjust unilaterally** — Twitch changed its subscription split from a 70/30 deal for select streamers to a 50/50 default, then introduced the Partner Plus program to restore a 70/30 rate for qualifying creators, showing the split is a platform-controlled term rather than a fixed market rate.
- **A point of leverage in competitive disputes** — Epic used the 70/30 app-store split's arbitrary Valve/Steam origin to challenge Google's justification for its rate, and Kick's more generous 95/5 split is a stated draw for streamers dissatisfied with Twitch's terms.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "revenue split" and "revenue share" only in the specific device-maker, app-store, and creator-payout deals described above, without defining the general concept. Outside the corpus, revenue sharing is defined as the distribution of the total revenue generated by the sale of goods and services among stakeholders or contributors, distinct from profit sharing (which splits only what remains after costs) (Wikipedia, "Revenue sharing," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenue_sharing).
