# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.



---


# Activision, Riot And Supercell's Abandoned Android Store Plans

Asked whether he believes Activision Blizzard really intended to build its own app store, Tim Sweeney said yes — Activision was building a store, with a large team of dozens of engineers building a mobile app store to launch on Android — and said that of the three companies, Riot is the strongest example, while he does not know about Supercell.

For Riot, Sweeney cited the documents in the case: Riot planned to distribute League of Legends directly through its website on mobile, exactly as it does on PC, and stuck to that plan until Google paid it off not to; at a minimum, he said, Google's payoff dissuaded Riot from distributing off Google Play. For Activision, his evidence is partly first-hand and partly documentary. Activision came to Epic and told Epic it was building the store; and after everything went down, Sweeney talked to an Activision employee close to that effort, working with the team building the store, who reported that the entire store team Activision had employed had been disbanded as soon as Activision signed its deal with Google. The Verge appended an editor's note that no such person was heard from at trial and that the interviewer would be eager to speak to them. Sweeney added that Activision was telling Google it was building the store, that Google's internal discussions said Google didn't want Activision building a competing store, and that after signing the deal Google staff were gleeful about having dissuaded perhaps their number one competitor at the time from launching its own store.



---


# Epic v. Google Is A Jury Trial

Epic and Google have to convince a jury, not the judge, which is totally different from how the Apple case played out — that one was a "bench trial."

The consequence is that persuasion cuts both ways and is hard to predict. All the evidence of tricky deals inside Google might sway a jury against the company; alternatively, Google scaremongering that sideloaded apps equal gaping security holes might sway a jury against Epic. Who knows.

The jury is also sealed off from coverage: Judge Donato explicitly told jurors they are in a "news-free bubble" through mid-December.



---


# Google's Project Hug Developer Payoff Program

Project Hug, as Tim Sweeney described it from the trial evidence, was a Google program that offered payoffs to developers so they would not pursue their own app stores or exclusive distribution — the same corrupt deal structure, in his account, that Google had tried on Epic when it wanted to pay Epic off to launch Fortnite on Google Play and not launch Epic's own store.

Its defining feature is scale and its trigger is Epic's refusal: as soon as Epic thwarted Google's effort, Sweeney said, Google went around to 27 different developers and offered each one a payoff to undermine any effort Epic made to get their games onto the Epic store exclusively. He named Activision, Riot and Supercell as developers that had direct distribution plans they were planning on and that Google paid not to pursue. Sweeney called these "just direct blatant violations of anti-competition law" and said it was crazy that a company of Google's scale would do that. He noted that as an Epic employee he had not been able to see Google's internal documents until the trial started — the lawyers could, but he saw almost all the key elements in the case at the same time the jury did — and that Project Hug was one of two things that stood out big time.



---


# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.



---


# Temu As The Top US iPhone App Of 2023

Temu, the Chinese e-commerce company, is Apple's most downloaded free app in the U.S. for 2023. Apple released an App Store feature on 12 December 2023 showcasing the top iPhone apps of the year, free and paid, as measured by app installs — its proxy for overall popularity. In that ranking, apps from Chinese-based companies have taken over spots previously held by U.S. tech giants like Meta and Google, with CapCut and TikTok, both from Beijing-based ByteDance, coming in at No. 3 and No. 5 respectively.

TechCrunch suggests the negative attention TikTok received during the year may account for its slip from being the No. 1 app last year to No. 5 this year, but says U.S. consumers have not sworn off Chinese apps by the looks of things, given Temu's No. 1 position.

Engagement data supports the point: figures from Apptopia, reported by Bloomberg, noted that consumers were spending 18 minutes per day in Temu's app compared with 10 minutes in Amazon, with younger users spending even more, at 19 minutes per day on average. While Temu attracts users with in-app games, its real draw may be its bargain prices, which have more appeal during an economic downturn, and it is also a heavily marketed app, just as TikTok was in the months leading up to its No. 1 ranking last year.

# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. # Sam Altman's Next Move After The OpenAI Firing

In the days after his firing, Sam Altman's destination was genuinely unsettled: on November 20, 2023 he and Greg Brockman announced they would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research team, yet on the same day both were reported to be still open to returning to OpenAI, and Altman was separately telling investors he planned to launch a new venture.

# OpenAI Board Composition And The Helen Toner Dispute

At the time of Sam Altman's ouster in November 2023, OpenAI's board of directors consisted of OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, tech entrepreneur Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner, the director of strategy at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology — and a clash between Altman and Toner is reported to have contributed to the crisis.

The New York Times reported that, before his ousting, Altman made a move to push out board member Helen Toner because he thought a paper she had co-written was overly critical of OpenAI. That, among other issues, led to OpenAI's predicament. The Times also indicated that negotiations to hire Altman back were continuing, but that one major sticking point remaining was "guardrails" intended to improve Altman's communication with the board.



---


# Dismissed Theories: A Murati Coup And A Personal Matter

TechCrunch pushes back on two explanations circulating for Altman's removal. The first is that interim CEO Mira Murati engineered the ouster: probably not — she seems cool, and anyway what CTO wants to be CEO?

The second is that the trigger was personal or legal rather than professional. When someone is kicked out in a hurry, it is not uncommon that there was some kind of unprofessional behavior in the workplace; some CEOs get a pass on things like having kids with direct reports, but not all. Altman also has three siblings, and his younger sister Annie has publicly accused him of abuse — allegations TechCrunch says it has no way of evaluating, and which involve private matters.

The premise both theories rest on is that the board's action had a personal or legal cause. TechCrunch's read on the board's language in dismissing Altman is that it was not a legal or personal problem that provoked the action, but a professional or business one.

# Sam Altman's Career And Public Profile

Sam Altman has a long history steering OpenAI: he co-founded the company alongside Peter Thiel, LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman and others, and initially served as a co-chair of OpenAI alongside Elon Musk, who left in 2018 to avoid a conflict of interest with Tesla.

Altman formerly headed the startup accelerator Y Combinator and also holds a seat on the board at Worldcoin, the ambitious cryptocurrency project. In the several months before his firing he played an active role in attempting to shape regulators' responses to AI, appearing at U.S. congressional hearings and meeting personally with world leaders including President Joe Biden, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz and French President Emmanuel Macron, among others, on an international policy tour.

His standing in the industry was reflected in the reaction to his ouster. Eric Schmidt posted on X: "Sam Altman is a hero of mine. He built a company from nothing to $90 Billion in value, and changed our collective world forever. I can't wait to see what he does next. I, and billions of people, will benefit from his future work- it's going to be simply incredible." His brother Jack Altman wrote: "More important than being one of the most brilliant and impactful people our industry has ever had Sam is one of the most generous and caring people I know. I've never met someone who has supported and lifted up more people around them than him. Couldn't be a prouder brother."



---


# Sam Altman Fired As OpenAI CEO In November 2023

Sam Altman was fired as CEO of OpenAI late on Friday, November 17, 2023, by the board of directors of OpenAI, Inc. — the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that acts as the governing body for OpenAI, the startup behind ChatGPT, GPT-4 and DALL-E 3. He both left the company's board of directors and stepped down as CEO, with chief technology officer Mira Murati stepping in as interim CEO.

OpenAI announced the shake-up in a post on its official blog; the company's management team was made aware shortly after. The blog post said Altman's departure followed a "deliberative review process by the board" which concluded that Altman "wasn't consistently candid in his communications" with other board members, "hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities," and that the board "no longer has confidence in [Altman's] ability to continue leading OpenAI." In a joint statement the board wrote that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity," said it remained "fully committed to serving this mission," thanked Altman for "his many contributions to the founding and growth of OpenAI," and said that "we believe new leadership is necessary as we move forward" and that Mira, "as the leader of the company's research, product, and safety functions," was "exceptionally qualified" as interim CEO. OpenAI said it would begin a formal search for a permanent CEO immediately.

Altman responded on X: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later." The removal came unexpectedly. OpenAI had just hosted its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, the week before with Altman emceeing; Altman had spoken at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference and at an Oakland, California event on the Thursday. According to The Verge and The New York Times, citing multiple internal sources, OpenAI employees learned of Altman's firing when it was announced publicly. The same change also saw co-founder Greg Brockman step down as chairman of the board while remaining OpenAI's president, reporting to Murati.



---


# OpenAI Board Negotiations Over Altman Reinstatement

Over the weekend that followed Sam Altman's firing, OpenAI's board held on-and-off talks about bringing him back as CEO; the talks repeatedly stalled, and at one point it was confirmed that Altman would not return and that new leadership would take hold.

The sequence ran roughly as follows. Investors — reportedly furious at the turn of events — exerted pressure on OpenAI's board to reinstate Altman, going so far as to recruit Microsoft, with Satya Nadella said to be sympathetic. On November 18 The Verge reported that the board had agreed in principle to resign and to allow Altman and Brockman to return, but it waffled, missing a deadline by which many OpenAI staffers were set to leave the company; Altman was said to be ambivalent about coming back and to be asking for "significant" governance changes. Bloomberg, citing sources close to the matter, reported that the board was in talks with Altman about returning as CEO as soon as that week, with discussions involving Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, one current board member, and possibly other directors. On November 19 The Information reported that Altman was expected to meet at OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters as executives pushed to have him reinstated, with Brockman invited to join though it was unclear whether he would.

Negotiations then hit a snag: Bloomberg reported that Brad Lightcap and Mira Murati, among others, were pushing the board to reinstate Altman, but the directors resisted, and as of midday Sunday the board had not resigned out of concern over who could replace them and was vetting candidates — one possible new addition being Salesforce co-CEO Bret Taylor. Later, according to The Information citing an internal memo sent by Sutskever, Altman would not be returning as CEO, and OpenAI appointed Emmett Shear, the co-founder of video streaming site Twitch, as interim CEO, replacing Murati. A number of investors and OpenAI employees had tried to bring Altman back after the sudden firing, but following a weekend of negotiations it was confirmed that he would not return; what that meant for ChatGPT's future and for the OpenAI DevDay announcements remained to be seen.



---


# Theory: An AGI And Mission Rift Between Altman And The Board

The proposition is that Altman's zeal for AGI, even absent a secret project or agreement, led to a major rift between him and the board. Altman is a proud techno-optimist and often speaks fondly of the possibilities of AGI, or artificial general intelligence, a theoretical software system that achieves human-like intellect and versatility. The board's statement pointedly includes that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity" and that new leadership was necessary.

The supporting observation is a directional one: it has been obvious to all that Altman took the company in a much more corporate direction from its origins, changing its legal status and aggressively pursuing enterprise and consumer applications, which does not sound a lot like the "mission" the board wants to advance.

What counts against it is timing. This shift did not happen today, and it certainly does not seem like a plausible reason for abruptly firing the CEO and a few others on a beautiful fall Friday afternoon — a gradual drift does not explain an abrupt dismissal.



---


# OpenAI Employee Revolt And Sutskever's Reversal

Nearly 500 of OpenAI's roughly 770 employees signed a letter saying they might quit unless the startup's board resigned and reappointed the ousted Sam Altman — a number that climbed to over 650 later that Monday — and, remarkably, the signatories included Ilya Sutskever, the chief scientist who had taken part in the removal.

Sutskever publicly reversed himself, publishing a post on X suggesting that he regretted his decision to remove Altman and that he would do everything in his power to reinstate Altman as CEO: "I deeply regret my participation in the board's actions. I never intended to harm OpenAI. I love everything we've built together and I will do everything I can to reunite the company." This was a reversal of the position he had taken days earlier. At an OpenAI all-hands meeting on the Friday afternoon, Sutskever had defended Altman's ouster, dismissing suggestions that pushing Altman out amounted to a "hostile takeover" and claiming that it was necessary to protect OpenAI's mission of "making AI beneficial to humanity."



---


# Induced AI's Plain-English Workflow Automation

Sam Altman is among the backers of Induced AI, an AI startup founded by two teenagers that aims to help businesses automate workflows in "previously unexplored" ways.

Manish reported the story in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023. Induced AI was founded that same year, and its product lets businesses type their back-office tasks into it in plain English, converting those instructions into pseudo-code in real time.



---


# Theory: A Long-Term Strategy Disagreement Over OpenAI's Economics

The proposition is that Altman and the board fell out over when OpenAI's money-losing growth strategy has to end. Despite being the hottest tech company in the world and everyone talking about ChatGPT, OpenAI is not exactly a sound business: it is shoveling money into the furnace as fast as it can by serving, by all accounts, a fantastically expensive product at bargain-bin prices. That is all well and good for a year or two, but at some point that strategy changes from a growth hack to an existential liability — so could Altman and the board have had irreconcilable differences on where that point lies?

TechCrunch judges this unlikely, and gives the disconfirming evidence: the company has been very deliberately pursuing this very publicly, confidently and on a long-term basis. Altman and the board seem to be in sync on this, at least for the present.



---


# Theory: Altman Circumvented The Board On A Deal

The prevailing theory floating around on November 18, 2023, based on the board's language and the way these giant tech companies work, is that Altman went around the board on a deal. "Not consistently candid" is a very diplomatic way of saying Altman lied.

The proposition: Altman — and potentially OpenAI President Greg Brockman, who stepped down as chairman simultaneously, then resigned — wanted to make a bold move that he knew the board would not like. It is not uncommon for these deals to be hammered out quietly in smoke- or vape-filled rooms and then presented as a fait accompli, but if it was controversial enough and the board found out about these maneuvers, it could be fuel for an ouster. The open question TechCrunch poses is what kind of deal would be big and dangerous enough for a summary dismissal of the CEO and famous face of the company, given the man was onstage two weeks earlier.

Microsoft is the natural candidate: few would be shocked if Microsoft, which is deeply embedded in OpenAI as an investor and customer, is a factor. Could Altman have been working with — or against — OpenAI's patron in secret? If Altman wanted to kill the golden goose by going independent, that might have activated the board's fiduciary or otherwise statutory duty; if he was negotiating some other deal, like an acquisition or deeper and more exclusive integration, it could also have caused the board to bristle, either at the idea itself or at being excluded. What would falsify it is weak: if Microsoft was as shocked as everyone else, as one report has it, it could hardly be the kind of high-stakes conspiracy some seem to be hoping for — but one must assume Microsoft would say that either way, since even if they had been working with Altman on a secret plan they could truthfully say they were surprised by his firing, and they "remain committed to our partnership."



---


# Sam Altman's Firing And Reinstatement

OpenAI's plans were very nearly smashed to pieces just before Thanksgiving when the OpenAI board of directors fired Sam Altman, arguing that he had not been "consistently candid in his communications with the board."

That firing didn't take. Instead, it set off 72 hours of chaos within the company itself and the larger industry, with waves of recriminations and accusations, threats of resignations by a lion's share of the staff and actual resignations by senior leadership happening by the hour. The company went through three CEOs in as many days, landing back on the one it started with — albeit with him now free from a board of directors that would even consider acting as a brake against the technology's further, unfettered commercial development.



---


# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."



---


# Sam Altman Reinstated As OpenAI CEO With A New Board

On November 21, 2023, OpenAI announced that it and Sam Altman had "reached an agreement in principle" for him to return as the company's CEO, alongside a restructured "initial" board of directors.

The new initial board named in the announcement comprised former Salesforce chief executive Bret Taylor as chair, former US Secretary of the Treasury Larry Summers, and Quora founder Adam D'Angelo. OpenAI posted: "We have reached an agreement in principle for Sam Altman to return to OpenAI as CEO with a new initial board of Bret Taylor (Chair), Larry Summers, and Adam D'Angelo. We are collaborating to figure out the details. Thank you so much for your patience through this." Altman also posted about the deal, saying his decision to join Microsoft on the Sunday "was the best path for me and the team"; since then, the new board's composition and Microsoft's support appeared to have been enough to bring him back to the company he co-founded. On November 29, OpenAI announced that Microsoft would gain representation on the new initial board in the form of a non-voting observer — it was not immediately clear who this observer might be, only that they would not have an official vote in board business.

The significance for ChatGPT, as TechCrunch framed it, is that the restructuring pushed aside the board members who were more focused on the nonprofit side of OpenAI and who held the most concerns over the commercialization of its tools.



---


# The OpenAI Board's Firing Of Sam Altman

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said on Friday, 2023-11-17, that it had pushed out its co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after a review found he was "not consistently candid in his communications" with the board of directors. "The board no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI," the artificial intelligence company said in a statement. Mira Murati, OpenAI's chief technology officer, would take over as interim CEO effective immediately while the company searched for a permanent replacement.

OpenAI declined to answer questions on what Altman's alleged lack of candor was about; the statement said only that his behavior was hindering the board's ability to exercise its responsibilities. Altman posted on X that Friday: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later."



---


# OpenAI Denial Of Malfeasance In Altman Ouster

OpenAI's own management pushed back against the inference that Sam Altman had been fired for wrongdoing, stating definitively that the board's decision was not a response to malfeasance and framing it instead as a communication breakdown.

The rebuttal came in an internal memo obtained by Axios and sent on the Saturday morning after the firing by OpenAI COO Brad Lightcap. Lightcap said the previous day's announcement "took [the management team] by surprise" and that management had had "multiple conversations with the board to try to better understand the reasons and process behind their decision," with discussions still ongoing as of Saturday morning. "We can say definitively that the board's decision was not made in response to malfeasance or anything related to our financial, business, safety, or security/privacy practices," Lightcap added. "This was a breakdown in communication between Sam and the board … We still share your concerns about how the process has been handled, are working to resolve the situation, and will provide updates as we're able."

The premise this attacks is the natural reading of the board's stated grounds — that a CEO removed for not being "consistently candid" must have done something wrong in the company's financial, business, safety or security and privacy conduct. Lightcap's memo concedes the communication problem while denying the conduct problem, and it also concedes that management itself did not understand the board's reasoning at the time.



---


# Greg Brockman Departure From OpenAI

OpenAI's longtime president and co-founder Greg Brockman was first removed as chairman of the board and then resigned from the company outright, citing "today's news" — the firing of Sam Altman on Friday, November 17, 2023.

By Brockman's own account, he got a text from OpenAI chief scientist and co-founder Ilya Sutskever shortly after noon on the Friday asking for a quick call. After Brockman sent a Google Meet link, he was told that he was being removed from the board as chairman "but was vital to the company and would retain his role" as president, and that Altman had been fired. Brockman then announced his resignation from OpenAI, sending a memo internally and publishing the text on X: "After learning today's news, this is the message I sent to the OpenAI team." He also posted jointly with Altman that "Sam and I are shocked and saddened by what the board did today," thanking the people they had worked with at OpenAI, their customers and their investors, and saying they were "still trying to figure out exactly" what had happened.

Brockman's account also places events the day before, on November 16: according to his post on X, Sutskever texted Altman on the Thursday evening about scheduling a Friday noon call, and Brockman alleges that Mira Murati, OpenAI's CTO and now interim CEO, was informed on Thursday night that Altman would be fired. Three senior OpenAI researchers resigned after Brockman, including director of research Jakub Pachocki and head of preparedness Aleksander Madry.



---


# Sam Altman's Side Ventures: Helion, Retro And Worldcoin

Altman has a number of possible next steps after leaving OpenAI, because even while running the company he placed large bets on several other ambitious projects.

Among them are Helion Energy, for developing fusion reactors that could produce prodigious amounts of energy from the hydrogen in seawater, and Retro Biosciences, which aims to add 10 years to the human lifespan using biotechnology. Altman also co-founded Worldcoin, a biometric and cryptocurrency project that has been scanning people's eyeballs with the goal of creating a vast digital identity and financial network.



---


# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# Altman's Argument On AI's Promise And Existential Risk

Sam Altman predicted that AI will prove to be "the greatest leap forward of any of the big technological revolutions we've had so far."

He paired that claim with its counterweight rather than leaving it alone: he also acknowledged the need for guardrails, calling attention to the existential dangers future AI could pose.



---


# Prediction: OpenAI Becomes A Product Company

TechCrunch predicts that after the leadership shake-up in November 2023, OpenAI will be a changed company — perhaps not outwardly, but the trickle-down effect of Sam Altman being more fully in charge will be felt at every level, manifesting above all in a "ship it" mindset.

The concrete test named is the GPT store, originally planned for launch in December 2023 but understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas. TechCrunch expects the "app store for AI" to be pushed hard as the platform to get your AI toys and tools from, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models, on the reasoning that OpenAI has an excellent model to work from in Apple's and will follow it all the way to the bank.

More broadly, the prediction is that the caution and academic reserve the previous board exerted will give way to an unseemly lust for markets and customers. Other major companies with AI efforts are expected to follow the same trend — for instance, Gemini/Bard horning in on a ton of Google products — but the writer suspects it will be more pronounced at OpenAI.



---


# The Analyst View That Altman's Exit Was Not A Business Problem

Forrester analyst Rowan Curran speculated that Altman's departure, "while sudden," did not likely reflect deeper business problems — attacking the inference from a shocking exit to trouble in the company's technology or commercial position.

"This seems to be a case of an executive transition that was about issues with the individual in question, and not with the underlying technology or business," Curran said.



---


# OpenAI Board's Merger Approach To Anthropic

During the leadership crisis, OpenAI's board of directors approached Dario Amodei, the co-founder and CEO of rival large-language model developer Anthropic, about a potential merger of the two companies, according to a report by The Information.

The approach was part of an effort by OpenAI to persuade Amodei to replace Altman as CEO. Amodei quickly turned down the CEO offer.



---


# Theory: A Financial Mismatch At OpenAI

The proposition is that some major mismatch in the financial department was the cause for dismissal. Could OpenAI be losing even more money than Altman admitted or projected? It seems impossible, TechCrunch writes, but the costs of running this operation have no precedent, nor really does the operation itself.

A variant, offered as purely speculative: what if Altman had been secretly pursuing an internal project, perhaps at significant cost, against the advice of the board and without the necessary safety measures that probably should accompany such research? It sounds a little wild, but firing your CEO like this is also a little wild.

What weighs against the family of financial theories is the difficulty of concealment: it is hard to imagine what Altman could have kept from the board and CTO that would be so damning. A separate possibility is that Altman was making personal investments in a way the board disagreed with — with OpenAI poised to be a kingmaker in the field, he would certainly be in a position of power. One would think that, as an ideologically driven person already rich beyond belief and at the head of the world's leading AI company, Altman would have risen beyond having to do this kind of side deal, or at the very least that scrutiny on him and those close to him would prevent them. But one can never be sure.



---


# Analyst Assessment Of Altman's Departure Impact

Gartner analyst Arun Chandrasekaran argued that Altman's exit "is indeed shocking as he has been the face of" generative AI technology — the ground for the shock being his public role rather than any operational gap.

Chandrasekaran qualified the consequence for the company itself: OpenAI still has a "deep bench of technical leaders," but its next executives will have to steer it through the challenges of scaling the business and meeting the expectations of regulators and society.



---


# Theory: A Security Or Privacy Incident At OpenAI

The proposition is that OpenAI experienced a major, perhaps pervasive, security issue that Altman downplayed. The circumstantial support: Microsoft reportedly suspended use of ChatGPT internally a few days before the firing, and OpenAI subsequently stopped allowing new signups. If there was a serious security problem in its biggest product and Altman downplayed it, that would obviously create distrust with the board. There is also the potential for misuse at scale with the enormous amount of personal data that travels through OpenAI's APIs and services.

What works against this theory is the identity of the replacement. CTO Mira Murati was just elevated to interim CEO in Altman's place, and it seems unlikely that anything security-related would go through the CEO and not the CTO, or that the two would be at odds to the point where one could be fired like this and the other swapped in to clean up the mess. As the board's statement notes, Murati is in charge of product and safety, among other things, so any significant snafu in that department would reflect on her as well as Altman.



---


# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.



---


# OpenAI's Board Composition In November 2023

The OpenAI board that fired Sam Altman consisted, the company said, of OpenAI's chief scientist Ilya Sutskever plus three non-employees.

Those three were Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, tech entrepreneur Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner of the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology.



---


# OpenAI's Founding And Its 2023 Board Crisis

The Rosewood hotel dinner led to the creation of a startup called OpenAI later that year; backed by hundreds of millions of dollars from Elon Musk and other funders, the lab promised to protect the world from Larry Page's vision. Thanks to its ChatGPT chatbot, OpenAI has fundamentally changed the technology industry and introduced the world to the risks and potential of artificial intelligence, and it is valued at more than $US80 billion, about $A123 billion, according to two people familiar with the company's latest funding round. Musk and Sam Altman's partnership did not survive, and the two have since stopped speaking. Altman's own gloss on such splits: "There is disagreement, mistrust, egos. The closer people are to being pointed in the same direction, the more contentious the disagreements are. You see this in sects and religious orders. There are bitter fights between the closest people."

The month before the 9 December 2023 article, that infighting came to OpenAI's boardroom: rebel board members tried to force out Altman because they believed they could no longer trust him to build AI that would benefit humanity, and over five chaotic days OpenAI looked as if it were going to fall apart until the board, pressured by giant investors and by employees who threatened to follow Altman out the door, backed down. The drama gave the world its first glimpse of the bitter feuds among those who will determine the future of AI, but years before the near meltdown there was a little-publicised but ferocious competition in Silicon Valley for control of the technology now quickly reshaping the world, from how children are taught to how wars are fought. That earlier story begins with DeepMind: five years before the Napa Valley party and two before the cat breakthrough on YouTube, Demis Hassabis, a 34-year-old neuroscientist, walked into a cocktail party at Peter Thiel's San Francisco town house and realised he had hit pay dirt, because there in Thiel's living room, overlooking the city's Palace of Fine Arts and a swan pond, was a chessboard; Hassabis had once been the second-best player in the world in the under-14 category, and said "I was preparing for that meeting for a year. I thought that would be my unique hook in: I knew that he loved chess."

# Which Travis Kelce Props To Play In Chiefs-Jets Week 4

Sporting News worked through FanDuel's Kelce-specific "Prop Stars" markets on 2023-09-28, recommending two of five. "Top of the Charts: Travis Kelce to have the Most Receiving Yards in the Game" at +140 — pass. The reasoning: the Jets know Kelce is trouble long before he even walks in and must slow down No. 87 to have a chance; New York's defense has been very good, though not quite great, over the last year and continues to improve, with Robert Saleh's troops holding opponents in check and giving their anemic offense a fighting chance, but the one thing Gang Green struggles to defend is the tight end — they were giving up the fifth-most receiving yards to the position that season at 56.3 and had just allowed Pharoah Brown a long 58-yard touchdown. Even so, +140 is a nice price for the best pass-catcher in the game, but there's too much blowout potential to warrant a flier. "Opening Act: Travis Kelce First TD Scorer" at +400 — bet on it, and the writers' favorite of all the specials: the Chiefs will likely score first whether they get the opening kickoff or not, while the Jets have an offensive coordinator who somehow underrated Micah Parsons and a team that refuses to take the training wheels off their former gunslinging quarterback, with Wilson turned into "Checkdown Charlie" by conservative coaching and no change expected early. "FriENDZONE: Travis Kelce to NOT score a TD" at +120 — pass, obviously, given the previous recommendation.

"Seemingly Ranch: Travis Kelce Last TD Scorer" at +550 — pass: ranch is a fine condiment beloved by many, which makes this wager something that should be seen as an insult to ranch fans everywhere; unless the Jets make it a close game or send it to overtime, it is hard to believe Kelce will even be on the field to score the last touchdown. "Platinum Performance: Travis Kelce to Score 3+ TDs" at +2500 — bet on it, with a small wager: when it comes to Kelce's greatest hits he prefers to save them for division rivals like the Raiders and Chargers, and he could be schmoozing in the suite when the second half begins rather than throwing blocks and catching footballs; but if the Jets keep it close they are prone to being exploited by players like Kelce, and with receivers lacking on the Chiefs sideline the tight end might put on a show typically only found in show business — having hosted "Saturday Night Live" back in March, Kelce is familiar with how to tell a story. Since the writers already have him scoring once, what's another two times to cash a monster long shot; don't count on it, but don't rule it out either, and bet responsibly.



---


# Josh Jacobs' And Breece Hall's 2023 Workloads

In the Nov. 12, 2023 Raiders-Jets game the two backfields diverged sharply: the Raiders largely turned to Josh Jacobs, who set season-best marks with 27 carries for 116 yards, while the Jets' duo of Breece Hall and Dalvin Cook was held to just 17 rushes for 54 yards.

Nine days later, in the Nov. 21 Week 12 running back rankings, both Jacobs and Hall were still trusted. Rounding out the top 10, the trio of Travis Etienne at the Texans, Josh Jacobs against the Chiefs and Breece Hall against the Dolphins were all looking to bounce back from disappointing Week 11 outings on the ground; Sporting News noted that all three backs had been mostly solid and that none had much to worry about in terms of backfield competition.



---


# Lions-Raiders Pregame: Carlson And St. Brown Active, Hoyer Inactive

The pregame log for the Oct. 30, 2023 Raiders-Lions "Monday Night Football" game reported two questionable players cleared to play and one backup quarterback ruled out. At 6:25 p.m. it noted, citing Adam Schefter and a league source, that Raiders kicker Daniel Carlson would play despite being listed as questionable with a groin injury — with the added question of whether the injury would change Josh McDaniels' decision-making. At 6:45 p.m. Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown was officially active after being listed as questionable with an illness. At 6:49 p.m. the blog reported Brian Hoyer inactive, leaving Aidan O'Connell as the Raiders' backup quarterback behind Jimmy Garoppolo.

Two matchup storylines followed. At 7:56 p.m. the blog observed that Josh Jacobs had not averaged more than 3.6 yards per carry in a single game that season and asked whether he could get going against a strong Lions run defense, noting it would be tough for Las Vegas to win without at least some production from the former first-rounder. At 8:07 p.m. it relayed the broadcast's point that the game was a homecoming for Michigan native Maxx Crosby, and that his play and that of fellow Michigan native Aidan Hutchinson would be pivotal.



---


# Jordan Love As A Week 5 2023 Start Against The Raiders

CBS Sports listed Jordan Love under "Start Him" for Week 5 of the 2023 season against Las Vegas: the claim is that Love has upside to get back to the 25-plus fantasy points he posted in Weeks 1-3, and the warrant is that the Raiders' track record against quarterbacks plus the return of Green Bay's injured personnel restore the conditions under which Love produced.

The grounds are personnel and opponent behaviour. Aaron Jones and Christian Watson return without snap limits, and guard Elgton Jenkins is back too. The Raiders deserve credit for trying — over the previous two weeks they led the NFL in pass-rush pressure rate and ranked 10th in blitz rate — but playing the weaker offensive lines of Pittsburgh and the Los Angeles Chargers helped boost those numbers, and quarterbacks still found success at 13.9 yards per catch and 7.07 yards after catch per reception over those two games, both bottom-three in the league. Both quarterbacks Las Vegas faced in Weeks 3 and 4 posted at least 22 fantasy points: Kenny Pickett, and Justin Herbert without his second-best receiver and without his top running back. The column's hunch is that the Raiders will keep blitzing and play a lot of gutsy man coverage behind it, having leaned man in two of their past three games and moved to heavy zone only against Denver in Week 1. Love has been a mixed bag against man — a terrible 39.4% completion rate but an outstanding 12.1% touchdown rate — and more man plus more blitzing could produce more rushing from Love, which he has shown he is willing to do.

The counterweight is his Week 4 loss to Detroit, which the column works through rather than ignores. The Lions' pass rush was too much for Love and the Packers line in the first half, Detroit played a lot of early zone and Love still threw into the teeth of it; he calmed down in the second half, took more of what the defense gave him and got into a groove before a bad read on a miscommunication with Romeo Doubs produced his second interception. # Most Valuable Player (MVP)

## Definition

In the corpus, MVP (Most Valuable Player) names the player judged most valuable to a team's or league's success, and the term surfaces at several distinct scopes: a formal season-long league award (NFL MVP, NBA MVP), a single-game honor (Super Bowl MVP), and an informal team-level or cross-sport label applied by media, players, and coaches.

## Context

At the league-season level, the NFL MVP and NBA MVP are formal annual awards contested among a small pool of star players. Sporting News's Dec. 5, 2023 awards-odds piece had Brock Purdy, Dak Prescott, and Jalen Hurts as the current NFL MVP favorites after Week 13, with C.J. Stroud and Jared Goff as the longshot cases. Separately, Yardbarker's Dec. 24, 2023 Christmas Day preview framed the Ravens-49ers game explicitly as "the decisive clash for the MVP Award," with Brock Purdy the heavy favorite (-230) and Lamar Jackson — the 2019 MVP — holding the second-shortest odds (+525). At the single-game level, MVP denotes a game-specific honor, as with Patrick Mahomes's two Super Bowl MVPs. At the team level, MVP is used informally by outlets like Yardbarker to name each team's most indispensable player at a season's midpoint — a designation that need not track the league-wide award and can go to a non-quarterback, as when Miami's Tyreek Hill or New England's Jabrill Peppers is named team MVP. The same informal usage crosses sports, as when an MLS goalkeeper calls forward Luciano Acosta "the MVP" of FC Cincinnati. MVP is also a standard sports-betting futures market: bettors wager on which player will win the season MVP award well before or during the season, alongside markets like Rookie of the Year and Offensive/Defensive Player of the Year.

## Background (external)

Beyond this corpus's sports-betting and news coverage, Wikipedia describes an MVP award more generally as an honor bestowed on the individual (or individuals, in case of a tie) "whose individual performance is the greatest in an entire league, for a particular competition, or on a specific team," recognizing one player's contribution within a team effort. (Source: Wikipedia, "Most valuable player," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Most_valuable_player, accessed 2026-09-02.)

## Key Characteristics

- **Multiple scopes** — the same "MVP" language covers a formal season-long league award (NFL, NBA), a single-game honor (Super Bowl MVP), and an informal team-level or sport-crossing designation used by media and players alike.

- **Betting futures market** — MVP odds are a standing futures category at sportsbooks (alongside moneylines, spreads, and other award markets), bet on well ahead of the outcome and repriced as the season's results accumulate.
- **Team-level MVP is unofficial** — team MVP picks (e.g., Yardbarker's AFC team-by-team roundup) are editorial judgments, not sanctioned awards, and can diverge sharply from who is in the league MVP conversation.

# Player Injury Report

## Definition

A player injury report is the periodic status listing an NFL team publishes during game week (and updates live on gameday) that tags each hurt or ailing player with a practice participation note and a game-status designation such as questionable, doubtful, or out, so broadcasters and fantasy managers know who is likely to play.

## Context

The corpus shows the report operating on two timescales: the pregame weekly cycle and the in-game live update. In the weekly cycle, CBS Sports' Week 13 injury roundup (doc_0289) and Sporting News' Week 10 fantasy injury updates (doc_0288) track players through the week's practice sessions — a player who is a full participant, limited participant, or a "DNP" (did not practice) on Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday accumulates a running designation that the team finalizes before kickoff. Ja'Marr Chase's Week 10 status is a clear case: he was listed as a DNP on Wednesday, logged back-to-back limited practices, and his final active call was left until a Sunday morning pre-game workout (doc_0288). During the game itself, CBS Sports' live-blog roundup shows teams issuing real-time in-game designations — "questionable to return," "doubtful to return," "ruled out" — when a player is hurt mid-contest, as with Cooper Kupp's ankle injury and Kenneth Walker III's oblique injury in the Week 11 roundup (doc_0113). The designations also interact with roster mechanics: a player can be activated off injured reserve to play (doc_0035) or, conversely, be placed on injured reserve, as De'Von Achane was during Week 6 (doc_0149).

## Key Characteristics

- **Tiered designations** — the standard tags observed in the corpus are full participant/limited/DNP during the week, collapsing into questionable, doubtful, or out for the final pregame report (doc_0289, doc_0288).
- **Live in-game updates** — beyond the pregame report, teams issue real-time calls like "questionable to return" or "ruled out for the remainder of the contest" when a player is injured during the game itself (doc_0113).
- **Roster-status linkage** — the report intersects with injured reserve moves: players can be activated off IR to play (doc_0035) or placed on IR after a lingering issue (doc_0149).
- **Coach commentary supplements the tag** — reporters attach head-coach quotes (e.g., Achane is "day-to-day"; it would be "a little aggressive" for Jefferson to play) to the bare designation to give fantasy audiences more color than the tag alone conveys (doc_0113, doc_0288).
- **Deadline-driven finality** — some designations resolve only hours before kickoff, e.g. Justin Jefferson needing activation by a Saturday 4 p.m. ET deadline to be eligible (doc_0288).

The counter-position to the Swift-Kelce media wave attacks its premise that the story is genuine and welcome, and it comes from within the fanbase and from commentators. Sporting News noted on 2023-09-28 that Travis Kelce had been catching a lot more than footballs lately and that fans everywhere had been swift to hop on the Taylor Swift bandwagon; the celebrity couple had been in the news for well over a week, and despite fatigue from many — Chris 'Mad Dog' Russo's rant being among the most vocal — companies like FanDuel just couldn't help but lean into a profitable storyline. The unresolved question the article poses is whether they are for real or whether this "Love Story" is just some extravagant publicity stunt.

Essentially Sports reported on 2023-10-25 that hardcore football fans were pretty much done with the NFL harping about Kelce and Swift. Reality TV star Rachel Lindsay, a longtime NFL fan, had recently slammed the "obnoxious" coverage, highlighting the "exhausting" uptick in Swifties obsessing over football — and that is offered as just one example of how fans were finding the fixation a little too disrespectful towards the sport.

# Brock Purdy's 49ers Career Trajectory

San Francisco 49ers franchise QB Brock Purdy is arguably the best quarterback in the 2022 NFL Draft class, despite being that draft's Mr. Irrelevant. He has had a dream start to his NFL career, remaining unbeaten and being one of the better young shot callers in the league; since breaking into the starting lineup he has made a mockery of his "Mr. Irrelevant" tag. The Iowa State University alum was the first Mr. Irrelevant to make a forward pass in a regular season game successfully, and it has been up from there.

Purdy finished his rookie season with five consecutive regular-season victories, completing a 10-game winning streak by San Francisco to close the season. He carried on his regular season form to the postseason, leading the 49ers to an NFC Championship Game against the Philadelphia Eagles; unfortunately, Purdy got hurt in the game, as the 49ers fell just short of a Super Bowl LVII appearance.

So far, Purdy has started the 2023 NFL season where he left off, opening the season with a 5-0 record. As of October 2023, the San Francisco 49ers were the only franchise unbeaten in 2023 alongside their NFC foes, the Philadelphia Eagles. No quarterback has done better than Brock Purdy in his draft class.

# 2023 NFL Defensive Player Of The Year: Danielle Hunter As The Longshot

Micah Parsons, Myles Garrett and T.J. Watt were the current favorites for 2023 NFL Defensive Player of the Year, with Danielle Hunter the longshot Sporting News argued at least deserved to be in the conversation, per its Dec. 5, 2023 awards-odds piece.

The grounds are Hunter's production and its effect on his team. Hunter led the league in tackles for a loss and was third in sacks with 13.5, behind Khalil Mack and Watt. Not only had he produced at a high level, but his play had been instrumental in the Vikings turning things around after a 1-4 start.

The warrant Sporting News offers is that name recognition, not performance, explains the gap in odds: Hunter may not have had the name recognition that Parsons, Garrett and Watt had, but he had played as well, if not better, that season. If he could continue to produce, he at least deserved to be in the conversation, if not to win.

# NFL Week 11 2023: Three Starting Quarterbacks Hurt, All Three Stayed Or Returned

In Week 11 of the 2023 NFL season, as reported by CBS Sports on 2023-11-19, three starting quarterbacks took injury scares and none of them ended the day sidelined for good. C.J. Stroud of the Texans left for a single play against the Cardinals after absorbing a hard hit, with backup Davis Mills entering in relief; Stroud did not receive an injury designation and returned after a quick check-in from trainers. Sam Howell of the Commanders received medical attention on the sidelines after enduring several hard hits to the upper body on a touchdown run against the Giants, was quickly cleared of a potential concussion and remained in the game, with veteran journeyman Jacoby Brissett listed as Washington's backup.

The most consequential case was Geno Smith of the Seahawks, who suffered an injury to his throwing arm after guiding a 16-7 lead over the Rams, showing frustration while trying to stretch the arm after a hit from Aaron Donald. Seattle quickly ruled him questionable to return with an elbow issue, and backup Drew Lock took over under center with 18 seconds left in the third quarter. Smith did return for the final drive of the game, in a losing effort. Head coach Pete Carroll said Smith will "make it back," and when asked whether that meant for Thursday's matchup against San Francisco, the coach said, "I would think so." The wider Week 11 context given by the same roundup: the week provided plenty of drama, from the Bears hanging with the Lions to the Giants getting a rebound from emergency quarterback Tommy DeVito, alongside another wave of unfortunate injuries.

# NFL Week 9 Player Prop Picks

Sporting News made three SuperDraft player prop picks for Week 9 of 2023: Rashee Rice OVER 45.5 receiving yards, Austin Ekeler OVER 29.5 receiving yards and Jahan Dotson OVER 45.5 receiving yards.

Rice (Chiefs vs. Dolphins in Germany) popped out as the first prop of the first game on Sunday morning, 9:30 a.m. in Frankfurt. The column loved the rookie receiver's big-play ability, consistently flashed over the previous month, during which he averaged over 55 receiving yards per game despite Kansas City's games being decided by an average of 11.8 points. It expected a tightly contested, high-scoring game with heavy playoff implications — potentially an AFC Championship preview — keeping Rice busy through all four frames, against a Dolphins defense that had allowed the fifth-most receptions and 12th-most yards to wideouts that season.

Ekeler (RB, Chargers @ Jets) was backed because the Chargers finally had their best player back to full health: he exploded for 123 yards and a touchdown against the Bears, a whopping 94 of them through the air as the PPR god gashed Chicago for chunk yardage several times. More of the same was expected from Justin Herbert and his back against a Jets defense allowing 46 receiving yards per game to running backs, sixth-most in the NFL.

Dotson (WR, Commanders @ Patriots) came full circle after making the preseason sleepers column, fading into early-season obscurity and re-emerging over the previous two weeks: with Curtis Samuel clearly not right the week before, the second-year wideout caught 8 of 10 targets for 108 yards and a touchdown, a stellar encore to his Week 7 line of five catches for 43 yards. The banged-up Patriots defense would focus primarily on stopping Terry McLaurin, which should open plenty of opportunities for Dotson.

# Daniel Garnero's Debut As Paraguay Head Coach

Daniel Garnero made his debut as Paraguay's new permanent head coach in the Oct. 12, 2023 qualifier against Argentina, having spent the last two years in charge of Paraguayan giants Libertad and taken over from Guillermo Barros Schelotto, who was let go after the September qualifiers just three days shy of his two-year hire anniversary.

The 54-year-old Garnero is an Argentine who made one appearance for the national team as a player and spent most of his career with Argentine club Independiente; he has managed at club level in Paraguay since 2015 with Sol de America, Guarani and Olimpia before Libertad. The Sporting News called it quite the test for his debut — taking on Lionel Messi and the defending World Cup champions, his home nation. Garnero set out his approach: "Vamos a jugar contra una selección que es la mejor del mundo. No solamente por logros, sino por idea colectiva y rendimientos individuales. Mi intención siempre es jugar con la pelota. Debemos ser inteligentes y agresivos en las recuperaciones" — his intention is always to play with the ball, and the team must be smart and aggressive in recoveries, which the blog called a bold claim.

Garnero rang the changes after Paraguay's defeat to Venezuela, making five alterations to that starting lineup. Ivan Ramirez came in at right-back for Robert Rojas for just his fourth international cap, the entire midfield three was swapped out with Mattias Espinoza, Alvaro Campuzano and Richard Sanchez entering, and Adam Bareiro took over at striker from Gabriel Avalos, earning his debut international cap. Forward Miguel Almiron is Paraguay's most prominent goalscoring threat and was in good form with three goals in his past five matches for Newcastle United. Paraguay had questions at goalkeeper, as mainstay Antony Silva had been phased out leaving three inexperienced internationals on the roster; New York Red Bulls starter Carlos Coronel, who earned his first two caps in the September matches, remained in net. Messi's Inter Miami teammate Diego Gomez was named to the Paraguay roster but was forced to withdraw due to injury.



---


# Paraguay's Outlook And Lineup Under New Coach Daniel Garnero

Paraguay went to Buenos Aires on Oct. 12, 2023 seeing themselves as real contenders for a 2026 World Cup place: they had not been close to qualifying for the last World Cup and had not reached a FIFA tournament since 2010, but with the 2026 field — and by extension qualifying across all federations — expanding this cycle, Los Guaranies would consider themselves genuine candidates, making points a premium in every match.

New head coach Daniel Garnero, making his debut, rang the changes after a defeat to Venezuela last time out, making five alterations to that starting lineup: the entire midfield was swapped out, and Adam Bareiro took over at striker, earning his debut international cap in place of Gabriel Avalos. The starting lineup (5-4-1) was C. Coronel (GK) — I. Ramirez, G. Gomez, Balbuena, Alonso, Espinoza — R. Sanchez, Campuzano, Almiron, Bareiro — Sosa.

Forward Miguel Almiron was Paraguay's most prominent goalscoring threat and was in good form with three goals in his past five matches for Newcastle United. The team had questions at goalkeeper: mainstay Antony Silva had been phased out, leaving three inexperienced internationals on the roster, and New York Red Bulls starter Carlos Coronel, who earned his first two caps in the September matches, remained in net. Lionel Messi's Inter Miami teammate Diego Gomez was named to the Paraguay roster but was forced to withdraw with injury.

# Gio Reyna's Return Under Berhalter, And His 45 Minutes Against Germany

Gio Reyna was called into the USMNT for the first time under Gregg Berhalter since their falling out at the 2022 World Cup, having recovered from a leg fracture suffered in summer Nations League duty under an interim head coach. The 20-year-old Borussia Dortmund playmaker's return was announced alongside that of defender Cameron Carter-Vickers, who had only just made his Celtic debut that season after a hamstring injury.

The working relationship had been a major talking point since the 2022 fallout: Reyna's lack of playing time at that World Cup was exacerbated by his parents' actions in the following weeks, which sparked a domestic violence investigation of Berhalter before his eventual re-hire as national team head coach. Berhalter had been forthcoming, admitting on his re-hire that the two had a "lot of work to do" while insisting time was needed to broach the situation, and later confirming they had broken the ice by phone. After the October roster release he confirmed they had spoken "weeks ago" on Zoom, said he appreciated Reyna's willingness to move forward, and — because Reyna had not yet played for his club that season — set the goal of getting him minutes so he could build fitness and return to Dortmund in the best position to begin his club campaign. Berhalter said they saw Reyna able to play three positions: central midfielder, attacking midfielder and winger, clarifying that his skill set fit a "between the lines" style of wide play rather than one glued to the touchline.

In the Oct. 14 friendly against Germany, Reyna looked sharp in the starting lineup in all the ways a young man can: unyielding energy, a surprising eagerness to cover the whole of the midfield, periodic flashes of skill, and bleach-blond hair that let viewers spot him instantly. He was exceptional throughout the first half — less influential than he might have been with greater access to the ball, but showing a welcome taste for covering ground to help on defense or retrieve the ball and launch an attack — while Weston McKennie was his typical self, particularly connecting with Christian Pulisic down the left. Playing 45 minutes was a victory of sorts after only 27 minutes in his one club appearance that season for Dortmund, having been injured in June with the U.S. and missed all of preseason and nearly two months of the Bundesliga. The one substantial element missing was being able to endure from starting to finishing. "The goal is to send him back to Dortmund in a really good spot," Berhalter said. "I think he played a good game, showed his quality. I think everyone in the first half played well. So it was good to see him, good to have him on the field." Many national team fans had sided with Reyna during the World Cup controversy; in this game they got what they argued for, but not what they wished.

# Germany's Decline And The Appointment Of Julian Nagelsmann

Germany entered their October 2023 friendly against the United States in a transitional phase, with Julian Nagelsmann having taken over as new head coach after Hansi Flick was unable to steer the team to safer waters in Qatar.

Germany are considered one of the preeminent national team programs in the world, but recent years have humbled Die Mannschaft. They had been eliminated in the group stage of two straight World Cup tournaments — an unthinkable slip in stature given they had never been bounced from any World Cup that early in history prior to 2018.

The Sporting News set that decline alongside the United States' own position: with the U.S. set to test themselves against one of Europe's most powerful sides, the opponents were entering a transitional phase as well.

# Manchester United's Injury List Before The Fulham Match

Manchester United were yet to recover from their large number of long-term injuries ahead of the November 2023 Fulham fixture, and had been fighting a battle to line up their best XI as players fell victim to one injury after another. Casemiro, who got injured during the international break, got back on the field against Newcastle United in the EFL Cup match, but was taken off at half-time with a new hamstring issue and would probably remain sidelined for weeks.

Other than Casemiro, Tyrell Malacia and Amad Diallo were suffering from knee issues, Lisandro Martinez was nursing a foot injury, Jadon Sancho was out due to disciplinary issues, and Luke Shaw was yet to recover from a muscle problem. Adding to that, Victor Lindelof was suffering from a bug that could see him miss the weekend's match.

On the other hand, Raphael Varane, who missed the previous match due to an illness of his own, could be back. Aaron Wan-Bissaka was also able to participate in the last match, coming on as a substitute, so he should be able to make a comeback. Marcus Rashford, Rasmus Hojlund and Bruno Fernandes could all see themselves in the starting lineup.

# The USMNT's October 2023 Friendlies Against Germany And Ghana

Gregg Berhalter and the U.S. men's national team scheduled friendlies against Germany and Ghana in October 2023 as they continued preparations for the 2024 Copa America and the 2026 FIFA World Cup. The U.S. first took on Germany in Hartford, Connecticut on October 14.

That match doubled as the debut for Germany's new head coach. The 15th-ranked Germans were under new management, so the USMNT served as the first match for Julian Nagelsmann, the 36-year-old who had been out of a job since departing Bayern Munich back in March. Most European countries were busy with Euro 2024 qualifying at that point, but Germany, as tournament hosts, qualified automatically, which opened their schedule for the friendly.

On October 17 the U.S. traveled to GEODIS Park in Nashville, Tennessee to face Ghana, two nations with a deep history of contentious matchups including three consecutive World Cup tournaments in 2006, 2010 and 2014.

# Messi's Four-Game Injury Absence And His 35-Minute Return

Lionel Messi missed four straight Inter Miami games with injury before returning off the bench for 35 minutes against FC Cincinnati on Oct. 7, 2023. He was left out entirely for the Oct. 4 trip to the Chicago Fire: 35 minutes before kickoff the lineups showed him not part of the squad, with Josef Martinez up front as Leonardo Campana was out with a knock. An hour before kickoff, Michelle Kaufman of the Miami Herald reported Messi "did not arrive with the team" to Soldier Field — a strong indication rather than outright confirmation that he would not play. Two hours out, Sporting News noted Gerardo Martino had played his cards extremely close to his chest each week about Messi's injury: asked about Jordi Alba's return, Martino said a timeline was in place, but asked about Messi's he refused to acknowledge whether one existed, saying "I understand your desire to know the exact timelines, but if I had the exact timelines I would share them. I just don't have them." Sporting News judged his involvement unlikely given recent matches but thought he could be more ready over the weekend against FC Cincinnati. Meanwhile Chicago was still feeling Messi fever, with Messi shirt vendors outside Soldier Field and the Fire media team joking that they had "the GOAT in the building."

Against FC Cincinnati he was available. Two hours before kickoff, well-connected Argentine journalist Gaston Edul had reported the night before that Inter Miami were likely to have Messi back in some capacity — "the idea is for Leo Messi to get minutes when Inter Miami plays FC Cincinnati" — which sounded like bench availability, alongside reporting that Messi was battling "fatigue" and a "scar tissue issue." Lineups 45 minutes out confirmed him on the bench, with a photo of his jersey hanging in his locker taken as a good indication he would return. Thirty minutes out, his availability was called a welcome sight for a club whose backs were against the wall and which had to win to stay alive. He entered in the 55th minute, replacing Tomas Aviles in a very attacking change with around 35 minutes to save Inter Miami's season, alongside Jean Mota for David Ruiz. By the time he stepped on the pitch, Inter Miami's early dominance had come and gone; Messi played a part but was unable to fully change the tide of the game.

Five days later, ahead of Argentina's World Cup qualifier, Sporting News noted Messi had been dealing with fitness concerns for weeks and had missed significant time for his club, but was on the national team roster and expected to play a part. According to a report from Argentina he would not start but was likely to play much or all of the second half. With Inter Miami's playoff run officially over, Argentina could feel better about deploying him for a full 90 minutes despite his recent fitness issues, knowing his club season was nearly over and months of rest lay ahead; he had missed the previous match against Bolivia and four Inter Miami games after that, then returned for a half-hour in the club's final fixture before the international break.

# Coaching Change

## Definition

A coaching change is the replacement of a team's head coach — by firing, mutual departure, or resignation — followed by the appointment of a successor, whether an outside hire, an internal promotion, or an interim/caretaker placeholder.

## Context

The corpus documents coaching changes across sports and settings: mid-season firings in the NHL and NFL, off-season managerial exits in club and international soccer/rugby, and speculative hot-seat coverage that treats a coach's job security itself as an ongoing storyline ahead of any actual move.

The Minnesota Wild "relieved head coach Dean Evason and assistant coach Bob Woods of their duties effective immediately," naming John Hynes as Evason's successor mid-season after a losing stretch left the team "far out of the playoff picture" (doc_0340).

Manchester United's Erik ten Hag was reported to be under mounting pressure, with Sporting News laying out replacement candidates — including permanent hires like Zinedine Zidane and Julen Lopetegui and a caretaker option in club legend Michael Carrick — "if Manchester United decide to pull the plug" on his tenure (doc_0315); the same piece notes United had already cycled through eight managers, including caretakers Ryan Giggs, Ralf Rangnick, and Carrick, since Alex Ferguson's 2013 retirement.

Carolina Panthers owner David Tepper's impatience with head coach Frank Reich was framed against his earlier in-season firing of Reich's predecessor, Matt Rhule, as precedent for how quickly an owner might act (doc_0474); Yardbarker's NFC "hot seat" roundup names head coaches such as New Orleans' Dennis Allen and Chicago's Matt Eberflus as under pressure for their job status ahead of any actual move (doc_0437).

In international coaching, the Springboks' World Cup-winning head coach Jacques Nienaber and director of rugby Rassie Erasmus departed together after South Africa's 2023 Rugby World Cup triumph, and All Blacks coach Ian Foster's tenure ended the same tournament with Scott Robertson set to take over (doc_0022); U.S. Soccer's appointment of Emma Hayes away from Chelsea to lead the USWNT followed a formal, multi-round search process after the prior head coach, Vlatko Andonovski, departed following a World Cup exit (doc_0108).

## Key Characteristics

- **Trigger is performance or results** — the Wild's move came after a 5-10-4 record and a seven-game winless streak (doc_0340); the Panthers' pressure on Reich stemmed from a 1-7 record and a struggling offense (doc_0474).
- **In-season vs. off-season timing** — some changes happen mid-season as an emergency reset (Wild firing Evason, doc_0340; the precedent of Carolina firing Rhule in-season, doc_0474), while others follow a season's end (Nienaber/Erasmus and Foster departing after the World Cup final, doc_0022; Hayes's move to the USWNT set for after her Chelsea season concludes, doc_0108).
- **Successor types vary** — a permanent outside hire (John Hynes for the Wild, doc_0340; Emma Hayes for the USWNT, doc_0108), a permanent internal promotion (Evason himself had been promoted to Wild head coach after the team fired Bruce Boudreau in-season, doc_0340), or a caretaker/interim stopgap (Michael Carrick's past spells in charge of Manchester United, doc_0315).
- **"Hot seat" speculation precedes the actual move** — media coverage frequently discusses a head coach's job security, and the club's history of prior changes, well before any change occurs, treating pressure itself as newsworthy (doc_0437, doc_0474).
- **The exiting coach's own track record and contract carry forward** — Evason's Wild contract obligations continued after his firing (doc_0340), and Reich's overall coaching record was reported inclusive of a prior in-season firing by the Colts (doc_0474).
