# Player Injury Report

## Definition

A player injury report is the periodic status listing an NFL team publishes during game week (and updates live on gameday) that tags each hurt or ailing player with a practice participation note and a game-status designation such as questionable, doubtful, or out, so broadcasters and fantasy managers know who is likely to play.

## Context

The corpus shows the report operating on two timescales: the pregame weekly cycle and the in-game live update. In the weekly cycle, CBS Sports' Week 13 injury roundup (doc_0289) and Sporting News' Week 10 fantasy injury updates (doc_0288) track players through the week's practice sessions — a player who is a full participant, limited participant, or a "DNP" (did not practice) on Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday accumulates a running designation that the team finalizes before kickoff. Ja'Marr Chase's Week 10 status is a clear case: he was listed as a DNP on Wednesday, logged back-to-back limited practices, and his final active call was left until a Sunday morning pre-game workout (doc_0288). During the game itself, CBS Sports' live-blog roundup shows teams issuing real-time in-game designations — "questionable to return," "doubtful to return," "ruled out" — when a player is hurt mid-contest, as with Cooper Kupp's ankle injury and Kenneth Walker III's oblique injury in the Week 11 roundup (doc_0113). The designations also interact with roster mechanics: a player can be activated off injured reserve to play (doc_0035) or, conversely, be placed on injured reserve, as De'Von Achane was during Week 6 (doc_0149).

## Key Characteristics

- **Tiered designations** — the standard tags observed in the corpus are full participant/limited/DNP during the week, collapsing into questionable, doubtful, or out for the final pregame report (doc_0289, doc_0288).
- **Live in-game updates** — beyond the pregame report, teams issue real-time calls like "questionable to return" or "ruled out for the remainder of the contest" when a player is injured during the game itself (doc_0113).
- **Roster-status linkage** — the report intersects with injured reserve moves: players can be activated off IR to play (doc_0035) or placed on IR after a lingering issue (doc_0149).
- **Coach commentary supplements the tag** — reporters attach head-coach quotes (e.g., Achane is "day-to-day"; it would be "a little aggressive" for Jefferson to play) to the bare designation to give fantasy audiences more color than the tag alone conveys (doc_0113, doc_0288).
- **Deadline-driven finality** — some designations resolve only hours before kickoff, e.g. Justin Jefferson needing activation by a Saturday 4 p.m. ET deadline to be eligible (doc_0288).

# Tyler Adams' Hamstring Injury Left The USMNT Without A Recognized No. 6

Captain Tyler Adams was the notable absence from the USMNT's October 2023 camp, sidelined with a frustrating long-term hamstring injury. He was initially injured playing for Leeds United back in March, and although he had finally recovered enough to make his Bournemouth debut in the EFL Cup in late September, he played just 20 minutes off the bench before suffering a setback that sidelined him again for the foreseeable future.

The absence mattered because Adams is the one proven defensive midfielder — a No. 6, in soccer jargon — on the USMNT roster. He had been absent from the national team since injuring his hamstring in the spring, and by the Oct. 14 friendly against Germany it was possible he would need a second surgery to address the issue.

Asked about him after that match, Berhalter told reporters: "Tyler's a great player. It's not nice to talk about guys that aren't here, though. I'd rather talk about the guys that are on the field."

# Open Questions on SST Patterns and Earth's Radiation Budget

The article argues that pressing, fundamental questions for climate dynamics concern how surface temperature patterns come about, how Earth's radiation budget depends on the details of those patterns, and the extent to which the two depend on each other.

Three tasks follow from that claim. First, understanding must improve of the drivers of sea surface temperature patterns — decadal coupled variability; the pace and spatial structure of ocean heat uptake; and forcing by aerosols, greenhouse gases, and volcanoes — as well as the relative timing of these drivers, with the goal of explaining historical patterns quantitatively and predicting their likely future evolution. Second, the dependence of local and remote top-of-the-atmosphere radiative fluxes on the magnitude, spatial scale, and sign (positive or negative) of surface temperature changes must be quantified. Third, it must be explained how ocean heat uptake and radiative feedback are connected on various timescales, both globally and regionally.



---


# Coupled Models Fail to Reproduce Observed Warming Patterns

Coupled climate models seem unable to simulate observed surface warming patterns across some key regions in which surface sensitivity modulates clouds: most importantly, models do not re-create observed cooling in the equatorial and subtropical eastern Pacific and Southern Ocean, and it is concerning that all models have the same sign of error in the trend patterns (Wills et al., 2022).

Coupled climate models simulate a freely evolving ocean surface and hence have their own expression of internal variability — one would not expect a coupled model to simulate El Niño events at the same time as they happened in nature, except by chance — which complicates comparisons between models and observations, especially on decadal timescales and beyond, for which little is known about the spectrum of internal variability in the real world. Even accounting for internal variability, the pattern failure persists, and models strongly disagree about the timescales over which future warming may occur in these regions. Limited knowledge of the drivers of surface warming pattern biases hampers the ability to evaluate them: it is not known whether the models' inability to reproduce observed trends is due to biases in how they represent the spectrum of internal variability, aerosol forcing, ocean-atmosphere interactions, deep and shallow atmospheric convection, Southern Ocean cloud-radiative properties, ocean thermocline depth, and ocean circulation, or something else entirely.



---


# Emerging Tools for Quantifying the Pattern Effect

Promising new tools and observations are beginning to emerge for quantifying the pattern effect: targeted model experiments and intercomparisons, extended global satellite observations of clouds and radiation, Argo floats sampling deep-ocean heat uptake, estimates of radiative imbalances before the year 2000, and new observational constraints on clouds' sensitivity to environmental controlling factors.

These developments encourage an optimistic outlook on the ability to quantify the pattern effect and its implications over the next couple of years. Working to solve these problems at the intersection of different disciplines and with input from different research communities will likely benefit related research into, for example, the sensitivity of tropical cyclones and future rainfall changes in the southwestern United States or in South America to surface warming patterns.



---


# Gen Z Mental Health And Climate Anxiety

Gen Z has the worst reported mental health of any generation: 45% of young people report having "excellent" or "very good" mental health, according to a 2018 report by the American Psychological Association. One of the major sources of that distress is climate change — nearly seven in 10 Gen Zers say they experience anxiety when viewing climate change content on social media, according to a 2021 Pew Research report.

They are not only reading about the effects of human-caused global warming but living through the consequences. The summer of 2023 reached record-breaking temperatures, with July the hottest month the planet has seen in over 100,000 years; Arizona experienced a monthlong heat wave with temperatures at or above 110 degrees every day; deadly fires broke out across the Mediterranean; suffocating smoke from Canadian wildfires blanketed New York City and the Northeast for days; and ice melt in the Arctic accelerated. Extreme heat is likely here to stay — and get worse — unless countries can rapidly reduce their carbon emissions, which is why Gen Z is more concerned with sustainability than any generation before them.

Greta Thunberg is the emblem the article offers: the 20-year-old has become one of the best-known environmental activists, famously speaking at the United Nations in 2019 with scathing words for world leaders. "You have stolen my dreams and my childhood with your empty words. And yet I'm one of the lucky ones," Thunberg said. "People are suffering. People are dying. Entire ecosystems are collapsing. We are in the beginning of a mass extinction, and all you can talk about is money and fairy tales of eternal economic growth. How dare you!"



---


# Gen Z News Distress Impairing Work Performance

Forty-six percent of young workers ages 18 to 26 say that they are regularly so distraught over what is happening in the news that they are unable to function at work, according to a 2023 Edelman report. The generational gradient is steep: by comparison, 38% of millennials, 24% of Gen Xers, and 19% of baby boomers and older generations say the same.

The article reads this as of a piece with the rest of the cohort's behavior — everything about their behavior communicates that Gen Z is just not okay with it, ranging from their widespread, hell-bent determination to find purpose in work and pushing their employers to have a social conscience, to a sense of despair over their own and the world's future finances. They have largely given up on saving money and instead dish out for little "treats" as a way to cope with the larger absurdity of 21st-century life.



---


# The US CLIVAR Pattern Effect Workshop, 2022

To foster work on the pattern effect across research communities, 140 scientists from around the world and from different disciplines gathered for a US CLIVAR (U.S. Climate Variability and Predictability Program) workshop in May 2022 in Boulder, Colorado.

The Eos article presents the current consensus that emerged during that workshop and raises questions that its authors say require urgent attention from scientists.



---


# "No Place Is Safe": Climate Impacts on Kalmus's Life

Kalmus concluded that "no place was safe" after a 2020 heat wave — considered nearly impossible if not for the influence of climate change — seared the Pacific Northwest for three days, killing hundreds of people, buckling roadways and sending overheated baby birds jumping from their nests to their deaths, in the very region where he had dreamed of making a life he thought might be buffered from the worst of climate change.

"It feels like it's worse than I thought it would be in 2023," Kalmus said, pointing to record-low Antarctic sea ice and record-high sea surface and land temperatures as signs that Earth systems could be shifting more quickly than the scientific community can grasp. In recent years climate change has begun to sting his personal life: in summer 2020 he sickened himself hiking in a California heat wave, then watched a wildfire burn a few miles from his California home, spewing smoke that left his voice raspy and his head aching, while the searing temperatures killed a dogwood tree in his front yard and his productivity slowed so that he could not focus on science. His family relocated to North Carolina for his wife Sharon's work, but the Pacific Northwest experience planted a seed: if he could not stop climate change and could not avoid it, could he at least find a better way to survive it? He knew what would not work — "I very quickly eliminated the idea of being a prepper — you know, hoarding beans and ammunition," he said — but he found himself daydreaming of a simpler life where he could keep bees, grow vegetables and press cider to drink on a Friday night, living closer to the land.



---


# Why Communicating Deep-Sea Science Matters

Jon Copley argues that communicating deep sea science matters because the deep sea is not somewhere people think about every day: we can go out at night and look at the sky and wonder what is going on up there, but you cannot glance into the deep sea in the same way, so it has become a realm of myth and darkness.

Even the names of the deepest parts — the abyssal plains and the hadal zone — evoke that kind of underworld, he says. The conclusion he draws is that it is nice to be able to shine a light on that for people and to highlight how our lives are connected to it.



---


# Paleorecords Must Account for the Pattern Effect

Just as the historical evolution of surface warming and the planet's radiation budget informs Earth's future only to a limited extent, analyses of paleorecords for recent and deep time intervals must account for the pattern effect to be applicable to climate projections of the future.

The supporting case is the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM): the cooling pattern during the LGM differed from the warming pattern observed currently, and from those expected for the next couple of decades and in the equilibrium following a doubling of carbon dioxide, not only in sign but also in the spatial distribution of magnitudes. Because the LGM currently provides the best constraint on the upper bound of equilibrium climate sensitivity (Sherwood et al., 2020), the details of the pattern effect matter greatly. Outstanding questions concern how representative pattern changes in the past century, the past millennium, or quasi-equilibrated times millions of years ago are of expected future changes; the paleorecord could further be crucial for understanding the timescales and relative importance of internal variability, forced response, and extratropical forcing to rates of warming or cooling in the equatorial Pacific in nature and in climate models.



---


# Gen Z Workplace Purpose And ESG Priorities

By 2030 Gen Z will account for nearly one-third of the U.S. workforce, but they are already radically redefining the meaning of work. Wanting a sense of purpose, they prioritize environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations in the workplace — which for them encompasses their companies taking accountability for their sustainability and environmental impacts, providing education and awareness for social issues, and ensuring diverse and inclusive boards and teams.

The behavioral evidence matches the stated priority: roughly two-thirds of Gen Zers say they frequently speak about important societal issues while at work, according to the Edelman report. They are also influencing their older coworkers when it comes to areas like work-life balance, fair pay, and employers' involvement on social issues.



---


# Evaluating Model Pattern Bias with Cloud-Resolving Models

The article argues that the advent of global coupled storm- and cloud-resolving models — which currently can simulate only a few months to years at a time — presents an exciting opportunity for evaluating model pattern bias, while acknowledging that their short runs make evaluation itself an open problem.

The most pressing question, on its account, is whether climate model simulations will be as far off from observations in the future as they have been relative to recent past conditions, and if so, how model biases in surface warming trends will be reflected in radiative feedbacks and global mean warming rates; it must also be quantified whether coupled models compensate for their bias in the surface warming pattern and radiative feedbacks through erroneous ocean heat uptake rates or aerosol forcings. For the new high-resolution models the difficulty is methodological: how to evaluate surface warming patterns and radiative feedbacks in these simulations and compare them meaningfully to observations and coarser-resolution models, knowing that even several decades are not enough to robustly detect a forced trend in some regions. And most pressing for the communities relying on coupled models' climate change projections is the question of the extent to which remaining carbon budgets with respect to global warming targets (Zhou et al., 2021), rates of near-term future warming, and detection and attribution efforts are contingent on the pattern effect.



---


# Equilibrium Climate Sensitivity and Its Uncertainty

Climate sensitivity quantifies how much Earth's surface warms in response to a doubling of carbon dioxide relative to preindustrial levels, and reducing the uncertainty in its estimates is one of the grand challenges in climate science.

The uncertainty is large because climate sensitivity aggregates myriad processes — from microscale aerosol-cloud interactions to planetary-scale atmospheric and ocean circulations — into one number, and clouds, which are notoriously difficult to measure and simulate, are the main driver of that uncertainty. Various lines of evidence are used to estimate climate sensitivity, including climate model simulations of varying complexity, observations over the past century, proxies that measure climate change in the distant past, and theory. The likely range of estimates was stubbornly constant at a distressingly imprecise 1.5-4.5 K for several decades, though the research community's efforts have recently chipped away at this range.



---


# Urban Heat Stress Disparity Across 481 US Cities

A new study published in One Earth showed that across 481 US cities, heat stress falls disproportionately on poor people and people of colour: "We found that the current disparity was quite consistent across cities: in more than 90% of the cities we considered, we found inequalities in heat exposure related to both income and race," said TC Chakraborty, an Earth scientist at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and the study's lead author.

The context is that when record temperatures and heat domes envelop wide areas of the United States each summer, people experience these extreme heat events differently. Those who live in historically marginalised neighbourhoods — where discriminatory land use and housing policies allowed segregation and racism to flourish — still face today a greater risk from high temperatures and from the health effects of heat stress. This kind of information can help city leaders use better measures of heat disparities and protect the populations at greatest risk of heat exposure.



---


# Youth Hopelessness As A Societal Sustainability Risk

Dayo Abinusawa, founder of London's Awa Business School and a former lecturer at Cambridge University's Judge Business School, warned that "a society where the young have little to no hope for the future is not a sustainable one." The grounds he offers are the material blockage facing young people: "How can young people build careers or wealth if they don't have jobs, and prices of goods and services continue to increase?"

The warrant joining the two is that a generation deprived of the means to build careers or wealth loses hope, and a hopeless young cohort undermines the society that produced it. The article leaves the consequence open: it remains to be seen what Gen Z will do when they come into decision-making positions in the workplace — perhaps they'll channel their rage and cynicism effectively, as some have already demonstrated.



---


# Protecting Populations Most Exposed to Extreme Heat

Public health measures and mitigation strategies are needed to protect the citizens at greatest risk from heat, especially as rising temperatures become more common — and studies of existing exposure disparities are the way to identify who those citizens are.

"Studies like this, which seek to understand more deeply the existing disparities in heat exposure, are important for identifying which communities are at greatest risk of suffering environmental changes related to climate change, such as extreme heat that keeps getting worse," said Neelima Tummala. Lara Whitely Binder, climate preparedness programme manager for King County, Washington, who was not involved in the research, located the cause: "Areas with fewer street trees, less access to green spaces — that is where you start to see the legacy of disinvestment and institutional racism that has come into play." Because the climate is changing and advancing, cities must from now on prepare for hotter summers and more frequent deadly heat waves by various means, both indoors and outdoors. "We not only need to better understand where it is hot, but also what the socioeconomic factors are for the inhabitants of those areas," Whitely Binder said. "We can begin to analyse what is in the heat islands and use that to start informing the policy decisions we are going to make."



---


# The Magnitude of the Observed Pattern Effect Is Disputed

Against confident use of the pattern effect, the article notes that the measurement and magnitude of the observed pattern effect are still debated and uncertain — the premise under attack being that the effect has a known, substantial size over the historical record.

The current best estimate is that the radiative feedback or damping under idealized, long-term carbon dioxide forcing is 0.5 ± 0.5 watt per square meter per kelvin weaker than the radiative feedback seen since the late 1800s (Andrews et al., 2022), and 0.5 watt per square meter per kelvin is similar in magnitude to the single radiative feedbacks that the pattern effect modifies. That wide range of uncertainty opens two contrasting possibilities. At one end, the pattern effect might have acted to retard global warming fairly strongly — in other words, mean global warming might have been much higher by now if the recent surface warming had come about in a different spatial pattern — which implies the pattern effect has the potential to influence future near-term warming rates strongly as the surface warming pattern evolves. At the other end, the pattern effect might have been negligible over the past century and might apply only over shorter timescales or in drastically different climate states. Difficulty in quantifying the effect stems from uncertainties in observed surface temperature trends, the magnitude of ocean heat uptake, and the short observational record of Earth's energy budget, while incomplete quantitative understanding of how clouds react to their environment and how these dependences are represented in the highly parameterized climate models further limits the ability to quantify the full range of the possible and recently realized pattern effect.



---


# Kalmus's Critique of Biden Climate Policy

Kalmus attacks the premise that President Joe Biden's record makes him a climate champion, arguing that the Inflation Reduction Act, Biden's signature climate bill, does too little to shut out the fossil fuel industry, and that rejoining the Paris accord is no achievement because "That Paris Agreement will take us to about 3 degrees Celsius of global heating. I don't think we'll have a civilization at 3 degrees Celsius."

His frustration extends beyond the administration: not his suburban neighbours in North Carolina, who continue to drive emissions-belching SUVs to big-box stores, and perhaps not even some in the science community, like those who kicked him out of the American Geophysical Union's annual fall meeting last year after he unfurled a banner and protested on the major science conference's biggest stage. The article supplies two checks on his claim. Rhodium Group, a nonpartisan think tank, estimates greenhouse gas emissions will drop 32%-42% below 2005 levels by 2030, well short of Biden's own benchmark for progress, with the inflation bill responsible for about a quarter of that projected decrease. And a 2022 United Nations report estimated global temperatures would rise between 2.1 and 2.9 degrees Celsius by 2100 if countries held to their climate commitments, while many countries remain off that pace.



---


# Jon Copley, Ocean Explorer

Jon Copley is a professor of ocean exploration and science communication at the University of Southampton in the U.K. who has completed dozens of dives to the darkest corners of the deep sea, and who dedicates much of his time to addressing the myriad questions and myths surrounding it.

Over the past 25 years Copley has travelled to the world's deepest hydrothermal vents, to Antarctica's icy "midnight zone" and to spectacular undersea mountain chains across the planet, and he says he is still amazed every time he encounters the strange life forms that thrive there. His new book, "Deep Sea: 10 Things You Should Know" (Orion Publishing, 2023), takes a fascinating look at some of the harshest habitats on Earth.



---


# Gen Z: Definition And Formative Events

Gen Z, as characterized in this account, is the cohort aged 11 to 26 as of October 2023 and the first fully digital native generation — the feature that discriminates it from every earlier cohort is not the scale of the history it has lived through but that it has been plugged into the world through the internet from such a young age. Social media posts are its lingua franca, and the "disturbing images" warning is one it is used to encountering there.

The formative events listed are dense. This generation has already lived through a once-per-century pandemic; the Jan. 6 insurrection, an event unseen for centuries in American politics, when armed right-wing extremists stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 following the election defeat of former President Donald Trump; the first major European ground war since World War II, in Ukraine; and market crashes in 2008 and 2020 that recall the Great Depression. Three years before the article, as Gen Z emerged into young adulthood, online videos of the murder of George Floyd shook the country in May 2020, resulting in a summer of violent Black Lives Matter protests and riots. School shootings have only increased in frequency since Columbine in 1999, with more students documenting the terror on their phones and sharing it online — one of them, the Parkland shooting of 2018, tragically created the first spokespeople of the post-millennial generation. Most recently, on Saturday, 2023-10-07, the Islamic militant group Hamas launched an unprecedented attack on Israel, resulting in the worst war the region has seen in 50 years; in three days more than 1,500 people died on both sides, and graphic, difficult-to-watch videos blanketed the internet.

The boundary case the account itself raises is that every generation has lived through era-defining historical events: millennials remember the 9/11 terrorist attacks and the U.S. invasion of Iraq, and baby boomers lived through the civil rights movement and the Vietnam War. What sets Gen Z apart is the medium — experiencing it all through videos, images, and articles online, which is shaping their mental health, workplace attitudes, and financial habits in visible ways.



---


# Historical Warming Does Not Bound Climate Sensitivity

The foremost implication of the pattern effect is that historically observed climate change does not constrain the upper limit of climate sensitivity (Sherwood et al., 2020; Forster et al., 2021).

The grounds for that claim are physical: the observed surface warming pattern caused feedbacks that were more stabilizing than the ones projected for the future. Warming was particularly pronounced in the sweet spots of the western Pacific and the subtropical eastern Pacific — a perfect combination for enhanced radiative damping — and in particular, low-lying cumulus clouds in the eastern Pacific covered a larger area and reflected more sunlight back to space than studies suggest they will in the future. The warrant joining the two is that a record produced under unusually stabilizing feedbacks cannot bound sensitivity under the different feedbacks expected later. More broadly, research on the pattern effect has exposed limitations of using equilibrium climate sensitivity to constrain future warming and, conversely, of using recently observed warming to constrain equilibrium climate sensitivity.



---


# The Model Versus Observation Climate Sensitivity Discrepancy

Early in the 2010s, a substantial discrepancy was noted between estimates of climate sensitivity derived from climate models and estimates based on the observed warming record and radiative balance, with the observation-based estimates pointing to much lower values than the model-derived ones.

Radiative balance here means the balance between incoming and reflected solar radiation and outgoing terrestrial radiation. A key breakthrough toward solving this conundrum has been the recognition of the pattern effect, the process whereby climate sensitivity depends on the geographic pattern of surface warming. This advance was rated as one of the most promising avenues for further constraining climate sensitivity in the future by Forster et al. (2021).



---


# Solar Cycle Maximum Forecast Revision

The major news about the sun in 2023 was that the solar maximum is arriving faster and will be more explosive than initially forecast: the peak would likely arrive by 2024 and be more active than the original prediction, and in October space weather scientists released an updated forecast for the current solar cycle that is more in line with what experts told Live Science.

When the current solar cycle began in 2019, forecasts from space weather scientists suggested that the solar maximum would arrive sometime from 2025 onward and be relatively weak compared with past solar cycles. Numerous warning signs early in the year — rising sunspot numbers, powerful X-class solar flares and changes in Earth's upper atmosphere — hinted that the solar cycle was not progressing as expected, and in June Live Science published an exclusive, in-depth feature on the upcoming solar maximum that laid out the revised picture. During the solar maximum the sun is much more chaotic than during the solar minimum. When the maximum does arrive, Earth can expect to be bombarded with more solar storms, resulting in frequent auroral displays, radio blackouts, potential satellite problems and disruptions to the migration patterns of some animals.



---


# Millennials As The New Boomer Homebuying Cohort

One of the key reasons for the resilience of the housing market in both the early 1980s and today is demographics: "Noticeably, demographics were favorable back then, with baby boomers having entered the prime homebuying age," Jeseo Park and her Bank of America team wrote, arguing that millennials are in a similar position today. The structure of the argument is that a large generation reaching prime homebuying age supplies a floor of demand that offsets rate-driven weakness — millennials are a giant generation all collectively coming of homebuying age nearly simultaneously, just like their boomer parents in the 1980s, and as Redfin puts it they are the biggest share of the "homebuying pie," purchasing about 60% of homes bought with mortgages during the past few years.

The relation Bank of America draws from this holds over a specific range. "Some sales activity should be supported by millennials reaching the prime homebuying age, and single-family building permits have steadily held up. This can help the housing market retain some of its momentum without falling apart," Park's team wrote. They believe low inventory of existing homes for sale combined with solid home sales to millennials could help put a "floor beneath home prices" — but that does not mean there won't be some near-term pain due to higher mortgage rates.



---


# Three Research Strands Behind the Pattern Effect

Three historically separate strands of research have highlighted the dependence of radiative feedbacks on the surface warming pattern, and they have converged over the past few years.

The first strand came from analyses of climate feedbacks and sensitivity in model simulations of unequilibrated, transient climate change: if feedbacks were constant, the expected equilibrium temperature change could be estimated using a very simple energy balance model that linearly extrapolates the relationship between global temperature change and radiative imbalance (Gregory et al., 2004), but when longer, fully equilibrated simulations became available it became evident that such methods systematically underestimate the actual equilibrium climate sensitivity — the reason being the evolution of the surface warming pattern, which initially emphasizes more stabilizing radiative feedbacks but later, during equilibration, emphasizes less stabilizing ones (Senior and Mitchell, 2000; Rugenstein et al., 2020). The second strand related the idea of constant feedbacks to efforts to estimate equilibrium climate sensitivity from the historical record: feedbacks calculated from observations, or from atmosphere-only model simulations forced with the observed surface warming pattern over the past couple of decades, imply less warming than those from model simulations with a fully interactive ocean, which have the freedom to create their own surface warming patterns (Gregory et al., 2020). The third strand came from oceanography, showing that the atmospheric cooling effect of ocean heat uptake differs depending on where it occurs — one unit of ocean heat uptake in high latitudes cools Earth more effectively than the same unit taken up by the low-latitude oceans, a difference that matters because the largest heat uptake by the ocean occurs at higher latitudes; this effect, termed ocean heat uptake efficacy, turns out to be another manifestation of the dependence of radiative feedbacks on surface temperature patterns (Winton et al., 2010; Lin et al., 2021). Their convergence highlights that understanding the pattern effect benefits from — and perhaps requires — contributions from virtually all climate research communities studying large-scale ocean-atmosphere coupling and the dynamics that set regional to global responses to external forcing.



---


# Heat Stress Correlation with Census Income and Race

Correlating the mapped heat indices with census data revealed that low-income neighbourhoods and residents of colour experienced higher temperatures and greater humidity, which together amplify heat stress, while census tracts with higher incomes suffered less heat stress.

Heat stress was also generally higher in areas with a greater percentage of Black and African American residents. A figure credited to TC Chakraborty of PNNL shows Baltimore census areas coloured by heat index and by the percentage of Black residents, and the comparison indicates that where a greater proportion of residents are Black, heat stress is higher.



---


# Global Water Scarcity Under Climate Change

More than one in every four people across the planet live in places without enough clean water, and climate change is making this worse: Earth's freshwater supply is falling, and by 2050 more than five billion people are expected to lack water at least one month per year.

Some shortages are due to warmer temperatures and less snow to feed into rivers, which puts stress on supplies of water for drinking and for growing crops. Whatever the cause, better water-slurping gels could make it easier to grow food in such water-stressed places, including those plagued by drought — and scientists have now created a new salty gel that sucks record-breaking amounts of moisture out of the air to make fresh drinking water, even in dry climates.



---


# Redlining Legacy and Present-Day Heat Disparity

The researchers compared their findings with historical data from 177 cities and found that today's heat disparity tracks 1930s lending discrimination: neighbourhoods generally graded "D" by lenders had a higher heat index than those graded "A."

The chain begins in the 1930s, when the US government rated neighbourhoods according to their investment worthiness. Many of the neighbourhoods housing poor and minority populations, especially Black and African American residents, were considered riskier investments and therefore received less funding for development and housing programmes. Today those marginalised neighbourhoods suffer far worse environmental conditions than other parts of their respective cities: they have less tree cover and experience higher surface temperatures than neighbourhoods that were not originally redlined. A 1938 Home Owners' Loan Corporation map of Brooklyn, New York shows neighbourhoods colour-coded by loan value, with areas in red marking places where banks and other lenders generally considered residents unworthy of inclusion in lending and home ownership programmes; those redlined districts had a disproportionate number of Black residents. "The disparities were pervasive," Chakraborty said, adding: "This result was very interesting — that this level of inequality and segregation correlated so strongly with the levels of heat disparity."



---


# The Myth That We Know Less About the Deep Sea Than Mars

The biggest, most pervasive myth about the deep sea, Jon Copley says, is the idea that we know almost nothing about it — the very popular claim that we know more about the moon or Mars than the deep ocean.

His rebuttal concedes exactly one premise and denies the rest: that claim is only really true for one very specific aspect of knowledge, having a detailed map of the terrain of a solid surface, because the moon and Mars are not covered in seawater, which blocks radar and means sonar must be used in the deep ocean. Apart from that, he says, we know far more about the deep ocean than about those other places. The deep sea has nonetheless become, in his phrase, a "realm of myth and darkness."



---


# Heat Index and Humidex Mapping Method

Rather than using satellite data to estimate land surface temperatures as previous urban heat studies had done, Chakraborty and colleagues assessed heat stress using the U.S. National Weather Service heat index and the Canadian meteorological service's humidity index (humidex), combining air temperature and humidity to better describe how the heat feels.

Using models that combine these variables was a more accurate way to catalogue the heat stress of US cities over the period 2014 to 2018.



---


# American Public Climate Worry Polling

A 2022 poll found that almost two-thirds of Americans say they have been affected by extreme weather they believe was at least partially due to climate change, and about 27% of Americans say they are "very worried" about climate change while another 27% just avoid the subject as best they can.

One in 10 Americans reported feeling symptoms of anxiety or depression over climate change. The article introduces these figures to make the point that climate change is weighing not only on scientists but also on everyday Americans.

Brown, DeVonta Smith and Dallas Goedert are still on the team — which inclines the writer to trust the production will return. The open question is whether Philly has a counterpunch if defenses have solved the scheme.

An executive framed the same trend in terms of how the Eagles now win: "People are going to crush Hurts and the offense. They are just churning the clock so much. It just feels like they are imposing their will on teams through the run game and through their short passing and it just hasn't taken off from an explosive passing standpoint, so when they play a team that can move the ball on them through the air, it presents some challenges."



---


# NFL Aggressiveness Versus Traditional Game Management

A longtime NFL executive challenged the analytics-driven push toward aggressive play-calling on 16 October 2023, asking whether coaches have "come too far with coaches wanting to 'win' the game instead of sometimes being more traditional" after the Eagles threw a killer interception on third-and-9 from their own 46-yard line while protecting a 14-12 lead against the Jets with two minutes left in the fourth quarter.

The premise attacked is not that aggression is generally wrong. Most would agree teams have gotten smarter in their handling of fourth-down situations, going for it when it makes sense instead of punting almost out of habit; making the aggressive play to win can absolutely be the smart play regardless of results, and it is progress when teams seriously wrestle with these questions, not just on fourth down but in all aspects of strategy. What the exec disputes is the automatic application of that reasoning to a particular game state: Philadelphia could have run the ball on third-and-9, then punted from around midfield, leaving the Jets with barely more than a minute remaining, no timeouts and Zach Wilson behind center facing a ferocious Eagles pass rush. "Are coaches not willing to go against the slight statistical benefit that WPA (win probability added) provides?" he asked. "Is it no longer OK to let your defense win the game when it clearly has a huge talent/performance advantage? This Eagles game was 14-12, not 37-35."

The inference the counter-argument targets is the neglect of situation-specific factors. In that game the Jets' offense had netted 19 yards on its previous three possessions, producing one field goal on a drive that gained 16 of those yards; the Eagles had already suffered three turnovers, and they knew Wilson would be taking over deep in his territory with very little time remaining. "To me, these are exactly the type of factors that a coach needs to consider when deciding," the exec said. "I think they were ignored here." A veteran coach added an incentive-based explanation — critics attuned to the trend toward aggressiveness pounce when teams pass up chances to go for the kill, coaches know team owners tend to be fans rather than football strategists and listen to those criticisms, which creates an incentive to go down swinging: "Everybody thinks they are playing Brady, Manning or Rodgers in two-minute. If before the game someone offered Philly to put its defense against Zach Wilson on a need-field-goal drive starting inside his own 15 with no timeouts and a minute left, you think they would have taken it?" The base rate is thin: the situation Philly faced was the seventh time since 2000 that a team leading by 1-2 points in the final two minutes faced third down with 7-10 yards to go from the minus-40 yard line to midfield with the opponent holding no timeouts; three of the seven passed, resulting in one first down, one sack and Hurts' interception, and of those three only the Eagles lost the game.



---


# The First Quarter Of Bengals 24, Bills 18

Cincinnati led Buffalo 14-7 after a high-scoring opening quarter on Nov. 5, 2023, having won the toss and taken the ball first. Trayveon Williams returned the opening kickoff to the 24; Burrow started with a checkdown to Joe Mixon for eight and another short pass Mixon took 15 yards to the Bengals' 47. Williams took the first two carries by a Bengal for seven and one, and Tanner Hudson — notable because much had been made of the tight end position after Irv Smith Jr.'s red-zone fumble the week before — caught a six-yard pass for a first down. Burrow dodged a sack, rolled left and flipped 18 yards to Tee Higgins at the Bills' 21, Mixon ran three up the middle and Burrow found Smith for 11 to the 7 and first-and-goal; at 8:30 p.m. Smith made a leaping grab over Jordan Poyer for a seven-yard touchdown, his first of the year, for 7-0.

Buffalo answered immediately. Ty Johnson returned the kickoff to the Bills' 15, Allen found Dalton Kincaid for five out of an RPO, then hit Stefon Diggs for nine on third-and-5 and again for a 34-yard strike, Diggs carving down the left sideline to the Bengals' 37. Allen scrambled and flipped a pass to Khalil Shakir that went 22 yards to the Bengals' 15, then connected with Kincaid for 13 to the Cincinnati 2, and at 8:39 p.m. rushed in for a two-yard touchdown — drawing a taunting flag as he ran through the right side — to tie it 7-7 with 6:03 left in the quarter.

Cincinnati retook the lead on a long drive. Williams returned to the Cincinnati 31; Burrow's throw to Ja'Marr Chase was broken up but he was roughed on the play for 15 yards; Andrei Iosivas, involved after back-to-back weeks with a touchdown, caught nine on a rollout and Mixon ran three for the first down at the Bills' 42. Facing their longest third down of the day at third-and-10 after a Mixon no-gain and a missed connection with Smith, the Bengals stayed perfect on third downs as Tyler Boyd caught 15 in front of the sideline to the Bills' 27, and Hudson's second catch went 13 to the 14. Burrow escaped the pocket and got the ball to Higgins, who dove for the pylon but was ruled out at the 2; Cincinnati then twice tried Chase, who was tackled at the 2 on a screen and could not hold a leaping grab in the end zone. At 8:52 p.m. Mixon bulldozed up the middle for a two-yard touchdown and a 14-7 lead. Buffalo took the ball at the 25 after a fair catch at the 2 with 35 seconds left, and James Cook's first rush of the game gained two to end the quarter.



---


# Why Sporting News Picked The Bills In Week 16

Sporting News' Dec. 21, 2023 preview picked the Bills, arguing that Buffalo would keep rolling because the Chargers' new coach could not right all his team's wrongs overnight.

The grounds are the state of each team: for Los Angeles, losing by less than 38 points would be a great place to start, an ironic benchmark set by the previous week's rout. For Buffalo, the expectation was that they would try to replicate their massive success running the ball the previous week against Dallas, and that the Los Angeles defense would begin sagging heavily in the second half. The warrant joining grounds to pick is the judgment that the Bills' ground-game formula travels: they can beat the Chargers through the air but would probably run a copy of their Week 15 game plan against L.A. and every team that came their way afterwards. The stated pick is the Bills.



---


# Lamar Jackson Ravens Midseason MVP

Yardbarker's Nov. 9, 2023 AFC midseason team MVP list named quarterback Lamar Jackson the Baltimore Ravens' MVP, concluding that he was the reason, once again, that Baltimore was a Super Bowl contender.

The grounds are his production and its timing: Jackson had inserted himself into the league MVP conversation during his team's four-game win streak, and the 2019 NFL MVP had thrown for 1,954 yards and nine touchdowns while posting 440 yards and five touchdowns rushing. The warrant is that dual-threat production concentrated in a winning run is what converts individual numbers into team contention.



---


# James Cook's Surge In Buffalo's Rushing Workload

Before Week 15 of the 2023 season James Cook had never rushed more than 17 times in a game; he then carried 25 times against Dallas for 179 yards and earned AFC Offensive Player of the Week, making Bills fans hopeful the offense would keep giving him more than 20 rushes a game.

The preview argued that with the Bills we often see several versions and levels of a team through the year, and with Buffalo it largely boils down to their ground game: Ty Johnson and Latavius Murray are serviceable running backs but lack the game-breaking speed and big-play ability Cook offers. Cook's 179-yard outburst coupled with backup Ty Johnson's shoulder injury in Week 15 were both expected to contribute to Cook garnering 20-plus touches in Week 16.



---


# Bengals 24, Bills 18 On Sunday Night Football

Cincinnati beat Buffalo 24-18 on Sunday Night Football on Nov. 5, 2023, by quarters of Bills 7-0-3-8 and Bengals 14-7-0-3, winning a fourth straight game after jumping to a 21-7 first-half lead and letting the defense limit the Bills to 11 points the rest of the way. Sporting News framed it as proof the Bengals were back: Cincinnati had started 1-3, including a pair of blowout losses in which it scored just three points against the Browns and Titans, and it had seemed Joe Burrow's calf injury would hold back the team in what appeared to be one of its best chances to finally win an elusive Super Bowl — but since the loss to Tennessee it had been the Bengals of old.

Fans expected an offensive showdown between two premier quarterbacks, and the first three drives suggested one. The Bengals scored an opening-drive touchdown in just nine plays, matched quickly by a Bills scoring drive of seven plays and 3:15, and Cincinnati re-took the lead on a 5:28 drive to close the first quarter. From there, "Mad Scientist" Lou Anarumo's defense kept Josh Allen and the Bills off balance for most of the rest of the game: their next four drives went punt, interception, punt, end of half. Burrow and the Bengals hit a few bumps in Buffalo territory but scored on their final drive of the half for a two-score halftime lead.

Buffalo picked up a field goal on the first drive of the second half and held Cincinnati to three points after the break, but it was not until 3:32 remained that Allen got the Bills back into the end zone, with a 17-yard strike to Stefon Diggs and a two-point conversion to make it a six-point game. Cincinnati then trusted No. 9 to put it away, starting the drive with a 32-yard deep shot to Tyler Boyd into Buffalo territory before Joe Mixon ran three times to pick up the final first down and let Burrow kneel it out.

In the highly anticipated rematch, Burrow again came out better than Allen in both the win column and the stat sheet: Burrow completed 31 of 44 passes for 348 yards with two touchdowns, while Allen went 26 for 38 for 258 yards with one passing touchdown and an interception, adding eight rushes for 44 yards and another score. With the win the Bengals moved into the final wild-card spot behind the Steelers and Browns, while the Bills were bumped to the outside of the AFC playoff race.



---


# Jacksonville Jaguars' Contender Readiness, 2023

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that the Jaguars, more than the other AFC contenders, seem early in their life cycle and still finding their way — which makes them a little harder to trust in big spots but also leaves greater space for growth.

The immediate scope condition is Trevor Lawrence's knee injury, the big concern coming out of that Sunday: if he is out, expectations shift dramatically, and the writer hopes the test results come back clear.

An executive gave the positive case, resting on coaching pedigree and experience rather than current form: "I like Jacksonville. Doug (Pederson) has a championship pedigree. This team is relatively young. They are scrappy. The fact that they have been there before gives them a chance. I think the quarterback is growing."



---


# Week 14 Standard-League Running Backs To Downgrade

Sporting News pushed back on several running backs whose Week 14 standard-league appeal looked better than the matchups warranted, publishing on Dec. 7, 2023.

The premise it attacks in each case is that a back's usual role guarantees production regardless of opponent. Sporting News was a tad worried about Buffalo second-year back James Cook (@ Chiefs), because Kansas City's front seven tends to be stout against speedsters but below-average against power backs; managers probably were not in a position to bench Cook, but should not expect massive numbers from a player who averaged just 2.7 yards per carry against the Eagles his last time out.

Zach Charbonnet (@ 49ers) faced a tough matchup and had a bruise on his knee, so Sporting News did not expect very fruitful results from the rookie if he started in Santa Clara. It also did not love Jerome Ford or Kareem Hunt (vs. Jaguars), since Jacksonville entered Week 12 allowing just 12.3 standard fantasy points per game to running backs, the third lowest in the NFL. And the standing verdict on Carolina held: do not start Chuba Hubbard or Miles Sanders (@ Saints) — it was even worse than usual that week, as New Orleans had a pretty hard-hitting front seven and the Bayou is no place for below-average offenses.



---


# T.J. Watt Steelers Midseason MVP

Yardbarker's Nov. 9, 2023 AFC midseason team MVP list named linebacker T.J. Watt the Pittsburgh Steelers' MVP, on the argument that he was the player who seemed to make the most of the plays Pittsburgh needed.

The grounds start with the team's oddity: the Steelers were the first team in NFL history to be outgained by their opponents in each of their first eight games and still have a winning record, at 5-3. It had not been pretty to watch, but Pittsburgh always made plays when needed. Watt's own line supports the attribution: the 2021 NFL Defensive Player of the Year was tied for the second-most sacks in the league with 9.5, and also had two forced fumbles, three fumble recoveries and one interception. The entry was written by Aaron Becker.



---


# Buffalo's AFC Wild Card Position Going Into Week 16

Going into Week 16 of the 2023 season, Buffalo was in the thick of the AFC wild card hunt at 8-6, trailing three other 8-6 teams — the Bengals, Colts and Texans — by tiebreakers.

The Bills were also riding high on the heels of their dominant 31-10 Week 15 home win over the Cowboys, led by running back James Cook's 25-carry, 179-yard, one-touchdown rushing bonanza. While Buffalo had had its ups and downs that year, the assessment was that if they made the postseason with their rushing game producing like this, they would be an extremely tough out.



---


# Jordan Poyer's Search For Purpose And Improbable Career

Despite a stellar career and a loving family, Jordan Poyer "felt like there was something missing" as recently as the previous year, The New York Times reported on 15 December 2023 — sobriety had not made him immune to anxiety and depression.

In the 2022 season he missed five games with elbow, foot, knee and rib injuries, and when the Bills lost to the Bengals in the divisional playoff round he felt responsible for not doing more. His angst ran deeper than football. "I still felt like there was something missing because I have this beautiful house, a beautiful family, everything anyone could ask for," he says. "I still felt a sense of unhappiness, a sense of not understanding who I was, and why I was the way I was. A part of me felt guilty just because I was living this way." He could not come to terms with why, despite all his shortcomings, he was in such an enviable position, and the questions that followed were what he had done to deserve it, whether he was justifying his good fortune, and whether there would be a greater purpose.

His football journey was improbable. No major college wanted him until Oregon State came in with a late offer to grayshirt, meaning his scholarship would not begin until January of his freshman year. He was chosen in the seventh round of the 2013 NFL draft, came into the league as a cornerback, was cut six games into his rookie season and then had to learn a new position with a new team. He took a blind-side hit that put him in hospital for two days with a lacerated kidney and a concussion, and his career could have been over then. Yet by now he has outlasted 191 of the 217 players drafted ahead of him, and he has not just survived in the NFL — he has thrived. In 2018 he saw a therapist for anxiety once a week; it was unfulfilling, and the answers were somewhere else.



---


# Ravens At 49ers, Christmas Day 2023: A Possible Super Bowl Preview

Baltimore Ravens (11-3) at San Francisco 49ers (11-3), at 8:15 p.m. ET, was easily the most hyped game of the week, Yardbarker previewed on 2023-12-24 — the top seed in each respective conference squaring off in what could be a Super Bowl LVIII preview as well as the decisive clash for the MVP Award. On the 49ers side, running back Christian McCaffrey: if Brock Purdy weren't playing at such a high level, and if the MVP weren't a quarterback-driven award, it would be difficult to argue against McCaffrey taking home the honors; he seemed poised to win Offensive Player of the Year, leading the NFL in rushing with 1,292 yards and in total yards per game at 128.6, and tied for first in touchdowns with 20. On the Baltimore side, tight end Isaiah Likely thriving in the starting role: the Ravens offense hadn't lost a step since losing Mark Andrews (ankle) in Week 11, largely due to Likely's emergence — the second-year tight end had averaged 64.3 yards over his last three games, particularly noteworthy since Andrews averaged 54.4 yards per game before his injury.

Should a defensive battle be expected? While both teams boast offenses ranking in the top five in yardage and scoring, this may not turn into a shootout: the Ravens defense had allowed the fewest points per game that season at 16.1 and the second-fewest total yards at 4,030, while San Francisco's unit ranked second in points at 16.7 and 10th in yardage at 310 per game. The 49ers defense might be slightly inferior statistically, but it could have more impact in this matchup — San Francisco had racked up an NFL-leading 25 turnovers and given up the second-fewest rushing yards at 1,252, which should help slow down the team with the league's most effective running game.



---


# Winning Too Soon And Coaching Regime Expectations

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that a bad team winning right away can be counterproductive, because early success resets expectations for fans and ownership and makes it less practical to take one step backward in the short term for a better shot at taking two steps forward down the line.

The test cases are the New York Giants and Minnesota Vikings, both of which exceeded expectations under first-year head coaches in 2022 and reached the playoffs, and both of which were struggling in their second seasons and facing difficult questions about the future. The grounds are that every head coach and general manager wants to win as much as possible, but the goal is to build for the long term, which can require time to do things with sustainability in mind — so whether early success helps or hurts could depend on how well the football leadership has communicated with ownership.

A veteran coach with experience on a half-dozen teams supplied the warrant from inside the building: "The best first year can be that 7-10 season where you show some promise. The Giants won a bunch of games early, people were heaping praise on the head coach, people get the expectation of what the quarterback can be. But oftentimes, you know different internally because you know the house you are living in. You are inside the walls every single day and you know where the roof leaks, where the foundation is cracked." Buffalo is offered as the managed version of the same situation: the Bills surprisingly reached the playoffs in their first season under Sean McDermott, a euphoric moment after a 17-year playoff drought, went 6-10 the next year, then began a steady rise behind Josh Allen and a top defense — but there isn't a Josh Allen on the Giants or Vikings. Minnesota in particular is in an interesting spot, with Kirk Cousins approaching free agency and playing well enough, most likely, to keep the Vikings from climbing too high in the draft order. "They already gave a contract to (tight end) T.J. Hockenson, and they are going to give one to (receiver) Justin Jefferson," an exec said. "Now, what? Are you going into the rookie pool and taking the fourth-best quarterback in the draft? You can look like Atlanta with (Desmond) Ridder pretty quick."



---


# NFL DFS Week 15 Defense And Special Teams Values

Sporting News' headline Week 15 2023 D/ST play was the Los Angeles Rams against the Commanders (DK $3,100, FD $4,300).

The Rams had been destroyed by MVP candidate Lamar Jackson and the high-flying Ravens in Week 14, but the column urged readers to push that out of their memory banks: before that game Sean McVay's squad had surrendered 20 or fewer points in four straight contests, and Aaron Donald and company had 17 sacks and six takeaways over their past six games, so they would be licking their chops looking across the line at Sam Howell — no quarterback had more interceptions than Howell, who had also taken 10 more sacks than any other signal-caller that season. More solid Week 15 D/ST plays listed were the Chicago Bears at Browns (DK $3,300, FD $4,100); the New York Jets at Dolphins (DK $2,700, FD $3,600); and the New England Patriots vs. Chiefs (DK $2,300, FD $3,200).



---


# The NFL Super Bowl Contender Landscape, Week 6 Of 2023

The New York Times' Pick Six column of 16 October 2023 addressed the key questions facing the ten teams with the shortest Super Bowl odds — the Chiefs, Eagles, 49ers, Bills, Bengals, Cowboys, Ravens, Lions, Dolphins and Jaguars — with one-third of the 18-week regular season nearly complete.

The prompt for the exercise was a weekend that changed the picture at the top. The San Francisco 49ers entered Week 6 riding a 15-game winning streak and looking unstoppable with a young quarterback, Brock Purdy, who was making the game look easy; they exited with a 19-17 defeat at Cleveland, injuries to key players and, for the first time that season, a question mark or two. The previously unbeaten Philadelphia Eagles also lost ugly that Sunday.

The season to that point had produced a set of contradictions the column set out to test. The Miami Dolphins had set NFL records for offense, only to lose by four touchdowns in their lone game against a true contender. The Kansas City Chiefs had won with defense, sometimes in spite of their offense. The Buffalo Bills had incurred devastating injuries. For each of the ten teams the column ran through what the writer thinks and what NFL insiders have to say.



---


# Jordan Poyer's Alcoholism And Sobriety

Jordan Poyer stopped drinking in March 2020, after downing a shot of tequila on March 13 in the Puerto Vallarta airport bar during a 12-hour flight delay, and his first significant temptation came that spring at a Bills defenders' gathering in Washington, D.C., where he put a shot of tequila down instead of drinking it, The New York Times reported on 15 December 2023.

The circumstances of that moment were public. With NFL team facilities closed because of COVID-19, Bills defenders met in Washington for a few days to train, study and bond; on the first evening cornerback Josh Norman welcomed the players to his home and out came the shots of tequila. When Poyer was handed one, he looked at it, then at his teammates, and put it down. Norman and the others, who had never seen him turn down a drink, were taken aback — "What?" one said. "Come on, Deejay Poyo!" Deejay Poyo was Poyer's alter ego, inspired by tequila and a turntable; for Poyer there was value in being someone else. His teammates did not know he had not put alcohol to his lips in about three months. "When I put that drink down for the first time, it was almost like I overcame a demon," Poyer says. The more time that passed, the less he wanted to drink; he has no desire for it now, and the smell of alcohol almost makes him gag.

The drinking began at Oregon State. Poyer spent his childhood in Astoria, Ore., a picturesque town on the mouth of the Columbia River not far from the Pacific Ocean, where his mother and stepfather worked at a juvenile detention center and raised him with a strict hand; when he was no longer under their watch, unsupervised as a freshman at Oregon State, he drank, and drank and drank. It never seemed to affect his play in college, where he was a consensus All-American, and despite continued drinking he made steady progress in his early NFL years. By then his drinking was out of control: he would down a six-pack of IPAs in 20 to 30 minutes for a quick buzz, and blacking out was a regular occurrence. His behaviour tested his marriage, though there was a draw between him and Rachel like a north pole to south. After the Bills lost to the Houston Texans in the wild-card round of the 2019 playoffs, Poyer was crestfallen and says he drank heavily every day for five weeks; at one point Rachel rid their home of all alcohol, but he would still sneak what he could, hiding it from her beneath bathroom cabinets and other places "like a child," she says. He was close to losing her. The drinking, he realised, was an attempt to relieve stress — stress from football expectations and stress from family life; he was a worrier, except with a drink in his hand. He went to an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting, then another, and another.



---


# Prisco's Week 12 Sunday Night And Monday Night Picks

Pete Prisco's Week 12 prime-time picks, published by CBS Sports on 2023-11-23, cover two games. For the Sunday 8:20 p.m. ET game on NBC and fubo, he argued the Chargers are having major issues right now and face one of the best teams in the league; the Ravens offense will miss tight end Mark Andrews, but the Chargers defense is perfect for any team throwing the football, so the Ravens will win it with a big game from Lamar Jackson. Pick: Ravens 30, Chargers 23.

For the Monday 8:15 p.m. ET game on ABC/ESPN and fubo, he noted both teams were coming off tough losses, with the Bears blowing a huge lead late — though it was more damning for the Vikings, a team that had been surging. His warrant: Minnesota's defense will be the difference as they get the best of Justin Fields. Pick: Vikings 24, Bears 14.



---


# Seahawks +6 At Ravens, Week 9

Sporting News took the Seahawks at +6 in Baltimore in Week 9 of 2023, predicting Ravens 26, Seahawks 23. The reasoning starts from the line itself: Baltimore's defense had been incredible of late and the Ravens seemed to be flying under the radar at 6-2, but the sportsbooks had clearly taken note of that run by giving the NFC West-leading Seahawks a full touchdown on the road — which looked like a great opportunity to back the underdog, considering Seattle had won two straight and gone 2-1 on the road, including a big win over the high-flying Lions in Detroit.

The supporting claims concern personnel trending upward. Geno Smith had not been the same Pro Bowl quarterback as in 2022 but had still shown moments of brilliance for Pete Carroll's squad, and with DK Metcalf and Kenneth Walker III a week closer to full health — and backup running back Zack Charbonnet looking on the verge of a breakout — the column liked Seattle to at least make a game of it. The Seahawks' defense had quietly been pretty good, and the offense was capable of fireworks when everything clicked. Bettors were told they could take an extra 1.5 points as insurance if they wanted, but the pick was Seattle to cover the +6.

Other Week 9 spreads the column liked were Patriots (-3) vs. Commanders and Raiders -1.5 vs. Giants.



---


# The Third Quarter Of Bengals 24, Bills 18

Buffalo scored the only points of the third quarter on Nov. 5, 2023, cutting Cincinnati's lead to 21-10 while both offenses stalled. Khalil Shakir brought the opening kickoff out to the 26 and Sean McDermott's stated aim of avoiding third-and-longs showed in a five-yard opening pass to Diggs. An ineligible-receiver-downfield flag brought up second-and-10, but Allen went back to Diggs, then twice to Kincaid — nine yards to the Bills' 41 and 11 more to Cincinnati's 48. Allen rifled a 15-yard pass to Diggs over Nick Scott's head to the Bengals' 33, dumped off to James Cook for eight, and Cook ran for seven and a first down into the red zone for the first time since Buffalo's opening drive, at the Cincinnati 17. Pressure then limited Allen on consecutive plays — an incompletion to Cooks to avoid a sack and a quick throw to Cook stopped after a yard — and on third-and-9 he could not connect with Gabe Davis in the end zone, so Tyler Bass drilled a 34-yard field goal at 10:13 p.m. for Bengals 21, Bills 10.

Cincinnati's response drive covered ground but ended empty. Williams returned the kickoff to the 16, though a penalty pushed the spot back to the Cincinnati 8. Mixon rushed for three and caught a pass for three, and a healthy Burrow showed his value on third-and-4 by scrambling for seven and the first down. Higgins caught a short pass and made several players miss up to the Cincinnati 43, but Burrow's deep shot to Chase was just short with Dane Jackson breaking it up, and after a Mixon dump-off lost a yard the Bengals faced third-and-11; Burrow looked Chase's way again and came up empty, leaving Chase with three catches for nine yards on seven targets, and Brad Robbins' punt pinned Buffalo at its own 9.

Buffalo could not escape. Allen threw quickly to Cooks for four, missed Diggs to the left, and after a timeout with the play clock at three seconds was flushed from the pocket and brought down by Trey Hendrickson for a yard, forcing a punt that Trenton Irwin fair-caught at the Bengals' 42 with 5:06 left in the quarter. Cincinnati moved again — Mixon's five-yard checkdown, an 11-yard Higgins catch to the Bills' 42, then, after Jordan Poyer blew up a pitch to Mixon for a four-yard loss, another nine-yard Higgins reception — but Burrow could not connect with Boyd on third-and-5, and after a timeout with 2:21 left the Bengals went for it on fourth-and-5 only for Drew Sample to be brought down three yards shy. Buffalo took over at its own 35, and Allen powered for a 10-yard run and hit Kincaid for 11 to reach the Cincinnati 44; back-to-back Cook plays of three rushing and six receiving set up third-and-1 at the Bengals' 35, and Allen sneaked left for three and the first down as the quarter ended.

qid: Which football club, discussed on both TalkSport and Sporting News, has both set an unwanted record by conceding 14 goals in the Champions League group stages and has been eliminated from European competitions following a defeat at their home ground, known as Old Trafford?
context:
# Manchester United's European Decline Since Ferguson

The Independent argued on 12 December 2023 that Manchester United's 1-0 defeat to Bayern Munich should have been a landmark low but instead felt grimly routine, because group-stage elimination has become the club's normal European outcome in the post-Ferguson era rather than an aberration.

The grounds are frequency and pattern. Manchester United, one of the grandest and richest names in this competition, have again gone out of the Champions League at the group stage; it is the third time it has happened since Sir Alex Ferguson, meaning it is their most common round of exit in that period. The night is presented as one more entry in a decade of disappointment in a competition in which this club rose to its most emotional heights — a low, but just part of that longer run.

The warrant is the gap between the occasion and the performance. These are not the sounds we are used to hearing after that Champions League theme; something does stir when the anthem is played at Old Trafford amid the lights — well, for most, that is, except the players. United should not be performing like this on what is supposed to be the classic European night at Old Trafford, and the display was a reminder that all they are going to have for some time are their memories. Having been involved in so many ludicrously chaotic matches, the biggest of all ended up being a non-event: this game never threatened to stir anything, and United never threatened at all. That, the argument runs, can now be talked about definitively, since it has been decisively ended.



---


# Manchester United's 2023/24 Champions League Elimination

Manchester United were out of Europe altogether after a limp display against Bayern at Old Trafford, where Kingsley Coman sealed a 1-0 win for Thomas Tuchel's side on the final day of Champions League group-stage play, per Sporting News on Dec. 12 and Dec. 13, 2023.

The Red Devils finished bottom of their four-team group, leaving them eliminated from Europe in their worst performance in the competition since 2005. On top of that, they set the record for most goals against in a Champions League group stage by an English club, with 15 conceded in their six games.

Their defensive record had collapsed as the season went on: from a Premier League standpoint they sat eighth in the English top flight, but their -5 goal differential was the worst of any club in the top 10.



---


# Manchester United's 2023-24 Champions League Group-Stage Record

Manchester United finished bottom of their 2023-24 Champions League group with four points, in fourth place, eliminated from European competition altogether rather than dropping into the Europa League, The Independent reported on 12 December 2023.

The decisive results came from outside the Bayern fixture. It was not Bayern who eliminated them: it was Galatasaray, who won at Old Trafford and scored six goals over 180 minutes against United, and FC Copenhagen, who qualified instead of them — Rasmus Hojlund's former club will be in the last 16 while his current one will not, making Copenhagen the anomalies in the draw, the outsiders with the spot that had seemed reserved for United. The second place United aimed for went instead to Copenhagen, a club with a fraction of United's budget, and that is where the damage was done. On the final night the Danish side's victory over Galatasaray ensured any United win would be irrelevant, leaving only a slim hope beforehand.

The campaign produced records of the wrong kind. When Coman scored, United became the first Premier League side to concede 15 goals in a Champions League group stage. United won a lone game in the competition, and even that required a penalty save to deny FC Copenhagen a draw. # Premier League

## Definition

The Premier League is the top tier of the English football league system, comprising 20 clubs, sitting above the Championship, League One, and League Two.

## Context

The corpus places the Premier League at the summit of a four-tier domestic pyramid: 20 Premier League clubs sit above the 24-club Championship, League One, and League Two, and this tier structure also determines entry rounds into the Carabao Cup (League Cup), where the 12 Premier League clubs not in European competition join at the second round and the remaining eight join at the third round.
Premier League clubs are also bound by league-wide financial rules: Everton were docked 10 points by an independent commission for breaching those rules with a £19.5m overspend in 2021-22, described as the biggest sporting sanction in Premier League history.
Match officiating in the league is overseen by the Professional Game Match Officials Limited (PGMOL), which has repeatedly apologised for VAR errors in Premier League fixtures, including a missed penalty in Manchester United's opening-weekend match against Wolves in the 2023/24 season.
Historical success in the competition is also tracked league-wide: Manchester United and Chelsea are named among only seven clubs to have won the "modern" Premier League, with Chelsea having won it twice since United's last title in 2012/13.

## Key Characteristics

- **Top of a four-tier pyramid** — 20 clubs, above the Championship (24), League One (24), and League Two (24).
- **Subject to league-wide financial rules** — breaches can trigger independent-commission points deductions, as seen with Everton's 10-point penalty for a 2021-22 overspend.
- **Officiated under PGMOL** — the body responsible for referees and VAR decisions across Premier League matches, including a public apology track record for errors.
- **A title tracked historically** — described in the corpus as having been won by only seven clubs in its "modern" era, used as a shorthand for a club's stature (e.g., Manchester United vs Chelsea).
- **Tracked match-by-match across a season** — referenced in the corpus via a club's progress through the campaign (e.g., a club's "11th Premier League match of the season").

# United's Squad Incoherence And Old Trafford's Decline

Barney Ronay argues that Manchester United's problem on the night of their Champions League exit was not spirit but coherence: the players stood up and died rather than lying down, but they looked like what they are — a muddled creation, stitched together out of parts and off-cuts.

The grounds are what was visible in the stadium and on the pitch. As the seconds ticked down at the end of a season-ender that felt like a gentle, even quite tender, act of sporting euthanasia, the only noise inside Old Trafford was Bayern Munich fans singing an impressively sustained version of Football's Coming Home, then Is This A Library? — to which Ronay answers no, it is more of a museum — before chanting "Auf Wiedersehen" at departing home supporters who had done pretty well to stick it out. In the second half United's back five was André Onana, Aaron Wan-Bissaka, Jonny Evans, Raphaël Varane and Diogo Dalot, an entirely random collection of players signed at various times by Ten Hag, José Mourinho, Ole Gunnar Solskjær and Alex Ferguson. By the end United had five academy players on the pitch with ages ranging between 17 and 35 — in outline evidence of internal good health, in reality another symptom of a machine that wants to function properly but has for so long been made to judder along at half-speed. The warrant is that the decay is institutional, not motivational, and it extends to the fabric of the place: when VAR happens at Old Trafford there is not even a VAR screen to say "VAR Check." The 1990s were a hell of a decade — they still are around there.
