# Harry Kane, The Striker Manchester United Did Not Sign

Harry Kane, the England captain and the forward Manchester United neglected to bid for in the summer, unlocked United's defence with a lovely flick to set up Bayern Munich's winner on 12 December 2023 — a reminder, The Independent wrote, of what could have been for United.

The comparison the reports draw is with the striker United did buy. Rasmus Hojlund has at least struck in the Champions League, but in domestic competitions he has been outscored 18-0 by Kane. United, cast out of continental competition altogether, became just the fourth English team to prop up a Champions League group when it concluded, and there was something predictable about the manner of their demise.

The Bayern game also showed one reason why Kane is at Germany's biggest club rather than England's: his side are through with ease and among the favourites for the competition, even if they do look lacking in a few areas.



---


# Harry Kane's 2023 Goal Tally And Bayern Munich Scoring Records

Harry Kane scored 52 goals in the 2023 calendar year for Bayern Munich, Tottenham and England, tied for second on TalkSport's list of the year's top scorers. A stunning 2022/23 season saw Bayern splash out over £100m to sign the Spurs legend in August, and Kane repaid the Bundesliga club's faith by breaking a number of records with his 25 goals in all competitions so far in the season.

The leading scorer in the German top flight with 22 goals, the Three Lions skipper set a new Bundesliga record the previous month by finding the back of the net 17 times in his opening 11 outings. Kane, who scored nine goals for England in 2023, is also the first player to register a hat-trick in their first outing against Borussia Dortmund. He is on course to score the most goals in a debut Bundesliga campaign as he hunts down Uwe Seeler's record of 30 for Hamburg in the 1963/64 season, and is on track to break Robert Lewandowski's record of 41 goals in a single season. He is adding assists too, as evidenced by his "filthy" effort against Man United in the Champions League. Like Mbappe, Kane could not overtake Ronaldo's calendar-year tally because of the German winter break.

Earlier in the season, in Bayern's 2-2 draw at RB Leipzig, Bayern earned a 57th-minute penalty against the run of play for a handball and Kane cut the deficit with his eighth league goal. Only Manchester City's Erling Haaland, when he played for Borussia Dortmund, had scored more often in his first six Bundesliga games, with nine goals.



---


# Bayern Munich 1-0 Manchester United At Old Trafford

Kingsley Coman scored the only goal of Bayern Munich's 1-0 Champions League win at Old Trafford just after the hour, from a delightfully sneaky round-the-corner pass by Harry Kane.

Bayern held the ball nicely and probed in neat, clipped, mannered attacks, with a lot seeming to hinge on how desperately they felt the need to twist that scalpel and whether they could really be bothered to take the thing to the wall. United defended well and their waves of pressing drew waves of applause; everyone there seemed to be trying. But with 58 minutes gone Copenhagen scored and United's hopes began to slip beneath the waves, and just over 10 minutes later Bayern made it 1-0 in Manchester: Coman was granted a huge expanse of time and space in front of the United goal, enough to set himself as though taking a penalty, and belted the ball into the corner. After all that pressure and all that tender hope, it looked a bit like a training goal.



---


# Tottenham's Premier League Record Of Failing To Win After Leading

OptaJoe recorded on 7 December 2023 that Tottenham had become the first side in Premier League history to fail to win five consecutive games despite going 1-0 up in each match, and the first to lose three consecutive home games despite going 1-0 up in each — a run the post summed up as "Spursy."

The Roar's report places that record in the table. Spurs had rebounded from three consecutive defeats with a stirring 3-3 draw at Manchester City over the weekend, but after this result they sat outside the Champions League qualification spots in fifth place, level with Manchester United.



---


# Newcastle vs Crystal Palace Preview, October 2023

Newcastle hosted Crystal Palace live on talkSPORT 2 at 3pm on 21 October 2023 on an impressive run of form across all competitions, having knocked last year's treble winners Manchester City out of the Carabao Cup and beaten Paris Saint-Germain 4-1 in the Champions League, talkSPORT previewed on 20 October.

The obstacle was the opponent's recent record against them: Crystal Palace proved unbeatable for Newcastle last season, with goalless draws in all three of their meetings across all competitions. Palace had been defensively impressive that term, keeping four clean sheets, and sat ninth in the table, just one place behind Newcastle, so they could vault the Magpies with a win.

On team news, Newcastle were without Joe Willock and Harvey Barnes through injury, but Sandro Tonali was available despite allegations of illegal betting that led to him being sent home from Italy's national team squad, and despite fears that he could be banned.



---


# Liverpool's Early-Season Form In 2023-24

By 20 October 2023 Liverpool had surpassed pre-season expectations of a new-look team: three points off the top, three goals scored in every Premier League home game, a 100% record in all competitions at Anfield, cruising through the Europa League group stage, and individuals shining.

The Guardian judged it not unreasonable of Jürgen Klopp, however, to expect much more as the season developed. Klopp framed the demand as intrinsic to his job: "You saw so many teams here growing in the direction we wanted and all became better step by step or the manager had to go," he said. "We will try together to get better step by step and show our real face more often than not."



---


# Recent Premier League Meetings Between Manchester United And Chelsea

Ahead of Chelsea's visit to Old Trafford in December 2023, their most recent Premier League away win against Manchester United was a 1-0 win in May 2013, per Sporting News on Dec. 5, 2023.

At that point Chelsea had won more Premier League games at Old Trafford — six — than any other side, but they proceeded to draw six and lose four of their next 10 trips to M16. Manchester United were at that time 11 Premier League games unbeaten against Chelsea since November 2017. However, the fact that seven of those matches ended all square had helped to make the game the most drawn fixture in Premier League history: some 19 of those draws featured goals for both teams, and a 1-1 draw in the fixture is the most common exact scoreline in Premier League history, occurring 14 times.

The listed recent results were: Premier League, May 25, 2023, Old Trafford, Man United 4-1 Chelsea; Premier League, Oct. 22, 2022, Stamford Bridge, Chelsea 1-1 Man United; Premier League, Apr. 28, 2022, Old Trafford, Man United 1-1 Chelsea; Premier League, Nov. 28, 2021, Stamford Bridge, Chelsea 1-1 Man United; Premier League, Feb. 28, 2021, Stamford Bridge, Chelsea 0-0 Man United; Premier League, Oct. 24, 2020, Old Trafford, Man United 0-0 Chelsea; FA Cup, Jul. 19, 2020, Wembley Stadium, Man United 1-3 Chelsea; Premier League, Feb. 17, 2020, Stamford Bridge, Chelsea 0-2 Man United; League Cup, Oct. 30, 2019, Stamford Bridge, Chelsea 1-2 Man United; Premier League, Aug. 11, 2019, Old Trafford, Man United 4-0 Chelsea.



---


# How Fierce Is The Manchester United-Chelsea Rivalry?

Sporting News argued on Dec. 5, 2023 that although matches between United and Chelsea have tended to be closely contested, they do not have as fierce a rivalry as the Red Devils do with the likes of Manchester City and Liverpool, or as the west London club holds with neighbours such as Tottenham and Arsenal.

The grounds are that the rivalry was intense only over a specific competitive window. Abramovich's takeover gave Chelsea a new level of wealth that temporarily turned them into the dominant force in the English game, briefly supplanting United, who had won the title in eight of the previous 12 Premier League seasons. Under the brash Jose Mourinho — an antagonist to his legendary United counterpart Sir Alex Ferguson — Chelsea embarrassed third-placed United in 2004/05, winning the trophy while finishing 18 points ahead of them and, at one point, forcing Ferguson's players to give them a guard of honour at Old Trafford because of the timing of their title win. United closed the gap to finish eight points behind Chelsea in second the following season, then returned to the top in 2006/07, with the deposed champions six points short of their total. Two points separated the teams as United won the Premier League again in 2007/08, and there would be one more changing of the guard to come when Chelsea finished first above United in 2009/10 — only for United to finish top a year later. That ultra-tight Champions League final encapsulated how close the rivalry had become in a competitive sense.

Both teams have won the Premier League since then, leaving United on a record 20 titles and Chelsea on six. Chelsea have won the Champions League and Europa League twice each, while United have won the former trophy three times and the latter once, and United's tally of 12 FA Cup triumphs is eight more than Chelsea have claimed. Both sets of supporters would be hoping their teams could become superpowers again after barren periods by their 21st-century standards: the rise of mega-wealthy Manchester City to become arguably the best team in the world had not helped, and nor had Liverpool's resurgence under Jurgen Klopp. United finished well off the pace albeit in a respectable third at the end of 2022/23, a season in which Chelsea came 12th — their lowest final position for 29 years.



---


# Newcastle's Elimination From The Group Of Death

Newcastle United were ejected from Europe altogether on the final matchday of the 2023-24 Champions League group stage, finishing with one win and five points after a second cruel comeback in as many games, The Independent reported on 13 December 2023.

For some 45 minutes, including half-time, they could savour the sight of a table that showed them in second, permitting them to imagine a date with Real Madrid or Bayern Munich in the knockout stages. And then, in little more than half an hour, they were out. Christian Pulisic's equaliser threatened to condemn them to the Europa League; Samuel Chukwueze's winner instead meant that spot went to AC Milan. The group of death went down to the dying minutes, but Newcastle have perished — they had savoured a return to Europe, but there will be no continental trips for them in the spring of 2024.

The report's assessment is that Newcastle can nevertheless depart the competition with heads held high: one win and five points seem meagre tallies for their contribution to the competition, and they have proof that it can be unforgiving and reasons to return. Their first Champions League campaign for two decades will surely not be their last for another 20 years. But it is over, and they are left to wonder about what might have been.



---


# Pre-Match Build-Up To Manchester United vs Chelsea, December 2023

Sporting News' countdown to kickoff at Old Trafford on Dec. 6, 2023 recorded the team-news surprise that Marcus Rashford started from the bench, along with Ten Hag's pre-match message about Chelsea's defending.

At 1 hour 30 mins until kickoff the blog noted Chelsea had won three of their last four Premier League away games but were without a league win at Old Trafford since 2013. At 1 hour until kickoff the team news was in: the eyebrow-raising decision from Erik ten Hag was that Marcus Rashford started from the bench, while Mauricio Pochettino started the former Man City man Cole Palmer. At 45 mins until kickoff the blog noted Raheem Sterling had failed to score in any of his 24 matches against Man United, and asked whether the night might be the ex-Liverpool and Man City player's.

At 30 mins until kickoff the warm-ups were underway at Old Trafford on a chilly night, and Ten Hag had just told MUTV that Chelsea do not "like to defend" and that United must take advantage of that. At 15 mins until kickoff the teams had headed down the tunnel at the Theatre of Dreams.



---


# Manchester United 2-1 Chelsea, December 2023

Manchester United got themselves back to winning ways with a 2-1 victory over Chelsea thanks to a superb Scott McTominay brace, per Sporting News on Dec. 6, 2023. The final score was Man United 2 (McTominay 19', 70'), Chelsea 1 (Palmer 45').

The victory remarkably put United within three points of rivals Manchester City, after the reigning champions were defeated by Aston Villa, and kept them in reach of the top four places.

McTominay became United's top scorer for the season with six goals, one ahead of Bruno Fernandes and Rasmus Hojlund. The Red Devils' captain had a first-half penalty saved by Robert Sanchez, and United's Danish striker was substituted after another Premier League game without a goal, despite making 11 appearances. United had now won their past 19 Premier League games at Old Trafford when scoring first, including all 16 under their Dutch manager.

# Critique Of Meta's App Store Parental Approval Proposal

The critique attacks the premise that moving approval to the app stores is a protection measure at all rather than a reallocation of blame. Meta's proposed "better way" of requiring parents to manage a teen's app downloads pushes the burden back to the app stores and to parents, who often today do not monitor or manage their teens' smartphone use.

TechCrunch grants the factual half of Meta's warrant and rejects the inference: while it is true that the app stores and smartphone makers would know the ages of their users, requiring parents to approve apps is the equivalent of overriding parental discretion and choice. Other entertainment ratings — like those for TV, movies or video games — are meant to be guidelines for parents, not laws, so Meta's position that apps are somehow different is a fairly extreme position to take.

Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit devoted to reigning in Big Tech, attacked the proposal's motive: "Instead of designing its products with kids' safety and privacy in mind, Meta would rather push blame onto parents and other companies to obscure the damage they've already done to young people. No one disputes that Google and Apple need to do more to protect children on their platforms, apps and devices. That fact does not absolve Mark Zuckerberg or Meta for years of willful negligence, and this announcement shows that the company's outright hostility toward protecting kids is sewn into the fabric of its profit model." Apple and Google did not return requests for comment.



---


# The 42-State Lawsuit Against Meta Over Harms To Young Users

A coalition of 42 states and D.C. is suing Meta over its harms to teens and young users, in part referencing findings from Meta whistleblower Frances Haugen. The former employee had provided to news outlets a treasure trove of documents that appeared to indicate Meta understood the harms it was causing — including things like body image issues among teens — but did not take action. Instagram head Adam Mosseri was later hauled before Congress in December 2021 to defend the app's teen safety record, but as of November 15, 2023 legislators had not come to any decision about how to regulate teen usage of these platforms.

The suit was filed in October 2023, and a newly unredacted version reported on November 27, 2023 alleges a troubling pattern of deception and minimization in how the company handles kids under 13 on its platforms, with internal documents that appear to show the company's approach to this ostensibly forbidden demographic is far more laissez-faire than it has publicly claimed. The lawsuit alleges a wide spread of damaging practices at the company relating to the health and well-being of younger people using it: from body image to bullying, privacy invasion to engagement maximization, all the purported evils of social media are laid at Meta's door — perhaps rightly, TechCrunch notes, but it also gives the appearance of a lack of focus.

In one respect at least the documentation obtained by the attorneys general of 42 states is quite specific, "and it is damning," as AG Rob Bonta of California put it. That is in paragraphs 642 through 835, which mostly document violations of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA — a law that created very specific restrictions around young folks online, limiting data collection and requiring things like parental consent for various actions, but which a lot of tech companies seem to consider more suggestion than requirement.



---


# Meta Researchers Avoided Documenting Under-13 Users

A potential smoking gun in the lawsuit is a series of anecdotes from Meta researchers delicately avoiding the possibility of inadvertently confirming an under-13 cohort in their work.

One wrote in 2018: "We just want to make sure to be sensitive about a couple of Instagram-specific items. For example, will the survey go to under 13 year olds? Since everyone needs to be at least 13 years old before they create an account, we want to be careful about sharing findings that come back and point to under 13 year olds being bullied on the platform." In 2021, another, studying "child-adult sexual-related content/behavior/interactions," said she was "not includ[ing] younger kids (10-12 yos) in this research" even though there "are definitely kids this age on IG," because she was "concerned about risks of disclosure since they aren't supposed to be on IG at all." Also in 2021, Meta instructed a third-party research company conducting a survey of preteens to remove any information indicating a survey subject was on Instagram, so the "company won't be made aware of under 13." Later that year, external researchers provided Meta with information that "of children ages 9-12, 45% used Facebook and 40% used Instagram daily."

During an internal 2021 study on youth in social media described in the suit, researchers first asked parents if their kids were on Meta platforms and removed them from the study if so. But one researcher asked, "What happens to kids who slip through the screener and then say they are on IG during the interviews?" Instagram Head of Public Policy Karina Newton responded, "we're not collecting user names right?" — in other words, TechCrunch notes, what happens is nothing. As the lawsuit puts it: "Even when Meta learns of specific children on Instagram through interviews with the children, Meta takes the position that it still lacks actual knowledge of that it is collecting personal information from an under-13 user because it does not collect user names while conducting these interviews. In this way, Meta goes through great lengths to avoid meaningfully complying with COPPA, looking for loopholes to excuse its knowledge of users under the age of 13 and maintain their presence on the Platform."



---


# Data Privacy

## Definition

Data privacy, across the corpus, is the recurring dispute over whether companies may collect, track, or profile people's personal information without their knowledge or consent.

That dispute plays out as regulatory enforcement against platforms: GDPR action against Meta's consentless ad tracking (doc_0107), COPPA litigation over Meta's collection of data from children under 13 (doc_0304), a "mass breach of privacy" allegation against TikTok's pre-consent tracking pixel (doc_0189), and California's CPPA extending opt-out and access rights to AI-based profiling (doc_0164).

## Context

In the corpus, data privacy surfaces as the recurring fault line between platforms that monetize personal data and the regulators pushing back on non-consensual collection. Norway's Datatilsynet issued an emergency GDPR ban on Meta running "personalized ads" without consent, then referred the case to the EU's Board to make the ban permanent across the single market, because Meta kept running tracking ads despite the order and a rejected court challenge (doc_0107). California's CPPA is drafting rules that would give residents opt-out and access rights over "automated decisionmaking technology," explicitly modeled on GDPR and expected to draw pushback from adtech and AI firms like Meta and OpenAI (doc_0164). The Age's investigation found TikTok's tracking pixel scraping site visitors' names, emails, and phone numbers before users clicked "I consent," prompting an Australian senator to call it a "mass breach of privacy" and demand a regulatory probe (doc_0189). Meta separately faces a 42-state lawsuit alleging it violated COPPA — the US law restricting data collection from children under 13 and requiring parental consent — by knowingly letting millions of underage users onto Instagram and Facebook while collecting their personal information (doc_0304).

## Key Characteristics

- **Consent is the legal hinge** — GDPR, as applied against Meta in Norway, turns on whether a company has a valid legal basis (consent, not "legitimate interest" or "contractual necessity") before tracking or profiling users for ads (doc_0107).
- **Pre-consent collection is the specific harm alleged against TikTok** — its pixel captured form-field data "often before clicking 'I consent'," unlike Google's and Meta's pixels, which the same test showed firing only after consent (doc_0189).
- **Children are a protected, heavily litigated category** — COPPA restricts data collection from users under 13 and requires verifiable parental consent, and Meta's alleged evasion of that requirement (ignoring reports, not disabling accounts, avoiding "actual knowledge") is the specific violation named in the unredacted lawsuit (doc_0304).
- **Regulators are extending consent/access rights into AI** — California's CPPA is drafting opt-out and access rights over automated decisionmaking technology and AI-based profiling, explicitly borrowing from GDPR's model (doc_0164).
- **Enforcement can escalate beyond a single national regulator** — Norway's local DPA used an emergency GDPR mechanism to bypass the "one-stop-shop" rule and force an EU-wide decision on Meta, showing that a single country's action can become bloc-wide policy (doc_0107).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the general legal concept the enforcement actions above are built on is the definition of "personal data" under GDPR.

GDPR.eu describes personal data as "any information that relates to an individual who can be directly or indirectly identified," a category spanning obvious identifiers like names and emails as well as location data and other online identifiers (GDPR.eu, "What Is GDPR, the EU's New Data Protection Law?", published by Proton AG with EU Horizon 2020 co-funding, accessed 2026-09-02: https://gdpr.eu/what-is-gdpr/).

# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.

# Meta's Under-13 Policy Versus Its Internal Growth Goals

An internal presentation called "2017 Teens Strategic Focus" appears to specifically target kids under 13, noting that children use tablets as early as 3 or 4, and that "Social identity is an Unmet need Ages 5-11." TechCrunch flags an important boundary on what this does and does not show. While Meta does not permit accounts to be run by people under 13, there are plenty of ways it can lawfully and safely engage with that demographic: some kids just want to watch videos from SpongeBob Official, and that is fine. What the law requires is that Meta must verify parental consent, and the ways it can collect and use their data are limited. So targeting under-13s as an audience is not by itself unlawful; the legal question is consent and data use.

# Shadowbanning

## Definition

Shadowbanning, as TechCrunch describes it, is when a platform "shadowbans, or limits the visibility of" a user's content without the platform notifying the user that anything has been restricted, so the user only discovers it by noticing a drop in views or reach.

## Context

In the corpus the term names the central accusation in the October 2023 controversy over Meta's handling of Palestine-related content: Instagram users accused Meta of shadowbanning their Stories about Palestine, and TechCrunch frames the belief that Meta "shadowbans, or limits the visibility of," such content as longstanding rather than new to that month.
The same allegation is cited beyond Meta's own platforms as a driver of platform choice: users turned to Snapchat's Snap Map for firsthand Gaza content specifically because accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content on Instagram and Facebook had eroded their trust in those platforms.
Meta's official response did not deny that reach had dropped; it denied the mechanism, attributing the reduced Story reach specifically to a global, content-neutral bug in Stories that re-shared Reels or Feed posts, and separately attributed a different global bug — one that had prevented some users from going live — to technical error rather than deliberate suppression tied to subject matter.

## Key Characteristics

- **Covert, not disclosed** — the defining feature reporters and users pointed to is that visibility drops silently, with no notification to the affected account; Bella Hadid described being "immediately shadowbanned" and her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million" with no explanation from the platform.
- **Detected by comparison, not confirmation** — users inferred shadowbanning by comparing engagement across their own posts (e.g., a user whose Stories fell from "100s of views to zero or a handful" and rebounded only after posting unrelated content like a cat photo), since the platform provided no direct evidence of restriction.
- **Contested mechanism** — Meta disputed that the effect was shadowbanning-by-design, attributing the reduced Story reach to a bug that "affected accounts equally around the globe" and "had nothing to do with the subject matter of the content," rather than confirming intentional visibility limits.
- **Trust-eroding beyond the platform itself** — the accusation pushed users toward alternative platforms (Snap Map) even though the accused conduct occurred on Instagram and Facebook, showing shadowbanning claims can shift audience behavior across platforms, not just within one.

# The State Patchwork Of Teen Social Media Laws

Meta's call to bring the app stores into the fight is, if anything, a response to the lack of action in Congress to pass online child safety regulations like the hotly debated KOSA (the Kids Online Safety Act), leaving U.S. states to individually create laws due to a void of federal guidelines.

Utah, for instance, passed a measure that will require social networks to give Utah parents access to their children's posts, messages and comments, and would block social media access during certain hours; the governor also signed a bill to prevent social media companies from adding features designed to addict minors to their platforms. A judge in Arkansas recently blocked a law that would have required parental permission for minors to create social media accounts. Beyond Meta, Montana also became the first state to ban TikTok, claiming the Chinese Communist Party was using TikTok to spy on Americans. Meta's threat, in terms of teen usage, is not one of a foreign power collecting private data on users, but rather risks to teen mental health, body comparison issues and exposure to sexual predators — and TechCrunch notes Montana could easily turn its eyes to Meta next, after the TikTok bill went through.

The overhead of managing apps to meet individual state regulations would be a headache for Meta, but Antigone Davis also argues it would lead to a lack of teen protection in some cases. "U.S. states are passing a patchwork of different laws, many of which require teens (of varying ages) to get their parent's approval to use certain apps, and for everyone to verify their age to access them," she wrote. "Teens move interchangeably between many websites and apps, and social media laws that hold different platforms to different standards in different states will mean teens are inconsistently protected," Davis said.

# The Digital Services Act

The Digital Services Act (DSA) is the European Union's pan-EU content moderation rulebook: a regulation that places governance obligations on digital services and platforms carrying user-generated content, with the aim of ensuring companies respond to reports of illegal content, and that layers heavier duties on the largest platforms. Its baseline obligations apply to digital services and platforms generally — respond diligently to notices of illegal content, clearly communicate terms and conditions to users, and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement of those terms.

The discriminating feature of the regime is its second tier. Platforms designated as "very large online platforms" (VLOPs) carry additional obligations to identify and mitigate systemic risks such as disinformation, gender-based violence, or negative effects on the exercise of fundamental rights. The Commission designated 19 VLOPs in April 2023, including Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram; X is also a designated VLOP. Compliance for VLOPs kicked in over the summer of 2023 — TechCrunch dates Meta's compliance start to August.

The regime's boundary case is disinformation itself. Unlike terrorism content, disinformation is not illegal in the EU per se. The DSA therefore does not reach it through the illegal-content removal route at all; it reaches it through the systemic-risk route, obliging a VLOP such as X to mitigate the risks attached to harmful falsehoods while separately acting diligently on reports of genuinely illegal content. The two duties run on different legal tracks even when they concern the same posts.

Penalties for confirmed breaches can be as high as 6% of global annual turnover, and the bloc holds a further power, in extremis, to block access to a service in the region for repeated infringements — meaning a platform that repeatedly fails to correct course could be shut off in the EU. TechCrunch illustrates the scale on both ends: Elon Musk last projected revenues of about $3 billion for 2023 for X, which by that example would cap a fine at up to $180 million, while in Meta's case the same 6% ceiling could run to multiple billions.

The regulation also contains a "crisis response" mechanism (Article 36) which enables the Commission to adopt rapid-fire measures on larger platforms in situations of "serious threat", such as war. As of TechCrunch's October 2023 reporting this part of the regulation was not yet operative: it would not start operating until February 17 of the following year, because it requires an advisory body — the European Board for Digital Services — to be operational before it can recommend that the Commission adopt a crisis response mechanism, and the Board's set-up was itself waiting on Member States to establish national Digital Services Coordinators, the bodies that oversee DSA compliance for non-VLOPs.

# Meta Bias Mechanisms

Meta's disproportionate suppression of Palestinian and Arabic content is produced by a stack of interacting mechanisms rather than any single fault: thin Arabic language resources, categorical policies that cannot handle nuance, a blanket prohibition on support for terrorist organizations, government partnerships that shape policy decisions, automated enforcement backed by "minimally trained humans," and an allocation of moderation resources that tracks regulatory pressure rather than need. TechCrunch set out this account on 19 October 2023, drawing chiefly on the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

The linguistic layer comes first. Meta struggles to navigate the cultural and linguistic nuances of Arabic, a language with over 25 dialects, and has been criticized for neglecting to adequately diversify its language resources. On top of that, the company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic — content that discusses violence without condoning it is the example given.

The policy layer compounds it. Meta forbids support of terrorist organizations, as most U.S.-based social media companies do, but struggles to moderate content around that prohibition, from user discourse to journalistic updates. Combined with the company's partnership with Israel to monitor posts that incite violence, the rule complicates matters for Palestinians living under Hamas' governance: as EFF points out, something as simple as Hamas' flag in the background of an image can result in a strike. Advocacy groups have separately raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions.

The enforcement layer supplies the inconsistency. Jillian York, EFF's director for international freedom of expression, blames automation and decisions made by "minimally trained humans," and says Meta's zero tolerance policy and imprecise enforcement often suppress content from or about conflict zones. The range of the effect is wider than Palestine: the site's moderation issues have negatively affected multiple non-English speaking regions, including Libya, Syria and Ukraine. "These rules can prevent people from sharing documentation of human rights violations, documentation of war crimes, even just news about what's happening on the ground," York said. "And so I think that is what is the most problematic right now about that particular rule, and the way that it's enforced."

The resourcing layer explains why the effect is unevenly distributed across languages. York says Meta has made more contact with regional Palestinian organizations since 2021 but has been slow to implement recommendations from EFF and other advocacy groups, and that it is "very clear" Meta is not putting the same resources behind Arabic and other non-English languages compared with the attention it gives countries that exert the most regulatory pressure. Moderation of English and other European languages tends to be more comprehensive, for example, because the EU enforces the Digital Services Act.

Meta contests the picture. In its response to the report, human rights director Miranda Sissons said the company was "assessing the feasibility" of reviewing Arabic content by dialect and that it has "large and diverse teams" who understand "local cultural context across the region," including in Palestine; responding to the escalating violence earlier that month, Meta said it had established a "special operations center" staffed with fluent Hebrew and Arabic speakers to monitor and respond to violating content. Despite those apparent efforts, Arabic is still disproportionately flagged as violating — as in the case of journalists reporting news in multiple languages.

# The GDPR Track Running Alongside The Consumer Complaint

As of November 30, 2023 the data protection question about Meta's pay-or-consent offer was unresolved and running on a separate track from the consumer complaint. "The company's approach also raises concerns regarding the GDPR," BEUC's Ursula Pachl noted, and a spokesman for BEUC told TechCrunch it might, at a later stage, file a complaint about Meta's data protection compliance with the relevant privacy authority once it has completed its own assessment of the issues — though he emphasized it was too early to say whether or not it would take that step.

In the meanwhile, Meta maintains that the model it has devised for obtaining users' consent to its ads processing complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) — although, TechCrunch notes, the adtech giant also said that when it was claiming performance of a contract and then legitimate interests for the processing, both of which were subsequently found to be incompatible with the GDPR.

TechCrunch's reading of the incentive: Meta is likely banking on another multi-year round of GDPR complaints, legal challenges and finally a referral to the CJEU, followed by another long wait before a ruling gets handed down, buying it several more years to run with its new legal basis fix and keep feeding its profits by doing what it likes with Europeans' data.

# Meta Response To Suppression Claims

Meta's rebuttal attacks the premise that any pattern of reduced reach for Palestine-related content shows deliberate suppression: the company says the reduced reach came from globally scoped technical bugs and from errors in good-faith enforcement, not from the subject matter of the posts. As reported by TechCrunch on 19 October 2023, Meta said it is closely monitoring its platforms for violations and may inadvertently flag certain content, but that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view."

The scope condition Meta sets around the whole dispute is its terrorist-organization rule: content praising or supporting Hamas — which governs Gaza and is designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union — is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms. This is stated in the aftermath of Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade cutting access to electricity, water and vital supplies, which have devastated Gaza.

Meta communications director Andy Stone declined to comment on the record and pointed TechCrunch to Meta's newsroom post about the conflict, updated on Oct. 18 with a statement addressing the shadowbanning claims. "Our policies are designed to keep people safe on our apps while giving everyone a voice," it said. "We apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice … We can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it."

The specific counter-explanations are two bugs, each claimed to be global and therefore content-neutral. Meta blamed technical errors for the removal of posts about Palestine during the 2021 conflict, and on the recent shadowbanning claims a company representative pointed TechCrunch to a Threads post by Stone: "We identified a bug impacting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts, meaning they weren't showing up properly in people's Stories tray, leading to significantly reduced reach. This bug affected accounts equally around the globe and had nothing to do with the subject matter of the content — and we fixed it as quickly as possible." Stone separately directed TechCrunch to the updated newsroom post, which said Meta identified and fixed a "bug" that prevented users from going live: "This was also a global issue that was fixed within a few hours. We understand people rely on these tools and we're sorry to anyone who felt the impact of these issues."

The rebuttal's reach is limited in ways the reporting records. It is unclear whether the bug affected accounts posting content unrelated to Gaza, while Instagram users have posted screenshots showing Stories about Palestine receiving significantly fewer views than other Stories posted the same day, and allege their view counts recovered when they posted content unrelated to the conflict. Meta's representative did not address the other accusations of censorship beyond Story visibility and did not respond to TechCrunch's follow-up questions; Meta initially did not respond to follow-up requests for comment. Asked about comments containing the Palestinian flag, Stone again pointed to the updated newsroom post, which did not directly address the issue, and he declined to comment on allegations of Meta disproportionately flagging Arabic news content, directing TechCrunch to the same post, which did not directly address those allegations either.

# DSA And DMA Oversight Of Meta's Ad Tracking

Meta's subscription plan faces three overlapping regimes, not one. As well as needing to comply with the GDPR, which delineates the qualities necessary for consent to be legal — such as that it is specific, informed and freely given — Meta is now also subject to the pan-EU Digital Services Act (DSA), which also sets conditions on larger platforms when it comes to tracking and profiling people for ads; so it won't just be data protection authorities making a call on whether Meta's subscription-or-tracking offer flies, since the European Commission is responsible for oversight of very large online platforms' DSA compliance.

Meta has also been designated as a so-called gatekeeper under the DSA's sister regulation, the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which also puts some limits on use of people's data for ads, and the Commission is the sole enforcer of the DMA. Meta is already in the Commission's sights over its approach to the DSA — the EU's executive has in recent days requested more information from the tech giant about its approach to content threats flowing from the Israel-Hamas war and about election security issues — but it remains to be seen whether the EU will apply the same close scrutiny to Meta's ad tracking offer.

# Content Moderation

## Definition

Content moderation, as the corpus uses the term, is the mix of platform policy and enforcement — written rules like Meta's Violence and Incitement policy and Community Guidelines, human reviewers, automated systems, and crowdsourced tools like X's Community Notes — that decides what user-generated content stays visible and how a platform acts on notices of illegal or rule-breaking material.

## Context

In the corpus, content moderation surfaces mainly as the practice EU regulators scrutinize under the Digital Services Act (DSA): the DSA's "very precise obligations" require platforms to be "timely, diligent and objective" in acting on notices of illegal content, and the European Commission's formal DSA proceeding against X names "content moderation" as one of the specific areas under investigation, alongside risk management, dark patterns, advertising transparency, and researcher data access (doc_0024; doc_0153).
It also appears as a site of contested practice and bias: Meta's moderation of Palestinian-related content during the Israel-Hamas war produced widespread allegations of shadowbanning and inconsistent enforcement across Arabic versus Hebrew content (doc_0106), while Meta separately described tightening its livestreaming and hostage-content moderation in direct response to that same conflict (doc_0335).
The term also frames platform-differentiation debates outside the EU: Kick's "light moderation" is cited as both a draw for streamers leaving Twitch and a source of safety controversy (doc_0405), Mozilla frames robust moderation and "trust and safety" as central to its fediverse strategy while noting a stricter-moderation rival (Pebble) failed to grow (doc_0026), and the US Supreme Court case over Texas and Florida laws turns on whether content moderation is a form of constitutionally protected "editorial judgment" (doc_0256).

## Key Characteristics

- **Policy plus enforcement** — moderation combines written rules (e.g. Meta's Violence and Incitement policy, Community Guidelines) with mechanisms to act on them: human reviewers, automated classifiers, and appeals processes (doc_0335; doc_0106).
- **Legally obligated for large platforms under the DSA** — the DSA requires timely, diligent, objective action on illegal-content notices, and imposes added systemic-risk mitigation duties (e.g. disinformation) on very large online platforms like X and Meta (doc_0024; doc_0335).
- **Can be outsourced/crowdsourced** — X replaced parts of its formal moderation function with the crowdsourced "Community Notes" system after gutting in-house enforcement teams, a shift EU regulators are explicitly assessing for adequacy (doc_0025; doc_0153).
- **Prone to inconsistency and bias** — Meta's own third-party report found Arabic content flagged as violating at higher rates than Hebrew content, and attributed this to uneven language/dialect resources and reviewer training rather than deliberate policy (doc_0106).
- **Contested as speech regulation** — in the US, whether moderation decisions constitute protected "editorial judgment" under the First Amendment is the central legal question in the Texas/Florida social-media laws before the Supreme Court (doc_0256).
- **A competitive and reputational lever** — platforms position their moderation stance (heavy vs. light) as a market differentiator (doc_0508; doc_0405), though the corpus notes stricter moderation alone did not guarantee growth for at least one platform, Pebble, which shut down after never gaining more than 20,000 users (doc_0026).

## Background (external)

The corpus repeatedly uses "content moderation" without ever stating a general definition for it. Content moderation, more broadly, is the systematic practice of screening user-generated content and applying a predetermined set of rules to determine whether it should be published, removed, or restricted — commonly for material judged irrelevant, obscene, illegal, harmful, or insulting — either by removing it outright, labeling it, or letting users filter it themselves (Wikipedia, *Content moderation*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# The Accredited Technology Clause And The Encryption Objection

WhatsApp, other encrypted messaging services, and digital rights groups reject the assumption that the Online Safety Act's CSAM-detection clause can be satisfied without breaking encryption: the section in question allows Ofcom to require online platforms to use so-called "accredited technology" to detect CSAM, and they say this scanning would require breaking apps' encryption systems and invading user privacy.

The objection is aimed at territory Ofcom has not yet reached. Today's consultation covers some of the act's least contentious ground, like reducing the spread of content that was already illegal in the UK. As Ofcom releases future updates it will have to take on touchier subjects, like content that is legal but harmful for children, underage access to pornography, and protections for women and girls — and, perhaps most controversially, it will need to interpret the section that critics have claimed could fundamentally undermine end-to-end encryption in messaging apps.

The matter is unresolved. Whitehead says Ofcom plans to consult on this next year, leaving the act's full impact on encrypted messaging uncertain.

Meta has internally tracked and documented under-13s, or U13s, in its audience breakdowns for years, as charts in the unredacted filing show. Internally, the numbers appear to be well documented. As the lawsuit alleges: "Meta possesses data from 2020 indicating that, out of 3,989 children surveyed, 31% of child respondents aged 6-9 and 44% of child respondents aged 10 to 12-years-old had used Facebook."
