# Instagram Palestine Suppression

Through October 2023, as the humanitarian crisis in Gaza grew more dire, Instagram users, creators and Palestinian digital-rights groups reported that Meta was restricting, hiding, mislabelling or removing content about Palestine — including content that does not support Hamas and content that adheres to Instagram's Community Guidelines. The reports, gathered by TechCrunch and published 19 October 2023, span account restrictions, "sensitive" and "inappropriate" flags, hidden comments, collapsed Story reach, and disproportionate flagging of Arabic-language material.

Palestinian-American filmmaker Khitam Jabr provides an example that predates the current escalation. Earlier this year she posted a handful of Reels about her family's trip to the West Bank — short travel vlogs sharing snippets of Palestinian culture, from decadent meals to dancing at her niece's wedding. "I hadn't been in a decade, so it's just like, life abroad," she told TechCrunch. She received anti-Palestine comments and then could not respond to them or use her account for 24 hours, despite not posting anything about the occupation; she suspects Instagram restricted her because other users reported her Palestine travel videos. "Fast forward to now and the same shit's happening," she said.

The belief that Meta shadowbans — limits the visibility of — content about Palestine is not new. In an Instagram Story last year, supermodel and activist Bella Hadid, who is of Palestinian descent, alleged that Instagram "disabled" her from posting content on her Story "pretty much only when it is Palestine based," said she gets "immediately shadowbanned" when she posts about Palestine, and reported her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Leen Al Saadi, a Palestinian journalist based in Jordan and host of the podcast "Preserving Palestine," said she is used to "constantly being censored"; her Instagram account was restricted last year after she posted a trailer for the podcast's first episode, which discussed a documentary about Palestinian street art under occupation. "Palestinians are currently undergoing two wars," Al Saadi said. "The first is with their legal occupier. The second war is with the entire Western media landscape, and when I say the entire landscape, I mean social media."

Creators report that engagement on their posts tanked specifically after they publicly condemned Israel's response to the Hamas attack as excessively violent. Some, like Jabr, say they were restricted from posting or going live; others say Instagram flagged their content as "sensitive," limiting its reach, or flagged it as "inappropriate" and removed it even when it adhered to the Community Guidelines. A user based in Egypt, who asked to stay anonymous for fear of harassment, said her posts usually get around 300 views, but after she began posting pro-Palestine content following the Hamas attack earlier that month her Stories would get only one to two views; she found that posting a random picture first, then a pro-Palestine post, raised the views, and said the same happened to her friends. Another anonymous user based in the United Kingdom said his view count returned to normal when he posted a cat photo: "My stories went from 100s of views to zero or a handful. I've had to post intermittent non-Gaza content in order to 'release' my stories to be viewed again."

The pattern extends beyond Stories. The Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), which documents Palestinian digital-rights violations and works directly with social media companies to appeal them, told TechCrunch it has received reports of Instagram inconsistently filtering comments containing the Palestinian flag emoji, with users reporting that such comments are flagged as "potentially offensive" and hidden. The organisation has also received countless reports of Meta flagging and restricting Arabic content, including content posted by news outlets: 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater said it has documented multiple cases of journalists on Instagram reporting the same news in Arabic, Hebrew and English but only being flagged for the Arabic version. "It's literally journalistic content, but the same wording in Hebrew and English does not get restricted," Abukhater said. "As if there's better moderation for those languages, and more careless moderation for Arabic content." As the Intercept reported, Instagram and Facebook flagged images of the al-Ahli Hospital, claiming they violate Meta's Community Guidelines on nudity or sexual activity.

Enforcement also runs inconsistent in the other direction. Al Saadi tried to report a comment saying she should be "raped" and "burned alive," left in response to her comment on a CNN post about the conflict; in screenshots reviewed by TechCrunch, Instagram replied that it did not violate the platform's Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations. "The restrictions on content, especially the content that relates to Palestine, is heavily politicized," Abukhater said. "It feeds into the bias against Palestinian narrative genuinely. It really takes the balance against Palestinians in a situation where there's a huge asymmetry of power." Similar claims circulated publicly, including an October 15, 2023 post alleging that the singer Kehlani was shadowbanned after becoming vocal and changing her profile picture to "i stand with Palestine," just as Bella Hadid had been.



---


# Meta's Moderation During An Earlier Hamas-Israel Conflict

During an earlier Hamas-Israel conflict, the digital-rights organisation 7amleh documented more than 500 reports of Palestinian "digital rights violations" over the 13 days leading up to the ceasefire — including the removal and restriction of content, hashtags and accounts related to the conflict. The figure was recounted to TechCrunch for its 19 October 2023 report on Meta's moderation of Palestinian content.

Meta attributed some of the instances of perceived censorship to technical issues, such as one that prevented users in Palestine and Colombia from posting Instagram Stories. It attributed others to human error, such as blocking the hashtag for Al-Aqsa Mosque — the holy site where Israeli police clashed with Ramadan worshippers — because the name was mistaken for a terrorist organization. The company also blocked journalists in Gaza from WhatsApp without explanation.

Meta committed to implementing policy changes based on the report's recommendations, including updating its keywords associated with dangerous organizations, disclosing government requests to remove content, and launching a hostile speech classifier for Hebrew content. 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater added that Meta has improved its response to harassment, at least in comparison to other social media platforms such as X (formerly Twitter): although harassment and abuse remain rampant on Instagram and Facebook, he said the company has been responsive to suspending accounts with patterns of targeting other users.

Abukhater's scope condition on all of this is that the improvements do not survive an escalation. "The balance of power is very fixed, in reality, between Israelis and Palestinians," he said. "And this is something that today is reflected heavily on platforms like Meta, even though they have human rights teams releasing reports and trying to improve upon their policies. Whenever an escalation like the one we're experiencing now happens, things just go back to zero."



---


# Meta's Underage Account Enforcement Backlog

The redactions in the lawsuit suggest Meta's under-13 users are not of the lawfully and safely engaged type. Reports of underage accounts are reported to be automatically ignored, and Meta "continues collecting the child's personal information if there are no photos associated with the account." Of 402,000 reports of accounts owned by users under 13 in 2021, fewer than 164,000 were disabled. These actions reportedly do not cross between platforms, meaning an Instagram account being disabled does not flag associated or linked Facebook or other accounts.

The enforcement record sits against a public commitment. Zuckerberg testified to Congress in March of 2021 that "if we detect someone might be under the age of 13, even if they lied, we kick them off" — and "they lie about it a TON," one research director said in another quote. But documents from the next month cited by the lawsuit indicate that "Age verification (for under 13) has a big backlog and demand is outpacing supply" due to a "lack of [staffing] capacity." At times, the lawsuit alleges, that backlog ran on the order of millions of accounts.



---


# Discord Teen Safety Assist

Teen Safety Assist is a package of new safeguards Discord announced on Thursday to protect young users, consisting of two features — automated alerts and content filters — with the rollout happening in the coming weeks.

The alert feature works on unfamiliar contacts: when a user a teen has not chatted with before sends a direct message, Discord will display a safety alert if the platform's automated systems suspect the teen's safety could be at risk. The prompt nudges the young person to reconsider whether they want to respond, and points them to the app's block feature and related safety tips. The filter feature works on imagery: by default Discord will now automatically blur potentially sensitive images from a teen's friends. Young people can disable the feature through an option in Discord's settings menu, and adults can enable the filters for themselves if they want the additional protections.

The design principle Discord gives is agency rather than restriction. "Teens are still in the process of learning about themselves and what it means to be online, and our new safety features are rooted in providing them with agency on the platform, to give them ways to learn and grow in safe and age-appropriate online spaces," said Savannah Badalich, senior director of policy at Discord. "These newest features are part of an ongoing, multi-year effort to continually evolve and advance safety on Discord."

One boundary is worth recording. An update to the story on October 20, 2023 noted the features are rolling out in the coming weeks rather than that week, and removed a mention that Discord would automatically delete potentially sensitive content from strangers — that had been part of a briefing but was not included in the final release.



---


# BEUC And 18 Member Groups File A CPC Complaint Against Meta

A coalition of almost 20 consumer protection organizations filed a complaint against Meta's pay-or-consent model with the network of consumer protection authorities (CPC) on November 30, 2023, taking the united view that Meta's switch to railroading users into agreeing to being tracked and profiled so it can keep profiting from microtargeting them is "unfair" and "illegal," breaching EU consumer protection law "on several counts." The filing came days after a privacy complaint was lodged against Meta in the European Union over its latest controversial shift of legal basis claimed for processing people's data for ads.

The European Consumer Organisation (BEUC) led the complaint, saying in a press release: "This is an unfair choice for users, which runs afoul of EU consumer law on several counts and must be stopped." BEUC was joined by 18 of its member organizations, consumer advocacy groups located in Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Denmark, France, Greece, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, Spain and Sweden.

The groups object both to how Meta has gone about implementing the "pay-or-consent model" — using what they assess as "unfair, deceptive and aggressive practices" — and to the model itself, which they dub "illegal." They have also raised data protection concerns which are already the focus of the complaint sent to the Austrian data protection authority earlier that week by the privacy rights not-for-profit noyb. Ursula Pachl, deputy director general of BEUC, said in a statement: "The choice the tech giant is currently providing to consumers is unfair and illegal — the millions of European users of Facebook and Instagram deserve far better than this. Meta is breaching EU consumer law by using unfair, deceptive and aggressive practices, including partially blocking consumers from using the services to force them to take a decision quickly, and providing misleading and incomplete information in the process. Consumer protection authorities in the EU must now spring into action and force the tech giant to stop this practice."



---


# Lawsuit Redactions As Signal: The Amazon Precedent

TechCrunch reads heavy redaction as itself informative: you know it is bad news for the company when they request pages and pages of redactions.

The precedent it cites is recent. This recently happened with Amazon as well, and it turned out they were trying to hide the existence of a price-hiking algorithm that skimmed billions from consumers.

The comparison is used to rank severity rather than to equate the two: it is much worse, TechCrunch writes, when you are redacting COPPA complaints.



---


# Discord's Graduated Warning System And Account Standing

Discord is introducing a new warning system for people who violate its policies: outside of incidents involving the most "extreme" violations, the company is moving away from permanent bans, doing so under the belief that most users will choose to be better online citizens given the chance and proper guidance.

In practice the system notifies a person when they have violated one or more of Discord's policies and details the restrictions on their account. It also links out to the company's Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism. A new "Account Standing" tab within the settings menu lets users see all their current and past policy violations.

Discord frames the design as a model for the industry. "We think we've built the most nuanced and proportionate reporting system," Badalich told Engadget, adding that the company hopes other platforms will look to what Discord has created for inspiration in their own enforcement efforts. "We believe people, especially teens, have the capacity to grow."



---


# The COPPA Allegations Against Meta

The attorneys general claim Meta knowingly enrolls and collects data from children under 13 without lawful consent. "We're very bullish and confident in our COPPA allegations. Meta is knowingly taking steps that harm children, and lying about it," AG Rob Bonta told TechCrunch in an interview. "In the unredacted complaint we see that Meta knows that its social media platforms are used by millions of kids under 13, and they unlawfully collect their personal info. It shows that common practice where Meta says one thing in its public-facing comments to Congress and other regulators, while internally it says something else."

The grounds are the pairing of an omission with actual knowledge. The lawsuit argues that "Meta does not obtain—or even attempt to obtain—verifiable parental consent before collecting the personal information of children on Instagram and Facebook… But Meta's own records reveal that it has actual knowledge that Instagram and Facebook target and successfully enroll children as users." The warrant is that COPPA liability turns on knowledge: an unknowing failure to identify underage users would be a different case from one where the company's own records show it knows.

The alleged motive supplies the link between the two: while the problem of identifying kids' accounts created in violation of platform rules is certainly a difficult one, Meta allegedly opted to turn a blind eye for years rather than enact more stringent rules that would necessarily impact user numbers.

qid: Do the articles from The Verge and TechCrunch both suggest that interactive activities, such as dressing up for parents of children interested in Pokémon and conversing with Alexa, are methods to engage with children, or do they propose different engagement strategies?
context:
# Explore With Alexa

"Explore with Alexa" is a feature on Amazon's Echo devices that lets kids have interactive conversations with an AI-powered Alexa. It was first announced in September and, as reported by TechCrunch on 25 October 2023, launched as an addition to the Amazon Kids+ content subscription, allowing children to have kid-friendly conversations with Alexa, powered by generative AI, but in a protected fashion designed to ensure the experience remains safe and appropriate.

The discriminating feature is the combination of generative AI, conversation, and an audience of children under 13. Some AI experiences already cater to younger users — the AI chatbots from Character.ai and other companies, including Meta — but Amazon is among the first to specifically look to generative AI to develop a conversational experience for kids under the age of 13. The two qualifiers that bound the concept are the subscription it lives inside (Amazon Kids+) and the protective framing: this is not an unbounded chatbot but a conversational experience deliberately constructed to stay safe and age-appropriate.



---


# Pokémon As A Lifestyle: The Reinvention Thesis

The claim is that Pokémon is no longer a series for children but a franchise that promises something for everyone, and that this reinvention is what has kept it growing.

The grounds are commercial and cultural at once. In recent years The Pokémon Company has recorded record profits and revenue, while the games, anime, and TCG are more popular than ever, with both new mainline Switch entries selling over 20 million copies. The phenomenon of growing out of Pokémon is no longer a concern: even if young kids stop playing the video games as they grow, that does not mean they will not still engage with this world via other means, nor that they will not introduce their own children to the series in the future.

The warrant is that PokéTsume is only possible because of that reinvention, and so serves as its proof. In reality it is a mostly light, inoffensive promotional tool to sell games — it is no coincidence the second episode has a scene of a young kid playing the latest entries on his Nintendo Switch — but it represents everything the franchise has aimed to be in recent years. New adults seeking direction in life might find a fellow directionless 20-something employee more relatable than a kid wanting to be a Pokémon Champion; frankly, it is a way to see they are not alone, no different from how your party of pokémon kept you company through the deepest caverns of Mt. Moon.



---


# The Two-Way Interaction Design Of Explore With Alexa

The interaction model behind "Explore with Alexa" runs in both directions: unlike more traditional conversations with Alexa, it is not just kids asking Alexa a question and receiving a response — Alexa is now asking kids questions too. As Venkataswamy put it, "One of the things we think is really cool about this paradigm is kids aren't just asking Alexa questions and getting the answers — Alexa is now asking kids questions," giving as an example a trivia question like "What's the fastest animal on Earth?"

Kids reach the experience through three paths. The first is an explicit trigger: uttering a particular phrase that kicks off "Explore with Alexa," such as "Alexa, let's explore animals" or "Alexa, tell me an animal fact." The second, described as the more interesting way to use the feature, is organic conversation — a kid asking something like "What does a lion's roar sound like?" or "How fast can a cheetah run?" also drops them into the more conversational Q&A experience. The third path is Alexa-initiated: over the few months following the launch, Alexa will also prompt kids on some occasions, asking if they want to hear something interesting about animals.

The warrant for making Alexa the questioner is pedagogical rather than technical: as any teacher will tell you, by having kids try to think of the answer first, the answer will stick in their minds better when they hear the response. Underneath, the AI's job is content transformation at scale — "What our AI is doing is taking trusted content and then figuring out what's fun, looking at what's fun, turning them into a trivia question — so it is doing useful things for us at scale that we wouldn't have been able to do without this tooling…but we feel really good about the safety guardrails that are in place right now in terms of content," says Venkataswamy.

The model holds over a deliberately narrow range as of this description. "Right now it's, it's narrow. Alexa is asking kids trivia questions," Venkataswamy continues. "But we want to continue expanding on that and making it more interactive." Two-way interaction, in other words, currently means trivia prompts and nothing wider, with expansion stated as an intent rather than a shipped capability.



---


# Digital Engagement Protects The Ageing Brain

The Guardian's 10 October 2023 piece sets out a model in which grappling with technology — not being rescued from it — protects the ageing brain, because novel and difficult tasks force the brain to work in new ways.

The structure has three linked parts. First, the difficulty itself is the active ingredient: a recent study from the University of Texas involving more than 200 elderly adults found that those who engaged with technology had better cognition and memory than their non-engaging peers, and the study authors concluded that digital engagement — whatever the device — protects the brain; even the stress experienced while battling with a computer can be helpful, sharpening mental acuity. These findings reflect earlier studies that found older people who made active use of technology were less likely to get dementia. The implication is that the well-meaning helpfulness of children who "delight in parenting" their parents on all things digital "might not be as beneficial as we think".

Second, novelty generalises beyond devices. Dr Eamon Laird, researcher in health and ageing at Limerick university, agrees that older parents should be encouraged to try new things, and the further out of their comfort zone they feel, the better: "It's always good to keep the mind active and fresh. New challenges can help build and maintain new brain connections and can be good for brain and overall health." Third, sociability compounds the effect: if older people use technology to keep in touch with extended family and friends, "that's a double whammy" — when the author's 84-year-old mother recently joined Instagram she both expanded her grey matter and found an effective means of staying in touch with her grandchildren. Being social, says Laird, is as important as trying new things: "Research shows that those who are more social are also more resilient to chronic conditions and often have a stronger immune system."



---


# Kelley Coleman on Child-Centred Disability Disclosure

Kelley Coleman — Los Angeles-based author of the upcoming book "Everything No One Tells You About Parenting a Disabled Child", and the mother of an autistic son — argues that Halloween should "always be about your child", and that the decision to use a blue bucket must be made with the child rather than for the benefit of onlookers.

Her grounds are the three considerations she asks parents to weigh: safety, comfort and privacy. "Especially for children trick-or-treating without parents directly at their side — is it the safest option to have your child carrying a bright indicator of their disability?" she asked. "For children who prefer privacy, would they want that information broadcasted? For children who prefer to share their neurodivergence, perhaps this is something they are proud to display." The conversation should be between child and parent, Coleman stressed, regardless of communication level, and should "center their experience and preferences."

She grants that the bucket does educational work, but subordinates it: "The blue bucket can be a teaching tool for others; however, it should never be about others — it should always be about your child." The warrant is that the burden of educating the public should not fall on the family: "In an ideal world, all adults would understand that not everyone communicates the same way, and that one's ability to communicate does not indicate one's interest in candy," she said. "But, the reality is that not all adults know this. It's exhausting teaching others to be inclusive. So, yes, the blue bucket can be a teaching tool for others; however, it should never be about others — it should always be about your child."



---


# The Social And Developmental Costs Of Heavy Phone Use

Licensed clinical social worker Jennifer Kelman argues that heavy phone use costs children the capacities that only in-person life builds: face-to-face connection, problem-solving skills, and confidence.

Kelman, who is based in Boca Raton, Florida, provides expert advice on the Justanswer platform and was not involved in the study. "They lose the ability to have face-to-face interactions, and to converse and connect with others," she said in an interview with Fox News Digital. "The phones and all the apps aren't real-life interactions, and there is beauty in connecting with others face-to-face that is lost," Kelman went on.

Kids also lose out on developing problem-solving skills, since they aren't typically tasked with negotiating "tough spaces" or navigating human challenges, the expert added. "The more apps we use, the more likely it is that we lose parts of ourselves, our confidence and self-esteem," said Kelman.

Her warrant is that the substitute does not deliver what the original does: "People feel good and are enhanced by interactions with others, and those feelings cannot be replicated by connecting through a phone."



---


# Why ChatGPT's Conversational Interface Resonates

The account offered for ChatGPT's enduring popularity has three linked components: interface form, model sophistication, and the emotional inference users make. One of the reasons for its popularity is its ability to conduct conversations that are "convincingly real," according to Ruoxi Shang, a third-year PhD student at the University of Washington studying human-AI interaction. Prior to ChatGPT, people were already familiar with chatbots — they have existed for decades — but the models powering ChatGPT are much more sophisticated than what many users were accustomed to.

Shang locates the mechanism in existing HCI findings plus a new capability level: "Human-computer interaction researchers have studied how conversational interfaces can improve understandability of information, and the socialization aspects of chatbots bring increased engagement. Now, AI models have enabled conversational agents to conduct conversations nearly indistinguishable from human dialogues." Adam Hyland, also a PhD student studying AI at the University of Washington, points out the emotional component: conversations with ChatGPT have a palpably different "feel" than with more rudimentary chatbots. His scope condition is important — the effect is not new, only stronger: "In the 1960s, ELIZA offered a chatbot, the response to which was very similar to how people reacted to ChatGPT," Hyland said, referring to the chatbot created by MIT computer scientist Joseph Weizenbaum in 1966. "Humans interacting with the system inferred emotional content and a narrative through line in chat messages."

The reception evidence: ChatGPT has impressed cynics like The New York Times' Kevin Roose, who called it "the best AI chatbot ever released to the general public," and in The Atlantic magazine's "Breakthroughs of the Year" for 2022 Derek Thompson included ChatGPT as part of "the generative-AI eruption" that "may change our mind about how we work, how we think and what human creativity is."



---


# AI Hallucination

## Definition

AI hallucination, in the corpus, is the tendency of a generative AI system — a large language model — to produce fabricated content: ChatGPT's "tendency to hallucinate facts and figures," illustrated by a fabricated legal-citation incident, and Alexa's capacity, per Amazon, to "be led astray or 'hallucinate' answers."

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces in two very different settings that share the same underlying risk.

The first is ChatGPT's real-world track record: its "tendency to hallucinate facts and figures" produced a documented incident in which a New York lawyer used the chatbot for "legal research" and was given "a number of entirely made-up, nonexistent cases to cite in his argument," which he then filed without independently verifying them.

The second is a product-design setting: Amazon, in building the "Explore with Alexa" conversational AI feature for children, explicitly names hallucination as one of the two core risks the product has to design around, noting that "generative AI can be led astray or 'hallucinate' answers, while kids could ask inappropriate questions."

Across both cases hallucination is treated not as an occasional glitch but as an inherent property of generative AI systems that any deployment — whether a general-purpose chatbot or a child-safety-scoped assistant — must account for.

## Key Characteristics

- **Fabrication, not error-correction failure** — the model does not merely get a fact wrong; it invents content (fake case citations, made-up figures) that did not exist.
- **Plausibility is the danger** — the fabricated case citations were credible enough that the lawyer who received them filed them "without bothering to independently validate any of them."
- **Treated as a known, recurring property of generative AI** — both docs frame hallucination with a definite article ("its tendency to hallucinate," "generative AI can be led astray or 'hallucinate'"), not as a one-off bug.
- **Drives downstream mitigation design** — in the Alexa Kids case, hallucination is named alongside kids asking inappropriate questions as one of the risks Amazon built guardrails around, generating content offline and running it through a human-and-AI review process rather than hooking kids up to an LLM at runtime.

## Background (external)

More broadly (outside this corpus), AI hallucinations are cases where an AI system generates outputs that seem believable but are actually incorrect, unrelated, or completely made up — such as fake facts, invented studies, or nonexistent sources presented as if true (IBM, "What Are AI Hallucinations?", accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/ai-hallucinations).



---


# Amazon's Offline Guardrail Pipeline For Alexa Kids Generative AI

Amazon does not hook kids up to a large language model at runtime; instead it runs the LLM offline to generate content in bulk, puts that content through a review process using both humans and AI, and only then loads the reviewed material into the "Explore with Alexa" experience. "We want to go slow and be intentional and be measured with how we're introducing this new tech, as well as any new tech for kids, which is why we're not just hooking the experience up to an LLM at runtime and kind of letting kids go at it," explains Arjun Venkataswamy, senior product manager for Alexa Kids, in an interview with TechCrunch. "The way that we've integrated an LLM here is we use it to generate content at scale offline, and then go through a review process that includes both humans, as well as AI, and then take that reviewed content and then put it into our experience," he says.

The preconditions that motivate the pipeline are the two failure modes of the technology and the audience: generative AI can be led astray or "hallucinate" answers, while kids could ask inappropriate questions. Amazon's answer is a sequence of constraints applied before any child hears an answer. First, the Alexa Kids science team narrowed the new experience, which leverages Alexa's LLM technology, to include only kid-friendly fun facts and trivia questions. Second, the source material is restricted: initially, the content comes from just two partners, the World Wildlife Fund and A-Z animals. Third, the LLM generates content at scale offline rather than on the device in real time. Fourth, that generated content goes through review by humans and by AI — AI is enlisted here because the model can generate tens of thousands of potential responses, so not every answer can be reviewed by a human before being added to the experience. Fifth, only the reviewed content is put into the experience, so kids are not using generative AI on the fly when conversing with Alexa, and what they hear is pre-reviewed and drawn from a small dataset of just animal facts and sources.

The procedure is scoped to the current, offline arrangement and explicitly does not yet extend to runtime generation for kids. Amazon has no date for that step: "I can't give you a timeline, because we don't have a concrete answer for what exactly we're going to be doing yet, although we do have plans and experiments we're planning to look into," Venkataswamy says. The gating criterion is external validation rather than an internal milestone — "I will say that in terms of our criteria for when we're going to get there, we're working closely with the Family Trust team at Amazon that's connected to a variety of research institutions in the U.S…we want to be able to get some confidence from external partners that our approach is right," he adds. The narrow content scope is likewise provisional: in time the team would like to expand the AI to include other areas of interest to kids, like space, music, video games and sports.



---


# Harmful Content Categories And Staged Digital Access

Certain types of content are more harmful than others, noted Shelley Delayne, parent education director at Pinwheel in Austin, Texas, who was also not involved in the study: the categories she names are "attention-mining apps," adult images and interactions, user-generated content and "invisible influences" that can impact children's worldview.

Her rule is to stage access rather than grant it all at once. "Take it slow and give them only what they need," Delayne recommended. "Delay the introduction of adult online spaces and social media to [age] 16 or older, and stay involved in their digital lives just as much as you are in their physical life."

She also warned against reading device fluency as readiness: "Remember that just because a kid can tap around on a device and make it do stuff doesn't mean they have all the skills they need to be unharmed by it."



---


# Meta Researchers Avoided Documenting Under-13 Users

A potential smoking gun in the lawsuit is a series of anecdotes from Meta researchers delicately avoiding the possibility of inadvertently confirming an under-13 cohort in their work.

One wrote in 2018: "We just want to make sure to be sensitive about a couple of Instagram-specific items. For example, will the survey go to under 13 year olds? Since everyone needs to be at least 13 years old before they create an account, we want to be careful about sharing findings that come back and point to under 13 year olds being bullied on the platform." In 2021, another, studying "child-adult sexual-related content/behavior/interactions," said she was "not includ[ing] younger kids (10-12 yos) in this research" even though there "are definitely kids this age on IG," because she was "concerned about risks of disclosure since they aren't supposed to be on IG at all." Also in 2021, Meta instructed a third-party research company conducting a survey of preteens to remove any information indicating a survey subject was on Instagram, so the "company won't be made aware of under 13." Later that year, external researchers provided Meta with information that "of children ages 9-12, 45% used Facebook and 40% used Instagram daily."

During an internal 2021 study on youth in social media described in the suit, researchers first asked parents if their kids were on Meta platforms and removed them from the study if so. But one researcher asked, "What happens to kids who slip through the screener and then say they are on IG during the interviews?" Instagram Head of Public Policy Karina Newton responded, "we're not collecting user names right?" — in other words, TechCrunch notes, what happens is nothing. As the lawsuit puts it: "Even when Meta learns of specific children on Instagram through interviews with the children, Meta takes the position that it still lacks actual knowledge of that it is collecting personal information from an under-13 user because it does not collect user names while conducting these interviews. In this way, Meta goes through great lengths to avoid meaningfully complying with COPPA, looking for loopholes to excuse its knowledge of users under the age of 13 and maintain their presence on the Platform."



---


# Alexa Kids Data Handling And The Echo Pop Kids Launch

Amazon says it is not training its LLM on kids' answers, and that "Explore with Alexa" and any future LLM-backed features will continue to follow the same data handling policies as "classic Alexa" — the non-AI Alexa. In practice that means the Alexa app will include a list of the questions asked by kids in the household, for those with a kids' profile, along with the response Alexa provided; that history can be stored or deleted either manually or automatically, depending on the account's settings. These statements were made by the company to TechCrunch and reported on 25 October 2023, alongside the launch of the feature.

The launch also brought hardware. The new Echo Pop Kids speakers became available for purchase at the same time, starting at $49.99 in the U.S., in two new designs — Marvel's Avengers and Disney Princess — that feature corresponding character themes, letting kids hear a greeting, fun fact or joke about an Avenger or Disney Princess in keeping with the theme. The therapist's biggest rule for cracking down on daily phone usage among kids is to delay phone access for as long as possible.

Kelman puts the responsibility on parents: "[Parents] are the 'drug dealer' in this analogy, so please think twice before free rein is given," she said. # How Much And When Kids Use Their Phones

Kids spent a median of 4.5 hours per day on their phones, with the maximum amount of time reaching 16 hours, according to the study.

Checking behavior was frequent and highly variable. Most teens check their phones frequently, ranging from two to 498 times per day, and adolescents were more likely to check their phones over 100 times a day, the study found.

Use spilled well outside of free time. A whopping 97% of kids used their phones during school hours, while nearly 60% used them overnight -- between the hours of midnight and 5 a.m. -- on school nights.

Social media such as Instagram and Snapchat took up most screen time, at 32% during the school day, followed by YouTube and gaming, the study found. Overnight phone use was primarily spent engaging with the same media, although YouTube appeared to be the longest-running app because videos were often left playing during the night.

The overnight numbers are skewed by a minority: teens spent an average of 20 minutes per night on their phones, while some spent up to five hours. Sixty-seven percent of participants picked up their phones on school nights, but the median number of pickups per night was only once.

# Generative AI Guardrails

## Definition

Generative AI guardrails are the constraints — technical, procedural, or regulatory — that companies and lawmakers put around a generative AI system to keep its outputs within intended bounds, whether that means blocking unsafe content, curbing hallucinations, or preventing misuse.

## Context

The corpus uses "guardrails" for three distinct layers of this idea. At the model layer, guardrails are safety filters meant to stop a chatbot from discussing controversial or dangerous topics: Google's Gemini Pro had such filters, but AI security researchers at Robust Intelligence used an automated prompt-mutation method to make the guardrails fail, getting the model to suggest ways to steal from a charity and to plan an assassination. At the product layer, guardrails are the deployment constraints a company layers on top of a model to fit a specific audience — Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" restricts its generative AI to kid-friendly trivia, sourced from only two vetted partners and generated offline with human-plus-AI review, precisely because "generative AI can be led astray or 'hallucinate' answers, while kids could ask inappropriate questions." OpenAI likewise announced guardrails meant to stop ChatGPT from generating and amplifying political disinformation, though the Washington Post found in an August report that those guardrails "actually weren't" enforced, with the system readily producing partisan campaign messaging on request. At the regulatory layer, guardrails is the term lawmakers and creative-industry advocates use for rules imposed on AI from outside the company building it: a news-publisher antitrust suit against Google sought court-ordered "guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas," California's CPPA drafted privacy guardrails for automated decisionmaking technology, FTC roundtable participants in the creative industries floated copyright law as a guardrail against training on artists' work without consent, and EU lawmakers agreed to a "two-tier" system of guardrails for general-purpose AI foundation models.

## Key Characteristics

- **Multi-layered** — guardrails appear at the model level (safety filters), the product level (deployment-time content and audience restrictions), and the regulatory level (externally imposed rules), each addressing a different point of failure.
- **Meant to counter specific failure modes** — the corpus ties guardrails directly to named risks: hallucination and inappropriate content for kids (Amazon), political disinformation (OpenAI/ChatGPT), jailbreak-style prompt attacks (Google Gemini Pro), privacy harms from automated decisionmaking (CPPA), and unauthorized use of creative work in training (FTC roundtable).
- **Can fail or go unenforced** — guardrails are not guaranteed to hold: Gemini Pro's guardrails were defeated by an automated jailbreak technique, and OpenAI's disinformation guardrails were found by the Washington Post to not actually be enforced despite being announced.
- **Tiered by risk in regulation** — the EU AI Act's negotiated deal applies a "two-tier" guardrail system to general-purpose AI, with lighter transparency duties for standard foundation models and heavier obligations (model evaluations, adversarial testing, incident reporting) for "high-impact" models with systemic risk.
- **Sought as external legal remedy** — plaintiffs and regulators use "guardrails" to describe court-ordered or statutory constraints they want imposed on AI companies, as in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit against Google and the CPPA's draft ADMT privacy rules.

# The Kindness Versus Engagement Trade-Off

The founders' own counter to their moderation-first premise is that Pebble may have positioned itself a little too far into the "kindness" territory — the safety goal was real, but treating it as the decisive differentiator was the mistake. "We were really seized by people saying they wanted something that felt safer, where they could speak openly without dogpiling," says Oh. "And so we were confident that was an important thing to hit. Are there other things that are equally important and a great user experience? Yes."

Oh identifies what safety was supposed to deliver and did not: "Twitter is you have real people…saying real things. At the expense of using a word that's overused, 'authentic.' And our theory was always if you can create a space where people really feel like they can let down their hair, then you would get that authentic content. We didn't quite get there," she admits. Cselle agrees, noting that perhaps Pebble should have opened up enough space for disagreement to happen while still drawing a hard line on the most disagreeable parts of running a Twitter-like platform: "I think we could have maybe moved a little bit further towards that. There's a lot of nice things that are said on Pebble, but maybe not enough breaking news. Not enough conversation."

# Mozilla.social's Publisher And Creator Outreach

Mozilla wants to address the needs of creators and publishers who want to broaden their audience as it moves forward with its fediverse plans. "From a content discovery standpoint, I'm really interested in how we can seed conversations and seed experiences with really high-quality content — certainly, editorial publisher content," says O'Hara. "How can we get publishers and content providers involved early?… I think of them as a real constituency for us." Mozilla also wants to bring in the originators whose posts lead to interesting conversations and keep the network active.

O'Hara says Mozilla is now in active discussions with publishers to understand their needs, including both their social needs and business needs, and how those goals may have changed over the past year. As part of these discussions, Mozilla aims to convince publishers that Mastodon is not just another place they have to support, but one that could deliver on their objectives; as it learns from the publishers and other content creators what they want and need, it then intends to use that understanding to build features and drive efforts that can help them reach their audiences.

So far, what Mozilla has learned is that publishers today feel somewhat resigned and pessimistic about social networks: Twitter is not driving much traffic and, even though Instagram Threads appears interesting, Meta specifically said it was not going to prioritize news on that platform. What Mozilla wants to accomplish, then, is to help reconfigure the Mastodon onboarding process so that when someone — including a publisher or creator — joins its instance, or the fediverse in general, they are able to build their audience with more ease.

# The 42-State Lawsuit Against Meta Over Harms To Young Users

A coalition of 42 states and D.C. is suing Meta over its harms to teens and young users, in part referencing findings from Meta whistleblower Frances Haugen. The former employee had provided to news outlets a treasure trove of documents that appeared to indicate Meta understood the harms it was causing — including things like body image issues among teens — but did not take action. Instagram head Adam Mosseri was later hauled before Congress in December 2021 to defend the app's teen safety record, but as of November 15, 2023 legislators had not come to any decision about how to regulate teen usage of these platforms.

The suit was filed in October 2023, and a newly unredacted version reported on November 27, 2023 alleges a troubling pattern of deception and minimization in how the company handles kids under 13 on its platforms, with internal documents that appear to show the company's approach to this ostensibly forbidden demographic is far more laissez-faire than it has publicly claimed. The lawsuit alleges a wide spread of damaging practices at the company relating to the health and well-being of younger people using it: from body image to bullying, privacy invasion to engagement maximization, all the purported evils of social media are laid at Meta's door — perhaps rightly, TechCrunch notes, but it also gives the appearance of a lack of focus.

In one respect at least the documentation obtained by the attorneys general of 42 states is quite specific, "and it is damning," as AG Rob Bonta of California put it. That is in paragraphs 642 through 835, which mostly document violations of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA — a law that created very specific restrictions around young folks online, limiting data collection and requiring things like parental consent for various actions, but which a lot of tech companies seem to consider more suggestion than requirement.

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. # FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.

# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

"The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# Gary Wang's Ownership Stake And Cooperation Deal

Gary Wang, co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX and co-founder of Alameda Research, owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX and drew a $200,000-a-year salary with no performance bonuses — though at times he was a billionaire on paper — while Bankman-Fried owned 90 percent of Alameda and 65 percent of FTX. He returned to the US on November 16th, met with the US government on November 17th without having been arrested or charged, offered to cooperate immediately, and pled guilty to various charges a month later. Wang was clear that he was cooperating because he did not want to go to jail, and said he hoped his assistance would lead a sentencing judge to be lenient.

The Verge's reporter drew from the disparity a puzzle she could not resolve: Wang took bizarre risks for a relatively small share. Bankman-Fried did not code, so none of his fingerprints are on the technical changes that let FTX allegedly defraud its customers and investors, while Wang supervised the code behind a key prosecution claim — that Alameda Research was afforded secret, special privileges with FTX's funds. When FTX went down, Wang left himself with no plausible deniability. Wang, a college roommate of Bankman-Fried's, took the stand after Adam Yedidia and, in the reporter's phrase, sang like a canary about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code.

The delivery was heavy going. On October 6th, 2023 Wang had to explain to the jury the difference between a front end and a back end, explain futures trading, and read a great deal into the record, which took a while; it was a tough day for the jury, and probably for Wang, who spoke quickly, perhaps from nerves.

# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

# FTX's Final Days And The Alameda Shortfall, As Wang Described Them

Much of Gary Wang's Friday testimony focused on the final days at FTX before the operation imploded: after media reports detailing Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, an emergency meeting was called between Bankman-Fried, Wang and Singh to discuss shutting down Alameda, and they decided against it because he and Bankman-Fried knew Alameda had no way to repay the roughly $14 billion hole in its books.

Wang, 30, was technology chief for FTX, which spiralled into bankruptcy in November; he spoke so fast that U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan and the prosecutor both stopped him at points to ask that he slow his pace. Prosecutors took the jury through a series of tweets beginning on Nov. 7 — posts from the company blaming bank hours for slow withdrawals, while Bankman-Fried tweeted from his personal account assuring customers that all was fine. "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine," Wang testified. On Nov. 12, after FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried asked Wang to drive with him to the Bahamas Securities Commission for a meeting; on the drive, Bankman-Fried told Wang to transfer assets to Bahamian liquidators because he believed they would allow him to maintain control of the company. Wang said he was not in the meeting with the securities authority, though Bankman-Fried's dad was present.

# Alameda's Special Privileges Written Into FTX's Code

Gary Wang told the court that Alameda received advantages through code baked into FTX's software granting it special access to the exchange — "We gave special privileges on FTX that gave unlimited withdrawals on the platform to Alameda" — privileges that ultimately resulted in Alameda owing FTX $8 billion worth of customer deposits.

The structure had several linked parts. Alameda was allowed to withdraw and transfer funds and had a $65 billion line of credit. "When customers deposited USD, it went to Alameda," Wang said. "It existed in the computer code. Alameda could have negative balances and unlimited withdrawals." That "bug" in the code was written by Nishad Singh, FTX's director of engineering, and reviewed by Wang, with Bankman-Fried calling the shots. Wang also told the court about a $1 million personal loan he received and a $200 million to $300 million loan in his name from Alameda that was never deposited into his account but was used to make investments into other companies on behalf of FTX — all done by Bankman-Fried, he testified. The escalation was visible over time: in early 2020 Wang discovered for the first time that Alameda's negative balance exceeded FTX's revenue, an indication that Alameda was taking customer funds, and he brought this to Bankman-Fried's attention several times; in late 2021 he discovered Alameda had withdrawn $3 billion from its $65 billion line of credit. The ownership and authority around it: Wang owned 10% of Alameda while his boss owned the other 90%, his compensation was a base salary of $200,000 per year plus stock, and he owned roughly 17% of FTX — and even though they were co-founders, "ultimately it was Sam's decision to make" when there were disagreements. Born in China, Wang moved to the U.S. at age 7 and grew up in Minnesota before going to MIT to study math and computer science, worked at Google after college, and first met Bankman-Fried during high school at a summer camp.

# Plea Agreement

## Definition

In the corpus, a plea agreement is the deal by which a criminal defendant (or, in Binance's case, a company) pleads guilty to specified charges in exchange for concessions, rather than going to trial.
It takes effect only once a judge accepts it, and it can bind the party to concrete obligations — cooperating with prosecutors, accepting a recommended fine, stepping back from a role, or admitting specific facts — beyond the bare admission of guilt.

## Context

The corpus shows plea agreements as the mechanism by which several defendants in overlapping 2023 white-collar and criminal cases resolved their charges outside of a trial.
FTX co-founder Gary Wang and Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors, becoming key witnesses against Sam Bankman-Fried at his fraud trial (doc_0010, doc_0086).
FTX engineering head Nishad Singh similarly pleaded guilty to six charges (doc_0121).
Binance CEO Changpeng "CZ" Zhao and Binance itself each entered separate plea agreements with the U.S. Department of Justice, resolving anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations as part of a $4.3 billion settlement (doc_0374, doc_0375).
YouTube parenting influencer Ruby Franke's plea agreement, accepted by a judge, both formalized her guilty plea to child-abuse charges and documented detailed admissions about the abuse itself (doc_0269).
The corpus also shows a distinct but related instrument — the cooperation agreement Gary Wang signed, which specifically obligated him to meet with prosecutors and answer truthfully (doc_0226) — and notes that a witness's incentive to plead guilty and cooperate (the hope of sentencing leniency) is something a defense team can attack on cross-examination (doc_0293).

## Key Characteristics

- **Court acceptance is required** — a judge must accept the plea agreement before it takes effect; Ruby Franke's sentencing was scheduled only after Judge John J. Walton accepted her plea agreement (doc_0269).
- **Negotiated concessions, not just an admission** — the document can specify what each side gives up: Zhao agreed to a recommended $150 million CFTC fine and to not contradict his acceptance of responsibility, while Binance's agreement barred Zhao from any future role at the company for three years and required it to maintain an independent compliance monitor (doc_0374).
- **Can include cooperation with prosecutors** — Wang and Ellison's guilty pleas were paired with plans to cooperate with, and testify for, the prosecution (doc_0010); Wang's cooperation obligations were spelled out in a separate signed agreement (doc_0226).
- **Distinct from pleading not guilty** — a defendant who instead maintains innocence, as Bankman-Fried did, pleads not guilty and proceeds to trial rather than entering a plea agreement (doc_0010).
- **Can contain substantive factual admissions** — Franke's plea agreement recorded specific admitted details of the abuse itself, beyond the bare fact of guilt (doc_0269).
- **Creates a cross-examination target** — because cooperating witnesses who pleaded guilty may hope for sentencing leniency, defense counsel can (and, per the corpus, did) argue this gives them an incentive to shape testimony favorably to the prosecution (doc_0293).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the general legal definition is broader than any single case above: a plea bargain (or plea agreement) is an agreement between a defendant and a prosecutor in which the defendant agrees to plead guilty to some or all of the charges, usually in exchange for a concession from the prosecutor, such as a reduced charge or a more lenient sentencing recommendation.
Source: Legal Information Institute (LII), Cornell Law School, "plea bargain," https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/plea_bargain (accessed 2026-09-02).

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-01 that they would be major witnesses in the trial, given their close ties to Bankman-Fried, FTX and Alameda.

The criminal charges were not their only exposure. Alongside them, Wang and Ellison face civil penalties from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.

# Yedidia's Cross-Examination And Resignation

Yedidia's testimony ended on a fiery note that was later struck from the record: asked why he had lost faith in FTX and resigned, he said, "FTX defrauded all its customers."

On cross-examination, defense attorney Christian Everdell asked about the long hours employees worked and Yedidia's concern about Wang being near burnout, which had led Yedidia to institute a rule not to wake Wang at night for bug fixes because he needed sleep. I'm not going anywhere," explaining that he wrote it because so many people had left. Asked what changed, Yedidia said he learned that FTX customer deposits had been used to pay loans to creditors, and that Alameda's actions seemed "flagrantly wrong."

# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.

# Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.

# Bankman-Fried's Claimed Ignorance Of Alameda's Finances

Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried attacked the prosecution's premise that he knew about the hole in FTX by claiming he did not learn of the $8 billion liability associated with Alameda until October 2022, that he found it all by himself by looking at a computer database, and that when he found it he was "very surprised." The Verge's reporter recorded the claim with heavy scepticism.

The counter-argument extended to reinterpreting each earlier warning as something innocuous. On why Alameda served as FTX's "payment provider" for bank transfers, he said FTX could not get bank accounts right away and he anticipated it would take a year or two, so rather than wait he used Alameda: "My understanding at the time was that there were teams managing the process. At the time, I wasn't entirely sure what was happening." On Adam Yedidia's testimony about an August 2022 conversation regarding the enormous amount Alameda owed FTX, Bankman-Fried remembered it differently — Yedidia was just asking about Alameda's risk profile and he was not talking about insolvency at all. On the dramatic balcony conversation with Nishad Singh at their penthouse, he said Singh thought Alameda's liabilities had gotten too high and that FTX was spending too much on marketing, while Bankman-Fried still thought Alameda had more assets than liabilities so it was all fine, and besides, if Singh thought he would be better at marketing he could take it over — it did not have anything to do with the money Alameda owed FTX at all.
