# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. Later Alameda's balance was more negative than FTT and the trading revenue combined, and Wang had further conversations with Bankman-Fried about it. Wang testified he knew at the time that Alameda was using FTX customers' funds and that he knew it was wrong.

The same gradual accommodation shows in Ellison's account. Choking back tears, she testified: "When I started working at Alameda, I don't think I would have believed you if you told me I would be sending false balance sheets to our lenders or taking customer money, but over time, it was something I became more comfortable with."



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Sassoon's Redirect And The Alameda All-Hands Recording

Prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's brief redirect of Caroline Ellison on October 12th, 2023 set a trap that opened the door to the jury hearing a secret recording of an Alameda all-hands meeting in which Ellison confessed to stealing billions of FTX customers' money at Bankman-Fried's direction. On direct examination, near the end, Sassoon had asked about the all-hands meeting without bringing up many specifics; during the cross, Mark Cohen asked Ellison what topics were covered in the meeting while avoiding details — which let Sassoon work the confession in on redirect. The judge then ruled in favour of the jury hearing the recordings, and the court briefly recessed; that was when Bankman-Fried's mother approached the defense lawyers.

The tape was set up by a short afternoon witness. Christian Drappi, a former Alameda software engineer who looked like a handsome funeral director in a black suit and tie, testified that when Binance CEO Changpeng Zhao announced on Twitter that he intended to acquire FTX, Ellison confessed the theft of customer funds to him and a few other employees. The all-hands took place the following day and was secretly recorded by an employee who had joined Alameda three days before. In the recording Ellison did indeed confess to stealing customer funds with Bankman-Fried's approval. Drappi said he resigned less than 24 hours after the meeting; the recording was later sent to him, and he sent it to the government.

The reporter's assessment was that Sassoon demolished any points Cohen had attempted to make and that she did not fully appreciate the cleverness until after Ellison left the stand and the jurors left the room. In the family seats, Joseph Bankman, the defendant's father and a senior advisor to FTX's philanthropic arm, was not in the room for the recording, and Barbara Fried looked unhappy, rubbing her left temple as though she had a tremendous headache.



---


# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.



---


# Defense Opening Statement: The Plane Metaphor

Defense attorney Mark Cohen answered the prosecution's opening not with evidence but with a metaphor: working at a startup, he told the jury with the energy of a patient father telling his obnoxious children a bedtime story, was like building a plane while flying it, and FTX the plane had flown right into the perfect storm of the crypto crash. The premise this attacks is the prosecution's claim of intentional theft — Cohen's counter was that Bankman-Fried "acted in good faith and took reasonable business measures," that FTX's and Alameda's business relationships were "reasonable under the circumstances," and, in the common white-collar defense form, that Bankman-Fried as CEO was simply too busy to oversee what everyone did every day. He also blamed Caroline Ellison and Binance CEO Changpeng "CZ" Zhao for the debacle.

The Verge's reporter judged the counter-argument self-defeating, because Cohen volunteered a fact the prosecution had not raised: FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit." That admission cuts against the good-faith premise — the lack of a risk officer kept elbowing her in the ribs as Cohen argued reasonableness, and the too-busy-to-supervise line made her more suspicious, since delegating oversight is exactly why you hire a risk officer. Cohen's own characterisation of his client worked the same way: Bankman-Fried was a math nerd who did not party, which paints a picture of someone deliberate, especially given that he left MIT immediately and went to work on Wall Street; a party-hardy trainwreck might plausibly overlook hiring a risk officer, but a deliberate person would not.

The context was that the defense had no plea to fall back on: the reporter had learned the day before that Bankman-Fried had never been offered a plea deal, since he and his attorneys had told the government they would not negotiate, which made her curious what evidence had made him so confident. The answer, she wrote, was instead a metaphor — and it is no good when your defense lawyer has just made you sound worse than the prosecution already did.



---


# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."



---


# The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse

FTX came apart in early November 2022 through a chain with four links: a leaked balance sheet revealed that Alameda's largest holding was FTX's own token in a quantity larger than the token's whole market, the disclosure destroyed confidence, the world's largest rival exchange pulled its holdings out, and the resulting bank run forced FTX and Alameda into Chapter 11 within days. TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account sets out the sequence: in early November 2022, that all changed.

Concerns surrounding FTX's liquidity grew after CoinDesk published a copy of Alameda's balance sheet, showing the firm held $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. The balance sheet showed that the $5.82 billion in FTT tokens that Alameda owned was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap, which was about $3 billion at the time — meaning Alameda purported to have more FTT tokens on its balance sheet than what existed in the world. Around the same time it was exposed, the world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, started pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT; Binance had held an equity position in FTX from 2019 to 2021. That withdrawal essentially triggered a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. mid-November 2022, Bankman-Fried resigned, and John J. Ray III, the Enron turnaround veteran, was appointed the new CEO.

The condition the whole mechanism rests on is the fragility of the underlying valuations. As TechCrunch put it on 2023-10-02, all of that activity came to a crashing end because the value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value — so when those valuations fell, they fell very, very hard. The chain therefore only runs as described where an asset is priced on expectation, held in size by a related party, and exposed to a counterparty large enough that its exit alone starts the run.



---


# Allow_negative: Alameda's Exemption From FTX Liquidation

"Allow_negative" was a column in FTX's account database that exempted Alameda Research — and only Alameda — from the exchange's automated liquidation, letting Alameda hold a negative balance and withdraw money its accounts did not have. Gary Wang testified that it originated in a code commit dated July 31st, 2019 under Nishad Singh's username, titled "OTC trades and transfers to special accounts." Written in Python, it added two columns to the account database, the relevant one being "allow_negative," a toggle that when on let the account go negative; the feature was switched on the same day by a second set of code also carrying Singh's username, and Wang said he supervised.

The structure it modified was FTX's risk management. As Wang explained it, a futures exchange is the middleman that lets strangers bet with each other: it sits between the two ends of the bet, paying the winner and collecting from the loser, which is why it requires collateral, and under some circumstances it automatically sells that collateral to limit its losses. On FTX this liquidation process was automated and took about 30 seconds to find the accounts that needed to be liquidated to minimize FTX's losses. Normal customers — the defense objected to "normal" and was overruled — could be automatically liquidated, but not Alameda. Wang testified that Bankman-Fried "told me a few times to make sure that Alameda's account is never liquidated on FTX," and that "the code addition was the result of those conversations." Alongside the exemption, Alameda could place orders faster than other users and held an enormous line of credit, and the court saw evidence that users may have unwittingly deposited money into Alameda rather than FTX.

The relation holds only for Alameda: no other customer trading on FTX had allow_negative privileges, and the same day the toggle was switched on in July 2019, Bankman-Fried tweeted that Alameda "is a liquidity provider on FTX, but their account is just like everyone else's" — a tweet shown in court, and to The Verge's reporter evidence that the fraud at FTX started very early, just months after FTX was founded. Bankman-Fried offered a competing origin story from the stand: FTX's big selling point was its "risk engine," which in 2020 was "effectively sagging under the weight" of the exchange's rapid growth so that time to liquidation stretched to minutes, and at one point the engine got stuck in a catastrophic feedback loop that would have created losses in the "trillions of dollars," with Alameda teetering on the brink of a liquidation that "would have disastrous consequences" for FTX. "At the time, I wasn't entirely sure what was happening," he testified, saying that because of that experience he suggested an "alert" or "delay" to keep Alameda from being liquidated by a bug, that allow_negative was the eventual result of that conversation, and that he did not know about it until very recently. The dates do not fit: allow_negative was coded and switched on in 2019, and the code was displayed in court in front of Bankman-Fried and the jury.



---


# Alameda Absorbed FTX's Losses, Including MobileCoin

Alameda Research functioned as FTX's sin-eater: when FTX took a loss, the loss was moved onto Alameda's balance sheet so that FTX would not look bad. Gary Wang testified that in 2021 FTX was facing a "several hundred million dollar" loss from an exploit in MobileCoin — apparently in April 2021, though Wang did not give a month — and Bankman-Fried directed him to have Alameda take it on instead, because FTX's balance sheets were visible to investors and Alameda's were not.

The relation was general, not a one-off. Ellison testified that her tenure as CEO of Alameda Research was an exercise in optics: when FTX took a loss in the hundreds of millions of dollars because a trader had exploited its system, Wang moved that loss onto Alameda's balance sheet, and FTX's "insurance fund," meant to keep traders from getting stuck with other traders' losses, was totally made up, with Alameda simply picking up the tab. The concealment held all the way to investors: Paradigm Capital's Matt Huang showed the court the balance sheets he had received from Bankman-Fried, and they did not include the loss, which should have appeared in the second-quarter numbers he was given — those instead showed $63 million in trading expenses and $63 million in "other expenses" for the quarter, and an estimated profit of $732 million.

Bankman-Fried offered a benign reading of the same arrangement from the stand: he said the MobileCoin loss, the one Wang said Alameda took to keep off FTX's balance sheet, was a totally innocent matter in which he thought it appropriate that Alameda take the position as a backstop liquidity provider.



---


# FTX's Spending Served Bankman-Fried's Status, Not Philanthropy

The Verge's reporter argued that at every turn the scams at FTX and Alameda led back to making Bankman-Fried more important — not to giving money away, as his stated Effective Altruism rationale claimed. The grounds are the pattern of what the money bought: Singh testified to more than a billion dollars spent on celebrity endorsements, which made FTX very famous even though the futures platform did not operate in the US; the political donations gave Bankman-Fried influence in the highest echelons of power; and Ellison testified to venture investments that gave him more dominance in the tech world.

The warrant joining the pattern to the conclusion is that spending reveals priorities better than statements do: it is easy to lie with words and harder to lie with money. Bankman-Fried went around telling people he wanted to make a lot of money in order to give it away, an idea of the Effective Altruism movement he affiliated himself with, but the amount he funneled to his Paper Bird vehicle alone was ten times the size of his philanthropic spending as outlined by the prosecution's expert Peter Easton — and all of it was vastly outweighed by his investments, the places where he could prove he was very smart by investing in the right companies early.

# Scott McTominay's Advanced Role And Goal Threat

Under Ten Hag, Scott McTominay functions as a marauding midfield engine and late-running goal threat with a licence to create overloads wherever he finds them — the job United once paid Paul Pogba to do.

The structure of the role differs from his previous, more conventional midfield positions. Against low blocks and structured defences — and, the piece notes, nobody is remotely accusing Chelsea of possessing one of those — he provides the extra body in a tightly marked penalty area; but he also pops up in the channels and on the wing, either supporting the man in possession or offering himself for the quick switch of play. The relation between that role and his output shows in the numbers: against Chelsea he scored his fifth and sixth goals of the season, having previously never got more than seven. The piece attributes this partly to opponents still not quite cottoning on to his goal threat — those late runs to the far post, the blur on the edge of the 18-yard box you do not spot until it is too late — and partly to how Ten Hag is using him. The range over which the relation holds is the current team: for all the undoubted leadership qualities of Bruno Fernandes and Harry Maguire, tactically it is McTominay running the show right now, a development with numerous interesting consequences. The Pogba comparison is drawn with the caveat that McTominay is a different kind of player with a different kind of skillset; Pogba's United career never quite worked out, largely — if you believe his most vehement critics — on account of his hair.

# The Three Concurrent Roles Of A Manchester United Manager

Barney Ronay models the Manchester United job as three concurrent roles — managing the past, managing the dysfunction of the present, and managing the everyday metrics on which the manager is judged.

First you must manage the past, which is constantly in the room and which skews every act, achievement and expectation. Second you must manage the dysfunction of the present, which expresses itself in every detail from a leaking stadium roof to the deep ills of a playing squad peopled with squatters and long-term missteps. Finally you get to manage the everyday metrics — team, results, style, energy, messaging: win things, improve players, create a coherent and happy internal culture, but do it during an unceasing takeover circus while star players sulk and brief against you, and while the ghost of Hamlet's father still skulks in the eaves. The three hold together only under those conditions; as of the December 2023 Champions League exit, Ronay judged, this felt like the end of one thing, perhaps even the beginning of the end of something else.

# Kevin Durant Sensitivity And Burner Account Criticism

Against the case that Durant is simply disrespected, Essentially Sports set out on Dec. 1, 2023 the counter-case that his own conduct and post-Warriors record explain much of the criticism — attacking the premise that the disregard is unearned.

His vulnerability to criticism and thin-skinned nature has on several occasions got the better of him: NBA legend Charles Barkley called Durant "sensitive" in an interview with 60 Minutes, saying "He's very sensitive. Great player. He's part of that generation who thinks he can't be criticized." That susceptibility became glaringly evident when he used a burner account in 2017 to defend himself on Twitter, and was exposed after inadvertently failing to switch accounts and posting a tweet through his verified account. Fans also criticize him for a lack of leadership and a lack of titles since leaving the Warriors: since his 2019 departure Durant has not secured an NBA title, and despite forming a formidable trio with Kyrie Irving and James Harden in Brooklyn, their best result was a second-round exit in the 2021 playoffs at the hands of the Milwaukee Bucks. Fans and media also strongly disapprove of his inclination to switch teams repeatedly even when he receives substantial support from the organizations — after the Brooklyn experiment did not work he requested a trade, and at the previous year's trade deadline the Nets traded him to the Suns, where despite teammates like Devin Booker and Chris Paul he again fell short of a title. His inability to clinch an NBA title without Curry and the Warriors has heightened the narrative questioning his status as an icon of the game.

# Kevin Durant Most Disrespected Superstar Claim

Essentially Sports argued on Dec. 1, 2023 that Kevin Durant stands as perhaps the most disrespected icon of the sport, on the grounds that his acknowledged talent and accolades are out of proportion to how he is regarded.

The grounds start with where he sits in the league's history. The NBA is home to the world's best basketball players and teams, and throughout its history iconic figures like Magic Johnson, Larry Bird, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Michael Jordan have left an indelible mark; but for the better part of the past two decades, players like Stephen Curry, LeBron James and Kevin Durant have dominated the NBA landscape. While LeBron James and Stephen Curry may have accumulated more championships and accolades, Durant is universally acknowledged as the best pure talent of his generation. The dispute the argument answers is that Durant divides opinions: some view him as the most skilled basketball player of his generation, others as a diva who rode the coattails of Stephen Curry to secure his two NBA championships. The warrant is that a careful consideration of Durant's game-changing impact and his multitude of accolades reveals a glaring gap between what he has done and how he is treated.

# Kevin Durant 2016 Move To Warriors Legacy

In the 2016 Western Conference finals, the Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook-led OKC Thunder faced the 73-9 Warriors and, after swiftly securing a 3-1 series lead, seemed poised for an NBA Finals appearance — but the Warriors orchestrated a remarkable comeback to win the series in seven games, meaning Durant would go trophy-less for another season, Essentially Sports recounted on Dec. 1, 2023.

In the 2016 offseason, Durant made the pivotal decision to join the very team that had defeated him. The move had profound consequences, leading to a shift in public opinion, with many labeling him a "snake" and "spineless." While Durant achieved the success he craved in the Bay Area, his decision to join the Warriors has permanently cast a shadow on his legacy.

# The Manchester United Crisis News Cycle Under Ten Hag

The Guardian's argument is that results at Manchester United no longer settle anything, because the club's crisis news cycle consumes wins as quickly as defeats: a stirring recovery against Chelsea bought Erik ten Hag only a few days' grace.

The grounds are the pattern of the week itself — rancour, rumour and recrimination, barbs in the press and barbs at the press, defeat at Newcastle followed by the Chelsea win and the startling realisation that United were three points behind Manchester City, all before Thursday. The warrant is a claim about the institution rather than the team: such is the way of things at football's most reliable content provider, and this beast must always eat, so the warm flume of goodwill would last only as long as it took for Dominic Solanke to run through on goal for Bournemouth on the Saturday afternoon, returning United to the grip of crisis and the now-familiar lexicon of surly unsourced stories about dressing room discontent. A second, related argument is that assessing any United manager requires filters: Ten Hag would of course take the blame for the early Champions League exit, and plenty of mistakes had been made, not least in the players the manager had been allowed to sign — but to be United manager is to undertake three concurrent roles.

# Kevin Durant Career Accolades And Scoring Ranks

Kevin Durant, as Essentially Sports characterized him on Dec. 1, 2023, stands as one of the most exceptionally skilled players in NBA history — a transcendent superstar across an illustrious 17-year career whose stellar performances have endeared him to millions of fans, yet who regularly faces disregard from both the media and fans, making him one of the most polarizing figures in basketball.

The discriminating feature is his physical and technical profile at entry: Durant rose to prominence in 2007, when the Seattle SuperSonics drafted him with the No. 2 pick, and the NBA had never witnessed a player possessing his unique skill set — a 6'11" forward renowned for his exceptional jump shot and lethal three-point accuracy, epitomizing the concept of a "Unicorn" in its truest sense. The record makes the disrespect more perplexing still: Durant has amassed 27,393 points in the regular season, ranking 11th in NBA history, and has contributed an additional 4,878 points in the playoffs, placing him 7th on the all-time list. He is a surefire future first-ballot Hall of Famer with a resume few can match — two NBA titles, two NBA Finals MVP awards, four scoring titles, and multiple selections to the All-Star and All-NBA teams.

# Erik Ten Hag's Position Under Ratcliffe

Erik ten Hag's team are treading water at precisely the wrong moment, The Guardian reported on 25 December 2023: Sir Jim Ratcliffe is taking charge of Manchester United's sporting department before making sweeping changes to the posts that will directly affect the manager.

Two lines of authority above Ten Hag are in play. Richard Arnold has left, despite officially staying until the end of the year, and into his role may come Jean-Claude Blanc, the CEO of Ratcliffe's Ineos Sport, as the man Ten Hag reports to. The report suggested an early tell of Ten Hag's standing in Ratcliffe's new empire: whether he is sounded out for his view on a prime factor in his ability to coach and manage the side to success, namely United's transfer policy.

# Manchester United's Defensive Imbalance: Ferdinand's Critique

Rio Ferdinand argued that Manchester United's European problems stem from a lack of balance in the team — they can score at will but make defensive mistakes that undo the game plan — and that the fix has to be applied over a period of games, not one or two, talkSPORT reported on 29 November 2023.

United had conceded 14 goals in the Champions League group stages, a new and unwanted record for the club that could get worse when they faced Bayern in the final match, while their 12 goals scored was the fifth-highest tally of any club — so the downfall was defensive. "I think they've got to look at themselves," said Ferdinand, a 2007/08 Champions League winner with United. "You can't go into a Champions League campaign and score nine goals in three away games and have one point at the end of it. I think that shows you that there's a lack of balance in the team at the moment. Yes they can get goals and yes they are attacking at will and creating chances, many of them coming through Bruno. But I think defensively, they just made mistakes, I think the goalkeeper today has to hold his hands up and say, 'Yep, I was at fault for a couple of goals. He should do better."

The warrant is that the tactical work was sound and the errors, not the plan, cost the points — and that repeated collapses leave a psychological residue. "I think the manager will be scratching his head and thinking, 'The game plan first-half worked perfectly,' and then all of a sudden they score a goal, it changes the dynamic of the game. # The INEOS Plan For Manchester United's Football Operations

Sir Jim Ratcliffe is demanding an executive role and overall control of Manchester United's day-to-day football matters, and plans to appoint his own sporting director, with former Tottenham and Southampton transfer guru Paul Mitchell one of the main names in the frame, talkSPORT reported on 18 October 2023.

# Ten Hag Rejects The Crisis Framing Of Manchester United's Season

Asked about a potential crisis at Manchester United after the Chelsea win, Erik ten Hag rejected the premise outright: "Crisis? Not for us. We keep calm. We know where we have to build. We are going in the right direction. This team is capable to be successful," per Sporting News on Dec. 6, 2023.

# Bruno Fernandes' Role Against Top Teams

Erik ten Hag argued on 28 October 2023 that Bruno Fernandes' contribution has to change against top opposition: he is at his best with a lot of the ball, so in games where United have less of it his job becomes taking whatever attacking moments arise and otherwise working hard for the team.

# Schmeichel's Criticism Of Manchester United's Lack Of Identity

Manchester United legend Peter Schmeichel attacked the premise that the defeat to West Ham on 23 December 2023 could be read as a performance at all: his counter is that there was no plan to the display, so the question of whether United played well before conceding does not arise.

Schmeichel lashed the team's lack of a plan and blasted them for looking slow against the Hammers. "It was just in many ways irrelevant. There was no plan to it," he said. # Ten Hag's Attacking Gamble And The Gaps It Leaves

The Guardian argues that Ten Hag is enacting a high-wire act — a daring gamble that United will gain more going forward than they lose going back — and that the Chelsea win is not yet evidence the gamble works.

The grounds are structural: if you commit a midfielder to McTominay's advanced role, you leave gaps elsewhere. One reason Chelsea found it so easy to play through United was that, with the forwards pushed high and McTominay as the secret sauce in the final third, there were open spaces every time they played through the press; Chelsea's goal was a case in point, two simple vertical passes straight through the centre via Mykhailo Mudryk to Cole Palmer, passes McTominay could see coming but could do precious little to stop. The warrant is that the result depended on finishing quality United cannot count on: on another night Chelsea score from one of these counterattacks, and in another game United face a better finisher than Nicolas Jackson, who for all his talent looks like a man playing football in a hall of mirrors. The bet is that lawless abandon will begin to resemble a sustainable attacking blueprint once Lisandro Martínez and Raphaël Varane come back, once Ten Hag brings the defensive line up 10 yards, once Rasmus Højlund hits some form and once Mason Mount gets up to speed — that he can shout down the noise in the short term while building something in the long term. In the raptured afterglow of a big win it felt like a gamble being won, but the writer's own caveat is to come back and check in a few days.



---


# Ratcliffe's Bid For A Manchester United Stake

As of 28 October 2023, Sir Jim Ratcliffe's bid to buy 25% of Manchester United for an inflated £1.3bn in return for control of football policy was expected to go through imminently, marking a new phase in the protracted sale of the club.

Erik ten Hag had overseen his squad through those recent weeks and, despite any implications the deal might have for the futures of his players, did not think the matter was a distraction. "Of course, they are committed to the club but especially they are committed to this team," Ten Hag said. "They want to be successful and are therefore aware you need [to focus on] the team, your teammates. That is how the players are thinking and they are not thinking about strategic reviews or structures or whatever."



---


# Paul Mitchell's Blueprint For A Manchester United Rebuild

Paul Mitchell argues that Manchester United must define an identity and a five-year blueprint and then hold to it, because consistency of decision-making over that period is what produces sustainable success — a blueprint he laid out while still at Monaco, reported by talkSPORT on 16 October 2023.

His grounds begin with context and end with comparison. "I think context is important to measure what Manchester United's current situation is, but I think they do need to get to the point of really putting down what Manchester United needs to be in the modern game," he explained. "We are a long time from the Sir Alex Ferguson era. Erik ten Hag is a top coach from Ajax but they need a top blueprint not only for now but for the next five years, and work towards that, and sometimes on that journey there are hard moments when you don't get the right results, even though you're doing the right things." The warrant is that results in the short run are a noisy signal: "You have to know that, over that period, the consistency of the decision-making will yield a good end result. I think we've seen that both Manchester City and Liverpool, that when you adopt that long-term strategy you can get real consistency and sustainable success."

The content of the blueprint is an identity statement spanning the whole club: "putting down their identity of what they want to be today, but most crucially what they want to be in five years' time, and where they want to be, and what they want to look like; from everything from young players, to the style of play, to the whole culture peace in Manchester United." There is a counter-consideration attached — almost certain to consult Ralf Rangnick before any approach from Ratcliffe, Mitchell may be warned off a club where long-term thinking has not existed — but should Ratcliffe get his man it could signal exactly the change in fortunes he and every supporter has been hoping for.



---


# United's Shot Dominance In The Win Over Chelsea

Manchester United's December 2023 win over Chelsea felt a lot tighter than it really was: United hung on inexplicably at the end despite enjoying 28 shots and an xG tally of 4.07.

For long periods United played some of their most authentically thrilling football of the season, a doctrine of relentless attack that had Diogo Dalot flying forward from right-back even as the minutes ticked down. It was also a game that felt more chaotic than it really was — the slippery, slingy nature of the play was largely by design, with United hollowing out their midfield to throw bodies forward and Chelsea hollowing out theirs to leave men up for the breakaway. It was a game that hung on United's determination to keep allowing Chelsea counterattacks and Chelsea's determination to keep messing them up, and above all on the curious main character energy of Scott McTominay.

# Jean-Claude Blanc and the United Chief Executive Challenge

The question The Guardian posed on 25 December 2023 is whether any chief executive can make Manchester United a best-in-class elite club again — and the candidate in frame is Jean-Claude Blanc, billed as the "Lionel Messi of business" by Nice's chief executive, Fabrice Bocquet.

Blanc's credentials are unusually broad for the role. He has an MBA from Harvard, and at 60 years old has been Juventus CEO and president, CEO at Paris Saint-Germain and at French Tennis, and the executive overseeing the Tour de France.

The boundary on those credentials is the club itself. The report argues that once Blanc, or whoever becomes Arnold's successor, is in place, it will dawn rapidly that United are a one-off hydra-headed beast of a club which is treacherously difficult to control. And there is the competitive gap: across town Manchester City have accrued six championships since United's last in 2013, and boast a commercial operation that leaves Ratcliffe's new concern light years behind.



---


# Erik Ten Hag Under Pressure In December 2023

Erik ten Hag faced a demanding week in early December 2023 amid reports indicating disunity within his team, and by mid-December the pressure around the Dutch boss continued to get more palpable as Manchester United's season continued to slip away.

On Dec. 6, 2023, Sporting News reported that the United manager had faced a demanding week amid reports indicating disunity within his team, and that his players did exceptionally well to block out the noise and focus on footballing matters. Two hours before kickoff against Chelsea the live blog noted it had been a relatively busy start to the week off the pitch for Ten Hag, and that it was time to see what happened on it. Sky Sports Premier League (@SkySportsPL) posted on December 5, 2023 that Erik ten Hag claimed there was not a good culture among staff and players before he joined Man United.

By Dec. 13, 2023, Sporting News framed the situation as one in which, as Manchester United's season continued to slip away, the pressure around Ten Hag continued to get more palpable.

# Erik Ten Hag's Selection U-Turns On Varane And Maguire

Erik ten Hag recalled Raphael Varane against Bayern Munich on 12 December 2023 after a 10-game absence during which both Luke Shaw and Jonny Evans had been preferred at centre-back to a World Cup winner, one of a series of selection reversals The Independent recorded that night.

Varane, summoned from what the report calls his inexplicable exile, performed with an assurance that made his omission all the odder. He is not the only case: with Harry Maguire and Scott McTominay, Ten Hag is compiling a group of players who were first out of his plans and then back in. During the match Maguire's injury forced him off the pitch, with 36-year-old Jonny Evans replacing him.

The significance attached to the pattern is about the manager's self-presentation: for a manager who likes to project an image of strong, decisive leadership, Ten Hag has had to reverse course rather too often — but then, the report concludes, his team are going backwards.



---


# Manchester United's 2023 Champions League Group Stage Exit

Ten Hag's United compiled arguably the worst performance by any English team in a Champions League group stage in 2023, finishing bottom of their group and shipping 15 goals — more than any other English team ever.

The Guardian conceded it was no Blackburn Rovers, but gave extra marks for United's pedigree, for the fact the group really was not much of a group, and for finishing bottom. There were also many moments of farce along the way, a six-part saga of chaos, collapse and laughter in the dark: Onana diving out of the way of the ball in Munich, Onana again diving out of the way of the ball in Istanbul, Casemiro's red card, lost leads in Manchester, and Marcus Rashford unfairly convicted of a venomous stamp in Copenhagen. And yet, with both group games blank at half-time on the final night, United were still just one goal away from going through to the last 16. Bayern, for all their own flaws, were basically a good version of whatever United were attempting to piece together: Kimmich-Goretzka-Musiala an A-grade version of Amrabat-McTominay-Fernandes, Manuel Neuer the thing Onana is trying so earnestly to be, and Bayern actually did go ahead and sign Harry Kane. From there United's season continued to narrow — they could not win the league, the Champions League or the Carabao Cup, leaving the FA Cup and the extended pursuit of fourth or even fifth place, although the state of the coefficient meant the thing that might keep Manchester United out of Europe the next season could be Manchester United being so bad in Europe that season.



---


# How The Goals Came In Manchester United 2-1 Chelsea

Erik ten Hag's side were dominant in the first half and finally pounced on Chelsea's inability to take control in midfield to open the scoring through Scott McTominay, per Sporting News on Dec. 6, 2023.

For the first goal, Mauricio Pochettino's men attempted to break at pace but Sofyan Amrabat made a vital interception and Fernandes found Alejandro Garnacho out wide; the youngster then cut the ball back to Harry Maguire, whose effort rebounded perfectly into the path of McTominay, and the Scotland international took one touch before blasting past Sanchez.

United led for the majority of the first 45 minutes but failed to build on their lead and were pegged back by the former Manchester City man Cole Palmer. The 21-year-old, who made the transfer from the Etihad Stadium to Stamford Bridge in August, stroked the ball into the far corner with deadly accuracy; it was his fifth Premier League goal of the season and his first from open play. United continued to put Chelsea under pressure in the second half and after numerous attempts McTominay headed powerfully past Sanchez. The Scotsman had seven shots, his most ever in a league game. Despite a flurry of late attacks driven by Reece James, Ten Hag's team stood strong and held on to see out the victory.



---


# Galatasaray Istanbul Hostile Atmosphere 1993

Former United defender Gary Pallister, injured for the 1993 game and watching from the stands, described the hostility in Istanbul as something he never experienced again: "That was our first foray in the Champions League and we were expected to go through. The hostility is something [to learn from] – I never experienced anything like that in the rest of my career. You look at that and think it can't get any worse." The Guardian reported his recollection on Nov. 27, 2023.

The intimidation extended well beyond the stadium. Pallister smiled at a bell boy at the team hotel and got a finger across the throat in response; Brian McClair had a cleaner bang on his bedroom ceiling in the night; and other players received numerous phone calls to disrupt their sleep. When it comes to pressure in the Champions League of late, United do not cope well, and there are few events trickier than a night in Istanbul — the current squad could face the same level of malevolence and needed to be prepared.



---


# Dalton Papali'i On All Blacks Leadership Vulnerability

All Blacks back-rower Dalton Papali'i described in the week before the 2023 World Cup final how senior players opening up emotionally in front of the squad had changed the group's mood, saying it made younger players want to play the game for them.

"It was quite special to hear some of the things those certain players said from the heart," he said. "You know, you think you know someone but once they open up and really be vulnerable in front of a team, it was quite special to hear. It was truly something special when you hear those boys open up. You know those leaders have been through a lot in their careers, the highs and the lows, the off-field and on-field stuff, and for them to open up, it sort of makes you feel welcomed and you want to play this game for them. There were a few tears and I think that's awesome to see, players showing vulnerability, just opening up about how much this tour and this sort of game means."

He set the moment in the context of the criticism the team had absorbed: "There were some (people) saying this is probably one of the most important games of All Blacks history. (The) All Blacks went through a bit of a hard path to get here, media, friends, family even criticising us and all that, and we stuck together. We weren't even said to be in the final and now look at us, we're here. Different players take it differently and some of the older players probably were hit a little bit harder and it was good to see just a bit of emotion and the want from them. Seeing that gives all the other players an extra two, three per cent to think 'OK, we are going to the well and we've got to give it our all'."

Papali'i said the All Blacks were intent on sending their leaders out on a high: "There's a few leaders in the team, it's going to be their last game in the jersey, so it's a big game for us and even the other players that are staying, knowing that we want to send those boys out on a high. How much they put into the jersey. We are standing on their…what's that quote? It's standing on the shoulders of giants."



---


# Manchester United's European Decline Since Ferguson

The Independent argued on 12 December 2023 that Manchester United's 1-0 defeat to Bayern Munich should have been a landmark low but instead felt grimly routine, because group-stage elimination has become the club's normal European outcome in the post-Ferguson era rather than an aberration.

The grounds are frequency and pattern. Manchester United, one of the grandest and richest names in this competition, have again gone out of the Champions League at the group stage; it is the third time it has happened since Sir Alex Ferguson, meaning it is their most common round of exit in that period. The night is presented as one more entry in a decade of disappointment in a competition in which this club rose to its most emotional heights — a low, but just part of that longer run.

The warrant is the gap between the occasion and the performance. These are not the sounds we are used to hearing after that Champions League theme; something does stir when the anthem is played at Old Trafford amid the lights — well, for most, that is, except the players. United should not be performing like this on what is supposed to be the classic European night at Old Trafford, and the display was a reminder that all they are going to have for some time are their memories. Having been involved in so many ludicrously chaotic matches, the biggest of all ended up being a non-event: this game never threatened to stir anything, and United never threatened at all. That, the argument runs, can now be talked about definitively, since it has been decisively ended.



---


# Paul Mitchell's Long-Term Recruitment Philosophy

Paul Mitchell argues that recruitment should be judged over the long term rather than by immediate returns, because young signings need time to settle and a player's prior record is better evidence than the narrative that forms around him in his first season — a case talkSPORT set out on 16 October 2023 using Heung-Min Son.

The grounds are Mitchell's own record and his stated standard. Having worked in football management for over a decade, his career has always been about the long term for his clubs, with the young signings he has made often only paying off after he has left. He frames the job as continuous improvement across the whole operation: "I want to continue to drive standards in each and every department. Psychology, sports science, nutrition, medicine, the way we travel, the way we refuel," he said, adding that "everything, every element I think we need to keep pushing to its maximum to try and be the best we possibly can."

The warrant joining evidence to claim is the Son case, which perfectly sums up his philosophy. "I took quite a lot of criticism in my first year at Tottenham for some of the decisions and Sonny was kind of at the centre of that," he explained. "Sometimes players need time, they're human beings, they need to settle, Sonny had a great track record at Hamburg and Leverkusen but there was this narrative that started to grow internally and externally that he wasn't a good finisher." He recalled telling a coach: "you're wrong, his history shows in two different clubs he's a very astute finisher off both sides." Son went on to be the 2022/23 Premier League top scorer, vindicating the judgement made against the prevailing internal and external narrative.



---


# Mr. Irrelevant: The NFL Draft's Final Pick

"Mr. Irrelevant" is the nickname given to the final pick of the NFL Draft. What distinguishes the title is purely positional: it attaches to whoever is selected last, regardless of the player or the team.

The Mr. Irrelevant title has been a staple of NFL Drafts since the 1976 Draft.



---


# Reece James Return From Injury Chelsea

Reece James was a constant menace to Blackburn's defence as he started for the first time since the opening day of the season on his return from injury, and Mauricio Pochettino admitted he was delighted to have his captain back, The Guardian reported on Nov. 1, 2023.

"He is one of the best full-backs in the world and to have been without him for so long has been difficult," Pochettino said. "But we need to be careful and little by little he will get back to full fitness."



---


# Manchester United Recent Champions League Failures

Thirty years on from Istanbul, United headed to Turkey knowing they had rarely been convincing in the Champions League in recent years, The Guardian reported on Nov. 27, 2023: a 3-1 away win against Paris Saint-Germain in the 2018-19 round of 16, after losing the home leg 2-0, was the last time they won a crunch match.

In 2020-21 they lost their final two group games and were eliminated, while back in 2015-16 Wolfsburg won the deciding group match to knock them out. United had done little learning in recent times, repeating the same failures in Europe's elite competition. It would not be a disgrace to lose against a good Galatasaray team, especially given Erik ten Hag was missing key players, but if the worst happened, everyone would need to come out of the experience stronger — regardless of the result, it should be a night of education about the demands of the Champions League.



---


# Carrick, Flick, Conte And Lopetegui As Manchester United Manager Candidates

Sporting News assessed four further candidates to replace Erik ten Hag on Dec. 13, 2023 — Michael Carrick, Hansi Flick, Antonio Conte and Julen Lopetegui — each with a case for and a specific reservation against.

Michael Carrick was the likeliest of those with direct Manchester United links: the former United midfielder made 316 appearances for the club over a 12-year Old Trafford tenure and was at Championship club Middlesbrough, his first permanent managerial appointment, where they sat 11th in the second tier as of mid-December, just three points back of the playoff spots in a crowded top half. Carrick's lack of experience was glaring, but hiring someone with deep knowledge of the club could be very enticing, and the fact he had not bombed in his first job was notable; the 42-year-old had also led the Red Devils before on a caretaker basis, installed in 2021 after Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's dismissal and leading the club to some big wins over Arsenal in league play and Villarreal in the Champions League before Ralf Rangnick took over.

Hansi Flick, the former German national-team manager, only lasted two years with Die Mannschaft before their failures at the 2022 World Cup caught up with him, yet he had big club experience, having led Bayern Munich first as an assistant under Niko Kovac and then for two years as manager, winning the treble in 2019/20 en route to being named UEFA Coach of the Year. The reservation is that Flick's lack of experience of any kind outside Germany — just one year abroad, as an assistant at Red Bull Salzburg — coupled with his struggles at national-team level could give some pause about bringing him to England for such a project position.

Antonio Conte, the former Chelsea and Tottenham boss, had not cropped up near the top of any betting lists, but Sporting News saw some sense in hiring the Italian: he had been out of work since his acrimonious departure from Tottenham that summer, after he seemingly shoved his way out of the club amid reports he was utterly miserable in London. While the idea of a control freak such as Conte taking over the Manchester United mess could easily be a recipe for disaster, the club could also seek out a fixer of his nature, hoping for an immediate boost they can build on once things crumble under the Italian, as they often do — though the Red Devils would likely have competition as he seemed to prefer working in his home country. Julen Lopetegui, the 57-year-old Spanish boss, represented maybe the perfect mix of experience, availability and interest: most known for his time in charge of the Spanish national team, where he succeeded Vincente del Bosque, he also had big club experience at Real Madrid, and had managed in the Premier League, seemingly on an upward trajectory at Wolves before abruptly leaving just days before the current season amid tension with the board. Therein lies the issue: he has left multiple positions in mysterious and awkward circumstances, with his Wolves exit reminiscent of his departure from the Spanish national team, where he suddenly departed just days before the start of the 2018 World Cup as news of his discussions with Real Madrid came to light — and between those two incidents and his failed tenures at Madrid and Sevilla, Sporting News asked whether he would be worth the risk at Old Trafford.

# The Woman In Me: Publication Details Of Britney Spears' Memoir

*The Woman in Me* is Britney Spears' memoir, published by Simon & Schuster on 25 October 2023 at $49.99 and reportedly written for a $US15 million ($23.3 million) advance; its defining subject is the conservatorship under which her father and others held almost complete control of her life for 13 years.

The Sydney Morning Herald's 1 October 2023 books preview describes the book as a candid account of a life in which the "huge-selling American singer has negotiated the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune in her 41 years", with the controversial conservatorship at its heart — an arrangement that nonetheless "still failed to stop it going off the rails many times" — and predicts it is sure to be a bestseller and exactly what her fans want.

The Guardian, reviewing the memoir on 24 October 2023, observes that it "feels fitting" the book is released a week before Halloween: however much was already known about the 13 years Spears lived under the conservatorship, her recounting of its imposition, life under it and her inability to escape it "is nothing short of a horror story", appalling "like something out of a Victorian novel, not the very real experiences of a thirtysomething in the last decade".

# Justin Timberlake's Apology And Support For Britney Spears

Justin Timberlake publicly apologised to Britney Spears on Instagram in 2021 after the documentary Framing Britney, which addressed the public scrutiny Spears faced during the 2000s, prompted criticism of how he had behaved following their breakup. Neither had ever acknowledged the rumours about why they split. His apology read: "I've seen the messages, tags, comments, and concerns and I want to respond. I am deeply sorry for the times in my life where my actions contributed to the problem, where I spoke out of turn, or did not speak up for what was right. I understand that I fell short in these moments and in many others and benefited from a system that condones misogyny and racism."

In June 2021 he also backed Spears after she testified publicly in a bid to end the conservatorship controlled by her father, Jamie Spears. At the Los Angeles court hearing, Spears alleged she had been forced to take lithium against her will and claimed the team managing her conservatorship had prevented her from having another baby by refusing to remove her IUD. Timberlake wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter: "After what we saw today, we should all be supporting Britney at this time. Regardless of our past, good and bad, and no matter how long ago it was. What's happening to her is just not right. No woman should ever be restricted from making decisions about her own body."

# Britney Spears On Body Scrutiny And Diet Control

The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account of *The Woman in Me* reports that Spears' body was treated as public property "from day one" and that, once she was under the conservatorship, her father policed her weight and every calorie she ate was recorded.

Between the videos for her debut single Baby, One More Time and Sometimes, the media noted her changing physique and concluded that the 16-year-old must have had breast implants rather than simply going through puberty. She noticed that talkshow hosts asked her about her chest while her boyfriend Justin Timberlake was asked serious questions about his music. Writing about shaving her head in a salon in 2007, she frames it as a "fuck you" to impossible beauty standards: "I'd smiled politely while TV show hosts leered at my breasts, while American parents said I was destroying their children by wearing a crop top."

That brief moment of freedom did not last: a year later she was ambushed into the conservatorship, which also exercised jurisdiction over her body. "No matter how much I dieted and exercised, my father was always telling me I was fat," she writes; punishing gym routines left her feeling "out of my mind", and her diet was monitored along with every other detail of her life while she went through the motions of her Las Vegas residency. "My body was strong enough to carry two children and agile enough to execute every choreographed move perfectly onstage. And now here I was, having every calorie recorded so people could continue to get rich off my body." On the other side of the conservatorship, she writes, freedom looks like being able to gain weight without anyone "shouting at me", eating chocolate again, and posting selfies — nude or clothed — on Instagram; people who do not understand the last of these, she suggests, have not been "photographed by other people thousands of times, prodded and posed for other people's approval".

# Britney Spears' Memoir On Early Fame And The Loss Of Freedom

In *The Woman in Me*, as summarised by The Guardian on 24 October 2023, Britney Spears describes how fame converted her childhood escape into confinement: by the age of 16 she was "public property", unable to go outside without being mobbed, and her love of singing and dancing had become a lucrative resource for other people.

Spears writes that as a child she escaped a difficult home life — her alcoholic father often rowing with her mother — into the outdoors, which "gave me a sense of aliveness and danger", and that performing made her feel invincible. By the time of her second album she wanted for so little; skinny-dipping with her dancers after playing Rock in Rio in January 2001 is one of her happiest memories, "a taste of rebellion and freedom, but I was just having fun and being a 19-year-old". After her split from Justin Timberlake she dreamed about quitting pop and opening a shop, and writes with hindsight that she "hadn't given myself enough time to heal from the breakup" — yet her requests for a break were not only turned down but interpreted as a potential sign of sedition to be quashed and interrogated.

In that restrictive environment small kindnesses took on outsized significance, such as Paris Hilton encouraging her "to have fun for the first time in a long time", which led to infamous nights out with the heiress and Lindsay Lohan; once again Britney was seen as stepping out of bounds and potentially damaging her earning potential. One night, after her mother babysat her sons, she returned home tipsy and Lynne Spears screamed at her: "The shame I felt killed my heart. I stood there, reeling, and thought, OK, I guess it's forbidden for me to party." As the restrictions tightened she acted out, and ended up legally denied her freedom for 13 years under a conservatorship controlled by her father.

# Britney Spears On Motherhood And Postpartum Depression

Spears writes in *The Woman in Me*, per The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account, that she suffered severe postpartum depression after her sons were born — depression she only recognised later — and that it left her suicidal: "I'll admit it, I felt that I couldn't live if things didn't get better."

When she became pregnant with her first son she initially thought it might protect her — "I wanted everyone to stay away: stand back! There's a baby here!" — but the paparazzi became more aggressive, particularly once she had her children in quick succession, becoming pregnant a second time three months after giving birth to her first. She felt hopeless about her ability to protect her sons: "I got a little depressed once I was no longer keeping them safe inside my body … I wanted them back inside me so the world couldn't get at them."

She has a keen sense of injustice about a contract with the public and the press that she never signed: "They just kept acting like I owed it to them to let the men who kept trying to catch me looking fat take photos of my infant sons." Her postpartum body and shots of her without makeup were treated as "some kind of a sin – as if gaining weight was something unkind I'd done to them personally, a betrayal. At what point did I promise to stay 17 for the rest of my life?" What she knows now, she writes, "is that every part of normal life had been stripped from me – going out in public without becoming a headline, making normal mistakes as a new mother of two babies, feeling like I could trust the people around me. I had no freedom and yet also no security."

# The Fan Movement And The 2021 End Of Britney Spears' Conservatorship

According to The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account of *The Woman in Me*, Spears first learned of the blossoming fan movement questioning her conservatorship from a nurse, called 911 in June 2021 to report her father for conservatorship abuse days before a probate court hearing, and was granted her freedom in November 2021.

A nurse showed her the fan movement that was spreading awareness of its suspicions that all was not right with the arrangement. Of speaking publicly at that point she writes: "My voice had been used for me and against me so many times that I was afraid nobody would recognise it now if I spoke freely."

When freedom came in November 2021, she says she felt shock, relief, elation, sadness and joy.

# Britney Spears' Confinement In A Solitary Rehab Facility

The passage The Guardian singles out on 24 October 2023 as the most upsetting in *The Woman in Me* is Spears' account of being locked up in a rehabilitation facility, put on lithium and subjected to relentless testing, where she "began to feel like I was being ritually tortured".

While confined she could not see her children or her dog, could not bathe or dress in private or shut the door to her room, and had set bed and waking times, alongside mandatory therapy. For blood tests, "the tech drawing my blood would be flanked by the nurse, a security guard and my assistant. Was I a cannibal? Was I a bank robber? Was I a wild animal? Why was I treated as though I were about to burn the place down and murder them all?" She wondered whether her family was trying to kill her, and, made slow and sclerotic, felt estranged from her own body: "If the idea of my being in that place was to heal, that was not the effect."

She writes that she is not scared of anything after that experience, "but it doesn't make me feel strong; it makes me sad. I shouldn't be this strong."

# The Woman In Me: Britney Spears' Memoir

The Woman in Me is Britney Spears' memoir, released on 24 October 2023 in both the US and the UK. Its publisher's press release describes it as "a brave and astonishingly moving story about freedom, fame, motherhood, survival, faith, and hope." The book is expected to cover the pivotal moments of Spears' life, including the high-profile legal battle to end her conservatorship, which was dissolved in November 2021 after 13 years.

Ahead of publication, the main point of anticipation was what the book would say about Spears' private life. Because she spent the 1990s and 2000s in heavily publicised romances, fans expected her to detail those relationships in the memoir, and in particular to share new material about her second husband, Kevin Federline.

# Arrested Development: Britney Spears' Child-Robot Model Of The Conservatorship

The Guardian's 24 October 2023 reading of *The Woman in Me* frames Spears' life as a structure of arrested development: she was "never allowed to be a real child, nor a real adult", and the conservatorship pushed her into what she calls a "child-robot" state in which she vacillated between girl, teenager and woman.

The relation holds across three phases she describes. In early fame, her 2001 single I'm Not a Girl, Not Yet a Woman is read as her most prescient recording, and after her split from Timberlake she likens herself to Benjamin Button: "Somehow that year, in becoming more vulnerable I started to feel like a child again." In the postnatal-depression phase the split deepens — "It was as if some part of me became the baby," she writes in an apologetic section about transferring her frustrations on to her interior decorator, "One part of me was a very demanding grown woman yelling about white marble, while another part of me was suddenly very childlike."

# Travis Kelce On Dating Taylor Swift In Public

In an interview with WSJ Magazine published on 20 November 2023, Travis Kelce spoke about his relationship with Taylor Swift, saying he admires her as a musician: "I've never been a man of words. Being around her, seeing how smart Taylor is, has been f***ing mind-blowing. I'm learning every day."

He also acknowledged the intense public attention his private life now attracts, noting he had "never dated anyone with that kind of aura around them" — but said he was not letting the media affect the relationship, and took his cue from how Swift handles it. "But at the same time, I'm not running away from any of it," he said. "The scrutiny she gets, how much she has a magnifying glass on her, every single day, paparazzi outside her house, outside every restaurant she goes to, after every flight she gets off, and she's just living, enjoying life. When she acts like that I better not be the one acting all strange."

context:
# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).
