# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.

# Class Action Settlement

## Definition

A class action settlement is an agreement that resolves a class-action lawsuit before (or instead of) a full trial verdict, typically trading a payment and/or changed business practices from the defendant for an end to the collective claim, in place of the class-wide monetary and injunctive relief a plaintiff would otherwise seek at trial.

## Context

The corpus shows the pattern most clearly in the Epic v. Google app store litigation: Google settled separately with all 50 U.S. state attorneys general and a number of consumers who had brought parallel antitrust claims, and reached a last-minute settlement with Match Group as well, leaving Epic Games as the only original plaintiff still pursuing trial.
Match's settlement let it take advantage of Google's "User Choice Billing" program — a reduced-commission alternative payment option — rather than continuing to litigate; Epic's CEO Tim Sweeney called Match "an awesome partner" and said he hoped Match "got out of their settlement what they needed to get for their business," contrasting Match's choice to settle with Epic's decision to keep fighting because it viewed cash settlements as insufficient while Google's "Google tax" remained in place.
The Helena World Chronicle class action against Google and Alphabet illustrates what a plaintiff seeks when a settlement has not (yet) been reached: the suit asks for damages plus an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent before using their data to train AI products, showing the class-wide monetary-and-injunctive relief that a settlement would otherwise substitute for.
The corpus also shows settlements shaping corporate behavior after the fact: Apple's earlier keyboard class-action settlement is cited as a factor that "tipped the scales" toward redesigning the MacBook Pro keyboard and dropping the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Substitutes for trial** — a settlement ends the case without a jury verdict; in the Google app-store litigation, settling with the state AGs, consumers, and Match Group left only Epic to actually go to trial.
- **Terms can stay undisclosed** — the corpus notes it was "not clear" what the AG/consumer settlement included, and Google would not say whether it had offered Epic a settlement.
- **Can substitute non-cash remedies for damages** — Match's settlement gave it access to a reduced-commission billing option rather than (or alongside) a cash payment, illustrating that settlements can trade behavioral/business-practice changes for dropped claims.
- **Not universally accepted by co-plaintiffs** — Epic explicitly declined to settle on cash terms alone, showing settlement is a choice each plaintiff or plaintiff group makes independently even within the same litigation.
- **Downstream business impact** — Apple's keyboard settlement is presented as a cost that influenced a later product redesign decision, showing settlements can have effects beyond the parties strictly bound by them.

# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# Google's News Content Payment Deal With Canada

In November 2023, the month before the Helena World Chronicle suit was filed, Google reached an agreement with the Canadian government under which the search giant would pay Canadian media for use of their content. Under the terms of the deal, Google will provide $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) every year to news organizations in the country, with funds distributed based on the news outlets' headcount.

Negotiations with Meta over the same Canadian law were still unresolved as of mid-December 2023. Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August, in light of the pressure to pay for content under the new Canadian law.



---


# Epic's Jury Verdict Against Google, December 2023

On Monday, a federal jury sided with Fortnite maker Epic Games in its fight to break Google's control over Android apps, surprising the world. The nine-person jury decided that Google has an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems, and that Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The outcome was striking because "walled garden" rival Apple almost entirely won a similar case two years earlier. For Tim Sweeney, this was, at last, a win.



---


# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.



---


# Epic v. Google Is A Jury Trial

Epic and Google have to convince a jury, not the judge, which is totally different from how the Apple case played out — that one was a "bench trial."

The consequence is that persuasion cuts both ways and is hard to predict. All the evidence of tricky deals inside Google might sway a jury against the company; alternatively, Google scaremongering that sideloaded apps equal gaping security holes might sway a jury against Epic. Who knows.

The jury is also sealed off from coverage: Judge Donato explicitly told jurors they are in a "news-free bubble" through mid-December.



---


# Project Hug, Agave And Banyan

The allegations made before trial suggest Google was playing loads of dirty tricks with names like "Project Hug," "Project Agave," and "Project Banyan," with Epic claiming it has seen evidence Google was paying off game developers and phone makers not to abandon its app store — to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars.

Google allegedly even toyed with the idea of buying Epic, to keep Fortnite from inspiring other game developers to abandon ship.



---


# Google's Secret OEM And Carrier Deals And Its Deleted Chats

Asked what surprised him in the courtroom, Tim Sweeney said the trial confirmed practices he had suspected since around 2018 — when some people called him a conspiracy theorist for saying so — including that Google leaked Epic's conversations to reporters to get negative stories written, paid other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores, and went around paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores.

Sweeney gave a concrete instance from Epic's own experience: when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with other smartphone manufacturers such as OnePlus and with carriers of all sorts, those partners told Epic they couldn't do a deal because Google had done a secret deal with them. He called it disconcerting to see the extent of bad-faith efforts inside a company of Google's size, saying you would expect a trillion-dollar company to have developed respectable processes and leadership structures providing checks and balances against wrongdoing. Instead, he said, Google employees were "rampantly destroying all their chats on these topics": long conversation threads would start to get into a spicy antitrust issue, somebody would point out that history was on, and the chat would go silent — history turned off so the documents would be destroyed. Sweeney said it was great to see all of that called out in detail at trial.



---


# The Epic v. Apple Ruling And Its Limited Weight Here

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. She also decided that Epic violated its developer agreement with Apple and would have to pay.

Epic did win something. Rogers barred Apple from keeping iPhone users in the dark about alternate ways they can pay for apps, and may have even allowed developers to add their own payment mechanisms.

The precedent's reach into the Google trial is limited in two specific ways. First, that was a different case — and it is not over until the Supreme Court weighs in or declines to take a look. Second, Google cannot tell jurors that Apple won its case, or that other plaintiffs settled; the judge in this case says so. Epic declined to answer on the record when asked about the Apple outcome.



---


# Simple Versus Complicated: Assessing The Opening Arguments

The claim after day one is that Epic's chances look better than they should, because the case may come down to simplicity: Google spent most of its first day attempting to explain complicated ins and outs of business, while Epic was able to paint a black-and-white picture of good and evil with itself as the clear underdog.

The starting expectation ran the other way. Walking into the courtroom on Monday morning it seemed impossible — if Epic could not prove Apple's walled iOS garden is a monopoly, how could the comparatively open Google do worse against the windmill-tilting Fortnite developer? The warrant that reverses that expectation is about jury persuasion rather than legal merit: a clearer picture beats a more accurate but more complicated one.

Things got complicated for both parties when the first two witnesses — Epic Games Store head Steve Allison and Yoga Buddhi CEO Benjamin Simon, who also appeared in the earlier Epic v. Apple trial — took the stand. Both Epic and Google spent a long, long time on subtle lines of questioning: you really had to read between the lines to see that Epic was trying to make a point about how Google's 70/30 revenue split is probably based on an arbitrary decision Valve made two decades ago with Steam, or that Google was trying to make the point that Epic, too, likely believed an app store provides more value than just payment processing and maybe deserves more money.



---


# Epic's Refusal Of Special Deals And Its 2019 Google Proposal

Asked whether he would have sued at all had Google offered 0 percent for Epic's own payments system or 4 percent for Google Play billing instead of a $147 million deal, Tim Sweeney answered no — Epic has always turned down special deals just for Epic, fighting on the principle that all developers should be given the same opportunities.

His grounds were a document in evidence: a 2019 email he sent to all of Google's senior executives, right before Fortnite launched the Marvel season and the Star Wars event featuring J.J. Abrams, saying Epic wanted to bring Fortnite to the Google Play Store in time for that event and wanted Google to allow Epic and all other developers to process certain payments and keep them all. Had Google said yes, Sweeney argued, it would have been awesome for all developers, the Android ecosystem would have become much stronger, and Google would be in a better position in the smartphone industry today; there would never have been a dispute because the problem would have been solved. The warrant tying this to the present is his claim that the fix has always been within Google's reach: Google makes several billion dollars a year in what he calls unfairly earned profits from imposing this tax, which is nothing compared to what it makes from search, and given all the other benefits it gets from Android, "Google could solve this problem today if they wanted to."



---


# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.



---


# Google's Knowledge Graph And Featured Snippets

As described in the Helena World Chronicle complaint, Google's Knowledge Graph is a database, launched in May 2012, from which Google draws a summary of content that it displays as a "Knowledge Panel" to the right of search results when a user searches for information on a topic. The complaint characterises it as one of Google's older question-and-answer technologies and treats it as part of the alleged harm to publishers, alongside newer AI technologies.

The complaint states that "Google compiled this massive database by extracting information from Publishers' websites — what Google calls 'materials shared across the web' — and from 'open source and licensed databases.'" By 2020, the Knowledge Graph had grown to 500 billion facts about 5 billion entities, but the complaint alleges that much of the "collective intelligence" Google tapped into was content "misappropriated from Publishers."

Featured Snippets are a distinct Google technology in which Google algorithmically extracts answers from webpages; the complaint cites them too, on the grounds that they shift traffic away from publishers' websites.



---


# The Epic v. Google Witness Lineup

A whole cast of intriguing people were set to be called as witnesses during the trial, going straight to the top of the org chart: Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Epic CEO Tim Sweeney are absolutely expected to attend.

Beyond the two chief executives, Android co-founder Andy Rubin might be deposed, and Google says the court will hear from current Android — and Chrome, and Chrome OS — boss Hiroshi Lockheimer. Google also says representatives from Apple, Netflix, Motorola, and AT&T should testify.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# Epic's Rebuttal Of Google's Leaked Email Summary

Pressed with the suggestion that the email Epic accused Google of leaking showed Epic was itself interested in a special deal, Tim Sweeney attacked the premise of the characterisation: Google did not leak the email, he said — it leaked "their ridiculously biased summary of it" to Abner Li at 9to5Google.

He supported the leak claim with trial testimony: Don Harrison testified that he didn't think Google leaked to the press, and was then presented with a document including Google's press team and Sameer Samat, head of all Android, summarising the articles that appeared as a result of Google's leaking of Epic's plans to the press. On the substance of the email, Sweeney said it is in evidence and is the same one he had already described: right before Christmas-ish 2019, with the new Marvel season and a lineup of Star Wars content planned, he asked Google's executives to let Fortnite come to the Google Play Store using Epic's own payment method and to open up the use of their own payment methods to all developers, not just Epic. The interviewer conceded the point, saying he had read that email in court and had not realised it was the same one, because it was so far off from what he had heard described as a "special billing exception."



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.

# Belgium-England: The Second Half And Wullaert's Penalty

Belgium won the game on 31 October 2023 through Tessa Wullaert's 85th-minute penalty, awarded by referee Esther Staubli after Georgia Stanway handballed Yana Daniels' 83rd-minute effort; Wullaert fired it into the bottom-left corner despite Mary Earps diving the correct way, Sport Grill reported.

England had the better of the half without converting. On the restart Fran Kirby quickly drew a foul from Kassandra Missipo, but Alessia Russo fumbled control from Chloe Kelly's free-kick and her shot was blocked; Nicky Evrard then saved Kirby's shot from Lucy Bronze's pullback pass in the 52nd minute as England continued to test the Red Flames' defence. Just past the hour mark England were given an almighty scare as Wullaert pounced on a through ball and side-stepped both Jess Carter and Millie Bright, only for Earps to block her shot with a stunning save.

Belgium were forced to defend for much of the last half-hour as Russo and Stanway saw shots denied, while substitute Rachel Daly nodded wide in the 80th minute from Keira Walsh's deep corner towards the left post. Sarina Wiegman's Lionesses were eventually made to pay for their wasted chances.



---


# Belgium 3-2 England: The Women's Nations League Result, October 2023

Tessa Wullaert's brace fired Belgium to a dramatic 3-2 home win over England in League A1 of the 2023-24 UEFA Women's Nations League, reported by Sport Grill on 31 October 2023.

Wullaert equalised for Belgium in first-half injury time before taking advantage of Georgia Stanway's handball to fire in an 85th-minute winning penalty.

The result put Belgium second in the group, one point ahead of England and two points behind group leaders the Netherlands, with those two rivals set to meet on 1 December in a blockbuster showdown.



---


# Belgium-England: First-Half Goals And Incidents

The first half in Leuven on 31 October 2023 finished 2-2: Laura De Neve curled Belgium ahead in the ninth minute, Lucy Bronze and Fran Kirby put England in front late in the half, and Tessa Wullaert levelled in first-half injury time, Sport Grill reported.

Having battled to a narrow home win the previous Friday, 27 October, England began on the front foot with a fourth-minute free-kick cleared by Belgium's Nicky Evrard. Belgium drew first blood in this Halloween encounter after Chloe Kelly was penalised for handball just outside the box, allowing De Neve to curl her ninth-minute free-kick straight into the near-top right corner beyond the reach of an outstretched Mary Earps. England struggled to mount a response as Belgium continued to soak up their pressure and hit them on the counter attack, until Alex Greenwood and Jassina Blom banged heads in the 18th minute as they tried to meet an aerial pass, halting play.

That lengthy delay reignited England's intensity, which paid off as Bronze drew a 36th-minute foul from Marie Detruyer and headed in from Kelly's subsequent free-kick two minutes later to restore parity. Kelly then fired wide in the 41st minute as Belgium were forced to substitute De Neve due to injury, which unsettled their defence; while Belgium's defence adjusted, Bronze's header a minute later from Keira Walsh's cross was fired wide on the rebound by Alessia Russo. England continued to press and got their reward in the 44th minute as Lauren Hemp was unleashed up the left flank by Walsh and found Kirby on the pullback to rifle in beyond Evrard and turn the tie around. England's lead lasted only seven minutes into 14 minutes of first-half injury time, as Wullaert was played through on the counter-attack by Janice Cayman to slot into the far left corner and pull Belgium level at the break.



---


# Harry Kane's 2023 Goal Tally And Bayern Munich Scoring Records

Harry Kane scored 52 goals in the 2023 calendar year for Bayern Munich, Tottenham and England, tied for second on TalkSport's list of the year's top scorers. A stunning 2022/23 season saw Bayern splash out over £100m to sign the Spurs legend in August, and Kane repaid the Bundesliga club's faith by breaking a number of records with his 25 goals in all competitions so far in the season.

The leading scorer in the German top flight with 22 goals, the Three Lions skipper set a new Bundesliga record the previous month by finding the back of the net 17 times in his opening 11 outings. Kane, who scored nine goals for England in 2023, is also the first player to register a hat-trick in their first outing against Borussia Dortmund. He is on course to score the most goals in a debut Bundesliga campaign as he hunts down Uwe Seeler's record of 30 for Hamburg in the 1963/64 season, and is on track to break Robert Lewandowski's record of 41 goals in a single season. He is adding assists too, as evidenced by his "filthy" effort against Man United in the Champions League. Like Mbappe, Kane could not overtake Ronaldo's calendar-year tally because of the German winter break.

Earlier in the season, in Bayern's 2-2 draw at RB Leipzig, Bayern earned a 57th-minute penalty against the run of play for a handball and Kane cut the deficit with his eighth league goal. Only Manchester City's Erling Haaland, when he played for Borussia Dortmund, had scored more often in his first six Bundesliga games, with nine goals.



---


# England's Olympic Qualification Heartbreak

Scoring six goals against Scotland on Dec. 5, 2023 was not enough to close the goal difference gap on the Netherlands, because the Dutch scored a fourth against Belgium deep in added time to secure top spot in the Nations League group ahead of England.

No one could question the effort, the heart or the drive of Sarina Wiegman's Lionesses in the game, but qualification hinged on a back and forth of goals in the final round of fixtures — England's against Scotland and the Netherlands' in their win over Belgium — a showdown that ended in an anxious wait and then complete heartbreak. An added-time save by Mary Earps at full stretch from a header by substitute Martha Thomas kept England in it. With the Netherlands having scored in the 91st minute, Bronze's powering header put England back in for two minutes, until the Dutch scored in the 95th to crush the Lionesses while they stood in a huddle waiting for news of the other game's result, the pain sweeping across their faces as it came through.



---


# Alex Greenwood's Head Injury Versus Belgium

Alex Greenwood was stretchered off after a clash of heads with Belgium's Jassina Blom on 31 October 2023, an incident that forced a 13-minute delay for medical treatment, Sport Grill reported.

The impact resulted in both players falling to the ground. Blom was eventually able to continue after concussion checks, while Greenwood was taken from the field on a stretcher.

England tweeted at half-time that Greenwood was conscious and talking to medical staff under observation: "Alex Greenwood is conscious and talking, and is being monitored by our medical staff," the Lionesses posted on October 31, 2023.

# PGMOL Apologies In The Opening Months Of 2023/24

Two incidents from the opening months of the 2023/24 Premier League season drew PGMOL admissions of error, per Sporting News on 2023-09-30. Manchester United 1-0 Wolves, August 14, 2023: Gary O'Neil's side were denied a late penalty after a foul from Andre Onana on Sasa Kalajdzic; despite a long VAR check, Wolves were not given the spot-kick in injury time and lost the match 1-0. After Onana clattered into Kalajdzic in the box, O'Neil thought a penalty would certainly be awarded, but instead the Wolves manager received a yellow card on the sidelines for his protests. PGMOL's Jonathan Moss did apologise for the mistake after the match, which O'Neil said he appreciated. Fans watching the game were in disbelief when the call was made, and similar incidents have happened since, including against United: Bruno Fernandes said he would wait for an apology — one that never arrived — after Cristian Romero was not punished for handball in the Red Devils' 2-0 loss to Tottenham, and plenty of onlookers debated the penalty won by Marcus Rashford in United's subsequent comeback win at home to Nottingham Forest.

Tottenham 2-1 Liverpool, September 30, 2023: Liverpool had their hearts broken as Joel Matip's stoppage-time own-goal gave Tottenham a 2-1 victory, with the Reds down to nine men after a red card to Curtis Jones and two bookings for Diogo Jota, looking to hang on at the death and nearly doing so until the cruel finish. However, the game could have turned out completely different had the VAR booth not committed a "serious human error" earlier in the match: soon after Jones was sent off in the first half, Luis Diaz scored to put Liverpool 1-0 up despite their disadvantage, but the flag went up for offside; replay seemed to show Diaz was onside, yet VAR Darren England ended his check without even drawing lines, and the decision stood. The PGMOL issued a statement after the match stating the goal should have stood.

# Romero's Red Card And Palmer's Penalty Equaliser

The defining moment of Tottenham vs. Chelsea on Nov. 6, 2023 came in the 31st minute, when a wild passage of play ended with Moises Caicedo's goal ruled out, Cristian Romero sent off on VAR review, and Cole Palmer converting the resulting penalty to level the scoreline at 1-1.

The sequence began with the ball pinging around the Tottenham penalty area, Spurs unable to clear after blocking multiple efforts, until Caicedo finally buried a long-distance effort with a low finish inside the left post. Despite initially appearing to count, the offside flag was raised extremely late, with the assistant referee determining, after a moment to think, that Nicolas Jackson was interfering with play from an offside position.

After a few looks, Oliver produced a straight red card for Romero's tackle and awarded Chelsea a penalty, which Palmer dispatched. # England 6-0 Scotland At Hampden: Match Report

England beat Scotland emphatically at Hampden on Dec. 5, 2023, taking an early lead from a Beth Mead corner headed in by an unmarked Alex Greenwood and building through a Lauren James masterclass.

Where England had played well for the opening 10 minutes against the Dutch only to be sucker-punched on the counter in the 12th minute, against Scotland there was no such risk: the visiting team took the lead to swing the pressure onto the Dutch, from Mead's corner. Moments later Lisa Evans went down in the box under pressure from Bronze, but appeals for a penalty were waved away with the right-back not having caught the forward's legs. England went close to a second, with the Dutch having taken the lead against Belgium, when James weaved into the box before delivering to Hemp at the far post, who lashed her effort off the base of a post from close range. Eight minutes later they doubled the lead: Mead's corner was cleared and sent back in by the Arsenal forward only to be cleared again, and while England players appealed for handball, James sent the ball goalward and it took a heavy deflection that wrongfooted Alexander and flew in. It was not pretty, but England were clawing away at the goal difference gap. A minute later James delivered in more characteristic style, curling a wonderful effort into the top corner from the edge of the area. In added time at the end of the half, James turned provider of the goal that put England top of the group once more, sweeping a cross to Mead at the far post for the forward to bring down and fire past a helpless Alexander. The goal that gave England a cushion came shortly after the restart, Georgia Stanway beating Corsie to the byline before sending the ball into the middle for Fran Kirby to turn in from close range — though the breathing room did not last long, with the Netherlands scoring once more. There was almost disaster for England when Earps failed to collect from the feet of Kirsty Hanson, but the Scotland forward sent her effort wide of the empty net with the angle closing.

# England's Defensive Brittleness And Dropped Points

Against the reading that England's Olympic exit turned on the final night in Glasgow, The Guardian argues the damage had been done in the preceding games — and that the underlying problem is defensive brittleness rather than attacking quality.

On the goal-difference framing, the counter-grounds are the earlier results: two poor goals conceded against the Dutch at Wembley, a 3-2 defeat in Belgium in October and a 2-1 loss to the Netherlands in September would all be full of regrets, so an extraordinary mountain remained that even a Lauren James masterclass and a gut-busting display from Lucy Bronze could not lift them over. The piece concedes there will be what-ifs either way, with the first goal conceded in Utrecht appearing offside in the buildup. On the attacking framing, the counter is that for large parts of the Wembley game England were not very good, and that for all their creativity and verve going forward perhaps the biggest flaw in the side is a lack of presence in the two penalty areas — the physicality and alpha energy to do the grunt work, to convert the crosses and to head them away. Individually, Jess Carter had a poor game and was withdrawn for Esme Morgan after half-time, Alex Greenwood over-committed for the first Dutch goal, and even the all-conquering Mary Earps plummeted to Earth with a poor first-half error. But beyond personnel, a basic brittleness seems to have crept into the team, a sense of melting surfaces and cracks in the ice: Sarina Wiegman talks a lot about defending against counterattacks because this is basically the key to the whole enterprise — cut off the counter and England's technical quality lets them easily dominate — and it is also the essential measure of how the team functions as a collective, in the efficiency of the press, the closing of angles and the command of space; Lineth Beerensteyn's two goals were the sort England simply were not conceding four months earlier. So England passed the ball around a bit and gave it away a bit and essentially ran around trying to feel normal again, and on countless occasions Kelly or Hemp would win a first or second ball, look up and see a penalty area empty of white shirts — issues not so much of tactics but of cohesion and energy: the timing of runs, and the sharpness required not just to anticipate where the ball is going to be but actually get there. You can still chase when running on fumes, but to create needs an idea and a vision, the clarity of mind to see the picture before it has materialised.

# Manchester United's 1-0 Defeat To Bayern Munich, December 2023

Manchester United lost 1-0 at home to Bayern Munich on the final Champions League group matchday, reported by The Independent on 12 December 2023, with Kingsley Coman scoring on 71 minutes from a Harry Kane assist to condemn United to a seventh home defeat of the season.

The goal came at near walking pace. Coman weaved his way through the centre, the ball was eventually worked to Kane, and the English forward clipped an artful ball back through for Coman, who finished emphatically. Bayern were already through and perhaps looking to make a point after their own 5-1 defeat to Eintracht Frankfurt, but did not even need to step it up to win; they were quite low-intensity themselves, and Coman's winner came from the forward almost walking through the middle of their team. Kane did not score but did set it up. Bayern still had more of the ball and more of the attacks, which was another tension for Ten Hag to overcome: United were playing in quite a controlled way when they were going to eventually have to go for it, yet Bayern were getting through that with relative ease, so the team almost looked like they were in two minds. Bruno Fernandes blazed United's best opportunity over the bar after good work from Aaron Wan Bissaka.

The atmosphere matched the performance. There was no energy or intensity; the Stretford End eventually implored United to "attack attack attack" but the complete absence of any such impulses left some of the stadium booing the side off at the end, and it was another utterly forgettable display in a drab game before a muted crowd. News came through shortly before the hour that Lukas Lerager had scored for Copenhagen, though it did not really change the atmosphere. In context this was far from United's worst performance of the season — nowhere near as bad as Bournemouth or Crystal Palace or Newcastle, or the other defeat to Newcastle, and not as self-destructive as they had been in Denmark and Turkey and at home to Galatasaray — and they were vaguely competent on the night. But they still lost, 24 years after Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's stunning intervention against the same opponent.

# Manfred's Rebuttal To Stripping The Astros' 2017 Title

Many thought taking away the World Series win, essentially nullifying 2017, was the best way to move forward; MLB thought otherwise, and Commissioner Robert Manfred's counter-argument attacked the workability of that remedy rather than the wrongdoing itself, per Essentially Sports on 2023-10-22. In his words: "Once you go down that road of changing what happens on the field, I just don't know how you decide where you stop." The premise he denied was that a clean line could be drawn around which on-field results to revise — and so the Commissioner's Trophy was still legitimate in the eyes of, well, the Commissioner.

A second strand of his objection was practical timing: by the time the controversy was uncovered, the Astros were well into establishing a streak of successful years, and Manfred called the process of stripping the Fall Classic title "difficult and impractical." Already unpopular among the masses, he made things worse for himself when he called the trophy a "piece of metal." He apologized later, but the team kept the championship victory.

# England 3-2 Netherlands At Wembley: Toone's Winner

Ella Toone's injury-time goal at 9.34 p.m. on a briskly cold Wembley night earned England three points against the Netherlands and kept their faintly glowing Olympic dream alive.

Throughout the Nations League campaign this had been an England team fighting its own sense of entropy, still giving everything and still trying the same plans and processes in the hope that eventually something would click — and it finally did. The goal breathed life into a team and a cycle, turning a moment that had felt like it was drawing to its natural conclusion into a rousing encore for a cast preparing for its final curtain; new challenges would come soon enough with European Championship qualifiers in the spring, but for now this iteration of the Lionesses still had tricks up its sleeve, talent and creativity to burn, and a fire that could scorch any team on the planet. They rallied spectacularly to salvage a match that looked cooked after 35 minutes, running on fumes and adrenaline, sustained by the sizzle of the Wembley crowd, the cold air on their skin and the flickering candle of qualification for Paris — an energy not really glimpsed since they reassembled that autumn, barely a month on from the trauma of Sydney, still a little dazed and concussed. Beth Mead came on for Chloe Kelly at half-time, Georgia Stanway moved further forward and made herself a menace in the penalty area, and the old buddies Toone and Alessia Russo teamed up off the bench; the Dutch retreated further and further into Wembley's wide open spaces, giving Lauren James the time and territory to dictate. James had a hand in all three goals, and as Toone ghosted in at the far post to provide the final flourish, Wembley screeched out one last call to arms.

# The VAR Intervention Window Before Play Restarts

VAR can only intervene in an incident before play restarts; once the game has resumed, the official cannot act on it. Sporting News invoked this window on Nov. 6, 2023 to explain why one passage of play in Tottenham vs. Chelsea was not reviewed at all.

It was unclear exactly why the incident went unreviewed, but the assumption offered was that the VAR official was likely not aware of it until play had already restarted, at which point he cannot intervene. The boundary condition Sporting News stresses is practical rather than legal: such incidents have to be caught before play restarts, which is extremely difficult to do as the game continues to flow.

# Red Cards And VAR Decisions In Tottenham Vs Chelsea

Tottenham finished the match with nine men after two dismissals, and referee Michael Oliver's game featured a string of contested VAR calls in both directions. Romero was lucky not to be sent off in the 21st minute after he retaliated with a kick on Levi Colwill following an initial shove on the Argentinean; he was later shown a red card, after a lengthy VAR review, for clipping Fernandez inside the box with a high-footed challenge that sent his compatriot to ground, with Oliver awarding Chelsea a penalty.

Sterling scored for Chelsea amid the earlier incident, seconds later, but his goal was ruled out for handball after his first shot rebounded off Porro onto his right arm before he put the ball away beyond Vicario. Fernandez and Thiago Silva then saw shots go wide for Chelsea, but tensions hit boiling point in the 28th minute as Moises Caicedo had an equalising goal disallowed due to Jackson interfering with play as the Colombian delivered his shot upon goal.

# College Football's "Best Versus Most Deserving" Debate

The New York Times argued on 3 December 2023 that college football has an identity crisis — whether the teams that play for the national championship should be the best or the most deserving — and that the 2023 selection forced the sport to confront it for the first time.

The grounds are historical. The crisis has existed since the inception of the College Football Playoff a decade ago, but never before had it come to a head the way it did that Sunday: in the nine years before that season, the best and the most deserving seamlessly became one, resulting in cut-and-dried decisions on which teams would make the field.

The warrant is that when the two criteria diverge, the choice exposes what the selection process actually is. With that one decision the committee didn't just choose teams in a given year — it revealed to the world the ugly truth about college football: this sport is a beauty contest where decisions on which teams can win the national title are sometimes made as much in a cozy hotel boardroom in Grapevine, Texas, as they are on the actual field.

# Playoff Seeding

Playoff seeding is the numbered ranking assigned to each team that has qualified for a postseason field, used to set which team hosts each game, which teams earn a bye, and how the bracket is arranged.

## Context

In the corpus, seeding shows up in two different forms depending on the sport's postseason structure.

For the NFL, Sporting News' Week 13 playoff-picture roundup builds seeding directly from division standings and tiebreakers: the No. 1 seed in each conference gets home-field advantage and the lone first-round bye, and teams below the four division leaders are ranked as wild-card "in the hunt" entrants — for example the Dolphins held the AFC's No. 1 seed on the conference-record tiebreaker over the Ravens, while the Cowboys, as a division runner-up, could finish "No. 1, No. 2 or No. 3" if they won their division or were "locked into No. 5" otherwise.

For college football, the corpus shows a different seeding mechanism entirely: the four-team College Football Playoff field is not set by a standings formula but by a selection committee that ranks and numbers teams by subjective judgment of "best" versus "most deserving" — the 2023 field was numbered 1. Michigan, 2. Washington, 3. Texas, 4. Alabama, with an unbeaten Florida State left out of the numbered field altogether.

MLB's postseason coverage in the corpus treats seeding's practical payoff — home-field advantage — as uneven in impact: The Athletic's ranking of playoff ballpark atmospheres notes that a Rangers team with nine fewer regular-season wins than the Rays still swept the Rays at the Rays' home ballpark, illustrating that seeding-conferred home-field advantage does not guarantee an edge.

## Key Characteristics

- **Numbered rank within a bracket** — each qualified team gets a single ordinal number (No. 1, No. 2, etc.) that determines its bracket position, as in the NFL's AFC/NFC seed lists and the CFP's 1-4 field.
- **Drives home-field advantage and byes** — in the NFL, the No. 1 seed in each conference gets the lone first-round bye and home-field advantage, a stake the corpus describes the Eagles as being "in real danger of losing" to the 49ers, while the Ravens held only a half-game lead for the same spot over three teams right behind them.
- **Built from different inputs by sport** — the NFL derives seeds from win-loss record, division titles, and tiebreakers (head-to-head, conference record); the CFP derives its numbered field from a committee's ranked judgment rather than a fixed statistical formula.
- **Division winners are seeded above wild cards** — the NFL's seeding format ranks all division leaders (seeds 1-4) ahead of the best non-division-winning teams (wild cards, seeds 5-7), regardless of overall record, as when the 6-6 Falcons held a division-winner seed while stronger wild-card contenders sat lower.
- **Home-field advantage from seeding is not decisive** — MLB coverage of the 2023 postseason shows the Rangers, with nine fewer regular-season wins than the Rays, sweeping the Rays at their home ballpark despite two of the smallest postseason crowds in the past 100 years there, so seeding sets the schedule and venue but not the outcome.

# Alabama, Texas And The SEC Selection Dilemma, 2023

The New York Times argued on 3 December 2023 that, as difficult as it would have been, the right thing for the CFP committee to do would have been to leave Alabama out — because Alabama lost a game at home and losses used to have consequences.

The dilemma the committee faced is easy to understand. Alabama is a one-loss SEC champion that beat Georgia on the Saturday, ending the Bulldogs' 29-game winning streak; Texas is a one-loss Big 12 champion that beat Alabama by 10 points in Tuscaloosa in September. Many fans were hoping the SEC would be left out entirely for the first time, but the committee — charged with picking the "best teams" — couldn't ignore what the ultra-talented Crimson Tide accomplished; and if Alabama goes, the committee could hardly leave out the team that beat it. It couldn't. That is probably the path of least resistance: outside of Florida State fans, the general population will move on convinced that the Playoff semifinals will be more entertaining with more high-level teams, and the best teams, as they say, won out.

The counter-case rests on consequences. Most of us know in our gut that the Crimson Tide — the most talented team, on paper, in the sport — are one of the four best teams, and Alabama is certainly equipped to win the whole thing. But Alabama, like peers Georgia and Ohio State, teams with a wealth of raw talent on their rosters, lost a game at home, and better teams have been left out in the past than this Alabama team because losses had consequences. Alabama's loss to Texas didn't have a consequence because we're enamored with the SEC and what it means to beat Georgia; it didn't matter that Alabama — though perceived to be an entirely different team in September — lost to the Longhorns. That game could have been a Playoff game in September. It turns out it was an exhibition.

# The CFP Committee's "Different Team" Justification For Florida State

The New York Times attacked the CFP committee's justification for omitting Florida State on 3 December 2023, arguing that CFP committee chair Boo Corrigan's statement — "Florida State is a different team. You look at who they are as a team without Jordan Travis — they are a different team" — is a well-informed opinion that is probably true, but is not a fact.

The premise under attack is that a team's quality without its injured starter can be reliably judged in advance. Choosing the best is entirely subjective and ultimately misleading given this is a sport that routinely features unpredictable results and unforeseen runs. The precedent cited is that the last time a team was relying on a third-string quarterback heading into the College Football Playoff — Ohio State in the inaugural season of the four-team field — it won the national title.

The rebuttal also concedes the disanalogy and then answers it. The difference between those Buckeyes and this Florida State team was that Ohio State won the Big Ten title game that year 59-0, while Florida State was in a close game with Louisville that was, quite frankly, not an enjoyable watch for people who love the excitement of big-time offense — perception, wrongly, became reality. Against that, one could make the case that Florida State is so good that it won a Power 5 conference championship game with a true freshman quarterback, and that in the CFP the Seminoles would have gotten second-string quarterback Tate Rodemaker back with a month to prepare for a semifinal game.

context:
# Manchester United 2-1 Chelsea, December 2023

Manchester United got themselves back to winning ways with a 2-1 victory over Chelsea thanks to a superb Scott McTominay brace, per Sporting News on Dec. 6, 2023. The final score was Man United 2 (McTominay 19', 70'), Chelsea 1 (Palmer 45').

The victory remarkably put United within three points of rivals Manchester City, after the reigning champions were defeated by Aston Villa, and kept them in reach of the top four places.

McTominay became United's top scorer for the season with six goals, one ahead of Bruno Fernandes and Rasmus Hojlund. The Red Devils' captain had a first-half penalty saved by Robert Sanchez, and United's Danish striker was substituted after another Premier League game without a goal, despite making 11 appearances. United had now won their past 19 Premier League games at Old Trafford when scoring first, including all 16 under their Dutch manager.



---


# Scott McTominay's Advanced Role And Goal Threat

Under Ten Hag, Scott McTominay functions as a marauding midfield engine and late-running goal threat with a licence to create overloads wherever he finds them — the job United once paid Paul Pogba to do.

The structure of the role differs from his previous, more conventional midfield positions. Against low blocks and structured defences — and, the piece notes, nobody is remotely accusing Chelsea of possessing one of those — he provides the extra body in a tightly marked penalty area; but he also pops up in the channels and on the wing, either supporting the man in possession or offering himself for the quick switch of play. The relation between that role and his output shows in the numbers: against Chelsea he scored his fifth and sixth goals of the season, having previously never got more than seven. The piece attributes this partly to opponents still not quite cottoning on to his goal threat — those late runs to the far post, the blur on the edge of the 18-yard box you do not spot until it is too late — and partly to how Ten Hag is using him. The range over which the relation holds is the current team: for all the undoubted leadership qualities of Bruno Fernandes and Harry Maguire, tactically it is McTominay running the show right now, a development with numerous interesting consequences. The Pogba comparison is drawn with the caveat that McTominay is a different kind of player with a different kind of skillset; Pogba's United career never quite worked out, largely — if you believe his most vehement critics — on account of his hair.



---


# How The Goals Came In Manchester United 2-1 Chelsea

Erik ten Hag's side were dominant in the first half and finally pounced on Chelsea's inability to take control in midfield to open the scoring through Scott McTominay, per Sporting News on Dec. 6, 2023.

For the first goal, Mauricio Pochettino's men attempted to break at pace but Sofyan Amrabat made a vital interception and Fernandes found Alejandro Garnacho out wide; the youngster then cut the ball back to Harry Maguire, whose effort rebounded perfectly into the path of McTominay, and the Scotland international took one touch before blasting past Sanchez.

United led for the majority of the first 45 minutes but failed to build on their lead and were pegged back by the former Manchester City man Cole Palmer. The 21-year-old, who made the transfer from the Etihad Stadium to Stamford Bridge in August, stroked the ball into the far corner with deadly accuracy; it was his fifth Premier League goal of the season and his first from open play. United continued to put Chelsea under pressure in the second half and after numerous attempts McTominay headed powerfully past Sanchez. The Scotsman had seven shots, his most ever in a league game. Despite a flurry of late attacks driven by Reece James, Ten Hag's team stood strong and held on to see out the victory.



---


# Harry Kane's 2023 Goal Tally And Bayern Munich Scoring Records

Harry Kane scored 52 goals in the 2023 calendar year for Bayern Munich, Tottenham and England, tied for second on TalkSport's list of the year's top scorers. A stunning 2022/23 season saw Bayern splash out over £100m to sign the Spurs legend in August, and Kane repaid the Bundesliga club's faith by breaking a number of records with his 25 goals in all competitions so far in the season.

The leading scorer in the German top flight with 22 goals, the Three Lions skipper set a new Bundesliga record the previous month by finding the back of the net 17 times in his opening 11 outings. # The Italy International Goalscoring Record Anomaly

The New York Times argued on 17 November 2023 that Italy's is perhaps the most surprising international goalscoring record: the claim is that Gigi Riva's relatively insubstantial haul of 35 goals, the mark to beat since the 1974 World Cup, has never been matched or even closely approached, and the warrant is that this reflects Italy's tactical shape and the distribution of its strikers rather than an absence of prolific forwards.

The comparative grounds establish that the record is low. No one has ever got particularly near Riva's total — Roberto Baggio and Alessandro Del Piero both reached 27, and that's as close as anyone has come. For context, four Englishmen have reached 35 goals in that period: Gary Lineker, Michael Owen, Wayne Rooney and Harry Kane; four Spaniards too — Raul Gonzalez, Fernando Torres, David Villa and David Silva — while Alvaro Morata, on 34, should get there shortly. Nor do current Italians look set to challenge it: Ciro Immobile, with 17, has less than half the tally, turns 34 in February and has been omitted from recent squads, and nobody in Luciano Spalletti's current squad has scored more than eight international goals.

The explanatory grounds are twofold. Italy's shortcoming clearly isn't about a complete lack of prolific strikers — Christian Vieri, Pippo Inzaghi and Luca Toni all scored heavily at club level — and sometimes it has been the opposite, with various strikers competing for a starting place so none got to dominate the national side for a decade; though around a decade ago there was simply a dearth of prolific Italian strikers to choose from, with Antonio Conte using Eder and Graziano Pelle up front at the 2016 European Championship. There are also tactical considerations: not only have Italy traditionally been the most defensive of the major European nations, but their attacking play has generally been based around using a second striker, with Baggio, Del Piero and Francesco Totti each the golden boy at various overlapping stages and Italy's No 9 often selected primarily to bring the best out of Italy's No 10.

# The Three Concurrent Roles Of A Manchester United Manager

Barney Ronay models the Manchester United job as three concurrent roles — managing the past, managing the dysfunction of the present, and managing the everyday metrics on which the manager is judged.

First you must manage the past, which is constantly in the room and which skews every act, achievement and expectation. Second you must manage the dysfunction of the present, which expresses itself in every detail from a leaking stadium roof to the deep ills of a playing squad peopled with squatters and long-term missteps. Finally you get to manage the everyday metrics — team, results, style, energy, messaging: win things, improve players, create a coherent and happy internal culture, but do it during an unceasing takeover circus while star players sulk and brief against you, and while the ghost of Hamlet's father still skulks in the eaves. The three hold together only under those conditions; as of the December 2023 Champions League exit, Ronay judged, this felt like the end of one thing, perhaps even the beginning of the end of something else.

Bayern still had more of the ball and more of the attacks, which was another tension for Ten Hag to overcome: United were playing in quite a controlled way when they were going to eventually have to go for it, yet Bayern were getting through that with relative ease, so the team almost looked like they were in two minds. The atmosphere matched the performance. There was no energy or intensity; the Stretford End eventually implored United to "attack attack attack" but the complete absence of any such impulses left some of the stadium booing the side off at the end, and it was another utterly forgettable display in a drab game before a muted crowd. News came through shortly before the hour that Lukas Lerager had scored for Copenhagen, though it did not really change the atmosphere. In context this was far from United's worst performance of the season — nowhere near as bad as Bournemouth or Crystal Palace or Newcastle, or the other defeat to Newcastle, and not as self-destructive as they had been in Denmark and Turkey and at home to Galatasaray — and they were vaguely competent on the night. But they still lost, 24 years after Ole Gunnar Solskjaer's stunning intervention against the same opponent.

# Terry McLaurin's Fantasy Outlook In Weeks 5 And 6 Of 2023

CBS Sports listed Terry McLaurin under "Start Him" in Week 5 of the 2023 season and then under "Sit Him" in Week 6, and the reversal turns on two things changing: the Commanders' targets diffused among three receivers, and the opponent shifted from a depleted Bears secondary to an ascending Falcons one in a low-total game.

The Week 5 case, published 4 October 2023 ahead of a home game with Chicago, holds that Washington may wish to win with a big dose of the run game — Brian Robinson is called a must-start — but that if the Bears put up any offense at all, McLaurin will be in position to put up nice numbers. Over the past three weeks he had led all Commanders wide receivers in targets and all Commanders players in receptions; he is the No. 1 guy, and his big Week 4 line of 8-86-0 plus an offensive fumble recovery for a touchdown would have been even bigger had Sam Howell placed a deep ball better on a play McLaurin was open for. Chicago was expected to play again without top outside cornerback Jaylon Johnson and safety Eddie Jackson — absences that had not led to a bonanza for Denver's receivers, since Russell Wilson spread the ball around — with rookies Tyrique Stevenson and Terell Smith lining up across from McLaurin most; if he remains the target leader he has the best shot at a big game. The pattern the column leans on: every top-target-earning receiver who plays mostly outside, like McLaurin, has found at least 10 PPR points in every game against the Bears, including Rashee Rice in Week 3 (seven targets, 5-59-0), Courtland Sutton in Week 4 (five targets, 3-27-1), Romeo Doubs in Week 1 (five targets, 4-26-2) and Mike Evans in Week 2 (eight targets, 6-171-1), those receivers combining to catch 18 of 25 targets, 72%, against Chicago. The breakdown lists Washington at home versus Chicago, the Commanders favoured by 6, an over/under of 44.5, an opponent ranked 19th versus wide receivers, 15.2 projected points, a 21st receiver ranking, and year-to-date totals of 21 receptions on 26 targets for 212 yards, one touchdown and 12.1 fantasy points per game. The verdict makes him a low-end WR2 worth the nod over George Pickens, Zay Flowers, Drake London and Jahan Dotson.

The Week 6 case, published 12 October 2023 ahead of a game at Atlanta, reverses it. McLaurin posted good numbers in only two games — Washington's 35-33 Week 2 win over Denver and its 34-31 overtime loss to Philadelphia in Week 4 — and this matchup carries an over/under of 42.5, tied for fourth-lowest of the week; adding the ascending secondary Atlanta seems to have and the Commanders' diffusion of targets makes him at best a low-end flex. The breakdown lists the Falcons favoured by 2.5, an opponent ranked 6th versus wide receivers, 12.1 projected points, a 37th receiver ranking, and year-to-date totals of 25 receptions on 31 targets for 261 yards, one touchdown and 11.4 fantasy points per game. In Week 5, even in a favourable game script where Washington trailed by three scores before halftime, McLaurin saw only five targets against Chicago's heavy zone coverage. On film, of the 10 third-down routes he ran, he drew extra coverage on four, got open on two where Howell threw elsewhere, and was a decoy on Curtis Samuel's touchdown; Howell was getting rid of the ball quickly and short as the Bears generated pressure, and by the end McLaurin's body language seemed dispirited. Washington throws to its wideouts on 58.7% of targets, below league average though not as low as Atlanta's 36.4%, and worse, McLaurin has just one more target (31) than Jahan Dotson (30), who has three more than Curtis Samuel (27) — all nearly even after five games, each having led in targets at least once. Atlanta is expected to play a heavy dose of zone, if only because Washington has struggled to be explosive against zone this year, and the Falcons gave a full dose of snaps last week to outside cornerback Jeff Okudah, not flawless but another sizable body against stronger perimeter receivers, so between Okudah and A.J. Terrell there isn't a matchup that's great for McLaurin. His own splits confirm the cap: an impressive 91.3% catch rate against zone but just 9.3 yards per catch on a sub-9.0 average depth of target, with a target share below 20% regardless of coverage. The verdict would rather roll the dice on Drake London, Tyler Lockett or Garrett Wilson.

# The Dallas Cowboys' 2023 Contender Credentials

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that it does not see where Dallas is better or going to get considerably better, especially on offense, though it conceded this was a tough time to evaluate the Cowboys fairly because they were so bad against San Francisco on a big stage in their most recent game.

The additional ground offered is cultural rather than statistical: every time the Cowboys enjoy success, they seem to enjoy it a little too much, which the writer treats as a reflection of their owner.

An executive located the problem in identity and consistency: "Run defense and consistency on defense, and then offensively, what is their identity? They just are not very good. Their best games are when they play great defense and get turnovers, but that is not going to happen enough, especially against the good teams." The warrant on both sides is that a contender needs a repeatable formula, and Dallas's best path — great defense plus turnovers — is not repeatable often enough against strong opposition.
