# Brock Purdy's Fantasy Outlook In Weeks 5 And 6 Of 2023

CBS Sports benched Brock Purdy in Week 5 of the 2023 season and then reversed itself in Week 6, admitting the first call was a mistake: the Week 5 argument was that Dallas' pressure plus man coverage created too much downside, and the Week 6 argument was that the author would not make the mistake of benching Purdy again after Dallas played zone and paid for it.

The Week 5 "Sit Him" case, published 4 October 2023, holds that it is safe to expect Purdy to feel a lot of pressure against the Cowboys, and that man coverage behind that pressure could create havoc that speeds him up; the column calls him consistent and the 49ers loaded, but treats this as one of those rare matchups with too much downside. After ranking him high early in the week the author moved him behind Anthony Richardson, Jordan Love and Trevor Lawrence, while keeping him ahead of Joe Burrow, Dak Prescott and Daniel Jones. The evidence for the downside: Dallas lost top cornerback Trevon Diggs and stayed red hot, leading the league in pass-rush pressure rate at 55.6% and ranking top-10 in blitz rate at 31.9%, which helped them into the top five in completion rate allowed (57.4%), passing touchdowns allowed (two) and missed tackles on pass plays (five, best in football); only Joshua Dobbs, who ran for 55 yards, had scored double-digit fantasy points against them, at 18, and their other victims were Daniel Jones, Zach Wilson and the Patriots quarterbacks. Dallas had also become one of the most aggressive defenses in the league, third from the bottom in zone-coverage snaps, having played heavy zone only in the closing quarters of blowout wins over the Giants and Jets — a completely different look from their January playoff meeting with Purdy, when they played zone on nearly 86% of snaps. In that playoff game the Cowboys pressured Purdy on 48.5% of dropbacks while blitzing just 21.2%, and Purdy completed 65% of his throws but struggled for 214 yards with no touchdowns. The counterweights the column concedes: San Francisco's 36.4% pressure rate allowed is only a shade worse than league average and is weighted by the Giants blitzing on 84.6% of Purdy's Week 2 dropbacks, a game in which Purdy still threw for 310 yards and two touchdowns without Brandon Aiyuk; Purdy had hit at least 20 fantasy points in eight of nine regular-season starts, which should be nine of nine but for a Week 2 touchdown ruled a lateral, and in nine of 11 including two playoff games, with at least 23 points in five of those nine including each of his past two; and the previous week he executed the offense flawlessly against Arizona, missing on one throw and again losing points to a pass ruled a lateral for a touchdown. His splits were strong against both man and zone — higher completion rate and yards per attempt against zone, four of his five passing touchdowns against man — but he was at his worst when pressured, completing 48.6% for 5.6 yards per attempt with a gaudy 18.9% off-target rate.

The Week 6 "Start Him" case, published 12 October 2023, is a correction. The author expected Purdy to struggle against a defense that pressured and played man; instead the Cowboys played a lot of zone and paid the price through the air, a choice a friend suggested was meant to avoid getting burned by long Christian McCaffrey runs. Against Cleveland, the combination of a hot 49ers defense and a Browns offense figuring to get stuffed should produce at least a game script for decent numbers, and the author would start Purdy over Trevor Lawrence, Geno Smith and Jared Goff. The breakdown lists San Francisco at Cleveland, the 49ers favoured by 7, an over/under of 37, an opponent ranked 1st versus quarterbacks, 16.5 projected points, an 11th quarterback ranking, and year-to-date totals of 1,271 passing yards, 24 rushing yards, 11 touchdowns, no interceptions and 23.4 fantasy points per game. In Week 5 Purdy beat one of the toughest pass rushes in football for four touchdowns on 24 attempts, with his seven incompletions comprising a drop, two balls batted at the line, a throwaway and two defensed passes, and an off-target rate of 0.0%. His 20-point streak extended to nine of 10 regular-season starts — 10 of 10 but for the lateral ruling — and 10 of 12 including playoffs, with at least 23 points in six of those 10 including each of his past three games. Cleveland has played the least zone coverage of any team in football, never even reaching 65% zone in a game and exceeding 70% in only three quarters all season, and had just watched Dallas play 90% zone while Purdy cooked them like BBQ chicken. The Browns rank third in pressure rate at 41.5% and blitz at an above-average 29.3%, but the Cowboys ranked higher and lost anyway; Purdy's pressured splits had improved to a 50% completion rate, 6.7 yards per attempt and a 15.9% off-target rate, and five of his seven passing touchdowns had come against man. Lamar Jackson's precedent is offered as the closing warrant: facing the Browns in their previous game he saw a ton of man coverage and heavy pressure yet threw two touchdowns and completed 79% of his passes for 9.8 yards per attempt without his starting left tackle and two of his top receivers, helped by his defense turning over an ill-prepared Browns offense.

# NFL Aggressiveness Versus Traditional Game Management

A longtime NFL executive challenged the analytics-driven push toward aggressive play-calling on 16 October 2023, asking whether coaches have "come too far with coaches wanting to 'win' the game instead of sometimes being more traditional" after the Eagles threw a killer interception on third-and-9 from their own 46-yard line while protecting a 14-12 lead against the Jets with two minutes left in the fourth quarter.

The premise attacked is not that aggression is generally wrong. Most would agree teams have gotten smarter in their handling of fourth-down situations, going for it when it makes sense instead of punting almost out of habit; making the aggressive play to win can absolutely be the smart play regardless of results, and it is progress when teams seriously wrestle with these questions, not just on fourth down but in all aspects of strategy. What the exec disputes is the automatic application of that reasoning to a particular game state: Philadelphia could have run the ball on third-and-9, then punted from around midfield, leaving the Jets with barely more than a minute remaining, no timeouts and Zach Wilson behind center facing a ferocious Eagles pass rush. "Are coaches not willing to go against the slight statistical benefit that WPA (win probability added) provides?" he asked. "Is it no longer OK to let your defense win the game when it clearly has a huge talent/performance advantage? This Eagles game was 14-12, not 37-35."

The inference the counter-argument targets is the neglect of situation-specific factors. In that game the Jets' offense had netted 19 yards on its previous three possessions, producing one field goal on a drive that gained 16 of those yards; the Eagles had already suffered three turnovers, and they knew Wilson would be taking over deep in his territory with very little time remaining. "To me, these are exactly the type of factors that a coach needs to consider when deciding," the exec said. "I think they were ignored here." A veteran coach added an incentive-based explanation — critics attuned to the trend toward aggressiveness pounce when teams pass up chances to go for the kill, coaches know team owners tend to be fans rather than football strategists and listen to those criticisms, which creates an incentive to go down swinging: "Everybody thinks they are playing Brady, Manning or Rodgers in two-minute. If before the game someone offered Philly to put its defense against Zach Wilson on a need-field-goal drive starting inside his own 15 with no timeouts and a minute left, you think they would have taken it?" The base rate is thin: the situation Philly faced was the seventh time since 2000 that a team leading by 1-2 points in the final two minutes faced third down with 7-10 yards to go from the minus-40 yard line to midfield with the opponent holding no timeouts; three of the seven passed, resulting in one first down, one sack and Hurts' interception, and of those three only the Eagles lost the game.

# Dallas Goedert As A Week 5 2023 Bust Candidate At The Rams

CBS Sports flagged Dallas Goedert as a "Bust Candidate" for Week 5 of the 2023 season at the Los Angeles Rams: the claim is that Goedert is a distant third in targets on the Eagles for a reason — he's not explosive in the least and the Philadelphia offense is much more concerned with its explosive components — and the warrant is that the Rams' recent tight end concessions came against secondary tight ends they barely covered, so they do not predict anything for Goedert.

The usage grounds are blunt. For three weeks in a row, with seven or fewer targets, Goedert has failed to reach even 50 receiving yards, and his target volume dipped from seven in Weeks 2 and 3 to four in Week 4, the same number as D'Andre Swift — and it shouldn't be lost on fantasy managers that since Swift became a staple in the Eagles offense, Goedert has taken a backseat. Coach Nick Sirianni again said "we need to get him the football," citing that plays designed for him wound up going to other Eagles because of how defenses played Goedert. The column's film review disputes that explanation: on his nine third-down routes in Week 4 there was nothing teams were doing to take him away, he still looked sluggish in his movements and didn't run many deeper routes, though on a couple he did get open and Jalen Hurts had better opportunities elsewhere. The mixed evidence from that game is that two targets came in the red zone and a third was a deep contested catch for 17 yards, while the fourth was dropped on a short throw. On the season Goedert has three red-zone targets and zero end-zone targets, and while there is always a shot he scores from short range, the Eagles like to run the ball near the goal line.

The matchup evidence is presented as a trap. The Rams got stung for two touchdowns to tight ends at Indianapolis the previous week, one on a 35-yard play where Mo Alie-Cox got matched up with defensive-end-turned-outside-linebacker Mike Hoecht, the other a five-yard toss to Andrew Ogletree, who ran past Hoecht off the snap for an easy score — but those players aren't considered primary tight ends like Goedert, so it's unlikely the Rams would cover Goedert the way they covered them, which is to say barely. Before Week 4, the Seahawks, Bengals and 49ers tight ends, including George Kittle, combined for eight non-PPR and 19 PPR fantasy points over three games against the Rams, whose pass stats against tight ends were much better before the Colts laid some numbers on them. The breakdown lists Philadelphia at the Rams, the Eagles favoured by 4.5, an over/under of 50.5, an opponent ranked 23rd versus tight ends, 9.3 projected points, a 12th tight end ranking, and year-to-date totals of 13 receptions on 19 targets for 88 yards, no touchdowns and 5.5 fantasy points per game. The verdict prefers Jake Ferguson and Zach Ertz in all formats, plus Kyle Pitts and Cole Kmet in non-PPR.

# Miles Sanders As A Week 5 2023 Sit At Detroit

CBS Sports listed Miles Sanders under "Sit Him" for Week 5 of the 2023 season at Detroit: the claim is that starting Sanders means hoping for a few long plays, perhaps through the air, plus a touchdown, and the warrant is that the Lions' run defense should keep him grounded while his own playing time is slipping away.

The grounds combine a collapsing role with collapsing efficiency. In Week 4 Sanders' playing time hit a season-low 43% of snaps as he continued losing third-down work to Chuba Hubbard; that has not crushed his reception totals, though his only game with more than four catches came with Andy Dalton under centre, and he played just 31% of Carolina's second-half snaps, a big change from Weeks 2 and 3 when his second-half snaps were much closer to Hubbard's. His yards per carry has tumbled like a bowling ball downstairs — 4.0 against the Falcons, 3.1 against the Saints, 2.7 against the Seahawks, 1.5 against the Vikings — and while those were tough matchups, the column says that doesn't make it a good look. Unsurprisingly he has two runs of 12-plus yards through four games and neither went more than 15 yards; the blame is shared, since Carolina's offensive line barely gave him any daylight last week or for much of the year, and defenses aren't yet scared of getting beaten by Bryce Young's arm. The breakdown lists Carolina at Detroit, the Lions favoured by 10, an over/under of 45, an opponent ranked 5th versus running backs, 9.9 projected points, a 25th running back ranking, and year-to-date totals of 158 rushing yards, 15 receptions, 81 receiving yards, one touchdown and 10.7 fantasy points per game.

The opponent evidence is the other half. Detroit is a tough matchup, giving up 2.9 yards per rush to running backs on the season, a top-three figure, as are its yards before contact allowed (0.49) and runs of 10-plus yards allowed (three); its 2.38 yards after contact per rush allowed is only fifth-best. Only Kenneth Walker, on the strength of two touchdowns, has managed more than five non-PPR and nine PPR points against these Lions. The column pre-empts the obvious historical objection: Detroit was strong against the run last year too when it went into Carolina and got absolutely pummelled by a Panthers run game that included Chuba Hubbard, and coach Dan Campbell accepted responsibility for that loss, saying the Lions "were not emotionally ready to go" — they should be this time, and besides, it is a different coaching staff in Carolina and clearly a different run game. The verdict prefers Jahmyr Gibbs, Dameon Pierce and Najee Harris to Sanders.

# NFL Week 11 Power Rankings, 25-32

At the bottom of Sporting News' Week 11 rankings on Nov. 13, 2023, the Green Bay Packers were 25th at 3-6 (previous week: 25), showing improved work from Jordan Love and his young weapons spreading the ball well in the passing game, but with run-defense woes and key holes in coverage that had all but doomed their playoff hopes. The Los Angeles Rams were 26th at 3-6 (26), hoping to find answers during a bye as Sean McVay's good early-season coaching job went by the wayside with key offensive injuries, needing Matthew Stafford to save face or the season would look a lot like 2022. The Tennessee Titans were 27th at 3-6 (27), with Will Levis going through rookie lumps after a dazzling debut as brutal offensive line woes exacerbated by injuries got to him and the whole offense — though the Titans still needed to keep starting him, since they could not overcome those systemic problems or those in overall pass defense.

The Chicago Bears were 28th at 3-7 (29): they do not care how they win, and should have been pleased their running game and defense bailed out a limited passing game with Tyson Bagent to secure another Week 10 win, hoping to finish strong with Justin Fields soon. The Arizona Cardinals jumped to 29th at 2-8 (32) after an immediate offensive spark with Kyler Murray and James Conner back, looking invigorated for Jonathan Gannon on defense and special teams and likely to finish strong and play a lot of spoiler. The New England Patriots were 30th at 2-8 (28), having tried to win by hiding Mac Jones and their quarterbacks in general and nearly pulling it off with a dominant running game and short-handed defense making plays, but without results in Germany ahead of a tough bye for Bill Belichick.

The New York Giants were 31st at 2-8 (30) and could flush away the season without Daniel Jones and Tyrod Taylor, with early and relentless injuries to the offense and a defense now falling apart too — the question being whether Brian Daboll would get a massive mulligan after his rookie playoff leadership. # Most Valuable Player (MVP)

## Definition

In the corpus, MVP (Most Valuable Player) names the player judged most valuable to a team's or league's success, and the term surfaces at several distinct scopes: a formal season-long league award (NFL MVP, NBA MVP), a single-game honor (Super Bowl MVP), and an informal team-level or cross-sport label applied by media, players, and coaches.

## Context

At the league-season level, the NFL MVP and NBA MVP are formal annual awards contested among a small pool of star players. Sporting News's Dec. 5, 2023 awards-odds piece had Brock Purdy, Dak Prescott, and Jalen Hurts as the current NFL MVP favorites after Week 13, with C.J. Stroud and Jared Goff as the longshot cases. Separately, Yardbarker's Dec. 24, 2023 Christmas Day preview framed the Ravens-49ers game explicitly as "the decisive clash for the MVP Award," with Brock Purdy the heavy favorite (-230) and Lamar Jackson — the 2019 MVP — holding the second-shortest odds (+525). At the single-game level, MVP denotes a game-specific honor, as with Patrick Mahomes's two Super Bowl MVPs. At the team level, MVP is used informally by outlets like Yardbarker to name each team's most indispensable player at a season's midpoint — a designation that need not track the league-wide award and can go to a non-quarterback, as when Miami's Tyreek Hill or New England's Jabrill Peppers is named team MVP. The same informal usage crosses sports, as when an MLS goalkeeper calls forward Luciano Acosta "the MVP" of FC Cincinnati. MVP is also a standard sports-betting futures market: bettors wager on which player will win the season MVP award well before or during the season, alongside markets like Rookie of the Year and Offensive/Defensive Player of the Year.

## Background (external)

Beyond this corpus's sports-betting and news coverage, Wikipedia describes an MVP award more generally as an honor bestowed on the individual (or individuals, in case of a tie) "whose individual performance is the greatest in an entire league, for a particular competition, or on a specific team," recognizing one player's contribution within a team effort. (Source: Wikipedia, "Most valuable player," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Most_valuable_player, accessed 2026-09-02.)

## Key Characteristics

- **Multiple scopes** — the same "MVP" language covers a formal season-long league award (NFL, NBA), a single-game honor (Super Bowl MVP), and an informal team-level or sport-crossing designation used by media and players alike.
- **Voting-panel awards lack fixed criteria** — the NBA MVP, for instance, is chosen by a panel of sportswriters and broadcasters (format since 1980, weighted 5/3/1 points for first/second/third-place votes) with no set selection rulebook, which is why outcomes are notoriously hard to predict and can produce "upset" winners.
- **Quarterback bias in NFL MVP framing** — corpus coverage repeatedly frames the NFL MVP as typically going to a quarterback from a top-seeded team, to the point that a non-quarterback like Christian McCaffrey is described as facing long odds "if the MVP wasn't a quarterback-driven award."
- **Betting futures market** — MVP odds are a standing futures category at sportsbooks (alongside moneylines, spreads, and other award markets), bet on well ahead of the outcome and repriced as the season's results accumulate.
- **Team-level MVP is unofficial** — team MVP picks (e.g., Yardbarker's AFC team-by-team roundup) are editorial judgments, not sanctioned awards, and can diverge sharply from who is in the league MVP conversation.

# Player Injury Report

## Definition

A player injury report is the periodic status listing an NFL team publishes during game week (and updates live on gameday) that tags each hurt or ailing player with a practice participation note and a game-status designation such as questionable, doubtful, or out, so broadcasters and fantasy managers know who is likely to play.

## Context

The corpus shows the report operating on two timescales: the pregame weekly cycle and the in-game live update. In the weekly cycle, CBS Sports' Week 13 injury roundup (doc_0289) and Sporting News' Week 10 fantasy injury updates (doc_0288) track players through the week's practice sessions — a player who is a full participant, limited participant, or a "DNP" (did not practice) on Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday accumulates a running designation that the team finalizes before kickoff. Ja'Marr Chase's Week 10 status is a clear case: he was listed as a DNP on Wednesday, logged back-to-back limited practices, and his final active call was left until a Sunday morning pre-game workout (doc_0288). During the game itself, CBS Sports' live-blog roundup shows teams issuing real-time in-game designations — "questionable to return," "doubtful to return," "ruled out" — when a player is hurt mid-contest, as with Cooper Kupp's ankle injury and Kenneth Walker III's oblique injury in the Week 11 roundup (doc_0113). The designations also interact with roster mechanics: a player can be activated off injured reserve to play (doc_0035) or, conversely, be placed on injured reserve, as De'Von Achane was during Week 6 (doc_0149).

## Key Characteristics

- **Tiered designations** — the standard tags observed in the corpus are full participant/limited/DNP during the week, collapsing into questionable, doubtful, or out for the final pregame report (doc_0289, doc_0288).
- **Live in-game updates** — beyond the pregame report, teams issue real-time calls like "questionable to return" or "ruled out for the remainder of the contest" when a player is injured during the game itself (doc_0113).
- **Roster-status linkage** — the report intersects with injured reserve moves: players can be activated off IR to play (doc_0035) or placed on IR after a lingering issue (doc_0149).
- **Coach commentary supplements the tag** — reporters attach head-coach quotes (e.g., Achane is "day-to-day"; it would be "a little aggressive" for Jefferson to play) to the bare designation to give fantasy audiences more color than the tag alone conveys (doc_0113, doc_0288).
- **Deadline-driven finality** — some designations resolve only hours before kickoff, e.g. Justin Jefferson needing activation by a Saturday 4 p.m. ET deadline to be eligible (doc_0288).

# Justin Fields As A Week 5 2023 Bust Candidate At Washington

CBS Sports flagged Justin Fields as a "Bust Candidate" for Week 5 of the 2023 season at Washington: the claim is that Fields is being started only for his passing, and the warrant is that a short-week trip behind the league's worst pass protection, with his designed rushing all but gone, removes the floor that usually protects his fantasy score.

The grounds separate the opponent from the circumstances. Washington itself is not that big a step-up in competition for Fields — but it is for his offensive line. The Commanders have a slightly below-average pass-rush pressure rate, with only one game all year above 30% (52.7% at Denver, where Russell Wilson still had a great game even discounting a Hail Mary touchdown catch), ranking seventh in sacks with 13 and 13th in pressures with 53, both around league average. Chicago, by contrast, ranks league-worst in pressure rate allowed at 47.4% of snaps — nearly one in every two dropbacks — and bringing back guard Teven Jenkins might help a little, but the unit is still struggling. The deep ball is the clearest upside: Washington ranks bottom-five in attempts, yards per catch and touchdowns allowed on throws of 15-plus air yards over the past three weeks, an area Fields can exploit, since he is tied for the most touchdowns on 15-plus air-yard throws this season with four and sits around league average in completion rate, attempts per game and expected points added per dropback. The weekly breakdown lists Chicago at Washington, the Commanders favoured by 6, an over/under of 44.5, an opponent ranked 23rd versus quarterbacks, 17.3 projected points, a 10th quarterback ranking, and year-to-date totals of 861 passing yards, 134 rushing yards, eight touchdowns, five interceptions and 20.4 fantasy points per game.

The bust risk rests on how Fields' Week 4 breakout was produced and on his vanished rushing. He posted his first-ever game with four passing touchdowns and over 300 yards against a Broncos defense devoid of a serious pass rush or pass-coverage skills through three quarters — a defense that had allowed season-best fantasy numbers to each of the past three quarterbacks it faced and was a terrific matchup for anybody. Once Denver generated heavy pressure in the fourth quarter Fields finished 5 of 11 for 50 yards, no touchdowns and two turnovers. On film he looked terrific for three quarters firing downfield from clean pockets, with an off-target rate of literally 0.0% and plays where he manipulated defenders with the threat of running before throwing over their heads, including Cole Kmet's short touchdown; by the fourth he was pressured, throwing off his back foot, throwing with too much velocity or out of sync with his target, and his off-target rate rose to 9.1%, closer to his 13.6% average over the first three games. The rushing collapse is the other prop removed: after seven designed runs in Week 3 he had just two designed runs in Week 4 for two total yards, and on the season 28 rushes for 134 yards and a score. Last season Washington got a season-best 57.1% pressure rate on Fields and blitzed him on 40.5% of dropbacks, and he still cleared nearly 20 fantasy points on one passing touchdown and one interception because he ran for 88 yards — the very cushion the column doubts he will have now. The verdict is comparative rather than absolute: Anthony Richardson and Jordan Love have more potential this week, Russell Wilson, Trevor Lawrence, Dak Prescott and Jared Goff do not, and you just might not have a better option than Fields.

# The NFL Super Bowl Contender Landscape, Week 6 Of 2023

The New York Times' Pick Six column of 16 October 2023 addressed the key questions facing the ten teams with the shortest Super Bowl odds — the Chiefs, Eagles, 49ers, Bills, Bengals, Cowboys, Ravens, Lions, Dolphins and Jaguars — with one-third of the 18-week regular season nearly complete.

The prompt for the exercise was a weekend that changed the picture at the top. The San Francisco 49ers entered Week 6 riding a 15-game winning streak and looking unstoppable with a young quarterback, Brock Purdy, who was making the game look easy; they exited with a 19-17 defeat at Cleveland, injuries to key players and, for the first time that season, a question mark or two. The previously unbeaten Philadelphia Eagles also lost ugly that Sunday.

The season to that point had produced a set of contradictions the column set out to test. The Miami Dolphins had set NFL records for offense, only to lose by four touchdowns in their lone game against a true contender. The Kansas City Chiefs had won with defense, sometimes in spite of their offense. The Buffalo Bills had incurred devastating injuries. For each of the ten teams the column ran through what the writer thinks and what NFL insiders have to say.

# Sports Betting As An Investment Mindset

Sporting News' best bets column argues that sports betting is not a gamble: with the right mindset, strategies and preparedness it is an investment, and the column said on Nov. 3, 2023 that it was loving its return on investment through seven weeks. On that view the activity is not a hobby but "a second job that allows us to punch in while we're sitting on our couch."

The grounds are the work that goes into it. Because the reader's goal is to boost their bankroll, the column's top priority is to help achieve that by putting in a ton of statistical research, attacking all the angles, uncovering betting trends and pinpointing value across all the sports betting sites each week — which is how it arrives at its best moneyline, spread, over/under and SuperDraft player prop bets for a slate it describes as featuring a plethora of lucrative opportunities.

# Kyle Pitts' Fantasy Outlook In Weeks 5 And 6 Of 2023

CBS Sports listed Kyle Pitts under "Sit Him" in Week 5 of the 2023 season and then under "Start Him" in Week 6, but the second call is deliberately hedged: after one good game against a zone-heavy defense, the author refuses to rush back to Pitts as a must-start because four really measly weeks preceded it.

The Week 5 case, published 4 October 2023 ahead of a home game with Houston, says it is hard to see the good in Pitts' game so far this season beyond his finding holes in zone coverage. Even Jonnu Smith has more red-zone targets than Pitts, three to two. On film there was no change in his explosiveness whatsoever: he was running at a slower-than-expected pace while the Jaguars still paid him plenty of attention defensively, a double whammy that left him without many targets; his longest opportunity was a well-placed deep ball from Desmond Ridder that he leapt for perfectly but couldn't secure to the ground, and he never separated from cornerback Tyson Campbell, with his best work coming on shorter routes against zone. Coach Arthur Smith said that week that Pitts isn't at 100%, adding "there are certain things, you see him, and he's doing really well right now and there are certain things that he can't [do well]. It's been a journey back. He's going to get there." The column concedes that if Smith is right then holding on to Pitts in fantasy makes sense, and that the matchup could create some receiving opportunities — maybe five catches for 50 yards, which is nothing to be excited about. The breakdown lists Atlanta at home versus Houston, the Falcons favoured by 2, an over/under of 41.5, an opponent ranked 18th versus tight ends, 7.6 projected points, a 13th tight end ranking, and year-to-date totals of 11 receptions on 21 targets for 121 yards, no touchdowns and 5.8 fantasy points per game. The verdict prefers Jake Ferguson, Zach Ertz and Dallas Goedert.

The Week 6 case, published 12 October 2023 ahead of a home game with Washington, upgrades him with an explicit cap on expectations: around 70 yards on six catches. If Week 5 had been Week 1 the author would have been encouraged and kept expectations high, but the matchup is a little tougher for Pitts and for Ridder, and teams have beaten the Commanders on deep shots to wide receivers rather than lumbering tight ends, so he is not convinced Pitts will maintain his target share or develop more explosive plays. In Week 5 Pitts came alive against Houston's zone-heavy defense with season highs in targets (11), catches (seven) and yards (87), his second game in three with a target share over 23% — though he played a season-low 53% of the snaps. Two things helped: he looked a little quicker off the snap and faster running straight, still lumbering when changing direction but perhaps slowly getting healthier, and Ridder seemed very comfortable throwing into tighter windows in zone coverage, the two showing good timing mainly on dig and out-breaking routes. Pitts continues to harvest a high average depth of target — 11.36 yards that week and 11.72 on the season, the highest among qualifying tight ends — while also carrying the lowest catch rate (56.3%) and worst yards after catch per reception (1.33) among them, with just 24 of his 208 yards coming after the catch. Washington plays zone at a slightly below-league-average rate, typically turning to man as soon as games get sideways, as in the second quarter the previous week or the fourth quarter against Buffalo; opponents average 32.0 pass attempts per game against them, ninth-fewest in football, and against tight ends who line up in the slot or out wide like Pitts the Commanders rank top-five in yards per catch and yards after catch per reception and have yet to allow a reception of 20-plus yards. They have allowed the seventh-most receptions on throws of 15-plus air yards, 19, but only two were caught by tight ends — Cole Kmet and Dallas Goedert — and neither went for more than 23 yards. The breakdown lists the Falcons favoured by 2.5, an over/under of 42.5, an opponent ranked 10th versus tight ends, 10.3 projected points, a ninth tight end ranking, and year-to-date totals of 18 receptions on 32 targets for 208 yards, no touchdowns and 7.8 fantasy points per game. The verdict still trots Pitts out over Logan Thomas, Dallas Goedert and Cole Kmet.

# 49ers Rout Cowboys 42-10 On Week 5 Sunday Night Football

San Francisco beat Dallas 42-10 at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, California on Sunday, Oct. 8, 2023, confirming that a 49ers team that had ended the Cowboys' season in each of the previous two years remained a level above its NFC counterpart. Jerry Jones had said earlier in the week that the game would show him how the Cowboys stacked up against the NFL's best; the answer, per Sporting News, was "not very well."

The 49ers carved up Dallas' defense on the opening drive and never let up. Brock Purdy threw four touchdowns in the rout, including three to George Kittle, and Christian McCaffrey scored for a 14th consecutive game as all of San Francisco's offensive weapons got involved. Defensively nobody had a larger impact than Fred Warner, who finished with an interception, a sack and a forced fumble. Dallas' offense looked much as it had in the previous season's playoff exit — uncomfortable and out of sorts — sluggish through the first half before unraveling when Dak Prescott threw three second-half interceptions. It got out of hand quickly enough that Sam Darnold entered the game for the 49ers with more than 12 minutes remaining. The quarter-by-quarter line was Cowboys 0-7-3-0 for 10 and 49ers 7-14-7-14 for 42.

Kickoff was 8:20 p.m. ET, which was 5:20 p.m. local time in Santa Clara. Going in, the two franchises had a long history, but San Francisco had won each of their last two meetings by knocking Dallas out of the playoffs, so a win would have carried psychological value for the Cowboys. Afterward, questions about whether Prescott and Dallas could get over the hump against the class of the NFC persisted, and although their wins had been dominant, Dallas already sat two games behind the Eagles in the NFC East. San Francisco moved to 5-0 with all of its major offensive weapons healthy and its defense living up to its billing; Kyle Shanahan's team would not face a team with a winning record until Week 10, though the Browns, Vikings and Bengals were described as far from automatic wins.

# The Detroit Lions' Defensive Improvement, 2023

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that the Lions' defensive improvement is real but not yet testable: Detroit is 11.3 EPA per game better on defense than the previous season, the second-largest gain for any team, yet the true measure will have to wait for the postseason.

The qualifications are built into the grounds. The schedule has something to do with the gain, and the 2022 defense was so bad that it couldn't stop Carolina, so the baseline was low. Looking forward, the remaining schedule features so many weak offenses — including Chicago twice, Green Bay, Denver and Las Vegas — that the improvement cannot be properly assessed before January. The writer nonetheless expects Detroit to win the NFC North and return to the playoffs, which will make the season successful no matter what happens from there.

An executive endorsed the team on the grounds of self-knowledge rather than personnel: "Yes, I do buy them. This is a league full of teams who do not really know who they are week to week. Detroit knows who they are, and they play to their identity. Anytime you know who you are and play to that style, you have a chance to be dangerous."

# Week 13 Dolphins-Commanders: Miami's Pass Rush Should Pass Its Post-Phillips Test

CBS Sports argues that the Dolphins pass rush, even after losing edge rusher Jaelan Phillips, should handle a leaky Commanders offensive line without giving up much in the way of deep completions. The grounds: with Phillips, the Dolphins ranked third in sacks with 38 and sixth in pass rush pressure rate at 39.9%, though both numbers were boosted by the defense's effort against a sagging Jets offense last Friday. Adding veteran Jason Pierre-Paul is described as not a cure-all, but he will help keep the Dolphins from being forced to blitz a ton week in and week out. On the other side, the Commanders offensive line has had some ugly showings lately — four sacks and a 49% pass rush pressure rate allowed against the Cowboys, four sacks and 32.7% pressure allowed against the Giants, and three sacks with 46.8% pressure allowed against the Seahawks — and, somehow, these results are better than what they were allowing through much of the first two months of the year.

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. # FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.

# Plea Agreement

## Definition

In the corpus, a plea agreement is the deal by which a criminal defendant (or, in Binance's case, a company) pleads guilty to specified charges in exchange for concessions, rather than going to trial.
It takes effect only once a judge accepts it, and it can bind the party to concrete obligations — cooperating with prosecutors, accepting a recommended fine, stepping back from a role, or admitting specific facts — beyond the bare admission of guilt.

## Context

The corpus shows plea agreements as the mechanism by which several defendants in overlapping 2023 white-collar and criminal cases resolved their charges outside of a trial.
FTX co-founder Gary Wang and Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors, becoming key witnesses against Sam Bankman-Fried at his fraud trial (doc_0010, doc_0086).
FTX engineering head Nishad Singh similarly pleaded guilty to six charges (doc_0121).
Binance CEO Changpeng "CZ" Zhao and Binance itself each entered separate plea agreements with the U.S. Department of Justice, resolving anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations as part of a $4.3 billion settlement (doc_0374, doc_0375).
YouTube parenting influencer Ruby Franke's plea agreement, accepted by a judge, both formalized her guilty plea to child-abuse charges and documented detailed admissions about the abuse itself (doc_0269).
The corpus also shows a distinct but related instrument — the cooperation agreement Gary Wang signed, which specifically obligated him to meet with prosecutors and answer truthfully (doc_0226) — and notes that a witness's incentive to plead guilty and cooperate (the hope of sentencing leniency) is something a defense team can attack on cross-examination (doc_0293).

## Key Characteristics

- **Court acceptance is required** — a judge must accept the plea agreement before it takes effect; Ruby Franke's sentencing was scheduled only after Judge John J. Walton accepted her plea agreement (doc_0269).
- **Negotiated concessions, not just an admission** — the document can specify what each side gives up: Zhao agreed to a recommended $150 million CFTC fine and to not contradict his acceptance of responsibility, while Binance's agreement barred Zhao from any future role at the company for three years and required it to maintain an independent compliance monitor (doc_0374).
- **Can include cooperation with prosecutors** — Wang and Ellison's guilty pleas were paired with plans to cooperate with, and testify for, the prosecution (doc_0010); Wang's cooperation obligations were spelled out in a separate signed agreement (doc_0226).
- **Distinct from pleading not guilty** — a defendant who instead maintains innocence, as Bankman-Fried did, pleads not guilty and proceeds to trial rather than entering a plea agreement (doc_0010).
- **Can contain substantive factual admissions** — Franke's plea agreement recorded specific admitted details of the abuse itself, beyond the bare fact of guilt (doc_0269).
- **Creates a cross-examination target** — because cooperating witnesses who pleaded guilty may hope for sentencing leniency, defense counsel can (and, per the corpus, did) argue this gives them an incentive to shape testimony favorably to the prosecution (doc_0293).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the general legal definition is broader than any single case above: a plea bargain (or plea agreement) is an agreement between a defendant and a prosecutor in which the defendant agrees to plead guilty to some or all of the charges, usually in exchange for a concession from the prosecutor, such as a reduced charge or a more lenient sentencing recommendation.
Source: Legal Information Institute (LII), Cornell Law School, "plea bargain," https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/plea_bargain (accessed 2026-09-02).

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# FTX's Fabricated Backstop Insurance Fund

Gary Wang testified on October 6th, 2023 that FTX lied about how much money was in its backstop fund, and the court was shown the code that generated the fake number published on FTX's website: it took the daily trading volume on FTX, multiplied it by a random number, divided it by a billion, and added the result to the number already displayed on the site. That figure had nothing to do with the actual amount of money in the insurance fund.

The fund mattered because of what FTX advertised. In many crypto networks, if someone lost enough money the exchanges could stick other traders with the losses too; FTX touted its automated liquidation as the way to avoid this, so that one customer going bankrupt would not affect the others. In the process of liquidating, FTX would try to sell the collateral on the open market, and if it could not finish, backstop liquidity providers would step in — market makers, including Alameda, which could be compensated for the losses they took from the backstop fund. Wang also testified that when there was not enough money in the fund, money was moved there from Alameda's accounts in order to pay the insurance out.

The prosecution's framing was that this was not merely a matter of Alameda holding special, secret privileges: it claimed those privileges were used to obfuscate basic elements of FTX's operations, exposing the exchange's supposed selling points as a lie.

# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# FTX

FTX was a crypto exchange that at its height was the third-largest in the world, backed by an unusually broad investor base and carrying enormous daily trading volume. Within two years, more than 80 investors provided about $2 billion in capital to FTX, helping Bankman-Fried propel his vision into a reality.

Its funding peaked in January 2022, when the company raised $400 million in a Series C round that boosted its valuation to $32 billion — its last round of public funding. Trades on FTX climbed up to $15 billion a day, and TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 piece notes that as that activity grew, SBF also got tied up in the corridors of political power. By the time his trial began, TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account framed the whole story as one question: how did the once third-largest crypto exchange get here?



---


# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.



---


# The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse

FTX came apart in early November 2022 through a chain with four links: a leaked balance sheet revealed that Alameda's largest holding was FTX's own token in a quantity larger than the token's whole market, the disclosure destroyed confidence, the world's largest rival exchange pulled its holdings out, and the resulting bank run forced FTX and Alameda into Chapter 11 within days. TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account sets out the sequence: in early November 2022, that all changed.

Concerns surrounding FTX's liquidity grew after CoinDesk published a copy of Alameda's balance sheet, showing the firm held $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. The balance sheet showed that the $5.82 billion in FTT tokens that Alameda owned was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap, which was about $3 billion at the time — meaning Alameda purported to have more FTT tokens on its balance sheet than what existed in the world. Around the same time it was exposed, the world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, started pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT; Binance had held an equity position in FTX from 2019 to 2021. That withdrawal essentially triggered a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. mid-November 2022, Bankman-Fried resigned, and John J. Ray III, the Enron turnaround veteran, was appointed the new CEO.

The condition the whole mechanism rests on is the fragility of the underlying valuations. As TechCrunch put it on 2023-10-02, all of that activity came to a crashing end because the value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value — so when those valuations fell, they fell very, very hard. The chain therefore only runs as described where an asset is priced on expectation, held in size by a related party, and exposed to a counterparty large enough that its exit alone starts the run.



---


# Binance's Market Position And Its 2023 Setbacks

Binance launched in June 2017 and within 180 days became the largest crypto exchange in the world. As of November 21, 2023 it had over $12.65 billion in trading volume during the past 24 hours — 532% higher than the $2 billion in trading volume from the second largest crypto exchange, Coinbase, according to CoinMarketCap data.

Binance has made headlines over the past year for a range of reasons, including Zhao's comments contributing to the collapse of FTX, which was once one of its top competitors.

Two commercial relationships also broke down in 2023. In April, Binance.US, its American sister company, broke off its $1.3 billion deal to buy crypto broker Voyager Digital's assets due to a "hostile and uncertain regulatory climate." And in August, Checkout.com cut ties with Binance over concerns about the crypto firm's alleged issues with anti-money laundering, sanctions and compliance controls; at the time, Binance's spokesperson said it does not agree with "Checkout's purported basis for termination and are considering our options for legal action."



---


# Prior SEC And CFTC Actions Against Binance

The DOJ charges against Binance came over five months after the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission accused the exchange and Zhao of lying to regulators about its operations, filing 13 charges against the defendants in the federal case.

The SEC's theory concerned the relationship between Binance and its U.S. arm: Zhao and Binance were allegedly "intimately involved" in directing the trading entity's business operations and providing crypto-related services to the Binance.US platform, which claims it is an independent exchange in the SEC filing.

In late March 2023 the U.S. CFTC also filed a suit against Binance, Zhao and its Chief Compliance Officer Samuel Lim for allegedly breaking trading and derivatives rules.



---


# FTX's Cooperating Witnesses

FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang and Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse, and both planned to cooperate with prosecutors. TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-01 that they would be major witnesses in the trial, given their close ties to Bankman-Fried, FTX and Alameda.

The criminal charges were not their only exposure. Alongside them, Wang and Ellison face civil penalties from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).



---


# Binance's $4.3B DOJ Resolution And CZ's Guilty Plea

Changpeng Zhao, also known as "CZ," the founder and CEO of Binance, is stepping down and has pleaded guilty to a number of violations brought on through the Department of Justice and other U.S. agencies; he appeared in a Seattle federal court on Tuesday, November 21, 2023 to enter his plea. Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has also agreed to pay about $4.3 billion to resolve the DOJ's investigations, the agency said in a press release that Tuesday.

As part of Binance's guilty plea, it has also reached agreements with the Department of Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), and will credit about $1.8 billion toward those resolutions.

The crypto exchange "admits it engaged in anti-money laundering, unlicensed money transmitting and sanctions violations," the DOJ release stated, calling it the "largest corporate resolution" that included criminal charges for an executive; Zhao pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an anti-money laundering program. "The message here should be clear: using new technology to break the law does not make you a disruptor, it makes you a criminal," U.S. Attorney General Merrick Garland said in a statement.
