# India vs Australia In The 2011 World Cup Quarter-Final

After so much Australian dominance in World Cup meetings with India, India finally got their revenge in the 2011 World Cup, defeating Australia by five wickets. Australia batted first and posted a target of 261 runs, courtesy of a 104-run knock off 118 balls by captain Ricky Ponting, losing six wickets in the process.

In the second innings Sachin Tendulkar, Yuvraj Singh and Gautam Gambhir scored three half-centuries as India chased down the target within 47.4 overs, losing 5 wickets. India went all the way to lift their second ODI World Cup trophy, defeating Sri Lanka in the final.



---


# India's 1987 World Cup Semi-Final Against England

India lost the 1987 semi-final to England by 35 runs at the Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai, on 5 November. Four years after 1983 the World Cup was being played outside England for the first time and India were hosting it, and in a coincidence India were up against England in the semi-finals once again.

England's Man-of-the-Match skipper Graham Gooch smashed 115 runs in 136 balls to lay a solid foundation for his team's fighting total of 254 for 6 wickets. India, one of the favourites to win the tournament, were very much on the path to victory while Mohammad Azharuddin, who top-scored with 64 runs, was at the crease; but with the fall of his wicket the Indian lower order collapsed like a house of placards.



---


# The 2011 World Cup: India's Last Hosting Before 2023

The last time India welcomed the ODI Cricket World Cup before 2023 was in 2011, when they were co-hosts with Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. Pakistan were barred from hosting due to terrorist attacks on the Sri Lankan team when touring the country a couple of years prior to the World Cup.

The 2011 World Cup was a tournament of many firsts. Australia's streak of remaining unbeaten in 35 World Cup matches was broken when they were defeated by Pakistan, having not lost a game since the 1999 tournament. It was also the first time two Asian teams were in the finals, as India became the first country to win a World Cup at home by defeating Sri Lanka in the decider.

Writing on Oct. 1, 2023, the Sporting News added that after a prolonged drought of ICC trophies, India were favourites to bring the trophy home again in 2023.



---


# The 1996 Semi-Final Abandonment And The Short 1999 Cycle

The 1996 World Cup, jointly hosted by India and Sri Lanka, produced what the Sporting News calls one of the most controversial episodes in the game: the two host teams met in the semi-finals at Eden Gardens, Kolkata, India's poor performance sparked an unruly crowd to protest against the home team, and Sri Lanka was declared the winner by default due to the halt in play.

Sri Lanka went on to win the trophy that year, and they were back to try and defend it three years later in England, rather than after the usual four-year gap.

The reason was a scheduling experiment. Following the 1996 event the ICC opted to try and revamp the schedule, with three years between events rather than four, but the move proved unpopular and 1999 was the only tournament to follow that pattern.



---


# India's Record Of World Cup Semi-Final Appearances

India first entered the semi-finals of the World Cup at the 1983 Prudential Cup in England, where they emerged as the tournament winners. They moved into the last-four stage on the next two occasions when the World Cup was held in India, in 1987 and 1996, and were in the semi-finals again in 2003 in South Africa. Eight years later they were in the last four at the 2011 World Cup as hosts, and repeated the feat in 2015, 2019 and 2023.

The summary statistic given on 11 November 2023 is that in their last six World Cups, India have been in the semi-finals on five occasions.



---


# India vs Australia In The 2015 World Cup Semi-Final At Sydney

Australia beat India by 95 runs in the second semi-final of the 2015 World Cup in Sydney on 26 March, which Zee Business describes as Australia's revenge for the 2011 quarter-final. Australia outplayed India in almost all departments of the game: Man-of-the-Match Steve Smith scored 105 runs in 93 balls and Aaron Finch 81 runs in 116 balls, taking Australia to 328 runs for 7 wickets in 50 overs, reported elsewhere in the same publication as a target of 329 with seven wickets lost. Umesh Yadav picked up four wickets for India.

In reply India needed a few big innings but, apart from skipper MS Dhoni with 65 runs in 65 balls, Shikhar Dhawan with 45 runs in 34 balls and Ajinkya Rahane with 44 runs in 68 balls, the batting order collapsed miserably; India crumbled within 233 runs in 46.5 overs, with Dhoni the highest scorer for the Indian side. James Faulkner picked up three wickets for Australia, with Mitchell Johnson and Mitchell Starc taking two wickets each. Australia went all the way to lift their fifth ODI World Cup trophy, defeating New Zealand in the final.



---


# India's 2011 World Cup Semi-Final Against Pakistan

India beat Pakistan in the second semi-final of the 2011 World Cup at the IS Bindra Stadium in Mohali on 30 March, bowling Pakistan out for 231 in 49.5 overs after posting 260 for 9 in 50 overs. The World Cup had returned to India after 1996, and fans from India and Pakistan could not have expected a better occasion than a World Cup for a meeting of the two teams.

Man-of-the-Match Sachin Tendulkar rose to the occasion with 85 runs, Virender Sehwag scored 38 and Suresh Raina remained unbeaten on 36; Pakistan seamer Wahab Riaz took 5 for 46 in 10 overs. In reply Misbah-ul-Haq with 56 runs and Mohammad Hafeez with 43 showed some resistance, but the lack of a big innings lower down the order hit Pakistan's prospects badly. India moved to the final and beat Sri Lanka to win their second World Cup title.



---


# India vs Australia: ODI World Cup Head-To-Head Record

As of 18 November 2023, India had faced Australia a total of 13 times in ODI World Cups, with the Aussies dominating on eight wins; India had, however, won the last two of those meetings, most recently in the league fixture of the 2023 World Cup in Chennai. The 2023 final was the fourth time India had qualified for an ODI World Cup final, whereas for Australia it was their eighth.

The article frames the fixture as a callback: two decades earlier these two goliaths of the cricketing world faced each other in the final of the ICC Men's ODI World Cup in Johannesburg, South Africa, and plenty of wounds are still to be healed for India because the defeat in the 2003 final against Australia still feels fresh. Writing before the result, it says it is only time to tell whether the Aussies will repeat history or whether India will write history by winning their third ODI World Cup.



---


# The ICC ODI Men's Cricket World Cup

The ODI Men's Cricket World Cup is the ICC's flagship championship — the Sporting News calls it the heart and soul of ICC Championships — and the 2023 edition was held in India from October 5 to November 19.

Its defining features are its organiser and its cycle: it is organised every four years by the International Cricket Council (ICC), and it is one of the most viewed sporting tournaments in the world.

The article that introduces it frames its purpose as a retrospective, taking a look at the history of the competition and some of the landmark moments that have helped make the World Cup what it is today, published on Oct. 1, 2023, ahead of the men's ODI showpiece.



---


# World Cup

## Definition

In the corpus, "World Cup" names a sport's top international championship, but its shape differs by sport: the ICC's men's ODI Cricket World Cup and World Rugby's Rugby World Cup (RWC) each crown a winner via a national-team final, FIFA's football World Cup is preceded by confederation qualifying such as CONMEBOL's, and Mikaela Shiffrin's Alpine skiing World Cup is tracked in the corpus as a tally of individual "World Cup wins" building toward an "overall World Cup" title rather than a single match.

## Context

In the corpus the term spans multiple sports and formats.
The ICC organises the Cricket World Cup "every four years," a men's ODI tournament whose 1975 edition (hosted by England, contested by eight teams including a composite East Africa/Sri Lanka side) established the pattern of a single-host, knockout-culminating event; the 2023 edition ran in India from October 5 to November 19, and its final pitted "two-time World Champions" India against "five-time World Champions" Australia.
World Rugby's Rugby World Cup (RWC) crowned the Springboks in the corpus's 2023 final — a 12-11 win over the All Blacks in France, reported under the headline "claim record FOURTH RWC"; the cited passage covers that single match and its aftermath, not the tournament's periodicity or hosting structure.
FIFA's World Cup operates on a longer cycle with a distinct qualification stage: national confederations such as CONMEBOL run "World Cup qualifying" matches (e.g., Argentina vs Paraguay for the 2026 tournament) years ahead of the finals themselves.
By contrast, the Alpine skiing World Cup that Mikaela Shiffrin dominates is not one tournament: the corpus counts her record in terms of individual "World Cup wins" and "five overall World Cup victories," a cumulative tally rather than a knockout final (see Background for how that circuit is structured).

## Key Characteristics

- **Governing-body run** — the corpus explicitly credits the ICC with organising the Cricket World Cup (doc_0409) and refers to the football World Cup as a "FIFA tournament" (doc_0105), with confederations such as CONMEBOL organising qualifying (doc_0105).
- **Periodic, at least for cricket** — only the Cricket World Cup's cadence is explicitly quoted in the corpus as "every four years" (doc_0409); the cited Rugby World Cup passage does not state a periodicity for the RWC.
- **National-team contest culminating in a final** — the cricket and rugby World Cups in the corpus each end in a single final: India vs Australia at Ahmedabad in 2023 (doc_0246), and the Springboks' 12-11 win over the All Blacks in France (doc_0022).
- **Separate qualification phase** — for football, "World Cup qualifying" is a distinct, multi-year stage (run per confederation, e.g. CONMEBOL) that precedes the finals tournament itself (doc_0105).
- **Not always a single event** — in individual sports such as Alpine skiing, the corpus describes "World Cup" wins accumulating toward an "overall World Cup" title for Mikaela Shiffrin (doc_0585) rather than a single match; the underlying season-long, points-based structure is documented externally (see Background).

## Background (external)

The FIS Alpine Ski World Cup that doc_0585 references is, per Wikipedia, a season-long circuit of races (roughly January to mid-March) rather than a single tournament.
Points are awarded to the top 30 finishers in each race (100 for first place, sliding to 1 for 30th, a system in place since the 1991-92 season), and the skier with the most cumulative points at season's end wins the overall title, symbolised by the "big crystal globe," with separate discipline titles awarded via smaller globes.

# India's 2003 World Cup Semi-Final Against Kenya

India beat underdogs Kenya by 91 runs in the last-four stage match in Durban on 20 March 2003. Man-of-the-Match India skipper Sourav Ganguly scored an unbeaten 111 runs in 114 balls and Man-of-the-Tournament Sachin Tendulkar an 111-ball 83, as India comfortably scored 270 for four wickets in 50 overs.

In reply Kenya were no match for Indian dominance: barring skipper Steve Tikolo, who top-scored with 56 runs, no Kenyan batsman could score more than 29, and Zaheer Khan took 3 wickets in 9.2 overs for just 14 runs. Though India breezed into the semi-finals easily, the tournament is also remembered for Kenya's best run in the World Cup, as a team from a country with limited cricket facilities and no proper grassroots structure reached as far as the semi-finals.

# The First ODI Cricket World Cup, 1975

England hosted the inaugural ODI World Cup in 1975 and held the event the following three times too, with the West Indies winning the first tournament.

The playing conditions were unlike the modern game: initially the game was played in cricket whites and with a red ball instead of a white ball. Eight teams took part in that inaugural tournament — India, Pakistan, England, Australia, West Indies, New Zealand and a composite team from East Africa and Sri Lanka. Current cricketing powerhouse South Africa was banned at the time from international sport due to its policy of racial segregation under the Apartheid system, and so did not take part in the first ODI World Cup.

The early honours went to two teams. The West Indies won the first tournament and defended the title in the second World Cup in 1979, while India's first taste of glory came when they clinched the trophy in 1983 by defeating the West Indies by 43 runs in the final.

# Jos Buttler's Reaction To The Sri Lanka Defeat

Speaking after England's defeat to Sri Lanka at the 2023 World Cup, captain Jos Buttler admitted his team had been "short of our best by a very long way" and said there was "no clear answer" as to how to turn their fortunes around.

His full comment placed the weight of the campaign on the captaincy: "It's incredibly tough, an incredibly disappointing tournament. As captain, you feel that a lot."

He also expressed personal and collective disappointment while ruling out a single fix: "We've been short of our best by a very long way. # India's 1983 World Cup Semi-Final Against England

India beat England by six wickets with 5.2 overs to spare in the semi-final at Manchester on 22 June 1983, storming into a World Cup final for the first time. India had lost in the first round of the 1975 and 1979 World Cups and were underdogs in the third World Cup, which was being held in England for the third consecutive time, but in that tournament India wronged many of their critics by reaching the semi-finals and playing the mighty hosts.

With the ball, skipper Kapil Dev struck three wickets while Roger Binny and Man-of-the-Match Mohinder Amarnath took two each as India restricted England to 213 all out in 60 overs. In reply Mohinder Amarnath played a useful innings of 46 and Yashpal Sharma scored a fine 61, while Sandeep Patil played a fiery innings of 51 not out in just 32 balls.

# ICC ODI World Cup 2023: Knockout Stage And Final

The two semi-finals that produced that pairing were India beating New Zealand by 70 runs on Wednesday, 15 November at the Wankhede Stadium in Mumbai, and Australia beating South Africa by three wickets on Thursday, 16 November at the Eden Gardens in Kolkata. # The 1987 ODI World Cup Format Change

The 1987 ODI World Cup brought two prime changes in the way the tournament was organised: a shift of venue from England to the Indian subcontinent, and games being played in 50 overs instead of 60.

The reason given for the shorter innings is climatic rather than sporting — the change in the number of overs was attributed to shorter daylight hours in Asia in comparison to England.

The 1987 tournament also had a new winner in Australia, who went on to defeat England by seven runs.

# England's 2023 World Cup Title Defence All But Dead

England's hopes of defending their World Cup crown were in tatters barely halfway through the 2023 tournament, with the 2019 champions sitting second-last of ten on the table on Oct. 26, 2023 and only mathematically able to scrape through to the semi-finals.

The trigger was a fourth abject loss in barely three weeks: an eight-wicket defeat to Sri Lanka in Bengaluru with nearly 25 overs to spare, after England were bowled out for a miserable 156. To reach the knockout stage they needed not only to turn their horrendous form around and win all four of their remaining matches, including an upcoming date with table-toppers and tournament favourites India, but also to hope for numerous other results, including Australia losing at least two and probably three of its own four games.

The Roar noted a hard deadline on that arithmetic: England's tournament might only stay mathematically alive until Sunday evening (AEST), when they faced the daunting challenge of tournament hosts India in Lucknow, with defeat certain to end their semi-final chances for good.

Michael Atherton argued in The Times that the Sri Lankan defeat officially represented the "end of an era" for English white-ball supremacy, describing the England players as looking "dazed and shell-shocked, unable to comprehend what has befallen them".

His grounds are cumulative rather than single-match: "Each defeat, now four in five matches, has chipped away at the confidence of a group of players at the end of a cycle. # India's 1996 World Cup Semi-Final Against Sri Lanka

India's 1996 semi-final against Sri Lanka at the Eden Gardens in Kolkata on 13 March was called off by the umpires with India reeling at 120 for eight in 34.1 overs, after crowd trouble interrupted the match and no respite came from the onlookers' side. The 1996 Cricket World Cup is known for Sri Lanka's emergence as a cricketing power on the horizon of world cricket and for the beginning of Sachin Tendulkar's extraordinary dominance in batting history.

India were favourites again in that first semi-final and raised their hopes by restricting Sri Lanka to 251 for 8 in 50 overs, despite Man-of-the-Match Aravinda de Silva's 66 and Roshan Mahanama's 58; India seamer Javagal Srinath took three top-order wickets including Sanath Jayasuriya and Romesh Kaluwitharana. Fans at the Eden Gardens cheered loudly while Tendulkar was at the crease, but once he fell for 65 with the team at 98, India suffered one of the worst collapses in the batting history of the World Cups, and the crowd turned angry and hostile towards Sri Lanka, creating a ruckus at the stadium. The long-lasting memories of the crowd's bad behaviour and of a weeping Vinod Kambli returning to the pavilion are still fresh in the memories of cricket fans of that generation.

# India vs Australia At The 1983 World Cup

India met Australia for the very first time at a World Cup in 1983 and lost that match by 162 runs. Australia posted a target of 321 runs courtesy of a brilliant 110 runs off 131 balls by Trevor Chappell, with Kapil Dev taking a fifer in that innings; India crumbled within 158 runs, with Ken MacLeay picking up six wickets for Australia.

# India vs Australia At The 1992 World Cup: The Rain-Affected One-Run Defeat

# ODI Cricket World Cup Winners List

Australia are the most successful nation in ODI World Cup history with five titles, ahead of India and the West Indies, who have two each, and England, Sri Lanka and Pakistan with one apiece.

By country the titles are: Australia 5 (1987, 1999, 2003, 2007, 2015); India 2 (1983, 2011); West Indies 2 (1975, 1979); England 1 (2019); Sri Lanka 1 (1996); and Pakistan 1 (1992). The list is current as of the Oct. 1, 2023 article, published before the 2023 tournament was played.

context:
# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.



---


# Meta Response To Suppression Claims

Meta's rebuttal attacks the premise that any pattern of reduced reach for Palestine-related content shows deliberate suppression: the company says the reduced reach came from globally scoped technical bugs and from errors in good-faith enforcement, not from the subject matter of the posts. As reported by TechCrunch on 19 October 2023, Meta said it is closely monitoring its platforms for violations and may inadvertently flag certain content, but that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view."

The scope condition Meta sets around the whole dispute is its terrorist-organization rule: content praising or supporting Hamas — which governs Gaza and is designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union — is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms. This is stated in the aftermath of Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade cutting access to electricity, water and vital supplies, which have devastated Gaza.

Meta communications director Andy Stone declined to comment on the record and pointed TechCrunch to Meta's newsroom post about the conflict, updated on Oct. 18 with a statement addressing the shadowbanning claims. "Our policies are designed to keep people safe on our apps while giving everyone a voice," it said. "We apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice … We can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it."

The specific counter-explanations are two bugs, each claimed to be global and therefore content-neutral. Meta blamed technical errors for the removal of posts about Palestine during the 2021 conflict, and on the recent shadowbanning claims a company representative pointed TechCrunch to a Threads post by Stone: "We identified a bug impacting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts, meaning they weren't showing up properly in people's Stories tray, leading to significantly reduced reach. This bug affected accounts equally around the globe and had nothing to do with the subject matter of the content — and we fixed it as quickly as possible." Stone separately directed TechCrunch to the updated newsroom post, which said Meta identified and fixed a "bug" that prevented users from going live: "This was also a global issue that was fixed within a few hours. We understand people rely on these tools and we're sorry to anyone who felt the impact of these issues."

The rebuttal's reach is limited in ways the reporting records. It is unclear whether the bug affected accounts posting content unrelated to Gaza, while Instagram users have posted screenshots showing Stories about Palestine receiving significantly fewer views than other Stories posted the same day, and allege their view counts recovered when they posted content unrelated to the conflict. Meta's representative did not address the other accusations of censorship beyond Story visibility and did not respond to TechCrunch's follow-up questions; Meta initially did not respond to follow-up requests for comment. Asked about comments containing the Palestinian flag, Stone again pointed to the updated newsroom post, which did not directly address the issue, and he declined to comment on allegations of Meta disproportionately flagging Arabic news content, directing TechCrunch to the same post, which did not directly address those allegations either.



---


# Meta's Moderation During An Earlier Hamas-Israel Conflict

During an earlier Hamas-Israel conflict, the digital-rights organisation 7amleh documented more than 500 reports of Palestinian "digital rights violations" over the 13 days leading up to the ceasefire — including the removal and restriction of content, hashtags and accounts related to the conflict. The figure was recounted to TechCrunch for its 19 October 2023 report on Meta's moderation of Palestinian content.

Meta attributed some of the instances of perceived censorship to technical issues, such as one that prevented users in Palestine and Colombia from posting Instagram Stories. It attributed others to human error, such as blocking the hashtag for Al-Aqsa Mosque — the holy site where Israeli police clashed with Ramadan worshippers — because the name was mistaken for a terrorist organization. The company also blocked journalists in Gaza from WhatsApp without explanation.

Meta committed to implementing policy changes based on the report's recommendations, including updating its keywords associated with dangerous organizations, disclosing government requests to remove content, and launching a hostile speech classifier for Hebrew content. 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater added that Meta has improved its response to harassment, at least in comparison to other social media platforms such as X (formerly Twitter): although harassment and abuse remain rampant on Instagram and Facebook, he said the company has been responsive to suspending accounts with patterns of targeting other users.

Abukhater's scope condition on all of this is that the improvements do not survive an escalation. "The balance of power is very fixed, in reality, between Israelis and Palestinians," he said. "And this is something that today is reflected heavily on platforms like Meta, even though they have human rights teams releasing reports and trying to improve upon their policies. Whenever an escalation like the one we're experiencing now happens, things just go back to zero."



---


# Meta Bias Mechanisms

Meta's disproportionate suppression of Palestinian and Arabic content is produced by a stack of interacting mechanisms rather than any single fault: thin Arabic language resources, categorical policies that cannot handle nuance, a blanket prohibition on support for terrorist organizations, government partnerships that shape policy decisions, automated enforcement backed by "minimally trained humans," and an allocation of moderation resources that tracks regulatory pressure rather than need. TechCrunch set out this account on 19 October 2023, drawing chiefly on the Electronic Frontier Foundation.

The linguistic layer comes first. Meta struggles to navigate the cultural and linguistic nuances of Arabic, a language with over 25 dialects, and has been criticized for neglecting to adequately diversify its language resources. On top of that, the company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic — content that discusses violence without condoning it is the example given.

The policy layer compounds it. Meta forbids support of terrorist organizations, as most U.S.-based social media companies do, but struggles to moderate content around that prohibition, from user discourse to journalistic updates. Combined with the company's partnership with Israel to monitor posts that incite violence, the rule complicates matters for Palestinians living under Hamas' governance: as EFF points out, something as simple as Hamas' flag in the background of an image can result in a strike. Advocacy groups have separately raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions.

The enforcement layer supplies the inconsistency. Jillian York, EFF's director for international freedom of expression, blames automation and decisions made by "minimally trained humans," and says Meta's zero tolerance policy and imprecise enforcement often suppress content from or about conflict zones. The range of the effect is wider than Palestine: the site's moderation issues have negatively affected multiple non-English speaking regions, including Libya, Syria and Ukraine. "These rules can prevent people from sharing documentation of human rights violations, documentation of war crimes, even just news about what's happening on the ground," York said. "And so I think that is what is the most problematic right now about that particular rule, and the way that it's enforced."

The resourcing layer explains why the effect is unevenly distributed across languages. York says Meta has made more contact with regional Palestinian organizations since 2021 but has been slow to implement recommendations from EFF and other advocacy groups, and that it is "very clear" Meta is not putting the same resources behind Arabic and other non-English languages compared with the attention it gives countries that exert the most regulatory pressure. Moderation of English and other European languages tends to be more comprehensive, for example, because the EU enforces the Digital Services Act.

Meta contests the picture. In its response to the report, human rights director Miranda Sissons said the company was "assessing the feasibility" of reviewing Arabic content by dialect and that it has "large and diverse teams" who understand "local cultural context across the region," including in Palestine; responding to the escalating violence earlier that month, Meta said it had established a "special operations center" staffed with fluent Hebrew and Arabic speakers to monitor and respond to violating content. Despite those apparent efforts, Arabic is still disproportionately flagged as violating — as in the case of journalists reporting news in multiple languages.

# Meta's Legal Basis Chain For Personalized Ads Under GDPR

Meta's justification for running personalized ads in the EU has moved through a chain of legal bases, each in turn rejected by regulators or courts, leaving consent as the only remaining option.

The chain runs as follows. Late in 2022 the European Data Protection Board settled a dispute between DPAs on a complaint against the legal basis the adtech giant claimed for running the ads; that led on, in January, to a final decision issued by the Irish DPC rejecting Meta's claim of contractual necessity to justify the processing. Since then Meta tried another switch of legal basis for the processing — to a claim of legitimate interests — but the EU's top court quashed that gambit with a ruling in July, related to a separate challenge brought by Germany's competition authority, which confirmed Meta cannot claim a legitimate interest to run its "personalized ads" in the absence of user consent.

That landmark strike was followed at the start of August by Meta announcing an "intention" to legalize its tracking ads business in the region by asking users for their permission. But it had still not done so, continuing to run unlawful ads — which is why the Norwegian DPA decided to take emergency action, pointing out that millions of EU people's rights are being infringed.

# Shadowbanning

## Definition

Shadowbanning, as TechCrunch describes it, is when a platform "shadowbans, or limits the visibility of" a user's content without the platform notifying the user that anything has been restricted, so the user only discovers it by noticing a drop in views or reach.

## Context

In the corpus the term names the central accusation in the October 2023 controversy over Meta's handling of Palestine-related content: Instagram users accused Meta of shadowbanning their Stories about Palestine, and TechCrunch frames the belief that Meta "shadowbans, or limits the visibility of," such content as longstanding rather than new to that month.
The same allegation is cited beyond Meta's own platforms as a driver of platform choice: users turned to Snapchat's Snap Map for firsthand Gaza content specifically because accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content on Instagram and Facebook had eroded their trust in those platforms.
Meta's official response did not deny that reach had dropped; it denied the mechanism, attributing the reduced Story reach specifically to a global, content-neutral bug in Stories that re-shared Reels or Feed posts, and separately attributed a different global bug — one that had prevented some users from going live — to technical error rather than deliberate suppression tied to subject matter.

## Key Characteristics

- **Covert, not disclosed** — the defining feature reporters and users pointed to is that visibility drops silently, with no notification to the affected account; Bella Hadid described being "immediately shadowbanned" and her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million" with no explanation from the platform.
- **Detected by comparison, not confirmation** — users inferred shadowbanning by comparing engagement across their own posts (e.g., a user whose Stories fell from "100s of views to zero or a handful" and rebounded only after posting unrelated content like a cat photo), since the platform provided no direct evidence of restriction.
- **Contested mechanism** — Meta disputed that the effect was shadowbanning-by-design, attributing the reduced Story reach to a bug that "affected accounts equally around the globe" and "had nothing to do with the subject matter of the content," rather than confirming intentional visibility limits.
- **Trust-eroding beyond the platform itself** — the accusation pushed users toward alternative platforms (Snap Map) even though the accused conduct occurred on Instagram and Facebook, showing shadowbanning claims can shift audience behavior across platforms, not just within one.

# Content Moderation

## Definition

Content moderation, as the corpus uses the term, is the mix of platform policy and enforcement — written rules like Meta's Violence and Incitement policy and Community Guidelines, human reviewers, automated systems, and crowdsourced tools like X's Community Notes — that decides what user-generated content stays visible and how a platform acts on notices of illegal or rule-breaking material.

## Context

In the corpus, content moderation surfaces mainly as the practice EU regulators scrutinize under the Digital Services Act (DSA): the DSA's "very precise obligations" require platforms to be "timely, diligent and objective" in acting on notices of illegal content, and the European Commission's formal DSA proceeding against X names "content moderation" as one of the specific areas under investigation, alongside risk management, dark patterns, advertising transparency, and researcher data access (doc_0024; doc_0153).
It also appears as a site of contested practice and bias: Meta's moderation of Palestinian-related content during the Israel-Hamas war produced widespread allegations of shadowbanning and inconsistent enforcement across Arabic versus Hebrew content (doc_0106), while Meta separately described tightening its livestreaming and hostage-content moderation in direct response to that same conflict (doc_0335).
The term also frames platform-differentiation debates outside the EU: Kick's "light moderation" is cited as both a draw for streamers leaving Twitch and a source of safety controversy (doc_0405), Mozilla frames robust moderation and "trust and safety" as central to its fediverse strategy while noting a stricter-moderation rival (Pebble) failed to grow (doc_0026), and the US Supreme Court case over Texas and Florida laws turns on whether content moderation is a form of constitutionally protected "editorial judgment" (doc_0256).

## Key Characteristics

- **Policy plus enforcement** — moderation combines written rules (e.g. Meta's Violence and Incitement policy, Community Guidelines) with mechanisms to act on them: human reviewers, automated classifiers, and appeals processes (doc_0335; doc_0106).
- **Legally obligated for large platforms under the DSA** — the DSA requires timely, diligent, objective action on illegal-content notices, and imposes added systemic-risk mitigation duties (e.g. disinformation) on very large online platforms like X and Meta (doc_0024; doc_0335).
- **Can be outsourced/crowdsourced** — X replaced parts of its formal moderation function with the crowdsourced "Community Notes" system after gutting in-house enforcement teams, a shift EU regulators are explicitly assessing for adequacy (doc_0025; doc_0153).
- **Prone to inconsistency and bias** — Meta's own third-party report found Arabic content flagged as violating at higher rates than Hebrew content, and attributed this to uneven language/dialect resources and reviewer training rather than deliberate policy (doc_0106).
- **Contested as speech regulation** — in the US, whether moderation decisions constitute protected "editorial judgment" under the First Amendment is the central legal question in the Texas/Florida social-media laws before the Supreme Court (doc_0256).
- **A competitive and reputational lever** — platforms position their moderation stance (heavy vs. light) as a market differentiator (doc_0508; doc_0405), though the corpus notes stricter moderation alone did not guarantee growth for at least one platform, Pebble, which shut down after never gaining more than 20,000 users (doc_0026).

## Background (external)

The corpus repeatedly uses "content moderation" without ever stating a general definition for it. Content moderation, more broadly, is the systematic practice of screening user-generated content and applying a predetermined set of rules to determine whether it should be published, removed, or restricted — commonly for material judged irrelevant, obscene, illegal, harmful, or insulting — either by removing it outright, labeling it, or letting users filter it themselves (Wikipedia, *Content moderation*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Norway's Ban On Meta's Consentless Tracking Ads

Norway's data protection authority asked a European Union regulator to take a binding decision on whether its emergency sanction on Facebook and Instagram tracking and profiling users for ad targeting without their consent should be made permanent and applied across the EU single market, not just locally.

The move could lead to a blanket ban on Meta running tracking ads without consent across the EU single market if the European Data Protection Board agrees the action is merited — though Meta may switch to asking users for permission to run "personalized ads" before any Board action, as it has claimed it intends to. The Datatilsynet issued its local ban on Meta tracking and profiling users without consent in July, using powers in the GDPR that enable concerned regulators to apply temporary measures, lasting three months, in their markets if they see an urgent need to act to protect citizens' data. Meta's lead regulator for the GDPR remains the Irish Data Protection Commission, which would normally lead on any enforcement, so the Norwegian DPA's emergency action circumvents the regulation's so-called "one-stop-shop" mechanism — and gives the Norwegian authority the option to refer ongoing concerns to the EDPB, as it has now done.

Meta has continued to flout the Datatilsynet order — which includes a daily fine of up to one million NOK (around $100,000) per day for non-compliance — ignoring the authority's requirement not to run tracking ads without permission, per a spokesperson for the DPA. The company instead sought a court injunction against the order, but earlier that month an Oslo court rejected Meta's arguments, affirming the DPA's right to act. Reached by email, the EDPB confirmed receipt of the authority's request: "The EDPB Secretariat will now assess completeness of the file. Once this assessment is complete, the deadline under art. 66(4) GDPR starts running and the Board will have two weeks to adopt its urgent binding decision," a spokeswoman said, declining to offer any steer on how long the Board's assessment would take.

# Shadowban Workarounds

As the war continued, social media users tried to find ways around the alleged shadowbanning on Instagram, using three supposed loopholes: misspelling flagged words, hiding text over unrelated images, and adopting pro-Israel signals they do not endorse. TechCrunch recorded the tactics on 19 October 2023, and describes them as supposed loopholes — user hypotheses about what evades the filters, not verified mechanics of Meta's systems.

The first tactic is orthographic: misspelling certain words, such as writing "p@lestine" instead of "Palestine," in hopes of bypassing any content filters. The second is visual: sharing information about Gaza as text superimposed over unrelated images, like a cat photo, so it will not be flagged as graphic or violent content. The third is signalling: creators have tried including an emoji of the Israeli flag, or tagging their posts and Stories with #istandwithisrael even when they do not support the Israeli government, in hopes of gaming engagement.

The precondition for all three is the belief that the platform is throttling Palestine-related posts, and the frustration behind them is widespread. Leen Al Saadi said her frustration with Meta is common among Palestinians, both in occupied territories and across the diaspora. "All we're asking for is to give us the exact same rights," she said. "We're not asking for more. We're literally just asking Meta, Instagram, every single broadcast channel, every single media outlet, to just give us the respect that we deserve."

# Data Privacy

## Definition

Data privacy, across the corpus, is the recurring dispute over whether companies may collect, track, or profile people's personal information without their knowledge or consent.

That dispute plays out as regulatory enforcement against platforms: GDPR action against Meta's consentless ad tracking (doc_0107), COPPA litigation over Meta's collection of data from children under 13 (doc_0304), a "mass breach of privacy" allegation against TikTok's pre-consent tracking pixel (doc_0189), and California's CPPA extending opt-out and access rights to AI-based profiling (doc_0164).

## Context

In the corpus, data privacy surfaces as the recurring fault line between platforms that monetize personal data and the regulators pushing back on non-consensual collection. Norway's Datatilsynet issued an emergency GDPR ban on Meta running "personalized ads" without consent, then referred the case to the EU's Board to make the ban permanent across the single market, because Meta kept running tracking ads despite the order and a rejected court challenge (doc_0107). California's CPPA is drafting rules that would give residents opt-out and access rights over "automated decisionmaking technology," explicitly modeled on GDPR and expected to draw pushback from adtech and AI firms like Meta and OpenAI (doc_0164). The Age's investigation found TikTok's tracking pixel scraping site visitors' names, emails, and phone numbers before users clicked "I consent," prompting an Australian senator to call it a "mass breach of privacy" and demand a regulatory probe (doc_0189). Meta separately faces a 42-state lawsuit alleging it violated COPPA — the US law restricting data collection from children under 13 and requiring parental consent — by knowingly letting millions of underage users onto Instagram and Facebook while collecting their personal information (doc_0304).

## Key Characteristics

- **Consent is the legal hinge** — GDPR, as applied against Meta in Norway, turns on whether a company has a valid legal basis (consent, not "legitimate interest" or "contractual necessity") before tracking or profiling users for ads (doc_0107).
- **Pre-consent collection is the specific harm alleged against TikTok** — its pixel captured form-field data "often before clicking 'I consent'," unlike Google's and Meta's pixels, which the same test showed firing only after consent (doc_0189).
- **Children are a protected, heavily litigated category** — COPPA restricts data collection from users under 13 and requires verifiable parental consent, and Meta's alleged evasion of that requirement (ignoring reports, not disabling accounts, avoiding "actual knowledge") is the specific violation named in the unredacted lawsuit (doc_0304).
- **Regulators are extending consent/access rights into AI** — California's CPPA is drafting opt-out and access rights over automated decisionmaking technology and AI-based profiling, explicitly borrowing from GDPR's model (doc_0164).
- **Enforcement can escalate beyond a single national regulator** — Norway's local DPA used an emergency GDPR mechanism to bypass the "one-stop-shop" rule and force an EU-wide decision on Meta, showing that a single country's action can become bloc-wide policy (doc_0107).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the general legal concept the enforcement actions above are built on is the definition of "personal data" under GDPR.

GDPR.eu describes personal data as "any information that relates to an individual who can be directly or indirectly identified," a category spanning obvious identifiers like names and emails as well as location data and other online identifiers (GDPR.eu, "What Is GDPR, the EU's New Data Protection Law?", published by Proton AG with EU Horizon 2020 co-funding, accessed 2026-09-02: https://gdpr.eu/what-is-gdpr/).

# Instagram Palestine Suppression

Through October 2023, as the humanitarian crisis in Gaza grew more dire, Instagram users, creators and Palestinian digital-rights groups reported that Meta was restricting, hiding, mislabelling or removing content about Palestine — including content that does not support Hamas and content that adheres to Instagram's Community Guidelines. The reports, gathered by TechCrunch and published 19 October 2023, span account restrictions, "sensitive" and "inappropriate" flags, hidden comments, collapsed Story reach, and disproportionate flagging of Arabic-language material.

Palestinian-American filmmaker Khitam Jabr provides an example that predates the current escalation. Earlier this year she posted a handful of Reels about her family's trip to the West Bank — short travel vlogs sharing snippets of Palestinian culture, from decadent meals to dancing at her niece's wedding. "I hadn't been in a decade, so it's just like, life abroad," she told TechCrunch. She received anti-Palestine comments and then could not respond to them or use her account for 24 hours, despite not posting anything about the occupation; she suspects Instagram restricted her because other users reported her Palestine travel videos. "Fast forward to now and the same shit's happening," she said.

The belief that Meta shadowbans — limits the visibility of — content about Palestine is not new. In an Instagram Story last year, supermodel and activist Bella Hadid, who is of Palestinian descent, alleged that Instagram "disabled" her from posting content on her Story "pretty much only when it is Palestine based," said she gets "immediately shadowbanned" when she posts about Palestine, and reported her Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Leen Al Saadi, a Palestinian journalist based in Jordan and host of the podcast "Preserving Palestine," said she is used to "constantly being censored"; her Instagram account was restricted last year after she posted a trailer for the podcast's first episode, which discussed a documentary about Palestinian street art under occupation. "Palestinians are currently undergoing two wars," Al Saadi said. "The first is with their legal occupier. The second war is with the entire Western media landscape, and when I say the entire landscape, I mean social media."

Creators report that engagement on their posts tanked specifically after they publicly condemned Israel's response to the Hamas attack as excessively violent. Some, like Jabr, say they were restricted from posting or going live; others say Instagram flagged their content as "sensitive," limiting its reach, or flagged it as "inappropriate" and removed it even when it adhered to the Community Guidelines. A user based in Egypt, who asked to stay anonymous for fear of harassment, said her posts usually get around 300 views, but after she began posting pro-Palestine content following the Hamas attack earlier that month her Stories would get only one to two views; she found that posting a random picture first, then a pro-Palestine post, raised the views, and said the same happened to her friends. Another anonymous user based in the United Kingdom said his view count returned to normal when he posted a cat photo: "My stories went from 100s of views to zero or a handful. I've had to post intermittent non-Gaza content in order to 'release' my stories to be viewed again."

The pattern extends beyond Stories. The Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), which documents Palestinian digital-rights violations and works directly with social media companies to appeal them, told TechCrunch it has received reports of Instagram inconsistently filtering comments containing the Palestinian flag emoji, with users reporting that such comments are flagged as "potentially offensive" and hidden. The organisation has also received countless reports of Meta flagging and restricting Arabic content, including content posted by news outlets: 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater said it has documented multiple cases of journalists on Instagram reporting the same news in Arabic, Hebrew and English but only being flagged for the Arabic version. "It's literally journalistic content, but the same wording in Hebrew and English does not get restricted," Abukhater said. "As if there's better moderation for those languages, and more careless moderation for Arabic content." As the Intercept reported, Instagram and Facebook flagged images of the al-Ahli Hospital, claiming they violate Meta's Community Guidelines on nudity or sexual activity.

Enforcement also runs inconsistent in the other direction. Al Saadi tried to report a comment saying she should be "raped" and "burned alive," left in response to her comment on a CNN post about the conflict; in screenshots reviewed by TechCrunch, Instagram replied that it did not violate the platform's Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations. "The restrictions on content, especially the content that relates to Palestine, is heavily politicized," Abukhater said. "It feeds into the bias against Palestinian narrative genuinely. It really takes the balance against Palestinians in a situation where there's a huge asymmetry of power." Similar claims circulated publicly, including an October 15, 2023 post alleging that the singer Kehlani was shadowbanned after becoming vocal and changing her profile picture to "i stand with Palestine," just as Bella Hadid had been.

# Meta's Legal Basis For Ad Tracking In The EU

The structure behind Meta's subscription move is a narrowing set of legal bases. The move follows years of privacy litigation, enforcements and court rulings in the EU, which have culminated in a situation where Meta can no longer claim a contractual right, nor legitimate interest, to track and profile users for ad targeting — although at the time of writing it is still doing the latter, meaning it is technically operating without a proper legal basis, and this summer Meta announced an intention to switch to consent.

The remaining relation is therefore singular: under regional data protection law the only available basis left for Meta's tracking and profiling ad business is to obtain freely given consent from users. The range over which that holds is exactly what is in dispute — the adtech giant's interpretation of free consent with this 'pay us or be tracked' subscription proposal will, justifiably, leave privacy advocates fuming, since the choice it's offering boils down to 'pay us money; or pay us with your privacy'.

# Dangerous Organizations and Individuals Policy

The Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy is the named enforcement category Meta cites when it removes content tied to groups that governments designate as terrorist organizations, most directly Hamas.
In the corpus its practical trigger is Hamas: content praising or supporting Hamas, which governs Gaza and is designated a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union, is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms.
Meta tracks enforcement of this policy as its own category, separate from its Violence and Incitement policy, reporting that it removed "seven times as many pieces of content on a daily basis for violating our Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy in Hebrew and Arabic alone" in the three days after October 7, 2023, compared with the two months prior.

## Context

In the corpus the policy is the mechanism through which Meta enforces against Hamas-related content during the Israel-Hamas war, and it is the recurring flashpoint in disputes over whether that enforcement is applied evenly.
Meta invokes the policy to justify removing content that praises or supports Hamas — Hamas being "designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union" — and Instagram separately cited a related "Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations" when it denied that a specific violent, threatening comment violated its rules, illustrating that the same policy family both blocks and, in users' eyes, under-enforces depending on the content.
The designation logic recurs beyond Meta's own platform actions: the corpus notes that Hamas is "considered a terrorist organization by the U.K., U.S. and other countries" in the context of the Web Summit/Cosgrave controversy, and that UNRWA operates "alongside Hamas, which Israel, the United States and other countries designate as a terrorist organization" in Gaza — showing the same underlying designation of Hamas driving both platform moderation policy and geopolitical characterization of the region's governing party.

## Key Characteristics

- **Named, tracked enforcement category** — Meta reports removal volumes specifically "for violating our Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy," distinct from its Violence and Incitement policy, letting the company cite a sevenfold daily increase in Hebrew/Arabic enforcement after October 7.
- **Anchored to external terrorist designations** — the policy's practical trigger in the corpus is content supporting Hamas, an organization the U.S., EU and U.K. designate as a terrorist group; the platform rule imports government designations rather than defining "dangerous" independently.
- **Contested in application** — Palestinian users and digital-rights advocates argue the policy (and its Community Guidelines "violence or dangerous organizations" language) is enforced inconsistently, citing a case where a violent, threatening comment was ruled not to violate it, and past instances where the Al-Aqsa Mosque hashtag was blocked after being "mistaken for a terrorist organization."
- **Localized to Arabic and Hebrew content** — the volume Meta cites for this policy is scoped specifically to Hebrew and Arabic content, not platform-wide, reflecting the languages most implicated in Israel-Hamas war content moderation.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Meta's own Community Standards describe the Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy more broadly than the Hamas-specific enforcement described above: it generally bars praise, substantive support, and representation of any individual or organization that Meta designates as dangerous, a designation list that spans terrorist organizations, hate organizations, criminal organizations, and other violence-inducing entities, not just Hamas.

# Analysis Of Meta's Delay Tactics On The Consent Switch

Meta's public "intention" to switch to consent is best read as a PR tactic for normalizing delay rather than as a compliance step, and the Norwegian referral to the EDPB may be what finally concentrates minds at the company on making good on its pledge sooner rather than later.

The grounds are in the shape of the announcement itself: Meta has sought to get ahead of events by using PR tactics that present a narrative in which it appears to retain some control — hence a blog post sketching a future "intention" to switch to consent, just without fixing a date, so keeping control of the timings and seeking to normalize the ongoing delay to rectifying its unlawful "personalized ads" — even as EU regulators have, collectively, forced the looming paradigm shift to its privacy-hostile business model. The warrant joining grounds to claim is that an undated intention imposes no constraint, so only external deadlines change behavior.

The bottom line is that in the not-too-distant future surveillance capitalism's poster child will — at least in a major international region for its business — have to end the consentless tracking and profiling it exploited for years to build up its adtech empire at the expense of web users' privacy. In the meanwhile, people in the EU's single market are once again being directed to wait on Ireland's DPC to enforce their privacy rights; but if the Irish authority is too slow to rectify Meta's lack of consent this time, there is now the backstop option of the Board stepping in a second time and finishing the job for it.

# BEUC's Consumer-Law Case Against Meta's Pay-Or-Consent Model

BEUC's summary of the issues identified with Meta's model under consumer protection law rests on four grounds, each attached to a distinct provision of consumer law.

First, aggression: Meta is partially blocking the use of Facebook and Instagram until users have selected one option or the other, which constitutes an aggressive practice under European consumer law; through persistence and by creating a sense of urgency, Meta pushes consumers into making a choice they might not want to take. Second, a mistaken belief about what the paid tier buys: many consumers likely think that by opting for the paid subscription as it is presented they get a privacy-friendly option involving less tracking and profiling, when in fact users are likely to continue to have their personal data collected and used, but for purposes other than ads.

Third, misleading framing: Meta provides misleading and incomplete information to consumers which does not allow them to make an informed choice, and is misleading them by presenting the choice as between a paying and a "free" option, while the latter option is not "free" because consumers pay Meta through the provision of their data, as past court rulings have already declared. Fourth, and the warrant tying the rest together, the absence of a real choice: given the market power of Meta's Facebook and Instagram services in the EU and the very strong network effects of social media platforms — since all your friends are on Facebook and Instagram — consumers do not have a real choice, because if they quit the services they would lose all their contacts and interactions built over the years; the very high subscription fee for "ad-free" services is also a deterrent, which likewise means consumers do not have a real choice.

# Irish DPC's Assessment Of Meta's Consent Model

Meta's lead regulator in the EU for the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC), told TechCrunch: "Meta notified the DPC on July 27 of its intention to implement an alternative, consent-based model in which users would be given a choice between ads-funded versions of its platforms, and subscription versions in which, in return for payment of monthly fee, it is said that users will not receive targeted advertising."

The regulator also set out the timing and its cause: "While February 2024 was initially identified by Meta as the earliest date by which its consent model would be operational, it agreed to bring forward that date to November 2023 at the direction of the DPC, the DPC having been concerned to ensure that changes would be implemented to the platforms as soon as practicable in light of earlier findings to the effect that Meta had failed to demonstrate its entitlement to rely on the legal bases on which it was then relying when processing users' data for behavioural advertising purposes. On the review itself: "Acting in consultation with its fellow European supervisory authorities, the DPC has been engaged in a detailed regulatory assessment of the consent-based model since it was first proposed by Meta in July. # The Digital Services Act

The Digital Services Act (DSA) is the European Union's pan-EU content moderation rulebook: a regulation that places governance obligations on digital services and platforms carrying user-generated content, with the aim of ensuring companies respond to reports of illegal content, and that layers heavier duties on the largest platforms. Its baseline obligations apply to digital services and platforms generally — respond diligently to notices of illegal content, clearly communicate terms and conditions to users, and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement of those terms.

The discriminating feature of the regime is its second tier. Platforms designated as "very large online platforms" (VLOPs) carry additional obligations to identify and mitigate systemic risks such as disinformation, gender-based violence, or negative effects on the exercise of fundamental rights. The Commission designated 19 VLOPs in April 2023, including Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram; X is also a designated VLOP. Compliance for VLOPs kicked in over the summer of 2023 — TechCrunch dates Meta's compliance start to August.

The regime's boundary case is disinformation itself. Unlike terrorism content, disinformation is not illegal in the EU per se. The DSA therefore does not reach it through the illegal-content removal route at all; it reaches it through the systemic-risk route, obliging a VLOP such as X to mitigate the risks attached to harmful falsehoods while separately acting diligently on reports of genuinely illegal content. The two duties run on different legal tracks even when they concern the same posts.

Penalties for confirmed breaches can be as high as 6% of global annual turnover, and the bloc holds a further power, in extremis, to block access to a service in the region for repeated infringements — meaning a platform that repeatedly fails to correct course could be shut off in the EU. TechCrunch illustrates the scale on both ends: Elon Musk last projected revenues of about $3 billion for 2023 for X, which by that example would cap a fine at up to $180 million, while in Meta's case the same 6% ceiling could run to multiple billions.

The regulation also contains a "crisis response" mechanism (Article 36) which enables the Commission to adopt rapid-fire measures on larger platforms in situations of "serious threat", such as war. As of TechCrunch's October 2023 reporting this part of the regulation was not yet operative: it would not start operating until February 17 of the following year, because it requires an advisory body — the European Board for Digital Services — to be operational before it can recommend that the Commission adopt a crisis response mechanism, and the Board's set-up was itself waiting on Member States to establish national Digital Services Coordinators, the bodies that oversee DSA compliance for non-VLOPs.

# "Pay Or Okay": The Cookie Paywall Model Meta Borrowed

The "pay or okay" model Meta is seeking to impose on EU users was not its invention. It was pioneered in Austria by the daily newspaper Der Standard, after which copycat cookie paywalls quickly sprang up on a raft of news publishers in Germany and elsewhere in the EU. noyb has been challenging this approach to GDPR consent since 2021, filing complaints with a number of data protection authorities and arguing the model forces newspaper readers to "buy back their own data at exorbitant prices."

The publisher case and the Meta case diverge on one feature. Some DPAs appear to have been sympathetic to local newspapers' use of cookie walls, seeing it as a way to support the production of journalism. When it comes to Meta, TechCrunch argues, that argument evaporates: Meta is definitely not in the journalism business, and moreover the adtech giant does not even need to produce content to pump around its social networks — it gets all that filler for free from the same users it is now demanding pay a fee if they want to use its services without being tracked and profiled for behavioral advertising, which makes Meta's model feel like even more of a rip off.

The legal boundary of the model remains unsettled. Back in April 2023, a decision by Austria's DPA on a noyb complaint about cookie paywalls said users must have the ability to say yes or no to specific data operations, meaning blanket consent is not an option. But the result left it unclear how cookie paywalls might be operated in a way that is GDPR compliant, and the privacy rights group vowed to fight the decision in court, predicting at the time that "the final decision on 'pay or okay' may be made by the European Court of Justice (CJEU) in the long run."

# Hashtag Blocking

Hashtag blocking is a content moderation technique in which a platform renders certain terms non-searchable, so that posts tagged with a blocked hashtag no longer surface in hashtag search results.

## Context

In the corpus the term appears in a TechCrunch report (2023-10-13) covering Meta's blog post responding to EU regulators' content-moderation warning over the Israel-Hamas war, where Meta lists hashtag blocking alongside other visibility-reduction measures — demoting potentially violating or borderline content in recommendations and reducing the visibility of potentially offensive comments — as one of the "other steps" it took to respond to the conflict. Meta applied hashtag blocking "to render certain terms related to the conflict non-searchable on its platforms," but its blog post did not specify which hashtags were being blocked.

## Key Characteristics

- **Search suppression, not removal** — the technique makes tagged terms non-searchable rather than deleting the underlying posts, distinguishing it from content takedowns.
- **Undisclosed scope** — Meta declined to specify which hashtags it was blocking in relation to the Israel-Hamas war, so the mechanism's actual coverage was opaque even in Meta's own disclosure.
- **Paired with other visibility levers** — the corpus presents it as one of a set of ranking/search measures Meta deployed together, alongside reduced recommendation of borderline content and reduced visibility of offensive comments.
- **Fallible in prior use** — Meta has previously misapplied a comparable hashtag block: during the 2021 Hamas-Israel conflict, it blocked the hashtag for Al-Aqsa Mosque, "mistaken for a terrorist organization." Following a third-party report on that conflict's moderation, Meta committed to policy changes such as updating its "keywords associated with dangerous organizations."

# Meta's EU Pay-Or-Consent Ad-Free Subscription

Meta's pay-or-consent model, rolled out in November 2023, is a binary offer to EU users of its social networks Facebook and Instagram: agree to being tracked and profiled by the behavioral ads business in order to continue or get free access to its products, or else pay a monthly subscription of at least €9.99 per month for an ad-free version of its mainstream social networks.

# Microtargeting

## Definition

In the corpus, microtargeting refers to using a platform's ad-targeting tools to aim political or advertising messaging at narrow, algorithmically selected audience segments — including by deliberately excluding groups defined by their interests or political views — rather than at a general audience.

## Context

In the corpus, microtargeting appears in two related EU controversies over data-driven ad targeting on major platforms.
Meta's "pay or consent" model is accused of forcing users to accept being "tracked and profiled" so the company can keep "profiting from microtargeting them," with nearly 20 consumer groups arguing this breaches EU consumer protection law.
Separately, the European Commission itself ran a microtargeted political ad campaign on X to build support for its CSAM-scanning proposal, which became the subject of a DSA-compliance investigation and a European Parliament committee hearing.
Both cases involve platforms designated Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) under the DSA — Facebook and Instagram in the Meta case, X in the Commission's campaign — though only the Commission's campaign was exposed using X's DSA-mandated ad-transparency tools, while the Meta case instead centers on a coordinated consumer-protection complaint.

## Key Characteristics

- **Exclusion-based mechanics** — technologist Danny Mekić's analysis of X's Transparency Report showed the Commission's campaign was configured to exclude specific interest groups (people interested in Julian Assange, in "nexit"/"brexit"/"spanexit," in figures like Viktor Orbán or Nigel Farage, and people interested in Christianity), after which the platform's algorithm found remaining users receptive to the message.
- **Echo-chamber effect** — Mekić described the resulting audience, once critical political and religious groups were filtered out, as "an uncritical echo chamber."
- **Regulatory exposure under the DSA** — the DSA prohibits using sensitive personal data, such as political opinions, to target ads; Mekić argued the Commission's campaign violated X's own advertising policy, the DSA, and the GDPR.
- **Basis for consumer-protection complaints** — separately, Meta's monetization of tracked-and-profiled user data for microtargeted advertising was central to BEUC's complaint that its pay-or-consent model is "unfair" and "illegal" under EU consumer law.
- **Exposed via VLOP transparency obligations** — the Commission's microtargeted campaign became visible only because Mekić used the public ad-transparency tools the DSA requires X, as a VLOP, to provide; Meta's microtargeting practice, by contrast, was already publicly known and became the basis of a separate consumer-protection complaint rather than something uncovered through ad-transparency tools.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, microtargeting is generally defined as the use of online data to tailor advertising or political messaging to individuals or small groups based on their personal characteristics or vulnerabilities, rather than addressing a broad, undifferentiated audience (Wikipedia, "Microtargeting," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microtargeting).

# Meta Crisis Response Measures

Following a content moderation warning from European Union regulators earlier that week, Meta published on 13 October 2023 an overview of how it is responding to risks on its platforms stemming from the Israel-Hamas war: a temporary expansion of its Violence and Incitement policy, prioritised livestream checks, demotion of borderline content, hashtag blocking, a special operations center, and a temporary suspension of strikes for some violations. The blog post frames much of this as "ongoing efforts" and rehashes some existing policies and tools, but the company confirms it made some changes in light of fast-moving events in Israel and Gaza.

The first change is the temporary expansion of the Violence and Incitement policy, in order to prioritize the safety of Israelis kidnapped by Hamas. Under it, Meta will remove content that "clearly identifies hostages when we're made aware of it, even if it's being done to condemn or raise awareness of their situation." Blurred images of victims are allowed, but, "in line with standards established by the Geneva Convention, we will prioritize the safety and privacy of kidnapping victims if we are unsure or unable to make a clear assessment."

The second is livestreaming. Meta says it is prioritizing checks on livestreaming functions on Facebook and Instagram, including watching for any attempts by Hamas to use the tools to broadcast footage of captured Israelis or other hostages. The precondition it invokes is prior violation history: "We recognize that the immediacy of Live brings unique challenges, so we have restrictions in place on the use of Live for people who have previously violated certain policies. We're prioritizing livestream reports related to this crisis, above and beyond our existing prioritization of Live videos." Meta drew the comparison to measures it took after the 2019 Christchurch attacks in New Zealand, when a single shooter livestreamed a killing spree targeting two mosques on Facebook. On the specific threat, it added: "We're also aware of Hamas' threats to broadcast footage of the hostages and we're taking these threats extremely seriously. Our teams are monitoring this closely, and would swiftly remove any such content (and the accounts behind it), banking the content in our systems to prevent copies being re-shared." The urgency is not hypothetical: in a particularly disturbing report on Israeli media that week, widely recirculated on social media, a girl recounted how she and her family learnt of her grandmother's death after Hamas militants uploaded a video of her dead body to Facebook, apparently using the dead woman's own mobile phone to post the graphic content to her Facebook page.

Further steps cover ranking and search. Meta says it is making it less likely that its systems will actively recommend potentially violating or borderline content, and reducing the visibility of potentially offensive comments; it is also applying hashtag blocking to render certain terms related to the conflict non-searchable on its platforms. The blog post does not specify which hashtags Meta is blocking in relation to the Israel-Hamas war.

Operationally, Meta says it established a special operations center staffed with experts, including Arabic and Hebrew speakers, to increase its ability to respond quickly to content reports, and that it is taking feedback from local partners such as NGOs on emerging risks and "moving quickly to address them."

Meta states the limit of the procedure itself: given the heightened attention and concern, it says non-violating content may be removed "in error." Its mitigation is to relax the penalty rather than the removal — "for some violations we are temporarily removing content without strikes, meaning these content removals won't cause accounts to be disabled" — and it says it continues to provide tools for users to appeal decisions they believe were wrong.

# DSA And DMA Oversight Of Meta's Ad Tracking

Meta's subscription plan faces three overlapping regimes, not one. As well as needing to comply with the GDPR, which delineates the qualities necessary for consent to be legal — such as that it is specific, informed and freely given — Meta is now also subject to the pan-EU Digital Services Act (DSA), which also sets conditions on larger platforms when it comes to tracking and profiling people for ads; so it won't just be data protection authorities making a call on whether Meta's subscription-or-tracking offer flies, since the European Commission is responsible for oversight of very large online platforms' DSA compliance.

Meta has also been designated as a so-called gatekeeper under the DSA's sister regulation, the Digital Markets Act (DMA), which also puts some limits on use of people's data for ads, and the Commission is the sole enforcer of the DMA. Meta is already in the Commission's sights over its approach to the DSA — the EU's executive has in recent days requested more information from the tech giant about its approach to content threats flowing from the Israel-Hamas war and about election security issues — but it remains to be seen whether the EU will apply the same close scrutiny to Meta's ad tracking offer.

# The GDPR Track Running Alongside The Consumer Complaint

As of November 30, 2023 the data protection question about Meta's pay-or-consent offer was unresolved and running on a separate track from the consumer complaint. "The company's approach also raises concerns regarding the GDPR," BEUC's Ursula Pachl noted, and a spokesman for BEUC told TechCrunch it might, at a later stage, file a complaint about Meta's data protection compliance with the relevant privacy authority once it has completed its own assessment of the issues — though he emphasized it was too early to say whether or not it would take that step.

Meta's lead data protection authority in the EU, Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC), had for several months been assessing its pay-or-consent offer but had yet to communicate a conclusion. In the meanwhile, Meta maintains that the model it has devised for obtaining users' consent to its ads processing complies with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) — although, TechCrunch notes, the adtech giant also said that when it was claiming performance of a contract and then legitimate interests for the processing, both of which were subsequently found to be incompatible with the GDPR.

TechCrunch's reading of the incentive: Meta is likely banking on another multi-year round of GDPR complaints, legal challenges and finally a referral to the CJEU, followed by another long wait before a ruling gets handed down, buying it several more years to run with its new legal basis fix and keep feeding its profits by doing what it likes with Europeans' data.
