# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# The Epic v. Apple Ruling And Its Limited Weight Here

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. She also decided that Epic violated its developer agreement with Apple and would have to pay.

Epic did win something. Rogers barred Apple from keeping iPhone users in the dark about alternate ways they can pay for apps, and may have even allowed developers to add their own payment mechanisms.

The precedent's reach into the Google trial is limited in two specific ways. First, that was a different case — and it is not over until the Supreme Court weighs in or declines to take a look. Second, Google cannot tell jurors that Apple won its case, or that other plaintiffs settled; the judge in this case says so. Epic declined to answer on the record when asked about the Apple outcome.



---


# Class Action Settlement

## Definition

A class action settlement is an agreement that resolves a class-action lawsuit before (or instead of) a full trial verdict, typically trading a payment and/or changed business practices from the defendant for an end to the collective claim, in place of the class-wide monetary and injunctive relief a plaintiff would otherwise seek at trial.

## Context

The corpus shows the pattern most clearly in the Epic v. Google app store litigation: Google settled separately with all 50 U.S. state attorneys general and a number of consumers who had brought parallel antitrust claims, and reached a last-minute settlement with Match Group as well, leaving Epic Games as the only original plaintiff still pursuing trial.
Match's settlement let it take advantage of Google's "User Choice Billing" program — a reduced-commission alternative payment option — rather than continuing to litigate; Epic's CEO Tim Sweeney called Match "an awesome partner" and said he hoped Match "got out of their settlement what they needed to get for their business," contrasting Match's choice to settle with Epic's decision to keep fighting because it viewed cash settlements as insufficient while Google's "Google tax" remained in place.
The Helena World Chronicle class action against Google and Alphabet illustrates what a plaintiff seeks when a settlement has not (yet) been reached: the suit asks for damages plus an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent before using their data to train AI products, showing the class-wide monetary-and-injunctive relief that a settlement would otherwise substitute for.
The corpus also shows settlements shaping corporate behavior after the fact: Apple's earlier keyboard class-action settlement is cited as a factor that "tipped the scales" toward redesigning the MacBook Pro keyboard and dropping the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Substitutes for trial** — a settlement ends the case without a jury verdict; in the Google app-store litigation, settling with the state AGs, consumers, and Match Group left only Epic to actually go to trial.
- **Terms can stay undisclosed** — the corpus notes it was "not clear" what the AG/consumer settlement included, and Google would not say whether it had offered Epic a settlement.
- **Can substitute non-cash remedies for damages** — Match's settlement gave it access to a reduced-commission billing option rather than (or alongside) a cash payment, illustrating that settlements can trade behavioral/business-practice changes for dropped claims.
- **Not universally accepted by co-plaintiffs** — Epic explicitly declined to settle on cash terms alone, showing settlement is a choice each plaintiff or plaintiff group makes independently even within the same litigation.
- **Downstream business impact** — Apple's keyboard settlement is presented as a cost that influenced a later product redesign decision, showing settlements can have effects beyond the parties strictly bound by them.

# Epic v. Google Is A Jury Trial

Epic and Google have to convince a jury, not the judge, which is totally different from how the Apple case played out — that one was a "bench trial."

The consequence is that persuasion cuts both ways and is hard to predict. All the evidence of tricky deals inside Google might sway a jury against the company; alternatively, Google scaremongering that sideloaded apps equal gaping security holes might sway a jury against Epic. Who knows.

The jury is also sealed off from coverage: Judge Donato explicitly told jurors they are in a "news-free bubble" through mid-December.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.



---


# The Epic v. Google Witness Lineup

A whole cast of intriguing people were set to be called as witnesses during the trial, going straight to the top of the org chart: Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Epic CEO Tim Sweeney are absolutely expected to attend.

Beyond the two chief executives, Android co-founder Andy Rubin might be deposed, and Google says the court will hear from current Android — and Chrome, and Chrome OS — boss Hiroshi Lockheimer. Google also says representatives from Apple, Netflix, Motorola, and AT&T should testify.



---


# Google's News Content Payment Deal With Canada

In November 2023, the month before the Helena World Chronicle suit was filed, Google reached an agreement with the Canadian government under which the search giant would pay Canadian media for use of their content. Under the terms of the deal, Google will provide $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) every year to news organizations in the country, with funds distributed based on the news outlets' headcount.

Negotiations with Meta over the same Canadian law were still unresolved as of mid-December 2023. Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August, in light of the pressure to pay for content under the new Canadian law.



---


# Epic's Jury Verdict Against Google, December 2023

On Monday, a federal jury sided with Fortnite maker Epic Games in its fight to break Google's control over Android apps, surprising the world. The nine-person jury decided that Google has an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems, and that Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The outcome was striking because "walled garden" rival Apple almost entirely won a similar case two years earlier. For Tim Sweeney, this was, at last, a win.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.



---


# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.



---


# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Openness And Sideloading

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google will also attack the foreclosure premise directly. It will note that, unlike Apple, it allows apps to be sideloaded on Android devices — something Epic takes advantage of today — and that this process is streamlined and helps keep users safe. Epic will claim in response that the process is made to be overly difficult for end users, with multiple steps involved and "scare screens" that warn users of the security risks involved with sideloading.

On discovery, Epic will suggest that Google hid items by allowing execs and employees to have "off the record" chats; Google will counter this as well, saying it has provided the court with thousands of chat logs and millions of documents. Google will ultimately push the notion that this case is not about competition but about money — that is, that Epic Games wants to reach the Play Store's 2.5 billion users without having to pay. As a Google blog post by Wilson White, VP, Government Affairs & Public Policy, put it: "Android's choice and flexibility work well for consumers and developers of all sizes. We look forward to making our case in court as we fight to keep our users safe from harm, partner with developers to grow their businesses, and keep the Android ecosystem thriving and healthy for everyone."



---


# Google's Secret OEM And Carrier Deals And Its Deleted Chats

Asked what surprised him in the courtroom, Tim Sweeney said the trial confirmed practices he had suspected since around 2018 — when some people called him a conspiracy theorist for saying so — including that Google leaked Epic's conversations to reporters to get negative stories written, paid other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores, and went around paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores.

Sweeney gave a concrete instance from Epic's own experience: when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with other smartphone manufacturers such as OnePlus and with carriers of all sorts, those partners told Epic they couldn't do a deal because Google had done a secret deal with them. He called it disconcerting to see the extent of bad-faith efforts inside a company of Google's size, saying you would expect a trillion-dollar company to have developed respectable processes and leadership structures providing checks and balances against wrongdoing. Instead, he said, Google employees were "rampantly destroying all their chats on these topics": long conversation threads would start to get into a spicy antitrust issue, somebody would point out that history was on, and the chat would go silent — history turned off so the documents would be destroyed. Sweeney said it was great to see all of that called out in detail at trial.



---


# The $360 Million Activision Payment And Its Evidentiary Weakness

The counter to Epic's headline number attacks the factual premise beneath it: the $360 million refers to an alleged payment that kept Activision from opening an app store that could compete with Google Play, but Activision told The Verge in 2022 that it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store" — and Google says it is now armed with the evidence to prove it.

Epic itself conceded a related point. On Monday Epic's attorney admitted Google "was too clever" to draw up contracts that specifically forced developers not to compete with the Play Store, so it is not clear how much of Epic's evidence will hold up on closer examination.

The narrative advantage may nonetheless survive the evidentiary weakness. The overall story Epic tells is compelling, and it is not clear Google's opening statement countered it: Google spent its 45 minutes attempting to explain that its dominance over the Android app market is not anything nefarious but simply the natural outcome of Google fiercely competing with the iPhone and its iOS App Store, where Google would like the court to believe the competition truly lies.



---


# Google's Auto-Deleted Chats And The Sanctions Ruling

Google employees up to and including CEO Sundar Pichai were caught setting sensitive chats to auto-delete to keep them out of a court's hands, and the court has already decided Google should be sanctioned in some way for making potential evidence disappear — enough that the judge has decided to explicitly tell the jury they are not seeing all the evidence.

Bornstein used it to plant persistent seeds of doubt in the minds of jury members: "All we know is whatever is in the destroyed chats, as bad as the documents are, is worse. Or at least it was worse, before they were destroyed."

The best Google could do in response was to plant its own feeble seed with the jury — "Is Epic using the chats to distract me from all the evidence I do see?" — alongside Pomerantz's legal point that it is true Google could have automatically saved all chats for all relevant employees, but just because Google did not save some chats did not mean it violated antitrust laws.

The issue is not confined to this case. It has also come up in the US v. Google antitrust trial in Washington, DC, still ongoing at the start of Epic's trial.



---


# Project Hug, Agave And Banyan

The allegations made before trial suggest Google was playing loads of dirty tricks with names like "Project Hug," "Project Agave," and "Project Banyan," with Epic claiming it has seen evidence Google was paying off game developers and phone makers not to abandon its app store — to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars.

Google allegedly even toyed with the idea of buying Epic, to keep Fortnite from inspiring other game developers to abandon ship.



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Epic's Rebuttal Of Google's Leaked Email Summary

Pressed with the suggestion that the email Epic accused Google of leaking showed Epic was itself interested in a special deal, Tim Sweeney attacked the premise of the characterisation: Google did not leak the email, he said — it leaked "their ridiculously biased summary of it" to Abner Li at 9to5Google.

He supported the leak claim with trial testimony: Don Harrison testified that he didn't think Google leaked to the press, and was then presented with a document including Google's press team and Sameer Samat, head of all Android, summarising the articles that appeared as a result of Google's leaking of Epic's plans to the press. On the substance of the email, Sweeney said it is in evidence and is the same one he had already described: right before Christmas-ish 2019, with the new Marvel season and a lineup of Star Wars content planned, he asked Google's executives to let Fortnite come to the Google Play Store using Epic's own payment method and to open up the use of their own payment methods to all developers, not just Epic. The interviewer conceded the point, saying he had read that email in court and had not realised it was the same one, because it was so far off from what he had heard described as a "special billing exception."



---


# Epic's Refusal Of Special Deals And Its 2019 Google Proposal

Asked whether he would have sued at all had Google offered 0 percent for Epic's own payments system or 4 percent for Google Play billing instead of a $147 million deal, Tim Sweeney answered no — Epic has always turned down special deals just for Epic, fighting on the principle that all developers should be given the same opportunities.

His grounds were a document in evidence: a 2019 email he sent to all of Google's senior executives, right before Fortnite launched the Marvel season and the Star Wars event featuring J.J. Abrams, saying Epic wanted to bring Fortnite to the Google Play Store in time for that event and wanted Google to allow Epic and all other developers to process certain payments and keep them all. Had Google said yes, Sweeney argued, it would have been awesome for all developers, the Android ecosystem would have become much stronger, and Google would be in a better position in the smartphone industry today; there would never have been a dispute because the problem would have been solved. The warrant tying this to the present is his claim that the fix has always been within Google's reach: Google makes several billion dollars a year in what he calls unfairly earned profits from imposing this tax, which is nothing compared to what it makes from search, and given all the other benefits it gets from Android, "Google could solve this problem today if they wanted to."



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Simple Versus Complicated: Assessing The Opening Arguments

The claim after day one is that Epic's chances look better than they should, because the case may come down to simplicity: Google spent most of its first day attempting to explain complicated ins and outs of business, while Epic was able to paint a black-and-white picture of good and evil with itself as the clear underdog.

The starting expectation ran the other way. Walking into the courtroom on Monday morning it seemed impossible — if Epic could not prove Apple's walled iOS garden is a monopoly, how could the comparatively open Google do worse against the windmill-tilting Fortnite developer? The warrant that reverses that expectation is about jury persuasion rather than legal merit: a clearer picture beats a more accurate but more complicated one.

Things got complicated for both parties when the first two witnesses — Epic Games Store head Steve Allison and Yoga Buddhi CEO Benjamin Simon, who also appeared in the earlier Epic v. Apple trial — took the stand. Both Epic and Google spent a long, long time on subtle lines of questioning: you really had to read between the lines to see that Epic was trying to make a point about how Google's 70/30 revenue split is probably based on an arbitrary decision Valve made two decades ago with Steam, or that Google was trying to make the point that Epic, too, likely believed an app store provides more value than just payment processing and maybe deserves more money.

# Playoff And Roster Stakes In Bears-Vikings On Monday Night

Heading into Week 13 on Nov. 27, 2023, the game was the difference between the No. 6 and No. 7 seed for the Vikings, with larger ramifications: a loss would leave the Packers, Rams and Saints trailing Minnesota by only a half-game in the wild-card race, while a win would keep the Vikings well within striking distance in the NFC North. After the 12-10 loss Minnesota (6-6) dropped to the No. 7 seed in the NFC with those three teams a half-game back; a win would have put the Vikings in position to compete for the division crown down the stretch, but merely holding a playoff spot would now be a battle for Kevin O'Connell's squad. Chicago's own hopes remained extraordinarily distant at 4-8.

The individual stakes centred on Justin Fields. Sporting News called the final six games critically important for a quarterback fighting to prove he is the Bears' franchise passer, and noted Chicago had a strong chance of landing the No. 1 overall pick in April's draft thanks to the Panthers' ugly season. On the night Fields flashed the good and the bad — excellent on Chicago's opening drive, though it ended without points, then undone by missed throws and costly turnovers that let the Vikings hang around — but when it mattered most he was poised and sealed the Bears' first win over an NFC North opponent since 2021. The Bears entered the night holding the No. 1 and No. 4 picks in the 2024 NFL Draft and would remain in those slots with or without a loss, thanks to the strength-of-schedule tiebreaker.

Availability shaped both sides. The Vikings were officially without Justin Jefferson, holding out their star receiver until they returned from their bye in Week 14, as Adam Schefter reported that day; D'Onta Foreman remained out for the Bears along with cornerback Tyrique Stevenson. Dobbs came in having shown good command of the Vikings' offense in three games since a trade out of Arizona, with an especially strong connection with T.J. Hockenson. Conditions were 15 degrees in Minnesota with a feels-like of 2, making the roof at U.S. Bank Stadium useful, and Vikings legend Adrian Peterson was in the building to watch his former team.



---


# Bears-Vikings Monday Night Broadcast Details

Chicago Bears vs. Minnesota Vikings kicked off at 8:15 p.m. ET (7:15 p.m. local time) on Monday, Nov. 27, 2023 from U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis, Minn., televised on ESPN, which has long held the broadcast rights to Monday Night Football. Joe Buck led the broadcast as play-by-play announcer with Troy Aikman as color analyst and Lisa Salters providing updates from the sidelines.

Streaming was available via ESPN+ or Fubo, which offers a free trial, with viewers in Canada able to stream every NFL game via DAZN.

The series history favored the home side: the Bears had not beaten the Vikings since 2020, with Minnesota 6-1 against Chicago over the previous four seasons, and the Vikings were 8-3 at home in the fixture since 2012.



---


# Bears 12, Vikings 10 On Monday Night Football

Chicago beat Minnesota 12-10 on Monday Night Football on Nov. 27, 2023, by quarters of Bears 0-3-3-6 and Vikings 0-3-0-7, ending what Sporting News called the honeymoon period for Joshua Dobbs in Minnesota. The folk-hero quarterback threw four interceptions, leading a sluggish offense that did not find its footing until the fourth quarter in a game Minnesota would not have needed many points to win.

The Bears' defense swarmed Dobbs all night, sacking him only twice but generating a great deal of pressure as the defensive backs made plays. Despite the barrage of turnovers, Chicago largely failed to capitalize, scoring only three points off the four Dobbs interceptions.

Chicago's own first turnover — a deflating fumble by Justin Fields when the Bears had a chance to extend their lead to two possessions — was quickly turned into a Vikings touchdown. That score looked like it might be the difference, particularly after Fields fumbled away the ball again on the next possession, but the Bears' defense put the ball back in his hands in the final minutes and Fields delivered. Facing 3rd & 10 outside field goal range, he hit an open D.J. Moore for a 36-yard gain; from there Chicago only had to kneel and let Cairo Santos, who drilled the 30-yard attempt with 10 seconds remaining, seal it.



---


# The Third Quarter Of Bears 12, Vikings 10

Chicago led 6-3 at the end of the third quarter on Nov. 27, 2023, having added a field goal while Minnesota gave the ball away again. Alexander Mattison, who had drawn the ire of Vikings fans all season, started the second half with a booming 21-yard run, but the Bears answered immediately by sacking Dobbs with Montez Sweat and Jaquan Brisker taking him down. Kevin O'Connell then went for it on 4th & 7 and Hockenson gained only six; the play looked good but the Bears' defense looked better, and Chicago took over with favorable field position.

The Bears converted that into points, though not efficiently. Roschon Johnson, impressive in spurts, picked up a first down to keep the drive alive, Fields ran up the middle for another, and then a questionable third-down call had Fields throw behind the line of scrimmage to D.J. Moore for nothing — leaving Cairo Santos to extend the lead with a field goal at 9:58 p.m. for Bears 6, Vikings 3.

Minnesota's running game worked and its passing game did not: Mattison had 19 yards three plays into the next drive. A hold by Jaylon Johnson gifted the Vikings a first down, but they still could not capitalize, with Ty Chandler unable to make T.J. Edwards miss on third down, sending Minnesota to a fourth-down attempt. At 10:08 p.m. Dobbs threw his third interception of the night, deflected by Jaylon Johnson and caught by Edwards — leaving the Bears, interestingly, with less favorable field position than an incompletion would have given them. Chicago then started to look respectable on third down again, completing to Moore to move deeper into Vikings territory, though it might still need another first down to give Santos a fair shot.



---


# The Fourth Quarter Of Bears 12, Vikings 10

The fourth quarter on Nov. 27, 2023 produced the game's only touchdown, two Justin Fields fumbles and a Cairo Santos field goal that won it 12-10 for Chicago. Late in the third-to-fourth quarter transition Byron Murphy broke up a Fields third-down pass and Santos — who had already missed from 48 that night — drilled a 55-yarder to make it Bears 9, Vikings 3.

Minnesota's offense kept turning the ball over. # Winning Too Soon And Coaching Regime Expectations

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that a bad team winning right away can be counterproductive, because early success resets expectations for fans and ownership and makes it less practical to take one step backward in the short term for a better shot at taking two steps forward down the line.

The test cases are the New York Giants and Minnesota Vikings, both of which exceeded expectations under first-year head coaches in 2022 and reached the playoffs, and both of which were struggling in their second seasons and facing difficult questions about the future. The grounds are that every head coach and general manager wants to win as much as possible, but the goal is to build for the long term, which can require time to do things with sustainability in mind — so whether early success helps or hurts could depend on how well the football leadership has communicated with ownership.

A veteran coach with experience on a half-dozen teams supplied the warrant from inside the building: "The best first year can be that 7-10 season where you show some promise. The Giants won a bunch of games early, people were heaping praise on the head coach, people get the expectation of what the quarterback can be. But oftentimes, you know different internally because you know the house you are living in. You are inside the walls every single day and you know where the roof leaks, where the foundation is cracked." Buffalo is offered as the managed version of the same situation: the Bills surprisingly reached the playoffs in their first season under Sean McDermott, a euphoric moment after a 17-year playoff drought, went 6-10 the next year, then began a steady rise behind Josh Allen and a top defense — but there isn't a Josh Allen on the Giants or Vikings. Minnesota in particular is in an interesting spot, with Kirk Cousins approaching free agency and playing well enough, most likely, to keep the Vikings from climbing too high in the draft order. "They already gave a contract to (tight end) T.J. Hockenson, and they are going to give one to (receiver) Justin Jefferson," an exec said. "Now, what? Are you going into the rookie pool and taking the fourth-best quarterback in the draft? You can look like Atlanta with (Desmond) Ridder pretty quick."

Denver turned an eight-point fourth-quarter deficit into a 21-20 win on Nov. 19, 2023, on a late Russell Wilson drive finished by Courtland Sutton. Wonnum sacked Wilson on the next third down, bringing on Will Lutz, who buried his fourth field goal of the day from 37 yards, going a perfect 4-for-4 to account for all of Denver's points, for Vikings 17, Broncos 12.

At 10:38 p.m. LB Josey Jewell brought pressure, Joshua Dobbs was hit as he threw and Broncos CB Ja'Quan McMillan intercepted, returning it nine yards, and Denver took over at the Vikings' 9-yard line. A 15-yard facemask penalty on Broncos WR Marvin Mims Jr. backed the offense up and the Vikings' defense held, so Lutz kicked again — a 28-yarder, his fifth make of the day, his side's lone source of offense, bringing Denver within one score at Vikings 17, Broncos 15 with 10:37 to play.

Minnesota answered with a long clock-eating drive kept alive by two gambles. What looked like a three-and-out was rescued by a fake punt on a gutsy call from head coach Kevin O'Connell, with Ty Chandler picking up 31 yards into Denver territory. Chandler then made a big gain on 3rd & 20 that appeared to be a first down; the spot was reviewed and overturned, ruling him just short and setting up 4th & inches, on which the Vikings went for it and Dobbs converted on a QB sneak. qid: Does the article from 'The Age' about Tyler Mitchell suggest that his career has been successful due to his early photography experiences, while the article from 'The Roar | Sports Writers Blog' about Graham Arnold indicates that his career choices involved staying with the Australian national team despite offers from Europe?

# Graham Arnold Socceroos Coaching Appearance Record

Graham Arnold would prowl the technical area for a 59th time on the Thursday, taking him clear of Frank Farina as the Socceroos' record-holder for matches coached, in a match against Bangladesh as 2026 World Cup qualifying started, The Roar reported on Nov. 13, 2023.

On the Tuesday, Football Australia CEO James Johnson, who had held firm on Arnold 20 months earlier, congratulated the coach on the impending record-breaking match. In a remarkable few weeks the previous year Arnold had gone from on the nose to a man revived; since then he had been linked to club jobs in Europe but opted to stick with the national team. Arnold, in his second stint as national team manager, also represented the Socceroos 56 times as a player and has been involved in national team coaching ranks since 2000, first as an assistant to Farina and then Guus Hiddink, before a brief period as caretaker coach in 2006. "It's certainly a proud moment and an achievement that I'll reflect on when the time is right," Arnold said. "I look at some of the names on that list – Farina, Arok, Thompson, Rasic – guys I played under or assisted in the early part of my coaching career, and it gives you some perspective on what a journey it's been so far."



---


# Tyler Mitchell On His Career Trajectory And Artistic Outlook

Interviewed by The Age ahead of the NGV Triennial and published on 27 November 2023, Mitchell says early success does not unsettle him — "The idea of the road ahead only excites me" — and that he deliberately allows himself space for quiet periods and for work that does not come off.

He traces his choice of medium to impatience: "I was impatient when I got started and just wanted to make visual things now, and I didn't want to wait for permission, or didn't want to wait on equipment, or didn't want to lug large amounts of equipment up flights of stairs. I just wanted to make something that I felt compelled by, immediately." His career has only blossomed in the years since the trip that started him in photography, and where some artists might feel trepidation at so much success so early, he is clear-eyed about the rhythm of a long career: there will be "very quiet, sleepy periods, and frenetic periods, or hyperactive periods", and it is "always refreshing as a young person to see how the career of a much older, more senior artist has really gone" — senior artists we know and love today "had decades where they were out of style, out of fashion, people thought their work was done, their best work was behind them, and yet, often had resurgences".

Crafting a career, he says, means "allowing space for bad and good, allowing space for artists to make and work through complicated and sometimes not-so-favourable ideas. And I try to give myself that same space. It's only about giving yourself grace and space and thinking one day at a time." Asked about a dream project or collaborator, he says there are too many; with one monograph behind him — 2020's I Can Make You Feel Good — he is hungry to make more.



---


# Graham Arnold Reflections On Coaching Development

Reflecting on his milestone, Graham Arnold said his 2006 caretaker period taught him a great deal about coaching and that, on reflection, he probably was not ready for it — as quoted by The Roar on Nov. 13, 2023.

"I think back to that caretaker period and how much I learnt about coaching; it was a challenging experience and one that on reflection I probably wasn't ready for. I'm grateful for the opportunity I was given and what it was able to teach me ahead of my pathway into club coaching," he said. "I was able to put lessons from that time into practice, develop and eventually return to the Socceroos much more prepared for the role. It's been a privilege to be part of the national team again with the benefit of that experience, and I'm immensely proud of what this group has been able to achieve in the last four years. In my opinion, there's no greater honour than representing your nation on the international stage. I look at the young players coming through the Socceroos system now full of pride in the work they've put in to get where they are, and the journey that's ahead of them. I've always loved being a part of the Socceroos culture and my desire to see Australia fulfil its footballing potential is still driving me to take this group to further success."



---


# James Johnson Tribute To Graham Arnold

Football Australia CEO James Johnson paid tribute to Graham Arnold in a statement marking the coach's milestone, calling him one of the greatest contributors to the Socceroos, as reported by The Roar on Nov. 13, 2023.

"Graham is one of the greatest contributors to the Socceroos," Johnson said. "He's been a constant in the Australian football landscape for more than 30 years as both a player and coach, being a part of some of the Socceroos most memorable moments. Anyone who knows Arnie will tell you he bleeds green and gold. His love for the Socceroos and football in Australia is both infectious and inspiring. That energy and passion is a huge element to the way he's able to lead and inspire our nation's best male footballers in some of our sport's most challenging arenas. On behalf of Football Australia, I'd like to congratulate Arnie on everything he's achieved in reaching this milestone and we look forward to him continuing to build on what is already an exceptional legacy."



---


# Graham Arnold 2022 World Cup Qualification Crisis

In March 2022 Graham Arnold seemed a dead man walking — the Socceroos' World Cup qualification campaign was lurching towards failure and the manager was being battered from all sides, The Roar recounted on Nov. 13, 2023.

Arnold's team had finished seven points off automatic qualification for Qatar after a shocking run of one win in seven games, leaving them facing an Asian playoff against the United Arab Emirates and then another against Peru to make the finals. While rumours swirled and ex-players and fans bayed for his blood, Football Australia took the pragmatic course and stuck by Arnold — a decision that likely had more to do with the lateness of the hour and financial considerations than any overwhelming faith in Arnie to turn around the fortunes. But he did just that, with qualification and an excellent run at the finals, bowing out to eventual champions Argentina after nearly taking them to extra time. He also got to answer critics like Mark Bosnich and Craig Foster, bluntly rejecting their negativity with a dismissive "who cares?" — which would have tasted sweet.



---


# Tyler Mitchell's Case For Lightly Staged Black Leisure Photography

Speaking to The Age in New York before the NGV Triennial and published on 27 November 2023, Tyler Mitchell argues that photography should not merely record how things are but imagine new realities — his "lightly staged" scenes of Black families at leisure are a deliberate challenge to the "visual regimes" that photojournalism reinforces.

His grounds are both art-historical and political. "I think that I am part of a longer lineage of black artists who have considered how they respond to the Western historical art canon, but also it's 2023, and it's a new day and I think beyond just responding to that canon, we're trying to use the limited language of pictures to try and imagine what personal and unencumbered freedom looks like for young black men and women today," he says. In one of his favourite works, A Glint of Possibility, a teenage boy hangs over a river on a tyre swing studying his own reflection — pensive and peaceful at once, relatable to anyone who has ever been a child on a tyre swing on a hot summer day, yet speaking to the turmoil and tension inherent in the experience of Black American teenage boys, whose lives can be destroyed or irrevocably altered even while doing unremarkable things such as walking home, playing in the park or talking to their crush. His work exists in the tension between what is possible and how things are; he describes it as "a consideration of joy, perseverance and self-determination against the backdrop of history". The Triennial's theme, "Magic, Matter, Memory", makes his pieces a logical inclusion: "A lot of my work meditates on being between a heightened reality, or potentially even a magical reality and an actual reality."

The warrant joining method to claim is his account of staging: "I'm creating what I call lightly staged moments… I'm setting up scenarios where these families are enjoying real moments of leisure in outdoor spaces, usually open pastures and fields, and those moments are meant to stand in for a meditation on what it means to enjoy leisurely outdoor nature as a black person." The context he names is the pandemic and the rise of the Black Lives Matter movement in the summer of 2020, when Black artists and activists sought to reframe a public debate about Black life and force new perspectives of peace, luxury and safety into the picture. He wants to challenge assumptions about certain people or cultures that are reinforced over and over: "I think that [photojournalism] is a well from which we all culturally – consciously or unconsciously – construct ideas of how people live around the world. My work is really about responding to, and questioning, and challenging those ideas." As a 20-year-old film student at New York University he became enamoured with still photography after signing up to a documentary photography course in Havana, Cuba, drawn to its accessibility after being frustrated by the time and money films required.



---


# Tyler Mitchell's Vogue Covers And NGV Triennial Works

Tyler Mitchell was just 23 when he became the first Black photographer to shoot the cover of American Vogue, photographing Beyoncé, and in November 2023 three of his works were on show in the NGV's Triennial exhibition, The Age reported on 27 November 2023.

His dreamy, delicately hued Beyoncé portraits spoke of a precocious visual talent, and in the five years since he has exhibited around the world, become an Instagram darling with more than 500,000 followers, and shot what became the most controversial vice-presidential portrait in living memory. When his portrait of Kamala Harris dressed in sneakers and casual clothing was chosen for the cover of Vogue for February 2021, the social media backlash was swift: critics questioned why his alternative image — in which Harris looked more vice-presidential — had not been used instead, and the magazine, bowing to outrage over the perceived lack of respect shown to the first woman to reach such high office, later issued a limited edition using the more formal shot. The controversy did little to dent the New York-based photographer's reputation as a rising star of the medium.

Of the three Triennial works, Picnic depicts a family gathering — young men throwing a football, a child lifted on shoulders, wicker baskets and a thermos, and in the background a darkened wood that perhaps hints at the fragility of a moment so peaceful and pure. In the others his figures are arranged across a sandy expanse in idealised depictions of Black American leisure: in Albany, Georgia a football flies through the air, a father in dress shirt and tails twirls a child, and a young boy rides a toy truck; Vastness focuses on a teenage boy standing patiently as his younger siblings stretch his wildly elongated sleeves out beside him, with a dog nearby sitting listening to a violinist. These carefully staged set-ups are evidence of Mitchell's desire to establish a new visual narrative for Black Americans.



---


# Paul Mitchell's Recruitment Career Record

Paul Mitchell is one of football's most respected executives, a recruitment specialist who has held head-of-recruitment or sporting-director roles at MK Dons, Southampton, Tottenham, RB Leipzig and Monaco, and who recently left the principality of Monaco — where he could well return for meetings with Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who is planning to appoint a sporting director, talkSPORT reported on 16 October 2023.

What distinguishes Mitchell is a scouting net cast far and wide and an eye for players before they are established. A former player in England's lower leagues, starring mainly for Wigan and MK Dons, he was moved upstairs at MK Dons and made his first big move by spotting future England regular Dele Alli after being named their head of recruitment in 2010. Two years later he joined Southampton in the same role, where Sadio Mane, Dusan Tadic, Graziano Pelle, Dejan Lovren and Victor Wanyama all went on to secure the Saints a bright future, make the club a fortune, become Champions League regulars and deliver a Premier League best finish — earning Mitchell a promotion to Tottenham in 2014. The north London side had just unsuccessfully splurged their world-record £85million from Real Madrid for Gareth Bale, so it looked like he could not have picked a worse time; yet Alli, Heung-Min Son, Toby Alderweireld, Eric Dier and Kieran Trippier set the side up for a bright future.

The boundary case in his record is Tottenham's boardroom. Mitchell left what he called his "dream job" after less than two years, reportedly due to chairman Daniel Levy's over-involvement in negotiations and the recruitment process — something that was not an issue at his next club, Leipzig, where Ralf Rangnick landed him and signings such as Dani Olmo, Christopher Nkunku and Amadou Haidara showed what he can do with the shackles off. Many of those signings starred in a run to the Champions League semi-finals in 2020, and in 2022 the club won its first ever trophy with a DFB Pokal. He left only to reach the pinnacle of his job, finally stepping up from head of recruitment to sporting director at Monaco. He was previously linked with Chelsea and Liverpool and, much like Ratcliffe, is from Greater Manchester; he remains good friends with Rangnick from their time together at Leipzig and last season made headlines when he was spotted at a youth team game while the German was interim coach at Man United.

# Mitchell Edwards AFL Draft Prospect 2023

Mitchell Edwards, profiled in Kevin Sheehan's top 40 for the 2023 AFL Draft as reported by The Roar on Nov. 15, 2023, is an exciting ruckman still growing into his body. State: Western Australia. # Paul Mitchell's Long-Term Recruitment Philosophy

Paul Mitchell argues that recruitment should be judged over the long term rather than by immediate returns, because young signings need time to settle and a player's prior record is better evidence than the narrative that forms around him in his first season — a case talkSPORT set out on 16 October 2023 using Heung-Min Son.

The grounds are Mitchell's own record and his stated standard. Having worked in football management for over a decade, his career has always been about the long term for his clubs, with the young signings he has made often only paying off after he has left. He frames the job as continuous improvement across the whole operation: "I want to continue to drive standards in each and every department. Psychology, sports science, nutrition, medicine, the way we travel, the way we refuel," he said, adding that "everything, every element I think we need to keep pushing to its maximum to try and be the best we possibly can."

The warrant joining evidence to claim is the Son case, which perfectly sums up his philosophy. "I took quite a lot of criticism in my first year at Tottenham for some of the decisions and Sonny was kind of at the centre of that," he explained. "Sometimes players need time, they're human beings, they need to settle, Sonny had a great track record at Hamburg and Leverkusen but there was this narrative that started to grow internally and externally that he wasn't a good finisher." # Andrew Redmayne Substitution In Peru Playoff

Graham Arnold's record-breaking achievement is conceivably down to one big ballsy call in the playoff against Peru, The Roar wrote on Nov. 13, 2023: with moments left in extra time against the South Americans, Arnold dragged Mat Ryan and replaced him with Andrew Redmayne, who saved the decisive spot kick — and also threw his opponent's water bottle, with cheat sheet attached, away from the goal.

Vincent Namatjira, 40 at the time of The Guardian's 16 October 2023 interview, has won some of Australia's most high-profile art prizes: the Ramsay art prize in 2019 for a Cook-inspired work, the Archibald prize in 2020 for his portrait of the AFL footballer Adam Goodes, and an Order of Australia medal.
