# Schumer's AI Insight Forum On Creative Copyright

On Wednesday November 29, 2023, US Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer held an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Insight Forum to discuss the importance and role of creative copyright and intellectual property in the development of AI — a sign that senior political figures in Washington are becoming increasingly interested in the impact of AI on the law.

Dennis Kooker, Sony Music Entertainment's President of Global Digital Business & US Sales, delivered a speech at the Forum outlining the major music company's position on AI and copyright law.



---


# YouTube's AI Music Incubator And Its Rightsholder Pledges

During its period of discussions with the majors, YouTube made a series of announcements aimed at the biggest issue for any rightsholder regarding AI-driven voice replication of artists: their ability to police it.

In August, YouTube and Universal Music Group jointly announced that the video platform was launching an "AI Music Incubator" — a program by which new tools and innovations would be developed at YouTube in close conjunction with artists and the music business; to progress the incubator, YouTube said it was working behind the scenes with a number of UMG-affiliated artists. Also in August, YouTube publicly committed to three principles or pledges behind its development of music-based generative AI tools. These pledges promised "appropriate protections… for music partners who decide to participate" in such tools, and promised "invest[ment] in the AI-powered technology" that, among other things, would help YouTube "protect our community of viewers, creators, artists and songwriters… [from] trademark and copyright abuse" — all of which seemed to hint at a desire to build a "Content ID"-style system on YouTube to control and police content made by cloning artists' voices. Then, earlier in November, YouTube announced it was developing a specific system for music partners allowing them to request the removal of content on its platform that "mimics an artist's unique singing or rapping voice."



---


# Broadcom Q4 Earnings Preview and VMware Integration

Broadcom (AVGO) was set to announce its Q4 results after Thursday's closing bell in the week following Seeking Alpha's December 3, 2023 preview, going in with shares up more than 67% for the year on the AI wave, a Buy consensus among sell-side analysts, and a Seeking Alpha Quant Rating that had transitioned to Strong Buy from Hold in mid-November.

The California-based semiconductor company's share gain far outpaced the broader market, which the preview read as underscoring its robust position and resilience in the then-current economic climate. Consensus estimates for the quarter were EPS of $10.96 and revenue of $9.28B, against an Earnings Insight record of beating both EPS and revenue estimates in eight consecutive quarters.

Two VMware developments framed the print. On the Friday before the preview, Broadcom announced plans to let go of 1,300 California-based VMware employees following the completion of its multi-billion-dollar acquisition of VMware on November 22 — a step in a $61B cash-and-stock diversification strategy moving the company from semiconductors toward the cloud. On the Wednesday before, a report surfaced that Broadcom was evaluating strategic alternatives for VMware's End-User Computing and Carbon Black cybersecurity units; that is a reported evaluation, not an announced divestiture.

Seeking Alpha author Mike Zaccardi supplied the bull case, contending that Broadcom offers tech and AI exposure at a lower price, with a strong semiconductor product portfolio and solid technical background, and that its earnings beat history, strong expense control and robust profitability make it an attractive investment. The same section of the week-ahead lists other companies reporting alongside Broadcom, including Lululemon Athletica (LULU), Dollar General Corporation (DG), Ciena Corporation (CIEN), Smartsheet (SMAR), Vail Resorts (MTN), Planet Labs PBC (PL), Guidewire Software (GWRE), The Cooper Companies (COO), HashiCorp (HCP), Lakeland Industries (LAKE), Greif (GEF), Liquidity Services (LQDT), GMS (GMS), Methode Electronics (MEI), Hooker Furnishings Corporation (HOFT), DLH Holdings (DLHC) and SecureWorks (SCWX), among others.



---


# The US Copyright Office's 2023 Study Of AI And Copyright

The US Copyright Office is spearheading one of the key US efforts to address AI and copyright: in the summer of 2023 it issued a call for submissions on the issue of AI and copyright, with the goal of putting together a study to "help assess whether legislative or regulatory steps in this area are warranted."

The call for submissions came as legislators and regulators around the world grappled with the many issues that had emerged since AI technology "went mainstream" about a year earlier. Numerous businesses involved in AI, and those with substantial copyright holdings, submitted their thoughts on the issue — including Universal Music Group and AI developer Anthropic.



---


# GPTs: OpenAI's Custom Chatbots And The Dev Day Announcements

GPTs are OpenAI's tool for building custom conversational, action-taking AI systems powered by OpenAI's models, including the models underpinning ChatGPT. They were announced at OpenAI's first-ever developer conference, held Monday, November 6, 2023, where the Microsoft-backed AI startup announced a host of new products — the more notable being tools to create custom "GPTs" (that is, domain-specific chatbots), new text-to-speech models, an API for the text-to-image model DALL-E 3, and an improved version of OpenAI's flagship model GPT-4, called GPT-4 Turbo.

What distinguishes a GPT from a prompt is that the knowledge is built in. With GPTs, a user can train a model on a cookbook collection, for example, so that it can answer questions about ingredients for a specific recipe; or they can give a model their company's proprietary codebases so that developers can check their style or generate code in line with best practices. Some of the initial GPTs, all created by OpenAI, include a Gen Z meme translator, a coloring book and sticker creator, a data visualizer, a board game explainer and a creative writing coach. ChatGPT can accomplish these tasks given carefully engineered prompts and foreknowledge, but purpose-built GPTs drastically simplify things — and might just kill the cottage industry that emerged around creating and editing prompts to feed to ChatGPT.

The consequence TechCrunch draws for ChatGPT itself is a change of role: with GPTs, ChatGPT could become more a gateway to a broader ecosystem of AI-powered chatbots than the end-all-be-all. GPTs introduce a level of personalization far beyond that ChatGPT offers today, and — once OpenAI sorts out its capacity issues — TechCrunch expects an explosion of creativity there. Will ChatGPT be as visible as it once was after GPTs flood the marketplace? Perhaps not; but it will not go away, it will simply adapt and evolve, no doubt in ways not even its creators can anticipate.



---


# DeepMind's Sale To Google And Facebook's AI Lab

Google offered $US650 million for DeepMind. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook offered a bigger payout to DeepMind's founders but would not agree to the conditions the founders had set, and DeepMind sold to Google.

Zuckerberg was determined to build an AI lab of his own and hired Yann LeCun, a French computer scientist who had also done pioneering AI research, to run it. A year after Hinton's auction, Zuckerberg and LeCun flew to Lake Tahoe for the same AI conference, and while padding around a suite at the Harrah's casino in his socks Zuckerberg personally interviewed top researchers, who were soon offered millions of dollars in salary and stock. AI was once laughed off; now the richest men in Silicon Valley were shelling out billions to keep from being left behind.

# Travis Kelce Invites Taylor Swift To Arrowhead

On 21 September 2023 Travis Kelce announced on The Pat McAfee Show that he had invited Taylor Swift to watch one of his games, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

He described the invitation in his own words: "I told her, 'I've seen you rock the stage in Arrowhead, you might have to come see me rock a stage at Arrowhead and we can see which one's a little more lit.' We'll see what happens in the near future."

The timeline then moves to the fated sighting of Swift at Arrowhead Stadium on the Monday, cheering on No. 87 with gusto.



---


# Taylor Swift's Arrowhead Appearance And Its Easter Eggs

At Arrowhead Stadium, the 12-time Grammy winner appeared to shout "let's f—ing go" after Travis Kelce scored a touchdown before chest-bumping other Chiefs fans, and fans then found a string of apparent Easter eggs around the visit, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

Because Swift is known for being an Eagles fan — she is originally from Pennsylvania and even references the team in Gold Rush — her outward support for Kelce's team seemed extra telling. Swifties were immediately on high alert, with some capturing Swift and Kelce leaving the stadium together. Extra observant fans noted that Kelce's blue and white post-game outfit was supposedly labelled the "1989 bedroom painting set", perhaps an intentional reference to Swift's 2014 album, which she was due to re-release in October; the paper suggests Swift's penchant for Easter eggs must be rubbing off on the tight end. They were also spotted in a "getaway car" together outside the stadium, potentially a nod to her 2017 track.

None of this actually confirms Swift and Kelce are dating, the piece notes. But regardless of whether it is a friendship or a romantic relationship, it has sent shockwaves through two massive cultural franchises, expanding the NFL's audience into uncharted territory — a cultural pairing on par with, and perhaps even bigger than, Kim Kardashian and Kanye West.



---


# Taylor Swift's Arrowhead Stadium Appearance, September 2023

Two days after Travis Kelce's 22 September 2023 charity event, the "All Too Well" singer was spotted cheering for the Kansas City Chiefs tight end from the box seats at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri, sitting next to Kelce's mother Donna and appearing to yell "let's f***ing go" in response to Kelce's third-quarter touchdown reception.

The Chiefs beat the Chicago Bears 41-10. After the game, Kelce was seen leaving the stadium in a blue and white splatter-paint denim suit, and eagle-eyed fans were quick to believe the outfit paid homage to Swift's forthcoming album 1989 (Taylor's Version), due for re-release on 27 October. According to photos and videos posted online, the two escaped the crowd at Arrowhead in Kelce's convertible, and the football star reportedly rented out Prime Social Rooftop in Kansas City for a post-game celebration with his family, his teammates and Swift.

A witness described the party to Entertainment Tonight: "Travis bought out the restaurant for his family and team. Taylor arrived, wearing a denim dress, and was seen snacking, having some cocktails and dancing alongside Travis. The two were very affectionate with one another but kept things fun and lighthearted. Travis' teammates also showed up to the after-party, as well as his mom, Donna Kelce. The party lasted until 2 am."



---


# Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift Dating Rumours in 2023

Speculation that Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift were dating began in July 2023, when Kelce confessed that he had tried and failed to give Swift a friendship bracelet bearing his phone number at one of her Eras Tour concerts; he later invited her on his podcast to one of his games at Arrowhead Stadium, an invitation she famously accepted on 24 September 2023, and she had attended three more of his games by 25 November 2023.

Kelce first told the bracelet story to his brother on their podcast back in July. "I was disappointed that she doesn't talk before or after her shows, because she has to save her voice for the 44 songs that she sings," he explained. "So I was a little butthurt I didn't get to hand her one of the bracelets I made for her. If you're up on Taylor Swift concerts, there are friendship bracelets and I received a bunch of them being there, but I wanted to give Taylor Swift one with my number on it."

The NFL star officially addressed the dating rumours during an episode of The Pat McAfee Show on 21 September 2023, in which he mocked his brother Jason Kelce for joking that he "100 per cent" believed his younger sibling was dating Swift. "It's hilarious how much traction this has actually gotten, right now it's like a game of telephone," Kelce said. "Where everybody's whispering in each other's ears and hearing random stuff. No one actually knows what's going on, especially when you got Jason Kelce on live television telling people just both sides - he doesn't know, it's true, this and that." He also said he remained open to pursuing a relationship with Swift, revealing that he had subtly asked whether she would attend one of his games: "I threw it out there, I threw the ball in her court. I told her, you know, I've seen you rock the stage in Arrowhead [Stadium], you might have to come see me rock the stage in Arrowhead and see which one's a little more lit. So, we'll see what happens in the near future."



---


# Travis Kelce's Moustache Remark And New York Visit

In August 2023 Travis Kelce hinted on the New Heights podcast that Taylor Swift would like his moustache — a clear suggestion he had made contact with her — and shortly afterwards took a week off training to visit New York City while Swift was re-recording her 1989 tracks there, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

The brothers were discussing the moustache Kelce grows every year in honour of the Chiefs' head coach, Andy Reid. Asked if he knew what Swift thought of the 'stache, he remained cheekily confident: "We're not going to bring up Taylor Swift in this episode," he says, "But something tells me she's going to like it."

The New York trip was reported by Vulture, and coincidentally happened to be while Swift was re-recording her 1989 tracks in the city.



---


# Taylor Swift's Attendance At Kansas City Chiefs Games

By early December 2023 Taylor Swift had attended five of Travis Kelce's games, including one on 3 December, often seated in the Kelce family suite — and since her first NFL appearance in September her occasional attendance had drawn pushback from NFL fans who believed her presence was distracting from the game itself. Swift told Time she has little sense of how much she is on screen: "There's a camera, like, a half-mile away, and you don't know where it is, and you have no idea when the camera is putting you in the broadcast, so I don't know if I'm being shown 17 times or once." She said she does not pay much attention to the cameras and fans around her because she is watching her boyfriend play.

Her answer to the criticism was direct: "I'm just there to support Travis. I have no awareness of if I'm being shown too much and pissing off a few dads, Brads, and Chads." Asked about the many Swifties who had started watching NFL games since she began dating Kelce, she joked: "Football is awesome, it turns out. I've been missing out my whole life." Her effect on the league was visible in October, when a Chiefs-Jets game she attended with famous friends became the most-watched Sunday NFL show since Super Bowl LVII in February 2023.



---


# Taylor Swift's Subsequent NFL Appearances And SNL Cameo

After her first Chiefs game, Taylor Swift kept appearing at Kansas City fixtures and made a Saturday Night Live cameo with Travis Kelce, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023.

On 1 October she went to her second consecutive Chiefs game, against the Jets — who, the timeline notes, technically play in New Jersey — showing up with famous friends Blake Lively, Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman after a week of reports that she would attend; the Chiefs won 23-20. On 12 October, one day after her movie premiere, Swift was in the house for the Chiefs' "Thursday Night Football" divisional matchup against the Broncos at Arrowhead Stadium, where she has performed herself and attended a game before; according to Al Michaels the game would have minimal Swift coverage, though there had already been a mention of the superstar.

On 15 October the two were spotted out in New York City together and then made a surprise appearance on "Saturday Night Live," with Kelce appearing in a skit about how much coverage Swift was getting during games while the singer introduced the musical act of the night, Ice Spice. On 22 October Swift attended her fifth Chiefs game, having now attended games broadcast across all five networks — CBS, NBC, Fox, ESPN and Amazon — watching the Chiefs face the Chargers on CBS in a Chiefs sweatshirt, seated next to Patrick Mahomes' wife, Brittany.



---


# NFL Broadcasters' Taylor Swift Lyric References

On 17 September 2023 Travis Kelce scored a touchdown against the Jaguars, prompting CBS announcer Ian Eagle to say "Kelce finds a blank space for the score" — a reference to Swift's 2014 hit Blank Space — and NFL Network's Rich Eisen followed with a slew of lyric references in a preshow, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

The suspicion that Swift and Kelce were spending time together in New York was seemingly confirmed in September when it was reported they had been "quietly hanging out" for months — the first, albeit tentative, confirmation from the media rather than from amateur Swiftie sleuths on social media. It was only a matter of time before the story entered the cultural zeitgeist, and it did so very quickly. Eisen's preshow references included "shake it off", "anti-hero" and "all too well", and Kelce acknowledged the tongue-in-cheek banter, commenting on a montage video of the preshow that Eisen posted to Instagram: "Well played Rich … Well played."

Suddenly football fans and Swifties were living through this surprising collision — Swift lyrics were infiltrating NFL game commentary, and her fans were furiously becoming football experts. All that needed to happen, the timeline says, was for Swift herself to infiltrate a game, determining once and for all whether there was anything to the rumours.



---


# The Swifties' Second Video: Operating A CD Player

In a second TikTok video the three young Swifties were captured using the CD player, which proved slightly easier to figure out than the case, FOX News Lifestyle reported on 11 November 2023.

All three girls can be heard "oohing" and "aahing" as they learn how to open the disc player.

"Whoa! That was fancy, guys. This is a fancy one," one of the girls can be heard saying in the TikTok video.



---


# Taylor Swift's Stated Approach To Public Scrutiny

Taylor Swift told Time in December 2023 that she has nothing to hide in her relationship with Travis Kelce, and defined what she means by a public relationship: "When you say a relationship is public, that means I'm going to see him do what he loves, we're showing up for each other, other people are there and we don't care. The opposite of that is you have to go to an extreme amount of effort to make sure no one knows that you're seeing someone. And we're just proud of each other." Although her love life makes headlines with every Kansas City Chiefs game she attends, the "Blank Space" singer said she is focused on being there for her partner rather than on concealing the relationship.

On scrutiny more broadly, the "Anti-Hero" singer said she tries not to let the paparazzi get to her even though so many of her outings with friends become headlines: "Over the years, I've learned I don't have the time or bandwidth to get pressed about things that don't matter. Yes, if I go out to dinner, there's going to be a whole chaotic situation outside the restaurant. But I still want to go to dinner with my friends." She described the change in her perspective over time: "Life is short. Have adventures. Me locking myself away in my house for a lot of years — I'll never get that time back. I'm more trusting now than I was six years ago."



---


# Swift And Kelce's Public Appearances Together

Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce appeared together publicly through the autumn of 2023, at his games, at her concerts, and away from both. On 22 October Swift returned to Arrowhead Stadium to watch the Kansas City Chiefs beat the Los Angeles Chargers — her fourth time attending one of Kelce's games amid ongoing reports that they were dating — and the pair seemingly confirmed the relationship there. Afterwards Chariah Gordon, the partner of Kelce's teammate Mecole Hardman Jr, posted an Instagram picture of Swift standing next to Kelce and reaching to kiss his cheek. Kelce also responded warmly when a fan shouted "Let's go Taylor's boyfriend" while he waited for an elevator, smiling slightly and pumping his fist into the air.

The couple were also photographed together away from stadiums, including a date earlier that month in New York City after their surprise appearances on the season 49 premiere of Saturday Night Live. Sources alleged to Entertainment Tonight that during that date Kelce got too close to Swift's security personnel and told her bodyguard to step aside; on his podcast Kelce explained what he had said and denied pushing anyone: "I placed my hand on the gentleman's back to let him know I was behind him. If I would have pushed him, he probably would have turned around and tased me." Kelce reciprocated the support in November by travelling to Buenos Aires, Argentina, for one of her Eras Tour shows, where Swift changed her "Karma" lyrics to "Karma is the guy on the Chiefs, coming straight home to me," laughing as fans screamed; after the show the "Style" singer was seen running into his arms and kissing him before he whisked her backstage.

# The Swift Effect: How 104 Million Swifties Could Complete The NFL's Revenue Target

Essentially Sports argues on 2023-10-25 that Taylor Swift's fanbase is, in arithmetic terms, exactly the audience the NFL needs to hit its revenue goal. The grounds: most of the 12-time Grammy Awardee's songs are about that warm fuzzy feeling and chemical reaction we call love, and those songs have earned the support of 103.7992 million Swifties in the world — a figure given to four decimal places, showing how much data exists on her. Football has 184 million fans, and the league generates $18 billion in revenue from those 184 million; if it adds 104 million (after rounding 103.7992) to that number, the article computes revenue of $28 billion — and just like that, the target will be met.

The supporting evidence is behavioural rather than purely arithmetical, and the article confronts the critics directly: while analysts like Stephen A. Smith may go around telling people they should be embarrassed for getting so invested in someone else's relationship, it is good business for the NFL. TMZ reported that #87's jersey sales skyrocketed 400% and his Instagram followers by 276%. Yahoo Finance reported a 53% rise in viewership among teen girls — a part of the population nobody would have thought in their wildest dreams the NFL would rope in. The October 1 matchup between the Chiefs and the Jets drew 27 million viewers and became the most-watched Sunday TV show since the last Super Bowl, which itself had an actual concert by Rihanna. An accompanying image credit shows Taylor Swift reacting while sitting next to Donna Kelce, watching the Kansas City Chiefs versus Chicago Bears game during the first half at GEHA Field at Arrowhead Stadium, Kansas City, Missouri.

# Travis Kelce's Criticism That The NFL Overdid Its Taylor Swift Coverage

Travis Kelce agreed on his podcast that the National Football League was overdoing its coverage of his rumoured girlfriend Taylor Swift, undercutting the league's implicit claim that leaning into the story was simply adding to the broadcast. Speaking after his game against the New York Jets on 1 October 2023, the 33-year-old Kansas City Chiefs tight end discussed the broadcast with his brother Jason, 35, on an episode of New Heights with Jason and Travis Kelce titled "The NFL Needs to Calm Down." The two addressed complaints from longtime football enthusiasts frustrated by constant Swift references during the game at MetLife Stadium: the league had promoted the fixture by speculating about whether the Grammy winner would attend, cameras panned constantly to the star-studded suite where Swift sat with Blake Lively, Ryan Reynolds, Sophie Turner and Hugh Jackman, and the NFL ran a special segment in which Carson Daly of The Voice attempted to explain football to "Swifties."

Asked plainly by Jason whether the NFL was overdoing it, Kelce first said "I think everybody is just, like, overwhelmed," and, pressed to set aside his feelings for Swift, hedged: "I think it brings a little more to the atmosphere, it brings a little bit more to what you're watching. But at the same time, I think..." His brother, the Philadelphia Eagles player, finished the thought — "They're overdoing it" — and Kelce agreed: "They're overdoing it a little bit, for sure. Especially my situation. I think they're just trying to have fun with it." Commenters under the New Heights video echoed the complaint: "I agree the NFL needs to calm down. Pissing off football fans is not how you repay your boi [sic] for all he's done for the sport"; "Pity Taylor. All she ever wanted was to watch the football game. Now she's being blamed and hated left and right"; "The NFL needs to seriously tone it down and let Trav and Tay explore this beautiful thing they have going on in peace."

# The Rio Postponement And The Death Of An Eras Tour Fan

A heat wave in Brazil forced Taylor Swift to postpone the second night of her Eras Tour shows in Rio de Janeiro in late 2023. The decision came after one of her fans, 23-year-old Ana Clara Benevides, died from a cardiac arrest during Swift's first performance in the country.

Swift told Time that performing for her fans regardless of circumstance is "part of my identity as a human." She said: "I know I'm going on that stage whether I'm sick, injured, heartbroken, uncomfortable, or stressed. That's part of my identity as a human being now. # Travis Kelce On Dating Taylor Swift In Public

He also acknowledged the intense public attention his private life now attracts, noting he had "never dated anyone with that kind of aura around them" — but said he was not letting the media affect the relationship, and took his cue from how Swift handles it. "But at the same time, I'm not running away from any of it," he said. "The scrutiny she gets, how much she has a magnifying glass on her, every single day, paparazzi outside her house, outside every restaurant she goes to, after every flight she gets off, and she's just living, enjoying life. When she acts like that I better not be the one acting all strange."

# The Taylor Swift And Travis Kelce Romance Overview

Rumours that singer Taylor Swift and Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce were dating ran for weeks and only intensified as Swift attended five Chiefs games during the season, according to CBS Sports' timeline of the rumoured romance published 12 October 2023.

The report gives the pattern of appearances. At the first game she attended the previous month, the Eras Tour singer was seen chatting with the tight end's mother, Donna Kelce, and cheering emphatically when No. 87 scored a touchdown. The week before publication she was in attendance to watch the Chiefs defeat the Denver Broncos in Week 6 on "Thursday Night Football." She was once again at Arrowhead Stadium, this time to watch the Chiefs take on another AFC West opponent, the Los Angeles Chargers.

# Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour Concert Film

"Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour," compiled from several Swift shows at Southern California's SoFi Stadium and directed by Sam Wrench, debuted on Friday, 2023-10-13, with advance ticket sales worldwide already past $100 million and an opening expected to launch at $100 million or possibly more. Movie theaters readied for an onslaught like they had never seen before: Swifties would descend, and dancing would be encouraged. By 2023-11-07 the almost three-hour film was the highest-grossing concert film of all time.

The film exists because the live tour was out of reach for most fans. Swift's camp was motivated to get it out even as her stadium tour continues internationally; the tour, projected by Pollstar to gross some $1.4 billion, crashed Ticketmaster's site, saw sky-high resale mark-ups and left many fans priced out. In July, Pitchfork reported that the average cost of a ticket for the North American leg was $3,801 — a 2,321% increase from her 2018 Reputation Stadium Tour, where the average resale price for North American shows was $157. The movie would be a way for millions more to experience the Eras Tour, offering up-close, intimate access to a show they never would have been able to attend otherwise, with adult tickets sold at $19.89 — a reference to her birth year and 2014 album, a re-recording of which was due out Oct. 27 — higher than the average movie ticket but several thousand less than many tickets to see Swift live, and with no Ticketmaster queue to wait in.

The release broke several theatrical norms. It arrived uncommonly fast, just a little over two months after the SoFi shows; speed was one reason Swift's father, Scott Swift, is said to have sought out a direct deal with AMC. Swift produced the film herself and, with 274 million followers on Instagram, didn't need a studio to promote it. After a premiere in Los Angeles on Wednesday, 2023-10-11, there were no advance screenings until the movie began playing at 6 p.m. local time Friday — where most wide-release movies open with Thursday showings and Friday daytime screenings.

# Concert Tour

## Definition

In the corpus, a concert tour is the live, multi-city, multi-date run of shows an artist performs — such as Taylor Swift's "ongoing 'Eras Tour'" and Beyoncé's "Renaissance" tour — that generates its own ticket revenue and can later be packaged, using footage from those shows, into a companion concert film for theatrical release.

## Context

In the corpus the term names both a live-event undertaking and, increasingly, the commercial engine behind an associated concert film: Taylor Swift's "ongoing 'Eras Tour'" is described as a 151-date stadium tour projected to gross about $1.4 billion, while Beyoncé's "Renaissance" tour is described as a "39-city, 56-show" run that "kicked off in Stockholm, Sweden in May and ended in Kansas City, Missouri in the fall" and made over $500 million while drawing over 2.7 million concertgoers.
Both artists' tours are directly tied to concert films — Swift's "Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour" and Beyoncé's "Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé" — which theatrical distributors built around footage and momentum from the live tour itself, so the tour functions in the corpus as the originating live event that a concert film later packages for wider audiences.
The corpus also frames touring as increasingly inaccessible: "concert tickets are more expensive than ever," with "inflation, Ticketmaster's monopolistic practices, and increased demand after COVID-related touring delays" cited as causes, and tours are described as never having been accessible to everyone because "geography, economics, health and safety concerns, and physical or mental ability" make stadium and arena concerts infeasible for large parts of a fanbase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Multi-city, multi-date structure** — Swift's Eras Tour spans 151 dates and Beyoncé's Renaissance tour spans 39 cities and 56 shows, both crossing international markets.
- **Repeatable show format** — each Eras Tour concert "spans over 180 minutes, with more than 40 songs from at least nine albums and 16 costume changes," performed against a fixed setlist that Swift memorized by "singing the entire set list out loud" during preparation.
- **Major revenue driver** — the Eras Tour is projected to gross roughly $1.4 billion and the Renaissance tour made over $500 million, figures separate from and larger than the box-office receipts of either artist's related concert film.
- **Rising ticket-access barriers** — average North American Eras Tour resale prices reportedly rose to $3,801, a "2,321% increase" over Swift's 2018 Reputation Stadium Tour average of $157, driven by inflation, resale-market dynamics, and pandemic-era touring delays.
- **Physical toll on performers** — Swift described committing to play a show "whether I'm sick, injured, heartbroken, uncomfortable, or stressed" absent "force majeure," and the tour's Rio de Janeiro leg was disrupted by a heat wave following a fan's death during a performance.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a concert tour is generally defined as a series of concerts by an artist or group of artists in different cities, countries, or locations, often named to distinguish one tour from another and to link a particular tour with a specific album or product. # The Timing Trade-Off In Rookie Of The Year Futures Betting

There is a fixed trade-off in when to bet NBA Rookie of the Year futures: the earlier you bet, the better the odds, but you bet without much information that could be key to an educated decision; conversely, if you wait for the data you need for an informed bet, the odds tighten and you see less of a return.

The mechanism is symmetric between bettor and book. When the lines are first released, the season has not started, so there are no statistics, trends or player news — the pre-season odds are so favorable precisely because even the oddsmakers lack the data to craft more specific lines. Once the season starts and you can see how the rookies are performing, you can gather the relevant data; but sportsbooks are gathering the same information and tighten the Rookie of the Year lines in response. So while you can better guess who will hoist the Wilt Chamberlain Trophy, the odds are tighter and your potential return reduced.

Stated as pros and cons: betting early gives an opportunity to find better value and betting odds that are fresh and unadjusted, but carries much higher risk because a player's performance, health and team dynamic can change through the season, and offers limited information. Waiting gives a lot more information for an informed bet and avoids betting on a player not remotely in contention, but reduces the opportunity to find value and the odds may not be as favorable. The range over which this holds is bounded by the individual: it is always important to take your risk tolerance into consideration while weighing the potential rewards, and no matter when you decide to wager, always gather as much information as possible before risking your money.

# How Sportsbooks Set And Move Betting Lines

The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services to set their lines and odds, while other sports betting apps simply copy those lines. The oddsmakers and services use computer models and algorithms that consider analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, matchup data and more to develop the lines and odds. Those lines are then subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that emerges before the game, and a book will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side.

The governing objective is balance rather than prediction. Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet, because that lets the book earn the small profit built into the odds and lines without worrying about which side wins. Sportsbooks want even betting so much that they will move a line or change the odds specifically to draw more bets to the other side.

The relation that matters to a bettor is that books do not all move together. The betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook: one book may be forced to move a line or change the odds because of the money it has taken while another is not, and the lines and odds may even differ right from the jump. That divergence is what creates the chance to book a bet at improved odds or a more favorable line.

The range over which this holds is narrow and specific. When a line moves for a legitimate reason such as an injury or roster move, every sportsbook jumps on board, and it is difficult to find value; when a line moves because of betting patterns, only the sportsbook that saw that betting makes the change, and that is the opportunity. Line shopping is the tool for spotting the second kind: choose a side, shop around at online sportsbooks, compare the lines and odds, and pounce when you find one offering something different and more favorable to your viewpoint.

# Why Moneyline Odds Change

Lines at sports betting apps change quickly for two primary reasons — public betting and new information — and sportsbooks adjust moneyline odds to stay profitable, balance their book and reflect the most current information about an event. Before setting odds oddsmakers gather extensive data, then release the finalized odds to the public; from that point a bettor can bet immediately or wait for shifts, though predicting those shifts is challenging.

The time dimension shows how an opening price drifts. Odds for the next Super Bowl champion released shortly after the previous Super Bowl are based mostly on the recently concluded season; as the new season approaches and teams make changes, the odds adjust to perceived championship chances, and as games progress the lines keep evolving with team performances.

The mechanism has five named drivers. Public betting patterns move a line because, when a significant amount of money lands on one team or participant, sportsbooks adjust the odds to balance their liability — making the price less favorable for the heavily-bet side and more favorable for the less-bet side to encourage even betting and reduce financial risk. New information matters because changes in player injuries, player substitutions or weather conditions alter the perceived outcome, and books adjust once such information becomes public. Professional bettors move lines because large wagers from sharp bettors often reflect insights or information that can influence the odds. Initial miscalculation is a fourth driver: sometimes the opening odds are perceived as offering value, and heavy betting on one side signals that the initial price was potentially "off," prompting an adjustment. Event dynamics is the fifth, applying to live betting placed while the event is in progress, where the evolving dynamics of the match lead to frequent changes.

# How To Open A Sportsbook Account, Download The App, And Place A Bet

The first thing you need before betting on the NBA Rookie of the Year Award, or any other bet, is an account at an online sportsbook — opening one is easy, quick and free, and can be done on a laptop, phone or tablet. The precondition to remember is location: it does not matter which state you live in when you sign up, but you must be within the state lines where sports betting is legal to make wagers, you must meet the legal age requirement (often 21), and you must adhere to all local and federal sports betting regulations. To bet through an app you must be within the state where that app is licensed.

The account steps run in order. # Sports Betting Odds

## Definition

Sports betting odds are the numbers a sportsbook posts alongside a wager to show the payout a bettor stands to win relative to their stake, and they are set by oddsmakers using computer models and analytics before being released to the public. The same underlying odds concept takes different shapes depending on the bet type — a moneyline price on who wins outright, a point spread price on a handicapped margin, and a totals (over/under) price on the combined score — and can be displayed in American, decimal, or fractional format.

## Context

In the corpus, odds are the common thread across every major bet type: moneylines, point spreads, totals, and prop bets all price outcomes with the same odds conventions, and combined-market previews such as college bowl coverage post moneyline, spread, and total odds side by side for a single game. Odds are not static — sportsbooks move them ("line movement") in response to public betting patterns, injury or roster news, and sharp/professional money, with the goal of balancing action on both sides of a bet so the book keeps its built-in profit regardless of outcome. Because different sportsbooks can carry different odds for the same event, bettors practice "line shopping" — comparing odds and lines across multiple sportsbooks before wagering to find the best price. Odds also extend beyond single games into futures and award markets, such as season-long odds on the NFL MVP race between Brock Purdy and Lamar Jackson.

## Key Characteristics

- **American odds format dominates U.S. listings** — a negative number (e.g., -110) shows the favorite and how much must be wagered to profit $100; a positive number (e.g., +250) shows the underdog and how much a $100 wager profits.
- **Three display formats carry the same price** — American, decimal (multiply the odds by the stake for total payout), and fractional (numerator = profit, denominator = stake) are alternative notations for identical odds.
- **Odds move for identifiable reasons** — sportsbooks shift a line or its odds because of lopsided public betting, new information (injuries, weather), sharp bettor action, or a perceived initial mispricing.
- **Odds differ by bet type but share the sign convention** — moneyline odds price the outright winner, point spread odds price a handicapped margin near even money, and totals odds price the over/under of a combined score; all three commonly display as American odds.
- **Line shopping exploits cross-sportsbook odds variance** — because oddsmakers and sportsbooks don't always move in lockstep, checking odds at multiple books before betting can secure a better price on the same wager.

# Point Spread Odds And Line Movement

Alongside a point spread, sportsbooks attach odds indicating the potential payout relative to the amount wagered, and those odds sit close to even because the spread itself is designed to level the playing field between the two teams. The same payout can be expressed in several formats: American (for example -110 or +110), Decimal (for example 1.91), and Fractional (for example 10/11), each a different way of stating the same potential return.

Point spread odds are not fixed once set; the shifts are commonly called "line movement." Lines move when the point spread or the odds attached to a particular bet change after sportsbooks have initially set them, and Sporting News identifies several drivers. The most common cause is an imbalance in the money being wagered on one side: if a significant majority of bettors back one team to cover, the top sports betting apps adjust the spread to make the other side more appealing and thereby balance the betting action. A second driver is unexpected events — injuries to key players, changes in team strategy, or significant weather events that might affect a game's outcome; for instance, if a star quarterback is announced as injured days before a big game, the spread might shift in favor of the opposing team. A third driver is information and public perception: when a piece of news or a prevailing sentiment about a team's increased chances of winning gains traction, it influences how people bet and leads sportsbooks to adjust their lines accordingly.

# Sony Music's Absence From "Dream Track"

Dennis Kooker's public statements on AI arrived a week after MBW pointed out a notable lack of endorsement from Sony Music Entertainment, and its artists, of YouTube's experimental AI project "Dream Track," which lets creators clone the vocals of successful musicians.

The initial cohort of stars involved in the project included recording artists signed to Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group — or labels within each of those two majors — but no Sony Music artists. In its earlier report MBW suggested that YouTube parent Google's recent submission to the United States Copyright Office, made in response to a request for written submissions as part of a study around copyright law and policy issues raised by AI systems, may have influenced Sony's absence from Dream Track.



---


# Sony Music's "Artist-Led" Approach To AI

Sources close to Sony Music's HQ in New York have suggested to MBW that the company is taking an "artist-led" approach to its experiments with any AI platform that can manipulate the work or voice of its roster — which is offered as the explanation for why Sony did not join Universal and Warner in "Dream Track."

The grounds are that Sony did not decline on principle. MBW understands that Sony Music, the recorded music arm of Sony Music Group, had like Universal and Warner been in discussions for months with YouTube over potentially licensing the experiment, and the company had shown its own willingness to experiment with generative AI music platforms that same week via an announcement about a project with David Gilmour, The Orb, and AI company Vermillio. In the case of Dream Track, MBW understands, Sony first offered the opportunity to participate to a number of its artists, but this group of acts did not show enthusiasm about participating. MBW notes that if one of these artists was Bad Bunny, signed to Sony's The Orchard, the reluctance is easy to see: the Puerto Rican superstar had expressed fury the other week about a popular track on TikTok that had cloned his vocal stylings via AI.



---


# YouTube's "Dream Track" Voice Cloning Experiment

On November 16, 2023 YouTube unveiled "Dream Track," an experiment enabling creators to clone the vocals, via AI tech and with official consent, of well-known stars.

Charlie Puth's voice is on there. John Legend's voice is on there. Demi Lovato's voice is on there. In fact the voices of a number of well-known recording artists signed to Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group — or labels within each major — are on there. Something conspicuous is not: any endorsement whatsoever from the world's second-biggest recording company, Sony Music Entertainment, or its artists.



---


# Which Artists Joined "Dream Track", And The Licensing Questions That Follow

MBW's closing observation is that the artists who agreed, with their record companies, to enter the YouTube "Dream Track" trial are stars — but in the case of both Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group they are, currently anyway, not the biggest megastars on either company's books.

The reasoning is that you might not expect, at this early stage, for the likes of UMG to put forward Drake, Taylor Swift, or The Beatles — or for WMG to put forward Ed Sheeran or Dua Lipa — to be guinea pigs in any early AI music experiments, even ones run by "friends" of the music industry like YouTube. From that observation MBW raises two open questions: whether there have been significant licensing payments made by YouTube to UMG and WMG for the right to play with the AI vocals of artists who have signed off on Dream Track thus far, and if so, whether these payments are being placed against any as-yet-unrecouped advances that some of these artists may have on their label accounts. More broadly, MBW poses a bigger question: when the day comes that YouTube asks the world's biggest superstars to wholeheartedly embrace "Dream Track", will Google's recent US Copyright Office filing give those superstars — and their record companies — pause for thought?



---


# UMG And WMG's Licensing Of "Dream Track"

Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group both dipped a toe into YouTube's "Dream Track" experiment — though not without caution — with UMG granting a limited license.

# The Material Reciprocity Principle In Music Royalties

Because of the EU-US asymmetry, European countries largely followed the "reciprocity principle" written into international copyright treaties such as the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty of 1996: in those countries where artists and labels are paid performance rights, there was no obligation to pay US artists and labels, since European artists did not receive those payments from airplay in the US.

The artists' groups' statement defends the principle in general terms, saying it "has proven vital in raising the level of copyright protection across the globe for decades."

# The EU-US Asymmetry In Recorded Music Performance Rights

At the heart of the dispute is a difference in how the US and the EU pay artists for terrestrial (non-satellite) radio broadcasts of music and recorded music played in bars and restaurants.

In Europe, when recorded music is played over terrestrial radio or in venues, performance rights payments must be made to the artists and labels behind the recording, as well as to the songwriters and publishers who own the composition behind the recording. In the US, by contrast, performance rights payments are made only to the songwriters and publishers, and not to artists and labels.

Robert Kyncl is the CEO of Warner Music Group, and the defining feature of his profile in the music business is that he came to it from 'Big Tech' — specifically from YouTube, where he was Chief Business Officer. That background is why, in the months before September 2023, he had been keeping a close eye on AI in the music industry.

His current role explains a second position associated with him: he has been pushing for price hikes at music streaming services. Both themes — AI in music, and streaming pricing — came up during Kyncl's Q&A session at the Code Conference in Laguna Niguel, California, on Tuesday 26 September 2023, as reported by Music Business Worldwide two days later.

# AI Developers Should Be Required To License Training Material

The NMPA's second demand is that AI developers be required to license the materials they use for training and keep records of them — not that music never be used for AI training, but that developers license it, not unlike how streaming services, bars and restaurants, or movie producers license music.

Many key players in the music industry and beyond have been adamant that using copyrighted works to train AI algorithms without authorization is copyright infringement, and a number of lawsuits have been launched against AI companies on these grounds. The NMPA's grounds for feasibility are practical: "Licensing musical works before training use is both required and practicable," the submission states, adding that "there are well developed processes in place for technology ventures to obtain free market licenses on a large scale." Scale is the operative condition, given that AI algorithms such as large language models are trained on countless millions or even billions of pieces of digital data. The NMPA points to existing activity as evidence that work on licensing "is already underway," citing news reports earlier in 2023 that UMG, along with Warner Music Group, were in talks with Google to secure licenses for artists' vocals and musical melodies to create AI-generated songs.



---


# Kyncl Prediction: Music Is the First Industry to Feel AI's Impact

Robert Kyncl's proposition, put at the Code Conference in September 2023, is that the music business will be out ahead of other industries in exploiting the potential of AI, and — out of necessity — also ahead on the question of how to regulate and monetise the use of AI by non-rights-holders. He attached a date to it: asked when that sea change would occur, he said "I would say within the next year you will see lots of evolution around AI… What you will likely see is increasing quality at a very fast pace."

His reasoning is structural rather than accidental. "Music – because it's so broadly distributed and it's so well aligned with the internet, because it's short format, it lends itself to recommendations, it's on all platforms – is generally first in most transformations and most innovations. So it digitizes first." He generalises from the previous cycle: "Whatever happened to the music industry 20 years ago is starting to happen in the movies and TV shows now. In the meantime, music emerged out of [digitization] better and stronger and more resilient. So, I would imagine the same will happen here, which is we'll likely be first."

The hypothesis is falsifiable on two fronts as stated. It fails if other industries, rather than music, lead on both exploiting and regulating AI; and it fails on its own timetable if the year following September 2023 does not bring the predicted rapid evolution and fast-rising quality in AI. Because the argument rests on music's broad distribution, short format and recommendation-friendliness, an AI transformation that arrives first in a long-format medium would also count against the mechanism he proposes.

# AfroFuture Rising Star Challenge Competition

The Rising Star Challenge is AfroFuture's annual flagship competition for unsigned and emerging artists in Africa, described by co-founder Abdul Karim Abdullah as the brand's way of supporting live music not only in Ghana but throughout Africa. Eligibility is limited to unsigned and emerging artists.

Entry and selection run in fixed stages. To enter, artists upload an original song to Audiomack and create an Instagram Reel that includes an introduction about the artist, their approach to music and the music-making process, and what they want their potential audience to know about their style of music. As a lead-up to the festival, 10 musicians are then chosen from a shortlist of 25 unsigned and emerging artists. From those, five finalists are chosen to perform on AfroFuture's Rising Star Stage alongside the festival's headliners. For the grand finale, one artist is selected for the ultimate prize — an exclusive recording agreement with Sony Music Africa for a single release. Winners additionally receive global distribution for their new single, marketing support such as a music video and more, free access to AfroFuture's recording studio, and mentoring and training from industry executives and leading musicians and producers.

In 2022 the format was extended with the Rising Star DJ Challenge, a call for DJs from across the diaspora to share their talents and win a place on the AfroFuture stage. Created in partnership with TuneCore to amplify the next generation of African superstars and find the next breakout DJ from the continent, it followed a different sequence: the top ten entries were selected by a panel of industry experts composed of TuneCore executives and AfroFuture DJs; once announced, fans across the world voted on social media to narrow the group down to three DJs; the top three finalists then battled it out at the AfroFuture Music Museum in Accra, Ghana on 27 December; and the contest winner performed at AfroFuture 2022 and walked away with a cash prize.



---


# AI Copyright And Training Disputes

Universal Music Group's answer to generative AI trained on its catalogue rejects the premise that such training is a neutral technical act, recasting it as a choice of allegiance: "The training of generative AI using our artists' music . . . begs the question as to which side of history all stakeholders in the music ecosystem want to be on: the side of artists, fans and human creative expression, or on the side of deep fakes, fraud and denying artists their due compensation," the label said after a song using AI to imitate Drake and The Weeknd, two of its artists, went viral.

A second objection cuts against the label framing itself. These same conversations and contradictions are manifesting across creative industries, but artists themselves don't always have a seat at the table — so an industry-level statement of grievance is not the same thing as artists speaking for themselves. Independent artists in particular are learning that their voices resonate louder when coming together across disciplines to push back against what Holland describes as an "extraordinary spectrum of exploitation" that leverages their work.

The dispute is not confined to music. In a roundtable hosted by the FTC that same week, the agency brought together figures from across creative industries — from voice acting and science fiction to screenwriting, music, illustration and even fashion — to delve into how generative AI is affecting creatives. TechCrunch reported the exchange on 2023-10-06.



---


# Why Spanish-Language Music Keeps Growing Globally

Asked what is driving the ability of Latin artists, particularly Latin American artists, to have global hits on distribution agreements without signing even licensing deals with major record labels, Alejandra Olea answers that Spanish-speaking music, from Spain and Latin America, just keeps getting bigger, and that Spanish and Latin artists have many more options to develop their audiences and monetize their music at each stage of their career.

The mechanism she gives has two linked parts. First, the world is one where music discovery and consumption are now primarily digital, artists have understood that, and they look for partners who get it too and whose expertise will allow them to leverage digital platforms to reach new and existing audiences wherever they are; artists like Iñigo Quintero and labels like Acqustic are prime examples of this profound shift within the Latin and the wider music industry. Second, the effect is strongest in Spanish-speaking markets, where music fans are among the most engaged audiences in the world, whether on digital platforms or on social media, and where music content is consumed with more frequency, in different formats, across multiple platforms and through different aspects related to the track.



---


# Music Streaming Price Hikes and Emerging Market Growth

Robert Kyncl told the Code Conference in September 2023 that the opportunity ahead of the music business is twofold: "One, the continued growth in emerging markets, and also the GDPs of those countries will be rising at the same time. So there's lots of growth there. And then there is the price elasticity optimization in mature markets."

Music Business Worldwide read that last point as a reference to the price hikes seen among all the major music streaming services over the past year or so, and to the growing belief within the music industry that streaming price hikes will be sustained — evidenced recently, at the time of writing in September 2023, by Deezer's second price hike within a year.



---


# Music Streaming Resilience Versus Streaming Video Downturn

Asked at the Code Conference whether the audio streaming business is likely to go through what streaming video is going through, Robert Kyncl's answer was unequivocal: "No. Music is much more resilient."

The grounds for the question were the state of streaming video. Netflix experienced its first-ever decline in subscriptions in 2022, though it has since roared back to health; the subscriber count of Disney+ appears to be in freefall; and talk is growing about ongoing consolidation of the many streaming video services that have come online over the past several years.

Kyncl's grounds for the contrast are the scale and speed of audio subscription growth rather than any claim about video. "So first, I think what happened in the last 15 years is incredible. They had literally zero people in the subscription model and now we have 700 million people in the world in the premium experience… which is incredible." He credited the path-forging to Spotify's Daniel Ek — "And I think really credit goes to Daniel Ek for forging the path for everybody. And then companies like Apple and YouTube and Amazon following and building up the [music] business. It's pretty incredible what has happened." The warrant tying this to resilience is that a market built from zero to 700 million premium subscribers across multiple competing platforms is structurally different from the video services now consolidating.



---


# The Digital-First Artist Development Model

The success of "Si No Estás" illustrates how much artist development has changed: social media and digital music services have now become the number one source of music discovery, and Believe has developed an innovative, AI and data-driven expertise to develop tracks and artists that Alejandra Olea describes as unique in the music industry.

The model's components and their relations are stated together: the key to success is great partnerships with the artist and their label, and being able to combine strong AI data-driven expertise to maximise momentum for an artist and a track at the right time with the right tools and the right partnerships, supported by both local and global teams. Olea singles out the last element as particularly important and truly one of Believe's strengths, being able to mobilise teams multi-locally and globally to accompany audience development for artists. The forward-looking claim attached to the model is that this is only the beginning for Iñigo Quintero and that Believe anticipates many more successes like his in future.



---


# European Artists' Projected Royalty Loss To US Rightsholders

A group of organizations representing musical artists in Europe has warned that an "anomaly" in EU law could soon result in artists losing up to 40% of the income they make from terrestrial radio broadcasts and other public performances of their music — and that because of a technicality in EU law, that lost income would largely go to US-based artists.

The groups include IMPALA, the trade association for European indie labels, and Adami, the French collective management organization for performers' rights. What the failure of the "reciprocity" principle means in practice is that US-based artists whose recordings are played on the radio in the EU will be able to collect performance royalties, while EU artists will continue to get nothing from their recordings being played in the US. Because royalties are paid from a collective pool of income, this will reduce payments to European artists by as much as 40% in some countries, the artists' groups said, as that is the share of US music played on the radio in those countries. IMPALA estimates that the annual loss to EU recorded music rightsholders from "reciprocity" protections not applying in Europe would amount to approximately €125 million (USD $137m) — money which would instead be handed to their US counterparts.

# Google Play Billing And The User Choice Billing Alternative

Google Play's billing arrangement, as of November 2023, has two tiers. The baseline requires apps to use Google's own first-party billing system and charges app developers a 15% to 30% commission on the sales it processes. The alternative is User Choice Billing, a program still in pilot testing, open to all developers who sell apps in the 35 markets where it is then available, including the U.S., which reduces the standard commission by 4% for companies who choose to use their own payment processing solution. Spotify and Bumble were the initial testers for the new system, first introduced in November 2022, and Match, as part of its settlement agreement, will also now take advantage of this option. Epic has declined to use it.

Google's defense of the commission rests on what it says the commission buys. It will argue that its commissions are not just tied to payment processing, but help it develop other features and controls to keep Android users safe and guide them to discovering new applications, as well as helping fund the tools and services developers need to build and grow their apps. Google also helps developers reach a broader audience beyond the mobile phone, with support for Android across platforms ranging from tablets to TVs to autos and more. And it notes that 99% of its developers qualify for a commission of 15% or less, based on their revenues — so the headline 30% is the boundary case, not the typical one.

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.

# The Epic v. Google Witness Lineup

A whole cast of intriguing people were set to be called as witnesses during the trial, going straight to the top of the org chart: Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Epic CEO Tim Sweeney are absolutely expected to attend.

Beyond the two chief executives, Android co-founder Andy Rubin might be deposed, and Google says the court will hear from current Android — and Chrome, and Chrome OS — boss Hiroshi Lockheimer. Google also says representatives from Apple, Netflix, Motorola, and AT&T should testify.

# Epic's Antitrust Claims Against Google Play

Epic's claim is that the Android operating system's Google Play Store constitutes an unlawful monopoly, and that Google is separately tying its Google Play payments platform to that store, keeping other potential app payment mechanisms from competing.

The grounds Epic offers are the frictions it says Google creates: Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that it has created an illegal monopoly which unjustly enriches Google while artificially driving up app prices because other stores cannot compete. The warrant joining that to the legal claim is the competitive-harm chain — no viable rival stores means no fee discipline, which means the "Google Tax" is paid either by developers or passed along to consumers. Epic wants to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods so developers are not stuck paying that tax.

Google's answer contests the warrant rather than the fees: it says Epic's demands would damage Android's ability to offer a secure user experience and to compete with Apple's iOS. Both sides agree the future of Google's app store could depend on this trial. Epic sued in 2020 after a fight over in-app purchase fees.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. Google's execution was uneven, though — it wound up spending much of its opening statement attempting to explain away its seemingly bad behavior as normal business practices and did not always succeed out of the gate.

# Hypocrisy On Both Sides Of The Courtroom

Each side's central talking point is undercut by its own conduct, so neither party's framing should be taken at face value. Epic says it is not in this for the money, only suing to end Google's monopoly — but Epic would surely profit if it does not have to pay Google's cut. Epic also looks set to argue that you are locked into Android after buying an Android phone, though switching back and forth between the platforms is easier than ever.

Google's talking points have the same problem. Google will say that every Samsung Galaxy phone has "a competing app store right there on the homescreen," even though Google apparently tried to quash that store too, fearing it could cost the company billions. Google was caught trying to play the China card in a pre-briefing with press, reminding journalists that Epic is 40 percent owned by Chinese company Tencent — even though Google itself allegedly considered teaming up with Tencent to eliminate the Epic threat. The parties cannot argue that in court, but Google can attempt to play the China card subtly: "Google may ask a witness once about Tencent's domicile," reads one of Judge Donato's orders.

In the same press briefing, Google suggested to journalists that Epic should have joined the company's "User Choice Billing" program if it wanted an alternative payment system, instead of suing — but that program did not exist until 2022, long after the lawsuit, and it only knocks 4 percentage points off Google's fee.

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google will also attack the foreclosure premise directly. It will note that, unlike Apple, it allows apps to be sideloaded on Android devices — something Epic takes advantage of today — and that this process is streamlined and helps keep users safe. Epic will claim in response that the process is made to be overly difficult for end users, with multiple steps involved and "scare screens" that warn users of the security risks involved with sideloading.

On discovery, Epic will suggest that Google hid items by allowing execs and employees to have "off the record" chats; Google will counter this as well, saying it has provided the court with thousands of chat logs and millions of documents. Google will ultimately push the notion that this case is not about competition but about money — that is, that Epic Games wants to reach the Play Store's 2.5 billion users without having to pay. As a Google blog post by Wilson White, VP, Government Affairs & Public Policy, put it: "Android's choice and flexibility work well for consumers and developers of all sizes. We look forward to making our case in court as we fight to keep our users safe from harm, partner with developers to grow their businesses, and keep the Android ecosystem thriving and healthy for everyone."

On Monday, a federal jury sided with Fortnite maker Epic Games in its fight to break Google's control over Android apps, surprising the world. The nine-person jury decided that Google has an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems, and that Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. In November 2023, the month before the Helena World Chronicle suit was filed, Google reached an agreement with the Canadian government under which the search giant would pay Canadian media for use of their content. # Revenue Split

## Definition

A revenue split, in the corpus, is the percentage pair — such as 70/30, 50/50, or 95/5 — by which a platform and a counterparty divide proceeds: Google's revenue share agreements (RSAs) with Android device makers and carriers, Google's 70/30 app-store split with developers, and Twitch's and Kick's subscription-revenue splits with streamers.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces across three unrelated disputes that share the same underlying mechanic: dividing proceeds between a platform and a counterparty. In the US v. Google antitrust trial, Google's revenue share agreements (RSAs) pay Android device makers and wireless carriers like Verizon a cut in exchange for setting Google Search and Chrome as defaults. In the Epic v. Google trial, Epic argued that Google's 70/30 app-store revenue split with developers is likely descended from an arbitrary decision Valve made with Steam two decades earlier, rather than from any principled calculation of the value Google's store provides. On the creator-platform side, Twitch's default subscription revenue split for Partners is 50/50, with a premium 70/30 tier once offered to select streamers before Twitch discontinued it in favor of ad revenue; rival platform Kick instead lures streamers away with a 95/5 split.

## Key Characteristics

- **Expressed as a ratio** — revenue splits are stated as two percentages that sum to 100, such as 70/30, 50/50, or 95/5, denoting each party's share.
- **Applies across different platform relationships** — the corpus shows the same mechanic governing device-maker default agreements (Google RSAs), app-store developer terms (Google/Epic 70/30), and creator subscription payouts (Twitch, Kick).
- **A lever platforms adjust unilaterally** — Twitch changed its subscription split from a 70/30 deal for select streamers to a 50/50 default, then introduced the Partner Plus program to restore a 70/30 rate for qualifying creators, showing the split is a platform-controlled term rather than a fixed market rate.
- **A point of leverage in competitive disputes** — Epic used the 70/30 app-store split's arbitrary Valve/Steam origin to challenge Google's justification for its rate, and Kick's more generous 95/5 split is a stated draw for streamers dissatisfied with Twitch's terms.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "revenue split" and "revenue share" only in the specific device-maker, app-store, and creator-payout deals described above, without defining the general concept. Outside the corpus, revenue sharing is defined as the distribution of the total revenue generated by the sale of goods and services among stakeholders or contributors, distinct from profit sharing (which splits only what remains after costs) (Wikipedia, "Revenue sharing," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revenue_sharing).
