# The October 2023 Cutoff Of Supplies To Gaza

Israel stopped allowing deliveries of food, fuel and other supplies to Gaza's 2.3 million residents on Oct. 10, 2023, and was reportedly preparing for a ground invasion; on Oct. 12, 2023 it warned 1.1 million Gaza residents in the northern section of the enclave to leave for the southern region in advance of that potential invasion. International aid groups warned that they could not deliver food and other basic services to people in the Gaza Strip and that a "dire" humanitarian crisis was set to worsen. Those groups provide food and other means of support to about 63% of people in Gaza.

What changed in October is the scope of the restriction rather than its existence. International aid groups now face the same problem in Gaza that local businesses and residents have encountered for about 16 years: a blockade that prevents civilians and items, like medicine, from easily moving into or out of the enclosed area, roughly 25 miles long. That 16-year blockade did not apply to the food and fuel that groups brought into Gaza. Now it does.



---


# The Israeli Blockade Of Gaza Since 2007

The Israeli blockade of Gaza is a set of permanent air, land and sea blockades that Israel set up around the enclave in 2007, one year after Hamas rose to political power. Its discriminating features are physical control of movement and of goods: Israel controls two physical checkpoints along Gaza which monitor both the entry and exit of people and trucks, limits the kind and quantity of materials that pass into Gaza, and generally prohibits Gazans who do not have work permits or special clearance — for medical purposes, for example — from entering Israel. Egypt, which borders Gaza on its southern end, also oversees one checkpoint that specifically limits people coming and going.

The blockade is not total, and its boundary cases matter. Israel has granted permits to about 17,000 Gaza residents to enter and work in Israel, and while trade continues, the food, fuel and medical supplies that people in Gaza use all first pass through Israel. Gaza is about the size of Philadelphia and requires trade with different businesses and countries in order to maintain and grow its economy, but it is heavily dependent on foreign aid — partially as a result of this blockade regime. Israel's restrictions intensified after Hamas' surprise attack on 20 Israeli towns and several military bases on Oct. 7, 2023, when Israel announced a broad blockade of imports into Gaza that stopped all food, fuel and medical supplies from entering the region.



---


# How The Blockade Produces Food Insecurity And Import Dependence In Gaza

About 64% of people in Gaza are considered food insecure, meaning they do not have reliable access to sufficient amounts of food — one of the several practical effects the blockade has for the average Gazan. The dependence has deepened over time: food as a percentage of Gaza's total imports has skyrocketed by 50% since 2005, when Israel first imposed a temporary blockade, while the amount of food the West Bank and Gaza actually produce has tumbled by 30% since then.

The mechanism suppressing local production is partly infrastructural damage. It is hard for Gaza to produce food within its own borders; one factor is that Israeli airstrikes hit Gaza's only power generation plant and main sewage treatment plant in 2008 and again in 2018. Those attacks resulted in the spread of sewage waste on land and in the water, destroying farmlands and food crops and threatening fish stocks in the ocean as well.



---


# Gaza's Economic Isolation And Poverty Indicators

More than 53% of Gaza residents were considered below the poverty line in 2020, and about 77% of Gazan households receive some form of aid from the United Nations and other groups, mostly in the form of cash or food. The Palestinian enclaves of the West Bank and Gaza — generally lumped together in economic analyses — both have small economies that together run a massive deficit of US$6.6 billion in losses each year, as the value of the imports they receive greatly outweighs the value of the items they produce and sell elsewhere.

Gaza's weak economy is caused by a number of complex factors, but the largest is the blockade and the economic and trade isolation it creates.



---


# Egypt's Strategic Value To Europe: Gas And Security

The war "underscores the important role Egypt has always played vis-a-vis security in and around Gaza," said Robert Satloff, executive director at The Washington Institute for Near East Policy — a role that is not lost on European governments.

Those governments woke up to Egypt's importance as a regional gas producer after Vladimir Putin's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. European officials visited to assess Egypt's potential as a gas supplier — with Israel's help — to supplant at least some Russian supplies.



---


# Gaza Sky Geeks Accelerator

Gaza Sky Geeks is an Alphabet-backed initiative based in Gaza that provides pre-seed investments, training and technology resources to Palestine's Gazan population, and has been a beacon of entrepreneurship in the region.

It is the largest tech hub in Palestine, providing a wide range of tech training at scale: in 2022, 5,000 coders and developers from across the West Bank and Gaza graduated from the program.



---


# Egypt's Role In The Israel-Hamas War And The Leverage It Creates

The war between Israel and Hamas has turned the spotlight on Egypt's role as a regional powerbroker, potentially winning it Western support as it tries to escape a grinding economic crisis. The structure linking the two is that Egypt's two assets in this conflict — long-held ties to Israel and a border with Gaza — make its stance decisive for outcomes the West wants.

Specifically, Egypt's position is shaping up as key to the fate of any refugees and to a sustained flow of aid for the besieged territory's 2 million residents, after Israel cut off crucial supplies in response to Hamas's deadly Oct. 7 assault. That dependence is what converts Egypt's geography and relationships into potential leverage over Western backing for its economy, as of the reporting date of 2023-10-22.



---


# UNRWA As A Parallel Government In Gaza

The United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East — UNRWA — is the biggest international aid group in Gaza, and over time it has evolved into a kind of parallel government alongside Hamas, which Israel, the United States and other countries designate as a terrorist organization. It is the second-largest employer in Gaza, following Hamas, and provides the bulk of the education, food aid and health care services for people in Gaza, in addition to 3 million other people registered as Palestinian refugees who live in Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, the West Bank and other places.

The scale of its service provision is what makes the "parallel government" description apt. UNRWA funds and runs a network of 284 schools in Gaza alone, employing over 9,000 local people as staff and educating over 294,000 children each year, and it runs 22 hospitals in Gaza that employ almost 1,000 health staff and record 3.3 million patient visits per year. Its schools are converted into humanitarian shelters in times of crisis, such as the current war, where people can go to get clean water, food, mattresses and blankets, showers and more. The precondition for this role is Gaza's weak economy and isolation because of the blockade, which mean it relies heavily on international aid organizations to provide basic services to residents.



---


# Israel-Hamas War Context, October 2023

As of TechCrunch's 2023-10-14 report, Israel is retaliating militarily against the attacks on its people, on its soil, and the hostages subsequently taken by Hamas — the ruling organization in Gaza that kidnapped at least 150 people and took them into Gaza during brutal attacks on Israel last weekend that killed 1,300 people. That strategy has seen Israel pummeling the "Gaza Strip" with bombs to eradicate it of Hamas and to get its hostages back, and over 1,500 people in Palestine so far have been killed as a result.

The tech industry in Israel — the country's biggest export and its biggest single contributor to GDP — is also taking a big knock, but inevitably the impact on the smaller and more fragile ecosystem in Gaza has been significantly more serious, and the physical, economic and societal destruction resulting from that leaves any future for the tech industry there in doubt: quite simply, there is no escaping the consequences of the war for anyone, let alone tech workers. Israel has now amassed soldiers near the north of Gaza ahead of an expected ground offensive into the densely populated enclave, and about 1.1 million people living in northern areas have been told to leave in the next day. The UN has warned of "devastating humanitarian consequences" from these latest moves, and a total blockade on the territory is being enforced with fuel, food and water running out; Israel says it won't lift the restrictions unless Hamas frees all hostages. TechCrunch notes the piece was later edited to include relevant information about the attacks by Hamas.



---


# Google Maps And Waze Halt Israel-Gaza Traffic Data

Google Maps and Waze stopped live traffic updates in Israel and the Gaza Strip at the request of the Israel Defense Forces, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-30. A Google spokesperson said the ability to see live traffic conditions and business information was halted temporarily out of "consideration for the safety of local communities."

There is precedent: Google did something similar in 2022 amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine, because the apps were being used to track military movements.



---


# Criticism Of UNRWA's Textbooks And Internal Governance

Against the case for funding UNRWA, defenders of the 2018 policy change that cut U.S. money cited UNRWA-published textbooks that allegedly glorified jihad — attacking the premise that the agency's educational work is politically neutral. UNRWA, for its part, maintained that as an outside organization it can only use the educational materials the country it is working in wants.

Two further lines of criticism target the agency's conduct rather than its curriculum. Some Republican politicians have said that UNRWA has "cozied up" to Hamas. And an internal UNRWA ethics committee has accused top staff at the agency of "sexual misconduct, nepotism, retaliation … and other abuses of authority" that created a toxic work environment.



---


# The Humanitarian Corridor Proposal For Gaza

A humanitarian corridor, as called for in Gaza by international aid groups and European Union officials, means a protected path specifically for civilians, aid workers and necessary basic items to pass through safely back and forth from Gaza to Israel and Egypt. Its defining features are protection and restricted purpose: it is not a general opening of the border but a designated safe route for particular people and goods.

As of 2023-10-13 the proposal remained only a proposal — there were no clear plans for such a protected pathway.



---


# Displacement And Casualties In Gaza As Of October 12, 2023

The number of people in Gaza displaced from their homes rose quickly over the days preceding Oct. 12, 2023, totaling over 330,000 on that date, with over two-thirds of them staying in UNRWA schools.

Since the war between Israel and Hamas began on Oct. 8, 2023, more than 1,500 Gazans had been killed and more than 5,300 injured, while Hamas attacks had killed more than 1,300 people in Israel and injured about 3,200 others. These are the figures as reported on 2023-10-13.



---


# Gaza Tech Infrastructure Destruction

The Palestinian tech ecosystem is now effectively gone, like the buildings in Gaza itself. "What is happening to tech in Gaza is that Israel is crunching it. Obliterating it," one source inside the territory told TechCrunch on 2023-10-14.

Ryan Sturgill, an American national and former head of the Gaza Sky Geeks (GSG) accelerator run by sponsor Mercy Corps, an NGO aid organization, described a dire situation on the ground after waves of shelling by the Israeli military: "The area around the the Mercy Corps building, which housed Gaza Sky Geeks, has been leveled. The structure is standing but blown out. The front of it is sort of ripped off." Video evidence posted on LinkedIn shows a blown-out building with the Mercy Corps sign. "Who knows what's going to happen. The offices are destroyed, the fiber lines are destroyed. The universities are destroyed. Three main universities in Gaza that produce all the computer science grads are leveled. I don't even know if people will ever be able to go back to Northern Gaza after what's happening today. The educational institutions that are there are gone," Sturgill added.



---


# Gaza's Internet Blackout And Connectivity

Internet connectivity in Gaza took a severe hit as the conflict between Israel and Hamas continued: Palestinian internet service provider NetStream reportedly collapsed due to a severe shortage of fuel supplies, while other providers such as Paltel and Mada Al Arab also faced serious connectivity issues. Although the situation remained precarious as of November 3, 2023, connectivity eventually was partially restored, and there are indications that the U.S. government is putting pressure on Israel to restore internet connectivity in Gaza. TechCrunch frames the stakes: when you think "essential services" you might think water, electricity and hospitals, but internet connectivity is increasingly important as the infrastructure that ties together the fabric of society.

The blackout was visible on Snap Map in real time. Some are concerned that internet access in Gaza, partially restored after Israel imposed a communications blackout, will be cut again. TikTok creator divergentredhed posted that she watched the blackout happen in real time on Snapchat: "Right there in Gaza it was like a hotspot of Snapchat Stories. It was yellow and green and red … all of it just went dark. The entire Gaza Strip went dark before my very eyes," she said. "I'm just going to spend the next few days uploading all of the content I have from Snapchat, from the people themselves."



---


# What Israeli Leaders Claimed The Gaza Barrier Would Do

At the time of the fence's completion, Israeli leaders argued that the barrier had already proved itself and would provide security to the region — claims that, as the article notes, rested on a threat model built around tunnels and ladders.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, then in opposition, referred mainly to the below-ground aspect: "Any time Hamas terrorists have tried to penetrate the border settlements through the tunnels, they were terminated underground. The below-ground barrier surrounding the Gaza Strip has already saved many lives." Then-Minister of Defense Benny Gantz said, "The barrier, which is a superior initial technological and inventive project that sets an iron wall, sensors and concrete between it and the residents of the south. It provides a sense of personal security that will allow this beautiful region to continue to grow." The reference scenario behind that confidence is identified by Yehoshua Kalisky, senior researcher at Tel Aviv University's Institute for National Security Studies: "The concept underlying the construction of an advanced technology fence relates to the Second Lebanon War, when Hezbollah surmounted a high fence with a ladder. This was the reference scenario. There was no thought that they would use aircraft here to cross it or that they would come with a heavy machinery, and simply breach it."



---


# Iran's State Funding Of Hamas

"The most significant way to finance terrorism is to finance countries, not fundraising campaigns," Ostrovitch-Levi says: campaigns have intensified greatly over the last month, but the core of the budget for Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis and Palestinian Islamic Jihad is Iran, in particular the Quds Force, the special forces of the IRGC.

The dependence is presented as decisive: Hamas has all kinds of additional sources of self-financing — businesses, associations, investments, and all kinds of arrangements it has tried to set up over the years — but "They need state funding, and without Iran they have no ability to exist." On scale: "As far as we know, the budget from Iran to Gaza is in the order of $100 million a year. Gaza could do very nice things with this money, make it even more beautiful than Dubai. But from what we know, most of this budget goes to the military wing of Hamas." Qatar is a distinct case: "Qatar transferred suitcases of cash to Gaza through Israel. Everyone knows this. This money allegedly went to pay salaries and civilian needs (education, health, infrastructure), and therefore Israel transferred it, so it's incorrect to say that it all went to fund terrorism." IMPA is charged with rooting out the sources of funding for terrorism, working together with the National Bureau for Counter Terror Financing of Israel (NBCTF) in the Ministry of Defense, which coordinates all activities to thwart terror financing, along with the Shin Bet, Military Intelligence Directorate (AMAN), and all other relevant intelligence and security agencies.



---


# Trade-Based Terror Financing Schemes

Another way to transfer money is trade — transferring goods, or inflating their value — a channel Israeli authorities have interdicted repeatedly at ports and crossings.

Two seizures illustrate the method. Only days before the November 2023 interview, containers of goods worth hundreds of thousands of shekels were seized at Ashdod Port, destined for Hamas merchants in Nablus and other cities, with the proceeds intended to finance Hamas operations. In August 2021, 23 tons of chocolate bars were seized in a joint operation by the NBCTF, AMAN and the Tax Authority at the Nitzana Border Crossing between Israel and Egypt; it was suspected the snack bars, destined for Gaza, were purchased with terror financing funds, with the proceeds from their sales earmarked for Hamas. A third affair combined trade and hawala: Hamas funds originating in Iran were transferred in cash to money changers in Turkey for transfer to Gaza, while Hamed al-Khachari, a Gazan money changer who worked for Hamas and was assassinated by Israel in 2019, located Gazan merchants who imported goods from Turkish companies and owed payment on them; they paid cash to Khachari, who transferred the money to Hamas in Gaza, while the money changers in Turkey received funds from Hamas abroad that were used to pay the Turkish companies.



---


# The Gaza Conflict's Information Environment, Late 2023

Israel has retaliated against Hamas' October 7 attack with unprecedented force against the Palestinian territory, claiming over 9,000 Palestinian lives according to Gaza Health Ministry numbers reported by the Associated Press, as of November 3, 2023.

Reporting capacity in the territory has been degraded on two fronts. The Committee to Protect Journalists reports that at least 30 journalists have been killed since Israel's bombardment and total blockade of the region began, and journalists in Gaza say that without consistent access to food, water and power it is becoming "impossible" to continue reporting.

At the same time, misinformation about the escalating violence is rampant on social media — so the shortfall in professional reporting coincides with an unreliable information supply.



---


# US Funding Of UNRWA Across Presidential Administrations

The U.S. has historically been the single-largest funder of UNRWA, a U.N. agency that relies on governments to support its work, giving more than $500 million to Palestinians from April 2021 through March 2022, including more than $417 million that went to UNRWA. U.S. support to UNRWA has fluctuated throughout different presidential administrations.

Total U.S. aid to the West Bank and Gaza peaked at $1 billion in 2009, after Israel sealed off the territory, and reached $1 billion in annual contributions again in 2013, when former Secretary of State John Kerry helped restart peace talks between Israel and Hamas. In 2018 the Trump Administration cut almost all of the money the U.S. typically gives to UNRWA, amounting to roughly 30% of the organization's total budget. The Biden administration then restored funding to UNRWA and other organizations helping Palestinians in 2021.



---


# Gaza As A Tech Outsourcing Hub

Gaza, despite being one of the most economically challenged regions in the world, has ironically always been a tech hub — not only for Palestine and Palestinians, but also for the world, with international companies having for many years sought out a presence there to collaborate with talented tech freelancers and the startups that gradually emerged from the region. According to sources who helped build those bridges, Nvidia, famed for its role in the new AI boom, has been working with at least 100 engineers from the region for years; tragically, the initiative to employ Palestinians in this outsourcing was that of Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, whose daughter was brutally murdered in the attacks by Hamas.

The hub's scale marks its boundary. Since at least 2008, TechCrunch has been covering technology companies out of Palestine, some serving their direct audience and some serving the tech world internationally, and Silicon Valley had taken an increasing interest in Palestine as a tech hub — but like the ecosystem itself, that interest is nascent: to date, those working in the region estimate that as much as $10 million has been invested in the Palestinian tech ecosystem. Notably, in 2017, Salesforce founder and CEO Marc Benioff joined Silicon Valley luminaries in backing the first-ever coding academy to be created in Gaza.

# Egypt's Refusal To Host Palestinian Refugees

President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi has rejected any suggestion that Egypt host Gazan refugees, even as the same Western governments now court him for help in alleviating the pressure on Gaza, suggesting instead that Israel take in Palestinians in its Negev desert: "They can transport Palestinians there until Israel implements its announced plan to destroy Hamas," he said on Wednesday, 2023-10-18. The core political ground is that "there is little to no constituency for going against decades of policy on not allowing Palestinian displacement," said Mirette Mabrouk of the Middle East Institute, while the inducements offered "might wind up becoming a political liability, especially in an election year."

Three further grounds support the refusal. Egypt already hosts some 9 million refugees and other migrants from countries including Syria, Sudan, Yemen and Libya. Opening a route for Palestinians may also present a new security risk in the Sinai peninsula, where the army has only just managed to get a handle on its fight with Islamist militants. And Jordan has also refused to accept more Palestinians, making it unlikely Egypt would become a regional exception and take in refugees many suspect may never be let back into Gaza — which would risk being seen in the Arab world as facilitating another mass displacement and betraying the Palestinian cause all Arab countries vocally espouse.

The warrant tying these grounds to the policy is that the domestic political cost outranks the economic one. While Egypt could absorb a certain number of people, the domestic political consequences would be "huge," said the Washington Institute's Robert Satloff: "The political leadership considers this a red line not to be crossed and would prefer to face worsening financial distress than accept a significant number of refugees."



---


# Easing Escalation Concerns Around Israel-Gaza In Late October 2023

Concerns about the conflict spreading more broadly have eased amid growing calls within Israel to rethink a ground invasion of Gaza, because of fears about the fate of some 200 hostages held there, the danger of retaliation by Hezbollah and the risk of Israeli military casualties.

The same 2023-10-24 wrap carried the quote of the day from Magellan chairman Andrew Formica, speaking as the group's chief executive stepped down abruptly amid the company's efforts to turn around its performance: "I think when you get to those decisions, you can then sit on them for a while… or you can say let's just deal with it [and] that's what we have done today."



---


# Snap Map As A Firsthand Record Of Gaza

As of November 3, 2023, the world was watching the humanitarian crisis in Gaza unfold in real time through firsthand accounts documented on, of all places, Snapchat. Amid calls for a ceasefire, TikTok and X (formerly Twitter) users were urging followers to view the devastation of Gaza for themselves on Snap Maps, which has displayed hot spots throughout northern Gaza since the Israeli airstrikes started in October 2023. You do not need an account to view Snap Map — the desktop version of the map is publicly accessible. "Snap Maps is a WEALTH of real-time information and is an important source for all journalists who aren't on the ground right now," X user inejmydarling posted.

Snap did not provide TechCrunch with hard data, but confirmed that since October 7 the company has seen a "moderate" increase in submissions to public Stories from Gaza, and said that more people from around the world are viewing content from the region. In the weeks since Israel's blockade of the territory began, screen recordings of the map, which displays bright red hotspots throughout northern Gaza, have been shared online.

The content itself is ordinary-hours documentation: in recent videos posted from Gaza City on Thursday night, users recorded bombings from their windows, and videos posted from the previous morning showed smoke rising from remaining buildings, demolished neighborhoods and people crowding around medical vehicles for treatment. As one X user wrote on October 29, 2023: "I'm begging you guys to please PLEASE check snap maps. Look at the difference between the living conditions just a few miles away. The people of Gaza are posting these publicly for us to see and share. Please listen to them. These are all from today. You can check yourselves."

# Meta Response To Suppression Claims

Meta's rebuttal attacks the premise that any pattern of reduced reach for Palestine-related content shows deliberate suppression: the company says the reduced reach came from globally scoped technical bugs and from errors in good-faith enforcement, not from the subject matter of the posts. As reported by TechCrunch on 19 October 2023, Meta said it is closely monitoring its platforms for violations and may inadvertently flag certain content, but that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view."

The scope condition Meta sets around the whole dispute is its terrorist-organization rule: content praising or supporting Hamas — which governs Gaza and is designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union — is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms. This is stated in the aftermath of Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade cutting access to electricity, water and vital supplies, which have devastated Gaza.

Meta communications director Andy Stone declined to comment on the record and pointed TechCrunch to Meta's newsroom post about the conflict, updated on Oct. 18 with a statement addressing the shadowbanning claims. "Our policies are designed to keep people safe on our apps while giving everyone a voice," it said. "We apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice … We can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it."

The specific counter-explanations are two bugs, each claimed to be global and therefore content-neutral. Meta blamed technical errors for the removal of posts about Palestine during the 2021 conflict, and on the recent shadowbanning claims a company representative pointed TechCrunch to a Threads post by Stone: "We identified a bug impacting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts, meaning they weren't showing up properly in people's Stories tray, leading to significantly reduced reach. This bug affected accounts equally around the globe and had nothing to do with the subject matter of the content — and we fixed it as quickly as possible." Stone separately directed TechCrunch to the updated newsroom post, which said Meta identified and fixed a "bug" that prevented users from going live: "This was also a global issue that was fixed within a few hours. We understand people rely on these tools and we're sorry to anyone who felt the impact of these issues."

The rebuttal's reach is limited in ways the reporting records. It is unclear whether the bug affected accounts posting content unrelated to Gaza, while Instagram users have posted screenshots showing Stories about Palestine receiving significantly fewer views than other Stories posted the same day, and allege their view counts recovered when they posted content unrelated to the conflict. Meta's representative did not address the other accusations of censorship beyond Story visibility and did not respond to TechCrunch's follow-up questions; Meta initially did not respond to follow-up requests for comment. Asked about comments containing the Palestinian flag, Stone again pointed to the updated newsroom post, which did not directly address the issue, and he declined to comment on allegations of Meta disproportionately flagging Arabic news content, directing TechCrunch to the same post, which did not directly address those allegations either.



---


# Gaza Tech Workers' Connectivity Collapse

"The tech sector is almost completely unable to function in Gaza right now," Iliana Montauk told TechCrunch on 2023-10-14. "Most people are in too much danger to be able to work; some have evacuated three times in the past 24 hours, moving from friend's house to family house, because each neighborhood they end up in is the next one being bombed. They usually receive warnings to evacuate their homes 10 minutes before a bombing, so they don't sleep and monitor the situation constantly ready to evacuate in a minute's notice."

On the technical side: "Most people have lost cell phone connections and internet access completely, or have some access to 2G only on their cell phones. Electricity is no longer being provided even for a few hours a day now, and people are running out of gas for their generators." Manara has around 100 software engineers in Gaza, some working remotely for tech companies in Silicon Valley/Europe.



---


# The Gaza Information War And The Hamas Narrative

Eylon Levy argues that the conflict is not only a kinetic war in Gaza but also an information war, in which the Hamas narrative is adopted far more easily than Israel's account is accepted. His first ground is a case of a claim that collapsed: the day after what he calls the bluff about the Al-Ahli hospital, which the Palestinians claimed had been hit by an Israeli missile killing 800 civilians but which in the end turned out to have been caused by a splinter group of Islamic Jihad, with no hospital destroyed and certainly not 800 people killed, he explained on Sky News that Hamas lies and makes up numbers, and the reporter asked him, almost speechless with surprise, whether he doubts Hamas' numbers. He describes such moments as intensely frustrating, recounting a BBC interview in which the interviewer told him "Hamas denies what you are saying", to which his answer is that of course Hamas denies this, since Hamas denies that it is even holding hostages, and Hamas massacres, beheads, rapes, burns families and then day and night denies that it did so. Some journalists around the world see that Hamas continues to lie about the biggest things when the whole truth is in front of everyone's eyes, and they continue to echo the lies.

His second ground is a structural claim about where information from Gaza comes from: it comes either directly from Hamas or from independent reporters and photographers who are part of the system in Gaza, and everyone knows that even if they are not affiliated with Hamas they are not free to present the full truth because they are not allowed to. The evidence he offers for the constraint is what is missing: there is not a single photo of a terrorist, not a single photo of a missile being launched from a densely populated area, from a mosque or a school, not even a single photo from the Hamas tunnels under Shifa; the reason is that these reporters, even if not explicitly on Hamas' side, operate under a dictatorial regime and cannot provide the information even if they wanted to, which is why he thinks it very important to keep reminding the world how biased the information reaching them is. Levy qualifies the argument explicitly: he does not want to give the impression that all interviewers are hostile and every question delusional, and he has many interviews with reporters who understand what is happening and simply want information and to hear the Israeli side, which is completely legitimate.



---


# Hamas Fundraising After October 7

Although it has been almost impossible to transfer money and goods to Gaza since October 7, with hawala shuttered and no trade, Hamas continues to raise funds — chiefly through Judea and Samaria and through online platforms abroad.

"The situation in Gaza is known, and nothing can be brought in, but fundraising activity continues in Judea and Samaria," Ostrovitch-Levi says. "It's also possible to make bank transfers to Judea and Samaria, and the fundraising activity hasn't stopped, because while the fighting is going on, they're continuing to fill their reserves for 'the day after' [the war]. We realize they're raising funds for their continued operations. Hamas is taking advantage of the current sympathy for the Gazans' situation, and is using online platforms, both of organizations whose business is crowdfunding, and also through the creation of fictitious projects to raise funds: throw-pillows, jewelry and whatnot, and more." All of this happens openly in Europe and other places around the world: "Hamas and Islamic Jihad carry out recruitment operations under the guise of humanitarian aid campaigns, and use Telegram, Twitter, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok to disseminate their announcements. The facade is always supporting humanitarian goals, but in practice it's about channels for funding individuals and entities connected directly to Hamas or Islamic Jihad." IMPA's goal is not only to stop individual fundraising but the entire interrelated chain, from fund-raiser to transferrer to recipient: "We have the ability to build the intelligence scenario, synchronize all the sources of information received, and delineate the money trail from abroad to Hamas. We're interested not only in who is running the campaign, the association or entity, but where the money is coming from, and where it's going. We need to stop all of the elements in this network."



---


# The Israeli Proposal To Temporarily House Gazans In Sinai

The Israeli government has spoken to counterparts in several countries about Egypt temporarily housing Palestinians fleeing the violence in Gaza, according to officials with knowledge of the matter. Israel suggested they could be moved to tent camps in the Sinai Peninsula — funded by the United Nations and the US — and then returned once military operations end, said the people. It is unclear whether Israel has put the idea directly to Egypt.

The reasoning behind the approach was economic. "Clearly the hope on Israel and the US's side had been that Egypt would accept economic incentives, at a time when it is suffering an economic crisis, to allow Gazans into Egypt," said Mirette Mabrouk, director of the Egypt program at the Washington-based Middle East Institute.

# Israel's Restraint Policy Toward Gaza

In an article five years before October 7, Brigadier General Eran Ortal argued that "Israeli restraint as regards proactive thwarting of offensive capabilities in the Gaza Strip stems from a clear Israeli strategy that strives to reduce the influence of the enemy on the current routine of life in Israel, even at the price of worsening of the threat in the future."

Ortal treated the policy as natural — "a Western nation cannot lead its life in an endless state of emergency" — but insisted that "alongside the understanding of the need for a containment policy, it must be recognized that the risks are high, as evidenced by the steeply worsening intensity of conflicts between Israel and the terrorist organizations in Gaza." His grounds are the adversary's adaptation: in recent decades Hamas and Hezbollah developed ballistic missiles and terror tunnels in response to Israeli policy that sought minimal friction with the enemy through separation and withdrawal from the security zone in southern Lebanon and the Gaza Strip. He points out that between Operation Pillar of Defense in 2012 and Operation Protective Edge in 2014, Israel significantly reduced targeted countermeasures against terrorist operatives, and none focused on Hamas operatives; his analysis is that because Iron Dome only came into use in 2011, the most dangerous threat posed by Gaza developed in the period preceding Operation Protective Edge. The understandings Israel reached with Hamas in 2012 were made "to stop the fighting," Ortal says, and to get life back to normal as quickly as possible — after air raid sirens sounded in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem for the first time since the Yom Kippur War and the education system shut down for more than a week. In 2018 Ortal wrote of "the barrier" that "it would be wrong to assume it will turn out to be more immune than its predecessors. The longer as we delay cutting the direct connection between the Hamas rockets and those of our other enemies, who make extensive use of this method of operation, and the idea of attacking our territory, the longer we will be condemned to watch from the sidelines and look at their constant enhancement." Ortal is currently in active military service and unavailable for interview.

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Criminal Trial

## Definition

In this corpus, "criminal trial" names the government's federal prosecution of Sam Bankman-Fried in Manhattan on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, in which prosecutors presented witness testimony to prove guilt while the defense contested it, U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan presided, and a jury returned the verdict.
The corpus uses the term specifically to distinguish this proceeding — and the format of Epic Games v. Google, a civil jury trial — from non-criminal, civil proceedings such as the Trump/Engoron case, which sought financial penalties rather than imprisonment.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal criminal trial in Manhattan, on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, presided over by U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan; the trial ran roughly six weeks, opening with jury selection on October 3, 2023 and opening statements the next day, and closing in a guilty verdict on all counts.
The proceeding follows a recognizable structure the corpus documents in sequence: jury selection, opening statements from prosecution and defense, the prosecution's case (fact witnesses like Adam Yedidia and Matt Huang, cooperating former co-conspirators Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison testifying under cooperation agreements, and expert testimony from accounting professor Peter Easton), cross-examination, the defendant's own testimony and cross-examination, closing arguments, and jury deliberation toward a verdict.
The corpus also shows what a criminal trial is not, by contrast: the parallel civil case against Donald Trump before Judge Arthur Engoron was a non-jury ("bench") trial brought by the New York attorney general seeking financial penalties, not imprisonment, and the corpus notes Manhattan prosecutors had considered and declined to bring a criminal case over the same underlying conduct — the state instead pursued civil fraud remedies. Epic Games v. Google is likewise a civil antitrust jury trial (Sherman Act, Cartwright Act claims) seeking injunctive and monetary relief, not a criminal prosecution, even though it shares the jury-trial format.

## Key Characteristics

- **Adversarial structure** — a prosecution (the government, e.g. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Danielle Sassoon, Nicolas Roos, and Thane Rehn in the SBF case) argues guilt while defense counsel (Mark Cohen, Christian Everdell) argues innocence or lack of criminal intent.
- **Jury as fact-finder** — a jury, not the judge, decides guilt; in the SBF trial the jury included a train conductor and a retired investment banker, and reporters repeatedly note what testimony "the jury saw" or "the jury will have to decide."
- **Burden and standard tied to criminal charges** — the prosecution must show the defendant's conduct was not just harmful but criminal; as one account puts it, "Just losing $8 billion is not a crime... But if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing... that's a crime," turning the case on proving intentional deceit and conspiracy rather than mere loss or business failure.
- **Cooperating witnesses and immunity/plea deals** — co-conspirators such as Gary Wang, Caroline Ellison, and witnesses like Adam Yedidia testified under cooperation agreements or legal immunity, a common feature of criminal trials involving multiple alleged participants.
- **Judge as referee, not fact-finder** — Judge Kaplan ruled on objections, instructed the jury on the law, and controlled testimony (e.g., telling the jury he was the "final authority" on the definition of "market manipulation"), while leaving the guilt determination to the jury.
- **Sentencing follows conviction** — a guilty verdict is followed by a separate sentencing phase; the corpus notes SBF's charges could put him in prison for the rest of his life and co-conspirator Gary Wang faced up to 50 years pending sentencing.
- **Distinct from civil trials** — civil proceedings (Trump/Engoron, Epic v. Google) can share elements like juries or trial-style testimony but seek monetary or injunctive remedies under a different legal standard, and can proceed without a jury at all (non-jury "bench" trial).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, a criminal trial is a court proceeding, initiated only by the government, in which the prosecution must prove the defendant's guilt "beyond a reasonable doubt" — a heavier standard than in civil cases — while the jury decides guilt and the judge oversees the proceeding and, on a guilty verdict, determines the sentence (U.S. Courts, "Criminal Cases," uscourts.gov, accessed 2026-09-02).

# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# Plea Agreement

## Definition

In the corpus, a plea agreement is the deal by which a criminal defendant (or, in Binance's case, a company) pleads guilty to specified charges in exchange for concessions, rather than going to trial.
It takes effect only once a judge accepts it, and it can bind the party to concrete obligations — cooperating with prosecutors, accepting a recommended fine, stepping back from a role, or admitting specific facts — beyond the bare admission of guilt.

## Context

The corpus shows plea agreements as the mechanism by which several defendants in overlapping 2023 white-collar and criminal cases resolved their charges outside of a trial.
FTX co-founder Gary Wang and Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors, becoming key witnesses against Sam Bankman-Fried at his fraud trial (doc_0010, doc_0086).
FTX engineering head Nishad Singh similarly pleaded guilty to six charges (doc_0121).
Binance CEO Changpeng "CZ" Zhao and Binance itself each entered separate plea agreements with the U.S. Department of Justice, resolving anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations as part of a $4.3 billion settlement (doc_0374, doc_0375).
YouTube parenting influencer Ruby Franke's plea agreement, accepted by a judge, both formalized her guilty plea to child-abuse charges and documented detailed admissions about the abuse itself (doc_0269).
The corpus also shows a distinct but related instrument — the cooperation agreement Gary Wang signed, which specifically obligated him to meet with prosecutors and answer truthfully (doc_0226) — and notes that a witness's incentive to plead guilty and cooperate (the hope of sentencing leniency) is something a defense team can attack on cross-examination (doc_0293).

## Key Characteristics

- **Court acceptance is required** — a judge must accept the plea agreement before it takes effect; Ruby Franke's sentencing was scheduled only after Judge John J. Walton accepted her plea agreement (doc_0269).
- **Negotiated concessions, not just an admission** — the document can specify what each side gives up: Zhao agreed to a recommended $150 million CFTC fine and to not contradict his acceptance of responsibility, while Binance's agreement barred Zhao from any future role at the company for three years and required it to maintain an independent compliance monitor (doc_0374).
- **Can include cooperation with prosecutors** — Wang and Ellison's guilty pleas were paired with plans to cooperate with, and testify for, the prosecution (doc_0010); Wang's cooperation obligations were spelled out in a separate signed agreement (doc_0226).
- **Distinct from pleading not guilty** — a defendant who instead maintains innocence, as Bankman-Fried did, pleads not guilty and proceeds to trial rather than entering a plea agreement (doc_0010).
- **Can contain substantive factual admissions** — Franke's plea agreement recorded specific admitted details of the abuse itself, beyond the bare fact of guilt (doc_0269).
- **Creates a cross-examination target** — because cooperating witnesses who pleaded guilty may hope for sentencing leniency, defense counsel can (and, per the corpus, did) argue this gives them an incentive to shape testimony favorably to the prosecution (doc_0293).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the general legal definition is broader than any single case above: a plea bargain (or plea agreement) is an agreement between a defendant and a prosecutor in which the defendant agrees to plead guilty to some or all of the charges, usually in exchange for a concession from the prosecutor, such as a reduced charge or a more lenient sentencing recommendation.
Source: Legal Information Institute (LII), Cornell Law School, "plea bargain," https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/plea_bargain (accessed 2026-09-02).

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.

# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. # Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.

# Bankman-Fried's Decision To Testify Backfired

The Verge's trial reporter argued that Bankman-Fried's choice to take the stand was a net loss for his defense: like Theranos' Elizabeth Holmes before him, he got on the stand to speak directly to his state of mind in a way no other witness can, but telling your side of the story opens you to a great many questions you might not want to answer on cross-examination — and, having watched a lot of crosses, she called Sassoon's the nastiest she had ever seen.

The warrant is what the charges turn on. The case hinged on conspiracy and intentional deceit: just losing $8 billion is not a crime, though it is very embarrassing, but if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing and how safe FTX was, that is a crime. Because state of mind was the contested issue, his own testimony became the evidence, and it did not hold: Sassoon had established the day before that he has a long history of dishonesty, and on October 31st, through a set of questions about what he did and did not do, she established that the story he told on direct examination was absurd. After a brief redirect by his own lawyers, resplendent with word salad, Bankman-Fried stepped down and the defense rested.

The direct examination had already supplied grounds. Beyond the two obvious lies the reporter counted him telling on the stand — about Alameda Research's name and about "allow_negative" — she was struck by how little he seemed to know about his own companies: apparently Singh, Wang, and Ellison were out there just doing whatever their little hearts desired, because Bankman-Fried was a CEO, but definitely not the kind that pays any attention to money at his crypto trading firm and futures exchange.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.

# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."

# Trump Motions to Dismiss the Fraud Case Rejected

Trump's lawyers asked the judge to throw out the case, and he denied the request. Their arguments attacked the attorney general's standing and the timing of the claims: they contend that James was not legally allowed to file the lawsuit because there is no evidence that the public was harmed by Trump's actions, and they also argued that many of the allegations in the lawsuit were barred by the statute of limitations.

Engoron, noting that he had "emphatically rejected" those arguments earlier in the case, equated them to the "time-loop in the film 'Groundhog Day.'"

# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." # SBF Taking The Stand As A "Hail Mary"

SBF taking to the stand in his own trial is a "Hail Mary" ahead of a verdict and potential sentencing for seven counts tied to fraud and money laundering. That is the claim former federal prosecutor Josh Naftalis made to TechCrunch in coverage published 2023-10-06.

The grounds Naftalis gives are that testifying is irreversible once it starts: "Once it goes to cross[-examination], he doesn't get to say, 'I'm done,'" he said. "He can't just walk out if he doesn't like how it's going." The warrant joining those grounds to the claim is that a defendant who takes the stand hands control of the questioning to the other side and cannot take it back — which is what makes the move a last-resort gamble rather than an ordinary defense choice.

Naftalis spoke at length about what comes next in the trial, and addressed common misconceptions about the prosecution and the defense, in the latest episode of TechCrunch's Chain Reaction podcast, which can be listened to on Apple Podcasts or Spotify.

# Sam Bankman-Fried's Federal Fraud Trial

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange FTX, is charged with seven counts of fraud and money laundering following the collapse of his cryptocurrency empire the previous year, and was on trial in New York in October 2023.

Two fixed points anchor the proceeding as CNBC described it on 2023-10-06. A U.S. judge revoked Bankman-Fried's bail at a hearing in a New York courthouse on August 11, 2023. And on Thursday, Oct. 5, 2023, Matt Huang, co-founder of Paradigm Operations LP, arrived at the New York court to appear in the case.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# Binance's $4.3B DOJ Resolution And CZ's Guilty Plea

Changpeng Zhao, also known as "CZ," the founder and CEO of Binance, is stepping down and has pleaded guilty to a number of violations brought on through the Department of Justice and other U.S. agencies; he appeared in a Seattle federal court on Tuesday, November 21, 2023 to enter his plea. Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, has also agreed to pay about $4.3 billion to resolve the DOJ's investigations, the agency said in a press release that Tuesday.

As part of Binance's guilty plea, it has also reached agreements with the Department of Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), and will credit about $1.8 billion toward those resolutions.

The crypto exchange "admits it engaged in anti-money laundering, unlicensed money transmitting and sanctions violations," the DOJ release stated, calling it the "largest corporate resolution" that included criminal charges for an executive; Zhao pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an anti-money laundering program. "The message here should be clear: using new technology to break the law does not make you a disruptor, it makes you a criminal," U.S. Attorney General Merrick Garland said in a statement.

# Trump's Other Criminal and Civil Cases 2023

Letitia James' lawsuit is one of several legal headaches for Trump as he campaigns for a return to the White House in 2024. He has been indicted four times in the six months to September 2023 — accused in Georgia and Washington, D.C., of plotting to overturn his 2020 election loss; in Florida of hoarding classified documents; and in Manhattan of falsifying business records related to hush money paid on his behalf.

Separately, the Trump Organization was convicted of tax fraud in 2022 in an unrelated criminal case for helping executives dodge taxes on extravagant perks such as Manhattan apartments and luxury cars, and the company was fined $1.6 million. One of the executives, Trump's longtime finance chief Allen Weisselberg, pleaded guilty and served five months in jail; he is a defendant in James' lawsuit and gave sworn deposition testimony for the case in May.
