# Britney Spears' Engagement To Jason Trawick

Britney Spears and Jason Trawick, a Hollywood agent who worked at WME, began dating in 2009 and became engaged in December 2011, but called off the engagement in January 2013 and announced they were going their separate ways.

Spears said in a statement sent by her representative to ABC News: "Jason and I have decided to call off our engagement. I'll always adore him and we will remain great friends." Trawick issued his own statement at the time: "As this chapter ends for us a new one begins. I love and cherish her and her boys and we will be close forever."

Travis Kelce broke his silence on Taylor Swift's Chiefs game attendance on his podcast on 27 September 2023, while saying he would not speak much more about the relationship, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023.

# Travis Kelce's Friendship Bracelet Overtures To Taylor Swift

Travis Kelce's public overtures to Taylor Swift began with friendship bracelets in mid-2023, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023, which dates the sequence precisely.

On 29 June, Kelce made a friendship bracelet to give to the newcomers at a camp for NFL tight ends, saying he was "taking a page out of Taylor Swift's book" — the timeline flags this as possibly where it all began. On 26 July, Kelce announced he had gone to Swift's highly anticipated concert but had not had the chance to meet the 12-time Grammy winner. "I was disappointed that she doesn't talk before or after her shows because she has to save her voice for the 44 songs she sings ... She doesn't meet anybody, or at least she didn't want to meet me, so I took it personal," Kelce said on an episode of the "New Heights" podcast he does with his brother, Philadelphia Eagles center Jason Kelce. He revealed that he had made a friendship bracelet — a fan tradition at her concerts — with his number on it to give to her, and when his brother asked whether it was his jersey number or his phone number, Kelce replied, "you know which one," adding: "If you're up on Taylor Swift concerts, there are friendship bracelets and I had received a bunch of them, but I wanted to give Taylor Swift one with my number on it." On 5 August, well before the two were rumoured to be dating, Kelce was asked his celebrity crush, and before he could answer the answer was given for him.

On 21 September, speaking on the Pat McAfee show, Kelce discussed the rumours and sounded somehow surprised people were talking about it: "It is hilarious how much traction this has actually got. It's like that old game in school called telephone where everybody is just whispering in each others ear, just hearing some random stuff. Especially when you got Jason Kelce on live television telling people just both sides." He then admitted he had invited Swift to one of his games, joking they would compete to see who put on the bigger show at Arrowhead Stadium: "I threw it out there, I threw the ball in her court and I told her you know, I've seen you rock the stage in Arrowhead you might have to come see me rock the stage in Arrowhead and see which one is a little more lit. We will see what happens in the near future." On 22 September, Kelce was spotted at his nonprofit charity event wearing a bracelet reading "Vigilante Sh--," the name of one of Swift's songs.

# Travis Kelce's WSJ Magazine Interview on Swift

In an interview with WSJ Magazine published on 20 November 2023, Travis Kelce described how much he admires Taylor Swift's skills as a musician and said he was not letting media attention affect the relationship.

"I've never been a man of words. Being around her, seeing how smart Taylor is, has been f***ing mind-blowing. I'm learning every day," he explained. Kelce acknowledged the public attention his personal life had received because he has "never dated anyone with that kind of aura around them", but specified that he was not letting the media affect his relationship.

"But at the same time, I'm not running away from any of it," he said. # The NFL's Defence Of Its Taylor Swift-Themed Promotion

The NFL defended its Swift-themed social media branding on 5 October 2023: the claim is that the Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce news is a pop cultural moment the league leaned into in real time, and the warrant is that it sits at the intersection of sport and entertainment and has produced an incredible amount of positivity around the sport.

The prompt was the branding itself. Swift coverage was everywhere and the league changed its X, formerly Twitter, bio to read "NFL (Taylor's Version)," a Swift lyric reference, while its Instagram account read "Chiefs are 2-0 as Swifties." Some found issue with these changes.

The league's statement gave its standing practice as the first ground: "We frequently change our bios and profile imagery based on what's happening in and around our games, as well as culturally. # Travis Kelce's Criticism That The NFL Overdid Its Taylor Swift Coverage

Travis Kelce agreed on his podcast that the National Football League was overdoing its coverage of his rumoured girlfriend Taylor Swift, undercutting the league's implicit claim that leaning into the story was simply adding to the broadcast. Speaking after his game against the New York Jets on 1 October 2023, the 33-year-old Kansas City Chiefs tight end discussed the broadcast with his brother Jason, 35, on an episode of New Heights with Jason and Travis Kelce titled "The NFL Needs to Calm Down." The two addressed complaints from longtime football enthusiasts frustrated by constant Swift references during the game at MetLife Stadium: the league had promoted the fixture by speculating about whether the Grammy winner would attend, cameras panned constantly to the star-studded suite where Swift sat with Blake Lively, Ryan Reynolds, Sophie Turner and Hugh Jackman, and the NFL ran a special segment in which Carson Daly of The Voice attempted to explain football to "Swifties."

Asked plainly by Jason whether the NFL was overdoing it, Kelce first said "I think everybody is just, like, overwhelmed," and, pressed to set aside his feelings for Swift, hedged: "I think it brings a little more to the atmosphere, it brings a little bit more to what you're watching. But at the same time, I think..." His brother, the Philadelphia Eagles player, finished the thought — "They're overdoing it" — and Kelce agreed: "They're overdoing it a little bit, for sure. Especially my situation. I think they're just trying to have fun with it." Commenters under the New Heights video echoed the complaint: "I agree the NFL needs to calm down. Pissing off football fans is not how you repay your boi [sic] for all he's done for the sport"; "Pity Taylor. All she ever wanted was to watch the football game. Now she's being blamed and hated left and right"; "The NFL needs to seriously tone it down and let Trav and Tay explore this beautiful thing they have going on in peace."

# Travis Kelce's Moustache Remark And New York Visit

In August 2023 Travis Kelce hinted on the New Heights podcast that Taylor Swift would like his moustache — a clear suggestion he had made contact with her — and shortly afterwards took a week off training to visit New York City while Swift was re-recording her 1989 tracks there, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

The brothers were discussing the moustache Kelce grows every year in honour of the Chiefs' head coach, Andy Reid. Asked if he knew what Swift thought of the 'stache, he remained cheekily confident: "We're not going to bring up Taylor Swift in this episode," he says, "But something tells me she's going to like it."

# Travis Kelce's "Breeder" Remarks On The New Heights Podcast

Travis Kelce, 34, made remarks about starting a family during a February 2023 episode of New Heights, the podcast he hosts with his brother Jason, that resurfaced in October 2023 amid his romance with Taylor Swift — after a source claimed to Yahoo Entertainment that the couple "have talked about kids" within the next year. In the episode, recorded while the Philadelphia Eagles and Kansas City Chiefs were preparing to meet in the Super Bowl, Jason asked their mother Donna which of her sons she was "rooting for." "You've said in the past to both of us that you root for me because I've given you grandkids," said Jason, who shares three children — Wyatt, four, Elliotte, two, and Bennett, seven months — with wife Kylie Kelce. "I've always known that you root for Travis. So who do you actually root for?"

Pressed again, "if in a battle to the death," Donna deflected by asking whom Jason would save if she and her husband Ed Kelce were stranded in the middle of the ocean, and said she could not pick which son to root against; Jason joked, "Remember if you choose me, Wyatt and Elliotte grow up without a father." Travis then chimed in about wanting his own family: "I gotta start breeding. I've gotta start breeding, to all the breeders out there." Jason replied "Please don't," and Donna advised: "Wait until you find the right person. Find the right person." Travis doubled down: "I'm gonna find a breeder, and I'm gonna get kids so that mom can love me again."

# The Kelce Brothers' Criticism Of NFL Swift Coverage

Travis and Jason Kelce said on 6 October 2023 that the NFL was doing too much with its Swift-Kelce coverage, a counter aimed not at showing celebrities at all but at the amount of it, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023.

Travis conceded the underlying value before rejecting the execution: "I think it's fun when they show who's at the game. I think it brings a little bit more to the atmosphere, brings a little bit more to what you're watching. But at the same time, they're overdoing it a little bit."

Jason attacked the league's inexperience by comparison with another sport: "I just think the NFL is not used to celebrities coming to the games. Like basketball has it all figured out. They're all courtside, they're sitting there. They show 'em once or twice, but then they get back to the game."



---


# Britney Spears' 55-Hour Marriage To Jason Alexander

Jason Alexander was Britney Spears' first husband: the two married at a wedding chapel in Las Vegas in 2004 and annulled the marriage only 55 hours after the ceremony. Alexander returned to the news in 2022 when he tried to attend Spears' wedding to Sam Asghari, and could be heard in a video saying he was going to crash the nuptials. "She's my first wife, my only wife," he reportedly told security. "I'm her first husband, I'm here to crash the wedding."

Alexander was arrested for trespassing, vandalism, and battery over the incident. A security guard later revealed in court that when Alexander crashed the wedding he also tried to enter Spears' bedroom.

qid: Does the article from FOX News - Entertainment suggest that Arnold Schwarzenegger and Reese Witherspoon advocate for a similar parenting style, as opposed to the article from The Independent - Life and Style which discusses the issue of parental controls with Roblox?
context:
# Celebrity Tough-Love Parenting In Hollywood

"Tough-love parenting" is FOX News Entertainment's 10 October 2023 label for the harsher styles some celebrities have described in interviews, prompted by the fact that Hollywood is a tough place to raise kids.

The category has two discriminating strands. The first is disciplinary severity: stars like Arnold Schwarzenegger, who admitted to being like a "drill instructor" when his kids were young, and Reese Witherspoon, who said she wants kids to deal with failure more directly.

The second is a wealth-and-gratitude strand: others, like Ashton Kutcher and Mila Kunis and Kristen Bell and Dax Shepard, are focused on keeping their kids grateful for growing up in famous families with wealth and privilege at their fingertips.



---


# Schwarzenegger's Warning On "A Generation Of Wimps"

Arnold Schwarzenegger warned on "The Howard Stern Show" that if young people are over-pampered, the nation may be "creating a generation of wimps and weak people", FOX News Entertainment reported on 10 October 2023.

His grounds are a claim about how character forms: "You can only strengthen your character and become a really strong person inside if you have resistance, if you fail, if you get up again and if you work hard."

The warrant joining the two is that pampering removes exactly the resistance, failure and effort he identifies as the mechanism of strength — so protecting children from hardship produces weakness rather than preventing it. The former California governor issued the warning recently, in the context of his own disciplinarian parenting.



---


# Roblox's Response On Its Parental Safety Tools

Roblox rejected the premise of Sarah Michelle Gellar's complaint that it lacks parental help, telling The Independent that such tools already exist and that the company was investigating her case. "We are looking into this case and we reached out directly to the user to help. We are committed to ensuring that our users have a positive experience on the platform," a spokesperson said.

The substance of the rebuttal is the provision the company says is already in place: "In partnership with safety groups, we've developed tools and resources like our Parent & Caregiver Guide and other helpful resources for parents to have conversations with their kids and teens about staying safe, spending controls and protecting their account. Our support team works with parents and users directly 24/7 and can be contacted with questions here," the spokesperson added, including a link to the company's support page.



---


# Arnold Schwarzenegger's "Drill Instructor" Discipline

Arnold Schwarzenegger recently admitted he had a "drill instructor" approach to parenting when his children were young, telling People while promoting his new book that he once burned his daughter Katherine's shoes in front of her, FOX News Entertainment reported on 10 October 2023.

Schwarzenegger, who shares four children with ex-wife Maria Shriver and also shares a son with Mildred Baena, the family's former housekeeper, recalled a moment when Katherine brought over her 3-year-old daughter Lyla and he saw the lesson passed down: "Katherine comes over with Lyla, and she says, 'Lyla, I told you already not to put the shoes there. Keep your shoes on, or you put them away, but you don't leave them there by the stand in front of the fireplace because you know what Daddy did? When I left my shoes there twice? The third time, he burned them in front of me and I cried,'" he said. Schwarzenegger said the story was "absolutely" true and took pride in knowing that Katherine uses the same methods, "which she cried over, and she complained about", with Lyla as well as her other daughter Eloise, both of whom she shares with husband Chris Pratt.

The 76-year-old described similar approaches with his eldest son Patrick. When Patrick was 9 and had not made his bed, Schwarzenegger threw his mattress off the balcony: "I opened up the door to the balcony, picked up the mattress and threw it down with the bedsheets, the pillows, everything. I said, 'Don't ever make someone come in and clean your room, clean your shower or make your bed… Because I taught you how to make the bed.'" He also battled over shower time with Patrick, feeling he was taking too long, and installed a timer similar to ones he had used in Munich: "And so when he got the shower on, and he was whistling and singing in there and thinking Daddy's not around, all the sudden the ice-cold shower came on. And all of a sudden, we heard downstairs the scream."



---


# The Social Media Reaction To Gellar's Roblox Feud

Many users on X, formerly known as Twitter, were surprised by Sarah Michelle Gellar's unexpected feud with the online gaming platform. Responding to her Instagram Story, one person said: "This is the most important beef of 2023." Another joked: "Buffy vs Roblox is where all this Millennial vs Gen Z discourse has been heading."

Reactions were not uniformly sympathetic. While one user agreed that "being hacked on Roblox is life ruining," another questioned why Gellar's 11-year-old son had access to his mother's credit card in the first place: "Oh please. That's not that bad. And I don't know why parents let their children use their debit/credit cards on games, like, make them pay themselves!"



---


# Gellar And Prinze's Strict Household Rules

Freddie Prinze Jr. said he and Sarah Michelle Gellar "are strict as hell" with their two children, and that Gellar has "100 rules" the kids know they cannot break, in a 2021 Us Weekly interview reported by FOX News Entertainment on 10 October 2023.

The "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" star and her husband have been married for more than 20 years and share two kids, aged 13 and 11 at the time of the 2021 interview. "Look, I don't believe in whooping kids. I've never whooped mine. My mom whooped me. They were, like, preventative whooping, so I know how to be strict," the "I Know What You Did Last Summer" star told the outlet. Of the rules he added: "They know they can't break [those rules]. Friendships come and go. I tell my kids all the time that family is forever. So, we have rules, and they've got to follow [them]."

Gellar told Us Weekly in 2020 that as parents their "expectations are a little higher than most": "I think [our children] know what the rules are. We have [family dinner] as many nights as we can. We have no phones at the table. We sit, we all have dinner together."



---


# Sarah Michelle Gellar's Complaint After Her Son's Roblox Account Was Hacked

Sarah Michelle Gellar, 46, publicly criticised Roblox on 4 December 2023 after her son's account on the platform was allegedly hacked, forcing her to cancel her credit card. The Buffy the Vampire Slayer star — who shares son Rocky, 11, and daughter Charlotte Grace, 14, with husband Freddie Prinze Jr — posted to her Instagram Story a screenshot from her iPhone showing a notification that her iCloud account "has been disabled" in the App Store and iTunes.

"This is what I've been dealing with after my son's @Roblox got hacked," she wrote. "I had to cancel my credit card and now my life is basically cancelled." The Cruel Intentions actor added a direct challenge to the company: "@Roblox Why don't you have better parental help?!?"



---


# Candace Cameron Bure's Strict But Loving Boundaries

Candace Cameron Bure described her parenting style to L.A. Parent as strict but loving — "We set firm boundaries, but there is always love and grace" — and said her goal is not to make her kids happy but to guide them into responsible adults, FOX News Entertainment reported on 10 October 2023.

The "Full House" star is a mom of three with husband Valeri Bure — Natasha, Lev and Maksim, all now in their early 20s — and spoke to the outlet when they were teenagers. "I hope my kids would say that I'm a loving mom," she said. "They would also describe me as strict." She continued: "I'm the mom that needs to meet the parents before my kids can go to a new friend's house. I want to know who they're with, where they're going. Even now that they're driving, I want them to text me when they arrive and when they're heading home."

Bure explained that they "work hard to keep our communication open and talk through any situation" and are "always willing to listen", but added: "I don't always say yes. My goal as a parent is not to make my kids happy but to guide them to be respectful, curious, responsible, resilient, kind, giving and thoughtful adults."



---


# Reese Witherspoon On Letting Children Fail

Reese Witherspoon argues that learning from failure "is actually a valuable tool that you can't take away from kids" — "You rob them if you don't let them sit in the discomfort of the experience" — speaking on the "Good Inside with Dr. Becky" podcast as reported by FOX News Entertainment on 10 October 2023.

Her grounds are her own upbringing. "I see this a lot with parents – I don't know when we stopped letting our kids fail. Like I learned so much from the paper I didn't turn in or the demerits I got, so I got detention. I was suspended from school," she recalled, adding: "And my parents didn't say, 'Uh, she didn't deserve that,' and take me out of school. They actually let me sit in it and feel uncomfortable." The Oscar winner, who shares her eldest children Ava and Deacon with ex-husband Ryan Phillippe and her youngest, Tennessee, with ex-husband Jim Toth, said she wants to see kids live with failure a little more.

The warrant is that discomfort teaches something removal cannot, including self-knowledge about limits. The "Walk the Line" star remembered comforting her daughter after she lost a basketball game while not shying away from the lesson: she said, "'Yeah, I know. I know that probably feels really bad,'" then added, "'You know what also? Maybe you're not good at basketball?'" Her daughter was slightly upset in the moment, but Witherspoon continued: "It's actually really important to learn what you're not good at."



---


# Kutcher And Kunis Keeping Their Children Grounded

Mila Kunis said she keeps her and Ashton Kutcher's children's privilege in check by reminding them that "Mommy and Daddy have money, but they're broke all the time", in a 2020 interview on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" reported by FOX News Entertainment on 10 October 2023.

The couple have been married since 2015 and share two children, daughter Wyatt, 9, and son Dmitri, 6. "That is not their bedroom, it is my bedroom that I'm letting them use, so they better take good care of it," she said with a laugh, continuing: "I say this in jest, but really they don't have things … they're raised on hand-me-downs from girlfriends' kids' clothing; we garden."

Kunis noted her kids are lucky to be born into a famous family and said she wants to ensure they are grateful: "Our kids are super-fortunate. Regardless, they were born at the right time to the right people, and I love them, but they're not going to be entitled a--holes."



---


# Roblox As An Online Game Platform

Roblox is a widely popular online game platform that "lets you play, create, and be anything you can imagine," according to its description on the Microsoft Store. Its defining features are that players customise characters and play minigames within the game, and that while the platform is free to download on a number of platforms — including Android and iOS smartphones, Xbox game consoles and Windows computers — players can also spend money on in-game items and customisations.

Its user base is young. According to TechCrunch, Roblox's millions of users range between the ages of eight and 18, with its key demographic between nine and 15 years old — the fact that makes parental controls and spending safeguards the recurring point of contention around the platform.



---


# Roblox Versus The Social Media Dopamine Critique

Asked at the Code Conference by Alex Kruglov, who runs the social gaming startup pop.in for a much older user base, what people will stop doing in order to spend their time on Roblox — a Clay Christensen "jobs to be done" question about who they are firing — and asked as a parent of three children, the middle of whom he described as treating Roblox like crack and being highly regulated by her parents, with Alex Heath adding "how dystopian is this going to be?", David Baszucki attacked the premise that all screen time is the same kind of screen time.

His answer was that Roblox is optimistic because, in the specter of social media, there is a wide range of things people do: some consume a lot of short video content and trigger dopamine; some do "compare my life with your life and accelerate FOMO"; and some do something closer to "my kid's on the phone with their friends — they're connecting, inventing, hanging out." He is somewhat optimistic, he said, that the future of Roblox's direction is the last of these: bringing people together when they cannot be together in real life.



---


# Kim Kardashian's Dispute With Roblox Over A Sex Tape Minigame

Sarah Michelle Gellar was not the first celebrity to publicly call out Roblox's parental controls. In the season one premiere of The Kardashians on Hulu, Kim Kardashian confronted the platform after her son Saint, eight, discovered what claimed to be unseen footage of her 2007 sex tape with her ex-boyfriend Ray J. Saint was playing Roblox on a family member's iPad when an icon of Kardashian's crying face appeared on screen; when he showed it to his mother, she pulled the iPad away after reading that the minigame had been registered under the username "KimsNewSexTape." In the episode Kardashian said she planned on "suing" Roblox for using her name and likeness: "I have all the time, all the money, and all of the resources to burn them all to the f***ing ground. This is supposed to be unreleased footage from my old tape, this is the last thing I want as a mom, for my past to be brought up 20 years later."

According to Polygon, the minigame's developer was reportedly banned from the platform when the episode aired in April 2022. A Roblox spokesperson confirmed to the outlet that the game existed but said the "referenced video was never available on our platform - we have strict moderation and policies to protect our community, including zero tolerance for sexual content of any kind which violates our Community Rules. The text reference to the tape that got around our filters was quickly taken down and fortunately visible only to an extremely small number of people on the platform. We also swiftly took down the associated experience and banned the community developer involved with the incident."



---


# Michele Borba on Labelling a Child

Parenting expert and child psychologist Dr. Michele Borba, commenting on the blue bucket controversy, told Fox News Digital that it is "always advisable not to label a child — unless it's for a positive reason."

Her ground is the effect of labels on the child: "Negative labels can impact a child's self-confidence," said the California-based psychologist. But she attaches an immediate limiting clause that keeps the judgment with the family: "But no one knows a child better than a parent."

The decision rule she proposes is therefore comparative rather than categorical: parents should consider whether the label hurts or helps their child interact with others. "For instance, is the child speech delayed? Does he have difficulty interacting with others or expressing his needs? Are others (including his peers) aware of the child's challenges?" she questioned. And the criterion that settles it is the child's own experience, not onlookers': "The ultimate goal is for the child to have a fun Halloween. The parents should never be concerned about others' responses; only do what is best for [the] child."



---


# The Sandwich Generation: Parenting Your Own Parents

The "sandwich generation" is The Guardian's 10 October 2023 name for today's midlifers who find themselves simultaneously parenting their children and their own parents — "In one breath we'll be begging our children to swap French fries for vegetables, and in the next breath we'll be urging our parents to exchange cake for sardines."

The defining feature is that parenting no longer starts and stops with our children, nor is it confined to those who have children: in a time of unrelenting change and ever-extending life, most of us will at some stage find ourselves "parenting" our own parents, and many — particularly those who had families later — will be doing both at once.

The condition that sharpens it is technological. The relentless pace of technology, accelerated by the Covid-19 pandemic, has made everything infinitely more complicated, leaving many older (and not-so-old) people baffled and frustrated; the author reports witnessing friends and family dashing to help parents with poorly designed online banking systems, unruly fridge alarms, "upgraded" software that has changed beyond recognition, apps and phones that do not function as expected, and numerous other technical challenges.



---


# Kristen Bell's Household Screen-Time Rules

Kristen Bell's screen-time rule is that her daughters are not allowed phones or screens at all during the week, with TV permitted on weekends on fairly liberal terms, FOX News Entertainment reported on 10 October 2023.

The rule as she states it: "They're not allowed to play with our phones or have any screens really. They are allowed to watch TV on the weekends, and we're pretty liberal with it, which I've been considering paying more attention to." The weekday ban has a predictable weekend consequence: "But since they're not allowed at all during the week, they will wake up at 6:30 on a Saturday morning, and they will watch TV until noon. I will also sleep until 9:45, which is really nice, and then get stuff done."

The limit Bell herself flags is the handover at the end: "But I will say, I notice how hard it is to pull them away from the TV at noon." She also admits the weekend rules get a little lax.



---


# Roblox's Dating Prediction

David Baszucki predicted at Roblox's developer conference, and repeated at the Code Conference in the interview published October 12th, 2023, that someday someone will build a dating app on Roblox: it will be very safe, it will be for 17-and-up people, and it will be an interesting way for people to connect. The proposition rests on a claimed market gap — there is probably a third of the population that will not go on Bumble or Tinder or Hinge or whatever, just because of awkwardness — and on a mechanism: in immersive 3D avatar-type communication, where one person can be Shrek and another Donald Duck, there is a breakdown of the friction and of the fear of a video call.

The prediction was hedged with a precondition. Baszucki said the company was very careful on that slide, pairing it with the 17-plus, ID-validated users in 17-plus experiences, so parents do not have a heart attack — given Roblox's history of safety and civility and its focus on that.

What would falsify it is straightforward from the way he framed it: if avatar-mediated interaction does not in fact reduce the awkwardness that keeps that third of the population off existing dating apps, or if no such app is built for the ID-validated 17-plus tier, the prediction fails.



---


# Hannah Keeley's Five Christmas Parenting Mistakes

"The biggest mistakes parents make at Christmastime" is a set of five holiday blunders identified by parenting expert Hannah Keeley, the Virginia-based expert who set them out in an email to Fox News Digital published on 9 December 2023.

The organising premise is that pressures are high for parents and caregivers around the holidays, which means there is room for error. Keeley identified the top five holiday blunders that parents often make, and presented them as things parents should try to avoid rather than as a diagnosis of any particular family.



---


# Kevin Federline's 2022 Comments And The Spears Camp's Rebuttal

Britney Spears and her camp rejected Kevin Federline's 2022 claim that their teenage sons were distancing themselves from her because of her social media posts, attacking both the causal premise and Federline's standing to make it public. In an August 2022 interview with ITV, Federline said the couple's sons found it "tough" seeing their mother sharing nude photos online — she had been posting such images while embracing her newfound freedom after the end of her 13-year conservatorship — adding: "I can't imagine how it feels to be a teenager having to go to high school." More than a decade after the marriage ended, the pair were still having ups and downs co-parenting their two teenage sons, Sean Preston and Jayden.

Spears attacked the causal claim in a statement on her Instagram Stories, denying that Instagram was the reason: "It saddens me to hear that my ex husband has decided to discuss the relationship between me and my children … As we all know, raising teenage boys is never easy for anyone. It concerns me the fact that the reason is based on my Instagram … It was LONG before Instagram … I gave them everything … Only one word: HURTFUL." Sam Asghari attacked the factual premise and Federline's motive, accusing him of using their sons to "vilify" his wife and claiming her ex-husband's "gravy train will end soon, which probably explains the timing of these hurtful statements"; he wrote on Instagram that "there is no validity to his statement regarding the kids distancing themselves and it is irresponsible to make that statement publicly." Spears' attorney Mathew Rosengart shifted the attack to Federline's own conduct, saying in a statement obtained by Variety that by posting private videos of Spears sternly speaking with her children without her consent he had created "legal issues" for himself: "Whether he realises it or not, Mr Federline has not only violated the privacy and dignity of the mother of his children, he has undermined his own children, whose privacy he should protect. Putting aside his ITV interview, Mr Federline's ill-advised decision to post an old video of his 11 and 12-year-old children was cruel, bottom of the barrel stuff. It was abhorrent." Rosengart added that "in addition to demeaning himself and violating societal norms, he has now also created various legal issues for himself, including, but not limited to, implicating cyber-harassment and cyber-bullying statutes, among other things."



---


# Sly

Sly, a Netflix documentary about Sylvester Stallone, was available to stream on Netflix in early November 2023. It runs 1 hour 35 minutes, is directed by Thom Zimny, and features Sylvester Stallone, Arnold Schwarzenegger, and Quentin Tarantino.

Polygon describes it as a close look at the life of one of the great American movie stars and film writers. Netflix's own synopsis, reproduced in Polygon's November catalog listing, frames it around origins and arc: his love of film began as an escape from a rocky childhood, and from underdog to Hollywood legend, Stallone tells his story in the documentary.



---


# Arturo Bejar's Critique Of Meta's Teen Safety Self-Regulation

In the absence of a legislative decision, Meta began regulating itself, adding new defaults and features that would restrict teens' access to content on its apps, protect their privacy and limit ad targeting to teens, as well as introducing parental controls. The premise under attack is that this self-regulation was sufficient.

In the weeks before November 15, 2023, a second Meta whistleblower, Arturo Bejar, came forward to express concerns that Instagram's approach to protecting teens was not working to keep them safe from sexual predators and unwanted sexual advances and harassment. Bejar had been hired as a consultant on the matter and eventually blew the whistle on Meta after seeing issues remain unresolved following years of work.

His argument essentially was that the improvements and safety features Meta was implementing were not enough and not effective — so the attack is on efficacy rather than on whether Meta acted at all, and its evidentiary weight comes from his having worked on the problem from inside for years.



---


# The Spears-Federline Child Support And Custody Disputes

In 2018 Kevin Federline asked Britney Spears for an extra $20,000 a month in child support, then, after months of court discussions, rejected her counter-proposal and doubled his request to $40,000 a month; a settlement was finally reached in September 2018, with Spears raising her payments to Federline from $20,000 to $35,000 a month.

The custody balance shifted the following year. Amid her father's health crisis and ongoing emotional distress, Spears voluntarily checked into a mental health treatment facility in 2019. Federline's attorney Mark Kaplan told Entertainment Tonight: "Kevin commends Britney for recognising that she needs to take a step back and that she is taking the reasonable steps to dealing with her situation in a responsible way. He wishes everyone well." That same year, Federline was granted 70 per cent custodial rights and Spears 30 per cent.



---


# The Smith Children: Jaden, Willow And Trey

Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith, married since 1997, share two children together — son Jaden, 25, and daughter Willow, 22 — while Will Smith also has a third child, son Trey, 30, from his first marriage to Sheree Zampino. The distinction matters for how the family is described: Jaden and Willow are the couple's own children, whereas Trey belongs to the earlier marriage and is Will's alone. Jaden, the couple's first child together, was born in July 1998; Willow was born in 2000.

Pinkett Smith credits both of her children with her own development, calling them "little gurus" who have taught her "a deep sense of self-acceptance." She made the remark in the October 2023 interviews surrounding her memoir, in which she also disclosed the couple's long separation. Speaking about that period, she insisted the marriage has never been an open one, saying that she and Will had "eliminated the chance of betrayal" while going on to live their "separate lives."



---


# Alexandra, Moving Home At 37 And Solo Motherhood

Alexandra moved back in with her parents at 37, stayed four months, and later returned for the first three months of her son's life after becoming a solo mother through fertility treatment — an experience she describes as both a privilege and a slide into infantilisation, The Age reported on 25 November 2023.

"While it was lovely to be taken care of, we all tend to regress when we're living with our parents. It's impossible not to feel infantilised, and there's a real tipping point where you start to lean into learnt helplessness," she says. She stayed for four months before moving out to house-sit a friend's place, then launched herself into dating to try to find a man to have a family with; after the roller-coaster of dating she decided to start fertility treatment on her own, and by the time it began she had found a stable job and was renting an apartment. When she got pregnant she was elated but also terrified about how she would raise a child on her own, financially and emotionally. Luckily, after she gave birth her parents invited her to live with them, so she moved back for the first three months of her son's life.

"While it was wonderful to have the emotional and practical support, after three months I felt that if I didn't get out there to live as an independent person, I would quickly lose any sense of what I was capable of. But I'm incredibly grateful for the time I had living with my parents; I know it's a huge privilege to have them as a safety net." She ended up writing a memoir, Inconceivable, about her journey to become a solo mum and the complexities of being a woman in her late 30s who has to start over and move back in with her parents: "I think while we're all embracing this contemporary feminist movement where women can create families of their own making, we're also realising that we need help, that parenthood can't happen alone."



---


# Using Santa as a Behaviour Bribe

Hannah Keeley argues that using a message of "be good or else" before Santa Claus comes down the chimney lowers parenting standards — a tactic she calls "stooping to Santa". "Don't lower your parenting standards to bribery, especially around a season and a character that is supposed to symbolize peace and goodwill on Earth," she said.

Two grounds support the claim. First, the bribe distorts the meaning of the holiday: the Santa bribe turns the focus of Christmas into "selfish gain on the part of your children". Second, it fails as parenting practice: "It's also lazy parenting, which never pays off in the long run," she said. "Being a mom is a professional career and deserves to be treated accordingly."

The alternative she prescribes follows directly: "Love your kids enough to learn how to manage their behavior appropriately and teach them self-discipline."



---


# Britney Spears' Conservatorship Under Jamie Spears

Britney Spears' conservatorship was a legal arrangement, entered into in February 2008, under which her father Jamie Spears took complete control over her assets. It followed a mental breakdown in 2008 that saw her placed on a 5150 psychiatric hold and left Kevin Federline with sole custody of their sons. The defining feature of the arrangement was the transfer of control not only over her finances but over her personal life, and it lasted until November 2021, when Spears was granted her freedom from it.

The turning point was Spears' testimony at her conservatorship hearing in June 2021, when she spoke publicly about her experience for the first time and called for those involved to be "put in jail." Federline expressed support for her after the testimony, saying he "only hopes the best for her because when the best for her is achieved, it's the best for their kids." His lawyer added in a statement at the time: "The best thing would be for their mom to be healthy and happy. And if either of those things aren't true, it doesn't provide for the best setting for custody to be exercised."



---


# Britney Spears And David Lucado

Two months after ending her engagement to Jason Trawick, Britney Spears began dating David Lucado, who worked at a legal firm; she announced their split in August 2014 by tweeting "Ahhhh the single life!", and her representative confirmed to People: "Yes, she's single." The breakup news came as TMZ alleged that Lucado had cheated on Spears and claimed that her father had purchased a video of the infidelity incident. The publication later reported that Lucado denied the cheating allegations, claiming he had been seeing the other woman while he and Spears were broken up.

Despite that history, Lucado defended his ex in a 2016 interview with the New York Times about her conservatorship. He told the paper: "If anyone knew the real Britney, they would know that she would rather be remembered for being the great mother she is rather than the artist she is." The publication noted that he again denied the infidelity claims made by Spears' father, and he added: "And if anyone could see her interactions with her kids, they would know that there is no need for a conservatorship over Britney's personal life."



---


# Parental Rules For Delaying And Limiting Phone Access

The therapist's biggest rule for cracking down on daily phone usage among kids is to delay phone access for as long as possible.

Kelman puts the responsibility on parents: "[Parents] are the 'drug dealer' in this analogy, so please think twice before free rein is given," she said. "Parents are giving their kids phones at young ages and kids are hooked quickly," she said. "Forget what friends are doing -- and delay this as long as you can," she advised.

If a cell phone is necessary due to schedules and after-school activities, a kid-safe starter phone like a Pinwheel could be a better alternative, Kelman suggested. "It's a phone that lets parents manage and monitor their usage, but there is no internet and only specific, parent-approved apps that can be turned on and off at will," she said.

She frames the tradeoff explicitly: "Better for your child to have a little FOMO [fear of missing out] than to have access to porn, become a victim of sextortion, or lose the ability to truly connect with other people." Parents should vet and monitor all content accessed by their kids, Kelman advised.



---


# Critique Of Meta's App Store Parental Approval Proposal

The critique attacks the premise that moving approval to the app stores is a protection measure at all rather than a reallocation of blame. Meta's proposed "better way" of requiring parents to manage a teen's app downloads pushes the burden back to the app stores and to parents, who often today do not monitor or manage their teens' smartphone use.

TechCrunch grants the factual half of Meta's warrant and rejects the inference: while it is true that the app stores and smartphone makers would know the ages of their users, requiring parents to approve apps is the equivalent of overriding parental discretion and choice. Other entertainment ratings — like those for TV, movies or video games — are meant to be guidelines for parents, not laws, so Meta's position that apps are somehow different is a fairly extreme position to take.

Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit devoted to reigning in Big Tech, attacked the proposal's motive: "Instead of designing its products with kids' safety and privacy in mind, Meta would rather push blame onto parents and other companies to obscure the damage they've already done to young people. No one disputes that Google and Apple need to do more to protect children on their platforms, apps and devices. That fact does not absolve Mark Zuckerberg or Meta for years of willful negligence, and this announcement shows that the company's outright hostility toward protecting kids is sewn into the fabric of its profit model." Apple and Google did not return requests for comment.



---


# Kristen Bell On A Shared Bedroom As Character Building

Kristen Bell argues that making her daughters share a bedroom builds character, because "to develop a good character, it's important to always be going through something" — told to Self in 2020 and reported by FOX News Entertainment on 10 October 2023.

The grounds are her expectation about their lives. Bell and Dax Shepard share two daughters, Lincoln, 10, and Delta, 8, and have been married for 10 years; the couple has been honest about the trials of raising their kids, especially keeping them grounded. "It's very important to me that they share a bedroom. I think their lives will be easier than most other people's on the planet," she said — so the difficulty has to be supplied deliberately.

The warrant is that shared constraint teaches negotiation and perspective: "I like the fact that they will have to figure out how to share a bedroom, figure out how to share your closet, figure out how to share your space. If that's the worst thing about your life, that you have to share a bedroom with your sister, you're going to be OK."

qid: Was there inconsistency in the portrayal of Sam Bankman-Fried's involvement in the FTX collapse between the TechCrunch report published on October 6, 2023, and the TechCrunch report published on October 7, 2023?
context:
# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Reaction To Lewis's Portrayal Of SBF

The backlash to Michael Lewis's 60 Minutes appearance attacks one specific premise of his account — that FTX was a sound business brought down only by an unwarranted loss of confidence — and, behind it, the inference that SBF's story is therefore a tragic fall rather than a fraud. The episode has fired up a lot of people, indignant at what they feel was too-easy treatment for someone who many believe brought down the whole crypto house. TechCrunch collected the reaction on 2023-10-02.

The premise is attacked head-on by Dan Held, who on October 2, 2023 quoted Lewis — "They had a great real business. If no one had cast aspersions on the business, if there hadn't been a run on customers deposits, they'd still be making tons of money" — and answered: "That's not true. They are not a bank, they're…", prefacing it with "Shameful that Michael Lewis is defending SBF." Ryan Selkis attacked the framing instead of the balance sheet, writing the same day that "The Michael Lewis interview is infuriating. SBF was a scumbag, and now we need to hear about his 'tragic fall' in the MSM because Sam told them he was an 'effective altruist' and people like Michael Lewis were so far up his ass they couldn't tell truth from fiction." Tobi Lutke attacked the coverage itself: "60 Minutes got rightly community noted here. How is it that SBF is still getting super positive media coverage when the media has nothing good to say about the founders that have actually created things and brought value into the world?"

Two qualifications sit against the backlash. Noff is defensive: she believes crypto is no worse than the stock market, which can also be manipulated and mishandled, adding that "Even when you identify corruption, I don't think that means we don't believe in the system in question." And TechCrunch's own reading is that the thing being attacked may not be quite what the critics take it for — Lewis's picture is a little less stark from the looks of the 60 Minutes episode, and it is not that clear at all whether SBF is getting a kicking or a coat of polish in the interview, given Lewis's celebration of SBF's self-proclaimed (yet not quite proven) idealism and the "Bankman-Fried-shaped hold in the world" that exists. The writer's closing point is that this confused message is very apt for cryptocurrency, where the process by which it works is forever murky and often misrepresented, at least to most people.



---


# FTX's Collapse And Bankruptcy, November 2022

FTX went bankrupt on November 11th, 2022, days after Gary Wang and Bankman-Fried had determined that about $8 billion in customer money was gone. On November 7th, Bankman-Fried tweeted "FTX is fine. Assets are fine," and another tweet in the thread said "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings." Wang testified flatly: "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine because FTX did not have enough assets for customer withdrawals."

Prosecutor Thane Rehn placed the trigger in the same month: when CoinDesk published its article in November 2022, people realized FTX was a house of cards, while Bankman-Fried was tweeting "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" and "We don't invest customer assets even in treasuries."

The day after the bankruptcy, on November 12th, Bankman-Fried directed Wang to send customer funds to Bahamian regulators. Customers could not take their funds off the exchange at that point because FTX had run out of money and its servers had been shut down. Bankman-Fried and his father met with lawyers while Wang waited outside with liquidators; the US lawyers wanted the remaining FTX assets transferred to the US, but Wang testified that Bankman-Fried told him to stall the US lawyers and transfer the funds to the Bahamian regulators instead, who were more likely to let him stay in control of the company. The collapse also propagated outward: the government put Zac Prince, the founder and former CEO of crypto lender BlockFi, on the stand just long enough to blame FTX's bankruptcy for BlockFi's subsequent bankruptcy.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. # Chapter 11 (Bankruptcy)

## Definition

Chapter 11 is the U.S. bankruptcy filing that insolvent companies in the corpus use to seek protection from creditors, and it does not guarantee a company survives: some filers are restructured under new leadership, while others wind down anyway once inside it.

## Context

In the corpus, Chapter 11 is the recurring endpoint for companies whose finances collapsed in 2022–2023. FTX and its trading-firm affiliate Alameda Research filed for Chapter 11 in the U.S. in mid-November 2022, after a published Alameda balance sheet exposed a huge FTT-token shortfall and a Binance-triggered bank run wiped out FTX's liquidity; the filing coincided with Sam Bankman-Fried's resignation as CEO and the appointment of Enron turnaround veteran John J. Ray III in his place. The same collapse pulled other crypto firms into Chapter 11: BlockFi filed in November 2022 and Genesis Global Trading followed in January, both noted by TechCrunch as part of the wider fallout from FTX's collapse. Outside crypto, WeWork filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in November 2023, listing over $18.6 billion of debt; TechCrunch's Week in Review opened its coverage of the filing with "as predicted," without stating when or on what basis it had made that prediction. SmileDirectClub took the same route but did not come back from it: the company shut down three months after its Chapter 11 filing, citing $900 million of debt — showing that a Chapter 11 filing in this corpus can precede either continued operation under new leadership (FTX) or an eventual full shutdown (SmileDirectClub).

## Key Characteristics

- **Used by companies of very different scale and sector** — from a $32-billion crypto exchange (FTX) to a flexible-office-space firm carrying $18.6 billion of debt (WeWork) to a smaller consumer startup (SmileDirectClub).
- **Often accompanies a leadership change** — FTX's filing came with Bankman-Fried's resignation and Ray's appointment as the new CEO to run the estate.
- **Does not guarantee the company continues operating** — SmileDirectClub shut down three months after filing, despite having gone through Chapter 11.
- **Can spread across a sector after one high-profile filing** — BlockFi's and Genesis Global Trading's Chapter 11 filings followed FTX's within months, both noted by TechCrunch as part of the wider fallout from FTX's collapse.
- **Distinct from Chapter 7**, the other U.S. bankruptcy chapter appearing in the same corpus's 2023 tech-layoffs list, which cybersecurity startup IronNet filed as it ceased all business activities.

## Background (external)

The corpus repeatedly names "Chapter 11" as the filing route without stating what the chapter itself legally entails. Chapter 11, formally Chapter 11 of Title 11 of the U.S. Code, is the reorganization bankruptcy: it lets a debtor continue operating as a "debtor in possession" while it develops a plan to restructure its debts and pay creditors, rather than immediately liquidating its assets — which is the province of Chapter 7 instead (United States Courts, *Chapter 11 - Bankruptcy Basics*, accessed 2026-09-02).

The Verge's reporter argued after Gary Wang's October 6th, 2023 testimony that Bankman-Fried's vanishing Signal messages might not help him as much as he had hoped, because the durable evidence was the code — and the code implicates him even without the messages. # The FTT Token And The "Sam Coins"

FTT was a token created by Bankman-Fried and Wang and issued by FTX, and it was one of several "Sam coins" — a nickname for tokens Bankman-Fried was heavily involved in and owned a lot of, either personally or through Alameda. Wang described FTT as being "sort of equity" in FTX, a characterisation The Verge's reporter suspected some crypto lawyers would dispute but that would probably please the SEC.

The distribution was lopsided from the start. Alameda got its war chest — 60 percent to 70 percent of the initial supply — for free, while seed investors got FTT at 10 cents a coin and FTT first listed at $1 a coin. Ellison testified that Bankman-Fried felt $1 per coin was psychologically important and directed her to buy up FTT using Alameda if the price fell below a dollar.

The discriminating feature of the Sam coins was that their book value was not realisable: they were almost certainly worth less than the value displayed on the balance sheet, because trying to sell them all at once would crater the prices. Bankman-Fried nonetheless directed Ellison to put those coins on the balance sheets Alameda showed to lenders, even though she felt doing so was "somewhat misleading." FTT also figures in the origin story of Alameda's negative-balance privilege: Wang said Bankman-Fried at first told him the code change letting an account go negative was to pay for expenses for the FTT token, but once implemented the ability to go negative was used for other things, including trading and unlimited withdrawals of FTX's trading fees and customer money.

# Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried attacked the prosecution's premise that he knew about the hole in FTX by claiming he did not learn of the $8 billion liability associated with Alameda until October 2022, that he found it all by himself by looking at a computer database, and that when he found it he was "very surprised." On the dramatic balcony conversation with Nishad Singh at their penthouse, he said Singh thought Alameda's liabilities had gotten too high and that FTX was spending too much on marketing, while Bankman-Fried still thought Alameda had more assets than liabilities so it was all fine, and besides, if Singh thought he would be better at marketing he could take it over — it did not have anything to do with the money Alameda owed FTX at all.
