# Adam Yedidia's Testimony And The $8 Billion Bug

Adam Yedidia, the prosecution's second witness, testified that in June 2022 he submitted a report to Bankman-Fried on Signal showing that $8 billion in customer money held in an internal database tracking cash wired to an Alameda account called "fiat at ftx.com" was missing.

Yedidia met Bankman-Fried in college at MIT and the pair remained close friends; assuming a robotic posture on the stand, he said he worked out of FTX's Hong Kong office from January to October of 2021 and then in the Bahamas until the collapse. He referred to a group Signal thread called "People of the House," referring to Bankman-Fried's $35 million penthouse where many employees lived; on who was paying the rent, Yedidia recalled Bankman-Fried saying he "assumed it's just Alameda paying for it in the end." Yedidia said Bankman-Fried had told him, before he began working in the Bahamas in 2019, that he and Ellison had had sex, and asked whether it was a good idea for them to date — Yedidia said no, and Bankman-Fried responded that he was expecting that answer. One of Yedidia's responsibilities was fixing the bug in the code that gave Alameda preferential treatment. He said he and Bankman-Fried spoke about the missing $8 billion at the pickleball court at the resort in Nassau, Bahamas, where he asked his boss if things were OK because it "seemed like a lot of money" from FTX customers was at risk. "Sam said, we were bulletproof last year. We aren't bulletproof this year," Yedidia testified; asked when they would be bulletproof again, Bankman-Fried said he was not sure, but it might be six months to three years. Yedidia said Bankman-Fried appeared "worried or nervous," which was atypical, but that he still trusted Bankman-Fried and Ellison to "handle the situation." On cross-examination, Christian Everdell, Bankman-Fried's attorney, focused on how Yedidia was the one responsible for developing and reviewing the code.



---


# The Mechanism Of FTX's Collapse

FTX came apart in early November 2022 through a chain with four links: a leaked balance sheet revealed that Alameda's largest holding was FTX's own token in a quantity larger than the token's whole market, the disclosure destroyed confidence, the world's largest rival exchange pulled its holdings out, and the resulting bank run forced FTX and Alameda into Chapter 11 within days. TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 account sets out the sequence: in early November 2022, that all changed.

Concerns surrounding FTX's liquidity grew after CoinDesk published a copy of Alameda's balance sheet, showing the firm held $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022. The balance sheet showed that the $5.82 billion in FTT tokens that Alameda owned was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap, which was about $3 billion at the time — meaning Alameda purported to have more FTT tokens on its balance sheet than what existed in the world. Around the same time it was exposed, the world's largest crypto exchange, Binance, started pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT; Binance had held an equity position in FTX from 2019 to 2021. That withdrawal essentially triggered a bank run on FTX. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. mid-November 2022, Bankman-Fried resigned, and John J. Ray III, the Enron turnaround veteran, was appointed the new CEO.

The condition the whole mechanism rests on is the fragility of the underlying valuations. As TechCrunch put it on 2023-10-02, all of that activity came to a crashing end because the value of cryptocurrencies on FTX was not banked to much more than speculation and the promise of higher value — so when those valuations fell, they fell very, very hard. The chain therefore only runs as described where an asset is priced on expectation, held in size by a related party, and exposed to a counterparty large enough that its exit alone starts the run.



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.

qid: Do 'The Age' and 'FOX News - Lifestyle' suggest that the actions of parents can lead to negative outcomes for their children, or do their claims point to different consequences of parental behavior?
context:
# "Grinchy Griping" and Child Egocentric Thinking

Hannah Keeley's model of why parents should not vent about holiday stress in front of their children has two components that process the same event differently. The "mom brain" is wired to process problems rapidly and move on to solutions. The "child brain", however, is wired to process a problem internally and take on the responsibility.

The relation between the two produces the mismatch: children up to the age of 9 process information egocentrically, which means that if there is a problem, they see themselves as the cause. So the same episode that a parent experiences as temporary venting is received by the child as attribution of blame: "Knowing this, make sure you don't do any 'grinchy griping' out loud to the children. You may see it as temporary venting, but they see it as, 'Mom is upset and I'm probably the reason.'"

The scope condition matters — the egocentric processing Keeley describes holds for children up to the age of 9. Within that range, the prescription is that parents should avoid "processing their frustration around the holidays audibly around the children", and should instead stay calm, find a reason to be grateful and vocalise it, even when frustrations accumulate.



---


# Michele Borba on Labelling a Child

Parenting expert and child psychologist Dr. Michele Borba, commenting on the blue bucket controversy, told Fox News Digital that it is "always advisable not to label a child — unless it's for a positive reason."

Her ground is the effect of labels on the child: "Negative labels can impact a child's self-confidence," said the California-based psychologist. But she attaches an immediate limiting clause that keeps the judgment with the family: "But no one knows a child better than a parent."

The decision rule she proposes is therefore comparative rather than categorical: parents should consider whether the label hurts or helps their child interact with others. "For instance, is the child speech delayed? Does he have difficulty interacting with others or expressing his needs? Are others (including his peers) aware of the child's challenges?" she questioned. And the criterion that settles it is the child's own experience, not onlookers': "The ultimate goal is for the child to have a fun Halloween. The parents should never be concerned about others' responses; only do what is best for [the] child."



---


# Online Predation And Sextortion Risk For Children

Kelman argues that children are structurally unable to protect themselves online, because their brains are not fully developed -- "so they aren't able to sniff out who is safe on the other end of the chat or the game."

Kelman stressed that kids "can't unsee what they have already seen," and that many adult apps may put kids "in harm's way."

The harm she names is coercive and self-perpetuating: "Kids are coerced into sending photos of themselves, often finding themselves victims of sextortion after they share the photos," the expert warned. "This leads to shame, despair and fear of telling their parents."



---


# Hannah Keeley's Five Christmas Parenting Mistakes

"The biggest mistakes parents make at Christmastime" is a set of five holiday blunders identified by parenting expert Hannah Keeley, the Virginia-based expert who set them out in an email to Fox News Digital published on 9 December 2023.

The organising premise is that pressures are high for parents and caregivers around the holidays, which means there is room for error. Keeley identified the top five holiday blunders that parents often make, and presented them as things parents should try to avoid rather than as a diagnosis of any particular family.



---


# Meta Researchers Avoided Documenting Under-13 Users

A potential smoking gun in the lawsuit is a series of anecdotes from Meta researchers delicately avoiding the possibility of inadvertently confirming an under-13 cohort in their work.

One wrote in 2018: "We just want to make sure to be sensitive about a couple of Instagram-specific items. For example, will the survey go to under 13 year olds? Since everyone needs to be at least 13 years old before they create an account, we want to be careful about sharing findings that come back and point to under 13 year olds being bullied on the platform." In 2021, another, studying "child-adult sexual-related content/behavior/interactions," said she was "not includ[ing] younger kids (10-12 yos) in this research" even though there "are definitely kids this age on IG," because she was "concerned about risks of disclosure since they aren't supposed to be on IG at all." Also in 2021, Meta instructed a third-party research company conducting a survey of preteens to remove any information indicating a survey subject was on Instagram, so the "company won't be made aware of under 13." Later that year, external researchers provided Meta with information that "of children ages 9-12, 45% used Facebook and 40% used Instagram daily."

During an internal 2021 study on youth in social media described in the suit, researchers first asked parents if their kids were on Meta platforms and removed them from the study if so. But one researcher asked, "What happens to kids who slip through the screener and then say they are on IG during the interviews?" Instagram Head of Public Policy Karina Newton responded, "we're not collecting user names right?" — in other words, TechCrunch notes, what happens is nothing. As the lawsuit puts it: "Even when Meta learns of specific children on Instagram through interviews with the children, Meta takes the position that it still lacks actual knowledge of that it is collecting personal information from an under-13 user because it does not collect user names while conducting these interviews. In this way, Meta goes through great lengths to avoid meaningfully complying with COPPA, looking for loopholes to excuse its knowledge of users under the age of 13 and maintain their presence on the Platform."



---


# Bonta: The Numbers Are For Impact, The Violation Is The Point

AG Rob Bonta's claim is that the scale of Meta's under-13 user base is rhetorical, not legal: any child at all makes the conduct illegal. It is difficult to extrapolate from the 2015 and 2020 numbers to today's, which as the evidence presented shows will almost certainly not be the whole story, but Bonta noted that the large figures are presented for impact, not as legal justification. "The basic premise remains that their social media platforms are used by millions of children under 13. Whether it's 30 percent, or 20 or 10 percent… any child, it's illegal," he said. "If they were doing it at any time, it violated the law at that time. And we are not confident that they have changed their ways."

Bonta also distinguishes the strength of the counts. The other complaints in the lengthy lawsuit have softer edges, such as the argument that use of the platforms contributes to poor body image and that Meta has failed to take appropriate measures, which is arguably not as actionable; the COPPA material is far more cut and dry. His evidence that notice was given: "We have evidence that parents are sending notes to them about their kids being on their platform, and they're not getting any action. I mean, what more should you need? It shouldn't even have to get to that point."

The warrant is a claim about design as choice: "These social media platforms can do anything they want. They can be operated by a different algorithm, they can have plastic surgery filters or not have them, they can give you alerts in the middle of the night or during school, or not. They choose to do things that maximize the frequency of use of that platform by children, and the duration of that use. They could end all this today if they wanted, they could easily keep those under 13 from accessing their platform. But they're not."



---


# Gellar And Prinze's Strict Household Rules

Freddie Prinze Jr. said he and Sarah Michelle Gellar "are strict as hell" with their two children, and that Gellar has "100 rules" the kids know they cannot break, in a 2021 Us Weekly interview reported by FOX News Entertainment on 10 October 2023.

The "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" star and her husband have been married for more than 20 years and share two kids, aged 13 and 11 at the time of the 2021 interview. "Look, I don't believe in whooping kids. I've never whooped mine. My mom whooped me. They were, like, preventative whooping, so I know how to be strict," the "I Know What You Did Last Summer" star told the outlet. Of the rules he added: "They know they can't break [those rules]. Friendships come and go. I tell my kids all the time that family is forever. So, we have rules, and they've got to follow [them]."

Gellar told Us Weekly in 2020 that as parents their "expectations are a little higher than most": "I think [our children] know what the rules are. We have [family dinner] as many nights as we can. We have no phones at the table. We sit, we all have dinner together."



---


# Using Santa as a Behaviour Bribe

Hannah Keeley argues that using a message of "be good or else" before Santa Claus comes down the chimney lowers parenting standards — a tactic she calls "stooping to Santa". "Don't lower your parenting standards to bribery, especially around a season and a character that is supposed to symbolize peace and goodwill on Earth," she said.

Two grounds support the claim. First, the bribe distorts the meaning of the holiday: the Santa bribe turns the focus of Christmas into "selfish gain on the part of your children". Second, it fails as parenting practice: "It's also lazy parenting, which never pays off in the long run," she said. "Being a mom is a professional career and deserves to be treated accordingly."

The alternative she prescribes follows directly: "Love your kids enough to learn how to manage their behavior appropriately and teach them self-discipline."



---


# The 42-State Lawsuit Against Meta Over Harms To Young Users

A coalition of 42 states and D.C. is suing Meta over its harms to teens and young users, in part referencing findings from Meta whistleblower Frances Haugen. The former employee had provided to news outlets a treasure trove of documents that appeared to indicate Meta understood the harms it was causing — including things like body image issues among teens — but did not take action. Instagram head Adam Mosseri was later hauled before Congress in December 2021 to defend the app's teen safety record, but as of November 15, 2023 legislators had not come to any decision about how to regulate teen usage of these platforms.

The suit was filed in October 2023, and a newly unredacted version reported on November 27, 2023 alleges a troubling pattern of deception and minimization in how the company handles kids under 13 on its platforms, with internal documents that appear to show the company's approach to this ostensibly forbidden demographic is far more laissez-faire than it has publicly claimed. The lawsuit alleges a wide spread of damaging practices at the company relating to the health and well-being of younger people using it: from body image to bullying, privacy invasion to engagement maximization, all the purported evils of social media are laid at Meta's door — perhaps rightly, TechCrunch notes, but it also gives the appearance of a lack of focus.

In one respect at least the documentation obtained by the attorneys general of 42 states is quite specific, "and it is damning," as AG Rob Bonta of California put it. That is in paragraphs 642 through 835, which mostly document violations of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA — a law that created very specific restrictions around young folks online, limiting data collection and requiring things like parental consent for various actions, but which a lot of tech companies seem to consider more suggestion than requirement.



---


# Teens' Own Reports Of Difficulty Managing Phone Use

More than two-thirds of all participants admitted they sometimes or often find managing their use of technology difficult -- or that they use it to escape "sorrow" or "negative feelings."

They also said they've missed sleep due to being on their phones at night.



---


# Harmful Content Categories And Staged Digital Access

Certain types of content are more harmful than others, noted Shelley Delayne, parent education director at Pinwheel in Austin, Texas, who was also not involved in the study: the categories she names are "attention-mining apps," adult images and interactions, user-generated content and "invisible influences" that can impact children's worldview.

Her rule is to stage access rather than grant it all at once. "Take it slow and give them only what they need," Delayne recommended. "Delay the introduction of adult online spaces and social media to [age] 16 or older, and stay involved in their digital lives just as much as you are in their physical life."

She also warned against reading device fluency as readiness: "Remember that just because a kid can tap around on a device and make it do stuff doesn't mean they have all the skills they need to be unharmed by it."



---


# The Sandwich Generation: Parenting Your Own Parents

The "sandwich generation" is The Guardian's 10 October 2023 name for today's midlifers who find themselves simultaneously parenting their children and their own parents — "In one breath we'll be begging our children to swap French fries for vegetables, and in the next breath we'll be urging our parents to exchange cake for sardines."

The defining feature is that parenting no longer starts and stops with our children, nor is it confined to those who have children: in a time of unrelenting change and ever-extending life, most of us will at some stage find ourselves "parenting" our own parents, and many — particularly those who had families later — will be doing both at once.

The condition that sharpens it is technological. The relentless pace of technology, accelerated by the Covid-19 pandemic, has made everything infinitely more complicated, leaving many older (and not-so-old) people baffled and frustrated; the author reports witnessing friends and family dashing to help parents with poorly designed online banking systems, unruly fridge alarms, "upgraded" software that has changed beyond recognition, apps and phones that do not function as expected, and numerous other technical challenges.



---


# Kelley Coleman on Child-Centred Disability Disclosure

Kelley Coleman — Los Angeles-based author of the upcoming book "Everything No One Tells You About Parenting a Disabled Child", and the mother of an autistic son — argues that Halloween should "always be about your child", and that the decision to use a blue bucket must be made with the child rather than for the benefit of onlookers.

Her grounds are the three considerations she asks parents to weigh: safety, comfort and privacy. "Especially for children trick-or-treating without parents directly at their side — is it the safest option to have your child carrying a bright indicator of their disability?" she asked. "For children who prefer privacy, would they want that information broadcasted? For children who prefer to share their neurodivergence, perhaps this is something they are proud to display." The conversation should be between child and parent, Coleman stressed, regardless of communication level, and should "center their experience and preferences."

She grants that the bucket does educational work, but subordinates it: "The blue bucket can be a teaching tool for others; however, it should never be about others — it should always be about your child." The warrant is that the burden of educating the public should not fall on the family: "In an ideal world, all adults would understand that not everyone communicates the same way, and that one's ability to communicate does not indicate one's interest in candy," she said. "But, the reality is that not all adults know this. It's exhausting teaching others to be inclusive. So, yes, the blue bucket can be a teaching tool for others; however, it should never be about others — it should always be about your child."



---


# Meta's Under-13 Policy Versus Its Internal Growth Goals

An internal presentation called "2017 Teens Strategic Focus" appears to specifically target kids under 13, noting that children use tablets as early as 3 or 4, and that "Social identity is an Unmet need Ages 5-11." One stated goal, according to the lawsuit, was specifically to "grow [Monthly Active People], [Daily Active People] and time spent among U13 kids" — a growth objective aimed at the age group Meta's own account rules exclude.

TechCrunch flags an important boundary on what this does and does not show. While Meta does not permit accounts to be run by people under 13, there are plenty of ways it can lawfully and safely engage with that demographic: some kids just want to watch videos from SpongeBob Official, and that is fine. What the law requires is that Meta must verify parental consent, and the ways it can collect and use their data are limited. So targeting under-13s as an audience is not by itself unlawful; the legal question is consent and data use.



---


# Parental Rules For Delaying And Limiting Phone Access

The therapist's biggest rule for cracking down on daily phone usage among kids is to delay phone access for as long as possible.

Kelman puts the responsibility on parents: "[Parents] are the 'drug dealer' in this analogy, so please think twice before free rein is given," she said. "Parents are giving their kids phones at young ages and kids are hooked quickly," she said. "Forget what friends are doing -- and delay this as long as you can," she advised.

If a cell phone is necessary due to schedules and after-school activities, a kid-safe starter phone like a Pinwheel could be a better alternative, Kelman suggested. "It's a phone that lets parents manage and monitor their usage, but there is no internet and only specific, parent-approved apps that can be turned on and off at will," she said.

She frames the tradeoff explicitly: "Better for your child to have a little FOMO [fear of missing out] than to have access to porn, become a victim of sextortion, or lose the ability to truly connect with other people." Parents should vet and monitor all content accessed by their kids, Kelman advised.



---


# The State Patchwork Of Teen Social Media Laws

Meta's call to bring the app stores into the fight is, if anything, a response to the lack of action in Congress to pass online child safety regulations like the hotly debated KOSA (the Kids Online Safety Act), leaving U.S. states to individually create laws due to a void of federal guidelines.

Utah, for instance, passed a measure that will require social networks to give Utah parents access to their children's posts, messages and comments, and would block social media access during certain hours; the governor also signed a bill to prevent social media companies from adding features designed to addict minors to their platforms. A judge in Arkansas recently blocked a law that would have required parental permission for minors to create social media accounts. Beyond Meta, Montana also became the first state to ban TikTok, claiming the Chinese Communist Party was using TikTok to spy on Americans. Meta's threat, in terms of teen usage, is not one of a foreign power collecting private data on users, but rather risks to teen mental health, body comparison issues and exposure to sexual predators — and TechCrunch notes Montana could easily turn its eyes to Meta next, after the TikTok bill went through.

The overhead of managing apps to meet individual state regulations would be a headache for Meta, but Antigone Davis also argues it would lead to a lack of teen protection in some cases. "U.S. states are passing a patchwork of different laws, many of which require teens (of varying ages) to get their parent's approval to use certain apps, and for everyone to verify their age to access them," she wrote. "Teens move interchangeably between many websites and apps, and social media laws that hold different platforms to different standards in different states will mean teens are inconsistently protected," Davis said.



---


# Under-13 Access To Age-Inappropriate Apps

Of the 85 participants under age 13, 68% used social media and had at least one app rated "teen" or higher, allowing access to "age-inappropriate experiences," the study suggested.

TikTok was the most popular app used by kids aged 11 and 12, while nearly half -- 45% -- of participants used apps with mature or adult-only ratings, such as porn sites, fantasy sports and betting apps, according to the study findings.



---


# Meta's Proposal: Parental Approval For App Downloads At The App Store

Meta wants to shift the burden of monitoring social media usage among teens back to the app stores — and to parents. In a blog post published November 15, 2023, Meta's global head of Safety, Antigone Davis, argued that parents should be responsible for approving their teens' app downloads, and staked Meta's position in supporting federal legislation that would require parental approval for app downloads for users under the age of 16.

The ground Meta offered is public opinion: it pointed to recent Pew research indicating that 81% of U.S. adults were in favor of requiring parental consent for teens to create social media accounts. TechCrunch's caveat is that while this may speak to popular opinion around parental sentiment, it does not mean that parents have thought through who should be responsible for preventing or allowing teens' access to social media, or how those apps should operate to protect teens.

The warrant tying the proposal to the app stores is one of existing capability: the app stores already have age guidelines, so it would seem to follow that they should also enforce them, if enforcement is to be regulated — or that seems to be Meta's thinking. TechCrunch also notes that a policy position like this is not something that would have been rushed out in a matter of days as a PR response to Bejar's claims, but something Meta has been stewing on for some time.



---


# The Holiday Martyr Parent

Hannah Keeley argues that it is important to keep the holidays well-rounded, and calls out "martyr moms" who are at their "peak performance" during Christmastime, putting everyone else before themselves: "They wear themselves out making sure everyone else has the perfect Christmas, but never put themselves on the receiving end," she said.

Her diagnosis of the cause is psychological rather than logistical: these parents "subconsciously compensate for a lack of self-worth and validate their role as a [parent] by creating too much busyness in their life." The warrant against the behaviour is that it yields nothing for anyone: "all that results from a mom who runs herself into the ground is just that: a mom who runs herself into the ground."

The remedy she offers is a question to interrogate the underlying belief: "If this is you, take a breath, put away the to-do list and ask yourself, 'What would I have to believe in order to have a relaxed and joyful Christmas?' Maybe we can use that as a guide to sit back and relax."



---


# Critique Of Meta's App Store Parental Approval Proposal

The critique attacks the premise that moving approval to the app stores is a protection measure at all rather than a reallocation of blame. Meta's proposed "better way" of requiring parents to manage a teen's app downloads pushes the burden back to the app stores and to parents, who often today do not monitor or manage their teens' smartphone use.

TechCrunch grants the factual half of Meta's warrant and rejects the inference: while it is true that the app stores and smartphone makers would know the ages of their users, requiring parents to approve apps is the equivalent of overriding parental discretion and choice. Other entertainment ratings — like those for TV, movies or video games — are meant to be guidelines for parents, not laws, so Meta's position that apps are somehow different is a fairly extreme position to take.

Sacha Haworth, executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit devoted to reigning in Big Tech, attacked the proposal's motive: "Instead of designing its products with kids' safety and privacy in mind, Meta would rather push blame onto parents and other companies to obscure the damage they've already done to young people. No one disputes that Google and Apple need to do more to protect children on their platforms, apps and devices. That fact does not absolve Mark Zuckerberg or Meta for years of willful negligence, and this announcement shows that the company's outright hostility toward protecting kids is sewn into the fabric of its profit model." Apple and Google did not return requests for comment.



---


# Schwarzenegger's Warning On "A Generation Of Wimps"

Arnold Schwarzenegger warned on "The Howard Stern Show" that if young people are over-pampered, the nation may be "creating a generation of wimps and weak people", FOX News Entertainment reported on 10 October 2023.

His grounds are a claim about how character forms: "You can only strengthen your character and become a really strong person inside if you have resistance, if you fail, if you get up again and if you work hard."

The warrant joining the two is that pampering removes exactly the resistance, failure and effort he identifies as the mechanism of strength — so protecting children from hardship produces weakness rather than preventing it. The former California governor issued the warning recently, in the context of his own disciplinarian parenting.



---


# Candace Cameron Bure's Strict But Loving Boundaries

Candace Cameron Bure described her parenting style to L.A. Parent as strict but loving — "We set firm boundaries, but there is always love and grace" — and said her goal is not to make her kids happy but to guide them into responsible adults, FOX News Entertainment reported on 10 October 2023.

The "Full House" star is a mom of three with husband Valeri Bure — Natasha, Lev and Maksim, all now in their early 20s — and spoke to the outlet when they were teenagers. "I hope my kids would say that I'm a loving mom," she said. "They would also describe me as strict." She continued: "I'm the mom that needs to meet the parents before my kids can go to a new friend's house. I want to know who they're with, where they're going. Even now that they're driving, I want them to text me when they arrive and when they're heading home."

Bure explained that they "work hard to keep our communication open and talk through any situation" and are "always willing to listen", but added: "I don't always say yes. My goal as a parent is not to make my kids happy but to guide them to be respectful, curious, responsible, resilient, kind, giving and thoughtful adults."



---


# Kutcher And Kunis Keeping Their Children Grounded

Mila Kunis said she keeps her and Ashton Kutcher's children's privilege in check by reminding them that "Mommy and Daddy have money, but they're broke all the time", in a 2020 interview on "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" reported by FOX News Entertainment on 10 October 2023.

The couple have been married since 2015 and share two children, daughter Wyatt, 9, and son Dmitri, 6. "That is not their bedroom, it is my bedroom that I'm letting them use, so they better take good care of it," she said with a laugh, continuing: "I say this in jest, but really they don't have things … they're raised on hand-me-downs from girlfriends' kids' clothing; we garden."

Kunis noted her kids are lucky to be born into a famous family and said she wants to ensure they are grateful: "Our kids are super-fortunate. Regardless, they were born at the right time to the right people, and I love them, but they're not going to be entitled a--holes."



---


# The Christmas "Give List" Versus the Wish List

Hannah Keeley argues that while building a wish list is fun for kids, the "give list" carries the moral importance: "Many parents make the mistake of teaching their children that Christmas is a time to make a 'wish list' and get what they want," she said.

The ground against a wish-list-only Christmas is its effect on children: "This is loads of fun, but can often create a big case of 'the gimmes' in your children." The warrant is a general principle about balance: "Life is balance. It's about receiving and giving."

The prescription follows: as parents guide their kids to create a wish list, Keeley encouraged them to spend equal time creating a list of gifts to give to family and friends. "Collaborate with them on what they want to give to the people they love, and encourage them to use their imagination and creative ability, not just your credit card," she said. "Even if it's a pine cone covered in peanut butter and bird seed for loved ones to use as a bird feeder, the gift came from the heart and a beautiful lesson was learned — that's the best Christmas gift of all."



---


# The Social Media Victims Law Center's Lawsuit Against Snap

In April 2023, the relatives of more than 65 victims, represented by the Social Media Victims Law Center, filed lawsuits against Snap, the parent company of Snapchat — an app known for its disappearing messages features, and the platform used by the vast majority of the suit's victims.

The suits are one expression of a wider response by bereaved parents. In their grief, victims' parents are motivated to end this crisis to prevent another family's suffering while also giving meaning to their loss, and many have launched awareness campaigns, founded educational programs and advocated for legislative change.

What is new is the venue: some parents are now taking to the civil courts, targeting the tech giants whose platforms facilitated their children's purchases of the pills that killed them.



---


# Reese Witherspoon On Letting Children Fail

Reese Witherspoon argues that learning from failure "is actually a valuable tool that you can't take away from kids" — "You rob them if you don't let them sit in the discomfort of the experience" — speaking on the "Good Inside with Dr. Becky" podcast as reported by FOX News Entertainment on 10 October 2023.

Her grounds are her own upbringing. "I see this a lot with parents – I don't know when we stopped letting our kids fail. Like I learned so much from the paper I didn't turn in or the demerits I got, so I got detention. I was suspended from school," she recalled, adding: "And my parents didn't say, 'Uh, she didn't deserve that,' and take me out of school. They actually let me sit in it and feel uncomfortable." The Oscar winner, who shares her eldest children Ava and Deacon with ex-husband Ryan Phillippe and her youngest, Tennessee, with ex-husband Jim Toth, said she wants to see kids live with failure a little more.

The warrant is that discomfort teaches something removal cannot, including self-knowledge about limits. The "Walk the Line" star remembered comforting her daughter after she lost a basketball game while not shying away from the lesson: she said, "'Yeah, I know. I know that probably feels really bad,'" then added, "'You know what also? Maybe you're not good at basketball?'" Her daughter was slightly upset in the moment, but Witherspoon continued: "It's actually really important to learn what you're not good at."



---


# Meta's Response To The Underage-User Allegations

Meta's rebuttal attacks the evidentiary basis of the unredacted complaint rather than the legal standard. In statements, the company said the suit "mischaracterizes our work using selective quotes and cherry-picked documents."

On the substantive allegation about under-13 accounts, Meta asserted that it does act on them once identified: "we have measures in place to remove these [i.e. under-13] accounts when we identify them." The premise it disputes is therefore inaction, not the existence of underage users.

Its defense on why identification is imperfect is a claim about the state of the art rather than about its own effort: "However, verifying the age of people online is a complex industry challenge."



---


# How Much And When Kids Use Their Phones

Kids spent a median of 4.5 hours per day on their phones, with the maximum amount of time reaching 16 hours, according to the study.

Checking behavior was frequent and highly variable. Most teens check their phones frequently, ranging from two to 498 times per day, and adolescents were more likely to check their phones over 100 times a day, the study found.

Use spilled well outside of free time. A whopping 97% of kids used their phones during school hours, while nearly 60% used them overnight -- between the hours of midnight and 5 a.m. -- on school nights.

Social media such as Instagram and Snapchat took up most screen time, at 32% during the school day, followed by YouTube and gaming, the study found. Overnight phone use was primarily spent engaging with the same media, although YouTube appeared to be the longest-running app because videos were often left playing during the night.

The overnight numbers are skewed by a minority: teens spent an average of 20 minutes per night on their phones, while some spent up to five hours. Sixty-seven percent of participants picked up their phones on school nights, but the median number of pickups per night was only once.



---


# Kristen Bell's Household Screen-Time Rules

Kristen Bell's screen-time rule is that her daughters are not allowed phones or screens at all during the week, with TV permitted on weekends on fairly liberal terms, FOX News Entertainment reported on 10 October 2023.

The rule as she states it: "They're not allowed to play with our phones or have any screens really. They are allowed to watch TV on the weekends, and we're pretty liberal with it, which I've been considering paying more attention to." The weekday ban has a predictable weekend consequence: "But since they're not allowed at all during the week, they will wake up at 6:30 on a Saturday morning, and they will watch TV until noon. I will also sleep until 9:45, which is really nice, and then get stuff done."

The limit Bell herself flags is the handover at the end: "But I will say, I notice how hard it is to pull them away from the TV at noon." She also admits the weekend rules get a little lax.



---


# Charlie Sheen Says He Is Raising His Twin Sons Alone

Charlie Sheen says he is currently raising his two youngest children, 14-year-old twins Max and Bob, on his own, telling People that most of his time lately has been spent on "doing single dad stuff". The boys' mother, Brooke Mueller, has struggled with drug addiction for several years, and Sheen said that recently she "has been trying to figure some stuff out on her end, so she's not in the picture too much right now." Mueller's representative declined to comment on the situation to Fox News Digital.

Sheen, who also has three daughters — one with a high school sweetheart and two with ex-wife Denise Richards — called his sons "really cool, really smart and really funny", but admitted they do have a bit of a problem "worshiping their devices". He laughed: "Although on the flip side, when they're doing that it gives me a little time to not be dragging them all over the city. But I also feel like the screens detract them from having other opportunities to expand their minds in other areas."

The history matters to the account: Sheen went through his own period of addiction several years ago, and Richards famously took the twins in at one point when Sheen and Mueller were both deemed incapable of caring for them. Now, as he prepares for a return to television and focuses so much on parenting, things seem to be looking up. Reported by Fox News Entertainment on 17 December 2023.

qid: Did the TechCrunch report on October 7, 2023, concerning Dave Clark's comments on Flexport, and the subsequent TechCrunch article on September 30, 2023, regarding Ryan Petersen's actions at Flexport, result in a change in the nature of the events reported?
context:
# Flexport Leadership Change And Layoffs

Logistics company Flexport is laying off 20% of workers, or about 600 people, topping off a spate of staff upheavals at the company, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-22.

The following week TechCrunch supplied the leadership context: Flexport founder Ryan Petersen had just taken back the CEO title after his hand-picked successor was pushed out. Petersen's big message has been getting the company's financial house back in order, and he has criticized former CEO Dave Clark of overspending, specifically around hiring and expanding too quickly. Petersen has spent the past month cutting costs, including laying off about 20% of its workers, or about 600 people.



---


# Flexport And Convoy Technology Acquisition Talks

Flexport is in talks to acquire the technology of Convoy, the once buzzy digital freight startup that abruptly shuttered after failing to find a buyer, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-30. The possible deal was reported by WSJ and came without other details, but still made TechCrunch's writer raise an eyebrow.

If Flexport acquires the technology, the company plans to restore Convoy's trucking services for as many customers and partners as possible, according to WSJ's source — which, TechCrunch notes, is going to cost money, prompting the question of whether Petersen's reign of financial frugality is already over.



---


# Flexport Leadership Turmoil

Dave Clark, the former Amazon executive who was ousted as CEO of Flexport just a year into the job, fired back at the company's founder and board, calling recent reporting on the logistics company "deeply concerning."

Clark made the comments on Monday of the week covered by TechCrunch's October 7, 2023 Week in Review, in a lengthy post on the social media site X. The post followed a CNBC report that had provided new information about his last days at Flexport. Flexport is described as a freight forwarding and customs brokerage startup valued at $8 billion.



---


# Dave Clark's Hiring And Flexport's IPO Plan

Clark arrived at Flexport in 2022 as the apparently perfect hire for a tech startup trying to disrupt the age-old logistics industry — he had built Amazon's logistics unit into a juggernaut that rivalled carriers like UPS and FedEx — and among his goals was to help Petersen prepare Flexport for an IPO, something the company had discussed doing within a two- to three-year window.

Since 2021 Petersen had been seeking a successor for then-operating chief Sanne Manders, in part to address what several ex-employees described as lingering issues with the company's troubled billing processes; fixing that was Clark's job. Petersen and Clark worked together as co-CEOs for the first six months, and in March Petersen transitioned to executive chairman — an arrangement meant to free Petersen up to do what he loved, "getting beers with customers," in the words of two former Flexport employees, while Clark, a self-described "builder at heart," was at the wheel. "There's a perfect complement of skill sets," Petersen told Forbes in June 2022. "Mine are much more creative, zero-to-one founder time, and Dave is the supreme executor and a legend in the supply chain world." Buying Deliverr was meant to be the first step in turning Flexport into a more full-scale logistics service. Shopify had acquired Deliverr in May 2022 for $2.1 billion, but the e-commerce software company was being hammered by Wall Street as its Covid pandemic pop faded, and by January 2023 CEO Tobias Lutke knew he needed to get rid of it; around that time Lutke first approached Petersen to float a deal, and Petersen told Clark he should engage with Shopify's team. Initial talks fell apart but resumed when Flexport executives learned Shopify was about to execute deep cost cuts and was eager to sell. Clark and Petersen flew to Miami to meet Shopify's leadership, and as a transaction neared, Clark — who had a reputation as a deft negotiator — got Shopify, already an investor in Flexport, to sweeten it with $40 million in cash and the framework for a $260 million convertible note that could help Flexport on its path to an IPO, according to an internal document analyzing the deal. The sale would be announced alongside Shopify's first-quarter earnings report on May 4. "We did not change the terms of a deal or rush it just to have it line up with an earnings call," Shopify said in a statement, adding that with Flexport "we are tightly mission-aligned to ensure the success of our merchants, which is why we chose to deepen our partnership with them earlier this year." The night before the announcement, Petersen appeared at a "Tech Talk" at Flexport's Bellevue, Washington office to pitch the "Flexport vision" to hundreds of people; asked whether Flexport would ever get into last-mile logistics, he paused, glanced at his watch, and said to keep an eye on the morning news, according to an employee who witnessed the exchange and a person told independently. The comment alarmed Clark and Flexport executives, who were concerned Petersen had disclosed material nonpublic information about a publicly traded company. Petersen did not respond to calls or messages from CNBC, the company declined to make him available for an interview, and a Flexport spokesperson did not respond to CNBC's question about whether Petersen was aware of concerns about his statement.



---


# Dave Clark's Ouster From Flexport

On Sept. 13, 2023, Flexport founder Ryan Petersen took the stage at North America's premier supply chain conference in Phoenix — exactly a week after he had forced out his hand-picked successor as CEO, ex-Amazon executive Dave Clark, so Petersen could once again run the show — and Clark, whom he had ousted just a year into the job, was sitting in the first few rows.

Petersen was surprised that Clark showed up, according to people with knowledge of the matter. Days earlier Petersen had excoriated Clark, alleging he had secretly expanded the company's headcount and taken on unnecessary leases without Petersen's or the board's knowledge, and posting on X, formerly Twitter, "Strategic Plan, Day 1: Make better decisions!" With Clark a few feet away, Petersen struck a different tone: "I think we're going to look back and go, 'Wow I'd probably do that all over again because of the progress that we've made,'" he said on stage, and personally commended Clark for orchestrating the $1.3 billion purchase of Deliverr from Shopify, announced in May, which picked up supply chain technology for last-mile deliveries. "I'm very, very lucky because I wouldn't have had the courage to go and do that acquisition, but I give all the credit in the world to Dave Clark," Petersen said. "There's no one probably in the world who would be better at running that last-mile e-com fulfillment network." The mixed messaging from the 43-year-old founder underscores the dysfunction surrounding the sudden firing of Clark, who previously spent 23 years at Amazon and built its mammoth logistics network on the way to becoming one of Jeff Bezos' top deputies. It is also indicative of a bigger challenge facing Flexport, whose software is designed to simplify transporting goods: valued at $8 billion by private investors in early 2022, just as the economy was turning and the 10-year tech bull market was ending, the company has been trying to operate in Silicon Valley startup growth mode while restraining expenses to reflect new economic realities and cope with supply chain bottlenecks. CNBC's account is based on conversations with people close to Clark and Petersen who requested anonymity, corroborated by internal documents and communications. Petersen has publicly said Clark overspent, overhired and overpromised, burned through cash and kept Petersen in the dark about key financials and an ambitious expansion into end-to-end supply chain tools for small and medium-sized businesses — something his allies echoed to CNBC. But documents viewed by CNBC and sources close to Clark undermine those claims, showing that Clark, who arrived when the company was struggling to bill customers and track containers, worked closely with the board and Petersen to implement decisions Flexport now suggests were ill-advised; evidence to support the claims of financial mismanagement is lacking, raising questions about whether that narrative was put forward to justify Clark's exit. A Flexport spokesperson rejected that characterization: "Ryan Petersen returned as CEO in order to restore Flexport's culture of customer engagement, and drive the growth and cost discipline required to return the company to profitability."



---


# Clark's Cease-And-Desist, The Political Friction, And The Firing For Cause

Clark's cease-and-desist letter cited two documents that had been presented to the board — a pre-acquisition financial analysis of the Deliverr deal, presented by the co-CEOs for board approval and shaped by multiple prior board meetings, and a review of Flexport's first-quarter numbers — both viewed by CNBC.

Clark's camp suggested other factors may have led to the abrupt firing, among them politics. Days after Clark was ousted, Petersen sent him a message, seen by CNBC, blasting one of his key female executives for wasting her days at the company on "far left-wing political activism"; the executive is a registered Republican. Trae Stephens, the Founders Fund partner, had also shared his contempt for that executive weeks before Clark's departure, a person familiar with the board told CNBC, and Stephens did not respond to a request for comment. Petersen is also a venture partner at Founders Fund, the firm started by Peter Thiel, a prominent supporter of President Trump's 2016 campaign who more recently bankrolled Senate candidates in Ohio and Arizona, and many of Thiel's closest confidantes at Founders Fund and elsewhere in venture are outspoken conservatives — though Petersen's sole public political contribution in 2023 was to a Democratic political action committee associated with Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia, and he does not talk much about politics. Clark has donated to candidates on both sides of the aisle; upon his departure The Wall Street Journal reported he was considering running for governor of Texas, but two people familiar with his thinking say that is not happening anytime soon. Flexport told CNBC that an employee's politics are not relevant in personnel decisions: "Ryan Petersen does not care at all about anyone's political or personal affiliations. That is their business. It is inappropriate for any employee to spend an excessive amount of time during work hours on activities unrelated to their role." A person familiar with the female executive said her noncorporate endeavors were largely related to charitable organizations. Clark has largely remained silent since he was forced to resign on Sept. 5, though in private he has expressed frustration at how his former team was treated, as many of his allies from Amazon who joined him at Flexport were summarily fired by Petersen shortly after his departure. On Sept. 13, Flexport chief legal counsel Chris Ferro contacted Clark to tell him his resignation a week earlier had not been accepted: instead, Flexport's board met the day after Clark resigned and voted to fire him for cause, though the board minutes did not yet reflect why. Ferro allegedly told Clark that Flexport would give him a block of 2 million shares — worth millions of dollars — if he signed a separation agreement including nondisclosure and nondisparagement clauses; Clark declined. Shortly after, Clark took the stage at the same Phoenix supply chain conference Petersen had spoken at earlier that day and did not hold back: "The only thing I really regret from the past year was I sort of picked the wrong founder. Basically, it was a place of extending my reputational halo to a group that, in my opinion, didn't deserve it. Largely, because about half the team was let go last week on Friday, the most brutal nonseverance packages I've ever seen in my life. It was about as disrespectful a way as humanly possible."



---


# The Flexport Forecast Dispute And The Contested Whistleblower Claim

A source close to Petersen told CNBC that a mid-August meeting in Texas went poorly for Clark because a so-called whistleblower — a senior finance executive — stepped forward shortly beforehand and told Petersen that the numbers being presented were "not real"; CNBC's reporting attacks the factual premise of that account, since documents seen by CNBC and conversations with people with direct knowledge of the board meeting make it clear that there were no substantiated whistleblower actions or allegations of financial impropriety.

The underlying dispute was about forecasts, not fraud. For much of the summer Clark had pushed then-CFO Kenny Wagers and his financial planning and analysis team to realign Flexport's year-end and 18-month forecasts, for obvious reasons: at the beginning of 2022 it cost around $14,500 to move a single container across the Pacific, and by late 2022 prices of ocean freight from Asia to the U.S. West Coast were down 90% from a year earlier due largely to weakening global demand — and because Flexport makes money charging fees for transporting goods, its business was getting hammered. But Wagers and Stuart Leung, a Flexport finance executive and close Petersen ally, were reluctant to pare back forecasts, frustrating Clark, who felt the projections were overly optimistic; Wagers and Leung did not respond to CNBC's interview requests. Clark ultimately prevailed, but the revised forecasts distressed Petersen, and Clark, Petersen and Wagers met in Texas in mid-August to fine-tune them. Flexport's spokesperson told CNBC: "There was no whistleblower nor was there any financial misconduct. Any allegations to the contrary are completely false." On Sept. 15, shortly after CNBC spoke with the Petersen source, legal counsel for Clark sent a cease-and-desist letter to Flexport instructing the company to preserve and retain all communications involving Clark's departure; the letter disputes the existence of a whistleblower and lists specific allegations as false and defamatory, including Petersen's claims that Clark was an unfit CEO because he overextended the company's lease obligations. Five hours after the letter was sent, the source close to Petersen contacted CNBC and asked to retract their statements and all details related to Clark's firing or the so-called whistleblower; CNBC declined to retract the statements. Petersen has since deleted several of his posts criticizing Clark.



---


# Flexport Versus Amazon In End-To-End Supply Chain Services

On Sept. 12, almost a week after Clark was fired, Flexport executives convened in Seattle to launch an end-to-end supply chain service allowing sellers to move products from factories to customers' doorsteps through integrations with major online marketplaces — and earlier that same day, just up the street, Amazon had unveiled a strikingly similar service in front of approximately 2,200 attendees at its annual Accelerate seller conference.

The project was spearheaded by Parisa Sadrzadeh, an executive vice president at Flexport whom Clark had poached from Amazon's logistics unit. Flexport had planned a booth at Accelerate but was told it could not be an exhibitor, which some staffers suspected was due to the competing supply chain products; Amazon said Flexport had discussed securing exhibit space months earlier but did not meet all the requirements to participate, and that its launch was not mentioned in those conversations. Flexport's own event was underwhelming: in a conference room about 50 people watched Sadrzadeh debut the service and then introduce Petersen, who spoke for roughly 20 minutes, according to Burak Yolga, co-founder of a digital freight forwarding company who attended. "Flexport announced pretty much the same thing that Amazon announced," Yolga said, adding that he left after about half an hour. The company had paid rapper Nelly $150,000 to perform at the event, but in the days beforehand Petersen opted to squash the performance because the optics were bad after his post about rescinding job offers — and Flexport still paid the artist. Beyond the public relations fallout from the Clark saga and any legal wrangling to follow, Flexport faces staffing turnover and a growing threat from Clark's former employer: it recently ousted Wagers as CFO, lost its human resources chief, and more layoffs are expected soon after the company cut 20% of its staff in January.



---


# Flexport's Board Composition

Flexport's board was made up largely of investors who were betting on the founder — a composition that matters because Clark's first quarterly board meeting as sole CEO was June 1 and his second was Aug. 31, days before he was forced out.

The board included Founders Fund's Trae Stephens, who had helped start defense-tech firm Anduril Industries, and Michael Ronen, who left SoftBank in 2020. Andreessen Horowitz was represented by Bob Swan, an operating partner at the firm and former CEO of Intel.



---


# Cruise's Nationwide Driverless Pause

Two days after California suspended its permits, Cruise decided to pause driverless operations in every market where it had started to charge for its robotaxi service, including Austin, Houston and Phoenix. TechCrunch's reporter, writing on 2023-10-30, found the decision surprising given how sources had described an all-hands meeting earlier that week led by co-founder and CEO Kyle Vogt: in that meeting, which came the day after the DMV suspended Cruise's permit, Vogt and other leaders told staff the company had not paused operations elsewhere besides California and gave no indication that it was planning to. Instead, Vogt told employees the company was re-evaluating how it discloses information to regulators to ensure it is clearly communicated, according to an account from sources who heard the call.

Cruise had even quietly launched driverless operations in Miami with just a few vehicles, a move that suggested the company was moving ahead despite its significant problems in California. As for what changed, TechCrunch offers two possibilities: perhaps Cruise execs were pressured by GM, or they looked around and realized that they were losing support from other states. Either way, Cruise said it's now going to examine "processes, systems, and tools and reflect on how we can better operate in a way that will earn public trust."



---


# Going Infinite: Michael Lewis's Account Of SBF's Political Dealings

Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, and details about Bankman-Fried's political dealings emerging from it include his alleged attempt to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president.

TechCrunch's team was focused on the Manhattan Federal Court for the trial of Bankman-Fried, the disgraced entrepreneur accused of orchestrating the collapse of the cryptocurrency exchange FTX; the Lewis book is the second channel through which the week's revelations arrived. The reporting is framed as allegation rather than established fact, and it comes from the book rather than from courtroom testimony. The item appeared in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023.



---


# X Post-Volume Discrepancy

X CEO Linda Yaccarino's post-volume figure contradicts Elon Musk's: speaking at an event in the week covered by TechCrunch's October 7, 2023 Week in Review, she claimed X was seeing 500 million posts per day on the platform, whereas in September Musk had said X users were creating 100 million to 200 million posts every day, excluding retweets.

The contradiction attacks the reliability of the platform's own content-volume claims rather than any single argument built on them: two of X's most senior figures, weeks apart, gave figures that differ by a factor of roughly two to five. TechCrunch does not adjudicate between them, closing the item with "So who's right? Beats us." The item also does not state whether Yaccarino's 500 million figure excludes retweets, as Musk's explicitly did — so part of the gap may be definitional and part may not.



---


# What Drove The ASX Rally On 10 October 2023

TMS Capital portfolio manager Ben Clark attributed the Australian sharemarket's strength to three things acting together: a calming bond market, a positive lead from Wall Street, and positive news out of China.

He set out how each fed through. "The bond market is retracing," he said. "There's also been strength in resource stocks amid rumours that the Chinese government might launch a substantial stimulus package." On the rates channel, Clark said interest-rate sensitive sectors climbed on increased probabilities of an easing in interest rates, because "Consumer discretionary and information technology companies are winners in lower-interest rate environments." Looking ahead, as more annual general meetings kicked off over the following weeks, Clark said he would be looking at trading updates, especially of companies that did not give solid guidance in their last update.



---


# Convoy's Digital Freight Shutdown

The digital freight broker Convoy told employees in the week before TechCrunch's 2023-10-22 report that it was shutting down, due to what executives described as a "massive freight recession." TechCrunch's takeaway: it turns out that disrupting the freight business is hard.

The abrupt closure wiped out investors, and comes about 18 months since the Seattle-based company raised $260 million in fresh funding that pushed its valuation to $3.8 billion.



---


# Faction Driverless Funding Round

Faction, the driverless tech developer, raised an undisclosed amount in a round led by TDK Ventures, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-30. Ducera Partners, Trucks Venture Capital and Fifty Years also joined the round.



---


# Dan Lewis's Convoy Founding Thesis

Convoy co-founder and CEO Dan Lewis's argument for starting the company was that trucking combined a very large money flow with unusually little startup competition — "I saw a massive opportunity and few people going after it," Lewis told TechCrunch. The former Amazon and Google executive, who has a background in strategy and management consulting, said that when he was struck by the urge to start a company, he researched the money-attracting industries of the world and then, using AngelList, saw how many companies were trying to disrupt those industries.

The grounds are the counts that search returned: thousands of companies working on industries ranging from telecommunications and fashion to video games and food, while billions of dollars were going into trucking each year but fewer than 30 startups showed an interest in the field. The warrant is that a large industry with few entrants is where opportunity concentrates. Asked later whether his method of deciding on a direction for a startup is still a good method, Lewis said, in short, yes. TechCrunch revisited the May 2022 interview on 2023-10-22, after Convoy's collapse.



---


# Zipcar's NHTSA Recall Fine

Zipcar is getting hit with a fine from the NHTSA for "renting vehicles with open, unrepaired recalls," TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-22.

One recall concerns 2015-2017 Ford Transit Vans, which continued to appear on Zipcar's platform despite safety issues with the vehicles.



---


# Anduril's Roadrunner Counter-Air Vehicle

Anduril, the controversial defense company co-founded by Oculus founder Palmer Luckey, has developed a new product designed to take on the proliferation of low-cost, high-powered aerial threats, TechCrunch reported on 9 December 2023.

Dubbed Roadrunner, it is a modular, twin-jet-powered autonomous vertical take-off and landing air vehicle, one version of which is capable of carrying a warhead. It can take off, follow and destroy targets or — if there is no need to intercept the target — autonomously maneuver back to base for refueling and reuse.



---


# Whether Founders Should Attend Events

TechCrunch's 2023-10-13 startups roundup argues that the question of whether founders should attend events cannot be settled by anecdote, and reports that a survey of more than 50 founders found no real consensus — only a set of pros and cons and circumstances in which the return on investment is decent.

The grounds are three competing pieces of evidence. A few months earlier, Alexis Ohanian, the co-founder of Reddit, tweeted that if he could go back in time and do one thing differently when he was building Reddit, he would have spent significantly less time attending events. The newsletter's author reports the opposite personal experience: he always regrets getting on a plane, or into an Uber, to go to an event, but on the way back he has never regretted it, because in his experience something magical always comes out of going. Against both, the TC+ team, being data-driven journalists, surveyed more than 50 founders to work out whether attending events still makes sense in 2023.

The warrant is the explicit rejection of anecdote as evidence: the TC+ team is "not interested in anecdotes, however: neither mine nor Alexis'," so a survey of many founders is treated as the thing that can answer the question where two conflicting personal accounts cannot. The reported result is deliberately non-committal — there is no real consensus, but there are good pros and cons — and the practical payoff is conditional rather than general: the article is worth reading to figure out in which circumstances a founder can expect a decent return on investment on event-going. The scope is founders and the year 2023.



---


# Gemini Pro's News Summarization Refusals And Stale Answers

Asked to summarise topical news in early December 2023, Gemini Pro often would not do it, despite having Google Search and Google News at its disposal. It seemed loath to comment on potentially controversial news topics, instead telling users to Google it themselves.

The TechCrunch reporter tried the same prompt and got a very similar response. ChatGPT, by contrast, gave a bullet-list summary with citations to news articles.

There was one partial exception, and it exposed a second problem: Gemini Pro did provide a summary of updates on the war in Ukraine when the reporter asked for one, but the information was over a month out of date.



---


# Nikola's Trevor Milton Arbitration Award

Nikola, the electric and hydrogen-powered heavy truck maker, was awarded $165 million from its founder and former executive chairman, Trevor Milton, in an arbitration proceeding, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-30.



---


# Rebelle Rally 2023 Rivian Win

At Rebelle Rally 2023, a 2,120-kilometer off-road and navigation competition in its eighth year, one Rivian team took first place in the 4x4 class — the first time an all-electric vehicle was on the top podium. The first place finishers, driver Lillian Macaruso and navigator Alexandra Anderson, are both employees of Rivian.

The event's conditions are unusual: it has become a proving ground of sorts for the 65 all-women teams who participate as well as for stock manufacturer vehicles, and GPS and other electronic devices are strictly prohibited. There were 10 vehicles out of the 65 that fell into the electrified category, such as the Jeep Wrangler Rubicon 4xe, and four of those — all of them Rivian R1T pickups — were electric. TechCrunch's Kirsten reported the result on 2023-10-22, noting she went looking at EVs, tech and, believe it or not, green hydrogen at a seemingly non-tech event.



---


# Bolt's SEC Probe Closed Without An Enforcement Recommendation

Bolt Financial and its co-founder Ryan Breslow were subpoenaed by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate whether the company violated any securities laws during its 2021 fundraising, and on August 23 the SEC said — in a letter viewed by TechCrunch — that it was not recommending an enforcement action for the company. Bolt CEO Maju Kuruvilla told TechCrunch in an interview that the one-click checkout company is putting the probe behind it and is moving on.

# Board Governance

In this corpus, board governance is illustrated by cases where a board of directors exercises (or conspicuously lacks) the power to oversee and remove a company's CEO: OpenAI's board firing Sam Altman, Flexport's board ousting Dave Clark, and FTX's absence of any board at all.

## Context

The corpus's clearest working example is OpenAI's board, which in November 2023 fired co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after "a deliberative review process" concluded he was "not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."
That framing treats board governance as a standing check on the CEO: the board's stated justification was not a business or legal failure but a breakdown in the information flow the board needs to do its job.
OpenAI's board itself sits atop a nonprofit structure that "preserved its nonprofit governance structure" even as the startup underneath pursued commercial growth, so the board's authority over the CEO ran through that nonprofit layer rather than ordinary shareholder control.
Board composition determines whose judgment gets exercised: OpenAI's board consisted of chief scientist Ilya Sutskever and three non-employee directors (Adam D'Angelo, Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner), and the subsequent standoff over reinstating Altman turned on negotiating a new board (Bret Taylor, Larry Summers, Adam D'Angelo) as a condition of his return.
The corpus also frames board governance by its absence: Paradigm co-founder Matt Huang testified he was "concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors" before investing anyway, though on cross-examination he said Bankman-Fried told him he didn't want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.
Flexport's board, by contrast, illustrates governance operating through composition rather than absence: a board "made up largely of investors who were betting on the founder" held quarterly meetings on June 1 and Aug. 31 before Clark was forced to resign on Sept. 5.

## Key Characteristics

- **Power to remove or reinstate the CEO** — OpenAI's board fired Altman outright, then negotiated the terms (including its own reconstitution) under which he could return.
- **Grounded in a formal duty to oversee, not just advise** — the board's justification for firing Altman was specifically that his conduct hindered "its ability to exercise its responsibilities," i.e., an oversight duty rather than a performance complaint.
- **Structure shapes authority** — OpenAI's nonprofit board sat above the commercial subsidiary, giving it authority that ordinary shareholder-elected boards would not have over a purely for-profit company.
- **Composition determines outcome** — who sits on the board (employee vs. non-employee directors, investor-aligned vs. independent) is itself a lever contested during crises, as seen in both the OpenAI reinstatement talks and Flexport's investor-heavy board.
- **Its absence is itself notable** — the corpus flags FTX's lack of a board of directors as a specific governance gap investors identified before FTX's collapse, distinguishing "no oversight body" from "an oversight body that failed."

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, corporate governance is generally defined as the mechanisms, processes, and relations by which corporations are directed and controlled by their boards of directors, managers, shareholders, and other stakeholders.
The widely cited Cadbury Report formulation puts it more simply: corporate governance is "the system by which companies are directed and controlled."
Source: [Corporate governance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_governance), Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02.

# Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)
