# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Gemini Pro's News Summarization Refusals And Stale Answers

Asked to summarise topical news in early December 2023, Gemini Pro often would not do it, despite having Google Search and Google News at its disposal. It seemed loath to comment on potentially controversial news topics, instead telling users to Google it themselves.

The TechCrunch reporter tried the same prompt and got a very similar response. ChatGPT, by contrast, gave a bullet-list summary with citations to news articles.

There was one partial exception, and it exposed a second problem: Gemini Pro did provide a summary of updates on the war in Ukraine when the reporter asked for one, but the information was over a month out of date.



---


# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.



---


# Google's Knowledge Graph And Featured Snippets

As described in the Helena World Chronicle complaint, Google's Knowledge Graph is a database, launched in May 2012, from which Google draws a summary of content that it displays as a "Knowledge Panel" to the right of search results when a user searches for information on a topic. The complaint characterises it as one of Google's older question-and-answer technologies and treats it as part of the alleged harm to publishers, alongside newer AI technologies.

The complaint states that "Google compiled this massive database by extracting information from Publishers' websites — what Google calls 'materials shared across the web' — and from 'open source and licensed databases.'" By 2020, the Knowledge Graph had grown to 500 billion facts about 5 billion entities, but the complaint alleges that much of the "collective intelligence" Google tapped into was content "misappropriated from Publishers."

Featured Snippets are a distinct Google technology in which Google algorithmically extracts answers from webpages; the complaint cites them too, on the grounds that they shift traffic away from publishers' websites.



---


# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.



---


# Google's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

In its report to the EU disinformation Code, Google — an early adopter of generative AI in search via its Bard chatbot — discusses "recent progress in large-scale AI models" which it suggests has "sparked additional discussion about the social impacts of AI and raised concerns on topics such as misinformation."

Google summarised its approach: "Google is committed to developing technology responsibly and has published AI Principles to guide our work, including application areas we will not pursue," adding, "We have also established a governance team to put them into action by conducting ethical reviews of new systems, avoiding bias and incorporating privacy, security and safety. Google Search has published guidance on AI-generated content, outlining its approach to maintaining a high standard of information quality and the overall helpfulness of content on Search. To help address misinformation, Google has also announced that it will soon be integrating new innovations in watermarking, metadata, and other techniques into its latest generative models. Google also recently joined other leading AI companies to jointly commit to advancing responsible practices in the development of artificial intelligence which will support efforts by the G7, the OECD, and national governments. Going forward we will continue to report and expand upon Google developed AI tools and are committed to advance bold and responsible AI, to maximise AI's benefits and minimise its risks."

On forward commitments over the next six months, Google's report states it has no additional measures planned for YouTube. With generative image capabilities rolling out internally over the next year, it commits Google Search to leveraging the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard to add metadata tags to images generated by Google AI, and notes: "Creators and publishers will be able to add a similar markup to their own images, so a label can be displayed in Search to indicate the images as AI generated."

# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.



---


# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.



---


# Google's News Content Payment Deal With Canada

In November 2023, the month before the Helena World Chronicle suit was filed, Google reached an agreement with the Canadian government under which the search giant would pay Canadian media for use of their content. Under the terms of the deal, Google will provide $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) every year to news organizations in the country, with funds distributed based on the news outlets' headcount.

Negotiations with Meta over the same Canadian law were still unresolved as of mid-December 2023. Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August, in light of the pressure to pay for content under the new Canadian law.



---


# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.



---


# The 42-State Lawsuit Against Meta Over Harms To Young Users

A coalition of 42 states and D.C. is suing Meta over its harms to teens and young users, in part referencing findings from Meta whistleblower Frances Haugen. The former employee had provided to news outlets a treasure trove of documents that appeared to indicate Meta understood the harms it was causing — including things like body image issues among teens — but did not take action. Instagram head Adam Mosseri was later hauled before Congress in December 2021 to defend the app's teen safety record, but as of November 15, 2023 legislators had not come to any decision about how to regulate teen usage of these platforms.

The suit was filed in October 2023, and a newly unredacted version reported on November 27, 2023 alleges a troubling pattern of deception and minimization in how the company handles kids under 13 on its platforms, with internal documents that appear to show the company's approach to this ostensibly forbidden demographic is far more laissez-faire than it has publicly claimed. The lawsuit alleges a wide spread of damaging practices at the company relating to the health and well-being of younger people using it: from body image to bullying, privacy invasion to engagement maximization, all the purported evils of social media are laid at Meta's door — perhaps rightly, TechCrunch notes, but it also gives the appearance of a lack of focus.

In one respect at least the documentation obtained by the attorneys general of 42 states is quite specific, "and it is damning," as AG Rob Bonta of California put it. That is in paragraphs 642 through 835, which mostly document violations of the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, or COPPA — a law that created very specific restrictions around young folks online, limiting data collection and requiring things like parental consent for various actions, but which a lot of tech companies seem to consider more suggestion than requirement.



---


# Associated Press And OpenAI's Licensing Deal

Select news outlets proved far more amenable to OpenAI than the authors suing it. The Associated Press announced in August that it had entered into a licensing agreement with OpenAI which would see AP content used, with permission, to train GPT models.

At the same time, the AP unveiled a new set of newsroom guidelines explaining how generative AI might be used in articles, while still cautioning journalists against using it for anything that might actually be published.



---


# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. Google's execution was uneven, though — it wound up spending much of its opening statement attempting to explain away its seemingly bad behavior as normal business practices and did not always succeed out of the gate.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.

# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.

# Whether Founders Should Attend Events

TechCrunch's 2023-10-13 startups roundup argues that the question of whether founders should attend events cannot be settled by anecdote, and reports that a survey of more than 50 founders found no real consensus — only a set of pros and cons and circumstances in which the return on investment is decent.

The grounds are three competing pieces of evidence. A few months earlier, Alexis Ohanian, the co-founder of Reddit, tweeted that if he could go back in time and do one thing differently when he was building Reddit, he would have spent significantly less time attending events. The newsletter's author reports the opposite personal experience: he always regrets getting on a plane, or into an Uber, to go to an event, but on the way back he has never regretted it, because in his experience something magical always comes out of going. Against both, the TC+ team, being data-driven journalists, surveyed more than 50 founders to work out whether attending events still makes sense in 2023.

The warrant is the explicit rejection of anecdote as evidence: the TC+ team is "not interested in anecdotes, however: neither mine nor Alexis'," so a survey of many founders is treated as the thing that can answer the question where two conflicting personal accounts cannot. The reported result is deliberately non-committal — there is no real consensus, but there are good pros and cons — and the practical payoff is conditional rather than general: the article is worth reading to figure out in which circumstances a founder can expect a decent return on investment on event-going. The scope is founders and the year 2023.

# Firefox's Decline: The Chrome Share Alternative Explanation

TechCrunch attacks the causal premise in Mozilla's Yahoo story — the inference that Firefox lost users *because* Yahoo was the default. As it puts it, that is not the full story.

Two grounds are offered. First, Yahoo was already well behind Google in terms of search technology at that point, so the switch conflated the default change with a pre-existing quality gap. Second, and more damaging to the inference, Firefox itself was very well behind Chrome: Chrome ended 2014 with nearly 50% market share and ended 2017 — when Google got prime default search position on Firefox — at nearly 65% of all web browser usage on desktop, with mobile even more skewed to Chrome. In other words, the number of Firefox users might have been declining for other reasons.

The counter also flags the interest at stake: pushing the blame on Yahoo certainly works in Google's favor here, since the story is being told in Google's defense.



---


# Anecdotal Evidence Undercuts Google's Gemini Pro Claims

Against Google's promises for Gemini Pro, TechCrunch's rejoinder on 7 December 2023 was blunt: "the anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise." The counter-argument attacks the evidential basis of the launch claims rather than the model's architecture, setting user experience after release against what Google said the model would do.

The grounds are the reception of the rollout itself. A "lite" version of Gemini, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard the day before the article, and it did not take long before users began voicing their frustrations with it on X, formerly Twitter.



---


# Google's Defense That Search Defaults Are Easy To Change

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. On Google's blog, president of global affairs Kent Walker said the search product was the favourite of users, browsers and device makers simply because it was the best in the business: "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," and "this lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today." Walker's supporting evidence is revealed preference when Google is not the default: when Mozilla made Yahoo! the default on Firefox, most users changed it to Google; and people setting up a Windows device frequently sidestep the Microsoft default — "Google" was the number one search query on Bing in 2021 — despite Microsoft making that very annoying to do. The Age's writer called this a compelling point, familiar to anyone who has dodged Microsoft's pleading while setting Chrome and Google as defaults on a new PC, but countered that all of these arguments ignore that Google and its competitors are not on an even playing field: the question remains why users prefer Google, and if the answer is that Google is simply better, the further question is whether that is down to its scale, longevity, ubiquity and all the user data it sucks up, which no other company could possibly match.



---


# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.

# Point Spread Variants By Team Sport

Spread betting is popular across sports but takes slightly different forms in each: football and basketball use a point spread, baseball calls it the "run line," hockey the "puck line," and soccer the "goal line." In every case the mechanism is the same — the favorite must win by more than the posted margin, and the underdog wins the bet by winning outright or losing by less than it.

In a hypothetical NFL spread with the Patriots as -5.5 favorites over the Steelers, a bet on the Patriots needs them to win by 6 or more points, while a bet on the Steelers wins if they win outright or lose by 5 or fewer. In a hypothetical NBA spread with the Warriors as -9 favorites over the Raptors, a Warriors bet needs a win by 10 or more points and a Raptors bet wins on an outright win or a loss by 8 or fewer; at Warriors 110, Raptors 104, Raptors bets win because they lost by only 6, whereas a 115-104 Warriors win covers the spread by 11 points.

In a hypothetical MLB matchup between the Yankees and Red Sox with the Yankees at -1.5 on the run line — baseball's point spread — a Yankees bet requires a win by 2 or more runs, and Red Sox bets win on a victory or a 1-run loss; Yankees 5, Red Sox 4 means Red Sox bets win, while a 6-3 Yankees win covers the run line with a 3-run margin. At NHL betting sites the "puck line" is akin to the point spread: with the Canadiens as -1.5 favorites over the Blackhawks, the Canadiens need to win by 2 or more goals, and Blackhawks bets win on an outright win or a one-goal loss; Canadiens 3, Blackhawks 2 means Blackhawks bets win because the one-goal victory does not cover 1.5, while a 4-1 Canadiens win covers by a 3-goal margin. In a hypothetical MLS game between LA Galaxy and Atlanta United with LA Galaxy at -1 on the goal line, the Galaxy need to win by 2 or more goals and Atlanta bets win on an outright win or a single-goal loss; LA Galaxy 2, Atlanta United 1 means Atlanta bets win, while a 3-1 Galaxy win covers with a 2-goal margin.

# Point Spread Odds And Line Movement

Alongside a point spread, sportsbooks attach odds indicating the potential payout relative to the amount wagered, and those odds sit close to even because the spread itself is designed to level the playing field between the two teams. The same payout can be expressed in several formats: American (for example -110 or +110), Decimal (for example 1.91), and Fractional (for example 10/11), each a different way of stating the same potential return.

Point spread odds are not fixed once set; the shifts are commonly called "line movement." Lines move when the point spread or the odds attached to a particular bet change after sportsbooks have initially set them, and Sporting News identifies several drivers. The most common cause is an imbalance in the money being wagered on one side: if a significant majority of bettors back one team to cover, the top sports betting apps adjust the spread to make the other side more appealing and thereby balance the betting action. A second driver is unexpected events — injuries to key players, changes in team strategy, or significant weather events that might affect a game's outcome; for instance, if a star quarterback is announced as injured days before a big game, the spread might shift in favor of the opposing team. A third driver is information and public perception: when a piece of news or a prevailing sentiment about a team's increased chances of winning gains traction, it influences how people bet and leads sportsbooks to adjust their lines accordingly.

# Sports Betting Odds

## Definition

Sports betting odds are the numbers a sportsbook posts alongside a wager to show the payout a bettor stands to win relative to their stake, and they are set by oddsmakers using computer models and analytics before being released to the public. The same underlying odds concept takes different shapes depending on the bet type — a moneyline price on who wins outright, a point spread price on a handicapped margin, and a totals (over/under) price on the combined score — and can be displayed in American, decimal, or fractional format.

## Context

In the corpus, odds are the common thread across every major bet type: moneylines, point spreads, totals, and prop bets all price outcomes with the same odds conventions, and combined-market previews such as college bowl coverage post moneyline, spread, and total odds side by side for a single game. Odds are not static — sportsbooks move them ("line movement") in response to public betting patterns, injury or roster news, and sharp/professional money, with the goal of balancing action on both sides of a bet so the book keeps its built-in profit regardless of outcome. Because different sportsbooks can carry different odds for the same event, bettors practice "line shopping" — comparing odds and lines across multiple sportsbooks before wagering to find the best price. Odds also extend beyond single games into futures and award markets, such as season-long odds on the NFL MVP race between Brock Purdy and Lamar Jackson.

## Key Characteristics

- **American odds format dominates U.S. listings** — a negative number (e.g., -110) shows the favorite and how much must be wagered to profit $100; a positive number (e.g., +250) shows the underdog and how much a $100 wager profits.
- **Three display formats carry the same price** — American, decimal (multiply the odds by the stake for total payout), and fractional (numerator = profit, denominator = stake) are alternative notations for identical odds.
- **Odds move for identifiable reasons** — sportsbooks shift a line or its odds because of lopsided public betting, new information (injuries, weather), sharp bettor action, or a perceived initial mispricing.
- **Odds differ by bet type but share the sign convention** — moneyline odds price the outright winner, point spread odds price a handicapped margin near even money, and totals odds price the over/under of a combined score; all three commonly display as American odds.
- **Line shopping exploits cross-sportsbook odds variance** — because oddsmakers and sportsbooks don't always move in lockstep, checking odds at multiple books before betting can secure a better price on the same wager.

# Sports Betting Terminology Glossary

CBS Sports set out the top Kentucky betting terms for new bettors on 13 October 2023, defining each bet type by what the bettor is actually wagering on and, in several cases, by a worked Kentucky example.

Against the spread means that instead of betting on an exact winner, the widely popular spread bet levels the playing field by letting you wager on how many points a team will win by: in basketball, if Kentucky is the 7.5-point favorite against Louisville then Kentucky covers by winning by 8 or more, while Louisville as the 7.5-point underdog covers by winning outright or losing by 7 or fewer. Money line is an elevated outright bet with odds adjusted to reflect a favored team and an underdog: if Kentucky is a -200 favorite against Florida you'd need to bet $200 to return $100, while Florida at +200 would return $200 on a $100 bet. An outright bet is the easiest wager to place and is perfect for horse racing, one of Kentucky's biggest sporting events — bettors choose one athlete, or thoroughbred, to win an entire event. An Over/Under has the sportsbook post an estimated total of both teams' final scores, with the bettor wagering on whether the actual final will be higher or lower: if the Over/Under for a Kentucky-Louisville basketball game is 125.5, you wager on the final total being Over 126 or Under 125. A player prop projects a player's stat at the end of a game and asks you to wager over or under that projection, with popular examples being how many touchdown passes a quarterback throws or how many three-pointers a basketball player hits; Kentucky is one of the 18 states that allows prop bets on collegiate athletes.

The remaining terms describe the market's participants and mechanics. The underdog is the team deemed less likely to win based on the odds, and a bet on one typically yields a larger return than a bet on the favorite; the favorite is deemed more likely to win, and bettors often pay a premium for backing one though they more often win outright. Consensus odds are generally defined as an average of all available betting markets, since different sportsbooks may price markets variably based on the action they've taken or their own interpretation of information. Futures markets encompass almost anything outside single-game bets — total regular-season wins, championship odds, MVP odds and more. A parlay requires two or more bets within a single wager, all of which must win: wagering $100 on a three-leg parlay at 6 to 1 odds could win $600 if all three legs win. Juice, also known as the vig or vigorish, is effectively the tax oddsmakers charge for handling a wager — if a book judges a game a virtual coinflip it may price both options at -110 to give itself a 10% rake on all the action. A push is a bet where neither the bettor nor the sportsbook wins: if an over/under for total points is set at 44 and both teams combine for exactly 44, the result is a push and the principal is returned. Live or in-game betting allows bets on several different markets in real time — in basketball, on the outcome of a quarter, individual statistics and live-updated spreads and totals.

# Determining A Point Spread Bet Outcome

To settle a point spread wager, compare the final margin of victory against the spread: the favorite covers by winning by a margin greater than the specified point spread, while the underdog covers by either winning the game outright or losing by fewer points than the spread. Those are the potential outcomes of a point spread wager as Sporting News sets them out.

Applied to a favorite that covers, suppose an NBA betting site has set the point spread for a Los Angeles Lakers-New York Knicks game at Lakers -7. This means the Lakers are the favorites and are expected to win by 7 points, so a spread wager on the Lakers requires them to win by more than 7. If the final score is Lakers 110, Knicks 100, the Lakers won by a margin of 10 points; since that is more than the 7-point spread, a bet on the Lakers wins.

Applied to a favorite that fails to cover, suppose an NFL betting site has set the point spread for a Chicago Bears-Miami Dolphins game at Bears -4, indicating the Bears are the favorites and are expected to win by 4 points; betting the Bears means betting they will win by more than 4. If the final score is Chicago Bears 24, Miami Dolphins 23, the Bears have won by only a 1-point margin. Since that is less than the 4-point spread, a bet on the Bears loses — despite winning the game, they failed to "cover" the 4-point spread, so those who wagered on them lost.

# Point Spread Push And Half-Point Lines

A "push" in point spread betting is the situation where the final result of an event exactly matches the set point spread, producing neither a win nor a loss for bettors; the wagers are typically refunded, so neither the bettor nor the sportsbook wins or loses money on that bet. Sporting News illustrates it with an NFL game in which the Dallas Cowboys are favored by 7 points against the Philadelphia Eagles: if the Cowboys win by exactly 7, bettors on either team experience a push and their wagers are refunded, because the Cowboys neither exceeded nor fell short of the 7-point spread.

Sportsbooks often employ half-points in their lines precisely to avoid this outcome, since they do not want to return bets. Had the example spread been Cowboys -7.5, the game could not possibly have ended in a push; half-point lines such as 7.5 or 6.5 remove the exact-match case entirely.

A tie in the literal matchup is a distinct boundary case from a push, and many spread bets still have winners and losers when one occurs. If the Cleveland Browns are -1.5 favorites over the Baltimore Ravens and the NFL matchup ends 21-21 after overtime, the Ravens win that spread bet, because the margin of victory of 0 was narrower than 1.5.

# Moneyline Odds Examples By Sport

Typical moneyline prices look the same across sports — a minus number on the favorite, a plus number on the underdog — but the shape of the market varies with the sport, most obviously where draws or large fields exist. In an NFL game between the Dallas Cowboys (-130) and the New York Giants (+110), the Cowboys are the favorites: a $130 bet on Dallas returns $100 profit if they win, while a $100 wager on the Giants earns $110 profit on an upset. An NBA game between the Los Angeles Lakers (-150) and the Miami Heat (+130) works the same way, with $150 on the Lakers profiting $100 and $100 on the Heat profiting $130.

Baseball and hockey illustrate slight favorites and even money. For an MLB game with the New York Yankees at -120 and the Boston Red Sox at +100, the Yankees are slight favorites — a $120 bet returns $100 profit — while the Red Sox are at even odds, so a $100 bet also returns $100 profit. For an NHL game with the Toronto Maple Leafs at -140 and the Chicago Blackhawks at +120, $140 on Toronto profits $100 and $100 on Chicago profits $120.

Soccer adds a third selection. In an MLS match between the Seattle Sounders (+110), the Draw (+230) and Atlanta United (+140), neither team is a clear favorite though the Sounders have slightly better odds: $100 on Seattle profits $110, $100 on the draw profits $230 if the match ends tied, and $100 on Atlanta profits $140. In soccer, the possibility of a draw is a common outcome to bet on, which is different from many other major sports.

Combat sports, tennis and golf round out the pattern. A UFC fight between Conor McGregor (-200) and Dustin Poirier (+170) pays $100 profit on a $200 bet on McGregor and $170 profit on a $100 bet on Poirier. A tennis match between Serena Williams (-150) and Maria Sharapova (+130) makes Williams the favorite, with $150 on her profiting $100 and $100 on Sharapova profiting $130. PGA Tour odds price individual golfers to win a tournament — Tiger Woods +500, Rory McIlroy +600 — so a $100 bet profits $500 or $600 respectively; in golf, with usually many players in the field, the odds can be much higher than in head-to-head matchups.

# Totals Bet Outcomes: Push And Overtime

An over/under wager has three potential outcomes: if the combined score exceeds the set total, the "over" bet wins; if the score is below the set total, the "under" bet wins; and if the combined score of the game matches the total exactly, the bet is typically considered a "push" and the wager is refunded.

A push therefore occurs when the combined score of a game matches the set total established by the bookmaker, meaning bettors neither win nor lose and their original wager is returned. To avoid this outcome, most sportsbooks employ half-points in their totals: by setting a total at 200.5 instead of 200, sports betting sites ensure that a game's combined score cannot possibly match the set total exactly.

Overtime is a separate boundary case. In most sports and with the majority of sportsbooks, overtime does count toward a totals wager; Sporting News advises always checking the specific rules of the sportsbook you are betting with to confirm, but says overtime is generally included in totals wagers.

# Over/Under Totals Bet Definition

A totals bet, commonly known as an over/under bet, is a wager on the combined score of both teams in a game: bookmakers set a predicted total score, and bettors choose whether the actual combined score will surpass it ("over") or fall short of it ("under"). Rather than picking the winner or the winning margin, totals betting asks only about the game's combined score, and it sits alongside point spreads and moneylines as a favorite option in sports betting.

The discriminating feature is that the bettor's only concern is whether the final combined score falls over or under the line set by oddsmakers — the identity of the winner is irrelevant. Sporting News illustrates with an NBA game whose total is set at 210.5 points: those who bet the "over" win if the combined score of the two teams is 211 or more, while those who bet the "under" win if the score totals 210 or less. The 0.5 ensures no chance of a tie, since teams cannot score in half-points.

The category is broader than points. Over/under bets involve wagering on whether a particular number will be over or under the figure the bookmaker set, and that number can be combined points scored in a game, total rounds in a fight, or total games in a tennis match.

# Point Spread Bet Definition

A point spread bet is a wager on the difference in score between two teams (or players) in a specific game or event, in which bookmakers assign the favored team a point spread or handicap intended to equalize the odds against the less-favored team. To place one, a bettor selects either the favored team or the underdog and predicts whether that side will surpass or fall short of the given spread; the odds on both sides are set to try to even out the money wagered on each.

The discriminating features are the two symbols and what they oblige each side to do. The "(-)" symbol denotes the favorite — the team expected to win, typically assigned a negative point value indicating the number of points by which it must win for a bet on it to succeed; the favorite has points deducted. The "(+)" symbol denotes the underdog — the team expected to lose, typically assigned a positive point value indicating the number of points it may lose by and still win the bet; the underdog has points added. Covering the spread means a team has surpassed the expectations the spread set and so won the bet: for the favorite, winning by more than the specified number of points; for the underdog, either winning outright or losing by fewer points than the spread. If the underdog wins the contest outright, it is also the spread winner.

The term "against the spread" carries two senses that mark a boundary case. Most generally, betting against the spread simply means placing a point spread bet at all — betting the underdog to win outright or lose by fewer points than specified, or betting the favorite to win by a margin greater than specified. In a secondary definition that distinguishes betting "with the spread" from betting "against the spread," the latter term means specifically that you are betting on the underdog. Sporting News notes that the best sports betting sites offer a daily menu of point spread bets across dozens of sports and events.

# The American Odds Format

American odds express a price as either a negative (-) or a positive (+) number, and they are the format most listings on the best online sports betting sites predominantly use — one of three types of odds, alongside decimal and fractional, that bettors encounter when researching and handicapping across platforms.

The negative numbers, which can seem perplexing at first, point to the team, player or option considered the favorite to win, and can also represent wagers that are less than even money; the negative figure tells you how much you need to bet to earn a profit of $100. Positive odds conversely signal the underdog, or bets offering more than even money, and the figure shows how much profit you will make on a $100 wager.

A worked moneyline example makes the arithmetic concrete. Imagine that on a top NFL betting site the New England Patriots are listed as -110 favorites while the New York Jets stand at +250. If you back the favorite and bet $110 on the Patriots and they win, you end up with $210 — your initial $110 stake plus the $100 profit you earned.

# Moneyline Outcomes: Win, Loss, Draw And Push

A moneyline wager can end in several ways: the most straightforward outcomes are a win or a loss, determined by whether the team or individual you backed was victorious or defeated, and there is also the possibility of a draw if the event ends in a tie. Winning is simply a matter of picking the eventual winner — bet on Boxer B in a bout between Boxer A and Boxer B, and if Boxer B wins you are paid based on the odds at the time you placed the wager. A loss means the side you backed did not win: bet $100 on Team A in an NBA game and, if Team B wins, the bet on Team A loses.

Some sports price the draw as its own selection. In soccer especially, games can end in a draw and bettors can wager on that outcome, so a moneyline typically shows three sets of odds — one for each team to win and one for the draw. For a match between Team A and Team B, the odds might read Team A +150, Draw +220, Team B +180; a $100 wager on "Draw" that lands returns $220 in profit on top of the $100 stake, totaling $320, while a win by either team loses the $100.

A tie handled as a "push" is a different case, and the scope condition matters. When a push occurs bettors are refunded their original wager, with no money won or lost; but sports that typically allow a tie, like soccer, often offer the draw as a bet instead, and if the game ends in a draw and you did not bet that option, you lose. It is therefore essential to understand the specific rules of the sportsbook and the sport to know how ties are handled. Finally, in most sports and with most sportsbooks — including new betting sites — overtime or any extra time or tiebreakers do count toward a moneyline bet, though you should always check your sportsbook's specific rules.

The grounds are how the lines are made and remade. Sportsbooks set game totals considering factors like recent performances, weather, and player status, and as new data emerges and betting trends develop, this line can shift — if many bettors choose the "over," the sportsbook might raise the total to balance the bets. The warrant joining grounds to claim is that line movements often reflect public betting sentiments and therefore offer insights to informed bettors: because a move encodes information the book has absorbed about data and about where the public money is, watching it tells the bettor something they did not otherwise have. Hence bettors must monitor any line changes before the game starts and strategize accordingly to optimize their betting success.

The argument stops short of endorsing either side of a totals bet in the abstract: neither wager holds a universal advantage, and success in over/under betting hinges on a thorough evaluation of both the set line and the competing teams.

# Totals Line Movement Drivers

The totals line can move, and Sporting News attributes that movement to four kinds of input: betting activity, injury updates, weather conditions, and other news and updates.

Betting activity is one of the most common reasons for line movement — a significant amount of money wagered on one side, either the over or the under, leads bookmakers to adjust the line to balance the action and protect themselves from potential losses. Injury updates work through the expected score: if a key player is injured or unable to play, that can influence the expected total score, leading bookmakers to adjust the line accordingly. Weather conditions matter in outdoor sports; heavy rain or snow in a football game might create expectations of a lower-scoring game, causing the line to move down. Finally, any other news that might affect team performance — changes in team strategy or recent performances — can influence totals lines.

# Handicap Betting In Tennis And Golf

In individual sports the point spread survives as a handicap denominated in the sport's own units: at tennis betting sites it is usually based on games or sets and is termed a "game handicap" or "set handicap," while in golf it appears as "stroke handicap" betting, akin to point spreads but measured in golf strokes.

# Why Moneyline Odds Change

Lines at sports betting apps change quickly for two primary reasons — public betting and new information — and sportsbooks adjust moneyline odds to stay profitable, balance their book and reflect the most current information about an event. Before setting odds oddsmakers gather extensive data, then release the finalized odds to the public; from that point a bettor can bet immediately or wait for shifts, though predicting those shifts is challenging.

The time dimension shows how an opening price drifts. Odds for the next Super Bowl champion released shortly after the previous Super Bowl are based mostly on the recently concluded season; as the new season approaches and teams make changes, the odds adjust to perceived championship chances, and as games progress the lines keep evolving with team performances.

The mechanism has five named drivers. Public betting patterns move a line because, when a significant amount of money lands on one team or participant, sportsbooks adjust the odds to balance their liability — making the price less favorable for the heavily-bet side and more favorable for the less-bet side to encourage even betting and reduce financial risk. New information matters because changes in player injuries, player substitutions or weather conditions alter the perceived outcome, and books adjust once such information becomes public. Professional bettors move lines because large wagers from sharp bettors often reflect insights or information that can influence the odds. Initial miscalculation is a fourth driver: sometimes the opening odds are perceived as offering value, and heavy betting on one side signals that the initial price was potentially "off," prompting an adjustment. Event dynamics is the fifth, applying to live betting placed while the event is in progress, where the evolving dynamics of the match lead to frequent changes.

# Fractional And Decimal Odds Formats

Fractional odds show two numbers separated by a slash (/) or a dash (-) — 5/1 or 5-1, say — where the first number, akin to a numerator, represents potential profit and the second, akin to a denominator, indicates the amount you need to stake. Put differently, the denominator tells you how much you must bet to earn a profit equivalent to the numerator. With 2/1 odds you would earn $2 for every $1 wagered; with 4/9 odds a bet of $9 would yield a $4 profit, so a winning $9 bet at 4/9 returns $13 in total — the $9 stake plus the $4 profit. These odds turn up occasionally, especially in contexts like horse racing, and are straightforward once you get the hang of them even if they initially look like a math problem.

Decimal odds are to betting what the metric system is to measurements: straightforward and user-friendly, with fewer intricacies than their American and fractional counterparts — though, just as the metric system is not universally embraced in the US, decimal odds can be overlooked there. To determine a bet's payout you multiply the decimal odds by the amount you are betting. If an NHL betting site has the Edmonton Oilers at 2.53 to beat the Detroit Red Wings, a $10 bet would yield a $25.30 return, comprising the $10 wager and $15.30 of profit.

The scope condition worth keeping is what the decimal calculation returns. It gives the total payout, not just earnings, so anyone tracking betting profits must subtract the original stake from the payout to get an accurate figure.

# How Sportsbooks Set And Move Betting Lines

The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services to set their lines and odds, while other sports betting apps simply copy those lines. The oddsmakers and services use computer models and algorithms that consider analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, matchup data and more to develop the lines and odds. Those lines are then subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that emerges before the game, and a book will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side.

The governing objective is balance rather than prediction. Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet, because that lets the book earn the small profit built into the odds and lines without worrying about which side wins. Sportsbooks want even betting so much that they will move a line or change the odds specifically to draw more bets to the other side.

The relation that matters to a bettor is that books do not all move together. The betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook: one book may be forced to move a line or change the odds because of the money it has taken while another is not, and the lines and odds may even differ right from the jump. That divergence is what creates the chance to book a bet at improved odds or a more favorable line.

The range over which this holds is narrow and specific. When a line moves for a legitimate reason such as an injury or roster move, every sportsbook jumps on board, and it is difficult to find value; when a line moves because of betting patterns, only the sportsbook that saw that betting makes the change, and that is the opportunity. Line shopping is the tool for spotting the second kind: choose a side, shop around at online sportsbooks, compare the lines and odds, and pounce when you find one offering something different and more favorable to your viewpoint.
