# Adam Yedidia's Testimony And The $8 Billion Bug

Adam Yedidia, the prosecution's second witness, testified that in June 2022 he submitted a report to Bankman-Fried on Signal showing that $8 billion in customer money held in an internal database tracking cash wired to an Alameda account called "fiat at ftx.com" was missing.

Yedidia met Bankman-Fried in college at MIT and the pair remained close friends; assuming a robotic posture on the stand, he said he worked out of FTX's Hong Kong office from January to October of 2021 and then in the Bahamas until the collapse. He referred to a group Signal thread called "People of the House," referring to Bankman-Fried's $35 million penthouse where many employees lived; on who was paying the rent, Yedidia recalled Bankman-Fried saying he "assumed it's just Alameda paying for it in the end." Yedidia said Bankman-Fried had told him, before he began working in the Bahamas in 2019, that he and Ellison had had sex, and asked whether it was a good idea for them to date — Yedidia said no, and Bankman-Fried responded that he was expecting that answer. One of Yedidia's responsibilities was fixing the bug in the code that gave Alameda preferential treatment. He said he and Bankman-Fried spoke about the missing $8 billion at the pickleball court at the resort in Nassau, Bahamas, where he asked his boss if things were OK because it "seemed like a lot of money" from FTX customers was at risk. "Sam said, we were bulletproof last year. We aren't bulletproof this year," Yedidia testified; asked when they would be bulletproof again, Bankman-Fried said he was not sure, but it might be six months to three years. Yedidia said Bankman-Fried appeared "worried or nervous," which was atypical, but that he still trusted Bankman-Fried and Ellison to "handle the situation." On cross-examination, Christian Everdell, Bankman-Fried's attorney, focused on how Yedidia was the one responsible for developing and reviewing the code.

# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.

# Bankman-Fried's Post-Bankruptcy Media Tour

After FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried went on an extensive media tour, doing interviews with The New York Times' Andrew Ross Sorkin and Good Morning America — and he kept giving interviews even under house arrest, including with The New Yorker.

The Verge's reading of his motive: Bankman-Fried seemed to think that if he just explained things, everyone would understand that what he did was a mistake, not a crime.

# Bail

## Definition

Bail is the term the corpus uses for Sam Bankman-Fried's pretrial release from custody: a $250 million bond that let him live under house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto instead of in jail while awaiting trial, and which a U.S. judge revoked in August 2023 (doc_0010, doc_0226).

## Context

The corpus's clearest illustration is Sam Bankman-Fried's case: after being arrested in the Bahamas in December 2022 and extradited to the U.S., he was released on a $250 million bail bond and confined to house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto (doc_0010). That release was not permanent — a U.S. judge revoked his bail in August 2023 after he was accused of intimidating former Alameda CEO Caroline Ellison by leaking her private diary, leaving him in custody by the time his fraud trial began that October (doc_0010, doc_0226). Bail is also treated as something a court can simply refuse to grant: one recap of the FTX saga notes flatly that "SBF has been denied bail" (doc_0030). The concept resurfaces around Bankman-Fried's co-defendants, where house arrest — the condition often attached to bail — is described as a lighter alternative to imprisonment that cooperating felons like Gary Wang, Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison might still face even without prison time (doc_0121).

## Key Characteristics

- **Conditional, not unconditional freedom** — release on bail came bundled with restrictions (house arrest at a fixed address) rather than free movement (doc_0010).
- **Financially secured** — Bankman-Fried's release required a $250 million bail bond, tying his liberty to a monetary guarantee (doc_0010).
- **Revocable** — a judge can revoke bail mid-proceedings for conduct that violates its terms, as happened after the Ellison intimidation allegations, moving the defendant from house arrest to detention (doc_0010, doc_0226).
- **Discretionary and sometimes denied outright** — courts can decline to grant bail at all, as they did for Bankman-Fried at least once during his case (doc_0030).
- **Distinct from post-conviction outcomes** — bail concerns pretrial release, while house arrest can separately appear as a possible post-conviction alternative to imprisonment for cooperating defendants (doc_0121).

## Background (external)

The corpus never defines "bail" itself — it only reports how bail applied in Bankman-Fried's case.
Per Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute, bail is "the money a defendant pays as a guarantee that they will show up in court at a later date," and release can be "conditioned on certain behavior of the defendant," such as staying away from an alleged victim (Cornell Law School LII, *Wex: bail*, accessed 2026-09-02).
A defendant's failure to comply "triggers the bond obligation and allows the court to keep any money given as security" (Cornell Law School LII, *Wex: bail*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# The FTT Token And The "Sam Coins"

FTT was a token created by Bankman-Fried and Wang and issued by FTX, and it was one of several "Sam coins" — a nickname for tokens Bankman-Fried was heavily involved in and owned a lot of, either personally or through Alameda. Wang described FTT as being "sort of equity" in FTX, a characterisation The Verge's reporter suspected some crypto lawyers would dispute but that would probably please the SEC.

The distribution was lopsided from the start. Alameda got its war chest — 60 percent to 70 percent of the initial supply — for free, while seed investors got FTT at 10 cents a coin and FTT first listed at $1 a coin. Ellison testified that Bankman-Fried felt $1 per coin was psychologically important and directed her to buy up FTT using Alameda if the price fell below a dollar.

The discriminating feature of the Sam coins was that their book value was not realisable: they were almost certainly worth less than the value displayed on the balance sheet, because trying to sell them all at once would crater the prices. Bankman-Fried nonetheless directed Ellison to put those coins on the balance sheets Alameda showed to lenders, even though she felt doing so was "somewhat misleading." FTT also figures in the origin story of Alameda's negative-balance privilege: Wang said Bankman-Fried at first told him the code change letting an account go negative was to pay for expenses for the FTT token, but once implemented the ability to go negative was used for other things, including trading and unlimited withdrawals of FTX's trading fees and customer money.

# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who pleaded guilty to their own charges. Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. The government has indicated FTX co-founder Gary Wang and engineering head Nishad Singh will also be among the witnesses called to testify about Bankman-Fried.

# Bankman-Fried's Claimed Ignorance Of Alameda's Finances

Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried attacked the prosecution's premise that he knew about the hole in FTX by claiming he did not learn of the $8 billion liability associated with Alameda until October 2022, that he found it all by himself by looking at a computer database, and that when he found it he was "very surprised." The Verge's reporter recorded the claim with heavy scepticism.

The counter-argument extended to reinterpreting each earlier warning as something innocuous. On why Alameda served as FTX's "payment provider" for bank transfers, he said FTX could not get bank accounts right away and he anticipated it would take a year or two, so rather than wait he used Alameda: "My understanding at the time was that there were teams managing the process. At the time, I wasn't entirely sure what was happening." On Adam Yedidia's testimony about an August 2022 conversation regarding the enormous amount Alameda owed FTX, Bankman-Fried remembered it differently — Yedidia was just asking about Alameda's risk profile and he was not talking about insolvency at all. On the dramatic balcony conversation with Nishad Singh at their penthouse, he said Singh thought Alameda's liabilities had gotten too high and that FTX was spending too much on marketing, while Bankman-Fried still thought Alameda had more assets than liabilities so it was all fine, and besides, if Singh thought he would be better at marketing he could take it over — it did not have anything to do with the money Alameda owed FTX at all.

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.

# Temu As The Top US iPhone App Of 2023

Temu, the Chinese e-commerce company, is Apple's most downloaded free app in the U.S. for 2023. Apple released an App Store feature on 12 December 2023 showcasing the top iPhone apps of the year, free and paid, as measured by app installs — its proxy for overall popularity. In that ranking, apps from Chinese-based companies have taken over spots previously held by U.S. tech giants like Meta and Google, with CapCut and TikTok, both from Beijing-based ByteDance, coming in at No. 3 and No. 5 respectively.

TechCrunch suggests the negative attention TikTok received during the year may account for its slip from being the No. 1 app last year to No. 5 this year, but says U.S. consumers have not sworn off Chinese apps by the looks of things, given Temu's No. 1 position.

Engagement data supports the point: figures from Apptopia, reported by Bloomberg, noted that consumers were spending 18 minutes per day in Temu's app compared with 10 minutes in Amazon, with younger users spending even more, at 19 minutes per day on average. While Temu attracts users with in-app games, its real draw may be its bargain prices, which have more appeal during an economic downturn, and it is also a heavily marketed app, just as TikTok was in the months leading up to its No. 1 ranking last year.

# The Decline In US VC Investment In China: The Data

China's USD investors continue to deploy capital in industries that are not in the crosshairs of U.S.-China competition, but overall their activity has dwindled significantly due to the changing regulatory and geopolitical currents, coupled with a slowing economy.

The year 2022 saw just $14.5 billion invested in Chinese companies by U.S.-headquartered VCs, compared to $45.4 billion the year before, according to a report from research firm PitchBook. The number of deals nearly halved to 595, and the share of deals with U.S. investor participation dropped to 18.2% in 2022 after hovering above 30% for half a decade.

The scaleback is most notable in prolific investors like Sequoia Capital China, which recently changed its name to HongShan after splitting off its China operation; despite its proactive move to decouple, Sequoia still faces scrutiny from the U.S. government over its decades of activity in China. For the first three quarters of 2023, HongShan completed just 47 deals, compared to 99 deals in the same period of 2022, according to Crunchbase data.

# US Export Controls On China And The Taiwan Flashpoint

Shen Yamei expected the Chinese side to bring up U.S. export controls and investment restrictions at that week's meeting. The Biden administration has restricted U.S. companies from selling high-end tech, primarily in semiconductors, to Chinese companies, and sought to curb U.S. investments in such Chinese tech; U.S. Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo said no to China's requests to reduce the controls on a trip in August and called them "matters of national security". Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng also raised the issues during preparatory meetings with U.S. Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen in San Francisco on 10 November, according to state media. Gabriel Wildau, managing director at consulting firm Teneo, wrote that "aside from Taiwan, export controls are Beijing's top concern, but there is no political space in Washington roll back existing controls", that "the immediate aftermath of the [Biden-Xi] meeting is likely to mark a cyclical high point for bilateral relations", and that the key question is whether that high point extends into a plateau or whether political pressures trigger a new cycle of deterioration, since the period from June had offered a window of opportunity to stabilise relations that may close after the meeting.

On Taiwan, the island is set to hold its presidential election in January, and a more pro-independence winner could stir more of Beijing's ire. Beijing considers Taiwan part of its territory with no right to independently conduct diplomatic relations, while the U.S. recognises Beijing as the sole government of China but maintains unofficial relations with Taiwan, a democratically self-governed island. # China's Data Laws And Government TikTok Device Bans

China's National Intelligence Law of 2017 requires all organisations and citizens to "support, assist and co-operate with the state intelligence work," which is the legal basis on which the Party can compel disclosure from domestically based companies.

# Banking-as-a-Service

## Definition

Banking-as-a-service (BaaS) is the label TechCrunch's coverage applies to platforms — Synapse and QI Tech — that let banks and fintech companies build financial services on top of them, rather than platforms that serve end customers as a bank would.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term through two TechCrunch items: Synapse, covered in the fintech newsletter The Interchange as a San Francisco–based company whose platform "enables banks and fintech companies to easily develop financial services," and QI Tech, covered in the general Startups Weekly newsletter as a Brazilian "banking-as-a-service platform" that raised a large Series B.

Both appear as fintech infrastructure providers rather than consumer-facing banks — Synapse sits behind other companies' financial products, and QI Tech's raise is framed as backing for the same kind of platform business in Brazil.

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform, not bank** — the BaaS provider "operates a platform enabling banks and fintech companies to easily develop financial services" rather than serving end customers directly.
- **Infrastructure for others' products** — Synapse's role is to let other banks and fintechs build financial services on top of it, positioning it as embedded infrastructure rather than a retail brand.
- **Investor interest despite volatility** — QI Tech's BaaS platform drew a $200 million Series B, the largest Brazilian raise across all sectors that year, around the same time Synapse laid off 86 people, or about 40% of its staff.
- **Exposure to macro conditions** — an earlier round of Synapse layoffs (18% of its workforce, per a June blog post from CEO Sankaet Pathak) was attributed to "the current macroeconomic conditions" affecting its clients and platforms, indicating BaaS providers' fortunes are tied to the health of the banks/fintechs building on top of them.

## Background (external)

Wikipedia's entry on Banking-as-a-Service defines it more generally: BaaS refers to offering banking products — like deposit accounts, loans, and credit cards — to customers through partnerships with non-bank or non-financial third parties, where the bank handles balance-sheet management (capital, liquidity, credit risk) while the partner, often a fintech, engages the customer directly through its own app, typically connecting to the bank's systems via APIs.

# Diablo 4 Barbarian Key Passive Build Archetypes

Barbarians are Diablo 4's only pure melee class, with the other classes having hybrid builds for multiple ranges, and Polygon's 2023-10-19 guide identifies four main ideas that all Barbarian builds stem from: Fury dumping, which was most popular in the game's pre-season; weapon swapping; Bleed; and Berserk.

Each archetype is anchored to a Key Passive. Fury dump builds use the Unbridled Rage Key Passive, which causes Fury spenders to cost double the Fury but deal more than double the damage, and obviously require very steady Fury generation since it is easy to starve yourself. Berserk builds use the Unconstrained Key Passive and are all about keeping the Barbarian in the Berserk stage at all times, which nets a hefty bonus — all Barbarian builds will likely use some skills that trigger Berserk, and Unconstrained just enhances the effect. Bleed builds use the Gushing Wounds Key Passive to create a critical strike heavy build that is great for whittling down groups of enemies with damage over time and explosions. Weapon swapping builds, which take advantage of the Walking Arsenal Key Passive, offer what is almost certainly the most unique playstyle for Barbarians: constantly swapping between skills and weapons to give yourself massive damage buffs.

The practical rule that follows is to have one of these Key Passives in mind when building and choose skills accordingly; skills that share certain aspects, like Bleed, are color-coded on the skill tree and can be found with the in-game search function. Other Barbarian builds let you take advantage of mechanics like Thorns or Shouts, but they still typically end with one of these Key Passives.

# BG3 Barbarian: The Damage Class

Polygon names Barbarian the best class for damage in Baldur's Gate 3. Barbarians are all about combat: they get light and medium armor and shields, but they also have the option to keep their AC up even without wearing armor.

For weapons, Barbarians get a wide range of heavy hitters such as battleaxes and warhammers. Every Barbarian gets the Rage ability, which lets them hit even harder and reduces damage during combat — and only during combat. At level 3 a Barbarian chooses from the Wildheart, Berserker, or Wild Magic subclasses. Wildheart lets you modify Rage with animal-themed tweaks such as healing, jumping, or a stampede; Berserker is a lot more straightforward and focuses on hitting extra things and on throwing; Wild Magic adds a magical flair to Rage with a random magical effect plus improved saving throws against magic for you and your allies. Berserker is the best subclass for a Barbarian, with the reasoning and the skill and feat picks left to Polygon's separate Barbarian build guide.

# Game Patch Notes

## Definition

Neither corpus article uses the phrase "patch notes," but both document the same underlying pattern: a studio bundling a slate of changes — new content, rebalancing, and quality-of-life fixes — under a single named or numbered update tied to a release date.
Polygon's Diablo 4 coverage lists that pattern for "Season 2"/"Season of Blood": leveling speed, new endgame bosses, a Nightmare Dungeon rework, mount handling, and Renown/gem-Stash changes, all bundled to arrive together on Oct. 17 (doc_0533).
Polygon's games-of-the-year piece shows the same pattern for Cyberpunk 2077's named "Patch 2.0," a systems-revamping update shipped alongside — but distinct from — the paid Phantom Liberty expansion (doc_0213).

## Context

The corpus's clearest example is Diablo 4's Season 2 update, "Season of Blood," reported by Polygon on 2023-10-04: alongside new vampire powers, Blizzard shipped a broad slate of quality-of-life changes covering leveling speed, endgame bosses, Nightmare Dungeon design, mount handling, and the Renown and gem/Stash systems, all set to arrive together on Oct. 17 as one seasonal patch.

Polygon's broader 2023 games-of-the-year piece shows the same pattern in a second game: Cyberpunk 2077's Phantom Liberty expansion arrived "alongside the sweeping Patch 2.0," which revamped the base game's role-playing progression systems, improved enemy AI, and "course-corrected a litany of other details" — a patch bundled with, but distinct from, the paid DLC content it accompanied.

## Key Characteristics

- **Versioned or seasonal framing** — changes are grouped under a single identifier (Patch 2.0, Season 2/"Season of Blood") rather than released piecemeal, per doc_0533 and doc_0213.
- **Mix of change types** — a single patch bundles new content (Diablo 4's five endgame bosses), rebalancing (faster leveling, reworked Nightmare Dungeon affixes), and quality-of-life fixes (Renown carryover, gems no longer taking bag space), per doc_0533.
- **Developer-explained rationale** — studios attach commentary to justify changes, as when Diablo 4's game director Joe Shely and associate director Joe Piepiora told Polygon the quality-of-life focus came from finally having time to react to player feedback, unlike the rushed first season (doc_0533).
- **Distinct from paid content** — a patch can ship independently of or alongside paid expansions; Cyberpunk 2077's Patch 2.0 revamped core systems while Phantom Liberty (the paid DLC) added new story content, and reviewers credit the patch as much as the DLC for the game's improved reception (doc_0213).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, this kind of update bundle has a generic industry name: release notes (also called patch notes).
Per Wikipedia, release notes "describe important information about a distribution of a hardware or software product" and typically include "a list of what is new in the release, including bug fixes and new features" (Wikipedia, "Release notes," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Diablo 4 Barbarian Leveling Build

This Barbarian leveling build, based on Lexyu's Barbarian leveling guide at IcyVeins and published by Polygon on 2023-10-19, is purely for leveling — allocating your 58 skill points between levels 1 and 50. As with most Barbarian leveling guides it uses Hammer of the Ancients as the primary skill, since it deals massive damage while remaining very cheap to cast, plus Frenzy, Death Blow, Rallying Cry, Leap, and Wrath of the Berserker. Readers wanting more on item affixes or other Legendary powers are pointed to the original IcyVeins guide.

Skills must be purchased in a specific order, because some require a number of allocated points in the tree to unlock, so new skills must be unlocked before existing ones are enhanced. The order is: Frenzy / Enhanced Frenzy; Hammer of the Ancients / Enhanced Hammer of the Ancients / Furious Hammer of the Ancients; Combat Frenzy; Rallying Cry / Enhanced Rallying Cry / Tactical Rallying Cry; Hammer of the Ancients (ranks 2-3); Leap / Enhanced Leap / Power Leap; Hammer of the Ancients (ranks 4-5); Death Blow / Enhanced Death Blow / Warrior's Death Blow / Death Blow (rank 2-5); Wrath of the Berserker / Prime Wrath of the Berserker / Supreme Wrath of the Berserker; Pit Fighter (ranks 1-3); Tempered Fury; Furious Impulse (ranks 1-3); Walking Arsenal; Hamstring; No Mercy; Expose Vulnerability (ranks 1-3); No Mercy (ranks 2-3); Swiftness (ranks 1-3); Thick Skin (ranks 1-3); Counteroffensive (ranks 1-3); Defensive Stance (ranks 1-3); Slaying Strike (ranks 1-3); Aggressive Resistance; and Prolific Fury.

Once the Weapon Expertise system unlocks, place the two-handed sword in your Technique slot, which causes all of your Hammer of the Ancients damage to make enemies Bleed.

At the start of a new character, complete three dungeons first to collect their Aspects, then place them on a piece of gear, ideally jewelry when possible — replacing these Legendaries with new versions using the imprint system every few levels. They are: Aspect of Ancestral Force from the Sunken Ruins dungeon in Scosglen, which makes Hammer of the Ancients quake outwards, dealing X% of its damage to enemies; Aspect of the Expectant from the Underroot dungeon in Scosglen, where attacking enemies with a Basic Skill increases the damage of your next Core Skill cast by X% up to X%; and Edgemaster's Aspect from the Oldstones dungeon in Scosglen, where skills deal X% increased damage based on Primary Resource when cast, with the maximum benefit at full Primary Resource.

# Final Fantasy 16

Final Fantasy 16, developed by Square Enix for PlayStation 5, is ranked 16 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31. Polygon's verdict is blunt: it kicks ass, taking players on a lavish, unadulterated Game of Thrones-esque adventure.

You play as a broody Clive Rosfield, a young man whose life's work is to protect his little brother Joshua; the story begins when Clive's life takes a turn for the worse and he vows to destroy the monster who ruined his and his family's legacy. Developed by Creative Business Unit III, Square Enix's internal team behind the MMORPG Final Fantasy 14, the game leans into patchwork territories of fantasy genre fare — palace intrigue, a whole lot of sex, and endless war between nations — then sprinkles in Final Fantasy elements like mother crystals, dazzling kaiju fights between summons known as Eikons in this iteration, and of course Chocobos.

Critic Ana Diaz notes the quality of the story in this long and linear character-driven RPG waxes and wanes, but calls the action combat among the best she has ever played: the gameplay grips you from the very beginning as Clive smoothly dashes, parries, and swings his giant sword and varied magic with a dazzling amount of style, and it did not just help her stick with the game but allowed her excitement to bubble over every time she took on a new mission.

# Diablo 4 Season 2 Nightmare Dungeon and Travel Changes

Nightmare Dungeons remain places to farm for better items and push builds to their limit in Diablo 4 season 2, but they are becoming much simpler and less grindy: the design team has reworked several Nightmare Dungeon affixes to make them less obnoxious, and Nightmare Sigils now teleport players directly into the dungeon instead of to the door. Polygon reported this on 2023-10-04.

Teleporting to Nightmare Dungeons is one thing, but players still need to ride their horses around the world to reach events like Helltides and the new seasonal activity, Blood Harvest.

Mounts have therefore also been improved in season 2: horses are now faster, and their dashes allow them to break through barricades in the roads. Game director Joe Shely told Polygon the mounts should be more intelligent as well, and will not get stuck on objects in the world as easily as before.

# Baldur's Gate 3

Baldur's Gate 3, developed by Larian Studios for PlayStation 5 and Windows PC, is ranked 2 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31, and Polygon says it hit at the perfect moment.

The timing argument has two parts. Despite the handful of truly great computer role-playing games released since the early 2000s — Larian itself made waves with its Divinity: Original Sin series in 2014 and 2017 — the genre had largely remained a modern niche; but Dungeons & Dragons has undergone something of a renaissance thanks to actual-play series like Critical Role and Dimension 20, and Larian had two years of player feedback with which to build its new masterpiece. That masterpiece launched in August and garnered the kind of attention that catapults a game from niche interests to widespread acclaim: old CRPG fans finally came home, the Mass Effect generation discovered a new kind of RPG, and D&D fans found an exceptional digital version of their beloved tabletop game to play alone or with their party in co-op.

Critic RG writes that like a good DM, the game teases out story beats that feel personal to you, cleverly luring you into experiences that seem like they would not make sense in anyone else's campaign; every act delivers quiet, memorable character moments and anxiety-inducing battles, all feeling organic, letting the game replicate as closely as a video game can D&D's best feature — the intoxicating sense that anything could happen at any moment. The best games that year told their stories in interesting ways, but Baldur's Gate 3 takes experimental storytelling to another level, with every choice and every new direction a simple success, fail, or crit away; one roll of the dice after another can take you all the way from a crashed Nautiloid to the city of Baldur's Gate itself, and it is the spinning whir of its d20 that defined video game storytelling in 2023.

# Dredge (Fishing Horror Game)

Dredge, developed by Black Salt Games for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X, is ranked 17 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31. Polygon describes it as a Lovecraftian horror experience masquerading as a simple fishing game.

The open ocean is filled with terrible creatures that can and will damage or destroy your boat, and each of the major islands you visit comes with its own evil sea beasts that must be dealt with if you want to progress the story or fish peacefully. The game ultimately tells a dark parable about loss, and how obsession can own you if you are not careful.

Critic RG argues what makes it one of the best games of 2023 is that under its foreboding story and twisted environments is a fishing game that grows more complex with every outing, centered on an upgrade system that feels amazing to progress through: as the dangers around you grow, so do your ship's capabilities, and adventuring into battles — metaphorical and otherwise — with the seas' most dastardly critters always yields upgrades that let you catch even better fish and build an even bigger boat. By 10 or so hours in, you feel like a commercial fisherman who happened upon something bigger and more foreboding than they could have imagined, having stared deep into some kind of black abyss only to escape forever changed.

Exquisite Biome, from game designer Caro Asercion and illustrator Si Sweetman, sits in the world-building TTRPG tradition but focuses specifically on ecological biomes and the creatures that populate them. # Diablo 4 Season 2 Endgame Bosses and Uber Uniques

Diablo 4's season 2 adds five new endgame bosses where players will spend their time at max level and earn some of the game's most powerful items: Grigoire The Galvanic Saint, the Echo of Varshan, The Beast in the Ice, the Dark Master, and the Echo of Duriel. Polygon reported this on 2023-10-04.

Each boss has its own laundry list of busy work to complete in order to unlock the encounter — such as completing Nightmare Dungeons above level 30 or completing Grim Favors — but each also comes with Unique rewards. Because the bosses each offer their own pool of Unique items, farming for a specific piece becomes easier: instead of running dungeons and hoping the desired item drops, players can gather all the materials, kill The Beast in the Ice, and repeat if they do not get what they wanted.

The Echo of Duriel is the most interesting of the five, since Duriel has a chance to drop the ultimate, super-rare uber Uniques that were previously almost impossible to acquire; to compensate, players must kill the four other endgame bosses each time they want to face Duriel.

Blizzard's designers did not build these bosses to be as tough as the ultimate Uber Lilith fight, but they should hopefully prove a challenge to most players while giving a targeted way to farm must-have items. The Echo of Duriel, who is level 100, will be the most difficult of the new bosses, and is the only way for players to farm Uber Uniques in Diablo 4. For players with more in-game gold than time, Blizzard confirmed in the interview that players will be able to trade with one another to get the items needed to summon Duriel and the other bosses.

# Dungeon Crawl Classics

Dungeon Crawl Classics, by Goodman Games, is picked in Polygon's 2023 roundup by Thilo Graf of AAW Games, who says that of the many RPG systems he runs and plays, precious few have had such a tremendous and lasting impact on his design and games.

Its defining features are aesthetics influenced by all-time greats like Leiber and Moorcock, volatile magic, a relatively flat power curve for a d20-based game, and an emphasis on the skill of the players rather than primarily rewarding the crafting of effective builds. Graf positions it between two poles: it is not as much of a heroic power fantasy as D&D 5e or Pathfinder, but neither is it as minimalist as many old-school games. With fickle gods, mutating magics, lucky scoundrels, and ferocious fighters, he says DCC feels like playing through a Bal-Sagoth or Eternal Champion song, and adds that it is easy to pick up if your group has any experience with D&D's third edition or Pathfinder. He also notes its influence on his own work: DCC's focus on simple, impactful rules was a core design inspiration for the almost system-neutral Survivalist's Guide to Spelunking for 5e, which he wrote with Douglas Niles and Stephen Yeardley, and he is pleased that DCC authors, judges, and players use that book too.

# Custom Character Versus Origin Character In Baldur's Gate 3

An Origin character in Baldur's Gate 3 is one of the NPCs from your party that you can simply choose and play as right from the start, whereas a custom character is one you build yourself by picking a race and background.

The discriminating feature is the trade between setup effort and narrative freedom. Playing an Origin character is a perfectly fine way to play if you would rather not go through the process of picking a race and background, but you are then limited to that character's predetermined story. A custom character is a bit more work at the beginning, yet gives you far more freedom to experience the entire story of Baldur's Gate 3. Polygon presents this as the decision to settle before moving on to the class rankings themselves.

# Diablo 4 Season 2 Renown and Gem Inventory Rework

Two of Diablo 4's other biggest pain points — gems and Renown — are also being addressed in season 2, as Polygon reported on 2023-10-04.

The grind to accrue Renown, the resource players get for completing activities in each area, is no longer something players will need to partake in every season: much like the Altars of Lilith change in season 1, players who have fully unlocked their Renown track with one character will never have to do it again. Previously players had to max out Renown — which all but required doing nearly every dungeon and most side quests in the game — every season in order to get all available Skill and Paragon Points. Unlike with the Altars of Lilith carryover, players will not need to first log into a character that has completed the Renown track in order to propagate that data to the rest of their account; associate game director Joe Piepiora said all of that data migration should happen without that extra step in season 2.

Polygon calls this yet another massive 180 on the Renown system from Blizzard in barely five months' time. Asked about the shift, Piepiora said players simply were not having fun redoing the grind every season, hence the move — as with the Altars last season — to alleviate the pressure on players to only play "efficiently."

As for gems, they will no longer take up bag space, as they are now considered crafting materials. That change comes alongside a massive upgrade to the Stash itself: Stashes now appear in more locations, including all minor towns with a Waypoint in them, and players can search their Stashes for specific items and affixes.

# There Is No Single Best Class In Baldur's Gate 3

Polygon argues that there is no single best class in Baldur's Gate 3 — "barrelmancer aside" — so the choice should be settled by how you want to play rather than by any ranking of raw power.

The grounds are twofold. First, the classes in Baldur's Gate 3, and in pen-and-paper D&D for that matter, are all fairly well-balanced. Second, the game gives you as many opportunities for creative problem solving as it does for punching, so a class that looks weak in a straight fight still has routes to succeed. The warrant joining grounds to claim is that when options are balanced and the game rewards more than one kind of solution, "best" collapses into "best for your intended playstyle." A further supporting point removes the risk of a bad commitment: even when playing solo you still manage the rest of your party, so you get to experiment with multiple classes at once rather than being locked into one. Polygon repeats the same argument verbatim in its Warlock build guide of 2023-12-01, so the position is stated across both articles.

# City Of Winter

City of Winter is a TTRPG with lightweight rules but a heavy emphasis on the kind of ephemera usually reserved for much crunchier games, recommended in Polygon's 2023 roundup by Ennie Award-winning entertainment journalist Linda Codega, who says she and her friends still talk about the weekend they spent playing it.

Because of that emphasis, creating space for the game is almost as important as who you choose to play it with. Characters travel along a cloth map illustrating a landscape with only the barest indications of topography; the focus instead relies on themes of assimilation, diaspora, and — most importantly to the narrative — baggage. As a family of immigrants, bound by blood or by choice, players describe their home and their traditions, and then, as a darkness comes from the west side of the map, they leave it all behind, choosing what traditions and rituals they pick up from the places they visit and what they hold on to from their homeland. Codega notes that very few games require such strict fidelity to the road laid out before you, but argues City of Winter uses that structure to facilitate the kind of deeply resonant character arcs and development many role-players crave. Her verdict: an astoundingly complex game in which bringing your best stories to the table leaves you with a sense of loss and belonging that seem to walk together, hand in hand.

# BG3 Monk: The Speed Class

Polygon names Monk the best class for speed in Baldur's Gate 3. Monks are a melee class kind of like Fighters, but with a lot more pizzazz: their best Ability is Dexterity, so their combat is more martial arts than swordplay.

Monks do not get armor and have only a limited set of weapons available, but they make up for it with Unarmed Strikes that deal extra damage. They take a little more finesse to play than Fighters. Monk subclasses unlock at level 3 and comprise Way of the Four Elements, Way of the Open Hand, and Way of Shadow. Way of the Four Elements mixes spells into your Monk abilities, using renamed spells from the caster classes; Way of the Open Hand expands your attacks to include things like knocking down enemies or pushing them with extra melee attacks; Way of Shadow makes your Monk sneaky and stealthy, effectively a ninja subclass. Polygon's recommendation is stated as "Way of the Open Palm is the best subclass for a Monk," with reasoning and skill and feat picks left to its separate Monk build guide.

# Super Mario Bros. Wonder

Super Mario Bros. Wonder, developed by Nintendo EPD for Nintendo Switch, is ranked 4 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31 — the first side-scrolling 2D platformer in the Super Mario Bros. line since New Super Mario Bros. U in 2012, and both a faithful rendition of the classic format and a complete reinvention of the series' irresistible formula.

# Diablo 4 Season 2 Experience and Leveling Changes

One of the most notable changes in Diablo 4's second season update is an increase in experience gains: Blizzard claims players will be able to reach the level cap of 100 about 40% faster than in Season of the Malignant, which had already increased experience gains compared with Diablo 4's launch. # Terry McLaurin's Fantasy Outlook In Weeks 5 And 6 Of 2023

qid: Does the TechCrunch article suggest a different level of transparency from Sam Altman with the board compared to the portrayal of his involvement with generative AI technology as described in the Fortune article?
context:
# OpenAI Board Composition And The Helen Toner Dispute

At the time of Sam Altman's ouster in November 2023, OpenAI's board of directors consisted of OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, tech entrepreneur Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner, the director of strategy at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology — and a clash between Altman and Toner is reported to have contributed to the crisis.

The New York Times reported that, before his ousting, Altman made a move to push out board member Helen Toner because he thought a paper she had co-written was overly critical of OpenAI. That, among other issues, led to OpenAI's predicament. The Times also indicated that negotiations to hire Altman back were continuing, but that one major sticking point remaining was "guardrails" intended to improve Altman's communication with the board.



---


# Theory: An AGI And Mission Rift Between Altman And The Board

The proposition is that Altman's zeal for AGI, even absent a secret project or agreement, led to a major rift between him and the board. Altman is a proud techno-optimist and often speaks fondly of the possibilities of AGI, or artificial general intelligence, a theoretical software system that achieves human-like intellect and versatility. The board's statement pointedly includes that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity" and that new leadership was necessary.

The supporting observation is a directional one: it has been obvious to all that Altman took the company in a much more corporate direction from its origins, changing its legal status and aggressively pursuing enterprise and consumer applications, which does not sound a lot like the "mission" the board wants to advance.

What counts against it is timing. This shift did not happen today, and it certainly does not seem like a plausible reason for abruptly firing the CEO and a few others on a beautiful fall Friday afternoon — a gradual drift does not explain an abrupt dismissal.



---


# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.



---


# Sam Altman's Career And Public Profile

Sam Altman has a long history steering OpenAI: he co-founded the company alongside Peter Thiel, LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman and others, and initially served as a co-chair of OpenAI alongside Elon Musk, who left in 2018 to avoid a conflict of interest with Tesla.

Altman formerly headed the startup accelerator Y Combinator and also holds a seat on the board at Worldcoin, the ambitious cryptocurrency project. In the several months before his firing he played an active role in attempting to shape regulators' responses to AI, appearing at U.S. congressional hearings and meeting personally with world leaders including President Joe Biden, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz and French President Emmanuel Macron, among others, on an international policy tour.

His standing in the industry was reflected in the reaction to his ouster. Eric Schmidt posted on X: "Sam Altman is a hero of mine. He built a company from nothing to $90 Billion in value, and changed our collective world forever. I can't wait to see what he does next. I, and billions of people, will benefit from his future work- it's going to be simply incredible." His brother Jack Altman wrote: "More important than being one of the most brilliant and impactful people our industry has ever had Sam is one of the most generous and caring people I know. I've never met someone who has supported and lifted up more people around them than him. Couldn't be a prouder brother."



---


# Altman's Argument On AI's Promise And Existential Risk

Sam Altman predicted that AI will prove to be "the greatest leap forward of any of the big technological revolutions we've had so far."

He paired that claim with its counterweight rather than leaving it alone: he also acknowledged the need for guardrails, calling attention to the existential dangers future AI could pose.



---


# Analyst Assessment Of Altman's Departure Impact

Gartner analyst Arun Chandrasekaran argued that Altman's exit "is indeed shocking as he has been the face of" generative AI technology — the ground for the shock being his public role rather than any operational gap.

Chandrasekaran qualified the consequence for the company itself: OpenAI still has a "deep bench of technical leaders," but its next executives will have to steer it through the challenges of scaling the business and meeting the expectations of regulators and society.



---


# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.



---


# The OpenAI Board's Firing Of Sam Altman

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said on Friday, 2023-11-17, that it had pushed out its co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after a review found he was "not consistently candid in his communications" with the board of directors. "The board no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI," the artificial intelligence company said in a statement. Mira Murati, OpenAI's chief technology officer, would take over as interim CEO effective immediately while the company searched for a permanent replacement.

OpenAI declined to answer questions on what Altman's alleged lack of candor was about; the statement said only that his behavior was hindering the board's ability to exercise its responsibilities. Altman posted on X that Friday: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later."



---


# Sam Altman's Side Ventures: Helion, Retro And Worldcoin

Altman has a number of possible next steps after leaving OpenAI, because even while running the company he placed large bets on several other ambitious projects.

Among them are Helion Energy, for developing fusion reactors that could produce prodigious amounts of energy from the hydrogen in seawater, and Retro Biosciences, which aims to add 10 years to the human lifespan using biotechnology. Altman also co-founded Worldcoin, a biometric and cryptocurrency project that has been scanning people's eyeballs with the goal of creating a vast digital identity and financial network.



---


# Sam Altman's Rise As The Face Of Generative AI

In the year since Altman catapulted ChatGPT to global fame, he became Silicon Valley's sought-after voice on the promise and potential dangers of artificial intelligence, and his sudden and mostly unexplained exit brought uncertainty to the industry's future. He helped start OpenAI as a nonprofit research laboratory in 2015, but it was ChatGPT's explosion into public consciousness that thrust him into the spotlight as a face of generative AI — technology that can produce novel imagery, passages of text and other media. On a world tour in 2023 he was mobbed by a crowd of adoring fans at an event in London.

He has sat with multiple heads of state to discuss AI's potential and perils. On Thursday, 2023-11-16, he took part in a CEO summit at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference in San Francisco, where OpenAI is based. At OpenAI's first developer conference the week before, Altman was the main speaker, showcasing a vision for a future of AI agents that could help people with a variety of tasks; days later he announced the company would have to pause new subscriptions to its premium version of ChatGPT because it had exceeded capacity.



---


# Sam Altman's Next Move After The OpenAI Firing

In the days after his firing, Sam Altman's destination was genuinely unsettled: on November 20, 2023 he and Greg Brockman announced they would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research team, yet on the same day both were reported to be still open to returning to OpenAI, and Altman was separately telling investors he planned to launch a new venture.

On November 20 Altman, Brockman and colleagues announced they would join Microsoft to lead a new AI research team, with Satya Nadella leaving the door open to other OpenAI staffers and saying they would be given the resources they needed should they choose to join. As reported by The Verge, however, Altman's move to Microsoft was not a done deal — both Altman and Brockman remained open to returning to OpenAI if the remaining board members who initially fired him stepped aside. At the same time, according to The Information, Altman had been telling investors he was planning to launch a new venture, with Brockman expected to join the effort in whatever form it took — possibly an AI chip startup. Altman also posted on X on November 18: "i love you all. today was a weird experience in many ways. but one unexpected one is that it has been sorta like reading your own eulogy while you're still alive. the outpouring of love is awesome. one takeaway: go tell your friends how great you think they are."

Nadella himself hedged. In a series of interviews he stepped back from earlier reporting that Altman and Brockman were headed to Microsoft, telling CNBC: "Obviously, we want Sam and Greg to have a fantastic home if they're not going to be in OpenAI," and saying he was "open" to them settling at Microsoft or returning to OpenAI should the board and employees support the move.



---


# Sam Altman's Career Before OpenAI

Sam Altman, 38 as of November 2023, is not trained as an AI engineer, yet has been seen as a Silicon Valley wunderkind since his early 20s. The defining credential of that earlier phase is that he was recruited in 2014 to take the lead of the startup incubator YCombinator.

The reputation attached to him at the time is captured in YCombinator co-founder Paul Graham's 2014 announcement that Altman would become its president: "Sam is one of the smartest people I know, and understands startups better than perhaps anyone I know, including myself." Graham said then that Altman was "one of those rare people who manage to be both fearsomely effective and yet fundamentally benevolent."



---


# Generative AI

## Definition

In the corpus, "generative AI" is the umbrella label applied to the 2023 AI boom's content-producing systems — OpenAI's ChatGPT (built on GPT-3.5/GPT-4) and Adobe's Firefly image and vector-graphics models are the flagship examples named — rather than a term the corpus itself formally defines.

## Context

The corpus treats "generative AI" as the umbrella term for the mainstream AI boom of 2023, distinct from the EU AI Act's regulatory term "general purpose AI" (GPAI), which lawmakers deliberately chose as a more technology-neutral label for "the most powerful models behind the current boom in generative AI tools" so the law would not be pinned to one architecture like transformers (doc_0525).
OpenAI built ChatGPT specifically "to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI," and its free, chat-based interface is credited with "taking generative AI mainstream" as a consumer product rather than a research artifact (doc_0047).
Enterprise adoption is depicted as cautious relative to vendor hype: a Morgan Stanley survey found 56% of CIOs said generative AI was affecting investment priorities, but only 4% had launched significant projects, most still in evaluation or proof-of-concept (doc_0160).
The technology spans well beyond chatbots — Adobe's Firefly generative AI models generate images and vector graphics for creative software (doc_0043), and Amazon executive Tye Brady discussed generative AI alongside humanoid robots and mobile manipulation as an input to robotics work (doc_0528).
The same capability that drives adoption also drives the corpus's recurring regulatory and creative-industry concerns: the EU warned that "widely accessible generative AI tools" pose disinformation risks to elections (doc_0248), and the National Music Publishers Association called generative AI "the greatest risk to the human creative class that has ever existed" in its copyright submission to the US Copyright Office (doc_0271).

## Key Characteristics

- **Illustrated by content-producing examples rather than defined outright** — the corpus shows the term through instances of new text, images, and vector graphics being produced from a prompt, illustrated by ChatGPT's text generation (doc_0048) and Firefly's image/vector generation (doc_0043).
- **Consumer breakout via chat interfaces** — ChatGPT's free, web-based chat interface is what took generative AI "mainstream," reaching the fastest adoption of any consumer app (doc_0047, doc_0048).
- **Enterprise adoption lags vendor hype** — large-company CIOs report slow, cautious rollout despite heavy vendor promotion, weighing API/SaaS costs against ROI (doc_0160).
- **Distinct from but overlapping "general purpose AI"** — EU lawmakers deliberately avoided calling the underlying models "generative AI" in law, choosing "general purpose AI" instead to stay technology-neutral rather than tied to transformer-based architectures (doc_0525).
- **Applies across domains beyond chatbots** — spans creative tools (Adobe Firefly) and robotics (Amazon's mobile manipulation work), per the corpus (doc_0043, doc_0528).
- **Focus of copyright and disinformation controversy** — named by the NMPA as a threat to the "human creative class" via unlicensed training data (doc_0271), and flagged by the EU as an election-disinformation risk requiring safeguards (doc_0248).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "generative AI" as a familiar shorthand without formally defining it. Per IBM, generative AI "is artificial intelligence (AI) that can create original content — such as text, images, video, audio or software code — in response to a user's prompt or request," distinguishing it from AI systems built only to classify or act on existing data (IBM, *What is generative AI?*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Theory: A Long-Term Strategy Disagreement Over OpenAI's Economics

The proposition is that Altman and the board fell out over when OpenAI's money-losing growth strategy has to end. Despite being the hottest tech company in the world and everyone talking about ChatGPT, OpenAI is not exactly a sound business: it is shoveling money into the furnace as fast as it can by serving, by all accounts, a fantastically expensive product at bargain-bin prices. That is all well and good for a year or two, but at some point that strategy changes from a growth hack to an existential liability — so could Altman and the board have had irreconcilable differences on where that point lies?

TechCrunch judges this unlikely, and gives the disconfirming evidence: the company has been very deliberately pursuing this very publicly, confidently and on a long-term basis. Altman and the board seem to be in sync on this, at least for the present.



---


# The Analyst View That Altman's Exit Was Not A Business Problem

Forrester analyst Rowan Curran speculated that Altman's departure, "while sudden," did not likely reflect deeper business problems — attacking the inference from a shocking exit to trouble in the company's technology or commercial position.

"This seems to be a case of an executive transition that was about issues with the individual in question, and not with the underlying technology or business," Curran said.



---


# Theory: A Financial Mismatch At OpenAI

The proposition is that some major mismatch in the financial department was the cause for dismissal. Could OpenAI be losing even more money than Altman admitted or projected? It seems impossible, TechCrunch writes, but the costs of running this operation have no precedent, nor really does the operation itself.

A variant, offered as purely speculative: what if Altman had been secretly pursuing an internal project, perhaps at significant cost, against the advice of the board and without the necessary safety measures that probably should accompany such research? It sounds a little wild, but firing your CEO like this is also a little wild.

What weighs against the family of financial theories is the difficulty of concealment: it is hard to imagine what Altman could have kept from the board and CTO that would be so damning. A separate possibility is that Altman was making personal investments in a way the board disagreed with — with OpenAI poised to be a kingmaker in the field, he would certainly be in a position of power. One would think that, as an ideologically driven person already rich beyond belief and at the head of the world's leading AI company, Altman would have risen beyond having to do this kind of side deal, or at the very least that scrutiny on him and those close to him would prevent them. But one can never be sure.



---


# Induced AI's Plain-English Workflow Automation

Sam Altman is among the backers of Induced AI, an AI startup founded by two teenagers that aims to help businesses automate workflows in "previously unexplored" ways.

Manish reported the story in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023. Induced AI was founded that same year, and its product lets businesses type their back-office tasks into it in plain English, converting those instructions into pseudo-code in real time.

# Sam Altman's Firing And Reinstatement

OpenAI's plans were very nearly smashed to pieces just before Thanksgiving when the OpenAI board of directors fired Sam Altman, arguing that he had not been "consistently candid in his communications with the board."

That firing didn't take. Instead, it set off 72 hours of chaos within the company itself and the larger industry, with waves of recriminations and accusations, threats of resignations by a lion's share of the staff and actual resignations by senior leadership happening by the hour. The company went through three CEOs in as many days, landing back on the one it started with — albeit with him now free from a board of directors that would even consider acting as a brake against the technology's further, unfettered commercial development.



---


# OpenAI's AI Chip Ambitions

The company has suggested that it might be entering the AI chip market at some point in the future, in an effort to shore up the speed and performance of its API services.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had previously pointed to industry-wide GPU shortages for the service's spotty performance, and producing its own processors might mitigate those supply issues while potentially lowering the current four-cent-per-query cost of operating the chatbot to something more manageable.
