# Sassoon's Redirect And The Alameda All-Hands Recording

Prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's brief redirect of Caroline Ellison on October 12th, 2023 set a trap that opened the door to the jury hearing a secret recording of an Alameda all-hands meeting in which Ellison confessed to stealing billions of FTX customers' money at Bankman-Fried's direction. On direct examination, near the end, Sassoon had asked about the all-hands meeting without bringing up many specifics; during the cross, Mark Cohen asked Ellison what topics were covered in the meeting while avoiding details — which let Sassoon work the confession in on redirect. The judge then ruled in favour of the jury hearing the recordings, and the court briefly recessed; that was when Bankman-Fried's mother approached the defense lawyers.

The tape was set up by a short afternoon witness. Christian Drappi, a former Alameda software engineer who looked like a handsome funeral director in a black suit and tie, testified that when Binance CEO Changpeng Zhao announced on Twitter that he intended to acquire FTX, Ellison confessed the theft of customer funds to him and a few other employees. The all-hands took place the following day and was secretly recorded by an employee who had joined Alameda three days before. In the recording Ellison did indeed confess to stealing customer funds with Bankman-Fried's approval. Drappi said he resigned less than 24 hours after the meeting; the recording was later sent to him, and he sent it to the government.

The reporter's assessment was that Sassoon demolished any points Cohen had attempted to make and that she did not fully appreciate the cleverness until after Ellison left the stand and the jurors left the room. In the family seats, Joseph Bankman, the defendant's father and a senior advisor to FTX's philanthropic arm, was not in the room for the recording, and Barbara Fried looked unhappy, rubbing her left temple as though she had a tremendous headache.



---


# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. Bankman-Fried is said to have directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers, and to have forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged. These are the government's allegations as presented in its opening statement, not established findings.



---


# Cohen's Cross-Examination Of Caroline Ellison

Mark Cohen's cross-examination of Caroline Ellison on October 12th, 2023 aimed at the premise that her direct testimony was reliable — she had recounted many conversations held in person or on auto-deleting messaging platforms, and she had an incentive to flip on Bankman-Fried in the form of possible leniency at sentencing — but The Verge's reporter judged that the defense absolutely biffed it. In Cohen's disorganized cross-examination he mostly bored the jury; at one point two different jurors appeared to be asleep, and midway through the morning the reporter began wondering whether there was a mercy rule for cross-examinations.

The lines of attack were opened and dropped. Cohen established that Bankman-Fried had a much larger appetite for risk than Ellison, that the two reacted differently to stress, and that they took different approaches to media — Ellison avoided it while Bankman-Fried sought it out — without building on any of it. He drew out that Alameda had one accountant in 2021 and hired two more junior accountants in 2022, and had a problem retaining accountants, then dropped that too. He appeared to be trying to suggest the government had coerced Ellison's testimony by getting her to plead guilty to defrauding investors, conduct she could not have been involved in since she did not prepare materials for them; unfortunately she said she had had conversations with investors as part of their due diligence, and Alameda was in any case taking on losses from FTX to keep FTX's balance sheet pristine. Cohen also pressed the hedge he had blamed her for not taking out in his opening — hedging being long crypto by selling Nasdaq futures — which raised the question of whether the defense was that she should have taken more customer funds, or taken them sooner.

Small failures accumulated. Cohen asked Ellison to define what "buy on the way down" meant as though it were a term of art, which seemed to puzzle her, and at other times he seemed to forget what she had testified to and brought up things she had not said; like FTX employee Adam Yedidia before her, Ellison was fastidious about making sure a question was clear and her answer precise. She appeared at one point to be toying with him: having testified on direct about the token Luna, she noted when Cohen asked about Terra/Luna that she had only spoken about Luna, leaving him to fumble the relationship between the two. There were many sidebars, enough that several jurors looked entertained when one occurred, and in one the day before the prosecution complained that Bankman-Fried was visibly scoffing at Ellison's answers, per the court transcript. What Cohen was up against was strong direct evidence: fake balance sheets, one sent to crypto lender Genesis, after which a Genesis representative texted Ellison to say he had spoken to Bankman-Fried — strongly suggesting Bankman-Fried knew the contents of the fake balance sheet. Afterwards, the defendant's mother Barbara Fried engaged Christian Everdell in an animated conversation, gesticulating and clearly holding a strong opinion; Everdell walked off and Cohen talked to her for a bit.

FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang and Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse, and both planned to cooperate with prosecutors. # The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."

# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.

# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# The U.S. Justice Department's Parallel Antitrust Suits Against Google

The Helena World Chronicle class action arrives alongside the filing of the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, and the complaint also references the Justice Department's 2020 civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

The two government cases concern different markets: search and search advertising in the 2020 suit are distinct from the digital ad technologies at issue in the more recent one.

# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.

# Google's News Content Payment Deal With Canada

In November 2023, the month before the Helena World Chronicle suit was filed, Google reached an agreement with the Canadian government under which the search giant would pay Canadian media for use of their content. Under the terms of the deal, Google will provide $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) every year to news organizations in the country, with funds distributed based on the news outlets' headcount.

Negotiations with Meta over the same Canadian law were still unresolved as of mid-December 2023. Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August, in light of the pressure to pay for content under the new Canadian law.

# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.

# "Go Big In Europe": Google's Post-Fine Search Quality Push

The government argued on November 10, 2023 that Google only endeavored to enhance its search engine in the European Union after it was hit by a €5 billion antitrust fine in 2018 — a claim internal documents revealed, according to Bloomberg.

The EU's antitrust order forced Google to offer Android phone users a screen with five search engine options to choose from, according to the DOJ. In response, Google enacted a plan its executives dubbed "Go Big in Europe," to enhance search results in France and Germany in 2019 and 2020 with more local content: news, post-game soccer video highlights, information on local television options for streaming, and pronunciation practice for different languages. The aim was to incentivize users to click on Google's home screen rather than the competition's.

That revelation effectively supports the Justice Department's argument that Google, without the push of competition, has little incentive to improve its products — a classic consequence in a monopoly.

# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.

# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

# Google's Knowledge Graph And Featured Snippets

As described in the Helena World Chronicle complaint, Google's Knowledge Graph is a database, launched in May 2012, from which Google draws a summary of content that it displays as a "Knowledge Panel" to the right of search results when a user searches for information on a topic. The complaint characterises it as one of Google's older question-and-answer technologies and treats it as part of the alleged harm to publishers, alongside newer AI technologies.

The complaint states that "Google compiled this massive database by extracting information from Publishers' websites — what Google calls 'materials shared across the web' — and from 'open source and licensed databases.'" By 2020, the Knowledge Graph had grown to 500 billion facts about 5 billion entities, but the complaint alleges that much of the "collective intelligence" Google tapped into was content "misappropriated from Publishers."

Featured Snippets are a distinct Google technology in which Google algorithmically extracts answers from webpages; the complaint cites them too, on the grounds that they shift traffic away from publishers' websites.

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.

# Google's Secret OEM And Carrier Deals And Its Deleted Chats

Asked what surprised him in the courtroom, Tim Sweeney said the trial confirmed practices he had suspected since around 2018 — when some people called him a conspiracy theorist for saying so — including that Google leaked Epic's conversations to reporters to get negative stories written, paid other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores, and went around paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores.

Sweeney gave a concrete instance from Epic's own experience: when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with other smartphone manufacturers such as OnePlus and with carriers of all sorts, those partners told Epic they couldn't do a deal because Google had done a secret deal with them. He called it disconcerting to see the extent of bad-faith efforts inside a company of Google's size, saying you would expect a trillion-dollar company to have developed respectable processes and leadership structures providing checks and balances against wrongdoing. Instead, he said, Google employees were "rampantly destroying all their chats on these topics": long conversation threads would start to get into a spicy antitrust issue, somebody would point out that history was on, and the chat would go silent — history turned off so the documents would be destroyed. Sweeney said it was great to see all of that called out in detail at trial.

# Gemini Pro's News Summarization Refusals And Stale Answers

Asked to summarise topical news in early December 2023, Gemini Pro often would not do it, despite having Google Search and Google News at its disposal. It seemed loath to comment on potentially controversial news topics, instead telling users to Google it themselves.

The TechCrunch reporter tried the same prompt and got a very similar response. ChatGPT, by contrast, gave a bullet-list summary with citations to news articles.

There was one partial exception, and it exposed a second problem: Gemini Pro did provide a summary of updates on the war in Ukraine when the reporter asked for one, but the information was over a month out of date.

# Epic's Opening Statement: Bribes And Blocks

Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's case that Android functions as an unlawful monopoly rested on characterising Google as a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" any attempt to compete with Android's Google Play store — with the resulting status quo being that the vast, vast majority of Android app installs come from Google Play, and only a tiny sliver is attributable to the Galaxy Store that comes preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

The grounds were money and conduct. Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's fat app profit margins — 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, says Epic — and pointed out several ugly-seeming ways Google has allegedly attempted to keep anyone from taking that money away, like paying game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers as Epic did with Fortnite. "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete. Literally gives them money and other things of value," said Bornstein. "It's like Google saying, 'Here's $360 million' — that's an actual number you'll hear about — why don't you sit this one out and let me win?"

The warrant linking payments to consumer harm was left mostly implicit on day one. The upshot for consumers, Epic's earlier legal filings have suggested, is that we pay higher prices for apps than we would if there were more competition and/or lower app store and payment processing fees; but while that will probably come up later in the trial, Epic chose to focus more on simply painting Google as the bad guy on day one.

# Google's Auto-Deleted Chats And The Sanctions Ruling

Google employees up to and including CEO Sundar Pichai were caught setting sensitive chats to auto-delete to keep them out of a court's hands, and the court has already decided Google should be sanctioned in some way for making potential evidence disappear — enough that the judge has decided to explicitly tell the jury they are not seeing all the evidence.

Bornstein used it to plant persistent seeds of doubt in the minds of jury members: "All we know is whatever is in the destroyed chats, as bad as the documents are, is worse. Or at least it was worse, before they were destroyed."

The best Google could do in response was to plant its own feeble seed with the jury — "Is Epic using the chats to distract me from all the evidence I do see?" — alongside Pomerantz's legal point that it is true Google could have automatically saved all chats for all relevant employees, but just because Google did not save some chats did not mean it violated antitrust laws.

The issue is not confined to this case. It has also come up in the US v. Google antitrust trial in Washington, DC, still ongoing at the start of Epic's trial.

# Epic's Rebuttal Of Google's Leaked Email Summary

Pressed with the suggestion that the email Epic accused Google of leaking showed Epic was itself interested in a special deal, Tim Sweeney attacked the premise of the characterisation: Google did not leak the email, he said — it leaked "their ridiculously biased summary of it" to Abner Li at 9to5Google.

He supported the leak claim with trial testimony: Don Harrison testified that he didn't think Google leaked to the press, and was then presented with a document including Google's press team and Sameer Samat, head of all Android, summarising the articles that appeared as a result of Google's leaking of Epic's plans to the press. On the substance of the email, Sweeney said it is in evidence and is the same one he had already described: right before Christmas-ish 2019, with the new Marvel season and a lineup of Star Wars content planned, he asked Google's executives to let Fortnite come to the Google Play Store using Epic's own payment method and to open up the use of their own payment methods to all developers, not just Epic. The interviewer conceded the point, saying he had read that email in court and had not realised it was the same one, because it was so far off from what he had heard described as a "special billing exception."

# Epic's Refusal Of Special Deals And Its 2019 Google Proposal

Asked whether he would have sued at all had Google offered 0 percent for Epic's own payments system or 4 percent for Google Play billing instead of a $147 million deal, Tim Sweeney answered no — Epic has always turned down special deals just for Epic, fighting on the principle that all developers should be given the same opportunities.

His grounds were a document in evidence: a 2019 email he sent to all of Google's senior executives, right before Fortnite launched the Marvel season and the Star Wars event featuring J.J. Abrams, saying Epic wanted to bring Fortnite to the Google Play Store in time for that event and wanted Google to allow Epic and all other developers to process certain payments and keep them all. Had Google said yes, Sweeney argued, it would have been awesome for all developers, the Android ecosystem would have become much stronger, and Google would be in a better position in the smartphone industry today; there would never have been a dispute because the problem would have been solved. The warrant tying this to the present is his claim that the fix has always been within Google's reach: Google makes several billion dollars a year in what he calls unfairly earned profits from imposing this tax, which is nothing compared to what it makes from search, and given all the other benefits it gets from Android, "Google could solve this problem today if they wanted to."

# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Epic v. Google Is A Jury Trial

Epic and Google have to convince a jury, not the judge, which is totally different from how the Apple case played out — that one was a "bench trial."

The consequence is that persuasion cuts both ways and is hard to predict. All the evidence of tricky deals inside Google might sway a jury against the company; alternatively, Google scaremongering that sideloaded apps equal gaping security holes might sway a jury against Epic. Who knows.

The jury is also sealed off from coverage: Judge Donato explicitly told jurors they are in a "news-free bubble" through mid-December.



---


# The Settlements That Left Epic Standing Alone

Other plaintiffs brought app store antitrust claims against Google and then all settled: all 50 state attorneys general and a number of consumers have tentatively settled, though it is not clear what the deal might include, and Match Group — the company behind Tinder, Match.com, OkCupid and other dating apps — just reached a surprise last-minute settlement too, one that makes it sound like Match effectively gave up. Epic stands alone.

Epic seems to have no interest in settling as long as the "Google tax" exists, and the company has repeatedly said it is not interested in cash. So far it has been willing to push these cases all the way through multiple appeals, cost be damned. It is not clear what Google could proactively offer that would satisfy Epic, since CEO Tim Sweeney has also publicly suggested that Google would simply circumvent any settlement it offers. If you want to see a vision of a future Epic would accept, look to the letter it sent to state attorneys general, laying out a settlement that would basically prohibit Google from doing the anticompetitive things Epic claims it did. Google would not tell The Verge whether it has offered Epic any kind of settlement.

# Apple Versus Google: A Contrast In Antitrust Conduct

Asked to compare the Apple and Google cases, Tim Sweeney summed up the difference as "Apple was ice and Google was fire" — arguing that Apple keeps all of its antitrust trickery internal to the company while Google had to go outside itself, and that the paper trail this produced is why the Google case played out differently.

His grounds are the mechanics of each scheme. Apple uses its own store and its own payments, and forces developers, OEMs and carriers to all have the same terms. Google, to achieve things with Android, went around paying off dozens of game developers not to compete and dozens of carriers and OEMs not to compete — and when many different companies do deals together, lots of people put things in writing, so it is right there for everybody to read. The warrant is evidentiary rather than moral: Sweeney said the Apple case would be no less interesting if Apple's internal thoughts and deliberations could be seen, but Apple was not putting it in writing whereas Google was, and he observed that because Google distributes Android as open source it had to put these deals more out in the open, even though it still wanted to keep them secret. He was careful not to let Apple off: he called Apple's restrictions on competition absolute — "thou shalt not have a competing store on iOS and thou shalt not use a competing payment method" — and said Apple should receive at least as harsh antitrust scrutiny as Google, adding that documents from both companies show them similarly self-serving in their deals.

# The $360 Million Activision Payment And Its Evidentiary Weakness

The counter to Epic's headline number attacks the factual premise beneath it: the $360 million refers to an alleged payment that kept Activision from opening an app store that could compete with Google Play, but Activision told The Verge in 2022 that it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store" — and Google says it is now armed with the evidence to prove it.

Epic itself conceded a related point. On Monday Epic's attorney admitted Google "was too clever" to draw up contracts that specifically forced developers not to compete with the Play Store, so it is not clear how much of Epic's evidence will hold up on closer examination.

The narrative advantage may nonetheless survive the evidentiary weakness. The overall story Epic tells is compelling, and it is not clear Google's opening statement countered it: Google spent its 45 minutes attempting to explain that its dominance over the Android app market is not anything nefarious but simply the natural outcome of Google fiercely competing with the iPhone and its iOS App Store, where Google would like the court to believe the competition truly lies.

# Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.



---


# Litigation Hold

## Definition

In the corpus, a litigation hold is the obligation the DOJ says Google was subject to during its antitrust trial — the obligation the DOJ accused Google of breaching by auto-deleting internal chat messages. What such a hold requires in general is given in Background (external) below, not in the cited corpus document.

## Context

In the corpus the term names the obligation Google was under during the DOJ's antitrust trial, and it is what makes Google's chat-deletion practice controversial rather than merely an ordinary retention policy: during Pichai's testimony the DOJ "touched on Google's policy of deleting internal chat messages, despite being subject to a litigation hold"; earlier, in February, the DOJ had accused Google of "systematically destroying chats through its history-off option, which deletes messages every 24 hours unless a user manually changed the setting."
Pichai's own account ties the hold directly to a change in Google's product defaults: he said he took action against the history-off default for chat in February specifically "to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold," and, when confronted with a 2021 message asking for history to be turned off in a group chat, said that exchange concerned a personnel matter and "had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with."

## Key Characteristics

- **The deletion dispute is the whole point** — the litigation hold is what turns Google's default chat auto-deletion (its "history-off" setting, deleting messages every 24 hours) from an ordinary retention policy into the DOJ's accusation of destroying material Google was obliged to keep.
- **Tied to the specific litigation** — the corpus frames the hold as arising from the DOJ's antitrust suit against Google, not as a general corporate record-keeping rule.
- **Distinguishes intentional destruction from routine practice** — the DOJ's accusation frames Google's chat auto-deletion as destruction of material Google was already obliged to preserve, not an ordinary retention decision.
- **Compliance is asserted, not self-evident** — Pichai maintained he "takes great care to comply with" the hold even while defending a 2021 request to turn off chat history, showing the same conduct can be read either as compliant or as evasive depending on intent.

## Background (external)

The corpus establishes that Google was subject to a litigation hold and disputes whether its conduct complied with it, but does not define the obligation itself. A litigation hold (also called a legal hold) is a process an organization initiates to preserve all forms of relevant information when litigation is reasonably anticipated, so that potentially relevant evidence is not lost, destroyed, or altered before or during a legal proceeding (Wikipedia, *Litigation Hold*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Trade and Free Agency

## Definition

Trade and free agency are the two channels by which professional sports rosters change hands outside the amateur draft: a trade moves a player between clubs in exchange for other players, picks, or salary-cap considerations while he is still under contract, and free agency is the period in which a player whose contract (or club control) has ended is free to negotiate and sign with any team, including his current one.

## Context

The corpus documents both mechanisms operating in parallel across MLB, NFL, NHL, and AFL. In baseball, the trade market and free-agent market are explicitly linked: Juan Soto is framed as a top trade candidate precisely because he is "entering his final year of club control" and the price to acquire him will only rise "now that he's a year and a half closer to free agency," and he was ultimately traded from the Padres to the Yankees at the 2023 Winter Meetings rather than reaching the open market at all. The Winter Meetings tracker shows signings (Eduardo Rodriguez to the Diamondbacks, Craig Kimbrel to the Orioles) and trades (Soto to the Yankees) being reported side by side as the offseason's two parallel transaction tracks. In the NFL, the corpus ties trades to a fixed calendar event — the "2023 trade deadline," before which the 49ers acquired Chase Young — while pending free agency (Kirk Cousins "approaching free agency," Michael Pittman Jr. "scheduled to be a free agent at season's end") is treated as a separate, later-arriving roster risk that mock-draft analysts weigh when projecting a team's draft needs. The NHL and AFL passages show the same free-agent path playing out for individual players: Patrick Kane was "traded last year at the deadline" and then, once his contract with the Rangers ended, "hit free agency for the first time in his career"; Adams and McStay are each described as having "arrived... as an unrestricted free agent."

## Key Characteristics

- **Contract-status distinction** — a trade moves a player who is still under contract to his current club; free agency begins only once that contract or club-control period has lapsed, as with Soto's approaching free agency versus his active trade candidacy.
- **Fixed deadlines govern trades** — leagues set a cutoff (the NFL's 2023 trade deadline, before which the 49ers acquired Chase Young; MLB's "summer deadline," which the Soto piece contrasts with the harder-to-project offseason) after which in-season trades are no longer permitted.
- **Compensation differs by channel** — trades exchange players, draft picks, or cap-related pieces between clubs (the 49ers sent a 2024 third-round pick for Chase Young), while free-agent moves are direct contract signings between a player and a new or returning club (Eduardo Rodriguez's four-year, ~$20M/year deal with Arizona).
- **A single player can pass through both channels sequentially** — Patrick Kane was traded away from Chicago at last year's deadline, then, once his Rangers tenure ended with a playoff exit, reached unrestricted free agency, illustrating that trade and free agency are sequential stages of the same player-movement pipeline rather than mutually exclusive categories.
- **Roster-planning implications extend beyond the transaction itself** — pending free agency (Cousins, Pittman) is treated by draft analysts as a signal of future roster need, just as trade acquisitions (Young) raise downstream questions about whether the move is a short-term "rental" or requires salary-cap restructuring to retain the player long-term.

# Shohei Ohtani's $700 Million Dodgers Contract

Shohei Ohtani agreed on Saturday 9 December 2023 to a 10-year, $700 million contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers, the largest contract in the annals of major North American team sports, his agency CAA announced and The New York Times reported.

Ohtani announced his decision on Instagram, ending years of feverish speculation about his future. The 29-year-old two-way sensation has captivated the industry since he left Japan for Major League Baseball heading into the 2018 season, doing things that appeared impossible in the modern era, feats that harkened back to Babe Ruth. As he travelled the country with the Los Angeles Angels that past summer, fans serenaded him with recruiting pitches, and when he entered free agency a dozen teams lined up, curious to see if they could meet his eye. Only one team could secure his services, and he will now be compensated for both his immense talent and his unparalleled star power.

The deal eclipsed the $360 million record for free agents set the previous winter by New York Yankees slugger Aaron Judge, and surpassed the record-setting $426.5 million extension of his former Angels teammate Mike Trout. It exceeded even contracts outside baseball, topping the $450 million deal inked by Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes, and outpaced soccer star Lionel Messi's $674 million contract, signed in 2017 when he was with FC Barcelona. Dodgers officials declined comment when asked if Ohtani had taken a physical, the final step before a deal can become official.

# Contract Extension

## Definition

A contract extension is a new agreement that lengthens (and typically updates the pay of) an existing player's or coach's deal with their current team before that deal expires, keeping them with the same organization rather than letting them reach free agency.

## Context

The corpus uses the term across coaching and playing contexts on both sides of an expiring-deal decision point: Jim Harbaugh is described as facing a choice between signing a contract extension at Michigan or leaving for the NFL, while Oregon State's Jonathan Smith received a contract extension through February 2029 (raising his salary to $4.85 million) only for Michigan State to hire him away regardless.
NFL coverage frames the extension as a retention tool used on a player nearing the end of his rookie or veteran deal: Chicago is noted as having "traded for and signed Montez Sweat to a lucrative contract extension," and Detroit's Jared Goff is described as "heading toward a likely contract extension" while still under contract with the Lions.
The corpus also surfaces a cautionary counter-case at Michigan State, where Mel Tucker's 2021 breakout season earned him a 10-year, $95 million contract extension shortly before his tenure collapsed amid misconduct allegations and a for-cause firing — illustrating that an extension is a bet on future performance, not a guarantee of it.
A related but distinct surface form in the corpus, "deal worth," reports the monetary value of a transfer or free-agent signing (e.g., Cole Palmer's move to Chelsea "in a deal worth around $A82 million," Casemiro's "four-year deal worth about £350,000 a week," Victor Caratini's "two-year deal worth $12 million") — these describe a new signing or trade, not the retention of an existing player by their current team, and so are adjacent to but not synonymous with a contract extension.

## Key Characteristics

- **Retention before expiry** — an extension is negotiated while the person is still under their current contract, pre-empting free agency (Harbaugh at Michigan, Goff at Detroit).
- **Term and pay change together** — extensions typically both lengthen the deal and raise pay, as with Jonathan Smith's extension through February 2029 at $4.85 million annually, and Tucker's 10-year, $95 million deal.
- **Used as a retention signal amid uncertainty** — Oregon State's athletic director called reaching an extension with Smith the program's "No. 1 priority" once speculation grew that he might leave, and Chicago signed Montez Sweat to a contract extension immediately after trading for him.
- **Not a guarantee of outcome** — an extension can precede departure anyway (Smith left Oregon State for Michigan State despite his extension) or precede collapse (Tucker was fired for cause not long after his extension).
- **Distinct from "deal worth" reporting** — corpus language describing a new signing or trade's dollar value ("deal worth $X") refers to acquiring a player, not extending an existing one.

# Shohei Ohtani's Free Agency Market Overview

As of Nov. 27, 2023 the Hot Stove dominoes had started to fall, but everyone who loves baseball — fans, players, coaches, front-office types and everyone else — was waiting on free agent Shohei Ohtani's decision about where he would sign his next contract.

Sporting News' framing rules out two possibilities. Ohtani had played his entire six-year MLB career with the Angels, but his teams had not even sniffed the postseason and he had made his desire to win crystal clear, so he would not be back. Nor did it seem likely he would chase every dollar possible and go solely by the highest offer, because he wants to win.

The conclusion is that the field is wide: lots of teams can meet Ohtani in that middle ground, offering both lots of money — he will absolutely sign the largest contract in baseball history — and lots of chances to compete for a World Series title, or two or three. It is a long list.

# The Deferral Structure Of Ohtani's Dodgers Contract

Ohtani will defer $680 million of his $700 million Dodgers contract, receiving only $2 million per year during the deal, according to a Dec. 11, 2023 report by Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic.

Under that structure the two-time MVP will receive $68 million per year, without interest, from 2034-43, making the present-day value of the contract much less than it originally appeared. The deal will still count as $46 million annually toward the luxury tax thresholds for Los Angeles, but Ohtani is nonetheless giving the organization much more flexibility than expected over the course of the contract.

# Major League Baseball (MLB)

## Definition

Major League Baseball (MLB) is the professional baseball league that the corpus treats as both a competitive structure of clubs and a governing body, exercising Commissioner-led authority to investigate and discipline rule violations while also running the season, postseason, and free-agent market that anchor the corpus's baseball coverage.

## Context

The corpus treats MLB as both the competitive league — teams, ballparks, postseason races, trades and free agency — and the governing body that polices it. The Houston Astros sign-stealing scandal shows MLB acting as regulator: the league investigated "68 people, including 23 Astros players," suspended general manager Jeff Luhnow and manager A.J. Hinch, fined the Astros $5 million (the maximum allowed), and stripped draft picks, all under Commissioner Robert Manfred, while declining to vacate the team's 2017 World Series title. The 2023 postseason coverage frames MLB as the league umbrella under which the annual Wild Card Series and Division Series are played across named ballparks (e.g., Minute Maid Park, Dodger Stadium, Citizens Bank Park). The 2023–24 offseason coverage — the Winter Meetings, the blockbuster Shohei Ohtani $700 million deal with the Dodgers and Juan Soto's trade to the Yankees — shows MLB's free-agency and trade system, where players move between the league's clubs. MLB also appears as a media and sponsorship platform: the collapsed FTX had its name "branded on Major League Baseball umpires' polos," and MLB Network figures (e.g., Alanna Rizzo, Tony Petitti) surface in coverage of on- and off-field controversies.

## Key Characteristics

- **League-and-regulator duality** — MLB is simultaneously the competitive structure of clubs and games and the disciplinary authority that investigates and punishes rule violations, as in the Astros case.
- **Commissioner-led governance** — Robert Manfred, as Commissioner, held final say on sanctions and publicly defended not stripping the Astros' World Series title, calling that step "difficult and impractical."
- **Structured season format** — clubs progress from a regular season into Wild Card and Division Series rounds before the World Series, the Fall Classic that decides the league champion.
- **Active free-agency and trade market** — MLB's offseason, including Winter Meetings, is where marquee free agents (Ohtani) and trade chips (Soto) change teams, shaping competitive balance for the following season.
- **Commercial visibility** — MLB's brand and personnel (umpire uniforms, MLB Network) are used by sponsors and broadcasters as evidence of the league's national reach, as seen with FTX's now-collapsed sponsorship deal.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Major League Baseball is documented as the highest level of professional baseball in North America: a league of 30 clubs (29 in the United States, 1 in Canada) split between the American League (formed 1901) and National League (formed 1876), which operated as separate legal entities until they merged into a single organization led by the Commissioner of Baseball in 2000.

Each club plays a 162-game regular season, and the champions of the two leagues meet in the World Series, a best-of-seven series first played in 1903.

# What The MLB Winter Meetings Are And Why The 2023 Edition Mattered

MLB's winter meetings are the window in which many of the top executives, players and agents all come together at the same spot, which makes them always a prime time for moves to happen, per Sporting News' 2023 tracker published Dec. 3, 2023.

The discriminating feature is the concentration of decision-makers and the chain reactions it produces. The previous year's winter meetings wound up being explosive: Aaron Judge, Justin Verlander, Trea Turner and Xander Bogaerts all came away with new contracts. The 2023 edition could wind up being similarly busy — there was a growing sense Shohei Ohtani could sign during the winter meetings, and a move of that magnitude could kick off the next wave of moves; there was also a number of top players on the trade market, including star Padres outfielder Juan Soto.

The 2023 meetings ran starting Sunday, Dec. 3 through Wednesday, Dec. 6, and were held in Nashville, with MLB's offseason expected to really kick into high gear over that span. Sporting News tracked all the latest news and rumors, following any signings and trades from Nashville.



---


# The Toronto Reports And Denials Of Dec. 8, 2023

On Friday, Dec. 8, 2023, a cascade of conflicting reports had Ohtani picking the Blue Jays and flying to Toronto, only for other reporters to place him at his home in Southern California with no decision made.

The sequence began with Dodgers Nation's J.P. Hoornstra reporting that Ohtani had selected the Blue Jays, who had reportedly won the sweepstakes; official details were not reported, though the report indicated the deal would shatter Mike Trout's record 12-year, $426.5 million contract. Sportsnet's Ben Nicholson-Smith countered that Ohtani had not yet made his decision and that there was no timeline, while noting Toronto was a finalist. MLB Network's Jon Morosi then reported that Ohtani, while not having officially picked a team, was headed to Toronto, after previous reports that he had picked the Blue Jays had since been denied. Hours after Morosi's report that the two-way star was headed to Toronto for a Friday meeting, USA Today's Nightengale and Sportsnet's Nicholson-Smith reported that Ohtani was at his home in Southern California; the Blue Jays remained finalists but his landing spot was not official. Morosi also reported that Ohtani was expected to make his decision soon, possibly as early as that Friday — coincidentally, Ohtani had made his original decision to sign with the Angels on Dec. 8, 2017, six years to the day.



---


# Relief Pitcher Signings At The 2023 Winter Meetings

Three veteran relievers found 2024 homes during the 2023 winter meetings — Craig Kimbrel with the Orioles, Kirby Yates with the Rangers and Chris Devenski with the Rays — per the reporting Sporting News carried in its tracker.

On Wednesday, Dec. 6, Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic reported the Orioles were bolstering their bullpen by signing Craig Kimbrel to a one-year, $13 million deal; Joel Sherman of the New York Post reported he had a $1 million buyout for 2025 and a $13 million club option. The 35-year-old right-hander amassed 23 saves in 69 innings in 2023 with a 3.26 ERA, and was sitting on 417 career saves, ranking eighth all-time, with a chance to vault all the way up to fourth — Francisco Rodriguez, fourth, at 437 and Kenley Jansen at 420 saves being the only other active reliever ahead of him. Rosenthal had reported earlier that Wednesday morning that Baltimore was "close" to a deal with the free agent and former Phillies closer; Baltimore would be without All-Star closer Felix Bautista for the entire 2024 season after he received Tommy John surgery in October, and even though stud reliever Yennier Cano had emerged as the top candidate to take the job, Kimbrel could bolster the back end of the O's bullpen.

On Tuesday, Dec. 5, Rosenthal reported that Kirby Yates, who would be 37 when the season began, was headed to the Rangers on a one-year deal; the right-hander, an All-Star closer for the Padres in 2019, posted a 3.28 ERA in 61 appearances for the Braves in 2023. Jeff Passan of ESPN reported that Chris Devenski, 33, agreed to a new one-year deal with the Rays that included a club option for 2025; Devenski began 2023 with the Angels but was released in late August and signed with Tampa Bay, posting a 5.08 ERA in 29 games for the Angels and dropping three full runs off that number in nine games with the Rays.



---


# Why The Franchise Tag May Not Suit Chase Young

The 49ers could try to slap Chase Young with the franchise tag if they're worried about paying him and Nick Bosa big bucks long-term — the tag was worth just under $20 million last season, so on its face it may look like San Francisco's best avenue toward keeping its Super Bowl window ajar.

The counter-consideration is cap mechanics: one-year deals are often complicated to fit into smaller amounts of salary cap space, so the 49ers would likely prefer to get a long-term agreement in place with Young to keep him.

The Sporting News' conclusion is that franchising him may not be worth the hassle — even though he is easily the team's best free agent in 2024.



---


# Shohei Ohtani's Free Agency Suitors And Finalists

Between Dec. 1 and Dec. 5, 2023, reporting narrowed Ohtani's field of suitors to the Dodgers, Blue Jays, Angels and Giants, with the Cubs — long viewed as one of his likeliest destinations — losing optimism and the Rangers, Red Sox and Mets already out.

Many of the top teams were expected to be in the mix, with the Dodgers and Cubs among those aiming to sign the two-time AL MVP and plenty of others expected to compete through the end. On Dec. 1, ESPN's Jeff Passan reported that the Rangers, Red Sox and Mets appeared to be out of the running while the Dodgers, Cubs, Blue Jays and Angels remained in the mix, with the Giants considered an unknown. On Dec. 4, MLB Network's Jon Morosi reported that the Braves were "engaged" in talks with Ohtani's camp, raising the prospect of a lineup with Ohtani alongside Ronald Acuna Jr., Ozzie Albies, Austin Riley and Matt Olson. The Athletic's Ken Rosenthal reported the same day that Ohtani was "believed" to have met with the Blue Jays at the team's complex in Florida, far from the meetings in Nashville, with Toronto pursuing both Ohtani and Juan Soto in hopes of striking a deal for one of the two stars, even as an earlier report that Monday indicated Ohtani was not expected to sign before the end of the Winter Meetings. On Dec. 5, USA Today's Bob Nightengale reported one high-ranking executive believed the Cubs' optimism about signing Ohtani had "now significantly wanted," leaving the Dodgers, Blue Jays, Angels and Giants as the remaining finalists; Jon Heyman of the New York Post reported that Ohtani had a "positive feeling about Toronto" before even meeting the Blue Jays on Monday, along with other cities and teams including the Dodgers, having been linked to Toronto and Los Angeles throughout the process. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts told reporters on Tuesday, Dec. 5 that the team had met with Ohtani for two to three hours over the weekend, that Ohtani was "clearly" the Dodgers' top priority and that the team was confident he would pitch again, though Roberts could not offer a timeline for the decision.



---


# Diamondbacks Land Eduardo Rodriguez On A Four-Year Deal

Left-hander Eduardo Rodriguez reportedly agreed to a four-year contract with Arizona worth around $20 million per year on Wednesday, Dec. 6, 2023, according to ESPN's Jeff Passan as carried in Sporting News' winter meetings tracker; the deal was still pending a physical per Passan's report.

Sporting News framed it as the reigning NL champions landing one of the free agent market's top pitchers.

A season earlier, Rodriguez posted a career-low 3.30 ERA across 152.2 innings with the Tigers and pitched to a 3.66 FIP. He decided to opt out of his deal with Detroit to test the free-agent market.



---


# Why Signing Ohtani Could Have Cost Toronto Bichette And Guerrero

The argument advanced in a Nov. 30, 2023 report by the New York Post's Jon Heyman is that signing Ohtani would not simply add to the Blue Jays lineup but could force them to subtract from it, with rivals believing Bo Bichette and Vladimir Guerrero Jr. could hit the trade block if Toronto landed the star.

The grounds are two facts about Toronto's roster and payroll: both infielders are free agents after the 2025 season, and signing Ohtani would add substantial payroll. The warrant joining those grounds to the conclusion is a cost calculation — given the added payroll of signing Ohtani, it is possible Toronto would view keeping the other two phenoms as too pricey. The argument concedes the tension in its own conclusion: trading the two infielders might seem counterproductive to signing Ohtani in the first place, since those two would be the biggest supporting bats in the lineup around him. The scope condition is that the Blue Jays were at the time one of the teams believed to still be among the strongest in the mix for Ohtani, so the whole chain was conditional on a signing that had not happened.



---


# An Early Ohtani Signing Would Reshape The Offseason

Reporting from Alden Gonzalez of ESPN on Nov. 11, 2023 raised the possibility that Shohei Ohtani could sign before the Winter Meetings, and Sporting News argued that pretty much everyone in baseball would love that to happen — because an early resolution benefits both the signing team and every other club.

For the signing team, the gains are commercial and competitive: it will kick the Ohtani hype machine into gear as soon as possible, with merchandise to sell, and the front office will use the signing to help lure other potential free agents, maybe even for a "play with Ohtani" discount. For the other teams, the warrant is opportunity cost — knowing Ohtani is off the board relatively soon into the offseason would allow them to shift to other priorities, like trading for Juan Soto or deciding which free-agent pitchers to pursue with the money that might otherwise have been earmarked for Ohtani.



---


# Gleyber Torres: The Trade Case Against Him, And Why His Own Numbers Rebut It

Essentially Sports argues on 2023-10-10 that the Yankees should not include Gleyber Torres in their 2024 reset, because his worth as a player outweighs the money his trade would save. The case for trading him: although it was a decent season for the second baseman, the lack of consistency brought him under scrutiny, and because he is in arbitration with the Yankees his trade chances rise — the team won't want to lose the opportunity to cash in some money from a trade. The context is a franchise in turmoil: the Yankees had been in the news since the league stage ended, first over the possibility of a third-party audit that was later shunted out, then over comments from Aaron Judge that drew attention to the workings of the team, conflicts and divisions between the core four, and now over assumptions of changes with the idea of cutting down the $300 million budget for the next season. Two specific reasons drive the interest in moving him: mlbtraderumors.com suggests Torres is expected to earn $15.3 million next year, so his trade could save the Yankees some money, and the Miami Marlins have been interested in him for a long time, giving the Pinstripes a good deal.

The rebuttal is the data. The 26-year-old avoided arbitration ahead of the 2023 season and signed a $9.95 million contract — a brilliant move given the requirements of the Bronx Bombers — and Torres fulfilled it for most of the season, finishing on a high with 90 runs, 25 home runs and 68 RBIs at an average of 0.273 and an OPS of 0.800. He also finished at the top of the batting charts for the team alongside captain Aaron Judge, clinching the most hits and recording an OBP of 0.347, and finished second in the fielding department behind the team's Gold Glove prospect Anthony Volpe, making 80 double plays with 563 chances created at a fielding percentage of 0.975. That performance was crucial in a season filled with injuries on both fronts. The conclusion: nothing worked well for the Yankees this season — their worst finish in seven years even with all the resources — and while the shift Brian Cashman is pressing encompasses alterations in both offensive and defensive personnel, they should refrain from including Torres because of his worth as a player; the $15 million expectation may sound huge, but it is not a big ask for the multibillion-dollar Yankees, and the 2009 champions can easily fulfill this request without constraining their spending.



---


# Role Player Signings And Trades At The 2023 Winter Meetings

Three secondary moves landed during the 2023 winter meetings — Victor Caratini to the Astros, Marco Gonzales re-routed from the Braves to the Pirates, and Wade Miley back with the Brewers — per the reporting Sporting News carried in its tracker.

On Tuesday, Dec. 5, Chandler Rome of The Athletic and Mark Feinsand of MLB.com reported veteran catcher Victor Caratini was headed to Houston on a two-year deal worth $12 million; the 30-year-old would serve as backup to new starter Yainer Diaz now that Martin Maldonado had moved on. Caratini had filled a similar role in Milwaukee the previous two years, slashing .259/.327/.383 with seven home runs in 62 games in 2023.

Also on Tuesday, Dec. 5, Jeff Passan of ESPN reported Marco Gonzales — acquired by the Braves in the trade that helped them land Jarred Kelenic on Sunday — was being re-routed to Pittsburgh for cash and a player to be named later. Gonzales, 31, was a decent rotation arm with 65 wins, 665 strikeouts and a 4.14 ERA over 893.0 innings pitched in his nine-year career. On Monday, Dec. 4, Ken Rosenthal reported that amid a turbulent offseason the Brewers would keep one piece of their rotation intact, as Wade Miley agreed to return on a one-year deal for 2024 with a mutual option for 2025; per ESPN's Jesse Rogers, Miley would make a base salary of $7 million the next season with the option at $12 million and a $1.5 million buyout. The 37-year-old lefty started 23 games for Milwaukee that year, going 9-4 with a 3.14 ERA.



---


# Rogers Communications Company Profile

Rogers Communications is Canada's largest wireless provider and the owner of a cable television empire, the Toronto Blue Jays baseball team, and other media and sports assets. The Rogers family's controlling stake in the public company is worth close to C$8 billion ($5.9 billion), according to calculations based on company filings for its 2023 annual meeting.

The company is inseparable from the prominent Toronto family behind it, and the court documents of October 2023 show that the fractures inside that family have never healed.



---


# The Guardians' Manager Search After Terry Francona's Resignation

Terry Francona announced his resignation following an 11-year tenure with Cleveland that included a 921-757 record (.549), six playoff trips and the 2016 AL pennant — a record that made him the winningest manager in franchise history, Essentially Sports reported on 2023-10-30. He had managed the Guardians until the conclusion of the 2023 season, but owing to health concerns he decided to put his wellbeing first.

Since Cleveland usually has one of the lowest payrolls in baseball, the team's lineup won't be receiving a lot of outside reinforcement. On the managerial hire itself, the Guardians are clearly not keen on getting someone from within MLB and are open to outside hires as well, as long as the new candidate can follow Terry's principles. One applicant slated for an interview was Craig Albernaz, the catching and bullpen coach for the San Francisco Giants, according to Paul Hoynes of Cleveland.com; despite lacking Major League managerial experience, the 40-year-old has led two championship-winning Tampa Bay Rays teams. Another likely candidate could be Carlos Mendoza, bench coach for the New York Yankees, who also lacks MLB managerial experience but at 43 is familiar with the Yankees system, suiting him well for Cleveland.

# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
