# Gaza As A Tech Outsourcing Hub

Gaza, despite being one of the most economically challenged regions in the world, has ironically always been a tech hub — not only for Palestine and Palestinians, but also for the world, with international companies having for many years sought out a presence there to collaborate with talented tech freelancers and the startups that gradually emerged from the region. According to sources who helped build those bridges, Nvidia, famed for its role in the new AI boom, has been working with at least 100 engineers from the region for years; tragically, the initiative to employ Palestinians in this outsourcing was that of Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, whose daughter was brutally murdered in the attacks by Hamas.

The hub's scale marks its boundary. Since at least 2008, TechCrunch has been covering technology companies out of Palestine, some serving their direct audience and some serving the tech world internationally, and Silicon Valley had taken an increasing interest in Palestine as a tech hub — but like the ecosystem itself, that interest is nascent: to date, those working in the region estimate that as much as $10 million has been invested in the Palestinian tech ecosystem. Notably, in 2017, Salesforce founder and CEO Marc Benioff joined Silicon Valley luminaries in backing the first-ever coding academy to be created in Gaza.



---


# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.

# DeepMind's Founding And Thiel's Investment

In 2010 Demis Hassabis and two colleagues, all living in Britain, were looking for money to start building "artificial general intelligence", a machine that could do anything the brain could do, at a time when few people were interested in AI because after a half-century of research the field had failed to deliver anything remotely close to the human brain. Some scientists and thinkers had nonetheless become fixated on AI's downsides, and many, including the three young men, had a connection to Eliezer Yudkowsky, an internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher who led a community calling themselves Rationalists or, later, effective altruists; they believed AI could find a cure for cancer or solve climate change but worried that AI bots might do things their creators had not intended, arguing that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators. Peter Thiel, enormously wealthy through an early investment in Facebook and his work with Musk in the early days of PayPal, had developed a fascination with the singularity, the science-fiction trope describing the moment when intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity, and with his funding Yudkowsky had expanded his AI lab and created an annual conference on the singularity; one of Hassabis' colleagues had met Yudkowsky years before and snagged them speaking spots at that conference, ensuring an invitation to Thiel's party, where Yudkowsky introduced Hassabis to Thiel. Assuming many guests would be trying to squeeze their host for money, Hassabis' strategy was to arrange another meeting: he told Thiel there was a deep tension between the bishop and the knight, pieces carrying the same value whose strengths the best players understood to be vastly different. Charmed, Thiel invited the group back the next day, gathering in the kitchen where their host, just finished with his morning workout and still sweating in a shiny tracksuit, was handed a Diet Coke by a butler; the three made their pitch and soon Thiel and his venture capital firm agreed to put £1.4 million, about $A2.7 million, into their startup, making him their first major investor.

They named the company DeepMind, a nod to "deep learning", a way for AI systems to learn skills by analysing large amounts of data, to neuroscience, and to the Deep Thought supercomputer from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, and by the spring of 2010 they were building their dream machine, wholeheartedly believing that because they understood the risks they were uniquely positioned to protect the world. Mustafa Suleyman, one of the three founders, said "I don't see this as a contradictory position. There are huge benefits to come from these technologies. The goal is not to eliminate them or pause their development. The goal is to mitigate the downsides." Having won over Thiel, Hassabis worked his way into Musk's orbit: about two years later they met at a conference organised by Thiel's investment fund, which had also put money into SpaceX, and Hassabis secured a tour of SpaceX headquarters, after which, with rocket hulls hanging from the ceiling, the two lunched in the cafeteria; Musk explained his plan to colonise Mars to escape overpopulation and other dangers on Earth, and Hassabis replied that the plan would work so long as superintelligent machines didn't follow and destroy humanity on Mars too. Musk was speechless, not having thought about that particular danger, and soon invested in DeepMind alongside Thiel so he could be closer to the creation of the technology.

# The OpenAI Board's Firing Of Sam Altman

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said on Friday, 2023-11-17, that it had pushed out its co-founder and CEO Sam Altman after a review found he was "not consistently candid in his communications" with the board of directors. "The board no longer has confidence in his ability to continue leading OpenAI," the artificial intelligence company said in a statement. Mira Murati, OpenAI's chief technology officer, would take over as interim CEO effective immediately while the company searched for a permanent replacement.

OpenAI declined to answer questions on what Altman's alleged lack of candor was about; the statement said only that his behavior was hindering the board's ability to exercise its responsibilities. Altman posted on X that Friday: "i loved my time at openai. it was transformative for me personally, and hopefully the world a little bit. most of all i loved working with such talented people. will have more to say about what's next later."

# AlphaGo As Evidence For AI Risk Concerns

Rationalists, effective altruists and others who worried about the risks of AI claimed the computer's win at Go validated their fears. The evidence cited is the pace of progress rather than the game itself: "This is another indication that AI is progressing faster than even many experts anticipated," wrote Victoria Krakovna, who would soon join DeepMind as an "AI safety" researcher, in a blog post.

The consequences inside DeepMind followed the same worry. Its founders were increasingly concerned about what Google would do with their inventions and in 2017 tried to break away from the company; Google responded by increasing the salaries and stock award packages of the DeepMind founders and their staff, and they stayed put. The ethics board never had a second meeting.

# USD Funds In China Turn To Overseas Deals

On a weekday afternoon at Red Rock Coffee, the café known for spotting venture capitalists in Silicon Valley, one is likely to overhear a few conversations in Mandarin. With China reopening its borders in spring 2023 following three years of COVID-19 restrictions, managers of U.S. funds in the country have been flocking to the Bay Area.

The trips themselves are not new; their purpose is. While these trips were routine before the pandemic, they have now taken on a fresh purpose of discovering deals beyond China.

As China's domestic investment appeal wanes, some investors start to look for opportunities beyond its borders. Rather than a complete departure, they are merely following the footsteps of Chinese talent who have already embarked on global expansion.

# Neural Networks And DeepMind's Atari Demonstration

A neural network is a complex algorithm created in the image of the human brain, essentially a giant mathematical system that spends days, weeks or even months identifying patterns in large amounts of digital data. First developed in the 1950s, these systems could learn to handle tasks on their own: after analysing names and addresses scribbled on hundreds of envelopes, for instance, they could read handwritten text. Flush with cash, DeepMind hired researchers who specialised in them.

DeepMind took the concept further, building a system that could learn to play classic Atari games such as Space Invaders, Pong and Breakout to illustrate what was possible. This got the attention of another Silicon Valley powerhouse, Google, and specifically Larry Page, who saw a demonstration of DeepMind's machine playing Atari games and wanted in. The boundary of what the field could then show was pushed again in the spring of 2012, when Geoffrey Hinton, a 64-year-old professor at the University of Toronto, and two graduate students published a research paper that showed the world what AI could do by training a neural network to recognise common objects such as flowers, dogs and cars.

# Chinese Capital Stigma In US Fundraising

A founder's Chinese links now operate as a screening filter in US fundraising, and the filter's scope keeps widening. Even having the Chinese branches of famed American VCs listed on the cap table might deter U.S. investors from funding Chinese founders in their backyard, three founders said; local investors are now shunning Chinese "links," of which the definition is ever evolving and broadening, at all costs to avoid geopolitical risks.

The reputational asymmetry compounds it. At home, the Western-educated and -trained Chinese entrepreneurs are darlings of local VCs; in Silicon Valley, they are little known to investors. Occasional media reports that stress their Chinese background further erode trust in potential investors and customers at a time when concerns about national security already run high.

A San Francisco-based Chinese founder set out the conditions under which the filter can be passed: "If you speak like a local, know how to pitch like a confident Silicon Valley founder, have not taken any money from Chinese VCs, have all your staff in the U.S., have generated good traction in the local market, and are working on getting a green card, you might get a chance to raise local money. Don't even think about it if you still run your R&D out of China."

# The OpenAI Board Ousts Sam Altman, November 2023

As reported on November 18, 2023, the OpenAI board had ejected billionaire and AI evangelist Sam Altman from his CEO role after an apparent vote of no confidence. The board's exact wording in a release issued that afternoon: Altman's "departure follows a deliberative review process by the board, which concluded that he was not consistently candid in his communications with the board, hindering its ability to exercise its responsibilities."

What followed was a whirlwind four days for OpenAI, the generative AI poster child behind the smash hit ChatGPT. The board ousted CEO and co-founder Altman and demoted president and co-founder Greg Brockman, who subsequently resigned, paving the way for what looked like a mutiny by staff insisting the founders be reinstated post-haste. By the time TechCrunch wrote again on November 21, 2023, Microsoft had already hired Altman and Brockman to head up a new internal AI unit — though, as things transpired, nothing had actually been signed yet, with rumors suggesting the ousted leaders might actually return to OpenAI after all, in some capacity at least.

TechCrunch cautioned on November 18 that the full truth would not be known for a long time, as the characters in the drama are likely to be NDA'ed up. Per various whispers and leaks, an all-hands meeting about the situation that afternoon did not produce any revelations beyond banal reassurances that the company is fine and they will get a fresh CEO soon.

# The Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act Of 2023

Tuesday's Senate AI forum followed the recent introduction of new AI legislation dubbed the Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act of 2023 (S. 3050), co-sponsored by Senators Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Mike Rounds (R-SD), Charles Schumer (D-NY) and Todd Young (R-IN).

The bill proposes AI bug bounty programs and would require a vulnerability analysis study for AI-enabled military applications. Its passage into law would also launch a report into AI regulation in the financial services industry, as well as a second report on data sharing and coordination.

The financial-services provision lands on a problem the SEC's own chairman has been lamenting. "It's frankly a hard challenge," SEC Chairman Gary Gensler told The Financial Times recently, speaking on the challenges the financial industry faces in AI adoption and regulation. "It's a hard financial stability issue to address because most of our regulation is about individual institutions, individual banks, individual money market funds, individual brokers; it's just in the nature of what we do."

# OpenAI's Nonprofit-To-For-Profit Structure

OpenAI started out as a nonprofit when it launched with financial backing from Tesla CEO Elon Musk and others, with stated aims to "advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return." That changed in 2018, when it incorporated a for-profit business, OpenAI LP, and shifted nearly all its staff into that business, not long after releasing its first generation of the GPT large language model for mimicking human writing.

Around the same time, Musk — who had co-chaired its board with Altman — resigned from the board, in a move OpenAI said would eliminate a "potential future conflict for Elon" due to Tesla's work on building self-driving systems. The resulting arrangement is a split one: OpenAI's board has preserved its nonprofit governance structure, while the startup it oversees has increasingly sought to capitalize on its technology by tailoring its popular chatbot to business customers.

# Schumer's AI Insight Forum On Creative Copyright

On Wednesday November 29, 2023, US Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer held an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Insight Forum to discuss the importance and role of creative copyright and intellectual property in the development of AI — a sign that senior political figures in Washington are becoming increasingly interested in the impact of AI on the law.

Dennis Kooker, Sony Music Entertainment's President of Global Digital Business & US Sales, delivered a speech at the Forum outlining the major music company's position on AI and copyright law.

# OpenAI's AI Chip Ambitions

The company has suggested that it might be entering the AI chip market at some point in the future, in an effort to shore up the speed and performance of its API services.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had previously pointed to industry-wide GPU shortages for the service's spotty performance, and producing its own processors might mitigate those supply issues while potentially lowering the current four-cent-per-query cost of operating the chatbot to something more manageable.

# OpenAI's Nonprofit Governance And Capped-Profit Structure

OpenAI's for-profit subsidiary, OpenAI Global, LLC, is fully controlled by OpenAI's nonprofit: the subsidiary is permitted to commercialize its technology, but it is subject to the nonprofit's mission of attaining artificial general intelligence (AGI), which OpenAI defines as AI that can "outperform humans at most economically valuable work."

The discriminating feature of this structure is where the power over AGI sits. The nonprofit OpenAI's board has the power both to determine when the company has achieved AGI and to exclude that AGI from IP licenses and other commercial terms — including terms with Microsoft, one of OpenAI's biggest investors and a steadfast integrator of OpenAI's technologies. OpenAI was founded as a nonprofit in 2015 but restructured in 2019 as a "capped-profit" company in order to raise capital, an acknowledgement of the huge costs associated with training cutting-edge AI systems. Altman underlined the point in an interview with the Financial Times in the week of his firing, saying he "hoped" Microsoft would increase its investment to help pay for "huge" imminent model training costs.

# The Paris AI Research Talent Pipeline

France's AI momentum is not a surprise, because a talent pipeline has been feeding it for years. Tech giants have historically set up AI research labs in Paris, as there is a large talent pool of PhD students in math, computer science and engineering. They usually graduate from Polytechnique, ENS or Inria, sometimes move to the U.S. for postdoctoral research, and then move back to France to join a research lab — so the loop runs school, US postdoc, return to a Paris lab.

The corporate labs anchoring that loop are specific. Facebook (now Meta) created its Paris research lab back in 2015 with Yann LeCun at the helm of the AI initiative; this research group is called FAIR, for Facebook Artificial Intelligence Research. Google followed suit with its own research center dedicated to AI in Paris.

The quality signal comes from a practitioner who had recently had a private meeting with some of the engineers and scientists working on AI projects: "The FAIR team is extremely impressive. Just look at what they've done with Llama," an entrepreneur told TechCrunch.

# OpenAI Board Composition And The Helen Toner Dispute

At the time of Sam Altman's ouster in November 2023, OpenAI's board of directors consisted of OpenAI chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, Quora CEO Adam D'Angelo, tech entrepreneur Tasha McCauley, and Helen Toner, the director of strategy at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology — and a clash between Altman and Toner is reported to have contributed to the crisis.

The New York Times reported that, before his ousting, Altman made a move to push out board member Helen Toner because he thought a paper she had co-written was overly critical of OpenAI. That, among other issues, led to OpenAI's predicament. The Times also indicated that negotiations to hire Altman back were continuing, but that one major sticking point remaining was "guardrails" intended to improve Altman's communication with the board.

# Theory: An AGI And Mission Rift Between Altman And The Board

The proposition is that Altman's zeal for AGI, even absent a secret project or agreement, led to a major rift between him and the board. Altman is a proud techno-optimist and often speaks fondly of the possibilities of AGI, or artificial general intelligence, a theoretical software system that achieves human-like intellect and versatility. The board's statement pointedly includes that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity" and that new leadership was necessary.

The supporting observation is a directional one: it has been obvious to all that Altman took the company in a much more corporate direction from its origins, changing its legal status and aggressively pursuing enterprise and consumer applications, which does not sound a lot like the "mission" the board wants to advance.

What counts against it is timing. This shift did not happen today, and it certainly does not seem like a plausible reason for abruptly firing the CEO and a few others on a beautiful fall Friday afternoon — a gradual drift does not explain an abrupt dismissal.

# DeepMind's Ethics Board And Its Single Meeting In 2015

When Musk invested in DeepMind he broke his own informal rule that he would not invest in any company he didn't run himself, and the downsides were already apparent when, only a month or so after his birthday spat with Larry Page, he again found himself face to face with his former friend. The occasion was the first meeting of DeepMind's ethics board on 14 August 2015, a board set up at the insistence of the startup's founders to ensure their technology did no harm after the sale. The members convened in a conference room just outside Musk's office at SpaceX, but that is where Musk's control ended: when Google bought DeepMind it bought the whole thing, and Musk was out, financially ahead but unhappy. Three Google executives now firmly in control of DeepMind were there, Page, Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder and Tesla investor, and Eric Schmidt, Google's chair, along with other attendees including Reid Hoffman, another PayPal founder, and Toby Ord, an Australian philosopher studying "existential risk".

The DeepMind founders reported that they were pushing ahead with their work but were aware the technology carried serious risks. Mustafa Suleyman gave a presentation called "The Pitchforkers Are Coming", telling the board that AI could lead to an explosion in disinformation and fretting that as the technology replaced countless jobs in coming years the public would accuse Google of stealing their livelihoods, so Google would need to share its wealth with the millions who could no longer find work and provide a "universal basic income". Musk agreed, but it was pretty clear the Google guests were not prepared to embark on a redistribution of their wealth: Schmidt said he thought the worries were completely overblown, and Page, in his usual whisper, agreed, arguing AI would create more jobs than it took away. Eight months later DeepMind had a breakthrough that stunned the AI community and the world, when a DeepMind machine called AlphaGo beat one of the world's best players at the ancient game of Go, a match streamed over the internet and watched by 200 million people across the globe, though most researchers had assumed AI needed another 10 years to muster the ingenuity to do that; the South Korean professional Lee Se-dol played Go against AlphaGo in March 2016.

# Israeli Tech Industry Boycott of Web Summit

In the days before 16 October 2023, a run of named technology figures publicly withdrew from Web Summit and, in several cases, pledged never to return, each citing Web Summit CEO Paddy Cosgrave's stance on the Israel–Hamas fighting. David Marcus, the longtime fintech entrepreneur and Meta executive, said in a tweet the previous day that he would never again attend, sponsor or speak at another Web Summit event: "Saddened by your ill-informed stance. You could've taken a more nuanced one, condemning these atrocities and calling for restraint. That would've been acceptable," he wrote. "You chose to support terrorists. As such I'll never attend/sponsor/speak at any of your events again." Keith Rabois, the Founders Fund partner and entrepreneur, went further than a single event, chiming in: "Will refuse to work with anyone who speaks at this conference in Qatar for the rest of my career."

Ori Goshen, the co-founder and co-CEO of AI21 Labs, announced on LinkedIn that he would no longer be giving a keynote at Web Summit, and grounded the withdrawal in two distinct complaints. "It's bad enough that summit CEO Paddy Cosgrave didn't see fit to express horror at the sickening atrocities committed by Hamas on October 7th," he said. "But as immoral as that is, Paddy Cosgrave chose to not only ignore these but instead post something against the policies of the Israeli government. Leaving aside his very partial understanding of history and geopolitics, this response was abhorrent. We at AI21 cannot be part of such indecency and moral bankruptcy. We will not attend WebSummit, and I will not give the keynote. #cancelwebsummit #standwithisrael"

The withdrawals then moved from individual companies to the state level when the Israeli ambassador to Portugal, Dor Shapiro, waded in. "Today, I wrote to the Mayor of Lisbon informing him that Israel will not participate in the #WebSummit conference due to the outrageous statements made by the conference CEO Paddy Cosgrave. Even during these difficult times, he is unable to set aside his extreme political views and denounce the Hamas terrorist activities against innocent people," he wrote, also on LinkedIn. "Dozens of companies have already canceled their participation in this conference, and we encourage more to do so."

Cosgrave's response over the same window moved in both directions. By 16 October he appeared to walk back his statement, writing nine days after Hamas invaded Israel: "We are devastated to see the terrible killings and the level of innocent civilian casualties in Israel and Gaza. We condemn the attacks by Hamas and extend our deepest sympathies to everyone who has lost loved ones. We hope for peaceful reconciliation." Under so much fire, however, he subsequently dug in his heels, tweeting afterward: "To repeat: War crimes are war crimes even when committed by allies & should be called out for what they are. I will not relent."

# OpenAI Board's Merger Approach To Anthropic

During the leadership crisis, OpenAI's board of directors approached Dario Amodei, the co-founder and CEO of rival large-language model developer Anthropic, about a potential merger of the two companies, according to a report by The Information.

The approach was part of an effort by OpenAI to persuade Amodei to replace Altman as CEO. Amodei quickly turned down the CEO offer.

# Sam Altman's Career And Public Profile

Sam Altman has a long history steering OpenAI: he co-founded the company alongside Peter Thiel, LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman and others, and initially served as a co-chair of OpenAI alongside Elon Musk, who left in 2018 to avoid a conflict of interest with Tesla.

Altman formerly headed the startup accelerator Y Combinator and also holds a seat on the board at Worldcoin, the ambitious cryptocurrency project. In the several months before his firing he played an active role in attempting to shape regulators' responses to AI, appearing at U.S. congressional hearings and meeting personally with world leaders including President Joe Biden, German Chancellor Olaf Scholz and French President Emmanuel Macron, among others, on an international policy tour.

His standing in the industry was reflected in the reaction to his ouster. Eric Schmidt posted on X: "Sam Altman is a hero of mine. He built a company from nothing to $90 Billion in value, and changed our collective world forever. I can't wait to see what he does next. I, and billions of people, will benefit from his future work- it's going to be simply incredible." His brother Jack Altman wrote: "More important than being one of the most brilliant and impactful people our industry has ever had Sam is one of the most generous and caring people I know. I've never met someone who has supported and lifted up more people around them than him. Couldn't be a prouder brother."



---


# Ohanian's Case for Techno-Optimism

Despite the problems with social media and the urgency, in terms of its impact on society, Alexis Ohanian argued in remarks reported on 31 October 2023 that there is still some hope — that the next generation of platforms can be built better, and that user appetite will itself turn against the current design. He gave two grounds. The first is who is building now: he noted that the founders his fund 776 invests in are much smarter and more aware of the issues than he ever was at their age, so perhaps the next platforms will still be addictive, but in a way that doesn't "further disrupt democracy." The second is a prediction about demand: he believes that after everything on social media becomes so perfectly curated for us, our brains will start to crave things that are not. The warrant tying grounds to conclusion is that the harms are contingent on choices made by a less aware cohort of founders working against an audience that had not yet tired of curation — change either and the outcome changes.

Ohanian drew the consequence out in terms of what comes after the feed: "I think we'll see a rebirth of live gatherings and in-person experiences…the bright side of this is that I hope it then gets us back in touch with our humanity, and the things that no amount of AI can replace." He was careful to mark the position as an aspiration held against resistance rather than a prediction of ease. "I want to be an optimist about it," he added. "And I think there's still a path forward but we're fighting against very, very strong human things. And if we can solve it, it will do so much good. It really, really will because we will find out we have more in common than not."

The optimism is bounded by a sharp rejection of one common defence of platforms — the town square. "The public square [analogy]…falls flat. Because if that then implies that it's a public square, which means like, what? a town or a city? If you're the person in charge of it, you're the mayor. But there's no democratic election," Ohanian pointed out. "You're a CEO. So then you're like the king? If you want to lean into the town square thing, fine. Just own it and say, yeah, it's a town square and I am the infinite dictator, tyrant of it."

# NFL Week 11 Power Rankings, 9-16

In Sporting News' Week 11 rankings of Nov. 13, 2023, the Jacksonville Jaguars were ninth at 6-3 (previous week: 4) after an NFC wake-up call against the 49ers, who were much more prepared coming off a Week 9 bye; Jacksonville needed to forget that debacle quickly, with a division double against Tennessee and Houston before facing Cincinnati. The Dallas Cowboys were 10th at 6-3 (11), having taken advantage of a "no contest" against the Giants at home with Dak Prescott continuing to ball as a passer and runner, needing to sustain the defense and running game in bigger games. The Seattle Seahawks were 11th at 6-3 (13), needing every ounce of their offense around Geno Smith to rally past the Commanders in a get-well performance that worked for him, Kenneth Walker and the receivers, with a defense that could be more consistent.

The Minnesota Vikings were 12th at 6-4 (14): new arrival Josh Dobbs kept producing the same offensive results the team had enjoyed with Kirk Cousins, thanks to more help from the running game for Kevin O'Connell and the defense overall under Brian Flores, making their 0-3 and 1-4 starts distant memories as they sought a sixth straight win in Week 11 against Denver. The Houston Texans were 13th at 5-4 (16), looking great with C.J. Stroud leading the offense and a running game now emerging, their defense making just enough plays to win high-scoring games — a legitimate playoff contender under rookie coach DeMeco Ryans.

The Cincinnati Bengals fell to 14th at 5-4 (7), battling key injuries that left little room for error, with Joe Burrow making key mistakes and the defense wilting against run and pass at home in the loss to the Texans. The Buffalo Bills were 15th at 5-5 (12) after falling into a trap game against the Broncos at home, losing because of more mistakes from Josh Allen, which their injury-hit defense could not tolerate. The Las Vegas Raiders jumped to 16th at 5-5 (22), hot after two consecutive wins for interim coach Antonio Pierce that brought flashbacks to the playoff push under Rich Bisaccia in 2021, putting them back in the AFC wild-card race with the Dolphins, Chiefs and Vikings ahead.

# Super Bowl

## Definition

In the corpus, the Super Bowl is the season-long reference point every team, player, and betting market is measured against — the game whose winners are still identified as "defending Super Bowl champions" months later (doc_0059) and which is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year" (doc_0201).

## Context

The corpus treats the Super Bowl as the horizon every team's season is measured against: the New York Times' Pick Six column frames one-third of the regular season through "the biggest questions facing Super Bowl contenders," ranking the Chiefs, Eagles, 49ers, Bills, Bengals, Cowboys, Ravens, Lions, Dolphins, and Jaguars by their Super Bowl odds (doc_0316).
Franchise identity is tied to it retroactively — the Cincinnati Bengals are described as having reached "a Super Bowl appearance in 2021" as the marker of the team's turnaround (doc_0071), and Travis Kelce is introduced as having "helped bring his team to Super Bowl victory in both 2020 and 2023" (doc_0044), with the Kansas City Chiefs subsequently referred to simply as "the defending Super Bowl champions" (doc_0059).
A Christmas Day matchup between the 49ers and Ravens is previewed explicitly as a "potential Super Bowl sneak peek" (doc_0003), showing how regular-season games get framed as previews of the eventual championship.

## Key Characteristics

- **Season-defining stakes** — teams and players are described relative to it long after the fact ("defending Super Bowl champions," "two-time Super Bowl MVP") (doc_0059, doc_0003).
- **Odds and futures market** — sportsbooks release "next Super Bowl champion" odds shortly after the previous Super Bowl concludes, and those odds shift through the season as teams change (doc_0061).
- **Special-event betting draw** — sportsbooks single out "Super Bowl betting lines" alongside World Series odds and March Madness as flagship special-event markets carrying their own promotional bonuses (doc_0072).
- **Peak prop-betting event** — the Super Bowl is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year," drawing "hundreds of prop bets" including exotic novelty props on the halftime show, the coin toss, and the color of the sports drink dumped on the winning coach (doc_0201).

# Playoff Seeding

Playoff seeding is the numbered ranking assigned to each team that has qualified for a postseason field, used to set which team hosts each game, which teams earn a bye, and how the bracket is arranged.

## Context

In the corpus, seeding shows up in two different forms depending on the sport's postseason structure.

For the NFL, Sporting News' Week 13 playoff-picture roundup builds seeding directly from division standings and tiebreakers: the No. 1 seed in each conference gets home-field advantage and the lone first-round bye, and teams below the four division leaders are ranked as wild-card "in the hunt" entrants — for example the Dolphins held the AFC's No. 1 seed on the conference-record tiebreaker over the Ravens, while the Cowboys, as a division runner-up, could finish "No. 1, No. 2 or No. 3" if they won their division or were "locked into No. 5" otherwise.

For college football, the corpus shows a different seeding mechanism entirely: the four-team College Football Playoff field is not set by a standings formula but by a selection committee that ranks and numbers teams by subjective judgment of "best" versus "most deserving" — the 2023 field was numbered 1. Michigan, 2. Washington, 3. Texas, 4. Alabama, with an unbeaten Florida State left out of the numbered field altogether.

MLB's postseason coverage in the corpus treats seeding's practical payoff — home-field advantage — as uneven in impact: The Athletic's ranking of playoff ballpark atmospheres notes that a Rangers team with nine fewer regular-season wins than the Rays still swept the Rays at the Rays' home ballpark, illustrating that seeding-conferred home-field advantage does not guarantee an edge.

## Key Characteristics

- **Numbered rank within a bracket** — each qualified team gets a single ordinal number (No. 1, No. 2, etc.) that determines its bracket position, as in the NFL's AFC/NFC seed lists and the CFP's 1-4 field.
- **Drives home-field advantage and byes** — in the NFL, the No. 1 seed in each conference gets the lone first-round bye and home-field advantage, a stake the corpus describes the Eagles as being "in real danger of losing" to the 49ers, while the Ravens held only a half-game lead for the same spot over three teams right behind them.
- **Built from different inputs by sport** — the NFL derives seeds from win-loss record, division titles, and tiebreakers (head-to-head, conference record); the CFP derives its numbered field from a committee's ranked judgment rather than a fixed statistical formula.
- **Division winners are seeded above wild cards** — the NFL's seeding format ranks all division leaders (seeds 1-4) ahead of the best non-division-winning teams (wild cards, seeds 5-7), regardless of overall record, as when the 6-6 Falcons held a division-winner seed while stronger wild-card contenders sat lower.
- **Home-field advantage from seeding is not decisive** — MLB coverage of the 2023 postseason shows the Rangers, with nine fewer regular-season wins than the Rays, sweeping the Rays at their home ballpark despite two of the smallest postseason crowds in the past 100 years there, so seeding sets the schedule and venue but not the outcome.

# NFC Playoff Seeding After Week 13 Of The 2023 Season

The Philadelphia Eagles held the NFC's No. 1 seed after Week 13 of the 2023 season, ahead of the San Francisco 49ers, Detroit Lions, Atlanta Falcons, Dallas Cowboys, Minnesota Vikings and Green Bay Packers, per Sporting News' Dec. 3, 2023 playoff picture.

At No. 1 were the Eagles (10-2), first place in the NFC East, who fell for the second time that season as their run of beating high-quality opponents in comeback fashion ended in getting routed by the 49ers at home; they now led the division by only one game over the Cowboys and were in real danger of losing home-field advantage and the lone bye to the 49ers too. At No. 2 were the 49ers (9-3), first place in the NFC West, whose red-hot ways since getting fully healthy around Brock Purdy after their bye continued with a dominant offensive performance against the Eagles — a statement that they were the new team to beat in the conference wherever they played — and who, up three games on the Rams and Seahawks, had another division title coming. At No. 3 were the Lions (9-3), first place in the NFC North, still in great shape to win the division with a three-game lead over the Vikings and the Packers after beating the Saints in New Orleans in Week 13, though looking more like the No. 2 seed would be their ceiling. At No. 4 were the Falcons (6-6), first place in the NFC South, in control of the NFL's weakest division thanks to beating the Saints and earning the head-to-head tiebreaker in Week 12; they got to .500 and increased their lead to a full game by beating the Jets in Week 13.

At No. 5 were the Cowboys (9-3), second place in the NFC East, who opened Week 13 by rallying to beat the Seahawks on Thursday night, keeping the heat on the losing Eagles ahead of them before hosting that team in Dallas in Week 14; they could finish No. 1, No. 2 or No. 3 if they won the division and were locked into No. 5 again otherwise. At No. 6 were the Vikings (6-6), second place in the NFC North, who jumped up a spot during their bye with the Seahawks losing on Thursday night to match their record, and who held the tiebreaker over the three other .500 NFC teams based on conference record — with the team in third place in their own division right behind them. At No. 7 were the Packers (6-6), third place in the NFC North, who moved into the final playoff spot thanks to having the second-best conference record after the Vikings, to whom they had already lost but would face again in Minnesota in Week 17; the Packers also held key wins over the Rams and Saints in the wild-card race.

# Playoff Stakes Of The Eagles-Seahawks Monday Night Football Game

The Eagles and Seahawks came into their Monday Night Football meeting on troubling losing streaks, and the NFC matchup carried important playoff implications, particularly for Philadelphia, per Sporting News on Dec. 18, 2023.

Philadelphia's two-game losing streak had dropped the Eagles to second place in the NFC East behind the Cowboys, who were also 10-3 but held the tiebreaker thanks to their slightly better divisional record. For a good stretch of the season the Eagles had appeared unstoppable and had been a favorite to return to the Super Bowl: after a surprising loss to the Jets in Week 6 — their first of the season — Philadelphia went on a five-game winning streak, impressively taking down top teams like the Dolphins, Cowboys and Chiefs. Most of those games were gritty, close wins, but the Eagles then dropped back-to-back games in blowout fashion to the 49ers and Cowboys, raising alarm bells among the Philly fanbase.

The Eagles were looking to rebound against a Seahawks team that had been reeling even worse, having lost four straight. Sitting four games behind the 49ers in the NFC West despite a disappointing season, Seattle still had a shot at a wild card playoff spot. After the Monday night game the Seahawks' schedule eased up a bit, with winnable games against the Titans, Steelers and Cardinals, but they could really have used a victory to give them confidence going into the final stretch.

# Around The League: The Eastern Conference Scoreboard That Squeezed Inter Miami

On the two October 2023 nights that decided Inter Miami's season, results elsewhere in the Eastern Conference ran against them. On Oct. 4, with 25 minutes to kickoff at Soldier Field, Sporting News noted the Chicago Fire were also fighting for a playoff spot, sitting 11th and able to jump into a postseason position with a victory — or with a draw plus outside help. Ten minutes before kickoff the other scoreboards were not going according to plan: Charlotte FC, 14th coming into the night, led Toronto FC 2-0, which for the moment jumped them above Inter Miami, and the New York Red Bulls were beating Eastern Conference leaders FC Cincinnati 2-0, a shocking result that momentarily lifted the Red Bulls above Chicago into 11th on 37 points.

Those matches finished badly for the chasing pack. The Red Bulls took a massive three points off FC Cincinnati with a 2-1 win, CF Montreal grabbed a last-gasp equalizer against the Houston Dynamo, and Charlotte FC pummeled Toronto FC 3-0 — not an ideal trio of results for others chasing a playoff spot.

Three days later, on Oct. 7, the most painful scoreline was again Montreal's. Inter Miami were nervous about results around the league, and CF Montreal's 2-0 lead over Portland meant they would be eliminated with anything less than a win; by the time Montreal led 3-0, Inter Miami had to win or they were officially out of the playoff race.

# Seahawks +6 At Ravens, Week 9

Sporting News took the Seahawks at +6 in Baltimore in Week 9 of 2023, predicting Ravens 26, Seahawks 23. The reasoning starts from the line itself: Baltimore's defense had been incredible of late and the Ravens seemed to be flying under the radar at 6-2, but the sportsbooks had clearly taken note of that run by giving the NFC West-leading Seahawks a full touchdown on the road — which looked like a great opportunity to back the underdog, considering Seattle had won two straight and gone 2-1 on the road, including a big win over the high-flying Lions in Detroit.

The supporting claims concern personnel trending upward. Geno Smith had not been the same Pro Bowl quarterback as in 2022 but had still shown moments of brilliance for Pete Carroll's squad, and with DK Metcalf and Kenneth Walker III a week closer to full health — and backup running back Zack Charbonnet looking on the verge of a breakout — the column liked Seattle to at least make a game of it. The Seahawks' defense had quietly been pretty good, and the offense was capable of fireworks when everything clicked. Bettors were told they could take an extra 1.5 points as insurance if they wanted, but the pick was Seattle to cover the +6.

Other Week 9 spreads the column liked were Patriots (-3) vs. Commanders and Raiders -1.5 vs. Giants.

# Point Spread Push And Half-Point Lines

A "push" in point spread betting is the situation where the final result of an event exactly matches the set point spread, producing neither a win nor a loss for bettors; the wagers are typically refunded, so neither the bettor nor the sportsbook wins or loses money on that bet. Sporting News illustrates it with an NFL game in which the Dallas Cowboys are favored by 7 points against the Philadelphia Eagles: if the Cowboys win by exactly 7, bettors on either team experience a push and their wagers are refunded, because the Cowboys neither exceeded nor fell short of the 7-point spread.

Sportsbooks often employ half-points in their lines precisely to avoid this outcome, since they do not want to return bets. Had the example spread been Cowboys -7.5, the game could not possibly have ended in a push; half-point lines such as 7.5 or 6.5 remove the exact-match case entirely.

A tie in the literal matchup is a distinct boundary case from a push, and many spread bets still have winners and losers when one occurs. If the Cleveland Browns are -1.5 favorites over the Baltimore Ravens and the NFL matchup ends 21-21 after overtime, the Ravens win that spread bet, because the margin of victory of 0 was narrower than 1.5.

# 49ers Rout Cowboys 42-10 On Week 5 Sunday Night Football

San Francisco beat Dallas 42-10 at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, California on Sunday, Oct. 8, 2023, confirming that a 49ers team that had ended the Cowboys' season in each of the previous two years remained a level above its NFC counterpart. Jerry Jones had said earlier in the week that the game would show him how the Cowboys stacked up against the NFL's best; the answer, per Sporting News, was "not very well."

The 49ers carved up Dallas' defense on the opening drive and never let up. Brock Purdy threw four touchdowns in the rout, including three to George Kittle, and Christian McCaffrey scored for a 14th consecutive game as all of San Francisco's offensive weapons got involved. Defensively nobody had a larger impact than Fred Warner, who finished with an interception, a sack and a forced fumble. Dallas' offense looked much as it had in the previous season's playoff exit — uncomfortable and out of sorts — sluggish through the first half before unraveling when Dak Prescott threw three second-half interceptions. It got out of hand quickly enough that Sam Darnold entered the game for the 49ers with more than 12 minutes remaining. The quarter-by-quarter line was Cowboys 0-7-3-0 for 10 and 49ers 7-14-7-14 for 42.

Kickoff was 8:20 p.m. ET, which was 5:20 p.m. local time in Santa Clara. Going in, the two franchises had a long history, but San Francisco had won each of their last two meetings by knocking Dallas out of the playoffs, so a win would have carried psychological value for the Cowboys. Afterward, questions about whether Prescott and Dallas could get over the hump against the class of the NFC persisted, and although their wins had been dominant, Dallas already sat two games behind the Eagles in the NFC East. San Francisco moved to 5-0 with all of its major offensive weapons healthy and its defense living up to its billing; Kyle Shanahan's team would not face a team with a winning record until Week 10, though the Browns, Vikings and Bengals were described as far from automatic wins.

# Seahawks-Giants First Half: Penalties, A Geno Smith Knee Scare, And A 14-3 Lead

Seattle led the Giants 14-3 at halftime of the Oct. 2, 2023 "Monday Night Football" game, in a first half marked by penalties, reversed calls and a knee injury scare for Geno Smith. Seattle won the coin toss and deferred; New York fair-caught the kickoff and started at its own 25 (8:15 p.m.). Jamal Adams' return was quickly threatened when he took a knee to the helmet and needed assistance getting off the field (8:22 p.m.), and he was ruled out for the remainder of the game at 8:35 p.m. New York's opening drive ended in a turnover on downs when Jones was stopped on a fourth-and-1 quarterback sneak from the Seahawks' 27 (8:25 p.m.).

The first quarter produced several oddities. Kenneth Walker III ran what appeared to be a 73-yard touchdown but, ruled not down, the play was called back and became a two-yard loss (8:28 p.m.). Seattle went three-and-out on a Kayvon Thibodeaux sack, and the Giants muffed the ensuing Michael Dixon punt but recovered it, taking over at Seattle's 34 (8:34 p.m.). Four straight Seahawks penalties left a drive starting first-and-20 (8:47 p.m.). Then at 8:54 p.m. Mario Edwards sacked Jones at the Giants' 15 and forced a fumble that Seattle recovered and returned to the New York 7. As time expired in the first quarter (8:56 p.m.), Smith rolled out and found DK Metcalf for his second touchdown of the year, and the extra point made it 7-0.

The second quarter brought fireworks and an injury. At 9:11 p.m. Smith caught his own batted pass and was pulled down out of bounds by Giants linebacker Isaiah Simmons; taking exception, Smith came back on the field and had words for safety Xavier McKinney, and he appeared slightly hobbled after the hit. Graham Gano made a 55-yarder at 9:23 p.m. to put New York on the board — since the start of the previous season Gano was 10-for-11 from 50 yards or longer. At 9:26 p.m. Smith was revealed to be in the medical tent with an undetermined injury, with Drew Lock taking snaps; by the two-minute warning Lock had moved Seattle to its own 48 while Smith left the tent for the locker room for further testing on his knee, his status questionable (9:30 p.m.). Lock then hit Noah Fant for a 51-yard completion to the one-yard line, Fant toeing the sideline (9:35 p.m.), and Kenneth Walker III punched it in from a yard out at 9:37 p.m. for his second touchdown of 2023, followed by a scrum between linemen producing offsetting penalties on Seahawks guard Anthony Bradford and Giants defensive end Leonard Williams. The half closed with New York committing its third and fourth special teams penalties of the night, handing Seattle the ball back after an intended fourth-and-4 punt; the Seahawks ran out the clock as boos rained down, and Seattle was also set to receive the second-half kickoff (9:47 p.m.). By halftime, Seattle fans could breathe a sigh of relief that their top signal-caller would be back under center, having avoided serious injury.

# The Dolphins' Record Comeback As A Heavy Favorite

The Miami Dolphins were the only team since 2000 to fall behind by 14 or more as a 13.5-point-or-greater favorite and still win and cover the spread, The New York Times reported on 16 October 2023.

The base is 223 teams since 2000 favored by at least 13.5 points in a regular-season or playoff game. Seventeen of those 223 fell behind by 14 or more, and six of the 17 won anyway. Only the Dolphins both won and covered the spread, which was 13.5 for that game — a new way to win a game, on top of the many that already existed.

# NFL Week 11 Power Rankings, 1-8

Sporting News' Week 11 power rankings, published Nov. 13, 2023 after a Week 10 in which five teams won on walk-off field goals and many games came down to the wire, put the Philadelphia Eagles first at 8-1 (previous week: 1). The Eagles enjoyed a bye trying to get healthier for a difficult stretch run in a top-heavy NFC, with games at the Chiefs (the Super Bowl 57 rematch), against the Bills, against the 49ers and at the Cowboys in the next four; they still looked like the conference team to beat, having proved they win in many ways around Jalen Hurts.

The Kansas City Chiefs were second at 7-2 (3), having had a good week off as they jumped back into the AFC's top seed and home-field advantage spot with the Ravens losing; already rolling defensively, they were expected to figure out more around Patrick Mahomes after the key Andy Reid bye. The Detroit Lions were third at 7-2 (5), becoming like the Eagles and thus the second-best team in the NFC: able to win shootouts with Jared Goff, Amon-Ra St. Brown and the passing game, to dominate with the running game, and to win with offense or defense, with Dan Campbell named coach of the year. The San Francisco 49ers were fourth at 6-3 (8) after a surprise offensive get-well game in Jacksonville with Brock Purdy leading the way and all his key supporting weapons doing damage even without Christian McCaffrey scoring, the biggest development being the defense going back to dominating a good offense.

The Baltimore Ravens were fifth at 7-3 (2): their offense was fine with Lamar Jackson's running and passing, but he could not afford big mistakes, which he made against the Browns, and the defense needed to pick up the pieces ahead of facing the Bengals on a short week. The Miami Dolphins were sixth at 6-3 (6), taking a much-needed bye to figure out how to beat the better teams, with a defense that should be getting better to support an often explosive offense and a likely Week 11 rebound against the Raiders. The Pittsburgh Steelers were seventh at 6-3 (9), playing the way Mike Tomlin wants with the running game rolling to big totals behind Jaylen Warren and Najee Harris and the defense doing what it needed, more against the pass than the run, in key moments. The Cleveland Browns were eighth at 6-3 (10), having proved they can win with defense in another way — with big plays — while showing more offensive pop when Deshaun Watson plays well and the running game does not slump, their playoff hopes looking much better after a stunning comeback against the Ravens.

# Giants At Eagles, Christmas Day 2023: Storylines To Watch

New York Giants (5-9) at Philadelphia Eagles (10-4), at 4:30 p.m. ET, was the middle game of the Christmas Day tripleheader, Yardbarker previewed on 2023-12-24. The first question is whether the Eagles defense can shake off the rust: appointing Matt Patricia as defensive play-caller didn't change much, with the defense giving up the third-most points in the NFL over their three-game losing streak, 95. Although the unit had reached its lowest point, there were reasons for optimism — New York ranked 31st among teams in points and yards per game that season and had surrendered a staggering 76 sacks, the third-most in a single season in NFL history, and the annual trip to Philadelphia had essentially been a scheduled loss for the Giants, whose last win at Lincoln Financial Field came in 2013.

The second question is whether quarterback Jalen Hurts and the Eagles offense can finally bounce back. The offense had struggled mightily over the last three games with Hurts' ineffectiveness playing a significant role: after averaging the third-most points in the NFL over the first 11 games at 28.2, the Eagles had scored four offensive touchdowns during the skid, three of which came via the "tush push." They might have difficulty throwing against a solid Giants pass defense but could alleviate some woes by running the ball efficiently, since New York gives up 131.6 rushing yards per game, the fourth-most in the league. The third question is whether Giants quarterback Tommy DeVito has any magic left: the Giants may have a terrible offense, but the unit has operated at its best under DeVito, an undrafted rookie and native of Cedar Grove, New Jersey, who had thrown for 858 yards, seven touchdowns and one interception in five games since being named starter, posting the 13th-highest passer rating in the NFL during that stretch at 97.3.

# Seahawks-Giants Second Half: Witherspoon's 97-Yard Pick-Six Ends The Contest

Seattle put the Oct. 2, 2023 "Monday Night Football" game away in the second half, winning 24-3 as Daniel Jones absorbed sack after sack. Geno Smith returned to the field for the Seahawks to start the half (10:03 p.m.). New York's defense forced a turnover on downs thanks to a major pass breakup from linebacker Micah McFadden, giving the Giants the ball at their own 15 (10:12 p.m.), but their drive was a three-and-out ending with Jones' sixth sack of the night, by eight-time Pro Bowler Bobby Wagner, and a punt from their own 12 (10:16 p.m.). Jason Myers missed a 53-yard field goal at 10:22 p.m., handing New York the ball at its own 34.

The decisive play came at 10:33 p.m. On fourth-and-1 from Seattle's 16, Brian Daboll had kept the offense on the field and Jones rolled out of play action for 11 yards to reach the five (10:30 p.m.); then Devon Witherspoon sat on an underneath route, intercepted Jones and returned it 97 yards for a touchdown, with the PAT good. What could have been a one-possession game became a three-score game, and Jones had two turnovers.

The rest was attrition. Wagner sacked Jones a seventh time to set up second-and-28 after a first-down penalty (10:45 p.m.); an eighth sack forced a punt on fourth-and-31 as fans began leaving the Meadowlands (10:48 p.m.); and after New York forced a three-and-out, Jones was sacked a ninth time on the first offensive play — a rough showing given Seattle had entered the week with just five sacks all season (10:56 p.m.). At 10:59 p.m. Seahawks safety Quandre Diggs intercepted Jones for his third turnover. Myers converted a 34-yard field goal at 11:04 p.m. for a three-touchdown lead with just over five minutes to play. Jones returned under center at 11:06 p.m., but was sacked for an 11th time at 11:09 p.m. for a turnover on downs, with Seattle taking over at the New York 35 and Drew Lock back in for Geno Smith. The game ended at 11:18 p.m. with Seattle 3-1 and New York 1-3; the Giants had now been dominated at home twice, following a 40-0 Week 1 blowout on "Sunday Night Football," and Jones' career primetime mark fell to 1-13, 0-3 on the season.

# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Engoron Summary Judgment That Trump Committed Fraud

A judge ruled on Tuesday 26 September 2023 that Donald Trump committed fraud for years while building the real estate empire that catapulted him to fame and the White House. Judge Arthur Engoron, ruling in a civil lawsuit brought by New York's attorney general, found that the former president and his company deceived banks, insurers and others by massively overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth on paperwork used in making deals and securing financing.

As punishment, Engoron ordered that some of Trump's business licences be rescinded, and said he would continue to have an independent monitor oversee the Trump Organization's operations. A Trump spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the ruling, and Trump has long insisted he did nothing wrong.

Fortune described the decision, which came days before the start of a non-jury trial in Attorney General Letitia James' lawsuit, as the strongest repudiation yet of Trump's carefully coiffed image as a wealthy and shrewd real estate mogul turned political powerhouse.



---


# The SBF Trial Proceedings

Sam Bankman-Fried is in court for alleged fraud and money laundering while leading crypto exchange FTX and sister company Alameda. TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 preview placed the case in the Manhattan Federal Court, describing the disgraced cryptocurrency entrepreneur as accused of orchestrating "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history": the multibillion-dollar collapse of FTX, the crypto exchange he founded and led. SBF, as he is known, has pleaded not guilty to some seven charges of fraud and conspiracy.

The trial kicked off with jury selection October 3. By TechCrunch's 2023-10-06 update the case was entering its next chapter, with proceedings resuming Thursday: as confirmed during a teleconference Wednesday, SBF would be taking the stand along with a handful of other witnesses, as the onus shifted toward the defense after the prosecution brought its case to its conclusion.

Access to the proceedings is limited: no devices are allowed, so reports are being physically put together within the courtroom, or sent to overflow rooms. The jury's composition ranges from a train conductor to a retired investment banker who attended Stanford University, and TechCrunch pointed readers to a special joint episode of its Equity and Chain Reaction podcasts for a better sense of the vibe between the jurors and the rest of the court.

A second account of the same events was arriving in parallel: "Going Infinite," a book by Michael Lewis chronicling the rise and fall of SBF, was set to debut on the first day of the trial.



---


# The Prosecution's Opening Statement Against Bankman-Fried

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." Rehn described a defendant who, as former CEO of FTX, oversaw a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure.

What followed was a roughly 30-minute story that repeatedly emphasized how Bankman-Fried allegedly stole customer funds to facilitate his jet-setting lifestyle, donate millions to political candidates, and finance risky bets. Rehn also directly contested the media framing of the defendant: he was not a crypto "boy" genius, as so many in the media — Fortune included — have written, but a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims." Rehn closed the characterization with a promise to the jury: "You will see the full picture."



---


# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.



---


# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Pre-Collapse Public Image Strategy

Before his fall, Bankman-Fried made himself out to be the Good Boy of crypto — the trustworthy face of a sometimes-shady industry — and he was very interested in publicity, sitting for many interviews both before and after the collapse of FTX.

The Verge attributes FTX's quick rise as an industry force at least in part to that appetite for attention: Bankman-Fried gave interviews freely and quickly rose to public prominence, positioning himself as an important, boyish face for crypto even though FTX hadn't been in the business as long as competing exchanges such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Gemini. At one point he told a colleague at FTX that "I honestly think it's negative EV" — possibly "expected value," as in poker — "for me to cut my hair. I think it's important for people to think I look crazy." Because he was so successful at this kind of public relations, his fall from grace became another mark against an industry already roiled by bankruptcies and scandals; The Verge adds that more trouble for the industry is likely to come from one crucial element of the fraud trial, the part where the government must prove intent.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. # Class Action

## Definition

A class action, as it appears across this corpus, is a single lawsuit pursued on behalf of a group of similarly affected people rather than filed by each person individually.

The corpus documents several such suits from 2023: FTX customers against crypto promoters including Paradigm, a news publisher against Google, consumers against PayPal, and the Authors Guild against OpenAI.

It also shows the mechanism can be blocked by contract, as with Uber's terms of use barring class actions in sexual-assault cases.

## Context

The corpus shows the mechanism used across very different disputes: FTX customers brought a class-action lawsuit accusing crypto investment firm Paradigm and other promoters of defrauding customers by promoting the exchange, publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet under the Sherman Act alleging AI tools like Search Generative Experience and Bard siphon off publishers' content and ad revenue, and consumers represented by law firm Hagens Berman filed a class action against PayPal over anti-steering rules that allegedly stifle competition from cheaper platforms like Stripe and Shopify.

The Authors Guild of America, representing Stephen King, John Grisham and 134 other authors, likewise filed its own class-action suit against OpenAI over unauthorized use of copyrighted books in training data, run in parallel to (but distinct from) comedian Sarah Silverman's separate, non-class suit.

Apple's earlier MacBook Pro keyboard class-action settlement is cited in the corpus as a business driver — the corpus notes the settlement cost probably factored into Apple's decision to redesign the keyboard, a change introduced alongside separate updates like a new camera and the removal of the Touch Bar.

## Key Characteristics

- **Collective standing** — a class action lets one or a few plaintiffs (e.g., Helena World Chronicle, the Authors Guild, unnamed FTX customers) litigate on behalf of an entire group with the same underlying grievance, rather than requiring each affected person to sue separately.
- **Can be contractually blocked** — the corpus shows companies can preempt this mechanism: under Uber's terms of use, class action lawsuits cannot be filed against the company in sexual assault cases, forcing survivors to litigate individually and preventing them from advocating for themselves collectively.
- **Used across dispute types** — the corpus applies the same mechanism to fraud (FTX), antitrust (Helena World Chronicle v. Google, PayPal anti-steering), and copyright (Authors Guild v. OpenAI) claims, showing it is a general procedural tool rather than one tied to a single area of law.
- **Settlement exposure shapes corporate behavior** — Apple's keyboard class-action settlement is presented in the corpus as a concrete cost that influenced a subsequent product redesign decision.
- **Defendants, not just plaintiffs, can be named as a group** — the FTX-related suit accuses Paradigm "and others" collectively of defrauding customers, showing the mechanism can target a class of co-defendants as well as aggregate a class of claimants.

## Background (external)

Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (Wex) defines a class action generically as "a procedural device that permits one or more plaintiffs to file and prosecute a lawsuit on behalf of a larger group, or 'class'" (Cornell Law School, Legal Information Institute, Wex: "class action," accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/class_action).

# Lobbying and Political Donations

Lobbying and political donations, in the corpus, are the practice of routing money to political candidates, parties, or officials to gain influence with regulators and lawmakers.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's use of FTX- and Alameda-linked funds for political spending during his rise, which became a prosecution theme at his fraud trial: TechCrunch reports he "had close ties to U.S. regulators and government officials, many of whom he donated to," and that Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" surfaced his "attempt to buy off Trump to get him to not run again for president" by discussing with Mitch McConnell how to "fund political candidates who were looking to offset Trump's influence in the Republican Party." At trial, prosecutor Thane Rehn told the jury Bankman-Fried used stolen customer funds to "donate millions to political candidates," and Nishad Singh, described as a longtime family friend of Bankman-Fried, pleaded guilty to charges that included counts "around his political donations." The practice also extended to those around Bankman-Fried: The Verge names "Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap" among the entities caught up in the case.

## Key Characteristics

- **Funding source under dispute** — the prosecution's theory was that the political donations were financed with misappropriated FTX customer deposits, not Bankman-Fried's own money.
- **Instrument of influence, not charity** — donations to candidates and officials are described alongside efforts to buy access (e.g., the reported offer to Trump), distinguishing them from Bankman-Fried's professed effective-altruism philanthropy.
- **Bipartisan reach** — the reporting describes both engagement with Democratic-aligned regulators/officials and an attempt to influence a Republican presidential race, i.e., donations spanning both parties.
- **Legal exposure** — political donations became a distinct criminal count (against Nishad Singh) and a recurring prosecution talking point against Bankman-Fried, showing the practice can carry direct legal consequences when the underlying funds are alleged to be stolen.
- **Family/associate involvement** — the practice was not confined to Bankman-Fried himself; his mother Barbara Fried's PAC, Mind the Gap, is named as part of the same political-spending network.
