# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Prior SEC And CFTC Actions Against Binance

The DOJ charges against Binance came over five months after the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission accused the exchange and Zhao of lying to regulators about its operations, filing 13 charges against the defendants in the federal case.

The SEC's theory concerned the relationship between Binance and its U.S. arm: Zhao and Binance were allegedly "intimately involved" in directing the trading entity's business operations and providing crypto-related services to the Binance.US platform, which claims it is an independent exchange in the SEC filing.

In late March 2023 the U.S. CFTC also filed a suit against Binance, Zhao and its Chief Compliance Officer Samuel Lim for allegedly breaking trading and derivatives rules.



---


# Theory: Altman Circumvented The Board On A Deal

The prevailing theory floating around on November 18, 2023, based on the board's language and the way these giant tech companies work, is that Altman went around the board on a deal. "Not consistently candid" is a very diplomatic way of saying Altman lied.

The proposition: Altman — and potentially OpenAI President Greg Brockman, who stepped down as chairman simultaneously, then resigned — wanted to make a bold move that he knew the board would not like. It is not uncommon for these deals to be hammered out quietly in smoke- or vape-filled rooms and then presented as a fait accompli, but if it was controversial enough and the board found out about these maneuvers, it could be fuel for an ouster. The open question TechCrunch poses is what kind of deal would be big and dangerous enough for a summary dismissal of the CEO and famous face of the company, given the man was onstage two weeks earlier.

Microsoft is the natural candidate: few would be shocked if Microsoft, which is deeply embedded in OpenAI as an investor and customer, is a factor. Could Altman have been working with — or against — OpenAI's patron in secret? If Altman wanted to kill the golden goose by going independent, that might have activated the board's fiduciary or otherwise statutory duty; if he was negotiating some other deal, like an acquisition or deeper and more exclusive integration, it could also have caused the board to bristle, either at the idea itself or at being excluded. What would falsify it is weak: if Microsoft was as shocked as everyone else, as one report has it, it could hardly be the kind of high-stakes conspiracy some seem to be hoping for — but one must assume Microsoft would say that either way, since even if they had been working with Altman on a secret plan they could truthfully say they were surprised by his firing, and they "remain committed to our partnership."



---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."



---


# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# Reaction To Lewis's Portrayal Of SBF

The backlash to Michael Lewis's 60 Minutes appearance attacks one specific premise of his account — that FTX was a sound business brought down only by an unwarranted loss of confidence — and, behind it, the inference that SBF's story is therefore a tragic fall rather than a fraud. The episode has fired up a lot of people, indignant at what they feel was too-easy treatment for someone who many believe brought down the whole crypto house. TechCrunch collected the reaction on 2023-10-02.

The premise is attacked head-on by Dan Held, who on October 2, 2023 quoted Lewis — "They had a great real business. If no one had cast aspersions on the business, if there hadn't been a run on customers deposits, they'd still be making tons of money" — and answered: "That's not true. They are not a bank, they're…", prefacing it with "Shameful that Michael Lewis is defending SBF." Ryan Selkis attacked the framing instead of the balance sheet, writing the same day that "The Michael Lewis interview is infuriating. SBF was a scumbag, and now we need to hear about his 'tragic fall' in the MSM because Sam told them he was an 'effective altruist' and people like Michael Lewis were so far up his ass they couldn't tell truth from fiction." Tobi Lutke attacked the coverage itself: "60 Minutes got rightly community noted here. How is it that SBF is still getting super positive media coverage when the media has nothing good to say about the founders that have actually created things and brought value into the world?"

Two qualifications sit against the backlash. Noff is defensive: she believes crypto is no worse than the stock market, which can also be manipulated and mishandled, adding that "Even when you identify corruption, I don't think that means we don't believe in the system in question." And TechCrunch's own reading is that the thing being attacked may not be quite what the critics take it for — Lewis's picture is a little less stark from the looks of the 60 Minutes episode, and it is not that clear at all whether SBF is getting a kicking or a coat of polish in the interview, given Lewis's celebration of SBF's self-proclaimed (yet not quite proven) idealism and the "Bankman-Fried-shaped hold in the world" that exists. The writer's closing point is that this confused message is very apt for cryptocurrency, where the process by which it works is forever murky and often misrepresented, at least to most people.



---


# Letitia James' History of Investigating Trump

Letitia James, who campaigned for office as a Trump critic and watchdog, started scrutinising his business practices in March 2019, after his former personal lawyer Michael Cohen testified to Congress that Trump exaggerated his wealth on financial statements provided to Deutsche Bank while trying to obtain financing to buy the NFL's Buffalo Bills.

Her office had previously sued Trump for misusing his own charitable foundation to further his political and business interests. Trump was ordered to pay $2 million to an array of charities as a fine, and the charity, the Trump Foundation, was shut down.



---


# VC And Lender Testimony As Collateral Risk For Crypto

The Verge argued that calling lenders, venture capitalists and customers to testify — necessary to establish the basis for some charges — might create collateral damage for the crypto industry beyond Bankman-Fried himself.

The grounds are the shape of the indictment and who it drags in: prosecutors allege that Bankman-Fried lied to FTX investors, so some of those investors may be called on to testify, which is not the kind of thing VC big shots generally enjoy. The worked example is Sequoia Capital: if Sequoia did due diligence around its investment in FTX, whatever Bankman-Fried told its partners could be important — was FTX already sending Alameda customer funds at that point, did Bankman-Fried know, and did he tell the VCs at the time? If he told them it wasn't happening, that would establish intent. Hermine Wong, the former head of policy at Coinbase and a former SEC regulator, adds that Binance was also an early investor in FTX and that former executives may be called on to testify as well.



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Decision To Testify Backfired

The Verge's trial reporter argued that Bankman-Fried's choice to take the stand was a net loss for his defense: like Theranos' Elizabeth Holmes before him, he got on the stand to speak directly to his state of mind in a way no other witness can, but telling your side of the story opens you to a great many questions you might not want to answer on cross-examination — and, having watched a lot of crosses, she called Sassoon's the nastiest she had ever seen.

The warrant is what the charges turn on. The case hinged on conspiracy and intentional deceit: just losing $8 billion is not a crime, though it is very embarrassing, but if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing and how safe FTX was, that is a crime. Because state of mind was the contested issue, his own testimony became the evidence, and it did not hold: Sassoon had established the day before that he has a long history of dishonesty, and on October 31st, through a set of questions about what he did and did not do, she established that the story he told on direct examination was absurd. After a brief redirect by his own lawyers, resplendent with word salad, Bankman-Fried stepped down and the defense rested.

The direct examination had already supplied grounds. Beyond the two obvious lies the reporter counted him telling on the stand — about Alameda Research's name and about "allow_negative" — she was struck by how little he seemed to know about his own companies: apparently Singh, Wang, and Ellison were out there just doing whatever their little hearts desired, because Bankman-Fried was a CEO, but definitely not the kind that pays any attention to money at his crypto trading firm and futures exchange.



---


# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who pleaded guilty to their own charges. Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. The government has indicated FTX co-founder Gary Wang and engineering head Nishad Singh will also be among the witnesses called to testify about Bankman-Fried.



---


# Alameda Research's Origins And Naming

Alameda Research was the cryptocurrency trading firm Bankman-Fried started in 2017 during a crypto bull run, and it was named for Alameda County in California, where its first office was set up. Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried said he knew "basically nothing" about cryptocurrency at the time but wanted to do arbitrage on it anyway, and that he is "somewhat introverted, naturally."

The name was chosen for cover. In his own words on the stand: "Effectively, we wanted to be under the radar at that point in time. I didn't want to call it Sam's Crypto Trading Firm or anything like that. We — there are a lot of competitors and people who we didn't particularly want to know what we were building out because they would race to do it. 'Research' was a sort of generic word, which filled out the company name. And that was — it was far better than the internal name that we had at that point, which was Wireless Mouse." The Verge's reporter noted she would find this more believable had she not already watched a video, played during Gary Wang's first day of testimony with Bankman-Fried and the jury present, of Bankman-Fried explaining on a podcast that the name made it easier to get a bank account.

The founding assembled the people later charged alongside him: Bankman-Fried went on a hiring spree, taking on Wang to program the computers, then Nishad Singh about a month after founding Alameda Research, and finally Caroline Ellison. Though Bankman-Fried was CEO and also majority owner, he wanted to be clear that he did not supervise Wang's direct work. After a run of wildly successful arbitrage — 50 percent to 100 percent annualized returns, per his testimony — he decided to found a cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, figuring he would fail and putting the chance of success at 20 percent, without defining the time period he had in mind.



---


# Crypto Contagion After FTX

FTX's collapse did not stay contained to FTX: the crypto industry as a whole suffered, and TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-01 that the collapse "was the first of many." BlockFi filed for Chapter 11 in November 2022, and Genesis Global Trading did the same in January.

The damage was reputational as well as financial. In TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 piece, Ayelet Noff — the CEO and founder of the public relations firm Sliced Brand, which represents a number of cryptocurrency businesses — gave this assessment: "He doesn't come off good at all here. You can tell he had no experience in management or handling such big undertakings. I think he was in way over his head." She continued: "I think he does a disservice to the whole community. He pushed back crypto adoption by at least a year or two. Each time one of these things happens it brings back the whole market. It's two steps forward and one step back."



---


# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

On Wall Street the vast majority of stocks fell under the pressure of high rates, including 90 per cent of those within the S&P 500. Big Tech stocks tend to be among the hardest hit by high rates, and they were the heaviest weights on the index: Apple fell 2.3 per cent and Microsoft lost 1.7 per cent. # The Rogers Governance Committee Investigation Of The 2021 Events

Rogers' corporate governance committee is conducting an investigation of the events that took place in 2021, documents show. The committee has asked for copies of "all correspondence" between Melinda Rogers-Hixon and former CEO Joe Natale, three other former executives, the five ousted directors, Martha Rogers, journalists and others, according to a letter to Rogers-Hixon included with the October 2023 court filing.

The stakes for her are explicit. "The investigation is intended to inform decisions that may be made about your status as a director of RCI," says the letter, signed by Robert Gemmell, a former Citigroup Inc. banker who is Rogers' lead director.

# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Rogers Communications' Rebuttal On Information Access

Rogers Communications denied the sisters' premise that they were improperly cut off from information, saying the company took "reasonable steps" to protect company information from a competitor. Spokesperson Sarah Schmidt added that Melinda Rogers-Hixon and Martha Rogers could have resolved the matter by choosing a different lawyer, "and they chose not to do so" — putting the cause of their exclusion on their own choice rather than on any vendetta.

The company also disputed that the courtroom was the right venue and that the dispute was harming the business. "This matter should be resolved privately," Schmidt said by email. "We've demonstrated that we will not be distracted by these actions — we have significant momentum in the market, our merger is tracking ahead of plan, and we remain squarely focused on doing what's right for our customers and stakeholders."



---


# The Rogers Family Boardroom Battle Of 2021

The bad blood inside the Rogers family spilled into full view in October 2021, when Edward Rogers publicly battled his sisters and his mother for control of the board and won in court. The result was that five Rogers Communications directors were fired and replaced by five allies of Edward Rogers. Soon after, then-CEO Joe Natale was sacked and replaced by Tony Staffieri, the former chief financial officer; Melinda Rogers-Hixon and Martha Rogers had opposed the CEO change.

This was not an isolated episode. The children of late founder Ted Rogers have frequently fought one another — sometimes driving down Rogers' stock price as investors grew worried about the company's governance.



---


# The Rogers Family Truce During The Shaw Takeover

In early 2022, Rogers family members agreed to temporarily shelve their disagreements, according to the October 2023 court filing, to avoid negative publicity as the company sought regulators' approval for the takeover of Shaw Communications Inc. The C$20 billion transaction was the company's biggest deal ever and among the largest corporate transactions in Canadian history. As part of that truce, Melinda Rogers-Hixon and Martha Rogers agreed not to participate in board discussions about the Shaw deal or receive materials on it, because of an argument about Rogers-Hixon's personal lawyer, whose firm also does work for Telus Corp., a competitor to Rogers and Shaw.

The Shaw takeover finally closed on April 3, 2023, and the Rogers siblings then engaged in talks "intended to resolve all issues between us," Rogers-Hixon stated in an affidavit, adding "I was hopeful all issues could be resolved without negative publicity." Those negotiations collapsed in September 2023. It isn't clear from the court filings whether the discussions included the possibility that any Rogers family members would sell their stake in Rogers Communications, leave their roles at the company, or exit the family trust that controls almost all of the voting shares of the public company.



---


# Rogers Communications Company Profile

Rogers Communications is Canada's largest wireless provider and the owner of a cable television empire, the Toronto Blue Jays baseball team, and other media and sports assets. The Rogers family's controlling stake in the public company is worth close to C$8 billion ($5.9 billion), according to calculations based on company filings for its 2023 annual meeting.

The company is inseparable from the prominent Toronto family behind it, and the court documents of October 2023 show that the fractures inside that family have never healed.

# Seller Complaints About Amazon's Fees And Pricing Policies

Many sellers have zeroed in on Amazon's pricing policies and rising fees as rightful areas of concern in the FTC's lawsuit.

Molson Hart, whose company Viahart sells toys on Amazon, has been a longtime critic of Amazon's pricing policies: he complained about how Amazon's seller fees impact pricing in a 2019 Medium post and later that year testified about his experience before a House committee. Hart said Amazon sales comprise about 90% of his business, meaning any hit those sales take on Amazon has a considerable impact. He recalled "24 anxious hours" in September 2022 when a third-party seller of his popular construction toy Brain Flakes listed the toy for a lower price on Target than it was offered on Amazon.

# The FTC's Antitrust Lawsuit Against Amazon

The Federal Trade Commission's sweeping 172-page antitrust lawsuit, filed in late September 2023, accuses Amazon of wielding its monopoly power to squeeze merchants and thwart rivals, which the agency alleges has led to artificially inflated prices and a degraded shopping experience for consumers.

The mechanism the FTC describes is an "anti-discounting strategy" backed by a "massive web-crawling apparatus that constantly tracks online prices" to stifle competition: Amazon punishes third-party sellers who offer cheaper products elsewhere by threatening to disqualify them from appearing in the buy box if it detects a lower price, and losing the buy box is an "existential threat" to sellers' businesses, the complaint alleges. The end result, the FTC argues, is elevated prices across the web — the company steadily hikes the fees it charges sellers and prevents them from discounting on other sites, so sellers often inflate their prices off Amazon, creating an "artificial price floor everywhere." The FTC is seeking to hold Amazon liable for allegedly violating anti-monopoly law but has not yet outlined the specific remedies it believes would best resolve its concerns; in antitrust cases, remedies are often determined only after a court finds the defendant liable. Amazon general counsel David Zapolsky responded in a blog post that third-party sellers set their own prices on the marketplace and that the company invests in tools to help sellers offer "competitive prices": "Even with those tools, some of the businesses selling on Amazon might still choose to set prices that aren't competitive. Just like any store owner who wouldn't want to promote a bad deal to their customers, we don't highlight or promote offers that are not competitively priced." Zapolsky argued the lawsuit could force Amazon to stop highlighting low prices, "a perverse result that would be directly opposed to the goals of antitrust law."

# Alphabet's Q3 2023 Results And Cloud Miss

Shares in Alphabet fell 6 per cent after hours after the Google parent delivered a mixed result: revenue climbed 11 per cent to $US76.7 billion with net income of $US19.7 billion thanks to a recovery in digital advertising revenue, but its closely watched cloud division — which houses its data storage business and many of its AI efforts — missed Wall Street expectations.

"Investors were disappointed by the relatively weak performance at its Google cloud platform, which is at risk of falling further behind" competitors' offerings, Jesse Cohen, a senior analyst at Investing.com, wrote in an email. During trading hours the S&P 500 slipped off session highs, led by losses in energy shares as oil slid below $US84 a barrel, but once again the index found support above the key 4200 mark; Verizon Communications, 3M and General Electric climbed on bullish forecasts, while Facebook and Instagram owner Meta dropped after being sued by California and dozens of other US states over harmful youth marketing claims. Bitcoin briefly topped $US35,000, and Treasury 10-year yields edged lower following Monday's intense volatility. Investors looking to the earnings season for a dose of good news were hanging their hopes on big tech: the five biggest companies in the S&P 500 — Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and AI chipmaker Nvidia — account for about a quarter of the benchmark's market capitalisation, and their earnings were projected to jump 34 per cent from a year earlier on average, according to analyst estimates compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence.

# Australian Market Resilience And The Range-Bound Reading

Novus Capital senior client adviser Gary Glover argued that the Australian sharemarket was surprisingly resilient following a negative lead from Wall Street and the latest inflation data, with markets starting to wake up to the fact that interest rates could stay higher for longer. His ground was the mismatch between the overseas move and the local one: "Considering the damage overnight in the US, Australian markets held on pretty well. I thought it would be a bigger down day across the board."

# ASX Stock And Sector Moves, Late September 2023

REITs, up 0.4 per cent, was the strongest sector on the Australian index in the session reported on 2023-09-26, as Goodman added 0.5 per cent and Dexus climbed 2.8 per cent. # The Rogers Sisters' Oppression Lawsuit Of 2023

Two members of the billionaire family that controls Rogers Communications Inc. — Melinda Rogers-Hixon and her sister Martha Rogers — sued the company, saying they had been frozen out of board meetings and blocked from getting information, and their court petition argues that the company has been "oppressive" to them. Melinda Rogers-Hixon says she is the target of a "personal vendetta" by her older brother, Rogers Chair Edward Rogers, according to a letter contained in the court filing: the siblings were close to an agreement that would have resolved their longstanding differences, but Edward Rogers reneged on it, according to her Sept. 20, 2023 missive, which was sent to Chief Executive Officer Tony Staffieri.

Both sisters said in documents that they are still being excluded from some parts of board and committee meetings and are being given redacted board documents. "I cannot properly perform my duties as a director if information that is provided to the rest of the directors is being withheld from me," Rogers-Hixon said in her affidavit. The two are seeking a judge's order to force the company to share information with them and to allow them to attend, in full, all meetings of the board as well as board committees they belong to. The court filing also suggests that Rogers-Hixon was forced out of her role as a director of Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment, the company that owns Toronto's professional hockey and basketball teams and in which Rogers Communications is a large minority investor.

Shares of Rogers extended losses on news of the lawsuit, closing down 2.2% to C$53.07 in Toronto; they had dropped 16% in 2023 to that point.

# Lawsuit Redactions As Signal: The Amazon Precedent

TechCrunch reads heavy redaction as itself informative: you know it is bad news for the company when they request pages and pages of redactions.

The precedent it cites is recent. This recently happened with Amazon as well, and it turned out they were trying to hide the existence of a price-hiking algorithm that skimmed billions from consumers.

The comparison is used to rank severity rather than to equate the two: it is much worse, TechCrunch writes, when you are redacting COPPA complaints.

# Amazon Q3 2023 Earnings Preview

Ecommerce and cloud giant Amazon was due to release its Q3 earnings on Thursday 26 October 2023 after the market close, with the quarter expected to focus on Amazon's cost-cutting initiatives, supply chain management and AI product deployment as potential positive factors for attracting investment in equities amid current market conditions.

Wall Street analysts held a consensus Strong Buy rating, but Seeking Alpha Quant Ratings assessed the company as a Hold; on a year-to-date basis Amazon shares had expanded by almost 50% in value. Grainger and more.

# Criticism Of The Focus On Far-Off AI Risk, And The FTC Probe

Some computer scientists have criticized the focus on far-off risks — the existential dangers Altman called attention to — as distracting from the real-world limitations and harms of current AI products. The premise attacked is that future catastrophic risk is the most urgent thing to attend to.

The concrete present-day case is already before a regulator: the U.S. Federal Trade Commission has launched an investigation into whether OpenAI violated consumer protection laws by scraping public data and publishing false information through its chatbot.



---


# ASX November 2023 Session and RBA Rate Expectations

In the Australian session reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 5 November 2023, energy companies were the main drag on the index, down one per cent, with Woodside off 0.8 per cent, Santos down 0.4 per cent and Ampol down 1.2 per cent, alongside coal miners Yancoal (down 1.7 per cent) and Whitehaven (down 2 per cent). "Westpac's results were better than expected, especially because it's been a bit of a perennial underperformer in the past few years," he said, adding that it set the tone for results from NAB and ANZ due to report in the following week. On his account the market had switched from pricing in an 80 per cent chance of a rate rise on the Tuesday to 50-50.

Other commentary framed the risk of a further increase. "Our view is that in the high likelihood there is another cash rate increase on Tuesday, that is going to be the nail in the coffin for consumer confidence," said CreditorWatch chief economist Anneke Thompson, amid warnings from some economists that another rate rise would dampen spending intentions just in time for Christmas. The same wrap noted that the men who built pubs and liquor juggernaut Endeavour Group into the world's largest poker machine operator had triggered a public spat over the future of a business they say has lost its way.

# Wall Street Movers At The End Of September 2023

Blue Apron soared 134.5 per cent after the meal kit company said it was being bought by Wonder Group for $US13 per share in cash in a deal valued at $US103 million ($160.2 million), while energy producers were on the losing end, hurt by the slide in oil's price.

Energy stocks in the S&P 500 fell 2 per cent as a group, more than double the loss of any of the other 10 sectors that make up the index; ExxonMobil fell 1.6 per cent and Schlumberger dropped 4.3 per cent — though energy stocks remain the market's standout performers since the summer. Shares of Ford and General Motors slipped after the United Auto Workers said it would expand its limited strike to include another facility for each, with Ford down 1.1 per cent and GM down 0.6 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 slipped 11.65 points to 4288.05, the Dow dropped 158.84 to 33,507.50, and the Nasdaq added 18.05 to 13,219.32. In sharemarkets abroad, indexes were modestly higher in Europe after exchanges were closed across much of Asia.

# Amazon Sellers Who Welcomed The FTC Case

On Amazon's own forum for merchants, Seller Central, several users cheered on the FTC and said they hoped the case would result in changes to the company's business practices.

Amazon's tense relationship with merchants has been well-chronicled over the years, with sellers expressing grievances over rising fees, an arcane suspensions process, and heightened competition on the marketplace from all sides including the e-commerce giant itself. "I think it's great, Amazon deserves it," one person commented, adding, "More should be coming on the way." Amazon in recent years made the forum anonymous, but users must have a seller account in order to post. Another post included a screenshot of a message Amazon sent to sellers the day after the FTC filed its complaint, which said, "As your partners, we know that this news may generate questions for you and our business together. This lawsuit does not change anything about our relationship with you or how we operate today." One user called it "BS verbiage," adding, "Businesses that sell in their store are indeed customers. And which of us has gotten good customer service?" Another described their last 12 months of selling on Amazon as "being up all night at an effing casino but I'm stuck, the drugs are starting to wear off, but I'm trying to break even on the mortgage payment I'm using to play. That's how it is selling on Amazon right now to me," and called it a "race to the bottom." "It's long overdue," another commenter wrote. "When they close me down, I'm applying for a job with the FTC." Still, others commented that the FTC's complaint is misguided: "Selling on Amazon is a life-changing opportunity and the amount of sellers that throw stones at the platform is astounding," one user wrote.

# ASX REITs And Company News, 24 October 2023

Real estate investment trusts (down 2 per cent) dropped further following the latest inflation data, with Mirvac (down 3.7 per cent) and Dexus (down 3.3 per cent) sliding lower, as the Australian sharemarket shook off a positive lead from Wall Street after hotter-than-expected inflation data raised the prospect of another interest rate rise at the Reserve Bank's next meeting.

Interest-rate sensitive sectors, including REITs and consumer companies, were among the weakest on the local bourse as investors digested the news. In other company news, shares in embattled funds manager Magellan dropped 3.5 per cent after the abrupt departure of its chief executive, David George. Infratil (down 3.6 per cent), Meridian Energy (down 2.7 per cent) and Resmed (down 2 per cent) were among the biggest large-cap decliners.



---


# Seller Skepticism That The FTC Picked The Right Issues

Even sellers sympathetic to regulating Amazon question the premise that the FTC's highlighted issues are the ones that would make the seller and consumer experience better. Scott Needham, who sells on Amazon and runs a product-finder tool for other Amazon sellers, said he was "surprised by some of the points that the FTC selected."

"I have over the years been very critical of Amazon," Needham told CNBC. "I've lost a lot of sleep because of some of the things that they have done. And the issues that they brought up, while they are interesting, they haven't created me a lot of pain." He was particularly puzzled by the claim that Amazon is coercive in how it encourages sellers to use Fulfillment by Amazon (FBA), saying many sellers "love FBA" for its compelling value in price and two-day shipping; for many, using FBA does not feel like a requirement, but they believe it will make their businesses "easier and more effective." "I think that the power that Amazon wields over sellers is considerable and absolutely worth looking into," Needham said. "But I'm not sure if this would actually change that." Scott Moller, an Amazon seller and co-founder of an agency that helps merchants run their storefronts, said the company has removed some of the challenges of running an online business: with FBA he can ship an item into an Amazon warehouse for $7.49 per package versus about $12 through a traditional carrier. "I don't have to have my own warehouse," said Moller, who sells grilling accessories under the brand Grill Sergeant. "I can use their staff, their storage, and I can instantly also take the data of advertising, so I can target ads." He also disputed the FTC's claim that Amazon has become littered with ads in search results, causing shoppers to wade through potentially less-relevant products of lesser quality: "We can tailor our ads to hit exactly the consumers we want. It's a perfect marriage of a transaction, and that's one of the beauties of what their marketplace offers." Needham's second objection is timing: he would have been more supportive if the case had been filed a few years ago, pre-pandemic — "I would have felt, yes Amazon is a monopoly… But actually after Covid, into 2023, ecommerce has had a lot of big changes. The competition is just not what it was in 2019." Competitors like Shopify and Walmart are increasingly viable alternatives for many categories of sellers, he said, not to mention rapidly growing Chinese e-commerce companies like Temu, and he has seen significant changes from Amazon as a result, among them a greater ability for sellers to communicate with buyers and offer select customers certain promotions — Shopify gives sellers much more control over customer communication, and although Amazon still controls the process, at least there is one. "I wish it was a clear-cut case," Needham said. "I have a vested interest in the marketplace doing really well, as a seller and as a service provider. And… this case, it doesn't make the marketplace better for sellers."



---


# Epic v. Google: What The Trial Is

Epic v. Google is the antitrust case in which Fortnite publisher Epic Games drags a tech giant into court alleging that its mobile app store is an illegal monopoly — and although Epic's parallel claims against Apple already got their day in court, the similar lawsuit against Google never did, which is why the case goes to trial on November 6th, a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued.

The déjà vu is the point of confusion the piece sets out to clear up: Epic already went to trial with Apple, resulting in a ruling where Apple mostly won, and its Llamacorn legal gambit failed to #FreeFortnite years ago. The distinction is that the Apple claims were heard and the Google ones were not.

An update dated December 15th, 2023 notes that the case is basically over by then.



---


# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.



---


# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.



---


# Big Tech Concentration In The S&P 500

"As these big tech stocks go, so does the overall market," David Trainer, chief executive officer of New Constructs, said before Microsoft and Alphabet's results — the core of a model in which a handful of heavyweights determine the index's direction.

The mechanism and its stress points were both visible in October 2023. On the upside, Trainer argued: "Strong big tech earnings may just be what's needed to end the stock market correction that started in late July. If big tech companies blow their numbers out of the water and provide strong guidance for future earnings, then we could see the stock market rally strongly through the end of the year." On the downside, rising rates have made already stretched big tech valuations look increasingly expensive, with the group remaining the most-crowded trade among fund managers according to Bank of America — prompting some investors to pay up for protection against a sell-off in Alphabet and Microsoft, two of the handful of heavyweights responsible for all of the S&P 500 Index's advance that year. The rate pressure was easing at the margin: the pain in long-duration growth stocks, fuelled in recent weeks by a relentless surge in Treasury yields, was finally on the verge of subsiding, and the yield on 10-year Treasuries was little changed at 4.85 per cent overnight. Oil closed at the lowest in more than a week amid signs the crude market's tightness had slackened and the Israel-Hamas war would remain contained for the time being, with West Texas Intermediate extending Monday's drop with a 2.2 per cent fall to $US83.59 a barrel, paring most of the gains made after Hamas's attack on Israel on October 7.



---


# Wall Street December 2023 Mixed Session

Most US stocks slipped in the overnight Wall Street session reported on 5 December 2023, though the market stayed near its highest level in 20 months after a mixed set of reports that kept alive questions about whether the world's largest economy can pull off a perfect landing in which it kills high inflation but avoids a recession. The S&P 500 edged down 0.1 per cent for its first back-to-back loss since October, the Dow Jones slipped 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 0.3 per cent.

Stocks fell more sharply in Asia amid worries about the health of China's economy, the world's second largest. US stocks and Treasury yields wavered after reports showed that US employers advertised far fewer jobs at the end of October than expected, while growth for services businesses accelerated more in the prior month than expected.

The underlying hope on Wall Street at the time was that the US economy was slowing from its recent hot pace by just the right amount: too much strength would give inflation more fuel, but too little would mean a recession. The Australian market's gains that day came after this mixed US session.



---


# Amazon's Buy Box Price Parity Enforcement: The Ripple Rug Case

Late in the day on Oct. 27, 2021, seller Fred Ruckel received an automated email telling him that his popular cat toy, the Ripple Rug, would no longer be shown in Amazon's all-important buy box — the area of the listing where shoppers click "Add to Cart" — because Amazon's software had detected the product being sold somewhere else for a cheaper price.

Ruckel is the sole seller of the Ripple Rug on Amazon, so the move all but ensured his product would disappear from the website, costing him thousands of dollars per day. The email, viewed by CNBC, read: "Below is a list of product(s) in your catalog that are not currently eligible to be the Featured Offer because they are not priced competitively compared to prices for those products from retailers outside Amazon." Unbeknownst to him, Chewy was running a discount promotion and had dropped the price of his product by a few dollars to $39.99 — less than the $43 offer on Amazon. The algorithm flagged it as a lower offer even though the item on Chewy cost $48.54 after shipping and taxes. Ruckel had to choose between lowering the price on Amazon or asking Chewy to raise the price of his product; he opted for the latter.



---


# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.



---


# Crude Oil Prices And The Qantas Senate Inquiry

Crude oil prices rose in the session reported on 2023-09-26, adding to worries about inflation: a barrel of benchmark US crude climbed 71¢ to $US90.39, and Brent crude, the international standard, added 67¢ to $US93.96 per barrel.

The day's quote came from the Qantas hearings. "The Senate committees have the power to summons witnesses within Australia but have no enforceable powers for witnesses who are overseas," said Senator Bridget McKenzie, after former Qantas boss Alan Joyce chose not to front the Senate select committee into the federal government's decision to reject extra flights from Qatar Airways, citing "personal commitments."



---


# The Epic v. Apple Ruling And Its Limited Weight Here

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. She also decided that Epic violated its developer agreement with Apple and would have to pay.

Epic did win something. Rogers barred Apple from keeping iPhone users in the dark about alternate ways they can pay for apps, and may have even allowed developers to add their own payment mechanisms.

The precedent's reach into the Google trial is limited in two specific ways. First, that was a different case — and it is not over until the Supreme Court weighs in or declines to take a look. Second, Google cannot tell jurors that Apple won its case, or that other plaintiffs settled; the judge in this case says so. Epic declined to answer on the record when asked about the Apple outcome.

qid: Has the perspective on managing dementia in 'The Guardian' articles shown a change from the time Susan Saunders was reported to be caring for her mother with dementia (published at '2023-10-10') to the more recent report on new Alzheimer’s drugs (published at '2023-12-17')?
context:
# Joining The Dementia Research Register For Trial Participation

Health coach Susan Saunders' advice, reported by The Guardian on 10 October 2023, is a two-step procedure for anyone with a parent in the early stages of dementia: investigate all the available research trials, and start by joining Dementia Research, a nationwide register that matches volunteers to research programmes.

The precondition is stated explicitly — the advice is for a parent in the early stages of dementia, not later ones — and Saunders speaks from experience, having found herself "parenting" her mother, who had dementia, while her own daughters were babies.

The scope of the advice as given is limited to finding and entering trials through that register; the source does not extend it to any other treatment step.



---


# The First Drugs to Treat the Cause of Alzheimer's

The arrival of the first drugs that treat the actual cause of Alzheimer's — rather than merely helping patients manage symptoms, which is all doctors have been able to prescribe until now — has been welcomed as a justifiable cause for excitement, although experts warn their use should be treated with some caution.

"The new drugs slow down the development of Alzheimer's by six months to a year and are useful only for those in the early stages of the condition, so they are certainly not miracle medicines," said David Thomas, head of policy at Alzheimer's Research UK. "However, after decades of research, they are the first to improve patients' lives directly, and that is a justifiable cause for excitement. If nothing else, they suggest we are probably on the right road to tackling Alzheimer's." The point was backed by neurologist Cath Mummery, of the Dementia Research Centre at University College London: "It has been a very long, hard road, but finally we have something positive to look at. That is very welcome."



---


# UK Dementia Burden and Projections

About a million people are living with dementia in the UK, and this is expected to rise to about 1.7 million by 2040; last year dementia took the lives of 66,000 people in England and Wales, and it is now the leading cause of death in Britain, with Alzheimer's accounting for two-thirds of cases.

The prospect of the new drugs has raised hopes that, after years of effort, scientists may be closing in on ways to directly tackle the UK's dementia crisis — a crisis whose projected growth the article describes as carrying potentially grim consequences.



---


# Delayed Alzheimer's Diagnosis: Patient Cases

Two families illustrate how long a dementia diagnosis can take: Mike Mackenzie-Smith waited over 10 years from the start of his symptoms, and Trina Armstrong waited six years from her first symptoms in 2006 before receiving the correct diagnosis.

Eleanor Mackenzie-Smith's father, Mike, has young-onset Alzheimer's, and his first symptoms were spotted 17 years ago, when Eleanor was 11. "However, it took over 10 years from the start of his symptoms and four separate tests between 2009 and 2017 to get my dad's final diagnosis, when he was 65. # The UK Dementia Diagnosis Bottleneck

The main problem facing doctors is the difficulty of pinpointing dementia not just in its early stages but even in its later phases: most cases are first presented to GPs, who then refer patients to memory clinics for a dementia test, but waiting times for appointments at these centres run up to two years on average.

Diagnosing Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia is usually based on pen-and-paper tests, followed by lumbar punctures and brain scans before a final diagnosis, and about 65% of cases are confirmed this way — meaning the remaining third of dementia cases are never diagnosed. Yet patients can only expect to receive treatments, including the new drugs, if their condition is identified.

# The Blood-Brain Barrier and Active Drug Transport

A major challenge for dementia treatment is the blood-brain barrier, which controls the movement of ions and molecules from the body to the brain and makes it difficult to get drugs into the central nervous system to tackle problems such as amyloid plaques.

Researchers are developing active transport methods for getting drugs across that barrier, said Cath Mummery: "For example, we are now exploring ways of helping drugs get into the brain much more efficiently, and that could have a major impact." Scientists caution that such developments will take years to realise, and that a great deal needs to be done in the short term to deal with dementia. "It is clear we have taken a step in the right direction but there is much more to do before we can have successfully dealt with these processes that are happening to our brains," said David Thomas. # Alzheimer's: The Lecanemab And Aducanumab Approvals

Leqembi, lecanemab, developed by Eisai in collaboration with Biogen, was the first and only approved drug for Alzheimer's, approved in July 2023, coming after several failed attempts and one controversial false start in recent years. Alzheimer's disease is characterised by amyloid beta deposits on brain cells leading to shrinking and loss of cognitive abilities, and despite a clear marker of amyloid plaques and a target area to work on, pharma companies failed to address plaque removal or to show a statistical improvement in cognitive functioning after plaque removal until this approval; Pfizer, Eli Lilly, Merck and many others faced failure in the space, and the amyloid theory itself was in question.

Biogen's aducanumab had a peculiar start: the company itself stopped development in 2019 but surprisingly pursued a high-dose study into 2021, after which the FDA gave the high-dose version an accelerated approval that faced sharp criticism, with three advisers resigning over the approval of a drug that could have cost $56,000 per annum to administer. With a "traditional" approval for the Eisai-partnered lecanemab, compared with the accelerated approval for aducanumab, Biogen has the first approved treatment, putting aducanumab on the backburner. On the critical marker of cognitive function improvement, lecanemab delivers lower degeneration compared to placebo: the treatment reduced clinical decline by 27 per cent at 18 months on clinical dementia scoring and delivered a 37 per cent improvement compared to placebo on the daily living scale. The article's verdict is that the development is satisfactory but a lot more progress remains to be made on the Alzheimer's treatment curve.

# Lecanemab and Donanemab: The Amyloid Drugs

Lecanemab, produced by Japanese pharmaceutical company Eisai, and donanemab, produced by Eli Lilly of the US, are the first medicines to stop amyloid from forming plaques in the brain — though they only slow, and do not ultimately halt, the progression of Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's disease is triggered by the buildup of a protein called amyloid in the brain, although symptoms may not appear for decades after this accretion has started, and scientists have tried for more than 20 years to find ways to stop amyloid from forming these plaques in the hope this would stop the disease's progression. Lecanemab was recently approved in the US and Japan, where treatments using it have already been launched; a second drug, donanemab, is expected to follow soon, and next year it is anticipated that the UK medical authorities will consider both of them for approval in Britain. # The UC San Diego Time-Restricted Feeding Study In Alzheimer's Mice

Participating in intermittent, time-restricted fasting could lead to a reduced risk of cognitive deterioration, a study published in the journal Cell Metabolism suggests: researchers at University of California San Diego School of Medicine adjusted the feeding schedule of certain groups of mice so that they only ate within six-hour windows each day, which the researchers noted would be equivalent to 14 hours of fasting for humans.

The framing question was about timing rather than content -- it has been proven that what people eat can help prevent or slow Alzheimer's disease, but the study asked about when they eat.

Compared to a control group of mice that ate on demand, the fasting mice showed improvements in memory, were less hyperactive in the evenings and had fewer sleep disruptions. They also were shown to have less buildup of amyloid proteins in the brain, which is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease.

The size of the effect exceeded what the team expected. "We were hopeful to see some improvements in pathology, but did not expect such profound effects in reducing plaques and inflammation and improving memory," a study author said. "The effects of time-restricted feeding on lower amyloid pathology were also measurable in blood using markers found in the clinic, which was another important finding."

# Allison Miller's Influenza, Sepsis And Leg Amputation

Allison Miller, a Virginia-based communications director who was a healthy 33-year-old at the time, lost her left leg above the knee after a case of influenza escalated into bilateral bacterial pneumonia, sepsis and septic shock; a decade later she described the sequence to Fox News Digital for an article published on October 18, 2023, which noted that this year marked ten years since those complications caused her life-changing loss.

The illness began with a sore throat and headache. When her symptoms got worse she went into urgent care for a chest X-ray, but it showed nothing alarming. "It looked like it was just some sort of run-of-the-mill stuff -- they gave me some prescription cough syrup and said to let them know if it got worse," she said. Back at home that night she started feeling worse and began having intense back pain. "Thinking it was the flu or something I could get over, I kept waiting to turn the corner -- like, this is the worst of it. It'll get better. And clearly that wasn't the case," she said. The next morning, when the back pain was causing her to have periodic blackouts, she managed to call a friend, who came over and called an ambulance. That is where her memory stops: "I remember being loaded into the ambulance -- and then I really don't remember a whole lot after that for about three weeks to a month thereafter. It just escalated very quickly."

As Miller would later learn, her influenza had caused bilateral bacterial pneumonia, which affects both lungs and is more severe than viral pneumonia. That led to sepsis, which quickly turned to septic shock. "All of my organs were shutting down," she said. "Within a short amount of time, I was in the ICU and they were doing everything they could. But ultimately, my last best chance was to be put on life support."

After five days on life support she experienced a rare complication. "A known complication of that form of life support is amputation," she said. "Some patients lose blood circulation, and that's what happened to me." Doctors ultimately had to amputate her left leg above the knee while she was still in a medically induced coma. "By the time I came out of it, it had been three weeks. I awoke in a very hazy position -- and I didn't have a left leg," she recalled. She spent another two months in the hospital and then had to do weeks of inpatient rehabilitation.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# Google's Parallel Antitrust Proceedings In Late 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was fighting antitrust on more than one front at once. The Epic Games case was not its only antitrust case in trial: Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the week before November 13, and on November 6 it went to trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games, which hoped to prove that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Separately, Google was involved in an antitrust lawsuit with the Department of Justice over its alleged search monopoly.

The Epic case had shed co-plaintiffs on its way to trial. Epic's lawsuit originally involved Match and several U.S. attorneys general, but Google reached a settlement with the attorneys general in October 2023 and with Match the week before November 6, so Epic fought the antitrust battle on its own. The lawsuit, held in the U.S. District Court in California's Northern District, would include testimony from a number of Google and Android execs, including CEO Sundar Pichai, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, as well as from Apple, Netflix and other Android developers. Epic, meanwhile, had lost its antitrust battle with Apple and was asking the Supreme Court to weigh in.

# Helena World Chronicle's Class Action Antitrust Suit Against Google

A class action lawsuit filed in the week of 15 December 2023 in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case was filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, which argues that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and their ad revenue through anticompetitive means, and it specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

Helena World Chronicle owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas. In the complaint it argues that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars."

Beyond damages, the suit asks for an injunction that would require Google to obtain consent from publishers before using their website data to train its general artificial intelligence products, including Google's own and those of rivals. It also asks that publishers who opt out of SGE still be allowed to show up in Google search results, among other things.

The law firm handling the case is Hausfeld, whose announcement states that "the anticompetitive effects of Google's scheme cause profound harm to competition, to consumers, to labor, and to a democratic free press," and that "Plaintiff Helena World Chronicle, LLC invokes the Sherman Act and Clayton Act to seek class-wide monetary and injunctive relief to restore and ensure competition for digital news and reference publishing and set up guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas in the new era of artificial intelligence."



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.
