# OpenAI's Three-Tier AI Safety Team Structure

OpenAI divides safety work across three teams distinguished by how far along a model is. In-production models are governed by a "safety systems" team, which handles, for example, systematic abuses of ChatGPT that can be mitigated with API restrictions or tuning. Frontier models in development get the "preparedness" team, which tries to identify and quantify risks before the model is released. Finally there is the "superalignment" team, which is working on theoretical guide rails for "superintelligent" models — which, as TechCrunch notes, we may or may not be anywhere near.

The discriminating feature between the tiers is thus the model's lifecycle stage: shipped, in development, or hypothetical future superintelligence.

# The Regulatory Gap Around Unapproved Aircraft Parts

Mary Schiavo's argument is that the regulatory perimeter stops in the wrong place: while plane and engine manufacturers, pilots and aviation companies are heavily regulated, distributors are not — and she pushed for tighter rules in the 1990s but was ignored.

Her grounds are her own casework and its stakes: "I've had cases where counterfeit parts have caused deaths. What's at stake is the safety of the lives of the flying public." The scope of the exposure, in her words, is total: "Literally, if it's on an aeroplane, it could be fake." Following her investigation various reforms came in, including a warning system to flag suspicious components — but not regulation of distributors. The current case is still running: the High Court case against AOG began on September 21 and is ongoing, and the UK's Civil Aviation Authority has said it is supporting the US Federal Aviation Administration and European Aviation Safety Agency in investigating the matter. A spokesman for CFM said: "We are working collaboratively with operators, so they can promptly remove the unauthorised parts from their engines in accordance with the recommendations issued by the regulatory agencies. We remain united with the aviation community in working to keep unapproved parts out of the global supply chain." B&H was approached for comment, and Zamora was approached for comment through friends and his barrister.

# Palestinian Content Moderation Distrust On Meta's Platforms

Users are also turning to Snapchat for information about Gaza as accusations of shadowbanning Palestinian content fuel distrust in platforms like Instagram and Facebook.

The policies themselves are not what separates the platforms: Meta's policies are not dissimilar to Snap's Community Guidelines, which prohibit pornographic content, content that advocates or advances terrorism, and content that portrays gratuitous or graphic violence.

What differs is the volume of complaint and the resulting user behavior. Allegations of censorship against Snapchat are not as frequent as they are against Meta's platforms, but many users are still urging others to screen record Stories posted from Gaza in case they are taken down.

# Discord Premium App Subscriptions And App Portability

Discord says it will begin rolling out Premium App Subscriptions to eligible developers in the UK and Europe, following a launch that began in the US a few weeks ago. On the subject of third-party apps, bots and plugins, the company said it is in the process of exploring how to make those accessible across nearly every part of Discord — it provided few details, but said the goal is to let people access their favorite apps and bots without those experiences being restricted to select servers.

The company describes the work as still experimental. "We're experimenting with a few different things, but the goal is for developers to reach more people with the awesome experience they're building. For users, we don't want them to be gated from having these custom experiences at their fingertips," Cherry Park, director of product marketing at Discord, told Engadget. "In terms of the way we architecture and build it, there are a couple of solutions. Some are easier, some are more difficult, and you're going to see us experiment with a few of them over the next few quarters."

Discord promised to share more about its efforts around app portability in the near future. In the meantime, Nitro subscribers will get a chance to test new features before they become available to the public.

# Foundation Model Reporting And Red-Team Disclosure Under The EO

The executive order sets out a reporting procedure for the most capable AI systems: a company developing any foundation model that poses a serious risk to national security, national economic security, or national public health and safety must notify the federal government when training the model, and must share the results of all red-team safety tests — and that information must be shared prior to the model being made available to the public, which could help reduce the rate at which companies unleash half-baked and potentially deadly machine learning products. The legal instrument used to compel this is the Defense Production Act.

Alongside red-team results, the EO also requires disclosure of the system's training runs — essentially its iterative development history. The purpose officials gave for the sequencing is verification: "What that does is that creates a space prior to the release… to verify that the system is safe and secure." The EO more broadly directs the establishment of new standards for AI safety and security, including reporting requirements for developers whose foundation models might impact national or economic security, and those requirements also apply in developing AI tools to autonomously implement security fixes on critical software infrastructure.

The procedure has a deliberately narrow scope. Administration officials were quick to point out that the reporting requirement will not affect any AI models currently available on the market, nor independent or small- to medium-size AI companies going forward, because the threshold for enforcement is quite high. It is geared specifically at the next generation of systems that the likes of Google, Meta and OpenAI are already working on, with enforcement on models starting at 10^26 petaflops — a capacity currently beyond the limits of existing AI models. "This is not going to catch AI systems trained by graduate students, or even professors," the administration official said.

The order was cast as a step past voluntary measures. "In response to the President's leadership on the subject, 15 major American technology companies have begun their voluntary commitments to ensure that AI technology is safe, secure and trustworthy before releasing it to the public," the senior administration official said. "That is not enough."

# Terms of Service

## Definition

Terms of Service (also called T&Cs or "terms and conditions") is the corpus's label for a platform's or vendor's own rulebook, as distinct from external regulation such as the DSA, which compels how that rulebook must be written and enforced (doc_0024).

The corpus applies the same label to two different domains: platform content-moderation rules — paired with, but not identical to, a separately named "Community Guidelines" document in Discord's warning system (doc_0505) — and the commercial fine print that online sportsbooks attach to sign-up and bonus offers (doc_0062, doc_0072).

## Context

In the corpus the term recurs wherever a platform's own rulebook — rather than a law — is the thing being disputed or regulated. The EU's DSA obliges platforms to "clearly communicate their T&Cs to users and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement," which is the legal hook the Commission uses against X over illegal-content handling (doc_0024). Breton's letter to X separately flags a change to X's "public interest policy" — the sub-rule governing when rule-breaking posts stay up for newsworthiness — as having left users "uncertain" about how X applies its own rules, illustrating that ToS content itself, not just its existence, is subject to DSA transparency requirements (doc_0025). On Meta's platforms, the operative rulebook is branded "Community Guidelines": Instagram removed and restricted Palestine-related posts that users say complied with those Guidelines, and Meta's own newsroom statements point back to the Guidelines and an appeals process as the mechanism for contesting enforcement (doc_0106). Snapchat's Community Guidelines are described as prohibiting pornographic, terrorism-advocating, or gratuitously violent content — a similarly-scoped rulebook to Meta's (doc_0124). Discord's new warning system links violators directly to its "Terms of Service, Community Guidelines and appeal mechanism," pairing the rulebook with a visible enforcement record (doc_0505). Outside content moderation, "terms and conditions" also names the commercial fine print — wagering requirements, banking limits, expiry windows — that online sportsbooks attach to sign-up and bonus offers, which users must accept before registering (doc_0062, doc_0072).

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform-authored, not statutory** — the rules originate with the service, distinguishing ToS from the regulations (e.g. the DSA) that constrain how it must be written and enforced.
- **Related but distinct rulebooks share the "terms" label** — "T&Cs" and "terms and conditions" name a platform's or vendor's own rules generally, while Meta and Snap label the content-moderation slice specifically "Community Guidelines"; Discord's warning system links to "Terms of Service," "Community Guidelines," and an appeal mechanism as three separate, companion items rather than one document (doc_0505).
- **Sub-policies can shift independently** — X's "public interest policy" changed without broader ToS changing, showing a rulebook is composed of adjustable sub-rules (doc_0025).
- **Transparency and enforcement is a regulatory target** — the DSA specifically requires clear communication of T&Cs and demonstrable enforcement, not merely that terms exist (doc_0024).
- **Disputed, uneven enforcement is a recurring failure mode** — users on Meta's platforms reported content removed despite compliance with Community Guidelines, and inconsistent enforcement (e.g. across Arabic vs. Hebrew content) became a trust and bias issue (doc_0106).
- **Domain-general usage** — the same "terms and conditions" label also covers non-moderation commercial conditions, such as wagering requirements attached to sportsbook bonuses (doc_0072).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "Terms of Service," "T&Cs," and "terms and conditions" throughout without ever stating a general definition for the term.

More broadly, terms of service — also called terms of use or terms and conditions — are the legal agreement between a service provider and its users: a person must agree to follow them to use the offered service, and for some websites they function simply as a disclaimer (Wikipedia, *Terms of service*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Generative AI Guardrails

## Definition

Generative AI guardrails are the constraints — technical, procedural, or regulatory — that companies and lawmakers put around a generative AI system to keep its outputs within intended bounds, whether that means blocking unsafe content, curbing hallucinations, or preventing misuse.

## Context

The corpus uses "guardrails" for three distinct layers of this idea. At the model layer, guardrails are safety filters meant to stop a chatbot from discussing controversial or dangerous topics: Google's Gemini Pro had such filters, but AI security researchers at Robust Intelligence used an automated prompt-mutation method to make the guardrails fail, getting the model to suggest ways to steal from a charity and to plan an assassination. At the product layer, guardrails are the deployment constraints a company layers on top of a model to fit a specific audience — Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" restricts its generative AI to kid-friendly trivia, sourced from only two vetted partners and generated offline with human-plus-AI review, precisely because "generative AI can be led astray or 'hallucinate' answers, while kids could ask inappropriate questions." OpenAI likewise announced guardrails meant to stop ChatGPT from generating and amplifying political disinformation, though the Washington Post found in an August report that those guardrails "actually weren't" enforced, with the system readily producing partisan campaign messaging on request. At the regulatory layer, guardrails is the term lawmakers and creative-industry advocates use for rules imposed on AI from outside the company building it: a news-publisher antitrust suit against Google sought court-ordered "guardrails to preserve a free marketplace of ideas," California's CPPA drafted privacy guardrails for automated decisionmaking technology, FTC roundtable participants in the creative industries floated copyright law as a guardrail against training on artists' work without consent, and EU lawmakers agreed to a "two-tier" system of guardrails for general-purpose AI foundation models.

## Key Characteristics

- **Multi-layered** — guardrails appear at the model level (safety filters), the product level (deployment-time content and audience restrictions), and the regulatory level (externally imposed rules), each addressing a different point of failure.
- **Meant to counter specific failure modes** — the corpus ties guardrails directly to named risks: hallucination and inappropriate content for kids (Amazon), political disinformation (OpenAI/ChatGPT), jailbreak-style prompt attacks (Google Gemini Pro), privacy harms from automated decisionmaking (CPPA), and unauthorized use of creative work in training (FTC roundtable).
- **Can fail or go unenforced** — guardrails are not guaranteed to hold: Gemini Pro's guardrails were defeated by an automated jailbreak technique, and OpenAI's disinformation guardrails were found by the Washington Post to not actually be enforced despite being announced.
- **Tiered by risk in regulation** — the EU AI Act's negotiated deal applies a "two-tier" guardrail system to general-purpose AI, with lighter transparency duties for standard foundation models and heavier obligations (model evaluations, adversarial testing, incident reporting) for "high-impact" models with systemic risk.
- **Sought as external legal remedy** — plaintiffs and regulators use "guardrails" to describe court-ordered or statutory constraints they want imposed on AI companies, as in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit against Google and the CPPA's draft ADMT privacy rules.

# The Digital Services Act

The Digital Services Act (DSA) is the European Union's pan-EU content moderation rulebook: a regulation that places governance obligations on digital services and platforms carrying user-generated content, with the aim of ensuring companies respond to reports of illegal content, and that layers heavier duties on the largest platforms. Its baseline obligations apply to digital services and platforms generally — respond diligently to notices of illegal content, clearly communicate terms and conditions to users, and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement of those terms.

The discriminating feature of the regime is its second tier. Platforms designated as "very large online platforms" (VLOPs) carry additional obligations to identify and mitigate systemic risks such as disinformation, gender-based violence, or negative effects on the exercise of fundamental rights. The Commission designated 19 VLOPs in April 2023, including Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram; X is also a designated VLOP. Compliance for VLOPs kicked in over the summer of 2023 — TechCrunch dates Meta's compliance start to August.

The regime's boundary case is disinformation itself. Unlike terrorism content, disinformation is not illegal in the EU per se. The DSA therefore does not reach it through the illegal-content removal route at all; it reaches it through the systemic-risk route, obliging a VLOP such as X to mitigate the risks attached to harmful falsehoods while separately acting diligently on reports of genuinely illegal content. The two duties run on different legal tracks even when they concern the same posts.

Penalties for confirmed breaches can be as high as 6% of global annual turnover, and the bloc holds a further power, in extremis, to block access to a service in the region for repeated infringements — meaning a platform that repeatedly fails to correct course could be shut off in the EU. TechCrunch illustrates the scale on both ends: Elon Musk last projected revenues of about $3 billion for 2023 for X, which by that example would cap a fine at up to $180 million, while in Meta's case the same 6% ceiling could run to multiple billions.

The regulation also contains a "crisis response" mechanism (Article 36) which enables the Commission to adopt rapid-fire measures on larger platforms in situations of "serious threat", such as war. As of TechCrunch's October 2023 reporting this part of the regulation was not yet operative: it would not start operating until February 17 of the following year, because it requires an advisory body — the European Board for Digital Services — to be operational before it can recommend that the Commission adopt a crisis response mechanism, and the Board's set-up was itself waiting on Member States to establish national Digital Services Coordinators, the bodies that oversee DSA compliance for non-VLOPs.

# Meta Crisis Response Measures

Following a content moderation warning from European Union regulators earlier that week, Meta published on 13 October 2023 an overview of how it is responding to risks on its platforms stemming from the Israel-Hamas war: a temporary expansion of its Violence and Incitement policy, prioritised livestream checks, demotion of borderline content, hashtag blocking, a special operations center, and a temporary suspension of strikes for some violations. The blog post frames much of this as "ongoing efforts" and rehashes some existing policies and tools, but the company confirms it made some changes in light of fast-moving events in Israel and Gaza.

The first change is the temporary expansion of the Violence and Incitement policy, in order to prioritize the safety of Israelis kidnapped by Hamas. Under it, Meta will remove content that "clearly identifies hostages when we're made aware of it, even if it's being done to condemn or raise awareness of their situation." Blurred images of victims are allowed, but, "in line with standards established by the Geneva Convention, we will prioritize the safety and privacy of kidnapping victims if we are unsure or unable to make a clear assessment."

The second is livestreaming. Meta says it is prioritizing checks on livestreaming functions on Facebook and Instagram, including watching for any attempts by Hamas to use the tools to broadcast footage of captured Israelis or other hostages. The precondition it invokes is prior violation history: "We recognize that the immediacy of Live brings unique challenges, so we have restrictions in place on the use of Live for people who have previously violated certain policies. We're prioritizing livestream reports related to this crisis, above and beyond our existing prioritization of Live videos." Meta drew the comparison to measures it took after the 2019 Christchurch attacks in New Zealand, when a single shooter livestreamed a killing spree targeting two mosques on Facebook. On the specific threat, it added: "We're also aware of Hamas' threats to broadcast footage of the hostages and we're taking these threats extremely seriously. Our teams are monitoring this closely, and would swiftly remove any such content (and the accounts behind it), banking the content in our systems to prevent copies being re-shared." The urgency is not hypothetical: in a particularly disturbing report on Israeli media that week, widely recirculated on social media, a girl recounted how she and her family learnt of her grandmother's death after Hamas militants uploaded a video of her dead body to Facebook, apparently using the dead woman's own mobile phone to post the graphic content to her Facebook page.

Further steps cover ranking and search. Meta says it is making it less likely that its systems will actively recommend potentially violating or borderline content, and reducing the visibility of potentially offensive comments; it is also applying hashtag blocking to render certain terms related to the conflict non-searchable on its platforms. The blog post does not specify which hashtags Meta is blocking in relation to the Israel-Hamas war.

Operationally, Meta says it established a special operations center staffed with experts, including Arabic and Hebrew speakers, to increase its ability to respond quickly to content reports, and that it is taking feedback from local partners such as NGOs on emerging risks and "moving quickly to address them."

Meta states the limit of the procedure itself: given the heightened attention and concern, it says non-violating content may be removed "in error." Its mitigation is to relax the penalty rather than the removal — "for some violations we are temporarily removing content without strikes, meaning these content removals won't cause accounts to be disabled" — and it says it continues to provide tools for users to appeal decisions they believe were wrong.

# Content Moderation

## Definition

Content moderation, as the corpus uses the term, is the mix of platform policy and enforcement — written rules like Meta's Violence and Incitement policy and Community Guidelines, human reviewers, automated systems, and crowdsourced tools like X's Community Notes — that decides what user-generated content stays visible and how a platform acts on notices of illegal or rule-breaking material.

## Context

In the corpus, content moderation surfaces mainly as the practice EU regulators scrutinize under the Digital Services Act (DSA): the DSA's "very precise obligations" require platforms to be "timely, diligent and objective" in acting on notices of illegal content, and the European Commission's formal DSA proceeding against X names "content moderation" as one of the specific areas under investigation, alongside risk management, dark patterns, advertising transparency, and researcher data access (doc_0024; doc_0153).
It also appears as a site of contested practice and bias: Meta's moderation of Palestinian-related content during the Israel-Hamas war produced widespread allegations of shadowbanning and inconsistent enforcement across Arabic versus Hebrew content (doc_0106), while Meta separately described tightening its livestreaming and hostage-content moderation in direct response to that same conflict (doc_0335).
The term also frames platform-differentiation debates outside the EU: Kick's "light moderation" is cited as both a draw for streamers leaving Twitch and a source of safety controversy (doc_0405), Mozilla frames robust moderation and "trust and safety" as central to its fediverse strategy while noting a stricter-moderation rival (Pebble) failed to grow (doc_0026), and the US Supreme Court case over Texas and Florida laws turns on whether content moderation is a form of constitutionally protected "editorial judgment" (doc_0256).

## Key Characteristics

- **Policy plus enforcement** — moderation combines written rules (e.g. Meta's Violence and Incitement policy, Community Guidelines) with mechanisms to act on them: human reviewers, automated classifiers, and appeals processes (doc_0335; doc_0106).
- **Legally obligated for large platforms under the DSA** — the DSA requires timely, diligent, objective action on illegal-content notices, and imposes added systemic-risk mitigation duties (e.g. disinformation) on very large online platforms like X and Meta (doc_0024; doc_0335).
- **Can be outsourced/crowdsourced** — X replaced parts of its formal moderation function with the crowdsourced "Community Notes" system after gutting in-house enforcement teams, a shift EU regulators are explicitly assessing for adequacy (doc_0025; doc_0153).
- **Prone to inconsistency and bias** — Meta's own third-party report found Arabic content flagged as violating at higher rates than Hebrew content, and attributed this to uneven language/dialect resources and reviewer training rather than deliberate policy (doc_0106).
- **Contested as speech regulation** — in the US, whether moderation decisions constitute protected "editorial judgment" under the First Amendment is the central legal question in the Texas/Florida social-media laws before the Supreme Court (doc_0256).
- **A competitive and reputational lever** — platforms position their moderation stance (heavy vs. light) as a market differentiator (doc_0508; doc_0405), though the corpus notes stricter moderation alone did not guarantee growth for at least one platform, Pebble, which shut down after never gaining more than 20,000 users (doc_0026).

## Background (external)

The corpus repeatedly uses "content moderation" without ever stating a general definition for it. Content moderation, more broadly, is the systematic practice of screening user-generated content and applying a predetermined set of rules to determine whether it should be published, removed, or restricted — commonly for material judged irrelevant, obscene, illegal, harmful, or insulting — either by removing it outright, labeling it, or letting users filter it themselves (Wikipedia, *Content moderation*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Johansson's Rebuttals To The Case Against The CSAM Scanning Proposal

Against opponents who characterise her CSAM-scanning proposal as mass surveillance, as a slippery slope, and as a law written around two vendors' technology, Ylva Johansson argued to MEPs that each of those premises is wrong: the proposal names no technology, would scan less than happens today, and forbids using detection for anything other than child sexual abuse. TechCrunch reported her answers on 25 October 2023, from her appearance before the committee.

The opposition she was answering had been aired earlier that week. A seminar organized by the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), an advisory body to the Commission on data protection law, heard from more than 20 speakers across civil society, academia and industry expressing deep misgivings about the Commission's approach — including a warning from the EDPS himself that the EU could be at a tipping point for freedom and democracy if it does not turn back from the plan to do non-targeted scanning of private messages. Johansson had been invited to participate in the seminar but declined to attend, and she did not offer a direct response to the EDPS' concerns at the hearing, instead countering a number of the arguments heard at the session.

Her first counter attacks the premise that the proposal is built around particular vendors. She denied that only Thorn and Microsoft have technology "that is necessary for the scanning", calling that claim "absolutely not true". "There are no specific technologies mentioned [in the proposal] and I think this is an important part. So there's no specific technology that's been favoured in this proposal," she told the committee, adding: "So many technologies are being developed all the time — while we are speaking — and they will continue to develop. So I think it's important that the legislation has to be technology neutral."

Her second counter attacks the inference from the proposal to mass surveillance. "My proposal would not mean that all communication will be scanned. Compared to the situation today it will be much more limited," she claimed, referencing the temporary ePrivacy derogation that currently gives messaging firms a legal basis to scan non-encrypted content for CSAM — a derogation intended to be replaced by the proposed regulation which, critics contend, will force platforms to scan end-to-end encrypted content too. "Today companies are allowed to scan if they search for child sexual abuse material. That's why we receive these 5.2 million videos and pictures and grooming attempts — 70% from private communication. If my proposal is adopted, this will be limited."

The warrant she offered for that comparison is the proposal's ordering of obligations: in-scope platforms are first required to deploy prevention measures to try to stop the spread of CSAM and/or prevent abuse of their tools by people intent on abusing children. "First comes prevention. Only if prevention is not enough, then you might be allowed to do detection — but only after a court decision," she said. "So only those that really cannot deal with the problem with mitigating measures… and only after a court decision and only during a specific period they will be allowed to do the detection. We will also limit the reporting so that we will also receive fewer but hopefully better reports."

Her third counter attacks the overreach and slippery-slope premises by pointing outside the proposal, to other EU laws acting as balancing checks on the scope of possible CSAM-scanning. "It's also important that we continue to comply with all relevant legislation. For example the GDPR and other requirements, there are no derogation from that in my proposal," she said. "It's also important — and I know that's been part of the debate — that it should not be a slippery slope. The proposal specifically prohibits using the detection technologies for any other purpose than the detection of child sexual abuse online — and only with verified indicators of child sexual abuse provided by the EU Centre."

That defensive strategy carries its own exposure. Given her reliance on pointing to the existence of a wider EU legal framework doing the heavy lifting and protecting Europeans' fundamental rights as a way to assuage critics, and given she is also invoking respect for the rule of law as a buttress against the risk of content-scanning mission creep, it is doubly relevant that the Commission now finds itself in a bind — forced to investigate whether its own officials ignored legal requirements in a bid to covertly sweep past critics.

# The Accredited Technology Clause And The Encryption Objection

WhatsApp, other encrypted messaging services, and digital rights groups reject the assumption that the Online Safety Act's CSAM-detection clause can be satisfied without breaking encryption: the section in question allows Ofcom to require online platforms to use so-called "accredited technology" to detect CSAM, and they say this scanning would require breaking apps' encryption systems and invading user privacy.

The objection is aimed at territory Ofcom has not yet reached. Today's consultation covers some of the act's least contentious ground, like reducing the spread of content that was already illegal in the UK. As Ofcom releases future updates it will have to take on touchier subjects, like content that is legal but harmful for children, underage access to pornography, and protections for women and girls — and, perhaps most controversially, it will need to interpret the section that critics have claimed could fundamentally undermine end-to-end encryption in messaging apps.

The matter is unresolved. Whitehead says Ofcom plans to consult on this next year, leaving the act's full impact on encrypted messaging uncertain.

# Disinformation

## Definition

Disinformation is false or misleading content spread online — distinct from the illegal-content category (like terrorism or hate speech) in that, per the corpus's account of EU regulation, disinformation "is not illegal in the EU per se," yet still counts as a *systemic risk* that large platforms must assess and mitigate.

## Context

The corpus's central storyline is the EU's escalating regulatory pressure on X (formerly Twitter) over disinformation tied to the Israel-Hamas war: the Commission's October 2023 warning and formal information request to Musk accused X of being used "to disseminate illegal content and disinformation" following the Hamas attacks, and a EU-commissioned study later found X had "the largest ratio of mis/disinformation posts" among major platforms.
Because X is a Digital Services Act (DSA) "very large online platform" (VLOP), the obligation to mitigate disinformation risk is legally binding on it even though the underlying falsehoods are not themselves illegal; the EU's voluntary Code of Practice on Disinformation (which Musk pulled X out of earlier in 2023) is treated by the Commission as a signal of DSA compliance on this exact risk.
Disinformation also surfaces as a generative-AI worry: Suleyman warned DeepMind's ethics board that AI "could lead to an explosion in disinformation," EU commissioner Vera Jourova flagged AI-generated disinformation as an election threat, and early fears that ChatGPT would be used "to generate disinformation on a massive scale" pushed European policymakers toward mandating security assessments of generative AI products.
Real-world examples in the corpus include a video-game clip falsely presented as Hamas missile footage circulating on X, and misinformation described as "rampant on social media" during the Gaza crisis, prompting some users to turn to Snap Map for unmediated, firsthand footage instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **Not illegal per se in the EU** — disinformation is treated as a systemic risk to be mitigated, not content that platforms are legally required to remove the way they must remove illegal content.
- **Distinct from "misinformation" but often paired with it** — the corpus uses both terms (e.g., "mis/disinformation posts," Mozilla's content-policy list of "misinformation" as a harm category), generally without a sharp technical distinction, though disinformation carries a stronger connotation of deliberate falsehood or manipulation (e.g., "Kremlin propaganda").
- **A VLOP systemic-risk obligation** — under the DSA, platforms designated VLOPs (like X) must proactively assess and mitigate disinformation risk, which is what makes an EU formal-information request or investigation possible even absent an illegal-content finding.
- **Measurable and comparable across platforms** — the EU's Code of Practice enabled a pilot study producing "structural indicators" (e.g., how easily disinformation content is found, how much engagement it gets) that let regulators rank X as worst among mainstream platforms.
- **A named risk of generative AI** — beyond social-media falsehoods, the corpus repeatedly frames disinformation as a downstream risk of AI text/image generation (ChatGPT, deepfakes), motivating both EU AI-Act-era safeguards and industry-side labeling commitments.

# TikTok's Synthetic Media Policy And Disinformation Measures

TikTok's report to the EU disinformation Code focuses on AI-generated content in the context of ensuring the "integrity" of its services, flagging a recent update to its community guidelines which also saw it modify its synthetic media policy "to address the use of content created or modified by AI technology on our platform."

The core rule is proactive disclosure: "While we welcome the creativity that new AI may unlock, in line with our updated policy, users must proactively disclose when their content is AI-generated or manipulated but shows realistic scenes," TikTok writes. It adds: "We continue to fight against covert influence operations (CIO) and we do not allow attempts to sway public opinion while misleading our platform's systems or community about the identity, origin, operating location, popularity, or purpose of the account. CIOs continue to evolve in response to our detection and networks may attempt to reestablish a presence on our platform. This is why we continue to iteratively research and evaluate complex deceptive behaviours and develop appropriate product and policy solutions. We continue to provide information about the CIO networks we identify and remove in this report and within our transparency reports here."

Commitment 15 in TikTok's report signs the platform up to "tak[ing] into consideration transparency obligations and the list of manipulative practices prohibited under the proposal for Artificial Intelligence Act." Under that pledge it lists being a launch partner of the Partnership on AI's "Responsible Practices for Synthetic Media" and contributing to the development of "relevant practices," and joining "new relevant groups" such as the Generative AI working group which started work that month. In the next six months it says it wants to further strengthen enforcement of its synthetic media policy and explore "new products and initiatives to help enhance our detection and enforcement capabilities" in this area, including in user education.

# Identity Verification

## Definition

In the corpus, identity verification covers two distinct uses on X (formerly Twitter): the legacy "verification" of notable accounts (the original Blue Check), and a newer bot-deterrence toolkit combining payment, phone, and ID verification. The corpus does not itself define the general term; see Background (external) below.

## Context

The corpus traces a shift in what verification means on X after Elon Musk's takeover. Musk ended legacy account verification and turned the Blue Check system into "a game of pay-to-play," one of a series of changes that made it harder for users to locate quality information on the platform and left them unable to tell "at a glance" whether a notable account's exchange was genuine — a gap that surfaced when a screengrab of an apparent exchange between Iran's supreme leader and an Israeli government account circulated without a reliable verification signal. Separately, in October 2023, X director of engineering Eric Farraro described a broader plan to fight bots that layers payment verification, phone verification, and ID verification on top of the new $1/year fee and X's existing heuristics and models for detecting fake accounts, framing identity checks as a way to raise the cost of automated account creation rather than a way to certify notability.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two distinct applications** — verifying an account belongs to a notable, authentic person or entity (the legacy Blue Check use), versus verifying an account is tied to a real payment method, phone number, or ID to deter mass bot creation (the 2023 anti-bot toolkit).
- **Layered, not standalone** — Farraro described ID verification as one option "as part of a larger strategy to fight bots," stacked alongside payment and phone verification and traditional heuristic/model-based detection, "not mutually exclusive" with the others.
- **Cost-raising rather than bot-proof** — the stated goal of ID/phone/payment verification was to make bot creation "difficult and expensive enough that it's less and less viable," not to eliminate bots outright.
- **Credibility function when applied to notable accounts** — removing legacy verification degraded users' ability to judge at a glance whether high-profile exchanges on the platform were genuine.
- **Anticipated arms race** — Farraro warned that AI would eventually be able to solve CAPTCHAs and generate content "undetectable by human or AI countermeasures," meaning verification-based defenses would need to keep evolving.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not offer a general definition of identity verification. Per Wikipedia's *Identity verification service* article, an identity verification service is "used by businesses to ensure that users or customers provide information that is associated with the identity of a real person" (Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02) — the general concept that both of the corpus's X-specific applications (notable-account verification and anti-bot payment/phone/ID checks) instantiate.

# Crisis Response Mechanism

## Definition

The crisis response mechanism is a provision of the EU's Digital Services Act (Article 36) that lets the European Commission adopt rapid-fire measures on very large online platforms (VLOPs) in situations of "serious threat," such as war.

## Context

The mechanism surfaces in the corpus as one of the DSA tools regulators point to while pressing X and Meta over content moderation during the Israel-Hamas war.
In the EU's formal request for information to X, the Commission separately asked X to report on "the activation and functioning of X's crisis response protocol" by October 18, 2023 — a company-level protocol distinct from, but referenced alongside, the DSA's own Article 36 mechanism.
Meta's coverage of the same period notes that the Article 36 mechanism cannot yet be adopted by the Commission because it is not operational: it needs a recommendation from an advisory body, the European Board for Digital Services, which in turn is waiting on Member States to stand up their national Digital Services Coordinators.

## Key Characteristics

- **Commission-adopted, not automatic** — the mechanism is a power the Commission "may adopt," triggered by a "serious threat" such as war, not a standing rule.
- **Scoped to larger platforms** — the corpus describes it applying to VLOPs, the same tier subject to the DSA's broader systemic-risk obligations.
- **Not yet operational as of October 2023** — activation depends on the European Board for Digital Services being operational, which in turn depends on Member States establishing national Digital Services Coordinators; the corpus gives a target start date of February 17 (the following year).
- **Distinct from a platform's own crisis protocol** — the corpus separately shows the Commission asking X to report on "the activation and functioning of X's crisis response protocol," a company-run process that is not the same thing as the Commission's Article 36 mechanism, though the two are easy to conflate.

# Ofcom's Recommended Practices And Enforcement For Illegal Harms

Ofcom recommends that in-scope platforms implement policies like not allowing strangers to send direct messages to children, using hash matching to detect and remove CSAM, maintaining content and search moderation teams, and offering ways for users to report harmful content. Ofcom estimates that around 100,000 services may fall under the wide-ranging rules, though only the largest and highest-risk platforms will have to abide by the strictest requirements.

The premise is consistency rather than novelty. Large tech platforms already follow many of these practices, but Ofcom hopes to see them implemented more consistently. "We think they represent best practice of what's out there, but it's not necessarily applied across the board," Whitehead says. "Some firms are applying it sporadically but not necessarily systematically, and so we think there is a great benefit for a more wholesale, widespread adoption."

The regulations also cover how sites should deal with other illegal harms like content that encourages or assists suicide or serious self-harm, harassment, revenge porn and other sexual exploitation, and the supply of drugs and firearms. Search services should provide "crisis prevention information" when users enter suicide-related queries, for example, and when companies update their recommendation algorithms they should conduct risk assessments to check that they are not going to amplify illegal content.

Enforcement runs through complaint and penalty. If users suspect a site is not complying with the rules, Whitehead says there will be a route to complain directly to Ofcom. If a firm is found to be in breach, Ofcom can levy fines of up to £18 million (around $22 million) or 10 percent of worldwide turnover — whichever is higher — and offending sites can even be blocked in the UK.

# Snapchat Design Features Alleged To Enable Drug Sales

The lawsuit against Snap claims that Snapchat's features facilitate practices like drug sales by connecting dealers to young customers while promising them safety from legal repercussions through anonymity.

Chief among those designs, according to Matthew Bergman, the lead attorney on the case, is the promise that a message will disappear not only for fellow users but also on the software's back end. That is the ground that turns a product feature into an enabler of crime: it prevents law enforcement officials from seeing the activity of a dealer even after the dealer has been identified.

The complaint names other features as problematic too: notifying individuals when another person screenshots their post, the ability to geolocate fellow users, and algorithms that suggest new connections based on demographics.

# War Duration and Scenarios Driving Israeli Growth Damage

Leo Leiderman's model of the war's economic damage has two drivers: duration and breadth. "First of all, the duration and character of the war will have a decisive impact on the depth of damage to the economy. Many studies, as well as past experience, indicate that the longer the war lasts, the broader will be the impact on the economy. It is also known that this connection between the length of the fighting and the economic damage might not be linear. And of course, the more the war widens to more fronts, the greater will be the economic damage."

He declined to quantify the effect. Asked on 12 October 2023 for a forecast of the consequences for growth, he said it was too early to make a quantitative estimate of the effects on the economy's growth in 2024 and 2025. Israel has a great deal of information about loss of growth and product in past episodes — the Yom Kippur War, the Lebanon War, two intifadas, various military operations, and the Covid pandemic — but in his view this is a completely different episode: "This is a new situation that has no precedent as far as the damage to the economy is concerned."

The range over which the model runs is therefore a spectrum of scenarios rather than a point estimate: "from a short war on the southern front only, to the nightmare scenario of a prolonged war with additional sectors involved." He noted the interview was taking place only on the fifth day of the war, and expressed the hope that the picture would start to become clearer.

# Azrieli Group's Office Portfolio In Q3 2023

Azrieli Group (TASE: AZRG) is one of the biggest companies in Israel's income-producing property sector, with 15 office buildings comprising 632,000 square meters of space and 97% occupancy.

In the week before 3 December 2023 Azrieli published its financial results for the third quarter of 2023, saying the company had not been impacted by the war. # AI21 Labs' Tel Aviv Office Lease

Less than a month before the war, Globes reported a huge deal in which Amnon Shashua's unicorn AI21 Labs announced it was leasing 7,000 square meters for NIS 15 million annually in Tel Aviv's Da Vinci project.

# Amot Investments' Portfolio And War Scenario Assessment

Amot Investments (TASE: AMOT), another of the biggest companies in the income-producing property sector, has 1.15 million square meters of office space for leasing with 93.5% occupancy and a further six projects in various stages of construction. # Israeli Economy in the First Week of the Gaza War

As the first week of fighting in the war in Israel's south drew to a close, the main index on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, the Tel Aviv 35, had fallen 6.4% over the week, with financial markets trying to gauge the damage the Israeli economy would sustain. Globes reported on 12 October 2023 that this was clearly a very significant event, but that the fog of war made it hard to estimate its full consequences.

The assessment came from Prof. Leo Leiderman, chief economic adviser at Bank Hapoalim and a professor of economics at Tel Aviv University, who set out for Globes his proposals for rehabilitating the economy and repairing the damage the war would cause. Asked what had been going through his mind in those first days, Leiderman said: "What most preoccupies me is not the economy but concern for the families of the soldiers, the wounded, and the captives, and solidarity with them. I have four relatives from Kibbutz Nir Oz who are still missing, and we have no information about them. I find it hard to understand how a war like this landed on us in a country as powerful as Israel. But we have no choice but to win."

# Egypt's Role In The Israel-Hamas War And The Leverage It Creates

The war between Israel and Hamas has turned the spotlight on Egypt's role as a regional powerbroker, potentially winning it Western support as it tries to escape a grinding economic crisis. The structure linking the two is that Egypt's two assets in this conflict — long-held ties to Israel and a border with Gaza — make its stance decisive for outcomes the West wants.

Specifically, Egypt's position is shaping up as key to the fate of any refugees and to a sustained flow of aid for the besieged territory's 2 million residents, after Israel cut off crucial supplies in response to Hamas's deadly Oct. 7 assault. That dependence is what converts Egypt's geography and relationships into potential leverage over Western backing for its economy, as of the reporting date of 2023-10-22.



---


# Egypt's Strategic Value To Europe: Gas And Security

The war "underscores the important role Egypt has always played vis-a-vis security in and around Gaza," said Robert Satloff, executive director at The Washington Institute for Near East Policy — a role that is not lost on European governments.

Those governments woke up to Egypt's importance as a regional gas producer after Vladimir Putin's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. European officials visited to assess Egypt's potential as a gas supplier — with Israel's help — to supplant at least some Russian supplies.



---


# Egypt's Refusal To Host Palestinian Refugees

President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi has rejected any suggestion that Egypt host Gazan refugees, even as the same Western governments now court him for help in alleviating the pressure on Gaza, suggesting instead that Israel take in Palestinians in its Negev desert: "They can transport Palestinians there until Israel implements its announced plan to destroy Hamas," he said on Wednesday, 2023-10-18. The core political ground is that "there is little to no constituency for going against decades of policy on not allowing Palestinian displacement," said Mirette Mabrouk of the Middle East Institute, while the inducements offered "might wind up becoming a political liability, especially in an election year."

Three further grounds support the refusal. Egypt already hosts some 9 million refugees and other migrants from countries including Syria, Sudan, Yemen and Libya. Opening a route for Palestinians may also present a new security risk in the Sinai peninsula, where the army has only just managed to get a handle on its fight with Islamist militants. And Jordan has also refused to accept more Palestinians, making it unlikely Egypt would become a regional exception and take in refugees many suspect may never be let back into Gaza — which would risk being seen in the Arab world as facilitating another mass displacement and betraying the Palestinian cause all Arab countries vocally espouse.

The warrant tying these grounds to the policy is that the domestic political cost outranks the economic one. While Egypt could absorb a certain number of people, the domestic political consequences would be "huge," said the Washington Institute's Robert Satloff: "The political leadership considers this a red line not to be crossed and would prefer to face worsening financial distress than accept a significant number of refugees."



---


# The Israeli Proposal To Temporarily House Gazans In Sinai

The Israeli government has spoken to counterparts in several countries about Egypt temporarily housing Palestinians fleeing the violence in Gaza, according to officials with knowledge of the matter. Israel suggested they could be moved to tent camps in the Sinai Peninsula — funded by the United Nations and the US — and then returned once military operations end, said the people. It is unclear whether Israel has put the idea directly to Egypt.

The reasoning behind the approach was economic. "Clearly the hope on Israel and the US's side had been that Egypt would accept economic incentives, at a time when it is suffering an economic crisis, to allow Gazans into Egypt," said Mirette Mabrouk, director of the Egypt program at the Washington-based Middle East Institute.

# Egypt's Economic Crisis And Its IMF Rescue Program

Egypt, which reached a deal with the IMF in December 2022, was as of October 2023 already in talks on boosting that rescue program to over $5 billion from $3 billion, people familiar with the discussions told Bloomberg that month. This is happening as the most populous Arab nation wrestles with its worst economic outlook in decades and President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi prepares for elections in less than two months' time — a combination that opens up opportunities for Cairo, though a host of domestic and regional considerations are seen ruling out any refugee deal.

According to Riccardo Fabiani, project director for North Africa with Crisis Group, it is possible the IMF's key shareholders in the US and Europe may pressure the Washington-based lender to soften its requirements and move ahead with the program despite Cairo's slow pace of reforms.

# Saudi Co-Leadership As Egypt's Way Out Of The Dilemma

One way out of Egypt's dilemma may be for it to offer Saudi Arabia a role co-leading the Palestinian issue for the Arab world in return for financial support, according to strategists. The proposition rests on Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman being willing: aware of domestic anger at Israel, he might welcome such an initiative to strengthen his regional profile — though he was absent from the Summit for Peace held in Cairo on Saturday, 2023-10-21, which is the one contrary indication the account records.

The fluid situation may offer Egypt other opportunities to take a mediating role that could be rewarded, Crisis Group's Riccardo Fabiani said. For now, Egypt will try to play a constructive part "in the hope that its contribution will be acknowledged by its international and regional partners and potentially rewarded economically," he said.

# Israel-Hamas Conflict: The Limited-Market-Impact Base Case

As of mid-October 2023, the Indian stock market's base case was that the Israel-Hamas hostilities would not escalate, and on that assumption the conflict was expected to have only a limited impact on markets. The grounds are threefold. First, the world can ill-afford another full-fledged war while economies are already battling high inflation and interest rates, an ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and a slowing China, which is precisely why many countries are trying to restrict any escalation; the market movement in the week before 14 October 2023 indicated that non-escalation was the presumed base case. Second, the US treasury secretary stated that the current conflict is not likely to significantly impact the global economic outlook. Third, history supports the same conclusion: a study of past conflicts between Israel and Hamas found that they tend to have limited impact on global financial markets, across crude oil, US 10-year yields, US equities and market volatility.

The warrant joining the evidence to the claim is that market impact tracks escalation, not the mere existence of hostilities: because the incentives of major countries point towards containment and because previous Israel-Hamas episodes transmitted little into the four channels that matter (oil, yields, equities, volatility), the priced-in outcome is a contained conflict. The argument is explicitly conditional on the non-escalation premise holding.

# Fiscal Cost Channels of the Israel-Gaza War

Leo Leiderman set out the war's cost to the Israeli budget as a set of direct and indirect channels: "As with any war, the current war has and will have direct and indirect impacts."

On the spending side, the war will substantially raise defence spending in the coming years for procurement of equipment, ammunition and advanced systems in accordance with the new needs. A second direct expense is payment for the reserve duty days of those mobilised. A third channel runs through financing costs: given current interest rate levels around the world, the cost of servicing public debt as a proportion of GDP will rise.

On the revenue side, he expects a decline in state revenues from taxation. The combined result of these channels is a rise in the fiscal deficit.

# Displacement And Casualties In Gaza As Of October 12, 2023

The number of people in Gaza displaced from their homes rose quickly over the days preceding Oct. 12, 2023, totaling over 330,000 on that date, with over two-thirds of them staying in UNRWA schools.

Since the war between Israel and Hamas began on Oct. 8, 2023, more than 1,500 Gazans had been killed and more than 5,300 injured, while Hamas attacks had killed more than 1,300 people in Israel and injured about 3,200 others. These are the figures as reported on 2023-10-13.

# Israeli Sectors Most Exposed to War Damage

Asked which industries the war would hit, Leo Leiderman put private consumption — particularly of services — at the centre: "A substantial decline can be expected in private consumption, particularly of services."

His mechanism runs through sentiment as well as income. The decline is not just because of damage to output and income but also for psychological reasons: distress, uncertainty and the possibility of prolonged reserve duty by some of the public will all affect consumer sentiment.

The exposed sectors he names are tourism, commerce, transport services, entertainment and restaurants. He also identified a vulnerable class of firm by analogy with an earlier shock: as in the Covid pandemic, the self-employed and small and medium-size businesses may be hurt, particularly those that operate with high leverage.

# Israel's Office Space Oversupply

Even before the war, the industry was talking about there being too large a supply of office space in Israel, and according to the Central Bureau of Statistics construction was begun on 3.56 million square meters of office space between 2020 and 2022. Avison Young Israel co-CEO Guy Amosi's grounds for concern are drawn from a live search: a company asked his firm to find 15,000 square meters and to map out options from Rishon Lezion to Kfar Saba, not looking in Tel Aviv where prices are high and where contracts were closed two years ago for NIS 150 per square meter; they found a huge number of projects in the area between Rishon Lezion and Kfar Saba, with millions of square meters being built, and Amosi says he really does not know who will occupy all those areas. He fears many areas in the central region could remain empty for a long time before they are occupied, and is particularly bothered by offices built without an anchor tenant to begin with, noting that even in Petah Tikva half a million square meters of new office space is being built.

The argument is qualified in two directions. Location still counts: Amosi sees an advantage in offices in a good location such as Park Naimi in the central region at Messubim Junction near Roads 4 and 1, and he points out that Midtown was written off when it was built next to Azrieli yet those are now the most sought-after towers, so everything is a question of how long it takes to occupy, and in the end everything will be occupied. He is also currently doing four or five deals for companies that must rent space, not large-scale, from firms ending contracts or growing and wanting more space. The causes he lists for the slowdown stack up: there was Covid and then a crisis in high-tech that led to a chain reaction of reduced spending, companies began to check every investment, interest rates rose and inflation is rampant all over the world, which he insists is not a local bubble, and above all this comes the war; but in general real estate works in waves and the wave will come again.

# Bank of Israel Interest Rate Policy During the War

Asked what the Bank of Israel should do at its interest rate decision on 23 October 2023, Leo Leiderman argued for holding: "As for cutting the interest rate, it's too early to consider that. The current interest rate is at the right level for the state of the economy, and together with the policy on exchange rates, it contributes to ensuring financial stability."

His first ground is that the inflation effect of the war is indeterminate. It was still too early to tell how the war would affect the rate of inflation in the short and medium term: just as there are new inflationary factors, such as the depreciation of the shekel, there will also be factors working in the opposite direction, given the expected decline in private consumption, tourism and other items.

His second ground extends his fiscal reasoning to monetary policy: as with fiscal policy, a country at war is allowed to deviate temporarily from the set inflation target. He judged that at the moment there was no surge in inflation expectations, and that the investment community is aware of the existence of index-linked assets and the exchange rate that can assist in hedging inflation risk. The warrant tying this to a hold rather than a cut is that financial stability, not inflation, is the binding objective while the shock is unresolved.

# Bank of Israel Thirty Billion Dollar FX Intervention

On the Monday of the week in which this 12 October 2023 interview was published, the Bank of Israel announced a dramatic plan to sell $30 billion of its foreign currency reserves to stabilise the shekel. By the time of the report the shekel had in fact recovered slightly and was trading at around NIS 3.96/$.

Leo Leiderman endorsed the move: "It's important to welcome the Bank of Israel's decision to intervene, as necessary, in the foreign exchange market, in order to ensure the market's regular operation." He also treated leadership continuity as stabilising, citing the decision to extend the term of Amir Yaron as governor at least for the duration of the war, and in his hope beyond it. He added that the banking system is stable with enough liquidity in the system, and that the behaviour of the investment community in Israel, including the financial institutions, indicates high confidence in the economy's resilience and financial strength — an "asset" he said a level-headed, correct economic policy must preserve.

# Why Israeli Office Rents Have Not Fallen

Asked why rents are not falling given huge supply and a fall in demand, the market's practitioners give two answers. Guy Amosi says prices have fallen by about 10% at most, and that those cutting rents are the ones who bought buildings in purchase groups like BSR City, where many individuals bought as a profitable investment; once construction of the building is finished and payments such as management fees, mortgage and property taxes drop, some owners think of selling, and in those places a drop in prices may be seen.

Or Ben Zvi Klein argues prices will not go down because people have learned lessons from the past: everyone was burned by Covid, and a property owner who gave a discount at the beginning of Covid realised it by the end, when the office opposite the one leased at a discount of NIS 100 per square meter was being rented out for NIS 140 per square meter. Property owners are not under pressure because they rented most of their space during the peak periods of 2021-2022; those who may be under pressure are companies trying to sublet their properties, where attractive prices are visible for fully furnished space. He qualifies the claim with a condition: Israelis have been living for years with fighting in the background, and if the war continues people may want to break a contract; but as the economy returns to work with kindergartens and schools opening there is a general feeling of an economy returning to normal alongside the war, and it is possible to start going to work. He draws the Covid parallel to its conclusion, that there was talk about whether people would return to work and in the end everyone returned to the office, and says he is optimistic about the office market in future.

# The Thesis That Egypt Is Too Big To Fail

Multiple economists, bankers and investors whom Bloomberg spoke with in October 2023 in Morocco, during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, saw Egypt as likely to receive some economic backing whatever its refugee stance. The crisis has reminded global players of the North African nation's status as a regional linchpin, entrenching the idea that it is too big to fail.

The warrant is regional instability rather than Egypt's own merits: the current conflict serves to highlight the growing instability on all sides of Egypt, in Libya, Sudan and now in Gaza. That confronts the US and Europe with the need to ensure that "Cairo remains a stable and reliable partner in the area" that "deserves external support," Crisis Group's Riccardo Fabiani said.

# Will Smith's Slap Of Chris Rock At The 2022 Oscars

In March 2022, at the 94th annual Academy Awards, Will Smith walked onto the stage and slapped the comedian Chris Rock, then yelled at him to "keep my wife's name out your f***ing mouth." The altercation followed Rock's joke — "Jada, I love you. GI Jane 2, can't wait to see you" — referring to Jada Pinkett Smith's shaved head, which is a result of her alopecia. It quickly became the most talked-about moment of the evening, with the pair initially appearing to laugh off the tense moment. Later that night, while accepting the award for Best Actor, Smith became teary and said he was a "fierce defender of his family."

The incident was reassessed in October 2023 after Pinkett Smith revealed the couple had been separated since 2016 and so were separated at the time of the ceremony. UK-based dating coach Jacob Lucas, quoted by The Independent, tied part of the surrounding controversy to that timing and questioned Smith's behaviour and word choice at the awards given the separation.

# Tim McGraw And Faith Hill's Marriage

Tim McGraw and Faith Hill, both 56, met in 1994, began dating in 1996 and married later that same year; they share three daughters — Gracie, 26, Maggie, 25, and Audrey, 21 — and by late 2023 had been married for nearly 30 years. McGraw joked to "Entertainment Tonight Canada" about how that reads in the industry: "I don't know if there's a key. We always say we're 27 years coming up, it's like 96 in show business. It's almost like dog years."

The distinguishing feature of their account is a rule set at the start rather than a technique applied since. Although he humbly denied having any "key" to a successful marriage, McGraw named the commitment the two made at the outset: "We just made a commitment early on, when we first decided we were getting married and having kids, that we wouldn't just walk out the door when problems arose."

# Counter-Argument: Separations Reschedule Problems Rather Than Resolve Them

UK-based dating coach Jacob Lucas attacks the premise that an indefinite separation is a constructive alternative to divorce, arguing instead that it merely postpones the breakup. Speaking to The Independent in October 2023, he acknowledged that not all separations end in resolutions: when couples stop living together it can create an emotional disconnect, and if a lack of connection already existed before they separated, the separation does not make those issues go away. In such cases, he believes, couples may be avoiding an inevitable breakup for the sake of comfortability. "They're not resolving their problems, they're rescheduling them," he said. "So, if you separate from someone, but you live in a separate house and you're still together, it seems to me you're just not letting go of the past because you want to stick to what's familiar. People stick to what they know, and it's like you have a tether to that person. Your brain's like: 'I cannot let go of them because I am scared of the unknown.' I don't think I've ever seen a couple separate and come back again."

Lucas also attacks the second premise — that a promise never to divorce is a strength. While he agrees both parties must be invested in a relationship, he warns that promising not to get a divorce could spark feelings of resentment down the line, and that an agreement of the kind the Smiths made could create a false narrative about divorce. He notes that fans do not know why the couple made that promise. His warrant is that the stigma the promise defends against is not real: "Getting divorced shouldn't feel like a taboo because people grow apart and that's fine. People get stuck in relationships because of their friends and family or societal pressure, and they worry about getting divorced. They think a divorce has a stigma to its name, which it doesn't, and they push aside the fact that they still essentially feel trapped with someone they don't want to be with."



---


# Expert Signs That It Is Time To End A Marriage

Asked when a couple should stop trying, relationship expert Susan Winter argues that the threshold is exhaustion of options rather than any particular grievance: "When there is no stone left unturned, or when they have tried every single combination possible to make the relationship function and yet it doesn't, that's the time to pull the plug. They've done their individual work and they have done the work together and ended up in the same place." Her warrant is that effort must have been made both separately and jointly; only when both routes converge on the same failure is the case closed. The Independent notes that every relationship is different, whether lived in the public eye or not, and that living separately may not be an issue for some couples at all.

Dating coach Jacob Lucas offers a different, behaviour-based test: "If you feel disrespected by your partner, feel humiliated, or were cheated on, you probably feel ready to split. I also think a real big one is, if you lose sexual attraction for your partner and you've actively tried to get it back and can't, it's time to go." Applied to the Smiths, the article sets out three open possibilities — the couple could stay separated, move back in together as a married pair, or get a divorce.

Two months after ending her engagement to Jason Trawick, Britney Spears began dating David Lucado, who worked at a legal firm; she announced their split in August 2014 by tweeting "Ahhhh the single life!", and her representative confirmed to People: "Yes, she's single." # Britney Spears And Kevin Federline: Marriage And Divorce

Britney Spears and Kevin Federline married in September 2004 after just three months of dating, in a surprise ceremony in Studio City, California, and Spears filed for divorce in November 2006 citing "irreconcilable differences." Sam Asghari filed for divorce from Britney Spears in August 2023 after only 14 months of marriage, listing the date of separation as 28 July 2023 and citing "irreconcilable differences." His statement read: "After six years of love and commitment to each other my wife and I have decided to end our journey together. Justin Timberlake publicly apologised to Britney Spears on Instagram in 2021 after the documentary Framing Britney, which addressed the public scrutiny Spears faced during the 2000s, prompted criticism of how he had behaved following their breakup. # Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# The Epic v. Apple Ruling And Its Limited Weight Here

In the Apple case both sides lost, but Epic arguably lost more: even though Apple has incredible power over the iPhone, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled the company did not have an unfair monopoly in that case, partly because she decided the relevant market for Fortnite was "digital mobile gaming transactions" rather than, say, iPhone apps. She also decided that Epic violated its developer agreement with Apple and would have to pay.

Epic did win something. Rogers barred Apple from keeping iPhone users in the dark about alternate ways they can pay for apps, and may have even allowed developers to add their own payment mechanisms.

The precedent's reach into the Google trial is limited in two specific ways. First, that was a different case — and it is not over until the Supreme Court weighs in or declines to take a look. Second, Google cannot tell jurors that Apple won its case, or that other plaintiffs settled; the judge in this case says so. Epic declined to answer on the record when asked about the Apple outcome.



---


# Epic Games v. Google Goes To Trial On November 6, 2023

Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite, went to trial with Google on November 6, 2023, hoping to convince a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. Match had settled its own antitrust lawsuit with Google the week before, but Epic's case proceeded.

This case differs slightly from Epic's battle with Apple on the same topic, because this time Epic cannot allege there is no other way to load apps onto Android devices, as it could with Apple: Android does allow for sideloading apps. Epic will suggest Google makes that process cumbersome, but the bulk of its arguments will center on what it believes are anticompetitive agreements between Google and device manufacturers and developers.

The precedent Epic's case relies on is a Microsoft case in which courts found Microsoft to have a monopoly over the operating system and to be abusing it, making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. To make its case, Epic plans to bring claims under Sections 1 and 2 of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, as well as California's anticompetitive laws, the Cartwright Act and the Unfair Competition Law. It will attempt to argue that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.



---


# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. Google's execution was uneven, though — it wound up spending much of its opening statement attempting to explain away its seemingly bad behavior as normal business practices and did not always succeed out of the gate.
