# Apple's 2023 Top iPad App And Game Lists

Apple's year-end App Store feature also includes separate lists of the top iPad apps and games, both free and paid, as well as top Apple Arcade games — the latter offering the only glimpse into Apple's subscription gaming store, which is otherwise a black box because it does not feature a Top Charts section like the larger App Store does.

There is some overlap with the iPhone lists, though streaming apps make a better showing among the free iPad apps: that list includes, in order, Max, YouTube and Netflix in the top three spots, with Disney+, Prime Video and Peacock at No. 5, 8 and 10 respectively. The full free iPad list ran: Max: Stream HBO, TV, & Movies; YouTube: Watch, Listen, Stream; Netflix; Google Chrome; Disney+; Goodnotes 6; TikTok; Amazon Prime Video; Temu: Shop Like a Billionaire; and Peacock TV: Stream TV & Movies.

# Google's Defense: Android Openness And Sideloading

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google will also attack the foreclosure premise directly. It will note that, unlike Apple, it allows apps to be sideloaded on Android devices — something Epic takes advantage of today — and that this process is streamlined and helps keep users safe. Epic will claim in response that the process is made to be overly difficult for end users, with multiple steps involved and "scare screens" that warn users of the security risks involved with sideloading.

On discovery, Epic will suggest that Google hid items by allowing execs and employees to have "off the record" chats; Google will counter this as well, saying it has provided the court with thousands of chat logs and millions of documents. Google will ultimately push the notion that this case is not about competition but about money — that is, that Epic Games wants to reach the Play Store's 2.5 billion users without having to pay. As a Google blog post by Wilson White, VP, Government Affairs & Public Policy, put it: "Android's choice and flexibility work well for consumers and developers of all sizes. We look forward to making our case in court as we fight to keep our users safe from harm, partner with developers to grow their businesses, and keep the Android ecosystem thriving and healthy for everyone."

# The Market Definition Fight In Epic v. Google

Market definition is the structural question on which the case turns: Epic claims Google has illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing," arguing that if you buy or develop for Android phones you are stuck paying the Google tax, while Google will say the real competition comes from Apple because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead.

The relation between definition and outcome is direct. If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google is on the road to victory; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape. A third path exists — the court could pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up doing. It is pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general, which is why the narrower Android framing matters so much to Epic.

Two observations sit outside the formal model but bear on how the fee looks. Google charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal or a credit card, which does seem like a lot; and though Epic cannot argue it in court, Apple was not able to explicitly justify a 30 percent fee to that case's judge. On the other hand, it does kind of seem like Epic wants something for nothing — Epic has not stated what kind of fee would actually be reasonable for Google to charge in exchange for placement in its store, and CEO Tim Sweeney seemingly suggests there should not be a Google fee at all if a developer wants to use its own payment system.

# Project Liberty: Epic's Deliberate Payment Bypass

Epic is the studio behind Fortnite, the extraordinarily popular free-to-play game, which makes money by selling in-game items with its virtual currency V-Bucks; until August 13th, 2020, if a player used an Android or iOS device and installed the game through an official app store, buying V-Bucks triggered an in-app payment fee to Google or Apple — fees critics call the "Google tax" or the "Apple tax," and which Epic definitely was not a fan of.

August 13th, 2020 was a very busy day. Epic announced it was bypassing Apple and Google's app store fees, deploying a hotfix update to Fortnite without either company's knowledge that let players buy V-Bucks directly through its own payment processing option at a discount. Apple and Google almost immediately reacted by kicking Fortnite off their app stores for breaking the rules. Then Epic was ready and waiting with two lawsuits and an attack ad depicting a Fortnite hero throwing a unicorn-llama hammer into a giant screen reminiscent of Apple's famous "1984" Macintosh ad. It was a striking publicity blitz followed by a lot of slow-moving court proceedings: the Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021 and a ruling came down that September, mostly decided in Apple's favor, though both parties are waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in, while the Google one was delayed again and again.

The premeditation is documented, and Google is countersuing over it. At trial Google pointed out how Epic hatched a secret plan called "Project Liberty" to quietly update Fortnite with code to bypass app store fees, get its app kicked off Apple's and Google's app stores, and sue. It showed out-of-context quotes from internal Epic communications — phrases like "How do we not look like the bad guys?", "Just planting the nefarious seed now" and "I mean everything we're attempting is technically a violation of Google's policy, right?" — to suggest Epic knew it was breaking bad at the time. An email from Epic CEO Tim Sweeney reads: "Here is our official plan for communicating with Google about bypassing the Google Play Store: SAY NOTHING TILL IT SHIPS."

Epic did not try to hide it in court. Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening statement, so by the time Google raised it, it had already been an hour since Epic admitted it intentionally broke Google's rules. "Epic decided to stand up because that's what you do to a bully," Bornstein told the jury.

# Payment Processor

## Definition

In the corpus, a payment processor is named as one of several distinct roles a company can hold in a transaction — the entity that handles the movement of payments — separate from being the customer, the merchant, or a market maker, even when a single company (like Alameda Research for FTX, or Google Play for its app store) plays more than one of those roles at once.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term across two very different settings: crypto-market infrastructure and app-store commerce.
In the FTX criminal trial, defense counsel Mark Cohen argued that Alameda Research "acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker" — the third role described in the corpus as a "financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies."
In fintech coverage, "payment processor" describes companies such as Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; the startup Rainforest is described as competing to win software-platform business away from these "legacy processors."
In the Epic v. Google trial, Google Play's own billing system is treated as the payment processor for in-app purchases, and the antitrust dispute centers on whether Google may tie that processing to app-store access; per Epic CEO Tim Sweeney, Google charges other developers 30% but struck a special deal letting Spotify pay 0% when it processes its own payments, or 4% when it uses Google's payment service instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **One of several roles a single company can hold** — the FTX defense listed "customer, payment processor, and market maker" as three separate roles Alameda played for FTX, distinct from being FTX itself.
- **A fee-generating, competitive service** — Google charges up to 30% for Play billing (discounted to 4%, or waived to 0% for self-processed payments, under Spotify's special deal), and a separate "User Choice Billing" program launched in 2022 knocks only 4 percentage points off Google's standard fee for developers using their own payment system; Rainforest, Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS compete for the equivalent software-platform and merchant business.
- **Built differently for different customer types** — Rainforest founder Joshua Silver argues that existing "modern processors" (incumbents like Fiserv and FIS) were built directly for merchants, not software platforms, and have had to retrofit their systems to handle software companies' payment-processing and reporting needs — the gap Rainforest positions itself to fill.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a payment processor is generally described as the intermediary that transfers payment data and messaging between the card-issuing bank, the merchant, and the acquiring bank to authorize and settle a transaction, and is typically categorized as either front-end (handling authorization) or back-end (handling settlement) (Wikipedia, "Payment processor," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Epic's Antitrust Claims Against Google Play

Epic's claim is that the Android operating system's Google Play Store constitutes an unlawful monopoly, and that Google is separately tying its Google Play payments platform to that store, keeping other potential app payment mechanisms from competing.

The grounds Epic offers are the frictions it says Google creates: Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that it has created an illegal monopoly which unjustly enriches Google while artificially driving up app prices because other stores cannot compete. The warrant joining that to the legal claim is the competitive-harm chain — no viable rival stores means no fee discipline, which means the "Google Tax" is paid either by developers or passed along to consumers. Epic wants to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods so developers are not stuck paying that tax.

Google's answer contests the warrant rather than the fees: it says Epic's demands would damage Android's ability to offer a secure user experience and to compete with Apple's iOS. Both sides agree the future of Google's app store could depend on this trial. Epic sued in 2020 after a fight over in-app purchase fees.

# Whether A VPN Is Worth It

Whether VPNs are worth it depends on how often you would actually use one for the standard use cases: if you travel a lot and rely on public WiFi or hotspots, are looking to browse outside your home country, or want to keep your traffic hidden from your ISP, then investing in a VPN will be useful — but even the best VPN services often slow down your internet connection speed, so they may not be ideal all the time.

The stronger claim is that a VPN should not be your main cybersecurity tool. The grounds are that VPN use can provide a false sense of security, leaving you vulnerable to attack, and that choosing just any VPN may leave you less secure than simply relying on your ISP — because the VPN could be based in a country with weaker data privacy regulation, be obligated to hand information over to law enforcement, or be linked to weak user data protection policies.

For users in professions like activism or journalism who want to really strengthen their internet security, Crandall suggests options like the Tor browser may be a worthwhile alternative: Tor is free, and while it is less user-friendly, it is built for anonymity and privacy.

# Rainforest's Embedded Payments For Software Platforms

Rainforest is an Atlanta-based startup that works with software companies to help them embed financial services and payments into their platforms, taking on incumbents such as Fiserv and FIS while also trying to take market share from other fintechs such as Stripe. Founded in 2022, it defines itself by a single restriction: it serves software platforms only.

The discriminating feature is that exclusive focus. CEO and co-founder Joshua Silver believes it gives the company an edge, because the alternative providers were built for a different customer: "None of the modern processors were built specifically for software platforms. Most of them were built directly for merchants, and they've all had to retrofit their platforms even to accommodate basic payment processing and reporting functions for software companies," he told TechCrunch. Rainforest accordingly captures volume as software platforms migrate off legacy processors such as Fiserv and FIS, and in doing so competes against companies like Stripe and its Connect product.

The boundary case that shapes the concept is how far a software company actually wants to go into finance. In an interview with TechCrunch, Silver respectfully disagreed with a16z general partner Angela Strange's 2019 statement that every company would become a fintech. In his view, most software companies do not actually want to be fintechs and deal with all the regulatory and compliance issues that go with that; they really just want to be able to accept payments and generate more revenue from being able to do so. Embedded payments in this sense is the narrow slice of fintech a software platform will adopt, not a wholesale transformation into one.

As of this October 2023 account, the startup had shown impressive growth in a short period, securing client commitments representing more than $500 million in processing, with much of the volume guaranteed.

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# MADA And RSA: Google's Two Android Distribution Agreements

Google binds Android device makers through two distinct contract types, described at trial on November 8, 2023 by Jamie Rosenberg, a Google employee who focuses on Android and Google Play, testifying in Google's defense. A mobile app distribution agreement (MADA) requires Android smartphone makers — like Samsung or Oppo — to pre-load a bundle of 11 Google apps on the device, including Search, Chrome and Play. Rosenberg's discriminating point about MADA is that the pre-loaded apps do not have to be the default choices.

A revenue share agreement (RSA) is the second and separate instrument. RSAs run with smartphone makers and also with wireless carriers such as Verizon, and unlike MADAs they do require the counterparty to set Google search and the Chrome web browser as defaults. So the boundary between the two is pre-installation versus default status: MADA buys presence on the device, RSA buys the default slot.

Rosenberg defended the arrangement on two grounds — that Google apps like Search are "best in class," and that the RSAs motivate other companies to make or sell more Android devices. He framed the broader competitive setting by saying the competition between Google and Apple is "as intense as it gets," per Bloomberg.

# Game Patch Notes

## Definition

Neither corpus article uses the phrase "patch notes," but both document the same underlying pattern: a studio bundling a slate of changes — new content, rebalancing, and quality-of-life fixes — under a single named or numbered update tied to a release date.
Polygon's Diablo 4 coverage lists that pattern for "Season 2"/"Season of Blood": leveling speed, new endgame bosses, a Nightmare Dungeon rework, mount handling, and Renown/gem-Stash changes, all bundled to arrive together on Oct. 17 (doc_0533).
Polygon's games-of-the-year piece shows the same pattern for Cyberpunk 2077's named "Patch 2.0," a systems-revamping update shipped alongside — but distinct from — the paid Phantom Liberty expansion (doc_0213).

## Context

The corpus's clearest example is Diablo 4's Season 2 update, "Season of Blood," reported by Polygon on 2023-10-04: alongside new vampire powers, Blizzard shipped a broad slate of quality-of-life changes covering leveling speed, endgame bosses, Nightmare Dungeon design, mount handling, and the Renown and gem/Stash systems, all set to arrive together on Oct. 17 as one seasonal patch.

Polygon's broader 2023 games-of-the-year piece shows the same pattern in a second game: Cyberpunk 2077's Phantom Liberty expansion arrived "alongside the sweeping Patch 2.0," which revamped the base game's role-playing progression systems, improved enemy AI, and "course-corrected a litany of other details" — a patch bundled with, but distinct from, the paid DLC content it accompanied.

## Key Characteristics

- **Versioned or seasonal framing** — changes are grouped under a single identifier (Patch 2.0, Season 2/"Season of Blood") rather than released piecemeal, per doc_0533 and doc_0213.
- **Mix of change types** — a single patch bundles new content (Diablo 4's five endgame bosses), rebalancing (faster leveling, reworked Nightmare Dungeon affixes), and quality-of-life fixes (Renown carryover, gems no longer taking bag space), per doc_0533.
- **Developer-explained rationale** — studios attach commentary to justify changes, as when Diablo 4's game director Joe Shely and associate director Joe Piepiora told Polygon the quality-of-life focus came from finally having time to react to player feedback, unlike the rushed first season (doc_0533).
- **Distinct from paid content** — a patch can ship independently of or alongside paid expansions; Cyberpunk 2077's Patch 2.0 revamped core systems while Phantom Liberty (the paid DLC) added new story content, and reviewers credit the patch as much as the DLC for the game's improved reception (doc_0213).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, this kind of update bundle has a generic industry name: release notes (also called patch notes).
Per Wikipedia, release notes "describe important information about a distribution of a hardware or software product" and typically include "a list of what is new in the release, including bug fixes and new features" (Wikipedia, "Release notes," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Google's Defense That Search Defaults Are Easy To Change

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. On Google's blog, president of global affairs Kent Walker said the search product was the favourite of users, browsers and device makers simply because it was the best in the business: "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," and "this lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today." Walker's supporting evidence is revealed preference when Google is not the default: when Mozilla made Yahoo! the default on Firefox, most users changed it to Google; and people setting up a Windows device frequently sidestep the Microsoft default — "Google" was the number one search query on Bing in 2021 — despite Microsoft making that very annoying to do. The Age's writer called this a compelling point, familiar to anyone who has dodged Microsoft's pleading while setting Chrome and Google as defaults on a new PC, but countered that all of these arguments ignore that Google and its competitors are not on an even playing field: the question remains why users prefer Google, and if the answer is that Google is simply better, the further question is whether that is down to its scale, longevity, ubiquity and all the user data it sucks up, which no other company could possibly match.

# Discount and MSRP

## Definition

In the corpus, a discount is the gap between a product's stated list price (which deal coverage also labels MSRP or the "usual"/"asking" price) and the lower sale price a retailer is currently charging, and deal-roundup articles cite that gap as the reason to call an offer a good buy.

## Context

The corpus's Cyber Monday and Black Friday deal-roundup articles repeatedly frame a sale item by naming its list price and then stating how far below that price the current offer sits, e.g. Engadget describes the third-generation AirPods as carrying "a list price of $169 but often sell for closer to $150, so this is $10 off the usual" once marked down to $140 — the discount is measured against the price the item "often" sells for, not only the official MSRP.
Outside deal journalism, the FTC's antitrust complaint against Amazon (doc_0002) treats discounting as a contested practice: Amazon's algorithm flagged seller Fred Ruckel's Ripple Rug as ineligible for the buy box after Chewy ran "a discount promotion" and dropped its price a few dollars below Amazon's $43 listing, illustrating how a single small discount elsewhere can trigger Amazon's price-parity enforcement.
Price-matching coverage (doc_0403) treats the same underlying concept — the difference between the listed price and a lower price found elsewhere — as the trigger for a retailer's price-match refund, though the article notes Amazon itself does not offer price matching.

## Key Characteristics

- **List price / MSRP as the reference point** — deal writers quote the item's list price (e.g. AirPods 3rd gen at $169, Apple Watch SE at $249) before stating the discounted price, so the discount is always expressed relative to that baseline.
- **"Usual" price can differ from MSRP** — Engadget distinguishes the official list price from what an item "often" or "regularly" sells for, and measures "off the usual" against the latter, meaning the advertised discount can be smaller than the gap from MSRP alone.
- **Discounts as leverage in enforcement** — in Amazon's marketplace, a competitor's discount (even just a few dollars) can cause Amazon's pricing algorithm to demote a seller's listing from the buy box, per the FTC's complaint.
- **Discounts as consumer protection** — price-matching and liberal return policies exist so a shopper who missed a discount at time of purchase can still recover the difference, though Amazon opts out of price matching specifically.
- **All-time-low framing** — deal coverage marks some discounted prices as new record lows (e.g. AirPods Max at $450), a stronger claim than an ordinary discount off list price.

## Background (external)

The corpus itself never formally defines "MSRP" or "discount"; it only uses the terms while reporting specific deals.
For general background, Wikipedia's "List price" article explains that a list price — also called MSRP, RRP, or SRP — is the price a manufacturer "notionally recommends that a retailer sell the product," and that such suggested prices are "sometimes unrealistically high, so the seller can appear to be offering a discount" (Wikipedia, "List price", https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_price, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Black Friday / Cyber Monday

## Definition

Black Friday and Cyber Monday are the paired retail sale events — the Friday after the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday and the Monday that follows it — that together anchor the start of the U.S. holiday shopping season, with retailers running discount campaigns across both dates and the days between them.

## Context

Retailers treat the two days less as isolated events than as bookends of a single extended sale window: Engadget reported that Amazon, Target, Best Buy, and Walmart all kicked off Black Friday-branded deals as early as late October 2023, so that "what was once a one-day event filled with limited-time deals has grown into a month-long event with a plethora of sales to sift through each day." Amazon itself began its Black Friday sale on Friday, November 17 — a week ahead of the calendar date — then switched to "Cyber Monday" branding in the early hours of Saturday, November 25, carrying many of the same discounts forward under the new label through the official close on Monday, November 27. Polygon likewise noted that the two named days (November 24 and 27 in 2023) no longer bound when the best prices actually appear, since retailers now front-load doorbuster-style deals across the preceding weeks. The pairing also functions as the header under which media outlets organize their own coverage: The Verge's "under $25" roundup groups both days together as one shopping period with "always a ton of hype about the discounts on big-ticket items."

## Key Characteristics

- **Two named days, one continuous season** — Black Friday (the day after Thanksgiving) and Cyber Monday (the following Monday) are distinct calendar dates, but retailer promotions now span from late October through the Monday close, blurring the boundary between them.
- **Retailer-driven timing shift** — multiple retailers (Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, Target) started Black Friday-branded deals days to weeks before the actual date in 2023, a strategy aimed at spreading out demand rather than concentrating it on one doorbuster day.
- **Deal carryover across the pairing** — items discounted for Black Friday commonly remain discounted, or are re-labeled, once Cyber Monday branding begins, rather than the two events offering wholly separate deal sets.
- **Broad retailer participation** — coverage spans Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and several other retailers, indicating the pairing is not a single-retailer promotion but an industry-wide sale convention.
- **High online-spend period** — the surrounding Thanksgiving-to-Cyber-Monday window ("Cyber Week") is tracked by analytics firms as a major driver of U.S. holiday online sales, with Thanksgiving Day alone producing billions in online spending as the de facto season opener.

# Noise-Cancelling Headphones

## Definition

In the corpus, "noise-cancelling headphones" (and earbuds with the same feature, often called "ANC" for short) is the headline spec used across shopping-guide roundups to rank and differentiate wireless headphone and earbud models — from Sony's WH-1000XM5, "our favorite pair of noise-canceling headphones" (doc_0369), down to open-design earbuds like the base AirPods that are explicitly called out as lacking ANC entirely (doc_0091, doc_0222, doc_0404).

## Context

Across the corpus, ANC is treated as the headline spec that separates flagship headphones and earbuds from budget or "open-style" designs, and it recurs in shopping-guide roundups (doc_0000, doc_0091, doc_0222, doc_0250, doc_0404, doc_0595, doc_0369, doc_0584) covering Cyber Monday, Black Friday, and Prime Day headphone deals. The Sony WH-1000XM5's ANC is ranked "among the better options we've tested" (doc_0404), while the WH-1000XM4 is repeatedly cited for its "powerful ANC" (doc_0595), and doc_0369 explicitly calls the WH-1000XM5 "our favorite pair of noise-canceling headphones." Apple's AirPods Pro and AirPods Max are described as having "effective" or "top-tier" ANC (doc_0222, doc_0404), while the base AirPods and AirPods (3rd gen), which use an open, unsealed design, are noted as lacking ANC and deep bass entirely (doc_0091, doc_0222, doc_0404). Bose's QuietComfort line (45, Ultra Headphones, Ultra Earbuds) is presented as a byword for strong ANC — "top-of-the-line" (doc_0000), "excellent" (doc_0250), and "outstanding" (doc_0404), and budget models like the Anker Soundcore Space A40 and Space Q45 are judged partly by how their "adaptive ANC" compares to pricier pairs (doc_0250, doc_0595). doc_0584 groups "noise-canceling headphones" together with tablets and smartwatches as one of the broad gadget categories seeing steep non-Amazon Prime Day discounts.

## Key Characteristics

- **Tied to a sealed design** — in the corpus, ANC goes with sealed-fit models: open-design earbuds (base AirPods, AirPods 3rd gen) that lack a sealed fit are described as having no ANC and weak bass response (doc_0091, doc_0222, doc_0404). (The active-vs-passive engineering mechanism is set out in Background (external).)
- **Gradations of strength** — the corpus treats ANC as a spectrum rather than binary: reviewers call the Bose QuietComfort Ultra Earbuds' ANC "the strongest we've tested from a true wireless model," rank the Sony WH-1000XM5's ANC as "among the better options," and describe cheaper models like the Anker Soundcore Space A40 as having ANC that "aren't quite as powerful as more expensive pairs" (doc_0250, doc_0404).
- **Adaptive/context-aware modes** — some newer models add "adaptive ANC" or "Adaptive Audio," which dynamically adjusts noise suppression based on the wearer's surroundings rather than applying a fixed level (doc_0222, doc_0250, doc_0595).
- **Paired with transparency mode** — ANC is frequently bundled with a complementary "transparency mode" that lets outside sound back in, letting the same device toggle between blocking and admitting ambient noise (doc_0091, doc_0222, doc_0404).
- **Purpose framing** — doc_0369 frames the buying decision around use case, describing noise-cancelling models as suited to "tun[ing] out noise so you can focus better," distinct from designs favoring situational awareness on flights or during workouts.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, active noise cancellation (ANC) is a defined engineering technique: a built-in microphone captures ambient noise, the system calculates the portion that would reach the ear, and "an opposing signal is then generated in the headphones to compensate for this component," reducing sound pressure at the eardrum through destructive interference — distinct from passive noise control, which reduces sound via "noise-isolating materials such as insulation, sound-absorbing tiles, or a muffler rather than a power source" (Wikipedia, "Active noise control," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Active_noise_control, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Walmart Cyber Monday 2023 Television Deals

WIRED's Walmart Cyber Monday roundup of 27 November 2023 recommended a spread of discounted TVs spanning Samsung's 8K QN900C, LG's C3 OLED and a large LG OLED, Samsung's Frame, and two Sony sets — the XR A90J and the X90L.

Restating that pick, WIRED says the set earns the gaming crown for its lightning-fast 9.2-millisecond response time and four HDMI 2.1 ports for connecting a PC, Xbox, PlayStation and Switch, and that outside gaming it works fantastically well, with perfect black levels and a great centre mount that helps place it on existing TV stands.

# Apple Price Adjustment Policy

Apple does not offer a price-matching policy: The Verge noted on October 25th, 2023 that while there have been some claims Apple will price-match up to 10 percent for products bought at certain major retailers, there is no official policy on the company's website.

What Apple does offer is a price adjustment on its own reductions. If Apple reduces its price on an Apple-branded product within 14 days from when you received your item, you can visit an Apple Store or contact the Apple Contact Center at 1-800-676-2775 to request a refund or get credit for the price difference. The exclusion that bounds it: this does not apply to special sales like Black Friday or Cyber Monday. Separately, buyers can still price-match Apple devices like the 15-inch MacBook Air elsewhere, assuming it is on sale.

# Walmart Cyber Monday 2023 Dolby Atmos Soundbar Deals

WIRED's Walmart Cyber Monday roundup of 27 November 2023 listed ten discounted soundbars, most of them Dolby Atmos systems: Bose's Smart Soundbar 600 and Smart 900, a multi-piece JBL system, the Klipsch Cinema 600, Polk's Audio Signa 4, Sony's HT-A5000, the Sonos Arc and Beam (Gen 2), a luxury Sennheiser model and Samsung's HW-Q800C.

Bose's Smart Soundbar 600 is described as a Mighty Mouse Dolby Atmos bar offering clear and expansive sound from a strikingly small frame, and unlike a lot of soundbars at its price it includes real up-firing drivers for immersive overhead effects, alongside good musicality, relatively punchy bass and great network streaming features. The JBL multi-piece system (8/10, WIRED Recommends) offers some of the best Dolby Atmos immersion you can buy plus fully wireless surround speakers that can sit behind you or double as Bluetooth speakers before reconnecting to the main bar for charging and playback. The Klipsch Cinema 600 is built from a speaker-like MDF cabinet paired with a massive 10-inch subwoofer driver, giving clear and powerful sound that is as good for music as for cinematic punch. Polk's Audio Signa 4 (7/10, WIRED Recommends) was already one of the most affordable Dolby Atmos soundbars of its kind, with true up-firing drivers, a wireless subwoofer for beefy bass and generally pleasing performance. Sony's HT-A5000 is pricey at full cost but a killer deal here, adding engulfing surround expansion, next-gen HDMI with VRR support for PS5 or Xbox Series X, multiple Wi-Fi streaming options, Dolby Atmos and DTS:X support and hi-res audio.

The Sonos Arc (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is WIRED's favourite soundbar for big home theatres, with three tweeters and eight mid-woofers for deep bass and full Dolby Atmos that bounces sound off walls and ceilings to mimic a surround setup; it was on sale at the same price during last year's holiday sales, but this is the lowest WIRED has tracked. The Sonos Beam (Gen 2) offers enhanced sound with Dolby Atmos support (with compatible TVs and streaming apps), a fast processor, an HDMI eARC port for high-definition audio, support for Alexa, Google Assistant and AirPlay 2, and pairing with other Sonos speakers for surround. Bose's updated Smart 900 adds better bass extension to an already great sound profile, with true up-firing drivers delivering expansive Dolby Atmos and virtual surround from a single unit, and this is the first time WIRED has seen its price drop. The luxury Sennheiser model is at the lowest price WIRED has seen — a hefty unit with no separate subwoofer, but with high-flying virtual surround and Dolby Atmos tricks, punchy grooves, sweet and smooth musicality and conveniences like Wi-Fi streaming and an analogue input. Samsung's HW-Q800C offers a lot from a two-piece system, mixing up-firing Dolby Atmos speakers with side-firing drivers for an engaging cinematic experience while its wireless subwoofer adds a hefty punch to effects and streaming music.

# Super Bowl

## Definition

In the corpus, the Super Bowl is the season-long reference point every team, player, and betting market is measured against — the game whose winners are still identified as "defending Super Bowl champions" months later (doc_0059) and which is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year" (doc_0201).

## Context

The corpus treats the Super Bowl as the horizon every team's season is measured against: the New York Times' Pick Six column frames one-third of the regular season through "the biggest questions facing Super Bowl contenders," ranking the Chiefs, Eagles, 49ers, Bills, Bengals, Cowboys, Ravens, Lions, Dolphins, and Jaguars by their Super Bowl odds (doc_0316).
Franchise identity is tied to it retroactively — the Cincinnati Bengals are described as having reached "a Super Bowl appearance in 2021" as the marker of the team's turnaround (doc_0071), and Travis Kelce is introduced as having "helped bring his team to Super Bowl victory in both 2020 and 2023" (doc_0044), with the Kansas City Chiefs subsequently referred to simply as "the defending Super Bowl champions" (doc_0059).
A Christmas Day matchup between the 49ers and Ravens is previewed explicitly as a "potential Super Bowl sneak peek" (doc_0003), showing how regular-season games get framed as previews of the eventual championship.

## Key Characteristics

- **Season-defining stakes** — teams and players are described relative to it long after the fact ("defending Super Bowl champions," "two-time Super Bowl MVP") (doc_0059, doc_0003).
- **Odds and futures market** — sportsbooks release "next Super Bowl champion" odds shortly after the previous Super Bowl concludes, and those odds shift through the season as teams change (doc_0061).
- **Special-event betting draw** — sportsbooks single out "Super Bowl betting lines" alongside World Series odds and March Madness as flagship special-event markets carrying their own promotional bonuses (doc_0072).
- **Peak prop-betting event** — the Super Bowl is called "the pinnacle for prop betting" and "the most prominent sports betting day of the year," drawing "hundreds of prop bets" including exotic novelty props on the halftime show, the coin toss, and the color of the sports drink dumped on the winning coach (doc_0201).

## Background (external)

The corpus never defines "Super Bowl" itself — it only reports how teams, players, and betting markets relate to it.
Per Wikipedia, the Super Bowl is "the annual championship game of the National Football League (NFL), serving as the final game of each NFL season" (Wikipedia, *Super Bowl*, accessed 2026-09-02).

On the New Heights podcast, Jason Kelce told his younger brother: "That's gotta be an NFL record right there," noting that about two million viewers were estimated to be female and joking, "I think a few of them might have been there for Deadpool and, uh, Taylor."

Merchandise moved as well: jersey sales for the Chiefs tight end reportedly spiked by 400 per cent, according to a report from the NFL's e-commerce partner, Fanatics, since Swift began attending her rumoured boyfriend's games.

# Travis Kelce's First Contact Attempt And The Eras Tour Bracelet

The first link between Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce was established in 2016 when Kelce played "Kiss, Marry, Kill" on AfterBuzz TV and said he would kiss Swift, and the first real contact attempt came in July 2023, when he tried and failed to give her a friendship bracelet with his number on it at her Eras Tour concert in Kansas City, The Age reported on 26 September 2023.

In the 2016 game Kelce — who helped bring his team to Super Bowl victory in both 2020 and 2023 — was given the options of Swift, Katy Perry and Ariana Grande, and said he would ultimately kill Grande, marry Perry and kiss Swift. That was about six years earlier, but it more recently set tongues wagging as fans wondered how long the plan for them to meet had been in the works.

Seven years on, things started to heat up: in July, speaking on the podcast he shares with his brother, New Heights, Kelce said he intended to give Swift a friendship bracelet with his number on it during her Eras Tour concert in Kansas City. The bracelet never made it to her wrist, nor his digits to her phone. "I was disappointed that she doesn't talk before or after her shows because she has to save her voice for the 44 songs she sings," he said. "She doesn't meet anybody, or at least she didn't want to meet me, so I took it personal[sic]." At that point any attraction seemed one-sided, but Kelce, exhibiting the tenacity typical of a professional sportsman, remained determined to get her attention — and the Kelce brothers could not stop talking about Swift on the podcast, her name popping up everywhere, including during conversations about facial hair.

# Travis Kelce's "Breeder" Remarks On The New Heights Podcast

Travis Kelce, 34, made remarks about starting a family during a February 2023 episode of New Heights, the podcast he hosts with his brother Jason, that resurfaced in October 2023 amid his romance with Taylor Swift — after a source claimed to Yahoo Entertainment that the couple "have talked about kids" within the next year. In the episode, recorded while the Philadelphia Eagles and Kansas City Chiefs were preparing to meet in the Super Bowl, Jason asked their mother Donna which of her sons she was "rooting for." "You've said in the past to both of us that you root for me because I've given you grandkids," said Jason, who shares three children — Wyatt, four, Elliotte, two, and Bennett, seven months — with wife Kylie Kelce. "I've always known that you root for Travis. So who do you actually root for?"

Pressed again, "if in a battle to the death," Donna deflected by asking whom Jason would save if she and her husband Ed Kelce were stranded in the middle of the ocean, and said she could not pick which son to root against; Jason joked, "Remember if you choose me, Wyatt and Elliotte grow up without a father." Travis then chimed in about wanting his own family: "I gotta start breeding. I've gotta start breeding, to all the breeders out there." Jason replied "Please don't," and Donna advised: "Wait until you find the right person. Find the right person." Travis doubled down: "I'm gonna find a breeder, and I'm gonna get kids so that mom can love me again."

# The NFL's Statement Defending Its Taylor Swift Coverage

Following criticism that the league was focusing too much on Taylor Swift, the NFL rejected the premise that its coverage had become disproportionate, in an official statement handed to People on 4 October 2023. It first defended the practice as routine: "We frequently change our bios and profile imagery based on what's happening in and around our games, as well as culturally. The Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce news has been a pop cultural moment we've leaned into in real time, as it's an intersection of sport and entertainment, and we've seen an incredible amount of positivity around the sport."

The league then attacked the proportionality claim directly, arguing that the Swift material was a small share of its output: "The vast majority of our content has remained focused on the game, our players and variety of other initiatives, including our Toy Story Funday Football alt-cast, the international games and more."

# Taylor Swift's Attendance At Kansas City Chiefs Games

By early December 2023 Taylor Swift had attended five of Travis Kelce's games, including one on 3 December, often seated in the Kelce family suite — and since her first NFL appearance in September her occasional attendance had drawn pushback from NFL fans who believed her presence was distracting from the game itself. Swift told Time she has little sense of how much she is on screen: "There's a camera, like, a half-mile away, and you don't know where it is, and you have no idea when the camera is putting you in the broadcast, so I don't know if I'm being shown 17 times or once." She said she does not pay much attention to the cameras and fans around her because she is watching her boyfriend play.

Her answer to the criticism was direct: "I'm just there to support Travis. I have no awareness of if I'm being shown too much and pissing off a few dads, Brads, and Chads." Asked about the many Swifties who had started watching NFL games since she began dating Kelce, she joked: "Football is awesome, it turns out. I've been missing out my whole life." Her effect on the league was visible in October, when a Chiefs-Jets game she attended with famous friends became the most-watched Sunday NFL show since Super Bowl LVII in February 2023.

# National Football League (NFL)

## Definition

In the corpus, the National Football League (NFL) is the professional football league covered as both a sports competition and a media business — its 2023 season tracked through AFC/NFC conference standings and playoff seeding, its "Thursday Night Football" package sold to Amazon Prime Video, and its revenue growth under Commissioner Roger Goodell, credited by Essentially Sports with a $27 billion revenue target for 2027.

## Context

The corpus treats the NFL as both a sports league and a media business: Essentially Sports traces its "humble beginnings in 1920" to its status as an "$18 billion juggernaut" today, with Commissioner Roger Goodell targeting $27 billion in revenue by 2027.
The same piece cites an estimate from Joe Pompliano that the NFL "will bring in $20 billion in revenue this year, more than the Premier League, La Liga, Bundesliga, Serie A, and Ligue 1 combined," and separately states outright that "the NFL is already the world's richest league."
Its season structure surfaces repeatedly in the corpus: standings are tracked by conference and division (AFC East/North/South/West, NFC East/North/South/West), with regular-season results determining division leaders and wild-card seeding heading into the playoffs.
Weekly games are also branded by broadcast window — most notably "Thursday Night Football" — which airs exclusively on Amazon Prime Video under an 11-year rights deal, with only the two competing teams' local markets exempted from needing a Prime subscription.
The league also anchors seasonal traditions distinct from other major U.S. leagues, most notably Thanksgiving Day games, which in 2023 drew an average of 34.1 million viewers across three games — a tradition the corpus contrasts with the NBA's Christmas Day slate — alongside a growing Christmas Day broadcast tradition of its own.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-conference structure** — teams are split into the AFC and NFC, each further divided into divisions, with standings and tiebreakers (head-to-head record, conference record) determining playoff seeding.
- **Regular season into playoffs** — the corpus's Week 13 standings coverage shows an 18-week regular season narrowing toward division leaders and wild-card contenders as the playoff picture takes shape.
- **Commissioner-led revenue strategy** — under Commissioner Roger Goodell, the league has set an explicit financial target ($27 billion by 2027) and, per the corpus, is already "the world's richest league."
- **Thursday Night Football broadcast rights** — the "Thursday Night Football" window airs exclusively on Amazon Prime Video under an 11-year deal, with local-market exemptions for the two competing teams.
- **Recurring scandal and safety scrutiny** — the corpus notes a history of controversies (Kaepernick's protest, domestic-violence cases, Deflategate, Bountygate, CTE concerns) running alongside active initiatives such as international games and the "Play Smart, Play Safe" concussion-safety program.
- **Holiday broadcast traditions** — Thanksgiving Day games are a fixture of the NFL calendar with viewership the corpus contrasts directly against the NBA's Christmas Day tradition.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the NFL is the highest level of professional American football: 32 teams split evenly between the American Football Conference (AFC) and National Football Conference (NFC), each with four four-team divisions.
Each season runs an 18-week regular season in which every team plays 17 games and takes one bye week, after which seven teams per conference enter a single-elimination playoff bracket whose conference-championship winners meet in the Super Bowl (Wikipedia, "National Football League," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League, accessed 2026-09-02).

# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. # Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.

# Remedies Sought Against Google And The Ripple Effect On Big Tech Cases

The government's argument in US v. Google is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, thereby hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The grounds offered for this is a data asymmetry: the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does every day, so exclusion from distribution compounds into a permanent quality gap for rivals.

The warrant joining the claim to the remedy is that if the deals are what starve rivals of data, then unwinding the deals and redistributing the data restores competition. On that logic, if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the search giant may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers; it may also be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers; and Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users. Enforcers want to show that antitrust law remains relevant and that even though Google is basically the God of the internet, it is still no match for U.S. law.

The Google outcome could also have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).
