# Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.



---


# "Go Big In Europe": Google's Post-Fine Search Quality Push

The government argued on November 10, 2023 that Google only endeavored to enhance its search engine in the European Union after it was hit by a €5 billion antitrust fine in 2018 — a claim internal documents revealed, according to Bloomberg.

The EU's antitrust order forced Google to offer Android phone users a screen with five search engine options to choose from, according to the DOJ. In response, Google enacted a plan its executives dubbed "Go Big in Europe," to enhance search results in France and Germany in 2019 and 2020 with more local content: news, post-game soccer video highlights, information on local television options for streaming, and pronunciation practice for different languages. The aim was to incentivize users to click on Google's home screen rather than the competition's.

That revelation effectively supports the Justice Department's argument that Google, without the push of competition, has little incentive to improve its products — a classic consequence in a monopoly.



---


# Consumer Search Startups And Switching Barriers

The premise attacked is that a better search product wins users. The cautionary case is Neeva, founded by former Google execs, which tried to convince people to switch to paid and private search with additional features; earlier in 2023 the startup shut down its consumer efforts and eventually got acquired by Snowflake.

Adii Pienaar, an investor in Deft, said that Deft has to give compelling reasons to users to switch to its service. His grounds are behavioral rather than technical: "Users' natural behavior for search is to follow the path of least resistance, i.e. most people just pick up their phone and just use the default search engine."

The conclusion he draws sets the bar Deft must clear: "For Deft to change that behavior, they will need to create a high-value proposition."



---


# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.



---


# Search Quality Complaints Explained By Data Volume Growth

The Age argued that the common online complaint that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago" could absolutely be true, but that it would be a stretch to blame the company's monetisation practices when there is a much simpler explanation: the sheer growth in the data Google has to index.

The grounds are the volumes. In 2013, people were creating around 9 ZB of data every year — nine zettabytes, or nine trillion gigabytes — which Google had to index constantly, whereas in 2023 it is more like 120 ZB. The warrant is a change in kind as well as quantity: not a whole lot of that is static websites as it was a decade ago; it is live information that may be nested within various services and apps, which is harder to index well. The article then turned to what actually happens when we search, noting that Google has published extensive information about its Search procedures, so it is not difficult to get the company's own take on what happens in the background when you send off a query.



---


# Firefox's Yahoo Default Search Switch, As Recounted By Mitchell Baker

On November 1, 2023, Mozilla CEO Mitchell Baker provided a defense of Google's quality as a search engine, even in "competitive" environments, by recounting how Mozilla "failed" when it switched Firefox's default search engine from Google to Yahoo. Baker was providing a recorded deposition for Google's defense, and she noted that Mozilla's users apparently wanted and expected Google.

The backstory: Yahoo inked a deal with Mozilla back in 2014 to pay the browser maker $375 million annually to be the default search engine on Firefox, at a time when Google was offering $276 million, said Baker. TechCrunch's verdict was that it was a bad deal.

Baker's account of why, according to Bloomberg: "I felt strongly that Yahoo was not delivering the search experience we needed and had contracted for." Yahoo had promised to reduce the number of ads and offer less user tracking, she said, but ended up gradually serving users more ads anyway. "The number of users who stayed with Firefox declined noticeably during the years when Yahoo was the default," said Baker.



---


# Why Traditional E-Commerce Search Has Degraded

Deft co-founder Zach Hudson told TechCrunch that there are a few plaguing problems with the traditional search experience that prevent users from finding a suitable item — that is, the claim is that search has gotten worse, not that users have gotten worse at searching.

He offers three grounds, each a different actor degrading the result set: "You have companies like Google and Amazon that continue to push the most relevant listings down so they can make more advertising dollars. Some easy searches are now hard because marketers have learned how to game these search engines. Plus, now you have AI content that is putting the burden on users to separate fact from fiction," he said.

The warrant tying them together is that each mechanism moves cost onto the user: platform ad incentives bury relevance, SEO gaming inflates the noise, and AI-generated content shifts verification work to the person searching.



---


# The DOJ Theory That Google's Default Deals Foreclose Search Rivals

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.



---


# Wired's Retracted Claim That Google Manipulates Search Queries

In October 2023, Wired posted an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — the example given being the replacement of a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear" — and Wired subsequently removed the article for not meeting its standards.

Google rejected the claim in very strong terms, saying the piece was misleading and inaccurate and denying that it ever altered search terms. The Age drew a lesson from the episode's reach: the degree to which the article was shared on social media and boosted in write-ups at other outlets shows just how willing people are to accept foul play on Google's part, and a suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling follows the company at all times. The article placed the episode in the wider context of the US case — which, having to prove Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo, could be an uphill battle for the government, but which offers everyone else a rare opportunity for insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share, and whether it is still focused on being the best or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money at the expense of product quality.



---


# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.



---


# Deft's Competitive Landscape: Search Incumbents

Given that it is building a search solution for e-commerce, Deft already faces challenges from Amazon and Google, both of which have shipped comparable features.

In September 2023, Amazon updated its visual search feature that lets users snap a photo of a product and search for similar items on the platform. Google released its multi-search feature in 2022, letting users fuse images and text — the same combination Deft offers.

Separately, Deft will also face competition from other startups like Objective, a Matrix Partners-backed startup building an API platform for multimodal search.



---


# Danny Sullivan, From Journalist To Google Liaison

After Cutts left, Google replaced him with a handful of people, none of whom could quite fill his shoes: "Those personalities sometimes were standoffish," Forrester said. "Some of them were superior. Some of them were a bit too wallflower."

One of the people Google brought in was Danny Sullivan, a former journalist who started Search Engine Land — the industry publication where Schwartz works — back in the 2000s. In 2009 Sullivan was described as "the closest approximation to an umpire in the search world," so when he published "A deep look at Google's biggest-ever search quality crisis" in 2017 and then took a job as Google's public liaison for Search only a few months later, it felt to some SEOs as though a congressperson working on gun safety legislation had quit to become an NRA lobbyist.

Forrester reports the suspicion without endorsing it. "There is a thread across the industry of people who believe that Google just made Danny an offer he couldn't say no to, and it was designed essentially to take his voice out of the conversation," he said. "I don't believe that's the case," he went on, but compared to Cutts, "I think that Danny specifically stays out of a lot of public conversations because he is in those private conversations with businesses."



---


# Google's Rebuttal To The Publisher Antitrust Suit

Google rejects the premise that it deprives publishers of readers and traffic. A Google spokesperson called the Helena World Chronicle lawsuit "meritless," and attacked the claim of foreclosure directly: "People have many ways to access information and news content today – through publishers' websites, dedicated apps, social media platforms, print papers and more. Google links people to publishers' websites more than 24 billion times each month – at no cost to them."

The rebuttal therefore contests two of the suit's premises at once: that Google is a bottleneck between readers and publishers, and that publishers are uncompensated, by pointing to the volume of free referrals Google sends.



---


# Google's Defense That Search Defaults Are Easy To Change

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. On Google's blog, president of global affairs Kent Walker said the search product was the favourite of users, browsers and device makers simply because it was the best in the business: "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," and "this lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today." Walker's supporting evidence is revealed preference when Google is not the default: when Mozilla made Yahoo! the default on Firefox, most users changed it to Google; and people setting up a Windows device frequently sidestep the Microsoft default — "Google" was the number one search query on Bing in 2021 — despite Microsoft making that very annoying to do. The Age's writer called this a compelling point, familiar to anyone who has dodged Microsoft's pleading while setting Chrome and Google as defaults on a new PC, but countered that all of these arguments ignore that Google and its competitors are not on an even playing field: the question remains why users prefer Google, and if the answer is that Google is simply better, the further question is whether that is down to its scale, longevity, ubiquity and all the user data it sucks up, which no other company could possibly match.



---


# Search As Private Infrastructure, Not A Public Library

The claim is that routing nearly all online information through a single private company has left us arguably worse off than before, because information that is controlled by a private business will always be subject to that business's bottom line — which is exactly why most countries around the world have libraries that are public institutions.

The grounds are a comparison with what the internet was supposed to be. In the beginning it was seen as an improvement on the spirit of the public library: an opportunity to transcend the gatekeepers controlling who could publish a book, allowing mankind to fully connect and share knowledge. Instead, nearly all online information runs through a single company, which assumes a veneer of civic utility, of impassive authority, when it is very much not a neutral entity.

Matt Cutts supplies the insider warrant that the veneer is doing work. "There were so many true believers at Google in the early days," he said. "As companies get big, it gets harder to get things done. Inevitably, people start to think about profit or quarterly numbers." He claimed that, at least while he was there, search quality always came before financial goals, but he believes the public underestimates how Google is shaping what they see: "I deeply, deeply, deeply believe search engines are newspaper-like entities, making editorial decisions." He speculated that the company did not want the public to think too hard about how search works because that awareness "encourages regulators and makes people realize, 'Oh, there's a lot of money here.'"

The consequence is epistemic rather than commercial. There has always been advertising and polemics from cranks, scammers, and liars, but now we see this stuff surfacing alongside truth and we cannot tell the difference, so we move through our lives with a greater sense of distrust and fear and insecurity. At the end of the day, it is Google's world, and the SEOs are only living in it.



---


# The Defense Of SEO As Legitimate Work

Barry Schwartz rejects the premise that the industry is filled with con artists: "There are a lot of scammers in every single business. It's just easier to call yourself an SEO than a doctor." Schwartz is an unbelievably fast talker and a prolific writer who has spent the past two decades covering SEO for the trade rag Search Engine Land, and both in conversation and in his work he has defended SEO as a legitimate, dignified pursuit: "The search community is filled with hard-working individuals working to help their clients' websites succeed in Google Search. That success is not done through dark, corrupt or shady tactics but rather hard, smart and thorough work."

Several people made a similar point: the best SEOs are the ones that follow Google's rules, which essentially ask you to make amazing websites without even thinking about Google. You are not supposed to make any attempt to artificially boost a website's ranking; you are supposed to be designing websites for human readers, not for the algorithm — and many SEOs do exactly this kind of work, rewriting copy, making a site load more quickly, and so on.

The defense has a limit the article presses on. The existence of good SEOs does not negate the presence of scammers and idiots and people who get ahead by violating Google's terms of service, just as the mild-mannered teacher's pet in a classroom does not negate the obnoxious shouting of the kids who refuse to behave; a few loud kids can easily drown everyone else out. Even Schwartz acknowledged the effect rule-breaking SEOs have had on the internet experience. Asked how he himself would find a reliable attorney — lawyers, accountants and contractors being particularly lucrative SEO customers because they are eager for attention from people going online for local recommendations — he answered: "I don't know if you can trust anything you read online. Maybe you ask a friend."



---


# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.



---


# Projected Publisher Traffic Losses From AI Search

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20% and 40% of their website traffic once Google's AI products fully roll out, according to a Wall Street Journal report noted by TechCrunch on 15 December 2023. That report also led with a modelling result from the online magazine The Atlantic: when The Atlantic modelled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user's query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic.

The stakes are set by how much publisher traffic Google currently supplies. According to data from Similarweb cited in the same coverage, Google today drives nearly 40% of publishers' traffic, so a shift to AI-answered queries could have a major impact on publishers' traffic going forward. The suit filed by Helena World Chronicle takes up precisely this question of how AI will impact publishers' businesses.

Some publishers are trying to get ahead of the problem: Axel Springer inked a deal with OpenAI in the same week to license its news for AI model training.



---


# Google's Most Lucrative Search Terms, Unsealed At Trial

Judge Amit Mehta ruled to make public a list that provides a glimpse of which search terms make Google the most money: 20 terms that were lucrative for the week of September 22, 2018. Revenue per search term, how many queries each of those terms got, and a separate list of popular search terms ordered by queries rather than revenue were all redacted, so the disclosure is a bare ranking without magnitudes.

The visible list, in order, is: iPhone 8; iPhone 8 plus; Auto insurance; Car insurance; Cheap flights; Car insurance quotes; DirecTV; Online colleges; AT&T; Hulu; iPhone; Uber; Spectrum; Comcast; Xfinity; Insurance quotes; Free credit report; Cheap car insurance; AARP; LifeLock.

TechCrunch read little surprise into it. Google and Apple have a long and mutually beneficial relationship even while competing, so three Apple search-related queries bringing in the big bucks is unsurprising — not least since September 22, 2017 was the official release date of the iPhone 8. Queries like "car insurance," "cheap flights" and "credit report" are perennial favorites and speak to how much Google dominates vertical search, that is, search in very specific market categories. As for LifeLock, the big Equifax data breach of 2017 was a hot topic in September 2017 and LifeLock was making a big push to win business with people who wanted to buy identity theft protection.



---


# Recommendation Algorithm

## Definition

Across the corpus, "recommendation algorithm" (and the closely related notion of algorithmic ranking/curation) names the automated mechanism a platform uses to control the visibility of content, products, or posts — and by extension, the mechanism regulators, courts, and users scrutinize when they suspect a platform is suppressing or favoring particular items.
No single corpus document offers a formal definition of the term; instead each shows the mechanism at work in a different dispute: Amazon's marketplace search ranking and "other products you may like" widget, Instagram's Stories/feed visibility, U.S. platforms' content-moderation feed curation, and Google's Featured Snippets extraction.

## Context

The corpus shows the same underlying mechanism operating across very different platform types, and shows regulators and courts converging on it from different angles.
On Amazon's marketplace, the EU's antitrust objections to the iRobot acquisition center on Amazon's ability to foreclose a rival's *algorithmic visibility* — delisting rival products, reducing their ranking in organic and paid results, excluding them from the "other products you may like" widget, or denying them labels like "Amazon's Choice" — since RVC buyers in France, Germany, Italy, and Spain rely on that in-marketplace ranking both for product discovery and for the final purchase decision.
The same document notes that Amazon's marketplace was separately designated a core platform service under the EU's Digital Markets Act, which imposes restrictions on self-preferencing.
On Meta's Instagram, users and digital-rights groups suspect a comparable but content-moderation-flavored version of the same idea — "shadowbanning" — where an algorithmic process silently lowers a post's visibility (e.g., Palestine-related Stories) without an explicit takedown.
In the U.S. Supreme Court's NetChoice cases (challenging Texas's HB 20 and Florida's SB 7072), the fight is over whether a platform's curation of what appears in a user's feed — a process now largely conducted algorithmically, generally with light human intervention or oversight — is a First-Amendment-protected editorial act that states cannot compel platforms to individually explain post-by-post.
Google's Featured Snippets, which algorithmically extract answers directly from publishers' web pages into search results, are cited in a news-publisher antitrust suit as a related mechanism: an algorithm that decides what content a user sees without the user visiting the original source, which publishers say siphons off their traffic and ad revenue.

## Key Characteristics

- **Ranking, not binary inclusion** — the algorithm typically operates on relative visibility (higher/lower placement in organic or paid results, inclusion in a "you may like" widget) rather than simple on/off access, which is what makes self-preferencing and shadowbanning hard to prove or disprove.
- **Automated with limited human oversight** — described in the NetChoice case as a process "largely conducted algorithmically now — generally with light human intervention or oversight," which is central to arguments that mandated per-decision human explanations would be impractical at the scale of "millions and millions of pieces of content a day."
- **Commercial leverage point** — on marketplaces, control over the recommendation algorithm doubles as a competitive lever: a platform that also sells its own products can use ranking, delisting, and widget exclusion to foreclose rivals, per the EU's ability-and-incentive theory of harm against Amazon.
- **Contestable but opaque** — content creators and merchants can suspect suppression (shadowbanning, reduced marketplace visibility) but the underlying ranking logic is not published, so claims tend to rely on circumstantial or anecdotal patterns rather than direct evidence.
- **Distinct from explicit content removal** — reduced algorithmic visibility (shadowbanning, lower ranking) is a softer, less visible action than outright delisting or takedown, and is treated differently in both platform policy and legal argument.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the general computer-science term for this kind of system is a "recommender system" (also called a recommendation algorithm, engine, or platform): a type of information filtering system that suggests items most relevant to a particular user, predicting user preferences to help them choose from large sets of options such as products, media, or content.
Source: "Recommender system," Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommender_system.

# Google's Knowledge Graph And Featured Snippets

As described in the Helena World Chronicle complaint, Google's Knowledge Graph is a database, launched in May 2012, from which Google draws a summary of content that it displays as a "Knowledge Panel" to the right of search results when a user searches for information on a topic. The complaint characterises it as one of Google's older question-and-answer technologies and treats it as part of the alleged harm to publishers, alongside newer AI technologies.

The complaint states that "Google compiled this massive database by extracting information from Publishers' websites — what Google calls 'materials shared across the web' — and from 'open source and licensed databases.'" By 2020, the Knowledge Graph had grown to 500 billion facts about 5 billion entities, but the complaint alleges that much of the "collective intelligence" Google tapped into was content "misappropriated from Publishers."

Featured Snippets are a distinct Google technology in which Google algorithmically extracts answers from webpages; the complaint cites them too, on the grounds that they shift traffic away from publishers' websites.

# Day Two Of The Bankman-Fried Trial: Jury Selection And The Courtroom Audience

On the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, the jury was selected on Wednesday morning, after which lawyers for the government and then for Bankman-Fried delivered opening statements that told two very different stories of the former FTX CEO's sudden rise and almost instantaneous fall. The central question framed by the proceedings was who Bankman-Fried, the former CEO of crypto exchange FTX, really is: a liar and a fraud, or someone who acted in good faith and, like many a startup founder, flew too close to the sun. That answer, the account notes, ultimately lies with the jury.

The day featured pointed allegations, a friend from MIT, and an audience replete with big names, including Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. Bankman-Fried himself spent most of the day in court staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys. The prosecution's account of his alleged crimes was described as featuring a study in contrasts.



---


# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

He was 31 years old and co-founded FTX in 2019; within a few years the once third-largest crypto exchange's valuation hit $32 billion at its peak, and the company is now trying to claw back any funds to distribute to creditors. Before the fall he was even compared to Warren Buffet, and many called him the white horse of crypto — a description TechCrunch notes it never applied to him.

Bankman-Fried, however, maintained his innocence. At The New York Times' DealBook Summit he appeared virtually from the Bahamas and said, "I didn't ever try to commit fraud on anyone; I was shocked by what happened this month"; in a published DM exchange with a Vox reporter he said he regretted filing for bankruptcy and thought that "regulators make everything worse." In January he pleaded not guilty to all counts, which include wire fraud, conspiracy to commit money laundering and conspiracy to misuse customer funds. He could face up to 115 years in jail if convicted on all charges.

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

# Alameda Research As The Alleged Conduit For FTX Customer Funds

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. The structure the government described works as follows: Caroline Ellison — Bankman-Fried's on-again off-again girlfriend and the CEO of Alameda — served as a front for the fund, and through that arrangement Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money, both cash and crypto.

Two further relations complete the alleged mechanism. # The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."

Thane Rehn, a prosecutor for the government, opened the case against Sam Bankman-Fried with the line "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world," and then argued that this appearance was false: "all of that, all of it, was built on lies," he declared to the jury, adding "Behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." # FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

# Proving Intent In The FTX Fraud Case

The government's case proceeds in two parts. The first is pretty simple and a little boring: prosecutors must show that certain transactions took place, using whatever records the Southern District of New York has for them.

The second part is where the drama is likely to come, says Christopher LaVigne, a litigation partner and co-chair of the cryptocurrency practice at the law firm Withers: prosecutors have to connect those transactions to Bankman-Fried, show that he knew what he was doing was wrong, and prove that he lied about it anyway. "What was he saying to his parents and his other advisors about this?" LaVigne asks. "What conversations happened between him and his co-conspirators that are now cooperating against him?" To further establish intent, the government can use Bankman-Fried's own words: the indictment calls his November 2022 tweets "false and misleading." "We had him going out directly to the internet," LaVigne says — if he wrote things on Twitter or said things in interviews that weren't true, that's more fodder for the case: "They can point to that and say, 'This is what he said, this is what actually happened.'" Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who pleaded guilty to their own charges. Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison, who was also sometimes Bankman-Fried's girlfriend, may play an important role — Bankman-Fried leaked her diaries to The New York Times and was consequently jailed for witness tampering. The government has indicated FTX co-founder Gary Wang and engineering head Nishad Singh will also be among the witnesses called to testify about Bankman-Fried.

# Lobbying and Political Donations

Lobbying and political donations, in the corpus, are the practice of routing money to political candidates, parties, or officials to gain influence with regulators and lawmakers.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's use of FTX- and Alameda-linked funds for political spending during his rise, which became a prosecution theme at his fraud trial: TechCrunch reports he "had close ties to U.S. regulators and government officials, many of whom he donated to," and that Michael Lewis's book "Going Infinite" surfaced his "attempt to buy off Trump to get him to not run again for president" by discussing with Mitch McConnell how to "fund political candidates who were looking to offset Trump's influence in the Republican Party." At trial, prosecutor Thane Rehn told the jury Bankman-Fried used stolen customer funds to "donate millions to political candidates," and Nishad Singh, described as a longtime family friend of Bankman-Fried, pleaded guilty to charges that included counts "around his political donations." The practice also extended to those around Bankman-Fried: The Verge names "Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap" among the entities caught up in the case.

## Key Characteristics

- **Funding source under dispute** — the prosecution's theory was that the political donations were financed with misappropriated FTX customer deposits, not Bankman-Fried's own money.
- **Instrument of influence, not charity** — donations to candidates and officials are described alongside efforts to buy access (e.g., the reported offer to Trump), distinguishing them from Bankman-Fried's professed effective-altruism philanthropy.
- **Bipartisan reach** — the reporting describes both engagement with Democratic-aligned regulators/officials and an attempt to influence a Republican presidential race, i.e., donations spanning both parties.
- **Legal exposure** — political donations became a distinct criminal count (against Nishad Singh) and a recurring prosecution talking point against Bankman-Fried, showing the practice can carry direct legal consequences when the underlying funds are alleged to be stolen.
- **Family/associate involvement** — the practice was not confined to Bankman-Fried himself; his mother Barbara Fried's PAC, Mind the Gap, is named as part of the same political-spending network.

# Matt Huang And Paradigm's FTX Investment

Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner of Paradigm, a crypto venture capital firm that invested over $275 million in FTX — a stake that was wiped out — was the third witness to take the stand, and testified about his firm's due diligence.

Huang told the court that Bankman-Fried assured him funds would be used for FTX and not Alameda, and that he was promised Alameda had no preferential treatment on the FTX platform, even though the hedge fund was one of its top traders. Huang said he was concerned about FTX's lack of a board of directors but eventually invested anyway. During cross-examination he said Paradigm pressed Bankman-Fried on the board issue and was told he did not want investors as directors but did plan on having a board with experts.

# Can Sun's Testimony On Fabricated Justifications

Former FTX lawyer Can Sun testified that during the days in November when the exchange imploded, Bankman-Fried — then trying to raise money from the private equity group Apollo, which wanted an explanation for what had happened — came to him and asked him to come up with justifications for the missing funds. That request, Sun said, "basically confirmed my suspicions that had been rising all day" that Bankman-Fried had purloined the funds.

Sun ran Bankman-Fried through possible explanations, including a margin loan program, and explained that none of them could fit the actual situation — for instance, Alameda had borrowed more from FTX than had ever been in the margin loan program. He said Bankman-Fried acknowledged their conversation with a "yup, yup": "I was expecting a bigger response, but it was very muted." After that, Sun testified, Singh spilled the beans that Alameda had withdrawn assets that included the customer funds. Sun quit the next day, and, like Yedidia, testified with immunity.

The jury then saw the fabrication deployed in public: a Good Morning America appearance by Bankman-Fried on December 1st, 2022, in which he tried to justify the missing funds through the margin loan program. The Verge's reporter called it such a flimsy excuse that even George Stephanopoulos could see through it, and described Sun's testimony as brief and explosive.

# Adam Yedidia's First Testimony And His Immunity Deal

Late in the afternoon of the second day of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, the government called Adam Yedidia to the stand, and lead prosecutor Danielle Sassoon disclosed that this college friend of Bankman-Fried had legal immunity during his testimony. Asked why he had made such a deal with the government, Yedidia answered: "I was concerned that I had unwittingly written code that contributed to a crime."

Yedidia, described as a fast-talking graduate of MIT, testified that he and Bankman-Fried were close friends in college. After Bankman-Fried left Jane Street — the high-frequency trading firm where the former billionaire got his start in finance after MIT — he persuaded Yedidia to join him, first as a trader at Alameda and then as a developer at FTX.

The testimony was cut short when the clock neared 4:30 p.m. and court adjourned for the day. Yedidia was scheduled to continue his testimony on Thursday, to be followed by Matt Huang, a former partner at the venture capital firm Sequoia Capital, and then by Gary Wang, a key Bankman-Fried lieutenant and one of the government's star witnesses.

# Criminal Trial

## Definition

In this corpus, "criminal trial" names the government's federal prosecution of Sam Bankman-Fried in Manhattan on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, in which prosecutors presented witness testimony to prove guilt while the defense contested it, U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan presided, and a jury returned the verdict.
The corpus uses the term specifically to distinguish this proceeding — and the format of Epic Games v. Google, a civil jury trial — from non-criminal, civil proceedings such as the Trump/Engoron case, which sought financial penalties rather than imprisonment.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal criminal trial in Manhattan, on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, presided over by U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan; the trial ran roughly six weeks, opening with jury selection on October 3, 2023 and opening statements the next day, and closing in a guilty verdict on all counts.
The proceeding follows a recognizable structure the corpus documents in sequence: jury selection, opening statements from prosecution and defense, the prosecution's case (fact witnesses like Adam Yedidia and Matt Huang, cooperating former co-conspirators Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison testifying under cooperation agreements, and expert testimony from accounting professor Peter Easton), cross-examination, the defendant's own testimony and cross-examination, closing arguments, and jury deliberation toward a verdict.
The corpus also shows what a criminal trial is not, by contrast: the parallel civil case against Donald Trump before Judge Arthur Engoron was a non-jury ("bench") trial brought by the New York attorney general seeking financial penalties, not imprisonment, and the corpus notes Manhattan prosecutors had considered and declined to bring a criminal case over the same underlying conduct — the state instead pursued civil fraud remedies. Epic Games v. Google is likewise a civil antitrust jury trial (Sherman Act, Cartwright Act claims) seeking injunctive and monetary relief, not a criminal prosecution, even though it shares the jury-trial format.

## Key Characteristics

- **Adversarial structure** — a prosecution (the government, e.g. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Danielle Sassoon, Nicolas Roos, and Thane Rehn in the SBF case) argues guilt while defense counsel (Mark Cohen, Christian Everdell) argues innocence or lack of criminal intent.
- **Jury as fact-finder** — a jury, not the judge, decides guilt; in the SBF trial the jury included a train conductor and a retired investment banker, and reporters repeatedly note what testimony "the jury saw" or "the jury will have to decide."
- **Burden and standard tied to criminal charges** — the prosecution must show the defendant's conduct was not just harmful but criminal; as one account puts it, "Just losing $8 billion is not a crime... But if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing... that's a crime," turning the case on proving intentional deceit and conspiracy rather than mere loss or business failure.
- **Cooperating witnesses and immunity/plea deals** — co-conspirators such as Gary Wang, Caroline Ellison, and witnesses like Adam Yedidia testified under cooperation agreements or legal immunity, a common feature of criminal trials involving multiple alleged participants.
- **Judge as referee, not fact-finder** — Judge Kaplan ruled on objections, instructed the jury on the law, and controlled testimony (e.g., telling the jury he was the "final authority" on the definition of "market manipulation"), while leaving the guilt determination to the jury.
- **Sentencing follows conviction** — a guilty verdict is followed by a separate sentencing phase; the corpus notes SBF's charges could put him in prison for the rest of his life and co-conspirator Gary Wang faced up to 50 years pending sentencing.
- **Distinct from civil trials** — civil proceedings (Trump/Engoron, Epic v. Google) can share elements like juries or trial-style testimony but seek monetary or injunctive remedies under a different legal standard, and can proceed without a jury at all (non-jury "bench" trial).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, a criminal trial is a court proceeding, initiated only by the government, in which the prosecution must prove the defendant's guilt "beyond a reasonable doubt" — a heavier standard than in civil cases — while the jury decides guilt and the judge oversees the proceeding and, on a guilty verdict, determines the sentence (U.S. Courts, "Criminal Cases," uscourts.gov, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.

# FTX's Final Days And The Alameda Shortfall, As Wang Described Them

Much of Gary Wang's Friday testimony focused on the final days at FTX before the operation imploded: after media reports detailing Alameda's business practices and its troubling ties to FTX, an emergency meeting was called between Bankman-Fried, Wang and Singh to discuss shutting down Alameda, and they decided against it because he and Bankman-Fried knew Alameda had no way to repay the roughly $14 billion hole in its books.

Wang, 30, was technology chief for FTX, which spiralled into bankruptcy in November; he spoke so fast that U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan and the prosecutor both stopped him at points to ask that he slow his pace. Prosecutors took the jury through a series of tweets beginning on Nov. 7 — posts from the company blaming bank hours for slow withdrawals, while Bankman-Fried tweeted from his personal account assuring customers that all was fine. "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine," Wang testified. On Nov. 12, after FTX declared bankruptcy, Bankman-Fried asked Wang to drive with him to the Bahamas Securities Commission for a meeting; on the drive, Bankman-Fried told Wang to transfer assets to Bahamian liquidators because he believed they would allow him to maintain control of the company. Wang said he was not in the meeting with the securities authority, though Bankman-Fried's dad was present.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Decision To Testify Backfired

The Verge's trial reporter argued that Bankman-Fried's choice to take the stand was a net loss for his defense: like Theranos' Elizabeth Holmes before him, he got on the stand to speak directly to his state of mind in a way no other witness can, but telling your side of the story opens you to a great many questions you might not want to answer on cross-examination — and, having watched a lot of crosses, she called Sassoon's the nastiest she had ever seen.

The warrant is what the charges turn on. The case hinged on conspiracy and intentional deceit: just losing $8 billion is not a crime, though it is very embarrassing, but if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing and how safe FTX was, that is a crime. Because state of mind was the contested issue, his own testimony became the evidence, and it did not hold: Sassoon had established the day before that he has a long history of dishonesty, and on October 31st, through a set of questions about what he did and did not do, she established that the story he told on direct examination was absurd. After a brief redirect by his own lawyers, resplendent with word salad, Bankman-Fried stepped down and the defense rested.

The direct examination had already supplied grounds. Beyond the two obvious lies the reporter counted him telling on the stand — about Alameda Research's name and about "allow_negative" — she was struck by how little he seemed to know about his own companies: apparently Singh, Wang, and Ellison were out there just doing whatever their little hearts desired, because Bankman-Fried was a CEO, but definitely not the kind that pays any attention to money at his crypto trading firm and futures exchange.

# Owen Teale's Missed Leading Man Opportunities

Owen Teale had several chances to become a leading man and each fell away — financing collapsed, an American star was demanded, and he chose family over Hollywood networking — The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 20 October 2023.

When The Fifteen Streets attracted a massive TV audience in Britain, Teale was offered a lead role in a movie playing a bare knuckle fighter, but the financing fell through and he signed up for a four-year stint with the Royal Shakespeare Company instead. Years later a producer offered him the lead in a big film being shot in Britain, but the money men demanded an American star and William Hurt got the gig. When Teale won a Tony Award in 1997 for his performance in Ibsen's A Doll's House, he was told he needed to spend time in Hollywood wooing producers and decided to fly home to his family in London instead: "My wife was about to give birth, so I said 'I'm off'. I'm sure part of it was I just didn't believe that I was going to waltz into leading man roles in Hollywood." Despite the plaudits, awards and steady offers of work, the piece observes, he has never been certain of his gifts — probably why he is so consistently good, since complacency is not in his nature.

He is far better at recognising brilliance in others, such as Toni Collette, with whom he worked on Dream Horse, a 2020 movie about an unlikely champion racehorse. "Toni just raised my game. That's a huge talent, huge," he says, shaking his head in wonder. "I recently received an award from BAFTA for the film and part of me thinks they should give it to Toni." He is happiest in a room full of actors working on a play, a film or a TV production: "What turns me on is the thought of collaborating with talented people. I'm very sociable with the rest of the company and fully intend to do that when I come to Melbourne."

# Owen Teale's Family And Recent Villain Roles

Owen Teale is a Welsh character actor whose recent parts are a run of menacing men — Lars Hutton in The Rig, Ser Alliser Thorne in Game of Thrones, Chief Inspector Philip Osborne in Line of Duty and the villainous sorcerer Peter Knox in A Discovery of Witches — The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 20 October 2023.

Reflecting on the chance encounter that sent him to drama school, he says: "I was going nowhere really. If I hadn't met those two young women I don't know what would have happened. But there have been so many points in my career, moments of pure chance, when things went my way. And if you can survive the moments when things don't go your way, you can make it." If you are not a diehard Game of Thrones fan his name may not be familiar, but his pale face, intense eyes and imposing physicality — he is 188cm in his socks — will be; he is a Zelig-like figure whose frequent stage and screen appearances invariably guarantee two things: the tale will be well told and bad stuff is going to happen.

He spoke from Leeds, where he was visiting his younger daughter Gracie, 21, who is studying art and design at the city's university; Eliza, 25, his other daughter with actor wife Sylvestra Le Touzel, is following in her parents' footsteps, and his son Ion, from his first marriage, recently made him a grandfather. Earlier that day he had been in Edinburgh shooting scenes for the second season of the supernatural TV thriller The Rig, in which his character Lars Hutton — an irascible bully and the man most likely to be chucked off the oil rig — has somehow made it back for the next instalment of the Amazon Prime drama.

# Owen Teale's Barry The Bear Route Into Acting

Owen Teale's acting career began with a car full of booze and a bear costume: suspended from his sixth-form college for organising a riotous Christmas party and in need of a job, he took work as a fairground mascot and was pointed towards drama school by co-workers, The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 20 October 2023.

"They held an investigation into the party and I was the first to be called in," says the 62-year-old Welsh actor, best known as gimlet-eyed master-at-arms Ser Alliser Thorne in Game of Thrones. "They'd found the empty bottles and people were falling over drunk. I said, 'yeah, I did it. It was me. I borrowed my mother's car, loaded it up with booze and smuggled it in'." Teale had no intention of joining his father at the limestone quarry that fed the steel works at Port Talbot; he wanted to escape South Wales and find a bigger world. A kindly teacher called Mr Davies suggested he might find work at Barry Island Pleasure Park, a fairground near Cardiff — "At the time, it was a rust bucket of a big wheel and one big dipper," Teale recalls. "But I went along and auditioned. I was hoping to be a magician's assistant or something like that, but they said 'you'd be great as the bear. Here's the costume'."

The role of Barry the Bear was deceptively hard: "His remit was to wander around the park greeting visitors, but you could only do an hour at a time because you sweated so much. I wore pyjamas under the costume to absorb the sweat, but it would fill the rubber hands. After a while, I'd get bored, sit on the big wheel and go round and round." The sight of a disconsolate, sweaty bear riding the ferris wheel caught management's attention and Teale was sacked — at which point a couple of co-workers, students from the Guildford School of Acting, suggested he audition at their alma mater. He was accepted, awarded a study grant, and Barry the Bear got a ticket out of Wales. He is due to play Scrooge in a Melbourne season of A Christmas Carol.

# Tate McRae's Greedy TikTok Breakthrough

Tate McRae's song Greedy went viral in August 2023 after being used in a video by popular TikToker Tube Girl and then in countless hair-flip transition clips, eventually amassing over 320 million streams globally, topping charts internationally and becoming the 20-year-old's proper breakthrough, The Age reported on 30 November 2023.

Until then her career, the review says, had "a stench of desperation about it" — a wild thing to say about someone only 20, but the description of an artist trading explicitly in classic pop moves while failing to grab the popularity such expression necessitates. The Calgary-born musician had already had a journey: a professionally trained dancer since 6, at 13 she finished third on the US version of So You Think You Can Dance and attracted record label attention with songs uploaded to YouTube. In 2020 her weeper You Broke Me First had a chart moment, leading to her 2022 debut I Used To Think I Can Fly, an intriguing album of thrashy bangers and post-Billie Eilish sad-pop featuring production from pop titans Greg Kurstin (Adele) and Finneas (Eilish). It had at least one could've-been smash — the spiky What Would You Do? — but, fairly listless despite her swaggering delivery, it failed to ignite with either mainstream audiences or pop aesthetes.

Greedy also landed her a slot on Saturday Night Live, "that pop superstar rite-of-passage", and sold out shows for her Australian tour the following November. That it was the song to push her to the next level is somewhat confounding, the reviewer writes: it is not particularly memorable and her debut had better tracks that slipped listeners by, but its sassy sentiment — "I would want myself", particularly suited to clips of youthful coming-of-age expression — caught on with the TikTok crowd, "which is how pop stardom happens these days". In another popstar move, McRae channelled an alter ego, Tatiana, who is "ballsy, loud and obnoxious", for Greedy's vibrant music video, a fun throwback to choreographed Y2K-era aesthetics with McRae dancing all lustily on a Zamboni.

# Fan Reactions To Owen Teale After Jon Snow's Death Scene

Owen Teale braced for hostility after Jon Snow's death was broadcast, expecting irate Game of Thrones fans who would hate him for "killing the goodness"; instead he was asked for endless selfies and impromptu recitations of Ser Alliser Thorne catchphrases such as "For the Watch!" or "Bas-terd!", The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 20 October 2023.

Once, a drunk emerged from a restaurant and stumbled towards Teale brandishing a knife; the actor braced himself, but the man simply wanted "Ser Alliser" to hold the utensil to his throat for a photo. On a visit to Uluru with his family, the tour guide caught sight of his face and exclaimed, "what are you doing here?" — "He just kept staring at me and I realised it was an Alliser Thorne thing," says Teale. "I said, 'I'm not going to kill anyone, I'm just an actor'. But it clearly troubled him that this person who had committed this awful crime had suddenly appeared." Teale has the grace to admit he enjoys this new level of celebrity: "People seem to realise that without the darkness of people like Ser Alliser, Jon Snow couldn't have shone as brightly as he did."

He was well into his 50s when he landed his highest-profile role, but it would be wrong to think of him as a late starter: in 1989, not long out of drama school, he starred in the hit television adaptation of Catherine Cookson's romance The Fifteen Streets, alongside Sean Bean, another young working-class actor who went on to become a leading man in Hollywood before playing Ned Stark in Game of Thrones. Asked whether he ever wishes he had followed Bean's trajectory, Teale replies: "Oh god, yeah. Absolutely. You instinctively think [playing leading men] will lead to feelings of success. But it never came my way. My cut of my jib wasn't quite right. It's about what your face does on screen I guess."

# Tate McRae's Think Later Reviewed

The Age's 30 November 2023 review argues that Think Later, Tate McRae's sophomore album, is best when it follows the Greedy template and is dragged down by an overemphasis on understated ballads imposed by producer Ryan Tedder's formula.

The grounds are track by track. The album is almost completely produced and co-written with Tedder (OneRepublic) and sports his hit-making trademarks "for better or worse" — pristine songcraft hooked around off-kilter concepts that cannot help but catch the ear, but punishingly midtempo, songs searching for gravitas over, say, fun; for an album supposed to be McRae's bold, confident, cheeky makeover, parts of it lack spark. Tellingly, the best songs — Exes, Hurt My Feelings and Guilty Conscience — follow the Greedy template of skittering Timbaland-style beats recalling Y2K-era pop, all syncopated and staccato and sultry kiss-offs to dumb boys; they feel strong and personally nostalgic, like McRae nodding to her countrywoman Nelly Furtado's classic mid-'00s run, but driven by McRae's playfulness. We're Not Alike shows another promising side, a post-punky thing built on an Interpol-ish riff that slyly builds into something anthemic, recalling her pal Olivia Rodrigo's sleeper Guts track Pretty Isn't Pretty.

The warrant is comparative: that these songs are so interesting is exactly what makes the ballads frustrating. Songs like opener Cut My Hair, Grave and Stay Done are slick but dour affairs, the classic Tedder formula. # How Owen Teale Sources Darkness For Scrooge And Alliser Thorne

Owen Teale's account of playing villains is a simple three-part mechanism: an inner "sense of nothingness" that appears when he is away from other people, which he channels into hatred on screen, and which he will summon again to make Dickens' Ebenezer Scrooge convincing in an upcoming Melbourne production of Jack Thorne's award-winning adaptation of A Christmas Carol, The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 20 October 2023.

The structure of the relation runs from his own sociability to its inverse. "It's true, I have started to play a lot of dark characters," he says, smiling, "and at first it was a great challenge because I'm quite a sociable fellow." Asked how he finds that darkness, he answers: "It's a sense of nothingness. In all honesty, I'm not very good at being completely on my own. I come alive when I'm with other people. So staying in hotel rooms away from my family isn't great and it doesn't get any easier. There's something empty and a bit scary within me when I'm not with people. I think that's where that stuff comes from." The interviewer's framing is that the avuncular man in amber-coloured spectacles and leather jacket on the line from Leeds is a master of darkness.

The range over which the mechanism holds is demonstrated by his most famous scene: when Ser Alliser Thorne drove a dagger into the heart of Game of Thrones' Byronic hero Jon Snow in the final episode of Season 5, he left the show's 10 million viewers in a profound state of shock. "There was Kit … who was so beautiful. And he's such a lovely man. # Danny Elfman's Return to Live Concert Performance

What brought Danny Elfman back to live performance — and rebirthed him as a man who could share a stage with Billie Eilish and Limp Bizkit's Wes Borland — was, in Polygon's view on 2023-10-13, Henry Selick's The Nightmare Before Christmas: a Burton-produced stop-motion project that was a black sheep for Walt Disney Animation before blossoming into a cult favorite, and, based on the last few years of Elfman's life, a transformative milestone.

In 2013 the former Oingo Boingo frontman returned to the stage at the Royal Albert Hall to perform his scores from Tim Burton movies with a full orchestral backup, including select numbers from The Nightmare Before Christmas, which he sang in full. The concert was such a hit that Disney invited him to appear alongside co-stars Catherine O'Hara, who voices Sally, and Ken Page, who voices Oogie Boogie, at the Hollywood Bowl in Los Angeles for a night purely dedicated to Nightmare — and that concert was such a hit that the group has performed it regularly every October since, and would do so again that Halloween.

The hype around his various Burton and Nightmare concerts sparked the idea among Coachella programmers that Elfman could play alongside pop acts of the moment. As Elfman tells it, there was immediate and obvious hesitation on his part, since he was not a rock star or a pop star or hip-hop star, but after watching Childish Gambino and Janelle Monáe unleash pure theatrical mayhem at Coachella 2019 he saw his way in, and the then-66-year-old began immediate work on a set blending his film music, Oingo Boingo hits, and experimental songs fit for a rowdy crowd. Polygon appended a correction noting that a previous version of the story said Elfman performed at Royal Albert Hall in 2014; he performed his Music of Tim Burton concert in 2013.

# Peter Gabriel's I/O, His First Solo Album In Two Decades

I/O is Peter Gabriel's first solo album of new original material in over two decades, The Age reported on 30 November 2023 — a gap so long that "some wags are calling it his Chinese Democracy", though the rarely punctual Axl Rose took a comparatively brisk 18 years to follow up Use Your Illusion.

Before the silence, Gabriel was seemingly everywhere: he popularised the massive, heavily gated drum sound that dominated the era and became one of world music's greatest champions by co-founding the WOMAD festival. And then he wasn't.

Some things have not changed. From the get-go, on opening track Panopticom, there is "that gunshots-in-an-echo-chamber drum sound" and the instantly recognisable fat, slithering tones of long-time bassist Tony Levin, and the subject matter is the familiar big-world thinking — in this case Gabriel's utopian idea of an infinitely expandable and accessible world database, "but, you know, one that doesn't peddle untruths". The title track could almost come from Coldplay, with its singalong chorus designed for arena crowds waving lit-up smartphones, while Gabriel sings "stuff coming out, stuff going in, I'm just a part of everything".

# Shameless Media: A Self-Funded Podcast Company Built On Pop Culture

Shameless Media is the Melbourne-founded company built by Michelle Andrews and Zara McDonald out of their passion for smart conversations about pop culture, launched in 2019 and home not just to the Shameless podcast but also to Everybody Has a Secret, Shameless Book Club and Love etc. As of this 7 October 2023 profile it has 1.1 million followers across social media, plus 1 million unique listeners and 2.5 million podcast downloads a month, and 11 staff.

Its defining financial feature is independence: for the first 10 months Shameless was a weekend project, researched and recorded around the pair's other jobs, and in those early days McDonald and Andrews were self-funded, buying their own podcasting equipment and spending just $70 to print advertising flyers. Even now they have never taken on any outside investment, and the company has been profitable from day one.

The origin story runs through their former employer. Nine years ago Andrews and McDonald were both 20 and working entry-level jobs in Melbourne at women's media company Mamamia, covering late shifts, often on weekends, and regularly sharing an Uber home; a friendship grew out of their shared love of pop culture. "We'd be watching the same TV shows and listening to the same podcasts," says Andrews, now 29. Their back-seat chats led to the idea for Shameless — "a pop culture podcast for smart people who love dumb stuff". The story of how they left Mamamia after having the idea rejected at the final hour has been told many times, but these days they rarely think of it. "It ended up being amazing for us that they didn't want the show," says Andrews. "We feel so far removed from that time," adds McDonald, also 29. They are now well known as the "Shameless girls".
