# I/O's Mortality Themes And Overlong Tracks

The Age's 30 November 2023 review argues that I/O is animated by a palpable sense of mortality but undermined by songs left "in the oven too long" — stretching to five, six and seven minutes and in need of an edit or at least a change in tempo.

The grounds for the first half of the claim are biographical and musical. Gabriel is 73, and he is mining a seam of material about taking stock, feeling at one with the world and the admittedly not-exactly-original realisation that love is all we need. This reaches its most intense moment in And Still, a song he wrote to deal with the death of his mother in 2016 — a fragile, delicate thing with an almost Nick Drake transparency, as he remembers leaning his head against her skin and the feeling of her brushing his hair as a young boy. The reviewer also notes that in the late '90s Gabriel collaborated with Randy Newman on That'll Do from the Babe soundtrack, and suggests that should Newman be indisposed for the next Pixar film, Gabriel's Playing For Time could easily slot in for the reflective, tear-inducing, life-affirming ballad Newman routinely provides at the end of the second act.

The grounds for the criticism are two named tracks: Olive Tree and Live and Let Live overload the "one with the world" barrow he is pushing — the former a Sting-like concoction that seems to be two different songs bolted together, the latter coming from a fine place, inspired by Nelson Mandela and The Elders project, but littered with cliches such as "When we can forgive, we can move on" and "An eye for an eye, again and again, until the whole world is blind". On top of all this there are two mixes of the album, a "bright-side mix" by Mark "Spike" Stent and a "dark-side mix" by Tchad Blake. "Yes, it's a lot to take in," the reviewer concludes. "But then, it's been a while in the making. And who knows when, or if, we'll get a follow-up?"

# Healy Denies The End Of Australian Women's Cricket Dominance

Alyssa Healy rejected the suggestion that the Test defeat to India showed Australia's unprecedented period of dominance was ending: her counter attacks the inference from a single result, arguing the loss is "probably not even a blip" because it came in a format and conditions the team is not familiar with.

Quizzed on the point after the loss, Healy was defiant. "It's probably not even a blip," she said. "It (Test cricket) is a format where we're not overly familiar with, in conditions that we're not familiar with. I see more positives out of this and than any sort of negativity."

She then challenged the standard being applied to the team, arguing that outside expectations have not kept pace with a squad in transition: "There is always a lot of expectation and external noise about our team and how we're performing. They are so used to seeing us winning, that I think, at times, they forget that we've actually seen quite a lot of change over the last 12 to 18 months. That kind of goes unnoticed external to our group."

# Dalton Papali'i On All Blacks Leadership Vulnerability

All Blacks back-rower Dalton Papali'i described in the week before the 2023 World Cup final how senior players opening up emotionally in front of the squad had changed the group's mood, saying it made younger players want to play the game for them.

"It was quite special to hear some of the things those certain players said from the heart," he said. "You know, you think you know someone but once they open up and really be vulnerable in front of a team, it was quite special to hear. It was truly something special when you hear those boys open up. You know those leaders have been through a lot in their careers, the highs and the lows, the off-field and on-field stuff, and for them to open up, it sort of makes you feel welcomed and you want to play this game for them. There were a few tears and I think that's awesome to see, players showing vulnerability, just opening up about how much this tour and this sort of game means."

He set the moment in the context of the criticism the team had absorbed: "There were some (people) saying this is probably one of the most important games of All Blacks history. (The) All Blacks went through a bit of a hard path to get here, media, friends, family even criticising us and all that, and we stuck together. We weren't even said to be in the final and now look at us, we're here. Different players take it differently and some of the older players probably were hit a little bit harder and it was good to see just a bit of emotion and the want from them. Seeing that gives all the other players an extra two, three per cent to think 'OK, we are going to the well and we've got to give it our all'."

Papali'i said the All Blacks were intent on sending their leaders out on a high: "There's a few leaders in the team, it's going to be their last game in the jersey, so it's a big game for us and even the other players that are staying, knowing that we want to send those boys out on a high. How much they put into the jersey. We are standing on their…what's that quote? It's standing on the shoulders of giants."

# Concert Tour

## Definition

In the corpus, a concert tour is the live, multi-city, multi-date run of shows an artist performs — such as Taylor Swift's "ongoing 'Eras Tour'" and Beyoncé's "Renaissance" tour — that generates its own ticket revenue and can later be packaged, using footage from those shows, into a companion concert film for theatrical release.

## Context

In the corpus the term names both a live-event undertaking and, increasingly, the commercial engine behind an associated concert film: Taylor Swift's "ongoing 'Eras Tour'" is described as a 151-date stadium tour projected to gross about $1.4 billion, while Beyoncé's "Renaissance" tour is described as a "39-city, 56-show" run that "kicked off in Stockholm, Sweden in May and ended in Kansas City, Missouri in the fall" and made over $500 million while drawing over 2.7 million concertgoers.
Both artists' tours are directly tied to concert films — Swift's "Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour" and Beyoncé's "Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé" — which theatrical distributors built around footage and momentum from the live tour itself, so the tour functions in the corpus as the originating live event that a concert film later packages for wider audiences.
The corpus also frames touring as increasingly inaccessible: "concert tickets are more expensive than ever," with "inflation, Ticketmaster's monopolistic practices, and increased demand after COVID-related touring delays" cited as causes, and tours are described as never having been accessible to everyone because "geography, economics, health and safety concerns, and physical or mental ability" make stadium and arena concerts infeasible for large parts of a fanbase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Multi-city, multi-date structure** — Swift's Eras Tour spans 151 dates and Beyoncé's Renaissance tour spans 39 cities and 56 shows, both crossing international markets.
- **Repeatable show format** — each Eras Tour concert "spans over 180 minutes, with more than 40 songs from at least nine albums and 16 costume changes," performed against a fixed setlist that Swift memorized by "singing the entire set list out loud" during preparation.
- **Major revenue driver** — the Eras Tour is projected to gross roughly $1.4 billion and the Renaissance tour made over $500 million, figures separate from and larger than the box-office receipts of either artist's related concert film.
- **Rising ticket-access barriers** — average North American Eras Tour resale prices reportedly rose to $3,801, a "2,321% increase" over Swift's 2018 Reputation Stadium Tour average of $157, driven by inflation, resale-market dynamics, and pandemic-era touring delays.
- **Physical toll on performers** — Swift described committing to play a show "whether I'm sick, injured, heartbroken, uncomfortable, or stressed" absent "force majeure," and the tour's Rio de Janeiro leg was disrupted by a heat wave following a fan's death during a performance.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a concert tour is generally defined as a series of concerts by an artist or group of artists in different cities, countries, or locations, often named to distinguish one tour from another and to link a particular tour with a specific album or product. (Wikipedia, "Concert tour," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concert_tour)

# Peter Gabriel From Genesis To Eighties Pop Ubiquity

Peter Gabriel spent much of the '70s at the forefront of prog-rock as the singer for Genesis, and then went on to personify big, shiny '80s pop, The Age noted on 30 November 2023.

In the Genesis years he created sprawling concept albums and wore a series of increasingly bizarre stage outfits "that suggested he had ingested a truckload of acid on the way to a Halloween party", and was one of the main reasons punk had to happen. The evidence of his subsequent ubiquity is specific: the most played video on MTV was Sledgehammer, his body slam of a hit from 1986; the song blaring from the boombox John Cusack held aloft under Ione Skye's window in the iconic scene from 1989's Say Anything was Gabriel's In Your Eyes; and, somewhat bizarrely, you can barely watch an old episode of Miami Vice without hearing a Gabriel song in the background.

The same column places this in a contemporary context via its other subject: with a pop landscape led by serious singer-songwriters like Taylor Swift, SZA, Olivia Rodrigo and Billie Eilish, Dua "go girl, give us nothing" Lipa, the fame-trolling Doja Cat and the introverted-to-the-point-of-obscurity PinkPantheress, the reviewer sees a vacancy for Tate McRae's particular set of popstar skills — she is a throwback in the classic singing-dancing Britney mould, and "if she's greedy enough, the platform feels like it's hers to grab". Of Gabriel the verdict is blunter: after two decades he returns "overcooked and overlong".

# Thanksgiving's Origin In A Grindhouse Fake Trailer

Eli Roth's slasher film Thanksgiving began 16 years before its 2023 release as a spoof movie trailer in the middle of Grindhouse, Quentin Tarantino and Robert Rodriguez's pulpy 2007 double-feature, The Age reported on 15 November 2023.

The original trailer — tagline "There will be no leftovers" — showed an axe-wielding pilgrim wreaking havoc on lusty teenagers around the backwoods of Plymouth, Massachusetts, and was inspired by the seasonal horror films of Roth's '70s and '80s youth such as Halloween (1978), My Bloody Valentine (1981) and Silent Night, Deadly Night (1984). "[Co-writer] Jeff Rendell and I, we grew up in Massachusetts, which is the birthplace of Thanksgiving; it's a huge deal there and in school it's really shoved down your throat – you go to these pilgrim recreation villages, there's a school play, a parade…" Roth explains. "So growing up we always thought, 'Why isn't there a Thanksgiving slasher film?' Grindhouse gave us the opportunity to try out all the kills we'd already had floating around in our heads." Campy, explicit and horrific, the trailer came to be touted by genre aficionados as "the best horror movie never made". "It's really down to the fans, badgering me year after year," Roth jokes of how it became a real movie. "Guilt-tripping and shaming me, it really works."

In a metatextual flip that cheekily ribs Hollywood's predictability, the 2023 film is framed as a modern-day reboot of the lost slasher film featured in the fake trailer: a killer is loose in modern-day Plymouth with an axe, a wrath and a creepy mask of the first US settlement's first governor, whose name was John Carver. "I mean, when history hands you a gift like that, how do you not use it?" jokes Roth. "It's a perfect slasher villain name and he was real, the governor on the Mayflower!" Despite Thanksgiving Day's heavy baggage — like Australia Day, many in the US have increasingly questioned the holiday's ties to colonial aggression — the key creative breakthrough came from something more contemporary: watching online "trample videos" from Black Friday shopping sales, traditionally held the day after Thanksgiving, which began proliferating on social media around a decade ago. "These Black Friday sales, they were never a thing when I was a kid. But now I know they're even in Australia, they're everywhere," says Roth. "The whole idea of Thanksgiving is you're supposed to be thankful for what you have and for your health, but then you just go out and kill your neighbour for a waffle iron."

# Eli Roth's Horror Filmography And Acting Roles

Eli Roth has helmed over 20 films as a director, more than double that as a producer, and has also appeared onscreen — notably as Sgt. Donny "The Bear Jew" Donowitz in Quentin Tarantino's Inglourious Basterds (2009) and, most recently, in 2023's comically maligned The Idol, where he played a wracked Live Nation rep, The Age reported on 15 November 2023.

He has been horror's most provocative maestro for decades, a filmmaker who finds sinister glee in pushing the envelope; it was his film Hostel (2005) that spawned the term "torture porn". Of returning to the slasher form he says: "Every time I make a horror movie, it's like a badge of honour for me. It's like, this is my chance to make a slasher film, you know? I grew up with Freddie, Jason, Michael Myers, Chucky – I loved those movies so much – and in the '90s, we had Ghostface and other slashers that were overlooked, like Mute Witness (1995) which is one of my favourites. I just thought, well, it's time for a new slasher. I want a new killer in town, so let's create another one." Recalling a Q&A screening for his feature debut Cabin Fever (2002) at Glebe's now defunct Valhalla cinema about 20 years earlier, Roth remembers "a kid coming up to me after, with his friend Angus, and we talked for half an hour about how much he loved the movie. And I was doing Angus' radio show the next day and that kid came up to me again and he's like, 'Yeah, I made a short film called Saw.' It was Leigh Whannell."

Although he was not involved in The Idol's troubled first incarnation, Roth says he enjoyed his experience on creator Sam Levinson's set — "You saw this negative stuff come up [in the press] and I'd be thinking, 'What are people talking about?'" He completed The Idol right before directing Thanksgiving and credits the experience with "switching up my brain to use another side of my creativity". "I think that's why I really am an actor's director and why actors like working with me, is that they know I understand what they go through," he says. "In the rehearsal process with the cast, or getting ready to do a scare scene, I want to give them the room to go off-script a bit until we find something interesting, and that's all from my personal experience as an actor."

# Ireland's 37-Phase Final Attack Against New Zealand

Ireland's last attack of the 2023 Rugby World Cup quarter-final ran to 37 phases and five minutes before ending in a turnover, with the 28-24 scoreline staring back at them from the giant screen. You could feel the desperation around the Stade de France, awash with green thanks to the Irish fans doing their part, as Ireland went through phase after phase after phase after phase hunting the try that could overturn the deficit.

The move started well inside their own half, with 77 minutes on the clock. It took in 37 gruelling phases of Bundee Aki grinding out extra yards with each punishing carry, Tadhg Beirne left at a literal standstill through tiredness, and Johnny Sexton — for the final time ahead of retirement — running the famous wraparound upon which he has built maybe the greatest Ireland career of all time.

But it ended, almost inevitably, with a turnover deep in the New Zealand 22, the ball being kicked to touch and the men in green sinking to the floor bereft.

# The QRU Refuses To Centralise Commercial Functions

The Queensland Rugby Union stopped short of wanting to hand over its commercial property, rejecting the step from high-performance centralisation to full centralisation: "While the QRU is very supportive of high-performance alignment, it will not agree to any proposal on centralising commercial or corporate functions."

The premise it attacks is that consolidating commercial operations under Rugby Australia would strengthen the game. The QRU's reason is local expertise: "The very strength of our State unions is the expertise they bring in their own markets. We are open to work on commercial initiatives together but will always retain our independence for the benefit of Queensland Rugby, its members and stakeholders."

It backed the position with its own financial and participation record. The letter cited a sustainable business model built through the elimination of legacy operating debt, four straight operating profits, and work in partnership with governments to deliver $31 million of improvements to Ballymore through the construction of the National Rugby Training Centre, home of the Wallaroos and Queensland Reds. It also pointed to 71,000 players across the state, including more than 16,000 female participants, 257 schools featuring rugby as part of their program, and the Hospital Cup and regional club competitions, as evidence the game was in good health in Queensland.

# The NSW Waratahs' Licence Handover To Rugby Australia

The New South Wales Rugby Union was in the latter stages of handing over its licence to Rugby Australia, The Roar revealed in the week before Oct. 10, 2023 — a move by which the NSW Waratahs, who were on the brink of insolvency, handed over their commercial and high-performance property.

The practical effect is that all male and female Waratahs players, including coaches and high-performance staff, as well as all commercial and operations staff, will run out of RA's office. NSW Waratahs chief executive Paul Doorn informed stakeholders of the decision the previous week.

RA is cognisant that not every Super Rugby franchise will follow suit immediately, but the governing body is hopeful that now one of the two biggest states has agreed to hand over the keys, others will follow swiftly, with the Melbourne Rebels expected to be next. RA chief executive Phil Waugh says building trust back between the governing body and the states is essential to their plans.

# The QRU's Position On High-Performance Centralisation

In the wake of the Wallabies' 2023 World Cup flop, the Queensland Rugby Union reaffirmed on Oct. 10, 2023 that it is committed to moving to a centralised high-performance model — but will not follow the NSW Waratahs in handing over the keys to Rugby Australia.

The QRU's stated commitment reads: "The QRU is committed to working with Rugby Australia to lead reform of our game at a high-performance level, and help Rugby Australia develop an improved game through high-performance centralisation." The letter defined the scope of that centralisation: it "would include a national player-contracting model, and alignment of key high-performance staff, such as coaching, strength and conditioning, and medical to operate as one national system." The letter, an open letter to members published on Wednesday morning by QRU chief executive David Hanham and chairman Brett Clark, also pointed to RA's involvement in Les Kiss' appointment as Reds coach — the former State of Origin winger turned coach, who has spent the best part of two decades coaching in Ireland and England, replacing Brad Thorn — as an example of the model in practice.

The QRU also expressed strong support for Rugby Australia to conduct a "fully independent and transparent top-to-bottom review of the Wallabies program and how it can be improved" in light of the historic first World Cup pool exit, adding: "It should also provide a clear view of what is needed in a leadership and governance framework to ensure we put the right people, in the right roles, in the right system." The Roar noted the boundary of the consensus: while all five Australian Super Rugby sides are fundamentally on board with moving to a centralised high-performance program, some states, including the ACT Brumbies as well as the QRU, don't want to give up their commercial assets.

# The Rugby Australia High-Performance Director Role And Its Remit

The Rugby Australia director of high-performance is the position at the top of the governing body's high-performance structure, described by chief executive Phil Waugh in December 2023 as the biggest job on his leadership team in terms of its impact on the general sentiment around the game in Australia.

Three duties define the role as described. First, the director oversees all of Australia's men's and women's high-performance programs. Second, the holder is tasked with "integrating" those programs, as Rugby Australia tries to centralise all of Super Rugby's high-performance programs. Third — and perhaps most pressing at the time — the director must build a list of coaching candidates to take over from Eddie Jones, with Rugby Australia wanting the new Wallabies coach set in stone by the start of Super Rugby.

The scope conditions attached are timing and seniority. Rugby Australia always said it wanted the role filled by Christmas, and Waugh's framing sets the standard for the appointment: "It's a big job. It's the biggest job on my leadership team in terms of the impact it has on the general sentiment around the game."

Rugby Australia was forced to take out a $40m loan from Ares to keep the game afloat, and as of Oct. 10, 2023 had around another $15m left to spend from it while looking to borrow up to another $60m.

The purpose of the additional borrowing is to be in the strongest possible position to capitalise on two major money-making events — the 2025 British and Irish Lions series and a home men's World Cup — and succeed. # Peter Horne's Appointment As Rugby Australia High-Performance Director

Rugby Australia was moving closer to naming World Rugby's director of high-performance Peter Horne as its new director of high-performance, a move The Roar reported on 11 December 2023 could also help land highly-regarded coach Joe Schmidt for the vacant Wallabies job.

The Roar had reported the previous week that Horne emerged as the leading candidate, and it is believed he edged out former Sydney University, Australian Sevens and Harlequins director of rugby Billy Millard for the role. The finer points of the negotiations were being worked out, with an announcement likely over the following week once Horne wrapped up a crucial series of meetings with World Rugby — he was leading World Rugby meetings with tier-two nations that week in Sydney, with former Fiji coach Simon Raiwalui in attendance before officially joining World Rugby. His appointment reflects Rugby Australia's desire to go down an administrative path rather than choose a former coach of any standing, as Millard would have offered, and Horne will sit at the top of the high-performance tree with the next Wallabies coach reporting into him.

His background is given in some detail. Horne joined World Rugby in 2015 as a general manager of high-performance before moving into his current role, and during that tenure the Sydneysider played an important role in setting up competitions, high-performance structures and pathways across developing countries. He also played a role in helping Super Rugby integrate Fiji Drua and Moana Pasifika into the competition. Those successes played out at the recent Rugby World Cup, with Chile, Fiji, Georgia and Portugal delivering encouraging performances that positively reflected World Rugby's desire to spread and build the game. He briefly worked at Saracens as a general manager.

# Eddie Jones' Case For Reforming The Australian Rugby System

Eddie Jones argued that the Wallabies' problems are systemic rather than confined to the national team, and that it was crucial for Rugby Australia to get alignment in the code from grassroots through to the top team — with Australia, a two-time world champion, then ranked 10th in the world.

His grounds are the gap he saw at the top of the game and the state of the layer beneath it: "You just got to watch the quarterfinals at the weekend. We're not at that level. And we can't pretend to be at that level. But can we be at that level by 2027? Yes, we can. We're definitely off the pace but the opportunity to get better is there." The warrant is that a team declines when the system under it stops supporting it: "This is not an unusual situation. You've got a team that was struggling for a period of time, you've got underneath it a system that's not supporting it and at some stage you bottom out. This is the opportunity now to change the team — as we've started with picking younger players with bright futures — and then we've got to look at the development system underneath as well. It's not a simple equation that the Wallabies are bad. Let's be serious about this. The Wallabies are not where they need to be but underneath that we need to fix the system to go forward. And if we can do that now we've got a rosy future." He also acknowledged the cost of that change and the fans' pain: "We feel all the supporters hurt and really appreciate the great support we had in France and back in Australia for the team… Sometimes the change you have to have is uncomfortable. It is quite difficult. And sometimes you have to go through this to get into a better state and I believe that the problems we've had particularly at the national team will put us in a better state going forward." Jones clearly believes he is the right man to carry Australia on: "I think I've got the foresight to see where we need to go. I've got the experience of being in difficult situations before."

Earlier, on Oct. 10, Jones advocated specifically for Australian rugby to move to a centralised model, believing the nation had fallen behind the rest of the world: "We're a state-based union that's run by the states, the national union wants to assume more responsibility and when things were going well, no one questioned that. But over the last period of time, they haven't been going so well and this tournament's probably been the icing on the cake where it's got to a stage where I think people, most people probably think there's time for change. But it's not going to go easy." He located the payoff in player development: "[It's] one of the key issues. We need to maximize the development of the players. At the end of the day, that's the key to success and alignment of your resources, for a small country. Because Australia, if you look at the history of rugby, when we were amateur, we were probably ahead of the game because we had the influence of rugby league. We had the influence of AFL and our players were more professional than the rest of the world." And: "I know what's going on and we need to get a better system of developing players. We need to develop better players and we need to develop a larger batch of better players and that only comes through changing the whole system."

# Jones Defends Leaving Cooper And Hooper Out Of The World Cup Squad

Against criticism of his squad selection, Eddie Jones said on Tuesday, Oct. 16, 2023 that he had no regrets about leaving experienced players such as Quade Cooper and Michael Hooper out of the side for the 2023 World Cup.

He conceded the critics' right to their view while rejecting its authority over his decision: "Everyone's got their own judgment and they're allowed to have that judgment."

His own reasoning rests on a longer horizon than the tournament just played: "My choice was that I decided to go with youth. And I stand by that because I think we've got a lot of good young players who are really going to benefit from that experience at the World Cup, and going forward to the 2027 World Cup."

# The Wallabies' 2023 Pool Exit And The Review That Followed

Eddie Jones' Wallabies became the first Australian side to bow out of a Rugby World Cup in the pool stages in 2023, and Jones accepted that a review would be required into the flop — a statement that, as The Roar put it, puts the ball firmly in Rugby Australia's court as far as his future goes.

Jones was named Wallabies coach at the start of the year as replacement for Dave Rennie, arriving with grand statements that his team could win the Rugby Championship, the Bledisloe Cup and make a smash and grab on the World Cup. None of those targets were achieved, and Jones changed his tune about building for the future when he named a young team for the doomed Cup campaign. He finished the year with a 2-7 win-loss record, the only two victories coming against lowly Georgia and Portugal.

He said the team — including coaches and players — had already completed their own review of the World Cup disaster, and that the next one would be "a formal review to be done by independent consultants" in which he was ready to participate. # Eddie Jones Commits To The Wallabies Job After The 2023 World Cup

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# Gary Wang's Ownership Stake And Cooperation Deal

Gary Wang, co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX and co-founder of Alameda Research, owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX and drew a $200,000-a-year salary with no performance bonuses — though at times he was a billionaire on paper — while Bankman-Fried owned 90 percent of Alameda and 65 percent of FTX. He returned to the US on November 16th, met with the US government on November 17th without having been arrested or charged, offered to cooperate immediately, and pled guilty to various charges a month later. Wang was clear that he was cooperating because he did not want to go to jail, and said he hoped his assistance would lead a sentencing judge to be lenient.

The Verge's reporter drew from the disparity a puzzle she could not resolve: Wang took bizarre risks for a relatively small share. Bankman-Fried did not code, so none of his fingerprints are on the technical changes that let FTX allegedly defraud its customers and investors, while Wang supervised the code behind a key prosecution claim — that Alameda Research was afforded secret, special privileges with FTX's funds. When FTX went down, Wang left himself with no plausible deniability. Wang, a college roommate of Bankman-Fried's, took the stand after Adam Yedidia and, in the reporter's phrase, sang like a canary about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code.

The delivery was heavy going. On October 6th, 2023 Wang had to explain to the jury the difference between a front end and a back end, explain futures trading, and read a great deal into the record, which took a while; it was a tough day for the jury, and probably for Wang, who spoke quickly, perhaps from nerves.

# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

In the prosecution's account offered by Thane Rehn, the key to Sam Bankman-Fried's alleged scheme was Alameda Research, a crypto hedge fund that Bankman-Fried also owned. # The Defense's Good-Faith Case For Bankman-Fried

Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, attacked the prosecution's central premise that his client was a liar who stole from customers, stating early in his opening statement that "Sam didn't defraud anyone." The defense's counter-picture is of a nerdy startup founder who acted in "good faith," not the prosecution's "cartoon of a villain"; Cohen repeatedly harped on Bankman-Fried's allegedly good-faith actions throughout his address to the jury. Bankman-Fried, whose cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, appeared in court as this argument was made.

Cohen also disputed the specific claim that Alameda Research was a covert conduit. Alameda was not subterranean or shady, he said; it was a successful hedge fund. FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, he argued, claiming that Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — that is, a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies.

The defense's warrant for reading failure as something other than fraud was an analogy Cohen employed throughout: "working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it," and businesses sometimes fail. He specifically pointed the finger at Ellison, the former CEO of Alameda, who he said did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. And when the walls came closing in and the aforementioned plane approached the "eye of the storm," Cohen argued, Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty — he was willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. "In the end, Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses," he concluded. "He didn't steal any money."

# Sam Bankman-Fried

Sam Bankman-Fried is the former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, whose highly anticipated criminal trial started on the Tuesday before TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. As one former federal prosecutor put it: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."

TechCrunch's 2023-10-02 summary of his standing on the eve of trial: SBF has been denied bail; his name is mud (or much worse) among those who have lost money in Alameda or FTX; and those who might not have had positions in these still blame him for other crypto woes, because he set off a ripple effect.

# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

# Sassoon's Redirect And The Alameda All-Hands Recording

Prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's brief redirect of Caroline Ellison on October 12th, 2023 set a trap that opened the door to the jury hearing a secret recording of an Alameda all-hands meeting in which Ellison confessed to stealing billions of FTX customers' money at Bankman-Fried's direction. On direct examination, near the end, Sassoon had asked about the all-hands meeting without bringing up many specifics; during the cross, Mark Cohen asked Ellison what topics were covered in the meeting while avoiding details — which let Sassoon work the confession in on redirect. The judge then ruled in favour of the jury hearing the recordings, and the court briefly recessed; that was when Bankman-Fried's mother approached the defense lawyers.

The tape was set up by a short afternoon witness. Christian Drappi, a former Alameda software engineer who looked like a handsome funeral director in a black suit and tie, testified that when Binance CEO Changpeng Zhao announced on Twitter that he intended to acquire FTX, Ellison confessed the theft of customer funds to him and a few other employees. The all-hands took place the following day and was secretly recorded by an employee who had joined Alameda three days before. In the recording Ellison did indeed confess to stealing customer funds with Bankman-Fried's approval. Drappi said he resigned less than 24 hours after the meeting; the recording was later sent to him, and he sent it to the government.

The reporter's assessment was that Sassoon demolished any points Cohen had attempted to make and that she did not fully appreciate the cleverness until after Ellison left the stand and the jurors left the room. In the family seats, Joseph Bankman, the defendant's father and a senior advisor to FTX's philanthropic arm, was not in the room for the recording, and Barbara Fried looked unhappy, rubbing her left temple as though she had a tremendous headache.

# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.

# Prosecution Allegations In The FTX Superseding Indictment

In a superseding indictment filed August 14th, prosecutors argued that Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection: that his statements that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies.

The indictment also says there were special features in FTX's code that "permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX," created at Bankman-Fried's direction, effectively exempting Alameda from the kinds of risk management other customers faced — while, the government alleges, "Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX." Bankman-Fried is accused of using "billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits" to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda's lenders. He allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial even though they aren't part of the charges brought. A second trial is scheduled for March 2024, with additional charges.

# Criminal Trial

## Definition

In this corpus, "criminal trial" names the government's federal prosecution of Sam Bankman-Fried in Manhattan on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, in which prosecutors presented witness testimony to prove guilt while the defense contested it, U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan presided, and a jury returned the verdict.
The corpus uses the term specifically to distinguish this proceeding — and the format of Epic Games v. Google, a civil jury trial — from non-criminal, civil proceedings such as the Trump/Engoron case, which sought financial penalties rather than imprisonment.

## Context

The corpus's central example is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal criminal trial in Manhattan, on seven charges of fraud and conspiracy tied to the collapse of FTX, presided over by U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan; the trial ran roughly six weeks, opening with jury selection on October 3, 2023 and opening statements the next day, and closing in a guilty verdict on all counts.
The proceeding follows a recognizable structure the corpus documents in sequence: jury selection, opening statements from prosecution and defense, the prosecution's case (fact witnesses like Adam Yedidia and Matt Huang, cooperating former co-conspirators Gary Wang and Caroline Ellison testifying under cooperation agreements, and expert testimony from accounting professor Peter Easton), cross-examination, the defendant's own testimony and cross-examination, closing arguments, and jury deliberation toward a verdict.
The corpus also shows what a criminal trial is not, by contrast: the parallel civil case against Donald Trump before Judge Arthur Engoron was a non-jury ("bench") trial brought by the New York attorney general seeking financial penalties, not imprisonment, and the corpus notes Manhattan prosecutors had considered and declined to bring a criminal case over the same underlying conduct — the state instead pursued civil fraud remedies. Epic Games v. Google is likewise a civil antitrust jury trial (Sherman Act, Cartwright Act claims) seeking injunctive and monetary relief, not a criminal prosecution, even though it shares the jury-trial format.

## Key Characteristics

- **Adversarial structure** — a prosecution (the government, e.g. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Danielle Sassoon, Nicolas Roos, and Thane Rehn in the SBF case) argues guilt while defense counsel (Mark Cohen, Christian Everdell) argues innocence or lack of criminal intent.
- **Jury as fact-finder** — a jury, not the judge, decides guilt; in the SBF trial the jury included a train conductor and a retired investment banker, and reporters repeatedly note what testimony "the jury saw" or "the jury will have to decide."
- **Burden and standard tied to criminal charges** — the prosecution must show the defendant's conduct was not just harmful but criminal; as one account puts it, "Just losing $8 billion is not a crime... But if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing... that's a crime," turning the case on proving intentional deceit and conspiracy rather than mere loss or business failure.
- **Cooperating witnesses and immunity/plea deals** — co-conspirators such as Gary Wang, Caroline Ellison, and witnesses like Adam Yedidia testified under cooperation agreements or legal immunity, a common feature of criminal trials involving multiple alleged participants.
- **Judge as referee, not fact-finder** — Judge Kaplan ruled on objections, instructed the jury on the law, and controlled testimony (e.g., telling the jury he was the "final authority" on the definition of "market manipulation"), while leaving the guilt determination to the jury.
- **Sentencing follows conviction** — a guilty verdict is followed by a separate sentencing phase; the corpus notes SBF's charges could put him in prison for the rest of his life and co-conspirator Gary Wang faced up to 50 years pending sentencing.
- **Distinct from civil trials** — civil proceedings (Trump/Engoron, Epic v. Google) can share elements like juries or trial-style testimony but seek monetary or injunctive remedies under a different legal standard, and can proceed without a jury at all (non-jury "bench" trial).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, a criminal trial is a court proceeding, initiated only by the government, in which the prosecution must prove the defendant's guilt "beyond a reasonable doubt" — a heavier standard than in civil cases — while the jury decides guilt and the judge oversees the proceeding and, on a guilty verdict, determines the sentence (U.S. Courts, "Criminal Cases," uscourts.gov, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# FTX's Bankruptcy And Leadership

The man who represented FTX before Congress after its failure told lawmakers the exchange had effectively no internal governance at all, and the prosecutor bringing the case called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes one of the biggest financial frauds in American history. TechCrunch reported both on 2023-10-01.

Ray represented the company during a House Financial Services Committee hearing regarding FTX. Asked whether the firm had significant risk management systems, Ray said at the time that "there were virtually no internal controls and no separateness whatsoever," and added that he did not "trust a single piece of paper" in the exchange's organization. Separately, in a press conference, U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called Bankman-Fried's alleged crimes "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."



---


# Caroline Ellison's Guilty Plea And First Day Of Testimony

Caroline Ellison, head of the hedge fund Alameda Research during its implosion along with FTX, took the stand on October 10th, 2023 having already pleaded guilty to criminal charges — fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud, and money laundering — and told the jury that Bankman-Fried "directed me to commit these crimes." She quantified the taking: "We ultimately took about $14 billion, some of which we were not able to pay back."

Her long-anticipated first day took the form of walking through a damning spreadsheet she had prepared for her ex and boss, now the defendant in a criminal fraud trial. She entered hunched in on herself, wearing a dusty rose dress with a gray blazer over it, looking less like an executive than like a girl who had borrowed her boyfriend's coat because she was cold. Asked by the prosecution to identify Bankman-Fried, she had trouble finding him and gazed around the courtroom for more than 20 seconds — apparently he was incognito with his new haircut — and when she did spot him she identified him as the one wearing a suit, which got chuckles from the rest of the defense table, also all in suits. She tilted her head down to answer questions and lifted it when she had finished each answer.

The defendant's own reaction registered the shift: Bankman-Fried had been vibrating slightly during Wang's testimony, and during Ellison's his bouncing became more noticeable. By the end of the day, The Verge's reporter wrote, the spreadsheet seemed like a sideshow.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Decision To Testify Backfired

The Verge's trial reporter argued that Bankman-Fried's choice to take the stand was a net loss for his defense: like Theranos' Elizabeth Holmes before him, he got on the stand to speak directly to his state of mind in a way no other witness can, but telling your side of the story opens you to a great many questions you might not want to answer on cross-examination — and, having watched a lot of crosses, she called Sassoon's the nastiest she had ever seen.

The warrant is what the charges turn on. The case hinged on conspiracy and intentional deceit: just losing $8 billion is not a crime, though it is very embarrassing, but if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing and how safe FTX was, that is a crime. Because state of mind was the contested issue, his own testimony became the evidence, and it did not hold: Sassoon had established the day before that he has a long history of dishonesty, and on October 31st, through a set of questions about what he did and did not do, she established that the story he told on direct examination was absurd. After a brief redirect by his own lawyers, resplendent with word salad, Bankman-Fried stepped down and the defense rested.

The direct examination had already supplied grounds. Beyond the two obvious lies the reporter counted him telling on the stand — about Alameda Research's name and about "allow_negative" — she was struck by how little he seemed to know about his own companies: apparently Singh, Wang, and Ellison were out there just doing whatever their little hearts desired, because Bankman-Fried was a CEO, but definitely not the kind that pays any attention to money at his crypto trading firm and futures exchange.



---


# FTX Ventures Was Funded By Alameda

Caroline Ellison testified that the money behind FTX Ventures came from Alameda Research, even though Bankman-Fried announced the fund publicly without naming its source: on January 14th, 2022 he tweeted, "We're launching a $2b venture fund: FTX Ventures!" She said he did not want to go public with where the funds came from, telling her he thought Alameda's brand was less good and that he did not want his name associated with it.

The Verge reported the episode on October 10th, 2023 as part of Ellison's testimony, framing it as FTX keeping cozy private ties with Alameda while publicly holding it at arm's length — an echo, the reporter wrote, of Bankman-Fried and Ellison's romantic relationship. The same distancing appears in another transaction: Alameda bought Robinhood shares for Bankman-Fried, who moved them to a vehicle called "Emergent Fidelity Technologies" to avoid association with Alameda.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Cross-Examination On The Missing $8 Billion

On October 31st, 2023, prosecutor Danielle Sassoon walked Bankman-Fried through his reaction to the FTX software bug fixed by Adam Yedidia — a bug that overestimated the amount Alameda owed FTX by about $8 billion — and to the discovery that, even after the bug was fixed, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. His response had been to direct alleged co-conspirator Caroline Ellison to repay third-party loans and to go on making investments. Bankman-Fried said he found out about the fiat@ftx account, the one that tracked how much Alameda owed FTX, in June 2022 while his senior staff was focused on fixing the software bug, but did not discover what the account was for until October.

Simple questions, The Verge's reporter wrote, nailed him to the wall. Had he given his employees at Alameda the direction not to spend FTX customer deposits? Had he put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money? Did he put in place any measures at Alameda to protect FTX customer money? No, no, and no — even though he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe. Asked who was making decisions to spend $8 billion of customer funds, he could not recall knowing anything about it; asked whether there were rules or requirements for how money borrowed from FTX would be returned, or rules for risk management, he said, "I was concerned with overall risk management." Asked whether he had called anyone in to ask who spent $8 billion, he said, "I wasn't trying to build out blame for it," saying he was focused on solutions; he fired no one. The court also saw an Alameda balance sheet from June 13th, 2022 that included the money it was borrowing from FTX as "ftx borrows," on which he seemed pretty hazy.

The June 2022 testimony resonated most with the reporter. Asked whether he had asked what "fiat@ftx" was, he said he did — but his employees told him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting," words she heard uttered aloud in a court of law. Yedidia — Bankman-Fried's college friend, Bahamas roommate, and FTX employee — had testified that he asked Bankman-Fried about the $8 billion hole on a padel tennis court in their luxury complex in June or July, and on the stand Bankman-Fried seemed to be trying to deny the conversation had ever taken place; it was not until Judge Lewis Kaplan intervened to ask whether Yedidia had ever told him about that money, in words or in substance, that Bankman-Fried admitted he had been told. "So it's your testimony that your supervisees told you to stop asking questions?" Sassoon asked, in a tone so level she could have been filing her nails. His parents were not there; the jurors watched attentively. Phrases like "hole isn't really the word I would use," and answering a question by saying he wanted "a few more qualifiers and scoping on it," led the reporter to conclude that if you know the meaning of the word "epistemology," you absolutely should not testify in your own defense.



---


# FTX's Fabricated Backstop Insurance Fund

Gary Wang testified on October 6th, 2023 that FTX lied about how much money was in its backstop fund, and the court was shown the code that generated the fake number published on FTX's website: it took the daily trading volume on FTX, multiplied it by a random number, divided it by a billion, and added the result to the number already displayed on the site. That figure had nothing to do with the actual amount of money in the insurance fund.

The fund mattered because of what FTX advertised. In many crypto networks, if someone lost enough money the exchanges could stick other traders with the losses too; FTX touted its automated liquidation as the way to avoid this, so that one customer going bankrupt would not affect the others. In the process of liquidating, FTX would try to sell the collateral on the open market, and if it could not finish, backstop liquidity providers would step in — market makers, including Alameda, which could be compensated for the losses they took from the backstop fund. Wang also testified that when there was not enough money in the fund, money was moved there from Alameda's accounts in order to pay the insurance out.

The prosecution's framing was that this was not merely a matter of Alameda holding special, secret privileges: it claimed those privileges were used to obfuscate basic elements of FTX's operations, exposing the exchange's supposed selling points as a lie.



---


# Alameda Research's Origins And Naming

Alameda Research was the cryptocurrency trading firm Bankman-Fried started in 2017 during a crypto bull run, and it was named for Alameda County in California, where its first office was set up. Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried said he knew "basically nothing" about cryptocurrency at the time but wanted to do arbitrage on it anyway, and that he is "somewhat introverted, naturally."

The name was chosen for cover. In his own words on the stand: "Effectively, we wanted to be under the radar at that point in time. I didn't want to call it Sam's Crypto Trading Firm or anything like that. We — there are a lot of competitors and people who we didn't particularly want to know what we were building out because they would race to do it. 'Research' was a sort of generic word, which filled out the company name. And that was — it was far better than the internal name that we had at that point, which was Wireless Mouse." The Verge's reporter noted she would find this more believable had she not already watched a video, played during Gary Wang's first day of testimony with Bankman-Fried and the jury present, of Bankman-Fried explaining on a podcast that the name made it easier to get a bank account.

The founding assembled the people later charged alongside him: Bankman-Fried went on a hiring spree, taking on Wang to program the computers, then Nishad Singh about a month after founding Alameda Research, and finally Caroline Ellison. Though Bankman-Fried was CEO and also majority owner, he wanted to be clear that he did not supervise Wang's direct work. After a run of wildly successful arbitrage — 50 percent to 100 percent annualized returns, per his testimony — he decided to found a cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, figuring he would fail and putting the chance of success at 20 percent, without defining the time period he had in mind.



---


# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.



---


# Allow_negative: Alameda's Exemption From FTX Liquidation

"Allow_negative" was a column in FTX's account database that exempted Alameda Research — and only Alameda — from the exchange's automated liquidation, letting Alameda hold a negative balance and withdraw money its accounts did not have. Gary Wang testified that it originated in a code commit dated July 31st, 2019 under Nishad Singh's username, titled "OTC trades and transfers to special accounts." Written in Python, it added two columns to the account database, the relevant one being "allow_negative," a toggle that when on let the account go negative; the feature was switched on the same day by a second set of code also carrying Singh's username, and Wang said he supervised.

The structure it modified was FTX's risk management. As Wang explained it, a futures exchange is the middleman that lets strangers bet with each other: it sits between the two ends of the bet, paying the winner and collecting from the loser, which is why it requires collateral, and under some circumstances it automatically sells that collateral to limit its losses. On FTX this liquidation process was automated and took about 30 seconds to find the accounts that needed to be liquidated to minimize FTX's losses. Normal customers — the defense objected to "normal" and was overruled — could be automatically liquidated, but not Alameda. Wang testified that Bankman-Fried "told me a few times to make sure that Alameda's account is never liquidated on FTX," and that "the code addition was the result of those conversations." Alongside the exemption, Alameda could place orders faster than other users and held an enormous line of credit, and the court saw evidence that users may have unwittingly deposited money into Alameda rather than FTX.

The relation holds only for Alameda: no other customer trading on FTX had allow_negative privileges, and the same day the toggle was switched on in July 2019, Bankman-Fried tweeted that Alameda "is a liquidity provider on FTX, but their account is just like everyone else's" — a tweet shown in court, and to The Verge's reporter evidence that the fraud at FTX started very early, just months after FTX was founded. Bankman-Fried offered a competing origin story from the stand: FTX's big selling point was its "risk engine," which in 2020 was "effectively sagging under the weight" of the exchange's rapid growth so that time to liquidation stretched to minutes, and at one point the engine got stuck in a catastrophic feedback loop that would have created losses in the "trillions of dollars," with Alameda teetering on the brink of a liquidation that "would have disastrous consequences" for FTX. "At the time, I wasn't entirely sure what was happening," he testified, saying that because of that experience he suggested an "alert" or "delay" to keep Alameda from being liquidated by a bug, that allow_negative was the eventual result of that conversation, and that he did not know about it until very recently. The dates do not fit: allow_negative was coded and switched on in 2019, and the code was displayed in court in front of Bankman-Fried and the jury.

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.
