Engadget suggests MasterClass could be a good gift option for people who love to learn or collect hobbies, as it provides access to hundreds of hours of video of masters of their craft explaining how they do their work, and some classes have exercises to complete as well, making it feel more like a real class. The deal was available until the end of the day on Black Friday proper.



---


# Classic Nintendo Franchise Picks For The Switch

Polygon's advice for a first-time Switch owner is to start with the modern-day Zelda, Mario, and Animal Crossing games, on the grounds that Nintendo is home to some of the most iconic gaming franchises.

The selection is explicitly a narrowing: it is hard to pick just a handful from this wealth of options, to say nothing of other iconic Nintendo series, so Polygon says it has narrowed the field to some of the platform's absolute best.



---


# Should You Upgrade To The Steam Deck OLED?

Polygon's reviewer concedes that for an existing Steam Deck owner the OLED model is technically an incremental improvement, but argues that the screen and the battery may still justify the double dip — and that for a heavy user the upgrade is inescapable.

The grounds are the two upgrades the review treats as more than cosmetic: the display and the battery life. The warrant is a usage-dependent one, made explicit through the reviewer's own case — someone who puts hundreds of hours into the Steam Deck each year converts an incremental gain into a large absolute one, so the more you play, the more the incremental case tips over into a purchase. For readers who do not already own a Steam Deck the argument is simpler and unconditional: the reviewer repeats that this is his favorite console ever, and it just got better.



---


# Travel And Language Learning Gift Cards

For a giftee in dire need of a screen break, The Verge's guide points to travel-oriented gifts ranging from the obvious, like airline gift cards, to national park passes.

A GetYourGuide gift card provides an easy way to take advantage of guided tours and tourist attractions around the world, letting a recipient explore volcanoes like Italy's Mount Etna or swim with sharks in Cape Verde. A Pack & Go gift card (Amazon and Target) covers almost everything needed on vacation: it can be used on a Southwest Airlines flight, to buy gas from Chevron or Texaco on a road trip, or to book an Airbnb or place a Grubhub order. For aspiring polyglots, a Rosetta Stone membership makes it easy to learn everything from French to Arabic to Japanese from home, with extras including speech recognition tech to get the accent right; Rosetta Stone is currently offering up to 50 percent off its plans, with the 12-month single-language tier starting at $126, $42 off. Finally, a gift card to a rideshare service like Uber (Amazon, Best Buy, Target) or Lyft (Amazon, Best Buy, Target) comes in handy for a ride to the airport — or if New Year's Eve plans include popping a few celebratory shots.



---


# Nintendo Switch OLED Smash Bros. Bundle Deal

The main Nintendo Switch deal for Black Friday 2023 bundles the $350 Nintendo Switch OLED with a digital copy of Super Smash Bros. Ultimate and a three-month individual subscription to Nintendo Switch Online for no extra cost, available at Walmart, Target, GameStop, Best Buy and Nintendo's own online store.

Smash Bros. Ultimate was released way back in 2018, so it's hard to call this an amazing deal, but the game remains one of the console's best and still typically retails between $50 and $60 on its own, while the Switch Online sub goes for $8. If you're late to the Switch bandwagon you could do much worse for a free pack-in game — but keep in mind that Nintendo is expected to unveil its next console at some point in 2024.



---


# Streaming Subscription Gifts For Film And TV Fans

For movie buffs and avid sports fans alike, The Verge's last-minute gift guide points to subscriptions that grant a giftee access to a wide range of content, including some catered toward anime diehards, horror lovers, and those looking for something more niche.

The example it details is the Disney Bundle at $15: a monthly, ad-supported subscription that grants access to Disney Plus, Hulu, and ESPN Plus for $14.99 a month, listed as $15 at Disney. The Verge's pitch for it is breadth of household appeal — sports fans can watch all the latest games while the rest of the family streams Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Ahsoka, and The Bear.



---


# Mario Kart 8 Deluxe

Polygon says no multiplayer Nintendo Switch list would be complete without mentioning the most recent edition of the 20-year Mario Kart series; it appears in the outlet's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

Though the game came out in 2017, it still reigns supreme as far as kart racing goes.

It also still gets new courses, such as the recent addition of Mario Kart 7's Rainbow Road.



---


# Kids' Toy And Playset Gifts 2023

The Verge's kids guide rounds up six toys: The Super Mario Bros. Movie Van Playset at $9.99+ (Amazon, Walmart, GameStop), the Pokémon Carry Case Playset at $33.99+ (Walmart, Target, Macy's), Furby at $49 (Amazon, Walmart), the Original Bazooka Bubble Gun at $32.39 (Amazon), the Nerf Perses MXIX-5000 Motorized Blaster at $59.99+ (Amazon, Walmart, Electronics Express), and the frog-green Quick Push electronic sensory fidget toy at $16.99 (Amazon).

It's been a big year for Mario — a new movie and a new Nintendo Switch game in Super Mario Bros. Wonder — so the Van Playset may scratch the itch for tykes who can't get enough of the plumber. The Pokémon Carry Case is a plastic backpack that unfolds to reveal a collapsible climbing wall, a sparring platform, and other arid environments for small two-inch plastic pokémon to play or battle in. The new Furby, a voice-activated animatronic plushie, has all kinds of responses, dances, and songs built in, and — most importantly for the guide — the resurrected '90s toy is a completely offline experience with no "smart" functionality, so a kid won't be pinging a cloud server every time they speak. The Bazooka Bubble Gun is a battery-powered blaster pumping out over 5,000 BPM — bubbles per minute. The Nerf Perses MXIX-5000 shoots soft foam balls as fast as eight pellets per second with a top-loading hopper that's equally fast and frantic to reload, with a warning to outfit kids with proper eye protection. The Quick Push froggy game with lights and sounds feels a bit like popping bubble wrap: recommended for ages three and up, and possibly a great fit for children who enjoy sensory toys.



---


# Xbox Series X Holiday Price Drop, 2023

As of 2023-12-09, Walmart and Amazon were offering the Xbox Series X as a standalone purchase for $349.99 — the same price as the earlier Diablo 4 Xbox Series X bundle, and a $150 discount off the standard price of the Microsoft console. Polygon's stated position is that nobody should pay more than $350 for an Xbox Series X during the holidays.

The trade-off is that this deal lacks a pre-packaged game, but Polygon notes plenty of sales were floating around to add excellent titles to an Xbox library without paying full price. Amazon was offering modest discounts on $50 Xbox Gift Cards at $45 each, with no stated limit on quantity, and Target had discounted three-month Game Pass Ultimate subscriptions to $44.99 from $49.99, giving access to a rotating library of titles for the Series X including Hi-Fi Rush, Cocoon, Venba, and Starfield.



---


# Ebook, Comic And Book Club Subscription Gifts

For a bibliophile whose tastes you don't know — or when you simply want to give more options than a single book — The Verge suggests a gift card to their favourite bookstore or a subscription like Kindle Unlimited, which grants members access to millions of ebooks and even select audiobooks.

Among the alternatives it rounds up: a Comixology Unlimited subscription for fans of Marvel and DC comics as well as manga like Fairy Tale, giving access to over 45,000 comics and graphic novels and more than 2,400 manga titles from a phone or tablet for $5.99 a month, with subscriber discounts on select digital books. A Book of the Month membership currently starts at $59.99 for a three-book plan, with the company curating five to seven bestsellers and classics for members each month so it's easy to choose something to read quickly. For readers who prefer brick-and-mortar shops, a Barnes & Noble gift card (Barnes & Noble, Amazon, or Best Buy) works, and for those who buy from local bookstores there's a Bookshop.org gift card. For those who prefer traditional newspapers and magazines, you can gift a subscription to The New York Times or The Washington Post, or to publications catering to specific interests like Cosmopolitan and National Geographic.



---


# Xbox Series X And Diablo IV Bundle Deal

The Xbox Series X bundled with Diablo IV dropped to $439 at Walmart for Black Friday 2023 — an all-time low for the bundle — reported by Engadget on 19 November 2023 and Mashable on 25 November 2023.

Engadget's framing: the console itself has a list price of $500 and the game is typically listed between $40 and $70, "so this is like getting a $60 discount on the console plus a free copy of the huge action-RPG". It also noted that Target was selling the same bundle with a $75 store gift card for $450.

Mashable's Walmart doorbuster roundup put the same $439 figure as the new all-time low, saying "you're basically getting a free copy of Diablo IV on top of a $60 discount on the Series X (which typically sells for $499.99 on its own)". The only other retailer matching it at the time of writing was the Microsoft Store itself, whose markdown "seems to have popped up recently in response to Walmart's doorbuster": a post on Xbox Wire had previously pegged its Black Friday price there at $509.99.



---


# Animal Crossing: New Horizons

Animal Crossing games have long been loved for their chill farming sim vibes and adorable villagers, and Polygon says Animal Crossing: New Horizons perfected the genre — a pick it rates great for newcomers to consoles and veterans of the genre alike.

The game sticks you on an island where you design a cute house, harvest materials, catch bugs and fish, and court animal villagers. Time passes as it does in real life, so the game paces itself perfectly for daily engagement, with tasks to accomplish and fees to pay Tom Nook, the raccoon who lends you all of your supplies and lodging. It is also social: you can visit other friends' islands, so friends who also have the game on Switch can give you a tour and lend a hand by gifting bells or other items.



---


# Music Streaming And Vinyl Subscription Gifts

Beyond the familiar Spotify gift cards (Amazon, Best Buy, or Target), The Verge highlights several other music gifts for a giftee who is a musician or who just loves to unwind with music.

Apple Music is listed at $25 as a great gift for the casual listener, offering more than 100 million ad-free songs with spatial audio and support for Dolby Atmos; there's no designated Apple Music gift card, so you buy a regular Apple gift card — which the guide counts as an upside, since the recipient can also put it toward the latest AirPods. For true audiophiles, a Tidal gift card (Walmart, PayPal, or Best Buy) allows streaming in the highest audio quality possible: the ad-free service starts at $10.99 per month, with $9 extra per month adding support for lossless FLAC audio, Dolby Atmos Music, and Sony's 360 Reality Audio formats. A Fender Play subscription suits someone who has always wanted to learn guitar, with a continuously updated catalog of hundreds of instructor-led video lessons; it typically starts at $9.99 a month, but an annual subscription can currently be gifted for $74.999, half off. A Vinyl Me, Please subscription sends records monthly in a chosen genre — hip-hop, rock, or jazz — with booklets about each record and access to exclusive discounts, with three-month subscriptions starting at $128 and including four records, one a limited-time bonus. Lastly, a Ticketmaster gift card lets a loved one see their favourite musicians live, whether that's Olivia Rodrigo, Bad Bunny, or The Rolling Stones.



---


# Suika Game

Suika Game, developed by Aladdin X for Nintendo Switch, is ranked 43 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31. Critic JL describes it as an engrossing 2048-meets-Tetris-with-physics fruit drop game that has become her go-to whenever she needs to kill some time, and credits VTubers with introducing her to it.

She specifies that she is talking about the official Nintendo Switch version, not the horrific ad-plagued knockoffs that have flooded the App Store.

What makes it special, in addition to its cutesy gameplay, is its quality as a social game: the same way people sit around and talk about their NYT Connections, they sit around and talk about their fruitless attempts at getting double watermelons or breaking the 3,000 point threshold. It is also a great game to watch — nothing is funnier than seeing somebody's Suika run go downhill in 30 seconds flat, which JL notes is a reason the game has taken the streaming world by storm.



---


# Diablo 3 (Switch Local Multiplayer)

Now more than a decade old, Diablo 3 is still a great local multiplayer choice, especially on the Switch, according to Polygon's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

The action RPG felt bombastic when it first came out but has become a very comforting grind game to share with friends.

Polygon's writer adds a reason the older game still matters on that platform: Diablo 4 has not made its way to Nintendo Switch.



---


# Nintendo Switch Sports

Nintendo Switch Sports gracefully takes up the mantle of Wii Sports, whose legacy — and banging soundtrack — Polygon says will never be forgotten. It appears in the outlet's 2023-10-20 list of the 35 best couch co-op games for Nintendo Switch.

It carries over many of the same classic sports, like bowling, golf, and tennis.

It also adds some new ones to the mix, like volleyball and chambara, which Polygon calls a great complement to Wii Sports' boxing — with the practical warning to make sure you have enough space around you so you do not accidentally hit your television.



---


# Apple Store Credit And Gift Card Promotion, November 2023

Apple's November 2023 holiday promotion is not a discount at all: instead of cutting prices, Apple gives buyers of select items a gift card of Apple Store credit to spend later, running from the time of WIRED's 25 November 2023 guide through 27 November, with up to $200 in credit available.

The defining feature is the substitution of future store credit for an immediate price cut. WIRED's framing is that Apple notoriously does not run sales on its own storefront; what it usually does instead is throw in a gift card for Apple Store credit when you purchase select items. The amount of credit scales with the product bought: buying an iPhone 14 or iPhone SE earns up to $75 in store credit, while buying a MacBook Air earns up to $200, with the full list of qualifying items published by Apple.

A separate and distinct mechanism runs at another retailer: Amazon has a sale on Apple gift cards, where each card has its own unique corresponding coupon code. WIRED's example is a $100 Apple Gift Card bundled with a free $15 Amazon credit using the code APPLET5USAP, with many other cards to choose from. This second offer is a discount on the gift card itself rather than Apple's own purchase-triggered store credit, so the two should not be confused.



---


# Vudu Digital Movie Storefront

Vudu is like a digital Blockbuster: a storefront with a huge catalog of films you can rent or buy, ranging from new releases such as Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Mutant Mayhem to beloved classics such as The Nightmare Before Christmas.

Its distinguishing feature as a gift is that, unlike some other gift cards on the market, Vudu's do not expire — so you can take your time and save them for a rainy day. Polygon frames them as compelling gifts for the cinephile in your life.



---


# Lil Gator Game

Lil Gator Game, developed by MegaWobble for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X, is ranked 35 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31.

Critic Chris Grant acknowledges that in an unprecedented year for game releases, readers may be surprised to see it this high on the list — and says he was just as surprised to find, in a moment of introspection, that it was one of his own favorite games of 2023.

At the risk of diminishing its accomplishments, he offers a comparison that should cut to the quick for interested parties: this is the most A Short Hike-alike he has discovered yet, a singular high he has been chasing for years. His recommendation is for a lazy weekend afternoon spent playing — not gaming, but playing, in the joyous, unstructured sense of a day in the park.



---


# Prime Day Console And Controller Deals, October 2023

The console highlight of The Verge's October 10th, 2023 Prime Day gaming roundup was the Microsoft Xbox Series X at $400, down from $500 — a 20 percent discount on a refurbished unit at Amazon. The Series X is Microsoft's flagship console, its most powerful and biggest option, focused on fast 4K gameplay, while the Series S is aimed at smooth 1440p performance and takes a disc-less approach. Also listed: Hallmark's Nintendo Entertainment System Console Ornament at $16.16, about $4 off at Amazon — a tiny NES replica holding a little copy of Super Mario Bros. that lights up and plays the classic Mario theme with sound effects when you press its power button.

Controllers made up most of the list. Razer's wired Wolverine V2 Chroma fell to a new low at Amazon at $87.99, $62 off; the Xbox controller has six remappable buttons — more than any other Xbox controller The Verge is aware of — plus clicky buttons and RGB lighting on the grips. The cheaper Razer Wolverine V2 in white, with a built-in USB cable and no RGB lighting, was $45.99 at Amazon, $54 off. The GameSir G7 wired controller for Xbox and PC was $35.99 at Amazon, $9 off, a straightforward third-party gamepad with two programmable rear buttons, clicky face buttons, and a paintable front shell attached with magnets; the GameSir T4 Kaleid was $33.59, $8 off, the first time the transparent wired controller with RGB lighting had gone on sale, with drift-free Hall effect sticks and compatibility with PC, Nintendo Switch, and Android. The 8BitDo Ultimate Bluetooth Controller was $56, down from $70, a 20 percent discount; it comes with its own charging dock, has remappable controls, works with the Nintendo Switch, Steam Deck, and Windows PCs via Bluetooth and 2.4GHz, and, unlike the 2.4GHz-only version, has drift-free Hall effect sticks. The RGB-ified PowerA Spectra Infinity Enhanced Wired Controller for Xbox and PC was $29.99 at Amazon, $15 off, and is one of the cheapest controllers around to sport hair trigger lockouts. The PDP Victrix BFG Wireless Controller for PlayStation 5, PS4, and PC, in its Call of Duty: Modern Warfare II-branded black-and-gold design, was $169.99 at Amazon, $30 off — a very versatile DualSense alternative for FPS and fighting games, with multi-stage hair triggers and sticks and face buttons that can be swapped for an Xbox-style layout or a six-button fightpad.

Steam Deck accessories also featured: the Jsaux Mod Case was $24, down from $30, a 20 percent discount — a protective modular system consisting of a base case with grippy texture, a built-in kickstand, a removable lid, and a rear mounting system that can attach a power bank using an adjustable strap or Jsaux's add-on cooling fan. Jsaux's 45W USB-C charger with a five-foot cable and included right-angle adapter, designed for the Steam Deck but also good for a Nintendo Switch or just about any USB-C phone or tablet, was $15.19 at Amazon, $3 off.



---


# Power Bank For The Steam Deck

Each Steam Deck console includes a 45 W USB-C wall adapter, so Polygon advises finding a power bank that can meet that power level when you are on the go — and says options that can do it exist.

The constraint to watch during your search is the charging spec: only batteries that support the PD 3.0 spec, including the two options Polygon recommends, can recharge the Steam Deck at its fastest speed.

qid: What company, recently reviewed by TechCrunch for its laptop that stands out like a desktop, also justifies its choice of default search engine on The Verge, while simultaneously enforcing uniform terms across its platform as described in another article by The Verge?
context:
# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [The Google Antitrust Case](google_antitrust_case.md)
- [The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced](google_default_hypocrisy_argument.md)
- [US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial](us_v_google_search_antitrust_trial_overview.md)



---


# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.



---


# US v. Google: Two Months Into The Search Antitrust Trial

As of TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup, the Justice Department's landmark antitrust case against Google was nearly two months old, and the trial record was still producing fresh revelations. TechCrunch framed it as one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

An earlier roundup had already surfaced that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms, and that Google tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Over the couple of weeks preceding this roundup, more of Google's inner workings came to light, including some of the search engine's most lucrative search queries, the shape of the revenue-share agreements between Google and Android OEMs, and why Expedia has a bone to pick with Google.



---


# The DOJ Theory That Google's Default Deals Foreclose Search Rivals

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.



---


# iPhone Setup And The Absence Of A Search Engine Choice Screen

Eddy Cue acknowledged on the stand that the ISA didn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup — and said he wouldn't want to do that anyway, because "we try to get people up and running as fast as possible" and "setup is just critical stuff."

Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw built to that answer through a series of questions about the iPhone setup process, using three screenshots: the Appearance screen that appears when you first boot up an iPhone so you can pick font sizes, the location-tracking prompt that appears when you open Maps, and the App Tracking Transparency pop-up that tells you when an app wants to collect your data. Cue objected to all of these being considered part of setup, but Bellshaw's point was that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, and that search could be one of them. Cue argued that showing people a bunch of search engines they had never heard of would just be a bad user experience — even he couldn't remember the names of some of the alternatives to Google — and said, "We make Google be the default search engine because we've always thought it was the best. We pick the best one and let users easily change it." The Verge noted that "easily" is a persistent point of contention in the trial: DuckDuckGo's CEO, who testified the week before, claimed it takes "too many steps" to switch.



---


# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.



---


# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.



---


# Google's Agreement Not To Promote Chrome To Safari Users

As part of its search deal with Apple, Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, according to Bloomberg — a restraint that mattered because Google would otherwise have been able to do this with banners, pop-ups and other annoying means in its other Google apps. The same agreement also meant that Apple never switched to a Google competitor, and never allowed users to choose their browser when setting up their iPhones.

The observation surfaced in the antitrust trial, where the amount Google spent on homepage market share has been a fixing point. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella even said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search, per The Information — a stated willingness to pay, not a deal that happened.

A second, related admission came from Google's side: Pichai admitted to attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device back in 2018, according to The Verge. His aim, as reported, was to make Google's and Apple's services so connected as to be inseparable.



---


# Why Traditional E-Commerce Search Has Degraded

Deft co-founder Zach Hudson told TechCrunch that there are a few plaguing problems with the traditional search experience that prevent users from finding a suitable item — that is, the claim is that search has gotten worse, not that users have gotten worse at searching.

He offers three grounds, each a different actor degrading the result set: "You have companies like Google and Amazon that continue to push the most relevant listings down so they can make more advertising dollars. Some easy searches are now hard because marketers have learned how to game these search engines. Plus, now you have AI content that is putting the burden on users to separate fact from fiction," he said.

# Google's Defense That Search Defaults Are Easy To Change

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. # What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. # Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.

# Very Large Online Platform (VLOP)

## Definition

A Very Large Online Platform (VLOP) is a service designated by the European Commission under the EU's Digital Services Act (DSA) as carrying obligations beyond the DSA's baseline, on the grounds of its scale. Designation is the discriminating feature: the DSA's general duties apply to digital services broadly, but a platform once designated a VLOP additionally must identify and mitigate the *systemic risks* its service poses — disinformation, threats to fundamental rights, and, for algorithmic services, the societal risks attached to their recommender systems. The parallel designation for search engines is the Very Large Online Search Engine (VLOSE).

## Context

In the corpus the term appears as the tier that triggers DSA enforcement against the largest platforms. The Commission designated Meta's Facebook and Instagram as VLOPs earlier in 2023, and designated X (formerly Twitter) a VLOP in April 2023; VLOP compliance obligations took effect over the summer of 2023. The Commission is the *sole enforcer* of the DSA over VLOPs, which is the basis on which it opened its own request for information and later a formal investigation into X, and weighed in on Meta's advertising consent model. Designation is also what obliges these platforms to mitigate the disinformation risks the EU raised around upcoming elections, and it is why the Commission treats the (voluntary) Code of Practice on Disinformation as underpinning the DSA, with its stated intention to transform the Code into a Code of Conduct forming part of a co-regulatory framework for addressing disinformation risks.

## Key Characteristics

- **Designation, not self-classification** — a service becomes a VLOP by a Commission decision, and only then carries the extra duties.
- **Systemic-risk duty** — beyond acting on illegal content, a VLOP must assess and mitigate systemic risks such as disinformation, even where the underlying content (e.g. disinformation) is not itself illegal in the EU.
- **Sole-enforcer model** — the European Commission, not national regulators, enforces the DSA against VLOPs directly.
- **Penalty exposure** — confirmed DSA breaches by a VLOP can draw fines of up to 6% of global annual turnover, with service blocking possible for repeated infringement.
- **Search-engine analogue** — VLOSEs are the equivalent designation for very large search engines, subject to the same systemic-risk logic.

## Background (external)

The corpus names VLOP designation but does not state the numeric threshold that triggers it. Per the European Commission, the DSA sets the bar at more than **45 million average monthly active users in the EU** (European Commission, *DSA: Very Large Online Platforms and Search Engines*, accessed 2026-09-02), and the first batch of VLOP/VLOSE designations was issued on **25 April 2023** (European Commission, *List of designated VLOPs and VLOSEs*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Recommendation Algorithm

## Definition

Across the corpus, "recommendation algorithm" (and the closely related notion of algorithmic ranking/curation) names the automated mechanism a platform uses to control the visibility of content, products, or posts — and by extension, the mechanism regulators, courts, and users scrutinize when they suspect a platform is suppressing or favoring particular items.
No single corpus document offers a formal definition of the term; instead each shows the mechanism at work in a different dispute: Amazon's marketplace search ranking and "other products you may like" widget, Instagram's Stories/feed visibility, U.S. platforms' content-moderation feed curation, and Google's Featured Snippets extraction.

## Context

The corpus shows the same underlying mechanism operating across very different platform types, and shows regulators and courts converging on it from different angles.
On Amazon's marketplace, the EU's antitrust objections to the iRobot acquisition center on Amazon's ability to foreclose a rival's *algorithmic visibility* — delisting rival products, reducing their ranking in organic and paid results, excluding them from the "other products you may like" widget, or denying them labels like "Amazon's Choice" — since RVC buyers in France, Germany, Italy, and Spain rely on that in-marketplace ranking both for product discovery and for the final purchase decision.
The same document notes that Amazon's marketplace was separately designated a core platform service under the EU's Digital Markets Act, which imposes restrictions on self-preferencing.
On Meta's Instagram, users and digital-rights groups suspect a comparable but content-moderation-flavored version of the same idea — "shadowbanning" — where an algorithmic process silently lowers a post's visibility (e.g., Palestine-related Stories) without an explicit takedown.
In the U.S. Supreme Court's NetChoice cases (challenging Texas's HB 20 and Florida's SB 7072), the fight is over whether a platform's curation of what appears in a user's feed — a process now largely conducted algorithmically, generally with light human intervention or oversight — is a First-Amendment-protected editorial act that states cannot compel platforms to individually explain post-by-post.
Google's Featured Snippets, which algorithmically extract answers directly from publishers' web pages into search results, are cited in a news-publisher antitrust suit as a related mechanism: an algorithm that decides what content a user sees without the user visiting the original source, which publishers say siphons off their traffic and ad revenue.

## Key Characteristics

- **Ranking, not binary inclusion** — the algorithm typically operates on relative visibility (higher/lower placement in organic or paid results, inclusion in a "you may like" widget) rather than simple on/off access, which is what makes self-preferencing and shadowbanning hard to prove or disprove.
- **Automated with limited human oversight** — described in the NetChoice case as a process "largely conducted algorithmically now — generally with light human intervention or oversight," which is central to arguments that mandated per-decision human explanations would be impractical at the scale of "millions and millions of pieces of content a day."
- **Commercial leverage point** — on marketplaces, control over the recommendation algorithm doubles as a competitive lever: a platform that also sells its own products can use ranking, delisting, and widget exclusion to foreclose rivals, per the EU's ability-and-incentive theory of harm against Amazon.
- **Contestable but opaque** — content creators and merchants can suspect suppression (shadowbanning, reduced marketplace visibility) but the underlying ranking logic is not published, so claims tend to rely on circumstantial or anecdotal patterns rather than direct evidence.
- **Distinct from explicit content removal** — reduced algorithmic visibility (shadowbanning, lower ranking) is a softer, less visible action than outright delisting or takedown, and is treated differently in both platform policy and legal argument.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the general computer-science term for this kind of system is a "recommender system" (also called a recommendation algorithm, engine, or platform): a type of information filtering system that suggests items most relevant to a particular user, predicting user preferences to help them choose from large sets of options such as products, media, or content.
Source: "Recommender system," Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommender_system.

---


# Closed Sessions Limited The Public Record Of Cue's Testimony

The Verge cautioned that what it reported was all the testimony it saw: like so many things in this trial, the star witness was kept mostly under wraps thanks to complaints and worries about revealing confidential numbers and corporate secrets.

Even so, the questions put to Eddy Cue were the ones the DOJ is going to keep asking: is Google really the best search engine, or is it just the one writing the biggest checks — and if those checks went away, what would the search engine market look like? On that counterfactual, Cue said Apple has never really thought about it, Google said Apple would be silly to do so, and the Justice Department thinks it's about time Apple starts doing so.



---


# Danny Sullivan, From Journalist To Google Liaison

After Cutts left, Google replaced him with a handful of people, none of whom could quite fill his shoes: "Those personalities sometimes were standoffish," Forrester said. "Some of them were superior. Some of them were a bit too wallflower."

One of the people Google brought in was Danny Sullivan, a former journalist who started Search Engine Land — the industry publication where Schwartz works — back in the 2000s. In 2009 Sullivan was described as "the closest approximation to an umpire in the search world," so when he published "A deep look at Google's biggest-ever search quality crisis" in 2017 and then took a job as Google's public liaison for Search only a few months later, it felt to some SEOs as though a congressperson working on gun safety legislation had quit to become an NRA lobbyist.

Forrester reports the suspicion without endorsing it. "There is a thread across the industry of people who believe that Google just made Danny an offer he couldn't say no to, and it was designed essentially to take his voice out of the conversation," he said. "I don't believe that's the case," he went on, but compared to Cutts, "I think that Danny specifically stays out of a lot of public conversations because he is in those private conversations with businesses."



---


# Google Warps The Web It Observes

The article's central claim is that Google, not the SEOs, defined the shape of the modern internet: you cannot be the most powerful observer in the world for two decades and not deeply warp what you are looking at.

The grounds are the structural impossibility built into Google's founding goal. The company started with a noble cause — trying to make the internet easier to navigate at scale — and did accomplish that, but in doing so it inadvertently and profoundly changed how the internet looked. The problem lay in Google trying to be an objective and neutral arbiter of an information landscape that was meant to pretend it did not exist: you cannot design a free, automated system to help people find information without some people trying to game that system.

The warrant that shifts responsibility away from practitioners is a comparison of scale and agency. For the past 25 years the internet as we know it has been almost entirely defined and controlled by Google; what the SEOs do matters for all of us on a daily basis, distorting how we perceive the world in ways we can hardly begin to imagine or understand, yet any money any SEO has made is a fraction of a crumb compared to Google's 10-layer cake. The company brings in hundreds of billions of dollars a year, profits that skew Google's choices and priorities — as Google's founders themselves wrote back in 1997, "we expect that advertising funded search engines will be inherently biased towards the advertisers and away from the needs of the consumers."

The writer reaches this position by way of Lily Ray, who seemed the most reasonable person she had spoken to — even granting that Ray calls herself a "thought leader" and changed her last name to improve her personal branding by more closely associating herself with her grandmother's uncle, the artist Man Ray. Maybe some people would say that is the kind of absurd behavior that merits being attacked by an alligator, but the writer was beginning to come down on the side of the SEOs, who seemed to have a lot less agency than she had first imagined.



---


# The SEO-Algorithm Update Cycle

Since the dawn of the internet there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search's ability to be useful, and it works in cycles: people doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.

The cycle has turned several times before the current moment of widespread disillusionment. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011 SEO was once again oppressively pervasive — TechCrunch published a story called "Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google," which argued that "Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers." In the next year Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

The same event reads oppositely from the two ends of the relation. While the public might have experienced each of these updates as a relief, Mapstead and his SEO compatriots saw them as devastating. "They change the rules instantly overnight, and then you're out of business," he said. "Here you're trying to rely on this business model to feed yourself and your family, and they're pulling the rug from underneath you, and you've gotta scramble to pay rent."



---


# Duane Forrester, Bing, And The Search Engine's View

Duane Forrester was at Microsoft from 2007 until 2015, where he helped launch and manage Bing, the perpetual underdog to Google's domination of online search; because he worked as an SEO both before and after his time at Microsoft, he sees the industry from both sides — like an aerospace engineer who spent a few years at the Department of Defense, left for the private sector, and now is much better at winning military contracts. He has a holistic understanding of the delicate push and pull between the SEOs desperate for clues on how to do their jobs better and the search engine trying to keep its secret-sauce algorithm proprietary.

He was the first stop because Google was slow to allow anyone to talk to the writer, possibly because of the giant PR clusterfuck that has been the company's past year: accused by the federal government of being a monopoly, increasingly despised by the public, losing ground to Reddit, TikTok, and large language models.

Like Schwartz, Forrester wanted to emphasize how hard everyone works. "I've lost track of how many people I know who built companies and sold them and have just, like, made wealth," he said. "That is not a 40-hour commitment in the week. That is a 400-hour commitment." For the record, there are 168 hours in a week.

His route in started young. These days Forrester lives in Los Angeles and asked to meet at one of his favorite restaurants, which felt like a British pub operated by Disney World, tucked away in a desert strip mall and covered in Anglophile paraphernalia including Union Jack flags, a mural of Big Ben, and a red phone booth. Over a full English breakfast he described growing up in rural Canada, where his parents owned a motel and he used to mess around with the pay phone outside, eventually figuring out how to finagle free long-distance phone calls: "And then it became, 'What else can I know how to do?'" By the '90s he was trading tips with other SEOs in online forums, and he still remembers the thrill of the very first SEO conference he attended, where he was asked to speak. "The people who got up onstage to talk were seen as somehow more knowledgeable, but I don't know that we felt that way," he said. "You all kind of knew you were making shit up."

As a former SEO, Forrester understood that the quality of Bing's search results would be affected by the work of SEOs, so it made sense to communicate with SEOs as much as possible. Cutts similarly tried to serve as a conduit between SEOs and Google, but Forrester felt Google projected an attitude he described as: "We know what we're doing, we will stop your attempts to game this, and you know what? We'll just kind of ignore you, and when you give us feedback, eh, we don't really care."

context:
# Sydney Swans' First AFLW Finals Berth

Sydney, winless in their debut season the previous year, secured eighth spot and their first AFLW finals berth in 2023 by storming home with three unanswered goals against Fremantle, The Age reported on 3 November 2023.

"Any club that's able to go from winless one year to a finals berth, it's incredible," Sydney co-captain Chloe Molloy told Fox Footy after the match. "You can see the emotion on the girls' faces. Coming into the season, the odds were against us. Just to get into the eight, we've managed to do that. We're stoked. It's pretty special for the club." Missing star ruck Ally Morphett to a season-ending wrist injury, Laura Gardiner stood tallest in the midfield — the 20-year-old off-season recruit from Geelong had the ball on a string with a game-high 33 disposals and 18 contested possessions — while Molloy (two goals), Montana Ham, Rebecca Privitelli and Brooke Lochland hit the scoreboard.

The Swans' rise had been signalled earlier in the season by a record-breaking win over the Western Bulldogs, propelled by a Chloe Molloy masterclass: after a five-goal second term that included a four-minute burst of three majors, Sydney had already brought up their largest score in an AFLW game by half-time, and while the Bulldogs held their own in the last quarter the damage was done. The total was also the biggest the Dogs had conceded in their history, topping the 83 Melbourne kicked against them in round three. Molloy, the Swans' star off-season recruit and a former Collingwood ace, was a class above, kicking 3.4 from her 28 possessions and playing a crucial role in setting up numerous other Sydney goals. "She was itching to get in there [in the midfield]," Swans coach Scott Gowans said. "We kept her forward deliberately. It was important Chloe played a good block of time forward so we could have a look at it." That weekend the Blues lost to Greater Western Sydney by two points, 8.1 (49) to 7.5 (47), denying Carlton the chance to leapfrog into the top eight.



---


# Sydney Swans Top The AFLW Attendance Charts

The Sydney Swans sat top of the AFLW attendance charts on 26 October 2023, less than two years after their first match in the women's league, with an average attendance of 4,365 from four games — 124 more than the next best club, Adelaide.

They were due to play their final home match of the regular season that weekend, a marquee pride match against Collingwood at Henson Park on the Sunday, where a crowd in excess of 4,000 was expected. Earlier in the season, 5,474 fans were at North Sydney Oval to watch the Swans' first AFLW victory.

Swans forward Bella Smith said the players were proud of the club's attendance record and grateful for the support: "We get there two hours before the start of the game and the hill [at Henson Park] is bare. When you come out for the first team warm-up, the hill is slowly filling and then by the time the first bounce gets around, it is full. You can hear it, the atmosphere is amazing."



---


# AFLW 2023 Finals Qualification And Week One Fixture

The 2023 AFLW finals eight was not decided until the final game of the regular season, when Sydney downed Fremantle by 22 points to leapfrog St Kilda into the final spot, The Age reported on 3 November 2023.

The Saints had kept themselves in the race with a 20-point win over Carlton earlier in the day, 7.4 (46) to 3.8 (26), and with only 0.4 of a percentage point separating Sydney in ninth and St Kilda in eighth, the Swans' win assured them of retaking eighth spot. Had the Saints qualified, it would have been their maiden finals appearance. Saints goalkicker Jesse Wardlaw had a heavy collision with Carlton's Keeley Sherar late in the final quarter of their clash.

The resulting week-one finals fixture was: on Saturday November 11, the First Qualifying Final, Adelaide v Brisbane Lions, 2.35pm local (3.05pm AEDT) at Norwood Oval, and the First Elimination Final, Gold Coast v Sydney, 6.15pm local (7.15pm AEDT) at Heritage Bank Stadium; on Sunday November 12, the Second Elimination Final, Geelong v Essendon, 1.05pm AEDT at GMHBA Stadium, and the Second Qualifying Final, Melbourne v North Melbourne, 3.05pm AEDT at Ikon Park.



---


# The Swans' Matchday Experience Model For Local Attendance

The Sydney Swans' attendance strategy, described on 26 October 2023 by executive GM of marketing Loretta Johns, has two linked components: target local communities, and make match days compelling for fans on and off the field.

The off-field half is delivered through food, entertainment and promotion. "Our team has put a lot of work into sourcing some wonderful food offerings, entertainment and activities for kids, while we've had a local focus in promoting our games," Johns said. At North Sydney Oval that means quince paste and hand-picked grapes, cheddar cheese and biscuits in a little box with beautiful wrapping — "they've really thought about what they're doing and made it an experience."

The local-community half works through partnership as a promotional channel, not just a supplier relationship. At Henson Park, the Swans' other home ground in Sydney's gentrified inner west, "they've gone to microbreweries in the local area and invited them in, but also promoted through their clientele to come to the football" — the local business both provides the offering and supplies an audience.



---


# The Swans' On-Field Turnaround Under Chloe Molloy

After a winless campaign in 2022, the Sydney Swans — led by ex-Collingwood player Chloe Molloy — were competitive in the 2023 AFLW season, winning their first match in round one and sitting within a game of the top eight with two rounds to play as of 26 October 2023.

The Swans recorded their highest total the previous round in a 14-12-96 to 6-3-39 defeat of the Western Bulldogs, the league's winless bottom side, with Molloy recording 17 score involvements to set a new AFLW mark. The Guardian noted the turnaround mattered because fans of Australian rules football in the Harbour City have a reputation for being fickle.



---


# AFLW Longer Quarters And Interchange Cap Rule Changes

In a bid to improve the spectacle of the AFLW, the league introduced longer quarters and an interchange cap in 2023 to help increase scoring, and according to Nicole Livingstone the effect has been positive.

"We've increased game time by eight minutes per match, on average, and we've had record scores across the rounds," she said on 26 October 2023. "Whereas leading into the season we hadn't scored more than 100 goals in a round, we've regularly been scoring over 100 goals in a round."

Livingstone also said the AFL was happy with the level of competition: "Our ladder, from position five to 13 — there's only a game separating it. It just shows that this is a really competitive competition."



---


# AFLW Crowds Short Of Season-Extension Targets

Average AFLW attendance in 2023 was a little over 2,500 a match — tracking approximately on par with previous seasons, with a finals uptick likely to come — but crowds were short of the targets that could accelerate the extension of the regular season, which grows from 10 games that year to 12 games by 2025.

The league enjoyed strong attendances in round one, partly attributed to the so-called Matildas effect, but some clubs struggled to attract fans in large numbers across the season: crowds of less than 1,500 were recorded in both traditional markets such as Melbourne and Perth and in areas targeted for growth such as Blacktown and the Gold Coast.

Against that backdrop, Nicole Livingstone, general manager of women's football at the AFL, said the Swans' off-field offering had tapped into something "uniquely Sydney" and helped make matches more attractive.



---


# The 'Matildas Effect' And Its Limited Impact On Domestic Women's Sport

The Guardian argued on 26 October 2023 that the popularity of the Matildas' run to the Women's World Cup semi-finals has had only a limited impact on support for domestic women's sport, because the early spike did not persist.

The grounds come from the A-League Women, which launched that month with a first round highlighted by a crowd of more than 11,000 in Sydney — but more modest attendances in subsequent games, including two sub-2,000 crowds in Perth, follow it. The warrant is that a durable effect would show up beyond the opening round; a large first-round crowd followed by small ones is consistent with novelty rather than converted support.

Nicole Livingstone, the AFL's general manager of women's football, made the same point from the league side, saying the "green and gold fever" associated with the Women's World Cup was a one-off and that the AFL has plans in place for long-term growth: "We'll continue to keep building the base and keep building the foundations and have it not just strong at year seven, season eight, but strong for generations to come."



---


# The Western Bulldogs' 2023 AFLW Season

The Western Bulldogs endured a dismal 2023 AFLW season, suffering their biggest-ever defeat — a 57-point loss to Sydney, 14.12 (96) to 6.3 (39), at Whitten Oval — and finishing with a single win, The Age reported on 20 October and 3 November 2023.

That Sydney defeat was the Bulldogs' eighth loss in a row, and they had just two rounds left to clinch a win, next playing 17th-placed West Coast and then top-four side North Melbourne. Richelle Cranston, for whom the Dogs are a third club after starting at Melbourne and having a stint with Geelong before heading to the Bulldogs the previous year, lined up in that match. For the Swans, the victory had them challenging for a top-eight spot alongside the likes of Gold Coast, Geelong, Collingwood, St Kilda and Carlton.

In the final round against the Kangaroos, Britney Gutknecht kicked the Dogs' only goal early in the last term to avoid a record for the lowest AFLW score in the history of the competition. The Dogs have plenty to work on for next season as they look to regain a competitive edge, which was lost after a finals berth the previous year; along with being in a rebuild, they were badly injury-hit that season and used 32 players, more than any other club.



---


# St Kilda's 2023 AFLW Finals Near Miss

St Kilda came within 0.4 of a percentage point of a maiden AFLW finals appearance in 2023: Fremantle ended their four-game streak with a comfortable 24-point win in October, and although the Saints won their do-or-die final-round match, Sydney's victory over the Dockers sealed the last spot, The Age reported on 20 October and 3 November 2023.

The Fremantle defeat was comprehensive. The Dockers dominated from the start to win 6.9 (45) to 3.3 (21) at Fremantle Oval, flying out of the gates from the first siren and producing their highest-scoring quarter of the season with 26 points in the opening term — conversely the most the Saints had conceded in any quarter that season. Aine Tighe set the tone with a brilliant goal less than 30 seconds into the first quarter, followed by two majors from Gabby O'Sullivan and another by Angelique Stannett; Ella Friend slotted a much-needed goal for the visitors to make it 4.2 (26) to 1.3 (9) at quarter-time. With less than a minute till the long break, captain Hayley Miller (two goals) kicked the only major of the second quarter for a 26-point half-time lead, and despite second-half goals from Tyanna Smith and J'Noemi Anderson the Saints struggled to eat into the deficit. Dana East was everywhere for Fremantle, leading the game in disposals (19) and contested possessions (11), alongside Orlagh Lally (19 disposals, five clearances), while Jaimee Lambert was the shining light for the otherwise subdued Saints with a game-high seven clearances and 13 contested possessions. Having been on the verge of making their first finals appearance, St Kilda (4-4) could now miss the top eight even if they beat the fourth-placed Brisbane Lions and the ninth-placed Carlton; Fremantle (4-4) faced reigning premiers Melbourne next before finishing against 11th-placed Sydney.

In the do-or-die match that followed, Georgia Patrikios showed her class with 25 disposals and eight contested possessions in a powerhouse display, while Hannah Priest was a brick wall in defence with nine intercept possessions. Abbie McKay worked overtime to counter Patrikios in the midfield, racking up 28 disposals and 12 clearances alongside Mimi Hill (30 disposals), and defender Keeley Sherar (17) toiled against a potent Saints attack, but her side was outclassed across the park. It was not enough: Sydney prevailed in a fierce tug-of-war with the Dockers to seal their first AFLW finals appearance, coming from four points down at half-time in a low-scoring game, with a third-term goal from Rebecca Privitelli sparking a 5.10 (40) to 2.6 (18) win on the Sunday at Fremantle Oval.

# Geelong Cats' 2023 AFLW Finals Qualification

Geelong secured their spot in the 2023 AFLW top eight and locked in home-ground advantage for the first elimination final with a 40-point win over Hawthorn, 9.6 (60) to 3.2 (20), at GMHBA Stadium, The Age reported on 3 November 2023.

The Cats finished sixth, the win boosting their percentage to a healthy 141.2, almost 40 ahead of Essendon, who sit one rung below them on equal points. Momentum was also in Geelong's favour after two big wins in a row, having demolished Richmond by 38 points the previous weekend. Against the Hawks they controlled ball movement from the get-go, kicking four goals straight to open the match and keeping their opposition goalless to half-time. Chloe Scheer was again the star in front of goals with three majors, and the Cats finished with seven individual goalkickers; Georgie Prespakis (35 touches, eight clearances) and Amy McDonald (23 touches, eight clearances) were a formidable midfield duo, while the retiring Renee Garing had a whopping 11 tackles. Overall it was a strong team effort from a side that will be hungry for a finals win — the previous year the Cats had an impressive home-and-away run but bowed out narrowly in an elimination final to North Melbourne.

Young defender Rebecca Webster had told this masthead earlier in the week how important the home crowd is come knockout finals. "Playing at GMHBA is like a massive advantage for us," said Webster. "We love going in those four walls. We train there three, four times a week. So having that familiarity of the ground is awesome ... So I would be super-excited to make finals for one, but then play at home would be just that extra and having all our support behind us really drives us on the field."

# North Melbourne's 2023 AFLW Top-Four Finish

North Melbourne secured a top-four spot for the 2023 AFLW finals with a one-way win over the Western Bulldogs, played almost entirely in the Roos' attacking half, The Age reported on 3 November 2023.

Star midfielder Ash Riddell had 36 touches and seven clearances and said she was excited to go up against Melbourne or Adelaide in the first weekend of finals depending on other results that round, as they were the only two sides who beat North that year. "I'm excited like I think the group's coming together really nicely and where really well-prepared compared to previous years," Riddell told Fox Footy. # Collingwood-Geelong's Wind And Rain Contest, 2023

Collingwood beat Geelong by six points at Victoria Park in a round-eight AFLW clash decided less by which side was better overall than by which could adapt best to the blustery wind and rain, The Age reported on 20 October 2023.

The Magpies survived a fourth-quarter comeback to stay firmly in finals contention, while the Cats now faced an uphill battle to finish in the eight in two weeks' time. Geelong scored just one point in the first quarter and had only 1.3 on the board at three-quarter-time before kicking two goals to none in the final term to close in. Magpies ruck Sabrina Frederick starred with 39 hit-outs, using her height to bring the ball to ground to the advantage of her midfielders, and said her side had been practising for games like this: "Even in the chaos, it's quite comfortable because we train it. We train what scenarios to do in what moments, and even though it's a bit crazy, it felt so calm. We put players in place and we know what we're doing. But close games are good ones, for everyone. We knew they were going to come out like that [in the last quarter]. When they're down, they're just going to give us everything." Frederick admitted at times she "couldn't see" and felt like she could be "blown away".

Geelong coach Daniel Lowther said the strong winds made it hard for his side to clear the ball out of their defensive 50-metre zone and to move the ball with any certainty around the ground. "At one point the rain hit our box, it was flowing," Lowther said. "Both teams had to fight in the conditions, but it didn't help the game. Our marking contest wasn't too flash, our ground ball representation was a bit hit and miss, so our defence were under a bit more pressure than they should have been, but they fought back really well." Collingwood next play a Sydney line-up including former Magpies star Chloe Molloy, while Geelong take on Richmond at Ikon Park.

# Erin Phillips' AFLW Retirement

AFLW great Erin Phillips played her last game at Alberton Oval, with Port Adelaide saluting her with a huge 58-point win over Greater Western Sydney, 13.10 (88) to 4.6 (30), on the Saturday, The Age reported on 3 November 2023.

The crowd — which included Phillips' father Greg and mother Julie, both in tears after the game, more family and friends, and Adelaide captain Chelsea Randall — erupted as the curtain came down on the three-time premiership player after eight seasons and 67 games. "It was an awesome game and four quarters of Port Adelaide footy … It was awesome to finish up like that," Phillips told Fox Footy after the win. The 38-year-old kicked a momentous goal from a set shot in the final quarter and was smothered by her jubilant teammates afterwards: "I don't think I've been as nervous to kick a goal in my life, to be honest," she joked. "But nah, it was awesome."

Earlier she told the ABC that she wanted her legacy to include doing everything she could to grow the game: "Hopefully I can be remembered as someone who took their opportunities, loved the game and was willing to do whatever it took to ensure the next generation was in a better position." On the same Saturday the competition said goodbye to a range of players including Western Bulldogs forward Richelle Cranston, who has battled stage five chronic kidney disease while playing that season and was chaired off the ground by teammates Isabelle Pritchard and Ellie Blackburn, and Hawthorn's Akec Makur Chuot, who played 40 games for three clubs.

# Caiden Cleary AFL Draft Prospect 2023

Caiden Cleary, profiled in Kevin Sheehan's top 40 for the 2023 AFL Draft as reported by The Roar on Nov. 15, 2023, is an in-and-under player who extracts the ball well from stoppages. State: NSW-ACT. State League Club: Sydney Swans Academy. Community Club: Sydney University. Date of Birth: 05/03/05. Height: 182cm.

His ferocious attack on the ball and his opponent helped set the tone for the Allies to dominate the midfield battle throughout the National Championships, and he was rewarded with All Australian honours. He averaged 29.2 disposals, 11.2 contested possessions and a team-high 6.8 tackles across four matches for the Allies, and showed excellent repeat speed and courage as well as clean hands playing both on the inside and outside. His 6:06 effort in the 2km time trial at the national Draft Combine showcased his elite endurance. He has been part of the Sydney Swans' Academy since the under-10s. Weapon: Contested ball-winning ability. AFL player comparison: Tim Taranto (Richmond).
