# Richmond Tigers' Comeback Win In Cairns, 2023

A late goal by Emelia Yassir helped Richmond to their first win in four games, an 11-point AFLW victory over Hawthorn, 6.5 (41) to 4.6 (30), at Cazaly's Stadium in Cairns on the Friday night, The Age reported on 20 October 2023.

Separated by one point at half-time and down by nine points entering the last quarter, the Tigers kept their finals hopes alive by limiting Hawthorn to just one point in the decisive final quarter. Midfield duo Monique Conti (35 disposals, seven clearances) and Grace Egan (28, 5) were typically influential for Richmond, while Hawthorn were led by Emily Bates (18, four) and Jasmine Fleming (18, one). "Richmond were just absolute beasts, especially their midfielders. They really worked hard all night," Hawthorn coach Bec Goddard said after the game. "Our work rate really dropped off and we just watched them play some really good footy. If you're a Hawks fan, you would've seen some really exciting moments of footy tonight. Keep getting excited. We are coming, we're growing, we're getting better."

Hawthorn's Irish ace Aine McDonagh kicked the opening goal before Tigers skipper Katie Brennan slotted two unanswered majors to celebrate her 50th game in style, and fellow 50-gamer Greta Bodey snatched her own goal before quarter-time. A skirmish erupted in the second term after Brennan took exception to a tackle by Mattea Breed on Laura McClelland; McClelland was gifted a 50-metre penalty following a bump against Sarah Hosking by Sophie Locke and converted from inside the goal square while players were occupied by the tussle. Bridie Hipwell kicked the only goal of the third quarter to give Hawthorn a game-high nine-point lead, before Richmond rebounded in the last term: Courtney Jones ended Hawthorn's three-goal run with her first touch of the night to cut the margin to three points, and Yassir, dogged by inaccuracy in front of goal, reduced the deficit to a single point before finally breaking through on her third attempt to put the Tigers six points ahead with 11 minutes left, after which Caitlin Greiser sealed the win with a massive goal from 45 metres. Elsewhere in the round, the Lions next play St Kilda before taking on reigning premiers Melbourne in the final round, having staked their claim as premiership contenders again, while Adelaide play top-four side North Melbourne next weekend before 18th-placed Western Bulldogs.

# Gold Coast Suns' Second AFLW Finals Appearance

Gold Coast booked their second AFLW finals appearance with a 14-point win over Essendon, 6.3 (39) to 3.7 (25), at Great Barrier Reef Arena on the Friday, finishing the regular season in fifth spot, The Age reported on 3 November 2023.

While their men's side have yet to make a finals appearance, this is the second time Gold Coast's women have clinched a play-off spot, having also done so in the cancelled 2020 season. Losing midfield powerhouse Charlie Rowbottom to an ankle injury proved no obstacle in the Suns' maiden clash with the Bombers, which kicked off pride round: unsung hero Lucy Single filled the Rowbottom-size gap with 25 disposals and six clearances across the field while also playing a crucial tagging role on Maddy Prespakis. The former rugby sevens player was well supported by Claudia Whitford (25 possessions) and Alison Drennan (22 touches). Prespakis was held to eight contested possessions, well below a season average of 14 per game, while Georgia Nanscawen proved a potent threat with 13 contested possessions and three score involvements.

The Bombers broke through first with a goal from Amber Clarke, but young talent Darcie Davies (two goals) responded after being gifted 50 metres from a protected-area infringement by Mia Bush. Daisy D'Arcy, Jacqueline Dupuy, Jamie Stanton and Davies attempted to break away from the low-scoring tug-of-war in the second with goals of their own, but two goals from Amelia Radford and Georgia Gee kept the hosts close, while defender Ellyse Gamble (nine intercept possessions) proved a roadblock for the Suns' attackers. Single lit up the park with a clinical slice through the corridor, dodging two tackles to put the ball in the hands of Georgia Clayden, who capped the centre clearance with the only major of the third term; with both sides goalless in the final quarter, the Suns cruised home.

# Melbourne (Narrm)'s 2023 AFLW Ladder Position

Reigning premiers Narrm reclaimed top spot on the AFLW ladder — and their position as flag favourites — by defeating third-placed North Melbourne by 23 points, 5.7 (37) to 2.2 (14), at Ikon Park on the Saturday night, The Age reported on 20 October 2023.

It was a hard-fought, low-scoring battle between two powerhouse sides that play a similar game style: each set up well, are fast and like a good dose of contested marking. Narrm controlled more of the game by tightening around the contest and being cleaner going forward, and defended extremely well by suffocating the opportunities North created. The Demons scored just one goal a quarter in the second half — Tyla Hanks in the third and Eden Zanker in the fourth — while the Kangaroos were goalless for three terms after leading by five points at the first change, their opening goals coming from Niamh Martin and Tess Craven. A crafty goal from Demons skipper Kate Hore to open the second term put her side up, and Melbourne never gave up the lead.

Hanks was pivotal for the Demons with 26 disposals, seven tackles and one goal, while her midfield partner Olivia Purcell had 28 touches, five clearances and five tackles. For the Roos, Ash Riddell led the disposal count with 31, and skipper Emma Kearney was crucial in defence. Hanks said that with the state of the competition they just had to take it week by week, but it was good to get the win: "We knew we were up against the best tonight. It's a nice feeling tonight."

# West Coast Eagles' Upset Win Over Essendon, 2023

West Coast withstood a late surge from Essendon to claim their second win of the 2023 AFLW season, 3.5 (23) to 2.7 (19), in a slugfest at the appropriately named Windy Hill on the Sunday, The Age reported on 20 October 2023.

The win came in a difficult week for the club. Eagles coach Michael Prior had caused controversy with comments following the previous week's 70-point loss to Melbourne, blasting the decision to pit strugglers West Coast against the defending premiers: "How we play that team is beyond me. That is what you get when you get fixturing like that." He later backtracked, but his comments put added pressure and focus on his team. "We've had a horror week back at home, and it's been really bloody tough on all of us, and Mick as well. I'm just really proud of the girls," West Coast captain Emma Swanson said post-game on the broadcast. "I can name the whole team. Everyone had their second in the last couple minutes. That was such a team effort, everyone had a moment there when they had to put their head over the footy and lay a tackle and not let it slip."

Aisling McCarthy and Amy Franklin drew first blood for West Coast within the opening five minutes while the hosts were kept goalless; the Bombers added only three behinds in the second term and the Eagles failed to score as the blustery conditions took their toll. Kellie Gibson broke the goal drought with the only major of the third quarter, before the home side came to life with the wind at their backs in the final term, skipper Bonnie Toogood and Amber Clarke reducing the margin to four points. Toogood continued to pepper the scoreboard, but the Eagles held on. Swanson (25 disposals, eight clearances) stood out, while Bombers workhorse Maddy Prespakis (30 disposals, nine clearances) was typically prominent alongside Georgia Nanscawen (21, six). With two rounds left, West Coast had a chance to build a winning streak against bottom-of-the-table Western Bulldogs; Essendon, slipping one place to sixth, had must-win matches against Carlton and Gold Coast on the road to the finals, and would be without Steph Cain, sidelined with a concussion after an elbow to the head from Swanson.

# Adelaide 36ers Beat Perth Wildcats 89-78 In Round 4

The Adelaide 36ers told each other some hard truths before responding in style with an 89-78 victory that handed the Perth Wildcats a third straight defeat, reported on Oct. 19, 2023.

Sitting in bottom spot with one win from five games coming into the match, and having lost at home to the Phoenix on the Thursday night, the 36ers players got together to draw a line in the sand. It worked: their effort, energy and desperation were dramatically improved against Perth, as was the execution and a focus on getting Isaac Humphries more involved inside. Humphries put up 26 points and eight rebounds in a match-winning performance, and coach CJ Bruton's shortening of the rotation to just eight players worked too. "We met as a playing group yesterday and talked through a lot of stuff," Humphries said. "We just wanted to come out today and put into action everything we talked about. We executed what the coaches needed from us tonight and we executed what we, as a playing group, wanted to execute as well."

The third straight defeat left the Wildcats struggling at 2-4 for the season. Coach John Rillie was focused on knowing they aren't playing well and that the improvement needs to start offensively: "We're not playing good basketball at this point in time. # Concert Tour

## Definition

In the corpus, a concert tour is the live, multi-city, multi-date run of shows an artist performs — such as Taylor Swift's "ongoing 'Eras Tour'" and Beyoncé's "Renaissance" tour — that generates its own ticket revenue and can later be packaged, using footage from those shows, into a companion concert film for theatrical release.

## Context

In the corpus the term names both a live-event undertaking and, increasingly, the commercial engine behind an associated concert film: Taylor Swift's "ongoing 'Eras Tour'" is described as a 151-date stadium tour projected to gross about $1.4 billion, while Beyoncé's "Renaissance" tour is described as a "39-city, 56-show" run that "kicked off in Stockholm, Sweden in May and ended in Kansas City, Missouri in the fall" and made over $500 million while drawing over 2.7 million concertgoers.
Both artists' tours are directly tied to concert films — Swift's "Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour" and Beyoncé's "Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé" — which theatrical distributors built around footage and momentum from the live tour itself, so the tour functions in the corpus as the originating live event that a concert film later packages for wider audiences.
The corpus also frames touring as increasingly inaccessible: "concert tickets are more expensive than ever," with "inflation, Ticketmaster's monopolistic practices, and increased demand after COVID-related touring delays" cited as causes, and tours are described as never having been accessible to everyone because "geography, economics, health and safety concerns, and physical or mental ability" make stadium and arena concerts infeasible for large parts of a fanbase.

- **Multi-city, multi-date structure** — Swift's Eras Tour spans 151 dates and Beyoncé's Renaissance tour spans 39 cities and 56 shows, both crossing international markets.
- **Repeatable show format** — each Eras Tour concert "spans over 180 minutes, with more than 40 songs from at least nine albums and 16 costume changes," performed against a fixed setlist that Swift memorized by "singing the entire set list out loud" during preparation.
- **Major revenue driver** — the Eras Tour is projected to gross roughly $1.4 billion and the Renaissance tour made over $500 million, figures separate from and larger than the box-office receipts of either artist's related concert film.
- **Rising ticket-access barriers** — average North American Eras Tour resale prices reportedly rose to $3,801, a "2,321% increase" over Swift's 2018 Reputation Stadium Tour average of $157, driven by inflation, resale-market dynamics, and pandemic-era touring delays.
- **Physical toll on performers** — Swift described committing to play a show "whether I'm sick, injured, heartbroken, uncomfortable, or stressed" absent "force majeure," and the tour's Rio de Janeiro leg was disrupted by a heat wave following a fan's death during a performance.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, a concert tour is generally defined as a series of concerts by an artist or group of artists in different cities, countries, or locations, often named to distinguish one tour from another and to link a particular tour with a specific album or product. # Comparing "Renaissance" And "The Eras Tour" As Concert Films

The two 2023 concert films sit at different scales and, in Comscore analyst Paul Dergarabedian's framing, should not be compared too closely: "Renaissance" opened at $21 million against the $92.8 million debut of "Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour" in October, yet both figures dwarf the previous concert-film ceiling, and the tours behind them differ by roughly a factor of three in gross.

The structural relations are these. No one expected "Renaissance" to match "The Eras Tour," which was wrapping up its theatrical run with over $250 million globally; prior to Swift, the biggest concert film debuts — titles held by Miley Cyrus and Justin Bieber for their 2008 and 2011 films — had not surpassed the unadjusted sum of $32 million, so $21 million remains a very good start for a concert film. On the touring side, the 39-city, 56-show "Renaissance" tour kicked off in Stockholm, Sweden in May and ended in Kansas City, Missouri in the fall, making over $500 million and attracting over 2.7 million concertgoers, while Swift's ongoing 151-date "Eras Tour" was expected to gross some $1.4 billion. "To have two concert films topping the chart in a single year is pretty unprecedented," Dergarabedian said. The limit of the comparison is his own: "Taylor Swift was a total outlier and the result of a very specific set of circumstances. These two films are similar in genre only."

# Box Office

## Definition

Box office, as used throughout the corpus, is the reported revenue figure for a film's ticket sales, cited either as a single weekend's opening or debut number or as a cumulative running gross toward a domestic or global total.
Beyoncé's "Renaissance" is described as having "topped the box office" with "a $21 million debut" from North American ticket sales on its opening weekend (doc_0173), and "Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour" is tracked the same way, launching with "$100 million" in advance sales (doc_0419) and later "surpass[ing] $250m at the global box office" (doc_0046).

## Context

The corpus reports box office in two recurring ways: as a snapshot of a single weekend's ranking (who "topped the box office" that weekend) and as a running cumulative gross that signals a film's overall commercial success or failure.
Concert films sit alongside conventional theatrical releases in this reporting: "Renaissance" and "The Eras Tour" are both measured in the same box-office terms as scripted films like "The Batman" (doc_0081) or Scorsese's "Killers of the Flower Moon" (doc_0192), and both were distributed through a direct deal with AMC Theatres rather than a traditional studio (doc_0419).
2023 industry-wide box office is also used as a barometer of the theatrical exhibition business: analyst Dergarabedian expected the two concert films to help lift the North American box office "to more than $9 billion in 2023," up from "$7.4 billion" in 2022 (doc_0419), and the "Barbenheimer" pairing of Barbie and Oppenheimer is credited with dominating "the 2023 box office and the cultural discussion" (doc_0094).
The term also appears in retrospective judgments of a film's commercial fate: Scorsese and De Niro's "The King of Comedy" (1983) is described as having been "a flop at the box office" despite positive reviews (doc_0193), while Tobe Hooper's "The Texas Chain Saw Massacre" (1974) "made over $30 million at the box office on a budget of around $140,000" (doc_0563), illustrating the term's use for both underperformance and outsized return relative to cost.

## Key Characteristics

- **Reported as a debut and as a cumulative total** — outlets cite both a single weekend's opening number (e.g., "$21 million debut," doc_0173) and a running gross accumulated over a film's release (e.g., "surpassed $250m," doc_0046).
- **Ranking-based** — weekend box office is reported competitively, with films described as "topping" or "ruling" the box office relative to other new releases that same weekend (doc_0173).
- **Applies to concert films alongside scripted releases** — the corpus tracks Beyoncé's and Taylor Swift's concert films using the same box-office vocabulary and comparisons applied to traditional Hollywood films (doc_0173, doc_0419, doc_0081, doc_0192).
- **Used as both a success and failure signal** — the same term describes a "flop" (doc_0193) and a low-budget film's outsized return (doc_0563), as well as a blockbuster's records (doc_0046, doc_0419).
- **Aggregated into industry-wide totals** — individual films' box office performance feeds into annual North American or global box-office totals used to gauge the health of theatrical exhibition (doc_0419, doc_0094).

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "box office" as industry shorthand for a film's ticket-sales revenue without ever defining the term itself.
Outside the corpus, a "box office" (or "ticket office") is literally a place where tickets are sold to the public for admission to an event; by extension, the term is used, especially in the film industry, as a metonym for the amount of business a production earns, and total movie ticket sales have been termed "box office" since at least 1904 (Wikipedia, *Box office*, accessed 2026-09-02).

"Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé" opened in first place at the North American box office with $21 million in ticket sales, according to estimates from AMC Theatres released Sunday and reported by Fortune on 2023-12-03.

# The Masters Dispute And The "Taylor's Version" Re-Recordings

When music mogul Scooter Braun acquired Taylor Swift's longtime label, Big Machine Records, in 2019, he also gained the rights to the master recordings of Swift's first six studio albums; in November 2020 Braun sold those masters to an investment fund in a deal believed to be worth over $300 million. Swift responded by re-recording her catalogue, and by the end of 2023 had released four "Taylor's Version" albums: Fearless (Taylor's Version) in April 2021, Red (Taylor's Version) in November 2021, Speak Now (Taylor's Version) in July 2023, and 1989 (Taylor's Version) in October 2023.

The Independent suggests it was that decision to re-record the catalogue that catapulted Swift into her 2023 success. Asked by Time about the success of her tour, Swift traced it back to two ordeals: "It's not lost on me that the two great catalysts for this happening were two horrendous things that happened to me. ---


# The Eras Tour's Scale And Taylor Swift's Preparation Regimen

Each Eras Tour concert spans over 180 minutes, with more than 40 songs drawn from at least nine albums and 16 costume changes, and in 2023 alone the career-spanning tour broke records and is estimated to have grossed over $1.4bn. The accompanying concert film, the Eras Tour movie, surpassed $250m at the global box office after its October opening weekend, and Swift's rumoured relationship with Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce caused a 400 per cent spike in NFL jersey sales.

Swift told Time what preparing for a show of that length required. "Every day I would run on the treadmill, singing the entire set list out loud," she said. "Fast for fast songs, and a jog or a fast walk for slow songs." She also stopped drinking and underwent three months of dance training, which she admitted is "not my strong suit." After a run of shows she takes a day to rest and recover: "I do not leave my bed except to get food and take it back to my bed and eat it there. It's a dream scenario."



---


# Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour Concert Film

"Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour," compiled from several Swift shows at Southern California's SoFi Stadium and directed by Sam Wrench, debuted on Friday, 2023-10-13, with advance ticket sales worldwide already past $100 million and an opening expected to launch at $100 million or possibly more. Movie theaters readied for an onslaught like they had never seen before: Swifties would descend, and dancing would be encouraged. By 2023-11-07 the almost three-hour film was the highest-grossing concert film of all time.

The film exists because the live tour was out of reach for most fans. Swift's camp was motivated to get it out even as her stadium tour continues internationally; the tour, projected by Pollstar to gross some $1.4 billion, crashed Ticketmaster's site, saw sky-high resale mark-ups and left many fans priced out. In July, Pitchfork reported that the average cost of a ticket for the North American leg was $3,801 — a 2,321% increase from her 2018 Reputation Stadium Tour, where the average resale price for North American shows was $157. The movie would be a way for millions more to experience the Eras Tour, offering up-close, intimate access to a show they never would have been able to attend otherwise, with adult tickets sold at $19.89 — a reference to her birth year and 2014 album, a re-recording of which was due out Oct. 27 — higher than the average movie ticket but several thousand less than many tickets to see Swift live, and with no Ticketmaster queue to wait in.

The release broke several theatrical norms. It arrived uncommonly fast, just a little over two months after the SoFi shows; speed was one reason Swift's father, Scott Swift, is said to have sought out a direct deal with AMC. Swift produced the film herself and, with 274 million followers on Instagram, didn't need a studio to promote it. After a premiere in Los Angeles on Wednesday, 2023-10-11, there were no advance screenings until the movie began playing at 6 p.m. local time Friday — where most wide-release movies open with Thursday showings and Friday daytime screenings.



---


# Concert Films Flatten The Fandom Hierarchy

Polygon argues that attending a concert in person does not make you a bigger fan, and that concert films are levelling the field by dropping some of the barriers of price, location, and accessibility — which is why they increasingly look like the future of pop music fandom.

The grounds start with what fans go for. The writer says she goes to a BTS concert to see BTS perform but also to be among other BTS fans who already understand why she cares so much about a Korean boy band: they trade freebies and photocards, help each other set up lightsticks, and share favorite songs or members. That sense of belonging is available whether in a stadium in Korea or a cinema at her local mall. The second ground is who actually gets in: fans able to attend the stadium and arena concerts of the biggest musical artists in the world are not necessarily more passionate — they just have a combination of luck and privilege that others lack — so using in-person attendance to enforce a fandom hierarchy misreads what it measures. She notes that BTS, Taylor Swift, and Beyoncé, whose concert film Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé hits theaters in December, all have massive fandoms that are geographically scattered and often stigmatized by a mainstream culture that belittles female-driven fan culture, and that in a time when in-person community is harder to come by and can mean pushing people's financial or physical limits, a filmed concert can feel like a gift. The conclusion is qualified: concert films may not be the future of pop music for everyone, but they are increasingly the future of pop music fandom — and that is a good thing, because pop music fandom is a way to find collective joy and connection in art, and anyone who wants in should be able to join the party.



---


# The AMC-Taylor Swift Direct Distribution Deal

Two of the biggest stars on the planet — Taylor Swift, and Beyoncé in December under a very similar arrangement — are heading into cinemas in first-of-their-kind deals made directly with AMC Theaters that circumvent Hollywood studios and which, for now, leave streamers waiting on the sidelines. The relation that defines the model is the revenue split and the window: ticket sales will be split 43% with theaters and 57% shared by Swift and AMC, with the lion's share of that going to Swift, and the film will play exclusively in theaters for at least 13 weeks — longer than many Hollywood releases do now.

AMC CEO Adam Aron has called the deal "a coup for AMC" on social media. Both AMC and representatives for Swift declined to discuss the film's release, so the terms above are the extent of what the parties have put on the record as of 2023-10-10.



---


# Biggest Concert Films: The Box Office Records

"Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour" is poised to become the biggest concert film ever in about two days of release, as of 2023-10-10. Not accounting for inflation, the mark belongs to 2011's "Justin Bieber: Never Say Never," which took $73.1 million across its entire run.

Accounting for inflation, the comparison is much harder: it will be more difficult for "The Eras Tour" to catch "Woodstock," which grossed $50 million in 1970, a total that translates to nearly $400 million today.



---


# Theatrical Exhibition Innovation During Industry Disruption

Paul Dergarabedian, senior media analyst for data firm Comscore, argues that disruption is itself the engine of change in exhibition: "Innovation comes out of challenging times in this business. We're seeing a lot of changes, some subtle, some not so subtle." His reading of the current moment is that the old constraints have lapsed — "It seems like, right now, there are no rules when it comes to being successful."

The conclusion he draws for theaters is a widening of what belongs on their screens: "It really opens up the idea that other types of content can play really well in a movie theater."



---


# The Paramount Consent Decrees And Their Termination

The Paramount consent decrees were antitrust restrictions governing movie distribution that regulated divisions between exhibition and distribution for more than 70 years. They were terminated in 2020 at the urging of the Department of Justice, with a two-year sunset period that ran until 2022 — which is what facilitated some of the changes now reshaping theatrical release, such as a movie distributed by a theater chain.

"Innovation had effectively been stunted," says Makan Delrahim, the former antitrust chief at the Justice Department who proposed ending the consent decrees. He believes "Taylor Swift: The Eras Tour" — as a movie distributed by a theater chain, with nontraditional ticket prices — could "fuel new business models to save the exhibitors." "There will be more appetite to experiment different models for theatrical distribution," Delrahim says. "The industry needs it and, frankly, so do consumers."



---


# Taylor Swift Named Time's 2023 Person Of The Year

Time named Taylor Swift its 2023 Person of the Year, announcing the choice on Wednesday 6 December 2023. The magazine said the honour followed an "editors' assessment of the individual who most shaped the headlines over the previous 12 months, for better or for worse," and explained its selection this way: "While her popularity has grown across the decades, this is the year that Swift, 33, achieved a kind of nuclear fusion: shooting art and commerce together to release an energy of historic force." She was chosen from a strong list of contenders that included Chinese President Xi Jinping, King Charles III, the live-action Barbie movie, and Vladimir Putin.

The recognition came at the end of a whirlwind year in which her Eras Tour dominated ticket sales. Swift told Time: "This is the proudest and happiest I've ever felt, and the most creatively fulfilled and free I've ever been. Ultimately, we can convolute it all we want, or try to overcomplicate it, but there's only one question... Are you not entertained?"



---


# US Weekend Box Office Top Ten, Early December 2023

Comscore's estimated Friday-through-Sunday ticket sales at U.S. and Canadian theaters for the first weekend of December 2023 ranked "Renaissance: A Film by Beyoncé" first at $21 million, ahead of "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" at $14.5 million and "Godzilla Minus One" at $11 million.

The remainder of the top ten ran: 4. "Trolls Band Together," $7.6 million; 5. "Wish," $7.4 million; 6. "Napoleon," $7.1 million; 7. "Animal," $6.1 million; 8. "The Shift," $4.4 million; 9. "Silent Night," $3 million; 10. "Thanksgiving," $2.6 million. These were estimates only — final domestic figures were to be released Monday.



---


# Movie Theaters' Pivot To Alternative Content

The mechanism that turned the once declared-for-dead multiplex into the go-to place for stars previously at home on Netflix is a supply problem meeting a format opportunity. When studios began diverting some of their titles to streaming platforms, movie theaters began thinking harder about how they could fill their screens — a question exacerbated in autumn 2023 by an actors strike that led to the postponement of big releases like "Dune: Part Two." Movie theaters are increasingly not just a marquee of movie showtimes but a big-screen stage for a variety of visual media: BTS released a concert film earlier in 2023 with higher ticket prices and limited showtimes, and the Metropolitan Opera has for years done popular live broadcasts in theaters.

Concert films are not themselves new — just the month before, the Talking Heads classic "Stop Making Sense" returned to theaters for a decades-later encore — but "The Eras Tour" heralds something new and potentially game-changing in the movie industry. The scope condition is important: few acts can do what Swift and Beyoncé can, and their expected success is unlikely to be replicated. Still, "The Eras Tour" could be the start of an expansion of what a movie theater can be — think the Sphere, only much cheaper and in most towns.

Greg Marcus states the underlying business redefinition: "You could say we're in the movie business, but really we're in the getting-together-with-other-people business. The more we do of it, the more the customers will think about it and the more talent will go: This is something I could do."



---


# The Rio Postponement And The Death Of An Eras Tour Fan

A heat wave in Brazil forced Taylor Swift to postpone the second night of her Eras Tour shows in Rio de Janeiro in late 2023. The decision came after one of her fans, 23-year-old Ana Clara Benevides, died from a cardiac arrest during Swift's first performance in the country.

Swift told Time that performing for her fans regardless of circumstance is "part of my identity as a human." She said: "I know I'm going on that stage whether I'm sick, injured, heartbroken, uncomfortable, or stressed. That's part of my identity as a human being now. If someone buys a ticket to my show, I'm going to play it unless we have some sort of force majeure."



---


# The Original 1989: Grammy Wins, Chart Longevity And A $250m Tour

The original 1989 became Taylor Swift's biggest-selling album to date despite being seen as a risk by her record label, won three Grammy Awards including Album of the Year, and has spent 325 weeks in the UK charts. Its supporting tour sold 2.2 million tickets and earned more than $250m at the box office, with almost the entire album played every night.

Featuring hits like Shake It Off, Blank Space and Style, the album was originally written during the 2013-14 Red Tour, with demos stored on Swift's phone in a folder named "Sailor Twips". Deluxe editions came with collectible Polaroids featuring Taylor's favourite lyrics. In 2015, she was one of the main stage headliners at Radio 1's Big Weekend.



---


# Holdover Performance Of Hunger Games, Trolls, Wish And Napoleon

On the first weekend of December 2023 the holdover titles behind "Renaissance" were led by Lionsgate's "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes," which fell to second place in its third weekend with an estimated $14.5 million and had by then earned over $121 million domestically.

"Trolls Band Together" landed in fourth place in its third weekend with $7.6 million, bringing its domestic total to $74.8 million. Fifth place went to Disney's "Wish," which fell 62% from its underwhelming first weekend, taking $7.4 million from 3,900 locations for a global total of $81.6 million. Disney's other major film in theaters, "The Marvels," was also winding down in its fourth weekend with a disastrous global tally of $197 million against the reported $300 million it cost to make and market the superhero film. In its second weekend, Ridley Scott's "Napoleon" earned an estimated $7.1 million from 3,500 locations; produced by Apple Original Films and distributed by Sony Pictures, the film starring Joaquin Phoenix had then made $45.7 million domestically against a $200 million budget.



---


# Taylor Swift Re-Records 1989 To Regain Control Of Her Masters

On Friday, Taylor Swift released a new version of 1989 — the biggest-selling album of her career and the record that definitively turned her into a pop star — re-recorded as the latest instalment of an ongoing campaign to regain control of her work after an investment company bought her master tapes in 2019. The BBC reported this on 13 October 2023, with the article itself noting a publication date of 27 October for the album's return.

This re-recording is described as the biggest and riskiest part of the project. Earlier remakes in the campaign were largely made with a live band, whereas 1989's pop landscapes are full of squelchy, processed synths and treated vocals, which makes them harder to reproduce faithfully. Alongside the re-recorded album, fans can hear five new tracks from the star's vault, expanding on the themes and relationships she explored on the original. The artwork for the re-recorded version has a beach vibe, in contrast to the Polaroid aesthetics of the original.



---


# BTS Yet To Come Concert Film

In February, K-pop septet BTS released a filmed version of their "Yet to Come" concert — a one-night-only performance for 50,000 fans in Busan, South Korea — and the concert film made more than $50 million worldwide.

The figure is notable because the show had already been given away once: it was previously streamed via the Korean platform Weverse, allowing a reported 49 million fans to watch at home. Polygon reports the theatrical release still cleared $50 million after that.



---


# Concert Film Versus Live Concert

Polygon's writer argues that seeing a concert film in a movie theater is not the same as attending a live concert but is not an inherently lesser experience either — a claim she grounds in having attended the BTS Yet to Come concert both in person and in cinemas.

Her case is that the concert film has value past its re-creation of a specific intersection of place, time, and performance: she went to theaters to relive a once-in-a-lifetime show, but the film version was also its own unique collective fan experience. The practical advantages she names are arriving at the theater just 20 minutes before showtime, being able to go with all her BTS fan friends this time, and watching in a theater full of fellow fans with BTS lightsticks in hand and a BT21 Tata headband on head, which gave the same sense of fandom camaraderie as the in-person concert. She concedes the losses: she missed some of the freedom of the in-person experience, such as choosing where to direct her attention across an expansive stage bedecked with intricate sets calling back to different eras in BTS history. But she argues the clarity and focus of detail in the film evened the score, giving a much closer view of the choreography and the members' interaction with a close-up camera intimacy she had not gotten in person, and letting her share those fandom moments not only with her cinema audience but with millions of other fans viewing the same film around the world. She adds that Yet to Come would stream on Amazon Prime Video starting November 9, further expanding the number of fans able to see it.



---


# Conditions At The BTS Busan Concert

Polygon's writer, who attended the Yet to Come show in Busan, reports that getting 50,000 people into a 20-year-old stadium was not simple: by the time BTS took the stage, most attendees had been in line for hours with limited access to bathrooms, water, or information about what was going on.

Once the concert started, conditions in the 3,000-strong standing areas got intense as fans pushed toward the stage, crowding people at the front and prompting BTS to alter plans to come down into the audience for their performance of their 2018 hit "IDOL." The writer notes this was not her first chaotic, stressful in-person stadium concert experience and doubts it will be her last, and states the scope condition plainly: she is able and willing to make that trade for the chance to see her favorite musical group perform, but not everyone is, even if they could get tickets.



---


# Barriers To Attending Live Concerts

Polygon models rising barriers to live concert attendance as the driver behind concert films finding expansive new footing: the harder it becomes to attend in person, the more the filmed version has to do.

On the price side, concert tickets are more expensive than ever, with inflation, Ticketmaster's monopolistic practices, and increased demand after COVID-related touring delays coinciding to create what the piece calls a perfect storm of ticket-buying agony. Beneath price sits a structural constraint that predates it: tours were never accessible to everyone, because geography, economics, health and safety concerns, and physical or mental ability make stadium and arena concerts — held only in major metropolitan areas, and only in certain countries — infeasible or unaffordable for large swaths of global pop music fandom. The third variable is demand: as fandom's role as a source of identity and community becomes more precious and more people than ever want to see certain concerts, the pressure on a fixed supply of seats increases while the barriers rise.



---


# Taylor Swift's Stated Approach To Public Scrutiny

Taylor Swift told Time in December 2023 that she has nothing to hide in her relationship with Travis Kelce, and defined what she means by a public relationship: "When you say a relationship is public, that means I'm going to see him do what he loves, we're showing up for each other, other people are there and we don't care. The opposite of that is you have to go to an extreme amount of effort to make sure no one knows that you're seeing someone. And we're just proud of each other." Although her love life makes headlines with every Kansas City Chiefs game she attends, the "Blank Space" singer said she is focused on being there for her partner rather than on concealing the relationship.

On scrutiny more broadly, the "Anti-Hero" singer said she tries not to let the paparazzi get to her even though so many of her outings with friends become headlines: "Over the years, I've learned I don't have the time or bandwidth to get pressed about things that don't matter. Yes, if I go out to dinner, there's going to be a whole chaotic situation outside the restaurant. But I still want to go to dinner with my friends." She described the change in her perspective over time: "Life is short. Have adventures. Me locking myself away in my house for a lot of years — I'll never get that time back. I'm more trusting now than I was six years ago."



---


# Travis Kelce's WSJ Magazine Interview on Swift

In an interview with WSJ Magazine published on 20 November 2023, Travis Kelce described how much he admires Taylor Swift's skills as a musician and said he was not letting media attention affect the relationship.

"I've never been a man of words. Being around her, seeing how smart Taylor is, has been f***ing mind-blowing. I'm learning every day," he explained. Kelce acknowledged the public attention his personal life had received because he has "never dated anyone with that kind of aura around them", but specified that he was not letting the media affect his relationship.

"But at the same time, I'm not running away from any of it," he said. "The scrutiny she gets, how much she has a magnifying glass on her, every single day, paparazzi outside her house, outside every restaurant she goes to, after every flight she gets off, and she's just living, enjoying life. When she acts like that I better not be the one acting all strange."



---


# HSF's Q4 2023 Catalogue Revenue Drivers

Away from the governance dispute, MBW reported on 19 December 2023 that Hipgnosis Songs Fund is enjoying quite a fanciable Q4 in the real world of the music business. The company is benefitting from its cuts on hit albums including Taylor Swift's "1989 (Taylor's Version)", via its acquired Jack Antonoff catalog, as well as Swift's "Lover", via its acquired Joel Little catalog.

Its investments in seasonal Christmas evergreens continue to pay off too, with cuts on Michael Bublé's Christmas album and, most famously, a share of Mariah Carey's perennial megahit "All I Want For Christmas Is You".



---


# Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift Dating Rumours in 2023

Speculation that Travis Kelce and Taylor Swift were dating began in July 2023, when Kelce confessed that he had tried and failed to give Swift a friendship bracelet bearing his phone number at one of her Eras Tour concerts; he later invited her on his podcast to one of his games at Arrowhead Stadium, an invitation she famously accepted on 24 September 2023, and she had attended three more of his games by 25 November 2023.

Kelce first told the bracelet story to his brother on their podcast back in July. "I was disappointed that she doesn't talk before or after her shows, because she has to save her voice for the 44 songs that she sings," he explained. "So I was a little butthurt I didn't get to hand her one of the bracelets I made for her. If you're up on Taylor Swift concerts, there are friendship bracelets and I received a bunch of them being there, but I wanted to give Taylor Swift one with my number on it."

The NFL star officially addressed the dating rumours during an episode of The Pat McAfee Show on 21 September 2023, in which he mocked his brother Jason Kelce for joking that he "100 per cent" believed his younger sibling was dating Swift. "It's hilarious how much traction this has actually gotten, right now it's like a game of telephone," Kelce said. "Where everybody's whispering in each other's ears and hearing random stuff. No one actually knows what's going on, especially when you got Jason Kelce on live television telling people just both sides - he doesn't know, it's true, this and that." He also said he remained open to pursuing a relationship with Swift, revealing that he had subtly asked whether she would attend one of his games: "I threw it out there, I threw the ball in her court. I told her, you know, I've seen you rock the stage in Arrowhead [Stadium], you might have to come see me rock the stage in Arrowhead and see which one's a little more lit. So, we'll see what happens in the near future."



---


# Marcus Corporation's Preparations For Eras Tour Screenings

Greg Marcus, chief executive and chair of the Marcus Corporation, headquartered in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, has been in the movie business for years but never expected to be urging moviegoers to take out their phones during a film — let alone crafting friendship bracelets in preparation for an opening weekend. In a promotion for his theater chain, he strings beads together while humming "Shake It Off."

"This is different," says Marcus. "Take your phone out. Take selfies. Dance, sing, get up, have a good time. We want to create an atmosphere." In his theaters, like many other chains, there will be friendship bracelet stations, and sound systems have been modified for more of a concert feel. While Marcus grants it will be strange to see an AMC logo before a film playing in his theaters, he doesn't particularly mind: "I'm just happy it's there."



---


# Taylor Swift And Joe Alwyn's Relationship And Breakup

In April 2023 it was revealed that Taylor Swift and British actor Joe Alwyn had broken up after six years of dating. The former couple were notoriously private: the Conversations with Friends star had previously said he did not want to discuss the relationship because doing so "feeds into a weird part of the culture."

Even so, the relationship generated constant rumours about Swift's personal life — enough that her publicist, Tree Paine, was forced to publicly deny some of them. Swift, arguably more famous now than ever before, said the constant attention and swarms of paparazzi would not stop her from living her life.

# Amazon Kindle Kids Edition Deal Listings

The Kindle Kids appears in The Verge's 2023 kids gift guide at $119.99 (Amazon, Best Buy) and in WIRED's Prime Day roundup at a price matching what it saw in July for the best Kindle for kids.

The Verge describes the latest Kindle Kids (2022) as offering young readers a sharp 6.2-inch display with adjustable front lighting, USB-C charging, and a battery lasting weeks on a single charge — with the best part being that Amazon's kid-ified ebook reader is ad-free and comes with a two-year warranty against accidental damage plus access to a ton of age-appropriate content. WIRED adds that this model is waterproof with adjustable warm lighting for reading at night, that a Warrior Cats special edition is available for $120, and that the standard Kindle Kids is also on sale and a bit cheaper at $80 ($40 off) but lacks the adjustable warm lighting and waterproofing. Whichever you get, Amazon throws in a protective case, a one-year subscription to Amazon Kids+, and a two-year no-questions-asked replacement guarantee.

# The Amazon Invite-Only Deals System

Invite-only deals are a system Amazon introduced during Prime Day in summer 2023 to make it easier for Prime members to access deals expected to sell out quickly, and the company brought it back for Prime Big Deal Days.

Its scope is limited but broad within that limit: the feature is only available on select products, though it has spread across a variety of categories and price points. The mechanics are simple — if a product is part of the system, a "Request Invite" button appears on the right-hand side, and clicking it gives you a chance to buy at the sale price. The important caveat is that there's no guarantee you'll receive the invite. WIRED points readers to its story on How to Shop Like a Pro During Amazon Prime Day for more on how the program works.



---


# Prime Day 2023 Amazon Echo, Kindle And Fire Deals

WIRED's Prime Big Deal Days roundup covers Amazon's own devices and store promotions: an Echo Dot (5th Gen) bundle that includes a free smart plug, Echo Show 8, Echo Studio, the Kindle Oasis, Kindle Scribe, and the Fire Max 11, alongside Amazon-brand and gift card offers.

On the store offers: a discount applies automatically at checkout once you meet a $40 order threshold on select Amazon-branded products, which range from home essentials like paper towels and batteries to snacks, office supplies, and over-the-counter medicines — an easy way to stock up on frequently used items cheaply. Gift card deals are only worthwhile if you'd be spending the money anyway, but with brands like Doordash, Instacart and Fandango featured, chances are there's a worthy discount; each card has a unique coupon code on its product page to enter at checkout. Amazon also has private-label clearance up to 55 percent off across 10 pages of random cheap items — D-cell batteries for $5, compostable plates for $8, giant crayons for $9, "a truly hideous fanny pack" for $12. On devices: the Echo Dot (5th Gen) is one of WIRED's favorite Alexa speakers, and this deal is especially nice because it comes with a free smart plug that typically sells for about $20 — not the same model, but a similar Kasa plug is the top pick in WIRED's Best Smart Plugs guide. Other Echo Show devices are on sale, but the Echo Show 8 is WIRED's favorite; it comes with a free trial of Alexa Together, an Amazon service aiming to replicate a caregiver's tasks that usually costs $20 per month, so set a reminder to cancel. The Echo Studio is the best-sounding Alexa speaker though pretty expensive, and this price matches a low seen just once before, with more powerful sound overall and changes especially noticeable on the low end. Among e-readers, the other Kindles are more affordable so there's no practical reason to spend on the Oasis unless you love physical page-turn buttons — and WIRED thinks it's probably due for an update soon. The Kindle Scribe (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is the first Amazon e-reader that lets you write on its enormous 10.2-inch screen like a regular notebook, though writing in the margins of books requires sticky notes, which is frustrating given the price (marking up books is better on the Kobo Elipsa). The Fire Max 11 (5/10, WIRED Review) is Amazon's biggest, nicest, and most overpriced Fire tablet, made much more palatable by this deal: the display and new fingerprint sensor are nice, as is using the keyboard without Bluetooth, but Fire OS leaves much to be desired, like a decent app store.



---


# iPad And Kindle Oasis Deals During Prime Big Deal Day

Apple's entry-level 2021 iPad with 64GB and Wi-Fi was $249, down from $329 — 24% off — at both Amazon and Walmart during the anti-Prime Big Deal Day sales.

That 2021 iPad has a 10.2-inch screen, an A13 Bionic chip, and a 12MP front camera that supports Apple's Center Stage feature; it is compatible with the first-gen Apple Pencil and the Smart Keyboard, and is the only iPad that still has a 3.5mm headphone jack. The newer 10th-gen iPad was on sale for $399.99, $50 off, with 64GB of storage and Wi-Fi at Best Buy and Walmart; unlike the last-gen model, the 2022 iPad sports a larger 10.9-inch screen, USB-C support and a faster processor. The 2019 Kindle Oasis with 8GB of storage and ads was available for $199.99, $50 off, at Best Buy; the 7-inch e-reader sports physical page-turning buttons and a waterproof 300ppi E Ink display but lacks the USB-C support found in newer Kindles.



---


# The Kindle Lineup And Ad-Supported Models

Amazon, one of the pioneers of the e-reader, has dominated the space for years with its ever-expanding Kindle lineup, which consists of several unique models with their own pros and cons. The bulk of the devices function as simple ebook readers; with the Kindle Scribe, however, Amazon looks to be moving beyond books and into the realm of writing — something that should make future Kindles function more akin to physical paper. The category itself is defined by what it leaves out: you can always read ebooks on a tablet or a phone, but those devices are multipurpose and can be used for a ton of things like surfing the web or doom-scrolling on Twitter, whereas e-readers, while niche, are designed to store all of your books in a virtual library with limited functionality.

The discriminating option across the lineup is advertising. Kindle e-readers come in different storage configurations, but there is also an additional option to buy the device with or without ads: ad-supported Kindles display personalized advertisements on the lock screen when the device is in sleep mode, or at the bottom of the homescreen when it is connected to Wi-Fi. You typically save about $20 by buying the ad-supported version, and if you decide to remove ads later you can make a one-time payment covering the difference to remove them.

The Verge's October 16th, 2023 guide lists each model currently available, noting that sometimes there is no deal on one or any of the products, in which case it gives the most recent sale price instead. It also flags an alternative route to savings: Amazon offers 20 percent off all of its Kindles when you trade in select devices, so there are still ways to save when no model is discounted.



---


# Kindle 2022 Base Model Deals

Amazon announced a new entry-level Kindle in 2022, designed to replace the 2019 model; starting at $99.99, it puts Amazon's base e-reader more in line with the most recent Kindle Paperwhite, with longer battery life, a 300ppi screen, USB-C charging instead of Micro USB, 16GB of storage by default, and a new "denim" color resembling the soft blue you might associate with jeans.

As of The Verge's October 16th, 2023 roundup, the ad-supported model had recently dropped to $79.99, $20 off, with three months of Kindle Unlimited included — but at the time of writing it could only be bought at Amazon, Best Buy, and Target for its full retail price. A bundle was still discounted: at Amazon, the Kindle with ads, a power adapter, and a fabric cover started at $134.97, $15 off. Regardless of whether you choose the standalone model or the bundle, The Verge wrote, the new Kindle remains a worthwhile option if you are looking to pick up an e-reader for less than the latest Paperwhite.

# Anker 321 Travel Power Strip

The Anker 321 Power Strip was $15, down from $26 — 42 percent off at Amazon. It is an all-in-one 20W USB-C power cube with three AC outlets, two USB-A ports, and one USB-C port, and it is deputy features editor Sarah Jeong's pick.

Her case for it starts from a specific failure. Nobody wants to carry a power strip or extension cord on vacation, and it is probably unnecessary in relatively modern buildings and definitely unnecessary while camping — but sometimes you stay in a charming historical hotel or a lovely cabin in the woods and discover at bedtime that the only electrical socket in the bedroom is in the corner farthest from the bed, with two lamps already plugged into it. Older buildings especially suffer from what she calls loose socket syndrome, where those convenient modern boxy socket extenders with five different USB and USB-C charging ports cannot stay in place and fall right out of the wall because they are too heavy. After one otherwise pleasant vacation spent charging her phone, watch, AirPods, and laptop in a weird corner of the room with the charging hub propped on a strategically balanced mountain of books and sham pillows, she bought this Anker combination extension cord and power strip.

It is not a full power strip — just a cube with a few sockets plus USB and USB-C charging ports at the end of a five-foot cable. It takes up extra space in her suitcase, but each trip has left her feeling vindicated about the purchase.

The design detail that matters is that the three prongs at the end of the cable are static rather than folding flat for easy packing, which is key because the loose sockets of older buildings reject the beautiful convenience of folding prongs. There are more than enough sockets for one person, and with some finagling — and maybe an extra charging brick — it can accommodate two people's devices. If you are traveling overseas, do not forget to buy a different plug type for the region or pack an adapter.

# Battery Life and Charging

## Definition

Battery life and charging is the pair of consumer-electronics specs — how long a device runs on a charge, and how fast and via what connector it refills — that reviewers and shoppers use to compare phones, earbuds, handhelds, smart glasses, and the power banks and cables that feed them.

## Context

Across the corpus, battery life and charging speed function as headline review criteria and buying-guide sort keys rather than a single defined term: Engadget's Steam Deck OLED review leads with "its battery life is better" as one of the device's core upgrades, and The Verge lists "improved battery life and audio" as a top pro for Amazon's third-gen Echo Frames. The charging half of the pair is increasingly organized around USB-C: Engadget notes that Apple's iPhone 15 line and the second-generation AirPods Pro both moved to USB-C charging, and Polygon's portable-charger guide treats USB-C Power Delivery wattage as the key spec for matching a power bank to a phone, tablet, Steam Deck, or laptop. Capacity for power banks is measured in mAh, per Polygon's guide, while device battery life is reported in hours (the Echo Frames reviewer logged about five hours of media playback and calls before hitting 30 percent) or in minutes of measured playtime (Engadget's Steam Deck OLED testing). Gogoro's battery-swapping business shows the same pair of concerns scaled up to electric vehicles: swapping a depleted battery for a charged one at a station is explicitly framed as a way to cut "charging time" relative to plugging in.

## Key Characteristics

- **Duration is measured empirically, not just claimed** — Engadget timed the Steam Deck OLED at four hours 23 minutes playing Hades versus two hours 42 minutes on the original LCD model under identical settings, a 62 percent gain that beat Valve's own 30-to-50-percent claim.
- **Charging speed is a distinct spec from capacity** — Valve advertises the Steam Deck OLED going from 20 to 80 percent in 45 minutes, a speed claim separate from its 50Whr battery capacity; Polygon likewise separates a power bank's mAh capacity from its wattage-based recharge speed.
- **USB-C is displacing proprietary connectors as the charging standard** — Apple's iPhone 15 and USB-C AirPods Pro, and the iPad's shift off Lightning to USB-C on its 10th-generation model, are all cited by Engadget as part of a single connector transition.
- **Power Delivery (PD) wattage governs compatibility between chargers and devices** — Polygon's guide notes that only power banks supporting the PD 3.0 spec can recharge a Steam Deck at its fastest rate, and that a laptop needs PD 3.1 and a compatible cable to reach 140 W charging.
- **Battery swapping is an alternative to plug-in charging at the vehicle scale** — Gogoro's network lets riders exchange a depleted battery for a charged one at a station instead of waiting to charge in place, which TechCrunch frames as a way to reduce charging time for EV adopters.

Rumors point to Apple unveiling more USB-C accessories as it shifts away from the Lightning port, with Gurman suggesting USB-C versions of the Magic Trackpad, Magic Mouse and Magic Keyboard will appear at the event.

This makes a lot of sense given the rest of the lineup. Apple ditched the Lightning port in all iPhone 15 models, started adopting USB-C on iPads several years back, and recently unveiled an Apple Pencil with a USB-C charging port.

The driver is regulatory: the change was prompted by European Union rules requiring a standard charging port on certain devices. Having the same port on all Apple devices and accessories will mean consumers have fewer types of cables to worry about.

# Black Friday / Cyber Monday

## Definition

Black Friday and Cyber Monday are the paired retail sale events — the Friday after the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday and the Monday that follows it — that together anchor the start of the U.S. holiday shopping season, with retailers running discount campaigns across both dates and the days between them.

## Context

Retailers treat the two days less as isolated events than as bookends of a single extended sale window: Engadget reported that Amazon, Target, Best Buy, and Walmart all kicked off Black Friday-branded deals as early as late October 2023, so that "what was once a one-day event filled with limited-time deals has grown into a month-long event with a plethora of sales to sift through each day." Amazon itself began its Black Friday sale on Friday, November 17 — a week ahead of the calendar date — then switched to "Cyber Monday" branding in the early hours of Saturday, November 25, carrying many of the same discounts forward under the new label through the official close on Monday, November 27. Polygon likewise noted that the two named days (November 24 and 27 in 2023) no longer bound when the best prices actually appear, since retailers now front-load doorbuster-style deals across the preceding weeks. The pairing also functions as the header under which media outlets organize their own coverage: The Verge's "under $25" roundup groups both days together as one shopping period with "always a ton of hype about the discounts on big-ticket items."

## Key Characteristics

- **Two named days, one continuous season** — Black Friday (the day after Thanksgiving) and Cyber Monday (the following Monday) are distinct calendar dates, but retailer promotions now span from late October through the Monday close, blurring the boundary between them.
- **Retailer-driven timing shift** — multiple retailers (Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, Target) started Black Friday-branded deals days to weeks before the actual date in 2023, a strategy aimed at spreading out demand rather than concentrating it on one doorbuster day.
- **Deal carryover across the pairing** — items discounted for Black Friday commonly remain discounted, or are re-labeled, once Cyber Monday branding begins, rather than the two events offering wholly separate deal sets.
- **Broad retailer participation** — coverage spans Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and several other retailers, indicating the pairing is not a single-retailer promotion but an industry-wide sale convention.
- **High online-spend period** — the surrounding Thanksgiving-to-Cyber-Monday window ("Cyber Week") is tracked by analytics firms as a major driver of U.S. holiday online sales, with Thanksgiving Day alone producing billions in online spending as the de facto season opener.

# Fraud

## Definition

Fraud, in the corpus's usage, is the criminal or civil charge of knowingly deceiving others — misrepresenting facts, misappropriating funds, or overstating value — for financial gain, and it recurs across the corpus as the central charge in several 2023 prosecutions rather than a single incident.

## Context

The clearest instance is Sam Bankman-Fried's federal trial: he faced seven counts of fraud and conspiracy for his role at collapsed crypto exchange FTX, including wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering and to misuse customer funds, and was ultimately found guilty on all seven counts including wire fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's civil allegation sharpened the charge's scope, framing FTX as a fraud "from the start" with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by [Bankman-Fried's] own misappropriation of customer funds," and U.S. Attorney Damian Williams called the alleged scheme "one of the biggest financial frauds in American history."
Fraud also appears outside crypto: Judge Arthur Engoron ruled in a civil suit brought by New York Attorney General Letitia James that Donald Trump "defrauded banks with 'fantasy'" by deceiving banks and insurers through years of overvaluing his assets and exaggerating his net worth to secure financing — a civil, not criminal, fraud finding that led to rescinded business licenses and continued independent monitoring rather than jail exposure.
A related but distinct offense sits alongside these cases: Binance and CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty not to fraud but to anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, paying $4.3 billion to resolve the charges — the corpus treats this as adjacent misconduct in the same 2023 wave of crypto-industry legal reckonings, but the DOJ's own framing (failing to maintain an anti-money-laundering program, not deceiving victims for gain) keeps it conceptually separate from fraud proper.

## Key Characteristics

- **Deception for gain** — the common thread across cases is knowingly misrepresenting facts (asset values, fund safety, company solvency) to obtain money or credit, as in Bankman-Fried's alleged misappropriation of FTX customer funds and Trump's overvalued asset filings.
- **Criminal and civil tracks both exist** — Bankman-Fried faced criminal wire-fraud and conspiracy counts with prison exposure, while Trump faced a civil fraud finding from Engoron with business-related penalties, not incarceration risk.
- **Often bundled with conspiracy or related charges** — Bankman-Fried's indictment paired substantive fraud counts with conspiracy counts (to commit money laundering, to misuse customer funds) rather than resting on fraud alone.
- **Distinct from anti-money-laundering violations** — Binance/Zhao's guilty plea was for AML program failures and sanctions violations, not for defrauding customers, illustrating that not all crypto-industry 2023 prosecutions in the corpus were fraud cases even though they are often discussed together.

# Testimony At The SBF Trial

Across the first three weeks of the trial, a run of former colleagues, an outside investor and a forensic accounting expert testified that FTX customer money flowed into Alameda Research and out again to other uses, and that FTX's investors were never told about the two firms' special relationship. TechCrunch's running coverage, published 2023-10-06, summarises each week.

In week one, FTX's co-founder and CTO Gary Wang testified Thursday on the extent to which Alameda Research was used for whatever purposes he and SBF saw fit: according to Wang, the crypto trading firm pulled funding directly from FTX customers, whose transactions would be funneled toward Alameda and then directed elsewhere. Thursday also brought testimony from Matt Huang, co-founder and managing partner at crypto investment firm Paradigm, which invested $278 million in FTX across 2021 and 2022 and is part of a class-action lawsuit accusing it and others of defrauding customers by promoting FTX. His testimony centered around being left uninformed about FTX's utilization of customer money to keep Alameda Research afloat — a practice Huang says would have halted his involvement — and covered his relationship with FTX stretching back to 2019.

Week two's standout testimony came from Alameda Research's former CEO Caroline Ellison, who claimed she took $14 billion from customers to repay debts to lenders, using them as a line of credit under the instruction of SBF. Ellison also went into detail about how a $2 billion venture fund, FTX Ventures, was funded by money that had previously been allocated to Alameda from third-party lenders. And though there are no charges of bribery in the case, she also testified to paying Chinese officials $150 million to restore access to $1 billion in frozen trading accounts.

The third week featured a couple of noteworthy moments for the prosecution. FTX's former general counsel Can Sun, like many of SBF's former colleagues, opted to cooperate with authorities and testified that SBF asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy. Robert Boroujerdi, managing director of the hedge fund Third Point, testified about his experience working with SBF and FTX in a partnership that ultimately resulted in a $60 million investment and a lack of awareness about the special relationship between Alameda Research and FTX; had he known of such a relationship, he testified, Third Point would not have invested in FTX in the first place. And earlier in the week, Peter Easton — a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom — testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX: much of that funding came from customers, and Easton testified that he found user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments or direct funding toward political causes and charities.

# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.

# Plea Agreement

## Definition

In the corpus, a plea agreement is the deal by which a criminal defendant (or, in Binance's case, a company) pleads guilty to specified charges in exchange for concessions, rather than going to trial.
It takes effect only once a judge accepts it, and it can bind the party to concrete obligations — cooperating with prosecutors, accepting a recommended fine, stepping back from a role, or admitting specific facts — beyond the bare admission of guilt.

## Context

The corpus shows plea agreements as the mechanism by which several defendants in overlapping 2023 white-collar and criminal cases resolved their charges outside of a trial.
FTX co-founder Gary Wang and Alameda Research CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors, becoming key witnesses against Sam Bankman-Fried at his fraud trial (doc_0010, doc_0086).
FTX engineering head Nishad Singh similarly pleaded guilty to six charges (doc_0121).
Binance CEO Changpeng "CZ" Zhao and Binance itself each entered separate plea agreements with the U.S. Department of Justice, resolving anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations as part of a $4.3 billion settlement (doc_0374, doc_0375).
YouTube parenting influencer Ruby Franke's plea agreement, accepted by a judge, both formalized her guilty plea to child-abuse charges and documented detailed admissions about the abuse itself (doc_0269).
The corpus also shows a distinct but related instrument — the cooperation agreement Gary Wang signed, which specifically obligated him to meet with prosecutors and answer truthfully (doc_0226) — and notes that a witness's incentive to plead guilty and cooperate (the hope of sentencing leniency) is something a defense team can attack on cross-examination (doc_0293).

## Key Characteristics

- **Court acceptance is required** — a judge must accept the plea agreement before it takes effect; Ruby Franke's sentencing was scheduled only after Judge John J. Walton accepted her plea agreement (doc_0269).
- **Negotiated concessions, not just an admission** — the document can specify what each side gives up: Zhao agreed to a recommended $150 million CFTC fine and to not contradict his acceptance of responsibility, while Binance's agreement barred Zhao from any future role at the company for three years and required it to maintain an independent compliance monitor (doc_0374).
- **Can include cooperation with prosecutors** — Wang and Ellison's guilty pleas were paired with plans to cooperate with, and testify for, the prosecution (doc_0010); Wang's cooperation obligations were spelled out in a separate signed agreement (doc_0226).
- **Distinct from pleading not guilty** — a defendant who instead maintains innocence, as Bankman-Fried did, pleads not guilty and proceeds to trial rather than entering a plea agreement (doc_0010).
- **Can contain substantive factual admissions** — Franke's plea agreement recorded specific admitted details of the abuse itself, beyond the bare fact of guilt (doc_0269).
- **Creates a cross-examination target** — because cooperating witnesses who pleaded guilty may hope for sentencing leniency, defense counsel can (and, per the corpus, did) argue this gives them an incentive to shape testimony favorably to the prosecution (doc_0293).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the general legal definition is broader than any single case above: a plea bargain (or plea agreement) is an agreement between a defendant and a prosecutor in which the defendant agrees to plead guilty to some or all of the charges, usually in exchange for a concession from the prosecutor, such as a reduced charge or a more lenient sentencing recommendation.
Source: Legal Information Institute (LII), Cornell Law School, "plea bargain," https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/plea_bargain (accessed 2026-09-02).

# Prosecution And Defense Arguments On Day Two Of The SBF Trial

On the second day of the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX, the prosecution argued that Bankman-Fried knowingly committed fraud, and it grounded that claim in motive: he did so, prosecutors said, to achieve great wealth, power and influence.

The defense countered with the opposite reading of the same conduct. Its claim was that the FTX founder acted in good faith, never meant to commit fraud or to steal, and basically got in over his head — an argument whose warrant is that inexperience and overreach, rather than intent, explain what happened. The two sides therefore contest intent rather than the underlying events, and the reporting on this exchange comes from Rebecca and Jacquelyn in TechCrunch's Week in Review of October 7, 2023, covering day two of the trial only.

# Sam Bankman-Fried's Charges And The Collapse Of FTX

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges.

FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried's frustration with other exchanges while he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. According to the SEC, FTX was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to Alameda, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds."

# FTX's Inner Circle: Family And Friends Implicated

The Verge's October 26th, 2023 account of the trial catalogued how everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world was caught up in the case. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud; "I love you Sam," he had texted at one point, "I'm not going anywhere" — that was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds, at which point he resigned. Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement, saying he had backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors, and pleaded guilty to six charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, told the court about the seven phony balance sheets she had created and was clear that Alameda took customer funds, that Bankman-Fried knew about it, and that he even invested them against her advice.

His family was drawn in too. Joe Bankman, his father, is among the people included in the "small group chat," the Signal group where the FTX inner circle strategized during the exchange's last days. Barbara Fried's political action committee, Mind the Gap, is among the entities that received FTX customer money as political donations; Fried and Bankman lived together in a Bahamas house purchased for them using FTX investor funds, according to a financial expert called by the prosecution, and in a lawsuit filed by FTX's bankruptcy estate the two are alleged to have been given $10 million of FTX customer funds. Gabe Bankman-Fried's nonprofit, Guarding Against Pandemics, got millions from FTX; he was also in a Signal group chat, Donations Processing, that Singh says was used to coordinate the transfer of FTX and Alameda money to various political causes, and in that chat he can be seen recommending that some donations be made "in the dark" to avoid public relations headaches. Singh also said Gabe had an assistant fly to the Bahamas with a stack of blank checks for Singh to sign.

The consequences outlast the trial. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons; even if they never do time — and they may very well be imprisoned or subjected to house arrest — their lives are irrevocably changed, not least by whatever restitution requirements they face, they are barred from taking certain kinds of jobs, and there is the publicity. Bankman, Fried, and Gabe Bankman-Fried's reputations are tarnished, and in the political arenas where they once operated they are suddenly undesirable. Beyond the courtroom, everyone who had money trapped on the exchange when it collapsed — as a result of Alameda purloining customers' funds — had their lives altered: even if they are made whole by the bankruptcy proceedings, that is still money they should have had access to at any time, which may mean houses that were not purchased, medical procedures left undone, and life savings lost. The reporter's summary: it is a Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw, the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.

# VC And Lender Testimony As Collateral Risk For Crypto

The Verge argued that calling lenders, venture capitalists and customers to testify — necessary to establish the basis for some charges — might create collateral damage for the crypto industry beyond Bankman-Fried himself.

The grounds are the shape of the indictment and who it drags in: prosecutors allege that Bankman-Fried lied to FTX investors, so some of those investors may be called on to testify, which is not the kind of thing VC big shots generally enjoy. The worked example is Sequoia Capital: if Sequoia did due diligence around its investment in FTX, whatever Bankman-Fried told its partners could be important — was FTX already sending Alameda customer funds at that point, did Bankman-Fried know, and did he tell the VCs at the time? If he told them it wasn't happening, that would establish intent. Hermine Wong, the former head of policy at Coinbase and a former SEC regulator, adds that Binance was also an early investor in FTX and that former executives may be called on to testify as well.
