# FTX Fraud Charges And The SEC's Allegation

Sam Bankman-Fried, the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX, faced seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy — specifically, two counts of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges — and the Securities and Exchange Commission alleged that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." The Verge repeated this framing at the head of each of its trial dispatches through October 2023, and in its October 28th, 2023 write-up reported that Bankman-Fried had been found guilty on seven counts including charges of wire fraud.

The boundary of the concept is the mix of charge types: the indictment paired substantive wire fraud counts with conspiracy counts rather than resting on a single offence, and the SEC's civil allegation about the exchange's origins ran alongside the criminal case rather than being part of it. The Verge's reporter, writing as the prosecution's case neared its end on October 26th, 2023, added an impression of the people the charges swept in: all the co-conspirators seemed oddly younger than their years, as though they had got stuck in the "math camp forever" environment Bankman-Fried created for them and simply failed to grow up.



---


# Gary Wang's Testimony At The FTX Fraud Trial

Gary Wang, the lesser-known co-founder of FTX, told a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday that he had committed financial crimes while working at FTX — including wire and commodities fraud — carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research and had been Bankman-Fried's girlfriend.

Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?" Wang responded, "Yes." Asked whether he saw any of the people he committed those crimes with in the courtroom, Wang — dressed in an oversized and wrinkled suit with a red tie and glasses — awkwardly stood up, looked around, and answered, "Yes"; asked who, he said, "Sam Bankman-Fried." He was one of two former friends of Bankman-Fried's from MIT who also worked at FTX while living with the founder in the Bahamas and who took the stand that week to testify against their former classmate, confidant and boss, a man who allegedly ran a crypto empire that defrauded thousands of customers out of billions of dollars. The trial, set to last six weeks, was to resume on Tuesday with key testimony expected from Ellison, considered the prosecution's star witness, who had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges. Bankman-Fried faces seven federal charges, including wire fraud, securities fraud and money laundering, that could put him in prison for the rest of his life. Thus far Bankman-Fried, 31, has remained mostly quiet in court, intently listening to witnesses and at times writing notes to his attorneys — but as Wang testified against him, he looked visibly upset, shifting his gaze from his former friend to the ground and at one point putting his head in his hands.



---


# Line Of Credit

## Definition

In the corpus, "line of credit" denotes the informal, undocumented facility FTX extended to its affiliated trading firm Alameda Research.

Caroline Ellison testified there was "no contract and no written terms," and that Alameda drew against it in increments of $100,000 to $10 million at a time to fund trading.

## Context

The corpus uses "line of credit" almost exclusively to describe the Alameda–FTX arrangement at the center of the SBF fraud trial. Gary Wang testified he set the facility up for Alameda and repeatedly raised its ceiling as the firm kept running against its limit — moving from "a few hundred million," to a billion, and eventually to an effectively unlimited figure that reached $65 billion. Caroline Ellison separately testified that Alameda used $14 billion drawn "as a line of credit" to repay debts to third-party lenders, on Bankman-Fried's instruction. Bankman-Fried, for his part, denied on the stand that he knew about the "effectively infinite" line of credit Alameda received from FTX, a denial The Verge's trial coverage called "peculiar," concluding that the CEO of a financial company simply didn't pay attention to finances.

## Key Characteristics

- **Draw-as-needed structure** — funds are accessed incrementally against a ceiling rather than disbursed as one loan, as when Ellison described draws of $100,000 to $10 million at a time.
- **No collateral, no contract** — Ellison testified the $65 billion facility "did not have to post collateral" and had "no contract and no written terms."
- **Escalating limit** — the ceiling was repeatedly raised over time as the borrower kept exceeding it, per Wang's account of the increases from a few hundred million to $65 billion.
- **Invisible to oversight** — the credit line "wasn't visible to FTX's auditors," per Ellison's testimony, despite its size.
- **Exclusivity** — Wang testified the facility was "unmatched by anyone else on FTX," making it a privilege specific to the affiliated firm rather than a standard customer product.

## Background (external)

The corpus illustrates the term through a single, irregular instance rather than defining it as a general banking product. Per Wikipedia, a line of credit is ordinarily a borrowing arrangement from a bank or financial institution that lets a customer access funds up to a set maximum whenever needed, is typically revolving so that repaid amounts can be redrawn without reapplying, and generally charges interest only on the amount actually withdrawn (Wikipedia, *Line of credit*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Alameda–FTX facility described in the corpus departs from that standard model in that it had no written agreement, no collateral requirement, and no independent oversight.

# Alameda Research's Origins And Naming

Alameda Research was the cryptocurrency trading firm Bankman-Fried started in 2017 during a crypto bull run, and it was named for Alameda County in California, where its first office was set up. Testifying on October 28th, 2023, Bankman-Fried said he knew "basically nothing" about cryptocurrency at the time but wanted to do arbitrage on it anyway, and that he is "somewhat introverted, naturally."

The name was chosen for cover. In his own words on the stand: "Effectively, we wanted to be under the radar at that point in time. I didn't want to call it Sam's Crypto Trading Firm or anything like that. We — there are a lot of competitors and people who we didn't particularly want to know what we were building out because they would race to do it. 'Research' was a sort of generic word, which filled out the company name. And that was — it was far better than the internal name that we had at that point, which was Wireless Mouse." The Verge's reporter noted she would find this more believable had she not already watched a video, played during Gary Wang's first day of testimony with Bankman-Fried and the jury present, of Bankman-Fried explaining on a podcast that the name made it easier to get a bank account.

The founding assembled the people later charged alongside him: Bankman-Fried went on a hiring spree, taking on Wang to program the computers, then Nishad Singh about a month after founding Alameda Research, and finally Caroline Ellison. Though Bankman-Fried was CEO and also majority owner, he wanted to be clear that he did not supervise Wang's direct work. After a run of wildly successful arbitrage — 50 percent to 100 percent annualized returns, per his testimony — he decided to found a cryptocurrency exchange, FTX, figuring he would fail and putting the chance of success at 20 percent, without defining the time period he had in mind.



---


# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.



---


# Cohen's Cross-Examination Of Caroline Ellison

Mark Cohen's cross-examination of Caroline Ellison on October 12th, 2023 aimed at the premise that her direct testimony was reliable — she had recounted many conversations held in person or on auto-deleting messaging platforms, and she had an incentive to flip on Bankman-Fried in the form of possible leniency at sentencing — but The Verge's reporter judged that the defense absolutely biffed it. In Cohen's disorganized cross-examination he mostly bored the jury; at one point two different jurors appeared to be asleep, and midway through the morning the reporter began wondering whether there was a mercy rule for cross-examinations.

The lines of attack were opened and dropped. Cohen established that Bankman-Fried had a much larger appetite for risk than Ellison, that the two reacted differently to stress, and that they took different approaches to media — Ellison avoided it while Bankman-Fried sought it out — without building on any of it. He drew out that Alameda had one accountant in 2021 and hired two more junior accountants in 2022, and had a problem retaining accountants, then dropped that too. He appeared to be trying to suggest the government had coerced Ellison's testimony by getting her to plead guilty to defrauding investors, conduct she could not have been involved in since she did not prepare materials for them; unfortunately she said she had had conversations with investors as part of their due diligence, and Alameda was in any case taking on losses from FTX to keep FTX's balance sheet pristine. Cohen also pressed the hedge he had blamed her for not taking out in his opening — hedging being long crypto by selling Nasdaq futures — which raised the question of whether the defense was that she should have taken more customer funds, or taken them sooner.

Small failures accumulated. Cohen asked Ellison to define what "buy on the way down" meant as though it were a term of art, which seemed to puzzle her, and at other times he seemed to forget what she had testified to and brought up things she had not said; like FTX employee Adam Yedidia before her, Ellison was fastidious about making sure a question was clear and her answer precise. She appeared at one point to be toying with him: having testified on direct about the token Luna, she noted when Cohen asked about Terra/Luna that she had only spoken about Luna, leaving him to fumble the relationship between the two. There were many sidebars, enough that several jurors looked entertained when one occurred, and in one the day before the prosecution complained that Bankman-Fried was visibly scoffing at Ellison's answers, per the court transcript. What Cohen was up against was strong direct evidence: fake balance sheets, one sent to crypto lender Genesis, after which a Genesis representative texted Ellison to say he had spoken to Bankman-Fried — strongly suggesting Bankman-Fried knew the contents of the fake balance sheet. Afterwards, the defendant's mother Barbara Fried engaged Christian Everdell in an animated conversation, gesticulating and clearly holding a strong opinion; Everdell walked off and Cohen talked to her for a bit.



---


# The Escalation Of Alameda's Negative Balance

Alameda Research first ran a negative balance on FTX in late 2019, and the amount it was allowed to go negative crept upward in steps, each one justified after the fact — the model of the fraud that Gary Wang's and Caroline Ellison's testimony described was escalation rather than a single decision. As The Verge's reporter summarised Wang's testimony: first it was okay to dip into FTX's profits, then it was okay to take more, then even more; first it was a little line of credit just to provide liquidity, then a bigger one, then an effectively limitless one.

The steps ran as follows. Because Alameda and FTX shared an open-plan office, Wang heard a trader ask Bankman-Fried whether it was okay to keep withdrawing money from the negative account, and Bankman-Fried said it was okay as long as the amount stayed lower than FTX's total trading revenue; he was CEO of both companies at the time. Around 2019 or 2020, Wang checked the database and found Alameda was negative by about $200 million, more than the $150 million FTX had made in revenue — which had to mean Alameda was taking customer money. Wang was surprised and discussed it with Bankman-Fried, who told him he just needed to take into account the value of FTT, the token the two of them had launched; Wang trusted his judgment and did not pursue it. Later Alameda's balance was more negative than FTT and the trading revenue combined, and Wang had further conversations with Bankman-Fried about it. Wang testified he knew at the time that Alameda was using FTX customers' funds and that he knew it was wrong.

The same gradual accommodation shows in Ellison's account. Choking back tears, she testified: "When I started working at Alameda, I don't think I would have believed you if you told me I would be sending false balance sheets to our lenders or taking customer money, but over time, it was something I became more comfortable with."



---


# Marc-Antoine Julliard's Testimony As FTX's First Witness-Victim

The prosecution's first witness at Sam Bankman-Fried's trial was not a blockbuster name or a former lieutenant-turned-cooperator like Caroline Ellison but a victim: Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader who lives in London and whose money got stuck on FTX. Julliard testified that on Nov. 8, 2022, in the crypto exchange's final few days, he tried to pull out almost $100,000 in cash and crypto, and that he was never able to. The withdrawal screenshots shown in court were of attempts to move $20,000 USD and about 4 Bitcoin, worth about $20,000 at the time — roughly $100,000 in total, inaccessible.

Julliard explained why he had chosen FTX in 2021 when he decided to invest in crypto, trading currencies like Bitcoin and Dogecoin there. He trusted FTX because Bankman-Fried came across as a leading figure of the industry; because the sheer volume of users mattered to him, and FTX was at the time among the top three biggest exchanges; and because major VC firms had invested. "They don't commit hundreds of millions without doing due diligence, checking the books, the accountancy of the firm, going through several compliance process[es], so that was a vote of confidence for me," he said. He also noted FTX's glossy ads — featuring Gisele Bündchen, for instance — which suggested a very high budget, and reasoned that it wouldn't make sense to spend that much money unless FTX had very strong financials. He opened an account, transferred in both regular money and cryptocurrency, and used the exchange to execute his plan of buying Bitcoin to sell back in five to ten years at higher prices.

In November 2022 things went bad. Julliard followed Bankman-Fried on Twitter and read aloud in court the "FTX is fine. Assets are fine" tweets, along with "FTX has enough to cover all client holdings. We don't invest client assets" and a few others, which gave him the impression that his money was there and that any problem might be technical — anti-spam measures — or regulatory. By the time he tried to get his money out on November 8th, it was too late. Cross-examining a customer whose money is gone is described as a thankless task, but Mark Cohen tried anyway, noting that Julliard was a licensed commodities broker who was trading in crypto because he didn't have to disclose it, that he knew crypto was new and risky, and that he didn't review the terms of service agreement he had assented to when making his FTX account. The next witness called was Bankman-Fried's former college and FTX roommate, Adam Yedidia.



---


# Bankman-Fried's Decision To Testify Backfired

The Verge's trial reporter argued that Bankman-Fried's choice to take the stand was a net loss for his defense: like Theranos' Elizabeth Holmes before him, he got on the stand to speak directly to his state of mind in a way no other witness can, but telling your side of the story opens you to a great many questions you might not want to answer on cross-examination — and, having watched a lot of crosses, she called Sassoon's the nastiest she had ever seen.

The warrant is what the charges turn on. The case hinged on conspiracy and intentional deceit: just losing $8 billion is not a crime, though it is very embarrassing, but if Bankman-Fried lied to customers and lenders about what he was doing and how safe FTX was, that is a crime. Because state of mind was the contested issue, his own testimony became the evidence, and it did not hold: Sassoon had established the day before that he has a long history of dishonesty, and on October 31st, through a set of questions about what he did and did not do, she established that the story he told on direct examination was absurd. After a brief redirect by his own lawyers, resplendent with word salad, Bankman-Fried stepped down and the defense rested.

The direct examination had already supplied grounds. Beyond the two obvious lies the reporter counted him telling on the stand — about Alameda Research's name and about "allow_negative" — she was struck by how little he seemed to know about his own companies: apparently Singh, Wang, and Ellison were out there just doing whatever their little hearts desired, because Bankman-Fried was a CEO, but definitely not the kind that pays any attention to money at his crypto trading firm and futures exchange.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Google's Defense That Search Defaults Are Easy To Change

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. On Google's blog, president of global affairs Kent Walker said the search product was the favourite of users, browsers and device makers simply because it was the best in the business: "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," and "this lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today." Walker's supporting evidence is revealed preference when Google is not the default: when Mozilla made Yahoo! the default on Firefox, most users changed it to Google; and people setting up a Windows device frequently sidestep the Microsoft default — "Google" was the number one search query on Bing in 2021 — despite Microsoft making that very annoying to do. The Age's writer called this a compelling point, familiar to anyone who has dodged Microsoft's pleading while setting Chrome and Google as defaults on a new PC, but countered that all of these arguments ignore that Google and its competitors are not on an even playing field: the question remains why users prefer Google, and if the answer is that Google is simply better, the further question is whether that is down to its scale, longevity, ubiquity and all the user data it sucks up, which no other company could possibly match.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# Apple's Privacy Stance Versus Google's Default Payments

Meagan Bellshaw's privacy line of questioning attacked the premise that Apple chose Google because Google had the best product: if Apple genuinely regards Google as bad on privacy, then something other than product quality must explain why Apple gives Google a central place on its platform.

Bellshaw asked Cue whether Apple believes user privacy is important, to which he said, "Absolutely." She then showed a series of emails and slides in which Cue and Apple railed against Google's privacy policies, and Cue readily agreed with them: "We've always thought we had better privacy than Google." He said one provision of the ISA was that Google had to allow people to search without logging in, and that Apple has done things in Safari and around its platforms to make it harder for Google or anyone else to track users. Bellshaw never quite said it, but The Verge read the DOJ's implication as this: Google is a privacy menace anathema to everything Apple believes is important to its users, yet Apple gives it that central place because Google pays so handsomely. She then asked Cue to review some of Apple's financial filings and whether it is true that the ISA represents a significant portion of Apple's profits. Cue's rebuttal was that this is not how Apple looks at it, because the framing doesn't account for all the work Apple did to make its platform so appealing that an agreement like this could work as well as it does.

# iPhone Setup And The Absence Of A Search Engine Choice Screen

Eddy Cue acknowledged on the stand that the ISA didn't allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup — and said he wouldn't want to do that anyway, because "we try to get people up and running as fast as possible" and "setup is just critical stuff."

Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw built to that answer through a series of questions about the iPhone setup process, using three screenshots: the Appearance screen that appears when you first boot up an iPhone so you can pick font sizes, the location-tracking prompt that appears when you open Maps, and the App Tracking Transparency pop-up that tells you when an app wants to collect your data. Cue objected to all of these being considered part of setup, but Bellshaw's point was that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, and that search could be one of them. The Verge noted that "easily" is a persistent point of contention in the trial: DuckDuckGo's CEO, who testified the week before, claimed it takes "too many steps" to switch.

# The Google Antitrust Case

The Google antitrust case is the U.S. government's trial over Google's dominance in the online search market, stemming from a 2020 antitrust claim, in which the government argues that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out competition in search or advertising and thereby to hinder competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products.

Its defining features are the conduct at issue and the defence offered against it. Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the trial, defending Google's business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine. Google's answer is that it is just doing business: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, and that, the company says, does not make its actions illegal.

The important boundary case is which Google antitrust matter this is. The 2020 search claim is separate from the one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to "halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google's monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising." The search case and the digital-advertising case are distinct proceedings and should not be conflated.

The trial is the venue in which the underlying numbers surface. Monday's hearing revealed plenty of juicy tidbits, including the $26.3 billion Google spent making itself the default search engine across platforms in 2021, and how Google tried to take it further and have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones.

# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.

# The DOJ Theory That Google's Default Deals Foreclose Search Rivals

The Justice Department's case against Google is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple, but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform.

The grounds the DOJ pressed through Eddy Cue's testimony were framed as a single question: whether Apple picked Google because it is the most lucrative choice or the best product. That question was a key part of Cue's testimony and, in The Verge's account, a key part of the DOJ's entire case. The warrant is the inference joining the two: if the defaults are bought rather than earned, then the network of default agreements, not product quality, is what keeps Google in place across platforms.

# What A Ruling Against Google Would Mean For Big Tech

A ruling against Google would not stop at Google: the remedy would likely resemble the Microsoft settlement and the outcome would ripple through the other pending Big Tech cases, because enforcers are using this trial to demonstrate that antitrust law can still take on the largest and most powerful companies in the world.

The grounds for the first half of that claim are the available remedies. If the judge rules against Google, the outcome could look a lot like the Microsoft deal, in which the computer company was required to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers, and was also banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with computer manufacturers. Google might likewise end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users — a remedy scaled to the disparity the DOJ has cited, that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday.

The grounds for the ripple effect are the cases already queued behind this one. The FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power. The DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products. And there is an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, in which the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is enforcers' own stake in the result: they will want to show that antitrust law is still relevant and can successfully take on the biggest, most powerful companies in the world, so a win here sets the template the neighbouring cases are argued against. The scope condition is that nothing was settled as of this report — the case is expected to continue for several weeks, bringing to a head one of the biggest fights in tech antitrust since the U.S. took Microsoft to trial in the 1990s.

# Antitrust

Antitrust is the label the corpus uses for a 2023 wave of U.S. and EU legal actions against dominant tech and payments companies — the FTC's suit against Amazon, the DOJ's *US v. Google* search-monopoly trial, Epic Games' Sherman Act/Cartwright Act suit against Google Play, Helena World Chronicle's Sherman Act/Clayton Act class action against Google, PayPal's anti-steering class action, and the EU's competition review of Amazon's iRobot acquisition.

## Context

The corpus documents a wave of parallel antitrust actions against major tech and payments companies in 2023. The FTC and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon, alleging it used its dominant position to inflate prices, overcharge sellers, and stifle competition via an "anti-discounting strategy" and buy-box penalties for third-party sellers who priced lower elsewhere; the FTC sought to hold Amazon liable for violating anti-monopoly law, with remedies to be determined only after a liability finding. Separately, the DOJ's *US v. Google* trial over Google's search dominance turned on the Information Services Agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices — Apple's Eddy Cue testified about the ISA's revenue-share renegotiation with Google (specific dollar figures were reserved for closed court sessions), while separate testimony from Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan put Google's 2021 default-placement payments at $26.3 billion total, with a New York Times report cited alongside that testimony putting Apple's share at roughly $18 billion; the DOJ argued Google's default-placement deals with Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla foreclosed rivals from the data needed to improve competing search products. Epic Games separately sued Google over Google Play's app-distribution and payment-processing practices, invoking Sherman Act Sections 1 and 2 alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. A class action by news publisher Helena World Chronicle accused Google of "anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others" over its use of publisher content in Knowledge Graph and AI search features. PayPal was hit with a class action alleging its anti-steering rules — modeled on tactics Visa and Mastercard abandoned after a DOJ antitrust suit — stifled competition from lower-cost payment platforms like Stripe. In the EU, regulators used antitrust competition-concern findings (a formal statement of objections) to scrutinize Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot over fears it would let Amazon foreclose rival robot-vacuum makers on its marketplace.

## Key Characteristics

- **Statutory basis** — in the U.S., Sherman Act Sections 1 (anticompetitive agreements) and 2 (monopolization) and the Clayton Act are the primary tools; the FTC additionally proceeds under anti-monopoly/unfair-methods-of-competition authority, and states can add their own statutes (e.g., California's Cartwright Act).
- **Conduct at issue** — cases target using dominance to raise prices or fees, penalize rivals' lower prices (Amazon's buy-box mechanism), pay for default placement to foreclose competitors (Google-Apple), restrict app distribution and billing options (Google Play), or impose anti-steering rules that block cheaper alternatives (PayPal).
- **Enforcers vary by jurisdiction** — DOJ and FTC (plus state AGs) bring U.S. federal cases; private plaintiffs can also bring antitrust class actions (Helena World Chronicle, PayPal consumers); the European Commission enforces EU competition law and can use a formal statement of objections short of blocking a deal to press for remedies.
- **Remedies are typically litigated after liability** — the FTC's Amazon complaint explicitly left remedies undetermined pending a liability finding, and the historic Microsoft case (the precedent both DOJ v. Google and Epic v. Google draw on) resulted in required API-sharing and a ban on anticompetitive, exclusive deals with computer manufacturers.
- **Merger review is a distinct antitrust track** — the EU's iRobot objections show competition authorities scrutinizing prospective mergers for foreclosure risk before a deal closes, separate from post-hoc conduct cases.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "antitrust" as a familiar label for these cases without defining the term itself. Per the Federal Trade Commission, U.S. antitrust law originates with the Sherman Act of 1890, a "comprehensive charter of economic liberty aimed at preserving free and unfettered competition," joined in 1914 by the FTC Act and the Clayton Act (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). Sherman Act Section 1 prohibits contracts, combinations, or conspiracies that restrain trade, and Section 2 addresses monopolization and attempted monopolization; the Clayton Act separately reaches practices like mergers that may substantially lessen competition, and the FTC Act prohibits "unfair methods of competition" (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02). The Department of Justice brings criminal Sherman Act cases, the FTC enforces the FTC Act against similar conduct, and state attorneys general and private plaintiffs can enforce parallel state antitrust statutes (FTC, *The Antitrust Laws*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Recommendation Algorithm

## Definition

Across the corpus, "recommendation algorithm" (and the closely related notion of algorithmic ranking/curation) names the automated mechanism a platform uses to control the visibility of content, products, or posts — and by extension, the mechanism regulators, courts, and users scrutinize when they suspect a platform is suppressing or favoring particular items.
No single corpus document offers a formal definition of the term; instead each shows the mechanism at work in a different dispute: Amazon's marketplace search ranking and "other products you may like" widget, Instagram's Stories/feed visibility, U.S. platforms' content-moderation feed curation, and Google's Featured Snippets extraction.

## Context

The corpus shows the same underlying mechanism operating across very different platform types, and shows regulators and courts converging on it from different angles.
On Amazon's marketplace, the EU's antitrust objections to the iRobot acquisition center on Amazon's ability to foreclose a rival's *algorithmic visibility* — delisting rival products, reducing their ranking in organic and paid results, excluding them from the "other products you may like" widget, or denying them labels like "Amazon's Choice" — since RVC buyers in France, Germany, Italy, and Spain rely on that in-marketplace ranking both for product discovery and for the final purchase decision.
The same document notes that Amazon's marketplace was separately designated a core platform service under the EU's Digital Markets Act, which imposes restrictions on self-preferencing.
On Meta's Instagram, users and digital-rights groups suspect a comparable but content-moderation-flavored version of the same idea — "shadowbanning" — where an algorithmic process silently lowers a post's visibility (e.g., Palestine-related Stories) without an explicit takedown.
In the U.S. Supreme Court's NetChoice cases (challenging Texas's HB 20 and Florida's SB 7072), the fight is over whether a platform's curation of what appears in a user's feed — a process now largely conducted algorithmically, generally with light human intervention or oversight — is a First-Amendment-protected editorial act that states cannot compel platforms to individually explain post-by-post.
Google's Featured Snippets, which algorithmically extract answers directly from publishers' web pages into search results, are cited in a news-publisher antitrust suit as a related mechanism: an algorithm that decides what content a user sees without the user visiting the original source, which publishers say siphons off their traffic and ad revenue.

## Key Characteristics

- **Ranking, not binary inclusion** — the algorithm typically operates on relative visibility (higher/lower placement in organic or paid results, inclusion in a "you may like" widget) rather than simple on/off access, which is what makes self-preferencing and shadowbanning hard to prove or disprove.
- **Automated with limited human oversight** — described in the NetChoice case as a process "largely conducted algorithmically now — generally with light human intervention or oversight," which is central to arguments that mandated per-decision human explanations would be impractical at the scale of "millions and millions of pieces of content a day."
- **Commercial leverage point** — on marketplaces, control over the recommendation algorithm doubles as a competitive lever: a platform that also sells its own products can use ranking, delisting, and widget exclusion to foreclose rivals, per the EU's ability-and-incentive theory of harm against Amazon.
- **Contestable but opaque** — content creators and merchants can suspect suppression (shadowbanning, reduced marketplace visibility) but the underlying ranking logic is not published, so claims tend to rely on circumstantial or anecdotal patterns rather than direct evidence.
- **Distinct from explicit content removal** — reduced algorithmic visibility (shadowbanning, lower ranking) is a softer, less visible action than outright delisting or takedown, and is treated differently in both platform policy and legal argument.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the general computer-science term for this kind of system is a "recommender system" (also called a recommendation algorithm, engine, or platform): a type of information filtering system that suggests items most relevant to a particular user, predicting user preferences to help them choose from large sets of options such as products, media, or content.
Source: "Recommender system," Wikipedia, accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recommender_system.

# ASPI's Analysis Of TikTok Pixel Data Aggregation Risk

Researchers at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute argue that the danger of TikTok's tracking pixel lies less in the type of data collected — which resembles what US tech giants gather — than in how that data can be aggregated and in who can ultimately reach it.

Jocelinn Kang, a technical specialist at the institute, said data from a tracking pixel could be aggregated across websites, apps and social media platforms, and that pixel tracking could identify users through their "browser fingerprint," a combination of their IP address, browser and system details. The linking gets sharper as identifiers accumulate: "However, when more identifying data such as email and phone number is associated with a user, their web activity can be better linked," Kang said.

Strategic Policy Institute researcher Samantha Hoffman said the data collected by TikTok's pixel was similar to that of US-based tech giants Google and Meta, but that the difference was "the intent." Advertising data had "incredible propaganda value," she said, and the warrant joining that to the risk is state access: "If you think about that, plus the access that TikTok is required to give the Chinese government, that's the problem." She notes TikTok itself made that access explicit — in November 2022 the company changed its privacy policy to state clearly that user data can be accessed by some employees from across the world, including China. "They talk about how even data collected overseas can be used by the company and its partners, and would be kept private unless security organisations make demands of it," Hoffman said. China's national intelligence laws allow the government to pull data upon request from companies based there.

# Google's Link-Based Ranking And The Market It Created

Google revolutionized search by evaluating websites based on links from other websites, seeing each link as a vote of relevance and trustworthiness — a structure that made the ranking of any page a function of what other pages pointed to it. The founders pledged to be a neutral navigation system with no ads: just a clean white screen with a search box that would bring people off the Google landing page and out to a helpful website as seamlessly as possible. Users quickly decided this link-based sorting methodology was superior to the existing search engines, and by the end of 1999 Google was handling the majority of online queries.

The model arrived in response to a documented problem. In 1997 an Italian professor published a journal article about what he called Search Engines Persuasion: "Finding the right information on the World Wide Web is becoming a fundamental problem," he wrote, and "a vast number of new companies was born just to make customer Web pages as visible as possible," which "has led to a bad performance degradation of search engines."

The relation between votes and rank held only as long as links were scarce and organic, and it did not. Mapstead, like many early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt: almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy — buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google's results rise.

# Data Privacy

## Definition

Data privacy, across the corpus, is the recurring dispute over whether companies may collect, track, or profile people's personal information without their knowledge or consent.

That dispute plays out as regulatory enforcement against platforms: GDPR action against Meta's consentless ad tracking (doc_0107), COPPA litigation over Meta's collection of data from children under 13 (doc_0304), a "mass breach of privacy" allegation against TikTok's pre-consent tracking pixel (doc_0189), and California's CPPA extending opt-out and access rights to AI-based profiling (doc_0164).

## Context

In the corpus, data privacy surfaces as the recurring fault line between platforms that monetize personal data and the regulators pushing back on non-consensual collection. Norway's Datatilsynet issued an emergency GDPR ban on Meta running "personalized ads" without consent, then referred the case to the EU's Board to make the ban permanent across the single market, because Meta kept running tracking ads despite the order and a rejected court challenge (doc_0107). California's CPPA is drafting rules that would give residents opt-out and access rights over "automated decisionmaking technology," explicitly modeled on GDPR and expected to draw pushback from adtech and AI firms like Meta and OpenAI (doc_0164). The Age's investigation found TikTok's tracking pixel scraping site visitors' names, emails, and phone numbers before users clicked "I consent," prompting an Australian senator to call it a "mass breach of privacy" and demand a regulatory probe (doc_0189). Meta separately faces a 42-state lawsuit alleging it violated COPPA — the US law restricting data collection from children under 13 and requiring parental consent — by knowingly letting millions of underage users onto Instagram and Facebook while collecting their personal information (doc_0304).

## Key Characteristics

- **Consent is the legal hinge** — GDPR, as applied against Meta in Norway, turns on whether a company has a valid legal basis (consent, not "legitimate interest" or "contractual necessity") before tracking or profiling users for ads (doc_0107).
- **Pre-consent collection is the specific harm alleged against TikTok** — its pixel captured form-field data "often before clicking 'I consent'," unlike Google's and Meta's pixels, which the same test showed firing only after consent (doc_0189).
- **Children are a protected, heavily litigated category** — COPPA restricts data collection from users under 13 and requires verifiable parental consent, and Meta's alleged evasion of that requirement (ignoring reports, not disabling accounts, avoiding "actual knowledge") is the specific violation named in the unredacted lawsuit (doc_0304).
- **Regulators are extending consent/access rights into AI** — California's CPPA is drafting opt-out and access rights over automated decisionmaking technology and AI-based profiling, explicitly borrowing from GDPR's model (doc_0164).
- **Enforcement can escalate beyond a single national regulator** — Norway's local DPA used an emergency GDPR mechanism to bypass the "one-stop-shop" rule and force an EU-wide decision on Meta, showing that a single country's action can become bloc-wide policy (doc_0107).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the general legal concept the enforcement actions above are built on is the definition of "personal data" under GDPR.

GDPR.eu describes personal data as "any information that relates to an individual who can be directly or indirectly identified," a category spanning obvious identifiers like names and emails as well as location data and other online identifiers (GDPR.eu, "What Is GDPR, the EU's New Data Protection Law?", published by Proton AG with EU Horizon 2020 co-funding, accessed 2026-09-02: https://gdpr.eu/what-is-gdpr/).

# Search As Private Infrastructure, Not A Public Library

The claim is that routing nearly all online information through a single private company has left us arguably worse off than before, because information that is controlled by a private business will always be subject to that business's bottom line — which is exactly why most countries around the world have libraries that are public institutions.

The grounds are a comparison with what the internet was supposed to be. In the beginning it was seen as an improvement on the spirit of the public library: an opportunity to transcend the gatekeepers controlling who could publish a book, allowing mankind to fully connect and share knowledge. Instead, nearly all online information runs through a single company, which assumes a veneer of civic utility, of impassive authority, when it is very much not a neutral entity.

Matt Cutts supplies the insider warrant that the veneer is doing work. "There were so many true believers at Google in the early days," he said. "As companies get big, it gets harder to get things done. Inevitably, people start to think about profit or quarterly numbers." He claimed that, at least while he was there, search quality always came before financial goals, but he believes the public underestimates how Google is shaping what they see: "I deeply, deeply, deeply believe search engines are newspaper-like entities, making editorial decisions." He speculated that the company did not want the public to think too hard about how search works because that awareness "encourages regulators and makes people realize, 'Oh, there's a lot of money here.'"

The consequence is epistemic rather than commercial. There has always been advertising and polemics from cranks, scammers, and liars, but now we see this stuff surfacing alongside truth and we cannot tell the difference, so we move through our lives with a greater sense of distrust and fear and insecurity. At the end of the day, it is Google's world, and the SEOs are only living in it.

# TikTok Pixel Pre-Consent Data Collection Test

Testing by The Age found that personal information typed into Australian websites was sent back to TikTok often before the user clicked "I consent" to the website's privacy policy.

The test was run by installing a browser extension and then visiting websites such as Sportsbet, Kmart, Beyond Blue and many others. On each site the testers went to sign up for an account, entering personal information including their full name, email address and phone number. Using Omnibug, they could see in real time that information being sent back to TikTok — and, crucially, that this often happened before consent to the site's privacy policy had been given.

The mechanism named in the report is a TikTok tool called "automatic advanced matching," which sees when a user enters text into a form field or a search box and, if it looks like an email address or phone number, scrapes that data.

# Firefox's Decline: The Chrome Share Alternative Explanation

TechCrunch attacks the causal premise in Mozilla's Yahoo story — the inference that Firefox lost users *because* Yahoo was the default. As it puts it, that is not the full story.

Two grounds are offered. First, Yahoo was already well behind Google in terms of search technology at that point, so the switch conflated the default change with a pre-existing quality gap. Second, and more damaging to the inference, Firefox itself was very well behind Chrome: Chrome ended 2014 with nearly 50% market share and ended 2017 — when Google got prime default search position on Firefox — at nearly 65% of all web browser usage on desktop, with mobile even more skewed to Chrome. In other words, the number of Firefox users might have been declining for other reasons.

The counter also flags the interest at stake: pushing the blame on Yahoo certainly works in Google's favor here, since the story is being told in Google's defense.

# Mozilla's Open Letter On AI Openness

The letter's claim is that openness makes AI safer, against the counter-position that proprietary control does. In an open letter published by Mozilla a few weeks before November 21, 2023, Meta's chief AI scientist Yann LeCun joined some 70 other signatories in calling for more openness in AI development, and the letter has since garnered more than 1,700 signatures. The backdrop is that Big Tech companies such as OpenAI and Google's DeepMind have called for more regulation, warning of catastrophic consequences if the AI levers were to meet the wrong hands — in other words, arguing that proprietary AI is safer than open source.

LeCun and his co-signatories disagree, and concede the risk before turning it around: "Yes, openly available models come with risks and vulnerabilities — AI models can be abused by malicious actors or deployed by ill-equipped developers. However, we have seen time and time again that the same holds true for proprietary technologies — and that increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous. The idea that tight and proprietary control of foundational AI models is the only path to protecting us from society-scale harm is naive at best, dangerous at worst." The warrant is that scrutiny, not secrecy, is what makes technology safe.

On a personal level, LeCun has accused the big-name AI players of trying to secure "regulatory capture of the AI industry" by lobbying against open AI R&D — an argument about motive rather than safety. And on a company level, Meta is doing all it can to encourage collaboration and "openness," recently partnering with Hugging Face to launch a new startup accelerator designed to spur adoption of open source AI models.

# Sam Altman's Career And Public Profile

Sam Altman has a long history steering OpenAI: he co-founded the company alongside Peter Thiel, LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman and others, and initially served as a co-chair of OpenAI alongside Elon Musk, who left in 2018 to avoid a conflict of interest with Tesla.

Altman formerly headed the startup accelerator Y Combinator and also holds a seat on the board at Worldcoin, the ambitious cryptocurrency project. # Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. # The Digital Services Act

The Digital Services Act (DSA) is the European Union's pan-EU content moderation rulebook: a regulation that places governance obligations on digital services and platforms carrying user-generated content, with the aim of ensuring companies respond to reports of illegal content, and that layers heavier duties on the largest platforms. Its baseline obligations apply to digital services and platforms generally — respond diligently to notices of illegal content, clearly communicate terms and conditions to users, and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement of those terms.

The discriminating feature of the regime is its second tier. Platforms designated as "very large online platforms" (VLOPs) carry additional obligations to identify and mitigate systemic risks such as disinformation, gender-based violence, or negative effects on the exercise of fundamental rights. The Commission designated 19 VLOPs in April 2023, including Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram; X is also a designated VLOP. Compliance for VLOPs kicked in over the summer of 2023 — TechCrunch dates Meta's compliance start to August.

The regime's boundary case is disinformation itself. Unlike terrorism content, disinformation is not illegal in the EU per se. The DSA therefore does not reach it through the illegal-content removal route at all; it reaches it through the systemic-risk route, obliging a VLOP such as X to mitigate the risks attached to harmful falsehoods while separately acting diligently on reports of genuinely illegal content. The two duties run on different legal tracks even when they concern the same posts.

Penalties for confirmed breaches can be as high as 6% of global annual turnover, and the bloc holds a further power, in extremis, to block access to a service in the region for repeated infringements — meaning a platform that repeatedly fails to correct course could be shut off in the EU. TechCrunch illustrates the scale on both ends: Elon Musk last projected revenues of about $3 billion for 2023 for X, which by that example would cap a fine at up to $180 million, while in Meta's case the same 6% ceiling could run to multiple billions.

The regulation also contains a "crisis response" mechanism (Article 36) which enables the Commission to adopt rapid-fire measures on larger platforms in situations of "serious threat", such as war. As of TechCrunch's October 2023 reporting this part of the regulation was not yet operative: it would not start operating until February 17 of the following year, because it requires an advisory body — the European Board for Digital Services — to be operational before it can recommend that the Commission adopt a crisis response mechanism, and the Board's set-up was itself waiting on Member States to establish national Digital Services Coordinators, the bodies that oversee DSA compliance for non-VLOPs.

# Platform Transparency After X Went Private

An EU investigation would, indirectly, be a key way for the public to gain significantly more transparency around how X is being used — and abused. That is TechCrunch's claim about what regulatory scrutiny of the platform would deliver beyond any compliance finding.

The grounds are a change in X's corporate status. Since Musk took Twitter private, the company no longer produces quarterly earnings reports, and it is not held as closely to account as a result.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is the substitution of one disclosure channel for another. Public-company reporting is what ordinarily forces periodic, public disclosure about a platform's operations and scale; taking the company private removed that channel and the accountability pressure attached to it. A regulatory investigation compels disclosure through a different route, so it would restore to public view information about the platform's use and abuse that the market no longer extracts.

# Tim Turk's NHL Protocol Observation Assessment

Tim Turk's evaluation method, which he calls an "NHL protocol observation assessment," runs new clients through specific drills that allow him to visualise their shooting actions from a technical standpoint — he calls each player's shot "like a fingerprint" — as described in The New York Times on 17 November 2023.

The opening step is stationary. Turk throws some pucks down in the slot and simply asks the player to shoot them stationary, so he can watch their body formation, hip and shoulder positions, spine angles, and puck preparation and positioning, paying particular attention to where the puck starts in their stance versus where it finishes.

The precondition implied by the name is that this is what he does with new clients rather than players he already knows, and the aim is observation and visualisation of an existing technique rather than correction of it.

# Climate Sweet Spots and Pattern-Dependent Feedbacks

Global mean radiative feedbacks depend not only on global mean temperature but on the spatial pattern of surface warming: a degree of global warming spread out evenly will cause a different radiative response than if that same warming were concentrated in a climate sweet spot — a location where surface warming produces efficient radiative damping.

For decades, researchers assumed that global mean radiative feedbacks mostly depend on global mean temperature (Gregory et al., 2004). The article's analogy is that applying a force uniformly over someone's entire body elicits a very different reaction than tickling the soles of that person's feet. A wide variety of processes affect the evolution of surface temperature, from greenhouse gas forcing and regional aerosol forcing to natural oscillations involving the ocean and atmosphere to the continental boundary conditions and the extent of ice sheets and sea ice, and the pattern of surface temperature change over the past 40 or so years featured a pronounced spatial structure, with some locations even cooling in spite of global mean warming on the order of 1 K. Feedbacks involving clouds and the atmospheric temperature structure are most sensitive to spatial differences in warming: deep convection in the warmest tropical regions readily communicates surface conditions upward throughout the troposphere (up to about 10-15 kilometers) and then horizontally across much of the globe, making the western Pacific a climate sweet spot. That warmer air sitting atop the relatively cool waters in the eastern Pacific or Southern Ocean acts to stabilize the lowermost troposphere, allowing more extensive low-lying stratus and stratocumulus clouds to develop, and because of their location and structure these low clouds efficiently cool the planet and offset some of the initial warming. Observations over recent decades show strong warming in regions of deep convection such as the western Pacific communicated throughout the troposphere, leading to strong warming aloft that enhances radiative emission to space, while parts of the eastern Pacific have cooled; warming aloft with cooling at the surface enhances lower tropospheric inversion strength in the eastern Pacific and promotes extensive shallow cloud cover that reflects solar radiation and keeps Earth relatively cool. Coupled climate models, by contrast, create their own surface warming pattern that differs from the observed one — warming aloft is less pronounced, lower tropospheric inversion strength is decreased and cloud cover is reduced through time, both of which lead to less efficient cooling near Earth's surface in models than in nature.

# Duane Forrester, Bing, And The Search Engine's View

Duane Forrester was at Microsoft from 2007 until 2015, where he helped launch and manage Bing, the perpetual underdog to Google's domination of online search; because he worked as an SEO both before and after his time at Microsoft, he sees the industry from both sides — like an aerospace engineer who spent a few years at the Department of Defense, left for the private sector, and now is much better at winning military contracts. He has a holistic understanding of the delicate push and pull between the SEOs desperate for clues on how to do their jobs better and the search engine trying to keep its secret-sauce algorithm proprietary.

He was the first stop because Google was slow to allow anyone to talk to the writer, possibly because of the giant PR clusterfuck that has been the company's past year: accused by the federal government of being a monopoly, increasingly despised by the public, losing ground to Reddit, TikTok, and large language models.

Like Schwartz, Forrester wanted to emphasize how hard everyone works. "I've lost track of how many people I know who built companies and sold them and have just, like, made wealth," he said. "That is not a 40-hour commitment in the week. That is a 400-hour commitment." For the record, there are 168 hours in a week.

His route in started young. These days Forrester lives in Los Angeles and asked to meet at one of his favorite restaurants, which felt like a British pub operated by Disney World, tucked away in a desert strip mall and covered in Anglophile paraphernalia including Union Jack flags, a mural of Big Ben, and a red phone booth. Over a full English breakfast he described growing up in rural Canada, where his parents owned a motel and he used to mess around with the pay phone outside, eventually figuring out how to finagle free long-distance phone calls: "And then it became, 'What else can I know how to do?'" By the '90s he was trading tips with other SEOs in online forums, and he still remembers the thrill of the very first SEO conference he attended, where he was asked to speak. "The people who got up onstage to talk were seen as somehow more knowledgeable, but I don't know that we felt that way," he said. "You all kind of knew you were making shit up."

As a former SEO, Forrester understood that the quality of Bing's search results would be affected by the work of SEOs, so it made sense to communicate with SEOs as much as possible. Cutts similarly tried to serve as a conduit between SEOs and Google, but Forrester felt Google projected an attitude he described as: "We know what we're doing, we will stop your attempts to game this, and you know what? # ChatGPT Overview And Significance

ChatGPT is OpenAI's text-generating AI chatbot, and it has taken the world by storm: what started as a tool to hyper-charge productivity through writing essays and code from short text prompts has evolved into a behemoth used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies for far more wide-ranging needs.

That growth propelled OpenAI itself into becoming one of the most-hyped companies in recent memory, even though CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return raised concerns about the company's direction and opened the door for competitors. The fallout was still settling, but it might empower competitors such as Meta and its LLaMA family of large language models, or help other AI startups get attention and funding as the industry watched OpenAI implode and put itself back together. Whatever the nefarious side of ChatGPT, it was clear that AI tools were not going away anytime soon: since its initial launch nearly a year earlier, ChatGPT had hit 100 million weekly active users, and OpenAI was investing heavily in it.

The capability boundary at the time was defined by model access and modality. GPT-4, which can write more naturally and fluently than previous models, remained largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users, although it could be accessed for free through Microsoft's Bing Chat in the Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome and Safari web browsers. Beyond GPT-4 and the OpenAI DevDay announcements, OpenAI had recently connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users, and with the integration of DALL-E 3, users could generate both text and images right inside ChatGPT.

# Peter Kalmus's Profile and Radical Turn

Kalmus, 49, thinks civilization is on the path to break down, that the Biden administration is clueless on climate, and that he might get fired from his job at NASA if he is arrested for a third time protesting what he views as downright madness: the continued use of fossil fuels.

Kalmus, whose strident tweets reach some 340,000 followers on X, is at the vanguard of a group of scientists who are increasingly disillusioned and growing convinced that more radical action is needed to wake up political leaders. He has been on a 15-year quest to halt climate change and has already oriented most everything in his life to minimize his own climate footprint and maximize what he can do to push society to change — and nothing has been enough. The changes he made were not enough: he wrote a book on climate change and chained himself to a Chase bank in protest of fossil fuel financing, and twice he has been arrested during climate protests. So this summer, as extreme heat and rainfall battered many American communities, he visited Maine searching for something different — not for climate solutions, but for new ways to withstand climate change's harms and to make peace with the grief that often feels inescapable for those who reckon with global warming daily; he visited Belfast, Maine in July and August to see the Possibility Alliance homestead as he looked for inspiration on how best to live with the effects of climate change. Now a married father of two teenagers, Kalmus is introspective, earnest and narrowly focused on climate change in both his personal and professional life; tall with an athletic build, a neat beard and a tangle of messy hair with a skunklike streak of white, he can sometimes come off like an overgrown teenager — the smartest person in the room, brimming with idealism and still indignant, with a zeal many adults can no longer muster, about how life's most annoying systems work, like the U.S. medical system, a symptom of what he calls the "capitalist death cult." His social media posts often evoke heartbreak: "We're in the process of losing basically everything," he wrote recently on X.
