# ChatGPT Legal And Privacy Controversies

ChatGPT has generated a run of legal and privacy controversies: an Australian mayor publicly announced he may sue OpenAI for defamation over ChatGPT's false claims that he had served time in prison for bribery, which would be the first defamation lawsuit against the text-generating service, and there have been other cases of ChatGPT accusing individuals of false crimes.

The libel exposure follows from how the models work: they do not know or care whether something is true, only that it looks true — a problem when the output is used for homework, and potentially libel when it accuses someone of a crime they did not commit. How troubling statements produced by ChatGPT will be handled was expected to play out over the following months as tech and legal experts tackled the fastest moving target in the industry. As of the article, there were no lawsuits specifically targeting ChatGPT, but OpenAI is involved in at least one lawsuit with implications for AI systems trained on publicly available data, which would touch on ChatGPT. There are also plagiarism issues: text-generating AI models like ChatGPT have a tendency to regurgitate content from their training data. Copyright in output sits with the user — the person who requested the input from ChatGPT is the copyright owner.

On privacy, OpenAI has said that individuals in "certain jurisdictions" such as the EU can object to the processing of their personal information by its AI models by filling out a form — the "OpenAI Personal Data Removal Request" — which includes the ability to request deletion of AI-generated references about them, although OpenAI notes it may not grant every request since it must balance privacy requests against freedom of expression "in accordance with applicable laws." In its privacy policy OpenAI makes a passing acknowledgement of the objection requirements attached to relying on "legitimate interest," pointing users to instructions on how to opt out of use of their information to train its models. ChatGPT chats are not public, but OpenAI disclosed a bug, since fixed, that exposed the titles of some users' conversations to other people on the service.

Other controversies span platforms and schools. Discord integrated OpenAI's technology into its bot Clyde, and two users tricked Clyde into providing instructions for making methamphetamine and napalm. CNET found itself in controversy after Futurism reported the publication was publishing articles under a mysterious byline completely generated by AI, and Red Ventures, the private equity company that owns CNET, was accused of using ChatGPT for SEO farming even where the information was incorrect. Several major school systems and colleges, including New York City Public Schools, have banned ChatGPT from their networks and devices, claiming the AI impedes the learning process by promoting plagiarism and misinformation — a claim not every educator agrees with.

# Mapping Platforms Disabled Live Features In Israel And Gaza

Snap Map is especially relevant because other mapping sites limited features in the region at the request of the Israel Defence Forces (IDF).

Google disabled live traffic conditions in Israel and the Gaza Strip for Google Maps and Waze in the week before November 3, 2023, Bloomberg reports, "out of consideration for the safety of local communities." Users can still use navigational features to get around but are not able to see real-time traffic data, according to Bloomberg, because live updates could reveal the Israeli military's movements.

The Hill reports that Apple Maps took similar action in compliance with the IDF's request.

# NHTSA Investigation Of Cruise Pedestrian Incidents

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has opened an investigation into GM subsidiary Cruise's AV system following several incidents involving pedestrians in San Francisco, TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-22.

The most recent of those incidents left a woman stuck under a Cruise robotaxi after being hit by a human-driven vehicle.

- [Bail](term_bail.md): Bail is the term the corpus uses for Sam Bankman-Fried's pretrial release from custody: a $250 million bond that let him live under house arrest at his parents' home in Palo Alto instead of in jail while awaiting trial, and which a U.S. judge revoked in August 2023 (doc_0010, doc_0226).

- [Banking-as-a-Service](term_banking_as_a_service.md): Banking-as-a-service (BaaS) is the label TechCrunch's coverage applies to platforms — Synapse and QI Tech — that let banks and fintech companies build financial services on top of them, rather than platforms that serve end customers as a bank would.
- [Battery Life and Charging](term_battery_life_and_charging.md): Battery life and charging is the pair of consumer-electronics specs — how long a device runs on a charge, and how fast and via what connector it refills — that reviewers and shoppers use to compare phones, earbuds, handhelds, smart glasses, and the power banks and cables that feed them.

- [Bot Detection](term_bot_detection.md): Bot detection is the set of technical and policy methods a platform uses to identify automated or fake accounts and unwanted bulk activity — spam, phishing, malware, and inauthentic engagement — and to make running them costly or infeasible.
- [Box Office](term_box_office.md): Box office, as used throughout the corpus, is the reported revenue figure for a film's ticket sales, cited either as a single weekend's opening or debut number or as a cumulative running gross toward a domestic or global total. # CSAM Scanning

## Definition

CSAM scanning is the practice of using detection technology — hash matching, or broader content-scanning systems — to find child sexual abuse material (CSAM) on a platform so it can be removed and, where required, reported.
CSAM itself is treated across the corpus as a category of illegal content, alongside terrorism content and fraud, that platforms and regulators single out from ordinary "harmful" content because hosting or transmitting it is against the law.

## Context

The corpus shows CSAM scanning arising in three distinct regulatory and platform contexts.
In the EU, the European Commission's home affairs commissioner Ylva Johansson is spearheading a CSAM-scanning proposal that would require in-scope platforms to deploy prevention measures first and, only if those are insufficient, detection measures after a court decision; she notes that companies today already scan non-encrypted communications for CSAM under a temporary ePrivacy derogation, and that her proposal is meant to be "technology neutral" rather than naming a specific vendor's tool.
In the UK, Ofcom's first Online Safety Act guidelines recommend that platforms use "hash matching" to detect and remove CSAM, and reserve a separate "accredited technology" power that could require services — including encrypted messaging apps — to scan for CSAM, which critics say would require breaking end-to-end encryption.
At the platform level, Discord's scrutiny over CSAM followed an NBC News investigation that identified 35 cases over six years of adults allegedly using the platform to kidnap, groom, or sexually assault minors, plus 165 cases of prosecutions for sharing CSAM or using Discord to extort sexual images from young users; Discord responded by banning teen dating servers, banning sharing of AI-generated CSAM, and rolling out Teen Safety Assist content filters, rather than describing a scanning system of its own.
Mozilla's planned fediverse instance separately lists CSAM as illegal content its trust-and-safety policies will act against, alongside hate speech and harassment.

## Key Characteristics

- **Detection technique, not one product** — the corpus describes hash matching as the recommended baseline technique (per Ofcom), while the EU proposal is explicitly framed as "technology neutral," naming no specific vendor's scanning tool.
- **Ordered obligation, not a first resort** — in the EU proposal, platforms must attempt prevention before detection/scanning is permitted, and only after a court decision.
- **Encryption tension** — both the EU proposal and the UK's "accredited technology" power are described as potentially requiring scanning of end-to-end encrypted messages, which critics argue is incompatible with maintaining that encryption.
- **Legal basis already exists for some scanning** — Johansson notes companies currently scan non-encrypted content for CSAM under an ePrivacy derogation, which her proposal would replace.
- **Distinct from policy/moderation responses** — Discord's post-scrutiny response (bans, content filters, Teen Safety Assist) is a moderation and policy response to CSAM risk rather than a scanning system per se, illustrating that "addressing CSAM" and "CSAM scanning" are not synonymous.

# Thai Food Near Me's Viral Moment

In March, before serving a single person, Thai Food Near Me went viral online for its name: a photo of the restaurant circulated on Twitter ahead of its opening, brown butcher paper still covering the windows. The restaurant's goofy name was enough to garner coverage on news sites, along with an influx of customers in the first crucial months of being open.

The viral tweet invariably summoned a chorus of overly friendly, all-lowercase-text replies from brands looking for attention, and the official account of Google Maps — the very entity the meme-y restaurant name is designed to outsmart — could not resist. # Game Patch Notes

## Definition

Neither corpus article uses the phrase "patch notes," but both document the same underlying pattern: a studio bundling a slate of changes — new content, rebalancing, and quality-of-life fixes — under a single named or numbered update tied to a release date.
Polygon's Diablo 4 coverage lists that pattern for "Season 2"/"Season of Blood": leveling speed, new endgame bosses, a Nightmare Dungeon rework, mount handling, and Renown/gem-Stash changes, all bundled to arrive together on Oct. 17 (doc_0533).
Polygon's games-of-the-year piece shows the same pattern for Cyberpunk 2077's named "Patch 2.0," a systems-revamping update shipped alongside — but distinct from — the paid Phantom Liberty expansion (doc_0213).

## Context

The corpus's clearest example is Diablo 4's Season 2 update, "Season of Blood," reported by Polygon on 2023-10-04: alongside new vampire powers, Blizzard shipped a broad slate of quality-of-life changes covering leveling speed, endgame bosses, Nightmare Dungeon design, mount handling, and the Renown and gem/Stash systems, all set to arrive together on Oct. 17 as one seasonal patch.

Polygon's broader 2023 games-of-the-year piece shows the same pattern in a second game: Cyberpunk 2077's Phantom Liberty expansion arrived "alongside the sweeping Patch 2.0," which revamped the base game's role-playing progression systems, improved enemy AI, and "course-corrected a litany of other details" — a patch bundled with, but distinct from, the paid DLC content it accompanied.

## Key Characteristics

- **Versioned or seasonal framing** — changes are grouped under a single identifier (Patch 2.0, Season 2/"Season of Blood") rather than released piecemeal, per doc_0533 and doc_0213.
- **Mix of change types** — a single patch bundles new content (Diablo 4's five endgame bosses), rebalancing (faster leveling, reworked Nightmare Dungeon affixes), and quality-of-life fixes (Renown carryover, gems no longer taking bag space), per doc_0533.
- **Developer-explained rationale** — studios attach commentary to justify changes, as when Diablo 4's game director Joe Shely and associate director Joe Piepiora told Polygon the quality-of-life focus came from finally having time to react to player feedback, unlike the rushed first season (doc_0533).
- **Distinct from paid content** — a patch can ship independently of or alongside paid expansions; Cyberpunk 2077's Patch 2.0 revamped core systems while Phantom Liberty (the paid DLC) added new story content, and reviewers credit the patch as much as the DLC for the game's improved reception (doc_0213).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, this kind of update bundle has a generic industry name: release notes (also called patch notes).
Per Wikipedia, release notes "describe important information about a distribution of a hardware or software product" and typically include "a list of what is new in the release, including bug fixes and new features" (Wikipedia, "Release notes," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Ofcom's First Guidelines Under The UK Online Safety Act

After the Online Safety Act's arduous multiyear passage through the UK's lawmaking process, regulator Ofcom published its first guidelines for how tech firms can comply with the mammoth legislation — a proposal, part of a multiphase publication process, outlining how social media platforms, search engines, online and mobile games, and pornography sites should deal with illegal content like child sexual abuse material (CSAM), terrorism content, and fraud.

The defining feature of the regime is a duty of care rather than a fixed rulebook. "What this does for the first time is to put a duty of care on tech firms to have a responsibility for the safety of their users," Ofcom's online safety lead, Gill Whitehead, told The Verge. "When they become aware that there is illegal content on their platform, they have got to get it down, and they also need to conduct risk assessments to understand the specific risks that those services might carry."

The guidelines' status is a discriminating detail. They are released as proposals so Ofcom can gather feedback before the UK Parliament approves them toward the end of next year, and even then the specifics will be voluntary: tech firms can guarantee they are obeying the law by following the guidelines to the letter, but they can take their own approach so long as they demonstrate compliance with the act's overarching rules — and, presumably, are prepared to fight their case with Ofcom.

The aim is to require that sites be proactive to stop the spread of illegal content and not just play whack-a-mole after the fact. It is meant to encourage a switch from a reactive to a more proactive approach, says lawyer Claire Wiseman, who specializes in tech, media, telecoms, and data.

# Regulatory Investigations Into OpenAI In 2023

OpenAI faced regulatory action on several fronts in 2023: Italy ordered ChatGPT blocked over GDPR concerns, Poland opened its own GDPR investigation, China's licensing regime pushed ChatGPT clients out of the App Store, and the FTC was reported to be investigating the chatbot's statements about people.

Italy moved first. Italy's data protection authority ordered OpenAI to stop processing people's data locally with immediate effect, saying it was concerned the ChatGPT maker was breaching the EU's General Data Protection Regulation and opening an investigation; OpenAI began geoblocking access to ChatGPT in Italy. The DPA then laid out what OpenAI needed to do for the order to be lifted, giving OpenAI a deadline of April 30 to complete the regulator's compliance demands, with a slightly more generous timeline of May 15 for a local radio, TV and internet awareness campaign. Poland's authority publicly announced it had opened an investigation regarding ChatGPT, accusing the company of a string of breaches of the GDPR.

In China, multiple generative AI apps were removed from Apple's China App Store ahead of the country's latest generative AI regulations, set to take effect August 15. Apple wrote in a letter to OpenCat, a native ChatGPT client: "As you may know, the government has been tightening regulations associated with deep synthesis technologies (DST) and generative AI services, including ChatGPT. DST must fulfill permitting requirements to operate in China, including securing a license from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). Based on our review, your app is associated with ChatGPT, which does not have requisite permits to operate in China."

In the United States, the FTC was reportedly in at least the exploratory phase of an investigation into whether ChatGPT made "false, misleading, disparaging or harmful" statements about people. TechCrunch reporter Devin Coldewey noted that such an investigation does not appear out of thin air — the FTC does not look around and say "That looks suspicious"; generally a lawsuit or formal complaint is brought to its attention and the practices described imply that regulations are being ignored, much as a person suing a supplement company over pills that made them sick can prompt an FTC investigation because there is evidence the company lied about side effects. Separately, FTC chair Lina Khan and fellow commissioners warned House representatives in a congressional hearing that modern AI technologies like ChatGPT could be used to "turbocharge" fraud: "AI presents a whole set of opportunities, but also presents a whole set of risks," Khan said. "And I think we've already seen ways in which it could be used to turbocharge fraud and scams. We've been putting market participants on notice that instances in which AI tools are effectively being designed to deceive people can place them on the hook for FTC action."

# India's Demographic Dividend Versus China's Decline

Brahma Chellaney, professor of strategic studies at the New Delhi-based Center for Policy Research, wrote in a recent article that as India's geopolitical, economic and cultural clout grows, so does its global footprint, and that China's "decline" — as some have begun to call the conclusion of the country's four-decade-long economic boom — opens new opportunities for the Indian economy and other developing and emerging countries.

The demographic relation is the pivot. Earlier in 2023 India reached a milestone when its population officially surpassed that of China, which had been the world's most populous country for more than 300 years. While China's shrinking, rapidly ageing population is likely to impede economic growth and may curtail its geopolitical ambitions, India — one of the world's youngest countries, with a median age of 28.2 — is poised to reap a huge demographic dividend.

Chellaney nevertheless places the driving force in growth rather than demography alone: while India's gross domestic product is still smaller than China's, the country is currently the world's fastest-growing major economy and is projected to account for 12.9 per cent of global growth over the next five years, surpassing the United States' 11.3 per cent share.

# The Clock Change And Road Accident Risk

The Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA) has called for the abolition of Daylight Saving Time on road-safety grounds, arguing that turning the clocks back increases the risk of road accidents because more people end up driving during the darker winter months. Its proposed remedy is to adopt British Summer Time permanently: "RoSPA is in favour of this proposal, and is calling for the government to adopt British Summer Time (GMT+1) all year. This would mean road users will no longer experience the sudden onset of darkness during their autumn commutes, potentially saving many lives."

The quantitative grounds come from RAC Foundation figures cited in support of abolishing DST: road traffic collisions increase by 19 per cent in the fortnight after the clocks go back one hour from British Summer Time, and reduce by 11 per cent when the clocks go forward.

# The EU's Urgent Warning Letter To X

The European Union fired a public warning at Elon Musk-owned X (formerly Twitter) for failing to tackle illegal content circulating on the platform in the wake of Saturday's deadly attacks on Israel by Hamas terrorists based in the Gaza Strip — an "urgent" letter from internal market commissioner Thierry Breton that TechCrunch described as a very swift test of the bloc's newly updated content moderation rulebook. Breton shared the letter publicly, tweeting on October 10, 2023: "Following the terrorist attacks by Hamas against 🇮🇱, we have indications of X/Twitter being used to disseminate illegal content & disinformation in the EU. Urgent letter to @elonmusk on #DSA obligations". TechCrunch's later account places the letter on the Wednesday.

The letter's substance was twofold. Breton said the bloc had seen "indications" from "qualified sources" that X was being used to disseminate illegal content and disinformation in the EU following Saturday's attacks, then reminded X of the DSA's "very precise obligations" on content moderation: "When you receive notices of illegal content in the EU, you must be timely, diligent and objective in taking action and removing the relevant content when warranted." Separately, the European Commission raised concerns about the spread of disinformation on X related to the terrorist attacks and their aftermath.

On the disinformation side Breton was specific about what had been reported and what he wanted done: "Public media and civil society organisations widely report instances of fake and manipulated images and facts circulating on your platform in the EU, such as repurposed old images of unrelated armed conflicts or military footage that actually originated from video games. This appears to be manifestly false or misleading information," he wrote. "I therefore invite you to urgently ensure that your systems are effective, and report on the crisis measures taken to my team."

TechCrunch's own characterisation of the platform at that moment was blunter than the letter's: rather than tackling the problem, it wrote, X "appears to be turning into an engine of disinformation" — one that had demonstrably enabled the very swift amplification of a smorgasbord of toxic fakes around the Israel-Hamas war, falsehoods that might be trying to manipulate opinion around the conflict, or otherwise exploit horrific events to drive engagement (clickbait) or for even more cynical and potentially harmful ends.

# Tesla Cybertruck Production Outlook

Tesla gave updates about its long-delayed Cybertruck alongside its Q3 2023 earnings: initial deliveries are set for an event at Giga Texas on November 30, and Elon Musk noted that scaling the Cybertruck will be hard and that it will take 18 months before the pickup is profitable. "I mean, we dug our own grave with Cybertruck," said Musk.

Musk also said Giga Texas will be able to produce about 250,000 Cybertrucks a year starting in 2025. TechCrunch attaches a caveat to that projection on 2023-10-22: Musk isn't great at making predictions — he initially said the Cybertruck would be on the market by 2021 — so some of these numbers should be expected to be pushed out too.

# The OPEC Letter Pressuring Members Against Phase-Out Language

There were hopeful signs the week before COP28's close, when draft documents included options to incorporate language calling on countries to phase out fossil fuel use — alongside an option not to include such a clause — until the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries sent a letter to its member states pressuring them to "proactively reject any text or formula that targets energy i.e. fossil fuels rather than emissions."

Following that letter, language that had previously called on countries to phase out fossil fuels vanished from subsequent draft texts. Backlash was swift: "This obsequious draft reads as if OPEC dictated it word for word," former US vice president Al Gore posted on X on the Monday. "COP28 is now on the verge of complete failure."

# The Claim That SGE And Bard Appropriate Publisher Content

The Helena World Chronicle lawsuit claims that Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The grounds are that Google's AI products both retain users and consume publisher content without permission.

On the Search Generative Experience, the suit argues that SGE offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode but ultimately keeps users in Google's "walled garden" as it "plagiarizes" their content. The warrant that turns this into a harm publishers cannot escape is that publishers also cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot — so opting out of the AI experience would mean opting out of search itself.

On Bard, the suit says Google's Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications," citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data. The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.

The case points to other concerns too, such as changing AdSense rates and evidence of improper spoliation of evidence on Google's part through its destruction of chat messages — an issue raised in the recent Epic Games lawsuit against Google over app store antitrust issues, which Epic won.

# Data Privacy

## Definition

Data privacy, across the corpus, is the recurring dispute over whether companies may collect, track, or profile people's personal information without their knowledge or consent.

That dispute plays out as regulatory enforcement against platforms: GDPR action against Meta's consentless ad tracking (doc_0107), COPPA litigation over Meta's collection of data from children under 13 (doc_0304), a "mass breach of privacy" allegation against TikTok's pre-consent tracking pixel (doc_0189), and California's CPPA extending opt-out and access rights to AI-based profiling (doc_0164).

## Context

In the corpus, data privacy surfaces as the recurring fault line between platforms that monetize personal data and the regulators pushing back on non-consensual collection. Norway's Datatilsynet issued an emergency GDPR ban on Meta running "personalized ads" without consent, then referred the case to the EU's Board to make the ban permanent across the single market, because Meta kept running tracking ads despite the order and a rejected court challenge (doc_0107). California's CPPA is drafting rules that would give residents opt-out and access rights over "automated decisionmaking technology," explicitly modeled on GDPR and expected to draw pushback from adtech and AI firms like Meta and OpenAI (doc_0164). The Age's investigation found TikTok's tracking pixel scraping site visitors' names, emails, and phone numbers before users clicked "I consent," prompting an Australian senator to call it a "mass breach of privacy" and demand a regulatory probe (doc_0189). Meta separately faces a 42-state lawsuit alleging it violated COPPA — the US law restricting data collection from children under 13 and requiring parental consent — by knowingly letting millions of underage users onto Instagram and Facebook while collecting their personal information (doc_0304).

## Key Characteristics

- **Consent is the legal hinge** — GDPR, as applied against Meta in Norway, turns on whether a company has a valid legal basis (consent, not "legitimate interest" or "contractual necessity") before tracking or profiling users for ads (doc_0107).
- **Pre-consent collection is the specific harm alleged against TikTok** — its pixel captured form-field data "often before clicking 'I consent'," unlike Google's and Meta's pixels, which the same test showed firing only after consent (doc_0189).
- **Children are a protected, heavily litigated category** — COPPA restricts data collection from users under 13 and requires verifiable parental consent, and Meta's alleged evasion of that requirement (ignoring reports, not disabling accounts, avoiding "actual knowledge") is the specific violation named in the unredacted lawsuit (doc_0304).
- **Regulators are extending consent/access rights into AI** — California's CPPA is drafting opt-out and access rights over automated decisionmaking technology and AI-based profiling, explicitly borrowing from GDPR's model (doc_0164).
- **Enforcement can escalate beyond a single national regulator** — Norway's local DPA used an emergency GDPR mechanism to bypass the "one-stop-shop" rule and force an EU-wide decision on Meta, showing that a single country's action can become bloc-wide policy (doc_0107).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the general legal concept the enforcement actions above are built on is the definition of "personal data" under GDPR.

GDPR.eu describes personal data as "any information that relates to an individual who can be directly or indirectly identified," a category spanning obvious identifiers like names and emails as well as location data and other online identifiers (GDPR.eu, "What Is GDPR, the EU's New Data Protection Law?", published by Proton AG with EU Horizon 2020 co-funding, accessed 2026-09-02: https://gdpr.eu/what-is-gdpr/).

# Google Local Search Ranking Factors

Google's public documentation says it uses three categories to rank results that are local to a searcher: relevance, distance, and prominence. To improve local ranking, Google encourages businesses to provide a trove of information on their profile — basics like updated hours of operation and accurate location details, but also responding to reviews, adding photos, and even posting individual items in stock to their Google page. The prominence measure in Maps includes data from the web: links to the business, how the business ranks in traditional search, and press coverage, for example. In this way SEO affects how a business appears in local search results, and news articles and links are one way Google tries to determine the relevance of a page — which is why reporters' inboxes are overrun with spammy requests to buy "guest posts" on their sites from marketers.

The model bounds what a keyword-matched business name can do. Asked whether naming a business after a search term works, Danny Sullivan, Google's public liaison for Search, said, "I doubt it": owners doing this might find success, but Google pulls in other data to serve results to users, like location, reviews, or ratings — a "hodgepodge of different things that we have that are out there." Sullivan added, "I've seen these kinds of things over the years, and they kind of make me laugh and have a bit of a chuckle. But I don't think they're really great marketing campaigns," and said Google's advice has always been that businesses should make decisions that serve their customers, not the platform.

The behaviour the names target is real even if the leverage is limited. The term "Thai food near me" is searched, on average, nearly a million times a month in the US, according to Semrush, a company that provides keyword research and other popular SEO tools; Semrush notes you will need referring domains and optimized content to compete for the term and grades it as "difficult" to rank for — competitive, but not even the hardest category. Adding "near me" to a search term is both a learned behavior and encouraged by Google, since "___ near me" is a top autofilled search suggestion on both Search and Maps and has become synonymous with Google, which is why the joke works. One anomaly showed the distance factor being outweighed: a search The Verge's reporter did in Google Maps for "Thai food near me" from Wisconsin surfaced the Manhattan restaurant as a suggestion above any local businesses, making it easier to find from the Midwest than from Brooklyn. Sullivan said this could be due to Google recognizing there is a business with an exact-match name that has some degree of notoriety that people are searching for in different areas, and that while it could encourage others to name businesses this way, he does not see it as an issue that needs addressing.

# StarNews Mobile As An African Mobile Video Network

StarNews Mobile is an African mobile video network that offers African content creators a platform for monetizing their work through a subscription model, and which had secured $3 million in pre-Series A funding as of 30 October 2023. As of that date the service was available in six African countries — Cameroon, where it started, plus Nigeria, Ghana, Congo, Benin and Ivory Coast.

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Telco Distribution

Telco distribution is a go-to-market model in which a content or service platform reaches and monetizes users primarily through partnerships with telecommunications operators (telcos) rather than through open platforms like YouTube or Instagram, letting the operator's existing subscriber relationship, billing rails and marketing reach stand in for the platform's own audience-acquisition and payment infrastructure.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces through StarNews Mobile, an African mobile video network that prioritizes distribution partnerships with major mobile operators MTN and Orange over conventional streaming platforms, because creators face revenue limitations on those existing platforms.

Founder Guy Kamgaing describes the underlying insight as coming from years of monetizing "jokes and horoscopes via telcos" through SMS/VAS campaigns, then applying the same telco relationship to video content that creators could not otherwise monetize on YouTube or other open platforms.

The corpus frames mobile operators as "pivotal in propelling content within Africa's media industry, with unmatched distribution capabilities," making close collaboration with them "imperative for establishing a solid presence in the market" — operators are cast as the gatekeepers of both reach and revenue in this market.

## Key Characteristics

- **Operator-led acquisition** — a significant portion of user acquisition comes through the telecom operators themselves, since it is a seamless process for an operator like MTN to message its own customers to encourage sign-up.
- **Airtime as payment rail** — subscribers pay using their mobile airtime rather than a card or bank-linked method, letting the platform inherit the operator's existing billing relationship with the user.
- **Operator as both channel and competitor** — operators simultaneously drive baseline data usage and upsell customers with their own in-house content, so a distribution partner is also competing with the operator's proprietary offerings for the same subscriber attention.
- **Fit-dependent, not guaranteed** — the partnership only holds where the operator's own creator strategy aligns with the platform's; a misalignment with an operator's strategy is enough to force an exit from an otherwise-served market.
- **Concentration of layers** — operators are described as taking the lead in this dynamic, with content creators or show organizers following, which lets a platform built on telco distribution combine distribution, monetization and content creation "at the local level" rather than ceding distribution control to a separate platform.

# Value-Added Services (VAS)

## Definition

Value-Added Services (VAS) is named in the corpus as the business area Guy Kamgaing spent ten years in before founding StarNews Mobile, described as "content monetization, particularly within the VAS (Value-Added Services) business."

The corpus's only illustration of that work is text/SMS-based campaigns monetizing content such as jokes and horoscopes in partnership with telcos.

The corpus does not itself define VAS as a general category; a broader definition, drawn from an external source, is given in Background (external) below.

## Context

The term surfaces in the corpus as the professional background that led StarNews Mobile founder and CEO Guy Kamgaing to launch the platform: he spent ten years in "content monetization, particularly within the VAS (Value-Added Services) business," running text/SMS-based campaigns before founding StarNews in 2017. That VAS experience is presented as the direct precursor to StarNews's model — Kamgaing describes having monetized "jokes and horoscopes via telcos for several years" before realizing the same telco relationships and monetization mechanics could be applied to creator content instead. The corpus does not itself define VAS beyond this SMS/text-campaign example, so the general definition below is drawn from external reference.

## Key Characteristics

- **Text/SMS-based campaigns** — the corpus's sole description of Kamgaing's VAS work is running text/SMS-based campaigns to monetize content, by his own account "jokes and horoscopes via telcos."
- **Ten-year background, later reused** — Kamgaing's VAS-era monetization techniques are described as the experience he drew on when he "realized" the same telco relationship could be applied to creator content, founding StarNews in 2017.
- **Depends on a telco relationship** — Kamgaing attributes his ability to monetize content to "a relationship with the telcos," the same kind of relationship StarNews later built with MTN and Orange.

## Background (external)

The corpus names VAS but does not define the category itself. Per Wikipedia, Value-Added Service is a telecommunications term for "all services beyond standard voice calls and fax transmissions" — non-core offerings that enhance a carrier's basic service and raise average revenue per user, delivered either directly by the network operator or through third-party content providers (Wikipedia, *Value-added service*, accessed 2026-09-02). Typical examples include ringtones and ringback tones, SMS-based premium content, mobile TV, location-based services, mobile advertising, and mobile money — the same SMS/text-campaign category Kamgaing describes working in (Wikipedia, *Value-added service*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Portfolio Management Services In India

Portfolio Management Services are a managed-account alternative available alongside AIFs to Indian HNIs, governed by guidelines that date back to 1993 but that have grown in popularity with HNIs only recently. The growing financialisation of savings, the formalisation of the economy and the growing prosperity of tier 2 and 3 cities have raised PMS AUM, excluding EPFO and PF money, to ₹5.28 lakh crore as of July 2023. Because the minimum investment is ₹50 lakh, this option too is available only to HNIs.

The discriminating features are drawn against mutual funds. Both PMS and mutual funds provide expert guidance in navigating volatile markets and seizing wealth-creating opportunities, but because mutual funds cater to retail investors their guidelines are relatively stringent and compliance is rigorous, whereas PMS investment guidelines are somewhat more flexible, allowing portfolio managers to outperform mutual funds. A second appeal to HNIs is ownership: in PMS the beneficial ownership of securities belongs to the investors, as opposed to mutual funds where ownership belongs to the fund. PMS comes in two variants, discretionary and non-discretionary; in the former the portfolio managers make all decisions, in the latter the investor does.

# The Twitter-Alternative Market

The market for Twitter alternatives is a crowded one, and its structure has two parts: a large field of rivals, and an incumbent whose network effect none of them has broken. On the rival side there are numerous services for consumers to try, including the open source-based platform Mastodon, a soon-to-be decentralized system from Bluesky, plus smaller startups like Spill, Spoutible and Post, as well as a new app from Meta called Instagram Threads.

Co-founder and CEO Gabor Cselle, who had exits to Google and Twitter prior to starting Pebble, blames that density in part: "I think the competitive landscape evolved faster than we had thought. I didn't think that quite as many people — established organizations and newcomers — would try to do the same thing that we were doing and in very similar ways." The second part of the model is the X factor: the default platform for short posts retains some pull, despite — or perhaps because of — new owner Elon Musk's antics, and though the company may not have yet succeeded from a business and financial perspective, it's been hard for others to duplicate its function as a breaking news platform and place for spirited debates. Pebble co-founder and CTO Michael Greer, previously Discord engineering head, states the general relation: "I think Threads and others have encountered this as well. # Banking-as-a-Service

## Definition

Banking-as-a-service (BaaS) is the label TechCrunch's coverage applies to platforms — Synapse and QI Tech — that let banks and fintech companies build financial services on top of them, rather than platforms that serve end customers as a bank would.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term through two TechCrunch items: Synapse, covered in the fintech newsletter The Interchange as a San Francisco–based company whose platform "enables banks and fintech companies to easily develop financial services," and QI Tech, covered in the general Startups Weekly newsletter as a Brazilian "banking-as-a-service platform" that raised a large Series B.

Both appear as fintech infrastructure providers rather than consumer-facing banks — Synapse sits behind other companies' financial products, and QI Tech's raise is framed as backing for the same kind of platform business in Brazil.

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform, not bank** — the BaaS provider "operates a platform enabling banks and fintech companies to easily develop financial services" rather than serving end customers directly.
- **Infrastructure for others' products** — Synapse's role is to let other banks and fintechs build financial services on top of it, positioning it as embedded infrastructure rather than a retail brand.
- **Investor interest despite volatility** — QI Tech's BaaS platform drew a $200 million Series B, the largest Brazilian raise across all sectors that year, around the same time Synapse laid off 86 people, or about 40% of its staff.
- **Exposure to macro conditions** — an earlier round of Synapse layoffs (18% of its workforce, per a June blog post from CEO Sankaet Pathak) was attributed to "the current macroeconomic conditions" affecting its clients and platforms, indicating BaaS providers' fortunes are tied to the health of the banks/fintechs building on top of them.

## Background (external)

Wikipedia's entry on Banking-as-a-Service defines it more generally: BaaS refers to offering banking products — like deposit accounts, loans, and credit cards — to customers through partnerships with non-bank or non-financial third parties, where the bank handles balance-sheet management (capital, liquidity, credit risk) while the partner, often a fintech, engages the customer directly through its own app, typically connecting to the bank's systems via APIs.

Source: Wikipedia, "Banking as a service," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banking_as_a_service, accessed 2026-09-02.

# Thai Food Near Me's Viral Moment

In March, before serving a single person, Thai Food Near Me went viral online for its name: a photo of the restaurant circulated on Twitter ahead of its opening, brown butcher paper still covering the windows. The restaurant's goofy name was enough to garner coverage on news sites, along with an influx of customers in the first crucial months of being open.

The viral tweet invariably summoned a chorus of overly friendly, all-lowercase-text replies from brands looking for attention, and the official account of Google Maps — the very entity the meme-y restaurant name is designed to outsmart — could not resist. # Creator Economy

## Definition

In the corpus, "creator economy" names the industry of livestreamers and other online creators whose income depends on platform-designed monetization mechanisms — subscription revenue splits, ad-revenue sharing, sponsorship deals, and creator-payment plans — and whose sustainability is treated as a live, contested question by the platforms, creators, and press covering it.

Corpus evidence for this usage: TechCrunch reports that VidCon hosted an industry leadership summit where "creator economy experts and creators" aired grievances about the state of the business, and a TechCrunch newsletter calls it "eye-wateringly hard to make money as a creator"; Spill frames paying creators for their cultural contributions as "especially important for Black creators in the creator economy."

## Context

The corpus surfaces the creator economy wherever a platform's monetization design meets an individual creator's livelihood. Twitch's Chief Monetization Officer describes the company's subscription splits, the Partner Plus tier, ad-revenue sharing, and sponsorship deals as the tools it uses to let livestreaming creators make a living, and frames its unique position as the platform where "viewers are directly supporting creators" through subscriptions, gifting, and cheering. Kick undercuts Twitch's model with a more generous 95/5 revenue split, pulling streamers who cannot make ends meet on Twitch's terms. Spill, a beta social app, frames paying creators for their cultural contributions — "especially important for Black creators" — as central to its pitch. YouTube's demonetization of SSSniperwolf under its "Creator Responsibility policies" shows the same economy's downside: a platform can cut off a creator's income unilaterally. And at VidCon, "creator economy experts and creators" convened an industry leadership summit specifically to "hash out their grievances with the state of the business," underscoring that the term names a recognized industry, not just a metaphor.

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform-mediated monetization** — creators earn through mechanisms platforms design and can change: Twitch's subscription splits, its Partner Plus program (70/30 split on the first $100,000 for eligible streamers), ad-revenue sharing, and sponsorship deals.
- **Precarious, individual-scale economics** — a TechCrunch newsletter argues it is "so eye-wateringly hard to make money as a creator" that venture-scale returns are unrealistic, favoring peer knowledge-sharing (like VidCon's summit or a creator-networking app) over creators raising venture capital.
- **Platform dependence cuts both ways** — a small streamer's income can collapse when a platform changes its split (Kelly's Twitch income fell from over $1,000/month to about $120 after Twitch cut the 70/30 deal), then recover on a rival platform with a friendlier split (over $1,000/month on Kick with far fewer subscribers).
- **Unilateral platform enforcement** — a platform can suspend a creator's monetization outright, as YouTube did to SSSniperwolf under its Creator Responsibility policies after doxxing accusations.
- **Recognized as an industry with its own advocacy** — VidCon hosted a dedicated leadership summit where "creator economy experts and creators" aired grievances about the state of the business, and platform-adjacent apps like Spill explicitly build creator-payment plans, in Spill's case foregrounding credit and pay for Black creators.

## Background (external)

Beyond the corpus, "creator economy" is a general industry term for a platform-driven economy in which creators produce content, products, or services and distribute them directly to their audience via social media and related technologies, building communities and monetizing their work through channels like advertising, sponsorships, sales, crowdfunding, and subscriptions.

Source: Wikipedia, "Creator economy" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creator_economy), accessed 2026-09-02.

# StarNews Mobile's $3M Pre-Series A Round

Janngo Capital, an Africa-focused venture capital firm, led StarNews Mobile's $3 million pre-Series A funding round announced on 30 October 2023, and the other notable investors included the soccer players Aurélien Tchouaméni of Real Madrid, Jules Koundé of Barcelona and Mike Maignan of AC Milan, all affiliated with the athlete representation agency Excellence Sport Nation. Kamgaing highlighted the shared African heritage of these players, underscoring their connection to StarNews' mission and their genuine interest in engaging with the African audience and investing in startups across the continent. They join the ranks of investors like Blaise Matuidi, a former French international who has previously invested in the Sudanese fintech company Bloom and currently heads Origins, a VC firm run in collaboration with other soccer players who serve as limited partners.

The round is aimed at creator payouts and market expansion. Kamgaing revealed that the platform distributed $1 million to content creators in the prior year while maintaining an average monthly payout of around $70,000 to those creators, and the fresh injection of capital serves as a significant uplift for Africa's creator economy — an underserved sector in African tech, despite startups like the e-commerce-focused Selar holding their own. The funding will equip the Los Angeles-based company, which then had 40 employees, to better support its creators and gradually enhance payouts in the coming years, a crucial step in bolstering the region's creative industry. In a press statement Kamgaing outlined expansion plans to strengthen the startup's dominant presence in Francophone Africa while quickly expanding across strategic markets like Nigeria and Ghana, and on the call he said StarNews is looking to be in 11 markets by next year.

Fatoumata Bâ, founder and executive chair of Janngo Capital, affirmed the firm's support for StarNews, accentuating the platform's unique positioning, strategic partnerships, technology and content. That support is rooted in the belief that StarNews is well-positioned to capitalize on the immense growth potential of Africa's creative industry, which she said is poised for a fourfold expansion by 2050 and the possibility to generate up to $20 billion in GDP.

Fernand Tchouameni, spokesperson and investment advisor for Aurelien Tchouameni, framed the investment in diaspora terms: "I am very excited and proud to back StarNews, the first media platform that supports African creators and tells the world the real African story. Being of Cameroonian descent, I can also see StarNews becoming a bridge to connect with the African diaspora, and I personally look forward to being on it."

# Fortnite's Live-Service Content Treadmill

Polygon's model, published 2023-10-19, is that around 2018 Twitch and its personalities turned Fortnite into a juggernaut so powerful that much of the gaming industry started molding itself in its image — and that what kept Fortnite from being a mere fad was not its approachable aesthetic and surprising gameplay but its model: where content expansions and adjustments previously took months or years and often cost money, Fortnite set a more cutthroat standard of free weekly content updates.

The conditions that made this possible were unique to Epic. It could swing ceaseless delivery because the bulk of its profits at the time came from its engine, which many games — including Fortnite's competitors — license; those deep pockets made Fortnite possible in the first place, since the bubbly shooter was initially a flop before Epic perfected the formula. The cadence also let Epic quickly adapt Fortnite to whatever was trending or novel, whether Among Us or Splatoon, and much like Roblox it became a game that could give you anything — and if Epic did not emulate it, the players would. "You can't replicate Fortnite's growth from, like, the [content creator] standpoint and also definitely from the developer standpoint," says a Twitch streamer turned game developer who requested anonymity because he is not authorized to discuss the popular AAA live-service shooter he works on.

Those conditions were immaterial to publishers who could only imagine profits: suddenly "live service" was everywhere, and games like Overwatch, which could not achieve a similar pace, were posed as disappointments by content creators.

The limit of the model is the audience it assumes. Developers say getting half their players to actually finish games is unusual and worth celebrating, because most people will never finish a game they start, and 22% of purchased games on Steam are unplayed outright — affected by factors like sales or Game Pass, but still telling. Per Statista, a reported 25% of players between 18 and 34 enjoy games between three and six hours a week, 28% play two hours or less, and 19% play between 13 to 24 hours or more; as fans get older they apparently spend less time in games, and in the most engaged age group half of all players only log a couple of hours or so per week in their favorite games.

# Global Rate Shock Risk to Emerging Market Debt

Rajan Jain, Head of Credit Research at SBI Caps, framed the open question in a note: whether the yield curve dynamics mean the US is moving to a structurally higher-rate economy versus the post-GFC normal remains moot, with important implications for investment demand and system risk.

The transmission he describes runs outward from US rates. These movements have had a cascading effect on global economies, which have seen routs in their respective bond markets besides a fresh round of currency depreciation.

The vulnerable case is specific: emerging market economies with large volumes of USD-denominated debt, which could be caught in a vicious circle where their external debt in local currency terms balloons due to a strong DXY while their servicing ability is impaired by tepid economic activity owing to high rates. The stress is not confined to them — even advanced economies have felt the heat, and the ECB and others have maintained a hawkish narrative, Jain said.

On Saturday, 2023-10-21, President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi hosted what was billed as a "Summit for Peace" in Cairo, with Middle East and European leaders in attendance — evidence of the international focus then trained on Egypt. # Web Summit and the Paddy Cosgrave Controversy

Web Summit, the big tech conference brand that runs events in several cities and whose 70,000-person flagship event in Lisbon was taking place the month after 16 October 2023, was running into a wall — a wall of outrage. Founders, investors and others from the technology community in Israel had gone ballistic over comments made by the founder and figurehead of Web Summit, Paddy Cosgrave, related to the fighting underway across Israel and Gaza, specifically his criticism of Israel's retaliatory actions. The anger with Cosgrave had gone viral, and on the day of reporting it looked like it was about to overrun promotion efforts for Web Summit. The situation also highlighted how Israel's tech industry, the country's most valuable and arguably best-known export, built on business development and relationships, has been willing to cut those ties in the battle of public opinion in this most polarizing of conflicts. "Here in Israel, we're basically now in rage mode after the first week of shock and awe," one tech source told TechCrunch. "We ain't got time to f_ck around with anyone remotely suggesting Israel needs to sit it out and not put an end to Hamas."

The trigger was the opening day of the war. It all started the day that Hamas busted through Israel's walls and rampaged through villages and a music festival on a murdering and pillaging spree, killing 1,400 people, mostly civilians; Hamas, the ruling party in the Palestinian territory, is considered a terrorist organization by the U.K., U.S. and other countries, and they also took 199 hostages back into Gaza. On that day, Cosgrave was in Doha, Qatar — the city where Web Summit would be holding its newest event in four months' time.

What Cosgrave posted, and what he left out, is the specific grievance. As some were taking to social media to express shock, or sympathy, or in some cases advocating for restraint, some took more critical stances; Cosgrave, for his part, posted data on X of the human cost of the Israel-Palestine conflict between 2008 and 2023, and it omitted the events and casualties of that weekend. That stirred debate, but Cosgrave did not acknowledge that the numbers were out of date or comment about the attacks in Israel. He instead proceeded, over the next several days — between posts about Qatar, political comments related to Ireland, and rugby reactions — to put out several more posts, all highlighting the opinion that Israel was taking an unjust approach.

As the posts racked up a range of alarming and extreme responses on both sides of the argument, Cosgrave doubled down. On the Friday he noted he was "shocked by the rhetoric and actions of so many Western leaders" in supporting Israel. But as attention mounted, the rejections to Web Summit started, too.

# The Gaza Information War And The Hamas Narrative

Eylon Levy argues that the conflict is not only a kinetic war in Gaza but also an information war, in which the Hamas narrative is adopted far more easily than Israel's account is accepted. His first ground is a case of a claim that collapsed: the day after what he calls the bluff about the Al-Ahli hospital, which the Palestinians claimed had been hit by an Israeli missile killing 800 civilians but which in the end turned out to have been caused by a splinter group of Islamic Jihad, with no hospital destroyed and certainly not 800 people killed, he explained on Sky News that Hamas lies and makes up numbers, and the reporter asked him, almost speechless with surprise, whether he doubts Hamas' numbers. He describes such moments as intensely frustrating, recounting a BBC interview in which the interviewer told him "Hamas denies what you are saying", to which his answer is that of course Hamas denies this, since Hamas denies that it is even holding hostages, and Hamas massacres, beheads, rapes, burns families and then day and night denies that it did so. Some journalists around the world see that Hamas continues to lie about the biggest things when the whole truth is in front of everyone's eyes, and they continue to echo the lies.

His second ground is a structural claim about where information from Gaza comes from: it comes either directly from Hamas or from independent reporters and photographers who are part of the system in Gaza, and everyone knows that even if they are not affiliated with Hamas they are not free to present the full truth because they are not allowed to. The evidence he offers for the constraint is what is missing: there is not a single photo of a terrorist, not a single photo of a missile being launched from a densely populated area, from a mosque or a school, not even a single photo from the Hamas tunnels under Shifa; the reason is that these reporters, even if not explicitly on Hamas' side, operate under a dictatorial regime and cannot provide the information even if they wanted to, which is why he thinks it very important to keep reminding the world how biased the information reaching them is. Levy qualifies the argument explicitly: he does not want to give the impression that all interviewers are hostile and every question delusional, and he has many interviews with reporters who understand what is happening and simply want information and to hear the Israeli side, which is completely legitimate.

# Egypt's Role In The Israel-Hamas War And The Leverage It Creates

The war between Israel and Hamas has turned the spotlight on Egypt's role as a regional powerbroker, potentially winning it Western support as it tries to escape a grinding economic crisis. The structure linking the two is that Egypt's two assets in this conflict — long-held ties to Israel and a border with Gaza — make its stance decisive for outcomes the West wants.

# Disinformation On X After The Hamas Attacks On Israel

In the days after Saturday's Hamas attacks on Israel, posts identified as false circulated widely on X, including footage repurposed from a video game and clips entirely unrelated to the conflict. TechCrunch reported the pattern in two articles, on 10 and 13 October 2023, drawing on fact-checkers, public media, civil society organisations and X's own safety account.

The observed content fell into several kinds. Graphic videos apparently showing terrorist attacks on civilians circulated on X from Saturday onward. Alongside them were posts purporting to show footage from the attacks inside Israel, or from Israel's subsequent retaliation on targets in the Gaza Strip, which fact-checkers identified as false. A number of videos posted since the attacks were identified as entirely unrelated to the conflict — including footage filmed the previous month in Egypt, and a clip from the video game Arma 3 posted with the false claim that it showed Hamas missile attacks on Israel. Shayan Sardarizadeh (@Shayan86) flagged the Arma 3 clip on October 9, 2023: "This video certainly doesn't show a new air assault on Israel by Hamas militants, because it's actually from the video game Arma 3."

The volume was substantial. In remarks via X's safety account, the company reported more than 50 million posts globally over the past two days that referenced the weekend's terrorist attack, underlining the scope of content generated.

Two conditions shaped the environment. First, the attacks themselves: Hamas militants inside Gaza got past border fences and mounted a series of surprise attacks on Israeli civilians and tourists, after which Israel's prime minister declared "we are at war" and its military retaliated by firing scores of missiles into the Gaza Strip. By Thursday afternoon, per TechCrunch's 13 October report, Hamas' attack had killed more than 1,200 people according to the Israeli Military, and at least 1,537 people had been killed in Gaza by Israel's retaliatory strikes according to the Gaza Ministry of Health. Second, amplification on the platform itself: Eliot Higgins (@EliotHiggins) wrote on October 10, 2023 that "a totally false claim about Israel bombing a church in Gaza" had gone viral "thanks to multiple blue tick accounts repeating an unverified claim that had no evidence to back it up", adding that "Musk has created a fundamental issue with Twitter's credibility in moments of crisis."

X's owner was himself part of the observed pattern: at one point Musk recommended that people follow accounts that had posted antisemitic comments and false information in the past, though he subsequently deleted the tweet in which he made the suggestion. A Wired report published the day before TechCrunch's 10 October article summed up the situation on the platform under the headline "The Israel-Hamas War Is Drowning X in Disinformation."

# The Middle East Conflict As A Market Risk In October 2023

Investors in October 2023 were treating the Middle East conflict as a conditional risk rather than an active one: with Israeli air strikes attacking Gaza on Tuesday and razing entire districts in the densely populated and impoverished enclave, markets were being sanguine, but the sanguine view was explicitly contingent on the fighting not spreading.

John Praveen, managing director and co-chief investment officer at Paleo Leon, set out the transmission both ways. "Everybody has one eye on the Middle East conflict and one eye on what's happening with bond yields. The decline in bond yields is the key driver today," he said. But that view could change if, for example, the fighting spread to other countries in the region: "If tensions escalate bond yields might decline further because they're a safe haven, but equities would sell off in that instance because of increased uncertainty and risk aversion." Other signals ran alongside. Billionaire investor Paul Tudor Jones told CNBC the current geopolitical environment was the "most threatening and challenging" he had ever seen following Hamas's attack on Israel over the weekend, and predicted the US will enter a recession early next year. The shekel regained its footing as the central bank duelled short sellers to contain the market fallout from Israel's conflict with Hamas. European gas prices jumped, with Finland on high alert as it suspects a gas pipeline leak in the Baltic Sea was caused by a deliberate act of destruction, fuelling concerns about the safety of Europe's energy infrastructure. And base metals sank amid fresh fears over property turmoil in China.

# Dangerous Organizations and Individuals Policy

The Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy is the named enforcement category Meta cites when it removes content tied to groups that governments designate as terrorist organizations, most directly Hamas.
In the corpus its practical trigger is Hamas: content praising or supporting Hamas, which governs Gaza and is designated a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union, is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms.
Meta tracks enforcement of this policy as its own category, separate from its Violence and Incitement policy, reporting that it removed "seven times as many pieces of content on a daily basis for violating our Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy in Hebrew and Arabic alone" in the three days after October 7, 2023, compared with the two months prior.

## Context

In the corpus the policy is the mechanism through which Meta enforces against Hamas-related content during the Israel-Hamas war, and it is the recurring flashpoint in disputes over whether that enforcement is applied evenly.
Meta invokes the policy to justify removing content that praises or supports Hamas — Hamas being "designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union" — and Instagram separately cited a related "Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations" when it denied that a specific violent, threatening comment violated its rules, illustrating that the same policy family both blocks and, in users' eyes, under-enforces depending on the content.
The designation logic recurs beyond Meta's own platform actions: the corpus notes that Hamas is "considered a terrorist organization by the U.K., U.S. and other countries" in the context of the Web Summit/Cosgrave controversy, and that UNRWA operates "alongside Hamas, which Israel, the United States and other countries designate as a terrorist organization" in Gaza — showing the same underlying designation of Hamas driving both platform moderation policy and geopolitical characterization of the region's governing party.

## Key Characteristics

- **Named, tracked enforcement category** — Meta reports removal volumes specifically "for violating our Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy," distinct from its Violence and Incitement policy, letting the company cite a sevenfold daily increase in Hebrew/Arabic enforcement after October 7.
- **Anchored to external terrorist designations** — the policy's practical trigger in the corpus is content supporting Hamas, an organization the U.S., EU and U.K. designate as a terrorist group; the platform rule imports government designations rather than defining "dangerous" independently.
- **Contested in application** — Palestinian users and digital-rights advocates argue the policy (and its Community Guidelines "violence or dangerous organizations" language) is enforced inconsistently, citing a case where a violent, threatening comment was ruled not to violate it, and past instances where the Al-Aqsa Mosque hashtag was blocked after being "mistaken for a terrorist organization."
- **Localized to Arabic and Hebrew content** — the volume Meta cites for this policy is scoped specifically to Hebrew and Arabic content, not platform-wide, reflecting the languages most implicated in Israel-Hamas war content moderation.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Meta's own Community Standards describe the Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy more broadly than the Hamas-specific enforcement described above: it generally bars praise, substantive support, and representation of any individual or organization that Meta designates as dangerous, a designation list that spans terrorist organizations, hate organizations, criminal organizations, and other violence-inducing entities, not just Hamas.
Source: Meta Transparency Center, "Dangerous Organizations and Individuals" Community Standard, accessed 2026-09-02, https://transparency.meta.com/policies/community-standards/dangerous-individuals-organizations/.

Josh Kopelman, the founder of First Round Capital, publicly doubted Cosgrave's conciliatory statement: "Hard to take this statement at face value — given all the tweets @paddycosgrave has been liking over the last few days. # Egypt's Refusal To Host Palestinian Refugees

President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi has rejected any suggestion that Egypt host Gazan refugees, even as the same Western governments now court him for help in alleviating the pressure on Gaza, suggesting instead that Israel take in Palestinians in its Negev desert: "They can transport Palestinians there until Israel implements its announced plan to destroy Hamas," he said on Wednesday, 2023-10-18. The core political ground is that "there is little to no constituency for going against decades of policy on not allowing Palestinian displacement," said Mirette Mabrouk of the Middle East Institute, while the inducements offered "might wind up becoming a political liability, especially in an election year."

Three further grounds support the refusal. Egypt already hosts some 9 million refugees and other migrants from countries including Syria, Sudan, Yemen and Libya. Opening a route for Palestinians may also present a new security risk in the Sinai peninsula, where the army has only just managed to get a handle on its fight with Islamist militants. And Jordan has also refused to accept more Palestinians, making it unlikely Egypt would become a regional exception and take in refugees many suspect may never be let back into Gaza — which would risk being seen in the Arab world as facilitating another mass displacement and betraying the Palestinian cause all Arab countries vocally espouse.

The warrant tying these grounds to the policy is that the domestic political cost outranks the economic one. While Egypt could absorb a certain number of people, the domestic political consequences would be "huge," said the Washington Institute's Robert Satloff: "The political leadership considers this a red line not to be crossed and would prefer to face worsening financial distress than accept a significant number of refugees."

# Meta's Moderation During An Earlier Hamas-Israel Conflict

During an earlier Hamas-Israel conflict, the digital-rights organisation 7amleh documented more than 500 reports of Palestinian "digital rights violations" over the 13 days leading up to the ceasefire — including the removal and restriction of content, hashtags and accounts related to the conflict. The figure was recounted to TechCrunch for its 19 October 2023 report on Meta's moderation of Palestinian content.

Meta attributed some of the instances of perceived censorship to technical issues, such as one that prevented users in Palestine and Colombia from posting Instagram Stories. It attributed others to human error, such as blocking the hashtag for Al-Aqsa Mosque — the holy site where Israeli police clashed with Ramadan worshippers — because the name was mistaken for a terrorist organization. The company also blocked journalists in Gaza from WhatsApp without explanation.

Meta committed to implementing policy changes based on the report's recommendations, including updating its keywords associated with dangerous organizations, disclosing government requests to remove content, and launching a hostile speech classifier for Hebrew content. 7amleh advocacy manager Jalal Abukhater added that Meta has improved its response to harassment, at least in comparison to other social media platforms such as X (formerly Twitter): although harassment and abuse remain rampant on Instagram and Facebook, he said the company has been responsive to suspending accounts with patterns of targeting other users.

Abukhater's scope condition on all of this is that the improvements do not survive an escalation. "The balance of power is very fixed, in reality, between Israelis and Palestinians," he said. "And this is something that today is reflected heavily on platforms like Meta, even though they have human rights teams releasing reports and trying to improve upon their policies. Whenever an escalation like the one we're experiencing now happens, things just go back to zero."
