# Meta Moderation Bias

TechCrunch's claim, published 19 October 2023, is that Meta has a moderation bias problem rather than a "bug": the suppression of Palestinian voices is the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The argument's careful qualifier is that intent is not asserted — the company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.

The first ground is Meta's own commissioned evidence. During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company's actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation.

The second ground is the pattern of disproportionate scrutiny during that outbreak. Amid the violence following the May 2021 court ruling to evict Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah, a neighborhood in occupied East Jerusalem, users across Facebook and Instagram accused Meta of taking down posts and suspending accounts that voiced support for Palestinians. The digital rights nonprofit Electronic Frontier Foundation described Meta's actions in 2021 as "systemic censorship of Palestinian voices," and in its 2022 report on Palestinian digital rights, 7amleh said Meta is "still the most restricting company" compared with other social media giants in the extent of its moderation of the Palestinian digital space.

The third ground is internal. That same month, a group of Facebook employees filed internal complaints accusing the company of bias against Arab and Muslim users; in internal posts obtained by BuzzFeed News, an employee attributed the bias to "years and years of implementing policies that just don't scale globally."

The fourth ground is the measured asymmetry between languages. At the recommendation of its Oversight Board, Meta conducted a third-party due diligence report about the platform's moderation during the May 2021 conflict. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. It noted that Meta's moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as for Hebrew, because the latter is a "more standardized language," and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is duration and convergence. Because the disparity is recurrent across separate escalations, is corroborated from inside the company as well as by outside nonprofits and by Meta's own commissioned reviewers, and is traceable to standing properties of the moderation system rather than to a one-off failure, it is better described as bias inherent in the processes than as an isolated technical error.

# Meta Crisis Response Measures

Following a content moderation warning from European Union regulators earlier that week, Meta published on 13 October 2023 an overview of how it is responding to risks on its platforms stemming from the Israel-Hamas war: a temporary expansion of its Violence and Incitement policy, prioritised livestream checks, demotion of borderline content, hashtag blocking, a special operations center, and a temporary suspension of strikes for some violations. The blog post frames much of this as "ongoing efforts" and rehashes some existing policies and tools, but the company confirms it made some changes in light of fast-moving events in Israel and Gaza.

The first change is the temporary expansion of the Violence and Incitement policy, in order to prioritize the safety of Israelis kidnapped by Hamas. Under it, Meta will remove content that "clearly identifies hostages when we're made aware of it, even if it's being done to condemn or raise awareness of their situation." Blurred images of victims are allowed, but, "in line with standards established by the Geneva Convention, we will prioritize the safety and privacy of kidnapping victims if we are unsure or unable to make a clear assessment."

The second is livestreaming. Meta says it is prioritizing checks on livestreaming functions on Facebook and Instagram, including watching for any attempts by Hamas to use the tools to broadcast footage of captured Israelis or other hostages. The precondition it invokes is prior violation history: "We recognize that the immediacy of Live brings unique challenges, so we have restrictions in place on the use of Live for people who have previously violated certain policies. We're prioritizing livestream reports related to this crisis, above and beyond our existing prioritization of Live videos." Meta drew the comparison to measures it took after the 2019 Christchurch attacks in New Zealand, when a single shooter livestreamed a killing spree targeting two mosques on Facebook. On the specific threat, it added: "We're also aware of Hamas' threats to broadcast footage of the hostages and we're taking these threats extremely seriously. Our teams are monitoring this closely, and would swiftly remove any such content (and the accounts behind it), banking the content in our systems to prevent copies being re-shared." The urgency is not hypothetical: in a particularly disturbing report on Israeli media that week, widely recirculated on social media, a girl recounted how she and her family learnt of her grandmother's death after Hamas militants uploaded a video of her dead body to Facebook, apparently using the dead woman's own mobile phone to post the graphic content to her Facebook page.

Further steps cover ranking and search. Meta says it is making it less likely that its systems will actively recommend potentially violating or borderline content, and reducing the visibility of potentially offensive comments; it is also applying hashtag blocking to render certain terms related to the conflict non-searchable on its platforms. The blog post does not specify which hashtags Meta is blocking in relation to the Israel-Hamas war.

Operationally, Meta says it established a special operations center staffed with experts, including Arabic and Hebrew speakers, to increase its ability to respond quickly to content reports, and that it is taking feedback from local partners such as NGOs on emerging risks and "moving quickly to address them."

Meta states the limit of the procedure itself: given the heightened attention and concern, it says non-violating content may be removed "in error." Its mitigation is to relax the penalty rather than the removal — "for some violations we are temporarily removing content without strikes, meaning these content removals won't cause accounts to be disabled" — and it says it continues to provide tools for users to appeal decisions they believe were wrong.

# The National Public Diplomacy Directorate

The National Public Diplomacy Directorate, headed by Moshe Aviv, is the body through which Israel's spokespeople and volunteers have been working around the clock in the weeks before 3 December 2023. Its defining operating rule, in Eylon Levy's account, is constant availability: "we try to be available 24/7". He gives the shift pattern as evidence, having been interviewed at six in the morning one Friday and finishing with a CNN interview at 2am the following morning, and having done four BBC interviews on one Saturday; and it is not just him, with Mark Regev doing interviews at all hours of the night and Tal Heinrich in the US being interviewed non-stop in prime time, as part of what Levy calls an amazing team of professionals.

Its second defining feature is inter-agency collaboration. The work is done with Israel Police, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the IDF Spokesperson, the Israel Prisons Service, the Shin Bet, the National Security Council, and the Ministry of Diaspora Affairs, which is responsible for producing items for digital channels. Levy says it is amazing to see every day, when all these bodies assess the situation together, how they put their egos aside, and that if any channel wants an official spokesperson for the Israeli government then they will be there, because they cannot abandon the battlefield.

# IMPA's Blocking Of A Hamas Fundraising Pipeline In Europe

Two weeks into the war, the Israel Money Laundering and Terror Financing Prohibition Authority received secret intelligence from two European countries warning that "A large, well-known organization is raising funds for Hamas through posts on social networks, and fintech company platforms outside Israel, under the guise of donations to Gaza residents" — and in a swift joint international action, at IMPA's request, one of the European countries blocked the organization's money pipeline by immediately freezing its financial activities.

The intelligence included the name of the organization, its fundraising methods, and the identity of the entities behind it, and the concern was that within days the millions of dollars raised would go directly to the military arm of Hamas. "We are talking about a matter of minutes here. From the moment the authorities in Europe received the information, and we requested the money be blocked, with no court orders or delay, they blocked the transfer of millions of dollars to one of the most active organizations, and from it to Hamas. This is a real-time deterrence," IMPA director general Adv. Ilit Ostrovitch-Levi said. "And then there was a domino effect. Following this blocking, more countries began to look around, and blocked funds intended for terror. All this information, which is now shared at an international level, leads to the closing of more and more Hamas funding pipelines, in real time. With worldwide cooperation, Israel's security and enforcement authorities are thwarting the transfer of millions of dollars earmarked for terrorism, every day."

# Meta Response To Suppression Claims

Meta's rebuttal attacks the premise that any pattern of reduced reach for Palestine-related content shows deliberate suppression: the company says the reduced reach came from globally scoped technical bugs and from errors in good-faith enforcement, not from the subject matter of the posts. As reported by TechCrunch on 19 October 2023, Meta said it is closely monitoring its platforms for violations and may inadvertently flag certain content, but that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view."

The scope condition Meta sets around the whole dispute is its terrorist-organization rule: content praising or supporting Hamas — which governs Gaza and is designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union — is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms. This is stated in the aftermath of Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade cutting access to electricity, water and vital supplies, which have devastated Gaza.

Meta communications director Andy Stone declined to comment on the record and pointed TechCrunch to Meta's newsroom post about the conflict, updated on Oct. 18 with a statement addressing the shadowbanning claims. "Our policies are designed to keep people safe on our apps while giving everyone a voice," it said. "We apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice … We can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it."

The specific counter-explanations are two bugs, each claimed to be global and therefore content-neutral. Meta blamed technical errors for the removal of posts about Palestine during the 2021 conflict, and on the recent shadowbanning claims a company representative pointed TechCrunch to a Threads post by Stone: "We identified a bug impacting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts, meaning they weren't showing up properly in people's Stories tray, leading to significantly reduced reach. This bug affected accounts equally around the globe and had nothing to do with the subject matter of the content — and we fixed it as quickly as possible." Stone separately directed TechCrunch to the updated newsroom post, which said Meta identified and fixed a "bug" that prevented users from going live: "This was also a global issue that was fixed within a few hours. We understand people rely on these tools and we're sorry to anyone who felt the impact of these issues."

The rebuttal's reach is limited in ways the reporting records. It is unclear whether the bug affected accounts posting content unrelated to Gaza, while Instagram users have posted screenshots showing Stories about Palestine receiving significantly fewer views than other Stories posted the same day, and allege their view counts recovered when they posted content unrelated to the conflict. Meta's representative did not address the other accusations of censorship beyond Story visibility and did not respond to TechCrunch's follow-up questions; Meta initially did not respond to follow-up requests for comment. Asked about comments containing the Palestinian flag, Stone again pointed to the updated newsroom post, which did not directly address the issue, and he declined to comment on allegations of Meta disproportionately flagging Arabic news content, directing TechCrunch to the same post, which did not directly address those allegations either.

# Kremlin Propaganda And Platform Countermeasures

EU values and transparency commissioner Vera Jourova warned in September 2023 that platforms must concentrate efforts to combat the spread of Kremlin propaganda, including in the context of looming EU elections the following year with the risk of Russia stepping up its election interference efforts.

"One of my main messages to the signatories is to be aware of the context. Russian war against Ukraine, and the upcoming EU elections next year, are particularly relevant, because the risk of disinformation is particularly serious," she said. "The Russian state has engaged in the war of ideas to pollute our information space with half-truth and lies to create a false image that democracy is no better than autocracy. Today, this is a multi-million euro weapon of mass manipulation aimed both internally at the Russians as well as at Europeans and the rest of the world. We must address this risk. The very large platforms must address this risk. Especially that we have to expect that the Kremlin and others will be active before elections. I expect signatories to adjust their actions to reflect that there is a war in the information space waged against us and that there are upcoming elections where malicious actors will try to use the design features of the platforms to manipulate."

The Commission's early analysis of Big Tech's Code reports produced three concrete counts. YouTube shut down more than 400 channels between January and April 2023 which were involved in coordinated influence operations linked to the Russian state-sponsored Internet Research Agency, and removed ads from almost 300 sites linked to state-funded propaganda sites. TikTok's fact-checking efforts now cover Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian and 17 European languages, including through a new partnership with Reuters; "In this context, 832 videos related to the war have been fact-checked, of which 211 have been removed," Jourova noted. And Microsoft reported that Bing Search had either promoted information or downgraded questionable information in relation to almost 800,000 search queries related to the Ukraine crisis.

# Disinformation

## Definition

Disinformation is false or misleading content spread online — distinct from the illegal-content category (like terrorism or hate speech) in that, per the corpus's account of EU regulation, disinformation "is not illegal in the EU per se," yet still counts as a *systemic risk* that large platforms must assess and mitigate.

## Context

The corpus's central storyline is the EU's escalating regulatory pressure on X (formerly Twitter) over disinformation tied to the Israel-Hamas war: the Commission's October 2023 warning and formal information request to Musk accused X of being used "to disseminate illegal content and disinformation" following the Hamas attacks, and a EU-commissioned study later found X had "the largest ratio of mis/disinformation posts" among major platforms.
Because X is a Digital Services Act (DSA) "very large online platform" (VLOP), the obligation to mitigate disinformation risk is legally binding on it even though the underlying falsehoods are not themselves illegal; the EU's voluntary Code of Practice on Disinformation (which Musk pulled X out of earlier in 2023) is treated by the Commission as a signal of DSA compliance on this exact risk.
Disinformation also surfaces as a generative-AI worry: Suleyman warned DeepMind's ethics board that AI "could lead to an explosion in disinformation," EU commissioner Vera Jourova flagged AI-generated disinformation as an election threat, and early fears that ChatGPT would be used "to generate disinformation on a massive scale" pushed European policymakers toward mandating security assessments of generative AI products.
Real-world examples in the corpus include a video-game clip falsely presented as Hamas missile footage circulating on X, and misinformation described as "rampant on social media" during the Gaza crisis, prompting some users to turn to Snap Map for unmediated, firsthand footage instead.

## Key Characteristics

- **Not illegal per se in the EU** — disinformation is treated as a systemic risk to be mitigated, not content that platforms are legally required to remove the way they must remove illegal content.
- **Distinct from "misinformation" but often paired with it** — the corpus uses both terms (e.g., "mis/disinformation posts," Mozilla's content-policy list of "misinformation" as a harm category), generally without a sharp technical distinction, though disinformation carries a stronger connotation of deliberate falsehood or manipulation (e.g., "Kremlin propaganda").
- **A VLOP systemic-risk obligation** — under the DSA, platforms designated VLOPs (like X) must proactively assess and mitigate disinformation risk, which is what makes an EU formal-information request or investigation possible even absent an illegal-content finding.
- **Measurable and comparable across platforms** — the EU's Code of Practice enabled a pilot study producing "structural indicators" (e.g., how easily disinformation content is found, how much engagement it gets) that let regulators rank X as worst among mainstream platforms.
- **A named risk of generative AI** — beyond social-media falsehoods, the corpus repeatedly frames disinformation as a downstream risk of AI text/image generation (ChatGPT, deepfakes), motivating both EU AI-Act-era safeguards and industry-side labeling commitments.

# The Thesis That Egypt Is Too Big To Fail

Multiple economists, bankers and investors whom Bloomberg spoke with in October 2023 in Morocco, during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, saw Egypt as likely to receive some economic backing whatever its refugee stance. The crisis has reminded global players of the North African nation's status as a regional linchpin, entrenching the idea that it is too big to fail.

The warrant is regional instability rather than Egypt's own merits: the current conflict serves to highlight the growing instability on all sides of Egypt, in Libya, Sudan and now in Gaza. That confronts the US and Europe with the need to ensure that "Cairo remains a stable and reliable partner in the area" that "deserves external support," Crisis Group's Riccardo Fabiani said.

# The EU's Urgent Warning Letter To X

The European Union fired a public warning at Elon Musk-owned X (formerly Twitter) for failing to tackle illegal content circulating on the platform in the wake of Saturday's deadly attacks on Israel by Hamas terrorists based in the Gaza Strip — an "urgent" letter from internal market commissioner Thierry Breton that TechCrunch described as a very swift test of the bloc's newly updated content moderation rulebook. Breton shared the letter publicly, tweeting on October 10, 2023: "Following the terrorist attacks by Hamas against 🇮🇱, we have indications of X/Twitter being used to disseminate illegal content & disinformation in the EU. Urgent letter to @elonmusk on #DSA obligations". TechCrunch's later account places the letter on the Wednesday.

The letter's substance was twofold. Breton said the bloc had seen "indications" from "qualified sources" that X was being used to disseminate illegal content and disinformation in the EU following Saturday's attacks, then reminded X of the DSA's "very precise obligations" on content moderation: "When you receive notices of illegal content in the EU, you must be timely, diligent and objective in taking action and removing the relevant content when warranted." Separately, the European Commission raised concerns about the spread of disinformation on X related to the terrorist attacks and their aftermath.

On the disinformation side Breton was specific about what had been reported and what he wanted done: "Public media and civil society organisations widely report instances of fake and manipulated images and facts circulating on your platform in the EU, such as repurposed old images of unrelated armed conflicts or military footage that actually originated from video games. This appears to be manifestly false or misleading information," he wrote. "I therefore invite you to urgently ensure that your systems are effective, and report on the crisis measures taken to my team."

TechCrunch's own characterisation of the platform at that moment was blunter than the letter's: rather than tackling the problem, it wrote, X "appears to be turning into an engine of disinformation" — one that had demonstrably enabled the very swift amplification of a smorgasbord of toxic fakes around the Israel-Hamas war, falsehoods that might be trying to manipulate opinion around the conflict, or otherwise exploit horrific events to drive engagement (clickbait) or for even more cynical and potentially harmful ends.

# Bad Blood, The Katy Perry Feud And Rolling Stone's Last Place

Bad Blood has the dubious distinction of taking last place in Rolling Stone's ranking of all 237 Taylor Swift songs — the BBC calls it a vendetta disguised as a pop song, with a ham-fisted chorus that lacks her usual melodic instincts. # Wildest Dreams: Imagining The End Before The Relationship Begins

Wildest Dreams is defined by anticipatory disillusion — Taylor Swift imagines the end of a relationship before it has truly begun, asking her partner, when it all goes wrong, "Say you'll remember me / Standing in a nice dress / Staring at the sunset." It belongs to a wider strand on 1989 in which growing up means letting go of youthful optimism: on one hand she has developed an ability to laugh off her critics, on the other she seems increasingly jaded about love.

Swift described the shift in her own terms to Rolling Stone: "The way I used to approach relationships was very idealistic. I used to go into them thinking, 'Maybe this is the one - we'll get married and have a family, this could be forever'. Whereas now I go in thinking, 'How long do we have on the clock before something comes along and puts a wrench in it, or your publicist calls and says this isn't a good idea?'" An early draft of the lyrics had the couple fleeing the city and blotting out the pressures of the world, an idea which eventually resurfaced in I Know Places.

# The Most-Searched Podcasts Ranking

PodBam released a list of the 40 most-searched podcasts, and The Joe Rogan Experience was number one, averaging 135,000 monthly searches on Google. Call Her Daddy followed with 106,000 and This American Life with 81,000. The Verge, reporting the list on October 25th, 2023, noted it was no surprise that Rogan came first.

# Shake It Off As A Defiant Response To Celebrity Takedown Culture

Shake It Off is a honking great party record — a 21st Century Hey Mickey, rattling like a bag of spanners, with a chorus that drills so far into your brain you start seeing lights. Like Blank Space, it is a response to celebrity takedown culture: Taylor Swift lists all of her supposed flaws ("She's an airhead!" "She dates too many men!") with a defiant "so what?", sounding much less bothered than the girl who had written Mean as a riposte to a snarky music critic three years earlier.

It was the last song recorded for 1989. Swift arrived at the studio with a challenge for her co-writers Max Martin and Johan "Shellback" Schuster: "We need drums that make even the person who's having a terrible night at the wedding [go], 'Oh, it's my song!'" Released as 1989's first single, it was accompanied by a video shot over three days under intense secrecy, codenamed Project Sparrow, that built on the lyrical conceit.

The video's premise came from real criticism of her dancing. "When I'm at award shows, I have the best time dancing [but] I'm really tall and lanky so I look a little bit like a baby giraffe learning how to walk," she told a group of young Swifties. "So all over the internet, it's like, 'Taylor Swift looks awkward when she dances'. And as soon as I wrote [Shake It Off] I knew I wanted to do an entire music video of me awkwardly dancing. I'm like, 'Yeah, I do dance awkwardly, but I'm having more fun than you.'"

# Very Important People: A Reboot Of CollegeHumor's Hello My Name Is

Very Important People is a Dropout show revealed in the fifth-anniversary announcement video and, in Sam Reich's telling, a reboot of something the company did 12 or 13 years ago on CollegeHumor called Hello My Name Is. # I Wish You Would: A 2am Song Whose Real Story Runs In Reverse

I Wish You Would is one of Taylor Swift's many 2am songs, powered by a choppy, unrelenting guitar line that mimics her thoughts as they race uncontrollably in the middle of the night. In the lyric she is pining for an ex, absent-mindedly driving down their street and wishing she had never hung up the phone or broken things off.

In real life, though, the story was reversed — that inversion is the song's defining twist. Swift told Rolling Stone the song was "about an ex who bought a house two blocks from hers", while a hidden message in the CD booklet said: "He drove past her street each night." # Out Of The Woods And The Snowmobile Crash Behind It

Taylor Swift confirmed in interviews that Out Of The Woods was based on a true story, and in her Rolling Stone cover story she said the crash it describes actually occurred on a snowmobile, "with an ex who lost control and wrecked it so badly that she saw her life flash before her eyes". The song's "twenty stitches in a hospital room" arrives after a middle 8 in which the couple seem to have made a clean getaway, and then car brakes are slammed.

Musically the track exemplifies one of 1989's strengths — how the music reflects the emotional tenor of the words, here frantic anxiety. As Taylor and her partner run from forces that seek to destroy them, they are pursued by pounding drums and rushing synths, and there is a desperation to her voice, as though she is repeating "everything's fine, everything's fine, everything's fine" against evidence to the contrary.

Swift framed the revelation as a message to the press: "It was almost like this very strange, subtle clue to the media that they don't know everything that happened in that relationship, and I can have something really major and traumatic happen to me and they don't know about it," she told NPR. # Wondery Podcasts On Freevee

On November 16, 2023 YouTube unveiled "Dream Track," an experiment enabling creators to clone the vocals, via AI tech and with official consent, of well-known stars.

# Celebrity Endorsement

In the corpus, "celebrity endorsements" is named directly only once — listed alongside "campaign trail rallies" as one of several online-campaign tactics that, on their own, are "not enough to engage voters online" — and everywhere else the corpus treats it as a family of concrete cases rather than a defined category: FTX's paid partnerships with athletes, Anna Wintour's sponsorship request to Sam Bankman-Fried, The Epoch Times' political endorsements and CPAC sponsorship, and Vivek Ramaswamy's TikTok launch via a Jake Paul endorsement.

## Context

The corpus documents celebrity endorsement as a recurring marketing and political tactic across unrelated domains. FTX bought "mainstream recognition with branding deals and partnerships," most visibly by partnering with celebrities like Tom Brady and his ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka; a follow-up account puts a price on two of those deals, with Tom Brady paid $55 million and Steph Curry $35 million to "lend FTX legitimacy and edge." Anna Wintour — described in the corpus as "the icy fashion doyenne" — separately reached out to Sam Bankman-Fried to ask him to sponsor her Met Costume Ball, a related but distinct pattern of soliciting a sponsor rather than a spokesperson. The Epoch Times pursued the same logic in politics rather than commerce: a hired Republican strategist "achieved the goal" of legitimizing the outlet by securing interviews and introductions with conservative politicians and media figures at the Conservative Political Action Conference, where the outlet was also billed as a "supporting sponsor." In the 2023 Republican presidential primary, Vivek Ramaswamy tried the same move digitally, launching his TikTok presence "with an endorsement from Jake Paul" to reach young voters. Corporate sponsorship of events and venues appears as a companion pattern to celebrity endorsement rather than a synonym for it: FTX separately bought the naming rights to the Miami Heat's home arena, and English football's League Cup has been renamed after a succession of corporate sponsors (Coca-Cola, Worthington's, Carling, and currently Carabao) with no celebrity attached.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transfer of legitimacy or attention** — the endorsing figure's fame is meant to "lend legitimacy and edge" to the endorsed brand, as stated of the Tom Brady and Steph Curry deals with FTX.
- **Often explicitly paid** — reported dollar figures ($55 million for Brady, $35 million for Curry) show the arrangement is frequently a straightforward commercial transaction, not a spontaneous show of support.
- **Can misfire when authenticity is doubted** — Jake Paul's endorsement of Ramaswamy "only drove animosity from TikTok viewers," because the Paul brothers have "a reputation of promoting anyone and anything for a paycheck," and viewers "immediately questioned how much Ramaswamy paid him."
- **Distinct from, but adjacent to, event/venue sponsorship** — naming-rights deals (FTX and the Miami Heat arena) and tournament title sponsorships (the Carabao Cup) trade a brand name for association with an audience, without necessarily involving an individual celebrity endorser.
- **Can trigger public backlash independent of the endorsed party** — Web Summit's corporate sponsors and speakers withdrew their association after the event's founder, Paddy Cosgrave, made controversial comments about the Israel-Hamas conflict, with fintech entrepreneur David Marcus vowing "I'll never attend/sponsor/speak at any of your events again," showing that sponsor/endorser relationships run in both directions and can be revoked.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, celebrity endorsement (sometimes called celebrity branding) is a marketing method that uses a famous person to promote something, on the theory that "the positive image of the celebrity transfers to the brand," boosting public attention and trust; its success typically hinges on how well the celebrity fits the product and how genuine the association seems. (Wikipedia, "Celebrity branding," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_branding)

# What A VPN Is, And What It Does Not Hide

A virtual private network masks your IP address and the identity of your computer or mobile device on the network, creating an encrypted "tunnel" that prevents your internet service provider from accessing data about your browsing history. It is not a one-size-fits-all security solution — it is just one part of keeping your data private and secure.

The boundary of what it covers is narrow. A VPN only hides information like your IP address, location and browser history; a common misconception is that VPNs can make you totally invisible online, but the VPN provider often still has access to all of that information, so it does not grant total anonymity. You remain vulnerable to phishing attacks, hacking and other cyberthreats, which you should guard against with strong passwords and multi-factor authentication. Roya Ensafi, assistant professor of computer science and engineering at the University of Michigan, told Engadget that VPNs do not protect against common threats like phishing attacks, nor do they protect your data from being stolen: much of the data or information is stored with the VPN provider instead of your ISP, which means using a poorly designed or unprotected network can still undermine your security. What they are good for is online privacy when connecting to an untrusted network somewhere public, because they tunnel and encrypt your traffic to the next hop.

Marketing claims are therefore the wrong test. Sweeping claims like military-grade encryption or total digital invisibility may not be totally accurate; instead Yael Grauer, program manager of Consumer Reports' online security guide, recommends looking for security features such as open-source software with reproducible builds, up-to-date support for industry-standard protocols like WireGuard (Consumer Reports' preferred protocol) or IPsec, and the ability to defend against attack vectors like brute force.

Are they safe? Generally yes — VPNs are a safe and reliable way to encrypt and protect your internet data — but like most online services the safety specifics vary from provider to provider, and you can use third-party audits, Consumer Reports reviews, transparency reports and privacy policies to understand your chosen provider. Engadget's guide tested nine of the best VPN services available and landed on five top picks. An update dated November 10, 2024 removed a mention of PPTP, a protocol that Grauer notes "has serious security flaws."

# Owen Teale's Barry The Bear Route Into Acting

Owen Teale's acting career began with a car full of booze and a bear costume: suspended from his sixth-form college for organising a riotous Christmas party and in need of a job, he took work as a fairground mascot and was pointed towards drama school by co-workers, The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 20 October 2023.

"They held an investigation into the party and I was the first to be called in," says the 62-year-old Welsh actor, best known as gimlet-eyed master-at-arms Ser Alliser Thorne in Game of Thrones. "They'd found the empty bottles and people were falling over drunk. I said, 'yeah, I did it. It was me. I borrowed my mother's car, loaded it up with booze and smuggled it in'." Teale had no intention of joining his father at the limestone quarry that fed the steel works at Port Talbot; he wanted to escape South Wales and find a bigger world. A kindly teacher called Mr Davies suggested he might find work at Barry Island Pleasure Park, a fairground near Cardiff — "At the time, it was a rust bucket of a big wheel and one big dipper," Teale recalls. "But I went along and auditioned. I was hoping to be a magician's assistant or something like that, but they said 'you'd be great as the bear. Here's the costume'."

The role of Barry the Bear was deceptively hard: "His remit was to wander around the park greeting visitors, but you could only do an hour at a time because you sweated so much. The sight of a disconsolate, sweaty bear riding the ferris wheel caught management's attention and Teale was sacked — at which point a couple of co-workers, students from the Guildford School of Acting, suggested he audition at their alma mater. Two of Diablo 4's other biggest pain points — gems and Renown — are also being addressed in season 2, as Polygon reported on 2023-10-04.

The grind to accrue Renown, the resource players get for completing activities in each area, is no longer something players will need to partake in every season: much like the Altars of Lilith change in season 1, players who have fully unlocked their Renown track with one character will never have to do it again. Previously players had to max out Renown — which all but required doing nearly every dungeon and most side quests in the game — every season in order to get all available Skill and Paragon Points. Unlike with the Altars of Lilith carryover, players will not need to first log into a character that has completed the Renown track in order to propagate that data to the rest of their account; associate game director Joe Piepiora said all of that data migration should happen without that extra step in season 2.

Polygon calls this yet another massive 180 on the Renown system from Blizzard in barely five months' time. Asked about the shift, Piepiora said players simply were not having fun redoing the grind every season, hence the move — as with the Altars last season — to alleviate the pressure on players to only play "efficiently."

As for gems, they will no longer take up bag space, as they are now considered crafting materials. # Downward Revision of the Solar Corona's Size

A study published in November 2023 revealed that the outer edge of the sun's atmosphere, or corona, does not extend out quite as far as previously thought, making the sun likely somewhere between 0.03% and 0.07% smaller than had been assumed.

Until recently, the best way to measure the sun's corona was to observe it during a solar eclipse, when it becomes clearly visible around the moon. New technologies have allowed scientists to measure the oscillations, or waves, that travel through the corona, and those waves do not travel quite as far as expected. The difference between the new findings and previous estimates is relatively small, but scientists say it could make a big difference in how the star is studied.

# India's Demographic Dividend Versus China's Decline

Brahma Chellaney, professor of strategic studies at the New Delhi-based Center for Policy Research, wrote in a recent article that as India's geopolitical, economic and cultural clout grows, so does its global footprint, and that China's "decline" — as some have begun to call the conclusion of the country's four-decade-long economic boom — opens new opportunities for the Indian economy and other developing and emerging countries.

The demographic relation is the pivot. Earlier in 2023 India reached a milestone when its population officially surpassed that of China, which had been the world's most populous country for more than 300 years. While China's shrinking, rapidly ageing population is likely to impede economic growth and may curtail its geopolitical ambitions, India — one of the world's youngest countries, with a median age of 28.2 — is poised to reap a huge demographic dividend.

Chellaney nevertheless places the driving force in growth rather than demography alone: while India's gross domestic product is still smaller than China's, the country is currently the world's fastest-growing major economy and is projected to account for 12.9 per cent of global growth over the next five years, surpassing the United States' 11.3 per cent share.

# TikTok's Claim To Be The Driving Force Behind Music Discovery

TikTok's argument, made by Global Head of Music Ole Obermann on the back of the Luminate findings, is that "TikTok is the driving force behind music discovery in the industry, and that TikTok users are active, engaged and highly valuable drivers of music industry revenues."

The stated motive for commissioning the research was to move beyond the anecdotal: "TikTok is already famous for being the launchpad for creating viral hits and breaking new artists, but we wanted to understand how TikTok and its users impact the music industry more broadly," Obermann said in a statement, adding that "Luminate's findings prove what we had long known." MBW places the study in a pattern: it is part of an ongoing effort by TikTok to highlight its growing role in the development of global music culture, and last year TikTok released a report asserting that 13 out of the 14 songs to reach number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 in 2022 were driven by viral trends on TikTok.

# The Digital-First Artist Development Model

The success of "Si No Estás" illustrates how much artist development has changed: social media and digital music services have now become the number one source of music discovery, and Believe has developed an innovative, AI and data-driven expertise to develop tracks and artists that Alejandra Olea describes as unique in the music industry.

The model's components and their relations are stated together: the key to success is great partnerships with the artist and their label, and being able to combine strong AI data-driven expertise to maximise momentum for an artist and a track at the right time with the right tools and the right partnerships, supported by both local and global teams. Olea singles out the last element as particularly important and truly one of Believe's strengths, being able to mobilise teams multi-locally and globally to accompany audience development for artists. The forward-looking claim attached to the model is that this is only the beginning for Iñigo Quintero and that Believe anticipates many more successes like his in future.

# TikTok's Expansion Into Music Services

TikTok has built out music-related services to the point that one could be forgiven for thinking the company plans to reinvent itself as part of the music industry — a distribution service, a streaming service, a live event, artist upload deals, an AI music app and a save-to-streaming feature, layered on in about eighteen months.

The pieces, as MBW listed them on 2023-11-21: in 2022 TikTok launched SoundOn, its own music distribution service, which has partnered with Believe-owned distro company TuneCore and Downtown Holdings-owned B2B tech and services company FUGA. In the summer of 2023 it launched TikTok Music, a premium-only streaming service initially available in Brazil and Indonesia featuring the catalogs of all three major global recording companies (Sony Music, Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group), and quickly expanded it to Australia, Mexico and Singapore, though without Universal's catalog. In October 2023 TikTok announced its first-ever live music event, "TikTok In The Mix," and in the same month struck a deal with Distrokid to have indie artists upload their music to TikTok Music and to Capcut, TikTok's video editing software, as well as to TikTok's Commercial Music Library, which offers a catalog of music for brands to use in TikTok ads. Meanwhile parent ByteDance has launched an AI music-making app, and most recently TikTok unveiled "Add to Music App," which enables users to save music they have discovered directly to their Apple Music, Amazon Music (Prime or Unlimited) or Spotify accounts. MBW reads these partnerships as TikTok moving away from what at times appeared to be a trying relationship with the music industry — in one notable incident, TikTok disabled the use of copyrighted music for users in Australia, in what the platform described as an experiment and many observers saw as a hardball tactic in its licensing negotiations with music rights holders.

# UNH Sequencing Discovery of a Previously Unknown Canine Germ

Researchers at the University of New Hampshire's Veterinary Diagnosis Laboratory and the Hubbard Center for Genome Studies told NBC News they have identified a pathogen that might be what is making pets sick, in a development that might help shed light on the illness, which has affected a variety of dog breeds.

The observation came out of genetic sequencing of two sample sets: an initial group of 30 dogs from New Hampshire who were infected last year, and then an additional 40 dogs from Rhode Island and Massachusetts who got sick this year. From those samples the researchers say they have discovered a previously unknown germ.

The bacterium was discovered after a painstaking search. As Needle described it, "After initial sequencing showed there were no known viral, bacterial or fungal pathogens, time consuming and dogged work by graduate student Lawrence Gordon showed that 21 of the initial 30 samples from New Hampshire had some genetic material from one atypical bacterial species." The finding therefore rests on a partial hit rate within the first New Hampshire cohort rather than on every sample.

An important condition on this report is its publication status: the UNH team is sharing its results prior to publishing a research article, hoping they will give veterinarians some information as they deal with other respiratory syndrome outbreaks. The account was reported by Yahoo News on November 21, 2023.

# Theory: An AGI And Mission Rift Between Altman And The Board

The proposition is that Altman's zeal for AGI, even absent a secret project or agreement, led to a major rift between him and the board. Altman is a proud techno-optimist and often speaks fondly of the possibilities of AGI, or artificial general intelligence, a theoretical software system that achieves human-like intellect and versatility. The board's statement pointedly includes that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity" and that new leadership was necessary.

The supporting observation is a directional one: it has been obvious to all that Altman took the company in a much more corporate direction from its origins, changing its legal status and aggressively pursuing enterprise and consumer applications, which does not sound a lot like the "mission" the board wants to advance.

What counts against it is timing. This shift did not happen today, and it certainly does not seem like a plausible reason for abruptly firing the CEO and a few others on a beautiful fall Friday afternoon — a gradual drift does not explain an abrupt dismissal.

# The 2023 Chemistry Nobel for Quantum Dots

The 2023 Nobel Prize in chemistry honours three scientists who discovered and created quantum dots: Moungi Bawendi, a chemist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge; Louis Brus, a chemist based at Columbia University in New York City; and Alexei Ekimov, a physicist now working at Nanocrystals Technology, Inc., in Briarcliff Manor, N.Y.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the honour on October 4, and the trio will split a prize of 11 million Swedish kronor, or about $1 million. The award recognises a peculiar class of matter: typically, matter made of the same kinds of atoms arranged in the same way has the same properties, but tiny specks called quantum dots can contain the same molecules yet have different colours and other qualities depending on their size. The ability to make a whole rainbow of quantum dots simply by tweaking their size makes them highly useful — they light up TV screens and help doctors see inside the body.

# The Miyake Event Solar Storm 14,000 Years Ago

In October 2023, researchers revealed that a superpowered solar storm known as a Miyake Event slammed into Earth around 14,000 years ago, and experts said it could have been the most powerful solar outburst ever to hit the planet.

The evidence came from fossilized tree rings recently unearthed in the French Alps: the preserved plants all had off-the-chart levels of radiation in the same rings, which showed they all soaked up the radiation at the same time, and only a powerful Miyake Event could explain the levels of radiation the team found. "A similar solar storm today would be catastrophic for our modern technological society," the researchers wrote.

# World of Warcraft Classic: Hardcore and Season of Discovery

World of Warcraft Classic, developed by Blizzard Entertainment for Mac and Windows PC, is ranked 40 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31, and critic Oli Welsh argues it is quietly, and paradoxically, where Blizzard is doing its most forward-thinking work.

Something very interesting started happening in the retro version of WoW that year. While Blizzard has been content to march one half of the game's community forward through its history of expansions, it started to come up with creative ways to keep the other half — the half that wants to stay in the game as it was at launch — engaged.

The first of these was Hardcore, a brilliant permadeath mode that instantly made this aging game both more dangerous and more social, resurrecting the spirit of its 2004 servers. The second, just launched at the time, is the wild Season of Discovery, which remixes and restructures the original WoW experience — interpolating staggered level caps, shuffling class roles — in ways Welsh says might just change MMO design forever.

# War Duration and Scenarios Driving Israeli Growth Damage

Leo Leiderman's model of the war's economic damage has two drivers: duration and breadth. "First of all, the duration and character of the war will have a decisive impact on the depth of damage to the economy. Many studies, as well as past experience, indicate that the longer the war lasts, the broader will be the impact on the economy. It is also known that this connection between the length of the fighting and the economic damage might not be linear. And of course, the more the war widens to more fronts, the greater will be the economic damage."

He declined to quantify the effect. Asked on 12 October 2023 for a forecast of the consequences for growth, he said it was too early to make a quantitative estimate of the effects on the economy's growth in 2024 and 2025. Israel has a great deal of information about loss of growth and product in past episodes — the Yom Kippur War, the Lebanon War, two intifadas, various military operations, and the Covid pandemic — but in his view this is a completely different episode: "This is a new situation that has no precedent as far as the damage to the economy is concerned."

The range over which the model runs is therefore a spectrum of scenarios rather than a point estimate: "from a short war on the southern front only, to the nightmare scenario of a prolonged war with additional sectors involved." He noted the interview was taking place only on the fifth day of the war, and expressed the hope that the picture would start to become clearer.

# Criticism Of The Wilma Mankiller Barbie's Inaccuracies

Critics attacked the premise that Mattel's Wilma Mankiller doll faithfully represents Cherokee culture, pointing to specific errors in the product and its packaging. Chuck Hoskin Jr, Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, told The New York Times that the doll's basket was not authentically Cherokee, and that the wrong sets of symbols for the Cherokee language were used on the packaging — with the result that the symbols read "Chicken Nation" rather than "Cherokee Nation." "To someone who doesn't read Cherokee syllabary, they're not going to notice it," he said. "To the Cherokee people for whom Wilma is of such enduring significance and we have such enduring love for her, to see our seal incorrect, it's very disappointing because it would not have taken much effort or thought to avoid that." Hoskin said he learned of the doll's creation six months earlier and that Mattel did not work directly with the Cherokee Nation, though he added the company has been understanding of the criticism. The tribe's own statement said: "Regrettably, the Mattel company did not work directly with the tribal government's design and communications team to secure the official Seal or verify it."

Cherokee women raised a second objection — that Mattel overlooked the problematic details on both the doll and the packaging. "Mixed emotions shared by me and many other Cherokee women who have now purchased the product revolve around whether a Wilma Barbie captures her legacy, her physical features and the importance of centering Cherokee women in decision making," Stacy Leeds, the law school dean at Arizona State University and a former Cherokee Nation Supreme Court justice, told The Associated Press in an email. Regina Thompson, a Cherokee basket weaver who grew up near Tahlequah, does not think the doll looks like Mankiller, and said Mattel should have used traditional pucker toe moccasins instead of black shoes and included symbols on the basket that Cherokees use to tell a story. "Wilma's name is the only thing Cherokee on that box," Thompson said. "Nothing about that doll is Wilma, nothing."

# Protecting Populations Most Exposed to Extreme Heat

Public health measures and mitigation strategies are needed to protect the citizens at greatest risk from heat, especially as rising temperatures become more common — and studies of existing exposure disparities are the way to identify who those citizens are.

"Studies like this, which seek to understand more deeply the existing disparities in heat exposure, are important for identifying which communities are at greatest risk of suffering environmental changes related to climate change, such as extreme heat that keeps getting worse," said Neelima Tummala. Lara Whitely Binder, climate preparedness programme manager for King County, Washington, who was not involved in the research, located the cause: "Areas with fewer street trees, less access to green spaces — that is where you start to see the legacy of disinvestment and institutional racism that has come into play." Because the climate is changing and advancing, cities must from now on prepare for hotter summers and more frequent deadly heat waves by various means, both indoors and outdoors. "We not only need to better understand where it is hot, but also what the socioeconomic factors are for the inhabitants of those areas," Whitely Binder said. "We can begin to analyse what is in the heat islands and use that to start informing the policy decisions we are going to make."

# Emerging Tools for Quantifying the Pattern Effect

Promising new tools and observations are beginning to emerge for quantifying the pattern effect: targeted model experiments and intercomparisons, extended global satellite observations of clouds and radiation, Argo floats sampling deep-ocean heat uptake, estimates of radiative imbalances before the year 2000, and new observational constraints on clouds' sensitivity to environmental controlling factors.

These developments encourage an optimistic outlook on the ability to quantify the pattern effect and its implications over the next couple of years. Working to solve these problems at the intersection of different disciplines and with input from different research communities will likely benefit related research into, for example, the sensitivity of tropical cyclones and future rainfall changes in the southwestern United States or in South America to surface warming patterns.

# The Internet As A Global Endocrine System

Buck's model of what we have actually built is a collective body that runs on data but does not behave computationally: the thing we are jacked into and collectively creating seems more like a global endocrine system than anything we might have visualized in the years while "cyber" was a prefix.

The proposal begins from a mismatch with the 1960s inheritance. The ecology and spirituality of the 1960s, which shaped and structured much of what we see as energy democracy and the good future today, told us we were all connected — globally networked, a fevered dream from the 1980s or 1990s with roots in the 1960s and before. Media theorist Geert Lovink reflects on a 1996 interview with John Perry Barlow, Electronic Frontier Foundation cofounder and Grateful Dead lyricist, in which Barlow described cyberspace connecting each and every synapse of all citizens on the planet. As Lovink writes: "Apart from the so-called last billion we're there now. This is what we can all agree on. The corona crisis is the first Event in World History where the internet doesn't merely play 'a role' — the Event coincides with the Net. There's a deep irony to this. The virus and the network ... sigh, that's an old trope, right?" Read through one cultural history it seems obvious we would reach this point of being globally networked, and that the Internet would not just play a role in global events like COVID-19 or climate change but shape them.

The relation Buck proposes is that the connectedness arrived, but manifesting late and not at all as imagined: our global body is neither a psychedelic collective consciousness nor an infrastructure for data transmission comprising information packets and code. We have made a collective brain that does not act much like a computer at all — it runs on data, code, binary digits, but acts emotionally, irrationally, in a fight-or-flight way, and without consciousness, operating as an emotional toddler rather than with the neat computational sensing capacity that stock graphics of "the Internet" convey. Thinking of it as data or information is the same as thinking that a network of cells is a person.

The observation may seem banal — Marshall McLuhan was talking about the global nervous system more than fifty years ago, and we have had enthusiasm about cybernetics and global connectivity over the decades plus a more recent revitalization of theory about networks and kinship and rhizomes. The irony is that with fifty years of talk on "systems thinking" we still have responses to things like COVID-19 or climate that are almost antithetical to considering interconnected systems, dominated by one set of expertise and failing to incorporate the social sciences and humanities. So: globally connected, yet divided into silos, camps, echo-chambers. Social media platforms act as agents, structuring our interactions and our spaces for dialogue and solution-building — and authoritarians know this, which is why they have troll farms that can manipulate the range of solutions and the sentiments about them.

Public policies attempt to fulfill one or more of three objectives: efficiency, equity, and stability. # Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# Balanced Versus Deficit Budget in Philippine Fiscal Practice

The DBM calls a budget balanced when revenues match expenditures or disbursements. National Government expenditures have always exceeded total revenues, resulting in annual budget deficits, the DBM declared, and "the National Government had to resort to borrowing to cover said deficits which resulted in the ballooning of foreign and domestic debts," the budget office admitted.

The boundary case is 1994: "in 1994, the government broke the deficit trend by posting a budget surplus of P16 billion through an aggressive privatization and revenue generation program and a prudent expenditure program. # Philippine National Government Budget Definition

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) defines the government budget as "the financial plan of the government…which shows what its resources are, and how they will be generated and used over the fiscal period. It refers to the income, expenditures and sources of borrowings of the National Government (NG) that are used to achieve national objectives, strategies and programs."

Its constitutional basis is Section 22, Article VII: "The President shall submit to the Congress within 30 days from the opening of every regular session, as the basis of the general appropriation bill, a budget of expenditures and sources of financing including receipts from existing and proposed revenue measures."

The National Government budget is the totality of the budgets of all government entities: the National Government itself, the non-financial government-owned and -controlled corporations (usually only the 14 major GOCCs), government financial institutions, local government units, the social security institutions (GSIS, SSS, military pensions, PhilHealth and others), the Oil Price Stabilization Fund, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and the Central Bank-Board of Liquidators. It is allocated for the implementation of government programmes and projects, the operation of government offices, payment of salaries of government employees and payment of public debts, with expenditures classified by expense class, sector and implementing unit of government.

Appropriations come from two sources: new general appropriations legislated by Congress for every budget year under the General Appropriations Act, and existing appropriations previously authorised by Congress. Under Article VI, Section 29 of the Constitution, no money can be withdrawn from the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law.

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.

# The Digital Services Act

The Digital Services Act (DSA) is the European Union's pan-EU content moderation rulebook: a regulation that places governance obligations on digital services and platforms carrying user-generated content, with the aim of ensuring companies respond to reports of illegal content, and that layers heavier duties on the largest platforms. Its baseline obligations apply to digital services and platforms generally — respond diligently to notices of illegal content, clearly communicate terms and conditions to users, and be able to demonstrate proper enforcement of those terms.

The discriminating feature of the regime is its second tier. Platforms designated as "very large online platforms" (VLOPs) carry additional obligations to identify and mitigate systemic risks such as disinformation, gender-based violence, or negative effects on the exercise of fundamental rights. The Commission designated 19 VLOPs in April 2023, including Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram; X is also a designated VLOP. Compliance for VLOPs kicked in over the summer of 2023 — TechCrunch dates Meta's compliance start to August.

The regime's boundary case is disinformation itself. Unlike terrorism content, disinformation is not illegal in the EU per se. The DSA therefore does not reach it through the illegal-content removal route at all; it reaches it through the systemic-risk route, obliging a VLOP such as X to mitigate the risks attached to harmful falsehoods while separately acting diligently on reports of genuinely illegal content. The two duties run on different legal tracks even when they concern the same posts.

Penalties for confirmed breaches can be as high as 6% of global annual turnover, and the bloc holds a further power, in extremis, to block access to a service in the region for repeated infringements — meaning a platform that repeatedly fails to correct course could be shut off in the EU. TechCrunch illustrates the scale on both ends: Elon Musk last projected revenues of about $3 billion for 2023 for X, which by that example would cap a fine at up to $180 million, while in Meta's case the same 6% ceiling could run to multiple billions.

The regulation also contains a "crisis response" mechanism (Article 36) which enables the Commission to adopt rapid-fire measures on larger platforms in situations of "serious threat", such as war. As of TechCrunch's October 2023 reporting this part of the regulation was not yet operative: it would not start operating until February 17 of the following year, because it requires an advisory body — the European Board for Digital Services — to be operational before it can recommend that the Commission adopt a crisis response mechanism, and the Board's set-up was itself waiting on Member States to establish national Digital Services Coordinators, the bodies that oversee DSA compliance for non-VLOPs.

# The Scope Of The EU's DSA Investigation Into X

Per the Commission, the EU's investigation of X covers four areas. The first is compliance with DSA obligations related to countering the dissemination of illegal content in the EU, notably in relation to the risk assessment and mitigation measures adopted by X, as well as the functioning of the notice and action mechanism for illegal content in the EU mandated by the DSA, including in light of X's content moderation resources.

The second is the effectiveness of measures taken by X to combat information manipulation, with a focus on the effectiveness of its "Community Notes" system of crowdsourcing fact-checking to aggregated views of users, who may vote to label disputed tweets with additional context. The EU said the probe will also look at the effectiveness of related policies mitigating risks to civic discourse and electoral processes.

The third is transparency requirements, with a focus on "suspected shortcomings" by X in giving researchers access to publicly accessible data as mandated by Article 40 of the DSA, and suspected shortcomings in its ads repository, the ads transparency library the regulation also mandates. # Cannabis Use in Pregnancy: JAMA Study Findings

A study published Tuesday, Dec. 12, 2023 in the journal JAMA suggests that using cannabis during pregnancy may come with a higher risk of poor outcomes such as babies being born small for their gestational age, with the risks highest for those who use the drug in both the first trimester and later in gestation, as opposed to only the first trimester.

"What I think this study evaluates, that has not been evaluated previously, is whether the timing and amount of exposure matters, and what we saw was that higher levels of cannabis exposure were associated with increased risks of adverse pregnancy outcomes," first study author Dr. Torri Metz, an associate professor of obstetrics and gynecology at University of Utah Health, told Live Science in an email; using cannabis in the first trimester still carries risk, but the findings hint that stopping within the first trimester could help prevent that risk from growing larger. Urine screening flagged 610 participants who had used cannabis in pregnancy — nearly 200 used cannabis only in the first trimester, while the rest tested positive both in the first trimester and later in pregnancy. Participants who used cannabis had a higher risk of experiencing at least one of the poor pregnancy outcomes, nearly 26%, compared with 17.5% in the group that did not use cannabis; the risk was highest for those who used cannabis late into pregnancy and also appeared to rise with the overall concentration of THC byproduct in a person's urine. The researchers initially considered the pregnancy outcomes as a group rather than separately because, as Metz put it, "we knew we did not have a large enough sample to examine all of these outcomes independently," but a secondary analysis zoomed in on specific outcomes and found cannabis use linked to a higher chance that a baby would be born small, while not linked to a higher risk of high-blood-pressure disorders in pregnancy. "I think this lends more evidence to the idea that there are potential risks, and really talk to patients about alternative methods of treating whatever it is they're hoping to treat with cannabis," Metz told JAMA in a podcast interview.
