At the LIBE committee hearing the journalist Apostolis Fotiadis testified that documents he and his colleagues obtained showed email threads granting a CSAM-scanning "key stakeholder" privileged access inside Johansson's department, and, under pressure from MEPs, the commissioner read out a list of her meetings with technology companies and child safety organizations. TechCrunch reported the session on 25 October 2023.

Fotiadis, one of the journalists involved in the investigation the committee was examining, had also been invited by the committee to participate in the exchange of views, and he took the opportunity to defend their reporting from direct public attacks by Johansson. In a blog post ahead of the hearing — which deploys a crisis-PR-esque headline claim of "setting the record straight" — she criticized the article as "a series of insinuations looking for a home", claiming it paired an outline of "a selection of meetings I had, of events I attended, or conferences I addressed" with "a conspiratorial tone" in an attempt "to create the impression of financial influence where there is none".

Asked by the LIBE committee about the accusation that the journalists had, essentially, been spreading disinformation — and specifically whether he believed Johansson and the Commission's response to it amounted to a restriction on media freedom — Fotiadis responded by saying he did not think that was the case. He went on to express surprise at how the Commission had reacted to the scrutiny, and at its instinct to deploy "spin-doctor" tactics to try to discredit the article rather than engaging with the substance of the concerns being raised. The Commission risks straying close to making attacks on journalists by using such tactics, Fotiadis warned, adding: "You cannot just dismiss everything by calling fake news" — before also noting that Johansson's office had declined multiple interview requests ahead of publication of the article.

On the substance of the reporting, Fotiadis said documents obtained by the journalists included email threads between Commission officials in Johansson's department, DG-Home, and a "key stakeholder" advocating for the use of technology for CSAM-scanning, which indicated what he described as "privileged access" that "speaks directly to cooperation" and goes "way beyond" mere consultation or exchange of views on the proposal.

He gave the committee the shape of that access. "It's an official chain discussing invitation, how the stakeholder would be able to allocate experts that would speak in workshops — first attended by representatives of the Member States, and then afterwards actually by ministers in the Council in a meeting chaired by commissioner Johansson. So when we say facilitate, it's obvious that the EU officials discuss what kind of experts will be available from this particular stakeholder to attend these meetings and to present the point of view, which seems to be a privileged access," he explained. "Also in the same email thread there's mention of EU officials being allocated to specifically attend the cooperation between the stakeholder and DG-Home on the proposal, which to our understanding is something that goes way beyond the level of consultations or exchange of views or exchange of opinions on the proposal and speaks directly to cooperation."

The committee then pressed Johansson about her contacts with companies and other lobbyists during the drafting of the CSAM proposal, with MEPs saying they wanted clear answers to the allegations of commercial interest and heavy lobbying when the Commission was setting up and drafting the proposal. In the event MEPs got some bare bones detail. Asked for a list of these contacts, the commissioner responded that she had met with Google six times; Microsoft, Meta and TikTok three times each; twice with Twitter (X); and once apiece with Apple and Amazon. She also said she had met with the child safety organizations Thorn (twice) and Brave Movement (twice), and with Tech Alliance and ICANN once apiece.

In wider responses related to concerns about how much commercial interest had influenced the Commission, Johansson highlighted her decision for the CSAM-scanning proposal to be "technology neutral" — meaning the draft regulation does not support any specific tech solution — with the suggestion being that EU lawmakers had resisted lobbying by companies for a law that would explicitly favor their existing tech tools.

# Initial Public Offering (IPO)

## Definition

In the corpus, IPO — used interchangeably with "going public" — names the transition several companies undergo or are preparing to undergo onto a public stock exchange: cybersecurity startup IronNet is reported to have "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," and pre-IPO funds are described as investing in "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" ahead of that transition.

## Context

The corpus uses IPO/going-public language across several unrelated stories, which is what makes the term a recurring hinge concept rather than a one-off mention: cybersecurity startup IronNet "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," after which its stock price kept declining from an initial post-IPO spike; Swedish fintech Klarna is described as "taking steps toward an eventual IPO," restructuring into a U.K. holding company as "an important early step in its plans for an initial public offering"; and logistics company Flexport's ousted CEO Dave Clark counted among his goals helping prepare the company for an IPO, with Flexport having discussed an IPO in a two- to three-year window. The term also appears in Indian investing coverage, where late-stage "pre-IPO funds" let investors buy into "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" before their public debut, distinct from "publicly traded equity" that Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are said to be uncorrelated with. Once a company is public, its "stock price" becomes a live signal of investor sentiment, as seen in the Rogers family's boardroom conflict driving down Rogers Communications' stock price, and in Coinbase — "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges — seeing its shares swing on Binance/FTX-related news.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transition event** — the corpus marks the same before/after line with "going public" and "publicly traded," as with IronNet going "public in August 2021" and Coinbase being "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges.
- **Preceded by preparation** — companies undertake preparatory steps beforehand, such as Klarna's legal-entity restructuring into a U.K. holding company, or Flexport's Dave Clark working toward the goal of helping the company get "IPO ready" within a two- to three-year window it had discussed.
- **Followed by market scrutiny** — once public, a company's stock price becomes a running scoreboard, as with IronNet's post-IPO stock decline and Rogers Communications' stock price reacting to boardroom disputes.
- **Investment-fund target** — "pre-IPO" or late-stage private equity funds exist specifically to let investors buy into companies before this transition, aiming to capture value at listing.
- **Not guaranteed to sustain value** — IronNet's case in the corpus shows an initial post-IPO price spike can be followed by a steep, sustained decline.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, an IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public: a privately held company becomes a public company by selling shares to institutional and retail investors, typically with investment banks acting as underwriters who arrange for the shares to be listed on a stock exchange, a process also known as "floating" or "going public." (Wikipedia, "Initial public offering," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering)

An EU investigation would, indirectly, be a key way for the public to gain significantly more transparency around how X is being used — and abused. That is TechCrunch's claim about what regulatory scrutiny of the platform would deliver beyond any compliance finding.

The grounds are a change in X's corporate status. Since Musk took Twitter private, the company no longer produces quarterly earnings reports, and it is not held as closely to account as a result.

# Fine / Penalty

In the corpus, a fine or penalty is the recurring instrument through which financial-market, antitrust, data-protection, and platform-governance enforcement is actually made to bite against a confirmed or admitted violation.

## Definition

Fine / Penalty is the label the corpus uses for the monetary sanctions regulators and prosecutors impose on companies and individuals after a confirmed or admitted rule violation — sized as a percentage of global annual turnover under the EU's DSA and CPC regimes, or as a fixed dollar amount tied to a settlement or guilty plea under U.S. agency actions such as the DOJ/Treasury/CFTC resolution with Binance and CZ.

## Context

The corpus shows two dominant penalty designs. First, EU digital regulation ties fines to a percentage of a company's *global annual turnover* rather than a fixed sum: the Digital Services Act (DSA) allows fines of up to 6% of global annual turnover for confirmed breaches, and a separate Consumer Protection Cooperation (CPC) enforcement track lets national consumer-protection authorities impose fines of up to 4% of global annual turnover for conduct pursued as a consumer-law violation. The Commission invoked the 6% DSA figure against X twice — once as a warning in October 2023 alongside its formal request for information into Israel-Hamas disinformation concerns (before any investigation had been opened), and again in December 2023 when it opened a formal DSA infringement proceeding against X over risk management, content moderation, and deceptive design. Second, U.S. enforcement in the corpus produces fixed-dollar or admission-linked penalties: Binance agreed to pay about $4.3 billion to resolve DOJ, Treasury (FinCEN), OFAC, and CFTC investigations into anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, with CEO Changpeng Zhao separately recommended for a $150 million CFTC fine as part of his guilty plea. Outside the DSA/antitrust cluster, Norway's Datatilsynet used a *daily* fine (up to roughly $100,000 per day) to compel Meta's compliance with a consentless-ad-tracking ban, illustrating that penalties can be structured as recurring pressure rather than a one-time sum. Historical fines also inform present conduct: the corpus notes that Google only invested in improving search quality in Europe after being hit with a €5 billion EU antitrust fine in 2018, and the U.S. government cited that history in the DOJ's antitrust trial to argue Google lacks intrinsic incentive to improve without competitive or regulatory pressure.

## Key Characteristics

- **Turnover-percentage basis (EU model)** — DSA fines scale with a company's global annual turnover (up to 6%), and the parallel CPC consumer-protection track caps at 4% of the same base, so penalty exposure grows with company size rather than being fixed.
- **Fixed-sum or negotiated basis (US model)** — U.S. agencies in the corpus (DOJ, CFTC, SEC) reach specific dollar penalties, often as part of a guilty plea or settlement, as with Binance's $4.3B resolution and CZ's $150M recommended fine.
- **Recurring/daily penalties** — some regulators (Norway's Datatilsynet against Meta) impose a fine that accrues per day of continued non-compliance, functioning as ongoing coercive pressure rather than a settled sanction.
- **Penalty as leverage before conviction** — the EU explicitly warned X of possible fines and blocking *before* opening a formal investigation, using the threat of a penalty as a compliance-forcing signal.
- **Downstream behavioral effect** — a fine already levied (Google's 2018 EU antitrust fine) can be cited years later as evidence a company's improvements were penalty-driven rather than voluntary.

## Background (external)

The corpus uses "fine" and "penalty" as familiar terms without defining them itself. Per the Cornell Law School Legal Information Institute (LII), a fine is "a monetary penalty that is issued for failing to comply with one's duties," and it falls under the broader category of penalty, which can be imposed by a court or an administrative agency in either a criminal or a civil context (LII, *Fine*, accessed 2026-09-02). In criminal law a fine may be imposed alongside or instead of incarceration for violating a statute, while in civil law it commonly follows a breach of contract or comparable duty (LII, *Fine*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Spider-Man Embodies Ordinary Struggle

Polygon argues that Spider-Man represents the basic human needs Thanksgiving is really about, even though very few readers have to balance photojournalist work, a fraught dating life, and pummeling Dr. Octopus.

The grounds are the character's circumstances. Peter Parker is often the most financially strapped among his Avengers buddies and frequently the loneliest too, and those are recognizable traits among many young people, even those without radioactive-spider powers: when you are growing up and trying to figure out the world, it is easy to feel lost and isolated. The seasonal hinge is that feelings of loneliness spike during the holidays, so there is a good chance a reader will feel even more like Peter Parker when late November rolls around. From his first comic book appearance, Spider-Man has been a reminder that life is hard and complicated and that being a superhero does not preclude anyone from experiencing ordinary frustrations, setbacks, and confusion. The conclusion the article draws is that however his Thanksgiving escapades turn out, they remind readers and viewers that the holiday is about the hope of mutual connection, support, and nurturing — even if the girl of your dreams is out of reach and the Green Goblin is on your case, a table, some friends, and Aunt May's turkey might make everything better for a little while.

# Alternative Investment Funds Under The SEBI Framework

Alternative Investment Funds are pooled vehicles launched in 2012 after the market regulator SEBI issued guidelines for their management, guidelines that enable AIFs to identify and make investment opportunities available to investors in the public and private markets. AIFs can, for example, invest in listed and unlisted equities via private equity, infrastructure assets, venture debt, stressed assets, start-ups and so on; it is from this breadth that the term "alternatives" came about. The guidelines divide these funds into three categories, I, II and III, to make it easier for investors to understand a fund's investment objective.

The discriminating feature against traditional funds is correlation: AIF returns are generally uncorrelated with publicly traded equity or debt markets, providing a natural hedge against volatility and genuine portfolio diversification. The boundary on who may invest is the minimum investment threshold of ₹1 crore, which makes AIFs available only to HNIs, though not all funds must collect ₹1 crore in a single transaction; they can collect the money in tranches, called drawdowns, over 2-3 years, and that drawdown mechanism makes these funds easy on the wallet. AIFs have amassed an AUM of ₹8.30-lakh crore in the 11 years since inception, demonstrating the shift of HNI money to this asset.

# The Thesis That Egypt Is Too Big To Fail

Multiple economists, bankers and investors whom Bloomberg spoke with in October 2023 in Morocco, during the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, saw Egypt as likely to receive some economic backing whatever its refugee stance. The crisis has reminded global players of the North African nation's status as a regional linchpin, entrenching the idea that it is too big to fail.

The warrant is regional instability rather than Egypt's own merits: the current conflict serves to highlight the growing instability on all sides of Egypt, in Libya, Sudan and now in Gaza. That confronts the US and Europe with the need to ensure that "Cairo remains a stable and reliable partner in the area" that "deserves external support," Crisis Group's Riccardo Fabiani said.

# Judicial Reform (Israel, 2023)

## Definition

Judicial reform, in the corpus, is the Israeli government's contested 2023 "bid for judicial reform" — a domestic political fight the corpus treats as a settled point of reference (a fault line the country was already living through before the Hamas attacks of October 7) rather than something it explains from first principles. What the reform actually proposed is set out only in the Background (external) section below, not in the cited corpus documents.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the reform twice, each time as backdrop to a different story rather than as its subject. In the Eylon Levy profile, the reform is the fault line of Levy's own pre-war life: he "was also active in the protests against the government's judicial reform," and Globes pressed him on the shift — "one day you are at a demonstration against the government and the next day you are its spokesperson" (doc_0413). In the TechCrunch piece on Israel's startup ecosystem, the reform is the fault line of the tech sector's pre-war life: "the tech industry led opposition to the government's bid for judicial reform," with companies and investors "already refusing to do business in the country with the prospect of the reforms getting pushed through," a boycott effort that "has been brought to a halt" once the war made the two sides of that debate "stand together for what they see as the significantly bigger fight and threat" (doc_0448).

## Key Characteristics

- **Government-initiated, not judiciary-initiated** — doc_0448 describes it as the government's "bid" for reform; both docs frame it as opposed from outside government (doc_0413, doc_0448).
- **Provoked street protests** — Levy is identified by his participation in "the protests against the reform," which he describes as "no secret" (doc_0413).
- **Provoked tech-sector opposition** — the tech industry "led opposition" to the reform bid, with some companies and investors already refusing to do business in the country over it, before the war began (doc_0448).
- **Superseded, not resolved, by the war** — doc_0448 frames the reform fight as merely "brought to a halt" by October 7, with opposing sides now "standing together" against what they see as a bigger threat, not as a dispute that was settled; doc_0413 echoes this, with Levy describing pre-war disputes as something Israeli society "pulled our hair out over" that now look small against the war.

## Background (external)

The corpus names the "judicial reform" and its protest and boycott fallout but does not describe what the reform itself proposed. Per Wikipedia, the reform package introduced by Justice Minister Yariv Levin and MK Simcha Rothman in January 2023 proposed giving the government majority control over the committee that selects judges, curbing the Supreme Court's power to strike down legislation (including Basic Laws), letting the Knesset override certain court rulings with a 61-seat majority, making government legal advisors' opinions non-binding, and eliminating "unreasonableness" as a ground for judicial review of administrative decisions — changes aimed at reducing judicial checks on the government and the Knesset (Wikipedia, *2023 Israeli judicial reform*, accessed 2026-09-02). Mass protests began almost immediately after the plan's introduction in January 2023, well before the events covered in the corpus.

# Egypt's Economic Crisis And Its IMF Rescue Program

Egypt, which reached a deal with the IMF in December 2022, was as of October 2023 already in talks on boosting that rescue program to over $5 billion from $3 billion, people familiar with the discussions told Bloomberg that month. This is happening as the most populous Arab nation wrestles with its worst economic outlook in decades and President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi prepares for elections in less than two months' time — a combination that opens up opportunities for Cairo, though a host of domestic and regional considerations are seen ruling out any refugee deal.

According to Riccardo Fabiani, project director for North Africa with Crisis Group, it is possible the IMF's key shareholders in the US and Europe may pressure the Washington-based lender to soften its requirements and move ahead with the program despite Cairo's slow pace of reforms.



---


# Egypt's Refusal To Host Palestinian Refugees

President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi has rejected any suggestion that Egypt host Gazan refugees, even as the same Western governments now court him for help in alleviating the pressure on Gaza, suggesting instead that Israel take in Palestinians in its Negev desert: "They can transport Palestinians there until Israel implements its announced plan to destroy Hamas," he said on Wednesday, 2023-10-18. The core political ground is that "there is little to no constituency for going against decades of policy on not allowing Palestinian displacement," said Mirette Mabrouk of the Middle East Institute, while the inducements offered "might wind up becoming a political liability, especially in an election year."

Three further grounds support the refusal. Egypt already hosts some 9 million refugees and other migrants from countries including Syria, Sudan, Yemen and Libya. Opening a route for Palestinians may also present a new security risk in the Sinai peninsula, where the army has only just managed to get a handle on its fight with Islamist militants. And Jordan has also refused to accept more Palestinians, making it unlikely Egypt would become a regional exception and take in refugees many suspect may never be let back into Gaza — which would risk being seen in the Arab world as facilitating another mass displacement and betraying the Palestinian cause all Arab countries vocally espouse.

The warrant tying these grounds to the policy is that the domestic political cost outranks the economic one. While Egypt could absorb a certain number of people, the domestic political consequences would be "huge," said the Washington Institute's Robert Satloff: "The political leadership considers this a red line not to be crossed and would prefer to face worsening financial distress than accept a significant number of refugees."



---


# Sunak's Net Zero U-Turn, September 2023

When British prime minister Rishi Sunak appeared in front of the hastily assembled press on September 20, the letter-crammed slogan on his lectern caused the country to squint: "Long-term decisions for a brighter future," it read. TechCrunch's 2023-10-13 commentary notes that there was little in the speech that followed that brought hope — certainly not concerning the technological fight for our future climate.

With the government's already infamous U-turn on its green pledges, announced the previous week, the nation joined in a consternated chorus with global leaders to lament the prime minister's short-sighted choice: Sunak has pushed back the British net-zero transition timeline by at least five years.



---


# Kishida's Pitch to Global Investors 2023

Japanese prime minister Fumio Kishida was preparing, in the week of 1 October 2023, to make his strongest ever push for a bet on Asia's biggest advanced economy, as BlackRock founder Larry Fink and other heads of global funds gathered in Tokyo for a series of events to attract investment. "I would urge you to evaluate what we are doing in my country, look at the underlying strength of our economy and our plans for the future and then invest in Japan," Kishida said in a recent speech at the Economic Club of New York.

The pitch followed a month of conferences on the same question. Throughout September, in Tokyo, New York, Hong Kong and London, the world's biggest investment banks hosted a series of conferences for the world's biggest investors, all gravitating around the theme of whether Japan is really back. The events were run by JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Mizuho, BNP Paribas and Jefferies, and according to both attendees and hosts the answer is now clearer than it has been in a very long time: Japan is back, but global investors may take a little more persuasion that it is truly back for the duration.



---


# Japan Asset Management Reform and NISA Expansion

Japan's government initiatives to make Tokyo more attractive for foreign asset managers have two components, reported by the Financial Times on 1 October 2023. Prime minister Fumio Kishida has promised major reform of the country's $5tn asset management industry, which would ease regulations that had made it difficult for foreign and new players to enter. Separately, the government plans to expand the Nippon Individual Savings Account (Nisa) tax-free investment scheme from the following year, in a bid to unlock $14tn in household financial assets that has long sat in cash and bank deposits.

These initiatives aid the efforts of Japanese businesses to demonstrate better governance. The distinguishing feature investors draw from the combination is a change in kind, not degree: "This is completely different from before," says Stefanie Drews, president of Nikko Asset Management. "In the past, allocation to Japan had been tactical but this time it is strategic and that is why it is much more meaningful."

# Fossil Fuel Lobbyist Access At COP28 In Dubai

The UN's decision to hold the summit in the United Arab Emirates, a major oil and gas producer, wound up giving the fossil fuel industry unprecedented access: there were more fossil fuel lobbyists in Dubai than at any climate conference in the 28 years the United Nations has convened it.

Industry representatives for fossil fuels outnumbered the delegations from every country present at the talks except the United Arab Emirates and Brazil. According to an investigation by the BBC and the Centre for Climate Reporting, COP28 president Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber even used his position to lobby for oil and gas deals with other governments.

# The Cairo Diplomatic Surge And The 2023 Summit For Peace

On Saturday, 2023-10-21, President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi hosted what was billed as a "Summit for Peace" in Cairo, with Middle East and European leaders in attendance — evidence of the international focus then trained on Egypt. The recent flurry of diplomacy centered on Cairo marked something of a return to Egypt's traditional role, figuring prominently in every discussion over power politics across the region in the latter half of the 20th century, when it rallied Arab forces and led the 1973 attack on Israel that triggered the Yom Kippur war, before the two countries signed a peace treaty and established full diplomatic relations in 1980 and went on to become strategic allies.

In the days since Hamas — which the US and Europe designate a terrorist group — launched its attack on Israel, El-Sisi was courted by a succession of world leaders. US President Joe Biden reaffirmed the two countries' "enduring, strategic partnership" in a call. Visiting Chancellor Olaf Scholz praised German-Egyptian unity in working to prevent a Middle East "conflagration." Chinese President Xi Jinping met Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly in Beijing.

# Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 Targets

The Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 aims for a deep economic and social transformation to reinvigorate job creation and accelerate poverty reduction by steering the economy back to a high-growth path, and two main performance indicators are identified and will be monitored by the National Government.

The first is for the country to graduate into upper middle-income class status within the term of the current administration, for which the economy must grow its per capita income above the threshold set by the World Bank, a gross national income per capita of at least $4,466; in 2022 the Philippines achieved a GNI per capita of $3,950. The second is to lower the poverty level from 18.1% in 2021 to single digits by 2028, the end of the term of the current administration. Both indicators require high growth rates, and for the next year through 2028 the government pencils the growth rate between 6.5% and 8%.



---


# The Private Sector's Role In Philippine Sustainable Development

Coming off the pandemic and given the current global economic climate, it is opportune for the government to proactively drive actionable policies and programs that focus on building the resiliency of the economy through sustainable development, with greater emphasis on addressing climate change. That is the article's conclusion about timing, and the accompanying claim is that navigating external and domestic economic headwinds will not be an easy feat for the administration.

The warrant for optimism is the private sector's role as an important catalyst for sustainable development: with the private sector sharing industry knowledge and resources and potentially even leading certain socio-economic programs and projects of the National Government, the hope is that AmBisyon Natin 2040, of long and healthy lives for Filipinos that are strongly rooted, comfortable and secure, will be achieved.

# The QRU's Position On High-Performance Centralisation

In the wake of the Wallabies' 2023 World Cup flop, the Queensland Rugby Union reaffirmed on Oct. 10, 2023 that it is committed to moving to a centralised high-performance model — but will not follow the NSW Waratahs in handing over the keys to Rugby Australia.

The QRU's stated commitment reads: "The QRU is committed to working with Rugby Australia to lead reform of our game at a high-performance level, and help Rugby Australia develop an improved game through high-performance centralisation." The letter defined the scope of that centralisation: it "would include a national player-contracting model, and alignment of key high-performance staff, such as coaching, strength and conditioning, and medical to operate as one national system." The letter, an open letter to members published on Wednesday morning by QRU chief executive David Hanham and chairman Brett Clark, also pointed to RA's involvement in Les Kiss' appointment as Reds coach — the former State of Origin winger turned coach, who has spent the best part of two decades coaching in Ireland and England, replacing Brad Thorn — as an example of the model in practice.

The QRU also expressed strong support for Rugby Australia to conduct a "fully independent and transparent top-to-bottom review of the Wallabies program and how it can be improved" in light of the historic first World Cup pool exit, adding: "It should also provide a clear view of what is needed in a leadership and governance framework to ensure we put the right people, in the right roles, in the right system." The Roar noted the boundary of the consensus: while all five Australian Super Rugby sides are fundamentally on board with moving to a centralised high-performance program, some states, including the ACT Brumbies as well as the QRU, don't want to give up their commercial assets.

# The Monetary And Fiscal Policy Coordination Debate

The case for coordination starts from what the two arms achieved together and then what they cost. Low interest rates and large-scale QE programs allowed treasuries to borrow on the cheap to finance stimulus campaigns, protecting labor markets, businesses and consumers from collapse — but the spending blowout throughout and since the pandemic, part critical emergency funding and part political need to show an all-hands-on-deck approach in crisis, contributed to the latest outbreak in inflation.

The problem now is that the same kind of pulling in the same direction is needed to restrain demand, while many governments are concerned that if they tighten policy too hard, voters will kick them out and replace them with populists or extremists. That is reviving questions about whether central banks can deliver price stability all on their own. "If we were designing optimal policy arrangements from scratch, monetary and fiscal policy would both have a role in managing the economic cycle and inflation, and that there would be close coordination," Philip Lowe said in his last speech as Australian central bank governor in September 2023. ECB President Christine Lagarde put it more conditionally at a panel discussion in June at the institution's annual economic forum: "It's true that there are circumstances where working hand in hand and supporting each other has proved helpful."

Economists surveyed by Bloomberg predict fiscal policy will somewhat counteract the Fed's efforts to rein in inflation in the US.



---


# US Equity Sector Moves On 10 October 2023

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.4 per cent to 33,739.30, the S&P 500 gained 0.5 per cent and the Nasdaq Composite added 0.6 per cent, with all 11 major S&P 500 sectors advancing — materials and consumer staples led the gains while technology was the slowest gainer, and energy was among the laggards after its more than 3 per cent rally on Monday.

A measure of US-listed Chinese shares added 3 per cent amid reports that the Asian nation is considering new economic stimulus. "Policymakers have begun to acknowledge a lesser need for further policy action given financial conditions have tightened considerably after the recent surge in Treasury yields," said Ben Jeffery at BMO Capital Markets. "This acknowledgment may have reduced angst around the need for additional rate increases." Investors would be watching for any hints in the September Fed meeting minutes, due Wednesday, that would suggest the Fed may not follow through with the last rise indicated in its economic projections, according to Anna Wong at Bloomberg Economics, who noted that two critical coming indicators for the US economy — Thursday's consumer price index and Friday's University of Michigan consumer-sentiment survey — may give a more definitive read.



---


# The Case For Preemptive Central Bank Response To Supply Shocks

One lesson Gita Gopinath, the IMF's No. 2 official, draws from the latest inflation episode is that policymakers mustn't assume that looking through supply shocks — as textbooks suggest — is the optimal response. Her recommendation follows directly: central banks should be ready to react preemptively, even when inflation hasn't yet spun out of control.

The warrant is the experience of the 2021-2023 inflation outbreak itself, and the argument has an immediate application: policymakers may be called into action soon on that front, should an escalation in the conflict in the Middle East hit oil deliveries.



---


# Saudi Co-Leadership As Egypt's Way Out Of The Dilemma

One way out of Egypt's dilemma may be for it to offer Saudi Arabia a role co-leading the Palestinian issue for the Arab world in return for financial support, according to strategists. The proposition rests on Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman being willing: aware of domestic anger at Israel, he might welcome such an initiative to strengthen his regional profile — though he was absent from the Summit for Peace held in Cairo on Saturday, 2023-10-21, which is the one contrary indication the account records.

The fluid situation may offer Egypt other opportunities to take a mediating role that could be rewarded, Crisis Group's Riccardo Fabiani said. For now, Egypt will try to play a constructive part "in the hope that its contribution will be acknowledged by its international and regional partners and potentially rewarded economically," he said.



---


# The Longest-Standing International Goalscoring Records

Only six countries' international goalscoring records have stood for more than 50 years, including Libya, Sudan and Guinea, and if only nations that have qualified for the World Cup are counted, just Denmark, Norway and Hungary have records lasting more than half a century, as reported by The New York Times on 17 November 2023.

Hungary's is perhaps the most impressive of them, considering Ferenc Puskas scored 84 goals in just 85 games and had his international career brought to a premature end at the age of 29 because of the Hungarian Revolution; he later represented Spain at the 1962 World Cup, having gone half a decade without playing international football.

The striking finding in the other direction is how many goalscoring records have been set recently. Sixty-four of the 211 nations' record goalscorers have appeared for them in 2023, and in terms of time since they were set the median goalscoring mark has stood for just seven years, a group that includes the Republic of Ireland's Robbie Keane and Paraguay's Roque Santa Cruz. Increased longevity due to superior fitness levels in the modern game is clearly a major factor, as is the number of relatively new nations on the FIFA list.



---


# The Post-Tightening Monetary Policy Autopsy Of 2023

After the most aggressive monetary-tightening campaign in four decades, academics and economic practitioners are running autopsies on what could have prevented the cost-of-living crisis and how to ensure the same mistakes won't be repeated. Markets have scrambled to price in high-for-longer interest rates, with a new war in the Middle East adding yet more risk to an already uncertain outlook confronting central bankers as they gather for their penultimate meetings of a tumultuous year.

The policy navel-gazing centers on three debates: how much flexibility central banks can allow in reaching their inflation targets, the effectiveness of asset purchases in the policy mix, and the merits of monetary and fiscal coordination. Bloomberg surveyed economists from around the world to gather views on those three debates. Their verdict: central banks won't break their economies in a rush to hit inflation targets, QE will be used more sparingly in the future, and fiscal policy risks countering the work of monetary authorities.

# OpenAI's Nonprofit-To-For-Profit Structure

OpenAI started out as a nonprofit when it launched with financial backing from Tesla CEO Elon Musk and others, with stated aims to "advance digital intelligence in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return." That changed in 2018, when it incorporated a for-profit business, OpenAI LP, and shifted nearly all its staff into that business, not long after releasing its first generation of the GPT large language model for mimicking human writing.

Around the same time, Musk — who had co-chaired its board with Altman — resigned from the board, in a move OpenAI said would eliminate a "potential future conflict for Elon" due to Tesla's work on building self-driving systems. The resulting arrangement is a split one: OpenAI's board has preserved its nonprofit governance structure, while the startup it oversees has increasingly sought to capitalize on its technology by tailoring its popular chatbot to business customers.

# What Israeli Leaders Claimed The Gaza Barrier Would Do

At the time of the fence's completion, Israeli leaders argued that the barrier had already proved itself and would provide security to the region — claims that, as the article notes, rested on a threat model built around tunnels and ladders.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, then in opposition, referred mainly to the below-ground aspect: "Any time Hamas terrorists have tried to penetrate the border settlements through the tunnels, they were terminated underground. The below-ground barrier surrounding the Gaza Strip has already saved many lives." Then-Minister of Defense Benny Gantz said, "The barrier, which is a superior initial technological and inventive project that sets an iron wall, sensors and concrete between it and the residents of the south. It provides a sense of personal security that will allow this beautiful region to continue to grow." The reference scenario behind that confidence is identified by Yehoshua Kalisky, senior researcher at Tel Aviv University's Institute for National Security Studies: "The concept underlying the construction of an advanced technology fence relates to the Second Lebanon War, when Hezbollah surmounted a high fence with a ladder. This was the reference scenario. There was no thought that they would use aircraft here to cross it or that they would come with a heavy machinery, and simply breach it."

# Bank of Israel Thirty Billion Dollar FX Intervention

On the Monday of the week in which this 12 October 2023 interview was published, the Bank of Israel announced a dramatic plan to sell $30 billion of its foreign currency reserves to stabilise the shekel. By the time of the report the shekel had in fact recovered slightly and was trading at around NIS 3.96/$.

Leo Leiderman endorsed the move: "It's important to welcome the Bank of Israel's decision to intervene, as necessary, in the foreign exchange market, in order to ensure the market's regular operation." He also treated leadership continuity as stabilising, citing the decision to extend the term of Amir Yaron as governor at least for the duration of the war, and in his hope beyond it. He added that the banking system is stable with enough liquidity in the system, and that the behaviour of the investment community in Israel, including the financial institutions, indicates high confidence in the economy's resilience and financial strength — an "asset" he said a level-headed, correct economic policy must preserve.

# The USWNT Head Coach Search Process In 2023

U.S. Soccer's 2023 head coach search ran through multiple rounds of evaluation, with the list of candidates becoming smaller each time, as described by The New York Times on 15 November 2023.

The stages are given in order. The first pass was driven purely by data, which was then whittled down to a double-digit list Matt Crocker was considering as of September, and then a final shortlist, which also included Tony Gustavsson, head coach of Australia; multiple sources confirmed both Hayes and Gustavsson flew to the U.S. for interviews. Initial contact with Hayes was made a couple of months before the announcement, early in the search, with all three top-level U.S. Soccer executives — Crocker, president Cindy Parlow Cone and CEO J.T. Batson — involved in those talks. A U.S. Soccer statement describes the interview process as involving "psychometrics and abstract reasoning tests, in-depth discussions of strategy, coaching philosophy and the current player pool, as well as evaluation on the reactions to pressure, culture-building and interactions with players and staff"; USMNT coach Gregg Berhalter went through a similar process, including an abstract reasoning test, when he was re-hired by Crocker earlier in 2023. Crocker said in September that the final interviews would include lengthy technical and tactical assessments as well as questions to determine cultural fit.

Two further details are recorded. The federation had also checked in on the availability of Sarina Wiegman, according to one source briefed on the situation, despite clear messaging from both the English FA and Wiegman herself in August: "I'm staying out of it. I've heard it (from the press officer) but no, I'm with England and I'm really happy with England, and I have a contract until 2025," Wiegman said, and a representative from her camp declined to comment. And on timing: part of the surprise around the hire and the six-month runway is down to U.S. Soccer's own messaging, since Crocker had said in a September meeting with U.S. reporters that he hoped to have a new head coach in place by December; he and the federation stayed fairly consistent on their desired start date since the role opened in August, but that became one of the major concessions made in selecting Hayes.

# The Israeli Proposal To Temporarily House Gazans In Sinai

The Israeli government has spoken to counterparts in several countries about Egypt temporarily housing Palestinians fleeing the violence in Gaza, according to officials with knowledge of the matter. Israel suggested they could be moved to tent camps in the Sinai Peninsula — funded by the United Nations and the US — and then returned once military operations end, said the people. It is unclear whether Israel has put the idea directly to Egypt.

The reasoning behind the approach was economic. "Clearly the hope on Israel and the US's side had been that Egypt would accept economic incentives, at a time when it is suffering an economic crisis, to allow Gazans into Egypt," said Mirette Mabrouk, director of the Egypt program at the Washington-based Middle East Institute.

# Netanyahu Declaration of War and Three Objectives

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on 7 October 2023 that since that morning Israel had been at war, and set out three objectives. The first was to clear out the hostile forces that infiltrated its territory and restore security and quiet to the communities that had been attacked.

"The second objective, at the same time, is to exact an immense price from the enemy, within the Gaza Strip as well," he said. The third objective was to reinforce other fronts so that nobody should mistakenly join this war.

He closed with an appeal for composure and unity: "We are at war. In war, one needs to be level-headed. I call on all citizens of Israel to unite in order to achieve our highest goal – victory in the war."



---


# Egypt's 1991 Gulf War Debt Forgiveness

Egypt secured forgiveness of half its $20.2 billion debt owed to the US and allies in 1991 — one of the most generous incidences of debt relief creditor nations have granted — in exchange for support for the anti-Iraq coalition during the Gulf war. This stands as a precedent of sorts for Cairo winning favors as a regional war raged.

The motives on the creditor side were specific: the US wanted to reward Egypt's President Hosni Mubarak for his pivotal role in lining up Arab nations against Saddam Hussein, and to reimburse Egypt for heavy financial losses in the war. Egypt also sent armed forces to participate.

# Philippine National Government Budget Definition

The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) defines the government budget as "the financial plan of the government…which shows what its resources are, and how they will be generated and used over the fiscal period. It refers to the income, expenditures and sources of borrowings of the National Government (NG) that are used to achieve national objectives, strategies and programs."

Its constitutional basis is Section 22, Article VII: "The President shall submit to the Congress within 30 days from the opening of every regular session, as the basis of the general appropriation bill, a budget of expenditures and sources of financing including receipts from existing and proposed revenue measures."

The National Government budget is the totality of the budgets of all government entities: the National Government itself, the non-financial government-owned and -controlled corporations (usually only the 14 major GOCCs), government financial institutions, local government units, the social security institutions (GSIS, SSS, military pensions, PhilHealth and others), the Oil Price Stabilization Fund, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and the Central Bank-Board of Liquidators. It is allocated for the implementation of government programmes and projects, the operation of government offices, payment of salaries of government employees and payment of public debts, with expenditures classified by expense class, sector and implementing unit of government.

Appropriations come from two sources: new general appropriations legislated by Congress for every budget year under the General Appropriations Act, and existing appropriations previously authorised by Congress. Under Article VI, Section 29 of the Constitution, no money can be withdrawn from the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law.

# The FLOPs Threshold For Systemic-Risk GPAI Classification

The EU AI Act classifies a general purpose AI as carrying systemic risk by reference to the compute used to train it — 10^25 floating point operations — but the Commission confirmed during a technical briefing with journalists that this is only an "initial threshold," and that it will have powers to update it over time via implementing and delegating acts, that is, secondary legislation.

The structure has three moving parts and one relation between them. First, the threshold is not intended to stand alone: the idea is for the FLOPs figure to be combined, over time, with "other benchmarks" that will be developed by a new expert oversight body to be set up within the Commission, called the AI Office. Second, classification is self-assessed: a Commission official said it will be up to makers of GPAIs to self assess whether their models meet the FLOPs threshold and therefore whether they fall under the rules for GPAIs "with systemic risk." Third, the number was picked to capture current generation frontier models, though the Commission claimed lawmakers did not discuss nor even consider whether it would apply to any models currently in play, such as OpenAI's GPT-4 or Google's Gemini, during the marathon trilogues.

The official put the uncertainty plainly during the press briefing: "There are no official sources that will say ChatGPT or Gemini or Chinese models are at this level of FLOPs. On the basis of the information we have and with this 10^25 that we have chosen we have chosen a number that could really capture, a little bit, the frontier models that we have. Whether this is capturing GPT-4 or Gemini or others we are not here now to assert — because also, in our framework, it is the companies that would have to come and self assess what the amount of FLOPs or the computing capacity they have used. But, of course, if you read the scientific literature, many will point to these numbers as being very much the most advanced models at the moment. We will see what the companies will assess because they're the best placed to make this assessment." They added: "The rules have not been written keeping in mind certain companies. They've really been written with the idea of defining the threshold — which, by the way, may change because we have the possibility to be empowered to change this threshold on the basis of technological evolution. It could go up, it could go down and we could also develop other benchmarks that in the future will be the more appropriate to benchmark the different moments."

# The IDF's "Small And Smart Army" Doctrine

For years the IDF has praised the ethos of a small and smart army, implicitly if not explicitly, presenting itself as a high-tech army through countless publicized technological projects — a concept not limited to the border fence or to intelligence, and not merely a product of Operation Protective Edge.

The institutional expression includes establishing a technological division, Shiloh, to coordinate the development of technologies for all branches of the army together with the Directorate of Defense Research & Development (IMOD DDR&D or MAFAT); Shiloh, currently subordinate to the Ministry of Defense, was established following State Comptroller reports about the lack of coordination and synchronization between the Ministry of Defense and IDF units. The doctrine also drove a new border defense concept based on sensors and other technologies for gathering intelligence and thwarting infiltration, strengthening the Air Force with additional aircraft and armaments, and strengthening the operational end of regular front units — all while closing down armored battalions and consolidating helicopter squadrons. Ground force technological capabilities were also addressed, such as improved coordination between the infantry and air forces in air-to-ground actions, or identifying terrorists and weapons in an urban environment. Prof. Eviatar Matania of Tel Aviv University's School of Political Sciences, Government and International Affairs, founder and first director general of the Israel National Cyber Directorate, identifies a problem at the outset: a large gap between the technology and the officers expected to implement it as part of the security concept. Matania traces the lineage: the IDF has always advocated technological advancement as part of a concept valuing quality over quantity — "This existed even during [Israel's first Prime Minister David] Ben-Gurion's time, because it was clear that we could not defeat the enemy in terms of quantity, and it also integrated well with saving human lives – an important pillar in the security concept – but at that time, innovation was expressed in tactical issues. After the Yom Kippur War, Israel pulled strongly in the direction of building military technological superiority, and this integrated well with the Israeli economy, which was gradually opening up to the world, and the computer revolution. This effort bore fruit as early as 1982, when we proved to the whole world that we could destroy most of the Syrian surface-to-air missile array using precision-guided weaponry. Israel's security concept was updated by Dan Meridor and Lt. Col. Ron Eldadi, with the addition of a fourth component, defense, to the three components of Israel's traditional national security doctrine as determined by Ben-Gurion: deterrence, warning, and decisive victory, leading to the development of systems such as the Iron Dome, and David's Sling (formerly called Magic Wand)."

# The Scale Of Israel's Technology Sector In 2022

Technology is, without question, a giant part of Israel's economy: in 2022 it contributed more than 18% of the country's GDP, the most of any single sector, according to the latest annual report from the Israel Innovation Authority at the time of writing in October 2023. A total of 14% of Israeli citizens work in high tech, which in a country of just 9.2 million people works out to about 1.3 million.

The startup base is correspondingly large. The active number of startups in the country is 9,000, third-highest in the world after the Bay Area and NYC, and over the last five years those startups collectively brought $95 billion into the country by way of venture capital. Combining the business development of startups with the larger tech companies operating in Israel — Intel, Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and many others have operations there — they collectively exported $71 billion in the prior year, 48.3% of the total amount exported across all industries.

# A Presidential Veto Of An ITC Import Ban Is Extraordinarily Rare

Experts told The Verge that Apple getting a presidential veto of the ITC ban would be like lightning striking the same place twice. "It is extraordinarily rare for the President to overturn a decision from the International Trade Commission and in my view, [it's] unlikely in this particular case," said Andrei Iancu, co-chair of the Council for Innovation Promotion and partner at Sullivan & Cromwell LLP, who was director of the US Patent and Trademark Office from 2018 to 2021.

The grounds are the standard for a veto: a company usually has to show a public interest or health policy basis, and that isn't the case here. "It's unlikely that the import exclusion order will be disapproved by the USTR and the president," said Smith Brittingham, partner at Finnegan, Henderson, Farabow, Garrett & Dunner, LLP. "The only real answer would be, 'Well, it's Apple.'" The apparent counterexample is handled rather than ignored: in 2013 then-President Barack Obama did veto an import ban on the iPhone after Samsung accused Apple of infringing its cellular data patents. But according to Ben Levi, Apple then had arguments it lacks now — the patents were considered standard and essential, so Apple could raise fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory licensing (FRAND) issues, and the Obama administration was concerned the ban would give Samsung "undue leverage"; the ban also only affected the iPhone 4 and older iPad models, since newer iPhones didn't use an infringing chipset. In the Apple Watch case Apple has none of those arguments. "In that case 10 years ago, Apple really rolled the dice and pulled the rabbit out of the hat. It's very unlikely for them to do that again," Levi said.

# Patent Litigation

## Definition

In the corpus, patent litigation is the set of formal legal proceedings companies use to fight over patent rights — a patent holder's lawsuit in federal district court and, in parallel, a case before the US International Trade Commission (ITC) — with remedies that can include a monetary verdict or an ITC import ban, and with the accused party able to counter-sue or get the asserted patents ruled invalid or unenforceable.

## Context

The corpus documents two concrete disputes that illustrate the mechanics of patent litigation. Sonos sued Google and won a $32.5 million verdict over patent infringement, but a federal judge later threw out that win after finding Sonos' patents "unenforceable and invalid" — showing that a litigation win is not final until it survives post-trial and appellate review. Separately, Masimo sued Apple in the US District Court for the Central District of California in 2020 for trade-secret theft and infringement of 10 patents related to pulse-oximetry (SpO2) sensing technology, and when that case dragged on, Masimo additionally filed a parallel case with the US International Trade Commission (ITC) in 2021; Apple counter-sued Masimo the following year. The ITC route matters because, unlike a district court, it can issue an import ban that blocks the accused product (the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2) from entering the US market, and any such ban is then subject to a 60-day presidential review period during which the President or US Trade Representative may veto it.

## Key Characteristics

- **Dual venues** — patent disputes can run in federal district court (damages, injunctions) and, in parallel, before the ITC (import bans), as in the Apple-Masimo dispute where Masimo pursued both.
- **Invalidity/unenforceability as a defense** — a defendant can defeat an infringement verdict after the fact by getting the asserted patents ruled unenforceable and invalid, as happened to Sonos' win against Google.
- **Countersuits** — litigation can escalate into cross-litigation, as when Apple sued Masimo back, alleging Masimo's own watch cloned Apple's design.
- **ITC import-ban remedy plus presidential review** — an ITC finding of infringement can trigger a ban on importing the infringing product, but the ban is not final until a 60-day presidential/USTR review period lapses without a veto.
- **Long timelines** — the Apple-Masimo dispute originated roughly a decade before the resulting Apple Watch import ban took effect, illustrating how a single patent dispute can span years across multiple proceedings.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, patent litigation is generally described as the process of enforcing patent rights, and it is decided exclusively by federal (not state) courts in the US.

Remedies available in such litigation typically include a permanent or preliminary injunction ordering the infringing act to stop, and a damages award such as a reasonable royalty.

A defendant can raise defenses including that the patent has expired, that it holds a license, or that the patent is invalid or unenforceable, and disputes may also end in a settlement that includes a licensing agreement.

# Innovation As Perpetual And Mundane

For successful products and businesses, innovation is perpetual: there is a never-ending search to find the next new thing that enhances the user experience, extends product reach, expands revenue, or all three simultaneously. Product design makes innovation less daunting and increases chances of success because it is a multidisciplinary process with structures and frameworks to catalyze innovation, and technologists have a role in that process extending beyond simply validating the technology or concept, which is their customary responsibility.

The discriminating feature of innovation is novelty, not grandeur. The word innovation has a simple meaning — to introduce something new or a novel method of doing something — yet we frequently inflate it to mean something magical, grandiose and world-changing, when it can just as easily be mundane and straightforward.

The boundary of the concept is set by where the "new" applies: it can be localized to a team, product, process or business unit, and the "novel" can be well-known and established practices that have simply not been incorporated into your workflow or product. Sometimes innovation comes from closing small gaps and is not always a grand eureka moment.

# Licensing Or US Manufacturing As Apple's Exit Routes

Two remaining routes out of the ban would cost Apple money: it could sit down with Masimo and hammer out a licensing deal for the infringed patents, or it could avoid the import ban altogether by manufacturing the watches within the US instead of overseas.

Neither is straightforward. On licensing, Masimo CEO Joe Kiani told The New York Times that Apple "had not engaged in licensing negotiations," and any settlement requires both parties to want one. "Apple is a tough nut to crack," said Smith Brittingham, noting that Apple is one of the most sued companies in Silicon Valley and that its large cash reserves make taking Apple to court a costly endeavor — Masimo has reportedly spent $60 million litigating the issue thus far. "I think they tend to hold out as long as possible in order to make it less appetizing to sue Apple." On domestic manufacturing, Andrei Iancu said Apple could simply decide to build the watches in the US, but that is a significant supply chain change unlikely to happen any time soon.

# The Four Layers Of The GenAI Tech Stack

Rick Grinnell, founder and managing partner at Glasswing Ventures, categorizes the generative AI landscape into four distinct layers in the firm's proprietary view of the GenAI tech stack: foundation model providers, middle-tier companies, end-market or top-layer applications, and full stack or end-to-end vertical companies. He was answering, in TechCrunch's 13 October 2023 survey of AI investors, whether startups will build striated solutions for individual layers of the LLM stack — models, pre-training solutions and fine-tuning tools — or pursue a more vertical approach.

The relations between layers are stated as market-structure predictions. At the foundational layer, providers like Alphabet/Google's Bard, Microsoft/OpenAI's GPT-4, and Anthropic's Claude show that the more significant players possess inherent advantages regarding data accessibility, talent pool and computational resources; this layer is expected to settle into an oligopolistic structure like the cloud provider market, albeit with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption. Above the model itself lies the largest market opportunity: companies that introduce AI-powered APIs and operational layers for specific industries will create brand-new use cases and transform workflows, and by embracing this technology to revolutionize workflows, these companies stand to unlock substantial value. Within the stack, most of the opportunity lies in the application layer, where the best applications will harness their in-house expertise to build specialized middle-layer tooling and blend them with the appropriate foundational models, and where startups can use speed to their advantage as they work to "innovate, iterate and deploy solutions" to customers.

The range over which the model holds is explicitly limited by market immaturity. The market is still far from being crystallized; LLMs are still in their infancy, with adoption at large corporations and startups lacking full maturity and refinement, and robust tools and platforms are needed to enable broader utilization among businesses and individuals. Startups have the opportunity here to act quickly, find novel solutions to emerging problems, and define new categories. Even large tech companies recognize the gaps in their services and have begun investing heavily in startups alongside VCs — these companies apply AI to their internal processes and thus see the value startups bring to LLM deployment and integration, as with the recent investments from Microsoft, Nvidia, and Salesforce into companies like Inflection AI and Cohere.

A dissenting position within the same survey bears on how much weight the layer model should carry for strategy. Edward Tsai, a managing partner at Alumni Ventures, offered a potentially "controversial opinion that VCs and startups may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market."

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# Dangerous Organizations and Individuals Policy

The Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy is the named enforcement category Meta cites when it removes content tied to groups that governments designate as terrorist organizations, most directly Hamas.
In the corpus its practical trigger is Hamas: content praising or supporting Hamas, which governs Gaza and is designated a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union, is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms.
Meta tracks enforcement of this policy as its own category, separate from its Violence and Incitement policy, reporting that it removed "seven times as many pieces of content on a daily basis for violating our Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy in Hebrew and Arabic alone" in the three days after October 7, 2023, compared with the two months prior.

## Context

In the corpus the policy is the mechanism through which Meta enforces against Hamas-related content during the Israel-Hamas war, and it is the recurring flashpoint in disputes over whether that enforcement is applied evenly.
Meta invokes the policy to justify removing content that praises or supports Hamas — Hamas being "designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union" — and Instagram separately cited a related "Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations" when it denied that a specific violent, threatening comment violated its rules, illustrating that the same policy family both blocks and, in users' eyes, under-enforces depending on the content.
The designation logic recurs beyond Meta's own platform actions: the corpus notes that Hamas is "considered a terrorist organization by the U.K., U.S. and other countries" in the context of the Web Summit/Cosgrave controversy, and that UNRWA operates "alongside Hamas, which Israel, the United States and other countries designate as a terrorist organization" in Gaza — showing the same underlying designation of Hamas driving both platform moderation policy and geopolitical characterization of the region's governing party.

## Key Characteristics

- **Named, tracked enforcement category** — Meta reports removal volumes specifically "for violating our Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy," distinct from its Violence and Incitement policy, letting the company cite a sevenfold daily increase in Hebrew/Arabic enforcement after October 7.
- **Anchored to external terrorist designations** — the policy's practical trigger in the corpus is content supporting Hamas, an organization the U.S., EU and U.K. designate as a terrorist group; the platform rule imports government designations rather than defining "dangerous" independently.
- **Contested in application** — Palestinian users and digital-rights advocates argue the policy (and its Community Guidelines "violence or dangerous organizations" language) is enforced inconsistently, citing a case where a violent, threatening comment was ruled not to violate it, and past instances where the Al-Aqsa Mosque hashtag was blocked after being "mistaken for a terrorist organization."
- **Localized to Arabic and Hebrew content** — the volume Meta cites for this policy is scoped specifically to Hebrew and Arabic content, not platform-wide, reflecting the languages most implicated in Israel-Hamas war content moderation.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Meta's own Community Standards describe the Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy more broadly than the Hamas-specific enforcement described above: it generally bars praise, substantive support, and representation of any individual or organization that Meta designates as dangerous, a designation list that spans terrorist organizations, hate organizations, criminal organizations, and other violence-inducing entities, not just Hamas.
Source: Meta Transparency Center, "Dangerous Organizations and Individuals" Community Standard, accessed 2026-09-02, https://transparency.meta.com/policies/community-standards/dangerous-individuals-organizations/.

In response, Google enacted a plan its executives dubbed "Go Big in Europe," to enhance search results in France and Germany in 2019 and 2020 with more local content: news, post-game soccer video highlights, information on local television options for streaming, and pronunciation practice for different languages. The aim was to incentivize users to click on Google's home screen rather than the competition's.

That revelation effectively supports the Justice Department's argument that Google, without the push of competition, has little incentive to improve its products — a classic consequence in a monopoly.

# Organized Labor's Pushback On AI Deployment

Organized labor's argument, voiced by AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler at the conclusion of Tuesday's Senate AI forum, is that AI's effect on workers depends entirely on whether workers are included in the process: "If we fail to involve workers and unions across the entire innovation process, AI will curtail our rights, threaten good jobs and undermine our democracy. But the responsible adoption of AI, properly regulated, has the potential to create opportunity, improve working conditions and build prosperity."

The grounds Shuler offered are that the technology is already being used against workers — "Working people are fighting back against artificial intelligence and other technology used to eliminate workers or undermine and exploit us" — so the warrant joining grounds to claim is that regulation plus worker participation is what separates the beneficial deployment path from the harmful one, rather than the technology itself deciding the outcome.

The same argument came from inside the industry. While Andreessen calls for AI advancement at any cost and Tegmark continues to advocate for a developmental "time out," rank-and-file AI industry workers pressed their own case ahead of the forum: on Monday, employees from two dozen leading AI firms published an open letter to Senator Schumer demanding Congress act to safeguard their livelihoods from the "dystopian future" that Andreessen's screed would require. "Establishing robust protections related to workplace technology and rebalancing power between workers and employers could reorient the economy and tech innovation toward more equitable and sustainable outcomes," the letter's authors argue. The previous month, Senator Ed Markey (D-MA) and Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) had called on leading AI companies to "answer for the working conditions of their data workers, laborers who are often paid low wages and provided no benefits but keep AI products online."

# Palestinian Tech Ecosystem Growth Before The War

Ryan Sturgill, who had been helping Palestinian tech startups raise capital in the West Bank and Gaza since January, described strong momentum before the war: "Until now, there had been a pretty significant growth. A lot of companies in Saudi Arabia have been setting up back offices [in Palestine] for development for all sorts of new companies and even apps that are now growing in the Gulf, because Saudi has been growing so quickly on the tech front. Nvidia, and other international companies, has outsourcing operations in Palestine. Apple has outsourcing operations, Microsoft has R&D, and they would even like to see those expand. There's companies that had 200 developers sitting in offices in Ramallah." He added: "I've talked to all of the heads of these different offices; most of them are in in Israel. They are very positive people who want to try to support the tech industry there and those efforts have been working well and growing."

One of the main Palestinian VC funds, Ibtikar, had recently raised its second fund of $30 million, and high-growth companies emerging from Palestine include Mena Analytics (data analytics, invested in by Flat6Labs); Olivery (last-mile logistics, Flat6Labs, Gaza Sky Geeks Ibtikar Fund); Coretava (employee and customer loyalty); and SellEnvo (an Amazon fulfillment partner). Iliana Montauk, a former director of Gaza Sky Geeks, said: "Before this escalation, the Gaza tech scene was growing. I was just in Riyadh and met companies that hire entire software development teams in Gaza. Upwork and other Silicon Valley companies are now hiring software engineers remotely from Gaza. In addition, some had left to work abroad at companies like Google, Amazon, Qualtrics, etc. Last time I was in Gaza a year ago, almost everyone I talked to asked me how they could get a job and leave Gaza. They were worried about more bombings and wanted to bring their children up in a place without such a high risk. These people just want to live normal lives."

Tchia, developed by Awaceb for PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, and Windows PC, is ranked 48 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31. It is an open-world adventure game set in a fictional version of the island nation New Caledonia, inspired by Awaceb's co-founder's childhood in the country.

Everything is filtered through the titular main character's eyes — eyes with a special power that allows her to transform into any animals or objects in her environment, whether birds, dolphins, a camera, or rocks.

Critic Nicole Carpenter notes the game is clearly inspired by The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild but ends up standing on its own because of the innovative shapeshifting mechanics. It is not as technically polished as a Nintendo title with hundreds of developers — Awaceb has a team of roughly a dozen — but it is hard to innovate in such a ubiquitous genre, and Awaceb managed to do just that.
