# Big Tech Concentration In The S&P 500

"As these big tech stocks go, so does the overall market," David Trainer, chief executive officer of New Constructs, said before Microsoft and Alphabet's results — the core of a model in which a handful of heavyweights determine the index's direction.

The mechanism and its stress points were both visible in October 2023. On the upside, Trainer argued: "Strong big tech earnings may just be what's needed to end the stock market correction that started in late July. If big tech companies blow their numbers out of the water and provide strong guidance for future earnings, then we could see the stock market rally strongly through the end of the year." On the downside, rising rates have made already stretched big tech valuations look increasingly expensive, with the group remaining the most-crowded trade among fund managers according to Bank of America — prompting some investors to pay up for protection against a sell-off in Alphabet and Microsoft, two of the handful of heavyweights responsible for all of the S&P 500 Index's advance that year. The rate pressure was easing at the margin: the pain in long-duration growth stocks, fuelled in recent weeks by a relentless surge in Treasury yields, was finally on the verge of subsiding, and the yield on 10-year Treasuries was little changed at 4.85 per cent overnight. Oil closed at the lowest in more than a week amid signs the crude market's tightness had slackened and the Israel-Hamas war would remain contained for the time being, with West Texas Intermediate extending Monday's drop with a 2.2 per cent fall to $US83.59 a barrel, paring most of the gains made after Hamas's attack on Israel on October 7.

# Kalmus's Critique of Biden Climate Policy

Kalmus attacks the premise that President Joe Biden's record makes him a climate champion, arguing that the Inflation Reduction Act, Biden's signature climate bill, does too little to shut out the fossil fuel industry, and that rejoining the Paris accord is no achievement because "That Paris Agreement will take us to about 3 degrees Celsius of global heating. I don't think we'll have a civilization at 3 degrees Celsius."

His frustration extends beyond the administration: not his suburban neighbours in North Carolina, who continue to drive emissions-belching SUVs to big-box stores, and perhaps not even some in the science community, like those who kicked him out of the American Geophysical Union's annual fall meeting last year after he unfurled a banner and protested on the major science conference's biggest stage. The article supplies two checks on his claim. Rhodium Group, a nonpartisan think tank, estimates greenhouse gas emissions will drop 32%-42% below 2005 levels by 2030, well short of Biden's own benchmark for progress, with the inflation bill responsible for about a quarter of that projected decrease. And a 2022 United Nations report estimated global temperatures would rise between 2.1 and 2.9 degrees Celsius by 2100 if countries held to their climate commitments, while many countries remain off that pace.

# Product Design In The AI And Spatial Computing Era

Product design is in a moment of profound change and redefinition as technologies like artificial intelligence and spatial computing dramatically affect computing experiences. The two technologies act on different layers: AI, especially, may have only minor impacts on interface design but will significantly impact the holistic product or ecosystem experience, whereas spatial computing will change human-computer interactions and unmoor our understanding of what a computer is.

The consequence for practice is that in this innovation cycle, product design requires a wider perspective of platforms and interconnections between technologies, creating a strong need for technologists and designers to be in the process together.

# ChatGPT Mobile App Launches And Revenue

ChatGPT's mobile apps, launched for iOS in May 2023 and Android in July 2023, topped 110 million combined installs and reached nearly $30 million in consumer spending, according to a market analysis by data.ai.

The rollout was staged by geography. OpenAI launched the ChatGPT app for iOS free to use, free from ads and allowing voice input, but initially limited to U.S. users; the app syncs history across devices so it knows what a user previously searched via the web interface, and it is integrated with Whisper, OpenAI's open source speech recognition system, for voice input. Within six days it topped 500,000 downloads. OpenAI then announced the app was available on iOS in the U.S., Europe, South Korea and New Zealand, and added 11 more countries — Albania, Croatia, France, Germany, Ireland, Jamaica, Korea, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Nigeria and the UK. The app was later expanded to more than 30 further countries: Algeria, Argentina, Azerbaijan, Bolivia, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Estonia, Ghana, India, Iraq, Israel, Japan, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Lithuania, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mexico, Morocco, Namibia, Nauru, Oman, Pakistan, Peru, Poland, Qatar, Slovenia, Tunisia and the United Arab Emirates. A new version brought native iPad support with full-screen mode optimized for the tablet interface, support for using the chatbot with Siri and Shortcuts, and drag and drop for pulling individual messages from ChatGPT into other apps. On Android, OpenAI first put up a "pre-order" page on Google Play and days later released the app live in the US, India, Bangladesh and Brazil; the Android app looks more or less identical to the iOS one in functionality, getting most if not all of the web version's features and syncing conversations and preferences across devices.

Revenue is large but not dominant, and growth has slowed. In September, OpenAI amassed 15.6 million downloads and nearly $4.6 million in gross revenue across its iOS and Android apps worldwide — a record $4.58 million month for the mobile app — but revenue growth dropped from 30% to 20% in September according to market intelligence firm Appfigures. OpenAI's chatbot app far outpaces all others on mobile devices in terms of downloads, yet it is surprisingly not the top AI app by revenue: several other AI chatbots, such as "Chat & Ask AI" and "ChatOn — AI Chat Bot Assistant," make more money than ChatGPT.

# Ray-Ban Meta: Design And Discreetness

The Verge's reviewer found the Ray-Ban Meta glasses both good-looking and genuinely inconspicuous — in many ways, she wrote, they feel like they belong in a spy movie, since James Bond always looks good and the gadgets Q gives him are discreet. The reason design matters is blunt: you will never wear a pair of smart glasses if they make you look like a low-rent Warby Parker model, and aside from the original Bose Frames she had never liked the way she looked in smart glasses before. That these are Ray-Bans and come in more styles than typical smart glasses is what changed it — while Wayfarers are considered universally flattering, rounder frames look better on her, and instead of the usual tortoiseshell or black she could pick a round, transparent blue frame with pink lenses, whose colors she wished were more noticeable in darker lighting but which popped in sunlight. She wore them dolled up for a wedding, in functional but hideous running gear, in sweatpants, and with leather jackets: they go with everything.

The discreetness has a specific shape. No one will know you are wearing tech on your face unless you walk around saying "Hey Meta" at the top of your lungs; nobody knew she was listening to EXO's EXIST album on her commute. There is some faint audio leakage at full volume, but full volume is only necessary to block out the squeaky rails of the New York City subway, and fellow commuters likely will not notice because they have AirPods in or the ambient noise is louder. More troubling, no one batted an eye whenever she took photos and videos in public or private areas. The capture button sits on the top of the right arm.

She compared the experience to Eggsy in Kingsman: The Golden Circle, who takes a call through his glasses during an important dinner and appears to everyone else as a dapper gent in snazzy frames while hearing and seeing things they cannot. Her version had no bombs to defuse, but the point stands: she spent a lot of time wearing these in public doing and listening to things that people looking straight at her were not aware of. # The Fashion Industry's Plus-Size Inclusivity Gap

2023 in fashion was especially devoid of inclusivity or plus-size models: according to Vogue's Business Size Inclusivity Report, only 0.6 per cent of looks shown throughout the autumn/winter 2023 fashion season were modelled by plus-size people — this despite the body positivity movement having made waves over the previous 10 years.

Plus-size models have long advocated for more inclusive sizing, both in stores and on the runway. Luxury brands and labels, however, often avoid creating plus-size fashion over claims that it is too expensive to make. "Designers won't make plus sizes unless it's for a photo opp where a thin person can be quirky," one commenter pointed out.

The gap persists despite the market's size. The plus-size clothing market was expected to reach $288bn in 2023, according to Future Market Insights, yet advocates maintain that they are unable to purchase clothing that is both sustainable and inclusive. "I have to wear fast fashion and high street to major red carpet moments, and that's great, but I want the option to wear high end items of my choosing and it's not available," Tess Holliday told Elle UK in 2019. "But it's either that or I run around naked. Plus-size fashion is not there yet."

# Tyler Mitchell's Vogue Covers And NGV Triennial Works

Tyler Mitchell was just 23 when he became the first Black photographer to shoot the cover of American Vogue, photographing Beyoncé, and in November 2023 three of his works were on show in the NGV's Triennial exhibition, The Age reported on 27 November 2023.

His dreamy, delicately hued Beyoncé portraits spoke of a precocious visual talent, and in the five years since he has exhibited around the world, become an Instagram darling with more than 500,000 followers, and shot what became the most controversial vice-presidential portrait in living memory. When his portrait of Kamala Harris dressed in sneakers and casual clothing was chosen for the cover of Vogue for February 2021, the social media backlash was swift: critics questioned why his alternative image — in which Harris looked more vice-presidential — had not been used instead, and the magazine, bowing to outrage over the perceived lack of respect shown to the first woman to reach such high office, later issued a limited edition using the more formal shot. The controversy did little to dent the New York-based photographer's reputation as a rising star of the medium.

Of the three Triennial works, Picnic depicts a family gathering — young men throwing a football, a child lifted on shoulders, wicker baskets and a thermos, and in the background a darkened wood that perhaps hints at the fragility of a moment so peaceful and pure. In the others his figures are arranged across a sandy expanse in idealised depictions of Black American leisure: in Albany, Georgia a football flies through the air, a father in dress shirt and tails twirls a child, and a young boy rides a toy truck; Vastness focuses on a teenage boy standing patiently as his younger siblings stretch his wildly elongated sleeves out beside him, with a dog nearby sitting listening to a violinist. These carefully staged set-ups are evidence of Mitchell's desire to establish a new visual narrative for Black Americans.

# Calls for Creative Experimentation in VTuber Agencies

"Agencies should allow for talents to experiment, so long as it isn't hurting anyone," the anonymous Nijisanji source told Polygon for its 2023-10-19 piece — the central claim of an argument that VTubing must reinvent itself and give talents more freedom to avoid further stagnation.

The grounds begin with content range: NagamiMugi says that if VTubers took cues from other content creators and explored options like lore analysis videos or short-form reviews, the scene would not be as stagnant. Mugi, who has dreams of going corporate and is already relatively successful with her own storefront hosting collaborations and merchandise featuring other VTubers and artists, has auditioned for several major agencies — and says one asked whether she would close down her business if she passed the interview phase and became one of its talents.

That is not entirely uncommon: the Nijisanji source mentions that some talents have been given strict restrictions on what content they can and cannot create once their contracts with the agency expire, though this varies between talents and what is agreed between talent and agency. So while agencies can be viable for a creator's long-term growth, that growth is often strictly tied to the avatar associated with the agency. Both Hololive and Nijisanji give creators very little freedom in terms of presentation, whereas newer agencies such as Idol allow talents to create their own concepts — which may feel overwhelming to some but lets the talents behind these models flex their creativity and create a persona that would not fit neatly into the clearly defined boxes some agencies slot them into.

The full statement adds a tolerance for failure: "Let people fail and still have that opportunity for growth in the future. More risk-taking and trying to branch out in other ways instead of simply just streaming or following preestablished methods." According to both people Polygon interviewed, this is an agreed-upon sentiment — that to prevent further stagnation, this not-so-niche form of content creation needs to reinvent itself and allow more freedom to its talents. Time will tell whether larger agencies like Hololive, which reported 50% growth in its 2023 financial report, and Nijisanji will let their talents break the mold.

# Gogoro's Rationale For Entering India

Gogoro co-founder and CEO Horace Luke wants to "go big" in India even as the Taiwanese company faces challenges in its home country, and his case rests on two claims about what India offers.

The first is market size: India is the world's biggest two-wheeler market, where 15 million to 20 million new two-wheelers hit the road every year. The second is leverage beyond India itself — Luke sees the world's most populous country as a launch pad that will accelerate Gogoro's global expansion into other markets, a tactic TechCrunch judged reasonable considering India is already on a spree to become a competitive manufacturing hub for all major international brands and products, from smartphones to satellites.

Speaking at the company's launch in New Delhi in December 2023, Luke said the company has picked India as a strategic market from which it can reach a number of new users and enter new markets, starting with neighboring Nepal.

# Taylor Swift's Subsequent NFL Appearances And SNL Cameo

After her first Chiefs game, Taylor Swift kept appearing at Kansas City fixtures and made a Saturday Night Live cameo with Travis Kelce, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023.

On 1 October she went to her second consecutive Chiefs game, against the Jets — who, the timeline notes, technically play in New Jersey — showing up with famous friends Blake Lively, Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman after a week of reports that she would attend; the Chiefs won 23-20. On 12 October, one day after her movie premiere, Swift was in the house for the Chiefs' "Thursday Night Football" divisional matchup against the Broncos at Arrowhead Stadium, where she has performed herself and attended a game before; according to Al Michaels the game would have minimal Swift coverage, though there had already been a mention of the superstar.

On 15 October the two were spotted out in New York City together and then made a surprise appearance on "Saturday Night Live," with Kelce appearing in a skit about how much coverage Swift was getting during games while the singer introduced the musical act of the night, Ice Spice. On 22 October Swift attended her fifth Chiefs game, having now attended games broadcast across all five networks — CBS, NBC, Fox, ESPN and Amazon — watching the Chiefs face the Chargers on CBS in a Chiefs sweatshirt, seated next to Patrick Mahomes' wife, Brittany.

# Gag City As A Free Marketing Win For Nicki Minaj

TechCrunch's writer argues that whatever its provenance, Gag City is a win for Nicki Minaj. Is it an authentic stan-led campaign to build hype, or a plant to game engagement for both the album and the brands? What is clear is that the viral moment is a win for Minaj, manufactured or not — it is free promotion, and as a lifelong Barb who spent her adolescence running a stan account for "Pink Friday," the writer counts it as one.

The reason the free promotion matters so much here is Minaj's history with brands. She is an artist who has been embroiled in controversy throughout her career, from posting bad takes about COVID vaccines to defending her husband Kenneth Petty, a convicted sex offender; she may be a brilliant artist, but her problematic history makes her far from the family-friendly public figure that brands are more likely to endorse. With Gag City, Minaj has brands doing all of her marketing for her.

The final ground is a contrast with the prevailing playbook. "Pink Friday 2" is an artistic marvel in itself, the writer says, but the free promotion it has received as a viral meme is particularly astounding: artists have spent the last few years trying to drum up engagement by making their songs trend on TikTok, which audiences have started to resist, whereas Gag City does not bank on being the viral song of the summer to drive streaming numbers — the bit is removed enough for non-stans to enjoy it, while still revolving around the album it is promoting.

# Capitol's International-First, Direct-To-Fan Campaign Model

Capitol Music Group's changed approach to artist campaigns is to engage directly with international partners earlier than ever before, rather than unfairly relying on its ex-US affiliates within UMG to do the heavy lifting early on, since those affiliates have their own local repertoire to work on. The stated reason for the early emphasis on international is to start the process of building revenue streams as early as possible, specifically brand building and direct-to-fan monetization.

The model's range is illustrated by Ice Spice: she still has not released her debut album, yet is recognised around the world through commercials, syncs in video games, TV and film, a big soundtrack presence, and innovative products on her own store, with Michelle Jubelirer pointing to the Ice Spice American Flag and Chia Pet as examples. The case shows the mechanism working before the usual album milestone, which is the point of moving the international and commerce work earlier in a campaign.

# I'm Sorry Did You Say Street Magic

I'm Sorry Did You Say Street Magic, by Caro Asercion, is a GM-less city-building game played by two to six people with a stack of index cards and your favorite writing utensils. Madison Durham, writer and journalist and staff writer at Reviewed, recommends it on the grounds that some of the most joyful moments in tabletop gaming come from creative collaboration — the magic of making something new with friends, be it a narrative, a character, a world, or in this case a city.

The whimsically illustrated rulebook lays out the tools by which you lay bricks for your city, weaving together your ideas and your fellow players' to establish Landmarks, Residents, and Neighborhoods, all on a quest to find the city's true names. Durham calls it a beautifully simple game, guided by a Compass which can be anything — literally — and says it is almost impossible to capture its magic in words because each session was so entirely unique, from the verdant turtle-city in the sky her group built out in stages to the haunted shell of a city they later used as their D&D setting. Her verdict: a perfect game full stop, but especially for those seeking to rekindle their creativity or simply to sit down and create with friends.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# India's Electric Two-Wheeler Market Conditions

India has a relatively small market for EVs, accounting for only 3.7% of the country's total automotive market as of December 2023. Electric scooters capture 90% of total EV sales in the country, but that is just about 5% of the overall two-wheeler market.

Policy is a mixed force. The Indian government has allocated billions of dollars in subsidies and discounts to attract manufacturers and commuters to EVs, but these benefits only remain in place for a short time, and some disruption due to changes in their structure has recently been seen in the electric two-wheeler market.

Gogoro, like other players in the EV market, is nonetheless bullish, since the Indian government has targeted 30% EV adoption by 2030. Gogoro's approach of considering India as a manufacturing hub will also likely appeal to the government and help the company shift some of its production from China and enter new markets.



---


# The Quiet Year

The Quiet Year is a repeat entry on Polygon's list — it appeared twice on the previous year's roundup, praised by Jay Dragon for its elegance and noted by Keerthi Sridharan for the way their game group used it as a prologue, a practice popularized by Friends at the Table and The Adventure Zone — and Em Friedman, associate professor of English at Auburn University and Polygon contributor, also uses it as a standard early in her TTRPG class.

Her reason for naming it the standout of 2023 is an unplanned test of the design. After running it for her niece, then 4, and nephew, 8, her nephew asked her to run "the skulls game" for his entire class. Though not intended for a dozen grade schoolers, the mechanics turned out to be a perfect framework for imagining how to work together: they ensure everyone gets to take their turn unimpeded by the commentary of others, they ritualize dissent and discussion, and they supply a glorious sheet of blank paper on which to draw the zombie chicken monster friend of your dreams. She adds that it fits in her pocket.

# Rupal Shah Hollenbeck, Check Point President

Rupal Shah Hollenbeck has led Check Point for almost two years as of November 2023, and is one of the few C-suite level women in tech: nearly 17% of tech companies currently have a woman serving as CEO, according to AnitaB.org, which supports women in computing and tech.

She is a seasoned executive. After Intel, where she spent more than two decades, she spent time at Oracle, and she sits on the board of Neythri Futures Fund, which invests in female founders tapping into a growing base of South Asian female leaders. Although she has been in tech for nearly 30 years, Seeking Alpha reports that it has not gotten easier to be a woman in a male-dominated industry.

# Style: Named For Harry Styles, Explained As A Song About Fashion

Style is an epic aural painting of windswept coastlines and propulsive wanderlust, supposedly named for Harry Styles, with whom Taylor Swift had a brief relationship in 2012 — many of 1989's songs were supposedly inspired by that relationship. Swift's own account differs: she says the song was inspired by fashion, and how certain items like a black dress or red lipstick will "never go out of style", which prompted her to write about the people who'll always be part of your life even after the flame of romantic love wanes. The BBC notes that this all sounds like a classic piece of deflection to a probing journalist.

Whichever interpretation you prefer, the song marks a shift in Swift's psychology, as she briefly admits to having been unfaithful — the discriminating feature that separates it from her earlier writing. "I would never have said anything like that on a previous album," she told Ryan Seacrest. "My previous albums have always been, 'I was right, you were wrong'. What happens when you grow up is you realise that the rules in a relationship are very blurred. It gets very complicated, very quickly."



---


# Shein's Missguided Acquisition and Valuation

As ASOS faced huge losses, it was reported in the week to 1 November 2023 that the Chinese-founded retailer Shein had acquired the UK company Missguided, with plans to "reignite" the online retailer — which had itself only been bought out of administration by Mike Ashley's Frasers Group a year and a half earlier.

Despite calls for boycotts from anti-fashion campaigners, Shein was at that point valued at around £53bn, having expanded globally and bought many of its rival brands. In 2022 it was the most-googled fashion brand in the world and made a reported £18.9bn in revenue, suggesting that fast fashion is not falling out of favour with consumers who want to find entire outfits on a budget.



---


# Humanoid Prototype Reality Check: Figure And Optimus

Against the scale of Figure AI's market claim stands the state of its actual hardware: at the moment, Brett Adcock's firm doesn't have a prototype that's ready for market. Founded just over a year before 2023-11-05 and having raised tens of millions of dollars, it had recently revealed only a 38-second video of Figure walking through its test facility in Sunnyvale, California.

The same gap applies to the highest-profile competitor. Tesla CEO Elon Musk is also trying to build a humanoid, called Optimus, through the electric car-maker's robotics division, but a hyped-up live demonstration in 2022 of the robot's awkwardly halting steps didn't impress experts in the robotics field. Seemingly farther along is Tesla's Austin, Texas-based neighbor Apptronik, which unveiled its Apollo humanoid in an August 2023 video demonstration.



---


# Clean: The Imogen Heap Collaboration That Closed 1989

Clean, co-written with indie-pop auteur Imogen Heap, was 1989's original album closer and is very much the palette cleanser its title suggests. For once the cavernous 1980s drums are swapped for the plucked keys of a Zimbabwean mbira, while a weary Taylor Swift emerges from the ruins of a relationship.

The song prompts one of her best lyrics, establishing drought as a metaphor for emotional desolation ("the flowers that we'd grown together died of thirst") before she is reborn in the cleansing waters of a rainstorm: "When I was drowning, that's when I could finally breathe / And by morning, gone was any trace of you, I think I am finally clean."

Its underlying idea is the necessity of pain, she told Popcrush: "For most people that I've known who've fought through struggle, a lot of them who have really just faced the pain head on have come out OK a lot faster than the ones who just pretended to be in denial of it."



---


# Thai Food Near Me's Customer Experience

For a group The Verge's reporter spoke with at Thai Food Near Me on an evening in August, the SEO plan had — at least practically — the intended effect. One of the diners, Travis, found the restaurant on Yelp when searching for nearby dining options after missing an earlier reservation elsewhere; several people in the group had heard about the restaurant when it went viral in the spring but had not realized it was in New York. The group agreed the food was good, even though they had not known what to expect, and said they would definitely consider coming back if they were in the area.

The channel, though, was not the one the owners planned for. Co-owner Robert Sampson says that for the first several months of being open, most people were coming in after seeing Twitter and Reddit posts, not Google results, while others would walk by outside, do a double take at the sign, and come inside. "After you get that initial bunch, you've got people who enjoyed their dining experience here," he says. "They'll tell all their friends and family if they liked it, and then those people come from word of mouth."

Despite the admittedly silly name, the reporter found it clear that co-owners Jirapraphanan and Sampson care about what they are serving: the restaurant is clean and stylish, and the menu, carefully designed by Jirapraphanan, features original dishes she had not seen at other places; her food was tasty, came out promptly, and she said she too would note the spot if she were in the area again and craving Thai food. Jirapraphanan wants people to come back because they actually like the food — the name is part, but not all, of the branding. "I want to be different from other Thai restaurants," he says. "I think it did more than we could have ever imagined it would do," Sampson says. The restaurant's owners are Jirapraphanan, Sampson, Natkitta Kornwaewwongcharoen, and Nat P Akethamwong.

# Taylor Swift Re-Records 1989 To Regain Control Of Her Masters

On Friday, Taylor Swift released a new version of 1989 — the biggest-selling album of her career and the record that definitively turned her into a pop star — re-recorded as the latest instalment of an ongoing campaign to regain control of her work after an investment company bought her master tapes in 2019. The BBC reported this on 13 October 2023, with the article itself noting a publication date of 27 October for the album's return.

This re-recording is described as the biggest and riskiest part of the project. Earlier remakes in the campaign were largely made with a live band, whereas 1989's pop landscapes are full of squelchy, processed synths and treated vocals, which makes them harder to reproduce faithfully. Alongside the re-recorded album, fans can hear five new tracks from the star's vault, expanding on the themes and relationships she explored on the original. The artwork for the re-recorded version has a beach vibe, in contrast to the Polaroid aesthetics of the original.

# Three Strategy Tips For NBA Prop Betting

Every bettor should develop their own strategies, but the Sporting News offers three tips for NBA props: pay attention to player and team news, keep an eye on usage and minutes, and shop for the best lines.

First, pay attention to player and team news. Oddsmakers use various information to develop their lines for games and players, and you should too — keep tabs on player news and injuries, when top players are being rested, how they performed in recent games, and more. Value in player and team props comes from gathering information from multiple sources and tracking how players and their teammates perform; for example, if one of the starting guards is questionable for a game, you might consider the other guard for increased points or assists since they will likely handle a heavier load.

Second, keep an eye on usage and minutes. Even slight increases to a player's average minutes can make a difference when betting player props, especially later in the season when aging veteran players tend to rest more. Stay informed on usage and minutes trends for the players you're considering, and use them to your advantage — some of the best players in the NBA were once on the bench for most games until small increases in playing time gave them a chance to shine.

Third, shop for the best lines, a tip that applies to every bet you make. Using multiple sportsbook accounts lets you find the best odds for every NBA prop bet, and even the smallest differences — one sportsbook at +125 and another at +135 — can make a difference in your profit.

# Why Nagelsmann, Scaloni, Southgate And Pochettino Do Not Add Up For United

Sporting News pushed back on four names circulating as possible Manchester United managers on Dec. 13, 2023, attacking in each case the premise that the candidate would actually be available or sellable.

Julian Nagelsmann's name had come up in betting circles, but Sporting News saw no sense in it actually taking place: Nagelsmann had only recently been hired as head coach of the German national team, meaning there was no chance he was available until after Euro 2024 at the earliest — and in that case it was likely that Germany had flopped at their own tournament, meaning his hire would probably be quite sour. "This one just doesn't add up."

Lionel Scaloni could conceivably become available at a moment's notice amid speculation of his potential exit with the defending World Cup champions, but this felt an unlikely pairing: should he leave Argentina, Scaloni had been open about his mental fatigue and was likely to take some time off from management, and in the event he returned quickly he had been heavily linked to Real Madrid as a possible replacement for Carlo Ancelotti, who was expected to become the next permanent Brazil head coach. It was hard to imagine that Scaloni — who seemingly craves stability and routine, has no experience at club level, and lacks ties to the Premier League or Old Trafford beyond a brief loan spell with West Ham as a player in 2006 — would be a match for Manchester United in any capacity.

Gareth Southgate, another currently employed national-team manager, had been linked to the United job before, but it would take a perfect storm for him to be installed, whether permanently or as an interim stopgap. Some believed he could be considered the following summer once the Euros were over, since it had been speculated Southgate could leave his England post after the tournament with his contract expiring in December the next year; however, it was also possible he would stay on for the 2026 World Cup cycle, particularly if England had a good tournament in Germany, in which case he would only be available for double duty on a temporary basis — simply too messy to outweigh the benefits, as Brazil's experience showed, where it had all gone wrong for Fernando Diniz despite his Copa Libertadores victory with Fluminense. Finally, if Todd Boehly proved to have just as itchy a trigger finger as Roman Abramovich at Chelsea, Mauricio Pochettino could become available — but would he really be a sellable hire, having just failed in London after bombing at PSG and departing Tottenham in acrimonious manner? It seemed unlikely United would be interested in someone who demands significant club control and would have just been fired from a struggling league rival.

# Coaching Change

## Definition

A coaching change is the replacement of a team's head coach — by firing, mutual departure, or resignation — followed by the appointment of a successor, whether an outside hire, an internal promotion, or an interim/caretaker placeholder.

## Context

The corpus documents coaching changes across sports and settings: mid-season firings in the NHL and NFL, off-season managerial exits in club and international soccer/rugby, and speculative hot-seat coverage that treats a coach's job security itself as an ongoing storyline ahead of any actual move.

The Minnesota Wild "relieved head coach Dean Evason and assistant coach Bob Woods of their duties effective immediately," naming John Hynes as Evason's successor mid-season after a losing stretch left the team "far out of the playoff picture" (doc_0340).

Manchester United's Erik ten Hag was reported to be under mounting pressure, with Sporting News laying out replacement candidates — including permanent hires like Zinedine Zidane and Julen Lopetegui and a caretaker option in club legend Michael Carrick — "if Manchester United decide to pull the plug" on his tenure (doc_0315); the same piece notes United had already cycled through eight managers, including caretakers Ryan Giggs, Ralf Rangnick, and Carrick, since Alex Ferguson's 2013 retirement.

Carolina Panthers owner David Tepper's impatience with head coach Frank Reich was framed against his earlier in-season firing of Reich's predecessor, Matt Rhule, as precedent for how quickly an owner might act (doc_0474); Yardbarker's NFC "hot seat" roundup names head coaches such as New Orleans' Dennis Allen and Chicago's Matt Eberflus as under pressure for their job status ahead of any actual move (doc_0437).

In international coaching, the Springboks' World Cup-winning head coach Jacques Nienaber and director of rugby Rassie Erasmus departed together after South Africa's 2023 Rugby World Cup triumph, and All Blacks coach Ian Foster's tenure ended the same tournament with Scott Robertson set to take over (doc_0022); U.S. Soccer's appointment of Emma Hayes away from Chelsea to lead the USWNT followed a formal, multi-round search process after the prior head coach, Vlatko Andonovski, departed following a World Cup exit (doc_0108).

## Key Characteristics

- **Trigger is performance or results** — the Wild's move came after a 5-10-4 record and a seven-game winless streak (doc_0340); the Panthers' pressure on Reich stemmed from a 1-7 record and a struggling offense (doc_0474).
- **In-season vs. off-season timing** — some changes happen mid-season as an emergency reset (Wild firing Evason, doc_0340; the precedent of Carolina firing Rhule in-season, doc_0474), while others follow a season's end (Nienaber/Erasmus and Foster departing after the World Cup final, doc_0022; Hayes's move to the USWNT set for after her Chelsea season concludes, doc_0108).
- **Successor types vary** — a permanent outside hire (John Hynes for the Wild, doc_0340; Emma Hayes for the USWNT, doc_0108), a permanent internal promotion (Evason himself had been promoted to Wild head coach after the team fired Bruce Boudreau in-season, doc_0340), or a caretaker/interim stopgap (Michael Carrick's past spells in charge of Manchester United, doc_0315).
- **"Hot seat" speculation precedes the actual move** — media coverage frequently discusses a head coach's job security, and the club's history of prior changes, well before any change occurs, treating pressure itself as newsworthy (doc_0437, doc_0474).
- **The exiting coach's own track record and contract carry forward** — Evason's Wild contract obligations continued after his firing (doc_0340), and Reich's overall coaching record was reported inclusive of a prior in-season firing by the Colts (doc_0474).

# The USWNT Head Coach Search Process In 2023

U.S. Soccer's 2023 head coach search ran through multiple rounds of evaluation, with the list of candidates becoming smaller each time, as described by The New York Times on 15 November 2023.

The stages are given in order. The first pass was driven purely by data, which was then whittled down to a double-digit list Matt Crocker was considering as of September, and then a final shortlist, which also included Tony Gustavsson, head coach of Australia; multiple sources confirmed both Hayes and Gustavsson flew to the U.S. for interviews. Initial contact with Hayes was made a couple of months before the announcement, early in the search, with all three top-level U.S. Soccer executives — Crocker, president Cindy Parlow Cone and CEO J.T. Batson — involved in those talks. A U.S. Soccer statement describes the interview process as involving "psychometrics and abstract reasoning tests, in-depth discussions of strategy, coaching philosophy and the current player pool, as well as evaluation on the reactions to pressure, culture-building and interactions with players and staff"; USMNT coach Gregg Berhalter went through a similar process, including an abstract reasoning test, when he was re-hired by Crocker earlier in 2023. Crocker said in September that the final interviews would include lengthy technical and tactical assessments as well as questions to determine cultural fit.

Two further details are recorded. The federation had also checked in on the availability of Sarina Wiegman, according to one source briefed on the situation, despite clear messaging from both the English FA and Wiegman herself in August: "I'm staying out of it. I've heard it (from the press officer) but no, I'm with England and I'm really happy with England, and I have a contract until 2025," Wiegman said, and a representative from her camp declined to comment. And on timing: part of the surprise around the hire and the six-month runway is down to U.S. Soccer's own messaging, since Crocker had said in a September meeting with U.S. reporters that he hoped to have a new head coach in place by December; he and the federation stayed fairly consistent on their desired start date since the role opened in August, but that became one of the major concessions made in selecting Hayes.

# Onana As An Extra Outfield Player

Erik ten Hag's model of André Onana treats the goalkeeper as a potential extra outfield player who can push progressively higher up the pitch — but subordinates that role to shot-stopping and makes it conditional on the opposition. "First the job of a keeper is to save, is to [guard] his goal, that's his main job and don't forget this," Ten Hag said on 28 October 2023. "But, yeah, he is a keeper who we can use as an extra player and if we are developing [more] he can be more progressive and even higher up the pitch — an extra player, so that's an advantage."

The idea comes from Uefa's technical report on Onana's display for Internazionale in May's Champions League final, which described him as a "holding midfielder" — a formulation that intrigues because it suggests an evolution of what Guardiola introduced to the domestic game, a No 1 in Ederson performing as a de facto extra defender to maintain fluidity along the backline. Onana was so advanced as to be a No 6 rather than, as the technical report posited, a "sweeper-keeper", able to take up residence in the middle third of his half as his team pushed deep into enemy territory.

The range over which the model holds is explicitly limited. Asked whether facing the champions had come too soon for Onana to function as "the extra man", Ten Hag said: "It also depends on the opposition, how strong is the press, for instance, and how good is the team around him. So if it's possible — in my philosophy he has to do it every game [but] it is not always possible, so you have to adapt and this what I make clear. Even if you're not playing well, if the team is not playing well, or you're not playing to the standards you expect, you still have to win — so find a way to win, be pragmatic."

# Draft Pick

A draft pick is the corpus's term for a team's claimed selection in a professional sports league's draft — either the numbered turn itself or the player obtained with it.

The corpus uses "draft pick" and its variants ("drafted," "first-round pick," "overall pick") to describe how teams acquire players and how each individual selection is later labeled, ranked, and judged by its number, round, and outcome.

## Context

The corpus uses "draft pick" and its variants ("drafted," "first-round pick," "lottery pick") across several leagues to describe how teams acquire young talent and how commentators later judge those acquisitions. In the NHL, the Chicago Blackhawks are described as having "drafted" Connor Bedard, and teammate Kevin Korchinski is identified as "the No. 7 overall pick in the 2022 draft, one of three first-round selections by Chicago that year" — showing picks are numbered by overall selection order and grouped into rounds. In MLB, pitcher Alek Manoah is called a "former first-round pick," used as a lens to argue he still carries trade value because he remains under team control. In the NFL, Brock Purdy's "Mr. Irrelevant" nickname marks him as the final pick of the 2022 NFL Draft, contrasted against the eight quarterbacks selected earlier in the same draft class, including Kenny Pickett (pick 20) and Chris Oladokun (pick 241) — illustrating that picks are graded individually against draft order. In the AFL, the term applies pre-selection: Kevin Sheehan's "top 40 prospects" list previews players before the 2023 AFL Draft is even held, drawn from the pool who attended the AFL Draft Combine.

## Key Characteristics

- **Ordered by pick number** — picks are numbered across the draft (e.g., Purdy was "Pick 262," Korchinski was "the No. 7 overall pick"), and that number is itself used to grade or rank the selection after the fact.
- **Organized into rounds** — the corpus distinguishes "first-round" picks (Manoah, Korchinski) from later-round or final picks (Purdy, "Mr. Irrelevant"), with round number signaling perceived talent tier at selection time.
- **Retrospective judgment attaches to the pick, not just the player** — Golden State's "draft misses" piece frames entire draft classes (2020, 2021) as successes or failures by comparing whom the team picked against whom they passed over (e.g., Kuminga picked one spot ahead of Franz Wagner), and tallies how many of a team's draft picks are still on the roster years later.
- **Selection status carries lasting team control** — a player's history as a draft pick is tied to a team's rights over him for a fixed period; Manoah's status as a "former first-round pick" is invoked because he remains "controllable for four more seasons" before reaching arbitration.
- **Pre-draft coverage treats prospects as pending picks** — outlets rank and profile players before the draft occurs (the AFL's top-40 list, built from Combine attendees), so "draft pick" also describes a prospect's anticipated slot, not only a completed selection.

## Background (external)

The corpus never defines "draft pick" itself — it only reports specific picks, their numbers, and the players attached to them.
Per Wikipedia's article on sports drafts, a draft is a system in which "teams take turns selecting from a pool of eligible players," and a pick "refers to a team's turn or selection right within the draft" that can itself "be traded between teams" (Wikipedia, *Draft (sport)*, accessed 2026-09-02).
Draft order is commonly set to promote competitive balance, either by reverse order of the previous season's standings — "the previous season's worst team picking first" — or via a weighted lottery among non-playoff teams intended to "discourage teams from tanking" (Wikipedia, *Draft (sport)*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# ASPI's Analysis Of TikTok Pixel Data Aggregation Risk

Researchers at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute argue that the danger of TikTok's tracking pixel lies less in the type of data collected — which resembles what US tech giants gather — than in how that data can be aggregated and in who can ultimately reach it.

Jocelinn Kang, a technical specialist at the institute, said data from a tracking pixel could be aggregated across websites, apps and social media platforms, and that pixel tracking could identify users through their "browser fingerprint," a combination of their IP address, browser and system details. The linking gets sharper as identifiers accumulate: "However, when more identifying data such as email and phone number is associated with a user, their web activity can be better linked," Kang said.

Strategic Policy Institute researcher Samantha Hoffman said the data collected by TikTok's pixel was similar to that of US-based tech giants Google and Meta, but that the difference was "the intent." Advertising data had "incredible propaganda value," she said, and the warrant joining that to the risk is state access: "If you think about that, plus the access that TikTok is required to give the Chinese government, that's the problem." She notes TikTok itself made that access explicit — in November 2022 the company changed its privacy policy to state clearly that user data can be accessed by some employees from across the world, including China. "They talk about how even data collected overseas can be used by the company and its partners, and would be kept private unless security organisations make demands of it," Hoffman said. China's national intelligence laws allow the government to pull data upon request from companies based there.

# Portfolio Management Services In India

Portfolio Management Services are a managed-account alternative available alongside AIFs to Indian HNIs, governed by guidelines that date back to 1993 but that have grown in popularity with HNIs only recently. The growing financialisation of savings, the formalisation of the economy and the growing prosperity of tier 2 and 3 cities have raised PMS AUM, excluding EPFO and PF money, to ₹5.28 lakh crore as of July 2023. Because the minimum investment is ₹50 lakh, this option too is available only to HNIs.

The discriminating features are drawn against mutual funds. Both PMS and mutual funds provide expert guidance in navigating volatile markets and seizing wealth-creating opportunities, but because mutual funds cater to retail investors their guidelines are relatively stringent and compliance is rigorous, whereas PMS investment guidelines are somewhat more flexible, allowing portfolio managers to outperform mutual funds. A second appeal to HNIs is ownership: in PMS the beneficial ownership of securities belongs to the investors, as opposed to mutual funds where ownership belongs to the fund. PMS comes in two variants, discretionary and non-discretionary; in the former the portfolio managers make all decisions, in the latter the investor does.

# The QRU's Position On High-Performance Centralisation

In the wake of the Wallabies' 2023 World Cup flop, the Queensland Rugby Union reaffirmed on Oct. 10, 2023 that it is committed to moving to a centralised high-performance model — but will not follow the NSW Waratahs in handing over the keys to Rugby Australia.

The QRU's stated commitment reads: "The QRU is committed to working with Rugby Australia to lead reform of our game at a high-performance level, and help Rugby Australia develop an improved game through high-performance centralisation." The letter defined the scope of that centralisation: it "would include a national player-contracting model, and alignment of key high-performance staff, such as coaching, strength and conditioning, and medical to operate as one national system." The letter, an open letter to members published on Wednesday morning by QRU chief executive David Hanham and chairman Brett Clark, also pointed to RA's involvement in Les Kiss' appointment as Reds coach — the former State of Origin winger turned coach, who has spent the best part of two decades coaching in Ireland and England, replacing Brad Thorn — as an example of the model in practice.

The QRU also expressed strong support for Rugby Australia to conduct a "fully independent and transparent top-to-bottom review of the Wallabies program and how it can be improved" in light of the historic first World Cup pool exit, adding: "It should also provide a clear view of what is needed in a leadership and governance framework to ensure we put the right people, in the right roles, in the right system." The Roar noted the boundary of the consensus: while all five Australian Super Rugby sides are fundamentally on board with moving to a centralised high-performance program, some states, including the ACT Brumbies as well as the QRU, don't want to give up their commercial assets.

# Line Movement As A Signal Of Betting Value

Sporting News argues that bettors should monitor line movement before a game starts, because line moves reveal where the value in a bet lies. The claim is stated for both markets it covers: point spread odds can and do change based on a combination of actual betting patterns, unexpected events, and shifts in public perception, and savvy bettors keep a close eye on these line moves, as they can offer insights into where the value lies in a particular bet.

The grounds are how the lines are made and remade. Sportsbooks set game totals considering factors like recent performances, weather, and player status, and as new data emerges and betting trends develop, this line can shift — if many bettors choose the "over," the sportsbook might raise the total to balance the bets. The warrant joining grounds to claim is that line movements often reflect public betting sentiments and therefore offer insights to informed bettors: because a move encodes information the book has absorbed about data and about where the public money is, watching it tells the bettor something they did not otherwise have. Hence bettors must monitor any line changes before the game starts and strategize accordingly to optimize their betting success.

The argument stops short of endorsing either side of a totals bet in the abstract: neither wager holds a universal advantage, and success in over/under betting hinges on a thorough evaluation of both the set line and the competing teams.

# Uber's Results As A Macro Signal For Startups

The claim is that Uber's quarterly results carry information beyond Uber, and that the same numbers support two readings. Against a backdrop of macroeconomic uncertainty, the former startup darling's results can be viewed as an indication that its business model has matured and is now in a stable, profitable and cash-generating position. On the other hand, under-performing demand results from a company as global as Uber could indicate that consumer spend is coming in lighter than anticipated.

The warrant for treating it as a signal at all is Uber's role in its sector: for startups in the transport and on-demand sectors, Uber's earnings are a regular informational zeitgeist, which is why it is worth understanding where Uber's revenue came from in the third quarter and how each of its top-line sources converted — or not — to bottom-line results.

TechCrunch's own reading: the vibe when discussing Uber's results internally was that it is a very profitable and healthy company today, albeit one not growing as fast as the market had hoped. # Graham Arnold Reflections On Coaching Development

Reflecting on his milestone, Graham Arnold said his 2006 caretaker period taught him a great deal about coaching and that, on reflection, he probably was not ready for it — as quoted by The Roar on Nov. 13, 2023.

"I think back to that caretaker period and how much I learnt about coaching; it was a challenging experience and one that on reflection I probably wasn't ready for. I'm grateful for the opportunity I was given and what it was able to teach me ahead of my pathway into club coaching," he said. "I was able to put lessons from that time into practice, develop and eventually return to the Socceroos much more prepared for the role. It's been a privilege to be part of the national team again with the benefit of that experience, and I'm immensely proud of what this group has been able to achieve in the last four years. In my opinion, there's no greater honour than representing your nation on the international stage. I look at the young players coming through the Socceroos system now full of pride in the work they've put in to get where they are, and the journey that's ahead of them. I've always loved being a part of the Socceroos culture and my desire to see Australia fulfil its footballing potential is still driving me to take this group to further success."

# Eddie Jones' Case For Reforming The Australian Rugby System

Eddie Jones argued that the Wallabies' problems are systemic rather than confined to the national team, and that it was crucial for Rugby Australia to get alignment in the code from grassroots through to the top team — with Australia, a two-time world champion, then ranked 10th in the world.

His grounds are the gap he saw at the top of the game and the state of the layer beneath it: "You just got to watch the quarterfinals at the weekend. We're not at that level. And we can't pretend to be at that level. But can we be at that level by 2027? Yes, we can. We're definitely off the pace but the opportunity to get better is there." The warrant is that a team declines when the system under it stops supporting it: "This is not an unusual situation. You've got a team that was struggling for a period of time, you've got underneath it a system that's not supporting it and at some stage you bottom out. This is the opportunity now to change the team — as we've started with picking younger players with bright futures — and then we've got to look at the development system underneath as well. It's not a simple equation that the Wallabies are bad. Let's be serious about this. The Wallabies are not where they need to be but underneath that we need to fix the system to go forward. And if we can do that now we've got a rosy future." He also acknowledged the cost of that change and the fans' pain: "We feel all the supporters hurt and really appreciate the great support we had in France and back in Australia for the team… Sometimes the change you have to have is uncomfortable. It is quite difficult. And sometimes you have to go through this to get into a better state and I believe that the problems we've had particularly at the national team will put us in a better state going forward." Jones clearly believes he is the right man to carry Australia on: "I think I've got the foresight to see where we need to go. I've got the experience of being in difficult situations before."

Earlier, on Oct. 10, Jones advocated specifically for Australian rugby to move to a centralised model, believing the nation had fallen behind the rest of the world: "We're a state-based union that's run by the states, the national union wants to assume more responsibility and when things were going well, no one questioned that. But over the last period of time, they haven't been going so well and this tournament's probably been the icing on the cake where it's got to a stage where I think people, most people probably think there's time for change. But it's not going to go easy." He located the payoff in player development: "[It's] one of the key issues. We need to maximize the development of the players. At the end of the day, that's the key to success and alignment of your resources, for a small country. Because Australia, if you look at the history of rugby, when we were amateur, we were probably ahead of the game because we had the influence of rugby league. We had the influence of AFL and our players were more professional than the rest of the world." And: "I know what's going on and we need to get a better system of developing players. We need to develop better players and we need to develop a larger batch of better players and that only comes through changing the whole system."

# National Football League (NFL)

## Definition

In the corpus, the National Football League (NFL) is the professional football league covered as both a sports competition and a media business — its 2023 season tracked through AFC/NFC conference standings and playoff seeding, its "Thursday Night Football" package sold to Amazon Prime Video, and its revenue growth under Commissioner Roger Goodell, credited by Essentially Sports with a $27 billion revenue target for 2027.

## Context

The corpus treats the NFL as both a sports league and a media business: Essentially Sports traces its "humble beginnings in 1920" to its status as an "$18 billion juggernaut" today, with Commissioner Roger Goodell targeting $27 billion in revenue by 2027.
The same piece cites an estimate from Joe Pompliano that the NFL "will bring in $20 billion in revenue this year, more than the Premier League, La Liga, Bundesliga, Serie A, and Ligue 1 combined," and separately states outright that "the NFL is already the world's richest league."
Its season structure surfaces repeatedly in the corpus: standings are tracked by conference and division (AFC East/North/South/West, NFC East/North/South/West), with regular-season results determining division leaders and wild-card seeding heading into the playoffs.
Weekly games are also branded by broadcast window — most notably "Thursday Night Football" — which airs exclusively on Amazon Prime Video under an 11-year rights deal, with only the two competing teams' local markets exempted from needing a Prime subscription.
The league also anchors seasonal traditions distinct from other major U.S. leagues, most notably Thanksgiving Day games, which in 2023 drew an average of 34.1 million viewers across three games — a tradition the corpus contrasts with the NBA's Christmas Day slate — alongside a growing Christmas Day broadcast tradition of its own.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-conference structure** — teams are split into the AFC and NFC, each further divided into divisions, with standings and tiebreakers (head-to-head record, conference record) determining playoff seeding.
- **Regular season into playoffs** — the corpus's Week 13 standings coverage shows an 18-week regular season narrowing toward division leaders and wild-card contenders as the playoff picture takes shape.
- **Commissioner-led revenue strategy** — under Commissioner Roger Goodell, the league has set an explicit financial target ($27 billion by 2027) and, per the corpus, is already "the world's richest league."
- **Thursday Night Football broadcast rights** — the "Thursday Night Football" window airs exclusively on Amazon Prime Video under an 11-year deal, with local-market exemptions for the two competing teams.
- **Recurring scandal and safety scrutiny** — the corpus notes a history of controversies (Kaepernick's protest, domestic-violence cases, Deflategate, Bountygate, CTE concerns) running alongside active initiatives such as international games and the "Play Smart, Play Safe" concussion-safety program.
- **Holiday broadcast traditions** — Thanksgiving Day games are a fixture of the NFL calendar with viewership the corpus contrasts directly against the NBA's Christmas Day tradition.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, the NFL is the highest level of professional American football: 32 teams split evenly between the American Football Conference (AFC) and National Football Conference (NFC), each with four four-team divisions.
Each season runs an 18-week regular season in which every team plays 17 games and takes one bye week, after which seven teams per conference enter a single-elimination playoff bracket whose conference-championship winners meet in the Super Bowl (Wikipedia, "National Football League," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League, accessed 2026-09-02).

The New York Times argued on 16 October 2023 that it does not see where Dallas is better or going to get considerably better, especially on offense, though it conceded this was a tough time to evaluate the Cowboys fairly because they were so bad against San Francisco on a big stage in their most recent game.

# Sputnik: A Russian Sci-Fi Horror Built On A Twisted Trolley Problem

Sputnik is Egor Abramenko's 2020 directorial debut, starring Oksana Akinshina, Fedor Bondarchuk and Pyotr Fyodorov, and available on Hulu — Polygon's pick if you are hungry for a great piece of contemporary Russian sci-fi horror not directed by Andrei Tarkovsky or Yakov Protazanov. Set in 1983 at the height of Cold War tensions, the film (whose title is Russian for "fellow traveler") centres on Tatyana, an uncompromising young psychiatrist with a staunch attitude regarding the ends justifying the means, who is recruited by the Soviet military to treat Konstantin, a wounded cosmonaut and the lone survivor of a mysterious satellite crash. Only on arriving at the remote hospital facility and interacting with him does Tatyana realise the horrifying truth: Konstantin did not return from space alone — his body has become the unwitting host to an organism unlike anything seen on Earth. Caught between her duty to study the creature and her desire to save Konstantin from further harm, she must make a hard decision on which the survival of all humanity may rest.

What makes the debut compelling is how it takes the basic premise of the "trolley problem" thought experiment and twists it repeatedly, and successfully, to dramatic emotional effect. Akinshina (The Bourne Supremacy) delivers a convincing performance as a woman forced to confront and overcome the uncompromising attitude that had once assured her success but now threatens another man's life, potentially everyone on the planet, and her own soul; Fyodorov delivers a sympathetically complex and on occasion implicitly sinister performance as a Russian "hero" torn between his perceived duty to his country and his emotional obligation to a loved one he all but abandoned before his most recent mission. The creature design is terrific, as are the cinematography and the score.

Its distribution history is part of why Polygon spotlights it: having previously been slated for a world premiere at the 2020 Tribeca Film Festival and subsequently dumped on video-on-demand in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, Sputnik is exactly the kind of rare gem of intellectually and viscerally stimulating horror that otherwise goes unappreciated if not given the opportunity to shine.

# The Post-Tightening Monetary Policy Autopsy Of 2023

After the most aggressive monetary-tightening campaign in four decades, academics and economic practitioners are running autopsies on what could have prevented the cost-of-living crisis and how to ensure the same mistakes won't be repeated. Markets have scrambled to price in high-for-longer interest rates, with a new war in the Middle East adding yet more risk to an already uncertain outlook confronting central bankers as they gather for their penultimate meetings of a tumultuous year.

The policy navel-gazing centers on three debates: how much flexibility central banks can allow in reaching their inflation targets, the effectiveness of asset purchases in the policy mix, and the merits of monetary and fiscal coordination. Bloomberg surveyed economists from around the world to gather views on those three debates. Their verdict: central banks won't break their economies in a rush to hit inflation targets, QE will be used more sparingly in the future, and fiscal policy risks countering the work of monetary authorities.

# Israel-Hamas Conflict: The Limited-Market-Impact Base Case

As of mid-October 2023, the Indian stock market's base case was that the Israel-Hamas hostilities would not escalate, and on that assumption the conflict was expected to have only a limited impact on markets. The grounds are threefold. First, the world can ill-afford another full-fledged war while economies are already battling high inflation and interest rates, an ongoing Russia-Ukraine war and a slowing China, which is precisely why many countries are trying to restrict any escalation; the market movement in the week before 14 October 2023 indicated that non-escalation was the presumed base case. Second, the US treasury secretary stated that the current conflict is not likely to significantly impact the global economic outlook. Third, history supports the same conclusion: a study of past conflicts between Israel and Hamas found that they tend to have limited impact on global financial markets, across crude oil, US 10-year yields, US equities and market volatility.

The warrant joining the evidence to the claim is that market impact tracks escalation, not the mere existence of hostilities: because the incentives of major countries point towards containment and because previous Israel-Hamas episodes transmitted little into the four channels that matter (oil, yields, equities, volatility), the priced-in outcome is a contained conflict. The argument is explicitly conditional on the non-escalation premise holding.

The third and most important demand is a consistent climate policy, and the author argues the impact of not having one is playing out in real time. # The Cairo Diplomatic Surge And The 2023 Summit For Peace

# Bank of Israel Interest Rate Policy During the War

Asked what the Bank of Israel should do at its interest rate decision on 23 October 2023, Leo Leiderman argued for holding: "As for cutting the interest rate, it's too early to consider that. The current interest rate is at the right level for the state of the economy, and together with the policy on exchange rates, it contributes to ensuring financial stability."

His first ground is that the inflation effect of the war is indeterminate. It was still too early to tell how the war would affect the rate of inflation in the short and medium term: just as there are new inflationary factors, such as the depreciation of the shekel, there will also be factors working in the opposite direction, given the expected decline in private consumption, tourism and other items.

His second ground extends his fiscal reasoning to monetary policy: as with fiscal policy, a country at war is allowed to deviate temporarily from the set inflation target. He judged that at the moment there was no surge in inflation expectations, and that the investment community is aware of the existence of index-linked assets and the exchange rate that can assist in hedging inflation risk. The warrant tying this to a hold rather than a cut is that financial stability, not inflation, is the binding objective while the shock is unresolved.

# Ukraine 2024 Mobilisation and Negotiation Prospects

Ukraine's Defence Ministry said in the week before 25 December 2023 that its main goal in 2024 is to boost its domestic defence industry in the face of uncertain future supplies from its Western allies. It has also changed conscription laws, foreseeing the need to bolster its forces, which are dwarfed in size by Russia's but are more highly trained and equipped. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that week that the military had asked for up to 500,000 additional conscripts, but that he needed to hear "more arguments" to support the sensitive and costly proposal.

On talks, CNBC reported that with both Ukraine and Russia investing heavily in the war it is unlikely there will be any negotiations to end the conflict or agree a cease-fire, because defence analysts argue that neither side would want to enter negotiations unless in a position of strength and able to dictate terms.

The condition that could change this is political. "In the case of a Republican winning the presidential election next year, especially if that's Donald Trump, who seems to be the front-runner, and [if] funding is decreased substantially, then there will be increased pressure on Ukraine to negotiate," Mario Bikarski, a Europe and Russia analyst at the Economist Intelligence Unit, told CNBC.

# Israeli Post-War Economic Rehabilitation Planning Proposal

Leo Leiderman proposed that, despite the uncertainty over how the war would develop, Israel should begin preparing a general economic plan for rehabilitating the economy after the war, alongside an emergency budget. The precondition he sets is that planning starts now rather than after the fighting ends: "this is the time to start preparing a general economic plan with a strategy for rehabilitating the economy after the war."

The scope of the planning he specifies is detailed and professional coverage of all aspects of rehabilitating the settlements that have been damaged or destroyed in the south, rehabilitation of infrastructure, the health system, and the civilian systems that need attention.

On execution, he proposes tasking the Bank of Israel and the Ministry of Finance Budgets Division with coordinating the work, with help from the various research institutes and from economists, engineers and professionals in academic institutions and in the private sector. ## Definition

Judicial reform, in the corpus, is the Israeli government's contested 2023 "bid for judicial reform" — a domestic political fight the corpus treats as a settled point of reference (a fault line the country was already living through before the Hamas attacks of October 7) rather than something it explains from first principles. What the reform actually proposed is set out only in the Background (external) section below, not in the cited corpus documents.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the reform twice, each time as backdrop to a different story rather than as its subject. In the Eylon Levy profile, the reform is the fault line of Levy's own pre-war life: he "was also active in the protests against the government's judicial reform," and Globes pressed him on the shift — "one day you are at a demonstration against the government and the next day you are its spokesperson" (doc_0413). In the TechCrunch piece on Israel's startup ecosystem, the reform is the fault line of the tech sector's pre-war life: "the tech industry led opposition to the government's bid for judicial reform," with companies and investors "already refusing to do business in the country with the prospect of the reforms getting pushed through," a boycott effort that "has been brought to a halt" once the war made the two sides of that debate "stand together for what they see as the significantly bigger fight and threat" (doc_0448).

## Key Characteristics

- **Government-initiated, not judiciary-initiated** — doc_0448 describes it as the government's "bid" for reform; both docs frame it as opposed from outside government (doc_0413, doc_0448).
- **Provoked street protests** — Levy is identified by his participation in "the protests against the reform," which he describes as "no secret" (doc_0413).
- **Provoked tech-sector opposition** — the tech industry "led opposition" to the reform bid, with some companies and investors already refusing to do business in the country over it, before the war began (doc_0448).
- **Superseded, not resolved, by the war** — doc_0448 frames the reform fight as merely "brought to a halt" by October 7, with opposing sides now "standing together" against what they see as a bigger threat, not as a dispute that was settled; doc_0413 echoes this, with Levy describing pre-war disputes as something Israeli society "pulled our hair out over" that now look small against the war.

## Background (external)

The corpus names the "judicial reform" and its protest and boycott fallout but does not describe what the reform itself proposed. Per Wikipedia, the reform package introduced by Justice Minister Yariv Levin and MK Simcha Rothman in January 2023 proposed giving the government majority control over the committee that selects judges, curbing the Supreme Court's power to strike down legislation (including Basic Laws), letting the Knesset override certain court rulings with a 61-seat majority, making government legal advisors' opinions non-binding, and eliminating "unreasonableness" as a ground for judicial review of administrative decisions — changes aimed at reducing judicial checks on the government and the Knesset (Wikipedia, *2023 Israeli judicial reform*, accessed 2026-09-02). Mass protests began almost immediately after the plan's introduction in January 2023, well before the events covered in the corpus.

# Why iPhone Discounts Come From Carriers, Not Retailers

WIRED's Apple Black Friday guide of 25 November 2023 sets out a simple structure for how iPhone discounting works: you typically will not see many iPhone deals from retailers, because the sales that do exist usually come from carriers — AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile — and are attached to conditions rather than offered as straight price cuts.

The relation running through this model is conditional rather than promotional. Carrier iPhone offers carry several requirements, such as being on an unlimited plan or opening a new cell line, so the discount is granted in exchange for a service commitment rather than being available to any buyer at checkout. That is what distinguishes iPhone pricing from the rest of the Apple lineup covered in the same guide, where straightforward retailer discounts are the norm.

The range over which the model holds is narrow and stated: it applies to current iPhones during the November 2023 holiday sales, and WIRED notes the exceptions itself, having laid out a few deals on older unlocked iPhone models alongside some carrier promotions for readers in the market for a new phone.
