# Wearable Device

## Definition

In this corpus, "wearable device" (or "wearable") is the umbrella term outlets use for a body-worn consumer or health-tech gadget — a smartwatch, fitness ring, fitness band, or medical-sensing device — interchangeably with specific products like the Apple Watch, Google Pixel Watch, Whoop 4, Ultrahuman Ring Air, and Acurable's respiratory monitors.

## Context

The corpus uses "wearable" as the umbrella term spanning consumer smartwatches (Apple Watch, Google Pixel Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch), fitness rings (Ultrahuman Ring Air), fitness bands (Whoop 4), and specialized medical-sensing gadgets (Acurable's respiratory monitors, the Willow Go wearable breast pump). Some wearables are purely consumer-facing fitness/lifestyle products sold through holiday deals coverage, while others sit at the boundary of consumer electronics and regulated medical devices — the Apple Watch's SpO2 blood-oxygen sensor and EKG feature are the clearest example, since they triggered patent litigation with medical device makers Masimo and AliveCor over the underlying sensing technology. Acurable is described explicitly as "a medical device company that makes patient-friendly wearable devices to diagnose and manage respiratory conditions at home," showing wearables also serving a clinical diagnostic role outside the smartwatch category.

## Key Characteristics

- **Body-worn form factor** — worn on the wrist (Apple Watch, Pixel Watch, Whoop 4, Galaxy Watch), finger (Ultrahuman Ring Air), or elsewhere on the body (Acurable's respiratory monitors, Willow Go breast pump).
- **On-board sensing** — wearables carry sensors such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, optical heart-rate sensors, and SpO2 (blood-oxygen) sensors; the Apple Watch Series 9's double-tap gesture, for instance, is detected from accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate data collected at the wrist.
- **Companion-app dependence** — many wearables (Whoop 4, Ultrahuman Ring Air) have no display of their own and instead offload data to a smartphone app for analysis and coaching.
- **Health/medical crossover** — some wearables function as, or overlap with, regulated medical devices: the Apple Watch's SpO2 and EKG features became the subject of ITC patent disputes with medical device makers Masimo and AliveCor, and Acurable markets its wearables as home-use medical devices to diagnose and manage respiratory conditions such as sleep apnea.
- **Rapid feature iteration** — newer models add capabilities like Sleep Profiles, abnormal heart-rate tracking, and gesture controls (double tap), often gated behind newer chips (the Apple Watch Series 9's S9 chip with four neural engines).

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the general definition is broader than any single corpus device: wearable technology comprises small electronic and mobile devices, worn on the body or built into clothing or accessories, that commonly detect and transmit information such as vital signs, sometimes with immediate biofeedback to the wearer (Wikipedia, "Wearable technology," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wearable_technology).

# MacBook Pricing And Discount Landscape

Apple sells MacBooks equipped with its own M-series chips in a wide range of sizes and price points, starting with the 13-inch MacBook Air from 2020 at $999 and going up to the latest 16-inch MacBook Pro starting at $2,499 — and, as The Verge put it on October 26th, 2023, finding a deal on a current Mac with an M1, M2, or even the new M3 chip, as well as the higher-end M3 Pro and M3 Max, is actually not that difficult.

The discriminating feature of Mac discounting is that it is episodic rather than continuous: Macs may not experience perpetual discounts, but it is not uncommon to see various current models discounted by as much as $400. The alternative route to savings is buying refurbished directly from Apple, which avoids waiting for the changing winds of deals; Apple's refurbished store provides a one-year warranty on all products and generally offers discounts of up to 15 to 20 percent off the price of a new unit.

One boundary case is explicitly excluded. The Verge does not recommend buying any older Intel-based Macs: retailers may try to tempt buyers with very low prices on leftover new or refurbished stock, but there is a reason nobody wants them anymore — they are completely outclassed by all the newer models, unless you have some super-niche Windows Boot Camp needs, and even then you should consider which Windows apps you really need and whether they work with Parallels.

# FTX's Absence Of A Chief Risk Officer

The Verge's trial reporter argued that FTX's lack of a chief risk officer was either evidence of stupidity or a deliberate choice — and, since stupidity was unlikely, that Bankman-Fried probably chose not to hire one because he was worried about what such an officer might find. The grounds are that FTX ran a business in which risk management is structurally central, and the warrant is that any competent operator of such a business knows this, so the omission has to be explained by intent rather than oversight.

The claim about centrality rests on what FTX was. FTX was named as it was because it was a futures exchange, which, to borrow Bloomberg columnist Matt Levine's phrase, "sits between the winners and losers of bets" — meaning FTX could not pay out what it owed the winners unless the losers paid up. Risk officers exist to identify a business's potential risks, monitor them, and mitigate them, and those risks run from reputational to regulatory to financial, to say nothing of the regulatory risks specific to crypto. As the reporter put it after Bankman-Fried's own testimony, risk is an inherent part of a futures exchange, which is even more like a casino than regular cryptocurrency, so not having a risk team when you are any kind of financial anything is certainly a choice — and especially a choice when you go around telling everyone your crypto exchange is very good and safe.

Two things sharpen the argument. First, the omission was conceded: Bankman-Fried testified that he made a point of "periodically" handling support tickets himself because "I worried if I didn't, I would lose touch with the actual concerns of the customers," while what he did not do was create a risk team — something he now characterises as a "big mistake." Second, the defense raised the subject itself. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen's opening told the jury FTX "didn't have a chief risk officer, which became an issue when the storm hit," and offered a metaphor of FTX as a plane; the reporter's response was that if FTX was a plane, it was a plane flying with a key component missing, and that bringing this up was a tremendous mistake because the prosecution had not mentioned it.

# Black Friday / Cyber Monday

## Definition

Black Friday and Cyber Monday are the paired retail sale events — the Friday after the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday and the Monday that follows it — that together anchor the start of the U.S. holiday shopping season, with retailers running discount campaigns across both dates and the days between them.

## Context

Retailers treat the two days less as isolated events than as bookends of a single extended sale window: Engadget reported that Amazon, Target, Best Buy, and Walmart all kicked off Black Friday-branded deals as early as late October 2023, so that "what was once a one-day event filled with limited-time deals has grown into a month-long event with a plethora of sales to sift through each day." Amazon itself began its Black Friday sale on Friday, November 17 — a week ahead of the calendar date — then switched to "Cyber Monday" branding in the early hours of Saturday, November 25, carrying many of the same discounts forward under the new label through the official close on Monday, November 27. Polygon likewise noted that the two named days (November 24 and 27 in 2023) no longer bound when the best prices actually appear, since retailers now front-load doorbuster-style deals across the preceding weeks. The pairing also functions as the header under which media outlets organize their own coverage: The Verge's "under $25" roundup groups both days together as one shopping period with "always a ton of hype about the discounts on big-ticket items."

## Key Characteristics

- **Two named days, one continuous season** — Black Friday (the day after Thanksgiving) and Cyber Monday (the following Monday) are distinct calendar dates, but retailer promotions now span from late October through the Monday close, blurring the boundary between them.
- **Retailer-driven timing shift** — multiple retailers (Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, Target) started Black Friday-branded deals days to weeks before the actual date in 2023, a strategy aimed at spreading out demand rather than concentrating it on one doorbuster day.
- **Deal carryover across the pairing** — items discounted for Black Friday commonly remain discounted, or are re-labeled, once Cyber Monday branding begins, rather than the two events offering wholly separate deal sets.
- **Broad retailer participation** — coverage spans Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and several other retailers, indicating the pairing is not a single-retailer promotion but an industry-wide sale convention.
- **High online-spend period** — the surrounding Thanksgiving-to-Cyber-Monday window ("Cyber Week") is tracked by analytics firms as a major driver of U.S. holiday online sales, with Thanksgiving Day alone producing billions in online spending as the de facto season opener.

# Hardware Device

## Definition

A hardware device, in this corpus, is a physical consumer electronics product — a smart speaker, handheld game console, smart glasses, or similar standalone gadget — that a company designs, manufactures, and sells as a distinct unit, as opposed to software or a service.

## Context

The corpus covers hardware devices from two angles: unveilings/reviews and retail deals. Google's annual "hardware event" is where the company unveils an entire slate of new devices at once — the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro phones, the Pixel Fold, Pixel Buds, and the Pixel Watch 2 — showing that "hardware" in this reporting names the physical product line a company ships, distinct from the software layered on top (Android 14, Bard, Google Assistant) that runs on it.

Retail-deal roundups organize hardware devices into shopping categories — Amazon's Cyber Monday guide lists separate sections for Echo/Fire TV/Kindle devices, speakers, headphones, tablets, and gaming gear — treating "speaker" as one device sub-category among several, not a synonym for hardware in general.

Smart glasses form a recurring device category: the Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses combine a camera, open-ear audio, and a voice assistant, while Amazon's Echo Frames center on giving hands-free access to Alexa, and both trace the category back to the Google Glass Explorer Edition as its 2013 origin point.

Handheld gaming hardware is treated the same way: the Steam Deck OLED is discussed as a physical device with its own chip, screen, and battery specifications, refreshed mid-cycle the way a phone or headphone line would be.

## Key Characteristics

- **Physical and purchasable** — a hardware device is a standalone unit with a price and a retail listing (the Echo Frames at $314.99, the Ray-Ban Meta glasses at $299, the Steam Deck OLED at $549), not a subscription or app.
- **Distinct from the software it runs** — Google's hardware event unveils devices (Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel Watch 2) separately from the software updates (Android 14, Bard) that ship alongside them.
- **Organized into device sub-categories** — retail guides split hardware into categories such as Echo/Fire TV/Kindle, speakers, headphones, tablets, and gaming, each reviewed and discounted on its own terms.
- **Defined by internal components** — reviews describe a device's identity through its chip, screen, and battery (the Steam Deck OLED's die-shrunk APU, 7.4-inch OLED panel, and 50Whr battery), the specs that distinguish one hardware generation from the next.
- **Ambiguous surface form** — "speaker" in the corpus denotes both an audio hardware device (a smart speaker) and the office of Speaker of the House; only the device sense belongs to this concept.

# NIO Q3 2023 Earnings Preview

NIO (NIO) was set to release its Q3 earnings before the bell on the Tuesday following Seeking Alpha's December 3, 2023 week-ahead preview, with the Wall Street consensus at Buy and Seeking Alpha's Quant Ratings holding at Hold because of concerns about profitability and valuation.

Consensus estimates going into the print were EPS of -$0.23 and revenue of $2.66B. The Earnings Insight attached to the preview is the important qualifier on those numbers: NIO had missed EPS estimates consistently in the past eight quarters and had missed revenue expectations in 50% of those quarters. The Quant system's two stated objections — profitability and valuation — are what separate it from the sell-side's Buy, and both are as of the December 3, 2023 preview date rather than the reported result.

# Prediction: Apple Enters The AI Market

TechCrunch predicts that 2024 is the year Apple makes its AI move. Apple has an established pattern of waiting, watching and learning from other companies' failures, then blowing in with a refined and polished take that puts others to shame, and the timing is right — not just because if it waits too long its competition may eat up the market, but because the tech is ripe for its kind of improvement.

The predicted shape of the product is specific. Expect an AI that focuses on practical applications of users' own data, using Apple's increasingly central position in their lives to integrate the many signals and ecosystems the company is privy to. There will likely also be a clever and elegant way to handle problematic or dangerous prompts, and although it will almost certainly have multimodal understanding — primarily to handle user images — the writer imagines Apple will totally skip media generation. Some narrowly tailored but impressive agent capabilities are expected too: "Siri, get a table for 4 at a sushi place downtown around 7 and book a car to take us" sort of thing.

The open question is branding: whether Apple will bill it as an improved Siri or as a whole new service, Apple AI, with a name you can choose yourself. Apple may feel the old brand is freighted with years of being comparatively incapable, but millions already say "hey Siri" every 10 seconds, so it is more likely the company will opt to keep that momentum.

# Organized Labor's Pushback On AI Deployment

Organized labor's argument, voiced by AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler at the conclusion of Tuesday's Senate AI forum, is that AI's effect on workers depends entirely on whether workers are included in the process: "If we fail to involve workers and unions across the entire innovation process, AI will curtail our rights, threaten good jobs and undermine our democracy. But the responsible adoption of AI, properly regulated, has the potential to create opportunity, improve working conditions and build prosperity."

The grounds Shuler offered are that the technology is already being used against workers — "Working people are fighting back against artificial intelligence and other technology used to eliminate workers or undermine and exploit us" — so the warrant joining grounds to claim is that regulation plus worker participation is what separates the beneficial deployment path from the harmful one, rather than the technology itself deciding the outcome.

The same argument came from inside the industry. While Andreessen calls for AI advancement at any cost and Tegmark continues to advocate for a developmental "time out," rank-and-file AI industry workers pressed their own case ahead of the forum: on Monday, employees from two dozen leading AI firms published an open letter to Senator Schumer demanding Congress act to safeguard their livelihoods from the "dystopian future" that Andreessen's screed would require. "Establishing robust protections related to workplace technology and rebalancing power between workers and employers could reorient the economy and tech innovation toward more equitable and sustainable outcomes," the letter's authors argue. The previous month, Senator Ed Markey (D-MA) and Representative Pramila Jayapal (WA-07) had called on leading AI companies to "answer for the working conditions of their data workers, laborers who are often paid low wages and provided no benefits but keep AI products online."

# Boston Dynamics AI Institute Ethics Research

The Boston Dynamics AI Institute is still in its infancy and therefore doesn't have much in the way of public facing research to show just yet, but it is doing a lot of hiring. In the week of TechCrunch's 2023-10-01 report, it announced that MIT's Kate Darling will lead research around "ethics and societal impact of robotics and AI."

According to the institute, Darling's team will explore immediate as well as long term questions on the implementation and use of robotics, impact on the workplace, infrastructure and other topics. The team will perform studies and experiments designed to generate data needed for others to make informed ethics and policy decisions, and will also develop a series of talks and workshops at the intersection of ethics, law, economics and robotics that will offer a platform for broad discussion.

# Worker Protections And Federal AI Hiring In The Executive Order

The Biden administration concedes that while the AI revolution is a decided boon for business, its capabilities make it a threat to worker security through job displacement and intrusive workplace surveillance, and the EO seeks to address these issues with "the development of principles and employer best practices that mitigate the harms and maximize the benefit of AI for workers," an administration official said. "We encourage federal agencies to adopt these guidelines in the administration of their programs."

The order also directs the Department of Labor and the Council of Economic Advisors to study how AI might affect the labor market and how the federal government might better support workers "facing labor disruption" going forward. Administration officials also pointed to the potential benefits AI might bring to the federal bureaucracy, including cutting costs and increasing cybersecurity efficacy. "There's a lot of opportunity here, but we have to ensure the responsible government development and deployment of AI," an administration official said.

On hiring, the administration launched a new federal jobs portal on Monday, AI.gov, offering information and guidance on available fellowship programs for people looking for work with the federal government. "We're trying to get more AI talent across the board," an administration official said. "Programs like the US Digital Service, the Presidential Innovation Fellowship and USA jobs — doing as much as we can to get talent in the door." The White House is also looking to expand existing immigration rules to streamline visa criteria, interviews and reviews for people trying to move to and work in the US in these advanced industries.

# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.

# The Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act Of 2023

Tuesday's Senate AI forum followed the recent introduction of new AI legislation dubbed the Artificial Intelligence Advancement Act of 2023 (S. 3050), co-sponsored by Senators Martin Heinrich (D-NM), Mike Rounds (R-SD), Charles Schumer (D-NY) and Todd Young (R-IN).

The bill proposes AI bug bounty programs and would require a vulnerability analysis study for AI-enabled military applications. Its passage into law would also launch a report into AI regulation in the financial services industry, as well as a second report on data sharing and coordination.

The financial-services provision lands on a problem the SEC's own chairman has been lamenting. "It's frankly a hard challenge," SEC Chairman Gary Gensler told The Financial Times recently, speaking on the challenges the financial industry faces in AI adoption and regulation. "It's a hard financial stability issue to address because most of our regulation is about individual institutions, individual banks, individual money market funds, individual brokers; it's just in the nature of what we do."

# Google's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

In its report to the EU disinformation Code, Google — an early adopter of generative AI in search via its Bard chatbot — discusses "recent progress in large-scale AI models" which it suggests has "sparked additional discussion about the social impacts of AI and raised concerns on topics such as misinformation."

Google summarised its approach: "Google is committed to developing technology responsibly and has published AI Principles to guide our work, including application areas we will not pursue," adding, "We have also established a governance team to put them into action by conducting ethical reviews of new systems, avoiding bias and incorporating privacy, security and safety. Google Search has published guidance on AI-generated content, outlining its approach to maintaining a high standard of information quality and the overall helpfulness of content on Search. To help address misinformation, Google has also announced that it will soon be integrating new innovations in watermarking, metadata, and other techniques into its latest generative models. Google also recently joined other leading AI companies to jointly commit to advancing responsible practices in the development of artificial intelligence which will support efforts by the G7, the OECD, and national governments. Going forward we will continue to report and expand upon Google developed AI tools and are committed to advance bold and responsible AI, to maximise AI's benefits and minimise its risks."

On forward commitments over the next six months, Google's report states it has no additional measures planned for YouTube. With generative image capabilities rolling out internally over the next year, it commits Google Search to leveraging the IPTC Photo Metadata Standard to add metadata tags to images generated by Google AI, and notes: "Creators and publishers will be able to add a similar markup to their own images, so a label can be displayed in Search to indicate the images as AI generated."

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# Figure AI's Purist Humanoid Market Thesis

Rival robot-makers like Figure AI take a more purist approach, on the idea that only true humanoids can effectively navigate workplaces, homes and a society built for humans. Figure also plans to start with a relatively simple use case, such as in a retail warehouse, but aims for a commercial robot that can be "iterated on like an iPhone" to perform multiple tasks and take up the work of humans as birth rates decline around the world.

The market claim rests on labor scarcity rather than cost substitution. "There's not enough people doing these jobs, so the market's massive," said Figure AI CEO Brett Adcock. "If we can just get humanoids to do work that humans are not wanting to do because there's a shortfall of humans, we can sell millions of humanoids, billions maybe."

# Tech Layoffs In March 2023

March 2023 was one of the heaviest months of the 2023 tech layoff wave, headlined by Accenture's plan to cut 19,000 jobs announced on March 23, Meta's confirmation on March 14 that it would cut 10,000 people, and Amazon's second big round of 9,000 job cuts announced on March 20.

The month opened on March 1 with Thoughtworks laying off about 4% of its global workforce, approximately 500 employees; Alphabet's Waymo issuing a second round of layoffs that year, which combined with the January cuts meant the self-driving technology company had let go 8%, or 209 employees, of its workforce; and Cerebral letting go 15% of its workforce, roughly 285 employees. On March 6 Atlassian announced it was laying off about 500 employees, 5% of its total workforce; SiriusXM said it had laid off 475 employees, 8% of its total workforce; and the Nigerian B2B e-commerce platform Alerzo confirmed it had laid off 15% of its full-time workforce, leaving about 800 employees at the startup, which had a headcount of more than 2,000 before a first round of layoffs in September 2022. In the week of March 10 more Salesforce employees learned they had been laid off; Salesforce first announced it was laying off 10% of the workforce in January but some employees did not know until February, and the company confirmed these later layoffs were part of the same 10%. Y Combinator announced on March 13 that its cuts would affect 20% of staff, 17 team members. On March 14 CEO Mark Zuckerberg confirmed rumors that Meta would cut 10,000 people from its workforce and around 5,000 open roles it had yet to fill. Klaviyo announced on March 15 that it had laid off 140 staff across all teams, and Course Hero announced on March 16 that it had cut 15% of staff, 42 people.

The second half of the month was busier still. On March 20 Amazon announced another round of substantial layoffs, with 9,000 people set to lose their jobs — TechCrunch heard around 10% of that total came from AWS — and as part of the round Amazon shut down DPReview; Twitch announced it would lay off 400 employees; and Livespace announced it had laid off at least 100 employees, about 2% of its workforce. On March 22 Indeed announced it would lay off 2,200 employees, 15% of its staff, and Roofstock announced it had laid off 27% of its staff, approximately 100 employees. Accenture announced on March 23 that it planned to cut 19,000 jobs, 2.5% of its workforce. On March 24 Bloomberg reported that more layoffs could be on the way at Salesforce, quoting chief operating officer Brian Millham, who indicated the company could add to the ongoing job cutting at the CRM leader and in tech generally; if the layoffs happened they would come on top of the 10% cut in January. On March 27 Disney revealed in an internal memo that there would be three rounds of layoffs, the first beginning that week, impacting approximately 7,000 employees as announced in February, and Microsoft laid off 559 workers from its Bellevue and Redmond operations; as part of its earlier announcement to lay off 10,000 people, Microsoft had also laid off an entire team dedicated to guiding AI innovation that leads to ethical, responsible and sustainable outcomes. On March 28 GitHub announced it had eliminated over 100 jobs in the South Asian market, laying off virtually its entire engineering team in India, which a GitHub spokesperson told TechCrunch was part of the streamlining effort disclosed in February to cut roughly 10% of its workforce by the end of Q1 2023; Lucid announced it was laying off 1,300 employees, 18% of its workforce, to be completed by the end of Q2 2023. Shift Technologies announced on March 29 that it had laid off 30% of its workforce in Q1 2023. On March 30 Unacademy announced it had laid off more than 350 roles, 12% of its workforce, just over four months after cutting about 350 roles in November, and Roku announced it was letting go of about 200 employees, 6% of its workforce, having laid off 200 U.S. employees back in November. On March 31 Netflix confirmed a "handful of layoffs" including two longtime executives, with the exact number unclear; Netflix was scheduled to report Q1 2023 results on April 18.

# DeepMind's Founding And Thiel's Investment

In 2010 Demis Hassabis and two colleagues, all living in Britain, were looking for money to start building "artificial general intelligence", a machine that could do anything the brain could do, at a time when few people were interested in AI because after a half-century of research the field had failed to deliver anything remotely close to the human brain. Some scientists and thinkers had nonetheless become fixated on AI's downsides, and many, including the three young men, had a connection to Eliezer Yudkowsky, an internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher who led a community calling themselves Rationalists or, later, effective altruists; they believed AI could find a cure for cancer or solve climate change but worried that AI bots might do things their creators had not intended, arguing that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators. Peter Thiel, enormously wealthy through an early investment in Facebook and his work with Musk in the early days of PayPal, had developed a fascination with the singularity, the science-fiction trope describing the moment when intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity, and with his funding Yudkowsky had expanded his AI lab and created an annual conference on the singularity; one of Hassabis' colleagues had met Yudkowsky years before and snagged them speaking spots at that conference, ensuring an invitation to Thiel's party, where Yudkowsky introduced Hassabis to Thiel. Assuming many guests would be trying to squeeze their host for money, Hassabis' strategy was to arrange another meeting: he told Thiel there was a deep tension between the bishop and the knight, pieces carrying the same value whose strengths the best players understood to be vastly different. Charmed, Thiel invited the group back the next day, gathering in the kitchen where their host, just finished with his morning workout and still sweating in a shiny tracksuit, was handed a Diet Coke by a butler; the three made their pitch and soon Thiel and his venture capital firm agreed to put £1.4 million, about $A2.7 million, into their startup, making him their first major investor.

They named the company DeepMind, a nod to "deep learning", a way for AI systems to learn skills by analysing large amounts of data, to neuroscience, and to the Deep Thought supercomputer from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, and by the spring of 2010 they were building their dream machine, wholeheartedly believing that because they understood the risks they were uniquely positioned to protect the world. Mustafa Suleyman, one of the three founders, said "I don't see this as a contradictory position. There are huge benefits to come from these technologies. The goal is not to eliminate them or pause their development. The goal is to mitigate the downsides." Having won over Thiel, Hassabis worked his way into Musk's orbit: about two years later they met at a conference organised by Thiel's investment fund, which had also put money into SpaceX, and Hassabis secured a tour of SpaceX headquarters, after which, with rocket hulls hanging from the ceiling, the two lunched in the cafeteria; Musk explained his plan to colonise Mars to escape overpopulation and other dangers on Earth, and Hassabis replied that the plan would work so long as superintelligent machines didn't follow and destroy humanity on Mars too. Musk was speechless, not having thought about that particular danger, and soon invested in DeepMind alongside Thiel so he could be closer to the creation of the technology.

# Microsoft's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

Microsoft — a major investor in OpenAI which has also baked generative AI capabilities into its own search engine — claims in its EU disinformation Code report that it is taking "a cross product whole of company approach to ensure the responsible implementation of AI."

The report flags Microsoft's "Responsible AI Principles," which it says it developed into a Responsible AI standard v.2, and Information Integrity Principles "to help set baseline standards and guidance across product teams." Microsoft continues: "Recognizing that there is an important role for government, academia and civil society to play in the responsible deployment of AI, we also created a roadmap for the governance of AI across the world as well as creating a vision for the responsible advancement of AI, both inside Microsoft and throughout the world, including specifically in Europe," committing to continue building on these efforts by developing new tools — such as Project Providence with Truepic — and inking partnerships, the examples it gives being the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) to combat the rise of manipulated or AI created media, EFE Verifica to track false narratives spreading in Spain, Latin America and Spanish-speaking populations, and Reporters Sans Frontières to use their Journalism Trust Initiative dataset in Microsoft products. "These partnerships are part of a larger effort to empower Microsoft users to better understand the information they consume across our platforms and products," it suggests, also citing media literacy campaigns and "cyber-skilling" which it says are "not designed to tell individuals what to believe or how to think; rather, they are about equipping people to think critically and make informed decisions about what information they consume."

On Bing Search, where Microsoft was quick to embed generative AI features — leading to some embarrassing early reviews which demonstrated the tool producing dubious content — the report claims a raft of mitigating measures: applying its AI principles during development and consulting with experts; engaging in pre-launch testing and a limited preview period and phased release; the use of classifiers and metaprompting, defensive search interventions, enhanced reporting functionality, and increased operations and incident response; and updating Bing's terms of use to include a Code of Conduct for users. The report also claims Microsoft has set up a "robust user reporting and appeal process to review and respond to user concerns of harmful or misleading content." For the next six months, the report does not commit Bing Search to any specific additional steps to address risk attached to the use of generative AI — Microsoft says only that it is keeping a watching brief: "Bing is regularly reviewing and evaluating its policies and practices related to existing and new Bing features and adjusts and updates policies as needed."

# The Schatz-Kennedy AI Labeling Act

Senators Brian Schatz (D-HI) and John Kennedy (R-LA) introduced legislation on Tuesday that would provide more transparency on AI-generated content by requiring clear labeling and disclosures — technology that could resemble the Content Credentials tag the C2PA and CAI industry advocacy groups are developing.

The bill, which its sponsors call the Schatz-Kennedy AI Labeling Act, would require generative AI system developers to clearly and conspicuously disclose AI-generated content to users. Those developers, and their licensees, would also have to take "reasonable steps" to prevent "systematic publication of content without disclosures." The bill would additionally establish a working group to create non-binding technical standards to help social media platforms automatically identify such content.

Schatz framed the measure plainly in a press statement: "Our bill is simple. If any content is made by artificial intelligence, it should be labeled so that people are aware and aren't fooled or scammed." Speaking on the Senate floor the same Tuesday, he added that the bill "puts the onus where it belongs: on the companies and not the consumers," and argued that "labels will help people to be informed. They will also help companies using AI to build trust in their content."

# The Biden AI Executive Order Of October 2023

The Biden Administration unveiled its next steps in addressing and regulating artificial intelligence development on Monday: an expansive executive order (EO) that seeks to establish further protections for the public as well as improve best practices for federal agencies and their contractors.

The order is framed as a whole-of-government instrument. "The President several months ago directed his team to pull every lever," a senior administration official told reporters on a recent press call. "That's what this order does, bringing the power of the federal government to bear in a wide range of areas to manage AI's risk and harness its benefits ... It stands up for consumers and workers, promotes innovation and competition, advances American leadership around the world and like all executive orders, this one has the force of law."

Its provisions are phased rather than immediate. The actions will be introduced over the next year, with smaller safety and security changes happening in around 90 days and more involved reporting and data transparency schemes requiring nine to 12 months to fully deploy. To keep that schedule, the administration is also creating an "AI council," chaired by White House Deputy Chief of Staff Bruce Reed, who will meet with federal agency heads to ensure the actions are being executed on time.

Google offered $US650 million for DeepMind. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook offered a bigger payout to DeepMind's founders but would not agree to the conditions the founders had set, and DeepMind sold to Google.

Zuckerberg was determined to build an AI lab of his own and hired Yann LeCun, a French computer scientist who had also done pioneering AI research, to run it. # The Clinical Benefits Of AI In Health Care

Patel views AI as a "powerful instrument" that helps magnify physicians' capabilities rather than replacing them, and he groups its clinical benefits into pattern recognition, volume handling, automation, early risk detection and personalized medicine.

Pattern recognition comes first. "One of AI's primary strengths is its ability to recognize patterns that might escape the human eye," he said. "Whether it's intricate anomalies in medical imaging or subtle patterns in patient histories, AI can pinpoint details that make a significant difference in diagnosis and treatment."

The technology also helps providers by sifting through and analyzing vast volumes of information, far more than what would be humanly possible, Patel said, and it automates mundane and routine tasks, allowing health care professionals to redirect their focus to the patient.

Early risk detection is another key benefit. "AI tools can predict potential health risks by analyzing a combination of genetic, behavioral and environmental factors, facilitating early interventions and potentially saving lives," Patel said.

AI can also help enable the delivery of personalized medicine and proactive preventative care. "By analyzing individual genetic makeup combined with lifestyle and environmental factors, treatments can be tailored to the unique needs of each patient," Patel said. "And by predicting potential health issues before they manifest, we can guide patients on preventive measures, fundamentally changing our approach from cure to prevention."

# The CPPA's Risk-Based Approach Versus The EU AI Act

The CPPA's approach to regulating ADMT is risk-based, per Soltani. That echoes another piece of in-train EU legislation, the AI Act — a dedicated risk-based framework for regulating applications of artificial intelligence which has been on the table in draft form since 2021 but is now at a delicate stage of co-legislation, with the bloc's lawmakers clashing over the not-so-tiny detail of how, or even whether, to regulate Big AI, among several other policy disputes on the file.

The relation TechCrunch draws between the two is one of comparative advantage under discord: given the disagreement around the EU's AI Act, as well as the ongoing failure of US lawmakers to pass a comprehensive federal privacy law — since there is only so much presidential Executive Orders can do — there is a plausible prospect of California ending up as one of the top global rulemakers on AI.

That relation holds only over a limited range. The impact of California's AI rules is likely to remain local, given its focus on affording protections and controls to state residents. In-scope companies might choose to go further, such as offering the same package of privacy protections to residents of other US states, but that is up to them; the bottom line is that the CPPA's reach and enforcement is tied to the California border.

# Critical Infrastructure And CBRN Provisions Of The AI Executive Order

The executive order encourages the Departments of Energy and Homeland Security to address AI threats "to critical infrastructure, as well as chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and cybersecurity risks," and it attaches those standards to money: "Agencies that fund life-science projects will establish these standards as a condition of federal funding, creating powerful incentives to ensure appropriate screening and manage risks potentially made worse by AI." In short, any developers found in violation of the EO can likely expect a prompt and unpleasant visit from the DoE, FDA, EPA or other applicable regulatory agency, regardless of their AI model's age or processing speed.

The order also looks to use AI defensively. In an effort to proactively address the decrepit state of America's digital infrastructure, it seeks to establish a cybersecurity program, based loosely on the administration's existing AI Cyber Challenge, to develop AI tools that can autonomously root out and shore up security vulnerabilities in critical software infrastructure. It remains to be seen whether those systems will be able to address the concerns of misbehaving models that SEC head Gary Gensler recently raised.

# Layoffs

## Definition

Layoffs are the employer-initiated, batch workforce cuts the corpus tracks through 2023's "techwide reckoning" — TechCrunch's running tally puts total tech-industry job losses at more than 240,000 for the year, driven by companies pivoting "from a growth mindset to one based on efficiency" (doc_0049).

## Context

Across the corpus, 2023 is depicted as a "techwide reckoning" year: TechCrunch's running tracker put total tech-industry job losses at more than 240,000 for the year, already 50% above 2022 and still climbing, with cuts driven by the biggest names in tech — Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Yahoo, Meta and Zoom — as well as startups across many sectors (doc_0049).
The phenomenon recurs across very different company situations: a cybersecurity startup that went public but "failed to gain traction" and later shuttered outright, laying off its remaining staff (IronNet, doc_0011); a browser maker cutting 9% of its workforce across departments (Brave Software, doc_0043); a music-streaming giant cutting roughly 1,500 jobs (17% of its workforce) in its third layoff round of the year while its CEO framed the move as "right-sizing" for "productive and efficient" operations (Spotify, doc_0334); and a logistics startup cutting about 20% of its staff (roughly 600 people) under its founder, who returned as CEO after ousting his "hand-picked successor" over alleged overspending (Flexport, doc_0536, doc_0537).
Layoffs also follow directly from an acquired or platform company's takeover events: X's (formerly Twitter's) 2022 change of ownership "saw major layoffs, including in content moderation and human rights," which the corpus ties to the platform's later inability to respond to disinformation reports (doc_0024).
In the video-game industry specifically, layoffs are described as one of three interlocking forces — alongside consolidation and unionization — reshaping the sector: an estimated 9,000-plus video-game jobs were lost in 2023 versus roughly 1,000 in 2022, with layoffs concentrated at recently acquired studios (doc_0050).

## Key Characteristics

- **Batch, employer-driven terminations** — layoffs affect many employees at once (e.g., Brave's 9%, Spotify's 17%, Flexport's 20%), distinguishing them from case-by-case firings (doc_0043, doc_0334, doc_0537).
- **Framed as cost/efficiency correction** — companies in the corpus consistently attribute layoffs to macroeconomic pressure and a shift "from a growth mindset to one based on efficiency," rather than to sectoral collapse (doc_0049).
- **Can accompany full shutdown** — the most severe outcome pairs layoffs with the company ceasing operations entirely, as with IronNet, which "has shuttered and laid off its remaining staff following its collapse" (doc_0011).
- **Recurrent, not one-time** — several companies underwent multiple rounds within the same year (Spotify's third round by December 2023; Flexport cutting 20% in January with "more layoffs expected soon" by October) (doc_0334, doc_0536).
- **Concentrated post-acquisition** — layoffs and closures are described as "the most extreme negative outcomes for an acquired indie studio," recurring after ownership changes (video games) or leadership takeovers (X) (doc_0050, doc_0024).

# Theory: An AGI And Mission Rift Between Altman And The Board

The proposition is that Altman's zeal for AGI, even absent a secret project or agreement, led to a major rift between him and the board. Altman is a proud techno-optimist and often speaks fondly of the possibilities of AGI, or artificial general intelligence, a theoretical software system that achieves human-like intellect and versatility. The board's statement pointedly includes that "OpenAI was deliberately structured to advance our mission: to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity" and that new leadership was necessary.

The supporting observation is a directional one: it has been obvious to all that Altman took the company in a much more corporate direction from its origins, changing its legal status and aggressively pursuing enterprise and consumer applications, which does not sound a lot like the "mission" the board wants to advance.

What counts against it is timing. This shift did not happen today, and it certainly does not seem like a plausible reason for abruptly firing the CEO and a few others on a beautiful fall Friday afternoon — a gradual drift does not explain an abrupt dismissal.

# Tech Layoffs 2023: Overview And Totals

The tech industry saw more than 240,000 jobs lost in 2023 — a total already 50% higher than the previous year and still growing — as last year's techwide reckoning continued.

Earlier in the year, mass workforce reductions were driven by the biggest names in tech: Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Yahoo, Meta and Zoom. Startups across many sectors also announced cutbacks through the first half of the year. Tech layoffs slowed in the summer and fall, but cuts appeared to be ramping up again. By a second measure, the running total of layoffs for 2023 based on full months to date is 224,503, according to Layoffs.fyi, and tech layoffs conducted to date that year already exceeded the total number of tech layoffs in 2022 according to the data in that tracker.

The explanation TechCrunch offers is macroeconomic rather than sectoral collapse: many economists have cautioned against fears of a recession, which would seem like a reason for optimism, but the momentum for a tech sector rebound has been slow to build, resulting in tech companies continuing to cut back on their workforces and pivoting from a growth mindset to one based on efficiency in the face of stubborn market conditions. TechCrunch frames its tracker — a comprehensive list of all known 2023 tech layoffs, updated monthly — as a way to understand the impact on innovation, which companies face tough pressures, and who is available to hire for businesses lucky enough to be growing, as well as a reminder of the deeply human impact of layoffs.

# Open Letter Calling For A Six-Month AI Training Pause

More than 1,100 signatories — including Elon Musk, Steve Wozniak and Tristan Harris of the Center for Humane Technology — signed an open letter calling on "all AI labs to immediately pause for at least 6 months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4."

The grounds the letter offers are that contemporary AI systems are now becoming human-competitive at general tasks, and that this raises questions no one has answered: "Should we let machines flood our information channels with propaganda and untruth? Should we automate away all the jobs, including the fulfilling ones? Should we develop nonhuman minds that might eventually outnumber, outsmart, obsolete and replace us? Should we risk loss of control of our civilization?"

The warrant that joins those grounds to the demand for a pause is a claim about legitimacy and about the burden of proof: "Such decisions must not be delegated to unelected tech leaders," and "Powerful AI systems should be developed only once we are confident that their effects will be positive and their risks will be manageable." On that principle, capability that has already reached human-competitive general performance is exactly the point at which development must stop until confidence is established.

# Non-Pneumatic And Concept Future Tires

A non-pneumatic tire replaces air pressure with modern composites to provide the right mix of stiffness and flex with significantly more durability — the near-future example being the Michelin Uptis, which Michelin says could reduce tire replacements by 20 percent. Variations of this theme have been in development for decades, but models are in testing now for consumer and industrial use.

The idea is one of several attempts to change the equation altogether, rather than only finding sustainable replacements for tire manufacturing compounds or researching what today's compounds do to our health.

A more radical and more distant vision is Goodyear's 2020 ReCharge concept, which proposed that a biodegradable tread could be recharged simply by inserting refillable capsules with seasonal compounds. As a concept it is pretty far out there, and Goodyear's Helsel confesses as much, calling them "purely conceptual designs" that "might never be produced as such" — but he says the non-pneumatic nature of those concepts, and the advanced sensors embedded within, are indicative of ongoing research into future tires.

Virtually every tire manufacturer is making at least token efforts to increase the usage of sustainable materials like guayule. Yokohama is using motorsports to develop its Advan A005 tire, which debuted at last year's Pikes Peak International Hill Climb and contains 33 percent sustainable materials including biomass-derived rubber; Michelin shod Porsche's prototype electric GT4 e-Performance racer with tires said to be 53 percent renewable, made with materials like strap steel and lemon peels.

# The Scale Of Tire Wear Particle Emissions

According to researchers at Imperial College London, our cars and trucks emit 6 million tons of tire wear particles every year — transportation detritus that goes into the air, the land, and the water. That figure ignores the nearly 250 million tires disposed of annually in North America, roughly half of which are burned.

The framing is that tires are the most important safety component on a car, yet there is increasing research that they are doing a good deal of harm too, leaving their mark on the environment slowly and surely, one mote of black dust at a time.

It is a depressing state of affairs, but there is room for optimism: every major tire manufacturer globally is raising its game — not only in terms of performance in the face of bigger, heavier electric cars but also in terms of environmental impact. Renewable materials are finding their way into modern tires, and there is even greener rubber on the horizon.

# Tire Lifespan, Scrappage And Retreading

Modern tires last a lot longer than they used to: "In the early 1970s, the typical wear life for a set of tires was approximately 20,000 miles in average driving conditions," Harrigle says. "Fast forward to today, and 80,000-mile wear warranties are relatively common."

The bad news is that we are still going through more tires than ever. Harrigle says we scrap 250 million tires every year in North America, and again about half are burned for fuel. Even the best tires eventually need replacing, either through wear or the kind of roadside debris that can ruin a tire and your entire day.

Reuse beats recycling. Retreading itself is nothing new, and while it has generally fallen out of favor for consumer tires, on the industrial side it can be a huge cost-saver — and environment-saver too. Jason Roanhouse, VP of North American Bandag operations at Bridgestone Mobility Solutions, says the company's retread business has saved 300 million tires from being thrown out, worth roughly 4 billion gallons of oil.

# What Drivers Can Do To Reduce Tire Pollution

Given that most of the relevant research is happening at an industry level, it is easy to feel helpless about the role we all play in contributing this pollution when we are just trying to get to work — but Molden suggests three things drivers can do in the interim: drive more slowly, drive more smoothly, and choose the right tires.

On the third, the rule of thumb is to match the tire to the car rather than to the price. According to Molden the tires your car was outfitted with when new will provide the best wear characteristics: "It's a bit like going to a flight in restaurants, and each course has a wine match to the food," he says. Perfectly paired tires may cost more than whatever you can get at a local discounter, but they will provide better wear and, ultimately, less pollution.

# Cutting Wear Mass May Raise Toxicity

Emissions Analytics' Nick Molden challenges the assumption that reducing tire wear mass is straightforwardly progress: "The reason I'm worried about that is I'm sure you can reduce that wear mass, but if you do that by making the compound more toxic, you could actually make the environmental impact worse."

The premise under attack is that mass of debris is the right measure of environmental harm; the analogy offered is that such a trade could be akin to increasing a car's fuel efficiency by switching to leaded fuel.

Molden's proposed remedy is knowledge rather than a specific target. He believes what is needed is better understanding, and to that end he recently created the Tyre Emissions Research Consortium, a LinkedIn group with about 1,000 members, with the intent of breaking down the silos individual researchers were working in.

# The Evolution Of Meltwater's Media Monitoring Business

Meltwater's business has evolved through three stages, each driven by a change in where the media lives: manual press clipping, digitized monitoring of print decline, and then social-media-era sentiment analysis over unstructured data.

The company's roots are in businesses where humans physically sifted through piles of newspapers daily to clip mentions of a company's name, collate those and send them to clients to help them track how they are being covered in the media. The decline of print media digitized that effort, and then the rise of social media turned it into a wider game — sentiment analysis — as words became structured and, more usually, unstructured data. The influx of a whole new set of tools to glean insight out of that data turned a media challenge into a technical one.

Meltwater's response was to build AI in-house and to acquire a stream of businesses in an analytics consolidation play. The most high-profile of these acquisitions was undoubtedly DataSift, the groundbreaking firm that was an early friend of Twitter's in monetizing its firehose, only for that relationship to turn sour. Companies like Meltwater are at a crossroads these days in technology terms.

# Silica As A Tire Filler

Silica is an increasingly important tire filler that both displaces less renewable materials and makes tires more efficient. "Conventional tires rely on carbon black to strengthen the rubber matrix as the tire is cured," says Dale Harrigle, Bridgestone's chief engineer for replacement tires. "In a tire that uses silica in the tread compound, a portion of the carbon black is removed and replaced with silica, which allows for increased wet performance and reduced rolling resistance."

Its sourcing is changing too. Silica traditionally comes from sand, but Goodyear, for example, is now using silica sourced from a rice processing byproduct called husk ash.

The combined result: less harmful rubber, more grip, better wear, and better range or fuel economy.

# 6PPD-Quinone And Coho Salmon Die-Offs

6PPD-quinone is a toxin that forms when 6PPD — an additive that helps tires resist environmental damage and so last longer between replacements — reacts with ozone, and a 2020 study from the University of Washington's Center for Urban Waters found that a dramatic decline in coho salmon populations was the result of it. The salmon have now been placed on some West Coast endangered lists.

The causal chain runs from road to water. "Shortly after birth, they were essentially going mad and dying," Molden says. "The researchers finally linked it to this compound in tires because it was happening after rainfall. The rainfall was washing all the accumulated tire material off the road into the harbors and into the shore."

The relation does not stop at fish. That is bad not just for the salmon and the Pacific Northwest's fishing industry — 6PPD-quinone is in us too, and it only comes from tires.

How far the harm extends is still open. "The product 6PPD-quinone, which was identified in late 2020, requires more research to understand what impact, if any, it may have on aquatic life or the environment," Goodyear SVP of global operations and CTO Chris Helsel says. That is hardly a mea culpa, but the tire industry genuinely has been an active partner in studying the problem.

# Tire And Road Wear Particles

Tires break down into tire and road wear particles, or TRWP — the black dust that accumulates on roads, though not permanently: when it rains, it is carried away. It is easy to imagine that the lost rubber simply disappears as tread patterns fade, but the truth is more terrifying.

The scale of where that material ends up is the striking part. A recent Pew Charitable Trusts report found that 78 percent of ocean microplastics are synthetic tire rubber, which makes efforts to cut down on microfiber pollution from our laundry seem a bit quaint.

The concern is not the particles alone but what they carry. "What you don't want is all these little wear particles full of all these nasty compounds settling in the environment and inside us and gradually leaching out their toxins," says Nick Molden, CEO of Emissions Analytics, an independent group focused on testing and data about the overall environmental impacts of transportation.

# Ford Racing Success As A Brand Marketing Engine

Mark Rushbrook described Ford's motorsport marketing as a chain that starts on the racetrack: success on track is the foundation of successful marketing programs, and everything downstream — credibility, fan engagement, pride of ownership and global road-car promotion — depends on it, as reported by Essentially Sports on 6 November 2023.

The first link is winning itself and its internal effect. "Yeah, winning is everything for us, just as a point of pride. It's certainly going to be a celebration in Dearborn. My phone has been blowing up with Ford family members and our senior executives already so excited about it. It means a lot internally to the customer because motorsports is so important to us." The second link is the credibility mechanism, which Rushbrook states as a precondition rather than a benefit: "That is the basis for successful marketing programs; it is success on the racetrack. So you have to win the races, you have to win championships to have that credibility, and for fans to engage with your brand and make them proud to have a Ford parked in their driveway or in their garage."

The third link is the transfer from race car to road car, and it holds across series rather than only in NASCAR. Ford's global marketing strategy leverages the Mustang's success in NASCAR as a tool to promote its road cars worldwide, and as the seventh-generation Mustang continues to be sold globally as a road car it races not only in NASCAR but in various international series, including Australia Supercars, Mustang GT3, Mustang GT4 and Dark Horse R with a Spec Challenge. In essence, Ford takes the benefits from any Mustang's racing success and uses it to market their cars globally — the report calls it a win-win situation for both the brand and racing enthusiasts, while noting that all this might not have come to pass were it not for a timely intervention by "The Captain."

VIIZR was announced in December 2021. Its ownership structure is what distinguishes it from an ordinary Ford product line: it was a separate company majority owned by Ford, with Salesforce as a minority investor.

# Doubts About The AI Alliance's Effectiveness

TechCrunch's counter to the AI Alliance's promise attacks the premise that a broad coalition can act at all: without the participation of so many major AI industry players — and lacking deadlines or even concrete objectives — can the AI Alliance succeed, and what would success even look like?

Two further grounds are offered. First, the vast number of competing interests, from healthcare networks such as the Cleveland Clinic to insurance providers such as Roadzen, will not make it easy for the Alliance's members to coalesce around a single, united front. Second, for all their talk of openness, IBM and Meta are not exactly the poster children for the future the Alliance's release depicts, which casts doubt on their sincerity.

The conclusion is held open rather than asserted: perhaps the writer is wrong and the AI Alliance will be a smash success, or perhaps it will crumble under mistrust and its own bureaucracy — time will tell.

# The Pure Research Model At Automaker-Backed Institutes

The model at stake is "pure research" — a bit of a loaded term, but a hopeful one: finding a method that can sustain research outside of the pressures of academia and corporate R&D. The relation it depends on is a funder willing to decouple a research institute from near-term product deadlines, and the range over which it holds is set by the parent company's own strategic bet.

Asked whether there is pressure from Toyota to productize, Pratt says, "There actually is not, and I'm not saying that just to be nice. I think one of the great things about companies that have existed for long times is that this isn't the first time that they've done R&D. Certainly most of the R&D budget inside of Toyota is spent figuring out how to make the next car or maybe the car five years from now. But there's this notion — and I'm sure Hyundai shares this — that we're at the once-in-a-century time for transformation in the car industry. Battery electric vehicles are much simpler to make than cars have been in the past — no engine, no transmission, etc. So, we're going to have to compete in a much fiercer way in cars. But also, can we use the skills, the dreams and the hopes of the company to go beyond cars? TRI's job is to actually think about [what's] next. What's next after cars, as well as some fancy stuff on cars."

# Tire Compound Composition And Its Performance Tradeoffs

A tire's composition breaks down, in general terms, into four parts. "Natural rubber and synthetic rubber each represent about 25 percent of materials used in tire manufacturing. Fillers, primarily carbon black and silica, represent an additional 25 percent," Bridgestone's Niaura says. "The remaining percentage consists of steel, textiles, oils, resins, and other ingredients used to cure the tire or serve as anti-degradants." How all of this factors into each manufacturer's specialty blends is complicated.

The relation between blend and behavior runs across three properties: by blending different components, manufacturers can adjust a tire's grip (how sticky it is), tread life (how long it lasts), and rolling resistance (how efficient it will make your car).

Those three have traditionally traded off against one another — high-grip tires are traditionally short-lived and inefficient — but thanks to sticky science and renewable materials, that is changing.

# Digital Twins Deployed for Sustainability Goals

The first trend IoT Analytics highlights is that companies are deploying digital twins to meet sustainability goals, with the pursuit of those goals acting as a tailwind macro factor for the digital twin market. Sustainability was discussed in approximately 21% of recent CEO earnings calls and has remained a consistent topic throughout 2023.

The mechanism is that digital twins simulate real-world conditions and deliver real-time information, so organisations can optimise resource usage, reducing carbon emissions and improving supply and transportation networks. Survey evidence supports the link: according to Capgemini Research Institute's 2022 digital twins report, 57% of organisations agreed that one of the key drivers for their digital twin investments was improving their sustainability, and 51% agreed that digital twins would help achieve their organisation's environmental sustainability goals.

A former VP at an industrial automation vendor quoted in the report frames the scope over which the relation holds: "Digital solutions provide the visibility, analysis, and insight needed to address the challenges inherent in sustainability goals. A digital twin strategy as part of an overall digitalization plan can be a crucial capability for asset-intensive industries and needs to encompass the entire asset lifecycle, process, and value chain from design and operations through maintenance and strategic business planning." The worked example is Aden, a Chinese integrated facility service provider, which created a digital twin for one of its commercial centres in Chengdu, China, designed to help facility managers inspect, maintain and repair building assets; its 3D simulations assist managers in visualising, predicting and optimising energy consumption, with expected benefits including lower annual energy consumption, water usage and waste.

# Dan Lewis's Convoy Founding Thesis

Convoy co-founder and CEO Dan Lewis's argument for starting the company was that trucking combined a very large money flow with unusually little startup competition — "I saw a massive opportunity and few people going after it," Lewis told TechCrunch. The former Amazon and Google executive, who has a background in strategy and management consulting, said that when he was struck by the urge to start a company, he researched the money-attracting industries of the world and then, using AngelList, saw how many companies were trying to disrupt those industries.

The grounds are the counts that search returned: thousands of companies working on industries ranging from telecommunications and fashion to video games and food, while billions of dollars were going into trucking each year but fewer than 30 startups showed an interest in the field. The warrant is that a large industry with few entrants is where opportunity concentrates. Asked later whether his method of deciding on a direction for a startup is still a good method, Lewis said, in short, yes. TechCrunch revisited the May 2022 interview on 2023-10-22, after Convoy's collapse.

# Scorsese and Leonardo DiCaprio's Collaboration

The defining relationship of Scorsese's 21st-century career is his partnership with Leonardo DiCaprio, which began with 2002's Gangs of New York — itself the final product of an interesting but ultimately flawed compromise between Scorsese and producer Harvey Weinstein. Polygon described the partnership on 2023-10-26.

Polygon models it as a symbiotic exchange that elevated both men: the industry outsider who needed a safe box-office bet to finally get his epic, expensive dream projects financed, and the teen heartthrob who needed an auteur with arthouse gravitas to take him seriously so the industry would.

To date the project has been wildly successful, producing six films over 21 years, and the first five — Gangs of New York, The Aviator, The Departed, Shutter Island, and The Wolf of Wall Street — are Scorsese's top five highest-grossing films, with the box office for Killers incoming.

The relationship extends beyond casting. Over the years the team-up has served as a true creative marriage, and the two men now share a manager in Rick Yorn, the man responsible for discovering DiCaprio. Polygon presents this as evidence DiCaprio has not "just" been a muse and a face on the posters: he has had a say in deciding which projects Scorsese takes on and has made significant decisions shaping Scorsese's stories — Scorsese entirely reimagined Killers of the Flower Moon after DiCaprio offered notes on an early draft of the script, including shifting focus to a different main character and moving DiCaprio into that role.

# Josh Arnold's GameStop Structural Unprofitability Critique

Seeking Alpha author Josh Arnold argued in the December 3, 2023 week-ahead that GameStop is a structurally unprofitable company, writing: "GameStop faces fundamental headwinds, including poor margins and declining sales, making it a structurally unprofitable company."

The premise this attacks is that GameStop's problems are cyclical or fixable within the current business — the assumption behind any bullish read of the shares. Arnold's grounds are two specific fundamental headwinds, poor margins and declining sales, and the word doing the work is "structurally": the claim is not that the company is losing money this quarter but that the loss-making is built into its economics, so a better quarter or a stronger tape would not overturn it. Scope conditions: this is one named Seeking Alpha author's stated view as quoted in a December 3, 2023 preview, offered without supporting figures in the passage.

# Digital Twin Market Size and Adoption 2023

IoT Analytics projects that the global digital twin market could grow at a compound annual growth rate of approximately 30% between 2023 and 2027, according to its Digital Twin Market Report 2023-2027 as summarised by IoT Business News on 18 November 2023.

Adoption data underpins that projection. 29% of global manufacturing companies have either fully or partially implemented their digital twin strategies, a noticeable increase from 20% in 2020, and the proportion of companies not contemplating implementation appears to have fallen to 9% in 2023, down from 33.6% in 2020. Supporting the trend, an analysis of job postings on SimplyHired suggests growing demand for digital twin expertise: postings mentioning "digital twin" increased by 11% in October 2023 compared with just two years prior, while openings for most other tech topics declined over the same timeframe. Among the 60 tech-related skill sets IoT Analytics tracked, digital twin-related skills experienced one of the most significant growths.

Against this backdrop the report notes eight notable trends helping to advance and promote digital twins, of which the article discusses four in detail: digital twins deployed to meet sustainability goals; digital twins employed as virtual sensors in complex conditions; partnerships between cloud hyperscalers and OT and simulation specialists; and initiatives promoting interoperability of digital twins across multifaceted systems. These trends are described as shaping the future of the market and influencing investment priorities for companies across various industries.

# Open Letter Calling For A Six-Month AI Training Pause

More than 1,100 signatories — including Elon Musk, Steve Wozniak and Tristan Harris of the Center for Humane Technology — signed an open letter calling on "all AI labs to immediately pause for at least 6 months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4."

The grounds the letter offers are that contemporary AI systems are now becoming human-competitive at general tasks, and that this raises questions no one has answered: "Should we let machines flood our information channels with propaganda and untruth? Should we automate away all the jobs, including the fulfilling ones? Should we develop nonhuman minds that might eventually outnumber, outsmart, obsolete and replace us? Should we risk loss of control of our civilization?"

The warrant that joins those grounds to the demand for a pause is a claim about legitimacy and about the burden of proof: "Such decisions must not be delegated to unelected tech leaders," and "Powerful AI systems should be developed only once we are confident that their effects will be positive and their risks will be manageable." On that principle, capability that has already reached human-competitive general performance is exactly the point at which development must stop until confidence is established.

# Israeli Tech Industry Boycott of Web Summit

In the days before 16 October 2023, a run of named technology figures publicly withdrew from Web Summit and, in several cases, pledged never to return, each citing Web Summit CEO Paddy Cosgrave's stance on the Israel–Hamas fighting. David Marcus, the longtime fintech entrepreneur and Meta executive, said in a tweet the previous day that he would never again attend, sponsor or speak at another Web Summit event: "Saddened by your ill-informed stance. You could've taken a more nuanced one, condemning these atrocities and calling for restraint. That would've been acceptable," he wrote. "You chose to support terrorists. As such I'll never attend/sponsor/speak at any of your events again." Keith Rabois, the Founders Fund partner and entrepreneur, went further than a single event, chiming in: "Will refuse to work with anyone who speaks at this conference in Qatar for the rest of my career."

Ori Goshen, the co-founder and co-CEO of AI21 Labs, announced on LinkedIn that he would no longer be giving a keynote at Web Summit, and grounded the withdrawal in two distinct complaints. "It's bad enough that summit CEO Paddy Cosgrave didn't see fit to express horror at the sickening atrocities committed by Hamas on October 7th," he said. "But as immoral as that is, Paddy Cosgrave chose to not only ignore these but instead post something against the policies of the Israeli government. Leaving aside his very partial understanding of history and geopolitics, this response was abhorrent. We at AI21 cannot be part of such indecency and moral bankruptcy. We will not attend WebSummit, and I will not give the keynote. #cancelwebsummit #standwithisrael"

The withdrawals then moved from individual companies to the state level when the Israeli ambassador to Portugal, Dor Shapiro, waded in. "Today, I wrote to the Mayor of Lisbon informing him that Israel will not participate in the #WebSummit conference due to the outrageous statements made by the conference CEO Paddy Cosgrave. Even during these difficult times, he is unable to set aside his extreme political views and denounce the Hamas terrorist activities against innocent people," he wrote, also on LinkedIn. "Dozens of companies have already canceled their participation in this conference, and we encourage more to do so."

Cosgrave's response over the same window moved in both directions. By 16 October he appeared to walk back his statement, writing nine days after Hamas invaded Israel: "We are devastated to see the terrible killings and the level of innocent civilian casualties in Israel and Gaza. We condemn the attacks by Hamas and extend our deepest sympathies to everyone who has lost loved ones. We hope for peaceful reconciliation." Under so much fire, however, he subsequently dug in his heels, tweeting afterward: "To repeat: War crimes are war crimes even when committed by allies & should be called out for what they are. I will not relent."
