# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# The AI Development Moratorium Open Letter

Not everybody was enthusiastic about the pace at which generative AI was being adopted. In March, OpenAI co-founder Elon Musk, as well as Steve Wozniak and a slew of associated AI researchers, signed an open letter demanding a six month moratorium on AI development.

The letter attacks the premise underlying the industry's integration wave — that faster deployment is straightforwardly good — by asking for development itself to be paused rather than merely regulated.

# Fotiadis Testimony And Johansson's Lobbying Contacts At The LIBE Hearing

At the LIBE committee hearing the journalist Apostolis Fotiadis testified that documents he and his colleagues obtained showed email threads granting a CSAM-scanning "key stakeholder" privileged access inside Johansson's department, and, under pressure from MEPs, the commissioner read out a list of her meetings with technology companies and child safety organizations. TechCrunch reported the session on 25 October 2023.

Fotiadis, one of the journalists involved in the investigation the committee was examining, had also been invited by the committee to participate in the exchange of views, and he took the opportunity to defend their reporting from direct public attacks by Johansson. In a blog post ahead of the hearing — which deploys a crisis-PR-esque headline claim of "setting the record straight" — she criticized the article as "a series of insinuations looking for a home", claiming it paired an outline of "a selection of meetings I had, of events I attended, or conferences I addressed" with "a conspiratorial tone" in an attempt "to create the impression of financial influence where there is none".

Asked by the LIBE committee about the accusation that the journalists had, essentially, been spreading disinformation — and specifically whether he believed Johansson and the Commission's response to it amounted to a restriction on media freedom — Fotiadis responded by saying he did not think that was the case. He went on to express surprise at how the Commission had reacted to the scrutiny, and at its instinct to deploy "spin-doctor" tactics to try to discredit the article rather than engaging with the substance of the concerns being raised. The Commission risks straying close to making attacks on journalists by using such tactics, Fotiadis warned, adding: "You cannot just dismiss everything by calling fake news" — before also noting that Johansson's office had declined multiple interview requests ahead of publication of the article.

On the substance of the reporting, Fotiadis said documents obtained by the journalists included email threads between Commission officials in Johansson's department, DG-Home, and a "key stakeholder" advocating for the use of technology for CSAM-scanning, which indicated what he described as "privileged access" that "speaks directly to cooperation" and goes "way beyond" mere consultation or exchange of views on the proposal.

He gave the committee the shape of that access. "It's an official chain discussing invitation, how the stakeholder would be able to allocate experts that would speak in workshops — first attended by representatives of the Member States, and then afterwards actually by ministers in the Council in a meeting chaired by commissioner Johansson. So when we say facilitate, it's obvious that the EU officials discuss what kind of experts will be available from this particular stakeholder to attend these meetings and to present the point of view, which seems to be a privileged access," he explained. "Also in the same email thread there's mention of EU officials being allocated to specifically attend the cooperation between the stakeholder and DG-Home on the proposal, which to our understanding is something that goes way beyond the level of consultations or exchange of views or exchange of opinions on the proposal and speaks directly to cooperation."

The committee then pressed Johansson about her contacts with companies and other lobbyists during the drafting of the CSAM proposal, with MEPs saying they wanted clear answers to the allegations of commercial interest and heavy lobbying when the Commission was setting up and drafting the proposal. In the event MEPs got some bare bones detail. Asked for a list of these contacts, the commissioner responded that she had met with Google six times; Microsoft, Meta and TikTok three times each; twice with Twitter (X); and once apiece with Apple and Amazon. She also said she had met with the child safety organizations Thorn (twice) and Brave Movement (twice), and with Tech Alliance and ICANN once apiece.

In wider responses related to concerns about how much commercial interest had influenced the Commission, Johansson highlighted her decision for the CSAM-scanning proposal to be "technology neutral" — meaning the draft regulation does not support any specific tech solution — with the suggestion being that EU lawmakers had resisted lobbying by companies for a law that would explicitly favor their existing tech tools.

# Prosecution Opening Statement By Thane Rehn

Assistant US attorney Thane Rehn opened the government's case by pointing at Bankman-Fried and telling the jury, "This man stole billions of dollars from thousands of people." Delivering the statement in the cadence of a high schooler reciting lines in a student play, Rehn dodged explaining cryptocurrency to the jury and instead punched hard on Bankman-Fried lying and stealing, listing the evidence to come: internal company files, what customers were told, the testimony of his co-conspirators, and his own words.

Rehn's narrative contrasted the lifestyle with its foundation. At this time last year, he said, Bankman-Fried had a luxury lifestyle as CEO of the crypto exchange FTX — he hung out with Tom Brady, was on magazine covers, lived in a $30 million penthouse, and spent time with world politicians. "All of that was built on lies," Rehn said. He also told the jury Bankman-Fried sold stock in FTX and borrowed millions from lenders by lying, and laid out the sequence familiar from the news: in May and June of 2022, Alameda Research — the crypto trading company ostensibly helmed by Caroline Ellison — did not have enough to pay its bills, so it pulled customer money to repay loans; by September the hole in the FTX balance sheet was so big that customers could never be repaid.

The Verge's reporter, writing on October 4th, 2023, recorded the defendant's demeanour as the counterpoint: she had never seen Bankman-Fried so still, with the characteristic leg-jiggling absent and only occasional glances at Rehn. His hair was shorn, the result of a haircut from a fellow prisoner per the Wall Street Journal, and he wore a suit bought at a discount at Macy's, also per the Journal; it hung on him, and he appeared to have lost some weight.

# Ohanian's Case for Techno-Optimism

Despite the problems with social media and the urgency, in terms of its impact on society, Alexis Ohanian argued in remarks reported on 31 October 2023 that there is still some hope — that the next generation of platforms can be built better, and that user appetite will itself turn against the current design. He gave two grounds. The first is who is building now: he noted that the founders his fund 776 invests in are much smarter and more aware of the issues than he ever was at their age, so perhaps the next platforms will still be addictive, but in a way that doesn't "further disrupt democracy." The second is a prediction about demand: he believes that after everything on social media becomes so perfectly curated for us, our brains will start to crave things that are not. The warrant tying grounds to conclusion is that the harms are contingent on choices made by a less aware cohort of founders working against an audience that had not yet tired of curation — change either and the outcome changes.

Ohanian drew the consequence out in terms of what comes after the feed: "I think we'll see a rebirth of live gatherings and in-person experiences…the bright side of this is that I hope it then gets us back in touch with our humanity, and the things that no amount of AI can replace." He was careful to mark the position as an aspiration held against resistance rather than a prediction of ease. "I want to be an optimist about it," he added. "And I think there's still a path forward but we're fighting against very, very strong human things. And if we can solve it, it will do so much good. It really, really will because we will find out we have more in common than not."

The optimism is bounded by a sharp rejection of one common defence of platforms — the town square. "The public square [analogy]…falls flat. Because if that then implies that it's a public square, which means like, what? a town or a city? If you're the person in charge of it, you're the mayor. # Marcus Urann, The "Cranberry King"

Marcus Libby Urann was the "Cranberry King" — a bookish boy from Maine who became an influential college scholar and a Boston attorney before giving up the bar for the bogs in 1906, FOX News Lifestyle reported on 23 November 2023.

He was born on 3 October 1873 to Marcus M. and Chestina Urann in Sullivan, Maine, a tiny Downeast town on Bar Harbor, and described himself in one letter as a "bookworm". He attended the University of Maine, where he became an undergraduate scholar of great renown and great vision, and became an attorney in Boston after graduation; in 1906 he decided to give that up to buy cranberry bogs in and around Cape Cod and Plymouth. He died on 1 April 1963 in Hanson, Massachusetts, where he rests in a family plot in Fernhill Cemetery. "I do believe that anyone can do anything that he really desires to accomplish," Urann wrote as a young man in 1924, explaining the history of Phi Kappa Phi, and he lived by that example throughout his life.

The defining summary is the one given in The Boston Globe's obituary of 4 April, which called him "a recognized giant of the cranberry industry" and dubbed him the "Cranberry King": "He bought his first cranberry bog on [Cape Cod] in 1906. During the next 30 years, he built his bog holding into a complex throughout southeastern Massachusetts." # Mar-a-Lago Valuation Dispute

Mar-a-Lago is the sharpest of the valuation disputes: Trump valued the Palm Beach estate as high as $739 million — more than 10 times a more reasonable estimate of its worth, Fortune reported in September 2023 — on the idea that the property could be developed for residential use, when deed terms prohibit that, Attorney General Letitia James said. The Age's November 2023 comparison put Trump's 2021 valuation at $US612.1 million, Bloomberg's 2023 valuation at $US240 million, and New York's 2021 valuation at $US27.6 million.

The gap turns on how the property may be used. Trump made a series of agreements with Palm Beach County and the National Trust for Historic Preservation for Mar-a-Lago to be used only as a club, giving up development rights, so Palm Beach values the property as a business on its tax rolls and in 2021 assessed it at $US27.6 million, lower than comparable residential properties; New York State argues this is the appraisal Trump should have been using. That figure drew objections: New York's estimated value "was a shock to the real estate community and anybody with any understanding of the island and its values," said Liza Pulitzer, a real estate agent at Brown Harris Stevens and a Palm Beach native. "It could easily fetch $US500 million or more." That assumes a buyer views it as a single-family residence; it is currently not zoned for such use, though Trump is able to reside there through a loophole designating himself an employee. Trump's legal team engaged an expert witness who argued a future buyer could do the same thing, and could reduce the club to a membership of one, though it is unclear whether Palm Beach would allow that without a change to zoning status.

The property's economics have also shifted. Historically Mar-a-Lago never made much money for the Trump Organisation, but it took in about $US41 million in revenue in 2022 according to Trump's most recent ethics disclosure, compared with $US21 million in 2019. Bloomberg values it at $US240 million based on a combination of comparable residential property sales in the area and its value as a business, reflecting uncertainty around its future status — uncertainty not shared by everyone: if the city and county allowed it, "there is no reason why it wouldn't be able to converted to a full-time private residence," said Eli Beracha, director of the Hollo School of Real Estate at Florida International University. # The University Response Gap To Faculty Online Abuse

The Verge's reporter argued that universities are failing faculty who are harassed online, and that the gap is not only procedural but attitudinal: deans and chairs are often unaware of how online abuse is affecting their faculty, and where campuses do respond they rely on policing and a punitive model rather than the well-being and mental health of the targets. "Deans and chairs are often unaware at all of how online abuse is actually affecting their faculty," Victoria O'Meara told her. "A lot of the attacks — while they may graduate to things like emails or even, in a horrible instance, people showing up on campus — they often start on social media."

The reporter grounded the claim partly in her own experience teaching journalism in academia for over a decade, watching threats to teachers grow worse. In 2015 she became concerned about a student who professed having a crush on her despite knowing she is married and who told a colleague about his sexual feelings toward her; she reported her concerns to the school, and his behavior escalated. He already had a criminal record including charges of sexual violence, talked about killing people and writing a book about it, and his reading responses turned dark, discussing rape and describing ideas of criminal activity along with a lack of empathy toward murder and disaster victims; frightened students reported his conduct as well. Her department, program directors, and humanities dean supported her, but when other officials got involved — the school police, the counseling center, and a campus dean — she was made to feel like an alarmist, and her own self-doubt crept in as she asked whether she had been too nice to him. "I don't find him scary," one campus official on the case said, and she was informed a plan would be made to help the individual graduate. She and her teaching assistant kept up instruction; though he was not allowed to attend class in person, she spent those weeks checking door locks and plotting how she might handle an attack on her class — an agonizing exercise for a journalist who has covered the immediate aftermath of college massacres such as the one that killed 32 people at Virginia Tech in 2007. Her assistant, a graduate student in the MFA program, said, "There were about two weeks where I couldn't sleep. I would have really bad nightmares. I was worried about the students, but also for myself and for you," and the experience helped her decide she did not want full-time university employment again. Neither of them realized at the time that, as employees, they could have reported the situation themselves to the Title IX office; instead, to avoid the student showing up unannounced, they moved their class of around 50 undergraduates to a secret, unlisted location — prevention spearheaded by program directors on the ground, not from the powers above.

The warrant is that the job now requires the exposure that produces the risk. Academics use Twitter, now known as X, and Facebook to collaborate and connect with researchers in their field, and some use TikTok or Instagram to promote their research; "It's not really possible anymore to be an active member of your research community without being on social media," O'Meara said, and accessibility online has only heightened scholars' visibility and vulnerability — at a time when funding agencies increasingly ask researchers to do more public engagement. # DeepMind's Sale To Google And Facebook's AI Lab

Google offered $US650 million for DeepMind. Mark Zuckerberg of Facebook offered a bigger payout to DeepMind's founders but would not agree to the conditions the founders had set, and DeepMind sold to Google.

Zuckerberg was determined to build an AI lab of his own and hired Yann LeCun, a French computer scientist who had also done pioneering AI research, to run it. A year after Hinton's auction, Zuckerberg and LeCun flew to Lake Tahoe for the same AI conference, and while padding around a suite at the Harrah's casino in his socks Zuckerberg personally interviewed top researchers, who were soon offered millions of dollars in salary and stock. AI was once laughed off; now the richest men in Silicon Valley were shelling out billions to keep from being left behind.

# Battery Life and Charging

## Definition

Battery life and charging is the pair of consumer-electronics specs — how long a device runs on a charge, and how fast and via what connector it refills — that reviewers and shoppers use to compare phones, earbuds, handhelds, smart glasses, and the power banks and cables that feed them.

## Context

Across the corpus, battery life and charging speed function as headline review criteria and buying-guide sort keys rather than a single defined term: Engadget's Steam Deck OLED review leads with "its battery life is better" as one of the device's core upgrades, and The Verge lists "improved battery life and audio" as a top pro for Amazon's third-gen Echo Frames. The charging half of the pair is increasingly organized around USB-C: Engadget notes that Apple's iPhone 15 line and the second-generation AirPods Pro both moved to USB-C charging, and Polygon's portable-charger guide treats USB-C Power Delivery wattage as the key spec for matching a power bank to a phone, tablet, Steam Deck, or laptop. Capacity for power banks is measured in mAh, per Polygon's guide, while device battery life is reported in hours (the Echo Frames reviewer logged about five hours of media playback and calls before hitting 30 percent) or in minutes of measured playtime (Engadget's Steam Deck OLED testing). Gogoro's battery-swapping business shows the same pair of concerns scaled up to electric vehicles: swapping a depleted battery for a charged one at a station is explicitly framed as a way to cut "charging time" relative to plugging in.

## Key Characteristics

- **Duration is measured empirically, not just claimed** — Engadget timed the Steam Deck OLED at four hours 23 minutes playing Hades versus two hours 42 minutes on the original LCD model under identical settings, a 62 percent gain that beat Valve's own 30-to-50-percent claim.
- **Charging speed is a distinct spec from capacity** — Valve advertises the Steam Deck OLED going from 20 to 80 percent in 45 minutes, a speed claim separate from its 50Whr battery capacity; Polygon likewise separates a power bank's mAh capacity from its wattage-based recharge speed.
- **USB-C is displacing proprietary connectors as the charging standard** — Apple's iPhone 15 and USB-C AirPods Pro, and the iPad's shift off Lightning to USB-C on its 10th-generation model, are all cited by Engadget as part of a single connector transition.
- **Power Delivery (PD) wattage governs compatibility between chargers and devices** — Polygon's guide notes that only power banks supporting the PD 3.0 spec can recharge a Steam Deck at its fastest rate, and that a laptop needs PD 3.1 and a compatible cable to reach 140 W charging.
- **Battery swapping is an alternative to plug-in charging at the vehicle scale** — Gogoro's network lets riders exchange a depleted battery for a charged one at a station instead of waiting to charge in place, which TechCrunch frames as a way to reduce charging time for EV adopters.

# Enterprise Browser And Cloud Data Security As Categories

Talon and Dig sit in two newer areas of the security market, which is what would make them especially attractive to a larger acquirer — and TechCrunch understands there appeared to be others previously looking at both.

Dig's category is securing data in the cloud, working across fragmented data spread over multiple clouds. That taps into a growing area of the market, since cloud spend is one of the only other areas where budgets are not being curtailed; it is a very crowded field, but also a prime opportunity to emerge as a leader in matching solutions to how companies are actually working in the real world.

Talon's category is the enterprise browser — a platform for large organizations to operate all of their apps and services, built from the ground up with security in mind. It is still relatively new in the market but has already started to catch on big with customers and competitors, Island being another company in the same space. "They're creating a new category that has the potential of being bigger than endpoint security altogether," one source said. "They're reinventing the operating system."

# Engadget's VPN Testing Methodology

To test the security specs of different VPNs and name its top picks, Engadget relied on pre-existing academic work through Consumer Reports, VPNalyzer and other sources, referenced privacy policies, transparency reports and security audits made available to the public, and considered past security incidents like data breaches.

The comparison criteria were price, usage limits, effects on internet speed, possible use cases, ease of use, general functionality and additional "extra" VPN features like multihop. The VPNs were tested across iOS, Android and Mac devices to see the state of the mobile apps across various platforms — Windows devices are also supported in most cases. Testers used the "quick connect" feature on each app to connect to the "fastest" provider available when testing internet speed, access to IP address data, and DNS and WebRTC leaks, which occur when a fault in the encrypted tunnel reveals requests to an ISP.

Three practical tests followed: a geoblocking test accessing Canada-exclusive Netflix releases, a streaming test watching a news livestream on YouTube via a Hong Kong-based VPN, and a gaming test playing on servers in the United Kingdom. Performing these tests at the same time also allowed the reviewers to test claims about simultaneous device use.

# Passkeys As The Default Google Sign-In Method

A passkey is a phishing-resistant alternative to a password that lets users sign in to accounts using the same biometrics or PINs they already use to unlock their devices, or with a physical security key. As TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-13, Google is now making passkeys the default sign-in method for all users.

Two features discriminate a passkey from a password. First, resistance to phishing is the property the definition leads with — it is what the mechanism is for, not an incidental benefit. Second, the credential is not something the user types and remembers: authentication reuses the device unlock factors, biometrics or a PIN, or else a separate physical security key. That gives three admissible forms of the same method, one of which is hardware the user carries rather than anything stored on the signing-in device.

The scope of the Google change as reported is the default, applied to all users — the default sign-in method, rather than the only one available.

# Mozilla's Open Letter On AI Openness

The letter's claim is that openness makes AI safer, against the counter-position that proprietary control does. In an open letter published by Mozilla a few weeks before November 21, 2023, Meta's chief AI scientist Yann LeCun joined some 70 other signatories in calling for more openness in AI development, and the letter has since garnered more than 1,700 signatures. The backdrop is that Big Tech companies such as OpenAI and Google's DeepMind have called for more regulation, warning of catastrophic consequences if the AI levers were to meet the wrong hands — in other words, arguing that proprietary AI is safer than open source.

LeCun and his co-signatories disagree, and concede the risk before turning it around: "Yes, openly available models come with risks and vulnerabilities — AI models can be abused by malicious actors or deployed by ill-equipped developers. However, we have seen time and time again that the same holds true for proprietary technologies — and that increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous. The idea that tight and proprietary control of foundational AI models is the only path to protecting us from society-scale harm is naive at best, dangerous at worst." The warrant is that scrutiny, not secrecy, is what makes technology safe.

On a personal level, LeCun has accused the big-name AI players of trying to secure "regulatory capture of the AI industry" by lobbying against open AI R&D — an argument about motive rather than safety. And on a company level, Meta is doing all it can to encourage collaboration and "openness," recently partnering with Hugging Face to launch a new startup accelerator designed to spur adoption of open source AI models.

# Acquisition

## Definition

Across the corpus, "acquisition" denotes one company buying another and taking ownership and control of it — whether framed as an all-cash purchase of a target's shares (Amazon–iRobot), an outright corporate purchase (OpenAI–Global Illumination, Microsoft–Activision Blizzard King, Palo Alto Networks–Talon/Dig), or referred to interchangeably as a "merger," "buy," or "deal."

## Context

The corpus uses "acquisition" (and its synonyms "purchase," "buy," "merger," "deal") across a wide range of industries and deal sizes, from an AI startup's first tuck-in purchase to a $69 billion mega-deal, showing the term denotes a general transaction type rather than one specific event.
Amazon's proposed acquisition of iRobot was priced as an all-cash offer, later cut by 15% during a lengthy EU antitrust review, illustrating how the announced acquisition price can move before a deal closes.
OpenAI's purchase of Global Illumination was described as the company's "first public acquisition," showing the term applies equally to small, non-controversial tuck-ins as to headline-grabbing mega-deals.
Microsoft's $69 billion purchase of Activision Blizzard and King — the largest acquisition in video game history — took nearly two years to clear antitrust review before completing, and the corpus notes Microsoft's prior $26 billion purchase of LinkedIn as an earlier acquisition of comparable scale.
In cybersecurity, Palo Alto Networks' pursuit of Talon Cyber Security and Dig Security for roughly $1 billion combined is framed as one of several "mega deals" and smaller tuck-ins (CrowdStrike–Bionic, IBM–Polar, Cisco–Splunk) that the corpus groups together as an industry-wide acquisition trend driven by consolidation pressure.

## Key Characteristics

- **Change of ownership and control** — the acquirer gains control of the target's assets, operations, or equity; in the iRobot case the EU's concern was specifically that Amazon would gain the ability and incentive to influence competitive outcomes on its marketplace once it controlled iRobot.
- **A negotiated price that can shift** — the iRobot deal's price fell 15% from its original $1.7 billion all-cash offer as the target took on more debt during a delayed close, showing acquisition price is not fixed until the deal actually closes.

- **Driven by consolidation dynamics** — in cybersecurity, acquisitions cluster as companies buy up specialized startups (e.g., Palo Alto pursuing Talon and Dig) partly in reaction to competitors' own acquisitions, a pattern the corpus explicitly attributes to a "swing" toward large all-in-one platforms.

# K.O. II Memory, Voice Limit And Missing Resampling

The K.O. II's practical ceiling is not its 64MB of memory but its 12-voice limit: the memory translates to about 11 minutes of samples at the 46kHz/16bit at which the device records — halved if you sample in stereo — whereas the voice limit means it can make only 12 sounds at once, so six stereo samples playing simultaneously already hits it.

Engadget's reviewer judged that even going all out, over five minutes of samples should be plenty for most songs, and that their own compositions weren't interesting enough to hit the voice threshold — but maximalists should keep it in mind. What sharpens the limit is a missing feature: resampling, the common technique of merging separate sounds down into one new sample to avoid hitting the voice limit on other devices, is also the technique for baking in effects and modulation. Since the K.O. II can only manage one master effect at any one time, its absence is all the more obvious, and it is possibly the biggest complaint among users the reviewer has seen so far, after fadergate. There are workarounds, but they involve recording out into another device and sampling that back in — and "no one should have a sampler for their sampler, not in this economy." # Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Foundation Model Reporting And Red-Team Disclosure Under The EO

The executive order sets out a reporting procedure for the most capable AI systems: a company developing any foundation model that poses a serious risk to national security, national economic security, or national public health and safety must notify the federal government when training the model, and must share the results of all red-team safety tests — and that information must be shared prior to the model being made available to the public, which could help reduce the rate at which companies unleash half-baked and potentially deadly machine learning products. The legal instrument used to compel this is the Defense Production Act.

Alongside red-team results, the EO also requires disclosure of the system's training runs — essentially its iterative development history. The purpose officials gave for the sequencing is verification: "What that does is that creates a space prior to the release… to verify that the system is safe and secure." The EO more broadly directs the establishment of new standards for AI safety and security, including reporting requirements for developers whose foundation models might impact national or economic security, and those requirements also apply in developing AI tools to autonomously implement security fixes on critical software infrastructure.

The procedure has a deliberately narrow scope. Administration officials were quick to point out that the reporting requirement will not affect any AI models currently available on the market, nor independent or small- to medium-size AI companies going forward, because the threshold for enforcement is quite high. It is geared specifically at the next generation of systems that the likes of Google, Meta and OpenAI are already working on, with enforcement on models starting at 10^26 petaflops — a capacity currently beyond the limits of existing AI models. "This is not going to catch AI systems trained by graduate students, or even professors," the administration official said.

The order was cast as a step past voluntary measures. "In response to the President's leadership on the subject, 15 major American technology companies have begun their voluntary commitments to ensure that AI technology is safe, secure and trustworthy before releasing it to the public," the senior administration official said. "That is not enough."

# Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)

## Definition

In the corpus, multi-factor authentication (MFA) is never defined on its own — it appears only as one item in a longer list of security practices that a source recommends or claims to already follow, alongside things like passwords, encryption, and security audits.

## Context

Engadget's VPN guide tells readers that a VPN alone does not cover them: because VPNs do not protect against phishing, hacking, or other cyberthreats, users should also maintain complex passwords and multi-factor authentication as part of their broader security routine. Keep Labs, in a statement provided to TechCrunch, lists multi-factor authentication alongside encryption in transit and at rest, regular security audits, and penetration testing as part of the company's layered approach to protecting patient medication data under HIPAA and PIPEDA.

## Key Characteristics

- **One layer among several** — in both corpus mentions, MFA is named in the same breath as passwords, encryption, or audits, never presented as sufficient on its own.
- **Complements, not replaces, other tools** — Engadget frames it as something users need in addition to a VPN, since a VPN does not defend against phishing or credential theft.
- **Used as a compliance signal** — Keep Labs cites its use of MFA as evidence of adherence to data-protection regulations (HIPAA, PIPEDA) and "highest standards" of security, in a self-reported statement rather than an independent audit.

## Background (external)

CISA (Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency, part of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security) describes MFA as "a layered approach to securing your online accounts and the data they contain," requiring a user to present two or more authenticators — something they know (like a password), something they have (like a phone or authentication app), or something they are (like a fingerprint or face scan) — before access is granted.

Source: CISA, "More than a Password" (https://www.cisa.gov/MFA), publisher: Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency, accessed 2026-09-02.

# Microsoft's Generative AI Disinformation Measures

Microsoft — a major investor in OpenAI which has also baked generative AI capabilities into its own search engine — claims in its EU disinformation Code report that it is taking "a cross product whole of company approach to ensure the responsible implementation of AI."

The report flags Microsoft's "Responsible AI Principles," which it says it developed into a Responsible AI standard v.2, and Information Integrity Principles "to help set baseline standards and guidance across product teams." Microsoft continues: "Recognizing that there is an important role for government, academia and civil society to play in the responsible deployment of AI, we also created a roadmap for the governance of AI across the world as well as creating a vision for the responsible advancement of AI, both inside Microsoft and throughout the world, including specifically in Europe," committing to continue building on these efforts by developing new tools — such as Project Providence with Truepic — and inking partnerships, the examples it gives being the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) to combat the rise of manipulated or AI created media, EFE Verifica to track false narratives spreading in Spain, Latin America and Spanish-speaking populations, and Reporters Sans Frontières to use their Journalism Trust Initiative dataset in Microsoft products. "These partnerships are part of a larger effort to empower Microsoft users to better understand the information they consume across our platforms and products," it suggests, also citing media literacy campaigns and "cyber-skilling" which it says are "not designed to tell individuals what to believe or how to think; rather, they are about equipping people to think critically and make informed decisions about what information they consume."

On Bing Search, where Microsoft was quick to embed generative AI features — leading to some embarrassing early reviews which demonstrated the tool producing dubious content — the report claims a raft of mitigating measures: applying its AI principles during development and consulting with experts; engaging in pre-launch testing and a limited preview period and phased release; the use of classifiers and metaprompting, defensive search interventions, enhanced reporting functionality, and increased operations and incident response; and updating Bing's terms of use to include a Code of Conduct for users. The report also claims Microsoft has set up a "robust user reporting and appeal process to review and respond to user concerns of harmful or misleading content." For the next six months, the report does not commit Bing Search to any specific additional steps to address risk attached to the use of generative AI — Microsoft says only that it is keeping a watching brief: "Bing is regularly reviewing and evaluating its policies and practices related to existing and new Bing features and adjusts and updates policies as needed."

# Foundation Model

## Definition

A foundation model is a large AI model — trained by a small set of well-resourced providers — that sits at the base of the generative-AI stack and is adapted or built upon by other tools and applications, rather than being the end product itself.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces in two distinct settings: market structure and government regulation. In a TechCrunch survey of venture capitalists on the emerging LLM stack, Glasswing Ventures' Rick Grinnell divides the generative-AI landscape into four layers — foundation model providers, middle-tier companies, end-market/top-layer applications, and full-stack vertical companies — with foundation models sitting at the base layer that middle-layer tooling and top-layer applications are built on top of. He names Alphabet/Google's Bard, Microsoft/OpenAI's GPT-4, and Anthropic's Claude as examples of this foundational layer. Separately, in coverage of the Biden Administration's AI executive order, "foundation model" is the regulatory unit the order targets: it directs new reporting standards specifically for developers whose foundation models might affect national or economic security.

## Key Characteristics

- **Base-layer position** — foundation models sit beneath the middle tier (fine-tuning, prompt engineering, orchestration) and the application layer in the GenAI tech stack; other companies build and compete on top of them rather than replacing them.
- **Concentrated provider set** — the layer is dominated by a small number of large players (Alphabet/Google, Microsoft/OpenAI, Anthropic), whose advantages in data access, talent, and compute are expected to push this layer toward an oligopolistic structure akin to the cloud-provider market, tempered by open-source alternatives.
- **Reused across applications** — applications "blend" foundation models with in-house middle-layer tooling to build specialized, defensible products, rather than starting from scratch.
- **Trigger for regulatory reporting** — under the White House AI executive order, a company training any foundation model that poses a serious risk to national security, economic security, or public health/safety must notify the federal government when training the model and share red-team safety test results before public release.
- **High-capability threshold for regulation** — the EO's reporting duty is scoped to a computational threshold (10^26 petaflops) beyond the capacity of existing models at the time, so it targets only the next generation of the largest foundation models, not models currently on the market or built by small/independent developers.

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.

# The M3 MacBook Pro Lineup And Its Configurations

The M3 MacBook Pro line covers all three new chips across two sizes: the 14-inch MacBook Pro can be configured with any of the M3, M3 Pro or M3 Max, while the 16-inch is limited to just the Pro and Max.

The new MacBook Pro, which went on sale that week, was announced at the Scary Fast event alongside a new iMac and several members of the M3 line — a big departure for Apple following rumors it had planned the initial M3 launch for WWDC, before the supply chain thought differently. Announcing the M3, M3 Pro and M3 Max at once affords the company options, though less so for the M3-only iMac. An M3 Ultra is presumably also on the way in the not-too-distant future, but will almost certainly be confined to desktops like the Mac Studio and Mac Pro owing to the limitations of system architectures; Apple also recently shot down rumors surrounding a 27-inch iMac.

On configurations and price, the M3 Max comes in both 14-core CPU/30-core GPU and 16-core CPU/40-core GPU flavors; the review unit was the latter, which also means 48GB of memory and 1TB of storage by default, and it is a $4,000 computer as configured. Bumping memory and storage up to 128GB and 8TB respectively comes to $7,200 — a hefty increase from the base level 14- and 16-inch models, which run $1,600 and $2,500 to start. Apple lowered the barrier of entry for the lowest end model, but upgrades add up quickly; this is a real investment, and a system likely to last a while. Apple is currently on a one-year upgrade cycle for its first-party M-series chips, but it is genuinely tough to imagine an advance as pronounced as the one from Intel to in-house silicon happening any time soon; there is no such thing as a future-proofed laptop, so the best you can hope for is good mileage, which certainly applies here.

Alongside building new chips, Apple has spent the last few years listening to consumers in a way it had not for decades: finally updating the camera, building a better keyboard — the class action settlement probably tipped the scales as well — and ditching the well-meaning but ultimately ineffectual Touch Bar altogether. The arrival of the new 14-inch signaled the merciful end to that technology, as the last Touch Bar Mac, the 13-inch Pro, was replaced by the new 14-inch model.

# Video Game Release

## Definition

A video game release is the point at which a title becomes available to the public to buy or play, and the terms attached to that moment — which platforms it launches on, whether it is exclusive or day-one on a subscription service, and how its price behaves over time — are as much a part of "release" as the launch date itself.

## Context

The corpus discusses release terms most directly around the Microsoft-Activision Blizzard deal: Bethesda's Starfield launched in September 2023 exclusively on PC and Xbox and was playable on Xbox Game Pass from day one, the pattern Microsoft is expected to repeat with future Call of Duty titles once Activision Blizzard's catalog moves to Game Pass. This is presented as a departure from the prior arrangement, in which Sony typically held early access to Call of Duty ahead of general release, including early access to the game, testing, and bonus features. Separately, Black Friday 2023 shopping coverage shows how release timing shapes a game's retail position after launch: a newly released PS5 title, Marvel's Spider-Man 2, was added to the $500 PS5 bundle for no extra cost without any qualification about the deal's value, while Super Smash Bros. Ultimate, released back in 2018 and still retailing for $50-$60 on its own, was also added free to a $350 Nintendo Switch OLED bundle but drew the caveat that its age made it "hard to call...an amazing deal."

## Key Characteristics

- **Day-one platform and service availability** — a release can be tied to specific hardware (Starfield: PC and Xbox only) and can be simultaneously playable on a subscription service like Xbox Game Pass "on the first day they release," rather than requiring a separate purchase.
- **Exclusivity windows precede or follow release** — before the Microsoft-Activision deal, Sony's arrangement with Activision gave it early access to Call of Duty ahead of the general public, plus early testing and bonus features; UK regulators required a 15-year carve-out (via Ubisoft's cloud-streaming rights) to prevent Activision Blizzard titles from becoming Xbox-exclusive after release.
- **Release age shapes how a free pack-in game is framed** — a title's distance from its release date affects how retailers' holiday bundles are perceived: the newly released, critically acclaimed Spider-Man 2 was added free to the full-price $500 PS5 bundle with no caveat, while the 2018-released Smash Bros. Ultimate — still worth $50-$60 on its own — was called out as making its $350 Switch OLED bundle "hard to call...an amazing deal" precisely because the pack-in game was five years old.
- **Distribution model (buy vs. access) is a release-time choice** — Microsoft's habit of putting blockbuster titles on Game Pass at release leaves buyers choosing between purchasing the game outright or paying a monthly fee to access it from day one.

# Roblox As An Online Game Platform

Roblox is a widely popular online game platform that "lets you play, create, and be anything you can imagine," according to its description on the Microsoft Store. Its defining features are that players customise characters and play minigames within the game, and that while the platform is free to download on a number of platforms — including Android and iOS smartphones, Xbox game consoles and Windows computers — players can also spend money on in-game items and customisations.

Its user base is young. According to TechCrunch, Roblox's millions of users range between the ages of eight and 18, with its key demographic between nine and 15 years old — the fact that makes parental controls and spending safeguards the recurring point of contention around the platform.

# Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty

Phantom Liberty, developed by CD Projekt Red for PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X, is ranked 15 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31. Polygon's claim is that, like the best DLC, it does as much to expand on the base game as it does to reframe it.

It arrived alongside the sweeping Patch 2.0, which revamped Cyberpunk 2077's role-playing progression systems, improved its enemy AI, and course-corrected a litany of other details; Phantom Liberty itself adds a whole new district to the dystopian world of Night City, complete with its own spy-thriller storyline.

Critic M. Mahardy's assessment is that the resulting Cyberpunk 2077 is not an entirely different beast than the one released in 2020 but is a more evolved one, delivering on the promise of building a hacker-samurai in a neon-infused open world replete with futuristic heists, daunting choices, and striking characters. Phantom Liberty and Patch 2.0 may not completely erase the memory of CD Projekt's initial botched release, but they come pretty damn close — three years after players first set foot in V's shoes, the game has finally justified the hype.

# Associated Press And OpenAI's Licensing Deal

Select news outlets proved far more amenable to OpenAI than the authors suing it. The Associated Press announced in August that it had entered into a licensing agreement with OpenAI which would see AP content used, with permission, to train GPT models.

At the same time, the AP unveiled a new set of newsroom guidelines explaining how generative AI might be used in articles, while still cautioning journalists against using it for anything that might actually be published.

# Game Patch Notes

## Definition

Neither corpus article uses the phrase "patch notes," but both document the same underlying pattern: a studio bundling a slate of changes — new content, rebalancing, and quality-of-life fixes — under a single named or numbered update tied to a release date.
Polygon's Diablo 4 coverage lists that pattern for "Season 2"/"Season of Blood": leveling speed, new endgame bosses, a Nightmare Dungeon rework, mount handling, and Renown/gem-Stash changes, all bundled to arrive together on Oct. 17 (doc_0533).
Polygon's games-of-the-year piece shows the same pattern for Cyberpunk 2077's named "Patch 2.0," a systems-revamping update shipped alongside — but distinct from — the paid Phantom Liberty expansion (doc_0213).

## Context

The corpus's clearest example is Diablo 4's Season 2 update, "Season of Blood," reported by Polygon on 2023-10-04: alongside new vampire powers, Blizzard shipped a broad slate of quality-of-life changes covering leveling speed, endgame bosses, Nightmare Dungeon design, mount handling, and the Renown and gem/Stash systems, all set to arrive together on Oct. 17 as one seasonal patch.

Polygon's broader 2023 games-of-the-year piece shows the same pattern in a second game: Cyberpunk 2077's Phantom Liberty expansion arrived "alongside the sweeping Patch 2.0," which revamped the base game's role-playing progression systems, improved enemy AI, and "course-corrected a litany of other details" — a patch bundled with, but distinct from, the paid DLC content it accompanied.

## Key Characteristics

- **Versioned or seasonal framing** — changes are grouped under a single identifier (Patch 2.0, Season 2/"Season of Blood") rather than released piecemeal, per doc_0533 and doc_0213.
- **Mix of change types** — a single patch bundles new content (Diablo 4's five endgame bosses), rebalancing (faster leveling, reworked Nightmare Dungeon affixes), and quality-of-life fixes (Renown carryover, gems no longer taking bag space), per doc_0533.
- **Developer-explained rationale** — studios attach commentary to justify changes, as when Diablo 4's game director Joe Shely and associate director Joe Piepiora told Polygon the quality-of-life focus came from finally having time to react to player feedback, unlike the rushed first season (doc_0533).
- **Distinct from paid content** — a patch can ship independently of or alongside paid expansions; Cyberpunk 2077's Patch 2.0 revamped core systems while Phantom Liberty (the paid DLC) added new story content, and reviewers credit the patch as much as the DLC for the game's improved reception (doc_0213).

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, this kind of update bundle has a generic industry name: release notes (also called patch notes).
Per Wikipedia, release notes "describe important information about a distribution of a hardware or software product" and typically include "a list of what is new in the release, including bug fixes and new features" (Wikipedia, "Release notes," accessed 2026-09-02).

# Foundation Model Reporting And Red-Team Disclosure Under The EO

The executive order sets out a reporting procedure for the most capable AI systems: a company developing any foundation model that poses a serious risk to national security, national economic security, or national public health and safety must notify the federal government when training the model, and must share the results of all red-team safety tests — and that information must be shared prior to the model being made available to the public, which could help reduce the rate at which companies unleash half-baked and potentially deadly machine learning products. The legal instrument used to compel this is the Defense Production Act.

Alongside red-team results, the EO also requires disclosure of the system's training runs — essentially its iterative development history. The purpose officials gave for the sequencing is verification: "What that does is that creates a space prior to the release… to verify that the system is safe and secure." The EO more broadly directs the establishment of new standards for AI safety and security, including reporting requirements for developers whose foundation models might impact national or economic security, and those requirements also apply in developing AI tools to autonomously implement security fixes on critical software infrastructure.

The procedure has a deliberately narrow scope. Administration officials were quick to point out that the reporting requirement will not affect any AI models currently available on the market, nor independent or small- to medium-size AI companies going forward, because the threshold for enforcement is quite high. It is geared specifically at the next generation of systems that the likes of Google, Meta and OpenAI are already working on, with enforcement on models starting at 10^26 petaflops — a capacity currently beyond the limits of existing AI models. "This is not going to catch AI systems trained by graduate students, or even professors," the administration official said.

The order was cast as a step past voluntary measures. "In response to the President's leadership on the subject, 15 major American technology companies have begun their voluntary commitments to ensure that AI technology is safe, secure and trustworthy before releasing it to the public," the senior administration official said. "That is not enough."

# Baldur's Gate 3

Baldur's Gate 3, developed by Larian Studios for PlayStation 5 and Windows PC, is ranked 2 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31, and Polygon says it hit at the perfect moment.

The timing argument has two parts. Despite the handful of truly great computer role-playing games released since the early 2000s — Larian itself made waves with its Divinity: Original Sin series in 2014 and 2017 — the genre had largely remained a modern niche; but Dungeons & Dragons has undergone something of a renaissance thanks to actual-play series like Critical Role and Dimension 20, and Larian had two years of player feedback with which to build its new masterpiece. That masterpiece launched in August and garnered the kind of attention that catapults a game from niche interests to widespread acclaim: old CRPG fans finally came home, the Mass Effect generation discovered a new kind of RPG, and D&D fans found an exceptional digital version of their beloved tabletop game to play alone or with their party in co-op.

Critic RG writes that like a good DM, the game teases out story beats that feel personal to you, cleverly luring you into experiences that seem like they would not make sense in anyone else's campaign; every act delivers quiet, memorable character moments and anxiety-inducing battles, all feeling organic, letting the game replicate as closely as a video game can D&D's best feature — the intoxicating sense that anything could happen at any moment. The best games that year told their stories in interesting ways, but Baldur's Gate 3 takes experimental storytelling to another level, with every choice and every new direction a simple success, fail, or crit away; one roll of the dice after another can take you all the way from a crashed Nautiloid to the city of Baldur's Gate itself, and it is the spinning whir of its d20 that defined video game storytelling in 2023.

# Product Launch

## Definition

Across this corpus, "launch" (and "launched") is used to describe a company unveiling, announcing, or first shipping a new product, feature, or device — the corpus does not itself define the term, but consistently applies it to this announce-and/or-ship moment (see Context).

## Background (external)

ProductPlan's product-management glossary defines a product launch as "a business's planned and coordinated effort to debut a new product to the market and make that product generally available for purchase," noting that launches also build anticipation, gather early-adopter feedback, and generate momentum beyond simply enabling sales (ProductPlan, accessed 2026-09-02, https://www.productplan.com/glossary/product-launch/).

## Context

Across the corpus, launches recur as the mechanism by which companies move a product from development into the market, and the term covers a spectrum from a single press event to a multi-year rollout. Google's annual hardware event unveiled the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro alongside the Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds and Pixel Watch 2, showing that a single launch event can bundle several products at once. Apple's "Scary Fast" event was anticipated as the venue for unveiling M3-powered MacBook Pros, a refreshed iMac, and new USB-C accessories, illustrating that launches are often previewed and rumored before the event itself. Amazon's "Explore with Alexa" was "first announced in September" and only became available afterward, alongside the Echo Pop Kids speakers being "available for purchase" at $49.99 — showing the announce-then-ship pattern explicitly. OpenAI's ChatGPT similarly moved through staged launches: an initial November 2022 release, then a paid ChatGPT Plus tier and plug-in/API support unveiled in March 2023, then further features (Enterprise, browsing, voice, GPTs) rolled out through the rest of the year. Valve's Steam Deck OLED was announced at a press event ahead of its device launch, with press being told units would be "available to order" on a specific date and begin shipping shortly after. Keep Labs' medication-storage device took years between its 2019 preorder campaign and "this week started shipping its first product to consumers," showing a launch can be delayed substantially between announcement and actual availability.

## Key Characteristics

- **Two-stage structure** — an "unveiling" or announcement stage (often at a press or hardware event) is followed by a separate "available for purchase" or shipping stage, and the gap between them can range from days to years, as with Keep Labs' multi-year gap between its 2019 preorder campaign and 2023 shipping date.
- **Bundling** — a single launch event frequently introduces multiple products or features together, as Google did with the Pixel 8 line, Android 14, and several accessories in one hardware event.
- **Pre-launch anticipation** — launches are frequently preceded by rumors and analyst predictions about what will be unveiled, as with the expected Apple "Scary Fast" event coverage of M3 chips and MacBook Pro refreshes before the event occurred.
- **Staged/iterative rollout** — for software products like ChatGPT, "launch" is not a single moment but a sequence of feature releases (Plus tier, plugins, Enterprise, voice, GPTs) unveiled over many months following the initial debut.
- **Concrete availability signals** — corpus reporting marks a launch's completion with specific, checkable facts: a price, an order date, or a shipping date, e.g. the Steam Deck OLED being "available to order on November 16th" with shipping "as orders start to roll in," or the Echo Pop Kids being "available for purchase, starting at $49.99."

# The M3 MacBook Pro Lineup And Its Configurations

The M3 MacBook Pro line covers all three new chips across two sizes: the 14-inch MacBook Pro can be configured with any of the M3, M3 Pro or M3 Max, while the 16-inch is limited to just the Pro and Max.

The new MacBook Pro, which went on sale that week, was announced at the Scary Fast event alongside a new iMac and several members of the M3 line — a big departure for Apple following rumors it had planned the initial M3 launch for WWDC, before the supply chain thought differently. Announcing the M3, M3 Pro and M3 Max at once affords the company options, though less so for the M3-only iMac. An M3 Ultra is presumably also on the way in the not-too-distant future, but will almost certainly be confined to desktops like the Mac Studio and Mac Pro owing to the limitations of system architectures; Apple also recently shot down rumors surrounding a 27-inch iMac.

On configurations and price, the M3 Max comes in both 14-core CPU/30-core GPU and 16-core CPU/40-core GPU flavors; the review unit was the latter, which also means 48GB of memory and 1TB of storage by default, and it is a $4,000 computer as configured. Bumping memory and storage up to 128GB and 8TB respectively comes to $7,200 — a hefty increase from the base level 14- and 16-inch models, which run $1,600 and $2,500 to start. Apple lowered the barrier of entry for the lowest end model, but upgrades add up quickly; this is a real investment, and a system likely to last a while. Apple is currently on a one-year upgrade cycle for its first-party M-series chips, but it is genuinely tough to imagine an advance as pronounced as the one from Intel to in-house silicon happening any time soon; there is no such thing as a future-proofed laptop, so the best you can hope for is good mileage, which certainly applies here.

Alongside building new chips, Apple has spent the last few years listening to consumers in a way it had not for decades: finally updating the camera, building a better keyboard — the class action settlement probably tipped the scales as well — and ditching the well-meaning but ultimately ineffectual Touch Bar altogether. The arrival of the new 14-inch signaled the merciful end to that technology, as the last Touch Bar Mac, the 13-inch Pro, was replaced by the new 14-inch model.
