# Jada Pinkett Smith's 2023 Disclosure Of A Seven-Year Separation

Jada Pinkett Smith revealed in October 2023 that she and her husband Will Smith had been separated for the previous seven years — that is, since 2016 — while remaining married. The disclosure came in an interview with People given while she was promoting her memoir Worthy; The Independent's timeline piece dates the publication to 11 October, while its other reports on the same interview date it 10 October. Pinkett Smith, 52, said of her 26-year marriage to the 55-year-old actor that the couple are "still figuring it out": "We've been doing some really heavy-duty work together. We just got deep love for each other and we are going to figure out what that looks like for us."

She anchored the timeline to the 2022 Academy Awards, when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock after the comedian made a joke about her appearance: at that moment, she said, the pair had already been separated for six years. The revelation was treated as major news — "sent shockwaves around the world," in The Independent's phrasing — because both Smiths had previously doubled down on their stance against divorce, so a lengthy separation raised a new question: when should a couple simply get a divorce?

# Wildest Dreams: Imagining The End Before The Relationship Begins

Wildest Dreams is defined by anticipatory disillusion — Taylor Swift imagines the end of a relationship before it has truly begun, asking her partner, when it all goes wrong, "Say you'll remember me / Standing in a nice dress / Staring at the sunset." It belongs to a wider strand on 1989 in which growing up means letting go of youthful optimism: on one hand she has developed an ability to laugh off her critics, on the other she seems increasingly jaded about love.

Swift described the shift in her own terms to Rolling Stone: "The way I used to approach relationships was very idealistic. I used to go into them thinking, 'Maybe this is the one - we'll get married and have a family, this could be forever'. Whereas now I go in thinking, 'How long do we have on the clock before something comes along and puts a wrench in it, or your publicist calls and says this isn't a good idea?'" An early draft of the lyrics had the couple fleeing the city and blotting out the pressures of the world, an idea which eventually resurfaced in I Know Places.

# The Gaza Information War And The Hamas Narrative

Eylon Levy argues that the conflict is not only a kinetic war in Gaza but also an information war, in which the Hamas narrative is adopted far more easily than Israel's account is accepted. His first ground is a case of a claim that collapsed: the day after what he calls the bluff about the Al-Ahli hospital, which the Palestinians claimed had been hit by an Israeli missile killing 800 civilians but which in the end turned out to have been caused by a splinter group of Islamic Jihad, with no hospital destroyed and certainly not 800 people killed, he explained on Sky News that Hamas lies and makes up numbers, and the reporter asked him, almost speechless with surprise, whether he doubts Hamas' numbers. He describes such moments as intensely frustrating, recounting a BBC interview in which the interviewer told him "Hamas denies what you are saying", to which his answer is that of course Hamas denies this, since Hamas denies that it is even holding hostages, and Hamas massacres, beheads, rapes, burns families and then day and night denies that it did so. Some journalists around the world see that Hamas continues to lie about the biggest things when the whole truth is in front of everyone's eyes, and they continue to echo the lies.

His second ground is a structural claim about where information from Gaza comes from: it comes either directly from Hamas or from independent reporters and photographers who are part of the system in Gaza, and everyone knows that even if they are not affiliated with Hamas they are not free to present the full truth because they are not allowed to. The evidence he offers for the constraint is what is missing: there is not a single photo of a terrorist, not a single photo of a missile being launched from a densely populated area, from a mosque or a school, not even a single photo from the Hamas tunnels under Shifa; the reason is that these reporters, even if not explicitly on Hamas' side, operate under a dictatorial regime and cannot provide the information even if they wanted to, which is why he thinks it very important to keep reminding the world how biased the information reaching them is. Levy qualifies the argument explicitly: he does not want to give the impression that all interviewers are hostile and every question delusional, and he has many interviews with reporters who understand what is happening and simply want information and to hear the Israeli side, which is completely legitimate.

# Celebrity Endorsement

In the corpus, "celebrity endorsements" is named directly only once — listed alongside "campaign trail rallies" as one of several online-campaign tactics that, on their own, are "not enough to engage voters online" — and everywhere else the corpus treats it as a family of concrete cases rather than a defined category: FTX's paid partnerships with athletes, Anna Wintour's sponsorship request to Sam Bankman-Fried, The Epoch Times' political endorsements and CPAC sponsorship, and Vivek Ramaswamy's TikTok launch via a Jake Paul endorsement.

## Context

The corpus documents celebrity endorsement as a recurring marketing and political tactic across unrelated domains. FTX bought "mainstream recognition with branding deals and partnerships," most visibly by partnering with celebrities like Tom Brady and his ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, Steph Curry, Shaquille O'Neal, and Naomi Osaka; a follow-up account puts a price on two of those deals, with Tom Brady paid $55 million and Steph Curry $35 million to "lend FTX legitimacy and edge." Anna Wintour — described in the corpus as "the icy fashion doyenne" — separately reached out to Sam Bankman-Fried to ask him to sponsor her Met Costume Ball, a related but distinct pattern of soliciting a sponsor rather than a spokesperson. The Epoch Times pursued the same logic in politics rather than commerce: a hired Republican strategist "achieved the goal" of legitimizing the outlet by securing interviews and introductions with conservative politicians and media figures at the Conservative Political Action Conference, where the outlet was also billed as a "supporting sponsor." In the 2023 Republican presidential primary, Vivek Ramaswamy tried the same move digitally, launching his TikTok presence "with an endorsement from Jake Paul" to reach young voters. Corporate sponsorship of events and venues appears as a companion pattern to celebrity endorsement rather than a synonym for it: FTX separately bought the naming rights to the Miami Heat's home arena, and English football's League Cup has been renamed after a succession of corporate sponsors (Coca-Cola, Worthington's, Carling, and currently Carabao) with no celebrity attached.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transfer of legitimacy or attention** — the endorsing figure's fame is meant to "lend legitimacy and edge" to the endorsed brand, as stated of the Tom Brady and Steph Curry deals with FTX.
- **Often explicitly paid** — reported dollar figures ($55 million for Brady, $35 million for Curry) show the arrangement is frequently a straightforward commercial transaction, not a spontaneous show of support.
- **Can misfire when authenticity is doubted** — Jake Paul's endorsement of Ramaswamy "only drove animosity from TikTok viewers," because the Paul brothers have "a reputation of promoting anyone and anything for a paycheck," and viewers "immediately questioned how much Ramaswamy paid him."
- **Distinct from, but adjacent to, event/venue sponsorship** — naming-rights deals (FTX and the Miami Heat arena) and tournament title sponsorships (the Carabao Cup) trade a brand name for association with an audience, without necessarily involving an individual celebrity endorser.
- **Can trigger public backlash independent of the endorsed party** — Web Summit's corporate sponsors and speakers withdrew their association after the event's founder, Paddy Cosgrave, made controversial comments about the Israel-Hamas conflict, with fintech entrepreneur David Marcus vowing "I'll never attend/sponsor/speak at any of your events again," showing that sponsor/endorser relationships run in both directions and can be revoked.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, celebrity endorsement (sometimes called celebrity branding) is a marketing method that uses a famous person to promote something, on the theory that "the positive image of the celebrity transfers to the brand," boosting public attention and trust; its success typically hinges on how well the celebrity fits the product and how genuine the association seems. (Wikipedia, "Celebrity branding," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celebrity_branding)

# Johansson's Rebuttals To The Case Against The CSAM Scanning Proposal

Against opponents who characterise her CSAM-scanning proposal as mass surveillance, as a slippery slope, and as a law written around two vendors' technology, Ylva Johansson argued to MEPs that each of those premises is wrong: the proposal names no technology, would scan less than happens today, and forbids using detection for anything other than child sexual abuse. TechCrunch reported her answers on 25 October 2023, from her appearance before the committee.

The opposition she was answering had been aired earlier that week. A seminar organized by the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), an advisory body to the Commission on data protection law, heard from more than 20 speakers across civil society, academia and industry expressing deep misgivings about the Commission's approach — including a warning from the EDPS himself that the EU could be at a tipping point for freedom and democracy if it does not turn back from the plan to do non-targeted scanning of private messages. Johansson had been invited to participate in the seminar but declined to attend, and she did not offer a direct response to the EDPS' concerns at the hearing, instead countering a number of the arguments heard at the session.

Her first counter attacks the premise that the proposal is built around particular vendors. She denied that only Thorn and Microsoft have technology "that is necessary for the scanning", calling that claim "absolutely not true". "There are no specific technologies mentioned [in the proposal] and I think this is an important part. So there's no specific technology that's been favoured in this proposal," she told the committee, adding: "So many technologies are being developed all the time — while we are speaking — and they will continue to develop. So I think it's important that the legislation has to be technology neutral."

Her second counter attacks the inference from the proposal to mass surveillance. "My proposal would not mean that all communication will be scanned. Compared to the situation today it will be much more limited," she claimed, referencing the temporary ePrivacy derogation that currently gives messaging firms a legal basis to scan non-encrypted content for CSAM — a derogation intended to be replaced by the proposed regulation which, critics contend, will force platforms to scan end-to-end encrypted content too. "Today companies are allowed to scan if they search for child sexual abuse material. That's why we receive these 5.2 million videos and pictures and grooming attempts — 70% from private communication. If my proposal is adopted, this will be limited."

The warrant she offered for that comparison is the proposal's ordering of obligations: in-scope platforms are first required to deploy prevention measures to try to stop the spread of CSAM and/or prevent abuse of their tools by people intent on abusing children. "First comes prevention. Only if prevention is not enough, then you might be allowed to do detection — but only after a court decision," she said. "So only those that really cannot deal with the problem with mitigating measures… and only after a court decision and only during a specific period they will be allowed to do the detection. We will also limit the reporting so that we will also receive fewer but hopefully better reports."

Her third counter attacks the overreach and slippery-slope premises by pointing outside the proposal, to other EU laws acting as balancing checks on the scope of possible CSAM-scanning. "It's also important that we continue to comply with all relevant legislation. For example the GDPR and other requirements, there are no derogation from that in my proposal," she said. "It's also important — and I know that's been part of the debate — that it should not be a slippery slope. The proposal specifically prohibits using the detection technologies for any other purpose than the detection of child sexual abuse online — and only with verified indicators of child sexual abuse provided by the EU Centre."

That defensive strategy carries its own exposure. Given her reliance on pointing to the existence of a wider EU legal framework doing the heavy lifting and protecting Europeans' fundamental rights as a way to assuage critics, and given she is also invoking respect for the rule of law as a buttress against the risk of content-scanning mission creep, it is doubly relevant that the Commission now finds itself in a bind — forced to investigate whether its own officials ignored legal requirements in a bid to covertly sweep past critics.

# Ohanian's Case for Techno-Optimism

Despite the problems with social media and the urgency, in terms of its impact on society, Alexis Ohanian argued in remarks reported on 31 October 2023 that there is still some hope — that the next generation of platforms can be built better, and that user appetite will itself turn against the current design. He gave two grounds. The first is who is building now: he noted that the founders his fund 776 invests in are much smarter and more aware of the issues than he ever was at their age, so perhaps the next platforms will still be addictive, but in a way that doesn't "further disrupt democracy." The second is a prediction about demand: he believes that after everything on social media becomes so perfectly curated for us, our brains will start to crave things that are not. The warrant tying grounds to conclusion is that the harms are contingent on choices made by a less aware cohort of founders working against an audience that had not yet tired of curation — change either and the outcome changes.

Ohanian drew the consequence out in terms of what comes after the feed: "I think we'll see a rebirth of live gatherings and in-person experiences…the bright side of this is that I hope it then gets us back in touch with our humanity, and the things that no amount of AI can replace." # PhilHealth's Earmarked Revenue Model As A Template For PhilEd

PhilHealth's financing model combines member premiums and local government subsidies for enrolled indigents with earmarked national revenues. It receives a share of the "sin taxes" collected from tobacco and sugar-sweetened beverages, justified on the ground that tobacco smokers and sugar-sweetened beverage drinkers impose an additional burden on the healthcare system and so must contribute to health services; in Fiscal Year 2022 this amounted to P74 billion. Under the Universal Health Care Law, PhilHealth also receives 50% of the government share from the income of the Philippine Amusement Gaming Corp. and 40% of the Charity Fund of the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office, which in 2022 amounted to P188 billion.

The proposal transposes that structure to education. In addition to the school vouchers funded under the Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act, the authors suggest PhilEd be allocated a share of the taxes imposed on extractive industries, on the argument that the depletion of natural resources can only be justified if the taxes collected enhance human resources. # The Latent HIV Reservoir Challenge

The core obstacle to curing HIV is that the virus builds resilient genetic reservoirs inside human cells: "The existing challenge in HIV treatment lies in the virus creating resilient genetic reservoirs within human cells," Elena Herrera-Carrillo, an associate professor of infectious disease at Amsterdam University Medical Centers, told Live Science.

The mechanism runs as follows. HIV infects immune cells that are normally used to fight infection in the virus's host, and uses an immune cell's machinery to insert its own DNA into the host's genome, which allows the virus to replicate. If an HIV infection is not treated, it can lead to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), which results in a severely weakened immune system and leaves the infected person highly vulnerable to other infections, cancers and early death. The reservoir phenomenon, known as "latent HIV," occurs when the virus infects a type of immune cell called CD4+ memory T cells, which can persist for decades. Herrera-Carrillo's lab focuses on using CRISPR to edit cells that harbor HIV reservoirs despite ongoing cART therapy, because cART can suppress viral replication but, if the treatment is interrupted, "the dormant proviruses can reactivate, making a cure elusive," she said. That relation — suppression holds only while therapy continues, and integrated proviral DNA survives it — is what defines the boundary of what current therapy can achieve.

# The COP28 Final Text's Language On Transitioning Away From Fossil Fuels

The Verge notes that every word in that phrase is pretty dirty: coal is the most polluting fossil fuel, one reason it's hard to ignore in a climate agreement, but a commitment to phase down its use is decidedly weaker than one to phase it out, and the wording mirrors a recent letter to participating governments from COP28 president Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, who is also the CEO of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company. # EU Enforcement Steps Against X Over DSA Compliance

Between 10 and 13 October 2023 the European Union escalated against Elon Musk-owned X in two steps: a public warning letter on Wednesday from internal market commissioner Thierry Breton, and then, late on Thursday, a formal request for information sent by the Commission under the Digital Services Act. Crucially, no investigation had been opened at that point — EU officials confirmed to TechCrunch that an investigation had not been taken, and TechCrunch substantially revised its original report to make clear that a formal request for information, while it could prefigure a formal announcement of an investigation, is not yet that formal technical step.

The warning came first. In his "urgent" letter, shared on X by Breton himself, the bloc sent the strongest signal yet that it believed Musk's platform was in breach of the DSA — though this was by no means Musk's first warning. Breton wrote that the EU had "indications" that X was being used to disseminate illegal content and disinformation in the EU following Saturday's attacks, then reminded the company of the DSA's "very precise obligations" on content moderation: "When you receive notices of illegal content in the EU, you must be timely, diligent and objective in taking action and removing the relevant content when warranted," he warned, adding, "We have, from qualified sources, reports about potentially illegal content circulating on your service despite flags from relevant authorities." He also took issue with a change X had made the previous night to the public interest policy under which it judges newsworthiness — the test for whether posts that infringe its rules may nonetheless remain on the site — which Breton said had left "many European users uncertain" about how X applies its own rules. That matters under the DSA because the regulation requires platforms to be clear and transparent about their rules and how they apply them, "particularly relevant when it comes to violent and terrorist content that appears to circulate on your platform." Breton further said X should have "proportionate and effective mitigation measures" in place to tackle "the risks to public security and civic discourse stemming from disinformation." The EU asked Musk to make contact with relevant law enforcement authorities and Europol and to "ensure that you respond promptly to their requests", flagged unspecified additional DSA compliance issues his team would raise "shortly" — "with a specific request" — and gave Musk a deadline of 24 hours to respond, stipulating that his answer would be added to the bloc's assessment file on X's DSA compliance. The letter closed: "I remind you that following the opening of a potential investigation and a finding of non-compliance, penalties can be imposed."

The formal request for information followed. It came after the Wednesday warning about reports of illegal content and disinformation targeting the Israel-Hamas war circulating on the platform, and after Twitter's CEO sent a high-level, non-specific response to that warning. The Commission said it was looking at X's compliance with the DSA across a number of areas — its policies and practices regarding notices on illegal content; complaint handling; risk assessment; and measures to mitigate the risks identified. In its press release the EU wrote that "This request follows indications received by the Commission services of the alleged spreading of illegal content and disinformation, in particular the spreading of terrorist and violent content and hate speech," adding that the ask also addressed other aspects of DSA compliance.

The request carried explicit deadlines and consequences. X had until October 18 to provide information about "the activation and functioning of X's crisis response protocol", and until October 31 to respond to the other requests. "Based on the assessment of X replies, the Commission will assess next steps," the Commission wrote. "This could entail the formal opening of proceedings pursuant to Article 66 of the DSA." The regulation also includes powers to impose fines for "incorrect, incomplete or misleading information in response to a request for information", and the EU added that "In case of failure to reply by X, the Commission may decide to request the information by decision. In this case, failure to reply by the deadline could lead to the imposition of period penalties." TechCrunch noted that the pace at which regulators were moving was a strong indication of the bloc's direction of travel, and that its revised report also corrected an error in the original which had referred to Interpol rather than Europol.

# SEO Conference Culture And Its Excesses

After years of being friends online, the SEOs were eager to let loose in person, giving off what Forrester described as "that vibe of a lot of young people with access to a lot of money. And it was like, no expenses spared in New York City."

For Forrester it was the start of a long career of keynote presentations and consummate schmoozing — Clay, the father of SEO, described him as "a cruise director" on the SS SEO. The circuit has treated him well: he has attended events in Napa, Hawaii, and Barbados among many others, as well as "an infinite number of private dinners and these types of things in every city you can think of, at the most lavish restaurants," he said. "I've lost track of how many Michelin-starred meals I've had, 'cause it's now in the dozens, from my time in this industry. And I'm not going to say no to the dinner that everyone's going to, that one company is sponsoring because it's a thank you to everybody who contributed to, whatever it was, you know? And you go and everybody has a good time. You talk about the industry, and that's it. And it becomes the stuff of legends."

Over the years he has seen it all, remembering "walking into hotel rooms and it's two o'clock in the morning, there's drugs and alcohol and everything everywhere, and there's a party going on." He marveled at the audacity of his fellow SEOs: "Somebody showed up and brought her Aston Martin to a conference and parked it at the front door. Immediately got a parking ticket." When he suggested she relocate the car before it got towed, she said she would just move it to the next parking spot and get another ticket — "It's cheaper for me to leave the car parked out front and use it as a way to start conversations with potential clients than it is for me to rent a suite at the hotel and get people to go to the suite to have the same conversation." Then she offered him a joyride around Seattle, and obviously he said yes.

Representing a search engine changed the rules. Once he represented Bing, Forrester more or less stopped drinking at conferences, as had long been the case for his counterpart at Google, an engineer named Matt Cutts, who helped build and then ran the company's web spam team before stepping back in 2014 and leaving in 2016.

In 2010 Demis Hassabis and two colleagues, all living in Britain, were looking for money to start building "artificial general intelligence", a machine that could do anything the brain could do, at a time when few people were interested in AI because after a half-century of research the field had failed to deliver anything remotely close to the human brain. Some scientists and thinkers had nonetheless become fixated on AI's downsides, and many, including the three young men, had a connection to Eliezer Yudkowsky, an internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher who led a community calling themselves Rationalists or, later, effective altruists; they believed AI could find a cure for cancer or solve climate change but worried that AI bots might do things their creators had not intended, arguing that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators. Peter Thiel, enormously wealthy through an early investment in Facebook and his work with Musk in the early days of PayPal, had developed a fascination with the singularity, the science-fiction trope describing the moment when intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity, and with his funding Yudkowsky had expanded his AI lab and created an annual conference on the singularity; one of Hassabis' colleagues had met Yudkowsky years before and snagged them speaking spots at that conference, ensuring an invitation to Thiel's party, where Yudkowsky introduced Hassabis to Thiel. They named the company DeepMind, a nod to "deep learning", a way for AI systems to learn skills by analysing large amounts of data, to neuroscience, and to the Deep Thought supercomputer from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, and by the spring of 2010 they were building their dream machine, wholeheartedly believing that because they understood the risks they were uniquely positioned to protect the world. The corpus also treats venture capital as an industry with its own geography and macro trends: Sand Hill Road as the physical center of Silicon Valley VC, Sequoia Capital as a "high-powered venture capital firm" whose former partner was among the witnesses lined up to testify in the FTX trial, Israeli startups drawing $95 billion in venture capital over the prior five years even as funding had already fallen 73% year-over-year in the first half of 2023 — a decline reported in July, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector — and US-headquartered VC investment into China collapsing from $45.4 billion to $14.5 billion between 2021 and 2022 amid Beijing's tech crackdowns and Washington's new restrictions on outbound U.S. investment in Chinese tech.

## Key Characteristics

- **Equity-for-capital exchange with startups** — VCs and VC firms fund privately held companies in return for an ownership stake, as with Thiel's firm taking a position in DeepMind and Accel leading Rainforest's seed round.
- **Staged by named rounds** — investment is tranched into seed, pre-Series A, and Series A/B/C/D rounds that track a company's maturity, illustrated by FTX's Series C, StarNews Mobile's pre-Series A, and Clearco's Series D.
- **Concentrated in identifiable firms and hubs** — a small set of named firms (Sequoia Capital, Accel, Index Ventures, Motier Ventures, Janngo Capital) and physical hubs (Sand Hill Road) recur as the deal-making core of the industry.
- **Sensitive to macro and geopolitical conditions** — VC deployment can swing sharply with regulatory crackdowns and geopolitics, as shown by the drop in US VC activity in China and the 73% year-over-year decline in Israeli startup funding reported in mid-2023, before the October Hamas attacks further disrupted the sector.
- **Distinct from the startups it funds** — the corpus consistently separates the VC firm/investor role (Sequoia, Accel, Janngo Capital, UpWest) from the founder/startup role it capitalizes, even when the same article covers both.

## Background (external)

More broadly, and outside what this corpus documents, venture capital is generally defined as a form of private-equity financing supplied by specialized firms or funds to startup, early-stage, and emerging companies judged to have high growth potential, in exchange for equity or an ownership stake (Wikipedia, "Venture capital," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venture_capital).

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# DeepMind's Ethics Board And Its Single Meeting In 2015

When Musk invested in DeepMind he broke his own informal rule that he would not invest in any company he didn't run himself, and the downsides were already apparent when, only a month or so after his birthday spat with Larry Page, he again found himself face to face with his former friend. The occasion was the first meeting of DeepMind's ethics board on 14 August 2015, a board set up at the insistence of the startup's founders to ensure their technology did no harm after the sale. The members convened in a conference room just outside Musk's office at SpaceX, but that is where Musk's control ended: when Google bought DeepMind it bought the whole thing, and Musk was out, financially ahead but unhappy. Three Google executives now firmly in control of DeepMind were there, Page, Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder and Tesla investor, and Eric Schmidt, Google's chair, along with other attendees including Reid Hoffman, another PayPal founder, and Toby Ord, an Australian philosopher studying "existential risk".

The DeepMind founders reported that they were pushing ahead with their work but were aware the technology carried serious risks. Mustafa Suleyman gave a presentation called "The Pitchforkers Are Coming", telling the board that AI could lead to an explosion in disinformation and fretting that as the technology replaced countless jobs in coming years the public would accuse Google of stealing their livelihoods, so Google would need to share its wealth with the millions who could no longer find work and provide a "universal basic income". Musk agreed, but it was pretty clear the Google guests were not prepared to embark on a redistribution of their wealth: Schmidt said he thought the worries were completely overblown, and Page, in his usual whisper, agreed, arguing AI would create more jobs than it took away. Eight months later DeepMind had a breakthrough that stunned the AI community and the world, when a DeepMind machine called AlphaGo beat one of the world's best players at the ancient game of Go, a match streamed over the internet and watched by 200 million people across the globe, though most researchers had assumed AI needed another 10 years to muster the ingenuity to do that; the South Korean professional Lee Se-dol played Go against AlphaGo in March 2016.

# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.

# The Schatz-Kennedy AI Labeling Act

Senators Brian Schatz (D-HI) and John Kennedy (R-LA) introduced legislation on Tuesday that would provide more transparency on AI-generated content by requiring clear labeling and disclosures — technology that could resemble the Content Credentials tag the C2PA and CAI industry advocacy groups are developing.

The bill, which its sponsors call the Schatz-Kennedy AI Labeling Act, would require generative AI system developers to clearly and conspicuously disclose AI-generated content to users. Those developers, and their licensees, would also have to take "reasonable steps" to prevent "systematic publication of content without disclosures." The bill would additionally establish a working group to create non-binding technical standards to help social media platforms automatically identify such content.

Schatz framed the measure plainly in a press statement: "Our bill is simple. If any content is made by artificial intelligence, it should be labeled so that people are aware and aren't fooled or scammed." Speaking on the Senate floor the same Tuesday, he added that the bill "puts the onus where it belongs: on the companies and not the consumers," and argued that "labels will help people to be informed. They will also help companies using AI to build trust in their content."

The withdrawals then moved from individual companies to the state level when the Israeli ambassador to Portugal, Dor Shapiro, waded in. "Today, I wrote to the Mayor of Lisbon informing him that Israel will not participate in the #WebSummit conference due to the outrageous statements made by the conference CEO Paddy Cosgrave. # OpenAI's Founding And Its 2023 Board Crisis

The Rosewood hotel dinner led to the creation of a startup called OpenAI later that year; backed by hundreds of millions of dollars from Elon Musk and other funders, the lab promised to protect the world from Larry Page's vision. The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# Dangerous Organizations and Individuals Policy

The Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy is the named enforcement category Meta cites when it removes content tied to groups that governments designate as terrorist organizations, most directly Hamas.
In the corpus its practical trigger is Hamas: content praising or supporting Hamas, which governs Gaza and is designated a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union, is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms.
Meta tracks enforcement of this policy as its own category, separate from its Violence and Incitement policy, reporting that it removed "seven times as many pieces of content on a daily basis for violating our Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy in Hebrew and Arabic alone" in the three days after October 7, 2023, compared with the two months prior.

## Context

In the corpus the policy is the mechanism through which Meta enforces against Hamas-related content during the Israel-Hamas war, and it is the recurring flashpoint in disputes over whether that enforcement is applied evenly.
Meta invokes the policy to justify removing content that praises or supports Hamas — Hamas being "designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union" — and Instagram separately cited a related "Community Guidelines against violence or dangerous organizations" when it denied that a specific violent, threatening comment violated its rules, illustrating that the same policy family both blocks and, in users' eyes, under-enforces depending on the content.
The designation logic recurs beyond Meta's own platform actions: the corpus notes that Hamas is "considered a terrorist organization by the U.K., U.S. and other countries" in the context of the Web Summit/Cosgrave controversy, and that UNRWA operates "alongside Hamas, which Israel, the United States and other countries designate as a terrorist organization" in Gaza — showing the same underlying designation of Hamas driving both platform moderation policy and geopolitical characterization of the region's governing party.

## Key Characteristics

- **Named, tracked enforcement category** — Meta reports removal volumes specifically "for violating our Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy," distinct from its Violence and Incitement policy, letting the company cite a sevenfold daily increase in Hebrew/Arabic enforcement after October 7.
- **Anchored to external terrorist designations** — the policy's practical trigger in the corpus is content supporting Hamas, an organization the U.S., EU and U.K. designate as a terrorist group; the platform rule imports government designations rather than defining "dangerous" independently.
- **Contested in application** — Palestinian users and digital-rights advocates argue the policy (and its Community Guidelines "violence or dangerous organizations" language) is enforced inconsistently, citing a case where a violent, threatening comment was ruled not to violate it, and past instances where the Al-Aqsa Mosque hashtag was blocked after being "mistaken for a terrorist organization."
- **Localized to Arabic and Hebrew content** — the volume Meta cites for this policy is scoped specifically to Hebrew and Arabic content, not platform-wide, reflecting the languages most implicated in Israel-Hamas war content moderation.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, Meta's own Community Standards describe the Dangerous Organizations and Individuals policy more broadly than the Hamas-specific enforcement described above: it generally bars praise, substantive support, and representation of any individual or organization that Meta designates as dangerous, a designation list that spans terrorist organizations, hate organizations, criminal organizations, and other violence-inducing entities, not just Hamas.

# Technology Dependence Creates Defense Blind Spots

Avner Barnea argues that relying on technology produces a specific cognitive failure: "When the thinking is that you don't need soldiers because there are monitors, you expect in advance that you will receive the warning about the threat via the technological means and no one imagines a situation in which the observation array would be neutralized. On the contrary, it is seen as invulnerable."

His grounds are that the enemy sees the same technology: "The problem begins when the enemy is also exposed to these means: RCWS are great, they are important and cost millions, but they are visible to everyone, and everyone knows where they are. Once you begin believing that the fence will stop all the relevant threats, you think even half a battalion on standby is enough. Technology greatly influences our way of thinking and is seen as the answer to everything — only no one ever asks themselves what the vulnerabilities are, and what is the backup plan for the doomsday scenario when the technology layer collapses." Barnea supports the pattern with a historical case, comparing Israel's sense of technological superiority with US activity during the Vietnam War between 1965 and 1968: "The Americans relied on massive aerial bombardment with precision bombs and napalm bombs that burned huge areas, and advocated the 'scorched earth' concept. They convinced themselves that the Vietcong could not withstand it. In practice, the North Vietnamese army studied the American activity. It dug tunnels, moved equipment and people between bombings, eventually enabling it to reach the important bases in the south of the country, and overwhelm the Americans. In fact, the US military so believed in the damage it was causing that they reported a far greater number of casualties on the other side than the actual number, which in turn created an illusion of victory. They told themselves, we have B-52 bombers, there's no way we can't win."

# The Iron Dome's Strategic Paradox

The Iron Dome was built with the strategic vision of giving decision-makers breathing room — allowing them not to react immediately to rockets but to have the flexibility to react at the right time, in the right place, in a range of ways — yet its success was paradoxical: it was so successful that it not only supported the decision-making process but fundamentally changed it.

Prof. Eviatar Matania puts the paradox as follows: up until October 7, the system "served as a very successful plaster to threats to a sovereign state, because what legitimacy would a state leader have for going to war when no citizens were harmed?" Brigadier General Eran Ortal, until recently commander of The Dado Center for Interdisciplinary Military Studies, also believes technological measures such as the Iron Dome and the barrier influenced decision-making in Israel, and in his estimation helped the political echelon conduct a policy of military restraint towards the Gaza Strip, which in turn allowed Hamas to strengthen and gain offensive capabilities. But even after Iron Dome, Israel found it difficult to stand up against significant disruption of daily life on the home front: "Despite the clear threat posed by Gaza, the decision makers preferred to avoid a policy that would mean returning a large part of the country's population to the reality of air raids and disrupted daily routines. The bottom line: the Iron Dome did not change the essential strategic situation; as firepower from the Gaza Strip developed, so did the terrorist organizations' ability to control daily life in Israel's hinterland, hold it hostage, and restrain Israel from taking proactive measures against them." Ortal asks rhetorically why the relative success of the Iron Dome did not translate into restoring Israel's freedom of action against Hamas, and names three factors: first, like any operational system, Iron Dome is not perfect — the enemy studies it and develops its own challenges against it, and decision makers recognized that Israel is not hermetically protected; second, the enormous cost of deploying and operating batteries significantly impedes a policy based on continuous rounds of violence; and third, as long as rockets are intercepted in the skies over Israel and not over Gaza, the Israeli home front still experiences sirens, security rooms and shelters, and disrupted routine living — so "even the complete success of the Iron Dome left daily life on the home front in the hands of the terrorist organizations."

EU values and transparency commissioner Vera Jourova warned in September 2023 that platforms must concentrate efforts to combat the spread of Kremlin propaganda, including in the context of looming EU elections the following year with the risk of Russia stepping up its election interference efforts.

"One of my main messages to the signatories is to be aware of the context. Russian war against Ukraine, and the upcoming EU elections next year, are particularly relevant, because the risk of disinformation is particularly serious," she said. "The Russian state has engaged in the war of ideas to pollute our information space with half-truth and lies to create a false image that democracy is no better than autocracy. Today, this is a multi-million euro weapon of mass manipulation aimed both internally at the Russians as well as at Europeans and the rest of the world. We must address this risk. I expect signatories to adjust their actions to reflect that there is a war in the information space waged against us and that there are upcoming elections where malicious actors will try to use the design features of the platforms to manipulate."

# Earnings Report

## Definition

In the corpus, an earnings report is the quarterly release of a company's headline financial results — revenue, earnings per share (EPS), and net income — set against Wall Street analyst consensus estimates, usually paired with forward guidance for the next period.
The corpus never defines the term directly; it is used throughout as the recurring, scheduled event that "earnings week ahead" previews list companies for, and that individual company writeups (Nike, Uber) report the results of.

## Context

The corpus treats earnings reports as recurring, scheduled events that markets track closely: Seeking Alpha's "earnings week ahead" roundups list which major companies — Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, Ford, GM and dozens of others — are due to report in a given week, alongside consensus EPS and revenue estimates analysts will measure the actual results against.
Individual reports such as Nike's and Uber's quarterly releases show the report's core anatomy in practice: headline revenue and EPS figures are compared against analyst expectations to produce a "beat" or "miss," net income is disclosed alongside the year-ago comparison, and management issues guidance for the following quarter or full year on the same release or earnings call.
The term also surfaces as a governance signal: the corpus notes that after Elon Musk took Twitter (X) private, the company stopped producing quarterly earnings reports, which reduced public transparency and accountability around the platform's business — an absence the EU's disinformation scrutiny of X is contrasted against.

## Key Characteristics

- **Periodic and scheduled** — earnings reports are issued on a recurring quarterly (or annual) cadence, well-known enough in advance that outlets publish "earnings week ahead" previews naming which companies report and when.
- **Benchmarked against consensus estimates** — headline metrics (EPS, revenue) are reported alongside analyst consensus figures, and the gap between actual and expected results is characterized as a "beat" or "miss," as with Nike beating on earnings/margin while missing on revenue, and Uber missing revenue and EPS expectations despite YoY growth.
- **Forward guidance is bundled in** — companies commonly pair the backward-looking results with guidance for the next quarter or full year (e.g., Nike maintaining full-year revenue-growth and margin guidance; Uber issuing gross-bookings guidance for Q4).
- **Segment-level breakdowns** — reports can disaggregate results by business unit or geography (Uber's ride-hailing, delivery, and freight segments; Nike's regional sales by North America, EMEA, and APAC), each compared to its own prior-year and expected figures.
- **A public-company accountability mechanism** — ceasing to publish earnings reports (as X did after going private) is treated in the corpus as a loss of the transparency and external accountability that public disclosure otherwise provides.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out what an earnings report formally is or how it relates to SEC filings. Per the Corporate Finance Institute, an earnings report is an official financial document a public company releases to summarize its financial performance for a period — showing revenue, net income, and EPS (also called the income statement or profit-and-loss statement) — together with management's guidance on present and future expectations; it typically accompanies the fuller periodic filings (annual Form 10-K, quarterly Form 10-Q) that public companies submit to the SEC, and results are judged against market analysts' estimates even though that comparison is not part of the filing itself (Corporate Finance Institute, *Earnings Report*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Equity Valuations Must Be Judged Against Rising Bond Yields

Equity valuations do not function in a silo, so with bond yields at multi-decade highs investors may have to assess current valuations not just against the last ten years' valuations but against prior periods as well. The ground is that investors have many options, including fixed deposits, bonds and real estate, and when other assets get more attractive one must assess the scope for valuation change in equities; as of 14 October 2023, interest rates and bond yields in many developed markets, including the US, were at their highest levels since 2007.

The warrant runs through the earnings yield an equity offers relative to a risk-free alternative. Near-zero interest rates and low bond yields made stocks with an earnings yield of a mere 1-2 per cent attractive for a foreign portfolio investor: stocks such as Asian Paints, Nestle India and ABB India traded at PEs of 65, 83 and 85 times respectively at the time of writing, implying earnings yields of 1.5 per cent for Asian Paints and 1.2 per cent for Nestle and ABB. Such earnings yields were fine for FPIs to hold when compared with zero interest income in their domestic market, but with US bond yields offering 5 per cent these may not be so attractive even when considering growth prospects. While Indian interest rates were always higher, investors in equities benefited from global investors' hunger for yields, and that advantage is diminishing today. The article states explicitly that this is not a recommendation on the stocks but pointers on factors to consider in making the relative valuation process more foolproof.

# Valuation

## Definition

Across the corpus, "valuation" denotes the dollar figure attached to a company at a given moment — most often the headline number a startup or company is described as "valued at" following a funding round or share sale.

The corpus also uses the term for the analytical output public-stock analysts arrive at by pricing a stock through one of two competing methods, relative valuation or absolute (DCF) valuation.

## Context

The corpus repeatedly ties valuation to funding rounds and their trajectory: FTX's valuation rose to $32 billion at its peak after a $400 million Series C round in January 2022, before its collapse into bankruptcy; Flexport was valued at $8 billion amid the turmoil around Dave Clark's ouster; Adaptive, an AI startup based in Amsterdam and co-founded by French AI researcher Julien Launay, was about to raise a seed round at a $100 million valuation; and OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27–29 billion valuation in April 2023, separate from an earlier Microsoft investment. Scalable Capital's $65 million raise came in at a "flat" $1.4 billion valuation — unchanged from its prior round despite the company being four to five times larger, illustrating that valuation is a negotiated figure set at the moment of a deal, not a mechanical output of size or growth alone. Separately, the corpus's "Fundamental Investing" piece treats valuation as a discipline: analysts price stocks either through absolute valuation (a discounted cash flow model, "an interesting story backed by credible and validated numbers") or relative valuation (comparing a stock's PE, P/B, or EV/EBITDA ratio against peers, "an interesting number backed by a credible and validated story"), with about 85% of equity research and 50% of M&A valuation work using the relative approach because full DCF modeling across hundreds of stocks is impractical.

## Key Characteristics

- **Point-in-time and deal-driven** — a valuation is set at the moment of a funding round or share sale (e.g., FTX's $32B peak after its Series C, OpenAI's $27–29B share sale, Scalable Capital's raise), not a continuously updated market price.
- **Can be "flat"** — a company can raise new capital at the same valuation as its prior round even after growing substantially, as Scalable Capital did at $1.4 billion despite being four to five times bigger than at its 2021 round.
- **Detached from later outcomes** — a peak valuation (FTX's $32 billion) does not protect against later collapse; valuation reflects investor sentiment and negotiated terms at the time, not guaranteed durability.
- **Two competing methodologies for public stocks** — absolute valuation (DCF, modeling a company's own cash flows) versus relative valuation (comparing multiples like PE, P/B, EV/EBITDA against peers, growth, and history); the corpus reports relative valuation as the more prevalent in practice despite absolute valuation being considered theoretically superior.
- **Applies across scales** — the term covers everything from a seed-stage AI startup ($100 million) to a crypto exchange or foundation model company (tens of billions of dollars), with the same basic concept of "worth implied by a deal" underlying both.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, valuation in finance is the general process of determining the worth of a potential investment, asset, or security, typically through discounted-cashflow, relative, or contingent-claim approaches. (Source: Wikipedia, "Valuation (finance)," accessed 2026-09-02.)

# Wearable Fitness Tracker

## Definition

A wearable fitness tracker is a wrist-worn device — spanning dedicated fitness bands such as the Fitbit Charge 6 and general-purpose smartwatches such as the Apple Watch and Google Pixel Watch — that uses onboard sensors to track a person's activity and health signals, including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), and wrist-motion data, and displays the results on-device (doc_0222, doc_0241, doc_0491).

## Context

In the corpus, the category shows up almost entirely through product coverage of the two dominant lines: Apple Watch (Series 9, Ultra 2, SE) and Fitbit/Google's Pixel Watch, alongside Samsung's Galaxy Watch and dedicated bands like the Fitbit Charge 6.
Reviewers repeatedly frame the Apple Watch as "an excellent fitness companion, offering comprehensive health and activity data," and describe the Apple Watch SE's "fitness features and tracking data" as "well-rounded" even though it omits pricier sensors like blood oxygen (doc_0104, doc_0091).
The Fitbit Charge 6 is described as a dedicated fitness tracker distinct from a smartwatch, with an AMOLED touchscreen for activity stats, built-in GPS for outdoor workouts, and week-long battery life (doc_0222).
The first-generation Google Pixel Watch is presented as a smartwatch whose fitness-tracking capability comes from native Fitbit integration, including FDA-cleared EKGs; the same article notes the first-gen model omits the Sleep Profiles, abnormal heart-rate tracking, and nightly SpO2 features that arrived with the second-generation Pixel Watch (doc_0069).
A separate corpus thread ties the category's sensor hardware directly to a patent fight: Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 use an SpO2 (blood oxygen saturation) sensor that Masimo successfully argued infringed its pulse-oximetry patents, leading the ITC to order an import ban on those two watches (doc_0241).
The corpus also documents how newer silicon expands what a wrist-worn tracker can sense and act on: the Apple Watch Series 9's S9 chip adds four neural engines that process wrist accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate sensor data to recognize the Double Tap gesture, a feature unavailable on older Apple Watches that lack that chip (doc_0491).

## Key Characteristics

- **Wrist-worn form factor** — the category covers both single-purpose bands (Fitbit Charge 6) and multi-purpose smartwatches (Apple Watch, Pixel Watch, Galaxy Watch) that add fitness tracking to broader smart functionality (doc_0222, doc_0069).
- **Core sensed metrics** — step count, heart rate, and activity/workout data are baseline across models; higher-end devices add blood oxygen (SpO2) sensing and GPS for mapping outdoor workouts (doc_0104, doc_0222).
- **Tiered sensor availability** — cheaper models in a lineup (e.g., Apple Watch SE) drop specialized sensors like the blood oxygen app while keeping core step/activity tracking, distinguishing entry-level from flagship tiers (doc_0091, doc_0104).
- **On-wrist signal processing is noisy** — detecting subtle wrist gestures and vitals requires filtering accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate data against motion artifacts from the arm, muscles, and individual differences in wrist size (doc_0491).
- **Sensor IP is contested territory** — the SpO2 sensor at the center of the Apple–Masimo dispute shows that the sensing hardware inside these devices can itself be the subject of patent litigation with real market consequences (an import ban) (doc_0241).
- **Ecosystem integration matters** — fitness data on a smartwatch is often powered by a partner platform (Fitbit integration on the Pixel Watch) rather than being built entirely in-house (doc_0069).

# Wearable Device

## Definition

In this corpus, "wearable device" (or "wearable") is the umbrella term outlets use for a body-worn consumer or health-tech gadget — a smartwatch, fitness ring, fitness band, or medical-sensing device — interchangeably with specific products like the Apple Watch, Google Pixel Watch, Whoop 4, Ultrahuman Ring Air, and Acurable's respiratory monitors.

## Context

The corpus uses "wearable" as the umbrella term spanning consumer smartwatches (Apple Watch, Google Pixel Watch, Samsung Galaxy Watch), fitness rings (Ultrahuman Ring Air), fitness bands (Whoop 4), and specialized medical-sensing gadgets (Acurable's respiratory monitors, the Willow Go wearable breast pump). Some wearables are purely consumer-facing fitness/lifestyle products sold through holiday deals coverage, while others sit at the boundary of consumer electronics and regulated medical devices — the Apple Watch's SpO2 blood-oxygen sensor and EKG feature are the clearest example, since they triggered patent litigation with medical device makers Masimo and AliveCor over the underlying sensing technology. Acurable is described explicitly as "a medical device company that makes patient-friendly wearable devices to diagnose and manage respiratory conditions at home," showing wearables also serving a clinical diagnostic role outside the smartwatch category.

## Key Characteristics

- **Body-worn form factor** — worn on the wrist (Apple Watch, Pixel Watch, Whoop 4, Galaxy Watch), finger (Ultrahuman Ring Air), or elsewhere on the body (Acurable's respiratory monitors, Willow Go breast pump).
- **On-board sensing** — wearables carry sensors such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, optical heart-rate sensors, and SpO2 (blood-oxygen) sensors; the Apple Watch Series 9's double-tap gesture, for instance, is detected from accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate data collected at the wrist.
- **Companion-app dependence** — many wearables (Whoop 4, Ultrahuman Ring Air) have no display of their own and instead offload data to a smartphone app for analysis and coaching.
- **Health/medical crossover** — some wearables function as, or overlap with, regulated medical devices: the Apple Watch's SpO2 and EKG features became the subject of ITC patent disputes with medical device makers Masimo and AliveCor, and Acurable markets its wearables as home-use medical devices to diagnose and manage respiratory conditions such as sleep apnea.
- **Rapid feature iteration** — newer models add capabilities like Sleep Profiles, abnormal heart-rate tracking, and gesture controls (double tap), often gated behind newer chips (the Apple Watch Series 9's S9 chip with four neural engines).

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the general definition is broader than any single corpus device: wearable technology comprises small electronic and mobile devices, worn on the body or built into clothing or accessories, that commonly detect and transmit information such as vital signs, sometimes with immediate biofeedback to the wearer (Wikipedia, "Wearable technology," accessed 2026-09-02, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wearable_technology).

# Battery Life and Charging

## Definition

Battery life and charging is the pair of consumer-electronics specs — how long a device runs on a charge, and how fast and via what connector it refills — that reviewers and shoppers use to compare phones, earbuds, handhelds, smart glasses, and the power banks and cables that feed them.

## Context

Across the corpus, battery life and charging speed function as headline review criteria and buying-guide sort keys rather than a single defined term: Engadget's Steam Deck OLED review leads with "its battery life is better" as one of the device's core upgrades, and The Verge lists "improved battery life and audio" as a top pro for Amazon's third-gen Echo Frames. The charging half of the pair is increasingly organized around USB-C: Engadget notes that Apple's iPhone 15 line and the second-generation AirPods Pro both moved to USB-C charging, and Polygon's portable-charger guide treats USB-C Power Delivery wattage as the key spec for matching a power bank to a phone, tablet, Steam Deck, or laptop. Capacity for power banks is measured in mAh, per Polygon's guide, while device battery life is reported in hours (the Echo Frames reviewer logged about five hours of media playback and calls before hitting 30 percent) or in minutes of measured playtime (Engadget's Steam Deck OLED testing). Gogoro's battery-swapping business shows the same pair of concerns scaled up to electric vehicles: swapping a depleted battery for a charged one at a station is explicitly framed as a way to cut "charging time" relative to plugging in.

## Key Characteristics

- **Duration is measured empirically, not just claimed** — Engadget timed the Steam Deck OLED at four hours 23 minutes playing Hades versus two hours 42 minutes on the original LCD model under identical settings, a 62 percent gain that beat Valve's own 30-to-50-percent claim.
- **Charging speed is a distinct spec from capacity** — Valve advertises the Steam Deck OLED going from 20 to 80 percent in 45 minutes, a speed claim separate from its 50Whr battery capacity; Polygon likewise separates a power bank's mAh capacity from its wattage-based recharge speed.
- **USB-C is displacing proprietary connectors as the charging standard** — Apple's iPhone 15 and USB-C AirPods Pro, and the iPad's shift off Lightning to USB-C on its 10th-generation model, are all cited by Engadget as part of a single connector transition.
- **Power Delivery (PD) wattage governs compatibility between chargers and devices** — Polygon's guide notes that only power banks supporting the PD 3.0 spec can recharge a Steam Deck at its fastest rate, and that a laptop needs PD 3.1 and a compatible cable to reach 140 W charging.
- **Battery swapping is an alternative to plug-in charging at the vehicle scale** — Gogoro's network lets riders exchange a depleted battery for a charged one at a station instead of waiting to charge in place, which TechCrunch frames as a way to reduce charging time for EV adopters.

# Sphere And ABBA Voyage As Two Models Of Immersion

The Sydney Morning Herald's 19 October 2023 report sets out a two-part model of immersive concert design: ABBA Voyage in London pushes its effects out toward the audience, while Sphere more wholly and subtly envelops it — the only approximate comparison available for either.

The relation holds because both are wholly enveloping experiences where lights, sound and special effects are blended to push the audience's senses to the limit; they differ in one key way, which is direction. ABBA's effects project outward, largely to play smoke and mirrors with the on-stage simulacrums; Sphere's surround the viewer. A second shared structural condition is the artist: "They are both legacy projects made by artists who have the career and track record to be able to look at these things objectively in a way that a younger performer perhaps wouldn't because it takes an entire lifetime of experience to make those kinds of choices and make it work," Williams says.

A third link is institutional. The two shows share the British music stage architecture firm Stufish, whose work ranges from the Queen's Platinum Jubilee to tours for Beyoncé and Jay-Z, Michael Bublé, Elton John and Madonna, as well as the ABBA Arena in London; Stufish partner Ric Lipson collaborated on the U2 project for Sphere along with artist Es Devlin and producer Brian Eno. Lipson also marks the limit of the model — the venues are not locked to one show: "With the ABBA Arena, it's absolutely designed for that show, but you could also imagine that building having another avatar show in there, or indeed a live performance where people would use the technology that's in the building as an immersive environment."

# SpO2 Sensors Are Not Essential To The Apple Watch

Against the assumption that losing blood oxygen sensing would gut the Apple Watch, The Verge's wearables reviewer argued that removing the SpO2 sensors wouldn't be the end of the world for Apple in the short term — betting that the average Apple Watch user forgets the blood oxygen features even exist.

The premise attacked is the feature's importance. Apple's blood oxygen features are mostly for wellness and sleep tracking, and are not that useful beyond determining a nightly baseline; the watch periodically takes SpO2 readings in the background, or the user can actively take a spot check, but Apple itself doesn't make wide use of these metrics — unlike the way the watch uses its EKG capabilities to detect atrial fibrillation. On consumer wearables generally, SpO2 features have no medical use cases; they are essentially for "entertainment" purposes, and The Verge has repeatedly reported that they should never be used as any sort of replacement for traditional pulse oximeters. The reviewer conceded one boundary case: if rumors that Apple is working on sleep apnea detection are correct, losing the sensors would make developing that feature harder. But such a feature would require a lengthy FDA clearance process, which makes more advanced health features a medium- to long-term concern — and it's very possible Apple will have a workaround by the time they are ready for consumers.

# The Third Place

The third place is a sociological term that refers to a physical space that isn't work or home, where people can socialize without the obligations of productivity. The membership test is simple: if you can hang out there, it's a third place.

The category has boundary cases in both directions. During the pandemic, virtual communities served as ad hoc third places in lieu of coffee shops, bookstores and gyms, and Twitch, which saw exponential growth during the pandemic, was one of them. In the other direction, a place can be plentiful and still fail the role: last year's San Diego-based TwitchCon, for all of its faults, took place in a walkable city abundant with nearby places to hang out, allowing attendees to bond, network and interact outside of the convention center, while there's no shortage of third places in Las Vegas — but for many TwitchCon attendees, nightclubs and casinos aren't accessible alternatives to San Diego's more casual venues.

# Sphere: Venue And Display Specifications

Sphere is a $US2.3 billion Las Vegas venue whose defining feature is an interior 16K x 16K spherical video surface — the highest-resolution LED screen ever made, with 268,435,456 pixels — inside what is otherwise a conventional concert space, The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 19 October 2023.

But when the lights go down everything changes: Sphere splits open around you to reveal a succession of environments, each more stunning than the one before, and the effect is overwhelming. # The S9 Chip's Neural Engines Enable Double Tap

Double tap requires the Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 because the new S9 features four neural engines for machine learning, which is what powers the gesture; on older watches, the related Assistive Touch feature ran on the main CPU. That is why double tap is unavailable on the older Apple Watches that support Assistive Touch — Series 4 or later, including the first-gen SE and Ultra — even though the gesture technically is not new.

The relation between the dedicated silicon and the outcome is quantified. "Because we're on a purpose-built part of the processor, we're not contending with all the other things the CPU is doing at any given time," says David Clark, senior director of Apple Watch software engineering; the result is that the Series 9 and Ultra 2 are 15 percent more accurate at detecting the double tap gesture, and the feature itself is much less power intensive.

The reason so much computation is needed is the noise in wrist data. At the most basic level, the algorithm that detects double tap is trained on data from the accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart rate sensor collected from the wrist. That is harder than it sounds: on top of calculating how light reflects off blood pumping through veins, smartwatch algorithms must account for the arm — plus muscles, veins, and tendons — physically moving during walking, running, and gesticulating, and no two people have the same body, so differences in wrist size and limb length have to be taken into consideration. Ironically, the years Apple put into improving heart rate helped cut through that noise: according to Clark, "the gaps in reliable signals for heart rate" were what his team used to confirm subtler motions like the double tap gesture. The requirement runs in both directions: "Reliability means that when you do the gesture, we're able to detect it," Clark says. "Reliability also means that when you're doing things that are almost like a tap, or a double tap, that we're not erroneously triggering the gesture. We got to make sure we're able to detect the right thing through by tuning these things with the right scenarios." So the algorithm must also differentiate when someone is in motion, the type of activity, and what other features they are using — streaming music or taking calls might seem unrelated, but the model must account for noise introduced by subsystems like LTE and Bluetooth, which is harder to do well when everything runs on the main CPU.
