# Steam Deck OLED Battery Life

Valve says the Steam Deck OLED battery lasts 30 to 50 percent longer than the original's depending on how you play, with an official claim of "three to 12 hours," and Engadget's November 2023 testing measured gains at the top of or above that range.

The original Steam Deck's short battery life was one of its downsides, maxing out at eight hours and only under ideal conditions. The OLED pairs a more-efficient processor with a 25 percent larger battery — 50Whr capacity against the original's 40Whr — and charges faster, going from 20 percent to 80 percent in 45 minutes by Valve's claim. Engadget tested with Hades, its reviewer's most-played game on the original: although Hades does not support HDR it pops on the OLED, with animations looking more fluid than on the LCD version, and the OLED lasted four hours and 23 minutes before dying, against two hours and 42 minutes for the original at the same settings of 800p with a 60 fps cap and similar brightness — a 62 percent improvement that surpasses Valve's own estimates. Engadget flags the confound: batteries degrade, and its LCD Steam Deck dated from the device's launch in early 2022, an 18-month-old unit at review time, which explains why its gains were more pronounced. A harsher stress test playing Elden Ring with everything maxed out gave the OLED two hours and 20 minutes, about 40 percent longer than the original. Polygon separately resolved the obvious ambiguity in Valve's 30-50% figure by asking whether the comparison was against a Steam Deck running original firmware, which had poor battery life, or the latest firmware; Valve's answer was the latter, so existing owners should expect the big improvements over their current experience. Polygon's conclusion is that the OLED screen makes for a fancier Steam Deck, but it is the battery life — plus tweaks throughout the design to carve out more of it — that lets the handheld truly deliver on its promise of a portable gaming PC.

# Sphere's Plug-And-Play Touring Economics

Ric Lipson argues that venues like Sphere make touring more "plug-and-play": because the immersive environment lives in the building, a production no longer has to bring its own structure, screen and sound system, The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 19 October 2023.

The grounds are the venue's own capacity — "The Sphere does a similar thing, [in that] you have a fully immersive space, the video screen in the Sphere is vast, it has a huge number of pixels, and you can immerse the audience within this environment" — set against an industry that has historically built its lucrative concert spin-off business on converting sports venues to rock concert stages. "It opens you up to thinking about performances in different ways, both from a creative point of view, from a business point of view, from a sustainability point of view, and the ability to not have to bring your own structure and screen and [sound system]," Lipson says.

The warrant is the contrast with current practice and the plan that follows from it: "We have Adele in Caesar's Palace right now, which again is another large show that immerses the audience, but we bring everything in and every time we load that show out, it takes a week or so. # The Bedside Charging Station Habit

News writer Jess Weatherbed got a charging station as a birthday present from her partner after several months of arguing over their sleeping arrangements — something about her trailing the charging cables for her devices in the bed being "dangerous" and "extremely uncomfortable."

# Creator Economy

## Definition

In the corpus, "creator economy" names the industry of livestreamers and other online creators whose income depends on platform-designed monetization mechanisms — subscription revenue splits, ad-revenue sharing, sponsorship deals, and creator-payment plans — and whose sustainability is treated as a live, contested question by the platforms, creators, and press covering it.

Corpus evidence for this usage: TechCrunch reports that VidCon hosted an industry leadership summit where "creator economy experts and creators" aired grievances about the state of the business, and a TechCrunch newsletter calls it "eye-wateringly hard to make money as a creator"; Spill frames paying creators for their cultural contributions as "especially important for Black creators in the creator economy."

## Context

The corpus surfaces the creator economy wherever a platform's monetization design meets an individual creator's livelihood. Twitch's Chief Monetization Officer describes the company's subscription splits, the Partner Plus tier, ad-revenue sharing, and sponsorship deals as the tools it uses to let livestreaming creators make a living, and frames its unique position as the platform where "viewers are directly supporting creators" through subscriptions, gifting, and cheering. Kick undercuts Twitch's model with a more generous 95/5 revenue split, pulling streamers who cannot make ends meet on Twitch's terms. Spill, a beta social app, frames paying creators for their cultural contributions — "especially important for Black creators" — as central to its pitch. YouTube's demonetization of SSSniperwolf under its "Creator Responsibility policies" shows the same economy's downside: a platform can cut off a creator's income unilaterally. And at VidCon, "creator economy experts and creators" convened an industry leadership summit specifically to "hash out their grievances with the state of the business," underscoring that the term names a recognized industry, not just a metaphor.

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform-mediated monetization** — creators earn through mechanisms platforms design and can change: Twitch's subscription splits, its Partner Plus program (70/30 split on the first $100,000 for eligible streamers), ad-revenue sharing, and sponsorship deals.
- **Precarious, individual-scale economics** — a TechCrunch newsletter argues it is "so eye-wateringly hard to make money as a creator" that venture-scale returns are unrealistic, favoring peer knowledge-sharing (like VidCon's summit or a creator-networking app) over creators raising venture capital.
- **Platform dependence cuts both ways** — a small streamer's income can collapse when a platform changes its split (Kelly's Twitch income fell from over $1,000/month to about $120 after Twitch cut the 70/30 deal), then recover on a rival platform with a friendlier split (over $1,000/month on Kick with far fewer subscribers).
- **Unilateral platform enforcement** — a platform can suspend a creator's monetization outright, as YouTube did to SSSniperwolf under its Creator Responsibility policies after doxxing accusations.
- **Recognized as an industry with its own advocacy** — VidCon hosted a dedicated leadership summit where "creator economy experts and creators" aired grievances about the state of the business, and platform-adjacent apps like Spill explicitly build creator-payment plans, in Spill's case foregrounding credit and pay for Black creators.

## Background (external)

Beyond the corpus, "creator economy" is a general industry term for a platform-driven economy in which creators produce content, products, or services and distribute them directly to their audience via social media and related technologies, building communities and monetizing their work through channels like advertising, sponsorships, sales, crowdfunding, and subscriptions.

Source: Wikipedia, "Creator economy" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creator_economy), accessed 2026-09-02.

# StarNews' Content Partnerships And Nigerian Growth

StarNews reported its most impressive retention rate in Nigeria among all of its markets, a market that in CEO Guy Kamgaing's assessment exhibits all the right metrics for exponential growth: acquiring users is relatively straightforward, the platform enjoys strong user engagement and stickiness, and monetization is thriving. Kamgaing, an ex-PwC consultant, said these initiatives highlight the power of strong partnerships in which telcos take the lead, followed by content creators or show organizers. He located StarNews' distinctiveness in holding all three layers locally: "Production without distribution is tough and tougher without monetization. We're able to have all three layers at the local level. We have offices in all the markets and the teams there are specifically working with creators on content production, which is unique." He added that the platform's content spectrum has expanded to establish significant partnerships with the likes of Sony and Universal in the region.

# Nike Wholesale Partner Relationship Reset

Nike's relationship with its wholesale partners has been rocky: as the company pivoted to a direct-to-consumer model, it focused on driving sales online and in its stores at the expense of its wholesale accounts. The dependency reasserted itself when Nike grappled with excess inventories throughout 2023 and relied on those partners to move the merchandise, and it has now restored its relationship with both Macy's and DSW — accounts it previously cut in favour of the DTC strategy.

The quarter's numbers reflect a sector-wide caution as well as Nike's own pivot. Some analysts expected wholesale revenue to be sluggish because excess inventories have been a problem throughout the retail industry, with some wholesalers being more particular in what they order to avoid another backlog. Wholesale revenue during the quarter was flat compared with the year-ago period at $7 billion.

The relationships are structured to avoid concentration, and both CEO John Donahoe and finance chief Matthew Friend made clear that Nike is ready to meet customers in all channels, including through wholesalers and directly. The company singled out Dick's Sporting Goods as a key partner and noted it is still in the process of resetting its business with Foot Locker, which has seen two quarters in a row of plunging sales and profits. Friend framed the portfolio rule: "Ultimately, we have a segmented portfolio of strong partners across price points and channels. With no single partner representing more than a mid-single digit of Nike's total business." Despite the shift in how it works with wholesalers, Nike insisted direct sales will pave the way to future growth: "While the ultimate landing spot of digital and direct isn't as clear, we do believe we're going to be a more direct and a more digital company, and a more profitable company. # Usage-Based Pricing

## Definition

In the corpus, usage-based pricing (also called consumption pricing) is the charging model that VCs discuss as the one whose "trajectory... has organically aligned with the needs of large language models," with OpenAI's per-token API pricing cited as the motivating example, in contrast to conventional periodic SaaS pricing.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces in a TechCrunch roundup of venture capitalists discussing how AI startups should charge for AI-powered tooling, prompted directly by "the OpenAI pricing schema based on tokens and usage."
Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures frames usage-based pricing as the model whose "trajectory... has organically aligned with the needs of large language models," because prompt/output sizes and per-user resource consumption vary significantly from one request to the next.
Lisa Calhoun of Valor VC makes the mechanism concrete: companies like OpenAI charge largely "by the token," which she calls "a very different metric than most cloud computing," and notes cost monitoring may be a key aspect of tracking that metric.
The same discussion frames usage-based pricing as one leg of a three-way choice facing AI startups, alongside conventional periodic SaaS pricing and hybrid structures that blend the two.

## Key Characteristics

- **Cost tracks consumption, not time** — charges scale with resource use (e.g., tokens processed) rather than a fixed subscription period.
- **Aligned with LLM cost structure** — the model fits large language models well because compute cost per request varies with prompt/output size and per-user resource utilization; OpenAI itself reportedly spends upward of $700,000 per day on compute, making usage-based allocation a way to recover those variable costs.
- **Unpopular for budgeting** — tying all costs to volume is "generally unpopular with end users," who prefer the predictability of a fixed periodic fee.
- **Not universal across AI products** — applications that don't rely on an LLM as a backbone, and that make no direct token calls to a model provider, tend to gravitate toward conventional periodic SaaS pricing instead.
- **Persists via hybrid structures** — as LLM adoption widens, vendors are expected to combine tiered periodic payments and usage limits for smaller customers with uncapped usage-based tiers for larger enterprises, rather than replacing usage-based pricing outright.
- **Tied to data dependency** — because large language technology remains heavily dependent on continuous data inflow, the source article argues usage-based pricing is unlikely to disappear even as the market matures.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, usage-based pricing (also called pay-per-usage) is a general software/SaaS revenue model: charges are calculated from measured consumption — "the number of users, transactions, amount of storage space used, or other metrics" — rather than a flat recurring fee, and Wikipedia notes many buyers favor it because they see themselves as "relatively light users of the software," while it can create revenue uncertainty and added billing overhead for the seller. (Wikipedia, "Software as a service," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_as_a_service)

# Total Addressable Market (TAM)

## Definition

Total addressable market (TAM) is the overall revenue opportunity a market represents — the size of the "pie" a company could theoretically capture — as distinct from market share, the slice of that pie a specific competitor has actually won.
The corpus uses "TAM" directly only once: in a TechCrunch roundup on AI startup strategy, after VC Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures argued that startups "may want to temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," the article's author adds, as an editorial aside rather than part of Tsai's quote, "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" — treating TAM as a measure of how much upside is still up for grabs regardless of who wins any single deal.
Far more often the corpus talks about the narrower, already-contested slice of a market — "market share" — across search, payments, betting, retail, crypto, autos, and music.

## Context

The corpus's clearest TAM reference sits inside a broader discussion of how AI startups should compete: Edward Tsai of Alumni Ventures told TechCrunch that startups might "temporarily reduce their focus on defensibility and increase their focus on products that deliver compelling value and focusing on speed to market," a view the article's author then glossed with "Presuming massive TAM, that could work!" and Rick Grinnell of Glasswing Ventures separately described the goal of "capturing market share or meeting a critical market need before competitors" — TAM as the size of the opportunity, market share as who is winning it.
The rest of the corpus's "market share" usage documents that same capture-and-defend dynamic in mature markets rather than emerging ones: Google's roughly 90% share of online search (and the $26.3 billion it paid in 2021 to secure default placement across Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to protect that share); Chrome's climb from nearly 50% of desktop browser usage at the end of 2014 to nearly 65% by the end of 2017, the same year Google regained the default-search slot on Firefox; Binance's share of the crypto-exchange market falling from over 60% to under 50% after its DOJ settlement; Reliance Retail's roughly 3% share of India's retail market against Walmart's roughly 10% of the US market; Capitol Music Group's "high-5%" US label market share; Tesla losing EV market share to rivals amid price cuts; and fintech Rainforest explicitly trying to "take market share" from Stripe and legacy processors Fiserv and FIS.
Sportsbooks entering new states (Kentucky, Vermont) frame their promotional bonus wars in the same terms — "fighting for market share" in a market that is still being carved up as it launches.

## Key Characteristics

- **TAM is the whole opportunity; market share is the captured slice** — the corpus's one TAM mention treats it as license to chase growth over defensibility, while every market-share mention describes a company's already-won or already-lost portion of a market.
- **Market share is measured differently by market** — percentage of search queries (Google's ~90%), percentage of desktop browser usage (Chrome's ~65%), percentage of exchange volume/assets (Binance's 60%→50% decline), percentage of retail floor space or sales (Reliance Retail's ~3% vs. Walmart's ~10%), and record-label percentage of a national market (Capitol Music Group's "high-5%").
- **Share can be bought as well as earned** — Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default-placement payments to Apple and other partners, and sportsbooks' signup bonuses in newly legalized states, are both framed as direct spend to acquire or defend market share rather than organic growth.
- **Share shifts are framed as zero-sum among incumbents** — Rainforest is described as taking share "from" Stripe, Fiserv, and FIS; EV rivals are described as taking share "from" Tesla; new entrants into Vermont and Kentucky sports betting are described as "fighting" each other for the same pool of bettors.
- **A large presumed TAM changes competitive strategy** — the corpus's TechCrunch commentary on VC Edward Tsai's view suggests that when the addressable opportunity is presumed to be very large, startups may rationally prioritize speed to market over building defensible moats, since there is enough unclaimed opportunity for multiple winners.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out the "total addressable market" acronym or define TAM's relationship to narrower measures. Per Wikipedia, TAM is the total market demand for a product or service, typically expressed in annual revenue or units, if 100% of that market were captured; it is conventionally narrowed first to a Serviceable Addressable Market (SAM, the portion a company could realistically reach) and then to a Serviceable Obtainable Market (SOM, the portion realistically obtainable), with market share denoting how much of the SAM/SOM a given competitor currently holds (Wikipedia, *Total addressable market*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# StarNews' African Telco Distribution Model

StarNews Mobile's growth model places mobile operators at its centre: operators are pivotal in propelling content within Africa's media industry, with unmatched distribution capabilities, so collaborating closely with them is imperative for establishing a solid presence in the market. To draw a parallel for how the operator landscape is structured, Guy Kamgaing described Orange as the "Apple" of Africa's telecommunications world and MTN as the "Google."

The relation runs in both directions. Over the past few years operators have been instrumental in driving data usage across the continent, and they simultaneously upsell their customers with in-house content or with content from partners like StarNews. On the strength of that arrangement StarNews carries an active subscriber base of over 4 million through its partnerships with MTN and Orange across six markets, alongside a community of more than 120 content creators. The model has a documented boundary: StarNews exited South Africa after a misalignment with MTN's strategy for engaging content creators, so the operator partnership holds only where the operator's own creator strategy aligns with the platform's.

This approach let StarNews expand its user base organically while securing nearly $8 million in funding — a $900,000 friends and family round, a $2 million seed investment and a $1.8 million extension — from an array of U.S., European and African VCs including Investisseurs & Partenaires (I&P), Snap via its Yellow Accelerator program, LoftyInc Capital, Graph Ventures and Expert Dojo.

Beneath the operator layer, the platform is structured around channels, with each creator having a dedicated channel. Kamgaing says the company works closely with creators by providing financial support and assisting in content production, and that it guides creators in their digital journey with support in digital acquisition. A significant portion of the company's user acquisition comes through the telecom operators themselves, because it is a seamless process for an operator such as MTN to send messages encouraging its customers to sign up to StarNews to watch social media personalities, including music artists, comedians and influencers. Sign-up is streamlined for convenience and is followed by a straightforward payment mechanism that allows users to pay with their airtime; this works across six different networks, each offering various bundles, weekly subscriptions and daily plans.

The model also determines what content travels well over it. Alongside creator-produced material, StarNews features deeply hyperlocal content spanning topics such as motorbike taxis in Cameroon or food recipes in Ivory Coast, plus genre-specific shows including the footballing competition African Cup of Nations and a program modeled after a singing reality competition, The Voice. StarNews leverages its operator partnerships to raise awareness and significantly boost user activations for these shows: in the 2021 edition of the African Cup of Nations (AFCON) the platform produced exclusive content straight from the event and acquired 600,000 new users, and the company's concert sponsorships at one point attracted 500,000 subscribers by offering them the chance to attend a Fally Ipupa concert.

# Enterprise Value Multiples

Enterprise value refers to the total value of a company or business, and the total value as perceived by the market is represented by the sum of its market cap plus net debt, which includes minority interest. What works in the case of EV is that it allows a capital-agnostic analysis: whether a company is funded only with equity or with a combination of equity and debt, the total value of the business is the same, because sources of funding do not matter. Using EV, the value of equity, the share price, is derived from the value of the business; since the capital structure of companies varies significantly, an EV approach enables valuing them on similar terms, arriving at the value of the business first and then subtracting net debt to reach the equity value. The advantage of EV-based metrics is that they give more options for valuing a company.

The boundary conditions are set by where in the statements one can anchor. Valuation accuracy is better the lower down the P&L and cash flow statement one can get to, but there are many times when company profits are low while operational performance, that is EBITDA, is not bad; in such cases, as revenue and EBITDA continue to grow, operating leverage will result in PE growing much faster than those two line items. Hence EV-based metrics are options to consider when equity-based valuation multiples do not give a clear picture. Where even EBITDA multiples are not clear, as was the case with many new-age company IPOs that were reporting losses even at the EBITDA level, investors have no option but to go further up the P&L to metrics like EV/revenue, or outside the P&L entirely to metrics like EV/subscriber.

# Wearable Fitness Tracker

## Definition

A wearable fitness tracker is a wrist-worn device — spanning dedicated fitness bands such as the Fitbit Charge 6 and general-purpose smartwatches such as the Apple Watch and Google Pixel Watch — that uses onboard sensors to track a person's activity and health signals, including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), and wrist-motion data, and displays the results on-device (doc_0222, doc_0241, doc_0491).

## Context

In the corpus, the category shows up almost entirely through product coverage of the two dominant lines: Apple Watch (Series 9, Ultra 2, SE) and Fitbit/Google's Pixel Watch, alongside Samsung's Galaxy Watch and dedicated bands like the Fitbit Charge 6.
Reviewers repeatedly frame the Apple Watch as "an excellent fitness companion, offering comprehensive health and activity data," and describe the Apple Watch SE's "fitness features and tracking data" as "well-rounded" even though it omits pricier sensors like blood oxygen (doc_0104, doc_0091).
The Fitbit Charge 6 is described as a dedicated fitness tracker distinct from a smartwatch, with an AMOLED touchscreen for activity stats, built-in GPS for outdoor workouts, and week-long battery life (doc_0222).
The first-generation Google Pixel Watch is presented as a smartwatch whose fitness-tracking capability comes from native Fitbit integration, including FDA-cleared EKGs; the same article notes the first-gen model omits the Sleep Profiles, abnormal heart-rate tracking, and nightly SpO2 features that arrived with the second-generation Pixel Watch (doc_0069).
A separate corpus thread ties the category's sensor hardware directly to a patent fight: Apple Watch Series 9 and Ultra 2 use an SpO2 (blood oxygen saturation) sensor that Masimo successfully argued infringed its pulse-oximetry patents, leading the ITC to order an import ban on those two watches (doc_0241).
The corpus also documents how newer silicon expands what a wrist-worn tracker can sense and act on: the Apple Watch Series 9's S9 chip adds four neural engines that process wrist accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate sensor data to recognize the Double Tap gesture, a feature unavailable on older Apple Watches that lack that chip (doc_0491).

## Key Characteristics

- **Wrist-worn form factor** — the category covers both single-purpose bands (Fitbit Charge 6) and multi-purpose smartwatches (Apple Watch, Pixel Watch, Galaxy Watch) that add fitness tracking to broader smart functionality (doc_0222, doc_0069).
- **Core sensed metrics** — step count, heart rate, and activity/workout data are baseline across models; higher-end devices add blood oxygen (SpO2) sensing and GPS for mapping outdoor workouts (doc_0104, doc_0222).
- **Tiered sensor availability** — cheaper models in a lineup (e.g., Apple Watch SE) drop specialized sensors like the blood oxygen app while keeping core step/activity tracking, distinguishing entry-level from flagship tiers (doc_0091, doc_0104).
- **On-wrist signal processing is noisy** — detecting subtle wrist gestures and vitals requires filtering accelerometer, gyroscope, and optical heart-rate data against motion artifacts from the arm, muscles, and individual differences in wrist size (doc_0491).
- **Sensor IP is contested territory** — the SpO2 sensor at the center of the Apple–Masimo dispute shows that the sensing hardware inside these devices can itself be the subject of patent litigation with real market consequences (an import ban) (doc_0241).
- **Ecosystem integration matters** — fitness data on a smartwatch is often powered by a partner platform (Fitbit integration on the Pixel Watch) rather than being built entirely in-house (doc_0069).

# Banking-as-a-Service

## Definition

Banking-as-a-service (BaaS) is the label TechCrunch's coverage applies to platforms — Synapse and QI Tech — that let banks and fintech companies build financial services on top of them, rather than platforms that serve end customers as a bank would.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term through two TechCrunch items: Synapse, covered in the fintech newsletter The Interchange as a San Francisco–based company whose platform "enables banks and fintech companies to easily develop financial services," and QI Tech, covered in the general Startups Weekly newsletter as a Brazilian "banking-as-a-service platform" that raised a large Series B.

Both appear as fintech infrastructure providers rather than consumer-facing banks — Synapse sits behind other companies' financial products, and QI Tech's raise is framed as backing for the same kind of platform business in Brazil.

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform, not bank** — the BaaS provider "operates a platform enabling banks and fintech companies to easily develop financial services" rather than serving end customers directly.
- **Infrastructure for others' products** — Synapse's role is to let other banks and fintechs build financial services on top of it, positioning it as embedded infrastructure rather than a retail brand.
- **Investor interest despite volatility** — QI Tech's BaaS platform drew a $200 million Series B, the largest Brazilian raise across all sectors that year, around the same time Synapse laid off 86 people, or about 40% of its staff.
- **Exposure to macro conditions** — an earlier round of Synapse layoffs (18% of its workforce, per a June blog post from CEO Sankaet Pathak) was attributed to "the current macroeconomic conditions" affecting its clients and platforms, indicating BaaS providers' fortunes are tied to the health of the banks/fintechs building on top of them.

## Background (external)

Wikipedia's entry on Banking-as-a-Service defines it more generally: BaaS refers to offering banking products — like deposit accounts, loans, and credit cards — to customers through partnerships with non-bank or non-financial third parties, where the bank handles balance-sheet management (capital, liquidity, credit risk) while the partner, often a fintech, engages the customer directly through its own app, typically connecting to the bank's systems via APIs.

# Telco Distribution

Telco distribution is a go-to-market model in which a content or service platform reaches and monetizes users primarily through partnerships with telecommunications operators (telcos) rather than through open platforms like YouTube or Instagram, letting the operator's existing subscriber relationship, billing rails and marketing reach stand in for the platform's own audience-acquisition and payment infrastructure.

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces through StarNews Mobile, an African mobile video network that prioritizes distribution partnerships with major mobile operators MTN and Orange over conventional streaming platforms, because creators face revenue limitations on those existing platforms.

Founder Guy Kamgaing describes the underlying insight as coming from years of monetizing "jokes and horoscopes via telcos" through SMS/VAS campaigns, then applying the same telco relationship to video content that creators could not otherwise monetize on YouTube or other open platforms.

The corpus frames mobile operators as "pivotal in propelling content within Africa's media industry, with unmatched distribution capabilities," making close collaboration with them "imperative for establishing a solid presence in the market" — operators are cast as the gatekeepers of both reach and revenue in this market.

## Key Characteristics

- **Operator-led acquisition** — a significant portion of user acquisition comes through the telecom operators themselves, since it is a seamless process for an operator like MTN to message its own customers to encourage sign-up.
- **Airtime as payment rail** — subscribers pay using their mobile airtime rather than a card or bank-linked method, letting the platform inherit the operator's existing billing relationship with the user.
- **Operator as both channel and competitor** — operators simultaneously drive baseline data usage and upsell customers with their own in-house content, so a distribution partner is also competing with the operator's proprietary offerings for the same subscriber attention.
- **Fit-dependent, not guaranteed** — the partnership only holds where the operator's own creator strategy aligns with the platform's; a misalignment with an operator's strategy is enough to force an exit from an otherwise-served market.
- **Concentration of layers** — operators are described as taking the lead in this dynamic, with content creators or show organizers following, which lets a platform built on telco distribution combine distribution, monetization and content creation "at the local level" rather than ceding distribution control to a separate platform.

# Equity Multiples Must Use Shareholder Line Items

An equity multiple is a ratio whose numerator is price per share or market cap, or a variation of the same, and whose denominator must be a line item that belongs to equity shareholders. The reasoning comes from the accounts: on any company's balance sheet the liabilities side is primarily made up of two line items, shareholder funds and borrowings, whereas a Profit and Loss statement has many line items, starting with revenue, followed by variable costs, fixed costs and taxes, and the only claim equity shareholders have for distribution or appropriation amongst themselves is what is left after paying taxes, namely net profit.

From this it follows that there are only three items attributable to equity shareholders: net profit from the P&L statement, book value or shareholder funds from the balance sheet, and free cash flows to equity from the cash flow statement. Any relative valuation multiple will be linked to these three items one way or another, and any other metric could be wrong and misleading. Hence it is very important to use the right multiples: when it comes to equity metrics, it always has to be price or market cap, or variations of the same, in the numerator, divided by line items attributable to equity holders, or variations of the same. The article accompanies this rule with a table of commonly used equity multiples for relative valuation.

# Wonder As A Return To 2D Mario Experimentation

Polygon argues that Super Mario Bros. Wonder shares the inventiveness of the earliest 2D Mario games and their disregard for what should and shouldn't be in a Mario game — making it, for middle-aged fans, a candidate for the first "true new Mario game" since Super Mario World in 1990. The grounds lie in a history the reviewer sets out: with each Super Mario Bros. on the NES and SNES, Nintendo's designers learned from the previous entry, cut what didn't work, made audacious additions (there was a time when adding a dinosaur named Yoshi felt like a gimmick), and gradually accumulated the pieces and tropes that would recur for the next thirty-plus years. Then, with Super Mario 64, 3D Mario games became the de facto labs for Nintendo's greatest experimentation — magical hats, water guns, galactic travel — while 2D Mario defaulted to a vessel for nostalgia, including the cheekily named New Super Mario Bros. series.

The warrant is that Wonder revives the old spirit specifically by letting the designers break their own machine. The traditional layer is intact — every level can be enjoyed as a loyal continuation of the plumber's work in the 2D platformer genre, which has kept a healthy cadence since the series debuted in 1985: dash from left to right, jump over pits, concuss enemies, collect the occasional power-up, and leap onto the flagpole that ends one level and unlocks the next. But the wonder of playing Super Mario Bros. in 1985 came from discovery, with Nintendo anticipating that players would climb outside the confines of the level and placing shortcuts in hidden crevices to reward the most rule-breaking players; badges now build on that freedom with skills that let you soar over towering enemies or use the Piranha Plant grappling hook to climb above the stage. "This is the most significant difference between 1985 and 2023," the reviewer writes: "Mario's creators have joined in the fun of breaking the machine." He imagines the game's origin as a notebook in which, since the '90s, every Nintendo developer wrote down each idea that "didn't fit the tone" or "wasn't Mario enough," until someone had the gall to say: "Let's turn this stuffed notebook of chaos into a game. # Criticism Of The Wilma Mankiller Barbie's Inaccuracies

Critics attacked the premise that Mattel's Wilma Mankiller doll faithfully represents Cherokee culture, pointing to specific errors in the product and its packaging. Chuck Hoskin Jr, Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, told The New York Times that the doll's basket was not authentically Cherokee, and that the wrong sets of symbols for the Cherokee language were used on the packaging — with the result that the symbols read "Chicken Nation" rather than "Cherokee Nation." "To someone who doesn't read Cherokee syllabary, they're not going to notice it," he said. "To the Cherokee people for whom Wilma is of such enduring significance and we have such enduring love for her, to see our seal incorrect, it's very disappointing because it would not have taken much effort or thought to avoid that." Hoskin said he learned of the doll's creation six months earlier and that Mattel did not work directly with the Cherokee Nation, though he added the company has been understanding of the criticism. The tribe's own statement said: "Regrettably, the Mattel company did not work directly with the tribal government's design and communications team to secure the official Seal or verify it."

Cherokee women raised a second objection — that Mattel overlooked the problematic details on both the doll and the packaging. "Mixed emotions shared by me and many other Cherokee women who have now purchased the product revolve around whether a Wilma Barbie captures her legacy, her physical features and the importance of centering Cherokee women in decision making," Stacy Leeds, the law school dean at Arizona State University and a former Cherokee Nation Supreme Court justice, told The Associated Press in an email. Regina Thompson, a Cherokee basket weaver who grew up near Tahlequah, does not think the doll looks like Mankiller, and said Mattel should have used traditional pucker toe moccasins instead of black shoes and included symbols on the basket that Cherokees use to tell a story. # Showing Up (Kelly Reichardt)

Showing Up is Kelly Reichardt's film starring Michelle Williams, Hong Chau, and John Magaro, ranked 10 on Polygon's best movies of 2023 list of 2023-10-07 and available for digital rental/purchase.

Lizzy, played by Michelle Williams, is a 30-something artist living on campus at her hometown art school who wants two things in life: time to prepare for her exhibition, and her landlord Jo, played by Hong Chau, to fix her hot water heater. Superficially there is little more to Lizzy's plight, for the better — Reichardt, who directed and co-wrote, never permits the stakes to rise too high or the plot to get too complicated, because the film at its core is about working artists working in less financially stable mediums such as ceramic figurines and trippy visual projections. Without plot filling the film, there is time to just be present in a beautiful Pacific Northwest scene.

Critic CP identifies Reichardt's genius as getting the audience giggling at the artists but never the art: it is funny to think an artist dedicated a year of her life to crocheting a jumpsuit, except then you see the outfit and it is beautiful, an intentional undermining of the punchline; a teacher smugly opines on ceramics, but each piece he holds up is so lovingly crafted that they confidently speak for themselves. That decision — rib artists, celebrate art — sets the tone: humans are artifice, a bunch of contradictory masks put on to match the situation and the crowd, but our creations, when we commit to a craft in whatever medium, are an expression of our most vulnerable selves. Reichardt knows that art created from a place of sincere intent deserves compassion and respect, even if its creator is still a desperate, self-conscious ball of anxiety.

# Banking-as-a-Service

## Definition

Banking-as-a-service (BaaS) is the label TechCrunch's coverage applies to platforms — Synapse and QI Tech — that let banks and fintech companies build financial services on top of them, rather than platforms that serve end customers as a bank would.

## Context

The corpus surfaces the term through two TechCrunch items: Synapse, covered in the fintech newsletter The Interchange as a San Francisco–based company whose platform "enables banks and fintech companies to easily develop financial services," and QI Tech, covered in the general Startups Weekly newsletter as a Brazilian "banking-as-a-service platform" that raised a large Series B.

Both appear as fintech infrastructure providers rather than consumer-facing banks — Synapse sits behind other companies' financial products, and QI Tech's raise is framed as backing for the same kind of platform business in Brazil.

## Key Characteristics

- **Platform, not bank** — the BaaS provider "operates a platform enabling banks and fintech companies to easily develop financial services" rather than serving end customers directly.
- **Infrastructure for others' products** — Synapse's role is to let other banks and fintechs build financial services on top of it, positioning it as embedded infrastructure rather than a retail brand.
- **Investor interest despite volatility** — QI Tech's BaaS platform drew a $200 million Series B, the largest Brazilian raise across all sectors that year, around the same time Synapse laid off 86 people, or about 40% of its staff.
- **Exposure to macro conditions** — an earlier round of Synapse layoffs (18% of its workforce, per a June blog post from CEO Sankaet Pathak) was attributed to "the current macroeconomic conditions" affecting its clients and platforms, indicating BaaS providers' fortunes are tied to the health of the banks/fintechs building on top of them.

## Background (external)

Wikipedia's entry on Banking-as-a-Service defines it more generally: BaaS refers to offering banking products — like deposit accounts, loans, and credit cards — to customers through partnerships with non-bank or non-financial third parties, where the bank handles balance-sheet management (capital, liquidity, credit risk) while the partner, often a fintech, engages the customer directly through its own app, typically connecting to the bank's systems via APIs.

# Embedded Finance

## Definition

In the corpus, embedded finance is the practice a software platform adopts when it integrates financial services and payments directly into its own product surface — exemplified by Rainforest, which "works with software companies to help them embed financial services and payments into their platforms."

## Context

In the corpus the term surfaces through Rainforest, an Atlanta-based startup that "works with software companies to help them embed financial services and payments into their platforms," positioning itself against incumbent processors Fiserv and FIS as well as fintech rival Stripe and its Connect product.
The concept is framed against a counter-claim from a16z general partner Angela Strange, who argued in 2019 that every company would eventually become a fintech; Rainforest's CEO Joshua Silver disagreed, arguing that most software companies do not want to become fintechs and absorb the associated regulatory and compliance burden — they simply want to accept payments and capture the associated revenue.
That disagreement marks the boundary of the concept in the corpus: embedded finance is presented as a narrow slice of financial functionality a software platform adopts, not a full transformation of that platform into a financial institution.

## Key Characteristics

- **Embedding, not becoming** — the software platform integrates financial services and payments into its own product surface; it does not itself become a bank or a fintech.
- **Processor-agnostic competitive layer** — providers enabling embedded finance (Rainforest, Stripe Connect) compete against both legacy processors (Fiserv, FIS) and each other for the same underlying volume.
- **Revenue motive over financial-identity motive** — per the corpus's framing, platforms adopt embedded finance to accept payments and generate revenue, not to take on the regulatory and compliance profile of a fintech.
- **Distinct from the platform's core compliance burden** — because the platform is embedding rather than becoming a financial company, it can avoid the "regulatory and compliance issues" Silver describes as the cost of the alternative "everyone is a fintech" path.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, embedded finance is a recognized industry term: Plaid defines it as "the integration of financial services, like payments, lending, or banking services, into non-financial offerings," letting users access financial tools within products they already use (Plaid, "What Is Embedded Finance?", https://plaid.com/resources/fintech/what-is-embedded-finance/, accessed 2026-09-02).

# FICCI-IBA Bankers Survey Credit Demand 2023

The seventeenth round of the FICCI-IBA survey was carried out for the period January to June 2023, with a total of 24 banks participating — public sector, private sector and foreign banks together representing about 79 per cent of the banking industry as classified by asset size.

Its backdrop was strong: the Indian economy posted an impressive 7.2 per cent growth in the financial year ended March 2023 and 7.8 per cent in the first quarter of the then-current fiscal year, while credit growth continued to rise, signalling robust demand conditions as well as banks' improved appetite towards retail borrowers. The health of the banking sector has witnessed an encouraging turnaround, marked by healthier bank balance sheets and a gross NPA ratio at a decade low.

The findings show long-term credit demand growing in sectors such as infrastructure, textiles, chemicals, food processing and metals, with iron and steel also seeing accelerated long-term loan disbursements in the past six months. Infrastructure is witnessing an increase in credit flow, with 67 per cent of respondents indicating an increase in long-term loans, against 57 per cent in the previous round. The outlook for non-food industry credit growth over the next six months is optimistic, with 42 per cent of participating banks expecting growth above 12 per cent, compared with 36 per cent in the previous round.

Alphabet was set to announce its Q3 results during Tuesday 24 October 2023's post-market session, with the search-engine giant having outperformed the broader market index at a 55% growth rate that year, surpassing the S&P 500's 12%.

# SoftBank Corp's Majority Stake In Cubic Telecom

Cubic Telecom, which provides a software-based networking solution for vehicles and other devices to link up with mobile networks in whichever country they happen to be, picked up €473 million ($513 million at the time) from SoftBank Corp, which took a 51% stake in the Dublin-based startup, valuing it at just over $1 billion (€927 million).

That effectively makes Cubic Telecom a consolidated subsidiary of SoftBank. Barry Napier stays on as CEO and will have a seat on the board; Daichi Nozaki, SoftBank's SVP of global business, plus two other SoftBank-appointed people, still unnamed, will join the board, with the remaining three board seats occupied by existing Cubic Telecom investors, which include CARIAD (the Volkswagen Group) and Qualcomm.

An important distinction: the investment comes from SoftBank Corp, not SoftBank Group, nor the company's storied Vision Fund known — and occasionally notorious — for its outsized venture deals. In this case the Japanese telecoms and IT division in Tokyo is putting in the money as a strategic investment. "In line with our 'Beyond Japan' strategic growth initiative, we are extremely pleased to be teaming up with Cubic Telecom to make a full-fledged entry into the fast-growing market for high-value IoT asset connectivity," said Junichi Miyakawa, president and CEO of SoftBank Corp, in a statement.

# Dave Clark's Ouster From Flexport

On Sept. 13, 2023, Flexport founder Ryan Petersen took the stage at North America's premier supply chain conference in Phoenix — exactly a week after he had forced out his hand-picked successor as CEO, ex-Amazon executive Dave Clark, so Petersen could once again run the show — and Clark, whom he had ousted just a year into the job, was sitting in the first few rows.

Petersen was surprised that Clark showed up, according to people with knowledge of the matter. Days earlier Petersen had excoriated Clark, alleging he had secretly expanded the company's headcount and taken on unnecessary leases without Petersen's or the board's knowledge, and posting on X, formerly Twitter, "Strategic Plan, Day 1: Make better decisions!" With Clark a few feet away, Petersen struck a different tone: "I think we're going to look back and go, 'Wow I'd probably do that all over again because of the progress that we've made,'" he said on stage, and personally commended Clark for orchestrating the $1.3 billion purchase of Deliverr from Shopify, announced in May, which picked up supply chain technology for last-mile deliveries. "I'm very, very lucky because I wouldn't have had the courage to go and do that acquisition, but I give all the credit in the world to Dave Clark," Petersen said. "There's no one probably in the world who would be better at running that last-mile e-com fulfillment network." The mixed messaging from the 43-year-old founder underscores the dysfunction surrounding the sudden firing of Clark, who previously spent 23 years at Amazon and built its mammoth logistics network on the way to becoming one of Jeff Bezos' top deputies. It is also indicative of a bigger challenge facing Flexport, whose software is designed to simplify transporting goods: valued at $8 billion by private investors in early 2022, just as the economy was turning and the 10-year tech bull market was ending, the company has been trying to operate in Silicon Valley startup growth mode while restraining expenses to reflect new economic realities and cope with supply chain bottlenecks. CNBC's account is based on conversations with people close to Clark and Petersen who requested anonymity, corroborated by internal documents and communications. Petersen has publicly said Clark overspent, overhired and overpromised, burned through cash and kept Petersen in the dark about key financials and an ambitious expansion into end-to-end supply chain tools for small and medium-sized businesses — something his allies echoed to CNBC. But documents viewed by CNBC and sources close to Clark undermine those claims, showing that Clark, who arrived when the company was struggling to bill customers and track containers, worked closely with the board and Petersen to implement decisions Flexport now suggests were ill-advised; evidence to support the claims of financial mismanagement is lacking, raising questions about whether that narrative was put forward to justify Clark's exit. A Flexport spokesperson rejected that characterization: "Ryan Petersen returned as CEO in order to restore Flexport's culture of customer engagement, and drive the growth and cost discipline required to return the company to profitability."

# Scalable Capital's $65M Flat-Valuation Round

Scalable Capital, a Munich startup that aims to make investing in financial markets accessible to a wider range of consumers, has raised €60 million in equity — $65 million at 7 December 2023 rates — at a flat valuation of $1.4 billion. Balderton led the round, with participation from HV Capital out of its new growth fund and other unnamed existing backers, and the company will use the funds to build out its business in the six countries where it is already active — Germany, Austria, Italy, France, Spain and the Netherlands — and to expand into more.

The valuation was the same as the last time Scalable Capital raised money: $180 million in 2021, in a round led by Tencent with BlackRock, HV and Tengelmann participating. That is despite the startup now being "four or five times bigger" than it was two years ago, according to co-CEO Erik Podzuweit, who co-founded the company with Florian Prucker.

"Yes, we are four or five times bigger than we were at the last round," Podzuweit said in an interview. "So like for like, obviously it's a very attractive deal for the investor. But in the current market environment, I think it's really cool that we managed to get to pull this off." He confirmed the company still has "the majority of the money from the last funding round" in the bank, but that the extra injection means it can be a little more aggressive: "We can do a bit more marketing, we can hire the top people but we also have a much bigger equity cushion." The company has now raised more than $345 million. TechCrunch updated the piece to correct the 2021 amount to $180 million rather than $140 million, and to specify the customer numbers and total raised after the company provided them post-publication.

# StarNews Mobile's $3M Pre-Series A Round

Janngo Capital, an Africa-focused venture capital firm, led StarNews Mobile's $3 million pre-Series A funding round announced on 30 October 2023, and the other notable investors included the soccer players Aurélien Tchouaméni of Real Madrid, Jules Koundé of Barcelona and Mike Maignan of AC Milan, all affiliated with the athlete representation agency Excellence Sport Nation. Kamgaing highlighted the shared African heritage of these players, underscoring their connection to StarNews' mission and their genuine interest in engaging with the African audience and investing in startups across the continent. They join the ranks of investors like Blaise Matuidi, a former French international who has previously invested in the Sudanese fintech company Bloom and currently heads Origins, a VC firm run in collaboration with other soccer players who serve as limited partners.

The round is aimed at creator payouts and market expansion. Kamgaing revealed that the platform distributed $1 million to content creators in the prior year while maintaining an average monthly payout of around $70,000 to those creators, and the fresh injection of capital serves as a significant uplift for Africa's creator economy — an underserved sector in African tech, despite startups like the e-commerce-focused Selar holding their own. The funding will equip the Los Angeles-based company, which then had 40 employees, to better support its creators and gradually enhance payouts in the coming years, a crucial step in bolstering the region's creative industry. In a press statement Kamgaing outlined expansion plans to strengthen the startup's dominant presence in Francophone Africa while quickly expanding across strategic markets like Nigeria and Ghana, and on the call he said StarNews is looking to be in 11 markets by next year.

Fatoumata Bâ, founder and executive chair of Janngo Capital, affirmed the firm's support for StarNews, accentuating the platform's unique positioning, strategic partnerships, technology and content. That support is rooted in the belief that StarNews is well-positioned to capitalize on the immense growth potential of Africa's creative industry, which she said is poised for a fourfold expansion by 2050 and the possibility to generate up to $20 billion in GDP.

Fernand Tchouameni, spokesperson and investment advisor for Aurelien Tchouameni, framed the investment in diaspora terms: "I am very excited and proud to back StarNews, the first media platform that supports African creators and tells the world the real African story. Being of Cameroonian descent, I can also see StarNews becoming a bridge to connect with the African diaspora, and I personally look forward to being on it."

# Uber's Results As A Macro Signal For Startups

The claim is that Uber's quarterly results carry information beyond Uber, and that the same numbers support two readings. Against a backdrop of macroeconomic uncertainty, the former startup darling's results can be viewed as an indication that its business model has matured and is now in a stable, profitable and cash-generating position. On the other hand, under-performing demand results from a company as global as Uber could indicate that consumer spend is coming in lighter than anticipated.

The warrant for treating it as a signal at all is Uber's role in its sector: for startups in the transport and on-demand sectors, Uber's earnings are a regular informational zeitgeist, which is why it is worth understanding where Uber's revenue came from in the third quarter and how each of its top-line sources converted — or not — to bottom-line results.

TechCrunch's own reading: the vibe when discussing Uber's results internally was that it is a very profitable and healthy company today, albeit one not growing as fast as the market had hoped. The fact that Uber's share price was up at the time of writing indicates investors are content thus far to excuse the small Q3 misses and keep their eyes more focused on year-over-year improvements and forward guidance — with more to say when Lyft's numbers arrive.

Brian Armstrong, CEO of Coinbase, slammed the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission and said the cryptocurrency exchange is looking to invest more outside of the U.S. A Coinbase spokesperson declined to comment for the CNBC story published 30 November 2023.

Armstrong told CNBC's Joumanna Bercetche earlier that week that the Binance settlement allows the crypto industry to move past a spate of scandals: "The enforcement action against Binance, that's allowing us to kind of turn the page on that and hopefully close that chapter of history," he said, adding, "I think that regulatory clarity is going to help bring in more investment, especially from institutions."

# Dave Clark's Hiring And Flexport's IPO Plan

Clark arrived at Flexport in 2022 as the apparently perfect hire for a tech startup trying to disrupt the age-old logistics industry — he had built Amazon's logistics unit into a juggernaut that rivalled carriers like UPS and FedEx — and among his goals was to help Petersen prepare Flexport for an IPO, something the company had discussed doing within a two- to three-year window.

Since 2021 Petersen had been seeking a successor for then-operating chief Sanne Manders, in part to address what several ex-employees described as lingering issues with the company's troubled billing processes; fixing that was Clark's job. Petersen and Clark worked together as co-CEOs for the first six months, and in March Petersen transitioned to executive chairman — an arrangement meant to free Petersen up to do what he loved, "getting beers with customers," in the words of two former Flexport employees, while Clark, a self-described "builder at heart," was at the wheel. "There's a perfect complement of skill sets," Petersen told Forbes in June 2022. "Mine are much more creative, zero-to-one founder time, and Dave is the supreme executor and a legend in the supply chain world." Buying Deliverr was meant to be the first step in turning Flexport into a more full-scale logistics service. Shopify had acquired Deliverr in May 2022 for $2.1 billion, but the e-commerce software company was being hammered by Wall Street as its Covid pandemic pop faded, and by January 2023 CEO Tobias Lutke knew he needed to get rid of it; around that time Lutke first approached Petersen to float a deal, and Petersen told Clark he should engage with Shopify's team. Initial talks fell apart but resumed when Flexport executives learned Shopify was about to execute deep cost cuts and was eager to sell. Clark and Petersen flew to Miami to meet Shopify's leadership, and as a transaction neared, Clark — who had a reputation as a deft negotiator — got Shopify, already an investor in Flexport, to sweeten it with $40 million in cash and the framework for a $260 million convertible note that could help Flexport on its path to an IPO, according to an internal document analyzing the deal. The sale would be announced alongside Shopify's first-quarter earnings report on May 4. "We did not change the terms of a deal or rush it just to have it line up with an earnings call," Shopify said in a statement, adding that with Flexport "we are tightly mission-aligned to ensure the success of our merchants, which is why we chose to deepen our partnership with them earlier this year." The night before the announcement, Petersen appeared at a "Tech Talk" at Flexport's Bellevue, Washington office to pitch the "Flexport vision" to hundreds of people; asked whether Flexport would ever get into last-mile logistics, he paused, glanced at his watch, and said to keep an eye on the morning news, according to an employee who witnessed the exchange and a person told independently. The comment alarmed Clark and Flexport executives, who were concerned Petersen had disclosed material nonpublic information about a publicly traded company. Petersen did not respond to calls or messages from CNBC, the company declined to make him available for an interview, and a Flexport spokesperson did not respond to CNBC's question about whether Petersen was aware of concerns about his statement.

# Gogoro's Rationale For Entering India

Gogoro co-founder and CEO Horace Luke wants to "go big" in India even as the Taiwanese company faces challenges in its home country, and his case rests on two claims about what India offers.

The first is market size: India is the world's biggest two-wheeler market, where 15 million to 20 million new two-wheelers hit the road every year. The second is leverage beyond India itself — Luke sees the world's most populous country as a launch pad that will accelerate Gogoro's global expansion into other markets, a tactic TechCrunch judged reasonable considering India is already on a spree to become a competitive manufacturing hub for all major international brands and products, from smartphones to satellites.

Speaking at the company's launch in New Delhi in December 2023, Luke said the company has picked India as a strategic market from which it can reach a number of new users and enter new markets, starting with neighboring Nepal.

# SoftBank's "Beyond Japan" Strategy Via The Cubic Partnership

SoftBank Corp's route to international expansion in this deal runs through a stake in a partner rather than through network build-out or carrier acquisition: it sees an opportunity to expand internationally not through costly builds of more network, or by acquiring other carriers, but by taking a stake in a partner it sees getting strong traction as an IT partner globally.

# Philippine Inflation In 2023 And The Government Response

In his second State of the Nation Address, President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr. singled out inflation as the country's most pressing problem. In the first nine months of 2023, inflation averaged 6.6%, far above the upper end of the 2-4% target range set by the BSP. If left unchecked, inflation could undermine growth: it not only increases costs to organizations but sets in motion second-round effects as workers start demanding higher wages, consequently increasing business costs and discouraging investments.

Inflation is partly driven by supply-side issues, and the government is allocating more resources to the agriculture sector to boost production. Marcos mentioned that the National Government had distributed 28,000 new tools and machinery to farmers, and that an additional 600 km of farm-to-market roads were laid down to support the 14 million hectares of farmland, enhancing farmer access to markets. He also signed Executive Order No. 28 in May, forming the Inter-Agency Committee on Inflation and Market Outlook, tasked with keeping inflation within government targets and boosting the economy.

# The Cancellation Of The GM–Honda Affordable EV Partnership

General Motors and Honda said in April 2022 that they would co-develop millions of small and affordable EVs, teasing sub-$30,000 electrics for North America and aiming to deliver them in 2027.

By October 2023 they canned the collaboration, vaguely citing "extensive studies and analysis" to explain the move. The announcement came as GM slowed its transition to EVs and Honda teased a "new global EV series" of its own.

# OpenAI Corporate Deals And Business Moves

Alongside its product releases, OpenAI made a series of corporate moves in 2023: a news-content partnership with Axel Springer, an indemnity promise to business customers over copyright claims, its first acquisition, a $300 million share sale, and a stalled attempt to trademark "GPT."

OpenAI struck a deal with the Berlin-based news publisher Axel Springer, which owns Business Insider and Politico, to "help provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools"; under it OpenAI will train its generative AI models on the publisher's content and add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT. Bowing to peer pressure, OpenAI also said it would pay legal costs incurred by customers who face lawsuits over IP claims against work generated by an OpenAI tool, though the protections seemingly do not extend to all OpenAI products, such as the free and Plus tiers of ChatGPT. In its first public acquisition in its seven-year history, OpenAI acquired Global Illumination, a New York-based startup leveraging AI to build creative tools, infrastructure and digital experiences; OpenAI wrote in a brief blog post, "We're very excited for the impact they'll have here at OpenAI. The entire team has joined OpenAI to work on our core products including ChatGPT."

On financing, OpenAI closed a $300 million share sale at a $27 billion to $29 billion valuation, with VC firms including Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Thrive and K2 Global picking up new shares according to documents seen by TechCrunch, and a source saying Founders Fund was also investing. That round was separate from a large Microsoft investment announced earlier in the year, which closed in January and is believed to be around $10 billion. On trademarks, OpenAI applied for a trademark for "GPT" — Generative Pre-trained Transformer — in December, and petitioned the USPTO to speed up the process, citing the "myriad infringements and counterfeit apps" beginning to spring into existence; the petition was dismissed because OpenAI's attorneys neglected to pay an associated fee and to provide "appropriate documentary evidence supporting the justification of special action," meaning a decision could take up to five more months.

A developing story as of October 2023 is the greenshoots of recovery in China, backed by domestic consumption during Golden Week and tourism related to the Asian Games. For now these seem to be buttressed on stimulus and base effects, as China is now fully open, and the long-term trajectory remains to be seen.

The near-term consequence is for commodities: in any case, for now this has provided a floor for commodity prices, especially base metals. Fickle commodity prices will also be victims of fresh geopolitical tensions in West Asia, which has pushed up Brent crude. Food prices could also play truant with climate change affecting cropping area worldwide, with sugar and rice prices booming, the note said.

# Philippine Investment Liberalisation And RCEP

Growth under the Philippine Development Plan is expected to be investment-led, driven by structural changes: the Corporate Recovery and Tax Incentives for Enterprises law, which lowered the corporate income tax rate, and amendments to the Public Service Act, Foreign Investment Act and Retail Trade Liberalization Act, which further liberalized the economy. The new legislation is expected to attract more local and foreign investment, especially in the liberalized sectors, and for the energy sector in particular the PSA amendments are envisioned to help raise the capital needed to speed up the country's energy transition to renewables.

The trade leg runs through the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership, a trading bloc encompassing the ten members of ASEAN and the ASEAN Plus One Free Trade Agreement partners Japan, China, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand, which is already in force for the Philippines and helps ease market access through trade and investment rules while supporting global and regional supply chains. The conditional relation is stated explicitly: the Philippines can potentially position itself as a regional manufacturing hub if the right incentives and policy measures are put in place to encourage local and foreign investors to participate. Together, trade and investment are expected to play an important role in attaining economic transformation, the second goal of the PDP.

# India's Electric Two-Wheeler Market Conditions

India has a relatively small market for EVs, accounting for only 3.7% of the country's total automotive market as of December 2023. Electric scooters capture 90% of total EV sales in the country, but that is just about 5% of the overall two-wheeler market.

Policy is a mixed force. The Indian government has allocated billions of dollars in subsidies and discounts to attract manufacturers and commuters to EVs, but these benefits only remain in place for a short time, and some disruption due to changes in their structure has recently been seen in the electric two-wheeler market.

Gogoro, like other players in the EV market, is nonetheless bullish, since the Indian government has targeted 30% EV adoption by 2030. Gogoro's approach of considering India as a manufacturing hub will also likely appeal to the government and help the company shift some of its production from China and enter new markets.

On the Monday of the week in which this 12 October 2023 interview was published, the Bank of Israel announced a dramatic plan to sell $30 billion of its foreign currency reserves to stabilise the shekel. By the time of the report the shekel had in fact recovered slightly and was trading at around NIS 3.96/$.

# Google's Defense: Android Openness And Sideloading

Google plans to push back at Epic's claim that it does not have competition in the app store business — the premise on which Epic's monopoly theory rests. It will point out that not only does the Play Store compete with Apple's App Store, which the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon too, but Android also supports competitive app stores like Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore.

Google will also attack the foreclosure premise directly. It will note that, unlike Apple, it allows apps to be sideloaded on Android devices — something Epic takes advantage of today — and that this process is streamlined and helps keep users safe. Epic will claim in response that the process is made to be overly difficult for end users, with multiple steps involved and "scare screens" that warn users of the security risks involved with sideloading.

On discovery, Epic will suggest that Google hid items by allowing execs and employees to have "off the record" chats; Google will counter this as well, saying it has provided the court with thousands of chat logs and millions of documents. Google will ultimately push the notion that this case is not about competition but about money — that is, that Epic Games wants to reach the Play Store's 2.5 billion users without having to pay. As a Google blog post by Wilson White, VP, Government Affairs & Public Policy, put it: "Android's choice and flexibility work well for consumers and developers of all sizes. We look forward to making our case in court as we fight to keep our users safe from harm, partner with developers to grow their businesses, and keep the Android ecosystem thriving and healthy for everyone."

# The Epic v. Google Witness Lineup

A whole cast of intriguing people were set to be called as witnesses during the trial, going straight to the top of the org chart: Google CEO Sundar Pichai and Epic CEO Tim Sweeney are absolutely expected to attend.

Beyond the two chief executives, Android co-founder Andy Rubin might be deposed, and Google says the court will hear from current Android — and Chrome, and Chrome OS — boss Hiroshi Lockheimer. Google also says representatives from Apple, Netflix, Motorola, and AT&T should testify.

# Google's Defense: Android Competes With iOS

Google's defense denies the premise that Android app stores are a market of their own: "You cannot separate the quality of a phone from the quality of the apps in its app store, and that means Google and Apple compete against each other," began Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz. If Google can convince the jury of that, it could be a winning argument, because obviously Google does not have a monopoly on app stores or phones in general.

Pomerantz's commonsense line was that Google cannot possibly have a monopoly on Android app stores when "every single Samsung phone comes with two app stores right on the homescreen," and that the download charts reflect user preference rather than exclusion: "When they show these charts that show all these downloads from Play and not from the Galaxy Store, that's what the Samsung phone users are choosing. They're touching Play. Nothing's keeping them from touching the Galaxy Store; it's just what works for them."

Google's second plank is openness relative to Apple. Epic promised to "show that Google has closed off each and every other option" to the Play Store during this trial, but Google points to the simple fact that it allows alternate app channels at all — something Android rival iOS does not. Pomerantz boasted that over a billion people have gone through the process Epic portrays as needlessly onerous to get apps outside the Play Store; Google told The Verge over email that this refers to how many users have enabled the Android sideloading flow, not necessarily followed through with an install. "A billion people have done it after getting notified of the potential risks," Pomerantz said. "That's because Android users have a real choice."

Google also argues about consequences: if Epic wins, according to Google, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps, and damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone because it arguably cannot run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. Google's execution was uneven, though — it wound up spending much of its opening statement attempting to explain away its seemingly bad behavior as normal business practices and did not always succeed out of the gate.

# Epic's Antitrust Claims Against Google Play

Epic's claim is that the Android operating system's Google Play Store constitutes an unlawful monopoly, and that Google is separately tying its Google Play payments platform to that store, keeping other potential app payment mechanisms from competing.

The grounds Epic offers are the frictions it says Google creates: Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that it has created an illegal monopoly which unjustly enriches Google while artificially driving up app prices because other stores cannot compete. The warrant joining that to the legal claim is the competitive-harm chain — no viable rival stores means no fee discipline, which means the "Google Tax" is paid either by developers or passed along to consumers. Epic wants to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods so developers are not stuck paying that tax.

Google's answer contests the warrant rather than the fees: it says Epic's demands would damage Android's ability to offer a secure user experience and to compete with Apple's iOS. Both sides agree the future of Google's app store could depend on this trial. Epic sued in 2020 after a fight over in-app purchase fees.

# Epic v. Google Is A Jury Trial

Epic and Google have to convince a jury, not the judge, which is totally different from how the Apple case played out — that one was a "bench trial."

The consequence is that persuasion cuts both ways and is hard to predict. All the evidence of tricky deals inside Google might sway a jury against the company; alternatively, Google scaremongering that sideloaded apps equal gaping security holes might sway a jury against Epic. Who knows.

The jury is also sealed off from coverage: Judge Donato explicitly told jurors they are in a "news-free bubble" through mid-December.

# Arturo Bejar's Critique Of Meta's Teen Safety Self-Regulation

In the absence of a legislative decision, Meta began regulating itself, adding new defaults and features that would restrict teens' access to content on its apps, protect their privacy and limit ad targeting to teens, as well as introducing parental controls. The premise under attack is that this self-regulation was sufficient.

In the weeks before November 15, 2023, a second Meta whistleblower, Arturo Bejar, came forward to express concerns that Instagram's approach to protecting teens was not working to keep them safe from sexual predators and unwanted sexual advances and harassment. Bejar had been hired as a consultant on the matter and eventually blew the whistle on Meta after seeing issues remain unresolved following years of work.

His argument essentially was that the improvements and safety features Meta was implementing were not enough and not effective — so the attack is on efficacy rather than on whether Meta acted at all, and its evidentiary weight comes from his having worked on the problem from inside for years.

# Google Play Billing And The User Choice Billing Alternative

Google Play's billing arrangement, as of November 2023, has two tiers. The baseline requires apps to use Google's own first-party billing system and charges app developers a 15% to 30% commission on the sales it processes. The alternative is User Choice Billing, a program still in pilot testing, open to all developers who sell apps in the 35 markets where it is then available, including the U.S., which reduces the standard commission by 4% for companies who choose to use their own payment processing solution. Spotify and Bumble were the initial testers for the new system, first introduced in November 2022, and Match, as part of its settlement agreement, will also now take advantage of this option. Epic has declined to use it.

Google's defense of the commission rests on what it says the commission buys. It will argue that its commissions are not just tied to payment processing, but help it develop other features and controls to keep Android users safe and guide them to discovering new applications, as well as helping fund the tools and services developers need to build and grow their apps. Google also helps developers reach a broader audience beyond the mobile phone, with support for Android across platforms ranging from tablets to TVs to autos and more. And it notes that 99% of its developers qualify for a commission of 15% or less, based on their revenues — so the headline 30% is the boundary case, not the typical one.
