# Nobel Prize

## Definition

In the corpus, the Nobel Prize is the award administered by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences for the physics, chemistry, and economics categories, exemplified by the 2023 chemistry prize given to Moungi Bawendi, Louis Brus, and Alexei Ekimov for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots.
Winners split a cash award of 11 million Swedish kronor (about $1 million), drawn from a bequest left by the prize's creator, Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel.

## Context

In the corpus the term appears centered on the 2023 chemistry prize, awarded to Moungi Bawendi, Louis Brus, and Alexei Ekimov for the discovery and synthesis of quantum dots, announced by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm on 2023-10-04.
That announcement sat within a week of prizes: the physics prize went to Anne L'Huillier, Pierre Agostini, and Ferenc Krausz on 2023-10-03, and the medicine prize went to Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman on 2023-10-02 for mRNA vaccine research, with literature, peace, and economics prizes following on subsequent weekdays.
The term also surfaces outside the sciences-announcement context: a financial column refers in passing to "Nobel Laureate" Paul Krugman to lend authority to an economics analogy, showing the label is used in the corpus as a general marker of eminence as well as a specific science-prize designation.

## Key Characteristics

- **Administered by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences** for the physics, chemistry, and economics categories, with nominations solicited a year in advance from thousands of university professors and scholars worldwide, and nominee deliberations kept confidential for 50 years.
- **Committee-driven selection** — a committee for each prize discusses candidates over a series of meetings before presenting proposals to the full academy for a vote.
- **Cash award** — laureates split a prize of 11 million Swedish kronor (about $1 million), funded by Alfred Nobel's bequest.
- **Multi-category, staggered announcements** — physics, chemistry, medicine, literature, peace, and economics prizes are announced on separate weekdays within the same week.
- **Confidentiality can be broken accidentally** — the 2023 chemistry winners were identified by Swedish media hours before the official announcement, after the academy sent an early press release "for still unknown reasons."
- **Used loosely as an honorific outside its own announcements** — commentary elsewhere in the corpus invokes "Nobel Laureate" status (e.g., of economist Paul Krugman) simply to signal authority in an unrelated argument.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, the Nobel Prizes are a set of six international awards — physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, peace, and economic sciences — managed by the Nobel Foundation and funded from Alfred Nobel's bequest, first awarded in 1901 and given annually (with rare exceptions, such as wartime gaps in 1940-1942); the economics prize was added later, in 1968, by Sweden's central bank in Nobel's memory. (Wikipedia, "Nobel Prize," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize)

## Corpus References

Corpus notes whose source text references this term (evidence-backed, from `term_links.json`):

- [Quantum Dot Size-Dependent Properties](quantum_dot_size_dependent_properties.md)
- [The 2023 Chemistry Nobel for Quantum Dots](quantum_dots_2023_chemistry_nobel_award.md)
- [How The 2023 Chemistry Nobel Laureates Reacted](reactions_of_2023_chemistry_nobel_laureates.md)
- [Reactions to the Quantum Dot Nobel](reactions_to_the_quantum_dot_nobel.md)



---


# The 2023 Nobel Prizes Across Categories

The 2023 chemistry prize sat in a week of announcements. On Tuesday, 2023-10-03, the physics prize went to French-Swedish physicist Anne L'Huillier, French scientist Pierre Agostini and Hungarian-born Ferenc Krausz for producing the first split-second glimpse into the super-fast world of spinning electrons. On Monday, 2023-10-02, Hungarian-American Katalin Karikó and American Drew Weissman won the Nobel Prize in medicine for discoveries that enabled the creation of mRNA vaccines against COVID-19.

The prizes in literature, peace and economics followed, with one announcement every weekday until Monday. The Nobel Prizes carry a cash award of 11 million Swedish kronor ($1 million) from a bequest left by the prize's creator, Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel.



---


# The 2023 Nobel Prize In Chemistry For Quantum Dots

Three scientists won the Nobel Prize in chemistry on Wednesday, 2023-10-04, for their work on quantum dots — tiny particles just a few nanometers in diameter that can release very bright colored light and whose applications in everyday life include electronics and medical imaging.

The laureates are Moungi Bawendi of MIT, Louis Brus of Columbia University, and Alexei Ekimov of Nanocrystals Technology Inc. They were honored for their work with the tiny particles that "have unique properties and now spread their light from television screens and LED lamps," according to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which announced the award in Stockholm.



---


# How The 2023 Chemistry Nobel Laureates Reacted

Moungi Bawendi told the news conference he was "very surprised, sleepy, shocked, unexpected and very honored," and asked about the leak, said he didn't know he'd been made a Nobel laureate until he was called by the academy. Louis Brus, a professor emeritus at Columbia, said he didn't pick up the phone when the early morning call came from the Swedish academy to notify him: "It was ringing during the night, but I didn't answer it because I'm trying to get some sleep, basically," he told The Associated Press. He finally saw the news online when he got up around 6 a.m. "I certainly was not expecting this," Brus said.

Alexei Ekimov is the former chief scientist at Nanocrystals Technology, a company based in New York where he started working in 1999. The Swedish academy credited him with demonstrating in the early 1980s that the size of copper chloride nanoparticles affected the colors in glass. "It was really nice that we got it after 40 years of work," Ekimov told the AP; his first publication on the topic was in 1981.



---


# Reactions to the Quantum Dot Nobel

Researchers welcomed the award: "They're the ones who built the foundation," said Warren Chan, a biomedical engineer and chemist at the University of Toronto in Canada, calling the prize well-deserved. "I'm really happy that the field is getting credit for really changing the world."

Chan and his colleagues found one of the first uses for quantum dots in the 1990s, using them to tag cells in lab experiments. He notes that the Nobel committee does not just look at past impacts of a discovery but also considers the effects it may have in the future, and quantum dots could have a whole medley of uses not yet explored; his own team is now using quantum dots to detect infections such as flu and HIV. "I was absolutely thrilled to see this," said Judith Giordan, president of the American Chemical Society. "We have three people recognized who brought this technology from a dream, a hope, a theoretical construct … all the way through synthesis and manufacture."



---


# The 2023 Chemistry Nobel for Quantum Dots

The 2023 Nobel Prize in chemistry honours three scientists who discovered and created quantum dots: Moungi Bawendi, a chemist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge; Louis Brus, a chemist based at Columbia University in New York City; and Alexei Ekimov, a physicist now working at Nanocrystals Technology, Inc., in Briarcliff Manor, N.Y.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the honour on October 4, and the trio will split a prize of 11 million Swedish kronor, or about $1 million. The award recognises a peculiar class of matter: typically, matter made of the same kinds of atoms arranged in the same way has the same properties, but tiny specks called quantum dots can contain the same molecules yet have different colours and other qualities depending on their size. The ability to make a whole rainbow of quantum dots simply by tweaking their size makes them highly useful — they light up TV screens and help doctors see inside the body.



---


# The Premature Leak Of The 2023 Chemistry Nobel Announcement

The suspense surrounding the academy's decision took an unusual turn when Swedish media reported the winners several hours before the prize was announced on 2023-10-04. The advance notice apparently came from a news release sent out early by mistake: Swedish media reported hours before the Wednesday announcement that the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences had sent out a news release identifying Bawendi, Brus and Ekimov as the latest Nobel laureates, and public broadcaster SVT said the release stated they were receiving the prize for the "discovery and synthesis of quantum dots."

After officially announcing the three winners, Secretary-General Hans Ellegren said the Swedish academy would investigate how the information got out in advance. "There was a press release sent out for still unknown reasons. We have been very active this morning to find out exactly what happened," he said. "This is very unfortunate and we deeply regret what happened."



---


# The Nobel Prize Nomination And Selection Procedure

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, which awards the physics, chemistry and economics prizes, follows an ordered procedure. First it asks for nominations a year in advance from thousands of university professors and other scholars around the world. Then a committee for each prize discusses candidates in a series of meetings. Finally that committee presents one or more proposals to the full academy for a vote.

The confidentiality rule bounds the whole process: the deliberations, including the names of nominees other than the winners, are kept confidential for 50 years.



---


# The Fiftieth Anniversary Of Equal Prize Money At The US Open

On Thursday, 2023-10-12, Billie Jean King and about 60 athletes were to celebrate the 50th anniversary of equal prize money at the U.S. Open and of the King-Riggs match, at her annual awards dinner for the Women's Sports Foundation in New York.

In August 2023, former President Barack Obama and first lady Michelle Obama attended the U.S. Open at Arthur Ashe Stadium to mark the pay equity milestone. "Let us remember all of this is bigger than a champion's paycheck," Michelle Obama said during the ceremony on opening night. "This is about how women are seen and valued in this world."



---


# The 2023 Laureates On Basic Research As The Motivation

Moungi Bawendi argued that curiosity, not application, is what drives the work: he said he was not thinking about the possible applications of his research when he started on quantum dots. "The motivation really is the basic science. A basic understanding, the curiosity of how does the world work? And that's what drives scientists and academic scientists to do what they do," he said.

Louis Brus made a compatible but qualified case. He was glad to see recognition for the area of chemistry he practices, and said the practical applications of quantum dots, like creating the colors in flatscreen TVs, were something he had hoped for when he started the work decades ago. His warrant for treating unpredictability as intrinsic: "Basic research is extremely hard to predict exactly how it's going to work out. It's more for the knowledge base than it is for the actual materials. But in this case, it's both."



---


# Trump's Backing Of Jim Jordan's Speaker Bid

To win over GOP colleagues, Jim Jordan relied on backing from Donald Trump — the party's front-runner in the 2024 election to challenge President Joe Biden — and on groups pressuring rank-and-file lawmakers for the vote. It was not enough, and in fact backfired on some. "Jim Jordan will be a great speaker," Trump had said on Tuesday, 2023-10-17, outside a courthouse in Manhattan where he is facing business fraud charges. "I think he's going to have the votes soon, if not today, over the next day or two."

The alliance behind that endorsement is long-standing. Jordan has been a top Trump ally, particularly during the Jan. 6 Capitol attack by the former president's backers who were trying to overturn the 2020 election he lost to Biden. Days later, Trump awarded Jordan a Medal of Freedom.



---


# The Cairo Diplomatic Surge And The 2023 Summit For Peace

On Saturday, 2023-10-21, President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi hosted what was billed as a "Summit for Peace" in Cairo, with Middle East and European leaders in attendance — evidence of the international focus then trained on Egypt. The recent flurry of diplomacy centered on Cairo marked something of a return to Egypt's traditional role, figuring prominently in every discussion over power politics across the region in the latter half of the 20th century, when it rallied Arab forces and led the 1973 attack on Israel that triggered the Yom Kippur war, before the two countries signed a peace treaty and established full diplomatic relations in 1980 and went on to become strategic allies.

In the days since Hamas — which the US and Europe designate a terrorist group — launched its attack on Israel, El-Sisi was courted by a succession of world leaders. US President Joe Biden reaffirmed the two countries' "enduring, strategic partnership" in a call. Visiting Chancellor Olaf Scholz praised German-Egyptian unity in working to prevent a Middle East "conflagration." Chinese President Xi Jinping met Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly in Beijing.



---


# The Biden-Xi San Francisco Summit, November 2023

After another rocky year of U.S.-China tensions, the two countries' presidents were set to meet in person that week for the second time since Joe Biden took office, at a summit on the Wednesday local time in San Francisco alongside the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting. CNBC, reporting from Beijing on 13 November 2023, called it a rare summit before the U.S. presidential election cycle kicks off in earnest, noting that taking a tough stance on China, the second-largest economy in the world, has become one of the few areas of bipartisan agreement and that Biden plans to run for reelection. Michael Hirson, head of China Research at 22V Research, said "the focus will be on expanding dialogue in order to low[er] tail risks in the relationship and prevent a crisis that neither leader is looking for", that flashpoints such as Taiwan and the South China Sea need to be managed carefully, and that for that reason the meeting is still important, especially ahead of a politically charged 2024 that will begin with an important presidential election in Taiwan in January and end with the U.S. presidential election. U.S.-China tensions have escalated over the last several years, beginning with tariffs under the Trump administration and spilling over into broader tech restrictions under the Biden administration.

Goodwill efforts increased in the weeks leading up to the summit: more direct flights between the U.S. and China are resuming from a low base; Chinese commodity importers in October signed the first agreements since 2017 to buy U.S. agricultural products in bulk, according to a release from the U.S. embassy in Beijing; and China's Ministry of Commerce announced the previous week that it was gathering information in an effort to address unequal treatment of foreign businesses in China versus domestic ones, a longstanding business complaint. On the cultural front, however, the three remaining giant pandas in the U.S. on loan from Beijing returned to China the previous week due to an expiring contract, pandas having been lent by China to countries around the world as a diplomatic tool.

# Earnings Report

## Definition

In the corpus, an earnings report is the quarterly release of a company's headline financial results — revenue, earnings per share (EPS), and net income — set against Wall Street analyst consensus estimates, usually paired with forward guidance for the next period.
The corpus never defines the term directly; it is used throughout as the recurring, scheduled event that "earnings week ahead" previews list companies for, and that individual company writeups (Nike, Uber) report the results of.

## Context

The corpus treats earnings reports as recurring, scheduled events that markets track closely: Seeking Alpha's "earnings week ahead" roundups list which major companies — Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, Ford, GM and dozens of others — are due to report in a given week, alongside consensus EPS and revenue estimates analysts will measure the actual results against.
Individual reports such as Nike's and Uber's quarterly releases show the report's core anatomy in practice: headline revenue and EPS figures are compared against analyst expectations to produce a "beat" or "miss," net income is disclosed alongside the year-ago comparison, and management issues guidance for the following quarter or full year on the same release or earnings call.
The term also surfaces as a governance signal: the corpus notes that after Elon Musk took Twitter (X) private, the company stopped producing quarterly earnings reports, which reduced public transparency and accountability around the platform's business — an absence the EU's disinformation scrutiny of X is contrasted against.

## Key Characteristics

- **Periodic and scheduled** — earnings reports are issued on a recurring quarterly (or annual) cadence, well-known enough in advance that outlets publish "earnings week ahead" previews naming which companies report and when.
- **Benchmarked against consensus estimates** — headline metrics (EPS, revenue) are reported alongside analyst consensus figures, and the gap between actual and expected results is characterized as a "beat" or "miss," as with Nike beating on earnings/margin while missing on revenue, and Uber missing revenue and EPS expectations despite YoY growth.
- **Forward guidance is bundled in** — companies commonly pair the backward-looking results with guidance for the next quarter or full year (e.g., Nike maintaining full-year revenue-growth and margin guidance; Uber issuing gross-bookings guidance for Q4).
- **Segment-level breakdowns** — reports can disaggregate results by business unit or geography (Uber's ride-hailing, delivery, and freight segments; Nike's regional sales by North America, EMEA, and APAC), each compared to its own prior-year and expected figures.
- **A public-company accountability mechanism** — ceasing to publish earnings reports (as X did after going private) is treated in the corpus as a loss of the transparency and external accountability that public disclosure otherwise provides.

## Background (external)

The corpus does not spell out what an earnings report formally is or how it relates to SEC filings. Per the Corporate Finance Institute, an earnings report is an official financial document a public company releases to summarize its financial performance for a period — showing revenue, net income, and EPS (also called the income statement or profit-and-loss statement) — together with management's guidance on present and future expectations; it typically accompanies the fuller periodic filings (annual Form 10-K, quarterly Form 10-Q) that public companies submit to the SEC, and results are judged against market analysts' estimates even though that comparison is not part of the filing itself (Corporate Finance Institute, *Earnings Report*, accessed 2026-09-02).

# Dave Clark's Hiring And Flexport's IPO Plan

Clark arrived at Flexport in 2022 as the apparently perfect hire for a tech startup trying to disrupt the age-old logistics industry — he had built Amazon's logistics unit into a juggernaut that rivalled carriers like UPS and FedEx — and among his goals was to help Petersen prepare Flexport for an IPO, something the company had discussed doing within a two- to three-year window.

Since 2021 Petersen had been seeking a successor for then-operating chief Sanne Manders, in part to address what several ex-employees described as lingering issues with the company's troubled billing processes; fixing that was Clark's job. Petersen and Clark worked together as co-CEOs for the first six months, and in March Petersen transitioned to executive chairman — an arrangement meant to free Petersen up to do what he loved, "getting beers with customers," in the words of two former Flexport employees, while Clark, a self-described "builder at heart," was at the wheel. "There's a perfect complement of skill sets," Petersen told Forbes in June 2022. "Mine are much more creative, zero-to-one founder time, and Dave is the supreme executor and a legend in the supply chain world." Buying Deliverr was meant to be the first step in turning Flexport into a more full-scale logistics service. Shopify had acquired Deliverr in May 2022 for $2.1 billion, but the e-commerce software company was being hammered by Wall Street as its Covid pandemic pop faded, and by January 2023 CEO Tobias Lutke knew he needed to get rid of it; around that time Lutke first approached Petersen to float a deal, and Petersen told Clark he should engage with Shopify's team. Initial talks fell apart but resumed when Flexport executives learned Shopify was about to execute deep cost cuts and was eager to sell. Clark and Petersen flew to Miami to meet Shopify's leadership, and as a transaction neared, Clark — who had a reputation as a deft negotiator — got Shopify, already an investor in Flexport, to sweeten it with $40 million in cash and the framework for a $260 million convertible note that could help Flexport on its path to an IPO, according to an internal document analyzing the deal. The sale would be announced alongside Shopify's first-quarter earnings report on May 4. "We did not change the terms of a deal or rush it just to have it line up with an earnings call," Shopify said in a statement, adding that with Flexport "we are tightly mission-aligned to ensure the success of our merchants, which is why we chose to deepen our partnership with them earlier this year." The night before the announcement, Petersen appeared at a "Tech Talk" at Flexport's Bellevue, Washington office to pitch the "Flexport vision" to hundreds of people; asked whether Flexport would ever get into last-mile logistics, he paused, glanced at his watch, and said to keep an eye on the morning news, according to an employee who witnessed the exchange and a person told independently. The comment alarmed Clark and Flexport executives, who were concerned Petersen had disclosed material nonpublic information about a publicly traded company. Petersen did not respond to calls or messages from CNBC, the company declined to make him available for an interview, and a Flexport spokesperson did not respond to CNBC's question about whether Petersen was aware of concerns about his statement.

# Clark's Cease-And-Desist, The Political Friction, And The Firing For Cause

Clark's cease-and-desist letter cited two documents that had been presented to the board — a pre-acquisition financial analysis of the Deliverr deal, presented by the co-CEOs for board approval and shaped by multiple prior board meetings, and a review of Flexport's first-quarter numbers — both viewed by CNBC.

Clark's camp suggested other factors may have led to the abrupt firing, among them politics. Days after Clark was ousted, Petersen sent him a message, seen by CNBC, blasting one of his key female executives for wasting her days at the company on "far left-wing political activism"; the executive is a registered Republican. Trae Stephens, the Founders Fund partner, had also shared his contempt for that executive weeks before Clark's departure, a person familiar with the board told CNBC, and Stephens did not respond to a request for comment. Petersen is also a venture partner at Founders Fund, the firm started by Peter Thiel, a prominent supporter of President Trump's 2016 campaign who more recently bankrolled Senate candidates in Ohio and Arizona, and many of Thiel's closest confidantes at Founders Fund and elsewhere in venture are outspoken conservatives — though Petersen's sole public political contribution in 2023 was to a Democratic political action committee associated with Sen. Joe Manchin of West Virginia, and he does not talk much about politics. Clark has donated to candidates on both sides of the aisle; upon his departure The Wall Street Journal reported he was considering running for governor of Texas, but two people familiar with his thinking say that is not happening anytime soon. Flexport told CNBC that an employee's politics are not relevant in personnel decisions: "Ryan Petersen does not care at all about anyone's political or personal affiliations. That is their business. It is inappropriate for any employee to spend an excessive amount of time during work hours on activities unrelated to their role." A person familiar with the female executive said her noncorporate endeavors were largely related to charitable organizations. Clark has largely remained silent since he was forced to resign on Sept. 5, though in private he has expressed frustration at how his former team was treated, as many of his allies from Amazon who joined him at Flexport were summarily fired by Petersen shortly after his departure. On Sept. 13, Flexport chief legal counsel Chris Ferro contacted Clark to tell him his resignation a week earlier had not been accepted: instead, Flexport's board met the day after Clark resigned and voted to fire him for cause, though the board minutes did not yet reflect why. Ferro allegedly told Clark that Flexport would give him a block of 2 million shares — worth millions of dollars — if he signed a separation agreement including nondisclosure and nondisparagement clauses; Clark declined. Shortly after, Clark took the stage at the same Phoenix supply chain conference Petersen had spoken at earlier that day and did not hold back: "The only thing I really regret from the past year was I sort of picked the wrong founder. Basically, it was a place of extending my reputational halo to a group that, in my opinion, didn't deserve it. Largely, because about half the team was let go last week on Friday, the most brutal nonseverance packages I've ever seen in my life. It was about as disrespectful a way as humanly possible."

# Initial Public Offering (IPO)

## Definition

In the corpus, IPO — used interchangeably with "going public" — names the transition several companies undergo or are preparing to undergo onto a public stock exchange: cybersecurity startup IronNet is reported to have "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," and pre-IPO funds are described as investing in "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" ahead of that transition.

## Context

The corpus uses IPO/going-public language across several unrelated stories, which is what makes the term a recurring hinge concept rather than a one-off mention: cybersecurity startup IronNet "fail[ed] to gain traction after going public in August 2021," after which its stock price kept declining from an initial post-IPO spike; Swedish fintech Klarna is described as "taking steps toward an eventual IPO," restructuring into a U.K. holding company as "an important early step in its plans for an initial public offering"; and logistics company Flexport's ousted CEO Dave Clark counted among his goals helping prepare the company for an IPO, with Flexport having discussed an IPO in a two- to three-year window. The term also appears in Indian investing coverage, where late-stage "pre-IPO funds" let investors buy into "mature companies preparing to list on the stock exchange" before their public debut, distinct from "publicly traded equity" that Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) are said to be uncorrelated with. Once a company is public, its "stock price" becomes a live signal of investor sentiment, as seen in the Rogers family's boardroom conflict driving down Rogers Communications' stock price, and in Coinbase — "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges — seeing its shares swing on Binance/FTX-related news.

## Key Characteristics

- **Transition event** — the corpus marks the same before/after line with "going public" and "publicly traded," as with IronNet going "public in August 2021" and Coinbase being "the only one that's publicly traded in the U.S." among major crypto exchanges.
- **Preceded by preparation** — companies undertake preparatory steps beforehand, such as Klarna's legal-entity restructuring into a U.K. holding company, or Flexport's Dave Clark working toward the goal of helping the company get "IPO ready" within a two- to three-year window it had discussed.
- **Followed by market scrutiny** — once public, a company's stock price becomes a running scoreboard, as with IronNet's post-IPO stock decline and Rogers Communications' stock price reacting to boardroom disputes.
- **Investment-fund target** — "pre-IPO" or late-stage private equity funds exist specifically to let investors buy into companies before this transition, aiming to capture value at listing.
- **Not guaranteed to sustain value** — IronNet's case in the corpus shows an initial post-IPO price spike can be followed by a steep, sustained decline.

## Background (external)

Outside this corpus, an IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public: a privately held company becomes a public company by selling shares to institutional and retail investors, typically with investment banks acting as underwriters who arrange for the shares to be listed on a stock exchange, a process also known as "floating" or "going public." (Wikipedia, "Initial public offering," accessed 2026-09-02: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_public_offering)

# Three Filipino Education Dreams And The PhilEd Programs

The proposal maps three Filipino education dreams onto three PhilEd programs. The first dream is to enroll in a chosen course in the school of one's choice, which will be funded by the School Vouchers Program, transferred from DepEd to PhilEd. The second dream, especially for Filipino parents, is to save enough money to fund the college education of their children, hence the prevalence of pre-need Educational Plans; because most pre-need companies went into bankruptcy, causing financial ruin and emotional distress to plan holders, there has been a massive market failure and government must intervene, but the intervention should not involve the government offering educational plans, rather insuring them. Just as the Philippine Deposit Insurance Corp. insures bank deposits, PhilEd would insure educational plans, and just as PDIC is funded from premiums paid by banks, PhilEd would fund this program from premiums paid by educational plan companies; PhilEd would be ideally suited to this because it could swap failed educational plans with school vouchers from its repository.

The third dream is based on the realization of Filipino school graduates that their learning must continue after they leave their alma maters, because in this modern age the fount of personal knowledge must continuously be replenished. The parallel drawn is with healthcare: Health Maintenance Organizations continuously monitor and minister to health, so Lifelong Learning Organizations are needed to continuously monitor and minister to learning; HMOs exist in the Philippines while LLOs do not. In partnership with international development agencies and the private sector, PhilEd would create this industry, with the international development agencies providing technical assistance grants to create the developmental and regulatory framework and the private sector organizing the LLOs, while PhilEd acts as the "bastonero" or project manager, managing the project as well as mobilizing government support and assistance.

Earnings season was slated to peak in the week of 23 to 27 October 2023, with a wide range of companies across various sectors reporting results, Seeking Alpha reported on 22 October. # Google's Most Lucrative Search Terms, Unsealed At Trial

Judge Amit Mehta ruled to make public a list that provides a glimpse of which search terms make Google the most money: 20 terms that were lucrative for the week of September 22, 2018. Revenue per search term, how many queries each of those terms got, and a separate list of popular search terms ordered by queries rather than revenue were all redacted, so the disclosure is a bare ranking without magnitudes.

The visible list, in order, is: iPhone 8; iPhone 8 plus; Auto insurance; Car insurance; Cheap flights; Car insurance quotes; DirecTV; Online colleges; AT&T; Hulu; iPhone; Uber; Spectrum; Comcast; Xfinity; Insurance quotes; Free credit report; Cheap car insurance; AARP; LifeLock.

TechCrunch read little surprise into it. Google and Apple have a long and mutually beneficial relationship even while competing, so three Apple search-related queries bringing in the big bucks is unsurprising — not least since September 22, 2017 was the official release date of the iPhone 8. Queries like "car insurance," "cheap flights" and "credit report" are perennial favorites and speak to how much Google dominates vertical search, that is, search in very specific market categories. As for LifeLock, the big Equifax data breach of 2017 was a hot topic in September 2017 and LifeLock was making a big push to win business with people who wanted to buy identity theft protection.

# Sweeney And Pichai's Settlement Talks

Asked about his settlement talks with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Tim Sweeney said he could not discuss their content, but that the two met for an hour and had a professional discussion in which they did not reach a settlement — they were, in his words, "rather far apart."

He explained the gap in terms of what Epic was asking for: free and fair competition for everybody, removal of the payments tie, and removal of the anticompetitive measures, which he said obviously leads to far better deals for consumers and developers. What Epic does not want is a special deal just for itself. Sweeney characterised Google's strategy so far, as visible from all these deals, as taking out potential competitors one at a time while they are still weak and small, before they build up or unite into a formidable force — and said Epic is not going to go along with something like that.

# Pet Fit For Life Plush Wand

Audience manager Kaitlin Hatton's dog Trudee — otherwise known as My Boss — is notoriously insistent on being the focus of her attention: at any given moment Trudee has 20 toys strewn about the apartment, but she will not play with them unless Hatton is watching, literally with no distractions, sitting within feet of her, just staring at her chew on her toys for hours on end.

The problem is not affection but enrichment: Hatton loves staring at her dog, but Trudee does not get the enrichment she deserves when her activity levels are tied directly to Hatton's ability to give her undivided attention.

That changed when she bought the Pet Fit For Life Plush Wand, which has a toy attached to a long chewable rope suspended from a metal pole. Now Hatton not only tosses the toy about the room from the comfort of her couch, but Trudee is so distracted by chasing it that she does not notice if Hatton is not making direct eye contact. It is a win-win.

The first full week of December 2023 carried a heavy corporate reporting calendar, with several significant companies slated to announce quarterly results between December 4 and December 8 — releases Seeking Alpha framed on December 3, 2023 as holding considerable implications for energy, software, retail, autos and semiconductors.

The companies scheduled to release financial figures that week included NIO (NYSE:NIO), GameStop (NYSE:GME), DocuSign (NASDAQ:DOCU), ChargePoint (NYSE:CHPT), Dollar General (NYSE:DG), C3.ai (NYSE:AI) and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO). # Letitia James' History of Investigating Trump

Letitia James, who campaigned for office as a Trump critic and watchdog, started scrutinising his business practices in March 2019, after his former personal lawyer Michael Cohen testified to Congress that Trump exaggerated his wealth on financial statements provided to Deutsche Bank while trying to obtain financing to buy the NFL's Buffalo Bills.

Her office had previously sued Trump for misusing his own charitable foundation to further his political and business interests. Trump was ordered to pay $2 million to an array of charities as a fine, and the charity, the Trump Foundation, was shut down.

# Gogoro's Rationale For Entering India

Gogoro co-founder and CEO Horace Luke wants to "go big" in India even as the Taiwanese company faces challenges in its home country, and his case rests on two claims about what India offers.

The first is market size: India is the world's biggest two-wheeler market, where 15 million to 20 million new two-wheelers hit the road every year. The second is leverage beyond India itself — Luke sees the world's most populous country as a launch pad that will accelerate Gogoro's global expansion into other markets, a tactic TechCrunch judged reasonable considering India is already on a spree to become a competitive manufacturing hub for all major international brands and products, from smartphones to satellites.

Speaking at the company's launch in New Delhi in December 2023, Luke said the company has picked India as a strategic market from which it can reach a number of new users and enter new markets, starting with neighboring Nepal.



---


# GameStop Q3 Earnings Preview, December 2023

Video game retailer GameStop (GME) was scheduled to post its Q3 earnings after the closing bell on the Wednesday of the week following Seeking Alpha's December 3, 2023 preview, with analysts expecting losses to narrow year over year on relatively flat revenue.

The two rating systems disagreed, and in the harsher direction than for most names in the same preview: Wall Street analysts recommended selling GME stock, while Seeking Alpha's Quant rating system advised only a Hold. Consensus estimates were EPS of -$0.08 and revenue of $1.18B — consistent with the narrowing-loss, flat-revenue expectation. The Earnings Insight is the notable qualifier: GameStop had beaten EPS estimates in only three of the past eight quarters and revenue expectations in five of those reports, so a beat was far from the base case going in.

# US Jobs And Services Data In Early October 2023

Wednesday's ADP report suggested private employers added 89,000 jobs last month, a much sharper slowdown in hiring than the 140,000 economists expected. The report does not have a perfect track record in predicting what the more comprehensive jobs report from the US government will say, which was due to arrive on the Friday. Mike Loewengart, head of model portfolio construction at Morgan Stanley Global Investment Office, said that "if Friday's report also shows the labour market is cooling, stock investors may worry a little less about indefinitely higher interest rates".

A second report on the economy said growth in US services industries slowed in September by a touch more than economists expected. The figures were reported by The Age on 4 October 2023 alongside a note that oil prices slumped overnight.



---


# Mapstead's AdultFriendFinder Exit And Facebook Car Pages

Lars Mapstead is a guy seemingly blessed with a never-ending mental stream of schemes: he helped start a handful of companies, including the once-ubiquitous hookup site AdultFriendFinder, which sold in 2007 for $500 million.

He tried to retire after that but got bored and started a couple of Facebook pages devoted to his passion for hot rods and custom cars. This was during the peak years for social media, and just as Bastilla had described back at the alligator party, Mapstead's "core knowledge of SEO" came in handy: before long his pages had 25 million followers. "I was basically just spamming Facebook with cars and articles about cars and sending traffic to banner ads, and that turned into $120,000 a month," he said. "And that was supposed to be my hobby!"



---


# Lumesner Carry-On Backpack

Audience manager Kaitlin Hatton committed to traveling more earlier this year and took a look at the gear she had that could be replaced after years of trekking the globe; her ratty old secondhand carry-on bag was the first thing to go, and after several days of weighing the pros and cons of various travel bags she stumbled on this Lumesner carry-on backpack on Amazon, which fit all of her needs.

It can carry a laptop, several days' worth of clothes, her 40oz Hydro Flask bottle, and more, and it even includes some packing cubes. It is very comfortable, and the weight is well distributed when it is completely full. It is also an inexpensive alternative to many name-brand carry-on bags.

So far she has used it on a handful of trips and the quality has held up. One drawback: it holds onto pet fur, so she had to add a small lint roller to her travel necessities — but that is just life while traveling with a dog anyway.



---


# Duane Forrester, Bing, And The Search Engine's View

Duane Forrester was at Microsoft from 2007 until 2015, where he helped launch and manage Bing, the perpetual underdog to Google's domination of online search; because he worked as an SEO both before and after his time at Microsoft, he sees the industry from both sides — like an aerospace engineer who spent a few years at the Department of Defense, left for the private sector, and now is much better at winning military contracts. He has a holistic understanding of the delicate push and pull between the SEOs desperate for clues on how to do their jobs better and the search engine trying to keep its secret-sauce algorithm proprietary.

He was the first stop because Google was slow to allow anyone to talk to the writer, possibly because of the giant PR clusterfuck that has been the company's past year: accused by the federal government of being a monopoly, increasingly despised by the public, losing ground to Reddit, TikTok, and large language models.

Like Schwartz, Forrester wanted to emphasize how hard everyone works. "I've lost track of how many people I know who built companies and sold them and have just, like, made wealth," he said. "That is not a 40-hour commitment in the week. That is a 400-hour commitment." For the record, there are 168 hours in a week.

His route in started young. These days Forrester lives in Los Angeles and asked to meet at one of his favorite restaurants, which felt like a British pub operated by Disney World, tucked away in a desert strip mall and covered in Anglophile paraphernalia including Union Jack flags, a mural of Big Ben, and a red phone booth. Over a full English breakfast he described growing up in rural Canada, where his parents owned a motel and he used to mess around with the pay phone outside, eventually figuring out how to finagle free long-distance phone calls: "And then it became, 'What else can I know how to do?'" By the '90s he was trading tips with other SEOs in online forums, and he still remembers the thrill of the very first SEO conference he attended, where he was asked to speak. "The people who got up onstage to talk were seen as somehow more knowledgeable, but I don't know that we felt that way," he said. "You all kind of knew you were making shit up."

As a former SEO, Forrester understood that the quality of Bing's search results would be affected by the work of SEOs, so it made sense to communicate with SEOs as much as possible. Cutts similarly tried to serve as a conduit between SEOs and Google, but Forrester felt Google projected an attitude he described as: "We know what we're doing, we will stop your attempts to game this, and you know what? We'll just kind of ignore you, and when you give us feedback, eh, we don't really care."

# Why Indian Investors Should Look To US Big Pharma

For cutting-edge tech and pharmaceutical exposure, the US is the place for Indian investors to look to, because Indian markets already give them access to growth in manufacturing, banking, commodity, services and IT, but not to that frontier. The grounds are structural: the US is the largest pharmaceutical market in the world, and by virtue of its size, its ideal IP protection laws and its deep-pocketed insurers, most of the cutting-edge innovation in pharma tends to be concentrated there. The warrant is that for investors and general readers alike one should be abreast of the latest pharmaceutical innovation taking place overseas, since the open questions of the field, whether a weight loss pill will be a reality, when HIV will be cured, and what the future of cancer treatments is, are being answered in that market.

The article's scope is set out with the argument: it highlights the largest unmet needs in medicine currently being addressed by US Big Pharma such as Merck, Gilead and Eli Lilly, and also by big players based in Europe, namely Novo Nordisk and Roche, and it lays down the basic framework for investing in or assessing US pharma and the stocks currently in focus.

# Emma Hayes Appointed USWNT Head Coach

U.S. Soccer made Emma Hayes' appointment as head coach of the U.S. women's national team official on Tuesday 14 November 2023, making her the 10th full-time coach of the programme, as reported by The New York Times on 15 November 2023.

The sequence began on 4 November, when Chelsea Women released a statement saying their coach was leaving at the end of the season to "pursue a new opportunity outside of the Women's Super League and club football" — Hayes had just entered her second decade in charge, and few knew where she would land. That same day The Athletic, among others, reported that her next job would be with the U.S. women's national team, leading a four-time World Cup and Olympic gold medal-winning programme into a new era. Hayes, who previously won six WSL titles in England, will not take charge until her final season with Chelsea is complete the following May. Sporting director Matt Crocker made the final decision to hire her after a search process that began in August, following the team's surprising exit in the round of 16 at the World Cup and the subsequent departure of head coach Vlatko Andonovski. Though Hayes is seen as one of the world's top coaches in women's soccer, the article notes the appointment still comes as something of a surprise.

Both sides gave statements. U.S. Soccer president Cindy Parlow Cone said: "She has tremendous energy and an insatiable will to win. Her experience in the USA, her understanding of our soccer landscape and her appreciation of what it means to coach this team makes her a natural fit for this role and we could not be more pleased to have her leading our women's national team forward." Hayes said: "This is a huge honor to be given the opportunity to coach the most incredible team in world football history. The feelings and connection I have for this team and for this country run deep. I've dreamed about coaching the USA for a long time so to get this opportunity is a dream come true. I know there is work to do to achieve our goals of winning consistently at the highest levels. To get there, it will require dedication, devotion and collaboration from the players, staff and everyone at the U.S. Soccer Federation."

# Healy Denies The End Of Australian Women's Cricket Dominance

Alyssa Healy rejected the suggestion that the Test defeat to India showed Australia's unprecedented period of dominance was ending: her counter attacks the inference from a single result, arguing the loss is "probably not even a blip" because it came in a format and conditions the team is not familiar with.

Quizzed on the point after the loss, Healy was defiant. "It's probably not even a blip," she said. "It (Test cricket) is a format where we're not overly familiar with, in conditions that we're not familiar with. I see more positives out of this and than any sort of negativity."

She then challenged the standard being applied to the team, arguing that outside expectations have not kept pace with a squad in transition: "There is always a lot of expectation and external noise about our team and how we're performing. They are so used to seeing us winning, that I think, at times, they forget that we've actually seen quite a lot of change over the last 12 to 18 months. That kind of goes unnoticed external to our group."

# The England Camp's Verdict On The T20 Series Defeat

Jos Buttler's verdict on the Dec. 21, 2023 series defeat was that England "probably didn't adapt quickly enough with the bat," having thought 160 would have been a decent score on a used wicket, but that it was a fantastic bowling effort in which they did well to hang in the game as long as they did.

Buttler added that Phil Salt had had a brilliant series and that England found out lots about themselves as a team; on the stop-clock experiment, he said it was only in the last game that they really noticed it, and that it was good to keep the game moving. The live blog's own summary was that England's miserable white-ball year ended with another series defeat, though plenty of good had come from this series, most notably Salt's performance — and that while there were a few slots to fill, most notably at No. 3, they were in reasonable shape ahead of the next year's World Cup. Reece Topley said: "We've had some high-scoring games, but the last game was almost the complete opposite of what happened here. We were probably just under par with the first-innings score but with the ball we were excellent, pushed them right to the end. I think it's been an amazing series. Both teams have played some unbelievable cricket. I was so excited turning up today, because it was basically a final and those are the games you want to play in and be on the right side of. The bottom line is you want to win this series, I want to win every series I can for England."

# West Indies Win The 2023 T20I Series 3-2

West Indies beat England by four wickets in the fifth and deciding T20 international on Dec. 21, 2023, taking the series 3-2 when Shai Hope pinged Chris Woakes over extra cover for six at 19.2 overs, with West Indies 133-6.

It was the 120th six of the series, and Hope played a gem of an innings, calmly anchoring West Indies in an increasingly nervous chase with a run-a-ball 43; England fought admirably to defend a below-par total and, but for Hope, would probably have done it. Cricket on TNT Sports posted that the win claimed the series 3-2 and a white-ball clean sweep. The Guardian's report framed the finish as the sequel to a very different match: Tuesday's ludicrous, record-smashing, high-scoring entertainment had been followed on the same surface by thrilling low-scoring entertainment and a different result claimed in very different style, eventually won with four balls to spare and in the most unfitting of ways — with a massive six — by Hope, again proving himself the right man for a run chase. A series marked by stunning power hitting, roaring run rates and an unexpected midway transformation in England's performances and prospects concluded with a 3-2 triumph for West Indies, who extended their supremacy over England at home to four series in three formats across nearly five years.



---


# First T20I In Barbados: Match Summary

West Indies beat England in the first T20 international in Barbados on Dec. 12, 2023, chasing down 171 with eleven balls remaining after England collapsed from 112-2 at the ten-over mark.

The Guardian's James Wallace called it an intriguing game that set up the T20I series nicely, and a real statement laid down by Rovman Powell and his men. West Indies were up against it early, with England crunching their way to 112-2 off the first ten overs, but Jos Buttler's side managed only 59 runs off the next ten, losing eight wickets along the way. A total of 171 was thirty or more shy of where England would have liked to end up, and so it proved as West Indies showed how muscular their own batting card is — the home side cleared the ropes fourteen times compared with England's six. Andre Russell and Rovman Powell found the stands with ease at the business end of the match to get West Indies over the line. # The First ODI Cricket World Cup, 1975

England hosted the inaugural ODI World Cup in 1975 and held the event the following three times too, with the West Indies winning the first tournament.

The playing conditions were unlike the modern game: initially the game was played in cricket whites and with a red ball instead of a white ball. Eight teams took part in that inaugural tournament — India, Pakistan, England, Australia, West Indies, New Zealand and a composite team from East Africa and Sri Lanka. Current cricketing powerhouse South Africa was banned at the time from international sport due to its policy of racial segregation under the Apartheid system, and so did not take part in the first ODI World Cup.

The early honours went to two teams. The West Indies won the first tournament and defended the title in the second World Cup in 1979, while India's first taste of glory came when they clinched the trophy in 1983 by defeating the West Indies by 43 runs in the final.

# The Rain Delay And DLS Position In The First T20I

Rain stopped play in the first T20I with West Indies on 108-4 after 12.4 overs and requiring 64 runs off 44 balls — crucially, six runs ahead of the Duckworth Lewis Stern rate, so that if the rain did not abate the home side would take the spoils.

The heavens cracked out of nowhere and the players scurried off as the covers were hauled on, with Hope on 27 and Powell on 6. The rain then began tailing off and a rope was dragged around the outfield to take off excess water. The Guardian's man in Barbados, Simon Burnton, reported a 9.35 p.m. restart with no overs lost, putting play about eight minutes away; the live blog understood 10.10 p.m. local time — 2.10 a.m. in London — to be the cut off for the match.

# England 132 All Out In The T20 Series Decider

England were bowled out for 132 in the deciding fifth T20I on Dec. 21, 2023, less than half the 267-3 they had made on the same surface two days earlier, leaving West Indies needing 133 to win the series.

The Guardian's live blog set the contrast starkly: Tuesday at Tarouba, England 267-3 with 19 sixes; Thursday, England 132 all out with five sixes. England assembled exactly the same players in exactly the same place and exactly the same situation — losing the toss, put in to bat — but this was an entirely different performance, on a wicket once so true that turned untrustworthy. The report suggested that as a tour enters its final days thoughts often turn to home, and perhaps the focus was not as laser-sharp as it might have been; whatever the reason, the pyrotechnics of the two previous matches never sparked. It took a fabulous delivery from Gudakesh Motie to end Phil Salt's run of absurd form with his score a modest 38, but some of the other wickets seemed a little careless: in the fourth over Jos Buttler casually turned a Jason Holder delivery to fine leg where Oshane Thomas was positioned, hands cupped, and Harry Brook tried to paddle-sweep Motie but sent the ball only a few feet into the air for an easy Nicholas Pooran catch, making it 70 for four one ball into the ninth over, at which point Liam Livingstone and Moeen Ali had to focus on disaster prevention rather than entertainment. Akeal Hosein's four overs went for just 20 and brought the wickets of Will Jacks and Moeen — the latter undone by a relay catch on the boundary after he and Livingstone added 40 for the fifth wicket — and Livingstone followed precisely two overs later, prodding the ball limply back to Motie, at which point things really fell apart, the last five wickets surrendered in 20 balls for just 11 runs. England were 109 for four after 14 overs and then the house fell down: in the 19th over Andre Russell, who bowled really well, finished with two for 25 and would have had three wickets in four balls had Hosein taken a tricky low chance at third man to dismiss Sam Curran; Adil Rashid was run out for 1 at 132-9, sacrificing himself just as in the 2019 World Cup final so that Curran could stay on strike with four balls remaining; and Curran clouted the next ball to long-off, caught by Rutherford off Holder for 12, to end the innings.

# World Cup

## Definition

In the corpus, "World Cup" names a sport's top international championship, but its shape differs by sport: the ICC's men's ODI Cricket World Cup and World Rugby's Rugby World Cup (RWC) each crown a winner via a national-team final, FIFA's football World Cup is preceded by confederation qualifying such as CONMEBOL's, and Mikaela Shiffrin's Alpine skiing World Cup is tracked in the corpus as a tally of individual "World Cup wins" building toward an "overall World Cup" title rather than a single match.

## Context

In the corpus the term spans multiple sports and formats.
The ICC organises the Cricket World Cup "every four years," a men's ODI tournament whose 1975 edition (hosted by England, contested by eight teams including a composite East Africa/Sri Lanka side) established the pattern of a single-host, knockout-culminating event; the 2023 edition ran in India from October 5 to November 19, and its final pitted "two-time World Champions" India against "five-time World Champions" Australia.
World Rugby's Rugby World Cup (RWC) crowned the Springboks in the corpus's 2023 final — a 12-11 win over the All Blacks in France, reported under the headline "claim record FOURTH RWC"; the cited passage covers that single match and its aftermath, not the tournament's periodicity or hosting structure.
FIFA's World Cup operates on a longer cycle with a distinct qualification stage: national confederations such as CONMEBOL run "World Cup qualifying" matches (e.g., Argentina vs Paraguay for the 2026 tournament) years ahead of the finals themselves.
By contrast, the Alpine skiing World Cup that Mikaela Shiffrin dominates is not one tournament: the corpus counts her record in terms of individual "World Cup wins" and "five overall World Cup victories," a cumulative tally rather than a knockout final (see Background for how that circuit is structured).

## Key Characteristics

- **Governing-body run** — the corpus explicitly credits the ICC with organising the Cricket World Cup (doc_0409) and refers to the football World Cup as a "FIFA tournament" (doc_0105), with confederations such as CONMEBOL organising qualifying (doc_0105).
- **Periodic, at least for cricket** — only the Cricket World Cup's cadence is explicitly quoted in the corpus as "every four years" (doc_0409); the cited Rugby World Cup passage does not state a periodicity for the RWC.
- **National-team contest culminating in a final** — the cricket and rugby World Cups in the corpus each end in a single final: India vs Australia at Ahmedabad in 2023 (doc_0246), and the Springboks' 12-11 win over the All Blacks in France (doc_0022).
- **Separate qualification phase** — for football, "World Cup qualifying" is a distinct, multi-year stage (run per confederation, e.g. CONMEBOL) that precedes the finals tournament itself (doc_0105).
- **Not always a single event** — in individual sports such as Alpine skiing, the corpus describes "World Cup" wins accumulating toward an "overall World Cup" title for Mikaela Shiffrin (doc_0585) rather than a single match; the underlying season-long, points-based structure is documented externally (see Background).

## Background (external)

The FIS Alpine Ski World Cup that doc_0585 references is, per Wikipedia, a season-long circuit of races (roughly January to mid-March) rather than a single tournament.
Points are awarded to the top 30 finishers in each race (100 for first place, sliding to 1 for 30th, a system in place since the 1991-92 season), and the skier with the most cumulative points at season's end wins the overall title, symbolised by the "big crystal globe," with separate discipline titles awarded via smaller globes.
Source: Wikipedia, "FIS Alpine Ski World Cup," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIS_Alpine_Ski_World_Cup, accessed 2026-09-02.

# Britney Spears On Body Scrutiny And Diet Control

The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account of *The Woman in Me* reports that Spears' body was treated as public property "from day one" and that, once she was under the conservatorship, her father policed her weight and every calorie she ate was recorded.

Between the videos for her debut single Baby, One More Time and Sometimes, the media noted her changing physique and concluded that the 16-year-old must have had breast implants rather than simply going through puberty. She noticed that talkshow hosts asked her about her chest while her boyfriend Justin Timberlake was asked serious questions about his music. Writing about shaving her head in a salon in 2007, she frames it as a "fuck you" to impossible beauty standards: "I'd smiled politely while TV show hosts leered at my breasts, while American parents said I was destroying their children by wearing a crop top."

That brief moment of freedom did not last: a year later she was ambushed into the conservatorship, which also exercised jurisdiction over her body. "No matter how much I dieted and exercised, my father was always telling me I was fat," she writes; punishing gym routines left her feeling "out of my mind", and her diet was monitored along with every other detail of her life while she went through the motions of her Las Vegas residency. "My body was strong enough to carry two children and agile enough to execute every choreographed move perfectly onstage. And now here I was, having every calorie recorded so people could continue to get rich off my body." On the other side of the conservatorship, she writes, freedom looks like being able to gain weight without anyone "shouting at me", eating chocolate again, and posting selfies — nude or clothed — on Instagram; people who do not understand the last of these, she suggests, have not been "photographed by other people thousands of times, prodded and posed for other people's approval".

# The Batman Part II (Matt Reeves)

The Batman Part II is dated Oct. 3 in Polygon's 2023-10-24 DC slate rundown, again with Robert Pattinson as the Caped Crusader, greenlit immediately after the first film's success.

Polygon frames the sequel against low expectations for its predecessor: the long, contentious history behind 2022's The Batman did not leave much room for hope, since it was one of those movies that got bounced from team to team for years, changing shape at every bounce, and looked destined to be driven more by market calculation than by a specific vision. Director and co-writer Matt Reeves nonetheless found an effective take on the Dark Knight that resonated with audiences and landed solidly at the box office, and DC immediately greenlit a sequel.

No plot details were clear at the time, though Pattinson and Reeves had been blue-skying about a lot of things they would like to do — the Court of Owls storyline, maybe, or Mr. Freeze, or Calendar Man.

# Ice Spice's Breakout And The Capitol-10K Partnership

Capitol Music Group has been a crucial partner, alongside Elliot Grainge's 10K Projects, in the rise of Ice Spice, a Best New Artist Grammy nominee who has secured no fewer than four Top 10 Billboard Hot 100 singles and over 2 billion global streams off an official debut release that is an EP. Michelle Jubelirer calls her "THE breakout artist of 2023", adding that she is the first artist since Olivia Rodrigo to achieve three Top 5 single debuts in her first four months and that she has just attained another Top 10 with "Barbie World" with Nicki Minaj, and saying they are just at the beginning of what is going to be a tremendous career of artistry and global popularity.

On the signing itself, Jubelirer sets the record straight about the dinner that led to the co-signing of Ice Spice by Capitol and 10K, teasing Grainge about his selective memory: present were Jubelirer, Grainge, Jeremy Vuernick and 10K co-presidents Zach Friedman and Tony Talamo, all of whom won the artist's heart as a team. She says that after decades working with artists it is a rare occasion when you sit with an artist and just know you are in the presence of a future global superstar, and that was and is Ice Spice; her early music was exciting and her explosive growth as an artist and cultural figure has already transcended the world of music, making her a household name, a testament to her talent and drive and to a real team effort between Capitol, 10K and her manager James Rosemond Jr. Jubelirer notes that Ice Spice is a strong woman who has aligned herself with other strong women, the article adding that Ice Spice also signed to Universal Music Publishing Group via UMPG Chairman and CEO Jody Gerson, a close Jubelirer colleague. On the ingredients for widening her audience since "Munch", Jubelirer points to her look, her flow, her lyrics and her collaboration choices, naming Taylor Swift, Nicki Minaj and PinkPantheress, and to the fact that she knows precisely who she is and what is right for her to do and not do, a rare quality at such a young age that lets her make the right choices at warp speed; EVP of Media Ambrosia Healey scored a major coup by getting her the season opener of Saturday Night Live, one of many big media appearances, and every department has played an integral role in the launch and development.

# Britney Spears' Memoir On Early Fame And The Loss Of Freedom

In *The Woman in Me*, as summarised by The Guardian on 24 October 2023, Britney Spears describes how fame converted her childhood escape into confinement: by the age of 16 she was "public property", unable to go outside without being mobbed, and her love of singing and dancing had become a lucrative resource for other people.

Spears writes that as a child she escaped a difficult home life — her alcoholic father often rowing with her mother — into the outdoors, which "gave me a sense of aliveness and danger", and that performing made her feel invincible. By the time of her second album she wanted for so little; skinny-dipping with her dancers after playing Rock in Rio in January 2001 is one of her happiest memories, "a taste of rebellion and freedom, but I was just having fun and being a 19-year-old". After her split from Justin Timberlake she dreamed about quitting pop and opening a shop, and writes with hindsight that she "hadn't given myself enough time to heal from the breakup" — yet her requests for a break were not only turned down but interpreted as a potential sign of sedition to be quashed and interrogated.

In that restrictive environment small kindnesses took on outsized significance, such as Paris Hilton encouraging her "to have fun for the first time in a long time", which led to infamous nights out with the heiress and Lindsay Lohan; once again Britney was seen as stepping out of bounds and potentially damaging her earning potential. One night, after her mother babysat her sons, she returned home tipsy and Lynne Spears screamed at her: "The shame I felt killed my heart. I stood there, reeling, and thought, OK, I guess it's forbidden for me to party." As the restrictions tightened she acted out, and ended up legally denied her freedom for 13 years under a conservatorship controlled by her father.

# Britney Spears On Conservatorship Restrictions And Swat Holds

The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account of *The Woman in Me* reports that the conservatorship ruled by Spears' father medicated and surveilled her, vetted her dates with background checks, blood tests and NDAs, and that she was twice confronted by a Swat team and subjected to a forced hospital hold.

Fearing Kevin Federline would take away access to her children, she locked herself in a bathroom with one of her sons: "Before I knew what was happening, a Swat team in black suits burst through the bathroom door as if I'd hurt someone," she writes, and she was placed under a forced hospital hold. Soon after, her mother invited her to her beach house because "the cops are after you"; when she arrived, so did another Swat team. "I'm a five-foot four-inch pop singer who calls everyone sir and ma'am… They treated me like I was a criminal or predator."

The conservatorship was ruled by her father, whom she alleges was "an alcoholic, someone who'd declared bankruptcy, who'd failed in business, who'd terrified me as a little girl". Her dates were required to agree to background checks and blood tests, to sign NDAs, and to receive a full rundown of her sexual history before the first date: "The insanity of this system kept me from finding basic companionship, having a fun night out or making new friends – let alone falling in love… It was just the worst thing that could possibly ever happen to my music, my career and my sanity." She acceded in order to retain access to her boys, while questioning how she could perform at such a high level if she was "so sick that I couldn't make my own decisions". Her father sent her to rehab and Alcoholics Anonymous because she had been taking over-the-counter energy supplements; the women at AA inspired her to try to take control of her life, but she hit more walls. He would not let her remove her IUD to start a family with her boyfriend and later husband Sam Asghari (they have divorced since she completed the memoir), and after she objected to a new dance move suggested for her Vegas residency she was sent to a solitary rehabilitation facility for two months — the most upsetting part of the book.

# November 10 Reporting On Punishment Day

On Friday, Nov. 10, 2023, reporters tracked Michigan's travel to Penn State hour by hour as the college football world waited for the Big Ten's decision, which ESPN's Heather Dinich reported was expected to be announced early Friday afternoon while the team left for State College at 1 p.m. CT ahead of Saturday's game. Dinich reported that sources indicated a Big Ten response was coming early that afternoon and that Michigan would leave at 1 and fly midafternoon out of Detroit after clearing security checks, per usual routine.

The decision came right down to the wire. Adam Rittenberg reported that Michigan's administration had not heard from the Big Ten as of that hour, that the team would begin preparations to leave for Penn State around 1 p.m. ET, and that going down to the wire with any discipline was, as several sources noted, not really fair to players. Austin Meek reported Harbaugh boarding the bus, and observers on the ground in Ann Arbor had him heading to the airport with his team as Michigan awaited word. Harbaugh's attorney Tom Mars told ESPN he fully expected Harbaugh to fly with the team: "I'm confident he's going to be on that plane one way or another."

Dinich also mapped the possible outcomes and a limit on the conference's own authority. She reported the punishment could be anything ranging from "indefinite suspension to public reprimand or lofty fine," and cautioned against assumptions while noting that a suspension was certainly on the table. She added that anything more than two games or a fine of $10,000 would require special permission from an executive board composed of league representatives.

# Jada Pinkett Smith's 2023 Disclosure Of A Seven-Year Separation

Jada Pinkett Smith revealed in October 2023 that she and her husband Will Smith had been separated for the previous seven years — that is, since 2016 — while remaining married. The disclosure came in an interview with People given while she was promoting her memoir Worthy; The Independent's timeline piece dates the publication to 11 October, while its other reports on the same interview date it 10 October. Pinkett Smith, 52, said of her 26-year marriage to the 55-year-old actor that the couple are "still figuring it out": "We've been doing some really heavy-duty work together. We just got deep love for each other and we are going to figure out what that looks like for us."

She anchored the timeline to the 2022 Academy Awards, when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock after the comedian made a joke about her appearance: at that moment, she said, the pair had already been separated for six years. The revelation was treated as major news — "sent shockwaves around the world," in The Independent's phrasing — because both Smiths had previously doubled down on their stance against divorce, so a lengthy separation raised a new question: when should a couple simply get a divorce?

# Billie Jean King's 2023 Activities And Ownership Stakes

Billie Jean King, who turns 80 in November 2023, is still globetrotting in support of more investment and equity in women's sports: in the three months before 2023-10-13 she attended the Women's World Cup in Australia, kicked off the player draft for the new women's professional hockey league in Toronto, and is opening an office in London for a tennis business venture involving the international Billie Jean King Cup.

She is part of ownership groups involved with the Los Angeles Dodgers, the NWSL's Angel City FC and the PWHL hockey league that starts in January 2024. She recently launched the production company "Pressure is a Privilege," a phrase associated with the 39-time Grand Slam winner, and is an executive producer and host of "Groundbreakers," a documentary about female athletes that airs on PBS on Nov. 21. There is also an effort by members of Congress to award King the Congressional Gold Medal, one of the highest U.S. civilian honors, given to individuals whose achievements have a lasting impact in their field.

# Blasphemous 2

Blasphemous 2, developed by The Game Kitchen for Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Windows PC, Xbox One, and Xbox Series X, is ranked 47 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31. Polygon's claim is that long gone are the days when the Metroidvania genre languished untouched for years on end, and that despite an influx of entries in recent years few have exhibited as much mastery as this one.

Building off the strong roots of the first game, Blasphemous 2 continues to use Spanish Catholicism as a narrative and aesthetic touchpoint, telling a twisted religious tale that is about as far from proselytizing as you can get.

Critic Russ Frushtick notes that after the success of the first game the developers focused on refining the combat, adding multiple weapons and bizarre, hidden customization options that let players take command of how their character rips this world to shreds. The last 2D Metroidvania he played with this much polish and charm was Hollow Knight; Blasphemous 2 might not reach those same heights, but it comes damn close.

# India's Record Of World Cup Semi-Final Appearances

India first entered the semi-finals of the World Cup at the 1983 Prudential Cup in England, where they emerged as the tournament winners. They moved into the last-four stage on the next two occasions when the World Cup was held in India, in 1987 and 1996, and were in the semi-finals again in 2003 in South Africa. Eight years later they were in the last four at the 2011 World Cup as hosts, and repeated the feat in 2015, 2019 and 2023.

The summary statistic given on 11 November 2023 is that in their last six World Cups, India have been in the semi-finals on five occasions.

# Taylor Swift's Subsequent NFL Appearances And SNL Cameo

After her first Chiefs game, Taylor Swift kept appearing at Kansas City fixtures and made a Saturday Night Live cameo with Travis Kelce, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023.

On 1 October she went to her second consecutive Chiefs game, against the Jets — who, the timeline notes, technically play in New Jersey — showing up with famous friends Blake Lively, Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman after a week of reports that she would attend; the Chiefs won 23-20. On 12 October, one day after her movie premiere, Swift was in the house for the Chiefs' "Thursday Night Football" divisional matchup against the Broncos at Arrowhead Stadium, where she has performed herself and attended a game before; according to Al Michaels the game would have minimal Swift coverage, though there had already been a mention of the superstar.

On 15 October the two were spotted out in New York City together and then made a surprise appearance on "Saturday Night Live," with Kelce appearing in a skit about how much coverage Swift was getting during games while the singer introduced the musical act of the night, Ice Spice. On 22 October Swift attended her fifth Chiefs game, having now attended games broadcast across all five networks — CBS, NBC, Fox, ESPN and Amazon — watching the Chiefs face the Chargers on CBS in a Chiefs sweatshirt, seated next to Patrick Mahomes' wife, Brittany.

Blackburn's fortunes since Andy Cole scored the winning goal that saw off Tottenham in the final of this competition more than 20 years earlier under Graeme Souness had seen the Lancashire club drop down to the third tier for a season before coming close to reaching the Championship playoffs in the past two campaigns, The Guardian reported on Nov. 1, 2023.

# Party Animals

Party Animals, developed by Recreate Games for Windows PC and Xbox Series X, is ranked 46 on Polygon's best video games of 2023 list of 2023-10-31. Critic Julia Lee's summary is that the Gang Beasts-esque wiggly physics mixed with the cute characters makes for a perfect party game of fluffy fighting.

She says she does not know how Recreate Games managed to render some of the cutest animals she has ever seen.

Nor does she know how they made her completely OK with picking up those cute animals and flinging them into black holes, poison clouds, or freezing tundras: the second the match starts, all those cute fluffy corgis, rabbits, kitties, and ducks become her enemies, and she will beat them with a bat until they cannot wake up anymore without thinking twice about it.

# The 1996 Semi-Final Abandonment And The Short 1999 Cycle

The 1996 World Cup, jointly hosted by India and Sri Lanka, produced what the Sporting News calls one of the most controversial episodes in the game: the two host teams met in the semi-finals at Eden Gardens, Kolkata, India's poor performance sparked an unruly crowd to protest against the home team, and Sri Lanka was declared the winner by default due to the halt in play.

Sri Lanka went on to win the trophy that year, and they were back to try and defend it three years later in England, rather than after the usual four-year gap.

The reason was a scheduling experiment. Following the 1996 event the ICC opted to try and revamp the schedule, with three years between events rather than four, but the move proved unpopular and 1999 was the only tournament to follow that pattern.
