# Prediction: AI-Generated Content Will Overwhelm Search

Daron Babin's proposition is that Google results will soon be even worse, dominated entirely by AI-generated crap designed to please the algorithms, produced and published at volumes far beyond anything humans could create — far beyond anything we had ever seen before.

The mechanism he gives is cost collapse at the bottom of the market: "All the assholes that are out there paying shitty link-building companies to build shitty articles now they can go and use the free version of GPT."

The prediction's strong form is that the volume is unstoppable: "They're not gonna be able to stop the onslaught of it," he said, then laughed and laughed, thinking about how puny and irrelevant Google seemed in comparison to the next generation of automated SEO. "You can't stop it!" What would falsify it is exactly that — Google proving able to stop the onslaught, so that results are not dominated by machine-produced content.

# The Blurred Line Between SEO And Spam

Lily Ray's rebuttal targets Sullivan's premise that the boundary is clean and that Google has not changed. Sullivan had tried to convince the writer that Google was not behaving differently and in fact had not changed its search criteria in any major way for the past 20 years: Google wanted you to make good websites, and that was that; everyone who tried to rank higher by messing with the algorithm would be blocked. Sullivan even insisted that what these rule-breakers did should not be called SEO — he deemed it all "spam," defining spam as "stuff that search engines don't like."

The objection is that the line between strategies that violate Google's terms of service and strategies that do not has always been blurry and inconsistently enforced. "I've never seen this much tension in the industry in terms of, like, what Google says to do and what people are doing and getting away with," Ray said. "If you're gonna tell us that this stuff doesn't work, make it stop working!"

Ray declines to make it a question of individual character. As much as she despises what this kind of SEO has done to the internet, she hesitated to condemn the actual people doing it: "I used to do those types of tactics, so I couldn't hate on anybody personally," she said. "If people have a problem with Google's results, they have to ask themselves, is it the fault of the SEOs? Or is this Google behaving differently than it used to?"

# Missy Ward, Daron Babin And Darren Blatt: The Early Operators

Three veterans at the alligator party illustrate how the first generation of SEO made its money. Missy Ward, in an orange bandage dress so tight she said she could not take full steps — ordered on Amazon and untried until the day of the party — started doing SEO in 1998, when it was "five girls and all dudes," and eventually sold her company for $40 million. She was patient about explaining the history of SEO and suggesting other people to talk to, and pointed the writer toward a man in a sky blue polo with a long-running SEO podcast.

That was Daron Babin, whose SEO career got going in 1994, before Google even existed. "The air of manipulation was insane," Babin said. "We had this weird community of geeks and nerds, and we all talked to each other about how we were beating the algorithms up. People were trying to outrank other people just for bragging rights."

The party's host, Darren Blatt, has been friends with Babin for decades — since the era when Darren "D-Money" Blatt would throw rap star-studded internet marketing shindigs during the Adult Video News Awards in Vegas, back when sex sites were among the most advanced in technology, and Babin was using SEO to promote offshore casinos and Viagra ("We were outranking Pfizer!"). Together, Darren and Daron managed to milk all three of the early online cash cows: porn, pills, and gambling.

The consulting turn came as the internet became more regulated and mainstream around the turn of the century, when Darren noticed Daron's SEO skills were increasingly in demand. # Google's Defense That Search Defaults Are Easy To Change

Google's answer to the DOJ's foreclosure theory attacks the premise that a default locks users in: being default was not determinative, because changing from Google Search to another provider is easy, so Google's position reflects user preference rather than the deals.

In court, John Schmidtlein referenced Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing that make those services easy to find, and both he and Eddy Cue argued that switching search engines is so easy as to be a non-issue; Meagan Bellshaw briefly stepped up to rebut that notion, and that was it for Cue's testimony. On Google's blog, president of global affairs Kent Walker said the search product was the favourite of users, browsers and device makers simply because it was the best in the business: "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," and "this lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today." Walker's supporting evidence is revealed preference when Google is not the default: when Mozilla made Yahoo! the default on Firefox, most users changed it to Google; and people setting up a Windows device frequently sidestep the Microsoft default — "Google" was the number one search query on Bing in 2021 — despite Microsoft making that very annoying to do. The Age's writer called this a compelling point, familiar to anyone who has dodged Microsoft's pleading while setting Chrome and Google as defaults on a new PC, but countered that all of these arguments ignore that Google and its competitors are not on an even playing field: the question remains why users prefer Google, and if the answer is that Google is simply better, the further question is whether that is down to its scale, longevity, ubiquity and all the user data it sucks up, which no other company could possibly match.

# Default Search Engine

## Definition

The default search engine is the search provider a device, browser, or platform is pre-configured to use unless a user actively changes the setting — the search box that runs when a person types a query without first choosing an alternative, such as Google on the iPhone's Safari address bar or Firefox's search bar.

## Context

The term is central to *US v. Google*, the DOJ's antitrust case, because default status is the mechanism through which Google secures the overwhelming share of search queries: the Information Services Agreement (ISA) between Apple and Google, in place since 2002/2003, makes Google the default on all Apple devices, and Google separately pays Samsung, Mozilla, and other partners for the same status.
Apple executive Eddy Cue testified that Apple's iPhone setup flow deliberately omits any search-engine choice screen, arguing that presenting users with unfamiliar alternatives would harm the setup experience, while conceding the ISA does not permit Apple to offer such a choice.
Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 on default-placement deals across browsers, phones, and platforms — about $18 billion of that to Apple alone — a scale that the DOJ used to argue Google understands the mechanism's value: internal 2007 data showed users who set Google as their homepage searched 15% more, while switching away dropped searches 27%.
The Mozilla/Yahoo episode shows the same mechanism working in reverse: when Firefox switched its default from Google to Yahoo under a 2014 deal, Mozilla's CEO testified that user retention declined, illustrating how disruptive changing the default can be even when a paying competitor is involved.
Outside the antitrust trial, the term also frames ordinary consumer behavior: an investor in e-commerce search startup Deft described users' "natural behavior" as following the path of least resistance and just using the default search engine, meaning challenger search products must offer a high-value proposition to displace that inertia.

## Key Characteristics

- **Set by agreement, not by user choice** — default status on major platforms (Apple's Safari/iOS, Android OEMs, Firefox) is typically established through commercial deals (e.g., the Apple-Google ISA, Yahoo-Mozilla's $375M/year deal) rather than user selection at setup.
- **Backed by large recurring payments** — Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 across partners to hold default placement, with roughly $18 billion of that going to Apple.
- **Technically reversible but rarely changed** — Apple and Google both argued switching is easy, but DuckDuckGo's CEO countered that it takes "too many steps" to switch, and Google's own 2005 complaint about Internet Explorer's defaults argued that "most end users do not change defaults," so default status functions as durable market power.
- **Distinct from pre-installation** — Google's separate push to get Chrome and Search merely pre-installed (not necessarily defaulted) on Android and iPhones shows default status is a stronger, more contested tier than simple presence on a device.
- **Drives user behavior even outside browsers** — the concept extends to any search product; consumers default to "the path of least resistance," which challenger search startups must specifically overcome.

# Barber Shop Near Me And Felix Silva

Felix Silva decided on the name Barber Shop Near Me after considering more than 20 other options for his Coral Springs, Florida, store in 2019. The name is meant to be neutral and memorable — another contender was "The Barber Shop" — but Silva fully leaned into the Google joke: the logo is a red location pin resembling Google's own, with a blue, white, and red barber pole pattern in the middle. "Before we opened, we just had a logo [on an Instagram account]," Silva says. "And we had some clients then tell us, 'Oh, man, before you guys opened we thought Google was coming to town.'"

Like Jirapraphanan of Thai Food Near Me, Silva had seen firsthand how a business's Google presence could help or hurt its chances of success. He frequently searches for keywords like "vegan" to find restaurants, and one time Google returned results for a restaurant that was not vegan but had a customer review containing the keyword, which was highlighted. "It was a light bulb moment… like, 'Okay, this is the path I need to take. I really need to dial in and focus on the online presence, specifically Google, because that is going to be the foundation of the business,'" Silva says.

# Why Traditional E-Commerce Search Has Degraded

Deft co-founder Zach Hudson told TechCrunch that there are a few plaguing problems with the traditional search experience that prevent users from finding a suitable item — that is, the claim is that search has gotten worse, not that users have gotten worse at searching.

He offers three grounds, each a different actor degrading the result set: "You have companies like Google and Amazon that continue to push the most relevant listings down so they can make more advertising dollars. Some easy searches are now hard because marketers have learned how to game these search engines. Plus, now you have AI content that is putting the burden on users to separate fact from fiction," he said.

The warrant tying them together is that each mechanism moves cost onto the user: platform ad incentives bury relevance, SEO gaming inflates the noise, and AI-generated content shifts verification work to the person searching.

# ICC World Cup 2023: Leading Wicket Takers

As listed on 18 November 2023, the leading wicket takers of the ICC Men's ODI World Cup 2023 were: 1. Mohammed Shami (IND), 7 matches, 23 wickets; 2. A Zampa (AUS), 11 matches, 23 wickets; 3. D Madushanka (SL), 9 matches, 21 wickets; 4. JJ Bumrah (IND), 11 matches, 20 wickets; 5. G Coetzee (SA), 8 matches, 20 wickets; 6. Shaheen Shah Afridi (PAK), 9 matches, 18 wickets; 7. M Jansen (SA), 9 matches, 17 wickets; 8. RA Jadeja (IND), 11 matches, 16 wickets; 9. Josh Hazlewood, 11 matches, 16 wickets; 10. MJ Santner (NZ), 10 matches, 16 wickets; 11. BFW de Leede (NED), 9 matches, 16 wickets.

The accompanying commentary gives the bowling detail, and for the top two names cites figures that differ slightly from the table. Shami announced his return to the World Cup by picking a fifer in the very first match he played for India, and is described as having picked up 24 wickets in just six matches while conceding just 257 runs, including three five-wicket hauls and a seven-wicket haul against New Zealand in the semi-final on Wednesday, 15 November at the Wankhede Stadium in Mumbai. Adam Zampa, the highest wicket-taker for the Aussies, picked up 23 wickets including three four-wicket hauls while conceding 515 runs. Dilshan Madushanka finished high on the list despite Sri Lanka's dreadful campaign, picking up 21 wickets and conceding 525 runs. Jasprit Bumrah took 20 wickets conceding 373 runs and had the best economy rate in the whole tournament at 4.06. The 23-year-old Gerald Coetzee picked up 20 wickets for the Proteas in eight matches conceding 396 runs. Shaheen Shah Afridi was the best bowler for Pakistan with 18 wickets conceding 481 runs in nine matches. Marco Jansen, standing 6 feet 7 inches tall and making full use of his height, took 17 wickets in nine matches conceding 450 runs. Ravindra Jadeja bowled beautiful spells especially in the middle overs, taking 16 wickets and conceding just 398 at an economy rate of 4.25 in 10 matches. The Australian pacer Hazlewood was phenomenal with the new ball, creating movement batters struggled with, and picked up 16 wickets in 11 matches. New Zealand's bowling mostly depended on Mitchell Santner, effective on the turning tracks of India, who picked up 16 wickets and conceded 449 runs in 10 matches.

# The Scotland Commitment Row And The Gulf In Class

Against the suggestion that Scotland's efforts at Hampden should be questioned — that a defensive collapse almost helped England towards a Team GB place at the Paris Olympics — The Guardian argues that would be unfair.

The premise it attacks is that Scotland's players were less than fully committed. The counter-grounds are, first, that the gulf in class between the European champions, ranked fourth in the world, and their neighbours to the north, ranked 23rd, is clear, and that the manager, Pedro Martínez Losa, has been unconvincing in charge — so the scoreline needs no explanation in terms of effort. Second, the accusations had already been rejected by the players: Lucy Bronze called the claim that Scotland players might feel conflicted, with Olympic qualification on the line for them as much as for England, "the rudest thing I've ever heard," and Scotland's captain Rachel Corsie called it "disrespectful" and "outrageous." Third, any doubt about Scotland's intentions was put to bed, temporarily at least, in the opening three minutes, with Bronze clattered into late twice as Scotland looked to make an early impression, that rare foray forward urged on by a vocal Scotland crowd. Wiegman, for her part, had urged her players to "go wild from the first minute" while cautioning "but you don't want to get erratic," and England came out of the blocks searching for an early goal to assert their authority. Among the crowd, after Lauren Hemp raced free on the right, a hopeful "Come on Lauren" was met with a thick, cheery Scottish "Shut up!" behind the press box.

# Billie Jean King's 2023 Activities And Ownership Stakes

Billie Jean King, who turns 80 in November 2023, is still globetrotting in support of more investment and equity in women's sports: in the three months before 2023-10-13 she attended the Women's World Cup in Australia, kicked off the player draft for the new women's professional hockey league in Toronto, and is opening an office in London for a tennis business venture involving the international Billie Jean King Cup.

She is part of ownership groups involved with the Los Angeles Dodgers, the NWSL's Angel City FC and the PWHL hockey league that starts in January 2024. She recently launched the production company "Pressure is a Privilege," a phrase associated with the 39-time Grand Slam winner, and is an executive producer and host of "Groundbreakers," a documentary about female athletes that airs on PBS on Nov. 21. There is also an effort by members of Congress to award King the Congressional Gold Medal, one of the highest U.S. civilian honors, given to individuals whose achievements have a lasting impact in their field.

# The Longest-Standing International Goalscoring Records

Only six countries' international goalscoring records have stood for more than 50 years, including Libya, Sudan and Guinea, and if only nations that have qualified for the World Cup are counted, just Denmark, Norway and Hungary have records lasting more than half a century, as reported by The New York Times on 17 November 2023.

Hungary's is perhaps the most impressive of them, considering Ferenc Puskas scored 84 goals in just 85 games and had his international career brought to a premature end at the age of 29 because of the Hungarian Revolution; he later represented Spain at the 1962 World Cup, having gone half a decade without playing international football.

The striking finding in the other direction is how many goalscoring records have been set recently. Sixty-four of the 211 nations' record goalscorers have appeared for them in 2023, and in terms of time since they were set the median goalscoring mark has stood for just seven years, a group that includes the Republic of Ireland's Robbie Keane and Paraguay's Roque Santa Cruz. Increased longevity due to superior fitness levels in the modern game is clearly a major factor, as is the number of relatively new nations on the FIFA list.

# The Selection Questions Facing Nagelsmann With Germany

The Sporting News argues that the biggest question raised by Julian Nagelsmann's first 26-man Germany squad is which formation he can actually play, because there are no natural right-backs on the roster.

The grounds are that every available fix costs something: he will either have to pigeonhole a centre-back — Antonio Rudiger or Niklas Sule — out wide, sacrifice Josh Kimmich's presence in midfield to move him back, or move Pascal Gross back, and none of those are ideal options. The warrant limiting the damage is that the shape matters less than the method: whether Nagelsmann deploys a 4-2-3-1 or a 3-2-4-1, the tactical approach will likely remain the same.

Two further selection tasks follow. Getting the best out of young superstar Jamal Musiala will be one of the most important aspects of Nagelsmann's tenure, as Musiala has blossomed into a world-class talent at Bayern Munich but the 20-year-old has just one goal in 23 international caps to this point. Nagelsmann will also look to introduce a few overlooked players, starting with Robert Andrich, who could factor into the midfield setup as a traditional No. 6, especially as Ilkay Gundogan enters the twilight of his career — and he will want to raise Kimmich's level of play back to old heights, as the ever-present Bayern star has seen his level drop in recent years for both club and country but remains a special talent.

# Haaland's Chase Of Norway's International Goalscoring Record

Erling Haaland was just six goals away from Norway's international goalscoring record, making it surely inevitable that he will soon be his nation's most prolific striker ever, as reported by The New York Times on 17 November 2023.

The report notes the two ways of reading the timing: on one hand it will have happened remarkably quickly, since Haaland only scored his first goals for Norway in 2020; on the other, this has been an incredibly long time coming. At this point Norway appear to have the most prolific striker in Europe, and it's not unreasonable to consider where Haaland might end up in the all-time international goalscoring charts worldwide, never mind just among his compatriots.

His rate is the striking figure, with a caveat attached. Haaland is averaging nearly a goal a game for his country, which will inevitably be difficult for the 23-year-old to sustain over his career, but is impressive even at this early stage: excluding countries who have never qualified for a World Cup, only Jorgen Juve, Gigi Riva, Ferenc Puskas and Poul Nielsen, plus Japan's Kunishige Kamamoto, hold their nation's international goalscoring records while also boasting a rate of 0.75 goals per game or more. Even Cristiano Ronaldo, the most prolific international goalscorer of all time with 127 for Portugal, boasts "only" 0.63 goals per game, a lower rate than Romelu Lukaku, Harry Kane and Aleksandar Mitrovic, which owes to his early days as a winger rather than a central striker. Considering how many hat-tricks Haaland scores for Manchester City, it's not beyond the realms of possibility that he could score six goals during this international break to move level with Juve, particularly given Norway's first fixture is a home friendly against the Faroe Islands that Thursday before a European Championship qualifier against Scotland in Glasgow on Sunday — though the Faroes' defence is less leaky than you might expect, having conceded more than three times in a game only twice in their last 22 outings.

# Travis Kelce's Friendship Bracelet Overtures To Taylor Swift

Travis Kelce's public overtures to Taylor Swift began with friendship bracelets in mid-2023, according to CBS Sports' timeline published 12 October 2023, which dates the sequence precisely.

On 29 June, Kelce made a friendship bracelet to give to the newcomers at a camp for NFL tight ends, saying he was "taking a page out of Taylor Swift's book" — the timeline flags this as possibly where it all began. On 26 July, Kelce announced he had gone to Swift's highly anticipated concert but had not had the chance to meet the 12-time Grammy winner. "I was disappointed that she doesn't talk before or after her shows because she has to save her voice for the 44 songs she sings ... She doesn't meet anybody, or at least she didn't want to meet me, so I took it personal," Kelce said on an episode of the "New Heights" podcast he does with his brother, Philadelphia Eagles center Jason Kelce. He revealed that he had made a friendship bracelet — a fan tradition at her concerts — with his number on it to give to her, and when his brother asked whether it was his jersey number or his phone number, Kelce replied, "you know which one," adding: "If you're up on Taylor Swift concerts, there are friendship bracelets and I had received a bunch of them, but I wanted to give Taylor Swift one with my number on it." On 5 August, well before the two were rumoured to be dating, Kelce was asked his celebrity crush, and before he could answer the answer was given for him.

On 21 September, speaking on the Pat McAfee show, Kelce discussed the rumours and sounded somehow surprised people were talking about it: "It is hilarious how much traction this has actually got. It's like that old game in school called telephone where everybody is just whispering in each others ear, just hearing some random stuff. Especially when you got Jason Kelce on live television telling people just both sides." He then admitted he had invited Swift to one of his games, joking they would compete to see who put on the bigger show at Arrowhead Stadium: "I threw it out there, I threw the ball in her court and I told her you know, I've seen you rock the stage in Arrowhead you might have to come see me rock the stage in Arrowhead and see which one is a little more lit. We will see what happens in the near future." On 22 September, Kelce was spotted at his nonprofit charity event wearing a bracelet reading "Vigilante Sh--," the name of one of Swift's songs.

# Ray-Ban Meta: Design And Discreetness

The Verge's reviewer found the Ray-Ban Meta glasses both good-looking and genuinely inconspicuous — in many ways, she wrote, they feel like they belong in a spy movie, since James Bond always looks good and the gadgets Q gives him are discreet. The reason design matters is blunt: you will never wear a pair of smart glasses if they make you look like a low-rent Warby Parker model, and aside from the original Bose Frames she had never liked the way she looked in smart glasses before. That these are Ray-Bans and come in more styles than typical smart glasses is what changed it — while Wayfarers are considered universally flattering, rounder frames look better on her, and instead of the usual tortoiseshell or black she could pick a round, transparent blue frame with pink lenses, whose colors she wished were more noticeable in darker lighting but which popped in sunlight. She wore them dolled up for a wedding, in functional but hideous running gear, in sweatpants, and with leather jackets: they go with everything.

The discreetness has a specific shape. No one will know you are wearing tech on your face unless you walk around saying "Hey Meta" at the top of your lungs; nobody knew she was listening to EXO's EXIST album on her commute. There is some faint audio leakage at full volume, but full volume is only necessary to block out the squeaky rails of the New York City subway, and fellow commuters likely will not notice because they have AirPods in or the ambient noise is louder. More troubling, no one batted an eye whenever she took photos and videos in public or private areas. The capture button sits on the top of the right arm.

She compared the experience to Eggsy in Kingsman: The Golden Circle, who takes a call through his glasses during an important dinner and appears to everyone else as a dapper gent in snazzy frames while hearing and seeing things they cannot. Her version had no bombs to defuse, but the point stands: she spent a lot of time wearing these in public doing and listening to things that people looking straight at her were not aware of. That comes with pros and cons — but at least, she noted, you need not fear looking like a total jabroni, as in the picture of her wearing the Bose Frames Tempo.

# Britney Spears On Body Scrutiny And Diet Control

The Guardian's 24 October 2023 account of *The Woman in Me* reports that Spears' body was treated as public property "from day one" and that, once she was under the conservatorship, her father policed her weight and every calorie she ate was recorded.

Between the videos for her debut single Baby, One More Time and Sometimes, the media noted her changing physique and concluded that the 16-year-old must have had breast implants rather than simply going through puberty. She noticed that talkshow hosts asked her about her chest while her boyfriend Justin Timberlake was asked serious questions about his music. Writing about shaving her head in a salon in 2007, she frames it as a "fuck you" to impossible beauty standards: "I'd smiled politely while TV show hosts leered at my breasts, while American parents said I was destroying their children by wearing a crop top."

That brief moment of freedom did not last: a year later she was ambushed into the conservatorship, which also exercised jurisdiction over her body. # DeepMind's Founding And Thiel's Investment

In 2010 Demis Hassabis and two colleagues, all living in Britain, were looking for money to start building "artificial general intelligence", a machine that could do anything the brain could do, at a time when few people were interested in AI because after a half-century of research the field had failed to deliver anything remotely close to the human brain. Some scientists and thinkers had nonetheless become fixated on AI's downsides, and many, including the three young men, had a connection to Eliezer Yudkowsky, an internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher who led a community calling themselves Rationalists or, later, effective altruists; they believed AI could find a cure for cancer or solve climate change but worried that AI bots might do things their creators had not intended, arguing that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators. Peter Thiel, enormously wealthy through an early investment in Facebook and his work with Musk in the early days of PayPal, had developed a fascination with the singularity, the science-fiction trope describing the moment when intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity, and with his funding Yudkowsky had expanded his AI lab and created an annual conference on the singularity; one of Hassabis' colleagues had met Yudkowsky years before and snagged them speaking spots at that conference, ensuring an invitation to Thiel's party, where Yudkowsky introduced Hassabis to Thiel. Assuming many guests would be trying to squeeze their host for money, Hassabis' strategy was to arrange another meeting: he told Thiel there was a deep tension between the bishop and the knight, pieces carrying the same value whose strengths the best players understood to be vastly different. Charmed, Thiel invited the group back the next day, gathering in the kitchen where their host, just finished with his morning workout and still sweating in a shiny tracksuit, was handed a Diet Coke by a butler; the three made their pitch and soon Thiel and his venture capital firm agreed to put £1.4 million, about $A2.7 million, into their startup, making him their first major investor.

They named the company DeepMind, a nod to "deep learning", a way for AI systems to learn skills by analysing large amounts of data, to neuroscience, and to the Deep Thought supercomputer from The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, and by the spring of 2010 they were building their dream machine, wholeheartedly believing that because they understood the risks they were uniquely positioned to protect the world. Mustafa Suleyman, one of the three founders, said "I don't see this as a contradictory position. There are huge benefits to come from these technologies. The goal is not to eliminate them or pause their development. The goal is to mitigate the downsides." Having won over Thiel, Hassabis worked his way into Musk's orbit: about two years later they met at a conference organised by Thiel's investment fund, which had also put money into SpaceX, and Hassabis secured a tour of SpaceX headquarters, after which, with rocket hulls hanging from the ceiling, the two lunched in the cafeteria; Musk explained his plan to colonise Mars to escape overpopulation and other dangers on Earth, and Hassabis replied that the plan would work so long as superintelligent machines didn't follow and destroy humanity on Mars too. Musk was speechless, not having thought about that particular danger, and soon invested in DeepMind alongside Thiel so he could be closer to the creation of the technology.

# Anthropic's Founding By Former OpenAI Researchers

Dario Amodei, a researcher with ties to the effective altruist community, had been on hand at the Rosewood hotel when OpenAI was born, and was leading the lab's efforts to build a neural network called a large language model that could learn from enormous amounts of digital text: by analysing countless Wikipedia articles, digital books and message boards it could generate text on its own, and it also had the unfortunate habit of making things up. It was called GPT-3 and was released in the summer of 2020, and researchers inside OpenAI, Google and other companies thought this rapidly improving technology could be a path to artificial general intelligence. Amodei was unhappy about the Microsoft deal because he thought it was taking OpenAI in a really commercial direction, and he and other researchers went to the board to try to push Altman out, according to five people familiar with the matter; after they failed, they left, worrying, like DeepMind's founders before them, that their new corporate overlords would favour commercial interests over safety.

In 2021 the group of about 15 engineers and scientists created a new lab called Anthropic, with the plan of building AI the way the effective altruists thought it should be done, with very tight controls. Anthropic disputes the account of the board approach: "There was no attempt to remove Sam Altman from OpenAI by the co-founders of Anthropic," said an Anthropic spokesperson, Sally Aldous. "The co-founders themselves came to the conclusion that they wished to depart OpenAI to start their own company, made this known to OpenAI's leadership, and over several weeks negotiated an exit on mutually agreeable terms." Anthropic accepted a $US4 billion investment from Amazon and another $US2 billion from Google two years later. After OpenAI received another $US2 billion from Microsoft, Altman and another senior executive, Greg Brockman, visited Bill Gates at his sprawling mansion on the shores of Lake Washington, outside Seattle; the Microsoft founder was no longer involved in the company day to day but kept in regular touch with its executives.

# The AI Risk Paradox Among Tech Billionaires

At the heart of the competition to build artificial intelligence is a brain-stretching paradox: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, and they have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The grounds are the shape of the debate itself. Eight years after an argument between Elon Musk and Larry Page, that argument seems prescient, because the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it, or at least inflict grave damage, has framed an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators about whether the technology should be controlled or set free.

That debate has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI, all of whom have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it. The narrative anchor is that Musk and Page stopped speaking soon after the party that summer, and that a few weeks later Musk dined with Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road.

# Hinton's 2012 Paper And The Lake Tahoe Talent Auction

Scientists were surprised by the accuracy of the technology built by Geoffrey Hinton and his students, and one who took particular notice was Yu Kai, an AI researcher who had met Hinton at a research conference and had recently started working for Baidu, the giant Chinese internet company; Baidu offered Hinton and his students $US12 million to join the company in Beijing, according to three people familiar with the offer. Hinton turned Baidu down but the money got his attention: the Cambridge-educated British expatriate had spent most of his career in academia except for occasional stints at Microsoft and Google and was not especially driven by money, but he had a neurodivergent child and the money would mean financial security. "We did not know how much we were worth," Hinton said, and after consulting lawyers and experts on acquisitions he came up with a plan: "We would organise an auction, and we would sell ourselves." The auction would take place during an annual AI conference at the Harrah's hotel and casino on Lake Tahoe. Google, Microsoft, Baidu and other companies were beginning to believe that neural networks were a path to machines that could not only see but also hear, write, talk and eventually think; Page had seen similar technology at Google Brain and thought Hinton's research could elevate his scientists' work, giving Alan Eustace, Google's senior vice president of engineering, what amounted to a blank check to hire any AI expertise he needed. Eustace and Jeff Dean, who led the Brain lab, flew to Lake Tahoe and took Hinton and his students to dinner at a steakhouse inside the hotel the night before the auction, where the smell of old cigarettes was overpowering, Dean recalled, and made the case for coming to work at Google. The next day Hinton ran the auction from his hotel room; because of an old back injury he rarely sat down, so he turned a trash can upside down on a table, put his laptop on top and watched the bids roll in over the next two days.

Google made an offer, so did Microsoft, and DeepMind quickly bowed out as the price went up. The industry giants pushed the bids to $US20 million and then $US25 million, according to documents detailing the auction; as the price passed $US30 million Microsoft quit, but rejoined the bidding at $US37 million, with Hinton saying "we felt like we were in a movie". Microsoft then dropped out a second time, leaving only Baidu and Google, who pushed the bidding to $US42 million and $US43 million, until finally at $US44 million Hinton and his students stopped the auction; the bids were still climbing but they wanted to work for Google, and the money was staggering. It was an unmistakable sign that deep-pocketed companies were determined to buy the most talented AI researchers, which was not lost on Hassabis at DeepMind: he had always told employees DeepMind would remain independent, believing that the best way to ensure its technology didn't turn into something dangerous, but as Big Tech entered the talent race he decided he had no choice and that it was time to sell. By the end of 2012 Google and Facebook were angling to acquire the London lab, according to three people familiar with the matter, and Hassabis and his co-founders insisted on two conditions: no DeepMind technology could be used for military purposes, and its AGI technology must be overseen by an independent board of technologists and ethicists.

# DeepMind's Ethics Board And Its Single Meeting In 2015

When Musk invested in DeepMind he broke his own informal rule that he would not invest in any company he didn't run himself, and the downsides were already apparent when, only a month or so after his birthday spat with Larry Page, he again found himself face to face with his former friend. The occasion was the first meeting of DeepMind's ethics board on 14 August 2015, a board set up at the insistence of the startup's founders to ensure their technology did no harm after the sale. The members convened in a conference room just outside Musk's office at SpaceX, but that is where Musk's control ended: when Google bought DeepMind it bought the whole thing, and Musk was out, financially ahead but unhappy. Three Google executives now firmly in control of DeepMind were there, Page, Sergey Brin, a Google co-founder and Tesla investor, and Eric Schmidt, Google's chair, along with other attendees including Reid Hoffman, another PayPal founder, and Toby Ord, an Australian philosopher studying "existential risk".

The DeepMind founders reported that they were pushing ahead with their work but were aware the technology carried serious risks. Mustafa Suleyman gave a presentation called "The Pitchforkers Are Coming", telling the board that AI could lead to an explosion in disinformation and fretting that as the technology replaced countless jobs in coming years the public would accuse Google of stealing their livelihoods, so Google would need to share its wealth with the millions who could no longer find work and provide a "universal basic income". Musk agreed, but it was pretty clear the Google guests were not prepared to embark on a redistribution of their wealth: Schmidt said he thought the worries were completely overblown, and Page, in his usual whisper, agreed, arguing AI would create more jobs than it took away. Eight months later DeepMind had a breakthrough that stunned the AI community and the world, when a DeepMind machine called AlphaGo beat one of the world's best players at the ancient game of Go, a match streamed over the internet and watched by 200 million people across the globe, though most researchers had assumed AI needed another 10 years to muster the ingenuity to do that; the South Korean professional Lee Se-dol played Go against AlphaGo in March 2016.

# Open Source

Open source, in the corpus's AI-industry usage, is the label companies apply to AI models, tools, and frameworks whose code or methodology they make available for outside use, positioned as the opposite pole from a "closed" or "proprietary" approach where a single company controls access.
The term is contested rather than binary: TechCrunch's own reporting shows companies claiming the "open source" label while attaching licensing restrictions, so the word functions as a marketing and strategic banner as much as a precise technical category.

## Context

The corpus uses "open source" mainly to describe a strategic fault line in generative AI between companies favoring open distribution of models (Meta, Mistral AI, Hugging Face, Stability AI) and companies favoring proprietary control (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Anthropic).
Meta's Yann LeCun and roughly 70 co-signatories published an open letter arguing that "increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous," directly rebutting the argument from OpenAI and Google DeepMind that proprietary AI is safer than open source.
A leaked internal Google memo ("we have no moat, and neither does OpenAI") treated the rise of open source AI models — following a Meta foundation model leak in March 2023 — as an existential threat to proprietary LLM providers, because openness lets a broader community collaborate and experiment in ways closed models cannot match.
Meta went on to co-found the AI Alliance with IBM to promote "open innovation" and "open source AI models and frameworks," while pointed omissions from that alliance's membership (Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Cohere, Adept) map directly onto the open-versus-closed divide.
The label also shows up outside the Meta/OpenAI rivalry: French startup Mistral AI builds "open source large language models," Giskard builds an "open source testing framework" for LLMs, OpenAI's own Whisper speech-recognition system is described as open source, and Auto-GPT is an open-source app built atop OpenAI's proprietary GPT models — showing open and closed components routinely coexist in the same AI stack.
One VC analysis of the generative AI tech stack expects the foundation-model layer to settle into an oligopoly "with the addition of a strong open source contingency that will drive considerable third-party adoption," treating open source as a distinct, persistent segment of the market rather than a transitional phase.

## Key Characteristics

- **Positioned against "proprietary" / "closed"** — the corpus consistently frames open source as the opposite pole from proprietary, centrally-controlled AI development.
- **Safety argument cuts both ways** — proprietary-AI advocates (OpenAI, Google DeepMind) argue closed control limits catastrophic misuse; open source advocates (LeCun and signatories) argue public scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous.
- **The label is contestable** — Meta calls Llama open source, but TechCrunch reports licensing terms (a ban on using Llama to train other models, and a special-license requirement for apps with over 700 million monthly users) that restrict use for large competitors, so the "open source" claim is disputed even by outlets covering it.
- **Used as coalition-building rhetoric** — the AI Alliance's founding materials cast "open innovation" and "open science" against a vision that would "relegate AI innovation... to a small number of companies with a closed, proprietary vision," turning openness into a membership and marketing signal.
- **Spans models, tools, and frameworks** — the corpus applies "open source" to LLMs (Mistral's models, Llama), a testing framework (Giskard), a speech-recognition system (Whisper), and a task-automation app (Auto-GPT), not just to full foundation models.

## Background (external)

Outside the corpus, "open source" has a formal technical definition: the Open Source Initiative (OSI) specifies that open-source software's distribution terms must satisfy ten criteria — including free redistribution, availability of source code, and permission to create derived works — and that access to source code alone is not sufficient to qualify (Open Source Initiative, "The Open Source Definition," https://opensource.org/osd, accessed 2026-09-02).
That formal criteria-based definition does not appear anywhere in the corpus; the corpus instead uses "open source" informally, as a contested marketing and strategic label rather than a precise technical category (see Definition and Key Characteristics above).

# Mozilla's Open Letter On AI Openness

The letter's claim is that openness makes AI safer, against the counter-position that proprietary control does. In an open letter published by Mozilla a few weeks before November 21, 2023, Meta's chief AI scientist Yann LeCun joined some 70 other signatories in calling for more openness in AI development, and the letter has since garnered more than 1,700 signatures. The backdrop is that Big Tech companies such as OpenAI and Google's DeepMind have called for more regulation, warning of catastrophic consequences if the AI levers were to meet the wrong hands — in other words, arguing that proprietary AI is safer than open source.

LeCun and his co-signatories disagree, and concede the risk before turning it around: "Yes, openly available models come with risks and vulnerabilities — AI models can be abused by malicious actors or deployed by ill-equipped developers. However, we have seen time and time again that the same holds true for proprietary technologies — and that increasing public access and scrutiny makes technology safer, not more dangerous. The idea that tight and proprietary control of foundational AI models is the only path to protecting us from society-scale harm is naive at best, dangerous at worst." The warrant is that scrutiny, not secrecy, is what makes technology safe.

On a personal level, LeCun has accused the big-name AI players of trying to secure "regulatory capture of the AI industry" by lobbying against open AI R&D — an argument about motive rather than safety. And on a company level, Meta is doing all it can to encourage collaboration and "openness," recently partnering with Hugging Face to launch a new startup accelerator designed to spur adoption of open source AI models.

# The Paris AI Research Talent Pipeline

France's AI momentum is not a surprise, because a talent pipeline has been feeding it for years. Tech giants have historically set up AI research labs in Paris, as there is a large talent pool of PhD students in math, computer science and engineering. They usually graduate from Polytechnique, ENS or Inria, sometimes move to the U.S. for postdoctoral research, and then move back to France to join a research lab — so the loop runs school, US postdoc, return to a Paris lab.

The corporate labs anchoring that loop are specific. Facebook (now Meta) created its Paris research lab back in 2015 with Yann LeCun at the helm of the AI initiative; this research group is called FAIR, for Facebook Artificial Intelligence Research. Google followed suit with its own research center dedicated to AI in Paris.

The quality signal comes from a practitioner who had recently had a private meeting with some of the engineers and scientists working on AI projects: "The FAIR team is extremely impressive. Just look at what they've done with Llama," an entrepreneur told TechCrunch.

# Musk's Founding Of OpenAI And His Departure

Convinced that Larry Page's optimistic view of AI was dead wrong, and angry at his loss of DeepMind, Musk built his own lab: OpenAI was founded in late 2015, just a few months after he met with Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Silicon Valley. Musk pumped money into the lab and his former PayPal buddies, Reid Hoffman and Peter Thiel, came along for the ride; the three men and others pledged to put $US1 billion into the project, which Altman, then 30, would help run, and to get started they poached Ilya Sutskever from Google, one of the graduate students Google had "bought" in Hinton's auction. Initially Musk wanted to operate OpenAI as a nonprofit, free from the economic incentives driving Google and other corporations, but by the time Google wowed the tech community with its Go stunt he was changing his mind about how it should be run: he desperately wanted OpenAI to invent something that would capture the world's imagination and close the gap with Google, and it wasn't getting the job done as a nonprofit.

In late 2017 Musk hatched a plan to wrest control of the lab from Altman and the other founders and transform it into a commercial operation that would join forces with Tesla and rely on supercomputers the car company was developing, according to four people familiar with the matter; when Altman and others pushed back, Musk quit and said he would focus on his own AI work at Tesla. In February 2018 he announced his departure to OpenAI's staff on the top floor of the startup's offices in a converted truck factory, three people who attended said; when he said OpenAI needed to move faster, one researcher retorted that Musk was being reckless, and Musk called the researcher a "jackass" and stormed out, taking his deep pockets with him. OpenAI suddenly needed new financing in a hurry: Altman flew to Sun Valley for a conference and ran into Satya Nadella, Microsoft's CEO, and a tie-up seemed natural, since Altman knew Microsoft's chief technology officer Kevin Scott and Microsoft had bought LinkedIn from Hoffman, an OpenAI board member; Nadella told Scott to get it done. The deal closed in 2019, leaving Altman and OpenAI with a for-profit company formed under the original nonprofit, $US1 billion in fresh capital, and Microsoft with a new way to build AI into its vast cloud computing service. Not everyone inside OpenAI was happy.

## Definition

In this corpus, "space mission" surfaces in two distinct forms: agency-run scientific observatories — NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory and the European Space Agency's (ESA) Solar Orbiter — that monitor the sun, and the interplanetary ambitions of a commercial launch company, SpaceX, whose founder Elon Musk described a plan to colonize Mars.

# Missy Ward, Daron Babin And Darren Blatt: The Early Operators

Three veterans at the alligator party illustrate how the first generation of SEO made its money. Missy Ward, in an orange bandage dress so tight she said she could not take full steps — ordered on Amazon and untried until the day of the party — started doing SEO in 1998, when it was "five girls and all dudes," and eventually sold her company for $40 million. That was Daron Babin, whose SEO career got going in 1994, before Google even existed. "The air of manipulation was insane," Babin said. "We had this weird community of geeks and nerds, and we all talked to each other about how we were beating the algorithms up. People were trying to outrank other people just for bragging rights."

The party's host, Darren Blatt, has been friends with Babin for decades — since the era when Darren "D-Money" Blatt would throw rap star-studded internet marketing shindigs during the Adult Video News Awards in Vegas, back when sex sites were among the most advanced in technology, and Babin was using SEO to promote offshore casinos and Viagra ("We were outranking Pfizer!"). Together, Darren and Daron managed to milk all three of the early online cash cows: porn, pills, and gambling.

The consulting turn came as the internet became more regulated and mainstream around the turn of the century, when Darren noticed Daron's SEO skills were increasingly in demand. "I told him that he was missing the boat, that he needed to be a consultant and charge a few grand," Darren said. Daron took the advice, asking for $2,000 a day, and watched his career explode — "I would wake up in a city and not know what time zone I was in." To slow the pace he raised his rate to $5,000 a day, but "it seemed the more I raised my rates, the more gigs I was getting." Ori Goshen, the co-founder and co-CEO of AI21 Labs, announced on LinkedIn that he would no longer be giving a keynote at Web Summit, and grounded the withdrawal in two distinct complaints. # Dave Clark's Hiring And Flexport's IPO Plan

Clark arrived at Flexport in 2022 as the apparently perfect hire for a tech startup trying to disrupt the age-old logistics industry — he had built Amazon's logistics unit into a juggernaut that rivalled carriers like UPS and FedEx — and among his goals was to help Petersen prepare Flexport for an IPO, something the company had discussed doing within a two- to three-year window.

Since 2021 Petersen had been seeking a successor for then-operating chief Sanne Manders, in part to address what several ex-employees described as lingering issues with the company's troubled billing processes; fixing that was Clark's job. Petersen and Clark worked together as co-CEOs for the first six months, and in March Petersen transitioned to executive chairman — an arrangement meant to free Petersen up to do what he loved, "getting beers with customers," in the words of two former Flexport employees, while Clark, a self-described "builder at heart," was at the wheel. "There's a perfect complement of skill sets," Petersen told Forbes in June 2022. "Mine are much more creative, zero-to-one founder time, and Dave is the supreme executor and a legend in the supply chain world." Buying Deliverr was meant to be the first step in turning Flexport into a more full-scale logistics service. Shopify had acquired Deliverr in May 2022 for $2.1 billion, but the e-commerce software company was being hammered by Wall Street as its Covid pandemic pop faded, and by January 2023 CEO Tobias Lutke knew he needed to get rid of it; around that time Lutke first approached Petersen to float a deal, and Petersen told Clark he should engage with Shopify's team. Initial talks fell apart but resumed when Flexport executives learned Shopify was about to execute deep cost cuts and was eager to sell. Clark and Petersen flew to Miami to meet Shopify's leadership, and as a transaction neared, Clark — who had a reputation as a deft negotiator — got Shopify, already an investor in Flexport, to sweeten it with $40 million in cash and the framework for a $260 million convertible note that could help Flexport on its path to an IPO, according to an internal document analyzing the deal. The sale would be announced alongside Shopify's first-quarter earnings report on May 4. "We did not change the terms of a deal or rush it just to have it line up with an earnings call," Shopify said in a statement, adding that with Flexport "we are tightly mission-aligned to ensure the success of our merchants, which is why we chose to deepen our partnership with them earlier this year." The night before the announcement, Petersen appeared at a "Tech Talk" at Flexport's Bellevue, Washington office to pitch the "Flexport vision" to hundreds of people; asked whether Flexport would ever get into last-mile logistics, he paused, glanced at his watch, and said to keep an eye on the morning news, according to an employee who witnessed the exchange and a person told independently. The comment alarmed Clark and Flexport executives, who were concerned Petersen had disclosed material nonpublic information about a publicly traded company. He was born on 3 October 1873 to Marcus M. and Chestina Urann in Sullivan, Maine, a tiny Downeast town on Bar Harbor, and described himself in one letter as a "bookworm". He attended the University of Maine, where he became an undergraduate scholar of great renown and great vision, and became an attorney in Boston after graduation; in 1906 he decided to give that up to buy cranberry bogs in and around Cape Cod and Plymouth. He died on 1 April 1963 in Hanson, Massachusetts, where he rests in a family plot in Fernhill Cemetery. "I do believe that anyone can do anything that he really desires to accomplish," Urann wrote as a young man in 1924, explaining the history of Phi Kappa Phi, and he lived by that example throughout his life.

The defining summary is the one given in The Boston Globe's obituary of 4 April, which called him "a recognized giant of the cranberry industry" and dubbed him the "Cranberry King": "He bought his first cranberry bog on [Cape Cod] in 1906. IoT Analytics projects that the global digital twin market could grow at a compound annual growth rate of approximately 30% between 2023 and 2027, according to its Digital Twin Market Report 2023-2027 as summarised by IoT Business News on 18 November 2023.

Adoption data underpins that projection. 29% of global manufacturing companies have either fully or partially implemented their digital twin strategies, a noticeable increase from 20% in 2020, and the proportion of companies not contemplating implementation appears to have fallen to 9% in 2023, down from 33.6% in 2020. Supporting the trend, an analysis of job postings on SimplyHired suggests growing demand for digital twin expertise: postings mentioning "digital twin" increased by 11% in October 2023 compared with just two years prior, while openings for most other tech topics declined over the same timeframe. Among the 60 tech-related skill sets IoT Analytics tracked, digital twin-related skills experienced one of the most significant growths.

Against this backdrop the report notes eight notable trends helping to advance and promote digital twins, of which the article discusses four in detail: digital twins deployed to meet sustainability goals; digital twins employed as virtual sensors in complex conditions; partnerships between cloud hyperscalers and OT and simulation specialists; and initiatives promoting interoperability of digital twins across multifaceted systems. # The Hypocrisy Argument: Google Became The Monopoly It Denounced

The DOJ's argument, pressed in cross-examination by Bellshaw, is that Google has become the monopoly it denounced years ago — that the company objected to a rival's search default when it was the one being shut out, and now defends the same arrangement when it is the beneficiary.

The grounds are Google's own 2005 letter. Cast your memories back to 2005, when Microsoft's Internet Explorer became the default search engine: Google's legal chief David Drummond sent Microsoft an angry letter saying that making Internet Explorer the search default was anticompetitive. After establishing that Google understands the inherent value of defaults, Bellshaw brought up Drummond's letter precisely to establish the hypocrisy of Google today. The letter declared that problems with a default setting are made worse by how changes to defaults are handled, and that most end users "do not change defaults."

The warrant is that the letter's reasoning has not changed hands with the market position. These are exactly the arguments that other search engine companies, like DuckDuckGo, Brave or Microsoft's Bing, make when they accuse Google of being anticompetitive by making deals with Apple and others — so if Drummond's reasoning was sound in 2005, it convicts Google now. The DOJ doubled down on this in the trial.

The same cross-examination pressed a second consistency question, on the litigation hold. Pichai said that he took action against the history-off default for chat in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, according to CNBC. Bellshaw then pulled up a message exchange in 2021 where Pichai asked for history to be turned off in a group chat. Pichai responded that he wanted to discuss a personnel matter and that the subject had nothing to do with the litigation hold, which he said he takes great care to comply with.

# Cranberry Industry Scale And Urann's Legacy

Marcus Urann turned a hyper-local fruit into an international industry — Ocean Spray reports today that fresh cranberries account for only 5% of the fruit's production — FOX News Lifestyle reported on 23 November 2023.

The United States is easily the world's largest grower of a fruit essential to the flavour of its national holiday dinner table: American farmers grow twice as many cranberries as No. 2 Canada and about 20 times the production of third-place Chile, according to data from the Cranberry Institute in Carver, Massachusetts, next to Plymouth. Wisconsin, meanwhile, surpassed Massachusetts decades ago as the nation's top cranberry grower. # Scorsese's Late-Career Genre Departures

Alongside the films that revisit his old themes, Polygon's 2023-10-26 piece identifies a set of radical departures in Scorsese's late era — films whose relation to his body of work is contrast rather than continuation.

2004's The Aviator is his most conventional movie to date, the most traditional, Oscar-baity, Old Hollywood biography he has made, and is best understood as a director-for-hire palate-cleanser after the odyssey of making the perpetually troubled Gangs of New York. 2010's Shutter Island is horror and suspense, an expert exercise in pure genre, part Hammer Films and part Alfred Hitchcock, and it also contains some of the most inventive, moving, and painterly visuals he has ever committed to film.

2011's Hugo is perhaps the hardest Scorsese film to imagine a younger Scorsese making: a 3D Robert Zemeckis-style family film that is also about the end of life and about immortality in art. He made it as a love letter to Georges Méliès, Harold Lloyd, and his own then-12-year-old daughter Francesca, and it seems designed to remind fathers of all the times they tried to introduce their kids to their favorite old films. Hugo is explicitly about Scorsese's legendary cinephilia in a way his earlier films are not, and it is sentimental in a way his work has never been before or since.

# Fotiadis Testimony And Johansson's Lobbying Contacts At The LIBE Hearing

At the LIBE committee hearing the journalist Apostolis Fotiadis testified that documents he and his colleagues obtained showed email threads granting a CSAM-scanning "key stakeholder" privileged access inside Johansson's department, and, under pressure from MEPs, the commissioner read out a list of her meetings with technology companies and child safety organizations. Fotiadis, one of the journalists involved in the investigation the committee was examining, had also been invited by the committee to participate in the exchange of views, and he took the opportunity to defend their reporting from direct public attacks by Johansson. In a blog post ahead of the hearing — which deploys a crisis-PR-esque headline claim of "setting the record straight" — she criticized the article as "a series of insinuations looking for a home", claiming it paired an outline of "a selection of meetings I had, of events I attended, or conferences I addressed" with "a conspiratorial tone" in an attempt "to create the impression of financial influence where there is none".

Asked by the LIBE committee about the accusation that the journalists had, essentially, been spreading disinformation — and specifically whether he believed Johansson and the Commission's response to it amounted to a restriction on media freedom — Fotiadis responded by saying he did not think that was the case. He went on to express surprise at how the Commission had reacted to the scrutiny, and at its instinct to deploy "spin-doctor" tactics to try to discredit the article rather than engaging with the substance of the concerns being raised. The Commission risks straying close to making attacks on journalists by using such tactics, Fotiadis warned, adding: "You cannot just dismiss everything by calling fake news" — before also noting that Johansson's office had declined multiple interview requests ahead of publication of the article.

On the substance of the reporting, Fotiadis said documents obtained by the journalists included email threads between Commission officials in Johansson's department, DG-Home, and a "key stakeholder" advocating for the use of technology for CSAM-scanning, which indicated what he described as "privileged access" that "speaks directly to cooperation" and goes "way beyond" mere consultation or exchange of views on the proposal.

He gave the committee the shape of that access. # Letitia James' History of Investigating Trump

Letitia James, who campaigned for office as a Trump critic and watchdog, started scrutinising his business practices in March 2019, after his former personal lawyer Michael Cohen testified to Congress that Trump exaggerated his wealth on financial statements provided to Deutsche Bank while trying to obtain financing to buy the NFL's Buffalo Bills.

Her office had previously sued Trump for misusing his own charitable foundation to further his political and business interests. Trump was ordered to pay $2 million to an array of charities as a fine, and the charity, the Trump Foundation, was shut down.

# Google Paid $26.3 Billion In 2021 For Default Search Placement

Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be everyone's default search engine. The figure was revealed by Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan when he testified in court on October 28, according to The Verge.

About $18 billion of that total went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023, and Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003 — so the payment is the current year of a two-decade arrangement, not a one-off. Questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said the decision was made with the consumer in mind: Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices, he said, according to The Verge.

The trial also produced evidence that Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, and that when they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%. The email summarizing that meeting, sent to Pichai as well as other Google leaders, read: "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share," according to The Verge.

# The Sony, Gilmour, The Orb And Vermillio AI Reissue Project

Kooker cited as an example a recent generative AI-powered project around a reissue and remix of an album; although he did not name it specifically, Sony Music Entertainment had recently announced a generative AI project with The Orb and David Gilmour, a partnership between Sony Music Entertainment, Legacy Recordings and AI company Vermillio.

"These artists are known for their cutting-edge experimentation in music," Kooker said. In other words, they respect intellectual property rights and want to work with rights holders in ways that enhance and protect the copyrighted works."

# The US Sound Recording Public Performance Right Gap

The US "is the only significant music economy in the world that does not have these full rights in their domestic legislation," the artists' groups said — the gap being a public performance right in sound recordings for terrestrial broadcast.

The legislative history explains the shape of the gap. The US Congress extended copyright protections to sound recordings in 1971, but those protections did not include a public performance right that would have ensured royalty payments to artists, producers and labels. In 1995, Congress passed the Digital Performance Right in Sound Recordings Act, which did include performance rights, but limited those rights to performances made "by means of a digital audio transmission," which does not include terrestrial radio.



---


# Which Artists Joined "Dream Track", And The Licensing Questions That Follow

MBW's closing observation is that the artists who agreed, with their record companies, to enter the YouTube "Dream Track" trial are stars — but in the case of both Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group they are, currently anyway, not the biggest megastars on either company's books.

The reasoning is that you might not expect, at this early stage, for the likes of UMG to put forward Drake, Taylor Swift, or The Beatles — or for WMG to put forward Ed Sheeran or Dua Lipa — to be guinea pigs in any early AI music experiments, even ones run by "friends" of the music industry like YouTube. From that observation MBW raises two open questions: whether there have been significant licensing payments made by YouTube to UMG and WMG for the right to play with the AI vocals of artists who have signed off on Dream Track thus far, and if so, whether these payments are being placed against any as-yet-unrecouped advances that some of these artists may have on their label accounts. More broadly, MBW poses a bigger question: when the day comes that YouTube asks the world's biggest superstars to wholeheartedly embrace "Dream Track", will Google's recent US Copyright Office filing give those superstars — and their record companies — pause for thought?



---


# Kyncl Prediction: Music Is the First Industry to Feel AI's Impact

Robert Kyncl's proposition, put at the Code Conference in September 2023, is that the music business will be out ahead of other industries in exploiting the potential of AI, and — out of necessity — also ahead on the question of how to regulate and monetise the use of AI by non-rights-holders. He attached a date to it: asked when that sea change would occur, he said "I would say within the next year you will see lots of evolution around AI… What you will likely see is increasing quality at a very fast pace."

His reasoning is structural rather than accidental. "Music – because it's so broadly distributed and it's so well aligned with the internet, because it's short format, it lends itself to recommendations, it's on all platforms – is generally first in most transformations and most innovations. So it digitizes first." He generalises from the previous cycle: "Whatever happened to the music industry 20 years ago is starting to happen in the movies and TV shows now. In the meantime, music emerged out of [digitization] better and stronger and more resilient. So, I would imagine the same will happen here, which is we'll likely be first."

The hypothesis is falsifiable on two fronts as stated. It fails if other industries, rather than music, lead on both exploiting and regulating AI; and it fails on its own timetable if the year following September 2023 does not bring the predicted rapid evolution and fast-rising quality in AI. Because the argument rests on music's broad distribution, short format and recommendation-friendliness, an AI transformation that arrives first in a long-format medium would also count against the mechanism he proposes.

# The Material Reciprocity Principle In Music Royalties

Because of the EU-US asymmetry, European countries largely followed the "reciprocity principle" written into international copyright treaties such as the WIPO Performances and Phonograms Treaty of 1996: in those countries where artists and labels are paid performance rights, there was no obligation to pay US artists and labels, since European artists did not receive those payments from airplay in the US.

The artists' groups' statement defends the principle in general terms, saying it "has proven vital in raising the level of copyright protection across the globe for decades."

# UMG And WMG's Licensing Of "Dream Track"

Universal Music Group and Warner Music Group both dipped a toe into YouTube's "Dream Track" experiment — though not without caution — with UMG granting a limited license.

Sir Lucian Grainge, Chairman and CEO of Universal Music Group, said of the decision: "We have a fundamental responsibility to our artists to ensure the digital ecosystem evolves to protect them and their work against unauthorized exploitation, including by generative AI platforms. At the same time, we must help artists achieve their greatest creative and commercial potential – in part by providing them access to the kind of opportunities and cutting-edge creative tools made possible by AI." Robert Kyncl, CEO of Warner Music Group and an ex-high flyer at YouTube, commented: "With each major leap in technology, the music industry navigates a fresh set of challenges and opportunities. It's not always the case that, from the outset, tech platforms partner with artists, songwriters, labels, and publishers to experiment, iterate, and find possible solutions. YouTube is taking a collaborative approach with this Beta. These artists are being offered the choice to lean in, and we're pleased to experiment and find out what the creators come up with."

# AfroFuture Rising Star Challenge Competition

The Rising Star Challenge is AfroFuture's annual flagship competition for unsigned and emerging artists in Africa, described by co-founder Abdul Karim Abdullah as the brand's way of supporting live music not only in Ghana but throughout Africa. Eligibility is limited to unsigned and emerging artists.

Entry and selection run in fixed stages. To enter, artists upload an original song to Audiomack and create an Instagram Reel that includes an introduction about the artist, their approach to music and the music-making process, and what they want their potential audience to know about their style of music. As a lead-up to the festival, 10 musicians are then chosen from a shortlist of 25 unsigned and emerging artists. From those, five finalists are chosen to perform on AfroFuture's Rising Star Stage alongside the festival's headliners. For the grand finale, one artist is selected for the ultimate prize — an exclusive recording agreement with Sony Music Africa for a single release. Winners additionally receive global distribution for their new single, marketing support such as a music video and more, free access to AfroFuture's recording studio, and mentoring and training from industry executives and leading musicians and producers.

In 2022 the format was extended with the Rising Star DJ Challenge, a call for DJs from across the diaspora to share their talents and win a place on the AfroFuture stage. Created in partnership with TuneCore to amplify the next generation of African superstars and find the next breakout DJ from the continent, it followed a different sequence: the top ten entries were selected by a panel of industry experts composed of TuneCore executives and AfroFuture DJs; once announced, fans across the world voted on social media to narrow the group down to three DJs; the top three finalists then battled it out at the AfroFuture Music Museum in Accra, Ghana on 27 December; and the contest winner performed at AfroFuture 2022 and walked away with a cash prize.

# Sony Music's Generative AI Principles For Congress

Dennis Kooker, Sony Music Entertainment's President of Global Digital Business & US Sales, asked Congress at the November 29, 2023 AI Insight Forum to embrace a set of five principles around generative AI, on the argument that "if copyrights are protected and enforced appropriately, we are at the beginning of a multi-decade marathon that will change the creative and commercial landscape for music."

The framing condition Kooker set is that "Music is a tremendous driver for AI technology, and AI technology presents a tremendous opportunity for the creative development of music. But these opportunities must be grounded by the human creators' vision with the machine assisting, not with the machine replacing the human creator." The principles are: Assure Consent, Compensation, and Credit — "New products and businesses built with music must be developed with the consent of the owner and appropriate compensation and credit. It is essential to understand why the training of AI models is being done, what products will be developed as a result, and what the business model is that will monetize the use of the artist's work. Congress and the agencies should assure that creators' rights are recognized and respected." Confirm That Copying Music to Train AI Models is Not Fair Use — "Even worse are those that argue that copyrighted content should automatically be considered fair use so that protected works are never compensated for usage and creators have no say in the products or business models that are developed around them and their work. Congress should assure and agencies should presume that reproducing music to train AI models, in itself, is not a fair use." Prevent the Cloning of Artists' Voices and Likenesses Without Express Permission — "We cannot allow an artist's voice or likeness to be cloned for use without the express permission of the artist. This is a very personal decision for the artist. Congress should pass into law effective federal protections for name, image, and likeness." Incentivize Accurate Recordkeeping — "Correct attribution will be a critical element to artists being paid fairly and correctly for new works that are created. In addition, rights can only be enforced around the training of AI when there are accurate records about what is being copied. Otherwise, the inability to enforce rights in the AI marketplace equates to a lack of rights at all, producing a dangerous imbalance that prevents a thriving ecosystem. This requires strong and accurate record keeping by the generative AI platforms, a requirement that urgently needs legislative support to ensure incentives are in place so that it happens consistently and correctly." And Assure Transparency for Consumers and Artists — "Transparency is necessary to clearly distinguish human-created works from AI-created works. The public should know, when they are listening to music, whether that music was created by a human being or a machine." MBW summarised the intended effect: "The principles will ensure that intellectual property businesses can succeed in this new world alongside tech partners, further advancing investment and expanding economic opportunities."

Kooker said Sony Music has "roughly 200 active conversations taking place with startups and established players" right now about building new AI-related products and tools, and that some of these conversations "also include potential equity investments which would accelerate the development of these companies."

Dennis Kooker used his November 29, 2023 speech to attack the premise of the tech industry's Copyright Office submissions directly, telling Senators that "based on recent Copyright Office filings it is clear that the technology industry and speculative financial investors would like governments to believe in a very distorted view of copyright."
