# The Digital-First Artist Development Model

The success of "Si No Estás" illustrates how much artist development has changed: social media and digital music services have now become the number one source of music discovery, and Believe has developed an innovative, AI and data-driven expertise to develop tracks and artists that Alejandra Olea describes as unique in the music industry.

The model's components and their relations are stated together: the key to success is great partnerships with the artist and their label, and being able to combine strong AI data-driven expertise to maximise momentum for an artist and a track at the right time with the right tools and the right partnerships, supported by both local and global teams. Olea singles out the last element as particularly important and truly one of Believe's strengths, being able to mobilise teams multi-locally and globally to accompany audience development for artists. The forward-looking claim attached to the model is that this is only the beginning for Iñigo Quintero and that Believe anticipates many more successes like his in future.

# Robert Kyncl, Warner Music Group CEO

Robert Kyncl is the CEO of Warner Music Group, and the defining feature of his profile in the music business is that he came to it from 'Big Tech' — specifically from YouTube, where he was Chief Business Officer. That background is why, in the months before September 2023, he had been keeping a close eye on AI in the music industry.

His current role explains a second position associated with him: he has been pushing for price hikes at music streaming services. Both themes — AI in music, and streaming pricing — came up during Kyncl's Q&A session at the Code Conference in Laguna Niguel, California, on Tuesday 26 September 2023, as reported by Music Business Worldwide two days later.

# Thesis That Music Labels Are Headed for Irrelevance

The argument, common among music business observers from the world of tech, is that record labels could in the long term be headed for irrelevance. Its grounds are the arrival of digital platforms, including open ones like YouTube and SoundCloud, together with the proliferation of indie music distribution platforms such as DistroKid and TikTok's SoundOn.

The warrant joining grounds to claim is a claim about what labels are for: in a world where anyone can record music using a desktop audio workstation (DAW) and upload it directly to YouTube, or to Spotify via a distribution platform, labels have little left to do. Recording and distribution — the functions the label historically supplied — are available to any artist directly, so on this reasoning the label's remaining role shrinks toward nothing. Music Business Worldwide presented this as the speculation that tech-world observers "like to" make, and as the position Warner Music Group CEO Robert Kyncl was answering at the Code Conference in September 2023.

# Sony Music's Absence From "Dream Track"

Dennis Kooker's public statements on AI arrived a week after MBW pointed out a notable lack of endorsement from Sony Music Entertainment, and its artists, of YouTube's experimental AI project "Dream Track," which lets creators clone the vocals of successful musicians.

The initial cohort of stars involved in the project included recording artists signed to Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group — or labels within each of those two majors — but no Sony Music artists. In its earlier report MBW suggested that YouTube parent Google's recent submission to the United States Copyright Office, made in response to a request for written submissions as part of a study around copyright law and policy issues raised by AI systems, may have influenced Sony's absence from Dream Track.

# More Diversity And More Women In Label Leadership

Asked what single thing she would change about today's music business, Michelle Jubelirer chose one issue out of several she could name: the industry needs more diversity at all levels and within all facets, particularly on the label side. Her ground is stated as a claim about capability rather than fairness alone, that diversity is a superpower, and she describes it as an ongoing process she has put a lot of focus on, along with doing what she can to increase the number of women at her company.

The supporting evidence is the scarcity at the top: there just are not enough women, particularly within the most senior ranks at the labels. Within UMG, Nashville Chair and CEO Cindy Mabe and Jubelirer herself run standalone label groups, and she says she knows Lucian agrees with her that there need to be more. She commits to continuing to do what she can to increase representation at Capitol Music Group and within the music business at large.

# AI Copyright And Training Disputes

Universal Music Group's answer to generative AI trained on its catalogue rejects the premise that such training is a neutral technical act, recasting it as a choice of allegiance: "The training of generative AI using our artists' music . . . begs the question as to which side of history all stakeholders in the music ecosystem want to be on: the side of artists, fans and human creative expression, or on the side of deep fakes, fraud and denying artists their due compensation," the label said after a song using AI to imitate Drake and The Weeknd, two of its artists, went viral.

A second objection cuts against the label framing itself. These same conversations and contradictions are manifesting across creative industries, but artists themselves don't always have a seat at the table — so an industry-level statement of grievance is not the same thing as artists speaking for themselves. Independent artists in particular are learning that their voices resonate louder when coming together across disciplines to push back against what Holland describes as an "extraordinary spectrum of exploitation" that leverages their work.

The dispute is not confined to music. In a roundtable hosted by the FTC that same week, the agency brought together figures from across creative industries — from voice acting and science fiction to screenwriting, music, illustration and even fashion — to delve into how generative AI is affecting creatives. TechCrunch reported the exchange on 2023-10-06.

# European Artists' Projected Royalty Loss To US Rightsholders

A group of organizations representing musical artists in Europe has warned that an "anomaly" in EU law could soon result in artists losing up to 40% of the income they make from terrestrial radio broadcasts and other public performances of their music — and that because of a technicality in EU law, that lost income would largely go to US-based artists.

The groups include IMPALA, the trade association for European indie labels, and Adami, the French collective management organization for performers' rights. What the failure of the "reciprocity" principle means in practice is that US-based artists whose recordings are played on the radio in the EU will be able to collect performance royalties, while EU artists will continue to get nothing from their recordings being played in the US. Because royalties are paid from a collective pool of income, this will reduce payments to European artists by as much as 40% in some countries, the artists' groups said, as that is the share of US music played on the radio in those countries. IMPALA estimates that the annual loss to EU recorded music rightsholders from "reciprocity" protections not applying in Europe would amount to approximately €125 million (USD $137m) — money which would instead be handed to their US counterparts.

# Sphere And ABBA Voyage As Two Models Of Immersion

The Sydney Morning Herald's 19 October 2023 report sets out a two-part model of immersive concert design: ABBA Voyage in London pushes its effects out toward the audience, while Sphere more wholly and subtly envelops it — the only approximate comparison available for either.

The relation holds because both are wholly enveloping experiences where lights, sound and special effects are blended to push the audience's senses to the limit; they differ in one key way, which is direction. ABBA's effects project outward, largely to play smoke and mirrors with the on-stage simulacrums; Sphere's surround the viewer. A second shared structural condition is the artist: "They are both legacy projects made by artists who have the career and track record to be able to look at these things objectively in a way that a younger performer perhaps wouldn't because it takes an entire lifetime of experience to make those kinds of choices and make it work," Williams says.

A third link is institutional. The two shows share the British music stage architecture firm Stufish, whose work ranges from the Queen's Platinum Jubilee to tours for Beyoncé and Jay-Z, Michael Bublé, Elton John and Madonna, as well as the ABBA Arena in London; Stufish partner Ric Lipson collaborated on the U2 project for Sphere along with artist Es Devlin and producer Brian Eno. Lipson also marks the limit of the model — the venues are not locked to one show: "With the ABBA Arena, it's absolutely designed for that show, but you could also imagine that building having another avatar show in there, or indeed a live performance where people would use the technology that's in the building as an immersive environment."

# UMG's USCO Filing Rejecting Fair Use For AI Training

Universal Music Group's response to the US Copyright Office rejected the notion that using copyrighted material to train large language models is "fair use" — a position MBW called unsurprising and the starkest possible contrast to Google's assertion that prohibiting or limiting the use of copyrighted materials for AI training would undermine the purpose of copyright and foreclose the opportunities of the technology.

The filing's own example puts the claim bluntly: "The wholesale appropriation of UMG's enormous catalog of copyright-protected sound recordings and musical compositions to build multibillion commercial enterprises [in AI] is anything but fair use."

# Each Album Needs Its Own Sound: Swift's Rule For Cutting Songs

Speaking in 2015, Taylor Swift defended a brutal pruning of 1989's original tracklist on a single principle: an album must have its own sound, and a song that does not fit that sound is cut no matter how good it is. "I just need each album to have its own sound and if it doesn't fit that sound, it doesn't matter if it's a great song to me," she told New York radio's The Todd Show in the Morning.

The operative test she described was backwards-looking rather than about quality: "There were so many songs I wrote for this album that were really good, but if I felt in any way that they would have belonged on my last album, Red, they got cut." She acknowledged the cost of applying the rule — "There are really, really good songs on the cutting room floor because they weren't innovative enough or new enough. It's so weird to look back on that - you've got heaping piles of discarded songs that I really loved when I wrote them and I still love now."

# Sony Music's "Artist-Led" Approach To AI

Sources close to Sony Music's HQ in New York have suggested to MBW that the company is taking an "artist-led" approach to its experiments with any AI platform that can manipulate the work or voice of its roster — which is offered as the explanation for why Sony did not join Universal and Warner in "Dream Track."

The grounds are that Sony did not decline on principle. MBW understands that Sony Music, the recorded music arm of Sony Music Group, had like Universal and Warner been in discussions for months with YouTube over potentially licensing the experiment, and the company had shown its own willingness to experiment with generative AI music platforms that same week via an announcement about a project with David Gilmour, The Orb, and AI company Vermillio. In the case of Dream Track, MBW understands, Sony first offered the opportunity to participate to a number of its artists, but this group of acts did not show enthusiasm about participating. MBW notes that if one of these artists was Bad Bunny, signed to Sony's The Orchard, the reluctance is easy to see: the Puerto Rican superstar had expressed fury the other week about a popular track on TikTok that had cloned his vocal stylings via AI.

# Google's Copyright Filing Against YouTube's Music Reassurances

MBW's counter to the idea that YouTube's rightsholder assurances settle the matter is that Google's take on copyright "harvesting" by generative AI models sits in odd contrast to the copyright-related reassurances YouTube was careful to make to the music industry during the pre-development, development, and trial launch of "Dream Track."

The premise attacked is that the platform relationship and the parent company's legal position can be read separately. MBW's sources close to Sony Music were keen to point out that the company's general ongoing relationship with YouTube and YouTube Music is a harmonious one — YouTube is now the second largest commercial partner of the major record companies, with a stated ambition to catch up with Spotify in the years ahead, and says it paid out over USD $6 billion to music rightsholders in the year to end of June 2022, with around $2 billion of that coming just from ads on user-generated content. However, the October US Copyright Office filing from Google has definitely put the cat amongst the pigeons at Sony Music HQ, as MBW is sure it has at the other two major record companies, because of its position that "Any prohibition or limitation on the use of copyrighted materials for purposes of AI training would undermine the purpose of copyright and foreclose the many opportunities that come with this technology." As well as part-explaining Sony Music's refusal to be included in Dream Track thus far, Google's USCO filing also perhaps explains the careful words selected by Robert Kyncl and especially Sir Lucian Grainge in their respective comments endorsing YouTube's AI experiment — Grainge's statement, after all, began: "We have a fundamental responsibility to our artists to ensure the digital ecosystem evolves to protect them and their work against unauthorized exploitation, including by generative AI platforms…"

# Discogs As Music Database And Marketplace

Discogs is the internet's foremost database of recorded music and one of the most extensive marketplaces available for physical music media, with every bit of it generated and offered by users. On it you can catalog your collection, look up information about even the most obscure artists, cross-check record store prices to see whether your local shop has a markup, and purchase records, typically at something close to their "market rate." For a devoted vinyl collector or an obsessive music fan — as is often the case, both — it is very nearly a lifestyle.

What distinguishes it is the way the database is built. Founded in 2000 by Intel programmer Kevin Lewandowski, it was initially conceived as something of a Wikipedia for recorded music, which it predates by a few months, and it has not changed a great deal since its conception besides the introduction of the marketplace in the mid-aughts. Sellers have to submit a record's information if it is not already in the database in order to sell it, which is how the database became so complete; many entries, even for deep obscurities, are fastidious, with album covers and liner notes scanned for inclusion and album credits fleshed out with hyperlinks that are almost more useful and thorough than the Wikipedia equivalent, plus reviews by devotees, and a lively forum where all these details get litigated. The Verge's example, from October 7th, 2023: the entry for a Japanese pressing of Thelonious Monk in Italy includes photos of the record jacket and both sides of the vinyl. Doug Martin, who started selling on Discogs in 2020, described the users as different from casual buyers: "Some people just buy records for the album art hanging on the wall... These were real fans listening to real music who cared about the format and the medium. That's what attracted me in the beginning."

Its boundary case is its own position between two internets. Discogs is a fairly clunky, definitely old-fashioned website devoted to even older technology — a vestige of an earlier, more idyllic internet that has spent the last decade walking the record-needle-thin line between 2020s algorithmically driven tech monolith and niche unprofitable obscurity. It became a central part of the music internet, surviving physical media's replacement by MP3s and then streaming and rebounding as interest in vinyl, CDs, and tapes did throughout the 2010s. It is an insular community in many ways, but it is also, and has always been, a money-making endeavor for both Discogs and the sellers who use it — and sellers say the site's old tech has started to wear on them while new fees and restrictions have made it harder to do business.

# Abdul Karim Abdullah's Path into the Music Business

Abdul Karim Abdullah's first experience in the music industry came when a member of his fraternity, Phi Beta Sigma Fraternity Inc., booked Big Sean at his alma mater, Syracuse University. "I remember how much I enjoyed the experience because I was fascinated by how everything came together and the process of creating and managing an event," he told Music Business Worldwide in October 2023.

From that experience he got his big break as a stage manager for a concert he pitched to W&R Productions for El and Joey B, two major Ghanaian artists, at the Gramercy Theatre. Those early experiences, he says, gave him the confidence he needed to create, plan and execute his own event, leaving only the question of how to fund his big ideas. From his first event to establishing AfroFuture, he says he has gained a tremendous amount of knowledge, and that it has been the driving force behind everything he does to create sustainable change not only for Ghana but for Africa at large.

# Sony Music's Deepfake Takedowns And Support For The No FAKES Act

Dennis Kooker reported in his November 29, 2023 speech that Sony Music Entertainment has to date sent "close to 10,000 takedowns to a variety of platforms hosting unauthorized deepfakes that SME artists asked us to take down."

He openly discussed the company's efforts to get unauthorized AI content removed from platforms online, and named the obstacle: "platforms are quick to point to the loopholes in the law as an excuse to drag their feet or to not take the deepfakes down when requested." Kooker commended the No FAKES Act policy drafted by senators earlier in 2023, which he explained "would create a federal property right in one's voice or visual likeness and protect against unauthorized AI-generated replicas."

# YouTube's "Dream Track" Voice Cloning Experiment

On November 16, 2023 YouTube unveiled "Dream Track," an experiment enabling creators to clone the vocals, via AI tech and with official consent, of well-known stars.

Charlie Puth's voice is on there. John Legend's voice is on there. Demi Lovato's voice is on there. In fact the voices of a number of well-known recording artists signed to Warner Music Group and Universal Music Group — or labels within each major — are on there. Something conspicuous is not: any endorsement whatsoever from the world's second-biggest recording company, Sony Music Entertainment, or its artists.

# The Sam Smith "Unholy" Campaign At Capitol

CMG, along with its colleagues at Capitol UK and the artist's team, was behind the Grammy-winning global smash that is Sam Smith's "Unholy", an unapologetically ribald banger from a singer who refuses to be pigeonholed as a sweet balladeer. Michelle Jubelirer says Sam drove the record from its creation through the decision for it to be the first single; she felt it was a huge leap forward, bold and brash and so distinctive from the first listen, and one of the strongest songs and records Sam had ever created.

Her own role was to marshal everyone in the company to come up with creative and strategic ideas to lead the global effort behind it, and to make sure the team, led by Arjun Pulijal, worked closely with Jo Charrington and her team at Capitol UK and with Sam's managers Jack Street and Sam Evitt. Digital marketing was key to the effort: the song is in the Top 3 of all-time creations and shares for a pre-release campaign, and the global teams worked together to connect that pre-release momentum to the biggest looks at the DSPs, in the media and at radio. Jubelirer calls it extremely gratifying that "Unholy" broke records at the streaming services and says the Grammy won with Kim Petras was well-deserved; she adds that Sam was the first new artist to break big at the company after it launched, that they are considered family, and that she wants Sam to be with the label forever and as much a part of its legacy as the great superstars who came before.
